->ON THOSE THINGS WITHOUT WHICH VISION CANNOT BE<-
->completed. Chapter Seven.<-

->*36. For the completion of vision, six things are primarily necessary.*<-

Now it has been declared above that the sight perceives nothing from visible things that are with it in the same air—in such a way that its perception of them is not by <term>refraction|the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another, such as from air into the eye</term>—unless these things are gathered together: and these are, that there be some space between them; and that the thing be opposite the sight, so that between any point of its surface which the sight perceives, and another point of the surface of the eye, there is an imaginable <term>straight line|Alhazen emphasizes that light travels in straight lines, a foundational principle of optics</term>; and that there be light in it; and that its body be of some size in respect to the power of the sense of sight; and that the medium be transparent air, of continuous transparency, and that there be no other non-transparent body in it; and that the visible thing be resistant to the sight—that is, that there be no transparency in it, or if there is, that it be thicker than the transparency of the air between it and the sight. The sight will not perceive a visible thing unless these six <term>intentions|essential conditions or requirements</term> are gathered together: and if the visible thing lacks even one of these conditions, it will not be perceived by the sight. The sight's need for each of these conditions is always due to some specific cause.

->*37. Distance between the sight and the visible object.*<-

The reason why the sight does not perceive a visible thing unless there is some distance between them, and does not perceive it when it is applied directly to the eye, is due to two causes. One of these is because the sight does not perceive a visible thing unless there is some light in it, and when it is applied to the eye—if it is not illuminated by itself—there will be no light on its surface near the eye: because the body of the eye, by its very position, then blocks the light from the object. However, things that are <term>luminous by themselves|self-lighting objects like stars or fire</term> cannot be applied to the surface of the sight: for things illuminated by themselves are the stars and fire, which cannot be placed against the surface of the eye. The second cause is because vision does not occur except from the part opposite the <term>opening of the uvea|the pupil of the eye</term> from the middle of the surface of the sight; and if the visible thing is applied directly to the eye, nothing will be placed over that part of the eye except a portion of the visible thing equal only to that part. Thus, if the sight perceived the visible thing by direct contact, it would not perceive anything except the part applied to the part opposite the opening, and it would not perceive the rest of the visible thing. And if the visible thing is moved over the surface of the eye until it touches the whole surface of the visible thing according to the middle part of the eye, it will perceive one part after another, and while it perceives the second part, it will not perceive the first part: and thus it cannot perceive the whole visible thing at once. And since this is so, the form of the visible thing will not be shaped within it. It is as if some visible thing were over a dense body, and in that dense body there was a hole of smaller size than the visible thing: if the visible thing were applied to the hole, it would only perceive the part placed under the hole. Then, if the visible thing is moved over the hole until part after another is perceived by the sight, its whole form is not shaped in the sight. If, therefore, vision were by <term>touch|Alhazen is refuting the ancient idea that vision works like a sense of touch through physical contact</term>, the sight would not perceive the whole visible thing, nor its figure and form, unless the visible thing were equal to the middle part of the surface of the eye through which vision occurs: nor could it perceive many visible things at the same time. But when there is some space between the sight and the visible thing, it can perceive the whole visible thing at the same time from a small part, even if the visible thing is large: and it can perceive many visible things together at the same time. And when the visible thing is distant from the sight, it is possible for light to arise upon the surface of the thing opposite the sight. For these two causes, therefore, the sight does not perceive any of the visible things unless there is some space between them.

->*38. Direct placement of the visible object before the sight.*<-

The reason why the sight does not perceive a visible thing which is with it in the same air and in the part opposite it, unless there is a straight line between any point of it and some point of the part of the surface of the eye through which vision occurs: is because it has been declared that vision does not happen except from <term>forms|the visual images or patterns of light</term> coming from the visible thing to the sight, and that forms are not perceived except according to straight lines; and for this cause the sight does not perceive a thing unless there is a straight line between them. And if dense bodies in between cut all the lines that are between them, the visible things will be hidden from the sight: and if that body cuts some of those straight lines, some part will be hidden from the sight which is at the extremity of the lines blocked by the dense body.

->*39. Light.*<-

The reason why the sight does not perceive a visible thing unless there is light in it is due to two causes: either because the visible forms do not extend through the air unless there is light with the color; or because the form of color extends through the air even though there is no light with it, but it does not act upon the sight with a perceptible operation except by means of light. And it is manifest that the form of light is more manifest than the form of color, and that light operates with a more manifest operation: and because the form of color is weak, it cannot operate upon the sight in the way that light operates. And the form of color,

When it reaches the sight, it always acts upon it through its own strength and the readiness of the sight to be affected by it. Because it is mixed with the form of color and is not distinguished from it, the sight does not perceive the form of light except when it is mixed with the form of color. Therefore, the sight does not perceive the color of a visible thing except from the color mixed with the form of light coming to it from the thing seen. Because of this, the colors of many visible things are altered in the eyes by the alteration of the light falling upon them. Since the form of color does not act upon the sight unless it is mixed with light, and there is no form of color unless there is light in it, the sight perceives nothing from visible things unless there is some light in them.

### 40. *The size of the visible thing.* <note>original: "Magnitudo rei uisibilis. 19 p 3."</note>

As to why the sight does not perceive a visible thing unless its body is of a certain size: it is because it has been demonstrated that the form of a visible thing does not reach the sight except through <term>pyramids|a cone-shaped volume of light rays with the object as the base and the center of the eye as the point</term>, whose tip is the center of the sight and whose base is the surface of the thing seen. This pyramid marks out a small part of the surface of the <term>sensing member|the part of the eye that actually perceives light, specifically the lens or retina</term>, in which the form of the visible thing is arranged. If the visible thing is extremely small, the pyramid between it and the center of the sight will be extremely small. Thus, the part marked out on the sensing member will be like a point, incredibly tiny. But the sensing power does not perceive a form unless the part of its surface where the form arrives is of a <term>sensible quantity|a size large enough to be detected by the physical limitations of the nerves</term> in relation to the whole member. The powers of the senses are finite. When the part of the sensing member where the form arrives is not of a sensible size compared to the whole, the sense will not feel the impression made upon it because of its smallness. Therefore, it does not perceive the form. Thus, a visible thing that can be perceived by the sight is one in which the pyramid formed between the thing and the center of the sight marks out a part of the surface of the <term>glacial humor|the crystalline lens, which medieval scholars believed was the primary organ of vision</term> that is of a sensible size in relation to the whole surface of the glacial humor. This perception will only extend as far as the sensing power reaches; it does not extend to infinity, and it varies according to the strength of the eye's power. When the pyramid formed between the thing and the center of the sight marks out a part of the glacial surface that is of an imperceptible size, the sight cannot perceive that thing. For this reason, the sight cannot perceive an extremely small object.

---

### 41. *The transparency of the body placed between the sight and the visible.* <note>original: "Perspicuitas corporis inter uisum & uisibile interiecti. 13 p 3."</note>

As to why the sight does not perceive a visible thing unless the body between the sight and the thing is <term>diaphanous|transparent or translucent, like air, water, or glass</term>: it is because vision only occurs from a form coming from the thing seen to the sight. Forms only extend through transparent bodies. Vision is not completed—even when the thing seen is in the same air as the sight and the perception is not by <term>refraction|the bending of light as it moves between different materials</term>—unless the air is continuous between the thing seen and no dense body cuts through the straight lines between them. This is because the form only extends through air of uniform transparency according to straight lines. For this reason, the sight does not perceive a visible thing that is in the same air and opposite to it, unless the air between them is transparent and of uniform transparency.

---

### 42. *The density and solidity of the visible.* <note>original: "Densitas ac soliditas uisibilis. 14 p 3."</note>

As to why the sight does not perceive a visible thing unless there is density (or some degree of density) in it: this is due to two causes. The first is that what is dense is colored, and it is from color that the form comes to the sight, from which the sight perceives the color of the thing. However, that which is perfectly transparent lacks color, and therefore cannot be perceived by the sight. The second cause is that the sight does not perceive a thing unless it is illuminated, and a "secondary form" comes from the light within it to the sight along with the form of color. This secondary form of light does not arise from light shining upon a body unless the light is <term>fixed|the idea that light must "stick" or "settle" on a surface to be reflected or perceived, rather than passing straight through</term> in that body upon which it shines. Therefore, when light is fixed in that body, a secondary form is produced from it. When light shines upon a very transparent body, it is not fixed in it, but passes through its transparency. Therefore, when a transparent body is opposite the sight and light shines upon it from the side where the sight is, the light passes through it and is not fixed on its surface; thus, there is no light on the surface opposite the sight from which a form could come to the eye. If the source of light shining on that transparent body is itself illuminated, its light will pass through the transparent body to the sight, but it will carry nothing with it of the transparent body's color, since a perfectly transparent body has no color. The sight will therefore perceive the illuminated body behind the transparent one, but it will not perceive the transparent body itself. This is because the sight does not perceive a thing that is perfectly transparent. When the transparency of a body is similar to the transparency of air, its condition is like that of air, and it is not perceived by the sight, just as air is not. Transparent bodies whose transparency is not thicker than the transparency of air are not perceived by the sight, because no form comes from them to the sight that can act upon the eye. A similar thing happens if there is a transparent medium other than air between the sight and the object, and the transparency of the object is not thicker than the transparency of that medium. But when the thing seen is dense, it will be colored; and when light shines upon it, it is fixed upon its surface. From its color and the light shining upon it, a form is created which extends through the air and transparent bodies. When this form reaches the sight, it acts upon it, and the sight perceives the object from it. When a visible thing is transparent, but less so than air, it will have a color according to its thickness; and when light shines upon it, the light will be fixed in it with a certain fixing,

A form will arise in the air from it, according to the color and light on its surface. When that form reaches the sight, it will act upon the sight, and the sight will perceive that thing seen. For this reason, the sight does not perceive visible things unless the visible object itself is dense, or has some degree of density in it. Thus, the causes have now been explained as to why the sight perceives nothing unless the aforementioned characteristics are combined. This explanation is what we intended to demonstrate in this treatise.

# THE SON OF ALHAZEN

## ALHAZEN’S OPTICS

->BOOK TWO.<-

It has been explained how vision occurs: *and it is the quality of the sense of sight arising from the form of light and color, which are in the thing seen, arranged just as they are on the surface of the thing seen. However, the sight perceives many "intentions" <note>Alhazen uses the term "intentio" to refer to properties or characteristics of an object, such as shape, size, or distance, that the brain must interpret</note> from visible things besides light and color. It was also explained in the first treatise [18 n] that vision only occurs through the directions of radial lines, and that radial lines differ in their arrangements; similarly, the arrangements of the forms coming upon them to the sight also differ. Furthermore, the perception of the sight from the thing seen does not happen in all bodies or in all visible things: rather, the quality of the sense of sight varies among visible things, and the quality of the sense of sight varies from a single thing seen according to its specific position and distance. We will divide this treatise into three chapters. In the first, we will explain the diversity of the arrangements of radial lines and distinguish their properties. In the second, we will explain all the properties perceived by the sight, and how the sight perceives each of them. In the third, we will explain the variation of the sight's perception of them.*

### ON THE DIVERSITY OF THE ARRANGEMENTS OF THE RADIAL
->lines, and the distinction of their properties.<-

#### Chapter One.

1. *The straight line connecting the centers of the parts of the sight is the axis of the optical pyramid. 18 p 3.*

It has already been explained in the first treatise [18. 20 n] that the radial lines—from whose directions the sight perceives visible objects—are straight lines whose ends meet at the center of the sight. And it has already been explained regarding the form of the eye [4 n 1] that the sensing member, which is the <term>glacialis|The crystalline lens of the eye, which medieval scholars believed was the primary organ of sight</term>, is situated over the end of the hollow of the nerve <note>The optic nerve</note> upon which the entire eye is built. This nerve only turns away from behind the center of the sight and behind the whole eye, at the opening located in the hollow of the bone <note>The optic foramen in the skull</note>. It has also been explained [7. 9 n 1] that a straight line passing through all the centers of the <term>tunics|The various layers or membranes of the eye, such as the cornea and retina</term> of the sight extends through the middle of the hollow nerve, and passes through the center of the opening in the front of the <term>uvea|In this context, referring to the pupil or the iris opening</term>. It has also been shown [5.13 n 1] that the center of this line does not change with respect to the whole sight, nor the surfaces of the eye's tunics, nor the parts of the sight. Therefore, a straight line passing through all the centers of the tunics of the sight always extends directly to the place where the hollow nerve (upon which the eye is composed) turns, in all states, whether the eye is in motion or at rest. Because this line passes through the center of the sight, the center of the opening in the front of the uvea, and the center of the uvea itself, it extends through the middle of the <term>pyramid|The visual cone or "pyramid of light" that connects the eye to the object being seen</term> whose tip is the sight. Since the circumference of the opening in the front of the uvea contains it, let us call this line the **axis of the pyramid**. It was also explained in that same first treatise [19 n] that the pyramid formed between the thing seen and the center of the sight marks out a part of the surface of the glacialis containing the entire form of the thing seen at the base of that pyramid. The form will be arranged on this part of the surface of the glacialis through the direction of the radial lines extending between the thing seen and the sight, according to the arrangement of the parts of the surface of the thing seen. Therefore, when the sight perceives a visible thing and its form reaches that part of the surface of the glacialis marked out by the aforementioned pyramid, every point of that form lies upon a radial line extending between that point and the point opposite it on the surface of the thing seen, along which the form comes to that point on the surface of the glacialis in a straight line. Thus, when the form of the thing seen is in the middle of the surface of the glacialis, the aforementioned axis will be one of the lines upon which the forms of the points on the surface of the thing seen travel; and that point...

# BOOK II OF OPTICS

...the point of the surface of the object seen, which is at the end of that axis, is the one whose form arrives upon that axis. It was demonstrated in the first treatise [26 n] that the forms perceived by sight extend through the body of the crystalline lens <note>original: "glacialis"</note> and into the hollow of the nerve upon which the eye is composed, reaching the common nerve <note>The optic chiasm, where the signals from both eyes meet</note>, which is at the middle of the interior of the brain. There, the ultimate sensor <note>The faculty of the soul or brain that finally "sees" the image</note> perceives the forms of visible things. Vision is not complete until the form arrives at the common nerve. The extension of forms from the surface of the crystalline lens through the body of the lens follows only the path of straight radial lines, because the lens only receives these forms according to the direction of radial lines.

---

<margin>2. The crystalline and vitreous humors differ in transparency. Thus, the visible form is refracted at the surface of the vitreous humor.</margin>
## *The crystalline and vitreous humors differ in transparency. Thus, the visible form is refracted at the surface of the vitreous humor.* 21 p 3.

The ultimate sensor only perceives the positions of the parts of the object seen according to their positions on the object's surface. Since the positions of the parts of the form relative to each other—specifically the form reaching the surface of the crystalline lens—match the positions of the parts of the object's surface relative to each other [18 n 1], and these forms extend as previously stated: vision will not be complete until the form on the surface of the lens reaches the common nerve with its parts arranged as they were on the lens, without any mixing. The form only travels from the lens surface to the common nerve by extending through the hollow of the nerve <note>The optic nerve</note> upon which the eye or crystalline humor is set. Therefore, if the form does not arrive in the hollow of this nerve in the same state it had in the lens, it will not arrive at the common nerve in that state either. 

Now, the form cannot extend from the lens surface to the nerve's hollow in perfectly straight lines while preserving the arrangement of its parts; for all these lines meet at the center of vision <note>The center of the eye's sphere</note>, and if they continued straight past the center, their positions would be inverted: right would become left, left would become right, top would become bottom, and bottom would become top. Furthermore, if the form extended along the radial lines, it would cluster together at the center of vision and become like a single point. Since the center of vision is in the middle of the whole eye, and ahead of the curve of the nerve's hollow: if the form were extended from the center of the eye as a single point along one line, it would reach the curve of the nerve as a single point. Thus, the whole form would not reach the curve, but only one point—the one at the tip of the pyramid's axis. If it were extended along radial lines and passed through the center, it would be inverted due to the crossing of the lines. 

Therefore, the form can only reach the nerve's hollow with its parts correctly positioned by following refracted lines that intersect the radial lines. Vision is thus only completed after the form arriving from the lens surface is refracted and extends along lines that cut across the radial lines. This refraction must happen before reaching the center, because if it happened after passing the center, the image would be inverted. It has already been shown [18 n 1] that this form travels through the crystalline lens along straight radial lines; since it cannot reach the nerve's hollow except by being refracted onto lines that intersect the radial lines, the form must be refracted as it passes through the body of the lens. 

It was previously stated [4 n 1] regarding the anatomy of the eye that the crystalline body has varying levels of transparency <note>original: "diaphanitatis"</note>, and that its back part, called the vitreous humor <note>original: "humor uitreus"</note>, has a different transparency than the front part. No part of the lens has a different shape from the front part except the vitreous body; it is a property of the forms of light and color to refract when they encounter a different body with a different transparency. Therefore, the forms only refract when they reach the vitreous humor. This body was given a different transparency from the front of the lens specifically so that the forms would be refracted within it. The surface of this body must be positioned before the center so that the forms are refracted there before they pass the center. This surface must also have a uniform arrangement <note>original: "consimilis ordinationis"</note>; for if it were not uniform, the form would appear distorted <note>original: "monstruosa"</note> due to the refraction.

---

<margin>3. The common section of the crystalline and vitreous spheres is either flat, or is part of a sphere larger than the crystalline sphere. It has a center different from the center of the eye.</margin>
## *The common section of the crystalline and vitreous spheres is either flat, or is part of a sphere larger than the crystalline sphere. It has a center different from the center of the eye.* 23 p 3.

A surface of uniform arrangement is either flat or spherical. This surface cannot be part of a sphere whose center is the center of vision; if it were, the radial lines would always be perpendicular to it, and thus the form would continue straight through them and not be refracted. Nor can it be part of a small sphere; for if it were, when the form refracted from it and moved further away, it would become distorted. Therefore, this surface is either flat or is a part of a sphere of a significant size, such that its sphericity does not interfere with the arrangement of the form. 

Thus, the surface of the crystalline humor—which is the common boundary between the vitreous body and the front crystalline body—is a surface of uniform arrangement positioned before the center of vision. All forms reaching the surface of the lens extend through the crystalline body along straight radial lines until they reach this surface. Upon reaching this surface, they are refracted along lines of uniform arrangement that intersect the radial lines. The radial lines do not...

ALHAZEN

...help in the arrangement of the forms of visible things, except at the crystalline lens <note>original: "glacialem"; the lens of the eye was historically called the "glacial" or "icy" humor due to its appearance</note> alone: because the beginning of sensation is at that member. And it was also demonstrated in the first treatise [15.16.18 n] that it is impossible for the form of a visible object to be arranged on the surface of the eye—given the image of the visible thing and the smallness of the sensing member—except by means of these lines. These lines, therefore, are nothing other than the instrument of sight, through which the perception of visible things is completed according to their actual being. However, the arrival of forms at the ultimate sensor <note>The "ultimum sentiens" refers to the faculty in the brain that finally processes the visual information</note> does not require extension according to the straightness of these lines.

### 4. *The crystalline humor receives light and color differently than other transparent bodies.* 22 p 3. The same 30 n 1.

The reception of forms in the sensing member is not like the reception of forms in transparent <term>diaphanis|bodies that allow light to pass through, such as glass or water</term> bodies: for the sensing member receives these forms and senses them, and they pass through it because of its transparency and the sensory power that is within it. It therefore receives these forms according to a sensory reception. Transparent bodies, however, do not receive these forms except by a reception intended for passing them on, and they do not sense them. And since the reception of the sensing body from these forms is not like the reception of transparent, non-sensing bodies, the extension of forms in the sensing body does not have to be according to the <term>verticationes|straight paths or directions of light rays</term> which transparent bodies require. Vision, therefore, is not restricted to the reception of forms from the directions of radial lines alone, except because it is a property of forms to be extended in transparent bodies along all straight paths. And when these forms have arrived at the sensing member in an orderly fashion, and are perceived by the sensing member in an orderly fashion, nothing remains afterward that requires those specific directions. Only the front part of the crystalline lens is restricted to receiving forms from the directions of radial lines; however, the posterior part, which is the vitreous humor <note>The clear gel-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina</note>, and the receiving power which is in that body, is not restricted by its sensation of these forms to anything except maintaining their arrangement.

### 5. *The crystalline and vitreous humors receive light and color differently.* 22 p 3.

And since this is the case, the quality of the vitreous humor's reception of forms is not like the reception or the quality of the front of the crystalline lens; and the receiving power in the vitreous is not the same receiving power as in the front part. And since the quality of the vitreous humor's reception of forms is not the quality of the front part of the crystalline lens, the refraction of forms at the surface of the vitreous humor occurs only because of the difference in the quality of sensory reception between these two bodies. Therefore, forms are refracted <note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another</note> at the vitreous for two reasons: one is the difference in transparency between the two bodies, and the other is the difference in the quality of sensory reception between these two bodies. If the transparency of these two bodies were the same, the form would extend into the vitreous body according to the straightness of the radial lines, because of the similarity in transparency; but it would be refracted because of the difference in the quality of sensation. Thus, the form would be monstrous due to refraction, or there would be two forms because of this arrangement. But when the difference in transparency confirms the refraction, and the difference in the quality of sensation confirms that refraction or bending, the form after refraction remains a single form. Because of this, the transparency of the vitreous body and the transparency of the front crystalline lens are different. Forms, therefore, reach the vitreous arranged according to their arrangement on the surface of the visible object; this body receives them and senses them, then the form is refracted because of the difference in transparency and the difference in the sensation of that body, and so the form arrives according to its proper disposition. Then this sensation and these forms are extended through this body until they reach the ultimate sensor. The extension of the sensation and the form in the vitreous body, and in the sensing body extended in the hollow of the nerve, to the ultimate sensor, is like the extension of the sense of touch or the sense of pain to the ultimate sensor; for the sense of touch and the sense of pain are only extended from the members through the fibers of the nerves and the spirit extended along those fibers.

### 6. *The vitreous humor and the visible spirit are endowed with almost the same transparency.* 22 p 3.

And when the forms of visible things reach the body of the vitreous humor, sensation is extended from that member into the sensing body, which is extended in the hollow of the nerve that continues between the eye and the front of the brain. According to the extension of sensation, the forms are extended, arranged according to their disposition, because the sensing body naturally preserves the arrangement of these forms. This arrangement is preserved in the sensing body because the arrangement of the parts of the sensing body that receive the parts of the forms, and the arrangement of the receiving power within the parts of the receiving body—both in the vitreous body and in every subtle body <note>Likely referring to the "spiritus" or visual spirit thought to inhabit the nerves</note> extended in the hollow of the nerve—is a similar arrangement. This being so, when the form reaches any point on the surface of the vitreous, it travels in a continuous path, and its position will not be altered in the cavity of the nerve in which the sensing body is extended. All these paths, through which all the points in the form travel, will be in a similar arrangement to each other; and all these paths will follow the curve of the nerve as it turns. During this turning, they will be arranged according to their arrangement before and after the turn, because of the quality of the sensation of that body; and thus the form will reach the common nerve according to its proper disposition. It is not possible for the extension of visible forms to the ultimate sensor to occur in any other way; for it is impossible for forms to reach the common nerve in their true being unless their extension happens in this manner. And when the forms are extended...

[...distributed] according to that arrangement, it is necessary that the form reaching any point of the glacial surface <note>original: "superficiei glacialis"; the crystalline lens</note> always be extended along the same direction <term>verticationem|the straight line or trajectory of a ray</term> to the same point of the common nerve <note>The "common nerve" refers to the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet</note> where the form arrives. However, the form reaching any point of the glacial surface always reaches the same point of the vitreous surface <note>The vitreous humor is the clear gel-like substance behind the lens</note>. From this, it follows that from any two points of similar position in respect to the two eyes, two forms are extended to the same point in the common nerve. It also follows from this that the sensing body, which is in the hollow of the nerve, must be somewhat transparent <term>diaphanum|allowing light to pass through</term> so that the forms of light and color may appear in it.

And it also follows that its transparency must be similar to the transparency of the vitreous humor, so that the forms are not refracted <term>refringantur|bent when passing from one medium to another</term> upon reaching the final surface of the vitreous humor near the hollow of the nerve; for when the transparency of two bodies is similar, the forms will not be refracted. It is not possible for the forms to be refracted at this surface because this surface is spherical. If the forms were refracted by this surface, they would only be moved a small distance from it and would immediately become monstrous <note>Meaning the image would be severely distorted or "deformed" beyond recognition</note>. Therefore, the refraction of forms cannot occur at this surface. And since the transparency of the sensing body in the hollow of the nerve is not different from the transparency of the vitreous humor, this lack of difference will not cause any variation in the form.

Even though the form is extended along with the extension of the sense, the transparency of the sensing body in the hollow of the nerve is not different from the transparency of the vitreous body. Now, the transparency of this body exists only so that forms may be extended in it according to the directions required by transparency, and so that it may receive the forms of light and color and that they may appear in it. For a body does not receive light and color, nor do forms of light and color pass through it, unless it is transparent or has some density <note>original: "spifsitudinis" (spissitudinis); meaning a subtle opacity or physical substance</note> within it. Light and color do not appear in a transparent body unless there is some density in its transparency; for this reason, the glacial lens is neither at the extreme of transparency nor at the extreme of density. Therefore, the sensing body in the hollow of the nerve is transparent, and in addition, there is some density in it. The form passes through this body because of its transparency, and the forms appear to the sensitive faculty because of its density. The ultimate sensor <note>The final processing power of the brain/soul</note> does not perceive the forms of light and color except from the forms reaching this body at the point where they reach the common nerve; it perceives light from the illumination of this body, and color from its coloration. In this manner, then, will be the arrival of forms at the ultimate sensor, and the perception of the ultimate sensor regarding them.

### *7. Only the axis of the optical pyramid is perpendicular to the common section of the crystalline and vitreous spheres. 24 p 3.*

After it has been declared that forms are refracted at the surface of the vitreous humor, let us say that the axis of the radial pyramid <note>The central ray of the cone of light entering the eye</note> cannot be slanted upon that surface, nor can there be any other line perpendicular to it. For if the axis were slanted upon this surface, when the forms reached this surface, they would be diversified in their arrangement, and their dispositions would be changed. Forms cannot reach the surface of the vitreous humor according to their true being unless the axis of the pyramid is perpendicular to that surface. 

For when the sight is opposite some visible thing, and the radial axis reaches the surface of that visible thing, the form of that visible thing will reach the surface of the glacial lens arranged according to the arrangement of the parts of the visible thing's surface. The form of the point at the extremity of the axis of the visible thing's surface will reach the point on the axis at the surface of the glacial lens [by 18 note 1], and the forms of all points of the visible thing's surface—whose distance from the point at the extremity of the axis is equal—will reach the points of the forms on the glacial surface whose distance from the point on the axis is equal. This is because all points reaching the glacial surface are on radial lines extended from the center of sight to the surface of sight, and the radial axis is perpendicular to the glacial surface. 

Therefore, all plane surfaces starting from the axis and cutting the glacial surface will be [by 18 proposition 11] perpendicular to that surface. And it has already been declared [3 note] that the surface of the vitreous humor is either flat or spherical, and its center is not the center of sight. If, therefore, the radial axis is slanted upon this surface and is not perpendicular to it, no plane surface will start from the axis perpendicular to this surface, except for one surface only; all remaining surfaces starting from the axis will be slanted upon it. For this is the property of lines slanted upon flat and spherical surfaces. 

Let us therefore imagine surface **a b c d**, starting from axis **a c**, and extending perpendicularly upon the vitreous surface **f g e**. It will therefore cut the vitreous surface and the glacial surface and will mark in them two common sections: in the glacial, **b d**, and in the vitreous, **e f**. Let us imagine two points, **b** and **d**, on the common section of this surface and the glacial surface, and let them be equally distant from the point on the axis. Let us imagine two lines starting from the center of the glacial, which is **c**, to these two points **b** and **d**, and let them be **c b** and **c d**. Therefore [by 1 proposition 11] these two

Therefore, it is not possible for the forms to reach the surface of the <term>vitreous|the vitreous humor, the jelly-like substance behind the lens</term> unless the arrangement of their parts corresponds to their true existence. Thus, it is not possible for the radial axis to be slanted upon the vitreous surface; it must, therefore, be perpendicular. Consequently, all the remaining radial lines will be slanted upon this surface, whether it be flat or spherical, since they intersect the axis at the center of the <term>glacialis|the crystalline lens or glacial humor</term>. None of these lines, therefore, pass through the center of the vitreous surface—if it were spherical—except for the axis alone, because it is perpendicular to it, and because the center of the crystalline surface is not the center of the vitreous surface.

### 8. *Vision through the axis of the optical pyramid is the most certain: through any other line, it is more certain the closer it is to the axis. 43 p 3.* <note>Reference to Proposition 43, part 3</note>

AND since it has been shown [in 2 n] that the forms reaching the surface of the crystalline lens will not reach the hollow of the nerve except after they have been refracted, and their refraction does not occur except at the vitreous surface; and since the axis is perpendicular to that surface, and all remaining radial lines are slanted upon that surface: when the forms reach the vitreous surface, all points upon it will be refracted, except for the point on the axis. For that point is extended along the straightness of the axis until it reaches the <term>place of gyration|the point where the optic nerve bends or enters the eye</term> of the hollow nerve [by 17 n 1]. Therefore, no form reaching the crystalline surface is extended to the hollow of the nerve in a straight line except for the axial point alone; all remaining points reach the hollow of the nerve along refracted lines. 

Therefore, when the sight perceives a seen object, and 그 object is positioned opposite the middle of the sight, and the axis is within the radial pyramid containing that seen object: the form of that seen object will reach the crystalline surface along the straightness of the radial lines. Then the forms are extended from that surface also along the straightness of the radial lines until they reach the vitreous surface. Then the axial point is extended from that surface along the straightness of the axis until it reaches the place of gyration of the hollow nerve, and all remaining points are refracted along lines that intersect the radial lines, but in a similar arrangement, until they reach the place of gyration of the hollow nerve. The form will therefore reach that place arranged according to its order on the crystalline surface, and arranged according to its arrangement on the surface of the seen object. But the condition of slanted forms is not like the condition of those extended straight, because the slanting will necessarily alter them by some degree. It follows from this condition, therefore, that the point reaching the place of gyration of the hollow nerve, which was extended along the straightness of the axis, is more accurately verified than all other points of the forms.

### 9. *An oblique radius of the optical pyramid, being closer to the axis, is refracted at smaller angles; one further away, at larger angles: and two equally distant, at equal angles. 36 p 3.* <note>Reference to Proposition 36, part 3</note>

FURTHERMORE, the refraction of points reaching the surface of refraction that are closer to the axial point is smaller, and for those further away, it is larger. This is because refraction only occurs according to the angles formed by the lines upon which the forms travel and the perpendiculars that are upon the surface of refraction. For lines forming smaller angles with the perpendiculars, the refraction will be according to smaller angles; and for lines forming larger angles with the perpendiculars, the refraction will be according to larger angles. Lines closer to the axis slant less upon the surface of refraction, and thus form smaller angles with the perpendiculars on the surface of refraction; and those further from the axis slant more upon the surface of refraction, and thus form larger angles with the perpendiculars. 

Forms whose refraction is smaller are more clearly manifested, and those whose refraction is larger, less so. Therefore, the point upon the axis reaching the place of gyration of the hollow nerve is clearer than all other remaining points, and that which is near to it is clearer than that which is further away. These forms are those which extend to the common nerve, and from them the <term>ultimate sentient|the final perceiving faculty of the mind</term> grasps the form of the seen object. And since this form reaching the place of gyration of the hollow nerve is of a diverse condition—namely, that the axial point is clearer than all remaining points, and what is closer to it is clearer than what is further—therefore the form reaching the common nerve, from which the sensitive power perceives the form of the seen object, will be of a diverse condition. Its point corresponding to the axial point on the surface of the seen object will be clearer than all remaining points of the form, and what is closer to this will be clearer than what is further. 

If the conditions of seen objects are brought forward, and the quality of the sight's perception of objects (which the sight perceives simultaneously) is distinguished from the quality of the sight's perception of the parts of a single seen object, they will be found to agree entirely with what we have declared. For when an observer is positioned opposite many visible things at the same time, and his sight is still and he does not move it: he will find the seen object opposite the middle of his sight clearer than those which are to the sides of that middle, and that which is closer to the middle will be clearer. Similarly, when an observer looks at a large seen object and his sight is positioned opposite the middle of that object and is still, he will perceive the middle of that object more clearly than its extremities. This will be well demonstrated when there are many visible things close together, and the observer is positioned opposite one of them (which will be the middle among those visible things) with a still gaze: for then he will perceive that middle with clear perception, and at the same time he will also perceive those things on its sides, but not clearly. ### *10. A visible object is perceived either by sight alone, by sight and reasoning, or by sight and prior knowledge. In hypothesis 3, book 1; below in book 4, propositions 59, 60, part 3.*

The sense of sight perceives nothing of visible things except within a body. In a body, many things are gathered together and many things happen to it; sight perceives many things in bodies that are within them or happen to them. Color is one of those things that happens to bodies, as is light, and the sense of sight perceives both of these in bodies. It also perceives other things besides these two, such as shape, position, size, motion, and others which we shall distinguish later. It also perceives the similarity of colors and their differences, and the similarity of light and its differences; likewise, it perceives the similarity of shapes, positions, and motions. The perception of all these is not achieved in a single way, nor is the perception of any of them achieved by the sense of sight alone. For when sight perceives two individuals at the same time who are similar in form, it perceives the individuals and it perceives that they are similar. However, the similarity of the two forms in the two individuals is neither the forms themselves nor one of them. Since sight perceives individuals from the forms coming to it from the two individuals, it perceives the likeness of the two individuals from the similarity of the two forms reaching the sight from the object. This likeness of the two forms is not the forms themselves, nor is it a third form specific to "similarity"; rather, the similarity of two forms is their agreement in some quality. Therefore, the similarity of two forms is not perceived except by the comparison of one to the other and by the perception of that in which they are similar. Because sight perceives similarity, and there is no "third form" in the eye from which it perceives similarity, it follows that sight does not perceive the similarity of two forms except by comparing one to the other. Since this is the case, the visual sense's perception of the similarity of forms and their difference is not through sense alone, but through the comparison of forms with each other. 

Also, when sight perceives two colors of the same kind, and one of them is stronger than the other—such as the <term>green of myrtle|a dark, saturated green</term> and the <term>green of lovage|a lighter, yellowish green</term>—it perceives that they are both green, and it also perceives that one of them is of a stronger greenness. It distinguishes between the two greens and perceives their similarity in being green, yet their difference in strength and weakness. But the distinction between the two greens is not the sensation of greenness itself, since the sensation of greenness comes from the "greening" of the sight <note>original: "uiridificatione uisus," an Al-Haytham concept where the eye is momentarily affected by the color it sees</note> by both greens. Sight perceives that they are of one kind; therefore, the perception that one green is stronger than the other, and that the two are of the same kind, is a "discerning" of the coloration in the eye, not the sensation of color itself. Similarly, when two colors similar in strength are of the same kind, sight perceives the two colors, perceives they are of the same kind, and perceives they are similar in strength. 

The arrangement of light is similar for the sight, since sight perceives light and distinguishes between strong and weak light. Therefore, the visual perception of the similarity of colors and their difference, the similarity of light and its difference, and the similarity of the outlines of the forms of visible things, their shape, their position, and their differences, occurs only by comparing them with each other, not by sense alone. 

Furthermore, the sense of sight perceives the <term>transparency|diaphanitatem</term> of transparent bodies, even those that are extremely transparent. But it does not perceive such transparency by any other means than by comparison. For transparent stones, whose transparency is slight, are not perceived by sight to be transparent until they are placed against the light and the light is perceived from behind them; then they are perceived to be transparent. Likewise, the transparency of any transparent body is not perceived by sight until either the body or the light behind it is perceived, and it is further perceived through "distinction" <note>intellectual discernment</note> that what appears from behind is different from the transparent body. The perception that what is behind the transparent body is different from that body is not a perception by sense alone, but a perception by <term>reason|rationem</term>. And since transparency is only perceived through a mental marking, it is therefore only perceived by distinction and reason. 

Even writing <note>scriptura</note> is not perceived except through the distinction of the forms of the letters, their composition, and the comparison of them to similar things which were known to the writer before. Similarly, many visible things, when the quality of the com- [composition] is considered...

the comprehension of these things is not achieved by the sense [of sight] alone, but through reasoning and <term>distinction|the mental faculty of discerning different properties</term>. And since this is the case, not everything perceived by sight is grasped by sense alone; rather, many <term>visible intentions|non-material properties of an object, such as its "horseness" or shape</term> are grasped through reasoning and distinction alongside the sensation of the seen form. Sight itself does not possess the power of distinguishing; rather, the <term>distinguishing power|a cognitive faculty of the soul or mind</term> discerns these things. It recognizes familiar animals, trees, plants, and stones when it has seen them or similar things previously. It recognizes all familiar "intentions" in visible things. Sight cannot grasp the <term>quiddity|the "what-ness" or essence of a thing</term> of any object except through cognition. Cognition, however, is not perception by sense alone, since sight does not recognize everything it has seen before. If sight perceives an individual and is then separated from them for a long time, and later sees them again without remembering them, it will not recognize them; for it only recognizes what it has known when it remembers. Therefore, if cognition were perception by sense alone, it would follow that whenever sight saw an individual it had seen before, it would immediately recognize them in the second viewing according to all their characteristics—but this is not so. Since cognition only occurs through memory, cognition is not perception by sense alone.

### *11. Vision through a prior concept occurs, in a way, through <term>syllogism|a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>. <note>original: "63 p 3"</note>*

Perception through cognition is a form of perception involving a mode of reasoning. This is because cognition is the perception of the similarity between two forms: the form which sight perceives during the act of recognition, and the form of that seen object (or one like it) which it perceived the first time. For this reason, cognition only happens through memory. If the first form is not present in the memory, sight will not perceive the similarity between the two forms, and thus will not recognize the thing seen. Cognition applies both to the form of an individual thing and the form of a species. Recognition of an individual comes from comparing the form of the individual perceived by sight to another form previously perceived. Recognition of a species comes from comparing the form of the seen object to other forms similar to individuals of its species perceived before. This perception of similarity is an act of reason, as it only arises from the comparison of one form to another. Therefore, cognition is nothing other than a mode of reasoning. 

However, this reasoning is distinguished from all other types of reasoning because cognition does not occur through a complete investigation of every detail present in the form, but rather through **signs**. When sight perceives some of the "intentions" within a form and remembers the first form, it immediately recognizes the object. This is not how everything grasped by reason works; many things grasped by reason are only understood after a complete investigation of all their inherent details. For example, when a scribe looks at the form of the letters *a b c*, he immediately perceives that it is *a b c*. From the perception that *a* comes first and *c* is last, he understands it is *a b c*. Similarly, if he sees **THE LORD** <note>original: "DOMINVS"</note> written, he immediately understands it through cognition and habit. Likewise, a scribe understands all familiar arrangements as soon as he sees them, without needing to distinguish one letter from another. This is not the case if a scribe looks at a strange written word he has never seen before; he will not understand that word until he has distinguished its individual letters, and only then will he grasp the word. Therefore, any form that sight has not seen before (nor anything similar to it), when perceived by sight, will not be understood by sight until it has distinguished all or most of the details of that form. A familiar form, however, is perceived by sight immediately upon the perception of certain signs within that form. Thus, what is grasped through cognition is grasped through a sign; but not everything grasped through reasoning is grasped through a sign. Most visible properties are only grasped through cognition. Neither the essence of a seen thing, nor that of any thing perceived by other senses, is understood except through cognition. The power of cognition is joined to the power of sense, and the perception of visible things is not complete without it. Yet cognition is not by sense alone. Thus, of the properties perceived by the sense of sight, some are perceived by sense alone, some by cognition, and some by reasoning and distinction.

### *12. Vision through reasoning usually occurs in a very short time. <note>original: "69 p 3"</note>*

Most visible properties perceived through reasoning and distinction are grasped in an extremely small amount of time. It is often not apparent that their perception involves reasoning and distinction because of the speed of the logic through which these properties are grasped. Indeed, shape, size, transparency of a body, and similar properties found in visible things are mostly perceived with great speed, and it is not realized then that their perception is through reasoning. Since the perception of these properties is through reasoning, it only happens through the manifestation of their positions and the habituation of the distinguishing power to these properties. Upon the arrival of the form, it grasps all the properties within it, and thus they are distinguished by it during the perception—

# ALHAZEN

...conclusion. Similarly, in argumentation and all forms of reasoning where the premises are universal and obvious, the <term>distinguishing power|the mental faculty of discerning different properties</term> does not require any significant time to grasp their conclusions; rather, the conclusion is understood by the intellect the moment the premise is presented. The reason for this is that the distinguishing power does not reason through the literal assembly and ordering of a proposition in the way an argument is constructed using spoken words. While a verbal argument depends on words and the specific sequence of statements to reach a conclusion, the reasoning of the distinguishing power is not like that. This power grasps a conclusion without needing words, and without needing the formal arrangement of statements or vocabulary. The verbal arrangement of an argument is nothing more than a way to describe the *process* by which the distinguishing power reaches a conclusion. In itself, the mind's grasp of a conclusion does not require those specific verbal forms or sequences.

Therefore, <term>visible intentions|non-material properties of an object, such as its shape, size, or "what-ness"</term> that are grasped by reason are, for the most part, understood very quickly. In most cases, it is not even apparent that the mind has performed a reasoning process at all. Furthermore, when these visible intentions are grasped through reasoning and discernment many times over, the distinguishing power comes to understand their meaning deeply. If it sees them again later, it will grasp them through <term>cognition|recognition based on prior experience</term> without needing to discern every single detail again. Instead, it uses only "signs" or cues, and reaches the conclusion through recognition without needing to repeat the entire logical argument. An example of this is a writer who, upon seeing a word for the first time, must look at it carefully, but recognizes familiar words instantly.

All intentions grasped by reason follow this same pattern when their premises are obvious and their conclusions are true. Once the soul understands a conclusion to be true and encounters it many times, that conclusion becomes like a "manifest proposition" (an obvious truth) to the mind. Thus, when the soul sees the premise, it immediately understands the conclusion without needing to repeat the formal reasoning.

Indeed, many "intentions" that the distinguishing power actually confirms through reasoning are mistakenly thought to be "first propositions" (axioms or self-evident truths). People believe these are grasped by nature and the intellect alone, rather than through reasoning. For example, it is commonly thought that the statement "the whole is greater than its part" is judged true by the very nature of the intellect, and that the grasp of its truth involves no reasoning. However, the mind cannot grasp that the whole is greater than its part until it has first understood the "intentions" of "whole" and "part," as well as the concepts of "greater" and "smaller." If the mind does not understand the concept of the parts, it cannot understand the concept of the whole. The "intention" of a "whole" is simply the totality of things, while the "intention" of a "part" is a single component. "Greater" is a relationship to something else; specifically, the "greater" thing is that which is equal to the other thing *plus* something more.

The proof that every whole is greater than its part is found by comparing them: the whole is found to be equal to the part while also having a remainder—the "more." Because the concept of "greater" aligns so perfectly with the concept of a "whole," the mind reasons that the whole must be greater than its part. Since this proposition can only be understood in this way, its comprehension is actually a result of reasoning, not just the "nature of the intellect." What *is* in the nature of the intellect is simply the ability to recognize the alignment between the concept of a "whole" and the concept of "greater" when they are compared.

The structure of this <term>syllogism|a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> is as follows: 
1. Every whole adds something to its part.
2. Everything that adds to another is greater than it.
3. Therefore, every whole is greater than its part.

The speed at which the distinguishing power reaches this conclusion is only because the universal premise is so clear. But the realization that the whole is greater than the part is still a result of reasoning. Because the universal premise is so obvious, the mind grasps the conclusion the moment it encounters the specific, minor premise (the observation that a specific whole adds to its specific part). 

Because the truth of this conclusion is so firmly established in the soul and present in the memory, the intellect accepts the premise without needing to repeat the logical steps, relying on recognition alone. Anything of this type is called a "first proposition" by people; it is thought to be grasped by the intellect alone, and that no process other than the intellect is needed to understand its truth. This mistake happens because the truth is grasped instantly. Therefore, syllogisms whose premises are universal and obvious are understood in a period of time so short it cannot be perceived. Once the reasoning has been performed enough times for the truth of the conclusion to be certified in the soul, that conclusion becomes as clear as a manifest proposition. In this manner, the distinguishing power grasps many intentions through reasoning in imperceptible time, without needing to repeat the logical steps.

### 13. *Vision by an anticipated notion occurs in time, and its nature is mostly ignored.*

->64. 69 p 3.<-

Furthermore, the nature of how we grasp visible intentions through reason and recognition is often not apparent. This is because the comprehension happens so quickly, and because understanding *how* we understood something requires a "second argument" (a reflection) after the "first argument" (the act of seeing). The distinguishing power does not use this second argument at the same time it is busy grasping a visible intention. It does not stop to analyze *how* it is perceiving that intention; indeed, it cannot do so because of the sheer speed with which it grasps intentions through recognition and arguments based on obvious premises.

# OPTICS BOOK II

...firm and certain in the soul. And because of this, the quality of how the truth of many true propositions is grasped through cognition is not felt. The root of the affirmation of their truth is through reasoning at the moment they occur. For when these propositions are presented to the <term>distinguishing power|the mental faculty that analyzes and compares sensory data</term>, it immediately judges them to be true through <term>cognition|recognition of something previously known</term>. But during this recognition, the mind does not inquire into how the truth was previously affirmed, nor does it inquire into how it understands that they are true at the moment they occur.

In the same way, the process of reasoning by which the distinguishing power understands the nature of its own grasp of an object is not an instantaneous argument. Instead, it requires careful consideration, because different types of perception exist: some occur through the very nature of the intellect, some through recognition, and some through active consideration and distinction. Therefore, the understanding of *how* we perceive, and what kind of perception it is, only happens through a process of reasoning and distinction that is not rapid. 

Because of this, the way we grasp visible things through reason often goes unnoticed during the act of seeing. Furthermore, a human being is naturally born to distinguish without difficulty and to reason without labor. A person does not perceive that they are reasoning except when the reasoning is difficult. When it requires no effort or specialized knowledge, one does not notice the act of logic. Therefore, habitual arguments—those whose premises are obvious and require no effort—are natural to humans. Because of this, when a person grasps the conclusions of such arguments, they do not perceive that they have reached them through a logical process.

Evidence that a human is born to reason—and that they reason without perceiving the act—can be seen in children as they first grow. They grasp many things just like a grown, discerning person, and they perform many actions through distinction. For example: when a child is shown two things of the same kind, such as two apples, and one is more beautiful than the other, he will take the more beautiful one and leave the other. But the choice of a more beautiful thing only happens by comparing one to the other, and by the understanding of beauty—what is beautiful and what is ugly. Similarly, when he chooses the more beautiful apple over one of lesser beauty, it signifies that he only chose it after a comparison and after grasping the form of each, as well as the logical point that the beauty of the more beautiful one surpasses the less beautiful one. This choice of the more beautiful apple is only possible through a universal proposition <note>original: "propositiõem uniuersalem"</note> stating: *That which is more beautiful is better; and that which is better is more worthy of being chosen.* Therefore, the child uses this proposition, yet does not perceive that he is using it.

Since this is the case, the child reasons and distinguishes; yet there is no doubt that the child does not know what an "argument" is, nor does he perceive whether he is reasoning or not when he does it. Indeed, if someone intended to teach him what an argument is, or what it means to reason, he would not understand. Because the child reasons yet does not know what reasoning is, it shows that the human soul is born to reason without difficulty or labor. Thus, a person does not perceive during the perception of a thing that it is happening through a process of logic. 

However, the <term>intentions|the secondary qualities of an object, like beauty, shape, or use, beyond just light and color</term> that are grasped by reason are only the obvious ones, whose premises are very clear. As for intentions whose premises are not very clear, and whose arguments require effort, a person might actually perceive that they are grasping them through reason when they result from a true exercise of distinction.

It has now been made clear from everything we have said that some intentions grasped by sight are understood by sense alone, some by distinction, and some by cognition, reasoning, and logic. The nature of how particular intentions are grasped by sight is usually not apparent because of the speed of recognition and the speed of the reasoning by which visible intentions are understood. The distinguishing power is born to reason without labor or difficulty, but rather by nature and habit; and that power does not need to repeat its reasoning when perceiving particular intentions that have been seen many times before.

### 14. *From a visible thing seen frequently, a general notion remains in the soul, by which any similar visible thing is perceived and recognized.* <margin>61 p 3.</margin>

**I**ntentions that have been seen many times are also grasped by the reasoning and distinction present in the soul, so that a person does not perceive them "settling" there; nor does their settling have a specific sensory beginning. This is because a person has <term>experience|knowledge gained through repeated observation</term> of grasping visible things. Experience is itself a form of distinction—specifically the distinction by which sensory intentions are understood. Thus, a person understands sensory intentions through reason and distinction, and acquires the meanings of those sensory objects. 

These sensory intentions are frequently presented to him in succession until they "rest" in his soul, even without him noticing them doing so. Thus, when a particular intention that has already settled in his soul appears, he will grasp it upon its arrival through recognition. Yet he does not perceive the quality of the perception, nor the quality of the recognition, nor how the knowledge of that intention came to rest in his soul. 

Therefore, all particular intentions that are grasped by reason and distinction and are frequently repeated have already been grasped by the person in the past. They have settled in the soul, and a "universal form" <note>An abstract concept or mental category</note> has been created, resting there, derived from each of these particular intentions. These intentions are therefore grasped without repeating the original argumentation and without the reasoning by which the truth of that intention was first understood. Nothing remains that requires repeated reasoning except to consider the particular intentions that are in those...

*15. There are twenty-two primary visible properties, to which all others are referred.*

Since all these things have been explained, we shall now begin to describe the qualities of the comprehension of each of the particular intentions perceived through sight, and the qualities of the arguments by which the **distinguishing power** <note>The "distinguishing power" (uirtus distinctiua) is the mental faculty Alhazen believes processes sensory data into logical understanding.</note> acquires those intentions grasped by the sense of sight. The particular intentions grasped by the sense of sight are many, but they are generally divided into twenty-two: and these are **light, color, distance, position, solidity, shape, size, continuity, separation and division, number, motion, rest, roughness, smoothness, transparency, identity, shadow, darkness, beauty, ugliness, similarity, and difference** in all particular intentions and in all forms composed of these particular intentions.

These, therefore, are all the things grasped by the sense of sight. If any visible property exists beyond these, it is categorized under one of them: for instance, **arrangement** is placed under position; **writing** and **painting** are placed under shape and order; **straightness, curvature, concavity, and convexity** are placed under shape; **multitude and fewness** are placed under number; **equality and increase** are placed under similarity and difference; and **cheerfulness, laughter, and sadness** (which are perceived from the shape of the face) are placed under shape. Likewise, **weeping** (which is contained in the shape of the face along with the motion of tears) is placed under shape and motion. **Moisture and dryness** <note>original: "humilitas & siccitas." The text likely intended "humiditas" (moisture) given the context of "liquiditate" (liquidity), though the scribe wrote "humilitas" (humility).</note> are placed under motion and rest, since moisture is grasped by the sense of sight—but it is not grasped by sight except through the liquidity of a moist body and the motion of one of its parts before another—and dryness is grasped by sight only through the lack of movement in the parts of a dry body and the absence of liquid motion. Similarly, every particular intention grasped by sight is categorized under the parts we mentioned before. And all visible intentions are as we have stated above.

*16. Vision is perfected when the visible form, received by the crystalline humor, reaches the optic nerve. [20 p 3. The same 25 n 1.]*

This being the case, the distinction and reasoning of the distinguishing power—and the recognition of forms and their signs—occur only through the recognition or distinction made by the distinguishing power from the forms arriving within the cavity of the **common nerve** <note>The "common nerve" (neruus communis) refers to the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet.</note> at the point where the **ultimate sensor** <note>The "ultimate sensor" refers to the final faculty of the brain that perceives the image.</note> grasps them, and through the knowledge of the signs of these forms. Thus, the sensing body extending from the surface of the sensing member <note>the eye</note> to the cavity of the common nerve (namely, the **visual spirit**) is sensing throughout its whole, because the sensitive power exists throughout that entire body. Therefore, when a form is extended from the surface of the sensing member to the cavity of the common nerve, every part of the sensing body will feel the form; and when the form reaches the cavity of the common nerve, it will be grasped by the ultimate sensor, and then distinction and reasoning will occur.

The sensitive power feels the form of the visible thing throughout the entire sensing body extended from the surface of the sensing member to the cavity of the common nerve, and the distinguishing power distinguishes the intentions that are in the form at the moment the ultimate sensor grasps the form. In this manner, therefore, the forms of visible things are grasped by the sensitive power, the ultimate sensor, and the distinguishing power. It will be clear from this arrangement that the sensitive power feels the location on the sensing member where the form arrives, because it does not feel the form except from the place where the form arrives. It has also been shown [25 n 1] that from every point on the surface of the **glacial** <note>The "glacial" or "glacialis" is the crystalline humor/lens, considered by Alhazen to be the primary organ of sight.</note> the form is extended along a single continuous path, accounting for any refraction or curvature, until it reaches a single point in the place where the form arrives in the cavity of the common nerve.

Because of this, the form arriving at a part of the surface of the glacial is extended from that part to another part of the cavity of the common nerve. The forms of various visible things perceived simultaneously are extended to specific locations in the cavity of the common nerve. The forms of all those visible things arrive at the cavity of the common nerve, and the arrangement of those forms relative to one another in the cavity of the common nerve will be the same as the arrangement of the visible things themselves relative to one another. Therefore, when the sight is directed toward a visible object, the forms of the light and color of that object arrive at the surface of the eye, and they arrive at the surface of the glacial, and they are extended according to determined paths (as we have said) according to their arrangement, shape, and form, until they reach the cavity of the common nerve. They are grasped by the sensitive power upon their arrival in the body of the glacial and upon their arrival in the entire sensing body, and the distinguishing power distinguishes all the intentions within them. The form of light and the form of color do not reach the cavity of the nerve except because the sensing body extended in the cavity of the nerve is colored by the form of color and light and illuminated by the form of light, and the form reaches the cavity of the common nerve; and
