...it will be a part of the sentient body, located in the **hollow of the common nerve** <note>The "common nerve" refers to the optic chiasm, the place where the nerves from both eyes meet. Alhazen believed this is where the two images from the eyes combine into one.</note>, where the form of the visible object arrives, colored with the color of that object and illuminated by the light present in it. If the visible object has one color, that part of the sentient body will be of one color; and if the parts of the visible object are of different colors, the parts of that sentient body in the hollow of the common nerve will be of different colors. The **ultimate sensor** <note>The "ultimate sensor" (ultimum sentiens) is the final faculty of perception, usually located in the brain, that "reads" the images delivered by the eyes.</note> perceives the color of the visible thing from the coloration it finds in that part, and it grasps the light of the visible thing from the illumination it finds in that same part. 

The **distinguishing power** <note>The "distinguishing power" (uirtus distinctiua) is the analytical faculty of the mind that interprets sensory data.</note> perceives many **particular intentions** <note>In this context, "intentions" are the individual characteristics or qualities of an object, such as its shape, size, or position.</note> found in the visible object by distinguishing the features within that form. It does this by observing the arrangement of the parts of the form, the shape of the container of the form, the shape of its individual parts, the variety of colors, positions, and arrangements within the parts of that form, and their similarities or differences. 

Furthermore, the light coming from a colored visible object to the sight does not come by itself without color, nor does the form of the color coming from a visible object reach the sight without light. The forms of light and color present in a visible object only arrive mixed together, and the ultimate sensor only perceives them as mixed. Nevertheless, the sensor still perceives the visible object as illuminated and recognizes that the light appearing in the object is distinct from its color; this recognition is an act of **distinction** <note>Meaning the mind is able to separate the concept of "light" from the concept of "color," even if they physically arrive at the eye at the same time.</note>. 

Distinction, however, belongs only to the distinguishing power, not to the sense itself. Yet, once the distinguishing power has grasped this intention, the concept rests in the soul and does not require a new logical argument every time a form appears. The soul knows that the light in an object is different from its color. The distinguishing power perceives that the **accidental light** <note>Light that falls onto an object from an outside source, rather than light generated by the object itself.</note> on a colored object is different from its inherent color because the light on a single object varies—sometimes it increases and sometimes it decreases. While this happens, the color itself remains the same; although the "sparkle" or brightness of the color may change according to the light, the category of the color does not change. Also, accidental light might reach a visible object through an opening; if that opening is blocked, the object becomes dark. Therefore, through the distinguishing power's observation of the variation of light on objects, and its observation of an object’s illumination and its occasional lack of light, the sight perceives that the colors in visible objects are distinct from the light that falls upon them. 

The form that the sensor perceives from a colored visible object is thus a mixed form made of light and color. But the distinguishing power understands that the color within it is distinct from the light within it. This understanding is a type of **recognition** <note>Original Latin: "cognitio." Alhazen argues that once we learn what a color is, we recognize it instantly rather than having to re-analyze it every time.</note> that occurs when the form reaches the sensor, since the soul already knows that the light in any mixed form of light and color is different from the color itself.

### 17. Among the visible species, the essence of light and color is perceived first. [Ref: 67 p 3].

The first thing the distinguishing power perceives among the properties assigned to a form is the **quiddity** <note>The "what-ness" or essential nature of something.</note> of the color. However, the quiddity of a color is only grasped by the distinguishing power through recognition when the color of the visible thing is a familiar one. This recognition of a color's nature by the power of distinction occurs by comparing the current form of the color to forms it has perceived before—that is, to similar colors. 

For when the sight perceives the color red and recognizes it as red, it only knows it is red because it recognizes it; and this recognition only happens by comparing its form to things it has perceived previously. If the sight had never perceived the color red until now, it would not know upon seeing it that it was "red." Therefore, when a color is among familiar colors, it is known by the sight through recognition; but if it is an unfamiliar color that the sight has never encountered before, the sight will not recognize it but will instead compare it to the most similar colors it already knows. 

The root of perceiving color, therefore, comes from sense alone; afterward, when the sight has encountered it many times, it is perceived through recognition—that is, what kind of color it is. Likewise, the quiddity of light is only grasped through recognition, for the sight recognizes the light of a fire and the light of the sun, and it distinguishes between them and the light of the moon. This perception of the nature of these lights is only possible through recognition. Consequently, everything perceived by the sense of sight beyond light and color is not perceived by sense alone, but through distinction and reasoning combined with sense. This is because everything grasped through distinction and reasoning requires the analysis of the different intentions found within the sensible form, and these intentions are only grasped alongside the sensation of the form itself.

### 18. Light and color are perceived by sight through themselves alone. [Ref: 59 p 3].

Light that exists in an illuminated body is perceived by sight on its own according to its being, both by itself and from the sensation itself. Both light and color in a body that is colored and illuminated by accidental light are perceived by the sight simultaneously and mixed, and by sense alone. Therefore, **essential light** <note>Light produced by the object itself, like the sun or a flame.</note> is grasped by the sensor from the illumination of the sentient body, and color is grasped from the alteration and coloration of the form of the sentient body, along with the perception of the accidental light mixed with that color. Thus, when the form of a color reaches it, the sensor perceives "colored light," but when the form of essential light reaches it, it perceives "light alone." These two things alone are grasped by the sight through sense alone.

### 19. Color itself is perceived before its specific essence. Likewise, any visible thing is perceived in itself before its specific essence. <note>original: "Color ex sese prius percipitur, quàm ipsius essentia." Referring to Proposition 68, Part 3.</note>

And we shall say again that the comprehension of color, as far as it is color, occurs before the comprehension of the **quiddity** <note>original: "quidditatis." This is a philosophical term meaning the "what-ness" or the specific nature and identity of a thing.</note> of that color. That is to say, the sight perceives color and senses that it is "colored" before it senses what *kind* of color it is. This is because when the form reaches the sight, the sight becomes "colored," and when the sight is colored, it senses that it is colored, and thus it senses color. Then, through the **distinction** <note>The mental process of telling things apart or identifying specific characteristics.</note> of the color and the comparison of it to colors known to the sight, it comprehends the specific essence of the color. Therefore, the comprehension of color simply as color comes before the comprehension of the specific essence of that color, and the comprehension of the specific essence of the color will occur through **cognition** <note>Mental recognition based on prior experience.</note>. 

The proof that the sight comprehends color as color before it comprehends the specific nature of the color is this: visible things with strong colors, such as deep green or dark brown and the like, when they are in a very dark place, are not comprehended by the sight in that place except as mere colors. Yet the sight senses that they are colors, even if it does not distinguish what kind of colors they are at the beginning of the perception. But when the place is not very dark, or if the sight looks intently for a long time, the sight eventually comprehends what kind of color they are; or it does so if the light is increased and intensified in that place. 

It is clear from this experiment, therefore, that the sight comprehends color as color before it comprehends what kind of color it is. What the sight perceives of the color at the very moment it reaches the eye is "coloration," and this coloration is like a darkness or a shadow when the color is subtle. If the visible thing consists of different colors, the sight will initially perceive from the form of that visible thing a darkness in the parts of different qualities—varying according to strength or weakness—appearing like shadows that differ in intensity. Therefore, the first thing the sight perceives from the form of color is the change in the sensing organ and its coloration, which is a darkness or something similar to darkness. Then the sensing faculty distinguishes that coloration. 

If the visible thing is well-illuminated, that color will be distinguished by the sight, and its specific essence will be comprehended, provided it is among the colors the sight has often perceived before. If it is a color it has perceived almost always, it will be comprehended in a shorter time—in a second instant, between which and the first instant (when it perceived color simply as color) there is no **sensible time** <note>A duration of time long enough for a human to consciously notice.</note>. However, if it is an unfamiliar color that the sight has not perceived before except rarely, or if it is in a dark place with weak light, its specific essence will not be comprehended by the sight except in a sensible amount of time. And if the visible object is dark and has only a small amount of light—like what is perceived at night or in very dark places—nothing will be distinguished by the sensing faculty except for darkness itself. 

It is therefore demonstrated, by the comprehension of colors in dark places, that the comprehension of color as color comes before the comprehension of its specific essence. Furthermore, the proof that the sight perceives color as color before it perceives what kind of color it is, is this: when the sight perceives a strange color it has never seen before, it comprehends that it is indeed "a color," yet it does not know what kind of color it is. After dwelling on it for a long time, it will liken it to the closest similar color. From these experiments, it is clearly demonstrated that the comprehension of color as color occurs before the comprehension of the specific essence of the color. It is also demonstrated from these experiments that the comprehension of the specific essence of color occurs only through the process of distinction. Therefore, that which the sight perceives by **sense alone** <note>Pure sensory input without the need for mental interpretation.</note> is nothing but color as color and light as light; beyond these, it perceives nothing by sense alone, but rather through distinction, reasoning, and cognition.

### 20. The essence of color is perceived in time. Likewise, the essence of any visible thing is perceived in time. <note>Referring to Proposition 70, Part 3.</note>

And let us also say that the comprehension of the specific essence of color does not occur except in time. For since the comprehension of the essence of color is only achieved through distinction and assimilation <note>Comparing a new stimulus to a known memory.</note>, and distinction only occurs in time, it follows that the comprehension of the essence of color only occurs in time. 

A clear proof that the comprehension of the essence of color only occurs in time is provided by what appears on a **spinning top** <note>original: "trocho." A "trochus" is a hoop or a top used in physical experiments.</note> during its motion. For when there are different dyes on the top, and those dyes are arranged as lines extending from the center of its visible surface and from its neck out to the edge of its circumference, and the top is spun with a strong motion, anyone who looks at it will perceive all its colors as if they were a single color, different from all the individual colors on it. It will look as if it were a color composed of all the colors of those lines. The viewer will not perceive the lines themselves, nor the diversity of the colors. At the same time, the viewer will perceive the top as if it were standing still when the motion is very strong, because any single point does not remain in the same place for a sensible amount of time. Instead, in a minimal amount of time, it rotates through the entire circumference of the circle along which it revolves. 

Therefore, the form of a point reaches the sight along the circumference of a circle in the eye, and the sight does not comprehend the color of that point in that minimal time except as the entire circumference of the circle reaching the eye; thus, it perceives the color of that point as a circle in that minimal time. Similarly, all the points on the surface of the top show that the sight perceives the color of each of them over the entire circumference of the circle along which that point moves in a minimal time. All points whose distance from the center is equal move, during the spinning of the top, along the same circumference of a single circle. It follows from this that the color of every one of those points whose distance from the center is equal appears over the circumference of that same circle in a minimal time, which will...

...the time of a revolution. For this reason, the colors of all the points in the entire circumference of that circle will appear mixed together. Because of this, the color of the surface of the **spinning top** <note>original: "trochus." This refers to a top or a potter's wheel used to demonstrate how colors blend when rotated rapidly.</note> is perceived as a single color mixed from all the colors that are on its surface. Therefore, if the sight had comprehended the **quiddity** <note>The "what-ness" or specific identity of the color.</note> of the color in a single instant, and did not require time to comprehend its essence, then in that single instant—and in every instant of time in which the top moves—the essences of all the colors on the top would have been distinct during the motion. Since it requires time to comprehend their essences, it perceives them during a portion of the time of a revolution; and in any given instant of the time of revolution during their motion, it perceives them just as it would perceive their essence when they are at rest. This is because the essences of all familiar visible colors are the same in rest and in motion, unchanging; in any instant in which the visible thing moves, its color does not change. And because the sight does not comprehend the essence of the colors on the surface of the top when the top moves with a rapid motion, but does comprehend it when the top is at rest or in slow motion, it follows that the sight does not comprehend the essence of a color unless that color is fixed in the same place for a **sensible time** <note>A duration of time long enough to be perceived by the senses.</note>, or moves through a space during a sensible time whose size does not cause a strange effect on the position of that color relative to the sight. It is therefore demonstrated by this situation that the comprehension of the essence of color does not occur except in time; and it will be shown by this situation that the comprehension of the essence of all visible things occurs only in time. Since the sight does not comprehend the essence of color—which is perceived by the sense alone—except in time, it follows that it especially requires time for the comprehension of **visible intentions** <note>original: "intentionum uisibilium." These are the secondary qualities or meanings derived from an object, like shape, size, or beauty, which require mental processing.</note> which are grasped through distinction and reasoning. Therefore, the comprehension of the essence of visible things, and comprehension through **cognition** <note>Recognition based on memory.</note>, and comprehension through distinction and reasoning, will only occur in time, though it is often in the smallest amount of time.

### 21. Light and color are perceived in their own right in time.

And we shall say that color as color, and light as light, are not comprehended by the sight except in time. That is to say, the instant at which the comprehension of color as color (and light as light) occurs is different from the first instant in which the air carrying the form reaches the surface of the eye. For color as color and light as light are not comprehended by the perceiver except after the arrival of the form in the sensing body; and they are not comprehended by the **ultimate perceiver** <note>The "sensing faculty" or the brain's processing center.</note> except after the arrival of the form at the hollow of the **common nerve** <note>original: "nerui communis." In medieval anatomy, this is the optic chiasm where the two optic nerves meet and visual information was thought to be unified.</note>. The arrival of the form at the hollow of the common nerve is like the arrival of light from **apertures** <note>original: "foraminibus." Window-like openings or holes.</note> through which light enters toward the bodies opposite those apertures. Therefore, the arrival of light from an aperture to the body opposite the aperture does not occur except in time, even though it escapes the notice of the senses. For the arrival of light from an aperture to the body opposite it cannot escape one of two ways: either the light reaches the part of the air neighboring the aperture before it reaches the next part, then the next, and so on until it reaches the body opposite the aperture; or the light reaches the entire medium of air between the aperture and the body (and the body itself) all at once. If the air receives light successively, the light would not reach the body opposite the aperture except through motion; but there is no motion except in time. If, however, the entire air receives the light all at once, the arrival of light into the air (after it was not there) still does not occur except in time, even though it escapes the senses. For when the aperture through which light enters is blocked, and then the obstruction is removed: the instant in which the obstruction is removed from the first part of the aperture, and in which the air in the aperture is uncovered to the light, is different from the instant in which the light reaches the air touching that part inside the aperture, and the air continuous with it in all arrangements. For light does not reach any part of the air inside an aperture that is covered against the light until some part of the aperture is uncovered to the light, and no part of the aperture is uncovered in less than one instant. But an **instant** <note>An "instant" was defined as a point in time with no duration, similar to how a mathematical point has no size.</note> cannot be divided. Therefore, none of the light reaches the interior of the aperture in that same instant in which the part of the aperture is uncovered. Because that which is uncovered of the aperture in one instant is not uncovered successively; nor is that which is uncovered in one instant a part of any quantity, since nothing is uncovered in one instant except a point lacking quantity, or a line lacking width, because an obstruction is not removed from something having length and width except successively. Therefore, it is through motion; but motion only exists in time. And that which is uncovered from the aperture in one instant lacks width: it is therefore a point or a line. But a point lacking quantity and a line lacking width are not parts of the air. A point lacking quantity and a line lacking width—which is the point uncovered from the aperture in an instant—is only the boundary of some parts of the air inside the aperture, not a part of the air itself. And a point lacking quantity does not receive light, nor does a line lacking width, because nothing receives light except a body. And since this is so, nothing of the light reaches the air inside the aperture in the instant in which the first part of the aperture is uncovered. Therefore, the instant—which is the point or the first instant in which the light reaches the air inside the aperture or a part of it—is different from the instant in which the first part of the aperture is uncovered. But between any two instants, there is time. Therefore, light does not reach from the air outside the aperture to the air inside the aperture except in time; but that time is greatly hidden from the sense because of the speed with which the forms of light are received by the air. And a similar thing happens in sight, when it is placed opposite...

...of the thing seen, whereas it was not so before, and the air carrying the form of the thing seen happens to touch the surface of the eye after not having touched it before: the form does not arrive from the air carrying it to the interior of the **common nerve** <note>original: "nerui communis." In medieval anatomy, this refers to the optic chiasm, where the two optic nerves meet and where it was believed the visual images from both eyes were unified.</note> except in a span of time. However, the sense lacks a way to perceive that time because of its extreme brevity, and the sense's own weakness in grasping that which is at the limit of smallness. Therefore, in respect to the sense, that time is like an instant. Furthermore, the sensing organ does not perceive the forms coming to it unless it is affected by them; it does not perceive color as color, nor light as light, until it undergoes a **passive impression** <note>original: "patitur." A philosophical term meaning the organ is "acted upon" by an external force, resulting in a change.</note> from the form of light and color. But the impression of the sensing organ by the form of light and color is a kind of alteration, and no alteration exists except in time. Therefore, the sight does not comprehend color as color, nor light as light, except in time.

And in the time in which the form is extended from the surface of the sensing organ to the cavity of the common nerve, there will be a comprehension of color as color, and light as light, by the sensing power which exists in the whole sensing body; and upon the arrival of the form in the cavity of the common nerve, there will be a comprehension of color as color, and light as light, by the **ultimate sensor** <note>original: "ultimo sentiente." The final faculty of the soul or brain that interprets the visual data sent from the eyes.</note>. Therefore, the comprehension of color as color, and light as light, occurs in a time following the time in which the form reaches from the surface of the sensing organ to the cavity of the common nerve.

Furthermore, the instant which is the first in which the form reaches the surface of the sight is different from the instant which is the first in which the air carrying the form touches the first point of the surface of the sight—when the sight is placed opposite the thing seen after it was not so, or after the eye has opened its eyelids after they were closed. For when this happens, the first thing from the air carrying the form of that visible object to touch the surface of the sight is a single point, or a line lacking width, then one part after another, until the air carrying the form touches the part of the surface of the sight where the form arrives. And at the contact of that point (lacking size) or that line (lacking width) with the surface of the sight, nothing of the form of light and color reaches the surface of the sight, because the smallest part of a surface upon which light or the form of color arrives must itself be a surface. Therefore, in the instant in which a point of the surface of sight touches the first point of the air carrying the form, nothing has yet reached the surface of the sight. Thus, the instant which is the first instant in which the form reaches the surface of the sight is different from the first instant in which the air carrying the form touches the surface of the sight, when the sight is turned toward the object and the eyelids are opened.

And since this is the case, the form of light or color does not reach any part of the sensing organ, nor the surface of the sight, except in time. Therefore, the sensor does not comprehend color as color, nor light as light, except in time—namely, that the instant in which the sense of color or light occurs is different from the first instant in which the air carrying the form touches the surface of the sight. Now, therefore, it has been declared from all we have said how the sight comprehends light as light, and how it comprehends color as color, and how it comprehends the **quiddity** <note>The essential nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> of light and color, and how it comprehends the quality of light.

### *22. The perception of the distance of a visible object differs from the perception of its location, and from the object in its place.*

<margin>Chapter 14, page 4.</margin>
But the distance of a visible object from the sight is not comprehended by the sight through sense alone; nor is the comprehension of the distance of a thing the same as the comprehension of its location; nor is the comprehension of a thing in its place derived only from the comprehension of its distance. For the location of a visible thing consists of three **intentions** <note>original: "intentionibus." In this context, it refers to the distinct concepts or properties the mind grasps about an object.</note>: namely, the distance, the direction in the universe, and the quantity of that distance.

The quantity of distance is different from the "intention" of distance as such. For the intention of distance between two bodies is the lack of contact; and the lack of contact means there is some space between those two bodies. The quantity of distance is the measurement of that space. Thus, the intention of distance, being distance, arises from position; it is not the same as the quantity of distance. Therefore, the comprehension of the intention of distance (the lack of contact) is different from the comprehension of the quantity of space (the measure of distance). And the comprehension of the quantity of distance comes from the comprehension of magnitude. The comprehension of the distance of a visible thing and the comprehension of its direction arise from the comprehension of its position. The quality of comprehension for each of these is different, because the lack of contact is different from direction. Therefore, the comprehension of the location of a visible thing is not the same as the comprehension of the distance of that thing. The comprehension of a visible thing in its place consists in the comprehension of five things: light, color, distance, direction, and the quantity of distance. None of these is comprehended by itself alone, nor is one comprehended after another; rather, all are comprehended together when they are grasped through **recognition** <note>original: "cognitionem." Instantaneous identification based on memory or prior knowledge.</note>, rather than through repeated reasoning.

### *23. Vision does not occur by rays emitted from the eye.* <note>Refer to Book 5, Proposition 3. See also note 23.</note>

From the comprehension of a visible thing in its place, those who propose "rays" have theorized that vision occurs through rays exiting the sight and reaching the thing seen, and that vision occurs through the tip of the ray. They have argued against the **physicists** <note>original: "physicos." Here referring to Natural Philosophers who argued for "intromission" (light entering the eye) rather than "extramission" (rays leaving the eye).</note>, saying: "If vision occurred through a form coming from the thing seen..."

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "re uisa" (the thing seen), which will begin the next page.</meta>

<summary>Alhazen argues that vision is a physical process of alteration that requires time, distinguishing the instant of contact from the duration of perception. He also separates the concept of distance into distinct mental "intentions," such as the absence of contact versus the actual measurement of space, and begins a critique of the theory that the eye emits rays to see.</summary>

...the thing seen to the sight, and that form reaches the interior of the sight: why is the thing seen perceived in its own place, which is outside the sight, even though its form has already reached the interior of the sight? And those [other theorists] did not know that vision is not completed by the sense alone, and that vision is not completed except through prior cognition and **distinction** <note>original: "distinctionem." In this context, it refers to the mind’s ability to discriminate, judge, and process visual data beyond mere sensation.</note>; and if prior cognition and distinction were not present, vision would not be completed in the sight. Nor does the sight comprehend *what* the thing seen is at the moment of looking: for the nature of the thing seen is not grasped by the sense alone, but through distinction, or cognition, or reasoning repeated during the act of seeing. If, therefore, vision were by sense alone, and if all the **notions** <note>original: "intentionibus." This is a technical term in medieval optics (translating the Arabic 'ma'na') referring to the individual properties of an object—like shape, size, or color—perceived by the mind.</note> that are in visible things were grasped by sense alone, the thing seen would not be perceived in its place unless something [from the eye] had reached the object, touching and sensing it. However, since vision is not completed by sense alone, but by distinction, reasoning, and cognition, it does not require—for the perception of the thing in its place—a sensing organ extended toward it and touching it.

*24. The distance of a visible object is perceived by distinction and anticipated notion. 9 p 4.*

Let us return, therefore, to describing the quality of visual perception, and let us say: the **distance** <note>original: "remotio." Literally "remoteness," referring to the spatial gap between the eye and the object.</note> of the thing seen is not perceived through itself, but through distinction. This notion is among those notions that rest in the soul through elapsed time, such that the perception does not leave the soul because of its great frequency and the repetition of it upon the **faculty of distinction** <note>original: "uirtutem distinctiuam." The mental power that classifies and understands sensory inputs.</note>. Therefore, there is no need for repeated reasoning in perceiving every visible thing. Nor does the faculty of distinction seek, during the perception of every visible thing, how the notion of the thing seen came to rest within it; for it does not distinguish the quality of the perception at the moment of perceiving every visible thing, and it does not perceive distance except along with other notions that are in the thing seen. It perceives distance during the perception of the thing seen through prior cognition.

How the faculty of distinction perceives distance through distinction is as I shall describe. When the sight is placed opposite a visible thing after it had not been opposite it, it perceives the thing; and when it is removed from that opposition, the perception is destroyed. Similarly, when the sight opens the eyelids after they have been closed, and it is opposite some visible thing, it will perceive that thing; and when it closes the eyelids, the perception is destroyed. And it is in the nature of the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectus." Here referring to the basic logical processing of the mind.</note> that what happens to be seen at a certain position, and is destroyed upon its removal, is not fixed inside the sight, nor is the thing causing it to happen located inside the sight. It is also in the nature of the intellect that what appears upon the opening of the eyelids and is destroyed upon their closing is not fixed inside the sight, nor is the cause of it inside the sight. 

When the faculty of distinction perceives that what occurs in the sight—by which the sight perceives the thing seen—is neither a fixed thing inside the sight nor is its cause inside the sight, it immediately understands that what occurs in the sight arrives from the outside, and its cause is outside the sight. And since vision is destroyed by the closing of the eyelids and by removal from opposition, and occurs upon the opening of the eyelids and upon opposition, the faculty of distinction understands that what is seen in the sight is not in contact with the sight. And when the faculty of distinction understands that what is seen is neither inside the sight nor in contact with the sight, it immediately understands that there is a distance between it and the sight; for it is in the nature of the intellect (or at the highest level of clear distinction) that everything which is not in the body, nor in contact with it, is distant from it. 

And this is the quality of the perception of the distance of the thing seen, insofar as it is distance. But the faculty of distinction does not need to divide these steps when perceiving the distance of a thing seen, for we have only done this for the sake of explanation. The faculty of distinction perceives the conclusion of this logic during vision without needing that step-by-step division. Therefore, from the perception of the thing upon opposition and the opening of the eyelids, and from its destruction upon the removal of opposition and the closing of the eyelids, the faculty of distinction understands that the thing seen is outside the sight and that it is not in contact with the sight. In this manner, the faculty of distinction understands that there is a distance between the sight and the thing seen. Then, because of the frequency and repetition of this notion, it remains at rest in the soul, such that the soul does not even notice its presence, nor the quality of its presence—namely, that all visible things are outside the sight, and that between any visible thing and the sight there is a distance. 

Therefore, the distance of the thing seen from the sight is not perceived except by a small distinction: namely, that the faculty of distinction understands that vision is due to a notion external to the sight. With this, when it has come to rest in the soul, the faculty of distinction understands that any visible thing perceived by the sight is outside the sight, and there is a distance between it and the sight. And also, as we said above, the perception of distance is not completed except with other factors; and in our discussion on the quality of the perception of **position** <note>original: "situs." Referring to the object's location in space relative to the viewer.</note>, it will be made clear how distance is perceived along with position, and how the thing seen is perceived in its own place.

For some are perceived through the sense of sight and their magnitude is certified, and some are perceived whose magnitude is not certified. ...the thing seen, and it is verified in every thing seen: however, the quantity of the **distance** <term>remotio: the physical space or "remoteness" between the eye and an object.</term> is not verified to the sight in every thing seen. This is because between some visible objects and the sight there are **ordered continuous bodies** <note>original: "corpora ordinata continuata." This refers to a continuous surface, like the ground or a floor, which provides a visual scale or "ruler" for the mind to judge depth.</note>; but between other things and the sight there are no ordered continuous bodies, nor does their distance relate to ordered continuous bodies. Therefore, regarding those things whose distance relates to ordered continuous bodies: when the sight perceives the ordered bodies that correspond to the distance of those visible things—that is, when it perceives the quantities of those bodies and grasps their measurements—it will grasp the quantities of the spaces that lie between their boundaries. And the space that is between the two boundaries of the body seen, which corresponds to the distance between the sight and the thing seen (one boundary being near the object and the other near the observer), is the distance of the thing seen from the sight, since it corresponds to the space between the eye and the object. Therefore, when the sight grasps the measure of that space, it will grasp the measure of the distance of the thing seen. Thus, the sight grasps the quantity of the distance of visible things (those whose distance relates to ordered continuous bodies) from the perception of the measurements of the ordered bodies corresponding to their distances.

Now, the distance of some of these visible things is **moderate** <term>mediocris: an intermediate distance where vision functions optimally; neither too close nor too far.</term>, while the distance of others is beyond moderation. Therefore, the distance of visible things that are at a moderate distance is grasped by the sight with a true, verified perception. This is because visible things at a moderate distance, with ordered continuous bodies between them and the sight, are perceived by the sight with true comprehension. And when the sight perceives these visible things with true comprehension, it perceives the ordered bodies lying between itself and those visible things with true comprehension. When it perceives these bodies truly, it perceives the spaces lying between their boundaries truly; and when it perceives those spaces truly, it will grasp the measures of the distances of the visible things corresponding to those spaces with true and verified comprehension. Therefore, regarding visible things whose distance corresponds to ordered continuous bodies and whose distance from the sight is moderate, the sight grasps the measures of their distances with a true and certain comprehension—and to say "certain" here means to the highest degree that the sense is able to grasp.

However, the measures of the distances of visible things that are beyond a moderate distance (even if their distance corresponds to ordered continuous bodies), if they are perceived by the sight at all, are not perceived with a true and verified comprehension. This is because visible things beyond a moderate distance are not grasped by the sight with true comprehension. Even when there are ordered continuous bodies between the sight and these things, the sight does not perceive all these bodies with true comprehension because of the extreme distance of their far ends, and because they exceed the moderation through which the sight verifies visible things. And when the sight does not perceive these bodies with true comprehension, it will not perceive the spaces lying between their boundaries with true comprehension. Consequently, it will not perceive the distances lying between itself and the visible things located at the ends of these bodies with true comprehension. Therefore, the quantities of the distances of visible things that are beyond a moderate distance (even where there are ordered continuous bodies between them and the eye) are not perceived by the sight with true comprehension.

Similarly, the distances of visible things whose distance does not relate to ordered continuous bodies are not perceived by the sight with true comprehension. This is why, when the sight perceives **clouds** in a flat plain or in places lacking mountains, it will estimate that they are at a great distance, comparable to that of the celestial bodies. Yet, when clouds are among mountains and are continuous with them, the peaks of the mountains might be covered by the clouds; and when the clouds stand apart from one another, the peaks of the mountains may appear higher than the clouds. The sight might even perceive parts of the clouds touching the summits of the mountains—and this may happen even with mountains that are not very high. From this **experiment** <note>original: "experimentatione." In medieval science, this often refers to a structured observation or a "thought experiment" used to prove a point.</note>, it appears that the distance of clouds is not "extraneous" (extremely far), and that many of them are closer to the earth than the peaks of mountains; thus, the common belief in their extreme distance is an error. This demonstrates that the sight does not grasp the measure of the distance of clouds over a plain, but the measure of their distance *is* grasped by the sight when they are among mountains and the peaks appear higher than them. This is also found in many visible things upon the face of the earth: namely, that the measures of distances not relating to ordered continuous bodies are not perceived by the sight.

The following experiment further clarifies this—namely, that the sight does not grasp the quantity of an object's distance unless its distance relates to ordered continuous bodies, and the sight perceives those intervening bodies and verifies their measurements. Imagine a house which the observer has not entered before the time of the experiment. Let there be a narrow **hole** <note>original: "foramen." Alhazen frequently uses pinholes or small apertures in his optical demonstrations.</note> in a certain wall of that house. Beyond that hole, let there be an empty space which the observer has not seen before. In that empty space, let there be two walls, one of which is closer to the hole than the other, with some amount of distance between those two walls. Let the closer wall cover a certain part of the more distant wall, while another part of the distant wall remains visible. Let the hole be elevated from the ground so that when the observer looks through it, he cannot see the surface of the ground that lies behind the wall containing the hole. Now, when the experimenter comes to this place and looks through the hole, he will see the two walls at once, but he will not perceive the distance that exists between them. If the distance of the first wall is great—an extreme distance from the hole—he will perceive the two walls as if they are touching each other, and he might even estimate that they are one continuous wall if their color is the same. Even if the first wall is at a moderate distance from the hole and it is perceived that they are two separate walls, it will still be estimated that they are close to each other or touching, and the distance will not be...

...the distance between them will be verified. <note>original: "tificabitur," the conclusion of "certificabitur" from the previous page.</note> And when the eye perceives the first wall, even when its distance is moderate, it may appear as if it were near the other wall: the eye will not verify its distance, and the distance between these two bodies will not be verified by the sense of sight in this way. This is because, prior to that moment, the eye had not seen that place nor those two walls; perhaps the sight will even perceive those two bodies as if they were touching, even if the observer previously knew there was a distance between them. 

And when the eye does not perceive the distance between two such bodies, it cannot perceive the magnitude of the distance of the furthest body, even though it perceives the **form** of that body. Since it does not perceive the magnitude of the distance of that body—even while perceiving the body itself—it will not perceive the continuous bodies that correspond to its distance. Thus, the eye does not perceive the magnitude of a visible object's distance with certainty merely from perceiving its form; rather, the eye perceives the magnitude of a visible object's distance only through **reasoning** <term>argumentationem: a mental process of inference or "logical" deduction by the mind, rather than a raw sensory input.</term>.

The eye, however, does not reason about any measure except through the process of comparison—either by comparing that measure to another already grasped by the sight, or to a measure perceived at the same time. There is nothing by which the eye can measure the distance of a visible thing and compare it, so as to truly grasp its measure, except through **ordered bodies** <note>original: "corpora ordinata." This refers to objects like floor tiles, trees, or the ground itself that act as a visual ruler.</note> that correspond to the distance of the object. If the eye measures distance by anything other than these bodies, the measurement will be a mere estimate and not certain. 

Therefore, the magnitude of an object's distance is not grasped by the sense of sight unless that distance corresponds to ordered, continuous bodies; for the eye perceives those bodies and their measurements. This experimentation we have described has many similar examples in visible things, such as with two trees standing in the manner we described for the walls, or a piece of wood placed crosswise over an opening, in the same way we spoke of the first wall.

The distances of visible objects that are separated from one another are grasped by the eye through the perception of the division that exists between them. Furthermore, the eye's perception of the distance *between* two objects is handled in the same way as the distance *from* the observer to the object. If there are ordered continuous bodies between two distinct visible things, and the eye perceives those bodies and their measures, it will grasp the magnitude of the distance between those things. But if not, it will not truly grasp the magnitude of the distance between them. Similarly, if there are ordered continuous bodies between two objects, but they are at a very great distance so that the eye cannot verify the measures of those bodies, then the measure between those two objects will not be verified.

Therefore, the distances of visible things from the eye are only perceived through the perception of the **faculty of discernment** <term>uirtus distinctiua: the cognitive power of the soul/mind that identifies, compares, and judges sensory data.</term>; for what happens in the eye during vision only occurs through some external influence. No magnitude of distance is grasped by the sense of sight with true comprehension, except for the distances of objects whose space corresponds to ordered and continuous bodies, provided that the distance is also moderate. In such cases, the eye simultaneously perceives the ordered bodies corresponding to the distances and verifies the measures of those bodies as they follow one another. 

Measurements of distance, other than these, are not verified by the eye. Regarding objects whose distances cannot be verified, some relate to ordered continuous bodies that the eye does perceive, yet the distance of their extremities is too great <note>original: "extranea," meaning "extraordinary" or "excessive."</note>. Other distances relate to ordered continuous bodies, but the eye does not perceive those bodies—whether the distances are great or moderate. Finally, some distances do not relate to ordered continuous bodies at all; these are objects very high above the earth at a great distance, which have no nearby objects or walls to provide a scale for their distance. 

All visible things are divided into these categories. When the eye perceives objects whose distances cannot be verified, the **faculty of discernment** immediately recognizes their distances according to **estimation** <term>æstimationem: a "best guess" or intuitive judgment based on experience.</term>, not according to precision. It compares their distance to the distance of similar objects seen before, relying on its reasoning about the **form** of the object. It compares the form of the thing seen to the forms of similar objects the eye has perceived before, whose distances have already been verified by the faculty of discernment.

Thus, it compares the distance of an object (whose distance is not currently verified) to the distance of similar objects seen previously. When the faculty of discernment cannot verify the specific outlines of an object's form, it compares the size of the whole form to the measures of known objects of equal size whose distances are already established. It likens the distance of the unverified object to the distance of those verified objects of similar measure. 

This is the utmost that the faculty of discernment can do in grasping the distances of visible things. Through this reasoning, it might perhaps find certainty in grasping distance, or it might err; and in those cases where it finds certainty, it does not necessarily know whether it has actually found the truth or not. This reasoning occurs at the highest speed because the faculty of discernment is so accustomed to grasping the distance of objects through reasoning and verification. And perhaps the faculty of discernment will estimate the distance of an object—if its distance corresponds to ordered bodies and is moderate—simply because of its habit of estimating or reasoning about the distances of things, and because of the speed...

And when the distance of the seen object is moderate, there will not be a great discrepancy between the estimation of the distance and the true distance. Therefore, when the eye perceives any seen object, the **discriminative faculty** <term>uirtus distinctiua: the mental power that processes sensory data to reach logical conclusions</term> immediately perceives its distance and the measure of that distance, according to its ability to grasp it—that is, either through certainty or through estimation—and immediately its distance will have a conceived measure in the soul.

Therefore, the measure of the distance between two visible objects—between which there are continuous ordered bodies that the eye perceives and whose measures it verifies—is a verified measure. But the measure of the distance between two visible objects—between which there are no continuous ordered bodies, or between which there are continuous ordered bodies but the eye does not verify their measures or does not perceive them—is not a verified measure.

According to these modes, therefore, the perception of the distances of visible objects occurs through the sense of sight. Also, bodies that correspond to the distances of **familiar visible things** <note>original: "uisibilium assuetorum," objects the observer sees every day and whose sizes are already known to the mind</note> (which are at familiar distances that the eye is accustomed to perceiving) are grasped by the eye, and their measures are verified because of their frequency. Because of this, the eye perceives the measures of their distances through recognition. For when the eye perceives some familiar visible object at a familiar distance, it recognizes it, knows its distance, and estimates the magnitude of its distance. Therefore, when it estimates the magnitude of the distance of such visible objects, the estimation will be nearly true, and there will not be a great difference between the estimation and the truth. Thus, the magnitude of the distances of familiar visible objects at familiar distances is perceived by the eye through recognition from the estimation of their magnitudes; and most distances of visible objects are perceived in this manner.

### *26. Position is perceived from the moderate distance of the visible position. 29 p 4.*

Position, which the eye perceives from visible things, is divided into three modes. The first is the position of the whole seen object relative to the eye, or the position of some part of the seen object relative to the eye; this mode is **opposition** <term>oppositio: the state of being directly in front of the eye or facing it</term>. The second is the position of the surface of the seen object facing the eye, and the position of the multiple surfaces of the seen object facing the eye (when the seen object has many surfaces and many surfaces appear to the eye); as well as the position of the boundaries of the visible surfaces, the position of lines, and the spaces between any two points or any two visible objects perceived simultaneously by the eye. The third mode is the position of the parts of the seen object relative to each other, the position of the boundaries of the surface relative to each other, and the position of the parts of the boundaries relative to each other: this mode is **arrangement** <term>ordinatio: the internal spatial order or layout of an object's parts</term>. Similarly, the position of different visible objects relative to each other is placed under this mode.

All positions perceived by the eye are therefore divided into these three modes. The position of anything that has a location relative to another thing is composed of the distance of that thing from the other, and the orientation of that thing with respect to the other. Therefore, the **opposition** of a seen object to the eye is composed of the distance of the seen object from the eye and the direction in which the object is located relative to the eye. The perception of the distance of a seen object has already been explained as a concept resting in the soul.

---

The true place of a seen object is perceived from the position of the seen object relative to the sight, since the eye only perceives a seen object through opposition. The places perceived by the sense are understood through discrimination. The discriminative faculty perceives all places through the **imagination**. Thus, when the eye is opposite some place and perceives a visible object, and the eye is later moved away from that place and faces another, the vision of that first object is destroyed; but when it returns again to face that place, the vision of that object returns. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the mind determines the position of an object. It follows the previous page's explanation that the soul uses reasoning to estimate distances, particularly when the visual field includes continuous, familiar objects to serve as a reference.</meta>

->OPTICS, BOOK II. 43<-

...when [the object] is opposite the eye during the perception of that seen thing: and when the sight is removed from being opposite that place, the vision of that seen thing is destroyed. Then, therefore, the **discriminative faculty** <term>uirtus distinctiua: the cognitive power that processes sensory data to reach logical conclusions</term> perceives that the seen object only exists in the part opposite the eye during the vision of that object. And it has also been declared [in Book 1, chapter 18, note 1] that the eye receives forms specifically from the **directions** <note>original: *uerticationibus*. This refers to the specific orientation or "line of sight" along which a ray of light travels.</note> of the radial lines, and that the eye itself is not affected by forms except from the directions of those lines alone. And it has also been declared [in Book 1, chapter 19, note 1] that the form is extended into the body of the eye according to the straightness of the **radial lines**. Therefore, when the form of the seen object reaches the eye, the sensing subject immediately feels the form, feels the part of the eye which the form reached, and feels the direction through which the form extends into the body of the sensing member. Thus, when the eye perceives the location of the form within itself, and perceives the direction through which that form was extended, the discriminative faculty immediately perceives the place into which, from which, and through which that direction was extended. Moreover, the place through which and from which that direction extends is the location where that seen object is. 

Therefore, from the perception of the part of the eye reached by the form of the seen object, and from the perception of the direction through which the form was extended (and by which the eye is affected by the form), the discriminative faculty perceives the true direction through which the form of the seen object was extended. And in this manner, the locations of visible things are distinguished: for distinct visible things are not distinguished by sight except by the distinction of different locations on the surface of the sensing member reached by the forms of those distinct visible things. 

The perception of the location of a seen object in this manner has a parallel in the sense of hearing: for the sensing subject perceives a voice through the sense of hearing, perceives the place from which the voice comes, and distinguishes between a voice coming from the right, a voice coming from the left, from the front, and from behind. Indeed, it even distinguishes between the locations of voices with a subtler distinction than that: it distinguishes between the location of a voice coming from a place directly opposite the face and a voice coming from a place oblique to that direction. The places from which voices come are not distinguished by the hearing except through the directions along which the voices reach the hearing. Therefore, the sense of hearing perceives voices and perceives the directions from which those voices come; and from the perception of the directions along which the voices reach the hearing, and along the straightness of which the voice strikes the hearing, the discriminative faculty perceives the place from which the voice comes. Just as the locations of voices are perceived by the sense of hearing and then by the discriminative faculty by means of hearing, so too the locations of visible things are perceived by the discriminative faculty through the sense of sight. 

And among those things by which it is declared that the sensing subject perceives the direction according to how the eye is affected by the form of the seen object, is that which is perceived in **mirrors** through **reflection**. For a seen object, which the eye perceives through reflection, is only perceived by the eye when it is in opposition to it; but its form reaches the eye according to the directions of straight lines, which are the radial lines extended from the eye toward the opposite part. Therefore, when the eye senses the form from the directions of the radial lines, it will judge the seen object to be at the extremities of those lines. This is because it perceives nothing of the accustomed visible things (which it always perceives) except at the extremities of imaginary lines between the eye and the seen object, which are the radial lines. From the perception of a seen object by the eye through reflection—even if it is not actually seen in that opposite position—and according to the straightness of the directions through which the reflected forms reach the eye, it appears that the sensing subject feels the direction through which the form comes and from which the eye is affected by the form. 

And when the sensing subject feels the direction of sight from which the eye is affected by the form, the discriminative faculty perceives the place in which that direction extends and will perceive the location of the seen object. Therefore, the location of the seen object will be perceived by the sensing subject in a broad sense through the perception of its position during vision; and it will be perceived by the discriminative faculty in a broad sense from the perception of the seen object's position during vision; and it will be perceived with a true and certified perception from the perception of the direction from which the eye is affected by the form of the seen object. 

Moreover, the **distance** <note>original: *remotio*. Literally "remoteness," referring to the spatial gap between the viewer and the object.</note> of the seen object is a **concept** <note>original: *intentio*. In medieval science, this refers to a mental image or "notion" formed by the soul.</note> that has already settled in the soul. Therefore, upon the arrival of the seen object's form at the eye, the discriminative faculty perceives the location of the seen object along with the resting concept of distance within itself; and the combination of distance and location is "opposition" [the state of being in front of the eye]. Thus, when the discriminative faculty perceives the location of the seen object and its distance, it simultaneously perceives its opposition. The perception of opposition, therefore, comes from the simultaneous perception of the location of the seen object and the perception of its distance. And the perception of location will be according to the manner we have described. 

Therefore, when the form of the seen object reaches the eye, the sensing subject will feel the location of the sensing member reached by the form, and the concept of distance is already resting within it. It will therefore perceive the location and the distance simultaneously upon the sensing subject's perception of the form. Thus, upon the sensing subject's perception of the form, the discriminative faculty will perceive its opposition. In the manner described, the perception of opposition will occur. It has also been declared [in note 10] how the eye perceives the form of the seen object by sense alone. Therefore, upon the arrival of the form of the seen object in the eye, the sensing subject will perceive the color of the seen object and its light, and the location of the eye that was colored and illuminated by that form; and the discriminative faculty will perceive its location and distance upon the sensing subject's perception of its light and color. And thus light and color, location and distance, are perceived simultaneously in a tiny amount of time. But location and distance are "opposites" [the external placement], and light and color are the form of the seen object, and from the perception of the form and the perception of the opposition, the perception of the seen object in its position opposite the eye is sustained. However, the location of the visible object in which it is perceived by the sight is then estimated, not verified, since a verified location is not perceived except through the verification of the quantity of its distance.

### 28. The direct and oblique position of a line, surface, and space is perceived from the equal and unequal distance of its boundaries. *31 p 4.*

The position of visible surfaces relative to the sight is divided into two types: namely, **direct opposition** and **obliquity** <note>original: *obliquationem*. This refers to a surface being tilted or slanted away from the viewer.</note>. A surface directly opposite the sight is one whose **radial axis** <term>axis radialis: the central, most powerful ray of light traveling from the center of the object to the center of the eye</term>—when the surface is perceived by the sight in direct opposition—meets some point on it and is simultaneously elevated above the surface at an equal angle. An oblique surface is one whose radial axis meets some point on it but is slanted, not elevated at an equal angle across all the various modes of tilting. The boundaries of visible surfaces, the lines that exist in things, and the spaces between visible objects (or parts of them) are also divided into two: one consists of lines and spaces cutting across the radial lines, and the other consists of lines and spaces that run parallel to the radial lines and correspond to them.

Lines and spaces cutting across the radial lines are divided by position into two: into obliquity and directness, following the division of positions and surfaces into these two types. A **direct line** is one where the radial axis reaches some point on it and is perpendicular to it. An **oblique line** is one where the radial axis, when it reaches a point on it, is slanted and not perpendicular. The sight perceives the directness or obliquity of surfaces and lines, and distinguishes between them, by perceiving the difference or equality in the distances of their extremities. For when the sight perceives the surface of a visible object and its extremities, and senses that the boundaries of the surface are at an equal distance from it—or that two opposite points are equally distant from the point of the surface at which the eye is looking—it perceives the surface to be directly opposite, and the discriminative faculty judges it to be direct.

But when the sight perceives the surface of a visible object and senses a difference in the distance of its extremities—finding no two places on the surface equally distant from the point it is looking at—it perceives the surface to be slanted in respect to itself, and the discriminative faculty judges it to be oblique. The same applies to the positions of lines and spaces: the sight perceives a line or space as direct when it senses the two distances of its two ends are equal, or that two points on the line are equidistant from the point being stared at. Conversely, the sight perceives obliquity when it senses the distances of the ends are unequal. This equality or difference is often perceived by the sensing subject through estimation and signs. In this way, the sight perceives obliquity and directness. 

Furthermore, when an entire surface or line is "direct" to the sight, it does not mean every individual part of it is directly opposite the eye; in fact, no part is perfectly direct except the part upon which the axis falls. When the radial axis moves across a "direct" surface or line, it becomes slanted relative to every part it passes over, except for that first point where it was perpendicular. Thus, every part of a directly opposite surface or line, when taken by itself, is actually oblique, except for that aforementioned central point; yet when the whole line or surface is taken together, it is called direct. When the point where the axis is perpendicular is in the exact middle of the surface or line, the object is at the peak of direct opposition. If that point is not in the middle, it is still direct, but not perfectly so; the closer the perpendicular point is to the middle, the more direct the opposition of the surface or line appears. Finally, the positions of lines and spaces parallel to the radial lines are perceived by the sight through the perception of their opposition. When the sight perceives the far ends of lines or spaces and the near ends close to the eye, it perceives their position and...

...[the sight] will perceive their extension along the line of opposition. Therefore, according to these modes, there will be a perception of positions, surfaces, lines, and spaces by the sight in relation to it. Some surfaces, lines, and spaces intersecting the **radial lines** <term>radiales lineae: the straight lines extending from the eye to the object, forming the visual cone</term> are of a very great slant relative to the radial lines, some are of a slight slant, and some are perpendicular to the radial lines: these latter are the surfaces, lines, and spaces directly opposite the sight. Now, the farther extremity of any surface, line, or space follows the part remote from the sight—specifically, the part following the ends of the radial lines—and the nearer extremity follows the part close to the sight, namely, the part following the sight itself. 

And when the sight perceives any line or space, it immediately perceives the two **"wherenesses"** <term>ubitates: the specific spatial locations or coordinates of points in space</term> following the extremities of that line or space. Similarly, when the sight perceives a surface, it perceives the "wherenesses" following the extremities of that surface through the perception of its extension in length and breadth. Therefore, when the sight perceives a surface slanted relative to the radial lines, and that surface is of a very great tilt, the sight will perceive the "whereness" following the farther extremity during the perception of the surface, and it will perceive it to be following the ends of the radial lines; and it will perceive the "whereness" following the nearer extremity, and perceive it to be following that which is near the sight. The same applies to a line or space of very great slant. 

And when the sight perceives that one of the two extremities of a surface, line, or space follows a location remote from the sight, and that the other extremity follows a location near the sight, it immediately perceives the remoteness of one of the two extremities and the proximity of the other. And when it perceives the remoteness of one and the proximity of the other, it immediately perceives the slant of the position of that surface, line, or space. Thus, the slant of surfaces, lines, and spaces that are tilted relative to the radial lines with an extreme slant is perceived by the sight through the perception of the two "wherenesses" of their extremities.

->*29. An oblique visible position appears direct from an immoderate distance. <note>original: "34 p 4" — likely a cross-reference to Proposition 34, Part 4 of a related geometric proof.</note>*<-

However, the tilt or direct opposition of lines, surfaces, and spaces of slight slant or directness is not perceived by the sight with a true, **verified perception** <note>original: *certificata*. Alhazen distinguishes between "estimation" and "verified" perception, where the latter is mathematically certain.</note>, unless their distance is moderate and they are seen in relation to **ordered bodies** <term>corpora ordinata: regular, structured objects in the environment, like floor tiles or a row of pillars, used as a visual scale</term> perceived by the sight. In such a case, the sight perceives the measures of the distances of those extremities from the measures of those [ordered] bodies, and it perceives the equality of the two distances of the two extremities of the surface, line, or space—or their inequality. This is because none of the "wherenesses" following the extremities of surfaces, lines, or spaces that are directly opposite (or only slightly tilted) follows the sight itself; rather, their opposite extremities follow locations to the right, left, above, or below. 

If, therefore, the sight does not perceive the measures of the distances of such things from the eye, it will not perceive the equality or inequality of the distances of their extremities; and if it does not perceive this, it will not perceive their slant nor their directness. Therefore, when surfaces, lines, and spaces are at a very great distance and their slant is slight, the sight cannot perceive their slant, nor can it distinguish between the slanted and the straight. This is because the quantities of the distances of surfaces, lines, and spaces whose distance is great are not verified by the sight, but are merely estimated. And when their distance is great and they are only slightly slanted, the difference between their remote opposite extremities is very slight, almost lacking in quantity compared to the total magnitude of their distance. 

And since the sight does not verify the quantities of the distances of their extremities, it will not perceive the diversity of distances between those extremities. When it does not perceive the diversity between the distances of the extremities of a surface, line, or space, it will estimate those distances to be equal and will not perceive the slant of that surface, line, or space; and when it does not perceive the slant, it will estimate it to be direct. Thus, a slight slant of surfaces, lines, and spaces whose distance is very great is not perceived by the sight. The sight, therefore, perceives all surfaces, lines, and spaces that are at a very great distance and minimal slant as if they were directly opposite; it does not verify their positions, nor does it distinguish between the slanted and the directly opposite, but perceives the slanted and the straight in the same way. 

Similarly, the positions of surfaces, lines, and spaces whose distance is moderate are not verified by the sight when they are not seen in relation to ordered bodies, or when the sight does not perceive the bodies related to their distances and does not verify the quantities of their distances. In such cases, the sight does not distinguish between their slant and their directness, but takes their position by estimation; perhaps it will estimate such a thing to be direct, even though it is slanted. But when surfaces, lines, and spaces are at a moderate distance, and their distances are seen in relation to ordered bodies, and the sight perceives those ordered bodies and their quantities, it will perceive the quantities of the distances of the extremities of those surfaces, lines, and spaces. It will then perceive the equality of the distances of their opposite extremities, if those extremities are equal, or their inequality...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 45 regarding how the eye judges the orientation and slant of objects.
