->BY ALHAZEN<-

...the inequality of them, if they are unequal. And when [the sight] grasps the equality of the distances of the ends of surfaces, or lines, or spaces, or their inequality, it will grasp the orientation of that surface, line, or space—or its slant—with a verified perception. Similarly, the slant of lines, surfaces, or spaces that have a very great tilt is not grasped by the sight unless they are at a moderate distance relative to their size. For the sight does not grasp the **wherenesses** <term>ubitates: a scholastic term for the specific "where" or spatial location of a point</term> of the extremities of a surface, line, or space unless it also grasps the extent of that surface, line, or space. But the sight only grasps the extent of a surface, line, or space when it is at a moderate distance relative to the size of that object.

Therefore, the slant of a surface, line, or space intersecting the **radial lines** <term>radiales lineae: the straight lines of sight originating from the eye</term> will be grasped by the sight through the perception of the locations of its extremities, provided the slant is very great. However, if the slant is slight, or if the object is directly opposite the eye, the sight will perceive it as slanted or straight based on the perception of the distances of its ends. Yet, the sight does not verify the quality of the positions of surfaces, lines, and spaces that are at a maximum slant unless it has verified the extent of their length. Nor does it verify the position of surfaces, lines, and spaces that have a slight slant or are directly opposite unless it verifies the distances of their ends and perceives whether those distances are equal or unequal. 

But the sight rarely verifies the positions of visible things with certainty; most of what the sight perceives regarding the positions of objects is grasped only through **estimation** <term>aestimatio: a mental judgment or "best guess" the brain makes when sensory data is incomplete</term>. Thus, the reliance of the sight in grasping the positions of visible things is based on estimation. 

Therefore, when a viewer looks and wishes to verify the position of a surface, a line, or a space within a visible object, they will observe the form of that thing and the quality of its extension. If the form of the visible thing containing that surface, line, or space is clear and verified, and the slant of that object is very great, the sight will truly grasp its slant by perceiving its extension and the two "wherenesses" of its ends. 

If the form is clear but the slant is not extreme, and its distance relates to **ordered bodies** <term>corpora ordinata: familiar objects in the environment, like floor tiles or columns, used as reference points</term>, the sight will look at the bodies corresponding to the distances of its extremities and consider their size. It will then grasp the distance of that surface, line, or space, and the degree of its slant or its direct orientation, by perceiving the distances of its ends. 

However, if the form of the visible object is not clear—or if it is clear but the slant is extreme and the distance does not relate to ordered bodies—the sight will not grasp the certainty of the position of such a surface, line, or space. And when the sight perceives an unclear form and finds that its distance relates to ordered bodies, it immediately realizes that the position of that surface, line, or space cannot be verified. 

These are the modes by which the sight grasps the positions of visible surfaces, and the positions of the lines and spaces upon them—specifically those that intersect the radial lines. As for the spaces between distinct visible objects at very great distances—namely, when the distance to both objects at the two ends of the space is very great—that space is perceived by the sight as if it were directly opposite, even if it is slanted. This happens because the eye cannot detect the difference between the distances of its extremities. 

If one of the two visible objects at the ends of the space is closer than the other, and the sight senses its proximity, it will perceive the space between them as slanted, based on what it grasps from the closeness of the nearer object and the distance of the farther one. But if one is closer and the sight does not perceive its proximity, it will not sense the slant of the space between them. 

Therefore, the position of surfaces, lines, and spaces intersecting the radial lines is not verified by the sight unless their distance is moderate; and even then, the sight does not always verify the equality or inequality of the distances of their ends. If the sight does not verify the equality or inequality of these distances, it cannot verify their position. Most of the positions of visible things grasped by the sight are grasped only through estimation. If they are at a moderate distance, there will not be a great difference between the position grasped by estimation and the true position; but if they are at a very great distance, the sight will not distinguish between what is slanted and what is direct. For when the sight does not grasp the inequality of the two distances of the two ends of a visible thing, it perceives them as equal, and thus judges the visible thing to be directly opposite. These, then, are the ways the positions of surfaces, lines, and spaces are perceived by the sense of sight.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the eye perceives the orientation and spatial arrangement of parts of an object. It transitions from the perception of flat surfaces to the perception of three-dimensional depth and the "corporeity" (solidity) of objects, explaining the role of both raw visual data and mental reasoning.</meta>

# OPTICS BOOK II

...[The parts of an object] are perceived by the sight through the comprehension of the locations on the eye where the forms of the parts arrive, and through the comprehension of the arrangement of those parts of the form reaching the sight, by means of the **discriminative faculty** <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua." This is the mental power that processes raw visual sensation into meaningful perception.</note>. For since the form of any part of the surface of a seen object reaches a specific part of the surface of the sensing organ <note>The "sensing organ" refers to the eye, specifically the crystalline lens according to Alhazen's theory.</note> where the form of the whole arrives: when the surface of the seen object consists of different colors, and there are differences between its parts by which they are distinguished from one another, the form reaching the sight will be of different colors, and its parts will be distinct according to the distinction of the parts of the surface of the seen object. And the sensing organ senses the form, and senses each of the parts of the form from the sensation of their colors and the light that is in them; and it senses the locations of the forms of the parts in the eye from the sensation of the colors and light of those parts.

The **discriminative faculty** grasps the order of those locations from the comprehension of the diversity of the colors of the form's parts, and from the comprehension of the differences between the parts. Thus, it perceives right and left, top and bottom, by comparing them with one another; and thus it also perceives what is touching and what is separate. However, the position of the parts of a seen object relative to one another in terms of **nearness and distance** <gloss>that is, according to protrusion and depth</gloss> are perceived by the sight from the comprehension of the amount of distance of the parts from the eye, and the comprehension of the diversity of the distances of the parts according to greater or lesser degrees. 

Indeed, the positions of the parts of a seen object, when they are at a moderate distance from each other, are perceived by the sight in terms of nearness and distance: and this happens when the sight grasps the amount of that distance, and perceives the inequality (or equality) between the distances of the parts from the eye. But if the sight does not verify the amounts of its distance, nor the amounts of the distances of its parts, the sight will not grasp the arrangement of its parts in terms of nearness and distance during the act of seeing. 

If, however, the object is among **familiar visible things** <note>original: "uisibilibus assuetis." Alhazen argues that we recognize shapes we already know through memory rather than pure calculation.</note> which are known to the sight, it will grasp the arrangement of its parts according to protrusion, depth, and the shape of its surface through recognition, not by sight alone. But if it is among **unfamiliar visible things** <note>original: "uisibilibus extraneis."</note> which the sight does not recognize, it will perceive its surface as if it were flat when it has not verified the amounts of the distances of its parts. This effect is apparent when the sight looks at some convex or concave body that is at a very great distance; for the sight then does not perceive the convexity or concavity, but perceives it as if it were flat. 

And the positions of the parts of a seen object's surface relative to one another—in the diversity of their **locations** <term>ubitatum: the "wheres" or specific spatial coordinates</term>, and in their separation and continuity—are not perceived by the sight except from the comprehension of the parts of the form reaching the eye, and the comprehension of the diversity of colors and differences by which the parts are distinguished, and from the comprehension of the arrangement of the parts of the form by the discriminative faculty. 

The positions of the parts of the surface of a seen object relative to one another in nearness, and also according to distance with respect to the eye, are not perceived by the sight except from the comprehension of the amount of distance of the parts, and from the comprehension of the equality and inequality of the amounts of those distances. Therefore, the arrangement of the parts of a seen object according to nearness and distance is perceived by the sight for those objects whose distances of parts are verified by the sight; but the arrangement of parts for those objects whose distances are not verified is not perceived. The arrangement of distinct parts of a seen object is perceived by the sight from the comprehension of the locations in the eye where the forms of those parts arrive, and from the comprehension of the distinction in the eye by the discriminative faculty. And it is the same for separate visible objects. 

Furthermore, the boundaries of the surface of a seen object, or of its surfaces, and their arrangement, are perceived by the sight from the comprehension of the part of the surface where its color and light reach the eye, and from the comprehension of the boundaries of that part, and the arrangement of the circumference of that part by the discriminative faculty. According to these modes, therefore, the sight perceives the positions of the parts of visible things, and the positions of the parts of visible surfaces relative to one another, and the positions of the boundaries of surfaces, and the positions of distinct parts of visible things relative to each other, and the positions of distinct visible objects relative to one another.

### 31. *The solidity of certain bodies is perceived by sight alone; of others by sight and reasoning together.* <note>original: "syllogismo." In medieval science, a "syllogism" often refers to an unconscious mental deduction or inference.</note>

**Corporeity** <note>original: "corporeitas." The quality of being a three-dimensional body.</note>, which is extension according to the three dimensions, is perceived by the sight in some bodies and not in others. Nevertheless, in a person capable of discrimination, the principle is already established that nothing is perceived by the sense of sight except a body; and thus when he perceives a visible object, he knows immediately that it is a body, even if he does not perceive the extension according to three dimensions. 

The sight perceives the extension of bodies according to length and width from the comprehension of the surfaces of the bodies facing it. When, therefore, it perceives the surface of a body, knowing that the visible object is a body, it immediately perceives the extension of that body according to length and width, and only the third dimension remains. Some bodies are contained by flat surfaces intersecting each other obliquely; some are contained by concave or convex surfaces; some are contained by surfaces of diverse shapes intersecting each other obliquely; and some are contained by a single round surface. Now, a body that is contained by intersecting surfaces, one of which is flat—when it is perceived by the sight, and its flat surface is facing the sight and is directly in front, and the remaining surfaces intersect that surface directly opposite, or are perpendicular to the surface directly opposite,

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the human eye and the mind (the "discriminative faculty") work together to interpret two-dimensional visual data as three-dimensional objects. It focuses specifically on "corporeity"—the quality of having physical volume and depth—and how factors like curvature and distance affect our perception of a solid body.</meta>

->ALHAZEN<-

...opposite, or slanted toward the narrow part at the back of the directly opposite surface: nothing will appear to the sight except for the directly opposite surface alone. Therefore, from such bodies, the sight does not grasp anything except length and width; it does not sense the **solidity** <note>original: "corporeitatem." This term refers to the three-dimensional volume or "body-ness" of an object, as opposed to a flat 2D shape.</note> of such things. However, in a body contained by surfaces that intersect one another, when its surface is opposite the eye but not in a perfectly direct opposition—and the intersection of that surface with another surface of that body is grasped by the sight so that it can see two surfaces at once—then its **solidity** will be perceived by the sight. This is because the eye will grasp the slant of the body's surface relative to its depth. Thus, it will perceive the extension of the body according to its depth, just as it perceived the extension in length and width from the slanted surface. In this way, it grasps the **solidity** of such bodies. 

The same occurs when one of the body's surfaces is directly opposite the sight, and there are surfaces intersecting that surface (or one of them) which are slanted toward the wider part at the back of the directly opposite surface. In such a body, the sight will grasp the directly opposite surface and the surface intersecting it at an angle, and it will also grasp the junction of those surfaces; thus, as we have said, it will grasp the **solidity** of that body. Generally, I say that any body in which the sight can grasp two intersecting surfaces will be perceived in its **solidity** by the sight.

Furthermore, in bodies where a convex surface is grasped by the sight—whether it is contained by one surface or many—the sight can grasp its **solidity** by perceiving the truth of it. For if a convex surface is opposite the sight, the distances of its parts from the eye will be unequal: its middle will be closer to the sight than its edges. When the sight grasps its convexity, it perceives that the middle is closer than the edges. Once it senses that the middle is closer and the edges are farther away, it immediately senses that the surface extends toward the viewer from the furthest points tending toward the back. Thus, it senses the extension of the body in depth relative to the directly opposite surface. It also grasps the extension of that body in length and width by grasping the extension of the convex surface in length and width. 

Similarly, if another surface of the body besides the one directly opposite is convex, and the sight grasps its convexity, it will also grasp its extension according to the three dimensions. If, however, the sight senses another surface of a body in which there is a concave surface, and senses its intersection with the concave surface, it will then sense the slant of that body’s surface. Once it senses that slant, it immediately senses its **solidity**. 

But if only the concave surface is grasped by the sight, and no other remaining surfaces appear, the sight will not grasp the **solidity** of that body. Nor will the sight grasp anything from such bodies except their extensions in two dimensions only; it will not sense the **solidity** of such bodies except through prior knowledge, not through the sensation of the three dimensions of that body. Even though a concave surface also extends in depth (due to the proximity of its edges to the eye and the distance of its center), this extension of depth is only perceived as the extension of a **void** <note>original: "uacuitatis." Alhazen distinguishes between seeing the volume of a solid object and seeing the "emptiness" of a hole or bowl.</note>, not the extension of the seen body itself to which the concave surface belongs. 

Therefore, the perception of **solidity** by the sight only comes from the perception of the slant of a body's surfaces. These slants of surfaces—by which it is signaled to the sight that bodies are indeed bodies—are only grasped by the sight in objects at a moderate distance. In bodies at a very great distance, whose distance cannot be certain to the sight, the sight does not grasp the slants of the surfaces, and thus it does not grasp their **solidity** through the sense of sight alone. For in such bodies, the sight does not grasp the relationship of the parts of the surfaces to one another; it only perceives them as flat. Consequently, it does not grasp the slants of the surfaces, and finally, it does not grasp the **solidity**. Therefore, the sight does not grasp the **solidity** of a body at a very great distance when its distance is not certain. It grasps the **solidity** of bodies from the perception of the slants of their surfaces, and these slants are only grasped in visible objects at a moderate distance where the arrangement of the parts of the surfaces relative to one another can be understood. Aside from these, the sight only grasps **solidity** through prior knowledge.

### ### 32. A circle is perceived by the position it occupies on the surface of the eye. <note>See Proposition 45, Book 4.</note>

The **shape** <note>original: "Figura."</note> of a seen object is divided into two types: the first is the shape of the outline (the circumference) of the surface of the seen object, or the outline of some part of it. The second is the shape of the **solidity** of the seen object, or the shape of the **solidity** of some part of it. This latter mode is the form of the surface of a seen object whose **solidity** is grasped by the sense of sight. Everything the sight grasps regarding the shapes of visible things is divided into these modes. 

The shape of the outline of a seen object’s surface is grasped by the perceiver from the perception of the outline of the **form** <note>In Alhazen's theory, the "form" is the spiritual/physical representation of the object that travels to the eye.</note> that reaches the hollow of the **common nerve** <note>original: "nerui communis." This refers to the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet, which Alhazen believed was the site of final visual integration.</note>, and from the perception of the outline of that part of the sensing organ's surface where the form of the seen object arrives; for the outline of the seen object's surface is figured in both of these places. Therefore, whichever of these places the perceiver attends to, they can grasp within it the

### *33. A spherical surface is perceived from the proximity of its middle parts and the equal distance of its extreme parts. 48 p 4.*

### *34. A concave surface is perceived from the distance of its middle parts and the equal proximity of its extreme parts. 49 p 4.*

The **concavity** <note>original: "concauitas." It is the same regarding the concavity of the boundaries of a surface when it is opposite the sight; however, the sight does not grasp the concavity of a surface when the concavity is oriented upward, or downward, or to the side, except when the concave surface is in a cut-away section and the curvature of its boundary appears toward the sight.

### *35. Flatness at a moderate distance directly opposite the sight is perceived from the equal distance of its parts and the similarity of their placement and order among themselves. 47 p 4.*

The **flatness** <note>original: "planities." Similarly, the straightness of the boundary of a surface is grasped when the boundary is opposite the sight. For the straightness of the boundary of a surface, and its archedness or curvature—when the surface is opposite the sight and the boundaries contain it—is grasped by sight from the arrangement of its parts among themselves. Therefore, the convexity of the surface of the thing seen which is opposite the sight, its concavity, and its flatness are grasped by sight from the grasping of the difference in distance of the parts of the surface, or their elevations, or their widths, and from the quantities of the excess of distance of the parts, or their elevations, or their widths among themselves. Similarly, the convexity, concavity, and flatness of any part of the thing seen is grasped by sight from grasping the excess of the distances of the parts of that portion, or the excess of their elevations or widths, or their equality. 

And for this reason, the sight does not grasp concavity and convexity except in visible objects whose distance is moderate. However, the sight grasps the proximity of certain parts of a surface and the distance of others through certain bodies intervening between itself and the surface, and through bodies that allow for the comparison of the distance of the parts, whose proximity and distance are verified by the sight. And when certain parts of the surface are prominent and others are deep, the sight will grasp the prominence and depth of those parts through the slanting of the surfaces of the parts, the sections of the parts, and their curvatures in the places of depth, and through the positions of the surfaces of the parts among themselves. And this will happen when the sight has not perceived that surface before, nor anything of this kind. But if that thing seen is among familiar visible objects, the sight will grasp its form and the form of its surface through prior knowledge. The form of a thing seen which is contained by surfaces intersecting one another and of different positions is grasped by sight from grasping the intersection of its surface, from grasping the position of each of its surfaces, and from grasping those surfaces among themselves. In cases where the position of the boundaries is not verified by sight, nor the angles (if they have angles), in those cases the sight will not verify the figures. Therefore, all figures of visible things are grasped by sight according to the methods we have declared.

### *36. Magnitude is perceived neither from the visual pyramid angle alone, nor from a comparison of the angle and distance. 27 p 4.*

Magnitude and the quantity of the thing seen are grasped by sight, but the quality of this grasping is based on **uncertain notions** <note>original: "intentionibus dubitabilibus." In medieval science, "intentions" are the secondary properties the mind infers from raw sensory data.</note>. Many people are of the opinion that the quantity of the magnitude of a thing seen is not grasped by sight except from the size of the **angle** that is formed at the center of the eye, which is contained by the surfaces of the **radial pyramid** <note>original: "pyramidis radialis." This is the "cone of vision" where the eye is the vertex and the object is the base.</note> whose base contains the thing seen. They believe that the sight compares the quantities of things seen to the sizes of the angles formed by the rays that contain the things seen at the center of the eye, and that it relies in its grasping of magnitude on nothing but the angles alone. 

And some of them are of the opinion that the grasping of magnitude is not completed by a comparison to the angles alone, but through consideration of the distance of the thing seen and its position in comparison to the angles. And the truth is that it is not possible for the grasping of the quantities of things seen by the sight to be based on a comparison to the angles which the things seen subtend at the center of the eye alone. For the same thing seen does not differ in quantity to the sight, even though its distances may differ by a not insignificant amount. When a thing is near the eye and the eye has grasped its quantity, and afterwards it is moved a short distance away from the eye, its quantity is not diminished to the sight as long as its distance is moderate. And the quantity of any familiar thing seen never differs to the sight when its distances differ, provided they are within moderate distances. Similarly, equal bodies at different distances—when their distance is moderate—

And similarly, if it is moved away from the sight by three or four cubits, it will not appear smaller, even though the angles formed at the eye change by a significant degree. Furthermore, if a square figure with equal sides and right angles is drawn on the surface of some body, and that body is raised until the surface containing the square is nearly parallel to the line of sight—so that the eye still perceives the square figure—the eye will perceive a four-sided figure with equal sides. Nevertheless, the angles subtended by the sides of the square at the center of the eye will be different when the center of sight is near the surface containing the square; yet the eye still perceives the sides of the square as equal. Similarly, when diameters are drawn in various positions within a circle, and the surface containing the circle is then tilted until it is nearly parallel to the line of sight, the angles subtended by the diameters of the circle at the center of the eye will vary greatly according to the different positions of the diameters. Yet, the eye perceives the diameters of the circle as nothing but equal, provided the distance of the circles is moderate. If, therefore, the perception of visible things were based only on a comparison to the angles formed by the visible objects at the center of the eye, then the equal sides of a square would not be perceived as equal, the equal diameters of a circle would not be perceived as equal, a round circle would not be perceived as round, and a single visible object would not be perceived as having a consistent size in different circumstances. Therefore, through experimentation with these concepts <note>original: "intentionum." In medieval science, an "intentio" is a mental representation or a specific property of an object perceived by the mind.</note>, it is clear that the perception of the sizes of visible things is not based on a comparison to the angles alone.

### 37. *The magnitude of a visible thing is perceived by the size of the part of the surface of the eye (where the form arrives) and the angle of the optic pyramid. 17 p 4.*

Since this has been demonstrated, let us clarify the nature of how magnitude is perceived. It has already been stated that the foundation for perceiving most sensible things lies in reasoning and discernment <note>original: "argumentationem & distinctionem." Alhazen argues that vision is not just a physical process, but a cognitive one involving the brain's ability to judge data.</note>. Magnitude is one of the properties perceived by reason and argumentation. The "root" or basis upon which the **faculty of discernment** <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua." This is the cognitive power of the soul/mind that distinguishes and interprets sensory data.</note> relies when judging the quantity of a visible object's magnitude is the size of the area of the eye where the form of the visible object lands. This area is determined and measured by the angle at the center of the eye, which is contained within the <term>radial pyramid</term> <note>The "radial pyramid" or visual cone is the imaginary cone of light rays extending from the eye to the boundaries of the object being seen.</note> that encompasses both the visible object and the part of the eye receiving the form. Therefore, the part of the eye where the form lands, and the angle contained by the radial pyramid covering that part, are the fundamental elements that the senses and discernment cannot avoid using to perceive the magnitude of a visible object. However, the faculty of discernment cannot rely on the consideration of the angle alone, or the part of the eye corresponding to that angle alone. For when a visible object is perceived by the eye while it is near, the perceiver will grasp the location on the eye where the form lands and the size of that location. Then, when that same object is moved further away, it will still be perceived, and the perceiver will again grasp the location on the eye where the form lands a second time, and the size of that location. It is evident that the first location on the eye and the second location differ in size, because the size of the form’s location on the eye depends on the size of the <term>visual angle</term> <note>The angle formed at the eye by the lines coming from the extremities of an object.</note> subtended by the object at the center of sight. The further away an object is moved, the narrower the pyramid containing it becomes, along with its angle and the area on the eye where the form lands.

### 38. *True visible magnitude is perceived by comparing the base of the angle and the length of the optic pyramid. 27 p 4.*

When the perceiver grasps the place where the form of the visible object lands and the size of that place, he will also perceive the shrinking of that place as the object moves further from the eye. This phenomenon <note>original: "intentio."</note> frequently returns to the sight: specifically, that visible things often move away from the eye (or the eye from them) and approach the eye. The sight perceives the objects and notes the shrinking of the forms' locations on the eye during removal, and the enlargement of those locations during approach. Therefore, to perceive the actual size of a visible object, the faculty of discernment adds the distance of the object to the angle of the radial pyramid at the center of the eye. Because this happens so frequently, it becomes settled in the soul's faculty of discernment that the further a visible object is removed, the more the area of its form on the eye and the angle it subtends at the center of the eye will decrease. Because of this, it is settled in the soul that the area where the form lands and the angle subtended by the object depend on its distance from the eye. Once this is settled in the soul, when the faculty of discernment judges the size of a visible object, it does not consider the angle alone, but considers the angle and the distance together—since it is settled in the mind that the angle only exists in relation to the distance. Therefore, the sizes of visible things are not perceived except through discernment and comparison. The comparison by which the size of a visible thing is perceived is the comparison of the base of the radial pyramid (which is the surface of the visible object) to the angle of the pyramid and to the length of the pyramid (which is the distance of the object from the eye). And the consideration of the [faculty of] dis-

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s argument from page 51 regarding the "faculty of judgment" (uirtus distinctiua). He is explaining how the mind calculates the true size of an object by looking at both the visual angle and the estimated distance, a concept now known in psychology as size constancy.</meta>

->ALHAZEN<-

The faculty of **judgment** <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; this refers to the cognitive part of the brain that processes raw visual data into meaningful perception</note> does not reside merely in the part of the surface of the sensing organ <note>the eye</note> where the form of the visible object arrives, but involves the consideration of the distance of that object from the surface of the sight. For the size of the area where the form arrives is determined solely by the size of the **angle** <note>the visual angle</note> formed at the center of the eye. In most cases, there is no functional difference between the distance of the object from the surface of the eye and its distance from the center of the eye. It has also already been demonstrated [referencing previous sections 18, 24, and 25] that the sensing faculty perceives the **directions** <note>term: <term>uerticationes</term> (directions/orientations), referring to the straight paths light travels from an object to the eye</note> which exist between the center of sight and the visible object—which are the directions of the radial lines—and it perceives their arrangement, the order of visible things, and the arrangement of the parts of the object itself. 

When the sensing faculty perceives these things, the faculty of judgment understands that as these directions extend further from the eye, the spaces between their extremities widen. This concept is already well-established in the soul. Furthermore, it is also settled in the soul that the further the radial lines extend from the eye, the smaller the visible object will appear at their ends <note>i.e., it takes up a smaller portion of the total visual field</note>. Therefore, when the sight perceives a visible object and its boundaries, it perceives the directions by which those boundaries are known. These directions are the lines forming the angle at the center of the eye which the object subtends, and they define the area of the eye where the form of the object arrives.

When the sight perceives these directions, the faculty of judgment imagines the extension of these lines from the center of sight to the limits of the visible object. When it simultaneously perceives the amount of distance to the object, it imagines the length of those lines and the size of the space between their ends. These spaces between the ends of the lines are the diameters <note>dimensions</note> of the visible object. When the faculty of judgment imagines the size of the angle, the length of the radial lines, and the size of the spaces between their ends, it perceives the **true size** of the visible object as it exists in reality.

The directions which extend between the center of sight and the boundaries of any visible object are perceived by both the sensing organ and the faculty of judgment. Both the sensing organ and the faculty of judgment perceive the size of the part of the eye where the form of that object arrives. Once the faculty of judgment perceives the directions of the radial lines, it understands their positions relative to one another, their proximity, and the nature of their extension. Nothing else is required to complete the perception of the object's magnitude except the **distance** of the object. 

It has already been explained regarding the nature of distance perception [section 24] that the distance of any visible thing is perceived by the eye either with certainty or by estimation. When the faculty of judgment perceives the positions of the radial lines containing the boundaries of the object, and the size of the area between those lines on the surface of the sensing organ—which is the size of the angle—and simultaneously imagines the distance of the object, it immediately combines the size of the angle and the distance. When it imagines the angle and the distance together, it perceives the size of the object based on both.

The faculty of judgment imagines the distance of any visible object perceived by the eye and imagines the directions containing its boundaries. Through this mental image, it conceives the form of a **pyramid** <note>original: "pyramis"; the "visual cone" or pyramid of light with the eye at the apex and the object at the base</note> containing the visible object, with the object itself forming the base. In this way, the size of the visible object is grasped. 

The proof that the perception of size occurs by comparing the magnitude to the distance is this: when the eye perceives two visible objects at different distances that subtend the same angle at the center of the eye—meaning the rays passing through the edges of the first reach the edges of the second, and the first does not completely hide the second—and the eye perceives the distance of each with certainty, the more distant object will always be perceived as larger than the closer one. The further away the distant object is (provided the eye can confirm its distance), the larger it will be perceived. 

For example: when someone looks at a distant wall at a moderate distance, and the eye confirms the distance and size of that wall, including its width; then if they place their hand before one eye between the eye and the wall and close the other eye, they will find that the hand covers a large portion of that wall. In this situation, they perceive the size of their hand and realize that the portion of the wall covered by the hand is much larger than the hand itself. The eye simultaneously perceives the directions of the radial lines and understands that the angle subtended by both the hand and the wall is the same; yet it also perceives that the part of the wall covered by the hand is much larger than the hand. 

Since this is the case, the faculty of judgment in that perception understands that the more distant of two objects subtending the same angle is of a greater size. Furthermore, if in that same situation one turns their gaze and looks at another wall even further away, and places their hand between the eye and that wall, they will find that the area covered on the second wall is even larger than what was covered on the first. 

And if one then looks at the **sky**, they will find that their hand covers half of what appears of the sky, or a very large portion of it. Nevertheless, the viewer will have no doubt that their hand is as nothing compared to the portion of the sky it covers according to the senses. It is determined from this experiment, therefore, that the sight does not perceive size...

<summary>Alhazen explains the "size-distance invariance hypothesis," arguing that we perceive the true size of an object by mentally combining the visual angle it creates on the eye with its perceived distance. He provides a famous experiment using one's hand to cover a wall or the sky to prove that we do not judge size by the visual angle alone.</summary>

He now explains the mechanics of how the "faculty of judgment" uses the ground and the human body as a ruler to determine these distances.</meta>

...the size of the visible object, except from a comparison of the size of the visible object to the amount of its distance, combined with a comparison to the angle—not from a comparison to the angle alone. And if the understanding of the amount of size were based on the angle alone, it would be necessary that two visible objects at different distances, subtending the same angle at the center of sight, would appear equal. But this is not the case. 

Therefore, the amount of the size of the visible object is not understood through judgment <note>original: "per distinctionem"; referring to the cognitive process of the faculty of judgment</note> except from the mental representation of the **pyramid** <note>original: "pyramidis"; this refers to the "visual cone" or pyramid of light rays with its base at the object and its apex at the eye</note> containing the visible object by the faculty of judgment, and from the mental representation of the size of the pyramid’s angle, and from a simultaneous comparison of the pyramid’s base to both the size of its angle and its length <note>the distance from the eye to the object</note>. And this is the nature of the understanding of size. 

Because of the visual habit <note>original: "consuetudinis uisus"</note> in judging the distances of visible things, when the sight senses the form and the distance of a visible object, it immediately imagines the location of the form and the amount of the distance; it then understands the size of the visible object by combining these two concepts. However, the amounts of the distances of visible things are categorized under the sizes that are perceived by sight. It has already been stated [in sections 24 and 25] that some amounts of distance are perceived with certainty, while others are estimated. Those that are estimated are perceived by comparing the distance of a visible object to the distances of similar objects whose distances have been verified. Those distances of verified quantity are those that correspond to **ordered and continuous bodies** <note>original: "corpora ordinata & continuata"; objects like the ground or a wall that provide a continuous visual link between the observer and the object</note>. From the perception of these ordered and continuous bodies corresponding to the sight, and from the verification of the sizes of those bodies, comes the verification of the distances of the visible things located at their extremities.

### *39. The magnitude of distance is perceived by common bodies placed between the sight and the visible object. [Referencing 10 p 4 and 25 n]*

It remains, therefore, to be explained how the sight perceives the amounts of the distances of visible things corresponding to ordered and continuous bodies, and how it verifies the sizes of those ordered and continuous bodies that correspond to the distances of visible things. 

The ordered and continuous bodies that correspond to the distances of visible things are, for the most part, parts of the **earth** <note>original: "partes terræ"; meaning the ground</note> and familiar visible objects perceived by the sight. Most frequently, it is the surface of the earth, and the body of the earth lies between the visible objects and the body of the person looking at them. The sizes of the parts of the earth lying between the observer and the visible objects on its surface—which correspond to the distance of those objects from the sight—are always perceived by the sight. This perception of the sizes of the parts of the earth lying between the observer and the objects is achieved solely through the sight’s own measurement of them, and through the measurement of parts of the earth distant from the observer against parts near to him whose sizes have been verified. 

Through the frequent perception of parts of the earth and their measurement by the sight, the sight understands the size of the parts of the earth at one’s feet through recognition and comparison to similar parts already perceived. Thus, when the sight looks at a part of the earth lying between itself and the thing seen, it recognizes its size because of the frequent perception of parts of the earth similar to it. 

This concept is one of those that the sensing faculty acquires from the onset of **intellectual stability** <note>original: "quiescentiæ"; referring to the period in early life when the mind begins to settle on and store stable concepts of the world</note>. In this way, the amounts of the distances of familiar visible things become shaped in the imagination and settled in the soul, so that a person does not even notice the process by which they are established. 

The origin of the perception of the parts of the earth lying between the sight and the visible objects is as follows. The starting point for that which is verified by sight is the ground at one's feet. The size of what is at one's feet is perceived by the sight and the faculty of judgment, and the sight verifies it using the **measure of the human body**. For that part of the earth at one's feet is always measured by a person without conscious intent—by his feet when he walks over it, and by his arm when he reaches his hand toward it. 

Everything on the earth near a person is constantly measured by the human body without conscious effort; the sight perceives that measure and senses it, and the faculty of judgment perceives and understands that measure. From this, it verifies the sizes of the parts of the earth continuous with the human body. Therefore, the sizes of the parts of the earth near the person are already understood by the sensing faculty and the faculty of judgment. Their forms are already conceived in the faculty of judgment and settled in the soul. 

The sight perceives these parts of the earth constantly, and the sensing faculty feels the **radial directions** <note>term: <term>uerticationes</term> (orientations/directions); the straight paths rays of light take from the eye to the object</note> that extend from the sight to the extremities of these parts during their perception. By considering the body of the earth through sight, the faculty understands the parts of the surface of the sensing organ <note>the eye</note> where the forms of these parts of the earth arrive; it understands the sizes of the parts and the sizes of the angles subtended by these parts of the sight. 

Indeed, the angles subtended by the parts of the earth near a person are understood by the sensing organ over the passage of time, and their forms are conceived in the soul. The lengths of the radial lines extending from the center of sight to the extremities of the parts of the earth near a person are perceived and verified by the sensing faculty and the faculty of judgment. Because the lengths of these radial directions are always measured by the human body without conscious intent: if a person stands erect and looks at the ground at his feet, the lengths of the radial lines will correspond to the height of the person’s stature. The faculty of judgment will then certainly understand that the distance lying between the sight and...

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s discussion on how the mind perceives the size and distance of objects. He is explaining that we do not judge distance in a vacuum; rather, we use the ground beneath our feet as a continuous "ruler" to bridge the gap between our eyes and a distant object.</meta>

# ALHAZEN

The part of the earth [where a person stands] is the measure of a man’s height; the lengths of the parts of the earth that are continuous with the human body are quantities understood and perceived by the **faculty of judgment** <note>original: "uirtutem distinctiuam"; the cognitive power that processes sensory data</note>, and their forms are settled in the soul. Therefore, when the sight looks at the part of the ground at the feet, the sensing power immediately perceives the **orientations** <note>original: "uerticationes"; the specific directions or lines of sight</note> reaching the ends of that part. The faculty of judgment then imagines the lengths of those visual lines reaching those extremities, as well as the sizes of the angles contained by those lines. When the faculty of judgment has imagined the lengths of the lines and the sizes of the angles they form, it understands the size of the space between the ends of those lines with certain comprehension. In this manner, the sizes of the parts of the earth are made certain through the sense of sight.

Next, the sizes of the parts of the earth following these—further away—are perceived by sight by comparing the lengths of the **radial lines** <note>the rays of light or lines of sight</note> extending to their ends with the lengths of the rays extending to the first parts nearest the man. Thus, the faculty of judgment compares the radial lines arriving at the third location to those arriving at the second (which are common to both the first and second parts of the ground), and it perceives how much the third ray has increased over the second. Once it senses this, it will perceive the length of the third ray, just as it understood the length of the second ray with certainty. Therefore, two rays containing a second part of the earth will be of a known length to the faculty of judgment, and likewise, their position will be known to it. When it understands the length of the two rays and their position, it understands the space between their ends with certain comprehension.

In this same way, the faculty of judgment also understands the sizes of the parts of the earth that follow the parts containing the feet. Furthermore, the parts following the feet are always measured by the human body; for when a man walks upon the earth, the ground he walks upon is measured by his feet and his paces, and the faculty of judgment perceives its size. When a man has passed through the place where he was, and the parts connected to his feet, and reaches those following parts, those following parts are also measured just as the previous ones were. He understands the following parts just as he understood the previous ones. This comprehension will undoubtedly be verified, and thus the first comprehension is made certain by this second comprehension. If its size was not made certain the first time, it will be made certain the second time. 

This **proportional measurement** <note>original: "commensuratio"</note> is always understood by the perceiver, and he uses it without conscious effort. But when sight looks at any part of the ground, the perceiver and the faculty of judgment understand this measurement by way of an "accident"—that is, without deliberate intent. Then, because of the frequency of this action, the sizes of the parts of the ground following the feet, and the sizes of those following them, are already made certain. In this way, the perceiver and the faculty of judgment acquire the sizes of the parts of the earth surrounding the man, lying between the sight and the objects seen. This acquisition begins when a person is at rest; subsequently, the sizes of the distances of familiar visible objects on the surface of the earth become settled in the sensing power and the faculty of judgment. 

Therefore, the comprehension of the distances of familiar objects on the surface of the earth occurs through recognition and comparing them to one another. That is to say, the comprehension of the sizes of distances is through an acquisition by the perceiver and the faculty of judgment—not that the viewer understands exactly how many **cubits** <note>a unit of length based on the forearm</note> are in any given distance, but he acquires a determined quantity from every distance and every part of the earth, and he compares the distances of visible objects he sees later to those determined quantities. Similarly, he acquires a determined quantity from a cubit or a **palm** <note>a unit of length based on the width of the hand</note>, and from any measured quantity. When a viewer perceives a space and wants to know how many cubits are in it, he compares the form of that space acquired in his imagination to the form of a cubit acquired in his imagination; through this comparison, he understands the size of the space in respect to the cubit.

It is also a human habit that when one wishes to verify a certain **notion** <note>original: "intentionem"; a mental concept or perceived characteristic</note>, he repeats his gaze, distinguishes its details, and considers it over time; through this, he understands that notion according to the truth. Therefore, when a viewer perceives an object on the surface of the earth and wants to verify its distance, he looks at the continuous part of the ground lying between himself and the object. The sight moves along its length, and thus the **radial axis** <note>the central, most acute line of vision</note> moves over that part, measuring it and perceiving it piece by piece. It perceives even its small parts when the distance of that final space is moderate. When the sight perceives the parts of the earth, including the small parts, the faculty of judgment understands the size of the whole space. Because of the movement of the radial axis over the space, the faculty of judgment verifies the size of the part of the eye where the form of that space arrives, the size of the angle that the space subtends, and the length of the ray extending to the end of the space. When these two notions are verified by the faculty of judgment, the size of the seen part of the earth is verified. 

In the same way, the lengths of bodies raised up from the earth and extending into the distance—such as walls and mountains—are perceived by sight just as the sizes of the parts of the ground are perceived. The distances of objects facing them are understood from the comprehension of their lengths. In this manner, sight verifies the sizes of the distances of visible objects when they are at moderate distances and are facing continuous, ordered bodies. However, certain visible objects on the surface of the earth are at a moderate distance...

This allows the faculty of judgment to verify visual angles and ray lengths, creating mental templates (like the cubit) to estimate distances automatically.</summary>

# BOOK II OF OPTICS.

...and the sizes of the parts of the earth lying between the eye and those objects are of moderate size; and there are some objects whose distance is very great and beyond moderation, and the sizes of the parts of the earth lying between the eye and those objects are of extraordinary magnitude. The sizes of the parts of the earth are grasped by the sight according to the methods we have described. Therefore, that which is near and of moderate size is perceived and **verified** <note>original: "certificatur"; confirmed with accuracy</note> by the sight, but the size of that which is at an extreme distance is not verified by the sight. This is because when the sight perceives spaces, it understands their sizes by sensing the increase in the length of the **radial line** <note>original: "radij"; the ray of light or line of vision</note> and by sensing the angles subtended by small parts of the space as the **radial axis** <note>original: "axis radialis"; the central, most acute line of vision</note> moves over that space. It will verify the size of the space as it senses the slight increase in the length of the ray and the small increase in the angle subtended by the space.

However, when the distance is very great, the eye will not sense a small increase in the length of the ray, nor will it sense the movement of the ray across a small part of a space that is extremely distant. It will not sense the angle subtended by a small part of that extreme distance, nor will it verify the length of the ray reaching the end of the space, nor verify the size of the angle subtended by that space. And since it cannot verify the length of the ray reaching the end of the space, nor the size of the angle subtended by that space, it cannot verify the size of the distance itself. Furthermore, when the distance is very great, small parts of the space at the far end are not perceived by the sight, nor distinguished by it, because a small quantity at an extreme distance remains hidden from view. Therefore, when the radial axis moves over a very distant space and reaches that extreme distance, it will pass over a small part of the space without the observer sensing its movement; for a small part at an extreme distance does not create a **sensible angle** <note>an angle large enough for the eye to detect</note> at the center of the eye. Thus, when the radial axis moves over a distant space and the sight senses that it has already passed some part of that space, the actual size of the part it passed will not be the size it perceives through the senses, but will be larger. The more the distance increases, the more the parts at the end of the space will remain hidden from the sight, and the areas over which the movement of the visual ray remains hidden will be larger. Therefore, the sizes of extreme distances upon the face of the earth are not verified by the sight, because it cannot verify the length of the ray reaching their end, nor the size of the angle subtended by that space.

### 40. A visible object near the sight is seen more accurately. <note>original Latin reference: 15 p 4</note>

Furthermore, the observer senses the verification of the size of a space because a visible object near the sight is seen with more certainty. This is because the forms of nearby visible objects are more manifest, and they are grasped by the sight with a clearer perception. Their color and light are more manifest, as are the positions of their surfaces relative to the eye, the positions of their parts, and the shapes of their parts and surfaces. If there is any **sketching** <note>original: "lineatio"</note>, or painting, or small details on them, they will appear more clearly to the sight. This is not the case with objects at an extreme distance; for the sight cannot verify the form of a seen object at a very great distance according to its true being, and will be in doubt regarding its color, light, and the shape of its surfaces, and nothing of its **subtle properties** <note>original: "subtilibus intentionibus"; fine details or characteristics</note> or small parts will appear. 

This fact is obvious to the senses. Therefore, when the sight perceives a space upon the face of the earth, it immediately senses—even before it sees the end of it or the objects at its end—whether that space is of a moderate distance or of an extreme distance. If it verifies the form of the end of the space, or the form of the object at the end, with clarity, and also distinguishes the size of that space in the manner previously described, then the **faculty of judgment** <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"</note> will also understand that the size of that space is verified based on the clear perception of the form at its end. However, if it does not verify the form of the end or the object at the end, it will not verify the size of that space. The faculty of judgment, in considering this space, will simultaneously understand that the size of this space is not verified, due to the hidden nature of the form at its end. 

Therefore, the sizes of the distances of visible objects are distinguished by the sight, and the quality of the perception of their sizes is verified during **active looking** <note>original: "intuitionem"; focused observation</note>. When an observer wishes to verify the size of a seen object and its distance, he will look closely at the distance and distinguish it; in this way, he distinguishes a verified distance from one that is not verified. Thus, there is no visual property whose size is truly verified unless the distances involve continuous, ordered bodies and the distances themselves are **moderate** <note>original: "mediocres"</note>. The sizes of such distances are grasped by the sight in the manner we have explained. Beyond these, distances are not verified by the sight but are **estimated and compared** <note>original: "æstimantur & assimilantur"</note>; that is, the sight compares the distance of the seen object to distances of similar, familiar objects that it has already verified. When the sight senses that the form of an object is hidden due to distance, it will doubt the size of that distance. A **moderate distance**, the size of which is verified by the sight, is one at the end of which no part is hidden from the sight that has a perceptible proportion to the whole distance. Likewise, a moderate distance relative to a seen object—where the sight perceives the true size of the object—is a moderate distance at the end of which no part of that object is hidden that has a perceptible proportion to the total size of the object when the sight looks at that part on its own. Therefore, in every space where any part...

<summary>Alhazen explains that the human eye can only accurately "verify" distances that are moderate; at extreme distances, the eye fails to detect the tiny changes in visual angles and ray lengths necessary for measurement. He defines a moderate distance as one where no significant part of the object or space is lost to the blurriness of distance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s investigation into how we judge distance. While the previous page focused on the physical scanning of the ground (the "radial lines"), this section explores how the mind uses mental shortcuts—specifically the memory of familiar objects—to estimate distance when a physical scan isn't possible or precise.</meta>

-> ALHAZEN <-

...length has a <term>sensible proportion<note>original: "proportionem sensibilem"; a ratio large enough to be detected by the senses</note></term> to the quantity of the length of the space, it is grasped by the sight; it does not escape the sight's notice in the parts of the space that are near its far end, unless that part lacks a sensible proportion to the length of that space. Every such space is of **moderate distance**. However, a distance that is beyond moderation in length is one where, at its far end, a quantity that has a sensible proportion to the total distance remains hidden. A distance is beyond moderation with respect to the sight when some quantity of the visible object is hidden that has a sensible proportion to the whole visible thing, or when some <term>intention<note>original: "intentio"; a technical term meaning a characteristic, attribute, or "form" of an object perceived by the mind</note></term> of that visible thing is hidden, the absence of which causes the <term>quiddity<note>original: "quidditatis"; the "what-ness" or essential nature of an object—knowing what the object actually is</note></term> of that visible thing to be hidden.

The sensing faculty also grasps the quantity of the distance of a visible object from the size of the **angle** that the visible object subtends. Since the sight perceives **familiar visible objects** <note>original: "uisibilia assueta"; objects the viewer sees often, like a person, a tree, or a house</note> located at familiar distances, the sight recognizes them immediately upon perceiving them. When the sight recognizes them, it also knows the quantities of their sizes, because the quantities of their sizes have already been **verified** <note>original: "certificatae"; confirmed as accurate through experience</note> by the frequent perception of these familiar objects and are already settled in the **imagination**. When the sight perceives a familiar object, it immediately grasps the part of the eye reached by the form of that visible object, which that part faces. 

And when the sensing faculty grasps the quantity of the size of the visible object through recognition, and grasps the angle that the visible object then subtends, it will grasp the quantity of the distance of that visible object in that specific arrangement; for the angle subtended by that visible object exists only according to the quantity of the distance. Just as the sensing faculty receives an indication of the quantity of size from the distance combined with that angle, so too does it receive an indication of the quantity of the distance from the known size combined with that angle. This is because that specific size cannot subtend that specific angle except from that same distance, or from a distance equal to it, and not from just any distance. 

When the sensing faculty has grasped the quantity of the distance of that familiar object many times and frequently at moments when the visible object subtends an angle similar to that one at the center of the eye—and has many times received an indication of the size of that object from the distance and the angle—the **discriminative faculty** <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the part of the soul or mind that reasons and judges sensory data</note> will understand the quantity of the distance in which it perceives the size of that object relative to that angle. Once the discriminative faculty understands the quantity of the visible object relative to that angle, and perceives in this distance the size of the object relative to that same angle, and recognizes the object and the size it previously grasped, and perceives the size of the angle it then subtends, it will know the quantity of the distance according to which that distance relates to that angle. 

Therefore, the sensing faculty grasps the quantity of the distances of familiar objects by comparing the angle to the size of the object; then, through repetition, the sensing faculty grasps the distance of a familiar object through recognition. The size of the angle subtended by a familiar object, combined with the recognition of that object, becomes a sign indicating the quantity of its distance. Most distances of familiar objects are perceived in this manner. This perception is not perfectly certain; nevertheless, there is no great difference between this estimation and a verified distance. It is from this kind of perception that the **mathematicians** <note>referring to Euclidean or Ptolemaic traditions which prioritized geometry over psychology</note> formed the opinion that the size of an object is grasped by the angle alone. 

When, therefore, the sight perceives familiar objects at familiar distances and knows their distances in this way, it will find the truth for the most part regarding their distances, or there will be no great difference between what it perceives and the true distances. However, in the case of **foreign visible objects** <note>original: "uisibilia extranea"; unfamiliar objects the viewer has no prior mental record of</note> which the sight does not perceive frequently, it errs for the most part; though by chance it may occasionally find something correct in what it perceives using this method. These, then, are the ways we have explained by which the distances of visible objects are grasped by the sense of sight.

### 41. *Visible magnitudes are surfaces, their parts, boundaries, and the spaces that are cast between distinct visible objects. 18 p 4.* <note>This heading likely refers to a specific theorem or proposition number in the manuscript's organization.</note>

Now that the quality of how we perceive distances has been explained, and the distances have been categorized, we shall now distinguish the **magnitudes** of visible things grasped by the sight, and how they are perceived. Let us say, then, that the magnitudes which the sight perceives when positioned opposite them are the quantities of visible **surfaces**, the quantities of parts of visible surfaces, the quantities of the **boundaries** of visible surfaces, the quantities of the spaces between the boundaries of parts of surfaces, and the quantities of the spaces between distinct visible objects. These are all the types of quantities the sight perceives when an object is placed before it. 

However, the quantity of the **body** <note>original: "corporeitas"; the 3D volume or bulk</note> of a visible object is not grasped by the sight when it is merely positioned opposite it, because the sight does not perceive the entire surface of a body at once; it only perceives the surface or surfaces facing it, however small the body may be. Even if the sight perceives the "bodiness" of the body, it does not grasp the quantity of its volume, but only the shape of its body. If, however, the body is moved, or the eye is moved so that the sight perceives the entire surface of the body through the senses, or...

<summary>Alhazen explains that the mind calculates distance by comparing the visual angle of an object with its known physical size stored in memory. He also defines "visible magnitude" as primarily consisting of surfaces and boundaries rather than full 3D volumes, which require movement to be fully understood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s discussion on how the mind perceives the physical properties of objects. Having previously explained how we estimate distance using familiar markers, he now moves to the perception of "corporeality"—the three-dimensional volume of an object—and the mechanics of how the eye scans an object to verify its size.</meta>

-> OPTICS, BOOK II. <-

...whether through visual appearance or through some sign: in that case, the <term>faculty of judgment<note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the part of the soul or mind that processes sensory data into logical conclusions</note></term> will grasp the dimensions of its <term>corporeality<note>original: "corporeitatis"; the three-dimensional volume or "body-ness" of an object</note></term> through a second process of reasoning, distinct from the simple reasoning used during the act of seeing. Similarly, if the faculty of judgment grasps the volume of any part of a body, it only grasps it through this secondary reasoning, beyond the basic reasoning of sight. Therefore, the quantities that the sight perceives through direct opposition are only the dimensions of the surfaces and lines that we have already defined. And it has already been shown [38 n] that the perception of size only occurs by comparing the base of the <term>radial pyramid<note>original: "pyramidis radialis"; the cone-shaped field of vision with the eye at the point and the object at the base</note></term> containing that size to the angle of the pyramid (which is at the center of sight) and to the length of the pyramid (which is the distance of the visible thing). It has also been shown [24. 25 n] that some distances of visible things are **verified** and some are **estimated**. The sizes of visible things whose distance is verified are perceived by the sight through a comparison of their sizes to the angles they subtend at the center of sight, and to their verified distances. Therefore, the perception of the dimensions of the distances of such visible things will be a verified perception. However, the dimensions of the distances of visible things whose distance is estimated and not verified are perceived by the sight through a comparison of their size to the angles they subtend at the center of sight, and to their estimated and unverified distances. Therefore, the perception of the dimensions of such distances will not be verified. 

When, therefore, the perceiver wishes to verify the size of any visible thing, they will move their sight over its diameters, and thus the <term>radial axis<note>original: "axis radialis"; the central, most powerful ray of vision passing through the middle of the eye</note></term> will move over every part of the visible thing. If the distance of the visible thing is among the greatest distances, the indistinctness of its form will immediately appear to the sense, and it will be clear to the perceiver that its size is not verified. But if the distance of the visible thing is among the moderate distances, the verification of its vision will immediately appear to the sense. If, then, the radial axis is moved over what is in such visible things, it will measure it with a true measurement, grasp its parts, and verify the dimensions of its parts. Through this motion, it will verify the size of the parts of the surface of the <term>sensing organ<note>original: "membri sentientis"; referring here to the retina or the sensitive part of the eye</note></term> upon which the form of that visible thing arrives, and the size of the angle of the pyramid which that part subtends. And when the perceiver wishes to verify the distance across a body that corresponds to its distance, they will, through motion, verify the size of the body corresponding to its distance, which is equal, according to the sense, to the lengths of the radial lines. When the perceiver has verified the size of the distance of the visible thing and the size of the angle contained by the pyramid surrounding the visible thing, they will verify the size of that visible thing itself.

### *42. The axis of the optical pyramid remains unchanged when the eye is moved. 53 p 3.*

The movement of the axis over the parts of a visible thing does not occur by the axis rotating away from the location of the center and moving by itself over the parts of the visible thing. For it has already been shown [[11 n 1 & 7 n]] that this line is always extended straight to the <term>place where the nerve rotates<note>original: "locum gyrationis nerui"; the point of rotation for the eyeball near the optic nerve</note></term>, upon which the eye is composed, and that its position relative to the sight does not change. Instead, the whole eye moves in opposition to the visible thing, and the middle of the place where the sense of sight is located is set opposite to every single part of the visible thing. Therefore, when the whole sight is moved in opposition to the visible thing, the axis will pass through every part of the visible thing. At that moment, the form of every part of the visible thing will be extended to the sight—when the axis reaches it—along the straightness of the axis. The axis will be fixed in its own place and will not change from its place with respect to all the parts of the whole eye. Its rotation will occur in its own arrangement during the motion of the whole sight at the location of the nerve, which is only at the hollow of the bone. When the sight wishes to observe a visible thing and begins to look at the edge of it, the end of the axis will then be upon the edge of the visible thing. In this arrangement, the larger part of the whole visible thing will be on a part of the surface of the sight that is declining or oblique from the axis toward some side other than where the axis is; for its form will be in its middle and at the location of the axis in the sight, and the rest of the form will be oblique or declining toward another side from the axis. Then, when the sight is moved after that arrangement over another diameter of the visible thing, the axis is transferred to the part following that part, and the form of the first part will decline toward the other <term>location<note>original: "ubitatem"; a technical term for 'where-ness' or position</note></term> opposite the location toward which the axis is moving. From then on, the form will not stop declining while the axis moves over that diameter, until the axis reaches the end of that diameter of the visible thing and the far edge of the visible thing opposite the first part. Therefore, the form of the whole visible thing in this arrangement will be oblique toward the location opposite the location toward which it was previously oblique, except for the last part, which was upon the axis and in the middle of the sight. The axis, throughout this entire motion, will be fixed in its position, and this motion will be extremely fast—in most cases it is imperceptible because of its speed.

### *43. The optical axis in its motion is never the base of an angle subtended by the surface of the visible thing, nor does it always bisect the angle subtended by any diameter of the visible thing. 54 p 3.*

The axis is not placed in its motion as the boundary of the angle that the visible thing subtends at the center of sight, nor does it cut the width of the angle subtended by any of the diameters of the visible thing. For this would not happen unless the axis moved by itself while the whole eye remained at rest, which is impossible. For the whole eye moves during the act of looking, and the axis moves by the motion of the eye.
