### 44. *The sight perceives the magnitude of the optical angle from the portion of the surface of the eye in which the form of the visible object is shaped. <note>original: "73 p 3"; likely a reference to a proposition in another optical text or a previous draft</note>*

The <term>sensing faculty<note>original: "sentiens"; refers to the sensitive part of the soul or the neurological capacity to receive sensory data</note></term> does not grasp the size of the angle subtended by the visible object at the center of the eye, except by grasping the size of that part of the surface of the eye where the form of the visible object is shaped, and by the mental representation of the angle which that part subtends at the center of the eye. For the sense of sight naturally understands the dimensions of the parts of the eye in which forms are shaped, and naturally envisions the angles subtended by those parts. However, the sensing faculty does not verify the form of a visible object, nor the magnitude of its size through the motion of the eye, except because through this motion it grasps each part of the visible object by its center and by the location of the <term>visual axis<note>original: "axis in uisu"; the central, most acute line of vision</note></term>. Through this motion, the form of the visible object moves across the surface of the eye, and thus the part of the eye's surface where the form was located changes; for during this motion, the form of the visible object will be in one part of the eye’s surface after another. And as often as the sensing faculty grasps the part of the visible object that is at the end of the axis, it simultaneously grasps the whole visible object, and it grasps the entire part of the eye's surface reached by the form of the whole visible object, and it grasps the size of that part, and it grasps the magnitude of the angle which that part subtends at the center of sight. Thus, the sensing faculty repeatedly grasps the magnitude of the angle subtended by that visible object. Therefore, the angle is verified by it; and thus the <term>faculty of judgment<note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the analytical power of the mind that processes sensory images into logical conclusions</note></term> will understand the magnitude of the angle and the magnitude of the distance, from which it grasps the true size of the visible object. It is according to this method, therefore, that the <term>focused observation<note>original: "intuitio"; a purposeful, scanning gaze rather than a passive glance</note></term> of visible things by the sight occurs, as well as the verification of the size of visible things through such observation.

### 45. *The direct and oblique position of a line, surface, and space is perceived from the equal or unequal distance of its endpoints. <note>original: "12 p 4. Idem 28 n."</note>*

Furthermore, when the sight grasps the lengths of the <term>radial lines<note>original: "lineae radiales"; the straight lines or rays of light extending from the eye to the object</note></term> which are between the eye and the edges of the visible object, or the parts of its surface, it senses the equality or inequality of those lengths. If the surface of the visible object grasped by the sight is <term>oblique<note>original: "obliqua"; slanted or tilted away from the viewer</note></term>, the eye will sense its slant from the perception of the inequality of the distances of its extremes. And if the surface is directly opposite, it will sense its directness from the perception of the equality of those distances. Thus, the magnitude of its size will not be hidden from the faculty of judgment; for the faculty of judgment understands, from the inequality of the distances of the diameters of the extremes of an oblique space, the slanting of the pyramid containing it. Therefore, it will perceive the increase in the size of its base due to that slant. The size of an oblique magnitude is not confused with a directly opposite magnitude through resemblance, except when the comparison is made to the angle alone; however, if the comparison is made to both the angle and the lengths of the radial lines lying between the eye and the edges of the visible object, the faculty of judgment will not hesitate regarding the magnitude of the size. Therefore, the sizes of magnitudes, lines, and spaces are grasped by the sight from the grasping of the distances of their endpoints, and from the grasping of their inequality or equality.

But the furthest distance of the <term>moderate distances<note>original: "remotionum mediocrium"; the range of distance within which an object can be seen clearly and its size accurately judged</note></term> with respect to a visible object, when that object is oblique, is less than the furthest of the moderate distances with respect to that same object when it is directly opposite. This is because a "moderate distance" is one in which no part of the object having a sensible proportion to the whole object is hidden from the sight. When a visible object is oblique, the angle contained by two rays going out from the eye to any part of that oblique object will be smaller than the angle contained by two rays going out to that same part and at that same distance when the object is directly opposite the sight. And a part having a sensible proportion to the whole visible object, when the object is oblique, is hidden at a smaller distance than the distance at which that same part is hidden when the object is directly opposite. Therefore, the furthest of the moderate distances for an oblique object is less than the furthest moderate distance for that same object when it is directly opposite; and the whole oblique object is hidden at a smaller distance than the distance at which it is hidden when directly opposite; and its perceived size diminishes at a distance smaller than the distance at which its size diminishes when it is directly opposite. Therefore, the sizes of visible things whose quantities are verified by the sight are those whose distance is moderate, and whose distance relates to continuous, ordered bodies; they are grasped by the sight through comparing them to the angles of the radial pyramids containing them and to the lengths of the radial lines. Moderate distances, however, depend on the position of the visible object—whether in a slant or in direct opposition. And the angles are not verified except through the motion of the eye looking over the diameters of the surface of the visible object, or

And the distance is verified through the movement of the sight over the body, corresponding to the distances of the extremities of that surface or that space. And generally, the form of the visible object and the form of the distance of the visible object—whose distance is moderate and relates to orderly, continuous bodies—reach the imagination together at the same time during the intuition of the visible object. This occurs because the sight grasps the body corresponding to the distance of the visible object at the same time as it grasps the visible object itself. Thus, the <term>discriminative faculty<note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the cognitive power of the soul that processes sensory data to reach logical conclusions</note></term> will grasp the magnitude of the visible object according to the quantity of its verified form of distance, which is joined with its own form.

The magnitudes of such visible things are only grasped by the sight with a true comprehension. Therefore, according to this manner which we have declared, the magnitudes of visible things are grasped through the sense of sight. As to why a visible thing is grasped at the greatest distance as a smaller quantity than its true quantity, and why it is grasped at the closest distance as a larger quantity than its true one, we shall declare in our discourse on the <term>errors of sight<note>original: "erroribus uisus"; a famous section of Alhazen’s work dealing with optical illusions and the psychological failures of perception</note></term>.

### *46. The separation of visible objects is perceived from the distinction of the forms that are impressed on different parts of the surface of the eye. <note>original: "99 p 4"; likely a reference to a specific proposition or page in a related manuscript</note>*

The separation that exists between visible things is grasped by the sight from the distinction of the forms of two bodies or two distinct visible things arriving at the eye. But in the separation that exists between any two distinct bodies, there is either light, or an illuminated colored body, or darkness. Therefore, when the sight has grasped two distinct bodies: the form of light, or the form of the color of the body, or the form of darkness which is in the place of separation, reaches that part of the eye lying between the two forms of the two distinct bodies arriving at the eye.

Indeed, light, color, or darkness will sometimes be in an intermediate body lying between two bodies and continuous with both bodies. If, therefore, the sight did not sense that the light, color, or darkness in the place of separation is not in a body continuous with both bodies on its sides, it will not sense the separation of the two bodies. Furthermore, the surface of either of those two bodies is oblique to the place of distance. In the place of separation, there will perhaps be an obliquity of the two surfaces of the two bodies, or the surface of one of the two bodies manifest to the sight, and perhaps not. When the obliquity of the two surfaces of the two bodies, or the surface of one of the two bodies, has been manifest to the sight, then the sight will sense the separation of the two bodies.

The sight therefore grasps the separation of bodies from the comprehension of the <term>intentions<note>original: "intentionum"; in medieval science, these are the secondary qualities or "meanings" grasped by the mind, such as distance, shape, or separation, as opposed to primary sensations like color</note></term> which we have mentioned: either from the comprehension of light in the place of separation, sensing that the light is from behind the two surfaces of the two distinct bodies; or from the comprehension of a colored body in the place of separation, sensing that this body is different from both of the distinct bodies; or from the comprehension of darkness in the place of separation, understanding that this is darkness and not a body continuous with the two bodies; or from the comprehension of the obliquity of both surfaces of the two bodies in the place of separation, or the obliquity of the surface of one of the two bodies.

Everything, therefore, that the sight grasps regarding the separation of bodies, it does not grasp except according to one of these intentions. Moreover, separation might exist between two distinct bodies, or between two bodies that are not entirely separate—namely, two bodies that are continuous in some parts and separate in others, such as the fingers, the limbs of an animal, or the branches of trees. In either situation, the sight does not grasp the separation except according to the modes we have declared.

Sometimes, separation is grasped through prior knowledge and experience, but that comprehension is not through the sense of sight itself. Some separation of bodies is wide, and some is narrow. Wide separation is usually not hidden from the sight because of the appearance of the body corresponding to the distinct distance, and because that body appears different from both distinct bodies, and because of the comprehension of light and the illuminated <term>void<note>original: "uacuitatis"; here referring to the empty space or gap between two objects</note></term> corresponding to the distance.

A small and narrow separation, however, is not grasped by the sight except at a distance in which a body whose magnitude is equal to the width of the distance is not hidden from the sight. If the distance between two bodies is narrow and hidden, and its distance from the eye is such that bodies of that size would be hidden, the sight will not grasp that distance. If the distance of the two bodies from the eye is a moderate distance, and the sight grasps the two bodies with a true comprehension—(moderate distance being that in which a sensible quantity is not entirely hidden relative to the total distance, and true comprehension being that in which there is no sensible difference between the sight and the truth of the object)—the width of the distance might still be of a quantity lacking a sensible proportion to the distance of the visible thing, and lacking a sensible magnitude relative to the two distinct bodies (since a separation might be the width of a single hair). In such a case, that tiny size does not produce a sensible distance in the sight. Therefore, the distance between visible things is grasped by the sight according to the modes we have declared.

### *47. The continuity of a visible thing is perceived by the absence of distance. <note>original: "100 p 4"</note>*

Continuity is grasped by the sight from the absence of distance. When the sight has not sensed distance in some body, it will grasp it as being continuous. And if there is a hidden distance in a body that is not grasped by the sight, the sight will grasp that body as being continuous, even though there is a division in it.

And sight perceives continuity, and distinguishes between continuity and <term>contiguity<note>original: "contiguitatem"; here meaning the state of two objects touching each other while remaining distinct entities, as opposed to being one continuous body.</note> through the perception of the gathering of the two boundaries of two bodies. And the sight does not judge contiguity unless after it has known that each of the two touching bodies is diverse from the other: because the difference that exists between two contiguous things is sometimes found in two continuous bodies. Therefore, if the <term>sensing subject<note>original: "sentiens"; refers to the person or the faculty of the soul performing the act of perception.</note></term> has not sensed that each of the two touching bodies is diverse from the other and distinct from it, it will not sense the continuity, and yet it will judge it as continuity.

### 48. Number is perceived from the distinction of visible things.

Number is indeed perceived by sight, as are the components of number. This is because sight perceives many visible things simultaneously in a single moment: and when the sight perceives their distinction, it perceives that each of them is diverse from the other, and thus it perceives a multitude. The <term>discriminative faculty<note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the cognitive power that processes sensory data to reach logical conclusions.</note></term> perceives number from this multitude. Number, therefore, is perceived by the sense of sight from the perception of many distinct visible things, when the sight perceives them simultaneously, understands their distinction, and understands that each of them is diverse from the others. It is according to this manner that number is perceived by the sense of sight.

### 49. Visible motion is perceived from the change of its position in sensible time.

Motion is perceived by sight from a comparison of the moved thing to another visible object. For when the sight perceives a moved visible thing, and perceives another visible thing along with it, it perceives its position relative to that other moved visible thing. And when that visible thing has been moved, and that other visible thing has not been moved, then through the movement of that moved visible thing, its position will be changed relative to the stationary visible thing. And when the sight perceives it, and perceives another visible thing with it, it perceives its position relative to that visible thing and understands its motion. Motion, therefore, is perceived by sight from the perception of the diversity of the position of the moved visible thing relative to another.

And motion is perceived by sight according to one of three modes: either from the relationship of the moved visible thing to many visible things; or from its relationship to a single visible thing; or from its relationship to the sight itself.

The first mode occurs when the sight perceives a visible thing and its motion, and perceives it in relation to some visible object; then it perceives it in relation to some other visible object different from the first, while the sight remains in its place: thus it senses the motion of that visible thing.

The relationship of a moved visible thing to a single visible object occurs when the sight perceives a moved visible thing and perceives its position relative to another visible object; then it perceives its position has changed relative to that other object: either that it is further away, or closer, or that it is in a different direction, while the sight remains in its place. This can also happen through a change in the position of some part of the moved visible thing relative to a stationary visible object, or by the change of its parts relative to that visible object. It is according to this last manner that the sight perceives the motion of a visible thing moving in a circle, when a person compares it to another visible object. Therefore, when the sight perceives the position of a moved visible thing, or the position of its parts, or the position of any one of its parts, it perceives the motion of the visible thing.

The relationship of the moved visible thing to the sight itself occurs when the sight perceives a moved visible thing and perceives its <term>location<note>original: "ubitas"; a philosophical term referring to the category of "where" or spatial placement.</note></term> and its distance from the eye. When the sight is at rest and the visible thing is moved, then the position of the moved visible thing relative to the eye will change. If, therefore, the motion of the visible thing is across a wide space, its location will change, and the sight will sense the change of location. And when the sight senses the change of its location while the eye is resting, it senses its motion. And if the motion of the visible thing is along the length extending between itself and the eye, then the visible thing will either move further from the eye or approach it. When the sight senses its receding or its approaching while the eye remains in its place, the sight senses its motion.

And if the motion of the visible thing is circular, the part of the visible thing that faces the eye must necessarily change; and when that part of the visible thing has been changed and the sight senses its change while the eye remains in its place, it senses the motion of the visible thing. It is according to these modes, therefore, that the sight perceives motion when the eye is fixed in its place.

Furthermore, the sight perceives motion according to any of these modes even if the eye itself is moving. This happens when the sight senses the diversity of the position of the moved visible thing, realizing that the diversity is not due to its own eye movement, and distinguishing between the change in position that happens to the object because of the object's own motion and the change in position that happens to it because of the eye's motion. Therefore, when the sight senses a change in the position of a visible thing and senses that the change is not because of the eye’s movement, it senses the motion of the visible thing.

Indeed, the <term>form<note>original: "forma"; the internal image or representation of the object being viewed.</note></term> of a moved visible thing also moves within the eye because of its motion; however, the sight does not perceive the motion of a visible thing from the motion of its form in the eye alone. Rather, the sight only perceives the motion of a visible thing from a comparison of that thing to another according to the modes we have explained. This is because the form of a stationary visible thing sometimes moves in the eye while the object remains at rest, and in that case, the sight does not perceive it as moving. For when the eye moves across a range of visible things, the form of every visible thing facing the eye will move across the surface of the eye during its movement, whether the object is resting or moving. And because the sight has already become accustomed to the movement of the forms of visible things on its surface while those things are at rest, it will not judge the motion of a visible thing simply because of the movement of its form, except when the form of some visible thing reaches the eye and the sight perceives a change in the position of the form of the moved visible thing relative to the form of another visible thing—or from the change of forms in the same place of the eye, as in circular motion. Motion, therefore, is not perceived by the sight except according to the modes we have distinguished.

*50. The nature of motion is perceived from the space through which a visible object moves.* <note>original: "Qualitas motus percipitur è spatio..."</note>

The understanding of the nature of motion arises from the perception of the space over which a visible object moves, provided the visible object moves as a whole. Sight confirms the nature of motion when it has confirmed the shape of the space over which the moving object travels. When a visible object moves in a circle, sight perceives its motion to be circular by perceiving the changing positions of its parts relative to the eye, or by observing how one part of the object points toward different visible things one after another, or toward different parts of a single visible object one after another, while the object as a whole remains in its place. If the motion of the visible object is composite—made of both circular and <term>local<note>original: "locali"; referring to linear movement from one place to another.</note></term> motion—sight perceives it as composite by observing the change in the parts of the moving object relative to the eye (or relative to another visible object) while simultaneously perceiving the movement of the whole object away from its original place. It is through these methods, therefore, that sight perceives the different types of motion of visible things.

*51. Visible motion is perceived within a sensible duration of time.*

Sight does not perceive motion except within time, because motion does not exist except in time, and every part of motion occurs only in time. Furthermore, sight only perceives the motion of a visible object by seeing that object in two different places or in two different <term>postures<note>original: "situs"; referring to the orientation or position of an object relative to its surroundings.</note></term>. However, the place and posture of a visible object do not change except over time. Therefore, when sight perceives a visible object in two different places or two different postures, it must be at two different moments. Between any two different moments, there is an intervening time. Thus, sight only perceives motion in time. 

We also say that the time in which sight perceives motion must be <term>sensible<note>original: "sensibile"; meaning a duration long enough to be consciously noticed by the senses.</note></term>. This is because sight only perceives motion by seeing the object in one place after another, or in one posture after another. When sight perceives a moving object in its second location and no longer sees it in the first location where it saw it before, it immediately senses that the moment it sees the object in the second place is different from the moment it saw it in the first. Therefore, it senses the difference between the two moments. The same is true when it perceives motion from a change in the object's posture. If it sees a moving object in a new orientation and not in the original orientation it saw previously, it immediately senses the difference between the two moments and the time that passed between them. Therefore, the time in which sight perceives motion is necessarily sensible. 

Now that these points have been clarified, let us summarize what can be gathered from them. We say that sight perceives motion by seeing a visible object in two different postures at two different moments, between which is a sensible amount of time; this is the nature of how sight perceives motion. Sight also perceives the differences in motion—such as speed, slowness, and uniform motion—by perceiving the spaces over which the moving objects travel. When sight observes two moving objects and perceives the spaces over which they move, and senses that one of the two spaces traveled in the same amount of time is greater than the other, it senses the <term>velocity<note>original: "uelocitatem"</note></term> of the object that crossed the greater space. When two spaces are crossed in equal times and sight senses the equality of those spaces, it senses the equal speed of the two moving things. Similarly, if sight senses that two spaces are equal but the times taken for the two movements are unequal, it will sense the greater speed of the object that crossed the space in less time. Likewise, when two moving objects cross equal spaces in equal times, and sight senses both the equality of the time and the equality of the spaces, it senses the equality of the two motions. We have now explained how sight perceives motion, distinguishes its types, and judges its equality or inequality.

*52. Rest is perceived when a visible object occupies the same posture and place during a sensible time.* <note>original: "Quies percipitur è uisibili..."</note>

Rest is perceived by sight from the perception of a visible object remaining in the same place and in the same posture over a sensible duration of time. Therefore, when sight perceives an object in the same place and in the same orientation at two different moments with a sensible time between them, it perceives the object as being at rest during that time. Sight also perceives the posture of a resting object relative to other visible things and relative to the eye itself. This is the manner in which sight perceives the rest of visible things.

*53. Roughness is perceived from light illuminating a rough surface.* <note>original: "Asperitas percipitur è luce..."</note>

Roughness is perceived by sight for the most part through the form of the light appearing on the surface of a rough body. This is because roughness is a variation in the positions of the parts of a body's surface. Because of this, when light shines upon the surface of such a body, the protruding parts will mostly cast shadows. When the light reaches the recessed parts, there will also be shadows there, while the protruding parts will be clearly lit and exposed to the light. Because shadows fall in the deep parts and no shadows fall on the protrusions, the pattern of light on the surface of that body will be varied. This is not the case on a flat surface, because the parts of a flat surface all have a similar orientation; when light shines upon them, the form of the light across the entire surface is uniform. Therefore, the form of light on the surface of a rough body is different from the form of light on a flat surface. Sight recognizes the form of light that is on the surface

...rough surfaces, and the form of light that exists on flat surfaces, through the frequent observation of both rough and flat surfaces. Therefore, when the visual sense perceives the light on the surfaces of a body in the manner it is accustomed to seeing on rough surfaces, it will judge that body to be rough; and when it perceives light on the surface of a body in the manner it is accustomed to seeing on flat surfaces, it will judge the surfaces of that body to be flat. And when the roughness is pronounced <note>original: "extranea"; in this context, it refers to roughness that is clearly visible or outside the norm of a smooth surface.</note>, the protruding parts will be of a certain size, and thus sight will grasp the prominence of those parts and understand the position of the body's surface by perceiving the distance between those parts. When sight perceives the diversity of the positions of the parts of a body’s surface, it perceives its roughness through the variation of light and the distance of their positions; from this, the body's roughness becomes apparent. 

If, therefore, the light falling upon a rough body comes from the side opposite the rough surface, and the light is strong, sight will not perceive the roughness of this body unless it perceives the prominence of certain parts and the depth of others. If the roughness of this body is pronounced—that is, very great—sight will perceive the distance between the parts and the diversity of their positions, and will perceive the roughness of the body for the most part. However, if the roughness is slight, and the parts are deep and the pores <note>original: "pori"; small openings or gaps in the surface texture.</note> of that body are of the ultimate smallness, it will mostly remain hidden from sight. Sight will never perceive the roughness of such a body except at great proximity with a careful gaze at the parts of the body’s surface. When sight distinguishes the distance between the parts of such a body, and their prominence and depth, it perceives its roughness. But if sight does not distinguish the distance of its parts, nor their prominence and depth, it will not perceive its roughness. Therefore, roughness is perceived by sight through the perception of the diversity of the positions of the parts of the body’s surface, or from the form of light that sight is accustomed to seeing on the surfaces of rough bodies. Sight also recognizes roughness through the prior knowledge of similarity. If sight perceives nothing in a body based on such similarity, it will judge its roughness. But sight often errs regarding roughness when it attempts to recognize it through this intention <note>original: "intentionem"; here meaning a mental concept or visual cue.</note>, for a surface may be polished <note>original: "tersa"; meaning wiped clean, smooth, or lustrous.</note> and yet its polish does not appear, because polish is only apparent from a specific position.

### 54. *Smoothness is perceived from the light illuminating a smooth surface.* <note>original: "Lenitas percipitur è luce lenem superficiem illuminante."</note>

Smoothness and the evenness of a body’s surface are perceived by sight for the most part from the form of light appearing on the surface of a flat body, which sight is accustomed to seeing on flat surfaces. When the light on the surfaces of a body is of a uniform form, sight recognizes the smoothness of the surface by it. Sight sometimes perceives smoothness through a careful gaze as well. Thus, when sight gazes at the surface of a flat body, it perceives the equality of its parts, and so perceives the smoothness. Polish, however (which is intense smoothness), is perceived by sight from the glinting <note>original: "scintillatione"; the sparkling or specular reflection of light.</note> of light on the surface of the body. Therefore, it is perceived by sight through the perception of the surface’s equality. This equality of the surface is perceived by sight for the most part from the similarity of the form of light on the body’s surface. Polish is perceived by sight from the glinting of light on the body's surface and from the specific position from which the light is reflected. And perhaps roughness and smoothness may be joined together on the same surface: specifically, that there may be parts of different positions on the surface of some body, both deep and protruding, and yet the individual parts of these protruding and deep sections are smooth relative to one another, or some parts are of a similar position, such that the whole surface is rough, while its parts, or some of them, are smooth. The roughness of such a surface is perceived by sight through the perception of the diversity of the positions of the protruding and deep parts, while the smoothness of the parts is perceived by sight on the surfaces of those individual parts. Sometimes sight perceives the smoothness of such parts through a careful gaze and from the perception of the uniformity of each of their surfaces. It is according to these modes that sight perceives smoothness, polish, and roughness.

### 55. *Transparency is perceived from the perception of a dense body placed beyond the transparent body.* <note>original: "Perspicuitas percipitur è perceptione corporis densi ultra corpus perspicuum positi."</note>

Transparency <note>original: "Diaphanitas"; the quality of allowing light to pass through.</note> is perceived by sight through reasoning, based on the perception of what lies beyond the transparent body. The transparency of a transparent body is not perceived by sight unless there is some density <note>original: "spissitudo"; a degree of opacity or physical thickness.</note> in it, and its transparency is "thicker" than the transparency of the air lying between the eye and the object itself. If, however, it is at the limit of transparency, sight will not perceive its transparency, and will perceive nothing but what is beyond it. But when there is some degree of transparency in it, it is perceived by sight because of the density within it, and its transparency is perceived from the perception of what is beyond it. For when there is light or an illuminated colored body beyond the transparent body, it will be seen through the transparent body. Sight does not sense the transparency of a body when it perceives what is beyond it, unless it senses that the color and light perceived through the transparent body are the light and color of the object *beyond* it, and not the color and light of the body itself; if however...

...not: it will not perceive the transparency <note>original: "diaphanitatem"; the quality of allowing light to pass through.</note> of a transparent body. Therefore, if there is no light beyond the transparent body, nor an illuminated object, nor light in its surroundings, and no light or color appears through it or in any other part: the transparency of that body is not grasped. This occurs when a transparent body is placed against some dense <note>original: "spisso"; thick or opaque.</note> body, and that dense body contains it or is viewed through it, and if the transparent body is also of a dark color: for then the sight does not perceive the transparency of this body. Similarly, when there is a dark place beyond the transparent body, and no light appears through it, its transparency will not be grasped. However, when the sight perceives that the color seen through the transparent body is the color of the object behind it, it will perceive the transparency of the transparent body. Likewise, when a transparent body has weak transparency, and the object behind it and the bodies around it have weak light: then its transparency is not grasped by the sight unless it is placed in a strong light. But when the sight recognizes the light beyond it: it will grasp the transparency. Thus, according to these modes, the sight grasps the transparency of transparent bodies.

### *56. Density is perceived by the lack of transparency. 143 p 4.*

Density <note>original: "spissitudo"; often used here to mean opacity or the lack of being see-through.</note> is grasped by the sight from the absence of transparency. Therefore, when the sight perceives a body and does not feel any transparency in it, it infers its density.

### *57. Shadow is perceived by the absence of one light and the presence of another. 145 p 4.*

Shadow is grasped by the sight in relation to an illuminating light, or a part of an illuminating light. For shadow is the deprivation of certain lights combined with the illumination of the shadowed place by an external light—a light different from the one the place is deprived of. Thus, when the sight perceives what is adjacent to the shadow, and there is a stronger light upon that adjacent body than the light in the place of the shadow, it will perceive the shadowing of that place and the lack of the light that shines upon the body near it. For when the sight perceives some light in a place, but that place lacks sunlight or some other strong light, it will perceive the shadowing of that place and its lack of sunlight or other strong light. Sometimes the sight will perceive the shadow's source, and sometimes the shadowing body is not immediately distinguished by it; but eventually, when the sight grasps the place where the light is weak, and perceives that the furthest bodies in that place of weak light have a stronger light than that weak light, it will immediately perceive the shadow of that place. In this manner, therefore, the sight grasps shadow.

### *58. Darkness is perceived by the deprivation and absence of light. 146 p 4.*

Darkness is grasped by the sight through reasoning based on the absence of light. When the sight perceives a place and does not grasp any light in it, it perceives its darkness.

### *59. Beauty is perceived both from individual visual properties and from several properties joined together in symmetry. 148 p 4.*

Beauty is grasped by the sight through the perception of particular properties <note>original: "intentionum particularium"; in medieval optics, "intentions" are the various features or notions—like shape, size, color—that the mind extracts from a visual image.</note>, the nature of whose perception has been explained before. For each one of the aforementioned particular properties creates by itself a certain mode of beauty, and the combinations of them also create other modes of beauty. The sight does not grasp beauty except in the forms of visible things, which are grasped through the sense of sight. The forms of visible things are composed of particular properties, the distinction of which has already been declared. And since the sight grasps forms by grasping these properties, it therefore grasps beauty by grasping these properties. 

The modes of beauty grasped by the sight in the forms of visible things are many. Some visible things have a single cause arising from the particular properties within the form; for some, the cause is nothing but the conjunction of properties with one another, rather than the properties themselves; and for others, the cause is composed of both the properties and their composition. The sight grasps every property that is in any form by itself, and it grasps them in combination, and it grasps their composition and conjunction. The sight therefore grasps beauty by returning to the perception of particular properties. If these particular properties create beauty, their combinations do so similarly. To say "to create beauty" is to induce a disposition in the soul, by which it appears to the soul that the thing being seen is beautiful. 

This will become apparent through a brief inspection: for light creates beauty, and because of this, the sun, moon, and stars appear beautiful; and there is no cause in the sun, moon, and stars for which they appear beautiful except their light. Light, therefore, by itself creates beauty. Color also creates beauty. For any brilliant color, such as green and rose and similar ones, will appear beautiful to the sight, and the sight takes delight in them. Because of this, dyed cloths, flowers, and greenery appear beautiful. Color, therefore, by itself creates beauty. Distance also sometimes creates beauty accidentally. For in some beautiful forms there are spots and wrinkles that create ugliness in the forms; and when they are far from the sight, those subtle properties that create

...ugliness in those forms, and when those [ugly] properties are hidden, the beauty of that form will appear. Similarly, in many beautiful forms, there are subtle properties through which the form is beautiful, such as its line-work and arrangement. Many of these properties are hidden from the sight at moderate distances; but when they are close to the sight, those subtle properties will appear to the sight, and the beauty of the form will be revealed. Therefore, distance and proximity create beauty. Position <note>original: "situs"; the orientation or placement of an object.</note> also sometimes creates beauty: and many beautiful properties do not appear beautiful except because of their order and position alone. For all orderly distinctions, such as point-work, do not appear beautiful except because of their order. And handwriting <note>original: "scriptura"; can refer to writing or calligraphy.</note> does not appear beautiful except because of its arrangement: for beauty exists only from the proper direction of the shapes of the letters and from their composition with one another. If, however, the composition of the letters and their arrangement were not according to a single proportion—for instance, if one were large and another small—then the writing would not be beautiful, even if the shapes of the letters were well-positioned in themselves. And sometimes writing appears beautiful when its composition is proportional, even if the letters themselves are not of the highest quality of arrangement. Similarly, many forms of visible objects do not appear beautiful except because of the arrangement and ordering of their parts with one another. 

Corporeity <note>original: "corporeitas"; the three-dimensional quality or "bulk" of a body.</note> also creates beauty: and because of this, the bodies of humans and many animals appear beautiful. Shape also creates beauty: and because of this, the moon, and the beautiful forms of humans and many animals, trees, and plants do not appear beautiful except because of their overall forms, or because of the shapes of their parts, or because of their figures, or because of the figures of the parts of the form. Magnitude also creates beauty: and because of this, the moon appears more beautiful than the stars, and large stars more beautiful than small stars. Division also creates beauty: and because of this, separate stars are more beautiful than extended stars <note>likely referring to clusters or nebulae</note>, and more beautiful than the stars of the galaxy <note>original: "galaxiæ"; the Milky Way.</note>: and because of this, distinct candles are more beautiful than a single fire. 

Continuity also creates beauty: and because of this, a continuous green field <note>original: "uiridale"; a garden or verdant area.</note> and continuous, thick plants are more beautiful than scattered ones. Number creates beauty: and because of this, regions of the sky with many stars are more beautiful than regions with few stars: and because of this, many candles in the same place create beauty. Human movement in speech also creates beauty. And human rest creates beauty: and because of this, seriousness <note>original: "grauitas"; a sense of weightiness or dignity.</note> and silence appear beautiful. Roughness creates beauty: and because of this, shagginess <note>original: "villositas"; the nap or pile of a fabric.</note> appears beautiful, such as the shagginess in many cloths. Smoothness creates beauty: and because of this, it appears beautiful in fabrics. 

Transparency creates beauty: and because of this, sparkling transparent objects appear so at night. Density <note>original: "spissitudo"; opacity or thickness.</note> creates beauty: since color, light, shape, line-work, and all beautiful properties appearing in the forms of visible objects are not grasped similarly by the sight except because of density and shadow. Shadow makes beauty appear: because in many forms of visible objects there are spots and subtle bodies that make them ugly; and when they are in the light of the sun, those spots will appear in them, whereby their beauty is hidden; but when they are in shadow or weak light, those spots and blemishes will be hidden: whereby their beauty is perceived. Furthermore, the iridescent patterns <note>original: "tortuoſitates"; literally "twistings" or "windings."</note> that appear in the feathers of birds, and in the cloth called *amilialmon* <note>An Arabic-derived term, likely referring to a type of iridescent or watered silk (Moire).</note>, do not appear in shadow or weak light. 

Darkness also makes beauty appear: for the stars do not appear except in the dark: and similarly, their beauty does not appear except in the blackness of night and in dark places, and it is hidden in the light of day; and stars in dark nights are more beautiful than on moonlit nights. Similarity <note>original: "consimilitudo"; symmetry or resemblance.</note> creates beauty: for the members of an animal of the same species, such as one eye to the other, do not appear beautiful except when they are similar; for eyes, when they are of different shapes—for instance, if one is round and the other elongated—will be at the peak of ugliness; and also if one is black and the other green, they will also be ugly; and similarly if one is larger than the other. And similarly if one cheek is sunken and the other prominent, they will be at the peak of ugliness. And similarly when one of the eyebrows is thick and the other thin, or one of them long and the other short, they will be ugly. Therefore, all members of animals of the same kind will not be beautiful except when they are similar. And similarly, letters and pictures do not appear beautiful except when the letters are of the same kind, and those parts of them that are of the same kind are similar. 

Diversity also creates beauty: for the shapes of the members of an animal are of diverse parts, and they are not beautiful except because of that diversity. For if the whole nose were of the same thickness, it would be at the peak of ugliness; and its beauty exists only because of the diversity of its two ends and its tapering shape <note>original: "pyramidalitatem"; a cone-like or pyramidal narrowing.</note>. Similarly, the beauty of eyebrows exists only when their ends are thinner than the preceding parts. Similarly, all members of animals, when they are looked upon, it is found that their beauty exists only from the diversity of the shapes of their parts. And similarly in writing: for if the parts of the writing were of equal thickness, they would not appear beautiful; for the ends of letters do not appear beautiful except when they are thinner than the rest. For if the ends of letters, their middles, and their connections were of one thickness, the writing would be at the peak of ugliness. Diversity, therefore, creates beauty in many forms of visible objects. 

It has now been declared from what we have said that each of these particular properties <note>original: "intentionum"; a technical term in medieval optics for the characteristics or "intentions" an object projects to the eye.</note>, when it is grasped by the sense of sight, sometimes creates beauty by itself. And when a discourse is made concerning many bodies inductively by themselves—when all bodies are considered—it will be found that any of these properties creates beauty in many places. And we have not said what we have said except for the sake of example, and so that other examples might be acquired through these. Nevertheless, these properties do not create beauty in all places, nor does one of these properties create beauty in every form in which it occurs...

...that property <note>original: "intentio"; referring here to a specific visual quality or "notion" perceived by the mind.</note>, but only in certain forms, and not in others. For example: not just any magnitude makes for beauty in any body of a certain size; and similarly, not just any color creates beauty; nor does a green color create beauty in every body which that color reaches; and similarly, not just any shape creates beauty. And each of those properties <note>original: "intentionum"</note> which we have mentioned creates beauty by itself, but in certain places and not in others, and according to certain modes and not others. These properties also create beauty through their conjunction with one another: for instance, beautiful handwriting <note>original: "scriptura"</note> is that in which the shapes of the letters are beautiful and their composition with one another is a beautiful composition; for handwriting in which these two properties are joined is more beautiful than handwriting in which only one of these two properties exists. The limit of beauty in writing, therefore, does not exist except through the joining of shape and position. And similarly, when shimmering colors and paintings are arranged in a harmonious order, they are more beautiful than colors and paintings lacking such harmony. 

And similarly, beauty appears in the form of humans and animals from the joining of particular properties that are in them. For a moderate size of the eyes combined with an almond shape <note>original: "amygdalata"</note> is more beautiful than an eye that has only size alone or only an almond shape. And similarly, the roundness of a face combined with a thinness and delicacy of skin and color is more beautiful than one without the other. And similarly, a smallness of the mouth combined with thinness of the lips and a moderate size is more beautiful than a small mouth with thick lips; and more beautiful than thin lips with a wide mouth. And this property <note>original: "intentio"</note> has much diversity and many modes. 

And when you have performed an induction <note>A logical method of drawing a general conclusion from specific instances.</note> of all modes of visible beautiful forms, you will find that the conjunction of particular properties within those forms creates modes of beauty in them which a single property does not create by itself. And beauty, for the most part, does not arise except from the conjunction of these properties with one another. Since the particular properties we have mentioned create beauty by themselves, they also create beauty through their joining together. 

And beauty also arises from another property besides these two properties we have already mentioned: and that is proportionality and harmony <note>original: "proportionalitas & consonoritas"</note>. For forms composed of different members and different parts have different shapes, different sizes, and different positions, as well as continuity and connection; and although many particular properties occur in each of them, they are not all proportional. For not every shape is beautiful with every other shape; nor is every size beautiful with every other size; nor is every position beautiful with every other position; nor every shape with every size; nor every size with every position. 

But each of the particular properties has a proportion with certain other properties and is asymmetrical <note>original: "asymmetra"</note> with others. For example: a snub nose <note>original: "simitas nasi"</note> combined with deep-set eyes is not beautiful; and similarly, a large nose with large eyes is not beautiful; and similarly, a protruding forehead with deep-set eyes is not beautiful; and similarly, a flat forehead with protruding eyes is not beautiful. Therefore, each of the members has a shape that makes its own form beautiful; and yet, the specific shape of any member only has proportion with certain shapes of the remaining members, and not with others. And a form becomes beautiful through the gathering of proportional shapes; and similarly through their sizes, positions, and their arrangement. 

For the size of the eyes, combined with the beauty of their shape, and with a moderate snubness of the nose, and with a size proportional to the size of the eyes, is beautiful. And similarly, the almond shape of the eyes, their sweetness, and the delicacy of their form; and if they are small, combined with a thinness of the nose and a moderation in the shape of its size, they will be beautiful. And similarly, the thinness of the lips with a delicacy of the mouth is beautiful when the delicacy of the mouth is proportional to the thinness of the lips: namely, that the lips are not at the extreme of thinness and the mouth is not at the extreme of smallness, but the smallness of the mouth is moderate and the lips are thin, and furthermore, proportional to the size of the mouth. 

And similarly, the width of a face, when it is proportional to the sizes of the features of the face, will be beautiful: namely, that the face is not at the extreme of width, and the features of the face are proportional to the size of the whole face. For when a face is wide with the greatest width, and the features within it are small and not proportional to its size, the face will not be beautiful, even if the sizes of the features are proportional [to each other] and their shapes are beautiful. And similarly, when a face is small and narrow, and its features are large—I mean the features of the face—the face will be ugly <note>original: "turpis"</note>. But when the features are proportional among themselves, and proportional to the measure of the width of the face, the face will be beautiful, even if the features themselves are not beautiful on their own; for proportionality alone creates beauty. 

When, therefore, the beauty of the shape of every part is gathered in a form, there will be a beauty of size and composition, and a proportionality of the members according to their shapes, sizes, and positions; and if they are furthermore proportional to the whole shape of the face and its size, it will be at the height of beauty. And similarly, handwriting will not be beautiful unless its letters are proportional in shape, size, position, and order. And it is the same with all modes of visible things in which different parts are gathered. And when you consider beautiful forms of all visible modes, you will find that proportionality creates beauty more than any other single property, or even any properties joined by themselves. ...due to the proportionality of those properties <note>original: "intentionum"; referring to the visual qualities or "notions" perceived by the mind</note> joined together. For beauty does not arise whenever those properties are combined; rather, it occurs in some forms and not in others. And this is because of the proportionality that exists between those properties. Beauty, therefore, does not exist except from specific properties, and its perfection exists only from the proportionality and harmony <note>original: "consonantia"</note> which occurs between those specific properties. Now, therefore, it has been made clear from everything we have said that beautiful forms perceived by sight are not beautiful except through the specific properties perceived by the sense of sight, their conjunction with one another, and their proportionality to one another. And sight perceives the aforementioned specific properties both in simple and composite forms. 

Therefore, when sight perceives some visible object, and there is some specific property in that visible object which creates beauty by itself, and sight observes that property on its own: the form of that property will reach the sensing organ <note>original: "membrum sentiens"; the part of the eye or brain that receives the visual image</note> after it is observed, and the faculty of discrimination <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the mental power that judges and distinguishes between sensations</note> will perceive the beauty of the visible object in which that property resides. Indeed, because the form of any visible object is composed of many properties from among those properties whose division we previously described: when sight perceives a visible object and does not distinguish the properties within it, it will not perceive its beauty. But when it distinguishes the properties within it, and if any of those properties are of a kind that creates beauty in the soul, sight will immediately perceive that property by itself upon observing it. And when it perceives that property by itself, that perception reaches the sensing organ, and thus the faculty of discrimination perceives the beauty within it; and through that perception, it perceives the beauty of that visible object. 

Therefore, when sight perceives some visible object, and in that object there is a beauty composed of joined properties, and sight has observed that object and distinguished the properties within it, and perceived the properties that create beauty through their conjunction or their proportionality to one another—and once that perception reaches the sensing organ and the faculty of discrimination compares those properties to one another—it will perceive the beauty of that visible object as something composed of the conjunction of the properties within it. Thus, sight perceives the beauty that exists in visible things from the composition of those properties with one another, according to the manner we have explained.

*60. Deformity <note>original: "Deformitas"</note> is perceived both from individual visible forms and from several joined together that are asymmetrical <note>original: "asymmetris"; lacking proportion</note> to one another.*

Ugliness <note>original: "Turpitudo"</note>, however, is a form lacking any beautiful property. For as it has already been said, specific properties create beauty, but not in all places, nor in all forms; they do so in some, and not in others. Similarly, proportionality is not in all forms, but in some and not others. Therefore, forms in which the specific properties do not create any beauty by themselves, nor through their conjunction, and in which there is no proportionality between their parts, lack all beauty: and thus they are ugly. For the ugliness of forms is the privation <note>original: "priuatio"; the absence or lack of a quality</note> of beauty in them. And perhaps beautiful and ugly properties are gathered together in the same form: but sight perceives beauty from the beautiful part, and ugliness from the ugly part, once it has distinguished and observed the properties within it. Ugliness is therefore perceived by sight in forms lacking all beauties, by the privation of beauty during the act of perception.

*61. Similarity is perceived from the agreement of visible things with one another.*

Likeness <note>original: "Consimilitudo"</note> is the equality of two forms or two properties in the respect in which they are similar. When, therefore, sight perceives two similar forms or two similar properties, it simultaneously perceives the likeness from the perception of each of those two forms or properties, and from the comparison of one to the other. Sight, therefore, perceives likeness in similar forms or properties from the perception of each form or property according to its own being, and from the comparison of them to one another.

*62. Dissimilarity is perceived from the privation of similarity and the agreement of visible things with one another.*

Diversity <note>original: "Diuerfitas"</note>, however, is perceived by sight in different forms from the perception of each of the different forms, from the comparison of one to the other, and from the perception of the privation of equality—that is, the likeness—between them. Diversity is therefore perceived by the sense of sight from the perception of each form and property by itself, from their comparison to one another, and from the sensation of the privation of equality by the percipient. Now we have completed and set forth the explanation of the nature of the perception of each of the specific properties which are perceived by the sense of sight. ### ON THE DIFFERENCE IN HOW SIGHT PERCEIVES PARTICULAR PROPERTIES. Chapter III.

*63. Sight perceives many visible species at the same time. 2 p 4.*

It has now been explained how sight perceives any of the particular properties which are understood through the sense of sight. Sight perceives nothing except the forms of visible things, which are bodies: but the forms of visible things are composed of the aforementioned particular properties, such as shape, size, color, position, order, and the like. Therefore, sight does not perceive any of these properties except through the perception of visible forms composed of particular properties. Sight perceives any of the visible forms according to the particular properties that exist within those forms: and sight perceives none of the particular properties on its own, because none of the aforementioned properties exists by itself. For all these particular properties are found only in bodies, and there is no body in which one of these properties exists alone without another. Therefore, sight perceives nothing but visible forms: but every visible form is composed of many particular properties. Thus, sight perceives in every visible form many particular properties, which are distinguished in the imagination <note>original: "imaginatione"; in medieval science, this refers to the internal sense that retains and processes sensory images</note>. Sight, therefore, perceives any particular property during the vision of a seen object as joined with another particular property; then, by distinguishing between the properties present in the form, it perceives each property by itself.

*64. Vision occurs through a glance or a fixed gaze. 51 p 3.*

It has also been explained and determined how sight perceives the forms of visible objects, which are composed of particular properties. Some particular properties from which visible forms are composed appear upon the first glance <note>original: "aspectum"; a general or superficial look</note> at the visible object, while others do not appear except after careful inspection <note>original: "intuitionem"; a deeper, more focused looking</note> and subtle consideration: such as fine writing, delicate lines, and the difference between very similar colors. Generally, all subtle properties do not appear to the sight upon the first glance at the visible object, but only after inspection and consideration. The form of a visible object perceived by the sense of sight is that which is composed of all the particular properties present in the form of the object which it is possible for the sight to perceive. Sight does not perceive the true form of a visible object except through the perception of all the particular properties that exist in the form of that object. Since this is the case, the true form of a visible object, in which there are subtle properties, is not perceived by sight except after careful inspection. And since sight does not perceive subtle properties except through inspection, and subtle properties do not appear to the sight at the first glance of the visible object: when sight perceives a visible object and perceives its form, and there are subtle properties in that object, these do not appear through a glance, but through inspection. Therefore, when sight perceives a visible object and there is no subtle property in it, it will perceive its true form; however, it will not be certain that the form is true until it has conducted a strong inspection of every part of that visible object, and verified that no subtle property exists in it; only then will it be certain that the form it perceives is the true form. Therefore, in all situations, sight does not verify the form of a visible object except through the consideration of all parts of the object and the inspection of all parts that can appear in it. Because this has been explained, let us say that the perception of visible things occurs in two ways: superficial perception, and perception through inspection, which looks deeply. For when the sight looks at a visible object, it perceives the manifest properties within it at first glance: then, if it inspects the object further and considers all its parts, it will verify its form. If, however, it does not inspect its parts, it will not achieve a verified perception of the form. That form which is in the sight will either be its true form (though the sight cannot be certain it is true), or it will not be its true form. Since this is so, the perception of visible things occurs in two ways: superficial perception, which happens at the first glance, and perception which occurs through careful inspection. Perception by the first glance is unverified perception; perception by careful inspection is the perception through which the forms of visible objects are verified.

*65. Vision by a glance occurs through any ray of the optical pyramid; but by a fixed gaze it occurs through the axis alone. 52 p 3.*

Having explained this, let us say that the inspection through which the true forms of visible objects are perceived occurs through the sight itself and through distinction. For it has already been explained regarding the distinction of radial lines [8 n.] that the forms which are perceived by the sight along the radial axis <term>radial axis: the central, most direct line of sight in the cone (pyramid) of light entering the eye</term>, and those near the axis, are more manifest and of greater certainty than those forms which are perceiv—

<summary>This page distinguishes between the "glance" (a superficial first look) and "inspection" (a focused gaze). Alhazen explains that true knowledge of an object's form requires examining all its subtle properties, which is best achieved along the central radial axis of vision.</summary>

...are perceived from the remaining lines of radiation <note>original: "uerticationibus"; this refers to the straight paths or rays of light extending from the object to the eye</note>. Therefore, when the eye is positioned opposite any visible object, and that object is not extremely small but has some size, and the eye is fixed in its position during the act of looking: that part of the visible object which is directly opposite the center of the eye—lying on or near the radial axis <note>The "radial axis" is the central line of sight where vision is sharpest, similar to the modern concept of the foveal line of sight</note>—will be perceived more clearly than the remaining parts of the object. The eye itself perceives this arrangement. For when it grasps the visible object as a whole, it finds the place opposite its center, whose form reaches the middle of the eye, to be clearer than the other parts. It was stated above that this phenomenon is apparent to the senses when the visible object is of a large size. 

Therefore, when the eye perceives the entire visible object, it finds that the form of the part opposite its center is clearer than all the remaining parts. And when it wishes to verify <note>original: "certificare"; to make certain or to obtain a clear, accurate image</note> the form of the visible object, it moves so that its center is placed opposite each individual part of the object. In this way, it grasps the form of every part through a clear and verified perception, just as it initially perceived the part opposite its center. Thus, when the perceiver wishes to verify the visible object, the eye moves so that its center is opposite each part of the object. 

Through this motion, the eye perceives the form of every part of the visible object quite clearly; the discriminating faculty <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the cognitive power that processes and judges sensory information</note> distinguishes all the forms coming to it, the colors of the parts, the diversity of colors, and the arrangement of the parts relative to one another. Generally, it distinguishes all the properties <note>original: "intentiones"; the specific characteristics like shape, size, etc.</note> of the visible object that appear through close inspection <note>original: "intuitum"</note>, as well as the form of the entire object composed of those properties. In this manner, there is a verification of each part of the visible object according to its actual being, and a verification of all the object's properties. 

The form of each part of a visible object is only verified after the eye moves over all its parts. Furthermore, the eye is naturally inclined toward the motion of inspection and toward making the radial axis pass over all parts of the visible object. Therefore, when the discriminating faculty seeks to inspect a visible object, the radial axis is moved over all its parts. Since subtle properties within that object do not appear except through the motion of the eye and the passage of the axis (or the radial lines near it) over every part, a verified form of the visible object does not reach the perceiver—when the object is of any significant size—except through this motion and the centering of the eye on each part. 

Even when a visible object is extremely small and not directly opposite the center of the eye, its inspection is not completed until the eye has moved so that the axis passes over it and the form of that object reaches the center of the eye, allowing the form to appear clearly. Since this is the case, the inspection by which the eye grasps the true forms of visible things perhaps occurs through the eye itself and perhaps through the process of discrimination together. Therefore, the perception of the true form of a visible object occurs only through inspection, and the inspection by which the form is verified is not completed except through the motion of the eye. When the body of a visible object is of some size, its inspection is only completed by the movement of the radial axis across all the diameters of the object. 

This is the meaning intended by the one who opined that "vision does not occur except through motion," and that "no visible thing is seen in its entirety all at once." For he intended to speak of verified vision, which cannot exist except through inspection, the motion of the eye, and the motion of the radial axis over all the diameters of the object. 

The way the perceiver verifies the form of a visible object through inspection and motion is this: when the eye is opposite the object, the perceiver grasps the whole form in that initial position through a general perception, but grasps the part at the end of the axis with a true and perfectly accurate perception, while the remaining parts are seen with a lesser degree of perception. Then, as the eye moves and the axis shifts from where it was to another part, the perceiver grasps the form of the entire object a second time, and specifically grasps the part now at the end of the axis in this second perception. The perception of this new part in the second position will be clearer than it was in the first. In this same state, the perceiver still grasps the other parts through some general perception. 

Similarly, when the axis moves to a third part, the perceiver grasps the whole object a third time, and the part at the end of the axis a third time. The perception of this part will be clearer than it was in the previous two positions, while still grasping the rest of the parts. Thus, through the motion of the eye over the parts of the object, the perceiver gains two things: one is the repeated perception of the whole object, and the second is a clear perception of each individual part via the radial axis or the area near it. Consequently, everything that is possible to appear from those parts becomes apparent to the sense. When the perceiver has frequently grasped the whole object and each of its parts, they grasp through this process everything possible to be perceived from that object. 

With this perception repeated many times through the doubling and iteration of the perception of the whole, the discriminating faculty distinguishes what appears regarding the colors, light, size, distance, shape, and position of the parts—noting the equality of those that are similar and the diversity of those that differ in these properties—and the order of parts among themselves. From the discrimination of all these properties and their comparison to known similar things, the faculty perceives a composite form made of them all. Thus, the composite form of all these properties is imprinted in the imagination, and so the form is verified.

### 66. The repetition of looking impresses visible forms more deeply into the mind and makes them more certain. <margin>58 p 3.</margin>

Furthermore, let us say that when sight perceives some visible object, and its form has been certified <note>meaning: made clear, accurate, and distinct</note> to the perceiver, the form of that visible object remains in the soul <note>original: "anima"; Alhazen uses this term to refer to the seat of cognitive processing and memory, which we would today call the mind.</note>. It is shaped in the imagination, and as the perception of the visible object is repeated, its form will be more fixed in the soul than the form of a visible object which sight has not perceived except once or rarely.

And when sight perceives a particular individual, and then perceives other individuals of that same kind, and the perception of individuals is frequently repeated, the form of that kind of thing will come to rest in the soul, and a universally shaped form will emerge in the imagination. 

The evidence for this—that forms of visible things remain in the soul and in the imagination—is as follows: When a person remembers someone they knew before, and has verified their form, and remembers the time and place they saw them with true memory, they immediately imagine the form of that person, the shape of their face, their position at that time, and the place where they saw them. They might even imagine other visible things present in that place at the moment they saw him. This is a clear sign that the form of that person and the form of that place are fixed in the soul and remain in the imagination. 

Because of this, when a person remembers a city they have seen, they will imagine the form of that city, the form of the places they visited there, and the forms of the individuals they knew in that city. Likewise, for all visible things they have seen: when they come to memory, the person will imagine the forms according to the way and state in which they were previously perceived. 

Therefore, the imagination of visible forms which a person has seen before—and now knows even when they are absent—is proof that the forms of visible things which the eye perceives reach the soul and are shaped in the imagination. 

The reason why the form of an object whose perception is repeated by sight is more fixed in the soul and imagination than a form that is not repeated is this: when an intention <term>intention: a medieval technical term (Latin: intentio) referring to the specific qualities or characteristics of an object—such as its shape, color, or distance—that are "intended" for the mind to perceive.</term> reaches the soul, the form of that intention immediately follows. If time passes and the intention does not return to the soul for a long time, perhaps that intention is forgotten, or some of the specific details within that intention are lost. But if it returns to the soul before it is forgotten, its form is renewed, and the soul uses the second form to recall the first. When the occurrence of that intention is repeated many times upon the soul, the soul remembers that intention better; thus, the intention becomes more fixed in the soul. 

Additionally, the first time an intention or the form of a visible object comes to the soul, the soul might not grasp all the details within that form, nor will it verify them; instead, it grasps only certain aspects. But when the form returns a second time, the soul perceives something in it that it did not catch the first time. The more the form is repeated to the soul, the more there will be revealed from it what did not appear before. 

When the soul has grasped the subtle details of a form and has verified its image, it will be more fixed in the soul and imagination than a form in which the soul did not truly grasp all the details. Even if the soul grasped all details the first time, when the form is repeated and the soul perceives those details a second time, it will be more certain that what it grasped the first time is the true form. A true, verified, and certified form is more fixed in the soul and imagination than an unverified one. 

Therefore, when the perception of a visible object is repeated many times, its form will be more certified in the soul and imagination, and through this fixing of the form, the soul is able to remember them. 

The clear proof that intentions and forms are more fixed when repeated is this: when a person wishes to memorize a speech or a verse of poetry by heart, they repeat the words of that intention many times, and so it is fixed in their soul. The more they repeat the reading, the more fixed it becomes in the soul and the further it is from being forgotten. If they read the verse only once, it will not remain fixed; if they read it twice, perhaps it will still not be fixed, or if it is, it will soon be forgotten. By experimenting with this principle, it is clear that the more the forms coming to the soul are repeated, the more they are fixed in the soul and the imagination.

### 67. From a visible thing seen more often, a general notion remains in the mind: by which any similar visible thing is perceived and recognized. <margin>61 p 3. Also 14 n.</margin>

The arrival of universal forms of visible types in the soul, and their shaping in the imagination, happens in this way: Every individual visible object has a form and shape in which all individuals of that kind are alike. These individuals differ only by particular intentions <note>specific characteristics</note> perceived by the sense of sight—though perhaps the color is the same in all such individuals. 

The form, shape, color, and all the intentions from which the form of any individual of a species is composed constitute the "universal form" of that kind. Sight perceives that form and that universal shape, and it perceives every intention in which all individuals of a species are alike across all individuals perceived of that species; it also perceives the particular intentions by which those individuals differ. Therefore, through the intuition <note>direct observation/scanning</note> of the perception of individuals...
