### 68. The essence of a visible thing is perceived from visible species, by the benefit of a form residing in the mind. <margin>66 p 3.</margin>

And the reliance of the perceiver <note>original: "sentientis," meaning the person sensing or the sensing faculty</note> in the perception of the quiddity <term>quiddity: the essence or "what-ness" of a thing</term> of visible things is based only on the forms arriving in the soul. This is because the perception of the quiddity of visible things does not occur except through recognition <note>original: "cognitionem"</note>; and recognition exists only from the comparison of the form which sight perceives just now to a second form that is in the imagination, drawn from the forms of visible objects which sight perceived before; and from the comparison of the perception of the form currently perceived to another of the forms arriving in the imagination. Therefore, the perception of the quiddity of a seen thing is nothing other than the perception of the likeness of the form of the seen thing to one of the forms resting in the soul and fixed in the imagination. 

Thus, the reliance of the perceiver in understanding the essence of visible things is based on the universal form reaching the soul; and its reliance in the recognition of individual visible things is based on the forms of individuals reaching the soul for each of the individuals which sight perceived before, and whose forms were previously conceived and understood by the imagination. And the distinctive faculty <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the part of the mind that compares and distinguishes data</note> naturally likens the forms of visible things during vision to the fixed forms seen in the imagination, which the soul acquires from the forms of visible things. 

Therefore, when sight perceives some seen thing, the distinctive faculty immediately seeks its likeness among the forms existing in the imagination; and when it finds in the imagination something similar to the form of that seen thing, it recognizes that seen thing and understands its quiddity. If it does not find a form similar to the form of that seen thing among the forms existing in the imagination, it will not recognize that seen thing, nor understand its quiddity. And because of the speed with which the distinctive faculty likens the form of the seen thing during vision, an error may perhaps occur, so that it likens the seen thing to another seen thing, when there is some intention <term>intentio: a specific property or characteristic, such as color, shape, or size</term> in the seen thing that is also in that other thing. Then, if it considers that seen thing with repeated inspection after this initial state and verifies its form, it will liken it to the form truly similar to it in reality, and it will be revealed a second time that it had erred in the first comparison. In this manner, therefore, the quiddities of visible things are understood through the sense of sight.

### 69. Distinct vision occurs either by a gaze alone, or by a gaze and an anticipated notion together. <margin>62 p 3.</margin>

And since all these points have been explained, let us now say that the perception of visible things through inspection will occur in two ways: perception by inspection alone, and perception through inspection with preceding knowledge. 

Perception that is by inspection alone is the perception of foreign visible things which sight has not seen before, or visible things which sight perceived before but does not remember seeing. For when sight perceives some seen thing which it has not previously perceived by looking, nor a seen thing of this species, and the observer wishes to verify the form of this seen thing, he will inspect it and consider through inspection all the intentions that are in it, and understand its true form through inspection. And since he did not previously perceive that seen thing, nor anything of this species, he does not recognize its form upon perceiving it; and in such cases, sight requires inspection to understand the proper form. Therefore, the verification of the form of such visible things is only through inspection alone. Similarly, when sight perceives some seen thing which it perceived before but does not remember, it will not recognize its form except through inspection. Therefore, the perception of such visible things will be by inspection alone. 

Perception, however, which is by inspection with preceding knowledge, is the perception of all visible things which sight perceived before, or of whose species sight perceived something before, such that the forms of their species and their individuals have reached the soul. Therefore, when sight perceives some seen thing which it perceived before, or a thing of a species it perceived before, it immediately understands its whole form upon looking at that seen thing; then, with a brief inspection, it understands its whole form, which is the universal form of the species. When it has previously perceived visible things of that kind, and the form of the species of that seen thing has reached its soul, and it remembers the universal form of that kind of seen thing, it recognizes the universal form which it perceives in that seen thing upon perceiving it. And upon the recognition of the universal form which it perceives in that seen thing, it immediately recognizes that seen thing specifically; then, when it has inspected the remaining intentions which are in that seen thing, it will verify its particular form. If, however, it did not perceive that seen thing before, or perhaps perceived it but does not remember the perception of it, it will not recognize the particular form; and when it does not recog-

### *70. Visual scanning occurs over time. <margin>56 p 3.</margin>*

Furthermore, comprehension through visual scanning <note>original: "intuitionem"</note> does not occur except over a duration of time. This is because scanning only happens through the act of distinction <note>original: "distinctionem"; the mind's process of sorting through visual data</note> and the movement of the sight; but distinction and movement only occur in time. Therefore, visual scanning only occurs over time. It has been declared above [12.13 n] that comprehension through recognition and comprehension through distinction only occur over time.

### *71. A visible object is perceived in less time when visual scanning and prior knowledge work together than by visual scanning alone. <margin>64 p 3.</margin>*

Because it has been declared [69 n] that the comprehension of visible things through scanning sometimes happens by scanning alone and sometimes by scanning with prior recognition—and because that which is grasped by scanning and recognition is only grasped over time—we say that comprehension which occurs through scanning combined with prior recognition or knowledge will, for the most part, happen in less time than the time required for comprehension by scanning alone. 

This is because forms existing in the soul <note>original: "anima"; here meaning the mind or memory</note> and present in the memory do not require every single intention within them to be recognized (the parts from which they are truly composed); instead, it is sufficient for their comprehension to grasp just one intention characteristic of them. When the "distinctive faculty" <note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the part of the mind that processes and compares sensory data</note> grasps a specific intention belonging to a form coming toward it, and it remembers the original form, it will recognize all the forms coming to it. This is because every intention that is specific to a form acts as a "defining sign" <note>original: "signum signans"</note> for those forms. 

For example: when the sight grasps an individual human being and perceives only the outline <note>original: "lineationem"</note> of his hand, it immediately understands that it is a human before it perceives the outline of his face or the outlines of his remaining parts. Similarly, if it perceives the outline of his face before grasping the rest. Thus, from the comprehension of certain intentions that are unique to the form of a human, the mind understands that the visible thing is a human without needing to grasp all the remaining parts; it grasps the remaining parts through prior knowledge from the forms residing in the soul—I mean the forms of humans. 

In the same way, when the sight grasps certain intentions unique to the particular form of an individual it has perceived before—such as a specific shape of the nose, or greenness in the eye, or the arching of the eyebrows—it will comprehend that individual and recognize it through the comprehension of the whole form. Likewise, one recognizes a horse by a certain spot on its forehead or by a variation in its color. Similarly, a writer <note>original: "scriptor"; likely referring to someone who reads or writes often</note>, when he grasps the form of a word, recognizes it superficially before he considers the particular letters. Likewise, all parts that a writer sees frequently and continuously are recognized by him from the comprehension of only a few letters. 

Therefore, visible things that the sight has perceived before, and whose forms it now recognizes and remembers, are grasped by the sight through signs. However, strange visible things that the sight has not perceived before—or things it perceived before but does not remember—are not like this. When the sight grasps a visible thing it has not seen before and perceives the outline of certain parts, it does not comprehend the quiddity of that thing from that alone, because the form of the remaining parts is not resting within the mind. Sight, therefore, does not grasp the certainty of a visible thing it has not seen before except by considering all its parts and all the intentions within it. Likewise, the form of a visible thing that the sight has perceived before but does not remember is not verified by it except after considering all the intentions within it. But the comprehension of [only] some intentions within a form occurs in less time than the comprehension of all intentions within a form. Therefore, vision which occurs through scanning with recognition...

And because of this, the sight perceives visible things with a very fast, accustomed comprehension in a time that escapes the senses; and there will not be, for the most part, a sensible duration of time between the presentation of the sight to the thing seen and the comprehension of the quiddity <term>quiddity: the "what-ness" or essential nature of an object</term> of the familiar thing seen. Familiar visible things are therefore perceived by the sight through signs and through previous knowledge. Thus, the perception of their quiddities will be, for the most part, in a sensible time.

### 72. General species of a visible thing are perceived more quickly than individuals.

Furthermore, the comprehension of the species <note>original: "speciei"; the general category or class</note> of a thing seen occurs, for the most part, in a shorter time than the individuality of the thing seen is perceived. And this is because when the sight perceives some individual human, it first perceives that it is a human before it perceives his particular form; and perhaps it will perceive that it is a human even if it does not perceive the features of the face, but from the uprightness of the body and the arrangement of the members of the body, it will perceive that it is a human, even if it has not seen the face. And similarly, the sight perhaps sometimes perceives the specific nature of the modes of some familiar visible things through certain signs which are appropriate to that species. But the perception of the individuality of a thing seen is not like this. For the individuality of a thing seen is not perceived except from the perception of particular intentions <term>intentions: the distinct properties or characteristics (like color, shape, or size) that the mind extracts from a visual image</term> which are appropriate to that individual, or from the perception of several of them. But the perception of several particular intentions which are appropriate to an individual are not perceived except after the perception of the universal intentions which are in that individual, or after the perception of several of them; or generally, the intentions which are in the universal forms of that kind of individual come before the intentions which are in its individual form; but the perception of a part occurs in less time than the time in which the whole is perceived. Therefore, the perception of the specific category of a thing seen by the sight is in less time than the time in which the individuality of that thing seen is perceived.

### 73. Among common visible things, some are perceived more quickly than others.

Furthermore, the time of the perception of the specific nature of familiar visible things varies. For some species of familiar visible things resemble other species, and some do not—such as the species of "man" and the species of "horse." For the form of the species of man does not resemble another species of animal, but it is not so with horses. For a certain horse resembles many animals in its total form. Therefore, the time in which the sight perceives the species of an individual human and perceives that it is a human is not the same as the time in which it perceives the species of a horse and perceives that it is a horse—especially when it perceives both at a certain distance. For when the sight perceives the individual of some human moving locally, it will immediately perceive that it is an animal from the movement, and from the uprightness of the body, it will perceive that it is a human; but it is not so when it perceives a horse. For when the sight perceives an individual horse moving itself, and perceives at the same time its movement and the number of its feet, it will not perceive from this that it is a horse; for those intentions exist in many quadrupeds which resemble the horse in many intentions, and especially in the mule; for the mule resembles the horse in many characteristics. For a mule is not distinguished from a horse except by intentions that are almost unmanifest, such as the features of the face, the extension of the neck, the speed of movement, and the length of its strides. If, however, the sight does not perceive some of these intentions through which a horse is perceived along with the perception of its whole form, it will not perceive that it is a horse. And the time in which the sight perceives the uprightness of a human body is not the same as the time in which it perceives the form of a horse with the particular intentions by which a horse is distinguished from another animal. Therefore, the perception of the species of man is in less time than the time in which the species of a horse is perceived; although both times are small, nevertheless one of them, according to all conditions, is greater than the other. And similarly, when the sight perceives a rosy color in the flowers of a certain garden, it will immediately perceive that the substances of those colors are roses because of the color proper to roses; and with this, that the color is in things existing in a garden, it is perceived before the perception of the roundness, and before the roundness of its petals, and the layering of its petals one over the other, and before the perception of all its intentions from which the form of a rose is composed. But it is not so when it perceives the greenness of myrtle in a garden; for when the sight perceives only the greenness of myrtle in a garden, it will not perceive that it is myrtle from the perception of the greenness alone, because many plants are green, and many

...plants that resemble a myrtle in their greenness and shape. Therefore, if the sight does not grasp the specific shape of its leaves, their thickness, and the specific characteristics belonging to a myrtle, it will not recognize it as being a myrtle. The time in which it perceives the shape of the myrtle's leaves and the features by which a myrtle is specifically identified—along with the perception of its green color—is not the same as the time in which it perceives only a rose-like color. 

Similarly, the essential natures <term>quiddity: the "what-ness" or essence of a thing</term> of all species that can resemble others are not perceived by sight except through great scrutiny <note>original: "intuitionem"; Alhazen uses this to mean a focused, scanning gaze</note>. However, an essence with little resemblance to others is perceived by sight with little scrutiny. The same applies to individuals: for an individual that does not look like another individual is perceived by sight through moderate scrutiny and through identifying marks <note>original: "signa"; characteristic features used for quick recognition</note>. But an individual that the sight knows but which resembles another individual—even if it is known—is only grasped by the sight through great scrutiny. 

Therefore, the species and the individual of all familiar visible things are perceived by sight through moderate scrutiny combined with previous knowledge. And their recognition will occur for the most part in a sensible amount of time <note>i.e., a duration of time that can be consciously felt by the observer</note>. Yet the time for their recognition varies according to the variety of their species and individuals: the recognition of a species will be faster than the recognition of an individual, and the recognition of a species with little resemblance to others will be faster than the recognition of a species with much resemblance. Similarly, the recognition of an individual with little resemblance will be faster than the recognition of an individual with much resemblance.

### 74. The time of gazing varies according to the variety of visible species. 56 p 3.

And the time of scrutiny varies according to the features <note>original: "intentiones"; here meaning the properties or characteristics of an object</note> that one examines in visible things. For example: when the sight perceives a many-legged animal with small feet, and that animal is in motion, it will perceive its motion through moderate scrutiny. Having perceived its motion, it will perceive that it is an animal. Then, through moderate scrutiny of the feet, it will perceive that it is many-legged from the perception of the distance between the feet. Thus, it will not immediately know the number of feet; if it wishes to know the number of feet, it will need a longer scrutiny and more time. Therefore, the recognition of its "animal-ness" will occur in a short time, and then the recognition of the multitude of feet will occur in a short time. But the number of feet will not be perceived unless the sight has scrutinized each individual foot and counted them, which cannot happen except in a span of time of some length; and the quantity of time will depend on the greater or lesser number of feet. 

Similarly, when the sight perceives a round shape within which is a many-sided shape <note>a polygon</note>, and the sides of that shape are small, and moreover there is not a very great difference between the various sides: upon perceiving the total shape, it will perceive it as being round, and will not immediately perceive that there is a many-sided shape inside it, because its sides were extremely small. When it has scrutinized the round shape with a deeper gaze, the many-sided shape within the round one will appear. Therefore, the recognition of the roundness of the shape will be faster than the recognition of the many-sided shape within it. Furthermore, upon perceiving this, the variation of the sides of this shape will not appear, nor will the sight distinguish whether they are equal or not. The inequality of the sides of the many-sided shape will not appear except after great scrutiny and in a span of time of some length. 

Also, when the observer wishes to examine the shape of the whole visible thing, it is enough for the sight to pass over the surface of the visible thing only. Similarly, when he wishes to examine the color of the visible thing, it is enough to pass the sight over it only. And similarly when he wishes to examine the roughness of the surface of the visible thing, or its smoothness, or its transparency, or its thickness. These are not the hidden, subtle features found in visible things, such as those in any particular parts of visible things: like the similarity of shapes and the size of parts, the diversity of sizes and colors and their similarities, and the arrangement of small parts among themselves. For these features are not perceived through scrutiny unless the sight is fixed upon each of the parts, considers the shapes of those parts, and compares one to another. This will not be completed in a short time or through a fast movement, but in a span of time of some length. Therefore, the time of scrutiny for the features of visible things varies according to the variety of the features being scrutinized.

### 75. Vision through anticipated notions and brief gazing is uncertain. 65 p 3.

And since this has been explained, let us say: that vision which occurs through previous knowledge, and through identifying marks and moderate scrutiny, is not a certified <note>original: "certificata"; meaning accurate, verified, or certain</note> perception. For the perception of a visible thing through previous knowledge and identifying marks only concerns the totality and universality of the visible thing in a general way. The distinguishing faculty <note>the part of the soul or mind that processes and interprets visual data</note> perceives the particular features in that visible thing according to the way it knew those visible things from the primary form of that thing existing in the soul. But these particular features in visible things change with the passage of time; thus, the sight does not perceive features that have changed in that visible thing through previous knowledge. 

When the change is hidden and not clearly manifest, it is not perceived by the sight at first glance; and if it is not very manifest, it is only perceived through scrutiny. For example: when the sight knows a certain man, and that man’s face was clear, and the sight had verified his form; then that man went away from the sight for a long time, and a spot happened to appear on his face, and that spot was hidden; and the sight perceived him after this condition: it will recognize him upon perception, but not because of the perception and

...perception and recognition of that person, he will not perceive a blemish on his face unless it is obvious; and if he has not scrutinized it <note>original: "intuitus"; referring to the act of *intuitio* or a focused, investigative gaze</note>, he will not perceive it according to its true state. But if he scrutinizes it with a more careful gaze, the blemish on the face will appear to him, and then he will perceive the person's form according to its true state. 

Similarly, when the sight perceives a certain tree and scrutinizes it, confirming its form, and then remains away from it for a long time while the tree grows and increases in size and its shape changes—if that change in the tree is slight—then if the sight returns to that tree and recognizes it, it will not perceive that slight change which occurred in it through recognition alone. If, however, he scrutinizes it a second time, and at the same time remembers the true form it had the first time, he will perceive the change that occurred in it and will confirm its form a second time. If he does not scrutinize it, that form which he perceives from that tree through previous recognition will not be the true form which it has at the second perception. 

In the same way, when the sight perceives a wall in certain places, and that wall is smooth and has paintings and carvings upon it, and the sight scrutinizes that wall and confirms its form, then leaves that place for a long time—if a change then occurs in that wall, such as a roughening of the surface or a darkening of certain paintings, and that change is not very obvious—then if the sight returns to that place and looks at that wall while remembering the first form, he will perceive the wall as it was at the first vision. But through recognition alone, he will not perceive the hidden change that occurred in it, and he will recognize its form as being without any change. Therefore, if some roughness has occurred in it, he will judge it to be smooth, just as it used to be; and if the paintings were first truly confirmed and have since changed, he will judge them as if they were still as originally confirmed. 

Indeed, all visible things around us are subject to change in color, shape, size, position, roughness, smoothness, the arrangement of parts, and according to many particular properties <note>original: "intentiones particulares"; in medieval science, these are the individual characteristics or "intentions" that the mind picks up from an object</note>, since their natures are changeable and prepared to be affected by what happens to them from the outside. And because change is possible in them, it is possible for that change to be perceived by the sight in all of them. Although there may be some change in them that cannot appear to the sight, there is nothing among them in which an external change cannot occur that could be visible. 

Since all visible things are prone to changes that can be perceived by the sight, no visible thing which the sight perceives now—and which was perceived before—is confirmed by the sight during the second perception (that is, the sight cannot be certain the second time) that it has not been changed, since change is possible in all visible things. Therefore, when the sight perceives some visible thing which it perceived before, scrutinizes it, confirms its form, and remembers its form from the previous perception, it will recognize it. If a manifest change has occurred in that visible thing, it will perceive that change upon viewing it; but if the change is not manifest, it will recognize the thing and judge it during recognition according to its first state. Thus, if it does not repeat the scrutiny, it will not be certain that the form it previously knew remains according to its true state, since it is possible that a hidden change has occurred in it which cannot appear except through scrutiny. Therefore, if it repeats the scrutiny, it will confirm its form; and if it does not repeat the scrutiny, the perception of that visible thing will not be confirmed. Perception of visible things through previous recognition, through signs, and through a brief glance, is therefore not true perception.

### **76. The true visible form is perceived by a focused gaze: by accurate consideration: and by diligent distinction of all visible properties. 57 p 3.**

The sight does not perceive a visible thing with true perception except through scrutiny of the visible thing during its perception, and through the consideration of all the properties <note>original: "intentionum"</note> that are in that visible thing, and through the distinction of all of them during the perception of that thing. 

Vision, therefore, occurs in two ways: vision at first sight, and vision which occurs through scrutiny. By vision at first sight, the sight perceives only the manifest properties of the visible thing, and the form of the visible thing is not confirmed by this kind of glance. Vision at first sight is sometimes merely "imaginary" <note>original: "phantastica"; related to the *phantasia* or the faculty of forming mental images of things not fully known</note> and sometimes involves previous knowledge. 

Vision that is "imaginary" is the vision of visible things which the sight does not recognize upon glancing at them, even though it scrutinizes them. Vision that is "imaginary" with previous knowledge is the vision of visible things which the sight has known before, but in which it does not scrutinize their properties. In neither of these dispositions will the sight perceive the truth of the visible thing through the imagination, whether it has prior knowledge of that thing or not. 

Vision through scrutiny also occurs in two ways: vision by scrutiny alone, and vision by scrutiny with previous knowledge. Vision by scrutiny alone is of visible things which the sight has not perceived before, or of which it does not remember the perception when it scrutinizes them now. Vision through scrutiny with prior knowledge is the vision of all visible things which the sight perceives and remembers having perceived when it scrutinizes their properties and considers all the features within them. 

This vision is divided into two modes: one of which is the accustomed vision of familiar visible things; this part occurs through "signs" <note>specific markers like a scar, a certain color, or a shape that allow for fast ID</note> which are perceived by a brief scrutiny and by the consideration of certain properties in that visible thing along with previous knowledge. This vision occurs for the most part in an "insensible time" <note>a duration so brief it cannot be consciously measured or felt</note>; and the perception...

...the perception of that which is understood in this way is not comprehension at the highest level of certainty. The second part, however, is achieved through the ultimate degree of scrutiny <note>original: "intuitionis"; referring to a focused, investigative gaze</note>, and by the consideration of all the <term>properties</term> <note>original: "intentionum"; in this context, the specific characteristics of an object like color, shape, or size</note> which are found in the visible object during its perception, and with previous knowledge. This usually happens over a perceptible amount of time, and that time varies according to the properties found in the visible object. Vision that occurs in this way—through which familiar visible things are understood with the highest degree of certainty—only happens through the scrutiny of all properties in the object, the consideration of all its parts, and the distinction of all its characteristics during the act of perception, whether the person has prior knowledge of that thing or not. This verification, in terms of the senses, is a "verified property"; it means reaching the limit of what can be accurately grasped by the sense. Alongside all of this, the perception of visible things depends on the strength of the eyesight, since the visual sense of the eyes varies between strength and weakness. Therefore, the perception of visible things occurs according to these modes, and these are all the ways in which things are seen. This is what we intended to explain in this chapter. We have now completed the categorization of all visible things and their properties, and we have explained all the means by which sight reaches the comprehension of these things. We have also distinguished all the parts into which the modes of vision are divided. These are the matters we intended to clarify in this treatise.

## ALHAZEN'S OPTICS
### BOOK THREE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring a seated figure and classical architectural elements.</image-desc>

The third treatise consists of seven chapters. *The first chapter is the preface. The second concerns the things that must be established before discussing deceptions of sight. The third is about the causes that lead to visual deceptions. The fourth deals with distinguishing between types of visual deceptions. The fifth concerns the qualities of visual deceptions that occur through sensation alone. The sixth concerns the qualities of visual deceptions that occur in recognition. The seventh concerns the qualities of visual deceptions that occur in reasoning.*

->PREFACE TO THE BOOK, CHAPTER 1.<-

1. *Sight is sometimes deceived in its perception of visible things. [See Book 1, Part 4]*

It was explained in the first and second treatises how sight perceives visible things as they truly are, provided the perception is conducted correctly: how it verifies the visual form, and how it understands and verifies each of the particular properties as they are. However, not everything perceptible by sight is understood exactly as it is, nor is everything that seems to be understood by the observer in truth correctly perceived. Instead, sight is often deceived in many of the things it perceives, understanding them in a way different from how they truly are. Sometimes the observer realizes they are being deceived even while it is happening; at other times, they do not, believing they are perceiving things correctly. For instance, when sight perceives an object from a great distance, its size will appear smaller than its true measure; when that object is perhaps very close to the eye, sight will perceive its size as larger than the truth. Furthermore, when sight perceives a square or a polygon from a distance, it will perceive it as round if its diameters are equal, or oblong if its diameters are unequal. If it perceives a sphere from a very great distance, it will perceive it as flat. Such examples are many and varied, and all things perceived by sight in this manner are deceptive. 

Moreover, when sight looks at a star, it perceives it as stationary, even though the star is moving at that time. When the observer returns to their scientific knowledge, they know that the star is moving while they watch it; as soon as the observer reflects on this, they immediately realize they were deceived in perceiving the star as being at rest. Similarly, when someone looks at an individual on the surface of the earth from a very great distance, and that individual is moving with a very slow motion and the observation does not last long, the observer will perceive the person as being at rest. If the observer did not previously know the person was moving, and does not watch for a long duration, they will not realize they are being deceived in perceiving the person as stationary; they will be deceived in this perception, yet will not realize it. Therefore, deception happens to the sight in many of the things it perceives; sometimes this is noticed, and sometimes not. Since it has been explained in the two preceding books how sight perceives visible things as they are, and in this chapter we have shown through examples that sight is often deceived, it remains to be explained why, when, and how these deceptions occur. In this treatise, we are concerned with the deceptions of sight regarding things it normally perceives correctly, and we shall explain the causes of this, the various types of deceptions, and how each deception happens.

### CONCERNING THOSE THINGS WHICH OUGHT TO BE PREMISED TO THE DISCOURSE
#### on the deceptions of sight. Chapter II.

2. *The axes of the optical pyramids of both eyes, passing through the center of the opening of the uvea <note>original: "foraminis uueae"; refers to the pupil, which is an opening in the uveal layer of the eye</note>, always converge at a single visible point; and they are perpendicular to the surface of the eye. 32. 33 p 3.*

It was declared in the first treatise [18 n] that sight perceives nothing among visible things except according to the refracted <term>radial lines</term> <note>original: "verticationes... linearum radialium"; the straight-line paths along which light or visual power is imagined to travel</note>: and that the order of visible things and their parts is not perceived except through the arrangement of these radial lines. It was also stated [27 n 1] that a single visible object, when perceived by two eyes simultaneously, is only perceived as one when its position relative to the two eyes is a similar position; and that if the position is different, then the single object will be perceived as two. However, every ordinary visible thing that is consistently perceived by both eyes is always perceived as one. Hence, it is necessary for us to explain how a single object is perceived by both eyes as one in most instances and in most positions; and how the position of a single object relative to both eyes will be similar in most instances and positions. We shall also explain how the position of a single object relative to both eyes can be a different position, and how this happens. We have already mentioned this in the first treatise [27 n] and explained it generally, but not specifically. Let us say, therefore, that when an observer looks at some visible object, then each eye will be in opposition to that object; and when the observer directs the pupil toward that object, then each eye directs the pupil toward that object with an equal direction. And when the sight is moved over the thing seen, then both eyes will move over it together. And when the sight directs the pupil toward the thing seen, then the **axes** of the two eyes will gather upon that seen thing, and will be joined at some point on its surface. And if the observer moves his sight across that seen thing, then those two axes will move together over the surface of that object and through all its parts.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the geometry of binocular vision. Two circles, labeled 'e' and 'g', represent the eyes. Two straight lines (the optical axes) extend from the centers of these circles and converge at a single vertex 'a' at the top. Below the eyes, a horizontal line represents an object or plane, with 'q' on the far left, 'x' on the far right, and 'z' marked in the center. Vertical lines drop from 'e' and 'g' to intersect this lower horizontal line at points marked by short cross-strokes.</image-desc>

And universally, the two eyes are equal in all their dispositions: and the <term>sensitive power</term> <note>the faculty or ability to perceive sensory input</note> that is in them is the same, and their action and passion <note>in medieval philosophy, "action" is what the eye does, and "passion" is what it receives or undergoes from the light</note> are always equal and entirely similar. And if one eye is moved to see, the other is immediately moved toward that object by that same motion: and if one eye rests, the other rests. It is impossible for one eye to move for the sake of seeing while the other rests, unless it is hindered. And it was declared in the past [19 n 1] that between any visible object and the center of the eye there is an **imaginary pyramid** in the vision, the vertex of which is the center of the eye and the base of which is the surface of the object which the eye perceives; and this pyramid contains all the radial directions from which it perceives that seen thing. Therefore, when the two axes of both eyes are joined at some point on the surface of the object, then the surface of the object is the common base for both radial pyramids formed between the two centers of both eyes and that object: and then the position of the point where the axes are joined is a similar position for both eyes, because it is opposite the two centers of both eyes, and the two axes which are between that point and the two eyes are perpendicular to the surface of the two eyes.

3. *The position of a visible object relative to each eye is usually a similar position. Therefore, the axes of the optical pyramids and the lines drawn from each eye to the meeting point of the two axes—made in a straight line perpendicular to each axis—are equal. 40. 42 p 3.*

Regarding what remains of the surface of the object, between any point on it and the two centers of both eyes, there are two lines whose position relative to the two axes will be a similar position in part: because all pairs of imaginary lines between the two centers of the two eyes and a point on the visible surface where the two axes of the two eyes join will decline from the two axes in the same direction. For every point on the surface of the object where the two axes join will decline from the point of union toward the same side; whereas the point of union itself is upon both axes. Furthermore, the distances of these lines from the two axes are equal: because all pairs of lines proceeding from the two centers of the two eyes to any point among the points very near to the point of union are equally distant from the two axes, as far as the sense can tell. For the two axes proceeding to the point of union will be equal, or there will be no sensible difference between them, provided the object seen is not extremely close to the eye and its distance from the sight is moderate. And the disposition of any point very near to the point of union is similar; that is, all pairs of lines proceeding from the two centers of the two eyes to any such point do not differ in length as far as the sense can tell, but will be almost equal.

**OPTICS, BOOK III.**

### 4. Two straight lines drawn from both eyes to the meeting point of the two axes, formed on a straight line oblique to each axis, are almost unequal. <note>Proposition 41, Book 3</note>

When two declining lines <note>original: "lineae declinantes"; lines of sight that deviate or angle away from the central optical axes</note> are joined on a surface in which the two axes are located, they will be unequal. For the line that exits from the point in which the two axes are joined to a point declining from it forms unequal angles with the two axes; and the two axes are equal in length, and the line coupling the two points is common to both. For this reason, the two declining lines will be unequal. However, this inequality is not perceived by the senses if the declining point is close to the point of conjunction <note>the point where the two optical axes meet</note>. But if the two declining lines are below or above the axes, they can be equal.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram illustrating the principles of binocular vision and optical convergence. At the top are two circles labeled 'e' and 'g', representing the eyes. From the centers of these eyes, several straight lines (representing optical axes and light rays) extend downward toward two parallel horizontal planes. Points on the upper horizontal line are labeled 'b', 'a', 'f', and 'h'. Points on the lower horizontal line are labeled 'c', 'm', 'k', 'n', and 'd'. The intersections of these lines form various triangles and quadrilaterals that model how different points on a surface are perceived by both eyes simultaneously.</image-desc>

For the two angles formed by the two axes with the line continuing the two points can be equal if the point is below or above the axes. And in the positions that exist between these two positions, the difference that exists between the two declining lines will be less than the difference between the first two declining lines; and thus there will be no difference between them that affects the sense. Therefore, the two lines exiting from the two centers of the two eyes to the points near the point where the two axes are joined do not differ much in length as far as the sense can perceive. The axes are equal, and the line that couples the point of conjunction with the declining point—to which the two lines from the two centers exit—is common to the two triangles formed from those lines.

Therefore, the two angles at the two centers of the two eyes, which are subtended <note>opposite to</note> the common line at the surface of the seen object, will be equal; or there is almost no sensible difference between them. These two angles will always be very small when the point is very close to the conjunction of the two axes. And since the two lines that exit to any point near the point of conjunction form equal angles with the two axes, then the distance of any two lines exiting to that same point from the two axes of the two eyes will be an equal distance. Therefore, the position of any point on the seen surface where the two axes of sight are joined—if it is near the point of conjunction—is a similar position <note>original: "positio consimilis"; a key term in Alhazen’s theory meaning the points correspond to the same relative location on each retina</note> in respect to the two eyes, both in direction and in distance from the two axes.

However, the arrangement of points far from the point of conjunction, deviating to one side from both axes, is as follows: the angles between the two lines exiting to any of those points and the two axes perhaps differ by some small amount; and the position of all such points far from the point of conjunction in respect to the two eyes is a similar position in direction only, but not in distance from the two axes. Therefore, the position of any seen point perceived by both eyes, when it is of some size and has nearby diameters <note>extent or dimensions</note>, is a similar position in direction and distance in the view of both eyes. Because of this, its form is established in two places of similar position by the two eyes.

And when the object perceived by both eyes has very large diameters, then the position of that point where the two axes join will be a similar position for both eyes. The closer those two points on the surface of the seen object approach [the center], the more their position for the two eyes will be similar in both direction and distance simultaneously. However, the points on the surface of that seen object that are far from the point of conjunction and deviating from both axes to one side have a similar position in direction for both eyes, but perhaps a similar position in distance, and perhaps not. Therefore, the form of the part that is at the point of conjunction of this seen object—and that which contains the point of conjunction, and that which is near to it—is established in two places of the two eyes in a similar position in all arrangements.

The forms of the remaining parts far from the point of conjunction, surrounding the part of similar position, will be established continuously with the form of the part of similar position; and thus the whole of the two forms is established in two places of the two eyes between which there is no great difference in position. If there is a difference, it will be at the edges only, and it will be slight because of the continuation of the two extremes with the two middle parts, which are of similar position. This occurs when the two eyes are fixed in opposition to the seen object, and the two axes are fixed on one point of it. But when the two eyes are moved over the thing seen, and the two axes are translated from that point and moved together across the surface of the seen object, then the position of any point of that object and the position of points near it—in respect to the two eyes at the conjunction of the two axes upon it—will be a very similar position. The form of any part of the seen object during the motion of the two axes across the surface will be in two places of similar position for the two eyes; and thus the form of all parts of the seen object during motion and intuition will be of a similar arrangement for both eyes.

Also, the form of that which is near to that seen object, if it is of small size, is established...

### 6. *If two straight lines from the middle of the common nerve are bounded by the straight line connecting the centers of the openings of the turn of the hollow nerves: they will form an isosceles triangle.* <note>Proposition 30, Book 3</note>

<image-desc>Geometric diagram located to the right of the following paragraph. At the top are two circles representing eyes, labeled 'n' and 'm'. A horizontal line 'l' sits above them. Lines from the centers of the circles converge at a point 'a'. Below this, horizontal lines are labeled with letters 'b', 'c', 'd', 'h', 'g', 'f', and a bottom line 'r s t'.</image-desc>

It was also declared in the second treatise [1. 42 n] that the radial axis <note>the central optical axis of the eye</note> in each eye is the same line, which is not changed: and that it passes through the centers of all the tunics <note>layers</note> of the eye, and extends straight through the centers of all the tunics to the middle of the place of curvature from the hollow of the nerve <note>the optic nerve</note> upon which the eye is composed, which is at the opening <note>foramen</note> located in the hollow of the bone: and that it is inseparable from all centers: and that its position at all parts of the eye is always the same position, not changeable during the movement of the eye, nor during its rest: and that the position of the two axes in the two eyes is a similar position in respect to both eyes, at the hollow of the common nerve <note>the optic chiasm</note>, from which the ultimate sense <note>the brain or the faculty of perception</note> perceives the forms of visible things. Let us therefore imagine a straight line coupling the two centers of the two openings which are in the two hollows of the two bones containing the two eyes: and let us imagine two lines exiting from the two centers of the two openings, extended in the two middles of the two hollows of the nerves. These lines, therefore, meet in the middle of the hollow of the common nerve: because the position of the two nerves with respect to the common nerve is a similar position [by 4 n 1] and the position of these two lines at the line coupling the two centers of the two openings will be a similar position: because the positions of the two nerves, with respect to the two openings, is a similar position [by 4 n 1] and thus the two angles, which are between these two lines and the line coupling the two centers of the two openings, will be equal [otherwise the position of the nerves would be dissimilar].

For the two axes pass through the centers of the two openings: indeed, they pass through the two midpoints of the cavities of the two nerves, at the place of the <term>convergence<note>original: "pyramidationis"; the point where the visual cone or "pyramid" meets.</note></term> of the two nerves. And the two axes from the location of the centers of the two openings up to the point of joining, which is on the common axis, will be equal; and their position relative to the common axis will be a similar position. Furthermore, the two parts of the two axes that extend from the centers of the two eyes to the point of joining will be equal. The distance of the two centers of the eyes from the openings of the two bones and from the centers of the two openings is an equal distance. And because this is so: the position of the point on the visible surface where the two axes are joined, relative to the two points through which the two axes pass, will be a similar position; and its distance from them will be equal. And the position of any two points on the surfaces of the two eyes—whose position relative to the two central points on the two axes of the two eyes is a similar position in both direction and distance—will be a similar position relative to that same point in the cavity of the common nerve. Their distance from it will be according to their distances from the two axes. Thus, the two forms that are fixed at the two points of similar position on the surfaces of the two eyes will reach that same point in the cavity of the common nerve itself, and they will be superimposed upon it at that point, and they will become one single form. 

And the position of each of the points of the visible surface that are around the point on the common axis is a similar position relative to the two axes of the two eyes. Therefore, the two forms of the visible object, in which the three axes are joined <note>The two optic axes and the common axis</note>, will be fixed in the two centers of the two surfaces of the eyes. And the two forms of the point where the three axes meet will be fixed at the two points on the two axes of the eye surfaces; then the two seen forms will reach the cavity of the common nerve; and the two forms that are at the two points on the two axes will reach the point on the common axis and become one single form. And any two forms that are at two points of similar position from the two eyes will reach the same point among the points surrounding the point on the common axis; and thus the two forms of the entire visible object will be superimposed on each other and become one form, and so one thing will be perceived as one. 

According to this method, therefore, the two forms that are fixed in the two eyes from one visible object—whose position relative to the two eyes is similar—become one form; and thus the perceiver grasps one sight, even though two forms are fixed from it in the two eyes. > 10. *The meeting of the optic axes on the common axis makes vision most certain; outside of it, it is more certain the closer it is to the axis. 44 p 3.*

Having explained this, it is now declared that the form of any perceived object, which is grasped by both eyes and at whose surface point the axes of the two eyes meet, is impressed upon two places on the surfaces of the two eyes, which are the two centers of the surfaces of the two eyes. Then, these two forms proceed from the two eyes to the concavity of the common nerve at the same location, and they are superimposed upon one another, and a single form is produced. The two forms of the point where the two axes meet on the visible object will be impressed on the two points that are on the two axes of the surfaces of the two eyes, and they will go from these two points to the point of the center of the concavity of the common nerve. This happens regardless of whether the point where the two axes meet is on the common axis or outside of it. However, when the visible object is on the common axis, and the two axes meet at a point on it that is on the common axis, then the two forms of that point will be more perfectly identical. For the distances of that point from the two points where the two forms of that point are fixed on the surfaces of the two eyes (which are those points on the axes) will be equal, because the two axes in this arrangement will be equal in length.

Similarly, the forms of any point near that point—whose distances from the two points where its forms are impressed are equal to the senses—will be more identical than the two forms of a visible object that is outside the common axis. For this reason, the form of a visible object on the common axis, when it is fixed in the concavity of the common nerve, will be more **verified** <note>original: "certificata"; meaning clear, certain, or accurately perceived.</note>. But when the visible object is outside the common axis, and the distance is not great, then its two forms, which are impressed in the two eyes, will not differ greatly. Therefore, its forms impressed in the concavity of the common nerve will not be seen as two. However, when the visible object is outside the common axis and is very far from it, even if the axes of the two eyes meet at some point on it, its form will be impressed in the concavity of the common nerve as a single form, and the form of the point where the two axes meet will be impressed at the point of the common center; yet, its form will not be verified, but **doubtful** <note>original: "dubitabilis"; meaning blurry, uncertain, or double.</note>.

Therefore, the form of the point of the visible object where the two axes meet will be impressed, in all arrangements, at the center point of the concavity of the common nerve, whether the point of meeting is on the common axis or outside it; the rest of the form of the visible object will be impressed around that center point. If the visible object is a very small body with narrow diameters, and it is on or near the common axis, then its form will be impressed in the concavity of the common nerve as a single, verified form; the position of any of its points relative to the two eyes is a similar position, as we explained before.

But if the visible object is a large body with wide diameters, even if it is on the common axis, then the form of that part near the place where the two axes join (which surrounds the point of union) will be impressed in the common nerve as a single and verified form, and the form of the remaining parts will be impressed continuously with the form of that part. Because of this, the form of the whole visible object will be impressed as one in all arrangements; however, the form of the extremities, and of those parts far from the point of meeting, will not be verified. This is because for every point far from the point of meeting, two forms are fixed at two points of similar position in respect to both eyes at the limit of similarity; but the form of any point far from the point of meeting is fixed at two points of the two eyes whose position relative to the two eyes is similar in part, and perhaps similar in distance from the two axes, and perhaps not similar in distance from the two axes.

The forms of those things whose distance is not similar will be fixed in the concavity of the common nerve at two points slanted from the center in one direction, and they will be two forms. If the visible object is of a single color, this will have almost no effect on it, because of the similarity of the color and the identity of the form. But if the visible object has diverse colors, or if there is a line, a painting, or subtle details on it, then this lack of similarity affects it. Therefore, the form of the extremities will be doubtful, not verified. When the visible object is a large body and the axes of both eyes are fixed and immobile on some point of it, then its form appears as one, and the place where the axes meet and what is near it will be verified and indubitable. The extremities, however, and those things near them, will not be verified for two reasons: one is that the extremities are perceived by rays far from the axis, and therefore they will not be clearly manifest. The second is that the form of every point is not established in the concavity of the common nerve at a single point, but there are some whose form is established at two points, not one. Thus, when the two axes are moved over all parts of this visible object, then its form will be verified. But if the visible object is outside the common axis and far from it, its form will not be verified. For the position of any point of it relative to both eyes is not a similar position, because of the inequality of the distances of this point from the two points on the surfaces of the eyes where its two forms are established, and from the two axes. *11. An object located between the optical axes—either directly in front of one eye and oblique to the other—is seen as double. 104. 103 p 4.*

And likewise, when both eyes grasp many visible objects at once, and the axes of both eyes converge simultaneously on one of those objects and remain fixed upon it: the remaining objects will be outside the two axes. If the object where the two axes meet is of very small size, then the form of that object in the <term>concavity of the common nerve<note>The optic chiasm, where the optic nerves from both eyes meet.</note></term> will be a single, clear form. If the object is upon the common axis, then its form will be more clearly verified than the form of an object that is outside the common axis, even if the two axes converge upon it.

Regarding the objects grasped by sight in that state which are near the object where the two axes meet: if they are also of very small size, a single form is established in the concavity of the common nerve, in which there will be no great uncertainty, for its form will be near the center. However, of those visible things grasped by sight in this state, whatever is far from the object where the two axes meet: its form is established in the concavity of that nerve as uncertain. In such a case, there will either be two forms interpenetrating each other (because they are in one area, whereby the inequality between their positions in distance will not be great, and thus the two forms will overlap), or the form of certain parts will be double, and the form of others will be single. Thus, the form of such visible objects will be uncertain in all arrangements, due to the diversity of the position of the rays going out to them, and because the rays going out to them will be far from the two axes.

The form of an object oblique to the two axes, and far from the place where the two axes meet, will not be clear as long as it remains far from that meeting point. However, when the two axes are moved and converge upon that object, then its form will be verified. Furthermore, when the two axes of the two eyes converge on a certain object, and these two eyes grasp another object closer to the two eyes than the object where the axes meet—or further away—and it is also between the two axes: then its position relative to the two eyes will be different in direction. For when it is between the two axes, it will be to the right of one axis and to the left of the other. The rays going out to it from one eye will be to the right of the axis, and those going out to it from the other eye will be to the left; thus its position relative to the two eyes will be different in direction. The form of such objects is established in the two eyes in two places of different position; and the two forms established in the two eyes will reach two different places in the concavity of the common nerve, on two different sides of the center. Because of this, they will be two forms and will not be superimposed on one another. Similarly, when an object is on one axis but outside the other, its form will be established in the concavity of the common nerve in two places: one in the center, and the other oblique to the center, and they will not be superimposed. Therefore, according to these modes, the form of visible objects is established in the two eyes and in the concavity of the common nerve.

*12. It is shown by an instrument that an object sometimes appears as one, and sometimes as double. 108 p 4.*

All these things we have said can be tested by an experiment, which will provide confirmation. Let a board of light wood be taken, the length of which is one cubit <note>roughly 18 inches or 45 cm</note> and the width four fingers. Let it be quite flat, even, and smooth. Let the lines of its length be parallel, and those of its width parallel. Let there be two diameters intersecting each other on the board. From their point of intersection, let a straight line be drawn parallel to the two edges of the length [by Euclid, Book 1, Prop 31]. Let there also be drawn from the point of intersection a straight line perpendicular to the first line placed in the middle [by Euclid, Book 1, Prop 11]. Let these lines be colored with bright dyes of different colors so that they appear clearly, but let the two diameters be of a single color.

Let a notch be made in the middle of the width of the board, at the end of the straight line placed in the middle and between the two diameters. This should be a rounded, somewhat tapered <note>original: "pyramidaliter"</note> cavity, so that the bridge of the nose <note>original: "cornu nati"; likely a transcription error for "cornu nasi"</note> can enter it when the board is placed against it, until the two corners of the board almost touch the centers of the surfaces of the two eyes, even if they do not quite touch. Let the board, therefore, be in the figure **a b c d**, the diameters **a d**, **b c**, and the point of intersection **q**. Let the line extended in the middle of the length be **h q z**, and the line cutting this line at right angles be **k q t**. Let the cavity in the middle of the width of the board be that contained by the line **m h n**. One of these objects should be set upright in the middle of the board at point $q$, and it should be fixed to the board so that it cannot be moved from its place; it must stand perfectly upright upon the board. Two other objects should be raised at the ends of the wide line at the two points $k$ and $t$. Thus, the three objects will be in a single <term>alignment<note>original: "uerticatione"; referring to the vertical plane or line of sight.</note></term>.

Once this is done, the experimenter should lift this board and place the <term>concavity<note>A notch or cutout in the board designed to fit the bridge of the nose.</note></term>, which is in the middle of its length, against the bridge of the nose and between the eyes, so that the bridge of the nose enters the concavity and is flush with the board. Next, the experimenter must look at the object placed in the middle of the board and keep his <term>gaze<note>original: "pupillam"; while literally "pupil," in this context it refers to the focused line of sight or the eye's attention.</note></term> fixed firmly upon it. The <term>common axis<note>An imaginary line projecting forward from the midpoint between the two eyes.</note></term>, which we defined earlier, will be superimposed on the line extending through the middle of the board’s length, which is line $h z$.

In this arrangement, the experimenter should observe everything on the surface of the board. He will find that each of the three objects at points $k, q, t$ appears as one. He will also find that the line $k q t$ appears as a single line. However, the line $h z$ extending along the length of the board will appear as *two* lines, intersecting at the object placed in the middle. Similarly, the two diagonal lines, when the experimenter observes them in this state, will appear as four; that is, each of them will appear doubled.

Next, the experimenter should shift his gaze to one of the other objects at points $k$ or $t$, so that the two axes meet at the object placed at the end. Then he should observe the arrangement again: he will find that each of the three objects still appears as one, and the line placed across the width also appears as one. However, he will find that the middle line extending along the length of the board appears as two, and each of the diagonals appears as two.

When the experimenter has understood these lines and the objects placed on the board, he should remove the two objects at points $k$ and $t$ and place them on the longitudinal line $h z$: one at point $l$, which is nearer to the eye, and the other at point $s$, which is beyond the object in the middle. Then he should return the board to its first position and direct his gaze to the object in the middle. He will then find that the two objects appear as four, and slanted away from the middle—two on the right and two on the left. He will see them upon the two lines which are in reality one line in the middle, but appear as two; he will find each pair of these four objects sitting upon one of those two lines.

Similarly, if he removes the two objects from this line and places them upon one of the two diagonals—one partway toward the eye and the other beyond the middle object—he will find those two appear as four, for each of the diagonals will appear double. Therefore, there will appear to be two objects on each of the lines that make up a single diagonal: one toward the eye and the other beyond the middle object.

Likewise, if he places two objects upon both diagonals, one on each diagonal, and places them on the side toward the eyes, he will find those two appear as four: two near and two remote.

Then the experimenter should remove the two objects from the board and place one of them on the edge of the board, beyond point $k$ and very close to it, such as at point $r$. Let the board be returned to its first position, and let him direct his gaze to the middle object; he will then find that the object placed at point $r$ appears as one.

Next, let him remove the object from point $r$ and place it on the edge of the board further beyond point $k$, at a point distant from $k$ such as point $f$. When he directs his gaze to the middle object, he will find that the object at point $f$ appears as two.

The experimenter will find everything we have described when he directs his gaze to the middle object, or to an object placed on the straight transverse line, or to any point on that line, as long as the two visual axes meet at the middle object or at some point on that transverse line.

If, however, the experimenter directs his gaze in that position to an object placed *outside* the transverse line, or to a point located outside that line, so that the two axes meet at some point away from the transverse line: then the object in the middle will be seen as two. If the other objects are at points $k$ and $t$, then each of them will also be seen as two. But as soon as the experimenter directs his gaze back to the middle object, or to any place on the transverse line, the arrangement immediately returns to what it was in the first figure.

Therefore, from point $b$ let the lines $b k, b r, b f$ be drawn. Thus, line $k b$ is greater than line $b t$ <note>original: "per thesin & 19 p 1"; by the hypothesis [of the setup] and Proposition 19 of Book 1 [of Euclid's Elements].</note>, and line $k q$ is equal to $q t$ <note>original: "ex thesi"; from the hypothesis.</note>. Thus, angle $t b q$ is greater than angle $q b k$ <note>original: "per 4 p geometriæ Iordani"; by the 4th Proposition of the Geometry of Jordanus [de Nemore].</note>. In triangle $b t k$, from the angle $t b k$ bounded by the unequal sides $b t$ and $b k$, the straight line $b q$ goes to the middle of the base $t k$; therefore, the angle $q b k$ bounded by that $b q$ and the longer side $b k$ is smaller than the angle $t b q$ bounded by the same $b q$ and the shorter side $b t$. And angle $t b q$ is equal to angle $k a q$ <note>original: "per 8 p 1"; by Proposition 8 of Book 1.</note>...

Therefore, angle $kaq$ is greater than angle $kbq$. Consequently, the distance of line $ak$ from the axis $aq$ is greater than the distance of line $kb$ from the axis $bq$. However, the difference between these two distances is slight, for the difference between the two angles $kaq$ and $kbq$ is small; thus, the individual object located at point $k$ is seen as one by both eyes when the axes meet at the object located at point $q$. The two lines $ak$ and $bk$ are equivalent to the two rays extending to the object at point $k$ when the two axes meet at the object at $q$. Similarly, the condition of the object at point $r$ is understood: since the rays extending to it will be in the <term>alignment<note>original: "uerticatione"; refers to the straight line of sight or orientation.</note></term> of the two lines $ar$ and $br$, it will be seen as one. The two angles $raq$ and $rbq$ do not differ greatly, and angle $kbr$ does not have a perceptible magnitude when point $r$ is very close to point $k$. It will therefore be demonstrated from this arrangement that a visible object—whose position relative to the two axes is the same in terms of direction, and whose rays extending to it from the two eyes do not differ greatly in distance from those axes—will be seen as one by both eyes. However, the angles $faq$ and $fbq$ differ by a very large amount, and the object at point $f$ will be seen as two, because the two axes meet at the object at point $q$. It will therefore be demonstrated from this arrangement that a visible object, for which the position of the rays extending from the two eyes differs by a very large amount in their distance from the two axes, is seen as two—even if its position relative to the two axes is the same in terms of direction. Furthermore, the position of line $hqz$ relative to the axes of the two eyes is different in terms of direction. For the rays extending to the segment $hq$ from the right eye are to the left of axis $aq$, while the rays extending to this same segment from the left eye are to the right of axis $bq$. Conversely, the rays extending to the segment $qz$ from the right eye are to the right of axis $aq$, and the rays extending to it from the left eye are to the left of axis $bq$. Thus, the rays extending to this line have different positions in terms of direction, though the distance from the two axes for any two rays extending to any point on that line from the two eyes is equal. This line, and everything placed upon it (except for the object placed in the center), always appears as two when the two axes meet at the object placed in the center. It has therefore been demonstrated from this arrangement that a visible object whose position relative to the two axes is different in direction always appears as two, even though the distances of the rays extending to it from the two eyes are equal to the two axes. For the distances of any two rays extending from the two eyes to any point on it will be in two different directions. For this reason, the two forms of any point on it will be established at two points in the <term>hollow of the common nerve<note>original: "concauitatis communis nerui"; this refers to the optic chiasm, where the images from both eyes are combined.</note></term> on two different sides of the center. The same applies to the arrangement of both diameters. Since the rays extending to either of them from the eye following it will be from the middle of the eye, near the axis, both below and above the axis, the rays extending to it from the other eye will be slanted away from the other axis. Those from the right eye to the left diameter will be to the left of the axis, and those from the left eye to the right will be to the right of the axis. The forms of these diameters, and all points and objects placed upon them, appear as two (except for the object placed in the middle) when the two axes meet at the central object.

### 13. *A visible object directly opposite the center of one eye but oblique to the other appears double.*

It will therefore be demonstrated from this that a visible object which, in respect to one eye, is opposite its center, but in respect to the other eye is slanted from the center, is seen as two. For the form of the point established in the center of one eye will reach the center <note>referring to the center of the common nerve or visual perception</note>, but the form of the point slanted from the center of the other eye will reach a point other than the center, and slanted from the center, according to the slant of the point on the surface of the eye.

### 14. *A visible object where the optical axes meet, or where rays near them meet, appears as one.*

From this experimentation and exposition, it is clearly demonstrated that a visible object where the two axes meet always appears as one. Furthermore, any visible objects where rays meet that have a similar position in terms of direction—and between which there is no great difference in distance from the two axes—also appear as one. But a visible object where rays of similar direction meet, but which have a very great difference in their distance from the two axes, appears as two. Likewise, a visible object perceived through rays of different directional positions appears as two, even if the distances of the rays extending to it from the two axes are equal. All these things occur while the two axes meet at a single visible object. All ordinary visible objects are opposite both eyes, and both eyes look at each of them. Therefore, the two axes of the two eyes always meet upon them, and the position of the remaining rays that meet at a common point on them is a similar position in terms of direction, and they do not differ in distance from the two axes by a very great difference. For this reason, any of the ordinary visible objects is seen by both eyes as one, and none of these visible objects is seen as two, except rarely. Indeed, no visible object is seen as two unless its arrangement relative to both eyes is different by a very great difference, either in direction, or in distance, or in both. Such a position for a single object relative to the two eyes does not occur with such a great difference except rarely. Therefore, the reason why every ordinary visible object is seen as one by both eyes has been demonstrated by both logic and experiment. Furthermore, when the experimenter removes the individual object from the middle of the board and looks at the center of the intersection in the middle of the board, and then observes the lines drawn on the board, he will find the two diameters appear as four. He will find two of those four are close to each other and two are far apart, and also that all of them intersect each other at the middle point—that is, the point of intersection of the two diameters located on the common axis.
