...each of those remote [diameters] appears more remote from the middle than it is in reality. Then, when the experimenter covers one eye: he will see two diameters, and he will see the space between them as larger than it is in reality, according to its <term>pyramidal projection<note>original: "pyramidationem"; refers to the cone of vision where rays of light form a pyramid with the eye at the apex.</note></term>. That part of it which is wider is the width of the table: and it will appear that the diameter remote from the middle is the diameter that follows the covered eye. From this, it is made clear that the two diameters which appear close together when vision occurs in both eyes are those which are seen by the following eye; and that the two remote diameters are those seen by <term>oblique vision<note>vision occurring through side-rays rather than the central axis.</note></term>. 

The closeness of two out of the four occurs because when the two <term>axes<note>the central lines of sight for each eye.</note></term> meet at an <term>individual object<note>original: "indiuiduo"; a specific point or small test object used in the experiment.</note></term> placed in the middle: then each of the diameters is perceived by the following eye through rays very close to the axis. Because of this, their forms in the concavity of the <term>common nerve<note>original: "communis nerui"; the optic chiasm, where Alhazen believed the visual images from both eyes were united into one.</note></term> will be very close to the center, and their point of intersection will be at that very center; hence they appear close to each other and to the middle. 

The remoteness of two out of the four, however, occurs because each of the diameters is also perceived by the other eye through oblique vision. Therefore, it is perceived through rays remote from the axis; and one is perceived by rays to the right of the axis, and the other by rays to the left of the other axis. Consequently, their forms will be established in the concavity of the common nerve at a distance. For they will be fixed in two opposite parts with respect to the center, and also remote from the center; hence the two diameters have two forms close to each other and two forms remote from each other. 

The reason why the remoteness of each of the distant ones from the middle is perceived as greater than its true remoteness is this: because the distance between the two diameters is perceived by each eye as greater than it is in reality. This becomes apparent when the experimenter covers one eye and looks through the other. The reason why, when the experimenter covers one eye and looks only through the remaining one, he finds the space between the two diameters wider than it is in reality, is because the space between the two diameters is perceived by each eye as being very close to the eye; and everything that is very close to the eye appears larger than it is in reality. The cause of this will be explained later when we speak of <term>deceptions of sight<note>optical illusions.</note></term>. 

From the consideration of the arrangement of the diameters on the table, and the objects placed upon them (not in the middle), it appears that every visible object placed upon the common axis, and perceived by the eye through the radial axis, is perceived in its true place, whether it is perceived by one eye and through one axis of the two eyes, or whether it is perceived by both eyes and both axes. And it is declared that every visible object perceived by one eye and through the radial axis, which is not on the common axis, is perceived in a place closer to the common axis than its true place; and this also follows for those things perceived through the remaining rays besides the axis. Since the eye perceives the visible thing as it is, and the form is established in the concavity of the common nerve in one place—continuous with itself according to the continuity of the visible thing—and since the visible point on the radial axis (when it is not on the common axis) is seen in a place closer to the common axis than its true place, then its remaining points are also seen in a place closer to the common axis than their true place, because they are continuous with the part at the end of the axis. 

And if the axes of the two eyes were to meet at some visible point outside the common axis, this same condition would also follow: namely, that it would be seen in a place closer to the common axis than its true place. But this position rarely happens. For when those axes of the two eyes meet at some visible point, then in most arrangements the common axis will pass through that visible point; and the axes of the two eyes will never meet at any visible point outside the common axis except through strain or some hindrance forcing the sight to do so. And this condition does not appear in ordinary vision. For when this happens in ordinary vision, it will occur in all visions continuous with that vision; hence the position of the visible objects relative to each other will not be changed because of this. And since the position of that visible object in respect to neighboring visible objects has not been changed, then the transformation of its place will not be apparent when it occurs in ordinary vision. Therefore, when this aforementioned path is considered, it will be made clear from that experiment that this follows in all visions in which the axes of the two eyes meet, which are outside the common axis.

The experimenter should also take three small, equal <term>parchment slips<note>original: "schedulas pergameni"; used as test targets for reading.</note></term>: and let him write some word in clear script on one; and on the others let him write that same part, in the same size and the same shape. Let him place one object in the middle of the table, as before; and let him also place another object at point *k*. Then let him attach one slip to the object in the middle of the table, and another at point *k*: and let him ensure its position is the same as the position of the first slip. Let him set the table as he did before, and direct the pupil to the slip that is in the middle of the object: and let him look at it. Then he will perceive the part written upon it with certain comprehension; and he will simultaneously perceive in that arrangement the other slip and the part written on it, but not as clearly defined as the similar part written on the middle slip, even though they are identical in shape, form, and size. 

Then, in this arrangement, the experimenter must take the third slip in the hand following point *k*: and let him place it in the <term>alignment<note>original: "uerticatione"; the line of sight or orientation.</note></term> of the two slips that are on the table, and in the straight line of the extension of the line that is across the width of the table (which is on the surface of the table, as far as the senses can tell), but let it be remote from the table. Let this alignment be called the <term>facial alignment<note>original: "uerticatio facialis."</note></term>. And let the experimenter ensure that the position of the third slip, and the position of the part on it when he places the slip, is similar to the position of the two slips on the table. Then let him fix both eyes on the slip placed in the middle, and direct the pupil toward it: and then indeed he will perceive the third slip, if it is not very far from the table; but he will perceive the form of the part on it as doubtful and not intelligible, and he will not find it as he found the form of the part similar to it in the middle of the table, nor as he found the form of the part at point *k*, while both eyes directed the pupil...

*15. A visible object at the intersection of the optic axes is seen most precisely; outside this point, it is seen more precisely the closer it is to the intersection. 45 p 3.*

It appears, therefore, from this consideration, that the clearest of the <term>facing visible things<note>original: "uisibilium facialium"; objects placed directly in front of the eyes rather than at an angle.</note></term> to the sight—those which are perceived by both eyes—is that which is at the meeting point of the two <term>axes<note>original: "axium"; the central lines of vision for each eye.</note></term>. That which is closer to the meeting of the two axes is clearer than that which is further away; the form of an object distant from the meeting of the two axes is not precise, even though it may be perceived by both eyes. Furthermore, it appears from this consideration that the clearest of facing objects perceived by a single eye is that which is seen through the <term>radial axis<note>original: "axem radialem"; the central ray of the visual cone where vision is sharpest.</note></term>. That which is closer to it is clearer than that which is more remote; and an object distant from the radial axis has a doubtful, unverified form.

*16. A large visible object is not seen entirely and equally at the same time. 48 p 3.*

Furthermore, it appears that the sight does not perceive a visible thing of wide diameter with true comprehension unless it moves the radial axis over all its diameters and all its parts, whether the perception is with both eyes or one. For when the sight is fixed directly opposite a visible object of very large diameter, it will not perceive the whole with true comprehension: but only that which is upon the axis and near it will be seen with certified comprehension. Its remaining parts, specifically those remote from the axis, will be perceived, but not with certainty, even if the object is facing the viewer, and regardless of whether the perception occurs with both eyes or only one.

...will see the writing more obscured than the first. Then, let him also tilt the <term>parchment<note>original: "pergamenum"; here referring to the slip of writing material used in the experiment.</note></term> gradually, so that its center is always at the point of intersection, and let him observe it continuously. He will then find that the writing becomes obscured as the parchment is tilted: and the more the parchment is tilted, the more the writing will be obscured, until the parchment approaches the line extended through the middle of the table’s length. At that point, the writing on the parchment will appear very doubtful, almost unintelligible, and <term>unverified<note>original: "non certificata"; lacking the sharpness required for the eye to be certain of the shapes of the letters.</note></term>. 

Next, the <term>experimenter<note>original: "experimentatorem"; the person conducting these optical tests.</note></term> should return the parchment to its first position and stand it upright along the polished width-wise line, cover one eye, and inspect the parchment with the remaining eye. He will then find the writing clear and legible. Then, let him tilt the parchment as he did before and inspect it with one eye; he will find the writing more obscured than when it was in the <term>facing position<note>original: "oppositionem facialem"; oriented directly toward the observer's face, perpendicular to the line of sight.</note></term>. Then, let him tilt the parchment more and more, little by little, and look at it many times. He will find that the more it is tilted, the more the written part is obscured, until the parchment approaches the diameter that follows the open eye. 

It will therefore be demonstrated from this consideration that the clearest of visible objects located upon the <term>radial axis<note>original: "axem radialem"; the central line of vision extending from the eye to the point of focus.</note></term> is that which directly faces the eye. Furthermore, an object whose position is more directly facing is clearer than one whose position is less so. That which is tilted away from the radial axis at a maximum angle is doubtful and unintelligible, whether the vision is with both eyes or only one. 

Next, the experimenter should return the <term>marker<note>original: "indiuiduum"; a specific object or point used as a visual target.</note></term> that was on the table and place it in the middle of the table, attaching it to the point of intersection as in the first consideration. Then, let him set the parchment upright on the other part of the line placed across the width in a direct facing orientation, and direct the pupil of both eyes toward the marker placed in the middle. In this arrangement, he will perceive the parchment and the writing upon it; however, that which is near the marker in the middle will be clear, while that which is far from it will be doubtful and obscured. The further it is removed from the marker, the more it is obscured. 

Again, the experimenter should tilt the parchment in this state so that it intersects the width-wise line at some point on its other part. Let it be a small tilt, and let him direct his gaze to the marker in the middle; he will then see the writing on the parchment more obscured than when it was facing him. Then, let him tilt the parchment further and direct his gaze to the marker in the middle; he will then see the writing as doubtful, neither clear nor legible. 

Next, the experimenter should cover one eye and look with only one eye. Let him return the parchment to its first position, standing it up on the part of the width-wise line that follows the observing eye, and direct the pupil of that one eye toward the marker in the middle. He will then perceive the writing on the parchment and will see that which is near the marker more clearly than that which is distant; he will see that which is furthest from the marker as doubtful and illegible. Then, let him tilt the parchment so that it intersects the width-wise line at the point where it was standing, and let him inspect the marker in the middle with that same eye. He will then see the writing on the parchment as more doubtful and illegible than when the parchment was facing him. 

Then, let him tilt the parchment more, little by little, and he will see that the more the parchment is tilted, the more the writing will be obscured. It appears, therefore, from this consideration, that an object in a facing position is clearer than one seen at an angle, even if the object is not on the radial axis but outside of it. Indeed, when an object is significantly tilted, it is greatly obscured, even if it is not on the radial axis, whether seen with both eyes or only one. 

Again, the experimenter should remove the marker from the table and stand the parchment at the edge of the table, placing its edge against the end of the table’s width, which is marked **c d**. Let him direct the pupil of both eyes toward the middle of the parchment; he will then find the writing clear and legible. Then, let him tilt the parchment so that it intersects the width of the table at point **z**, which is in the middle of the table's width, and direct the pupil of both eyes to the middle of the parchment. He will then see the writing more obscured than before. 

Then, let him increase the tilt of the parchment little by little; he will see the writing become obscured gradually, so much so that if the tilt of the parchment is maximized, he will see the writing as very obscured in the same way it was when observed in the middle of the table. The same occurs if he observes it in this place with one eye. 

Next, the experimenter should place the marker on point **z** and stand the parchment on the other part of the width at the edge of the table, just as he did in the middle of the table. Let him direct his gaze toward the marker placed in the middle, look at the parchment, and consider the writing. He will see the same condition as he saw when it was in the middle of the table, whether considered with both eyes or one. 

Then the experimenter should also test the small slips of paper mentioned before at the edge of the table. He will see the same condition in them as when they were in the middle: namely, that the part in the middle slip is clearer than the part in the slip removed from the middle. The further the slip is from the middle, the more the part will be obscured. However, he will see that the distance from the center at which the part placed at the edge becomes obscured when the observation is at the edge of the table is proportional to the distance from the center at which the part at the edge becomes obscured when the observation is in the middle of the table. This is because it follows the distance of the rays exiting to the edge from the axis. Therefore, the ratio of the distance at which a form placed at the edge becomes obscured to the form placed in the middle, is the same ratio whether the observation is in the middle of the table or at its edge. Similarly, even if the experimenter removes the table and places the parchment...

...in which there is writing at a greater distance than the length of the table, and where one is still able to read the writing: if it is placed <term>facing the sight<note>original: "faciale uisui"; oriented directly toward the viewer's eyes.</note></term>, and he looks at it; then if he tilts it in its place, he will find the writing becomes obscured. And if he tilts it further, it will be more obscured, so much so that if he tilts it a great deal, until its position is close to the path of the rays extending to its center, then he will see the writing on the <term>parchment<note>original: "pergameno"; the writing surface used in the experiment.</note></term> very hidden—so much so that it cannot be read. He will see this whether it is viewed with both eyes or with only one.

Then, if someone moves the second slip and pulls it away little by little from the slip at which he is directing his pupil, he will find that the more distant the form of the part on the edge of the slip is from the second slip, the more it is obscured, until it becomes entirely illegible. And similarly, if he considers these two slips with only one eye, he will find the same result.

### 17. *A visible object directly facing the sight is seen most certainly; a tilted one less so, in proportion to its tilt. 33 p 4.*

**I**t is therefore declared from all these observations that the most clear of visible things at all distances is that which lies upon the <term>radial axis<note>original: "axem radialem"; the central, straight line of vision from the eye to the object.</note></term>. That which is closer to the axis is clearer than that which is further from it. Furthermore, a visible thing removed from the axis by a great distance has a <term>doubtful form<note>original: "dubitabilis formę"; blurred or uncertain, where the mind cannot quite make out the details.</note></term> and is not <term>verified<note>original: "certificabilis"; cannot be confirmed with precision by the visual sense.</note></term>, regardless of whether the vision is with one eye or both. 

Additionally, a facing object is clearer at all distances than a tilted object. The more the position of the visible thing approaches a facing position, the clearer it will be. A visible thing tilted upon the radial lines with extreme obliquity has a form that is very doubtful and not verified by the sight, whether the vision is with one eye or both, and whether the object is on the axis or off the axis. 

Now, the reason why a very tilted object is of a doubtful form—even though its distance is moderate and its size is perceived as it is—and why a facing object is clearer than a tilted one, is this: because the form of a very tilted object is established on the surface of the eye in a <term>compressed<note>original: "congregata"; literally "gathered together," referring to the optical foreshortening where a surface appears thinner as it is tilted away.</note></term> manner due to its tilt. For when the object is very tilted, the angle which it <term>subtends<note>original: "subtendit"; the angle formed at the eye by the two lines coming from the edges of the object.</note></term> at the center of the eye will be small. The part of the eye where the form is established will be much smaller than the part where it would be established if it were facing the sight. Its small parts are subtended at the eye by angles so tiny they are imperceptible due to the extreme tilt. For when a small part is greatly tilted, the two lines outgoing from the center of the eye to its edges become almost like a single line. 

Therefore, the sensing power does not perceive the angle contained between them, nor the specific part it occupies on the surface of the eye. A very tilted object will be doubtful because its form, impressed in the eye, will be compressed with the greatest density; its small parts will be imperceptible, and therefore its form will be doubtful. For this reason, if there are <term>subtle details<note>original: "subtiles intentiones"; fine features, such as the serifs of letters or small textures.</note></term> in such an object, they will not be grasped by the sight because of the obscurity of its small parts and the compression of the form. 

A facing object, however, is the opposite. Its form, as established in the eye, will be arranged just as it is on the surface of the object. Its small parts, which can be perceived by the eye, will be clear and ordered on the surface of the eye according to their arrangement on the object's surface; thus the form will be clear and not doubtful. Universally, subtle details, small parts, and the arrangement of parts are not perceived with true perception unless the form is impressed upon the surface of the <term>sensing member<note>original: "membri sentientis"; the eye, specifically the retina/uvea in Alhazen's model.</note></term>, and each part is established on a perceptible part of that surface. 

When a visible thing is very tilted, its form is not properly impressed in the sight, nor are the forms of its small parts fixed on the perceptible part of the eye. This only happens when the object is facing the eye, or when its tilt is slight and it is at a moderate distance. 

The perception of the size of a very tilted object, however—as it truly is, provided it is at a moderate distance even if the tilt is extreme—does not come from the form impressed in the eye alone. Rather, it comes from reasoning beyond the form: specifically, the perceiver recognizes the difference in distance between the two ends of the object, while also perceiving the measure of the form. When the sight perceives the difference in distance between the two ends of a very tilted object and notes the great difference between them, the <term>discriminating faculty<note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the cognitive power that interprets visual data to make sense of the world.</note></term> immediately imagines the position of that object. It calculates its size according to the difference in distance of its two ends, the measure of the part of the eye it occupies, and the angle it subtends—not solely from the visual form itself. 

Once the discriminating faculty perceives the difference in the two ends and the degree of tilt, it immediately realizes the compression of the form. It therefore perceives the object's true size by sensing the quantity of its tilt, rather than by the size of the compressed image. Yet, the small parts and subtle details within the object cannot be perceived by reasoning if the sight has not first sensed those parts or details. 

Thus, the obscurity of a form happens because of its compression in the eye and the resulting obscurity of its small parts. The clarity of a form at a moderate distance is due to the impression of the form in the eye as it truly is, allowing the eye to sense its small parts. Therefore, the reason why the form of a very tilted object is doubtful, while the form of a facing object is clear, has been declared. Having explained these things, we must now begin the discussion on the deceptions of sight, explaining their causes and varieties.

# ALHAZEN ON THE CAUSES BY WHICH DECEPTION HAPPENS TO SIGHT. Chapter 3.

### 18. *Eight things are necessary to complete vision: each of which must be <term>proportionate<note>original: "symmetrum"; meaning balanced or fitting in scale.</note></term> to the visible object to avoid <term>visual errors<note>original: "allucinationes"; in this context, it refers to any optical deception or failure to see clearly, rather than modern psychiatric hallucinations.</note></term>. 1. 2. 13. 14. 15. 16. 19. 56 p 3. 1 p 4. See 36 n 1.*

**I**t was declared in the first book [36 n] that in order for the sight to directly comprehend the forms of a visible body, a combination of certain things is necessary, which are: Distance, Facing Position, Light (not too weak), Solidity of the body, its Magnitude, and the Transparency of the intervening air; for if any of these are lacking, there will be no vision. It is also clear from the second book [12. 13. 20 n] that the sight can comprehend nothing from bodies except in time. Time, therefore, is one of the things necessary for vision to occur. Similarly, the infirmity of the eye hinders sight; wherefore Health will be one of the necessities. Furthermore, it has already been explained in the preceding part [15. 17 n] that a body shifted far from the <term>visual axis<note>original: "axe"; the direct line of sight from the center of the pupil to the object.</note></term> is hidden from the sight; and if it is greatly tilted at that time, it will not be fully comprehended. Therefore, Position is necessary for the completion of vision, since full comprehension does not occur except in a determined position.

There are, therefore, eight things necessary for the operation of sight: Distance, Position, Light, Magnitude of the body, Solidity, Transparency of the air, Time, and the Health of the sight. And each of these has a <term>latitude<note>original: "latitudinem"; a range or span within which the factor allows for clear perception.</note></term> proportioned to the thing seen. For example, a certain body is fully comprehended from one distance, but not fully from another; and between those distances is a great latitude in which the full comprehension of that body occurs, which is the latitude of distance with respect to a body of such size; and the larger the body is, the greater the latitude of its distance will be. In the same way, when the tilt of some body is great, the marks or small parts within it are not comprehended; but if a body in which the marks or parts are larger or less minute is seen at that same tilt, they will be comprehended. In a lesser tilt of the first body, its small details will be seen; and there is a latitude between these tilts. Similarly, a small body placed near the axis is seen, but if moved far away, it is hidden; yet at that same distance, a larger body will be seen. It is clear, therefore, that Position has a latitude proportioned to the magnitude of the body and its small details.

It is clear that Light has a latitude: for when the strength of light is great, it obscures the appearance of the body; and likewise its weakness does the same; but the appearance of bodies will be clear in intermediate lights. Furthermore, in a certain light, some parts of a body are comprehended, and in that same light other very minute parts are hidden, which would be seen in a greater light. Therefore, the latitude of light is proportioned to the magnitude of the body. Magnitude of the body also has a latitude: for if the parts of the thing seen are not proportional to the whole, they will be hidden from the sight; but if they are proportional, and the total body is small, they will still be hidden. Hence, in birds and minute animals, we do not perceive some small parts, even though they are proportional to them; but if the visible body is large and its parts are proportional, they will be seen accordingly. Therefore, the latitude of the magnitude of the visible thing is proportioned to the total body of which it is a part.

Solidity, moreover, has a latitude proportioned to the thing seen. For if there is a sharp color in some body, even if it is of little <term>solidity<note>original: "soliditatis"; in Alhazen's optics, this refers to opacity or the quality of being a non-transparent surface that can reflect light.</note></term>, it can be seen; which would not happen if the color were dull while the same solidity remained. Transparency of the air has a latitude. For if air that is slightly dense, such as a flame or smoke, is placed between the sight and some writing, the writing will not be discerned, yet the parchment will still be seen; and so it is in other things of this kind. Therefore, this latitude is proportioned according to the things seen. Time has a latitude. For if someone looks through a hole at a body that passes by instantly, it will not be perceived. Similarly, the motion of a <term>spinning top<note>original: "trochi"; a common mechanical example in medieval optics to show how speed blurs perception.</note></term> (because it is very fast) is not noticed in a very small amount of time. The same happens in a very small motion. Health has a latitude. For in a certain infirmity, the minute parts of a visible body are hidden, but in a lesser one, they are perceived.

And generally, any state in which the form of the thing seen is not verified as it is in truth, is a state that has departed from the <term>moderate range<note>original: "temperantia"; a state of balance or "just right" conditions.</note></term> proportioned to that visible thing. A visible thing’s state departs from the moderate range in distance either because of its greatest excess of distance or its greatest decrease. In Position, the departure from the moderate range occurs through the greatest distance from the axis, through the diversity of the body's position with respect to the two eyes, or through its greatest tilt. In Light, the departure from the moderate range is caused by its greatest strength or too much weakness. In Magnitude, by the diminution of the quantity of the visible thing. In Solidity, by the intensification of transparency. In Air, by its too great thickness. In Time, by its shortest duration. In Health, by the greatest weakness of the sight, or its change according to sickness.

However, the moderate range has a latitude, which will be revealed thus. When some body is seen, and it is moved a little further from the sight or brought closer: as long as it is seen differing from the truth by an imperceptible proportion, it is still within the moderate range; and so it remains until the change of appearance is proportional and sensible. The latitude of the moderate range in any of these is also measured according to its proportion to the other seven, and according to the color and the smallness of the parts of the body. Therefore, the latitude of the moderate range of distance is observed according to the color, and according to the small details which are in the body, and according to the light, and the six other things which have been mentioned. According to the variety of color: since a body of strong and sharp color is perceived from a greater distance than one of a dark and weak color. Hence, the greater latitude of the moderate range of distance is proportioned more to a strong color than to a weak one. Similarly, if there are notable marks in the visible body, they will be comprehended from a greater distance than if they were very small. Hence, there is a greater moderate range of distance with respect to notable parts of the body than with respect to minute ones. In like manner, the moderate range of distance is greater for a body directly facing [the sight] than for...

In the same way, the <term>latitude of balanced distance<note>original: "temperamenti longitudinis latitudo"; the functional range of distance within which an object can be clearly perceived.</note></term> is greater in strong light than in weak light. It is also greater if the body seen is large rather than small. Similarly, a very solid body is perceived from a greater distance than one that is less solid. Thus, the balance of distance is proportioned to the solidity of the body. The balance of distance is also proportioned to the quality of the air: for the thickness of the air hides bodies from the sight at a certain distance, whereas clarity reveals them at that same distance or even a greater one. The balance of distance is also proportioned to the quantity of time. For the motion of a body is perceived at a certain distance in a certain amount of time, and it will be perceived from a greater distance if given more time. Consider these things, adapt them to each case, and you will be able to see it easily: the balance of any of these is likewise proportional to all the others, and you will see what has been said through each individual instance. Therefore, when each of those things which have been listed is within the "latitude" of its balance, the truth of the form of the thing seen will appear just as it is in reality. However, when the form does not appear as it is in truth, either one of the aforementioned conditions has departed from its balance, or several of them have. Therefore, the reason why the sight errs in the comprehension of forms is nothing other than the departure of one or more of the aforementioned conditions from their balanced range. And these were the things to be said on this part.

### ON DISTINGUISHING THE ERRORS OF SIGHT. Chapter 4.

*19. In vision, error occurs either by sight alone, by a preconceived notion, or by reasoning.*

It is plain from the second book <gloss>[ 10 n ]</gloss> that the comprehension of things occurs through sense, knowledge, and <term>reasoning<note>original: "syllogismum"; in medieval optics, this refers to the unconscious mental process of inferring properties (like distance or size) from visual data.</note></term>. When an error happens in those things whose comprehension occurs through sense alone, we know it is an error of sense only. But when someone errs in those things comprehended through knowledge, the error will be in knowledge only. If, however, someone errs in those things comprehended through reasoning, the error will be in reasoning only. The sense acquires only light and color, as has been said <gloss>[ 17 n 2. ]</gloss> Knowledge, however, offers those things which were previously seen and held in the sight—for example, the light of the sun is recognized because it has been seen many times, and a distinction is made between the light of the sun and the moon. And although the comprehension of light happens through sense alone, the distinction of light occurs through knowledge. Similarly, the recognition of shapes occurs through knowledge, such as a triangle, a square, a circle, and other similar things. Likewise the recognition of roughness, smoothness, shadow, beauty, and the like. Through reasoning occurs the comprehension of those things which we explained above, even though the sense does not fully "know" them. Every comprehension of things is contained under one of these three modes; and when an error occurs in the comprehension of forms, it only happens in one of these. 

An error of sense occurs if a body, in which there is a great diversity of particular colors, meets the sight under very weak light—such as a garment decorated with different and tiny colored pictures—it will appear to be of a single color. This will be an error in the sense because the light has departed from its balanced range, while the other conditions have not. In knowledge, an error occurs when a known man is seen at a great distance and is judged to be another person who is also known; thus, seeing a brother from a certain distance, one thinks he sees his father, or something in this manner. This is an error in knowledge due to the departure of distance alone from its balanced range. In reasoning, an error occurs as when, because the clouds are moving, the motion is judged to be the moon's. This error happens from an imbalanced distance. For when the distance of the thing seen is within a balanced range, this does not happen: just as we see a stick fixed in the bottom of the water with the water flowing over it as unmoved even in motion, and we perceive the motion of the passing water. The aforementioned error in the moon's motion occurs when the clouds are many and continuous. The cause of this is: because as was shown above, <gloss>[ 49 n 2 ]</gloss> motion is not comprehended except by observing the approach of something to something else, or its departure. When there are few clouds, we can discern their motion because of the apparent approach or departure of each one relative to a star. But when the sky is covered with clouds, we do not discern their motion because of their continuity; nevertheless, we see the moon now in one part and now in another, from which we conclude that the moon itself is moving with a very rapid motion. In the same way, there will be error through a position that has departed from its balance, and through each of the eight conditions mentioned above in comprehension by sense, by knowledge, and by reasoning.

From the preceding it is clear that comprehension by sense does not occur except for light and color only. Therefore, error does not happen to the sense except in light and color. Nor does it happen through light or color except because of its imbalanced weakness or strength; or because of tiny and...

...the diversity of weak things. And this diversity of colors in weak light reaches the eye as something dark or shadowy; this also occurs in strong light when the substance of the colors is very small. Distance <note>original: "longitudo"</note> induces sensory error when the distance of the body from the sight is moderate, yet there are tiny parts within the body of different colors for which that specific distance is unbalanced <note>original: "intemperata"; outside the range where they can be clearly distinguished</note>. For that body will appear to be of only one color, because the distance is beyond the balanced range <note>original: "extra temperantiam"</note> with respect to the particular parts, even if all other factors remain balanced. This is a sensory error, as the sense of sight is what perceives color. Position <note>original: "situs"</note> causes the sense to err when the slant of the visible body is very great; its tiny particles will be hidden from view. If there is a diversity of colors in those tiny parts, the body will appear as a single uniform color. This error happens because of position alone. The same error occurs from an unbalanced position when the distance of the tiny parts from the visual axis is great. Very weak light causes error, for it hides the particles of a body from the sight and presents a uniform dark color; but if the light were returned to a balanced state, the diversity of colors or the smallness of the parts would not be hidden, since the light alone was positioned outside the balance. This would not appear so if the smallness of the parts did not exceed the balanced range. Solidity is a cause of sensory error if it is weakened, as in crystal; thus, when a colored body is placed behind it, the crystal seems to be affected by that color because its low solidity has strayed from the balance. This would not happen if the crystal were more solid. Sensory error proceeds from the transparency <note>original: "raritas"</note> of the air when a flame comes between the sight and an opposing body; even if the body seen is of a strong color, it will appear dark. In this case, only the transparency of the air has exceeded the balance. Time is a cause of error; for if the sight is directed suddenly toward a body of diverse colors, a single color will appear until the duration of inspection is prolonged—I am speaking of the light under which the body is perceived being not strong. For in weak light, the sight is not immediately transformed by each of the particular colors, as would happen in strong light. Sometimes the sight itself presents an error: for when strong light falls upon the eye, the sight is harmed, and immediately turning toward the color of some body, it perceives it as dark until it remains there a little while and the injury recedes. In the same way, when an infirmity of the eye is present, the truth of the colors will be hidden from the sight. Thus, the error arises solely from the quality of the sight departing from its balanced state. It is clear, therefore, that errors happen to the sight according to any of the aforementioned factors. And these occur in the sense alone, since the perception of colors happens through the sense alone.

### ON THE QUALITIES OF VISUAL DECEPTIONS THAT OCCUR IN KNOWLEDGE AND RECOGNITION. Chapter VI.

*21. Error occurs through an anticipated notion: when an anticipated form is wrongly compared <note>original: "asimilatur"</note> to a visible object because of a lack of proportion <note>original: "asymmetriam"</note> among the individual factors that complete the vision.*

---

<margin>[14. 67 n]</margin>
It was stated in the second book [14. 67 n] that the identification <note>original: "definitio"; the process of recognizing or defining what an object is</note> of a thing is acquired only through knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note>. For identification arises from the similarity or dissimilarity of one thing to another in its common form. It is the role of knowledge to compare a thing present to the sight with a form previously seen and stored in the mind; and from this comparison, the identification of any thing is acquired. Knowledge is divided into knowledge of a universal idea, or an individual one, or both. Every error of knowledge will be an error in one of these, or in both. Therefore, when some thing appears as something else, or as a different species than it truly is, there will be an error in assigning its identification. This error does not happen unless one of the aforementioned conditions is outside its balanced range. An error of knowledge regarding distance occurs if a known man is seen from a great distance; he will perhaps appear to the viewer as someone else he knows. Thus, sometimes a viewer seeing Peter says it is Martin, even though it is established that both are known to him. There is an error in the common form if someone sees a horse from a certain distance and thinks he sees a donkey. There is error in both forms (individual and common) if someone sees a horse known to him from a very great distance and thinks he sees a donkey known to him. In the same way, a triple error occurs with trees: in individuals, in common forms, or in both. Thus, sometimes one almond tree is thought to be another; sometimes from a great distance a pear tree is thought to be an almond tree; sometimes Peter's pear tree is believed to be Martin's almond tree. This same triplicity of error due to distance happens very often with clothes, stones, and other things. Sometimes an unknown thing is seen, and an error in knowledge occurs; for instance, if someone sees a fire far away in the air, he perhaps thinks he is seeing a star. It is clear that every such error falls under "knowledge," since in these cases an identification of the thing seen is assigned which is not truly there. It is also evident that the aforementioned error happens because the distance exceeds the balanced range. For if the distance were reduced to a balance, while the other causes of error remained as they were, the aforementioned error in knowledge would not occur. Position introduces error to knowledge when a body is very far from the visual axis; there will not be a certain perception of the form. Thus, sometimes in this position Peter will be thought to be Martin, or a horse will be thought to be a donkey. In this uncertainty, perhaps truth will be chosen, or perhaps falsehood. Since judgment is uncertain in this state, the choice will be accidental. It happens fur-

It concludes the analysis of sensory and cognitive errors and begins Chapter 7, which focuses on errors in the logical reasoning (syllogism) the mind performs during the act of seeing.</meta>

# BOOK III OF OPTICS

h 4
<meta>catchword: And</meta>

An error occurs from an unbalanced position <note>original: "ex intemperamento situs"</note>: for once the position is restored to a balanced state, the judgment derived from knowledge will not err. In the same way, when a body is at a great slant, its tiny parts cannot be confirmed. This results in errors of shape, color, and size. For perhaps a square appears circular, creating an error in both quantity and color. A departure of light from its balanced range also induces an error of knowledge. Indeed, excessive weakness of light brings about an error of form. This is why errors occur in the twilight regarding animals, clothing, or trees—specifically a triple error: either in the specific individual, in the species, or in both. This would not happen in balanced light. Furthermore, if the light departs from a balanced range proportioned to the sight but is used in an opposite way, the aforementioned error occurs even if the light is not unbalanced in itself. This happens with a certain bird called *aluerach* in Arabic <note>original: "aluerach"; likely referring to a bioluminescent insect or bird, or perhaps a firefly</note>; for it cannot be seen except at night. In its case, the light departs from the balanced range relative to it, but it is perceived at night like a fire; yet during the day, since it is not fully discerned, it might be mistaken for a butterfly (which it resembles). Thus, an error in the definition of a thing occurs from unbalanced light.

Size <note>original: "quantitas"</note> situated outside the balanced range causes knowledge to err. Hence, an ant is sometimes thought to be a grain-fly because of its smallness, and sometimes for the same reason a mustard seed is thought to be watercress. Solidity <note>original: "soliditas"</note> departing from the balanced range causes error, as when a red body is placed against a crystal while the other side of the crystal is facing the sight; the viewer will judge the color of the crystal to be red. This is an error of knowledge, as it concerns the definition of the color. The rarity of the air <note>original: "raritas aeris"; its transparency</note> being too diminished is a cause of error; thus, in its thickness, an error in the definition of a thing occurs. Similarly, if a body is placed between the eye and the object whose rarity is outside the balanced range compared to the balanced rarity of air—such as glass—the color of the opposite body will be judged as a mixture of its own color and the color of the glass. Thus, there is an error in the definition of color. In the same way, if a very thin cloth is placed before the eye and a body is seen behind it, the color of the body will appear mixed.

But a question arises: how can a mixture of colors appear after the cloth is placed there, since the partial colors of the body reach the eye only through the holes of the cloth, and no color reaches the eye from the cloth except from its threads, through which the colors of the body do not pass? The truth of the matter is this: although the partial colors of the body arrive separately and fall onto their own locations, and are not mixed with the colors of the threads (rather, the colors of the threads are separate from them both inside and outside the sight, and no confusion happens there), nevertheless, because the points where the surface color of the body and the color of the thread fall are very close together—with no sensible distance between them—they appear as a single point. Thus, the colors appear there as one mixed color. If, however, the holes in the cloth are large, the truth of both the cloth and the body's color will be discerned without mixture. The more compressed the tightness of the holes, the more truly the mixture will appear. Thus, when a body is seen behind a woolen cloth, the mixture of colors will appear most consistent with the color of the threads. For the holes of woolen cloth are inherently tight, and because they are covered with fibers <note>original: "pilis"; hairs or nap</note>, they are made even tighter.

Similarly, when a performer <note>original: "ioculator"</note> makes wooden puppets move, their shadows appearing to someone looking through a fine linen cloth (as is often done) will look like birds or animals matching the shapes of the puppets. This error in assigning a definition only happens because of the diminution of the air's rarity <note>i.e., the obstruction by the cloth</note>. A duration of time outside the balanced range is also a cause of error in knowledge. For if someone looks through a hole at a body passing with fast motion, they do not fully grasp the form of the body. This results in an error in the individual, the species, or both, as with horses, men, and trees. Similarly, this happens even without a hole, as when someone suddenly sees something that immediately vanishes from sight; they will err in grasping its form. This error stems from time alone.

The sight itself causes error: if the light of the sun descends strongly upon a deep green color or an intense red, the sight is harmed; and when the person then looks at something else, that thing will appear different than it truly is, or of another color, because of the presence of the injury. Many similar errors occur in this way. Likewise, in cases of eye sickness, a horse sometimes appears to be a donkey. This triple error mentioned before occurs in many things. It is clear, then, that there is an error in knowledge from the immoderation of the sight alone. The errors that occur in the sight's knowledge according to the individual causes of visual error are therefore clear.

### ON THE QUALITIES OF VISUAL DECEPTIONS THAT OCCUR IN SYLLOGISM AND REASON. Chapter VII.

->22. An error is made in reasoning <note>original: "syllogismo"</note> because of the lack of proportion <note>original: "asymmetriam"</note> of the individual factors that complete vision.<-

Most of those things grasped by sight are acquired through reasoning <note>original: "syllogismo"</note>, as was shown in the preceding book; and there has already been an explanation of those things grasped through reasoning, and how from these, a composition of individual forms occurs to the sense. When, therefore, an error happens in any of those factors, there will be an error in the comprehension made through reasoning. Now, the division of error in reasoning is two-fold: it will be either in the propositions <note>the premises of the mental "calculation"</note> or in their gathering <note>the logical connection</note>. In the propositions, it is three-fold: either a false one is taken for a true one, or a particular one for a universal one, or an error is made in the comparison of propositions. For example: if there are parts in a visible thing that appear and parts that are hidden, which are nonetheless perceivable by sight, if the sight fixes its intention upon it while those parts precede the viewer, the viewer concludes only from those parts he acquires in the visible thing. Even when he considers some conclusions that happen to that thing, he judges them to happen to it based only on the visible parts, since he does not account for any others. But when he fixes a diligent gaze upon the visible thing, he perceives the parts previously hidden and recognizes the error. I will therefore enumerate the errors of those things which the sight grasps through reasoning, which are twenty-two in number, so that the errors in reasoning may be made clear.

This page begins a detailed list of how excessive distance (longitudo) distorts our perception of an object's distance, position, solidity, shape, and size.</meta>

->ALHAZEN<-

And this shall be the enumeration according to each of the eight causes previously mentioned, and first according to distance.

### 23. *Immoderate distance creates errors in individual visual forms. Regarding remoteness. 16 p 4.*

I say, therefore, that distance exceeding the balanced range <note>original: "temperamento"; referring to the "just right" conditions for sight</note> causes the viewer to err regarding distance: just as happens when someone looks at very remote trees; although they are far apart from one another, they will nevertheless seem almost joined, or at least be judged close to each other. For the same reason, it happens that stars are sometimes thought to be almost joined, even though in truth they are very far apart. Because of this, the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> are judged by men to be on the same surface as the fixed stars, even though they are very far removed from them. There is, therefore, an error in distance because the distance has exceeded the balanced range. And this is an error in logical deduction <note>original: "syllogismo"; Alhazen uses this term to describe the mind's unconscious reasoning process during sight</note>, since the comprehension of distance occurs only through such deduction.

### 24. *Regarding position. 44.59.61.62.97 p 4.*

Distance outside the balanced range induces an error of position: for at such a distance, a slanted body will appear straight; and because of this, a square body slanted at this distance will appear oblong. In the same way, a circular form will appear oblong <note>i.e., elliptical</note> when slanted at this distance. Nor does this error happen except from the hiding of the slant, which is concealed at such a great distance. For if the slant were apparent, there would be no reason why the truth of the body’s form would be hidden. Therefore, there is an error in position alone due to the immoderation of distance. And this is the reason why the position is unknown: the excess of one of the rays falling on the side of the square over the length of the other ray is not proportional compared to the total removal of the body from the sight—I mean a sensible <note>perceptible</note> proportion; hence, because the difference is imperceptible, one ray is not judged to be any longer than the other. Indeed, the form of a square is thought to be oblong because its one side, not being slanted with respect to the sight, falls upon a part of the eye, and the form of the slanted side falls upon a smaller part, since it is under a smaller angle. And the perception of this kind of smallness will be according to the degree of the square's slant. And since the slant is not noticed, one side will be judged larger than the other because it is under a larger angle. Consequently, the shape will appear oblong. For the same reason, in a circular form, one diameter appears larger than the other; hence it is thought to be oblong. And this error is from the imbalance of distance; it would not happen if the distance were balanced. If, however, the distance—though unbalanced—is not very great, but the slant of that body is sharp, the viewer will perhaps perceive the slant, but not the truth of the slant; rather, he will judge it to be less than it is, and compare the slant of the side with the angle under which it is perceived; hence the quantity of it will appear smaller than it is, and thus the shape of the square will still be thought oblong, but less so than before.

### 25. *Regarding solidity and shape. 98.97.95.50.65 p 4.*

An excess of distance generates an error of three-dimensionality <note>original: "corporeitatis"; literally "bodiness" or solidity</note>. Three-dimensionality, however, comes from the arrangement of the visual form, and the knowledge of three-dimensionality is grasped from the knowledge of this kind of arrangement. When, therefore, an error occurs in three-dimensionality, it will be in the arrangement of the form or forms; for example, if the form of a curved body appears flat from a certain distance, or a flat one is judged to be curved. And this appearance will be in the shape. Shape is therefore the arrangement of the forms of a body. The arrangement of forms also receives its position; hence three-dimensionality is included under shape and position; thus an error of position and shape carries within it an error of three-dimensionality. Moreover, an error of shape happens without an error of position due to the immoderation of distance. For example, a shape of many equal sides <note>A polygon</note>, directly opposite the sight at an unbalanced distance, appears circular; for no other reason, indeed, than that the angles of the shape are imperceptible to the sight. For that distance hides from the sight parts that are proportional to the whole, even if it does not hide the whole. By the same logic of error, a curved line is judged straight from this distance. For the greater closeness of one part of the curved line to the sight over the closeness of a more remote part of the same line is not perceptible; because the curving of the parts is hidden, even though no error occurs in the position of that line. Similarly, a sphere seen from this distance will be judged as a flat form. Because the closeness of its bulge <note>original: "tumor"</note> exceeds the closeness of the edges by an amount imperceptible from this distance; hence the closeness of the parts is judged equal, and thus the form appears flat. This is why the sun and moon are thought to be flat surfaces by those watching; which erroneous perception of shape would be excluded if the distance were balanced.

### 26. *Regarding size. 28 p 4.*

There will be an error in the size of a body from unbalanced distance: because it will seem much smaller than it is in truth. And the reason for this thing is: because, as we have said, unbalanced distance is that which hides from the sight parts that are proportional to the whole, even by a perceptible proportion. And when there is a hiding of parts perceptible to the sense, the angles into which they fall will not be felt, even though they are proportional to the total angle. Hence, when the visual axis <term>The central line of sight from the eye to the object</term> scans the thing seen, many lines and many parts of it are hidden from it. Therefore, the total appearance is made smaller. Furthermore, the size of a part of any body is not considered except according to the size of the angle into which it falls; and the size of the angle is observed according to the part cut in the sight <note>The image projected on the eye</note>; and the quantity of the cut part is judged according to the two terminal points of that part; and those points are perceptible and proportional to the cut part. Since from such a distance the thing seen is judged according to boundaries proportional to the whole thing seen—for otherwise those boundaries would not be perceptible—and the boundaries of the cut part are directly opposite the proportional boundaries of the part seen. Therefore, those terminal points of the cut part hide the perceptible parts of the thing seen. When, therefore, the axis proceeds over the individual parts of the thing, perceptible parts are hidden from the individual parts; and so the whole quantity of the thing appears smaller. However, when a body is seen from a balanced distance, the terminal points of the cut part are very small, and almost imperceptible compared to it...

compared to the object itself. For in a balanced distance, the viewer's judgment selects boundaries for the visible things that are not imperceptible; hence, the parts proportional to the whole are not hidden. For this reason, the body does not appear smaller than its true reality. Furthermore, as was said previously <note>original: "38 n 2"; a cross-reference to an earlier proposition</note>, magnitude is not grasped in a body except from the comparison of its distance <term>length<gloss>longitudo; in this context, the distance from the eye to the object</term> and the visual angle. It has already been stated that from immoderate distance, the angle appears smaller because it is smaller in truth.

But there is no clear discernment of the remoteness. It has already been shown above <note>original: "39 n 2"</note> that moderate remoteness is perceived through intervening bodies, but immoderate remoteness is not. Therefore, since the remoteness of the visible thing is unknown, the mind perhaps compares it to a known distance and estimates it to be less than it is. Consequently, it is thought to be smaller due to both the smallness of the angle and the estimation of distance being less than the reality; this is the source of error regarding the size of the body. And the more the distance is increased, the more the error prevails. Indeed, the distance can be increased so much that the size of the body is estimated as almost a single point. If the distance increases further, that body will be hidden from sight.

In a similar way, the hiding of a body happens at a balanced distance, not because of the remoteness itself, but from the weakness of the body’s color. It is clear that hiding occurs due to weak color, because if a body of the same size but with a strong color were placed in the same spot at that same distance, it would not escape the sight like the body with weak color did. Therefore, sometimes it is not distance or diminished size that hides a body from view, but the weakness of color alone.

Furthermore, the hiding of a body sometimes happens because its color is similar to the color of the bodies positioned between it and the eye; and this happens even at a balanced distance. Thus, a white body placed at a distance is not discerned when snow has fallen over the surface of the intervening ground, but it is perceived once the snow is removed. It is obvious that the hiding was due to this identity of colors. For if a body of equal size but a different color were placed before the sight at the same distance, it would not be hidden. Therefore, when any object placed before the sight is not perceived, the cause of the hiding could be the excess of distance—which directs a form to the eye that is imperceptible or nearly a point—or, if the form does fall upon a perceptible part of the sight, it might still bypass the vision either because of the faintness of the color or the similarity of color between the visible thing and the intervening bodies.

Furthermore, an error in the size of a visible thing occurs even at a balanced distance. For when a body is at a moderate distance and is seen, its minute parts will be hidden from view—parts which appear at a shorter distance, though perhaps not fully, and as they are moved a little further away again, they are seen even less fully. The fullness of comprehension is diminished as the increase in remoteness grows stronger, until the hiding of the parts occurs, even though that distance does not exceed the "balanced" range. Again, at an immoderate distance, some part is fully grasped while some of its smallest parts are hidden. This is because the distance has exceeded the balance proportioned to those parts, even if it has not exceeded it with respect to the whole body or the grasped part. And although this distance may be known to the person, an error still occurs in the comprehension of the size of the parts; this is because of the angle under which the part is grasped, the capacity of which is estimated to be smaller than the truth. The cause of it appearing smaller is that the terminal points of the cut-off part hide a portion of the sight and constrict the capacity of the angle.

Therefore, when the distance of a visible thing is immoderate, an error in its size arises in two ways: from the smallness of the angle and from the uncertainty of the distance. At a balanced distance, however, there will be an error in the size of minute parts due only to the error of the angle. These are the reasons why a body is estimated as smaller than it is at a balanced distance.

Sometimes, an immoderate distance induces an error of greatness <note>Thinking an object is larger than it actually is</note>. Thus, at an immoderate distance—specifically a minimum distance, when the visible body is very close to the eye—the body will seem to be of a larger size than at a balanced distance, or than it is in truth; and this is for a twofold reason. For, as was said <note>original: "38 n 2"</note>, the intellect considers the distance and the angle, and from these it <term>deduces<gloss>syllogizat; Alhazen’s term for the mind's rapid, unconscious reasoning</term> the size of the body. At this closeness, the angle of the <term>visual pyramid<gloss>the cone of light rays extending from the object to the eye</term> is very large; and the distance of the body is only estimated from the surface of the eye to the surface of the body. For the distance penetrating into the interior of the eye from the visible body cannot fall into the eye’s estimation, since its interior part is not subject to the rays, nor can it be measured by the sight.

The sight, therefore, deduces the size from the capacity of the angle and the total distance. However, the true remoteness of the body is measured according to a line proceeding from the center of the eye to the body, since the consideration of the angle is made with respect to that center. At a balanced distance from the body, the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> of the eye—by which the true distance of the body exceeds the apparent distance—is imperceptible compared to the total distance of the body. Hence, it does not cause an error in the estimation of distance. But when the body is right next to the eye, the magnitude of the radius will be proportional to the distance of the body in a perceptible ratio. For it will sometimes be larger, sometimes equal, sometimes smaller, but in a significant proportion, such as half or something similar. Thus, in the proximity of a visible thing, the excess of the pyramidal angle and the perceptible smallness of the estimated distance relative to the true distance lead to the appearance of greatness in the body.

->*27. On division, continuity, and number. [See 109 p 4]*<-

An immoderate extension of remoteness introduces an error of distinction. For if a wall is seen from afar, and there is a dark color on a part of it, the viewer will believe that color to be a separation between parts; thus, what is continuous will be judged as discrete because of this error. Similarly, if tall grass grows near that wall, a distinction of parts will perhaps be seen where a part was hidden from view by the grass; hence the wall will not be considered a continuous thing. In the same way, when the sun's light falls on a wall and is not very strong, if some body casts a shadow that falls on the wall, the same error regarding the separation of parts without an interval will occur. It is clear, therefore, that the error of distinction in the <term>deduction<gloss>syllogismo</term> arises from the immoderation of remoteness. A distance that has gone beyond the balanced range is the cause of an error of continuity. For bodies seen from afar that are similar to each other in color are believed to be continuous when they are actually just near each other.

Having previously discussed size and continuity, he now examines how distance distorts our perception of movement, texture, and transparency.</meta>

ALHAZEN

From this it happens that the boards of a wall or a bench sometimes appear continuous, even though they are divided from one another by a small—I say—distinction. And this also happens in the immoderate distance of the thing seen; that is, a distance so great that the perception of such a small distinction is lost. And so, from this error of distance, that which is discrete is believed to be continuous. And since the perception of number depends on the observation of continuity and discretion, an error in number occurs: either unity appears in things that are separate, or a plurality is imagined in a single thing.

### 28. Regarding motion and rest. <note>original: "138 p 4"</note>

When the distance departs from a moderate range, it creates an error in [perceiving] motion. If someone moves toward the direction in which they see the moon, the sun, or some star, even after much movement, they see the moon just as far ahead as it was at the start of their journey. They conclude that the moon itself is moving in the same direction and receding from them, and that this is why the distance remains the same. This error happens even if the moon is actually hurrying in the opposite direction. The reason for this error is this: it is known to the viewer that among objects here on earth, if two bodies are positioned so that one moves in a certain direction, if the spatial relationship <term>site<gloss>situs; the relative position or posture</term> of one remains the same in respect to the other, then the second must be moving in the same direction and at an equal speed. But one should not assume this about the moon and stars. Since the viewer cannot perceive the change in position of the person moving relative to the star, the mind secretly draws a logical conclusion <term>syllogistically<gloss>syllogistice; using a formal logical argument</term> based on premises long known to it: that there is motion, while the actual change in the viewer’s position relative to the star remains hidden. Because the path a person covers by their own movement is not proportional to the vastness of the star, the tiny increase in closeness to the star is not sensible at such a distance. The same error occurs with the movement of clouds; for the movement of the moon is believed to be very fast [when clouds pass it], even though it is not, as we explained above <note>original: "19 n"</note>.

A departure from a balanced distance also causes an error regarding rest. If someone seen from far away moves with a slow motion, they will be thought to be standing still. This is why we believe the "wandering stars" <note>the planets</note> are motionless, even though they possess great speed. This is the common estimation regarding the stars: because the paths they travel, even over a long time, are not perceivable to the sight from such a great distance. Therefore, as their position relative to the viewer remains seemingly the same, they are judged to be at rest. In the same way, if a body at a distance moves directly along the line of sight—approaching the eye or receding from it—it will be thought motionless unless its motion is very forceful. This error occurs because, as shown above <note>original: "49 n 2"</note>, motion is only perceived in a body when it is seen first with one object and then with another. Here, this perception is excluded because the path the moving object travels along the visual rays is imperceptible from such a great distance.

### 29. Regarding roughness and smoothness. <note>original: "141 p 4"</note>

Excessive distance creates an error of roughness <term>asperitas<gloss>roughness or texture</term>. This is why, in the hair of a painted image seen from an immoderate distance, roughness is perceived when the painting is finely detailed. Because it is known that roughness exists in real hair, the mind concludes it is similarly present in the painting because of the detail of the form. The same error occurs in painted garments and the fur of animals that are expressively depicted. In all these cases there is no roughness, but rather an extreme smoothness. And although light reflects off smooth bodies but not off rough ones, light is sometimes seen reflecting in a painting, yet this does not exclude the opinion of roughness. This is because the observer is certain that sometimes roughness and reflection occur together in the same body—as happens in a person's hair that is very black and well-washed; for light is reflected in it, even though it is rough. Thus, from this similarity, an error occurs in estimating the roughness of a painting due to an immoderate distance relative to the painted body. Smoothness cannot be perceived in a painting unless the view is very clear. Thus, distance, compared to the moderation of other things, is ill-suited for perceiving smoothness.

An error in [perceiving] smoothness also happens from excessive distance. If a body with a slight roughness is placed before the sight from a great distance, it will be thought smooth. For roughness is only perceived in a body from the diversity of the positions of its parts—either those standing out in the light or those depressed in shadow, as explained above <note>original: "53 n 2"</note>. From such a distance, the difference in position between the raised and lowered parts, or the casting of shadows, is not perceived. Therefore, it is judged to be smooth.

### 30. Regarding thinness and density. <note>original: "144 p 4"</note>

From an immoderate distance <note>in this case, being too close</note> arises an error of thinness <term>raritas<gloss>rarity; here meaning thinness, transparency, or lack of density</term>. When a needle or something very thin is held up near the eye, although it appears larger to the sight than it truly is, it nonetheless hides nothing of the opposite wall or any other body behind it. Therefore, since the perception of thinness in a body arises because we can see something behind it, a needle held up (or something similar) will be judged to have "thinness" because the whole wall can be seen behind it. Why the needle appears larger when placed near the eye is clear from what was said above. But why, at such closeness, it hides nothing of the opposite wall is because such a small distance, relative to the needle's ability to hide things, is immoderate. If that needle is moved just a little further from the eye, it will hide a part of the wall larger than the needle itself. The cause of this will be more fully explained.

From an overabundance of distance, an error of solidity occurs. If someone looks at a "thin" <note>transparent or perforated</note> body from far away, and a colored or dark body is placed behind it, that body will not be thought thin, but solid. This is an error: because the viewer does not perceive anything behind that body, and since the nature of a thin thing is that a solid thing can be seen through it, the mind concludes the body is not thin, but solid.

### 31. Regarding shadow and darkness. <note>original: "147 p 4"</note>
