It is clear that this error happens because of too much distance. Because of excessive distance, the error of darkness creeps in. For if a white body is seen from afar, in which there is a large black part, darkness will perhaps be perceived in that part; from this, the conclusion is made that there is a hole in that body directly in that part, through which the darkness existing behind that body appears to come out.

### 32. Regarding beauty and deformity. <note>original: "150 p 4"</note>

Distance exceeding the moderate range is the cause of error regarding beauty and ugliness. For when something is looked at from far away, if there are small spots on it that make it ugly, because they are hidden by the distance, it is judged to be beautiful; for a conclusion is made only from what is visible, and the spots are hidden while the beautiful parts appear. Similarly, if a thing is seen from such a distance that there are pictures on it—but small ones that give beauty to the whole—since the causes of the beauty are hidden from sight, that thing will be judged ugly, since the judge <note>the mind or the visual faculty</note> takes their judgment only from what is apparent.

### 33. Regarding similarity and dissimilarity. <note>original: "153 p 4"</note>

From excessive distance, errors happen in the similarity and dissimilarity of bodies. For if the sight is directed at bodies far away that are similar in color, even if there are small marks or lines on them that are unlike and different from each other, when these escape the sight, the bodies will be judged entirely similar. Conversely, if there is a difference in the overall colors of the bodies, but there are small marks on them that are similar, they will be judged entirely dissimilar. And an error will occur: because the conclusion is made only from what is apparent.

### 34. Immoderate position creates errors in every visible type. Regarding distance. <note>original: "16 p 4"</note>

Position that goes beyond the moderate range <term>site<gloss>situs; the relative position or posture of an object relative to the eye</term> induces error in any of those things which are perceived through a <term>syllogism<gloss>syllogismus; a logical deduction where the mind reaches a conclusion based on visual premises</term>. Regarding length: as when two bodies are seen, one of which is directly behind the other so that one covers a part of the other, and a part of the rear one stands out—and this happens at a moderate distance, though not very certain, nor are there other bodies between them: the measure of the distance of one to the other will not be fully estimated. This is an error in the syllogism, since the distance is perceived only through a syllogism; but it is due to the position because, if one did not hide part of the other but both were exposed entirely to the sight—so that the path between them fell upon different rays, not the same one—the distance of one from the other would be discerned. And this error is from the lack of moderation in position alone; for when the position is restored to moderation (the other parts remaining unchanged), such an error does not happen.

### 35. Regarding position. <note>original: "44 p 4"</note>

A position outside the moderate range brings error to [perceiving] position itself. For when the <term>visual axis<gloss>axis uisualis; the central, most direct line of sight</term> falls on a body at a moderate distance opposite the sight, and another body is taken that is very far from the axis and tilted slightly over the <term>conceptual line<gloss>linea intellectualis; an imaginary geometric line used to calculate angles</term> upon which the axis falls perpendicularly: the viewer will not perceive the tilt of that body because the position has gone outside the moderate range. For there is no full perception of bodies placed far from the axis <note>as per section 15</note>. And in this error, the sight will judge what is tilted to be straight.

### 36. Regarding shape. <note>original: "97. 96. 61. 62 p 4"</note>

There is an error in shape through position. For if a circular body, like a cup or a small dish, is far from the axis and tilted slightly over the conceptual line we mentioned: its tilt will be hidden, and one of its diameters will be perceived under a larger angle than the other. For the one that appears straight corresponds to a larger angle than the tilted one. And because the difference of one angle over the other is notable, the straight diameter is judged larger than the tilted one; thus the circular shape of the body will be judged oblong. By a similar error, a square shape will be thought oblong when its side directly opposite the eye appears larger than the tilted side. And this is an error in the syllogism. For it puts forward propositions in which there is falsehood, namely: that neither of the sides is tilted; and that things seen from the same distance under the same and unequal angles are unequal; and that a form whose one side is unequal to the other is oblong. From this, an error is concluded, not the truth of the shape.

### 37. Regarding size. <note>original: "28 p 4"</note>

From the same cause, it is clear that there is an error in quantity when one circular diameter of a body appears larger than another diameter of the same body to which it is equal. Further, an error in size happens in another way from immoderate position alone: when someone placed high up looks down from that height at people walking who are equal to each other, arranged in a line one after the other. The ray falling on the first will undoubtedly be lower than the ray falling on the second; and as the distance of any of them from the first increases, the height of the ray falling on them will be greater. Therefore, the ray falling on the last one will be higher than on any other. Thus, the last one will be judged by the viewer to be the largest of all. I say this happens if the space of ground between any two is hidden from the sight, so that the measure of the height of the men cannot be perceived in comparison to the visible ground. There will be an error in the syllogism: because it errs in the premises, one of which is: "Whatever things appear higher in the field of vision are larger"—and this is not found in all things, but in most. And it is an error from immoderation of position, in respect to the perception of the size of a thing so arranged. For if the ray falling on the first were parallel to the ground, and the same ray fell on every other in its path, this error would have no place.

<summary>Alhazen explains how extreme distance and poor viewing angles cause the mind to make logical errors when judging beauty, shape, and size. He describes how tilted circles look like ovals and how people in a line can appear taller than they are if the ground between them is hidden.</summary>

While the previous page focused on errors caused by extreme distance, this section examines how the "position" (the angle and placement of an object relative to the eye) and "immoderate light" (too much or too little) lead the mind to make false deductions about what it sees.</meta>

ALHAZEN

### 38. On division, continuity, and number. <note>original: "109 p 4"</note>

In the perception of boundaries, error arises from an extreme position: for if an object is tilted at a great angle relative to the visual rays, and there are visible black or very dark spots on it, they will perhaps be thought to be holes. Thus, a division will be judged to exist between the parts near this darkness, even though there is a unified continuity there. If, however, there are visible dark lines on this body, they will be judged to be borders dividing it, even though they are continuous. Thus, the error happens because of the tilt of the body. In the case of continuity, an error will arise from position: if several walls are placed before the sight, one arranged behind the other with a small distance between them, and they all fall upon the same visual ray, the space between them will perhaps be hidden from the viewer. For this reason, they will be thought to be continuous when they are actually divided. This would not happen if the position of the walls were changed so that they were not perceived under the same ray. Error is introduced in number by an immoderate position when a single body is seen as two: and this happens when the position of the body is different with respect to the two eyes. In the same way, a plurality is judged in a single body when the object seen falls between the two visual axes, as was shown above <note>original: "11 n." — a reference to a previous proposition on double vision</note>. This is an error in mental reasoning <note>original: "syllogismo" — Alhazen uses this to describe the brain's logical processing of visual data</note>: for the viewer assumes there are different bodies seen externally when the visual form falls upon different locations within the eyes. From this, the mind concludes there is a difference where there is actually identity.

### 39. On motion and rest. <note>original: "138 p 4"</note>

In the case of motion, error arises from position, as when someone looking from a boat running in a river sees trees on the riverbank that are far from the visual axis; they will be thought to move. But if the axes are directed straight at them, they will be seen as motionless. In the case of rest, error suggests itself through position: when a thing is seen, such as a wheel, which is turning with a very fast motion but is far from the visual axis, it will appear motionless. It is clear that the error is due to position, because if the position is changed, its motion will be perceived; thus the error is from the immoderate position alone.

### 40. On roughness and smoothness. <note>original: "141 p 4"</note>

In the case of roughness, position causes error. For if light is reflected from finely painted hair, and the eye is not in the place of reflection, a perception of roughness will occur in them, even though there is only smoothness. The error is from position alone: for when the sight is fixed under the reflected light, roughness is not perceived in the body being seen. In the case of smoothness, error will arise from position: when something is far from the visual axis and there is a small amount of roughness in it, it will appear smooth; yet the viewer could perceive its roughness if the position were brought back to a moderate state.

### 41. On transparency and solidity. <note>original: "144 p 4"</note>

In transparency <note>original: "raritate" — literally 'thinness' or 'rarefaction'</note> and solidity, error happens from an immoderate position. For if a tilted light descends into a glass full of wine, and the passage of the light through the glass is hidden from the sight, and there is a great tilt of that light away from the incoming rays, and it is hidden from the viewer that there is wine in the glass vessel, the viewer will estimate the wine to be a solid body, unified with the vessel. This error does not happen when the passage of light through the glass vessel is obvious. Thus, the error in position regarding transparency and solidity.

### 42. On shadow and darkness. <note>original: "147 p 4"</note>

Regarding shadow and darkness: when a body is far from the axis, if there is a dark part in it, it will perhaps be thought to be a shadow; and if some other body is placed around it, the shadow will be estimated to proceed from that body. If, however, there is a very black part in that body, a hole will perhaps be estimated in the place of the blackness, through which the darkness comes out. This would not happen in a body placed in a moderate position.

### 43. On beauty and deformity. <note>original: "150 p 4"</note>

In the case of beauty and deformity, error happens from position: when a body is remote from the visual axis and there are many tiny spots on it that disfigure it, they will be hidden, and beauty will be judged in the body. For this reason, a freckled face <note>original: "facies lentiginosa"</note> seems beautiful in this position. Similarly, in this slanted position, the spots adhering to the moon are hidden from the viewer; thus, beauty is attributed to the moon when inspected in this way. If, however, there are pictures on the body being seen that give it beauty, and the body is not beautiful except because of their presence, since they themselves are hidden from the sight in this state, the body will be judged deformed. And this is an error in mental reasoning, because the conclusion of deformity or beauty is made only through appearances.

### 44. On similarity and dissimilarity. <note>original: "153 p 4"</note>

In the case of similarity and dissimilarity, error arises from position. For if two things agreeing in shape, appearance, and color are placed far from the axis, but there are small and dissimilar marks on them, an all-encompassing similarity will be judged in them, since those marks are unknown to the viewer. If, however, there is a difference between them in appearance, shape, and color, but there are similar marks on them, they will be thought entirely dissimilar, even though there is some similarity between them. Thus is the error in similarity and dissimilarity, on account of a conclusion made only from appearing things. And in all the aforementioned cases, error is produced from the immoderate position alone: for when it is placed within a moderate range, with other things remaining as they are, the erroneous estimation does not happen.

### 45. Immoderate light creates errors in each visible species. On distance. <note>original: "161 p 4"</note>

Light departs from the boundaries of moderation, and for this reason alone, in all things whose perception is acquired through mental reasoning, error is produced in length <note>distance</note> because of the smallness of the light. For if an arrangement of people is made at a moderate distance that is not very certain, so that one is behind the other, and the sight is applied to this arrangement at night: they will seem to cling to each other, and the distance between them is unperceived because of the weakness of the light.

<summary>Alhazen explains how the angle of view (position) and the intensity of light lead the mind to misinterpret physical qualities like continuity, motion, and beauty. He famously notes that a freckled face or the moon's surface can appear clear and beautiful simply because the observer's position hides small imperfections.</summary>
<keywords>visual axis, double vision, optical illusions, perception of motion, transparency, freckles, moon spots, low-light errors, Alhazen, Optica</keywords>

which would be apparent if the light were strong; these men, if they move in the same direction with equal motion, will always be thought to move together.

### 46. In position. <note>original: "44 p 4"</note>

**I**n position: as when, on a night that is not totally dark, something slightly turned away from the sight is placed before the eyes. The straightness of its position will be judged [incorrectly] because of the weakness of the light departing from the <term>balanced state</term> <note>original: "temperamento" — in medieval optics, this refers to the ideal or "moderate" conditions (light, distance, size) required for accurate perception.</note>.

### 47. In shape and size. <note>original: "97. 28 p 4"</note>

**S**imilarly, a shape with many equal sides will appear circular when seen at night, because the light is too weak to reveal the angles. In the same way, a sphere seen this way is thought to be a flat surface, because the protrusion of its parts is hidden from the sight. In size: as when a man is inspected at night and a forest is seen, or a wall remote from him; the man will appear close to the forest or the wall, since the distance between them is hidden from the sight, even though it may be very great. And perhaps the same [visual] ray will fall upon the man’s head and the height of the forest, depending on the amount of distance from the forest; and in this position, they will appear to be of the same height. Or perhaps the man will appear taller; this would not happen if the light were in its balanced state, because the distance from the man to the forest would be discerned, and the height of each would be measured according to the ground appearing between them.

### 48. In division, continuity, and number. <note>original: "109 p 4"</note>

**I**n distinction, number, and continuity, there will be error from the weakness of light. As if a tablet is seen at night upon which there is a drawing of dark lines; the viewer will perhaps think the divisions are cracks or fissures. And thus there is an error in distinction, because what is continuous appears divided. And in number, because a plurality is seen in a single thing. Similarly, when the sight is in a reflection of strong light: if bodies placed at a small distance from each other are brought near, they will appear continuous. And thus there is an error in continuity, because of light that is either too strong or too weak.

### 49. In motion and rest. <note>original: "138 p 4"</note>

**I**n motion and rest, error happens because of light. For if at night the sight perceives a man and a forest remote from him, the distance from the man to the forest will be hidden; and if the viewer moves toward that man, the more he approaches him, the more clearly he will see that distance. Hence, whereas previously the man appeared to be right with the forest, when the viewer approaches him, he seems further removed from the forest. And since it is certain to the viewer that the forest remains unmoved, he will <term>deduce</term> <note>original: "syllogizabit" — Alhazen views vision as a form of rapid, unconscious logical deduction or "syllogism" performed by the mind.</note> that the man seen is walking away from the forest, even though the truth is that he is stationary. This error would not happen in balanced light. In rest: as when a man seen at night is not fully perceived; hence, if he is seen only slightly, it is not discerned, and his motion will be thought to be rest.

### 50. In roughness and smoothness; rarity and density; shadow and darkness. <note>original: "141. 144 p 4"</note>

**I**n roughness and smoothness, there will be error. For roughness seen at night is perhaps judged as smoothness, or vice versa, depending on the quality of the thing seen. In rarity and density <note>Rarity and density here refer to the porosity or "thickness" of a material's substance.</note>: at night, a very "rare" (porous) body will be judged to have diminished rarity, because since a full perception of the solid cannot be made behind it, the reduction of its rarity will be thought to block the path of the sight. A body that is only slightly rare, however, will appear solid. In shadow and darkness: if there are dark parts on a white wall and the light of a candle falls upon that wall, the viewer will perhaps judge that darkness to be a shadow; and it will perhaps seem to him that the apparent shadow proceeds from a neighboring wall. Thus, there is an error in the estimation of shadow. Similarly, if there is a deep blackness in a part of a wall, it will perhaps be judged to be the void of a hole providing a path for the "emerging darkness." And if the whole surface of a wall is affected by intense blackness, the whole will perhaps be thought to be darkness itself, as happens with a wall covered in soot from a fire and seen in weak light.

### 51. In beauty and ugliness; similarity and dissimilarity. <note>original: "150. 153 p 4"</note>

**I**n beauty and ugliness: it is clear that a beautiful face is seen at night even if there are spots on it, such as freckles. And if there are subtle paintings on the thing seen, which are the causes of its total beauty, when they are hidden from sight in the night, the thing will appear ugly. In similarity and dissimilarity: in bodies of the same kind, color, and shape, in which there is a partial difference through hidden marks, in weak light an absolute similarity will be judged. And if the bodies are different in kind, color, and shape, but there is a partial conformity in some marks: because of the hiding of the marks due to the weakening of the light, an absolute difference of the bodies will be judged. And it is clear that in all the aforesaid, the error happens from the weakness of light alone, since when it is located within the limits of balance, error does not happen, other things being equal.

### 52. Immoderate size creates errors in each species of visible things. In distance. <note>original: "16 p 4"</note>

**Q**uantity [size] departs from balance, and that departure is the cause of error in all things for which the mind's deduction provides assurance. There will be an error in distance <note>original: "longitudine" — often used for the distance between the eye and the object.</note> from the aforesaid cause: as if two men are seen from a balanced distance, though one that is the maximum for their kind, and one is slightly in front of the other; the path situated between them will not be discerned. Hence one of them will appear to be right next to the other. And error happens because their distance [from each other], being very small, is not proportional to their total elongation from the sight, even if that elongation is balanced. There is, however, an error in distance, because those men will be judged by the eye to be equally remote; and thus the quantity of one distance is [judged] greater than it is in truth. Hence the error in distance.

### 53. In position. <note>original: "44 p 4"</note>

**I**n position, there is error because of the smallness of quantity. For if a mustard seed is tilted away from the eye, it nevertheless appears straight: because of its excessive smallness, the tilt of this seed cannot be detected relative to the <term>imaginary line</term> <note>original: "lineam intellectualem" — a theoretical axis used in medieval optics to calculate the geometry of vision.</note> upon which the common axis falls perpendicularly. This is because the distance between this line and the edges of the seed is not fully discerned, as it is minimal. And it is according to this distance that the tilt of the seed over that line is considered. The tilt of a visible thing is always considered according to this line with respect to both eyes. Thus, there is an error in position resulting from immoderate quantity.

<margin>2</margin>
### 54. In shape and size. <note>original: "97. 28 p 4"</note>

**I**n shape: For when a visible object is very small and has angles, the angles will be hidden from the sight; thus its form, though it is not so, might be estimated as round or long. And if there is a slight curvature in it, it will escape the sight, and its surface will be estimated as flat; from which it is clear that there is an error in shape. In size: Immoderate quantity brings about error. For if two bodies are presented to the sight, one of which slightly exceeds the other in length alone, or in width, they will by chance be judged equal in every dimension. And this is an error: because the <term>excess</term> <note>original: "excrementum" — in this context, the mathematical difference or "leftover" amount by which one thing exceeds another.</note> of one dimension over the other has escaped the limits of <term>balance</term> <note>original: "temperantiae" — the ideal state where an object is large enough and close enough to be seen accurately.</note> with respect to the sight, since it is imperceptible to it because of its excessive smallness. Because of this, measurements are necessary so that the sizes of bodies may be verified, since certainty is not acquired through sight alone.

### 55. In division, continuity, and number; motion and rest. <note>original: "109. 138 p 4"</note>

**I**n division, error occurs. For with a hair sticking to glass, a division and crack will appear to be in the glass, even though there is true continuity there; and this arises from the thinness of the hair, for if a thick substance were sticking to the glass, a crack would not be estimated in it. In continuity: For if thin sheets of parchment of equal width are held before the sight and well-pressed together, and the viewer does not know they are sheets, he will judge them to be continuous and to form a single body. The cause of the error is the quantity of the space lying between the sheets, which is not perceived by the viewer because of its smallness. And the cause of error in number will be the same as that of continuity. In motion: For if two things move, one of which moves a little faster than the other, the viewer will think their motion is equal, because the excess of one over the other is imperceptible to the viewer. Similarly, the quantity of the excess of the path which one travels over that which the other travels is imperceptible to the sight. Hence, an equality of paths and motions is judged. In rest: For when something very small is presented to the sight, perhaps some part of it will move, and the object itself will be judged unmoved, since the motion of the part escapes the sight.

### 56. In roughness and smoothness; rarity and density; shadow and darkness. <note>original: "141. 144. 147 p 4"</note>

<margin>[53 n 2]</margin>
**I**n roughness and smoothness: For when a very small thing meets the sight, smoothness will perhaps be judged where there was roughness, and vice-versa. Because, as has been said, roughness is not perceived in a body except by the shadow of certain parts over others, or their protrusion and the depression of others; all of which will be hidden from the judgment of the viewer because of the excessive smallness of the body. In <term>rarity</term> <note>original: "raritate" — in medieval physics, "rarity" refers to low density or transparency, while "solidity" refers to opacity and density.</note> and solidity: For if anyone looks at a very small polished body from which light can be reflected, such as a pearl, it will be judged to be similarly "rare" [transparent], though it is not. Similarly, upon seeing a very small "rare" body behind which a solid body is not perceived, it will be thought to be solid. In shadow and darkness: For if on a white wall opposite the sight there is a distinction of very black dots, with light applied to the sheets but falling directly on the wall or near it, the individual dots will be estimated by the viewer to be individual holes, behind which darkness breaks out. Hence, there is an error with the estimation of darkness from the smallness of the dots alone, which would not happen if the blackness, however intense, infected a large part of the wall. But if the blackness in those dots is not so intense, those dots will indeed be reckoned as holes in which there is shadow, since the light does not penetrate them, as usually happens when light falls upon the appearance of many holes. Hence, an error of shadow arises from the diminution of the dots alone.

### 57. In beauty and ugliness; similarity and dissimilarity. <note>original: "150. 153 p 4"</note>

**I**n beauty and ugliness: When, because of their smallness, spots disfiguring a seen body are hidden from the sight, an erroneous judgment of beauty occurs, because it is taken from appearances only. Just as there is an error in ugliness when, because of smallness, the paintings that bring grace to the seen thing are hidden. In similarity and dissimilarity: For when very tiny marks among some bodies are the causes of similarity or dissimilarity, because they pass by the sight due to their smallness, an all-encompassing similarity or dissimilarity will be judged, and the judgment will be taken from appearances only. In all the aforesaid, there is an error in the <term>syllogism</term> <note>original: "syllogismo" — Alhazen uses this term to describe the unconscious mental process of deduction by which the brain interprets visual signals.</note> arising from the smallness of the body; for when that size is balanced, no error occurs, all other things being equal.

### 58. Immoderate solidity creates errors in individual visible species. In distance and position. <note>original: "16. 44 p 4"</note>

**S**olidity sometimes departs from the balanced state and induces error in any of those things which are perceived through the syllogism. In length [distance]: For if the solidity of a body is minimal—that is, if it is very "rare" [transparent], such as pure crystal, and there is a bright body with strong light behind it—the crystal will not be perceived, but the body will be perceived through it as if there were no medium in between. Hence, since it is as if there were no acquisition of the "rare" [transparent medium], there will not be a full perception of its length [distance] from him. Hence, an error in length. Wherefore, if the position of a "rare" body is tilted, the tilt will be hidden from the viewer, and it will be judged...

perhaps its straightness will be misjudged. From this arises an error in position, and even an error in length: because one of its ends will be thought to be of the same length as the other, even when they are different.

### 59. In size and shape: division, continuity, and number. <note>original: "28. 97. 109 p 4" — references to other sections or propositions in the text.</note>

Next, because the size of a body is understood from its length and the width of the angle under which it is seen: if the length is unknown, an error in size occurs. In a similar way, there will be an error in shape. For if there are corners on a body, they will be hidden from the viewer; thus, a hexagonal shape might be thought to be spherical. If indeed there is a slight curvature in a body, it will go unnoticed, and the body will be judged to be flat. There will also be an error in distinction. For if a black line is drawn through a body of great <term>rarity</term> <note>original: "raritatis" — in medieval science, this refers to low density or high transparency, such as glass or clear air.</note>, the body will appear divided at the place where the line falls. If, however, there are two such bodies separated by a small distance, they will be thought to be continuous. Thus, there is an error in continuity. And it is clear that from these things, there will be an error in the understanding of number: since either one thing will appear as many, or many will appear as one.

### 60. In motion and rest. <note>original: "138 p 4"</note>

In motion, an error will occur from an immoderate degree of transparency: if a very transparent body, such as crystal, is placed before an opening, and the edges of this body are hidden from sight, and another object moves behind this body: the viewer will think the transparent body is moving, even though it is stationary. This would not happen if the body were moderately solid. In rest, an error happens from the same lack of moderation. For if a very transparent body is held in the hand, touching the hand, and it is moved within the hand with a revolving motion while the hand remains still—provided that some division between it and the hand is visible—that body will be judged to be motionless. This is because motion in it cannot be understood except by a change in the position of its parts relative to the hand. And because there is a total similarity in its parts, or so it seems, one cannot discern the position of any of its parts due to its transparency; therefore, neither can its motion be discerned.

### 61. In roughness and smoothness: transparency and density. <note>original: "141. 144 p 4"</note>

In roughness and smoothness: For if there is a slight roughness in a very transparent body, it will perhaps be thought smooth. If, however, it is smooth, and a rough body or a body of various colors is placed behind it, this transparent and smooth body will be estimated as rough. Thus, there is an error in smoothness. In transparency: For if behind a very transparent body there is another body that is not very transparent and is colored with a strong color, the first will not appear very transparent, but its transparency will be estimated according to the transparency of the object placed behind it. Thus, glass placed over other glass does not appear as transparent as it would if it were presented to the sight alone. Thus, there is an error in transparency. If, however, a solid body is placed behind the first transparent one, the first will be judged solid; hence an error in solidity. In the same way, if a very transparent vessel contains wine, since no light or other body is perceived behind it, perhaps the whole thing—glass and wine—will be judged to be one solid body.

### 62. In shadow and darkness. <note>original: "147 p 4. 67 p 10"</note>

In shadow, there will be an error due to transparency. For when the light of the sun descends into a house through some opening and falls upon a glass window, while that house is in shadow, a shadow will appear upon that window, even though in truth light falls upon it. This light would indeed be perceived if the body of the window were solid: because it would not pass through, and so would appear upon the solid surface. Thus, there is an error in shadow. In darkness: When the light of the sun does not descend into the water of a river or into the sea, as happens in the morning and evening hours: even if there is clarity in the water, it will appear dark; and the clearer it is, the darker it will be thought to be. This happens because the upper part of the water casts a shadow upon the next lower part, and that part upon the next lower one, and so on through each layer down to the bottom. And although the shadow of each individual part is small in itself, yet joined together they create one very large shadow, just as clearly happens with the color of wine: for in a small quantity of wine the color is weak, but in a large quantity, even if of the same kind, it is strong. Moreover, the reason why darkness appears in the clarity of the sea when it casts a shadow is this: intense clarity produces intense transparency; hence it grants the sight a deeper penetration. From this comes the acquisition of more parts of the sea that create shadows, because the perception of aggregated shadows leads to the belief in darkness. If, however, the sea is turbulent, the sight will penetrate only a little because of the diminished transparency, and it will perceive only a small part of the water; and although it creates a shadow, since the shadow itself is faint, the color of that part overcomes the shadow. For in turbid water color appears, while in clear water none appears; thus, both because of the color of the turbid water and because of the faintness of the visible shadow, darkness is not perceived in the water. Hence the turbid water will appear colored, and the clear water dark. However, when a ray of the sun falls upon the face of the sea, since a passage is open to it through the water's transparency, every appearance of darkness and shadow is cast away.

### 63. In beauty and deformity: similarity and dissimilarity. <note>original: "150. 153 p 4"</note>

In beauty and deformity: For if in a very transparent vessel there are small particles or engravings that bring beauty to it, and turbid or foul wine is poured into that vessel, the causes of the beauty will be hidden; and the vessel will be judged deformed, as sometimes happens with a glass vessel. Conversely, if some particles deform such a vessel, and clear, bright wine of a beautiful color is poured into it, the causes of the deformity will be hidden, and the vessel will be thought beautiful, even though it is deformed. In similarity and dissimilarity: If two very transparent vessels agree in shape, kind, and transparency, but differ in some of their parts...

arrangement, and are filled with wine of the same color and the same clarity: the causes of their difference will be hidden, and they will be judged as entirely similar. If, however, there is a difference between them in kind and form, but they agree in some partial aspects and are filled with similar wine: they will be thought entirely dissimilar. Thus, an error in similarity and dissimilarity occurs because the judgment is taken from appearances alone. And in all the aforementioned cases, the error happens solely from the lack of moderation in <term>solidity</term> <note>original: "soliditatis" — referring here to the opacity or density of the objects or the liquid within them</note>; for while the other factors remain as they are, no error occurs once these are restored to a moderate state.

### 64. Immoderate clarity of the medium creates errors in every kind of visible quality: in distance, position, shape, size, division, continuity, and number. <note>original: "16. 44. 97. 28. 109 p 4"</note>

When the <term>rarity</term> <note>original: "raritas" — in medieval science, this refers to the thinness or transparency of a medium like air.</note> of the air falling between the sight and the object seen goes beyond the boundaries of its proper moderation, it generates an error in all those things which the sight confirms through <term>inference</term> <note>original: "syllogismum" — Alhazen uses this to describe the mental process of concluding what an object is based on visual cues.</note>. Regarding distance: for if the air is frosty and dark, as often happens in the morning hours, a tower placed at a moderate distance from the sight will be estimated to be further away than it truly is. Thus, there is an error in distance. The cause is this: because the length of the ground below, by which the measure of the tower’s distance is taken, is not perceived; the ground is hidden because of the diminished transparency of the air. Thus, the lack of clarity is the cause of the error. Furthermore, if a visible body is slightly tilted in such air, the tilt will be hidden, though it would be clear in bright air. Thus, there is an error in position. And if there is a slight bump on the body, it will appear flat in such air; and if there are corners on the body, they will be hidden. Thus, the judgment of shape will be erroneous. In size, there will be an error from such air: because the object seen will appear larger than in moderate air, just as happens to bodies perceived through the transparency of water. And if there is something like a black line on a body, it will be thought to be a division of parts. Thus, there is an error in division. And if there are two bodies separated from each other by a small space, they will appear continuous in this air. Thus, there is an error in continuity. And from these things, it is evident that there is an error in number.

### 65. In motion, rest, roughness, smoothness, transparency, density, shadow, darkness, beauty, deformity, similarity, and dissimilarity. <note>original: "138. 141. 144. 147. 150. 153 p 4"</note>

In motion: for if two things are seen in such air, one of which moves a little faster than the other, their motions will perhaps be judged to be equal, whereas in moderate air the excess of one over the other could be discerned. This error is due to the hidden difference of the path of one over the path of the other. In rest: for if someone sees water flowing through such air at a moderate distance, but not very close, they will judge it either unmoved or, if its flow is strong, moved less than it actually moves. In roughness and smoothness: because in this air, a rough thing will appear smooth because the causes of the roughness are hidden. And when a polished thing is seen, since the reflection in it is not discerned, it will be estimated to be rough. In shadow: for if a white body is seen through this air, in which there are small round black particles, and the light of a fire falls upon that body—provided this air is interposed—a shadow will appear in those places, or perhaps they will be thought to be holes providing a way for darkness to break out. Thus, there is an error in shadow and darkness. Because of this air, a <term>rare</term> body will appear less rare, and perhaps will be thought solid. And so there is an error in solidity and rarity. In beauty and deformity, it is because of the particular features that grace or deform a body being hidden in this air. In similarity and dissimilarity, it is because the particular causes of difference or agreement between two bodies do not appear. And in all these, the error arises from the immoderate lack of clarity in the air alone; when other things remain unchanged, it would not happen in moderate air.

### 66. Immoderate time creates errors in every kind of visible quality: in distance, position, shape, and size. <note>original: "16. 44. 97. 28 p 4"</note>

Time placed outside the limits of its moderation is a cause of error in every detail which the sight confirms by inference. In distance: for if someone suddenly looks at something far from a tower, which is immediately snatched away from sight, they cannot fully discern the length between it and the tower; it will perhaps be judged either less distant from the tower than it is in truth, or more. The cause is this: because in that instant of time, the intermediate ground between the tower and the thing seen—by which the measure of distance is taken—is not perceived by the viewer; or because in a short time, the <term>visual axis</term> cannot discern the intermediate path. Thus, it cannot be fully perceived. And so, there is an error in distance. In position: when something suddenly meets the sight and immediately recedes, it will perhaps be thought straight when it is tilted, or vice-versa. In shape: if there is a slight bump in a thing seen suddenly, it will be hidden, and the thing will be thought flat, or the corners will be hidden if they are present. In size: for if someone moves a burning torch with a very swift motion within a small path, so that it often goes and returns through it, the path of the motion will appear to be made of fire; because the motion of the torch from one end of the path to the other happens as if in an instant. Thus, because of the shortness of time, neither the size nor the motion of the torch can be discerned. Hence, there is also an error here in motion.

### 67. In division, continuity, number, rest, and motion. <note>original: "109. 138 p 4"</note>

In division: for if something seen suddenly is turned away from the sight, and there is a black line on it, that blackness will be thought to be a division of parts. And if bodies that are touching or very close are seen suddenly, they will be estimated to be continuous, as happens with the planks of benches when inspected suddenly. Thus, there is an error in continuity. In motion: when one of two things moves a little faster than the other, the motions perceived in a small amount of time will be judged equal, since the difference is not perceivable in such a sudden glance. In rest: for if something moves slightly, it will not be seen to move when viewed suddenly; because the path which it traverses in the time of its perception is imperceptible to the sight on account of its smallness. Moreover, it was explained above <insert>[51 n 2]</insert> that it is not perceived...

# BOOK III OF OPTICS.

<note>original: "OPTICAE LIBER III"</note>

...motion is not perceived in a body except in a sensible amount of time. A similar error occurs with a small wheel: when it is turned very rapidly, it appears to be motionless, since the perception of its revolution cannot happen in a time as short as the time it takes for a single rotation. The same error occurs with a **spinning top** <note>original: "trocho" — a child’s toy like a top or hoop used in experiments on persistence of vision</note>. Hence an error of rest occurs because the change in position of the parts of the top cannot be discerned; therefore, neither can its motion. And if the top is of a single color, it is clear that the motion will not be perceived. If, however, it is of many different colors, the motion will still not appear, since the diversity of colors is hidden and, because of the excessive speed, a certain confused unity of colors is presented instead.

### 68. On roughness, smoothness, rarity, density, shadow, darkness, beauty, deformity, similarity, and dissimilarity. <note>original: "141. 144. 147. 150. 153 p 4"</note>

Regarding roughness: for when something rough is seen suddenly, it will perhaps be thought smooth, and if seen in this way, neither smoothness nor roughness can be discerned in it. Hence arise doubt and error. Regarding **rarity** <term>rarity: the transparency or thinness of a substance</term>: for when light falls weakly and infrequently upon a body, if it is seen suddenly and the slant of the light is not perceived, the body will perhaps be thought to possess an apparent rarity at its very edge. But if the sight is applied for a slightly longer time, the slant will be perceived as the cause of that appearing faint rarity. Regarding **solidity** <term>solidity: the opacity or density of an object</term>: for if someone looks intently at a rare <note>transparent</note> body and does not discern the passage of light behind it, he will think it is solid. Regarding shadow: if there are brownish parts on a white wall and the light of a fire falls upon it, those parts seen suddenly will be thought to be shadows. If, however, their blackness is seen intensely, they will be judged as holes full of darkness. Regarding beauty and deformity: because in such a short time the minute causes of beauty and ugliness are not perceivable—just as it happens when someone looking through a hole gazes at a face, they sometimes judge it to be foul or beautiful, or vice versa. And the same error occurs when the object seen is moved while the eye remains still. Regarding similarity and dissimilarity: because the particular causes of similarity and dissimilarity remain hidden. And in all these things, the error occurs solely from immoderate time; whereas in the aforementioned cases, no error would occur if the time were reduced to a moderate state.

### 69. Weakness of sight creates errors in every kind of visible quality: in distance, position, size, shape, division, continuity, and number. <note>original: "16. 44. 28. 97. 109 p 4"</note>

Debility and lack of moderation in the sight brings about error in each thing perceived by **inference** <term>inference: original "syllogismum," the mental process by which the brain interprets visual data</term> in the sight. Regarding length <note>distance</note>: for if two bodies are placed before the sight, one of which is a strong color and farther away, and the other a weak color and closer to the eye—since the perception of length is only made by a comparison to some intervening bodies—the weakness of sight will make that comparison uncertain. And because it is certain to a person that the sight is more reliable from closer locations than from more remote ones, the observer concludes that whichever of these bodies appears more certain to him must be the closer one. And it is plain that to a weak sight, a strong color is more certain than a weak one, even if it is slightly further away. The same error occurs even when the sight is moderate: for from a great distance, a body whose color is strong is judged closer than one whose color is weak, even if it is not much further away. The weakness of sight also errs in position. For if a body is slanted from some distance, even if the distance is moderate, and the slant is small, it will be unknown when the distance is fully perceived. And the uncertainty of the quantity of length also introduces an error of position. Regarding shape: because a slight bulge and a complex angle are hidden by the weakness of sight. And if there is a black line on a body, it will be judged as a division or a crack; conversely, contiguous bodies will be judged as one continuous whole. Hence errors in division, continuity, and number. By the same cause of error, a **squinting person** <note>original: "strabo" — someone with strabismus or crossed eyes</note> judges one thing as two, if there is a deformity in only one eye. For the thing seen has a different position relative to his two eyes. If, however, there is a deformity in both his eyes, when they happen to move, a difference of position will perhaps occur in them relative to the thing seen, and thus one thing appears as a plurality.

### 70. On motion and rest. <note>original: "138 p 4"</note>

Regarding motion: for if someone spins around in a circle many times, when he stops, he thinks the walls are moving. This is because, when the viewer moves, the internal visual force is moved; and although the viewer has stopped, the visual force does not stop immediately, but its motion continues while the viewer is at rest; and because of this, the estimation that the objects seen are moving arises. We see an example of this motion in a spinning top: for the top continues to revolve for a long time after the hand of the mover is at rest. There is also an illness <note>vertigo</note> in which everything seems to spin to the sufferer. Regarding rest: when a body of similar parts, such as certain **clock wheels** <note>original: "rotae horologiorum"</note>, revolves with a small rotation, a weak sight does not perceive its motion, which a moderate sight would indeed perceive. If, however, the revolution is great, it is not perceived even by a moderate sight. But if a moving body is made of dissimilar parts, as in a mill wheel, then a weak sight will perceive the motion; however, if the revolution of the wheel is rapid, the motion will be hidden from the weak sight. Since the parts of the wheel are very dissimilar, that dissimilarity is not fully perceived in the speed—and it is through the dissimilarity of parts that the perception of their motion occurs.

### 71. On roughness, smoothness, rarity, density, shadow, darkness, beauty, deformity, similarity, and dissimilarity. <note>original: "141. 144. 147. 150. 153 p 4"</note>

Regarding roughness and smoothness: because the sight will perhaps judge something slightly smooth as rough, or vice versa, if there is a dissimilarity between the forms of rough and smooth. Regarding rarity: when there is little solidity in a rare body, it will be judged as greater than it truly is by a weak sight. Regarding solidity: if there is a strong color in a rare body, or behind it, and the rarity is not very great, the sight will think it is solid. Regarding shadow: darkish marks on a wall appear as shadows to this sight when light falls upon it; and if they are very black, they will appear as holes in which there is darkness. In...

...concerning deformity and beauty: similarity and dissimilarity, because the specific causes of beauty or ugliness, similarity and dissimilarity, are hidden from the sight. And there is error in all the aforementioned things due solely to the weakness of sight.

72. *In vision, errors are created sometimes from single factors that complete the vision: at other times from many together, none of which would create an error by itself. <note>original: "15 4 p 4" — a cross-reference to related propositions.</note>*

We have already explained how error happens in **syllogism** <term>syllogism: here, the unconscious mental process of deduction where the brain interprets sensory data to identify an object</term>, according to each of the causes of visual error in any of the parts acquired through deduction; we have examined every mode of error and provided an example for each. And although there is a vast multitude of visual errors, they can all be reduced to the modes we have described and the examples proposed in order. We have also identified errors according to whether each occurs from only one cause. Sometimes, however, an error is introduced not by one cause alone, but by two or more.

For example: if something is moved at a great distance with a slow motion, it will suddenly appear to the sight to be motionless. Yet that motion could be perceived at a moderate distance even by a quick sight; or, even at that extreme distance, the motion would not be hidden if the time of inspection were moderate. Therefore, the error arises from two **immoderate conditions** <note>original: "intemperantijs" — an imbalance or lack of moderation in the physical circumstances of the observation</note>, neither of which is sufficient on its own: the combination of the three factors produces the error. 

If a body of various colors is revolved slowly while held at a great distance, under weak light, and for a short time, the body will be judged to be standing still. But if it is observed at the same distance and under the same light for a moderate amount of time, the motion will be understood. Similarly, it will not be hidden at a moderate distance under the same light and in a short time; and it can even be perceived at that same distance under a strong light. Generally, among all errors happening to the sight, neither one nor many combined can escape the causes we have named. For every form of a visible thing is composed of those qualities we have enumerated. And since the sight acquires nothing from visible things except some of these qualities, no error happens in sight except in one of them. 

Every error that occurs in knowledge happens because the intellect considers the things it perceives to be similar to things it has perceived in some way, or dissimilar. Every error in specific details will be either in the sense, in knowledge, or in the syllogism; it must be in one of these, or two, or all three. And whatever error occurs in these three will only be through an error of sight in the individual parts. It is now clear that error of sight in specific details only occurs because of the causes we have assigned, either from one of them alone or from many.

# BY THE SON OF ALHAZEN
## THE OPTICS OF ALHAZEN
### BOOK FOUR.

*This book is divided into five parts. The first part is the introduction to the book. The second explains that reflection happens to light from polished bodies. The third concerns the manner in which the form is reflected. The fourth shows that the perception of forms from polished bodies occurs only through reflection. The fifth concerns the manner of perceiving forms through reflection.*

### INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK. CHAPTER I.

1. *Vision happens in three ways: directly, reflected, and refracted. <note>original: "In præf. 1. 3. 10 Libr." — referencing the preface and previous books.</note>*

In the first three books, we have already explained the manner in which the sight perceives forms when the vision is direct, and we have listed every single thing the sight perceives in visible objects. However, the acquisition of sight is diversified in three ways: either directly, as we have said; or through **reflection** <term>reflection: light bouncing off a surface, such as a mirror</term> in polished bodies; or through **penetration** <term>penetration: now commonly called refraction; light passing through transparent media like water or glass</term>, as in rare substances, whose transparency is not like that of air. Vision cannot be diversified except in these three ways. In these latter two ways, the sight perceives the same qualities in visible things that we exposed above and whose acquisition in direct vision we made clear. Perhaps in these cases, the sight falls into error or follows the truth. In this book, we will identify when the acquisition of forms occurs through reflection, how that reflection happens, what the position of the reflected lines is, and we will first set forth certain essential properties.

### THAT REFLECTION HAPPENS TO LIGHT FROM POLISHED BODIES. CHAPTER II.

2. *Light and color are reflected from any point of a polished surface in straight lines. <note>original: "1 p 5"</note>*

It is clear from the first book <note>original: "1.2.3.14.18.19 n"</note> that light from a luminous body—whether its own light or accidental light—is directed onto every body opposite to it; and in the same way, color is sent out when light is upon it.

Thus, when a polished body is placed opposite a luminous body, light mixed with color is sent to it, and the light is reflected with the color, whether it be strong or weak, primary or secondary. That reflection occurs in strong light can be made evident: if an iron **mirror** <note>original: "speculum ferreum"</note> is placed opposite a strong light, and if a wall is placed opposite the mirror so that the diverted (not direct) light falls upon it, a strong reflected light will be seen on the wall. This light will not be seen in that same place if the mirror is removed or moved; rather, it will change according to the motion of the mirror...

the place of reflected light on the wall. Therefore, it is clear that reflection occurs in strong light. In weak light, it can be easily demonstrated: if within a house, through a single **aperture** <term>aperture: a small hole or opening, often referred to as a "foramen" in Latin optical texts</term> at some distance from the ground (but not much), the light of day—not direct sunlight—descends upon some body; and around that body an **iron mirror** <note>original: "speculū ferreum" — in the medieval period, mirrors were often made of polished steel or iron rather than glass</note> is placed; and around the mirror some white body is set: a greater light will appear on the second white body than would be there without the mirror. This increase is due solely to reflection from the mirror, since if the mirror is removed, only the weak secondary light will appear on the white body. Furthermore: if a diligent gaze is fixed upon the lines through which the light is sent from the first body into the mirror, one can observe their inclination upon the mirror; and at that same point on the lines, the inclination of the reflection is the same. It is a property of reflection that the inclination and the angle of the incoming and reflected lines are the same. But if the white body is moved from the place of reflection to another spot, no increase of light will be seen on it around the mirror, nor can it be seen except in that specific position. Therefore, it is plain that this specific position is a property of reflection. This same thing can be seen in secondary light: if the aforementioned mirror is made of silver, and a third white body is placed on the other side of the mirror, secondary light will indeed appear on the third body, and a greater light will appear on the second body. It is clear that the cause of this increase is reflection alone. Moreover, the reflection of light will be evident in every place: where a strong light descends through some aperture upon a body, by applying a mirror to the light and placing a white body opposite it in the manner described above. Truly, we shall explain the location of reflection and the position of the lines. It has already been shown in the first book <note>original references to "1.2.3.14.18.19 n" — these likely refer to specific propositions or chapters in Book I</note> that reflected light follows the straightness of lines; therefore, reflection from polished bodies occurs according to the process of straightness in its proper position.

### *3. Light and color flow together mixed from any point of a colored surface to any point of an opposite polished surface. <note>original: "2 p 5" — Proposition 2 from the source text</note>*

Furthermore: It is clear from the above that secondary light proceeding from an illuminated body, moving as accidental light, carries the color of the body with it. From every illuminated or luminous body, therefore, color is sent mixed with light to opposite polished bodies, and is reflected mixed into the appropriate part. Proof of this can be made if, within a house with only one aperture, light descends upon a body of a strong and beautiful color; and an iron mirror is placed around it, and around the mirror a concave body like a **cup** <note>original: "scyphi modū" — shaped like a drinking bowl or chalice</note>, inside which is a white body. Let this vessel be adjusted at the point of reflection so that the reflected light falls upon the white body: the color of that first body upon which the light first descended will indeed appear on the surface of the white body. This will not happen if the white body is placed outside the proper position of reflection. You will find this proven according to various kinds of colors, such as in sky-blue, redness, greenness, and the like. Therefore, it is plain that color mixed with light is sent back, and the appearance of the reflected color is clearer if the mirror is silver.

### *4. Reflection weakens light and color: and altogether the whole visible form. <note>original: "3 p s" — likely Proposition 3</note>*

The reason why this proof (namely, the perception of reflected color) might not appear when a mirror is placed opposite any body, but requires a white one, is this: as stated above, weak colors (even though sent together with light) are not perceived. For the forms that are reflected are weaker than the forms from which the reflection originates. This can be seen in this light: when a strong light falls into a mirror and is reflected onto a wall, the light on the wall will appear weaker than the light on the mirror, and the proportion between them is notable. The same will be clear in weak light in a similar way, as in the house in the first arrangement: if we place a third white body in the spot of the iron mirror, or near it, a greater light will appear on this body than on the second; this would not happen unless reflection weakened the light. But someone might say the cause of this is the blackness of the iron mirror, which, mixed with the light falling into the mirror, shadows it, and so the light reflected on the second body appears weak and dark; whereas light only descends onto the third body placed in the mirror's spot from the first body, mixed with no blackness. But that this is not the cause is clear from this: if a silver mirror is placed in the spot of the iron one, the same proof occurs. In like manner, the reflected color will be weaker than the color from which the reflection is made; this can be seen in the house and the vessel as before: if a white body is placed in the spot of the mirror, or near it, the color will appear stronger on it than on the white body placed inside the vessel. The same will be clear if a silver mirror is used instead of an iron one. Therefore, reflection weakens both lights and colors: but colors more than lights, according to both mirrors. This is because colors arrive weaker than lights; hence they are easily made even weaker in reflection. Furthermore: when a weak color reaches a mirror, it is mixed with the color of the mirror itself; thus the reflected color will appear weak and dark. And forms are weaker when reflected than at the point of reflection; and reflection is the cause of the weakness.

### *5. Reflected light and color are weaker than primary light and color: but stronger than secondary ones, when they are at an equal distance from the same source. <note>original: "4 p 5" — likely Proposition 4</note>*

Someone might say that the weakening of forms in reflection is due only to their distance from their origin. But it will be explained that even if the direct light and the reflected light are at an equal distance from the source, the reflected light will still be weaker. Let a ray of the sun enter a house through an aperture: let an iron mirror smaller than the aperture be placed opposite the aperture in the air, and let the remaining light from the aperture fall upon a white body on the ground; and let the light reflected from the mirror fall upon a raised white body. Observe this: let the distance from the aperture to both the raised and the lying body be the same. The light on the raised body will indeed appear less than the light on the body lying on the ground. No cause can be assigned for this decrease except reflection alone. The same happens if the mirror is silver. The same can be seen in color: for let the light of the sun in a house descend through an aperture upon a body of a strong color, to which a mirror is applied, and another concave body within which is a white body upon which the reflection falls; and let another white body of the same kind be placed in the house, similar to the one in the concave vessel, and let the distance be...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book IV regarding the properties of reflected light. It transitions from general observations about the intensity of reflected color and light to formal definitions of polished surfaces and the construction of an experimental instrument used to prove the laws of reflection.</meta>

<page-num>104</page-num>
<header>ALHAZEN</header>

...of this white [object] from the colored body upon which the light from the aperture <term>aperture: a small hole or "foramen" that allows a controlled beam of light to enter a dark room</term> falls, at the same distance of the white [object] located in the hollow from the colored body, and at the same distance of the mirror from it: then the color will be perceived as weaker on the white [object] inside the hollow than on that which is outside, even though they are equally distant from their origin (that is, from the colored body). The cause of this is that reflection weakens color. Furthermore: reflected light is stronger than secondary light <term>secondary light: light that has been scattered or diffused from a surface, rather than directly reflected by a mirror-like surface</term>, even when they are at the same distance from their origin. For when reflected light falls upon some body, if another similar body is placed outside the path of reflection at the same distance from the mirror, less light will be seen upon it than upon the first. This same thing will be clear in a house: if a mirror is placed on the ground directly in the path of the aperture so that it receives all the light from the aperture, the light will be stronger upon a body placed in the path of reflection than upon another similar body outside this path at the same distance from the mirror. In the same way, if the light from the aperture exceeds the size of the mirror and falls around the mirror onto the ground or a white body, and another body is placed at the same distance from that spot as the reflected body is from the mirror: the light on it will appear weaker than on the body in the path of reflection. The same happens with color; if a body is at the same distance from the mirror outside the path of reflection as a similar body within the path of reflection: the reflected color will appear on the body in the path of reflection, while perhaps none will appear on the other. If the mirror is made of iron <note>original: "ferreum" — polished steel or iron was the standard material for mirrors in the medieval period before silvered glass became common</note>, the color will appear very slight or not at all. But if the mirror is silver, some color will appear upon it, yet it will be very weak and far weaker than on the body in the path of reflection. Thus, it is clear that the forms of light and color are reflected from polished bodies and are weakened in reflection: direct forms are stronger than reflected ones when they share the same origin and distance, and reflected forms are stronger than secondary ones under the same conditions.

### ON THE MANNER OF REFLECTION OF FORMS FROM POLISHED BODIES. Chapter III.

*6. Definitions of smoothness, the polished surface, and perpendicular incidence. From definition 5, book 5.* <note>These references in italics are likely additions by the 1572 editor, Friedrich Risner, pointing to mathematical definitions.</note>

A polished body is one that is very smooth on its surface. Smoothness <note>original: "læuitas"</note> means that the parts of the surface are continuous, without a multitude of pores. Intense smoothness exists where there is great continuity of surface parts and the pores are small and few. The limit of smoothness is the total absence of pores and the absence of division between parts. Therefore, polishing is the continuous smoothing of surface parts with rare and tiny pores; the goal of polishing is the true continuity of parts and the absence of pores. In all polished surfaces, even if they have different shapes, reflection occurs, and the manner and property of reflection are the same. This property is that reflection occurs from every polished surface and from any point upon it. Given any point on the surface from which reflection occurs: the line of the form’s approach to that point and the line of reflection will be in the same plane as the perpendicular line <note>original: "perpendiculari"</note> drawn from that point. These lines will maintain the same position relative to the perpendicular and will have equal angles <note>This is the fundamental law of optics: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection</note>. By "perpendicular," I mean the line that is perpendicular to the surface that touches (is tangent to) the polished body at that point. These two lines and the perpendicular are in a single plane that falls orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> upon the surface tangent to the polished body at the point of reflection. If, however, the line through which the form approaches the mirror falls perpendicularly upon it, the form is reflected back along that same line and no other. This is a property of every reflection in every polished body. Therefore, if the polished body is flat, the surface tangent to the point of reflection will be one and the same as the surface of the body itself. But if it is a cylindrical mirror, polished either on the inside or outside, the contact between the mirror’s surface and the tangent surface will be a single line along the length of the cylinder. The same applies to a conical (pyramidal) mirror polished inside or out. In a spherical mirror, whether polished inside or out, the tangent surface touches at only a single point.

*7. Construction and use of the instrument of reflection. [Reference to Euclid's Elements]*

We shall now explain how this manner of reflection in all mirrors can be demonstrated to the eye. Take a thick plate of brass <note>original: "tabulam æneam"</note> to ensure it is firm; let its length be no less than twelve digits <note>original: "digitis" — a unit of measure roughly equal to the width of a finger, approx. 0.75 inches</note>, and its width six digits. Let a line be drawn parallel to the edge of its length. Near that edge, at the midpoint of this line, place the foot of a compass and draw a semicircle with a radius equal to the width of the plate. Then [according to Proposition 11, Book 1 of Euclid] draw a line from the center point perpendicular to the diameter just made; this line will be the radius that divides the semicircle into two equal parts [according to Proposition 33, Book 6]. On this radius, take a measure of one digit, and placing the compass foot on the center, draw a second semicircle based on the remaining part of the radius (with a radius of five digits).

Next, mark a measure of one digit on the radius, and from that marked point near the center, draw a line parallel to the diameter of the semicircle or the edge of the plate [according to Proposition 31, Book 1]. ### 8. Construction of the seven regular mirrors. <note>original: "8 p 5," likely a reference to Proposition 5 of Book 8 in an earlier draft or related text</note>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram located on the right side of the text block. It consists of a rectangle containing several horizontal and vertical partitions forming a grid-like structure. Various points and areas are labeled with letters: 'P' is at the top center; 'k' is below it; 'c' and 'q' mark the left and right ends of a horizontal line; 'z' and 'x' are points on a central vertical axis, with 'y' further down; and 'b' is at the bottom center. **F**urthermore, let seven iron mirrors be fabricated: one of which is flat; two are spherical (one concave, polished on the inside, the other on the outside); two are pyramidal (one polished on its face, the other in its cavity); and two are cylindrical <note>original: "columnaria"</note> (one concave, the other polished on its surface). 

The flat mirror shall be circular, and its diameter shall be three fingers. The cylindrical mirror polished on its surface should be bright and perfectly polished; the diameter of the circle of its length shall be six fingers, which is its base. The length of the cylinder, however, shall be three fingers. In the base of the cylinder, take a chord of three fingers' length; likewise, in the opposite base of the same cylinder, take an equal and opposite chord, so that the lines produced from the ends of one chord to the ends of the other are straight. Let this cylinder be cut according to the path of these lines, so that a portion of the cylinder remains whose ends are segments of chords. The height of the axis of the remaining portion should be less than the height of half a finger. (By "axis," I mean the line produced from the midpoint of the arc to the midpoint of the chord). 

For the concave cylinder, the length shall be three fingers and the diameter of its base six fingers; in it, let a chord of three fingers be taken, and let the section be made just as in the first one; the height of the axis of the remaining part shall be less than the height of half a finger. In all these mirrors, let there be exquisite polishing and absolute uniformity. 

In the pyramidal mirror, let the diameter of the base be sought; its size should be six fingers, the chord three, and the length four and a half fingers. Let the section be made according to straight lines, and let the height of the portion's axis be less than half a finger. Understand this to apply to both pyramidal mirrors. 

The spherical mirror should be a portion of a sphere whose diameter is six fingers, and the diameter of the base of this mirror three fingers; the height of the axis will be less than half a finger. Do the same for the concave spherical mirror. 

Then, you shall make seven flat wooden rulers <note>original: "regulas"</note> whose sides are parallel and orthogonal at the ends to the greatest possible extent. Let the length of the rulers be six fingers and the width four. Afterward, let one of the rulers be fitted to the square so that it falls orthogonally upon the lower surface of the square cavity, and see that it enters the square easily, lest it be changed by being squeezed. Let the point of the brass plate fall upon the face of the side of the ruler, and where it joins it, let a mark be made. From the assigned point, let a line parallel to the sides of the ruler be drawn to the ends of the ruler, so that this line is the longitudinal line of the ruler.
