### 9. The position and placement of the regular mirrors in the reflection instrument. <note>Cross-references to related propositions: 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 of Book 5.</note>

Once these things are completed, let a **flat mirror** <note>original: "speculum planum"</note> be fitted to one of the rules: it should be such that the rule is hollowed out according to the thickness of the mirror, so that the surface of the mirror is on the same plane as the surface of the rule. This must be done so that the midpoint of the mirror's surface is placed directly under the midpoint of the rule's surface, and so that the line dividing the rule's surface into two equal parts also divides the mirror's surface into equal parts, and so that the parts of the mirror are continuous with the dividing line; and let this be observed to the utmost limit of possibility.

Next, a **cylindrical mirror** <note>original: "speculum columnare"; literally "column-like"</note> polished on its outer face <note>i.e., a convex cylindrical mirror</note> should be applied to one of the rules so that its midpoint falls upon the midpoint of the rule, and so that a line taken along the length of the mirror, dividing it into equal parts, is continuous with the parts of the longitudinal line of the rule's surface, dividing it equally, and so that the middle line of the mirror's length is on the surface of the rule. This can be achieved in this way: let the arcs of both bases of the mirror be divided into equal parts, and from the marked point of division let a line be drawn to the opposite marked point, and let it be fitted and made continuous with the middle lines of the length.

A **concave cylindrical mirror** should be fitted to a rule so that the middle line of its length, taken according to the equal division of the arcs of the bases, is parallel to the middle longitudinal line of the rule; and also so that the chords of both arcs, along with the ends of the longitudinal line, are on the surface of the rule.

A **conical mirror** <note>original: "pyramidale speculum"; in medieval optics, "pyramidal" usually refers to a cone</note> polished on the outside <note>convex</note> should be applied to a rule so that its apex <note>original: "acumen"</note> is at the end of the middle longitudinal line of the rule, and the line dividing the section of the cone into equal parts—specifically the one drawn from the vertex to the midpoint of the arc of the base—should be on the surface, continuous with the remaining part of the middle longitudinal line of the rule.

A **concave conical mirror** should be applied to a rule so that its apex is directly in line with the middle longitudinal line of the rule, while the chord of the arc of the base is on the surface of the rule, and the line drawn from the vertex to the midpoint of the arc of the base is parallel to the middle longitudinal line of the rule. Since the length of the cone is four and a half fingers, there will remain one and a half fingers from the length of the rule.

To fit a **spherical mirror** polished on the outside <note>convex</note> to a rule: let a circle be made on the rule according to the size of three fingers; its center should be the midpoint of the rule. Let the mirror be fitted so that the midpoint of its surface is on the surface of the rule, and on the midpoint of the rule's middle longitudinal line. This can be known by applying another sharp rule <note>original: "regula acuta"; a straightedge with a tapered edge</note>, equal to this one in length and divided equally, and applied to the middle longitudinal line of the rule, so that the midpoint of this sharp rule touches the midpoint of the spherical mirror.

A **concave spherical mirror** is fitted by making a circle on the rule of three fingers' size, whose center is the midpoint of the rule. Once the circle is hollowed out, let it be placed so that the circle of the mirror's base is on the surface of the rule, and the midpoint of the mirror's cavity is directly opposite the midpoint of the rule, and the diameter of the mirror's base is continuous with the middle line of the rule. This shall be weighed <note>measured/calibrated</note> as follows: Let a point be marked on a sharp rule, and from that point let the length of the radius of the mirror’s base be noted on both sides. This sharp rule is then applied to the middle line of the rule so that the point marked on it is directly opposite the midpoint of the mirror’s cavity, and the diameter made on it coincides with the diameter of the base.

When these things are done, on the radius of the brass plate that divides the triangle into equal parts, let a length be marked from its tip equal to the axis of this concave mirror, and let a point be made. The axis is identified thus: Let the sharp rule be applied to the surface of the mirror so that the sharp edge is directly over the middle line of the length, with its point set directly over the midpoint of the concave mirror. Then let a straight and thin needle fall perpendicularly from that point on the sharp rule into the mirror; it will descend indeed onto the center point of the cavity. Let a point be marked on the needle which, after its descent, the cavity of the rule touches; and let the rule be slightly tilted so that the mark on the needle can be made more accurately. According to the length of the needle from the point marked on it, measure from the tip of the brass plate on the line dividing the triangle, and make a point.

Next, you should make this rule enter the concave square so that the tip of the brass plate descends upon the mirror, and the sharp rule should be used to mark a point on the line dividing the triangle that has been touched by that sharp rule when the tip of the triangle has descended to the surface of the cavity. Mark the point; this second point will be less distant from the tip than the first. For the surface of the brass plate is distant from the surface of the ring or plate in which the concave square is located by two fingers minus half a grain of hordei; however, the midpoint of the rule is directly opposite the midpoint of the concave mirror, which is indeed distant from that same plate surface by two fingers. Therefore, when the tip of the plate descends orthogonally, it will not fall upon the midpoint of the cavity, which is the end of the axis, but upon a higher point. Thus the proposition is clear. Let a point be marked on the concave mirror where the tip of the brass plate falls, and having extracted a small hole at that point, descending orthogonally, to this indeed...

### *10. A ray oblique to a flat mirror is reflected to the opposite side; and it makes the angles of incidence and reflection equal. <note>Refers to Book 5, Proposition 10.</note>*

Let the rule, upon which the flat mirror is placed, be inserted into the ring until the pointer of the brass plate falls upon the mirror, and let the rule be fixed in the concave square. Beneath the rule, let something be placed to give it stability so that it does not wobble. Then, let parchment be placed over the apertures, and let an impression be made with a finger so that they are stopped up, and you can perceive the impression; let a mark for the aperture be made on the parchment with ink <note>original: "incausto"</note> or something else. One of the apertures, however, should be left open—one that is slanted and not over the middle of the rule—and let the open aperture be exposed to a ray of the sun. The comprehension of this matter will be more certain if it is exposed to a sunbeam entering through a hole in a house <note>i.e., a camera obscura setup</note>. 

Therefore, when the ray entering the aperture reaches the mirror, you will see it reflect toward that [other] aperture, looking along the line of the brass plate that contains an angle—with the line dividing the triangle into equal parts—equal to the angle formed by the line from the uncovered aperture with that same semi-diameter of the plate. If, however, you expose the aperture into which the reflection occurs to the ray, covering the first one, you will see the ray reflected back into the covered one. 

But if a hollow iron column <note>a small metal tube or pipe</note>, which we directed to be made to the size of the apertures, is placed in the hole (and let a little wax be put around it so that it stands more firmly), the light will descend through the hollow of the column just as it descended through the aperture, and it will be reflected into the aperture corresponding to it. The descent and reflection will occur over the lines of the brass plate in the same manner as before. And if we move the column to the second aperture, we will see the light reflected into the first. However, the light descending through the column will be weaker than the light through the aperture without the column. Yet one may see the same mode of reflection in the weaker light. Let the aperture be stopped with wax so that a small empty space remains around its center: and the reflection of the light will be seen in a similar aperture around the center. In the same way, if you block the hollow of the column with wax so that only the very end of the axis remains, the light will descend upon the axis of the column and be reflected to the center of a similar aperture. In the same way, with the other column placed, when the light descends upon the axis of one aperture, it will be reflected upon the axis of the similar one. For the center of the aperture is directly opposite the axis: and since the reflection of the light falls on the center, and does not move except along a straight line, it must proceed according to the axis.

### *11. A ray perpendicular to the mirror is reflected back upon itself. <note>Refers to Book 5, Propositions 11 and 12.</note>*

With each of the apertures stopped up except for the middle one, which falls directly over the brass plate: let a columnar stick be made to the size of the aperture, and let its extremity be sharpened so that only the end of its axis remains, and let it descend through the aperture to the mirror, and let the point where it falls be marked. Then let a ray of the sun descend through that aperture; it will indeed fall upon the marked point and create a circle around it. Therefore, let a point be marked at the edge of this circular light, and according to the size of the line lying between the marked points, let a circle be made. This circle will indeed be larger than the circle of the aperture, because the passage of light entering through an aperture is in the manner of a pyramid <note>original: "pyramidis"; meaning the light cone diverges as it travels</note>. 

From this it is clear that light descending along the axis is reflected back upon the same axis. Nevertheless, a circular light will appear around the interior base of the aperture, of greater capacity than the incident light or ray, and also of greater light than the circle of the interior light; and it is clear that this light is produced by reflection. However, it is not through the reflection of the light descending along the axis, as can be shown from this: if both bases of the aperture are stopped up so that only the path of the axis remains, and the sun's ray descends through the path of the axis, that circular light will not appear around the interior base of the aperture. Therefore, it did not proceed from the reflected light of the axis. 

Furthermore, as we supposed above, that the rule should fall orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> into the concave square: if it is moved slightly from there so that the rule is tilted—such that the end further from the square is lower than the ray descending upon the middle aperture—it will not fall perpendicularly upon the mirror; and the reflected light will appear removed from the middle aperture. The greater the tilt, the further the reflected light will be removed from the aperture. But if the rule is returned to its upright position, the reflected light will be seen around the interior base of the aperture as before. It is clear, therefore, that when light falls perpendicularly upon the mirror, it returns to the aperture through which it entered. But when the light of the axis falls at a tilt, it will not be reflected to the aperture through which it entered; yet the center of the light will always appear upon the line of the concave surface of the ring, perpendicular to the brass plate and descending through the center of the middle aperture. Whatever has been said regarding the first two slanted apertures, understand the same for each; and what has been said regarding the flat mirror concerning light descending through either a slanted or middle aperture—whether the rule is straight or tilted—understand the same for other mirrors.

### *12. In mirrors—convex, concave: spherical, conical, cylindrical—the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. <note>Refers to Book 5, Propositions 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 20.</note>*

If, however, the rule in which the cylindrical mirror <note>original: "speculum columnare"; literally 'columnar mirror'</note> is polished on the outside is tilted in the square so that it does not fall orthogonally upon the square, but is tilted toward the right or left side:

The falling light will be seen to extend only over the aforementioned line, and it will be reflected to the middle aperture; and around its interior base, a circular light larger than the interior circle will be seen, just as was observed with the flat mirrors. You will be able to see the same in pyramidal mirrors. In like manner, in spherical mirrors, with the light descending through the middle aperture, let a circle be made on the surface of the rule according to the size of the circle already mentioned; and the light will be seen to extend over this circle and be reflected to the middle aperture in the manner already described. What has been said concerning natural light <note>direct sunlight</note> can also be seen in accidental light <note>original: "luce accidentali"; secondary light reflected from a surface like a wall rather than coming directly from the source</note>. Let a house with a single opening be placed opposite a wall onto which a ray of the sun descends, and let the instrument be applied to the opening. When, therefore, the accidental light enters through an aperture other than the middle one, it will be seen to reflect through the opposite one; and if the instrument is adjusted so that it enters through two apertures, it will be reflected through two similar ones. But so that you may be able to weigh <note>examine/measure</note> the light when it enters directly, place white parchment above it and tilt the instrument until you see the light falling upon the parchment; for in mirrors, the fall of accidental light is not fully grasped because of its weakness. The same things will be evident in this light as were evident in natural light; for there is no difference in their nature, except that one is strong and the other is weak. It is clear, therefore, that lights approaching mirrors through different lines are reflected through different lines; and that those incident according to a straight perpendicular return according to the same; and that the deviation of the lines of reflection is equal to the deviation of the lines of approach <note>the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection</note>.

### 13. The surface of reflection is perpendicular to the plane tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection. <note>Refers to Book 5, Proposition 25.</note>

It is also clear that the lines of reflected and incoming light are in the same surface which is orthogonal <note>perpendicular</note> to the surface of the polished body, or to the surface tangent to the point of the polished body from which reflection occurs. If the light comes upon the perpendicular, it is reflected upon the perpendicular; and into whatever point it falls, it is reflected in a perpendicular surface above the surface tangent to that point. The reflected line always maintains an angle with the perpendicular over that point equal to the angle which the incoming line includes with the same perpendicular.

The proof of this matter is as follows: because it is clear [by propositions 10, 11, and 12] that if any light descends through some aperture, it is reflected through another corresponding to it; and if the aperture is constricted so that it remains almost as a single axis, it is reflected through the axis of the corresponding one; and if a change is made in the descent of the light, it is reflected through the lines by which it had previously descended. And it is clear [from the construction of the reflection instrument] that the corresponding apertures have the same position with respect to the center. Since light does not proceed except through straight lines, it is clear that it is reflected through lines of the same position with respect to the middle of the aperture as the lines of descent. Whence, when it approaches through an orthogonal line, it is reflected through that alone. Wherefore, the lines of reflection always preserve the same position as the lines of descent with respect to the surface tangent to the point of reflection. This is true whether in substantial <note>direct/primary</note> or accidental light, whether strong or weak, and generally in all.

And we shall show this identity of position. We already know that the surface of the rule falls upon the plate in which we made the square orthogonally. Therefore, the middle line of the square plate is orthogonal to the line common to its intersection and the rule, and to the line of the rule's width. The square plate is parallel to the brass plate, and its line—that is, of the concave middle square plate—is parallel to the middle line of the brass plate, which is the line produced from the center of the brass plate and dividing the semicircle into equal parts. The line common to the surface of the brass plate and the surface of the rule, in which the line of width is, is parallel to the line common to the concave plate and the rule [by Book 1, Proposition 28; for the line of the rule's length cuts the lines of width at right angles]. Therefore, the middle line of the brass plate will fall perpendicularly upon the common line of the rule and the brass plate. And the rule is perpendicular to the surface of the square, and the surface of the square is parallel to the surface of the brass plate. Therefore, the surface of the brass plate is orthogonal to the surface of the rule; and the middle line of the rule's width is perpendicular to the middle line of the rule's length; and similarly, the middle line of the brass plate is perpendicular to the same. Thus, the middle line of the brass plate is perpendicular to the surface of the rule and to the middle line of its length; it is therefore perpendicu-

For the distance of the centers from the surface of the brass plate is the same—that is, half a barleycorn <note>original: "grani hordei"; a medieval unit of measurement approximately 1/3 of an inch</note>—and the diameter of the aperture is one barleycorn. This is done in the same way for each aperture. Therefore, the lines produced from the point of the rule where the axis falls to the center of two opposing apertures—which are parallel to the two lines extended from the center of the brass plate to the ends of the diameters of those same apertures—maintain an equal angle with these lines <note>according to Proposition 10 of Book 11.</note>

And if a line is raised from the end of the axis to the center of the aperture, it will be in the surface descending through the center, and it will be parallel to the middle line of the brass plate <note>according to Proposition 6 of Book 11</note>; since the lower line lying between their heads is perpendicular to the brass plate, and equal to the upper line lying between those same heads and perpendicular to the brass plate—and it is parallel to it. Similarly, the line from the center of the middle aperture to the end of the axis of the cylindrical rod is parallel to the middle line of the brass plate; and that line is perpendicular to the rule, and therefore so is this one <note>according to Proposition 8 of Book 11.</note> Therefore, this line and the other forming the angle are parallel to the middle line of the brass plate, and to the other line on the brass plate forming the remaining angle. Thus, the corresponding partial angles are equal to one another <note>according to Proposition 10 of Book 11.</note> Therefore, the middle line of the brass plate divides its angle into equal parts. Thus, the line from the center of the middle aperture divides its angle into equal parts. And since it is certain that light entering a tilted aperture moves through those lines containing the angle, it is clear that all light is reflected through lines which, along with the lines of descent, are in a surface orthogonal to the surface of reflection, making an angle with the perpendicular line equal to the angle which the perpendicular contains with the lines of descent; and that light descending perpendicularly is reflected back along the perpendicular. 

This is a general rule for all light. If, however, the rule is tilted—not on its side, but at its head—so that the axis of the middle aperture is not perpendicular to the rule, the light will be reflected and seen upon the line of the ring’s height, perpendicular and passing through the center of the aperture. The greater the tilt, the greater will be the distance of the reflected light from the aperture or the axis; and if the tilt is decreased, the distance will decrease, until the position of the rule returns to straightness and the light is reflected upon that perpendicular. That the axis of the middle aperture and the line of reflection are in the same surface, orthogonal to the surface of reflection during this tilt, is clear from this: for the axis of the middle aperture is perpendicular to the width of the rule—that is, to the common line of the rule's surface and the surface descending through the centers of the apertures—and the middle line of the plate (namely the ring) is parallel to this axis, and parallel to the middle line of the brass plate. And the middle line of the brass plate is perpendicular to the width of the rule, and to the common line of the surface of the rule and the surface of the brass plate. Therefore, the surface in which they reside—the middle line of the brass plate and the axis of the middle aperture—is also orthogonal to the surface of the rule. And in this surface is the perpendicular line in the height of the ring <note>according to Proposition 7 of Book 11</note>, since it passes through the ends of the parallel lines, namely the middle of the brass plate and the axis of the middle aperture. It is evident, therefore, that reflected light which appears in the perpendicular of the ring's height is reflected along a line which, together with the axis through which the descent occurs, is in a surface orthogonal to the surface of the rule. 

Therefore, when light descends onto a flat mirror, reflection occurs according to lines having the same inclination to the surface of the mirror; and these lines, with the perpendicular, are in a surface orthogonal to the mirror’s surface. In the case of an external columnar [cylindrical] mirror, the proof is exactly the same as in the flat one: namely, that the pointer of the brass plate falls perpendicularly upon the line of the mirror’s length; and similarly, the cylindrical rod descends upon the same; and the part of that line between these points of contact is orthogonal to the brass plate. And always, whether the light descends through the middle aperture or a tilted one, its reflection and its descent will be in the same surface, orthogonal to the surface tangent to the line of the mirror’s length. 

In an external pyramidal mirror, since the surface of the rule is in the same surface as the line of the pyramid’s length (just as in the columnar mirror), the position of the lines of the surface and the mode of reflection will be the same as in a flat mirror, and the proof is exactly the same. 

In a concave columnar [cylindrical] mirror, the pointer of the brass plate descends to its middle line of length, and the axis of each aperture falls upon the same; the part of that line between these points of contact is orthogonal to the surface of the brass plate. The axis of the aperture and the middle line of the brass plate are orthogonal to the surface tangent to that mirror at the line of length (which is the place of reflection) and are parallel to the surface of the rule. Thus, the method of proof is the same as before: namely, that reflection and descent are in the same surface, orthogonal to the surface of the place of reflection; and that they have the same inclination; and that descent through the middle causes reflection...

From which it is certain that this is not from a property of the light or the shape of any particular mirror, but from a certain common property of a polished thing and of any light. If, however, light should descend through different apertures to any point, a different reflection will be seen, and a diversity of angles consistent with its descent; and so it is in all cases.

### 14. Between the visible object and the mirror, innumerable pyramids are formed with alternating bases and vertices. <note>original: "22 p 5"</note>

It is manifest from the things above [2. 3 n] that if a polished body is placed opposite a luminous body: light from every point of the luminous body falls upon every point of the polished body. Thus, upon every point of the polished body falls a pyramid <term>pyramid: in medieval optics, this refers to a cone-shaped bundle of light rays with a point at one end and a surface at the other</term>, whose sharp point is in that point, and the surface of the luminous body is the base. And from every point of the luminous body proceeds a pyramid, whose sharp point is in that point, and the base is the surface of the polished body. If, however, some point is understood to be between the luminous body and the polished body: the light of the luminous body will indeed come to that point in the manner of a pyramid, whose sharp point is in that point, and the sides of this pyramid proceeding until they fall upon the surface of the polished body, create a pyramid. Whence in the understood point there will be the sharp points of two pyramids, whose bases are the surfaces of the luminous body and the polished body. And if a pyramid is understood at any intermediate point, whose base is the surface of the polished body, and the lines of this pyramid proceed: that which they occupy of the surface of the luminous body—that is, from which the light proceeded to the polished body—will be according to two pyramids whose sharp points are in the understood point; and whatever light proceeds in these two pyramids, proceeds and is included in the first two pyramids. And from the luminous body, light proceeds toward the mirror according to parallel lines: but these lines are included in the first two pyramids; and through whatever lines light is moved toward the mirror, the lines of reflection observe entirely the same placement which the lines of the motion of light had. Whence if light is moved through parallel lines, it is reflected through parallel lines; and light falling upon the polished body in the manner of a pyramid is reflected, observing the manner of the same pyramid. And when light descends from a luminous body through some aperture to a polished body: if a point is understood in the surface of the aperture on the side of the luminous body, from which point two pyramids are understood—the base of one in the luminous body, the other in the polished body—from the base of the pyramid alone whose base is the luminous body, light comes to the polished body over that point.

Similarly, if a point is understood in the surface of the aperture on the side of the polished body, in which are the sharp points of two pyramids, one toward the mirror, the other toward the luminous body: from the base of the pyramid alone which is the base in the luminous body, light reaches the mirror over this point; and from the part of the luminous body common to these two pyramids, light reaches the part of the mirror common to the two pyramids. Light also comes from the luminous body to the mirror through parallel lines: but through whichever lines it reaches, reflection happens in the manner aforesaid: and any lines of reflection observe the placement of the lines of the descent of light looking toward them: and in every reflection, the identity of the form of light that was on the polished body is observed; and these things we shall explain hereafter with an evident explanation.

### 15. Light reflected from a more distant polished surface is weakened in three ways.

Furthermore: it was clear [4. 5 n] that the further light is elongated from its origin, the more it is weakened; it was also clear that continuous light is stronger than dispersed light. Therefore, when light proceeds from some point of a luminous body toward the surface of a mirror in the manner of a pyramid, the more it is elongated from that point, the greater will be its weakness for a twofold reason: both because of elongation from its origin, and because of dispersion <note>The spreading of the rays over a larger area</note>. When, however, that light is reflected from some point of the mirror, it becomes weaker in a threefold way: because of the reflection itself which weakens it, because of the elongation from the place of reflection, and because of dispersion. If indeed reflected light from a mirror is gathered into some point: it will indeed become stronger because of the gathering <note>convergence</note>, but it will be weakened because of the reflection and elongation. If, therefore, the gathering of light restores to it as much strength as the reflection and elongation take away: the gathered reflected light will be of the same strength as it is at the surface of the mirror; if indeed the gathering adds less strength than those two diminish: it will be weaker; and if it adds more, it will be stronger. Similarly, if a pyramid proceeds from the surface of a luminous body to some point of the mirror: the light proceeding according to this pyramid-shape will be weaker because of elongation, but stronger because of gathering. If, however, the gathering can overcome the elongation: the light gathered at a point of the mirror will be stronger than a single light coming from the luminous body through one line—I say "single" because to any point of a line...

If, however, the distance outweighs the concentration: the light of a polished point will be less than the light of a single line taken alone; and if the concentration outweighs the distance: it will be stronger. Moreover, the lights that approach a mirror from a luminous source along parallel lines will be weaker than those approaching in another manner: because, being weakened on account of the distance, they are not concentrated onto the mirror, but are moved in reflection along parallel lines; hence they are weakened by both reflection and distance. ### *16. Light and color are reflected along physical lines, endowed with a certain width. <note>original: "Lux & color reflectuntur per lineas physicas, latitudine quadam praeditas"</note> 3 p 2. 8 p 5.*

<margin>b</margin> Furthermore: every line through which light is moved from a luminous body to an opposing body is a <term>sensible line<note>Latin: "linea sensualis." In medieval science, this refers to a physical ray that can be perceived by the senses, which must have a non-zero thickness to be visible.</note></term>, not without width. For light does not proceed except from a body, since it does not exist except in a body. But in the smallest light that can be taken, there is width, and in the line of its progress there is width; and in the middle of that sensible line, there is an <term>intellectual line<note>Latin: "linea intellectualis." This is a mathematical abstraction—a line with no width—used for geometric proofs.</note></term>, and its other lines are parallel to that one. And if the smallest of lights is divided: neither part of it will be light, but both will be extinguished and will not appear. If, however, the minimal light is doubled, or multiplied further, and being compacted it is divided into equal parts: each part of it will be light. If indeed the division is made into unequal parts: one part of it will be light, the other not at all. Moreover, the minimal light proceeds onto the minimal part of a body that light can occupy, and its progress is according to the intellectual line in the middle of the sensible line, with its extremities parallel to it. And the minimal light falls not upon an <unclear>intelligible</unclear> point of the body, but a sensible one, and it is reflected along a sensible line whose width is equal to the width of the incoming sensible line. And if a middle reflected intellectual line is understood within that sensible line: it will have the same position over the place of reflection as the middle intelligible line of the incoming sensible line has. And any intellectual line in the reflected sensible line observes exactly the same position with the intelligible line of the other sensible line corresponding to it. Therefore, in all light, the ratio of intellectual lines and points is observed, even though light does not proceed from them or through them [individually]: and in this manner shall be the reflection of light.

### *17. The reflection of light and color made from a rough surface mostly escapes the sight. <note>original: "Reflexio lucis & coloris à superficie aspera facta, plerunq. fugit visum"</note> 1 p 5.*

Furthermore: the reason why reflection occurs from polished bodies and not from rough ones is this: because light, as we have said, does not approach a body except by the swiftest motion, and when it reaches a polished surface: that position ejects the light from itself. A rough body, however, cannot eject it, because there are pores in the body which the light enters; but in polished bodies it finds no pores. Nor does this ejection happen because of the strength or hardness of the body, for we see reflection in water; rather, this repulsion is a property of the <term>polish<note>Latin: "politurae." Alhazen argues that smoothness, not hardness, causes the "rebound" effect of light.</note></term>. Just as it happens in nature that something porous falling from a height onto a hard stone is returned upward: and the less the hardness of the stone upon which it falls, the weaker the return of the falling object will be; and the falling object always returns toward the part from which it proceeded. Truly, in sand, on account of its softness, the return that happens in a hard body does not occur. If, however, there is a polish within the pores of a rough body: nevertheless the light entering the pores is not reflected; and if it should happen to be reflected, it is dispersed, and because of the dispersion it is not perceived by the sight. In like manner, if the raised parts in a rough body were polished: a dispersed reflection will occur, and for this reason it will be hidden from the sight. If indeed the prominence of the parts is so small that its position is almost the same as the depressions: its reflection will be perceived as if in a polished body, not a rough one, though less perfectly.

### *18. The rays of incidence and reflection agree in the similarity of their position. Therefore, the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. <note>original: "Radii incidentiae & reflexionis, situs similitudine conueniunt. Itaq. anguli incidentiae & reflexionis aequantur"</note> 20 p 5.*

The reason why the reflection of light occurs according to a line of the same position as the line through which the light itself approaches the mirror is this: because light is moved with the swiftest motion; and when it falls upon the mirror, it is not received, but a fixed place in that body is denied to it. And since the force and nature of the prior motion still persists in it, it is reflected toward the part from which it proceeded, and according to lines having the same position as the prior ones. We can see a likeness of this thing in natural motions, and even in accidental ones. If we allow a heavy spherical body to descend from some height perpendicularly onto a polished body: we will see it reflected over the perpendicular through which it had descended. In accidental motion: if some mirror is raised according to the height of a man and fixed firmly to a wall, and a spherical body is fastened to the tip of an arrow, and the arrow is projected by a bow into the mirror in such a way that the elevation of the arrow is equal to the elevation of the mirror, and the arrow is parallel to the horizon: it is plain that the arrow approaches the mirror along a perpendicular, and its return will be seen upon that same perpendicular. If, however, the motion of the arrow were along a line slanted toward it, it will be seen to reflect not through the line through which it came, but through a line parallel to the horizon, just as the other was, and of the same position with respect to the mirror and with respect to the perpendicular in the mirror. That the motion of reflection happens to light because of the resistance of the polished body is clear: because when the repulsion or resistance is stronger, the reflection of the light will be stronger. Moreover, why the same motion of reflection and its approach occurs, this is the reason: when a heavy body descends along the perpendicular, the repulsion of the polished body and the motion of the descending weight are directly opposite to each other, and there is no motion there except the perpendicular; and the resistance happens through the perpendicular: therefore the body is repelled according to the perpendicular. Whence it returns perpendicularly. But when a body descends along a slanted line: the line of descent falls between the perpendicular of the surface of the polished body passing through that point, and the line of its surface orthogonal to this

this [line] is the perpendicular: and if the motion were to penetrate beyond the point where it falls, so that it found a free passage, this line would indeed fall between the perpendicular passing through the polished surface and the line orthogonal to that perpendicular on the surface; it would observe the measure of its position with respect to the passing perpendicular and with respect to the other line, which is orthogonal to that perpendicular. For the measure of the position of this motion is composed of its position relative to the perpendicular and its position relative to the orthogonal line. But repulsion proceeding along the perpendicular—since it cannot repel the motion according to the measure it has relative to the perpendicular passing through the polished surface, because it does not enter even a little—therefore repels it according to the measure of position relative to the perpendicular which it holds relative to the orthogonal line. And when the regression of the motion has the same measure of position relative to the orthogonal line as it had previously to the same from the other side, it will similarly have the same measure of position relative to the passing perpendicular as it had before. But a heavy body in its return, when the motion of repulsion is finished, descends by its own nature and tends toward the center <note>The center of the Earth, i.e., gravity</note>. Light, however, having the same nature of reflecting—since it is not natural for it to ascend or descend—is moved in reflection along the line it began until it reaches an obstacle that causes the motion to stop. And this is the cause of reflection.

->19. *That color mixed with light is reflected is shown by a reflecting instrument. <note>original: "Colorem luci permixtum reflecti, reflexionis organo ostenditur."</note> 3 p 5.*<-

It is also clear from the above that colors move together with lights; hence there will be a reflection of color just as there is of light. And if you wish to see the proof of this according to the method assigned in the second part, you may. However, through the instrument made to denote this reflection, you will not see it fully on account of the weakness of the color. For color is weakened by distance, by reflection, and by the aperture through which it enters. That an aperture weakens it is clear from this: because light appears greater after a large aperture than after a small one. In like manner, when the apertures are narrow, the color after reflection will appear either not at all or very slightly. Nevertheless, if you wish to see it in the aforementioned instrument: make a silver mirror; for in an iron mirror the color appears weaker, since in reflection it is mixed with the reflected light, which is a mixture of the descending light and the slight light of the iron mirror, and the iron color mixed with the reflected color weakens it. Indeed, in a house with only a single aperture, let the aforementioned instrument be kept, and let a white wall be placed opposite the house, and let the instrument be fitted to the aperture of the house. Let the width of this aperture be such that it can occupy two apertures of the instrument, through one of which the white wall opposite the house is viewed; and let a body of strong color be placed against the perceived part of the wall, and let the part of the wall be seen through the other aperture of the instrument. Therefore, when light enters through the apertures of the instrument, the color will be seen to reflect through that aperture you are looking into which is opposite the colored body, and not at all through the other; and thus it will happen for any aperture opposite the body. And those things said regarding the reflection of light can be considered in the reflection of color. Now, the width of the aperture of the wall occupied two apertures of the instrument applied to it so that more light might descend onto the mirror and the reflected color might appear better. And since color is weakened when directed through an aperture, and similarly when reflected, when it falls upon a body opposite the sight, a second [weakening] will be perceived. Hence, if after reflection it falls upon a white body applied to the aperture of coloration, perhaps on account of the weakness the sight will not grasp it; but if a second sight is applied to the aperture of coloration, perhaps it will be grasped, since the first will be seen, not the second.

## CHAPTER IV. That the perception of forms from polished bodies happens by reflection. <note>original: "QVO'D COMPREHENSIO FORMARVM E' CORPORIBVS politis fiat reflexione. Cap. IIII."</note>

->20. *Both opinions are false: that rays sent from the sight to the mirror and then reflected to the visible object perceive the image; and that an image already imprinted on the mirror flows from there to the sight. <note>original: "Falsa est utraq; opinio: & radios à uisu ad speculum missos, indeq; ad uisibile reflexos, imaginem percipere: & imagine in speculo iam antè impressam inde ad uisum manare."</note> 23. 24 p 5.*<-

Many disagree on the manner of the perception of a <term>form<note>Latin: "forma." In this context, it refers to the visual image or the "species" of an object being viewed.</note></term> in polished bodies. Hence some of them think that rays go out from the sight to the mirror, and return from the mirror, and perceive the form of the thing in the return. Others affirm that the form of the body is imprinted on the mirror opposite it, and is therefore seen in it, just as the perception of their natural forms happens in bodies. But that it is otherwise is manifest from this: because if someone sees themselves in some part of a mirror and moves to another part, they will not see themselves in the first part, but in the second. This would not happen if their form were fixed in the first part. In the same way, if they move to a third part, the place of the appearance of the form will change, nor will it appear in the first or second part. Furthermore, when some body is seen and the viewer is moved from that position, it can happen that they do not see that body in that mirror, even though they see the whole surface of the mirror. This certainly would not be the case if the form were imprinted in the mirror, since the mirror is seen and does not change its place, and the body is similarly unmoved, and its form would dye the mirror just as before. And so that it may clearly appear that this does not happen from the perception of a [fixed] form: let half of the apertures of the instrument be blocked, and let there be some writing in one of the blocked ones. If the mirror of the ruler <note>A component of his experimental apparatus</note> is inspected through the aperture looking toward the writing, the writing will be perceived in the mirror; through any other [aperture], not at all. But if the form of the writing were imprinted on the mirror, it could be perceived through any aperture of the instrument. In a similar way, in cylindrical mirrors, the position of the writing will be perceived only through the aperture looking at the blocked aperture in which the writing is. Indeed, in pyramidal and spherical mirrors, the position and magnitude of the writing will be changed. Furthermore, with the cylindrical mirror removed and the ruler placed directly upon its bases, the face of a man positioned directly in it will appear. But if the ruler is raised or greatly tilted, it will appear distorted. It is clear, therefore, that the perception does not happen from a fixed form in the mirror, since the thing seen in mirrors is not perceived unless the sight is in the position of reflection.

### ->CHAPTER V. ON THE MANNER IN WHICH FORMS ARE PERCEIVED FROM POLISHED BODIES.<-

21. *A visible image is perceived through the reflection of a visible form from a mirror to the sight.* <note>Reference to Proposition 24, Book 5.</note>

It has already been made clear in the preceding section <note>original: "3 n," likely referring to a previous note or proposition</note> that if a bright, colored body is placed opposite a mirror, light and color proceed from every point of it to the entire surface of the mirror and are reflected along their own specific lines of reflection. Therefore, from a chosen point on the body opposite the mirror, light and color proceed to the mirror in the form of a continuous pyramid <note>Alhazen uses "pyramid" to describe what we would modernly call a "cone" of light spreading from a source</note>, the base of which is the surface of the mirror. This form is reflected along lines that hold the same position as the lines of approach, and after reflection, there will be continuity just as there was in the approach. 

And if the surface of a body <note>meaning the eye or an observer's body</note> meets these reflected lines, because of their continuity, the whole surface will be occupied so that no vacuum remains between them. If, therefore, the form of that body moves toward the mirror along those reflected lines and reaches the base of the pyramid—since the lines of the pyramid are in the same position as the reflected lines—the form will be reflected through the lines of the pyramid and will be entirely gathered at the chosen point. Whenever the form of any body comes to a mirror along certain lines, if those lines are in the same position as the lines of the pyramid from the chosen point to the mirror (meaning those lines corresponding to them), the form will move through that pyramid to the chosen point. If the sight is at that chosen point, it will see the body to which that form belongs. 

It was declared above <note>Propositions 2.17 and 2.18</note> that the acquisition of a form in a mirror occurs in a determined position. Therefore, the proper and natural position for the acquisition of sight through reflection is this: that the lines of the form's approach to the mirror have the same position as the lines of the pyramid from the center of the sight to the ends of those lines (namely, each line with its corresponding counterpart). The perception of a reflected form does not happen except in this position. It is clear, then, that according to this arrangement of lines alone, the perception of forms occurs. 

It is also clear that light and color proceed from a bright colored body to the mirror and are reflected; nothing proceeds from the body except light and color. It is evident, therefore, that such a form is perceived from light and color alone. And since the form, composed of color and light, moves according to the aforementioned observation of position, it is superfluous to say that rays go out from the eye to the mirror and are reflected according to the aforementioned position, as has been said by many <note>Alhazen is here rejecting the "extramission" theory held by many Greeks, including Euclid and Ptolemy, who believed the eye emitted rays to "touch" objects</note>. This mode of reflection is therefore not contrary to the teaching of geometers, but in harmony with it, since the position of rays is observed in it geometrically, even while rejecting the opinion of "outgoing rays." 

This method has been clear to me alone until now. Truly, since the form proceeds from a bright body to the mirror according to a variety of positions (because of the lines conceived from every point of the body to the whole surface of the mirror), there will be a reflection of the same form through various pyramids, whose apexes are different points and whose bases are the mirror's surface, observing the position of the lines of the form's motion. Because of this, it happens that at the same hour, with the mirror fixed, the same form of a body is perceived by different people upon whose gazes the apexes of the reflected pyramids fall. Similarly, if the same eye moves over those apexes of the pyramids, the same form will appear to it from different places, even while the mirror remains unmoved. But when different people perceive the same form in a mirror, their gazes fall upon different locations on the mirror. For they cannot perceive the forms of different points from the same point of the mirror. 

It was also said <note>Proposition 3</note> that light proceeds from every point of a body to every point of a mirror. Thus, over every point of the body is the apex of a pyramid whose base is the surface of the mirror; and every point of the mirror's surface is the apex of a pyramid whose base is the entire surface of the body. Therefore, the form of the body will be at every point of the mirror, through lines proceeding in different directions that cannot intersect. And the form approaching any point of the mirror from the body through a pyramid will be reflected through a pyramid.

22. *If the visible object and the mirror agree in the similarity of their shape and position, a true and distinct image is seen.* <note>Reference to Proposition 35, Book 5.</note>

And although the same iteration of a form is multiplied over the surface of the mirror without number—since the total form coincides with every part and every point, and there is no separation in those forms but rather an inseparable continuity in reflection—nevertheless, because the total form does not fall upon different parts of the mirror [in the same way], it is directed toward different locations according to the identity of its position, where the sight perceives it. Therefore, when the shape of the mirror is similar to the shape of the body, there will be a fulfillment of the body's form and figure in the mirror. Because in a mirror of the same shape as the body, the form of the first point is directed to the first point of the mirror, the second to the second, and so on for all corresponding points; thus, there will be a total figure of the figure on the mirror's surface. This does not happen in a mirror of a different shape. 

Similarly, if any part of the mirror is taken which has the same shape as the body, the fulfillment of the body's figure will be in it. And since there are infinite such parts of the mirror, there will be infinite reflected forms of the body, but proceeding to different points from which the sight perceives the form. Since, therefore, the perception of the form occurs according to this arrangement of lines, there is no "fixing" of the form proceeding from the body onto the surface of the mirror. This happens in this manner in all mirrors, but most accurately in plane mirrors; in others, however, a certain diversity occurs due to an error of sight, according to the aforementioned mode. And any sight, according to the aforementioned mode, perceives from one point of the mirror only one point of the body; nor is the same point of the body perceived by two different sights in the same point of the mirror.

<summary>Alhazen explains that images in mirrors are formed by "pyramids" of light and color reflecting to the eye, rather than rays emitted from the eye. He demonstrates that while an object's form hits every point of a mirror, an observer only sees the specific points that reflect directly to their eye based on geometric position.</summary>

### 23. *The plane of reflection contains four points: the visible point, the point of reflection, the point of sight, and the terminus of the perpendicular line drawn from the point of reflection to the plane that touches the mirror at that same point. Thus, this perpendicular is common to all planes of reflection.* <note>The numbers 27 p 5, 6 p 6, etc., are cross-references to other propositions in this or related optical treatises.</note>

Furthermore, if a mirror is placed opposite the sight, and a pyramid <note>The author uses the term "pyramid" to describe what modern optics calls a "cone" of light spreading from a single point.</note> is imagined extending from the center of sight to the surface of the mirror, let a point be chosen on that surface. If a line of the pyramid is imagined from the center of sight to that point—since infinite lines can be drawn from that point—if one of them has the same position relative to the side of the pyramid and holds an equal angle with the perpendicular, then reflection can occur from any chosen point on the mirror. I say, therefore, that among the lines drawn from the chosen point, there is a line that has the same position as the side of the pyramid and holds an equal angle with the perpendicular at that point. That line is the side of an imagined pyramid meeting the surface of the object from that point; whatever falls upon the end of that line, when it comes through it to the chosen point, will be reflected to the sight along the aforementioned side of the pyramid. This side of the pyramid and the line produced from that point will be in the same plane, which is orthogonal <note>meaning "at a right angle"</note> to the surface touching the mirror at 그 point. I say this when there is an inclination of the side of the pyramid over the chosen point. For if it falls perpendicularly upon the surface touching the mirror at the chosen point, the side of the pyramid produced from the center of sight will be reflected back onto itself and return to the sight at the origin of its motion <note>original: "per 11 n."</note>.

In a plane mirror, what we have said is clear. Since a ray falls on any point of a flat surface, a perpendicular line can be raised from 그 point above that surface. From the center of sight, a line can be imagined falling perpendicularly onto the same flat surface (or its extension). By geometric rules <note>original: "per 35 d 1," likely referring to Euclid's Elements</note>, these two perpendiculars will be in the same plane because they are parallel <note>original: "per 6 p 11"</note>. A line drawn from the end of one to the end of the other on the flat surface will form an angle with both and will be in the same plane with both. The ray that rises from that line will hold an acute angle with the perpendicular of the mirror, and similarly with the perpendicular of the sight. <note>The text notes that angle *d c e* is acute because it is part of the right angle *d c a*, and this equals *a e c* because lines *a e* and *d c* are parallel.</note> And if a line of the flat surface is imagined to be produced in the other direction, passing perpendicularly over the ends of the perpendiculars, it will form a right angle with the perpendicular of the mirror on the other side. Therefore, an acute angle can be cut from that right angle equal to the acute angle which the ray holds with that same perpendicular. These two angles are in the same plane. Thus, the incoming ray and the reflected ray are in the same plane, specifically the plane of the aforementioned perpendiculars. When another point is observed, the same arrangement of rays and perpendiculars will occur: one from the center of sight, the other from the point seen. In every plane of reflection, therefore, there is a meeting of four points: the center of sight, the point perceived, the end of the perpendicular drawn from the center of sight, and the point of reflection. All planes of reflection intersect at the imagined perpendicular from the point of reflection; this perpendicular is common to all planes of reflection. Since the same occurs for any point inspected on a flat surface, there will be a similar reflection from all points in the same manner.

### 24. *If the sight is outside the surface of a convex spherical mirror, or a surface continuous with it, the common section of the base of the optical pyramid and the surface of the mirror will be the circumference of a "small circle" on the sphere.* <note>Reference to Proposition 3, Book 6. A "small circle" is any circle on a sphere's surface that does not pass through the center, unlike a "great circle" or equator.</note>

In spherical mirrors, what we have said will be evident: when a spherical mirror is placed opposite the sight (and "opposite" means the sight is not on the surface of that mirror or a surface continuous with it). When this mirror is inspected, the part of it grasped by the sight will be a part of the sphere enclosed by a circle smaller than a great circle. This circle is created by the motion of a ray touching the surface of the sphere if it is moved in a circuit, staying tangent to the sphere until it returns to the first point where the motion began. If we imagine surfaces intersecting through the diameter of the sphere (starting from the pole of the aforementioned circle), any arc of the spherical surface common to these surfaces—imagined from the pole of the circle to the circle itself—will be less than a quarter of a great circle. This is because a line drawn from the center of the sphere to the end of the ray touching the sphere (which is at the aforementioned circle) holds a right angle with the ray by reason of tangency <note>original: "per 18 p 3," referring to Euclid's rules on tangents</note>. It therefore holds an acute angle with the semi-diameter produced from the pole of the circle <note>original: "per 17 p 1"</note>, and the arc lying between the pole and the circle corresponds to this angle. <note>The text concludes that the periphery *c s* is less than a quadrant of the sphere's maximum circumference, citing the "Spherics" of Theodosius, a classical Greek work on the geometry of the sphere.</note>

# ALHAZEN

[...the circle is distant from its pole by a quadrant of the circumference of a great circle: the circumference described on the spherical surface by the rotation of a ray from a single point of sight touching the sphere will be smaller than the circumference of a great circle.] <note>This concludes a proof from the previous page regarding the "great circle," which is the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, sharing the same center and radius.</note>

***25. If of two straight lines from the point of sight, one touches a convex spherical mirror and the other cuts through the center: the tangent line, rotated around the fixed cutting line, will define a segment of the mirror's surface from any point of which a reflection to the sight can occur. And the centers of the sight and the mirror, the points of reflection, and the visible points all lie within the plane of reflection. 2. 5. 6 p 6.*** <note>These numbers are cross-references to other propositions in the text.</note>

I say, therefore, that from any point of this portion <note>The "portion" refers to the segment of the sphere's surface visible to the eye.</note> a reflection can occur. For when any point of it is taken: the diameter of the sphere imagined from that point will be perpendicular to the flat surface touching the sphere at that point [by the 4th theorem of the 1st book of Spherics]. And this is the proof of that matter. If two surfaces are imagined cutting the sphere through the diameter taken from the chosen point: the lines common to the surface of the sphere and these surfaces are circles of the sphere passing through the chosen point [by the 1st theorem of the 1st book of Spherics]. And if two lines are imagined touching these circles at the chosen point: the diameter will be perpendicular to both lines [by the 18th proposition of the 3rd book]. Therefore, it is perpendicular to the surface in which those lines lie [by the 4th proposition of the 11th book].

And when a ray falls upon the chosen point: it will be in the same plane as the diameter of the sphere whose end is the chosen point [by the 2nd proposition of the 11th book], and the line imagined from the center of sight to the center of the sphere—which indeed passes through the pole of the circle (and is the ray falling perpendicularly upon the surface of the sphere) [because by the 4th theorem of the 1st book of Spherics it is perpendicular to the plane touching the sphere at that point]—is similarly in the same plane [by the 2nd proposition of the 11th book]. And from these three lines, a triangle will be formed. And the ray falling upon the chosen point forms an acute angle with the diameter of the sphere from the outside; since this ray is higher than the ray touching the sphere, it will cut the sphere when it is understood to be extended. And the surface touching the sphere at the chosen point will be lower than this ray; and it will cut between the sphere and the sight, the viewed diameter—that is, the line imagined from the center of sight to the center of the sphere, passing through the pole of the circle.

Wherefore, since the diameter of the sphere is perpendicular to the surface touching the point: it will hold an angle greater than a right angle on the inner side with the ray descending to the point; wherefore [by the 13th proposition of the 1st book] on the outer side it will hold with it an angle less than a right angle. And when extended, it will be perpendicular to the surface touching the exterior [by the 4th theorem of the 1st book of Spherics]. Therefore, from the right angle which it holds with the surface on the other side of the ray, an acute angle can be cut off equal to that which the ray includes with that diameter; and these three lines and the two included angles will be in the same plane [by 6, 13 n.].

Therefore, from the chosen point of the segment, a line can be produced in the same plane as the ray falling on that point, and the perpendicular line in the surface touching the point, and at an equality of angles with that perpendicular. And the form <term>forma</term> <note>Alhazen uses "forma" (form) to describe the light or image-information traveling from the object to the eye.</note> of the point moved toward the surface of the mirror through that ray will meet that line. Therefore, it has the same position as the line that can be reflected [by 12 or 18 n.]. And the plane in which these lines lie will be perpendicular to the surface of the sphere at the touching point [by 13 n.]. And this must be understood for any point of the segment. Therefore, in every plane of reflection, there will be the center of sight, the center of the sphere, the point of reflection, and the reflected point. And all these surfaces will intersect upon the line drawn from the center of sight to the center of the sphere. And for any plane of reflection and the surface of the sphere, the common line will be a circle of the sphere [by the 1st theorem of the 1st book of Spherics]. And all these circles will intersect at the point of the sphere where the diameter of sight falls, which is above the pole of the segment's circle. However, when a ray falls upon the mirror perpendicularly to the surface at the point where the ray hits the sphere (and that ray is the diameter of sight through the pole of the segment's circle to the center of the sphere), reflection to the sight occurs along the same ray back to the source of the ray's movement [by 11 n.].

***26. If two planes from the center of sight are drawn through the sides bounding the visible surface of a convex cylindrical mirror: they will touch the mirror and form a common section at the sight parallel to the axis of the mirror. 2. 3 p 7.***

In columnar <note>A "columnar" mirror refers to what we now call a cylinder.</note> mirrors, however, what we have said will be clear. Let a columnar mirror, polished on the outside, be placed opposite the eye (that is, the opposition is such that the sight is not on the surface of the column, nor on a surface continuous with it). And let us imagine a plane from the center of sight to the surface of the column, cutting the column along a circle equidistant from the bases of the column. And in this plane, let two lines be taken touching the circle of the section at two opposite points; from each of those points let a line be produced along the length of the column; and let two planes be imagined in which these two lines of length lie, and the two lines drawn from the center of sight touching the circle of the section. I say that these surfaces will touch the column. For if it were said that one of them cuts it: it is clear that the section is along the line of the length of the column in which the surface falls [by the 21st definition of the 11th book]. and similarly there will be a section along the line of length

### BOOK IV OF THE OPTICS

opposite to this column; and the circle of the section passes through these two longitudinal lines <note>A "longitudinal line" refers to a straight line running along the length of the cylinder's surface, parallel to its central axis.</note>: and the line touching the circle of the section—since it lies in some surface—cuts the column along certain longitudinal lines that are parallel to each other. And if it passes through one of them, it will pass through the other, and with an equality of angles. Therefore, since it passes through the point where the circle of the section cuts the first longitudinal line, it will also pass through the point where another longitudinal line touches this circle, and thus it cuts the circle. Therefore, it does not touch it [as a tangent], which is contrary to the hypothesis. It is clear, therefore, that those two surfaces touch the mirror, and what falls between them on the surface of the mirror is what appears to the sight. Moreover, since the intersection of those two surfaces occurs at the center of vision, they will cut each other, and the common line of section will pass through the center of vision and will be parallel to the axis of the column. For since the axis of the column is orthogonal <note>Orthogonal: meeting at a right angle (90 degrees).</note> to the circle of the section [by the converse of Proposition 14, Book 11 <note>original: "per conuersam 14 p 11"</note>] and the longitudinal lines of the column are orthogonal to the same circle [by Proposition 8, Book 11, for the sides of a cylinder are parallel to the axis, which is perpendicular to the circle of the section by Definition 21, Book 11], the surfaces touching the column along these lines will also be orthogonal to the same circle [by Proposition 18, Book 11], and therefore also to the surface cutting the column in that circle. For this reason, the common line of these surfaces is orthogonal to the same surface [by Proposition 19, Book 11] and therefore parallel to the axis of the column [by Proposition 6, Book 11].

***27. If a straight line drawn from the center of vision to a point on the visible surface of a convex cylindrical mirror is continued, it will cut into the mirror.*** <note>Propositions 4 and 5 of Book 7.</note>

I say, therefore, that for whatever point is chosen in the visible section of the mirror, a line produced from the center of vision to that point will cut the mirror. Since the longitudinal line of the column understood to be at the chosen point will pass through the circle of the section and touch it at a point, if a line is drawn from the center of vision to that point, it will cut the mirror, because it falls between the lines touching this circle. Therefore, the surface proceeding from the center of vision, in which this line lies, will also cut the mirror. Since the line drawn from the center of vision to the chosen point is in the same surface, that line will cut the mirror; and thus any line understood from the center of vision to that portion of the mirror cuts the mirror. In the same way, any line understood from the common line passing through the center of vision to this portion cuts the mirror. Hence, any surface touching the mirror at some line of the visible portion cuts the surfaces that touch the extremities of the portion; and none of all the surfaces touching the portion reach the center of vision, but rather extend between the sight and the mirror.

***28. In a convex cylindrical mirror, reflection to the sight can occur from any point on the visible surface.*** <note>Proposition 25 of Book 7.</note>

I say, therefore, that light can be reflected from any point of this portion. For given a point, let a circle be made upon it parallel to the bases of the column. If, therefore, the surface proceeding from the center of vision and cutting the surface of the column parallel to the base cuts it along this circle, and the line drawn from the center of vision to the center of the circle passes through the given point, the reflection of the form of that point will occur along that same line to the origin of the line [by Note 11 <note>original: "per 11 n"</note>], because that is the axis of vision perpendicular to the axis of the column [by Definition 21, Book 11 and Proposition 29, Book 1]. Moreover, if any point is taken through which the axis passes perpendicular to the axis of the column, the reflection of that point will occur along that same axis [by Note 11]. But if the chosen point lies beyond the axis, whatever line is drawn from the center of the circle (which is parallel to the bases) through that point to the tangent surface at the longitudinal line of the column passing through that point, it will be orthogonal to the axis [by Definition 21, Book 11 and the converse of Proposition 14, Book 11]. Therefore, it is orthogonal to the longitudinal line passing through that point [by Proposition 29, Book 1]. And since the sight is higher than the surface touching the point, the line drawn from the center of vision to the chosen point will hold an acute angle with that perpendicular drawn from the point to the center of the circle. This is on the outer side, because it has an obtuse angle on the inner side; and from the right angle which that perpendicular holds with the line of the surface touching the circle [by Proposition 18, Book 3], an acute angle equal to this one can be cut away. That perpendicular and the center of vision are in the same surface; therefore, they are also in the same surface as the line drawn from the center [of the circle] to the point. Thus, the reflected line will be in the same surface as the line drawn from the center to the point. And this surface will be orthogonal to the surface touching the mirror at that point, since the perpendicular falls orthogonally upon this surface; such will be the surface of reflection.

There is, however, a difference between the lines common to the surfaces of reflection and the surface of the column. For when reflection occurs through the same ray, that same ray will fall orthogonally upon the axis, and the common line...
