...of the intersection of the surface of the column and the surface of reflection, it will be a straight line—specifically, the side of the column—whenever the diameter of the column lies within the surface of reflection. This is evident because the composition of a column is formed by the movement of a surface with equidistant sides around one stationary side <note>By [Definition 21, Book 11] of Euclid’s *Elements*. Alhazen describes the generation of a cylinder by rotating a rectangle.</note>. Whence, for a surface cutting the column in which the axis is located (that is, the stationary side), the intersection line with the surface of the column will be the "moving side" <note>This "moving side" is a longitudinal line on the cylinder's surface.</note>. And I say that of all possible surfaces of reflection, there is only one in which the intersection with the surface of the column is a straight line. This is because only a single surface can be conceived that contains both the axis of the column and the center of vision, and no more.

### *30. If the eye is outside the surface of a convex cylindrical mirror, in a plane of the visible object perpendicular to the axis: the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror will be a circle: and there is only one such circle in the same visible surface from which reflection to the eye can occur. [Proposition 9. 17 p 7].*

If, however, the surface of reflection is parallel to the bases of the column, the intersection line will be a circle <note>By [Theorem 5 of Serenus, *On the Section of a Cylinder*]. Serenus was a 4th-century mathematician who specialized in the geometry of cylinders and cones.</note>. And this is the only surface that has a circular intersection with the surface of the column. This is because, in every reflection, the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of reflection is the diameter of the circle that is parallel to the bases of the column. There cannot be more than one circle on the column’s surface parallel to the bases that also shares the same surface with the center of vision.

### *31. If the eye is outside the surface of a convex cylindrical mirror, in a plane of the visible object oblique to the axis: the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror will be an ellipse: and multiple points can exist in the same visible surface from which reflection to the same eye may occur. [Proposition 10. 18 p 7].*

However, all other surfaces of reflection cut through the column and the axis of the column. Since the perpendicular line drawn from the point of reflection cuts the axis of the column, the lines common to these surfaces and the surface of the column are the "sections" <note>Specifically "conic sections," which geometers like Apollonius defined as the shapes formed when a plane intersects a cone or cylinder.</note> which geometers assign to columns and pyramids.

### *32. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror is the side of the cylinder or a circle: the reflection made from any point of the common section will always occur in that same surface. [Proposition 19. 20 p 7].*

When the intersection of the surfaces of the column and the reflection is a straight line, at whatever point on that line the eye gazes, the reflection will occur in that same surface in which the axis lies. This is because there is only one surface touching the column along that longitudinal line. At whatever point on this line is chosen, the perpendicular drawn from it to the axis will be in the same surface as the axis; and this line will be orthogonal to the surface that is tangent to the surface of the column. (For because the side of the cylinder is parallel to the axis [by Definition 21, Book 11], the straight line perpendicular to the axis will also be perpendicular to the side [by Proposition 29, Book 1]. It is also perpendicular to the line touching the circle described through that same point on the side [by Proposition 18, Book 3]. Therefore, it will be perpendicular to the plane touching the mirror [by Proposition 4, Book 11].) But the center of vision is in a surface orthogonal to that same tangent surface, because the center of vision, the intersection line, and the axis of the column are all in one surface [by 6. 11 η] and that is the only surface orthogonal to that tangent surface [by Proposition 13, Book 11]. Therefore, all reflections made from the points of this line are in the same surface of reflection. 

Likewise, when the intersection line of the surface of reflection and the column is a circle, at whatever point on that circle the object is seen, the reflection occurs in one and the same surface. This is because any perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection will be the diameter of this circle, and therefore lies in the surface of this circle. The point of vision is similarly situated, and this surface is orthogonal to the surface tangent to any point chosen on this circle. Therefore, in this surface alone will the reflection of any point of the aforementioned circle occur.

### *33. From one point of the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror, one visible point is reflected to one eye in the same surface. [Proposition 22 p 7].*

However, if any other intersection line is chosen, reflection will not occur in that same surface of reflection except from one single point of this line. This is because the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection is orthogonal to the longitudinal line of the column passing through that point [by Definition 3, Book 11], and thus also to the axis [by Proposition 29, Book 1]. That perpendicular is the diameter of the circle parallel to the bases of the column. The surface of reflection and that circle intersect each other, and their common line is the diameter of that circle. That diameter is perpendicular to the surface touching the column at that point, and it is inclined <note>original: "declinata," meaning slanted or at an angle rather than perpendicular.</note> toward it. Therefore, that surface of reflection will also be inclined toward the axis. In a flat surface inclined toward some line, only one line can be conceived as falling orthogonally upon it. But if reflection were to occur from two points of the surface of reflection in the same surface, there would be two lines in that surface orthogonal to the axis, which is impossible since that surface is inclined toward it. For the perpendicular from the point of reflection falls into the circle parallel to the bases of the column and into a point on the axis, and it is the common section of the circle's surface and the reflection's surface. If, therefore, reflection were to occur from another point of the common line in the same surface, another perpendicular drawn from that other point would be the diameter of another circle of the column parallel to this one, and it would fall upon a point of the axis where the surface of reflection does not fall. And so it must be understood in all surfaces of reflection: that from only one point of the common line does reflection occur in the same...

### BOOK 4 OF OPTICS

...the same surface, with respect to the same sight: since with respect to two eyes, reflection can occur from two points on the surface of the mirror, such as at the ends of the diameter of a circle that is perpendicular to the section itself. However, with respect to a single eye, this does not happen: because those two points cannot be perceived simultaneously by the same eye; for it is always necessary that the visible part of the cylinder <note>original: "columnæ"</note> be less than half.

### 34. *If a straight line from the point of reflection is perpendicular to a convex cylindrical mirror: when continued inward, it will pass through the center of the circle parallel to the bases: and vice versa. [Proposition 21, Book 7].*

It is clear from what has been said before that the perpendicular understood at the point of reflection, if produced outward and inward, forms the diameter of the circle. Because if it did not: since it is established that the diameter of the circle passing through that point is perpendicular to the surface tangent to the cylinder <note>original: "columnam"</note> at that point [as shown in 32] and similarly perpendicular outward: there will be [by Book 1, Proposition 14 of Euclid's *Elements*] continuity between these perpendiculars, and they will form a single line. Because if it were not the case that the diameter produced outward was perpendicular to that surface, it would happen that two perpendiculars were erected from the same point of the surface [contrary to Book 11, Proposition 13]. Therefore, in every surface of reflection, the meeting of four points is evident: the center of sight; the point on the axis where the perpendicular falls; the point of reflection on the mirror; and the point from which the form of the body proceeds.

### 35. *If from a viewpoint outside the surface of a right convex conical mirror (or its continuation), a straight line makes an acute angle with the vertex of the axis: two planes drawn through straight lines from the viewpoint that are tangent to the mirror and the conical sides passing through the points of contact will be tangent to the mirror, and they will bound the visible surface (less than half) from which reflection to the viewpoint occurs. [Propositions 1 and 2, Book 7].*

In conical <note>original: "pyramidalibus"</note> mirrors polished on the outside and standing perpendicular to their bases, the viewpoint is positioned opposite: so that the sight is not on the surface of the mirror, nor on its continuation. Depending on the position of the eye relative to the conical mirror, the size of the part perceived in it will be determined. Therefore, if we imagine a ray from the center of the eye to the end of the axis of the cone—that is, to the vertex <note>original: "acumen"</note>—we can imagine a surface from the center of sight cutting the cone into a circle parallel to the base of the cone. We then imagine two lines from the center of sight tangent to that circle at opposite points, from which we draw lines along the length of the cone. Thus, the surface formed by one of these longitudinal lines and one of the tangent lines to the circle will be tangent to the cone. If it were to cut the cone, it would touch a point other than the point of tangency of the circle; let a longitudinal line be drawn over that point, and both that point and the vertex of the cone are simultaneously in this surface. Therefore, that line will be in this surface and will pass through some point of the circle; that point is therefore in this surface and in the circle. Thus it is on the common line of the circle and the surface; but that line is tangent to the circle: therefore the tangent passes through two points of the circle, which is impossible [and contrary to Book 3, Definition 2]. It remains, therefore, that this surface is tangent to the cone. And generally, every surface in which lines meet—tangent to some point of the cone and the longitudinal line passing through that point—is tangent to the cone along that longitudinal line. We have, therefore, two surfaces proceeding from the center of the eye that are tangent to the cone, between which is the portion of the cone visible to the eye in this position: and it is less than half of the cone, because the lines tangent to the circle include a part of it that is less than half.

<note>This diagram illustrates Proposition 35. Point 'b' represents the eye looking at a cone with vertex 'a'. The lines from 'b' grazing the sides of the cone (at 'f' and 'g') define the boundaries of what the eye can see.</note>

### 36. *If a straight line from the viewpoint is perpendicular to the vertex of the axis of a right convex conical mirror: two planes drawn through straight lines tangent to the mirror at the endpoints of the diameter of a circle parallel to the base, and the conical sides passing through the points of contact, will be tangent to the mirror: and they will bound the half-visible surface from which reflection to the viewpoint occurs. [Proposition 89, Book 4].*

If, however, the line drawn from the center of sight to the vertex of the cone holds a right angle with the axis, and a circle is imagined cutting the cone parallel to the base: the line common to this circle and the surface (in which the axis of the cone and the center of sight are located) will be perpendicular to the axis of the cone. This is because the axis is perpendicular to the surface of the circle [by the converse of Book 11, Proposition 14: so that by Book 11, Definition 3, the axis of the cone is perpendicular to all lines by which it is touched in the plane of the circle]. And upon this common line, let a diameter perpendicular to this line be drawn through the center of the circle; and from the endpoints of this perpendicular diameter, let two tangents to the circle be drawn, and also two lines up to the vertex of the cone. The two surfaces in which these two lines and the tangents are located will be tangent to the cone in the manner described before.

*37. Therefore, in this position, the sight perceives a part of the pyramid greater than half.

*39. If a straight line from the sight to the vertex of a right convex conical mirror is aligned with the axis, the entire conical surface will be visible. [Witelo, Book 4, Prop. 92].*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a right circular cone (referred to as a pyramid in the text) viewed from an angle. It includes the vertex, an axis line through the center of the circular base labeled 'c', and a line 'k' along the lateral surface. Points are labeled with lowercase letters.</image-desc>

And if the line falling from the center of sight to the end of the axis enters the pyramid: I say that no point on the entire surface of the pyramid is hidden from sight. For if any point is taken on the surface of the pyramid, let a line be understood from the center of sight to that point, and another from that point to the apex of the pyramid. These two lines, together with the line drawn from the center of sight to the end of the axis (which enters the pyramid), define a triangular surface. This triangle lies in a plane that cuts the pyramid, since every surface containing a line that enters the pyramid must cut it.

The line drawn from the center of sight to the chosen point cuts the longitudinal line <term>longitudinal line: the slant height or a line drawn from the apex to the base along the surface</term> that runs from that point to the apex. Of the lines in the surface where these two lines exist, there are only two lines on the surface of the pyramid: namely, this longitudinal line from the point to the apex, and another opposite it, which divides the angle formed by this line and the line entering the pyramid. Therefore, that opposite line, extended outside the pyramid, cuts the line from the center to the chosen point. Consequently, this line cuts two lines, which are the only lines from this surface that lie on the pyramid’s surface: one outside the pyramid and the other at the chosen point.

Therefore, even if extended to infinity, it will not meet any of those lines; thus, the chosen point is not hidden from sight, according to the method stated above. In this position, therefore, none of the planes touching the pyramid will pass through the center of sight; instead, each will cut the line from the sight to the end of the axis entering the pyramid, between the sight and the pyramid, specifically at the end of the axis.

When, however, the line of sight is applied to the longitudinal line of the pyramid, none of the planes touching the pyramid reach the center of sight except the one that touches the pyramid at that specific line. All other touching planes will cut that line between the sight and the vertex of the pyramid. Similarly, in a position where two tangent planes pass through the center of sight, any plane touching the pyramid on the visible portion (which lies between the two visual tangents) turns away from the center of sight. Wherever a visual line falls on any point of that portion, it will cut the pyramid because it falls between the two visual tangents. The surface containing this visual line and the longitudinal line of the pyramid will cut the pyramid, and this visual surface will be continuous with every surface of the pyramid in this portion, and thus also with the sight.

*49. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex conical mirror is a conical side, then reflection can occur from any visible point on the surface to the sight. [Witelo, Book 7, Prop. 31].*

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram showing a cone on a circular base with various lines of projection, reflection, and tangency. Geometric points are labeled with letters g, d, h, e, n, i, z, k, and x.</image-desc>

I say, therefore, that in any position, reflection can occur from any point. For let a point be taken, and imagine a circle passing through that point, parallel to the base of the pyramid. The diameter of this circle starting from this point will be perpendicular to the axis [by Prop. 5, Book 11 <note>original: "per 5 d 11"</note>], since the axis is perpendicular to the surface of the circle [by Prop. 18, Book 11, and the converse of Prop. 14, Book 11].

Therefore, the longitudinal line drawn from the point to the apex of the pyramid forms an acute angle with the diameter, and an acute angle with the end of the axis in the same surface [by Prop. 32, Book 1, because the angle formed by the axis and the semi-diameter *g d* is a right angle]. Let the visual line falling on the point be in the surface containing the longitudinal line and the axis; at that point, let a perpendicular be drawn to the longitudinal line. This perpendicular will indeed meet the axis [by Axiom 11]. A triangle will be formed from this perpendicular, the axis, and the longitudinal line.

At that point, imagine a tangent line, and on the diameter of the circle we made, imagine another diameter perpendicular to it. This will be perpendicular to the axis itself, and to the surface in which the axis and the first diameter lie [by Prop. 4, Book 11]. This second diameter is parallel to the tangent line [by Prop. 28, Book 1], since the tangent is perpendicular to the first diameter [by Prop. 18, Book 3]. Thus, the tangent line is perpendicular to the surface containing the axis and the first diameter [by Prop. 8, Book 11]. Therefore, it will be perpendicular to the first perpendicular we made [by Definition 3, Book 11], and so that first perpendicular falls orthogonally upon the surface touching the pyramid where the point was taken. Therefore, if the visual line falling on the chosen point follows the path of the perpendicular, it will indeed be orthogonal to the surface...

...the cone <note>original: "pyramidem"; the author uses "pyramid" to refer to what we now call a cone</note> at the point of contact, and the reflection of the form will occur along that same line [by proposition 11]. However, if it deviates from the perpendicular path, it will indeed form an acute angle with the perpendicular at the chosen point; and another line of sight can be produced from that point in the same surface, which maintains an angle equal to this one with the perpendicular, since the perpendicular is orthogonal to the tangent surface. Furthermore, any line falling orthogonally upon the tangent surface at the chosen point passes to the axis [by proposition 11 on the axis: for it is perpendicular to the side of the cone: because, since by thesis it is perpendicular to the plane touching the cone at the side by proposition 6 or 35, it will be perpendicular to the side itself by definition 3]. And if an orthogonal line is drawn from the axis to this surface, the interior and exterior perpendiculars will form a single line [by proposition 14 of Book 1]. For if not, since the interior perpendicular, when produced outward, is also perpendicular to the surface, it would happen that two perpendiculars are erected from the same point upon the same surface in the same direction [which contradicts proposition 13 of Book 11]. It is clear, therefore, that from any visible point on the surface of the cone, a reflection can occur at equal angles. And when the tilted line meets it, the form comes to the mirror along this line and is reflected to the sight along the other; and these lines are in the same orthogonal surface, above the surface tangent to the cone at the point of reflection [by propositions 6 and 13]. And this is the **plane of reflection**, in which four points are always contained: namely, the center of the sight, the point seen, the point of reflection, and the endpoint of the perpendicular.

> 41. *The common section of the planes of reflection and of a convex conical mirror is either a side of the cone or an ellipse; but it is never a circle. [Proposition 12 of Book 7].*

The common lines of the plane of reflection and the surface of the cone vary. For when the visual ray is continuous with the axis of the cone—that is, when the entire axis and the perpendicular passing to the axis are within the plane of reflection—the common line of the plane of reflection and the surface of the cone will be the **longitudinal line** <note>Also known as the generatrix</note> in this position. Since any plane in which the whole axis exists has this common line with the surface of the cone [as is clear from definition 18 of Book 11]. In every other position, a single longitudinal line of the cone will be common: specifically, the one that is in the plane containing the center and the axis. And when the center of sight is not directly aligned with the axis, there will be only one such plane; and every other common line will be a conic section, not a circle. For if it were a circle, the plane of that circle would be in the plane of reflection. And because the axis is orthogonal to that circle [by definition 18 of Book 11, and the converse of proposition 14 of Book 11], since every circle of the cone is parallel to the base [by theorem 4 of Book 1 of Apollonius’s *Conics*], the sides of the cone would be tilted relative to the circle, and thus relative to the plane of reflection. Therefore, in that plane, a perpendicular cannot be drawn to the longitudinal line of the cone; but [by propositions 6 and 12] a perpendicular drawn to the surface touching the place of reflection is in the plane of reflection, and is perpendicular to the longitudinal line [as was shown in the previous number], since any tangent surface touches along the longitudinal line [by propositions 6 and 35]. An impossibility therefore occurs [against proposition 13]. Thus, it remains that all other common lines of reflection are conic sections.

> 42. *If the common section of the planes of reflection and of the convex conical mirror is a side of the cone, reflection from any of its points will always occur in the same plane. [Proposition 19 of Book 7].*

And when the common line is a longitudinal line, from whatever point of that line reflection occurs, it will be in the same plane as the reflection from any other point. Since a perpendicular drawn from any point of this line will reach the axis [as shown in number 40], and the center of sight, the point of reflection, and the point on the axis will be in the plane of reflection. Therefore, in this plane, reflection occurs from any point.

> 43. *If the common section of the planes of reflection and of the convex conical mirror is an ellipse: reflection to the sight can occur in the same plane from one or two points of any visible surface. [Proposition 34 of Book 7].*

If, however, the common line is not a longitudinal line, I say that reflection occurs in the same plane either from one point of the common line, or from only two. Since a perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection reaches the axis and falls upon some point of it [as was evident in number 40], and by imagining a circle through the point of reflection, the circle will cut the axis orthogonally. (Because the circle is parallel to the base by theorem 4 of Book 1 of Apollonius’s *Conics*, the axis will be perpendicular to it, by definition 18 and the converse of proposition 14 of Book 11.) And because the perpendicular maintains an acute angle with the axis, the perpendicular will be tilted relative to the circle, and if rotated around, it will always be equal. Hence a secondary cone is formed, whose base is the circle and whose apex is the point on the axis where the perpendicular falls. Therefore, the plane of reflection either touches this cone or cuts it. If it touches it: I say that reflection can only occur in that same plane from the chosen point of reflection. For the plane that the plane of reflection touches will touch this secondary cone along the perpendicular, which is the orthogonal line in the plane of reflection [by propositions 6 and 35]. And if lines are drawn from the apex of the total cone to the common section of the plane of reflection and the total cone, they will fall upon the circle (which is the base of the imagined cone) before they fall upon the section—except for one, which falls upon the point of reflection. If, therefore, reflection were to occur from another point of the common section, the line drawn from that point to the apex of the imagined cone would be perpendicular to the longitudinal line of the cone—

...of the cone <note>original: "pyramidis"; here the author uses "pyramid" to describe a geometric cone</note>, passing through that point [as was shown before]: but the line from the tip <note>original: "acumine"; the vertex of the cone</note> of the conceptual cone to the point of the circle, through which that line of length <note>a "line of length" or "longitudinal line" is a line drawn from the vertex to the base along the surface of the cone</note> passes, is without doubt perpendicular to it. Therefore, another line forms an acute angle with this line, not a right angle. [Otherwise, the three angles of a rectilinear triangle would be greater than two right angles, contrary to Proposition 32 of Book 1: which follows as an absurdity from concluding right angles at *c r i* and *c i r*.] If, however, the surface of reflection cuts the conceptual cone, it will cut the circle that forms the base at two points. [For since the common section of the ellipse (which by the thesis is the surface of reflection) and the circle (which is the base of the conceptual cone) is a straight line by Proposition 3 of Book 11, bounded by two points: the ellipse therefore cuts the circle at two points, namely the ends of that straight line.] I say that these are the only points in the entire common section from which reflection can occur in that same surface. Since from both of those points, a line drawn to the tip of the conceptual cone is perpendicular to the line of length passing through its own point. For from whatever other point of the section a line is drawn to the tip of that cone, it will form an acute angle with the line of length passing through it, since the perpendicular forms a right angle with that same line of length in the circle. And the lines drawn from the tip of the conceptual cone to the points of the section which fall between the tip of the mirror and the circle will make obtuse angles with the lines of length toward the side of the tip of the total cone; and those drawn to points lying between the circle and the base of the mirror will make acute angles with the line of length on the side of the mirror's tip, and obtuse angles on the side of the base. Therefore, reflection cannot occur from any of these points.

*44. If the sight <note>the observer's eye or point of view</note> is on the concave surface of a spherical mirror: it will see the whole [surface]: if inside or outside: sometimes a hemisphere, sometimes more, sometimes less: if at the center: it will see only itself. [Cross-references to related propositions 71, 72 of book 4; 4 of book 8.]*

In concave spherical mirrors, if the eye is within the concavity of the mirror, the entire surface of the mirror will appear to it. But if it is outside, it can perceive a portion of it greater than half—specifically, that portion defined by the circle of the sphere which is touched by two rays drawn from the center of vision. However, if the eye is at the center of this mirror, no reflection will occur from any point of the mirror except back into itself. Since any line drawn from the center of a sphere to the sphere's surface is perpendicular to the surface tangent to the sphere at that point [by Proposition 25 or Theorem 4 of the Spherics]: therefore, in this position, the eye will perceive nothing by reflection except itself [by Proposition 11].

*45. If the sight is outside the center of a hollow spherical mirror: a visible object can be reflected from any of its points to the sight: except for that point where a straight line drawn from the sight through the center of the mirror falls. [Cross-references 6; 3 of book 8.]*

If, however, the eye is placed outside the center of the sphere, a reflection of another visible object can occur from any point of the mirror, except from the point where the diameter—drawn from the center of vision to the sphere through the center of the sphere—falls. This is because the diameter falls orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> upon the surface tangent to the sphere [by Proposition 25, and therefore it is reflected back into itself by Proposition 11]. But taking any other point, let a diameter be drawn to it from the center of the sphere, and a line from the center of vision. An acute angle will be included between these lines: since the visual line falls between the diameter and the tangent surface at that point, which is outside the sphere. And whether the eye is inside the mirror or outside, the visual line falls inside the mirror because it falls between the visual lines tangent to the circle of the sphere's portion. Thus, if the diameter *g b* and the line of reflection *g a* are joined and continued to the periphery, the angle *a g b* will be acute [by Proposition 31 of Book 3 and Proposition 32 of Book 1]. Since the diameter forms a right angle with the tangent [by Proposition 18 of Book 3], let an acute angle be cut from it, equal to the aforementioned one in the same surface; I say, therefore, that the line of reflection falls inside the mirror. This is because the common line of the mirror and the surface of reflection is a circle, forming with the diameter an acute angle greater than any rectilinear acute angle [by Proposition 31 of Book 3]. And this mode of reflection will exist at every single point. It is clear from this that in every surface of reflection there will be: the center of vision, the center of the mirror, the point of reflection, the point being seen, and the end of the diameter drawn from the center of vision through the center of the sphere; and that the line common to all surfaces of reflection and the surface of the mirror is a circle; and that reflection can occur from any point of that common line in the same surface.

ALHAZEN

### *46. In a concave cylindrical mirror, the surface of reflection contains four points: the eye, the visible object, the point of reflection, and the axis, onto which the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection falls.* <margin>Proposition 3 of Book 9; Proposition 83 of Book 4</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a vertical cylinder. A horizontal circular or elliptical cross-section is drawn in the middle. Points are labeled: 'a' at the center of the top circular face, 'b' at the center of the bottom face, 'c' on the right edge of the middle cross-section, and 'd' on the left side of the cylinder's surface. Lines represent optical paths or geometric projections connecting these points, illustrating principles of reflection in a concave cylindrical mirror.</image-desc>

**I**n concave cylindrical mirrors <note>original: "speculis columnaribus"; literally "columnar mirrors," the standard term for cylinders</note>, the entire mirror can be perceived if the eye is located inside it. However, if the eye is situated outside, a portion larger than half of the mirror will be visible—specifically that which lies between two surfaces proceeding from the center of vision and touching <note>tangent to</note> the cylinder. Let us consider a surface proceeding from the center of vision that is parallel to the bases of the cylinder. This surface will either intersect the cylinder or it will not. If it intersects, the line common to this surface and the cylinder will be a circle [according to the 5th theorem of Serenus's *On the Section of a Cylinder*]. The visual line passing through the center of this circle will fall perpendicularly upon the surface that touches the cylinder at the point where the line falls [as was demonstrated in section 32]. Reflection will then occur along that same line back to its origin [according to section 11]. Therefore, since a straight line (which, by Proposition 1 of Book 11, exists in a single plane) passes through the points of the eye, the visible object, the reflection, and the axis (where the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection falls), that line itself will be within one plane of reflection. Whatever other point is chosen, a line drawn perpendicularly from that point will fall upon the axis [as was clear in section 40]. The visual line falling on that point will form an acute angle with the perpendicular line [as shown in the preceding section], since it lies between the perpendicular and the tangent. It is clear that this line falls within the mirror because it falls between the surfaces touching that portion. Therefore, in the same surface of reflection, we can determine an acute angle from the angle which the perpendicular makes with the tangent, equal to the aforementioned acute angle. The line of reflection containing this angle will fall within the cylinder, since it falls between the perpendicular and the longitudinal line <note>a line running the length of the cylinder</note> passing through the end of the perpendicular. Thus, in the surface of reflection, there will be the center of vision, the point of reflection, the visible point, and the point on the axis where the perpendicular falls.

### *47. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the concave cylindrical mirror is a side of the cylinder or a circle, the reflection made from any point of that section will occur in the same surface.*

**A**nd if the eye is positioned in such a way that the common line of the surface of reflection and the surface of the cylinder is a longitudinal line, then from whatever point on that common line reflection occurs, it will be in one determined surface common to all these reflections—specifically the one in which the center of vision and the entire axis of the cylinder are located, as was said above regarding the non-concave <note>convex</note> cylindrical mirror [section 32]. Similarly, if the common line is a circle, all reflections made from points of that circle will proceed in the same surface, as was evident in other circles.

### *48. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the concave cylindrical mirror is an ellipse, the same visible object can be reflected to the same eye from multiple points of that section in the same surface.* <margin>Proposition 9 of Book 9</margin>

**I**f the cylindrical section is the common line, reflection will occur from two of its points in the same surface, although in the previously discussed cylinders [section 33] reflection occurred from only one point in a single surface with a single eye. This is because, in those cases, the points of the section facing each other (through which the circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder passes) were hidden from the eye. When one of those points was seen, the other was hidden due to the appearance of a smaller portion of the cylinder. But in these [concave mirrors], a larger portion of the cylinder is visible; hence, from a single viewpoint, the points marking the ends of the diameter of the circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder are perceived.

### *49. If the eye is inside a concave conical mirror, its entire surface will be seen; if it is outside and a straight line from the eye is continuous with the axis or the side of the cone, the whole interior will be hidden.* <margin>Proposition 5 of Book 9; Proposition 3 of Book 8</margin>

**I**n concave pyramidal <note>meaning conical</note> mirrors, if the eye is inside the mirror, it will see the whole of it. But if the eye is outside, and a line drawn from the center of vision to the tip <note>apex</note> of the pyramid enters the pyramid or is joined to a longitudinal line of the pyramid, nothing of the mirror will be seen. This is because any other line drawn from the eye to the pyramid will fall on the exterior surface of the pyramid, thus hiding the interior surface. However, if a portion of the pyramid is removed, a part of the pyramid can be seen—specifically the larger part falling between the tangent surfaces drawn from the center. And if the line from the center of vision is perpendicular to the surface touching the pyramid and is continuous with the axis, the common lines (as was said of other pyramidal mirrors) will be either longitudinal lines of the pyramids or sections. In these, reflection can occur from two points of the section in the same surface with respect to the same eye. In the surface of reflection, there will be the center of vision, the visible point, the point of reflection, and the point of the axis where the perpendicular falls.

<meta>This page concludes the fourth book of Alhazen’s Optics, focusing on how light behaves inside conical mirrors, and introduces the fifth book, which begins the systematic study of where images appear to be located (the "place of the image").</meta>

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF OPTICS.

*50. If the eye is placed opposite the base of a concave conical mirror, a visible object placed inside the mirror will be seen. Proposition 6 of Book 9.*

However, if a complete pyramidal <note>original: "pyramidale"; used here to describe the cone shape</note> mirror is placed opposite the eye, and the eye is positioned toward the base, it will perceive nothing except what is inside the mirror. This is because the perpendicular forms an acute angle with the line drawn from the eye to the mirror at the base; consequently, the reflection occurs toward the point <note>the vertex</note> of the cone. [For the reflected ray leans toward the side opposite the ray that falls obliquely on the mirror, according to the 10th theorem.] Thus, all reflected lines will fall inside the pyramid, and whatever is placed inside the pyramid can be seen. But if a portion of the mirror is removed along its length, then external objects can be perceived, since a path is opened for the lines of reflection to exit. Similarly, if the pyramid is cut like a ring so that the vertex is removed, the lines will have a free entrance and external things will appear. Furthermore, if the eye is positioned toward the concave surface of the mirror, it can perceive more external objects than if it were at the base, because a wider path is provided for the incoming lines.

*51. From any single point on any mirror, only one point of a visible object is reflected to one eye. Propositions 29, 30, and 31 of Book 5; also Proposition 37 of Book 5; also in the prefaces of Books 1, 5, and 10.*

Furthermore: if a single point on any mirror is chosen, it is impossible for more than one point of a form to be perceived through it by the same eye. This is because only one surface <note>plane</note> passes through the perpendicular and the center of vision, and there is only one line from the center of vision to that point. There is only one acute angle formed by the perpendicular line, and only one acute angle in that same surface equal to it [otherwise a part would equal the whole, which contradicts Axiom 9]. Therefore, there is only one line that makes an equal angle with the perpendicular; and when that line reaches the object, the form of another point cannot be carried through it, since the point in front hides the one behind it. 

However, two eyes can perceive two distinct points at the same point on the mirror. This is because an infinite number of surfaces can be identified intersecting along the perpendicular; in any of these surfaces, two equal acute angles can be formed around that perpendicular. 

Now, therefore, we have explained the property of reflection, and likewise the specific nature of every mirror. When the eye perceives forms through reflection, it does not realize that this acquisition happens via reflection. Reflection is not a property of the eye itself; even if the eye is removed, the form still proceeds from the object to the mirror and is reflected in the manner described. If it happens that the eye is in the location where those reflected lines gather, the eye will perceive that form at the heads of those lines. The form exists in the mirror not as if it had arrived there, but as if it were the mirror’s own natural form. 

Furthermore: sometimes the eye perceives forms in mirrors on the surface itself, sometimes inside the mirror, and sometimes beyond it. The apparent location of the form will depend on the shape of the mirror and the position of the visible object. The form will always be perceived in its own specific location even if the position of the eye and the mirror changes; however, the distance of that location from the surface of the mirror will vary according to the shape of the mirror. This location of the form is called the **place of the image** <term>locus imaginis: the position where a virtual image appears to the observer</term>. And the form itself is called the **image**. The eye perceives the visible thing in the place of the image. We shall discuss that location and its specific properties in each of the mirrors we have listed, and we shall assign the causes for why visible things are perceived in that place; this we shall do in the following book, if God wills.

## ALHAZEN'S OPTICS
### THE FIFTH BOOK.

This **BOOK** is divided into two parts. The first part is the prologue of the book. The second part concerns images.

->PROLOGUE OF THE BOOK. CHAPTER I.<-

*1. An image is a visible form reflected from a polished surface. In the definitions of Book 5.*

It is clear from the fourth book [Theorem 2] that the forms of visible things are reflected from polished <note>original: "politis"; smooth or mirrored</note> bodies, and the eye perceives them in these polished bodies because of reflection. It has also been shown [Theorems 20 and 21 of Book 4] how the perception of things occurs through the reflection of forms. The eye perceives the visible thing in a fixed location, provided the position of the object relative to the eye does not change. The form perceived in a polished body is called an **image**. In this book, we will explain the locations of images in polished bodies; we will say how knowledge of these locations is acquired and how they may be found through logical reasoning <note>original: "syllogisticè"</note>.

->ON THE LOCATIONS OF IMAGES. CHAPTER II.<-

*2. In a plane mirror, the image is seen at the intersection of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. Proposition 37 of Book 5.*

The location of the image of any point is the point at which the line of reflection intersects the perpendicular line understood to be drawn from the point of the visible object to the line tangent to the common line of the mirror's surface,

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s investigation into the "place of the image" (locus imaginis). Having finished the Fourth Book on the general principles of reflection, he now provides geometric proofs for why images in plane and convex spherical mirrors appear where they do—specifically at the intersection of the reflected ray and the perpendicular line dropped from the object to the mirror surface.</meta>

# ALHAZEN

...or to the surface continuous with the mirror and the surface of reflection. And we shall demonstrate these things. Let a plane mirror be taken and placed parallel to the horizon; let a straight, polished rod <note>original: "lignum"; literally wood, but here referring to a physical rod used as an experimental object</note> be erected upon the mirror. Let the size of the mirror be such that the whole rod can be seen; for unless the whole appears, an error will occur. Let a certain black point be marked on the rod. To the sight, a rod equal to this one will indeed appear beyond the mirror, continuous with this rod and perpendicular <term>orthogonal<gloss>meeting at a right angle</gloss></term> to the mirror. In the appearing rod, the marked point will appear just as far from the surface of the mirror as the same point is distant in the actual rod above.

And if the rod is tilted over the mirror, the appearing image will seem tilted with that same inclination. The point marked in the appearing image will seem equally distant from the surface of the mirror. And if from the marked point a rod is erected perpendicularly above the mirror, this rod will also be seen from the appearing point perpendicularly above the mirror and continuous with this perpendicular. The same will happen for several points marked on the rod. The same will happen entirely whether the mirror is raised or lowered. It is clear, therefore, through this, that the image of a seen point appears on the perpendicular drawn from the seen point to the surface of the mirror.

And in this mirror, the line which is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror is also perpendicular to the common line of the mirror's surface and the surface of reflection. The same can be shown in a pyramid <note>Alhazen uses "pyramid" to refer to both cones and pyramids; here he describes a solid object standing on a base</note> standing perpendicularly on its base, whose flat base is applied perpendicularly to a plane mirror. Another continuous pyramid will appear, and the base of these pyramids will be the same, and their apexes <note>original: "acumina"</note> will be equally distant from the mirror. It is clear that if a straight line is drawn from apex to apex, it will be perpendicular to the base, and thus to the mirror, since the surface of the mirror and the base are the same. Therefore, the vertex of the pyramid will be seen on the perpendicular drawn from it to the mirror.

Similarly, from whatever point of the pyramid a line parallel to the axis is drawn, it will fall on the corresponding point in the appearing pyramid; and that line will be perpendicular to the base and the surface of the mirror [by Proposition 8 of Book 11 of Euclid's Elements]. Therefore, the image of any point of the pyramid falls on the perpendicular imagined from that point to the surface of the mirror. But whatever point is placed opposite a plane mirror, one can imagine a pyramid of which that point is the vertex [by Proposition 14 of Book 4], which pyramid is perpendicular to its base and also to the surface of the mirror or continuous with it. One can also imagine another pyramid opposite this one, sharing the same base, and the perpendicular from vertex to vertex will be at a right angle to the mirror. Therefore, the image of any point opposite the mirror falls on the perpendicular drawn from the point to the surface of the mirror or its continuation.

But [by Proposition 21 of Book 4] it is clear that in mirrors the perception of forms does not occur except through lines of reflection. Therefore, the image of a seen point falls on the line of reflection; and any such line is straight. Therefore, the image of any point falls on the point of intersection of the perpendicular drawn from that point to the surface of the mirror and the line of reflection. And in plane mirrors, the common line of the surface of the mirror and the surface of reflection is one line with the line touching the place of reflection. Therefore, it is clear that in plane mirrors, the location of the image is the point of intersection of the perpendicular from the seen point to the line touching the common line of the mirror's surface and the surface of reflection, and the line of reflection.

*3. In a spherical convex mirror, the image is seen at the intersection of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. Proposition 11 of Book 6.*

In spherical mirrors polished on the outside <note>convex mirrors</note>, what we have said will be clear. Let a large mirror surface of this kind be sought, in which the form of a slender rod, erected perpendicularly upon it, may appear. The form of the rod will indeed appear continuous with the rod itself. A marked point will appear in the form of the rod, distant from the surface of the mirror according to its distance from the same in the actual rod. And if the rod is slenderer at one end than at the other, its form in this mirror will indeed appear pyramidal; this is an error of sight, which we will explain later.

Furthermore: let a pyramid be made perpendicular to a circular base of perfect curvature, and let it also be applied to this mirror. A pyramid will indeed be seen continuous with this one, erected on the same base, but smaller than the original. That it appears as a pyramid is clear from the fact that all lines from the appearing image of the vertex to the circle of the base seem equal. And if the pyramid is tilted slightly over the mirror from the position in which it is entirely seen—so that some part of it is hidden, provided the place of reflection on the mirror is exposed to sight—the image of the pyramid will still appear. And if the sight is moved further from the mirror or closer, provided it falls on the line drawn from the place of reflection to the eye, the image of the pyramid will be perceived. But the approach or retreat along this line will be such that the place of reflection is noted, and a line is drawn from that mark to the location of the eye, along which the movement occurs.

However, since the image of the perpendicular pyramid is over the base of the pyramid, and the base is one of the circles in the sphere, the line drawn from the vertex of the pyramid to the vertex of the image will be perpendicular to the sphere and will pass through its center [by Propositions 6 and 8 of Book 1 of the Conics <note>Apollonius of Perga’s Conics, a foundational text on geometry</note>]. It will be perpendicular to the sphere, pass through the center of the sphere, and be perpendicular to the surface touching the sphere at the point through which this line passes [by Theorem 4 of Book 1 of the Spherics, or Proposition 25 of Book 4]. Similarly, it will be perpendicular to the line touching the circle of the sphere passing through that point [by Definition 3 of Book 11]. This tangent is the line common to the surface of reflection and the surface touching the sphere at that point; and this line touches the circle of the sphere common to the surface of the sphere and the surface of reflection. Therefore, the line drawn from the vertex of the pyramid to the vertex of the image is perpendicular to the tangent line—the line common to the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror—which is a circle. Therefore, the image of the vertex is seen on this perpendicular. And it is clear [by Proposition 21 of Book 4] that the image of the vertex is on the line of reflection. Wherefore...

### 4. In convex cylindrical and conical mirrors, the image is seen at the intersection of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. [Proposition 37, Book 5].

In mirrors that are cylindrical <note>original: "columnatibus"; literally columnar</note> and polished on the outside, those things we said regarding the rod and the pyramid do not appear: because a straight line in these mirrors does not appear straight; this is a common error of sight, the cause of which we will assign later. However, it happens that the aforementioned location of the image can be seen at a single point of the body in this way. Using the instrument from the previous book <note>Alhazen’s specialized apparatus for measuring angles of reflection</note>, let a ruler be inserted, to which the cylindrical mirror is fixed, so that the middle line of the mirror's section is on the surface of the ruler, and this ruler does not pass through the brass plate, but falls orthogonally upon it, so that the height of the ruler is above the line dividing the triangle of the brass plate. Once the erection is made on this plate, let it be filled with wax and smoothed to a flat surface so that it is in the same surface as the plate; this is to ensure the ruler is more certainly perpendicular to the plate. 

Next, let a sharp ruler be sought, and its end sharpened, and let the sharpness of this ruler be applied to the middle surface of the ring of the line, and let it descend according to this line, and where it falls upon the ruler, let a mark be made. Afterward, let a needle <note>original: "acus"; used here as a precise pointer or object of sight</note> descend, in which a small white object is fixed: and let this be at the end, so that the needle does not descend all the way to the ruler. Let the sight be applied so that it is in the surface of the ruler, and let one eye be closed: the image of the object will indeed be seen on the line stretched from the marked point to the tip of the needle: which line is indeed perpendicular to the surface of the ruler, which surface touches the cylinder in the line of its length: and it is perpendicular to the line of the cylinder's length which is in the surface of the ruler: and it is the common line of the surface of the ruler and the surface of reflection: and in the surface of reflection are the line of length and the perpendicular line. 

And if the position of the sight is changed, and the sight is rotated around the surface of the ring: things will appear as before: the object, the image of the object, and the needle all on the same line. And that line is perpendicular to the middle line of the cylinder's length: and this is a perpendicular in the surface of reflection: because the surface of the ring cuts the cylinder at a circle parallel to the base of the cylinder: and the sight is in this surface. And we shall prove later that when the sight and the seen object are in a surface parallel to the base of the cylinder, that is the surface of reflection. In this position, the line common to the surface of the cylinder and the surface of reflection is a circle: and the perpendicular in which the image and the object are seen falls orthogonally upon the line tangent to this circle. 

Once these things are done, let the needle be removed from its place, and let the sharp ruler be placed over the middle line of the ring, so that it falls upon the middle line of the ruler's length, and let the sharp ruler be fixed firmly to the surface of the ring with wax. Afterward, let the ruler in which the mirror is placed be removed, and let the sharp ruler be taken, and let its sharp edge be applied to the middle line of the ruler's length, and let a mark be drawn with ink upon the mirror following the path of the sharp edge. Then let a small wax triangle be taken, one side of which is equal to the height of the ruler in which the mirror is held, and let the thickness of this triangle be moderate, and let the surfaces of this triangle be as flat as possible: and let the triangle be applied firmly to the cylinder's ruler beneath the base of the ruler, and let its side equal to the height of the ruler be placed upon the side of the base of the ruler. 

When it is so arranged, the height of this triangle will be above the base of the cylinder equal to the ruler. And to create a flat surface in the manner of the ruler's surface, let the triangle be enclosed between the ruler and the flat surface, and pressed until it is well flattened, and let the sharp ruler be placed upon the surface of this triangle, and let the end of this triangle be cut with the ruler's sharp edge; its end will then be a straight line, and this line will be the base of the ruler in which the mirror is located. Afterward, let the ruler be placed upon the surface of the plate that is in the instrument, and let the end of its base which is in the length (which is the side of the wax triangle) be placed upon the line which is in the length of the plate, just as was done before: and the surface of the ruler in which the mirror is located will be orthogonal to the brass plate: and this surface cuts the brass plate along the line which is in the surface of the mirror: and this surface touches the surface of the mirror along the line which is in the surface of the mirror: and this is the surface of the ruler in which the mirror is: and the angle of the sharp ruler adhering in the middle of the line of the ring's surface, in which surface the mirror will be, will be tilted toward the part where the head of the triangle is: because the ruler raised one part of it with the body of the triangle, and the other part, which is after the head of the triangle, is the surface of the brass plate: and the line which is in the middle of the mirror will be tilted. 

And when the side of the wax triangle is upon the line which is in the length of the brass plate: the ruler in which the mirror is will be moved: and the side of the triangle in this motion, if it is upon the line of length of the brass plate, shall proceed or recede until the angle of the sharp ruler meets some point of the line of the mirror's surface, until the sharp ruler is fixed; and let the line made on the mirror with ink be removed: and let a point be made on the surface of the mirror directly in line with the head of the sharp ruler, and let the sharp ruler be removed, and the needle be applied, and let the needle be on the middle line of the ring's surface, and let it be forced to adhere with wax: the conceptual line from the needle to the point marked on the surface of the mirror will be perpendicular to the surface of the ruler, which touches the surface

I will complete the mirror upon the marked point, and the perpendicular upon any line drawn from that point into the surface tangent <term>tangent<gloss>a line or surface that touches a curve or solid at a single point without crossing it</gloss></term> to the mirror. *5. Of the straight lines falling from the same visible point onto a plane or convex mirror: the perpendicular is the shortest. [Proposition 21, Book 1].*

If lines are drawn from a seen point to the surface of a mirror: that which is perpendicular is shorter than any other. Because any other line first intersects the common line of the surface tangent to the mirror (upon which the perpendicular falls orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note>) and the surface of reflection, before it reaches the mirror: and any line drawn from the seen point in this surface to this common line is greater than the perpendicular [by Proposition 19, Book 1] because it faces a larger angle [namely the right angle *a e f* in triangle *a e f*]. Thus the proposition is clear.

*6. In a concave spherical mirror, the image is seen at the intersection of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. [Proposition 37, Book 5].*

In concave spherical mirrors, some images are perceived beyond the mirror; some on the surface; and some on this side of the surface. Of these, some are perceived in truth <note>accurately or clearly</note>, and some besides the truth <note>distorted or illusory</note>. All those whose truth is perceived appear in the place where the perpendicular and the line of reflection intersect; which will be shown as follows. Let a pyramid <note>original: "pyramis"; in this context, it refers to a cone</note> be made, and let its axis be orthogonal to the base: and let the diameter of the base be less than half the diameter of the sphere: and let the line of the pyramid's length <note>the slant height</note> be greater than that same semi-diameter: and let it be cut from the side of the base to its quantity <note>its measure</note>, namely the semi-diameter: and let a circle be made upon the section: and let the pyramid be cut upon this circle.

Afterwards, in the middle of the mirror, let a circle be made to the size of the base of the remaining pyramid: and let the pyramid be fitted to this circle and fixed with wax. Then let the sight be placed in a position where it can perceive the image of the pyramid: and let light be applied so that the perception becomes more certain: you will not see the pyramid joined to this, but you will perceive it extended beyond the mirror: whence a certain continuous pyramid will appear, whose base is beyond the mirror, and part of it is the wax pyramid. And if a line of length <note>a line drawn down the side of the cone</note> is marked on this pyramid with ink: this line will be seen to extend over the surface of the appearing pyramid. And since the vertex of the pyramid is the center of the sphere: the line drawn from the vertex according to the length of the pyramid will be perpendicular to the line tangent to any circle of the sphere passing through the head of the line [for every side of the cone is equal to the semi-diameter of the sphere by construction: therefore the vertex of the cone is the center of the greatest circle in the sphere, whose semi-diameter is the side: and so by Proposition 18, Book 3, it is perpendicular to the tangent line]. Therefore, every line of length of the appearing pyramid is perpendicular to the line tangent to the common line of the surface of reflection and the surface of the sphere: which common line is indeed a circle [by Theorem 1 of the Sphaerics] and every point of the pyramid is seen in this perpendicular: and every perpendicular is in the surface of reflection [by Proposition 23, Book 4]: since the seen point and its image are in the perpendicular and in this surface: and every image is perceived in the line of reflection [by Proposition 21, Book 4]. Therefore, the image of any point of the pyramid will be at the point of intersection of the perpendicular...

However, the points whose images are perceived in front of the mirror—that is, between the eye and the mirror—occur when a line drawn from any of those points to the center of the mirror intersects the width of the path lying between the eye and the mirror. And so that this may be seen: let a pyramid <note>original: "pyramis"; likely a small triangular or conical marker used in the experiment</note> be taken from the middle of the mirror and placed to the side; its vertex will be the center of the mirror, and the distance of the eye should be greater than the radius of the sphere. The form of the head of the stick will then appear in front of the mirror, closer to the eye than the vertex of the pyramid; and the vertex of the pyramid, the head of the stick, and the image of the head will all lie on the same straight line.

The line passing through these two points lies within the surface of reflection. The common line <note>The intersection of the mirror's surface and the plane of reflection.</note> is a circle, and this line will be the diameter of that circle because the center of that circle is the center of the sphere. Therefore, this line will be perpendicular to the line tangent to the circle at the head of this line [according to Theorem 18, Proposition 3], and this line passes through the point being seen and its image. Thus, any point seen in front of the mirror is grasped on the same line as its center and its image; and any point is seen on the line of reflection [according to Theorem 21, Note 4]. Consequently, it is seen at the point of intersection of the perpendicular and the line of reflection. 

Those things whose true form is grasped in these mirrors are those whose images appear beyond the mirror or in front of its surface; besides these, there are no others which the eye perceives in truth in this mirror, for the objects themselves prevent their true images from appearing. The images that appear on the surface of this mirror belong to the final classification, and we shall explain these when we speak of the errors of vision. Therefore, any point truly perceived in this mirror appears at the meeting of the perpendicular and the line of reflection; indeed, this perpendicular passes from the observed point to the center of the sphere and falls at a right angle <term>orthogonaliter<gloss>at a 90-degree angle</gloss></term> onto the tangent of the common line.

### *7. In concave cylindrical and conical mirrors, the image is seen at the meeting of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. [Theorem 37, Prop 5].*

In concave columnar <note>original: "columnaribus"; referring to cylindrical mirrors</note> mirrors, the image varies: sometimes its location will be on the surface of the mirror, sometimes beyond it, and in all these cases, it will sometimes be grasped truthfully and sometimes not. When you wish to perceive the location of the image in these mirrors, do as you did with the exterior cylindrical mirrors. Let a ruler be employed in which there is a concave column, just as was used above, and likewise a needle, and a small body at the tip of the needle. Let the sight be placed opposite in the middle of the circle and in the middle of the surface of the ring; let the eye be raised slightly from the surface of the ring and look until it sees the image of the body. It should grasp the form of the body, the body itself, and a point marked on the mirror on the same perpendicular line to the mirror's surface—and this is done through a sensory syllogism <note>original: "syllogismum sensualem"; a term used by Alhazen to describe the mind's automatic, logical deduction based on visual data.</note>. 

The image will be beyond the mirror, and the reflection will be from a point on the straight line that is in the middle of the mirror. Then, let the sight be positioned on the surface of the ring, but away from the center, until it sees the image of the small body; it will indeed see it in front of the mirror. It will see the body, its image, and the point marked on the mirror all on one straight perpendicular line, which is perpendicular to the straight line tangent to the circle parallel to the base of the mirror at the marked point on the mirror’s surface. The surface of this is the surface of reflection in this position, which is the face of the ring, and the point of reflection is a point on that circle. 

Afterward, let another needle be held by hand, at the tip of which is a small body; let it be placed on the surface and the axis in such a way that the body and the marked point are on the same line, according to the sensory syllogism. Let the eye be on the surface of the ring, between its head and the middle; it will indeed see the image of the body, and it will see this image and its body and the marked point on the surface of the mirror all on the same straight line. If, however, the straight line is inclined with the small triangle we made, and the eye is in the middle of the ring, it will see the image in front of the mirror, but on the same straight line as the body and the marked point. This reflection will be from the cylindrical sections, since the mirror is inclined; and we know [from Theorem 21, Note 4] that the image is not perceived except on the line of reflection. It is clear, therefore, that the location of the image is where the perpendicular intersects the aforementioned line of reflection when truth is perceived. Even if the certainty of the image is not grasped, the nature of these images will be consistent with the images of truth. In the same way, you will be able to see the image in concave pyramids <note>conical mirrors</note> at the meeting of the perpendicular with the line of reflection. It is clear, therefore, that in all mirrors, images are perceived in the aforementioned place, which is likewise called the "location of the image."

### *8. The image in any mirror is seen at the meeting of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. [Theorem 37, Prop 5].*

Now, we shall declare the cause of why visible things are perceived through reflection in the locations of their images, and why the image lies upon the perpendicular drawn from the visible thing to the mirror’s surface. When the eye acquires a form through reflection, it acquires it immediately without certainty, and it acquires length through estimation; and it may perhaps grasp this length in truth through diligent attention, or perhaps not. We explained this in the second book [Notes 24, 25, 38, 39], and it was said there that...

the common line between the surface of the cylinder <term>cylinder; original: "columnae"</term> and the surface of reflection will be a straight line, specifically the side of the cylinder, provided that the diameter of the cylinder lies within the surface of reflection. This is evident because a cylinder is composed of the motion of a surface with parallel sides around one fixed side [according to Book 11, Definition 21]. Therefore, for a surface cutting the cylinder in which the axis—that is, the fixed side—is located, the common line between that surface and the cylinder's surface will be the moving side. And I say that of all the surfaces of reflection, there is only one in which the common line with the cylinder's surface is a straight line. This is because only one surface can be imagined in which both the axis of the cylinder and the center of sight are contained, and no more.

*30. If the eye is outside the surface of a convex cylindrical mirror, in a plane of the visible object perpendicular to the axis: the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror will be a circle; and there is only one such circle in the same visible surface from which reflection to the eye can occur. [Corresponding to Proposition 9, or 17 in Part 7].*

**If**, however, the surface of reflection is parallel to the bases of the cylinder: the common line will be a circle [according to Theorem 5 of Serenus’s *On the Section of a Cylinder* <note>Serenus of Antinoupolis was a 4th-century mathematician known for his work on cylinders and cones.</note>]. This is the only surface that has a circular common line with the surface of the cylinder. This is because in every reflection, the perpendicular to the surface tangent to the point of reflection is the diameter of the circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder; and there can be only one circle parallel to the bases on the cylinder's surface that is in the same plane as the center of sight.

*31. If the eye is outside the surface of a convex cylindrical mirror, in a plane of the visible object oblique to the axis: the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror will be an ellipse: and several points can exist in that same visible surface from which reflection to the same eye occurs. [Corresponding to Proposition 10, or 18 in Part 7].*

**All** other surfaces of reflection, however, intersect both the cylinder and the axis of the cylinder; since the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection intersects the axis of the cylinder. The common lines between these surfaces and the surfaces of the cylinder are the "sections" <note>conic sections like parabolas or hyperbolas</note> that geometers assign to cylinders and pyramids <term>pyramids; here meaning cones</term>.

*32. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror is the side of the cylinder, or a circle: reflection occurring from any point of that common section will always occur in the same surface. [Corresponding to Propositions 19 and 20 in Part 7].*

**When** a straight line is common to the surfaces of the cylinder and the reflection, whatever point on that line the eye looks at, reflection will occur in the same surface in which the axis lies. This is because there is only one surface tangent to the cylinder along that longitudinal line; and at whatever point on this line is chosen, the perpendicular drawn from it to the axis will be in the same surface as the axis. This line will be orthogonal to the surface tangent to the cylinder's surface. [For since, by Book 11, Definition 21, the side of a cylinder is parallel to the axis: a straight line perpendicular to the axis will be perpendicular both to the side (by Book 1, Proposition 29) and to the straight line tangent to the circle described through that same point on the side (by Book 3, Proposition 18). Therefore, by Book 11, Proposition 4, it will be perpendicular to the plane tangent to the mirror.] But the center of sight is in a surface orthogonal to that same surface: because the center of sight, the common line, and the axis of the cylinder are all in one surface [by Propositions 6 and 13], and there is only one surface orthogonal to that surface [by Book 11, Proposition 13]. Therefore, all reflections from points on this line occur in the same surface of reflection. Truly, when the common line of the surface of reflection and the cylinder is a circle, reflection will occur in one and the same surface from whatever point of that circle is seen. This is because any perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection will be the diameter of this circle: therefore it is within the surface of this circle, and the point of sight is similarly so; and this surface is orthogonal to the surface tangent to whatever point of this circle is taken. Therefore, the reflection of any point of the aforementioned circle will be in this surface alone.

*33. From one point of the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror, one visible point is reflected to one eye in the same surface. [Corresponding to Proposition 22 in Part 7].*

**But** for any other common line chosen: reflection will not occur in the same surface of reflection except from only one point of this line. This is because the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection is orthogonal to the longitudinal line of the cylinder passing through that point [by Book 11, Definition 3], and therefore also to the axis [by Book 1, Proposition 29]. That perpendicular is the diameter of a circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder; and the surface of reflection and that circle intersect one another; and the line common to them is the diameter of that circle. That diameter is perpendicular to the surface tangent to the cylinder at that point, and the surface of reflection intersects that longitudinal line of the cylinder where the tangency occurs, and it is slanted toward it. Therefore, that surface of reflection will also be slanted toward the axis. In a flat surface slanted toward a given line, only one line can be imagined falling orthogonally upon it. But if reflection were to occur from two points of the surface of reflection in the same surface: there would be two lines of that surface orthogonal to the axis, which is impossible, since that surface is slanted toward it. For the perpendicular from the point of reflection falls into the circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder and into a point on the axis, and it is the common section of the circle's surface and the surface of reflection. If, therefore, reflection were to occur from another point of the common line in the same surface: another perpendicular drawn from that other point would be the diameter of another circle of the cylinder parallel to this one, and it would fall into a point on the axis where the surface of reflection does not fall. ### 34. *If a straight line from the point of reflection is perpendicular to a convex cylindrical mirror: when continued inward, it will pass through the center of the circle parallel to the bases: and vice versa. [Corresponding to Proposition 21 in Part 7].*

It is clear from the preceding that the perpendicular understood at the point of reflection, when produced outside and inside, forms the diameter of the circle. This is because if it did not: since it is established that the diameter of the circle passing through that point is perpendicular to the surface tangent to the cylinder at that point [as shown in number 32] and similarly perpendicular outside: there will be [by Book 1, Proposition 14] continuity between these perpendiculars, and they will form one line. Because if it is not the case that the diameter produced outside is perpendicular to that surface: it would happen that two perpendiculars are raised from the same point of the surface [which is impossible, contrary to Book 1, Proposition 13]. Therefore, in every surface of reflection, the meeting of four points is evident: the center of sight; the point of the axis on which the perpendicular falls; the point of reflection in the mirror; and the point from which the form of the body proceeds.
