### 35. *If a straight line from a viewpoint located outside the surface of a right convex conical mirror, or on its continuation, makes an acute angle with the vertex of the axis: two planes drawn through straight lines from the viewpoint, touching the mirror and the conical sides, passing through the points of contact, will touch the mirror, and will bound a visible surface less than half, from which reflection to the sight occurs. [Corresponding to Propositions 1 and 2 in Part 7].*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a cone with vertex marked 'a' at the top. To the left, a point 'b' represents the eye or viewpoint. Lines from 'b' extend towards the cone, tangent to a circular cross-section at points 'c' and 'e'. Points 'g' and 'd' are also marked on this circle, with 'd' on the vertical axis descending from 'a'.</image-desc>

In pyramidal mirrors <term>pyramidal; Alhazen uses "pyramis" to refer to a cone</term> polished on the outside and standing perpendicular to their bases, the position of the sight is opposite: so that the sight is not on the surface of the mirror, nor on its continuation. According to the position of the sight with respect to the pyramidal mirror, the size of the part perceived in it will be determined. Therefore, if a ray from the center of the eye to the end of the pyramid's axis—that is, to the vertex <note>original: "acumen intellectus," the understood peak</note>—makes an acute angle with the axis on the side of the pyramid: we will imagine from the center of sight a surface cutting the pyramid across a circle parallel to the base of the pyramid. We will then imagine two lines from the center of sight, tangent to that circle at opposite points, from which we will draw lines along the length <note>the "slant height" or lateral edges</note> of the pyramid. Therefore, the surface formed from one of these longitudinal lines and the other tangent to the circle will touch the pyramid. 

For if it were to cut into the pyramid: it would touch another point than the point of contact of the circle. Let a longitudinal line be produced through that point; that point and the peak of the pyramid are simultaneously in this surface. Therefore, that line will be in this surface, and it will pass through some point of the circle. That point is therefore in this surface and in the circle: thus it is in the common line of the circle and the surface. But that line is tangent to the circle: therefore the tangent passes through two points of the circle which it touches, which is impossible [and contrary to Book 3, Definition 2 of Euclid's Elements]. It remains, therefore, that that surface touches the pyramid. And generally, every surface in which a line meeting a tangent at some point of the pyramid, and a longitudinal line passing through that point, touches the pyramid along the longitudinal line. We have, therefore, two surfaces proceeding from the center of the eye, touching the pyramid, between which is the portion of the pyramid appearing to the sight in this position: and it is less than half of the pyramid: since the lines tangent to the circle enclose a part of it less than half.

[Corresponding to Proposition 89 in Part 4].*

If, however, the line drawn from the center of sight to the peak of the pyramid holds a right angle with the axis, and a circle cutting the pyramid parallel to the base is imagined: the line common to this circle and the surface in which the axis of the pyramid and the center of sight are located will be perpendicular to the axis of the pyramid. This is because the axis is perpendicular to the surface of the circle [by the converse of Book 11, Proposition 14: thus by Book 11, Definition 3, the axis of the cone is perpendicular to all lines by which it is touched in the plane of the circle.] And upon the common line, let a diameter perpendicular to this line be drawn through the center of the circle: and from the ends of this perpendicular diameter let two tangents to the circle be drawn: and also two lines up to the peak of the pyramid. The two surfaces, in which these two lines will be with the tangents, will touch the pyramid in the manner previously described.

### 39. *If a straight line from the eye to the vertex of a right convex conical mirror is continued with the axis: the entire conical surface will be visible.* <note>Reference to Proposition 92 of Book 4.</note>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a right circular cone. An axis line connects the apex 'a' to the center of the base 'c'. A transversal line 'k-r-t' intersects the side of the cone, illustrating how visual lines interact with the slanted surface.</image-desc>

And if a line falling from the center of sight to the end of the axis enters the cone: I say that no point on the entire surface of the cone is hidden from sight. For, having taken any point on the surface of the cone: imagine a line from the center of sight to it, and another from it to the apex of the cone. These two lines enclose a triangular surface with the line drawn from the center of sight to the end of the axis, which enters the cone; and this triangle is in a surface cutting the cone: since every surface in which there is a line entering the cone cuts it. But the line drawn from the center of sight to the chosen point cuts, at that point, the longitudinal line <note>The "line of longitude" or generator of the cone; essentially the straight line running from the tip to the base along the surface.</note> drawn from it to the apex of the cone. And of the lines on the surface in which these two lines lie, there are only two lines on the surface of the cone: namely this longitudinal line, drawn from the point to the apex, and another opposite one, cutting the angle included by this [line] with the line entering the cone. Therefore, that opposite line, produced outside the cone, cuts the line drawn from the center to the chosen point. Thus, this line cuts two lines, which are the only lines of this surface that are on the surface of the cone: one outside the cone, the other at the chosen point. Therefore, if produced to infinity, it will not meet any of those lines; hence the chosen point is not hidden from sight, according to the method stated above. In this position, therefore, none of the surfaces tangent to the cone will pass through the center of sight, but each will cut the line from the sight to the end of the axis entering the cone, between the sight and the cone: and it is at the end of the axis. When, however, the line of sight is applied to a longitudinal line of the cone: none of the surfaces tangent to the cone belongs to the center of sight except that which touches the cone at the aforementioned line: and all tangent surfaces will cut that line between the sight and the vertex of the cone. Similarly, in the position where two tangent surfaces of the cone pass through the center of sight: any surface touching the cone in the visible portion of the cone, which lies between the two tangents, diverges from the center of sight: and upon whatever point of that portion a visual line falls: it will cut the cone, since it falls between two visual tangents: and the surface, in which this visual line and the longitudinal line of the cone lie, will cut the cone: and this visual surface will be continuous with any surface of the cone in this portion: and thus with the sight.

...the cone <note>original: "pyramidem"; the author uses the term for a pyramid to describe a cone.</note> touching at that point, and the reflection of the form will occur through the same line [by proposition 11]. If, however, it deviates from the path of the perpendicular, it will indeed make an acute angle with the perpendicular at the chosen point. Another line can be drawn from that point on the surface of that visual line which maintains an equal angle with the perpendicular, since the perpendicular is at a right angle to the tangent surface. Any line falling perpendicularly upon the tangent surface at the chosen point passes to the axis [by proposition 11 regarding the axis: for it is perpendicular to the side of the cone; because, as stated in the thesis, it is perpendicular to the plane touching the cone at its side by proposition 6 or 35, it will instead be triple <note>This likely refers to a specific geometric ratio in the author's source text.</note> to the perpendicular side]. And if a perpendicular is drawn from the axis to this surface, the interior and exterior perpendiculars will form a single line [by proposition 14, book 1]. If this were not so—since the interior perpendicular, when extended outward, is also perpendicular to the surface—it would happen that two perpendiculars are raised from the same point on the same surface in the same direction [which contradicts proposition 13, book 11]. It is clear, therefore, that from any point on the surface of the cone being viewed, reflection can occur with equal angles. When the slanted line meets the surface, the form comes to the mirror along this line and is reflected to the sight along the other. These lines are in the same <term>orthogonal surface</term> <note>A plane that meets another at a right angle (90 degrees).</note>, standing upon the surface tangent to the cone at the point of reflection [by propositions 6 and 23]. This is the **plane of reflection**, in which four points are always contained: namely, the center of the sight, the point being seen, the point of reflection, and the end of the perpendicular.

### 41. *The common section of the planes of reflection and the convex conical mirror is either a side of the cone or an ellipse, but never a circle. [Proposition 12, book 7].*

The common lines where the plane of reflection and the surface of the cone intersect vary. For when the visual ray is continuous with the axis of the cone—that is, when the entire axis and the perpendicular passing through the axis are within the plane of reflection—the common line between the plane of reflection and the surface of the cone will be the <term>line of longitude</term> <note>The straight line running from the apex of the cone down its side to the base, also called a "generator."</note> in this position. This is because any surface containing the entire axis has this line in common with the surface of the cone [as is clear from definition 18, book 11]. In every other position, there will be only one such line of longitude in common, specifically the one in the plane containing the center of sight and the axis. When the center of sight is not directly aligned with the axis, there will be only one such surface; and every other common line will be a <term>conic section</term> <note>original: "sectio pyramidalis"; a curve formed by the intersection of a plane and a cone.</note>, not a circle. If it were a circle, the plane of that circle would be within the plane of reflection. Since the axis is perpendicular to that circle [by definition 18, book 11, and its converse in proposition 14, book 11], and since every circle of the cone is parallel to the base [by proposition 4 of the first book of <note>original: "Apollonij"; referring to Apollonius of Perga, a Greek mathematician known as 'The Great Geometer' for his work on conics.</note> Apollonius’s *Conics*], the sides of the cone would be slanted over the circle. Thus, they would be slanted over the plane of reflection, meaning a perpendicular to the line of longitude of the cone could not be drawn in that plane. But [by propositions 6 and 13] the perpendicular drawn to the surface touching the point of reflection is in the plane of reflection, and it is perpendicular to the line of longitude [as shown in the previous number], since every tangent surface touches along a line of longitude [by propositions 6 and 35]. Therefore, an impossibility occurs [contradicting proposition 13]. It remains, then, that all other common lines of reflection must be conic sections.

### 42. *If the common section of the planes of reflection and the convex conical mirror is a side of the cone, the reflection from any point on that line will always occur within that same plane. [Proposition 19, book 7].*

When the common line is a line of longitude, a reflection occurring from any point on that line will be in the same plane as the reflection from any other point. This is because a perpendicular drawn from any point on this line will touch the axis [as shown in number 40], and the center of sight, the point of reflection, and the point on the axis will all be in the plane of reflection. Therefore, reflection from any point happens within this plane.

### 43. *If the common section of the planes of reflection and the convex conical mirror is an ellipse: reflection to the eye can occur in the same plane from one or two points of the visible surface. [Proposition 34, book 7].*

If, however, the common line is not a line of longitude: I say that reflection occurs in the same plane either from only one point of the common line, or from only two. Since a perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection will reach the axis and fall upon some point of it [as was clear in number 40], if we imagine a circle passing through the point of reflection, that circle will cut the axis at a right angle [because the circle is parallel to the base by proposition 4 of Apollonius’s *Conics*; thus the axis is perpendicular to it by definition 18 and the converse of proposition 14, book 11]. And because the perpendicular maintains an acute angle with the axis, the perpendicular will be slanted over the circle; if rotated around, it will always be equal. Thus, a cone <note>original: "pyramis"</note> is formed, whose base is the circle and whose apex is the point on the axis where the perpendicular falls. Therefore, the plane of reflection either touches this cone or cuts it. If it touches it: I say that reflection can occur in that same plane only from the chosen point of reflection. For it is plain that the plane of reflection will touch this cone along the perpendicular, which is the orthogonal line in the plane of reflection [by propositions 6 and 35]. And if lines are drawn from the apex of the total cone to the common section of the plane of reflection and the total cone, they will fall upon the circle (which is the base of the imagined cone) before they reach the section—except for the one line that falls on the point of reflection itself. If, therefore, reflection were to occur from another point of the common section, the line drawn from that point to the apex of the imagined cone would be perpendicular to the line of longitude of the cone—

*44. If the eye is located within the hollow surface of a spherical mirror: it will see the whole thing; if inside or outside: sometimes a hemisphere, sometimes more, sometimes less; if at the center: it will see only itself. Propositions 71, 72 of Book 4; Proposition 4 of Book 8.*

IN concave spherical mirrors, if the eye <note>original: "uisus"; literally "the sight," used here to mean the observer's eye or viewpoint.</note> is within the concavity of the mirror: the entire surface of the mirror will appear to it. But if it is outside: it will be able to perceive a portion of it larger than half; specifically, that which is formed by the circle of the sphere which two rays drawn from the center of the eye touch. However, with the eye existing at the center of this mirror, reflection will not occur from any point of the mirror except back into itself. Since indeed any line drawn from the center of the sphere to the sphere is perpendicular to the surface touching the sphere at 그 point [by Proposition 25 or Theorem 4 of the *Spherics*], therefore in this position the eye will perceive nothing by reflection except itself [by Proposition 11].

*45. If the eye is outside the center of a hollow spherical mirror: a visible object can be reflected from any of its points to the eye, except for that point upon which the straight line drawn from the eye through the center of the mirror falls. Proposition 6; Proposition 3 of Book 8.*

IF, however, the eye is placed outside the center of the sphere: reflection of another visible object can occur from any point of the mirror, except from that point where the <term>diameter</term><note>A line passing through the center of the mirror and the observer's eye.</note>, drawn from the center of the eye to the sphere through the center of the sphere, falls. This is because the diameter falls orthogonally upon the surface touching the sphere [by Proposition 25, and therefore it is reflected back into itself by Proposition 11]. But if another point is taken, let a diameter be drawn to it from the center of the sphere, along with a line from the center of the eye. From these lines, an acute angle will be enclosed; because the visual line falls between the diameter and the surface touching the point, which is naturally outside the sphere. And whether the eye is inside the mirror or outside, the visual line falls inside the mirror, because it falls between the visual lines touching the circle of the portion of the sphere. Thus, if the diameter *g b* and the line of reflection *g a* are connected and continued to the periphery, the angle *a g b* will be acute by Proposition 31 of Book 3 and Proposition 32 of Book 1.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a spherical mirror with center c. A viewpoint f is located outside a segment of the circle. Lines of reflection are drawn from f to points on the circumference (g, d). A horizontal diameter passes through points a, c, and b, illustrating the geometry of reflection and angles within a concave surface.</image-desc>

Therefore, since the diameter maintains a right angle with the tangent [by Proposition 18, Book 3], an acute angle equal to the aforementioned one is cut from it in the same surface. I say, therefore, that the line of reflection falls within the mirror, since the common line of the mirror and the surface of reflection is a circle, maintaining with the diameter an acute angle greater than any rectilinear acute angle [by Proposition 31, Book 3]. And this mode of reflection will exist at every single point. It is clear from these things that in every surface of reflection there will be: the center of the eye; the center of the mirror; the point of reflection; the point seen by the eye; and the end of the diameter drawn from the center of the eye through the center of the sphere. Furthermore, the common line of all surfaces of reflection with the surface of the mirror is a circle, and reflection can occur in that same surface from any point of that common line.

### *46. In a concave cylindrical mirror, the surface of reflection contains four points: the eye, the object, the point of reflection, and the axis, where the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection falls. <note>References: 3 p 9. 83 p 4.</note>*

**I**n concave cylindrical mirrors <note>original: "speculis columnaribus concauis"</note>, the entire mirror can be seen if the eye is located inside it. However, if the eye is outside, a portion larger than half of the mirror will be visible—specifically, the part lying between two surfaces extending from the center of vision and touching <note>term: "contingentes" (tangent to)</note> the cylinder. Let us imagine a surface extending from the center of vision that is parallel to the bases of the cylinder. This surface will either intersect the cylinder or it will not. If it intersects, the common line between this surface and the cylinder will be a circle <note>according to Theorem 5 of Serenus's *On the Section of a Cylinder*</note>. The visual line passing through the center of this circle will fall perpendicularly upon the surface touching the cylinder at that point [as demonstrated in number 32]. Reflection will then occur along that same line back to its origin [according to number 11]. Thus, since a straight line (which, by Proposition 1 of Book 11, lies in a single plane) passes through the points of the eye, the object, the reflection, and the axis where the perpendicular falls, that line itself will be within a single plane of reflection. Whatever other point is chosen, a line drawn perpendicularly from that point will fall upon the axis [as shown in number 40]. The visual line falling on that point will form an acute angle with the perpendicular line [as shown in the previous number], since it lies between the perpendicular and the tangent. That this line falls inside the mirror is clear from this: it falls between the surfaces touching that portion. Therefore, in the same surface of reflection, we can determine an acute angle from the angle the perpendicular makes with the tangent, equal to the aforementioned acute angle. The line of reflection containing this angle will fall inside the cylinder, because it falls between the perpendicular and the longitudinal line <note>The "line of length" or "latus" running down the cylinder's side.</note> passing through the end of the perpendicular. Thus, the center of vision, the point of reflection, the object being seen, and the point on the axis where the perpendicular falls will all be in the surface of reflection.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circular cross-section within a rectangular frame. A vertical line passes through the center point 'f', with 'a' at the top of the circle and 'e' at the bottom. Point 'b' is located on the bottom edge of the frame. Points 'd' and 'c' are on the left and right edges of the circle respectively, connected by a horizontal line passing through the center 'f'. Other rays or lines are drawn within the circle originating from point 'f'.</image-desc>

### *47. If the common section of the reflection surfaces and the concave cylindrical mirror is a side of the cylinder or a circle, the reflection from any point of that section will occur in that same surface.*

**A**nd if the eye is positioned in such a way that the common line between the surface of reflection and the surface of the cylinder is a longitudinal line, then reflection from any point on that common line will occur in one determined surface. This surface is common to all these reflections—namely, the one in which the center of vision and the entire axis of the cylinder are located, as was said above regarding the non-concave cylindrical mirror [number 32]. Similarly, if the common line is a circle, all reflections made from points on that circle will proceed in the same surface, as is evident in other circles.

### *48. If the common section of the reflection surfaces and the concave cylindrical mirror is an ellipse, the same object can be reflected to the same eye from multiple points on that surface. <note>Reference: 8 p 9.</note>*

**A**nd if the intersection with the cylinder is a common line <note>referring here to an elliptical section</note>, reflection will occur from only two of its points in the same surface. This is true even though, in the convex cylinders mentioned earlier [number 33], reflection occurred from only one point in a single surface for a single eye. The reason is that in the former case, the points of the section facing each other (through which the circle parallel to the bases passes) were hidden from the eye; when one of those points was seen, the other was hidden due to the appearance of the smaller portion of the cylinder. But in these [concave mirrors], a larger portion of the cylinder is visible. Hence, from a single eye, the points terminating the diameter of the circle parallel to the cylinder's bases can be perceived.

### *49. If the eye is inside a concave conical mirror, its entire surface will be visible. If it is outside and a straight line from the eye is continuous with the axis or the side of the cone, the entire surface will be hidden. <note>References: 5. 2. 9. 3 p 9.</note>*

**I**n concave conical mirrors <note>original: "speculis pyramidalibus concauis"; the author uses the term for pyramid to describe a cone.</note>, if the eye is inside the mirror, it will see the whole mirror. But if it is outside, and a line drawn from the center of vision to the tip <note>original: "acumen"; the apex.</note> of the cone enters the cone or aligns with the longitudinal line of the cone, nothing of the mirror will be seen. This is because any other line drawn from the eye to the cone will fall on the exterior surface of the cone; therefore, the interior surface will be hidden. However, if a portion of the cone is removed, the part of the cone falling between the tangent surfaces drawn from the center—specifically the larger part—can be seen. And if the line from the center of vision is perpendicular to the surface touching the cone and is continuous with the axis, the common lines will be (as mentioned regarding other conical shapes) either the longitudinal lines of the cones or sections. In these, reflection can occur from two points of the section in the same surface relative to the same eye. In the surface of reflection, there will be the center of vision, the point seen, the point of reflection, and the point on the axis where the perpendicular falls.

<meta>This page concludes Book 4’s geometric analysis of conical mirrors and begins Book 5, which transitions from the physical laws of reflection to the study of "images"—specifically where and how the mind perceives an object to be located after its light has bounced off a surface.</meta>

<header>BOOK 4 OF OPTICS.</header>

*50. If the eye is placed opposite the base of a hollow conical mirror: a visible object placed inside the mirror will be the only thing seen. <note>References: 6 p 9.</note>*

**B**ut if an entire pyramidal mirror <note>term: "speculum pyramidale" (In this context, Alhazen uses 'pyramidal' and 'conical' interchangeably to describe cone-shaped mirrors.)</note> is placed before the eye, and the eye is on the side of the base, it will perceive nothing except what is inside the mirror. This is because the perpendicular line forms an acute angle with the line drawn from the eye to that perpendicular on the side of the base. From this, reflection occurs toward the side of the apex <note>original: "acuminis" (the sharp point or tip of the cone)</note> [for the reflected ray leans toward the side opposite the ray of incidence, falling obliquely, according to number 10]. Consequently, all reflected lines will fall inside the pyramid, and whatever is placed inside the pyramid can be seen. However, if a portion of the mirror is removed along its length, exterior objects can indeed be perceived, as an exit is opened for the lines of reflection. Similarly, if the pyramid is cut like a ring so that the vertex is removed, the lines will have free entry and exterior objects will appear. If the eye is on the side of the mirror's concave surface, it can perceive more exterior objects than from the side of the base, because a wider path is given to the lines of incidence.

*51. From any single point of any mirror, only one point of a visible object is reflected to a single eye. <note>References: 29. 30. 31 p 5. also 37 p 5: also in the prefaces of books 1, 5, and 10.</note>*

Furthermore: taking any point on any mirror, it is impossible for the form of more than one point to be perceived in it by the same eye. Since only a single surface <note>term: "superficies" (here meaning a geometric plane)</note> passes through the perpendicular and the center of vision, and there is only one line from the center of vision to that point, there is only one unique acute angle formed with the perpendicular line, and only one unique acute angle in that same plane equal to it [otherwise a part would equal the whole, contrary to Axiom 9]. Therefore, there is only one unique line that makes an equal angle with the perpendicular; and when that line reaches a part of an object, the form of another point cannot be carried along it, since the point in front hides the one behind it. However, with two eyes, two point-forms can be grasped at the same point of the mirror, since infinite planes can be taken intersecting each other along the perpendicular, in any of which two equal acute angles can be carried around the perpendicular.

We have now declared the property of reflection, and likewise the specific property of any mirror. When the eye perceives forms through reflection, it does not notice that this acquisition happens by means of reflection. For reflection does not happen because of a property of the eye; even if the eye is removed, the form proceeds no less from the body to the mirror and is reflected in the manner described. If it happens that the eye is in the place where the reflected lines gather, the eye will grasp that form at the heads of these lines; and the form is in the mirror not as if it had just arrived, but as if it were a natural form of the mirror. 

Furthermore: sometimes the eye acquires forms in mirrors on the surface alone, sometimes inside the mirror, and sometimes beyond it. The apparent location of the form will depend on the shape of the mirror and the position of the visible thing. The form will always be perceived in its own proper place, even if the position of the eye and mirror is changed; and there will be a difference in the distance of the form's location from the mirror's surface according to the different shapes of the mirror. This location of the form is called the **location of the image** <note>original: "locus imaginis"</note>. And the form itself is called the **image**. The eye perceives the visible thing in the location of the image. We shall discuss that location and its properties in each of the mirrors we have enumerated, and we shall assign the causes for why visible things are perceived in that place; and this we shall do in the following book, God willing.

# BY ALHAZEN THE SON
## OF ALHAYZEN, OPTICS
### BOOK FIVE.

This book is divided into two parts. The first part is the preface of the book. The second is concerning images.

### PREFACE OF THE BOOK. CHAPTER I.

*1. An image is a visible form reflected from a polished surface. <note>Defined in the 5th book.</note>*

**I**t is clear from the fourth book [number 2] that the forms of visible things are reflected from polished bodies, and the eye perceives them in polished bodies because of reflection; and it was shown [numbers 20 and 21 of Book 4] how the acquisition of things happens through the reflection of forms. The eye perceives the visible thing in a determined place, primarily when there is no change in the position of the visible object relative to the eye. The form perceived in a polished body is named an **image**. In this book, we shall explain the locations of images from polished bodies, and we shall say how the knowledge of these locations is acquired and how it may be found through logical reasoning <note>original: "syllogistice" (meaning by geometric or logical deduction)</note>.

### ON THE LOCATIONS OF IMAGES. CHAPTER II.

*2. In a plane mirror, the image is seen at the intersection of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. <note>Reference: 37 p 5.</note>*

**T**he location of the image of any point is the point in which the line of reflection intersects the perpendicular understood to be drawn from the point of the visible object onto the line tangent to the common line of the mirror's surface...

...or to the surface continuous with the mirror, and the surface of reflection. And we shall declare these things. Let a flat mirror be taken and placed parallel to the horizon: and let a straight and polished rod be erected upon the mirror. Let the size of the mirror be such that the whole rod can be seen; for unless the whole appears, there will be an error. Let some black point be marked on the rod. To the sight, there will indeed appear a rod equal to this one "beyond" the mirror, continuous with the physical rod and <term>orthogonal</term> <note>at a 90-degree right angle</note> to the mirror. On the appearing rod, the marked point will appear, and it will be as far distant from the surface of the mirror as the same point is distant on the upper rod. If the rod is tilted over the mirror, the appearing image will be seen tilted with the same inclination; and the marked point in the image will appear equally distant from the surface of the mirror. And if from the marked point another rod is erected orthogonally to the mirror, this rod will also be seen from the appearing point orthogonally to the mirror, and continuous with this orthogonal line. The same happens with several points marked on the rod. And the same happens entirely whether the mirror is raised or lowered. It is clear through this, therefore, that the image of a seen point appears on the <term>perpendicular</term>, drawn from the seen point to the surface of the mirror. And in this mirror, the line which is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror is also perpendicular to the common line of the mirror's surface and the surface of reflection.

The same can be shown with a <term>pyramid</term> <note>In medieval geometry, this term often refers to a cone as well as a pyramid.</note> that is orthogonal to its base, whose flat base is applied orthogonally to a flat mirror. For another pyramid will appear continuous to it, with the base of these pyramids being the same, and their <term>apexes</term> <note>the sharp tips</note> being equally distant from the mirror. It is clear that if a straight line is drawn from apex to apex, it will be perpendicular to the base, and thus to the mirror, since the surface of the mirror and the base are the same. Therefore, the vertex of the pyramid will be seen on the perpendicular drawn from it to the mirror. Similarly, from whatever point of the pyramid a line is drawn parallel to the axis, it will fall to a point looking back at it in the appearing pyramid; and that line will be perpendicular to the base and to the surface of the mirror <note>original reference: "per 8 p 11," likely referring to Euclid’s Elements, Book 11, Proposition 8.</note>. Therefore, the image of each point of the pyramid falls on the perpendicular imagined from that point to the surface of the mirror. But whatever point is placed opposite a flat mirror, one can imagine a pyramid of which that point is the vertex <note>ref: per 14 n 4</note>, which pyramid is orthogonal to its base and also to the mirror's surface (or a surface continuous with it). One can also imagine another pyramid opposite this one, having the same base, where the perpendicular from vertex to vertex will be orthogonal to the mirror. Therefore, the image of any point opposite the mirror falls on the perpendicular drawn from the point to the surface of the mirror, or to its continuation. But it is clear <note>ref: per 21 n 4</note> that in mirrors, the grasping of forms does not happen except through the lines of reflection. Therefore, the image of the seen point falls on the line of reflection; and any such line is straight. Thus, the image of any point falls at the point of intersection of the perpendicular (drawn from that point to the mirror surface) and the line of reflection. And in flat mirrors, the line common to the mirror surface and the reflection surface is the same line as the one <term>tangent</term> <note>original: "contingente" (touching at a single point)</note> to the place of reflection. Therefore, it is clear that in flat mirrors, the location of the image is the point of intersection of the perpendicular from the seen point to the tangent line and the line of reflection.

### 3. *In a convex spherical mirror, the image is seen at the meeting of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. <note>ref: 11 p 6.</note>*

In mirrors that are polished on the outside of a sphere, what we have said will be clear. Let a large mirror surface of this kind be sought, in which the form of a slender staff, erected perpendicularly upon it, may appear. Indeed, the form of the staff will appear continuous with the staff itself; and a marked point will appear in the form of the staff, distant from the surface of the mirror according to its distance from the same in the physical staff. And if the staff should be more slender at one end than the other, its form will indeed appear pyramidal in this mirror—which is an error of sight <note>original: "error uisus"</note> that we shall assign later. Furthermore, let a pyramid be made orthogonal to a perfectly circular base, and let it also be applied to this mirror. A pyramid will indeed be seen continuous to this one, erected on the same base, but smaller than the original. That a pyramid appears is clear from this: that all lines from the appearing image of the vertex to the circle of the base appear equal. And if the pyramid is tilted slightly over the mirror from the position in which the whole is seen—so that some part of it is hidden, while the place of reflection in the mirror is still exposed to the sight—the image of the pyramid will still appear from there. And if the eye moves further from or closer to the mirror, as long as it stays on the line extended from that place to itself, the image of the pyramid will be perceived. But this approaching or receding should be done along this line, so that the place of reflection is noted, and a line is drawn from the mark to the location of the eye, along which the movement occurs. Truly, since the image of the pyramid is orthogonal to the base of the pyramid, and the base is a circle among the circles on the sphere, the line drawn from the vertex of the pyramid to the vertex of the image will be orthogonal to that circle and will pass through its center <note>ref: per 6.8 d 1 conicorum</note>. It will also be orthogonal to the sphere, passing through the center of the sphere, and will be perpendicular to the surface tangent to the sphere at the point through which this line passes <note>ref: per 4. th. 1 sphær. uel 25 n 4</note>. It will similarly be orthogonal to the line tangent to the circle of the sphere passing through that point <note>ref: per 2 d 11</note>. And this tangent is the common line of the surface of reflection and the surface tangent to the sphere at that point; and this line touches the circle of the sphere, which is common to the surface of the sphere and the surface of reflection. Therefore, the line drawn from the vertex of the pyramid to the vertex of the image is perpendicular to the tangent line, which is the line common to the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror (which is a circle). In this perpendicular, therefore, the image of the vertex is seen. And it is clear <note>ref: per 21 n 4</note> that the image of the vertex is on the line of reflection. Wherefore...

# OPTICS, BOOK V.

The image of the vertex <note>original: "uérticis"; the highest point or a specific point of an object</note> will be understood to be at the intersection of the line of reflection and the **perpendicular** <note>a line at a 90-degree angle</note> drawn from the vertex to the sphere, or to the tangent—the circle common to the surface of the sphere and the surface of reflection. Moreover, by taking any point opposite this mirror, one can imagine a <term>pyramid</term> <note>the cone of light or visual rays</note> orthogonal to the surface of the mirror, or to the surface continuous with it, whose vertex is the chosen point [according to Proposition 14, Book 4]. The line from that point to the image of that point will be in the surface of reflection and perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, or its continuation in the manner previously stated: because the object point and the image are always together in the surface of reflection [according to Proposition 23, Book 4]. Therefore, the line drawn from the object point to its image is also there.

4. In convex cylindrical and conical mirrors, the image is seen at the intersection of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. Proposition 37, Book 5.

In column-shaped <note>cylindrical</note> mirrors polished on the outside, those things we said regarding the wood and the pyramid do not appear: for a straight line in these mirrors appears not straight; and this is a common error of sight, the cause of which we shall assign later. It happens, however, that in only a single point of the body one may see the predicted location of the image, in this manner. Using the instrument of the preceding book, let a **ruler** be inserted, to which the cylindrical mirror has been fixed, so that the middle line of the mirror's section is on the surface of the ruler. This ruler should not pass through the **brass plate**, but should fall upon it <term>orthogonally</term> <note>at a right angle</note>, so that the height of the ruler is above the line dividing the triangle of the brass plate. Once this plate is erected, let it be filled with wax and smoothed to a flat surface, so that it is in the same plane as the plate; this is to ensure the ruler is more accurately directed perpendicular to the plate.

Then, let a sharp ruler be sought, and its end sharpened; apply the sharpness of this ruler to the middle of the surface of the ring's line, and let it descend along this line, and where it falls upon the ruler, let a mark be made. Afterward, let a **needle** descend, upon which a small white body is fixed; and let this be at the end, so that the needle does not descend all the way to the ruler. Then, let the eye be positioned so that it is in the plane of the ruler, and let one eye be closed. Indeed, the image of the body will be seen on the line drawn from the marked point to the sharp point of the needle. This line is perpendicular to the surface of the ruler, which surface touches the column <note>the cylinder</note> along its length-line; and it is perpendicular to the length-line of the column which is on the surface of the ruler. It is also the common line of the ruler’s surface and the surface of reflection. In the surface of reflection are both the length-line and the perpendicular line. 

If the position of the eye is changed, and the sight is rotated around the surface of the ring: the body, the image of the body, and the needle will appear just as before and on the same line. And that line is perpendicular to the middle length-line of the column; and this is the perpendicular in the surface of reflection, because the surface of the ring cuts the column at a circle parallel to the base of the column, and the eye is in this surface. We shall prove later that when the sight and the object body are in a surface parallel to the base of the column, that surface is the surface of reflection. In this situation, the common line of the surface of the column and the surface of reflection is a circle; and the perpendicular, in which the image and the body are seen, falls orthogonally upon the line tangent to this circle.

When these things are completed, let the needle be removed from its place, and let the sharp ruler be placed over the middle line of the ring, so that it falls upon the middle length-line of the ruler, and let the sharp ruler be firmly fixed to the surface of the ring with wax. Afterward, let the ruler holding the mirror be removed, and take the sharp ruler and apply its sharpness to the middle length-line of the ruler, and following the path of the sharpness, draw a line with **ink** upon the mirror. Then, let a small **wax triangle** be taken, one side of which is equal to the height of the ruler in which the mirror is placed. Let the thickness of this triangle be moderate, and the surfaces of this triangle be as flat as possible. Let the triangle be firmly attached to the column-ruler under the base of the ruler, and let its side equal to the ruler's height be placed upon the side of the ruler's base. When it is thus, the height of this triangle will be above the base of the column equal to the ruler. 

To make the surface flat like the ruler’s surface, let the triangle be enclosed between the ruler and a flat surface and pressed until it is well flattened. Upon the surface of this triangle, let the sharp ruler be placed, and the end of this triangle be cut with the sharpness of the ruler; its end will then be a straight line, and this line will be the base of the ruler in which the mirror is held. Afterward, let the ruler be placed upon the surface of the plate that is in the instrument, and let the end of its base—which is along the length, being the side of the wax triangle—be placed upon the line which is along its length. This surface touches the surface of the mirror along the line on the mirror's surface; and this is the surface of the ruler in which the mirror is held. The angle of the sharp ruler, adhering to the middle line of the ring's surface (in which surface the mirror will be), will be inclined toward the part where the head of the triangle is; because the ruler raised one part of it with the body of the triangle, and the other part, which is after the head of the triangle, is the surface of the brass plate; and the line which is in the middle of the mirror will be inclined. 

When the side of the wax triangle is on the line which is along the length of the brass plate, the ruler in which the mirror is held will be moved. If the side of the triangle in this motion is on the length-line of the brass plate, let it proceed or recede until the angle of the sharp ruler meets some point on the line of the mirror's surface, until the sharp ruler is fixed. Let the line made with ink on the mirror be removed, and let a point be made on the surface of the mirror directly opposite the head of the sharp ruler. Let the sharp ruler be removed, and let the needle be applied, and let the needle be on the middle line of the ring's surface, and be forced to adhere with wax. There will be an imaginary line from the needle to the marked point on the surface of the mirror, perpendicular to the surface of the ruler, which touches the surface...

# OPTICS, BOOK V.

...[the perpendicular] and the line of reflection. Moreover, the points whose images are perceived in front of the mirror—that is, between the eye and the mirror—occur when a line drawn from any one of them to the center of the mirror intersects the width of the path lying between the eye and the mirror. To see this, let a <term>pyramid</term> <note>often used here to refer to a cone or a conical pointer used in experiments</note> be removed from the middle of the mirror and placed to the side; the vertex will be the center of the mirror, and the distance of the eye should be greater than the semi-diameter of the sphere. Then, take a slender white stick and stand it in the mirror so that the center of the mirror is directly between the head of the stick and the center of sight. Direct the gaze to the point of the mirror from which a line drawn to the vertex of the pyramid lies between the head of the stick and the eye. The form of the head of the stick will appear in front of the mirror and closer to the eye than the vertex of the pyramid. The vertex of the pyramid, the head of the stick, and the image of the head will all be on the same straight line. This line is perpendicular to the line tangent to the common line of the mirror's surface and the surface of reflection <note>original: "superficiei reflexionis"</note> [according to Book 4, Proposition 25], since the surface of reflection passes through the center and the point of sight. The line passing through these two points is in the surface of reflection. The common line is a circle, and this line will be the diameter of that circle, since the center of that circle is the center of the sphere. Therefore, this line will be perpendicular to the line tangent to the circle at the head of this line [according to Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 18]. This line passes through the point seen and its image. Thus, any point seen in front of the mirror is understood to be on the same line as the center and its image, and any point is seen on the line of reflection [according to Book 4, Proposition 21]. Therefore, it is at the point of intersection of the perpendicular and the line of reflection. Those things whose true nature is understood in these mirrors are those whose images appear beyond the mirror or in front of its surface; besides these, there are no others which the eye perceives in truth in this mirror, for they themselves prevent their true images from appearing. The images that appear on the surface of this mirror are from the final division, and we shall explain these when we discuss the errors of sight. Therefore, every point truly perceived in this mirror appears at the meeting of the perpendicular and the line of reflection; this perpendicular indeed passes from the point seen to the center of the sphere and falls orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> upon the tangent, the common line.

*7. In concave cylindrical and conical mirrors, the image is seen at the meeting of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. Proposition 37, Book 5.*

In concave cylindrical <note>original: "columnaribus concauis"</note> mirrors, the image is varied: for sometimes its location will be on the surface of the mirror, sometimes beyond it; and in all these cases, sometimes it will be truly perceived, and sometimes not. When you wish to perceive the location of the image in these: do just as you did with the exterior cylindrical mirrors. Let a ruler be used in which there is a concave cylinder, just as was used above, and likewise a needle, and a small body at the tip of the needle. Let the eye be placed opposite in the middle of the circle and in the middle of the surface of the ring. Let the eye be raised slightly from the surface of the ring, and let it look until it sees the image of the body, and let it grasp the form of the body, the body itself, and the point marked in the mirror on the same perpendicular line above the surface of the mirror; and this is done through a <term>sensory syllogism</term> <note>original: "syllogismum sensualem"; a process where the brain instinctively calculates distance and position based on visual data</note>. The image will be beyond the mirror, and the reflection will be from a point on the straight line that is in the middle of the mirror. Then let the eye be placed on the surface of the ring, but away from the center, until it sees the image of the small body; it will indeed see it in front of the mirror. It will see the body, its image, and the point marked in the mirror on one straight perpendicular line, above the straight line tangent to the circle parallel to the base of the mirror, at the point marked on the mirror's surface. The surface of this is the surface of reflection in this foreground area, and it is the surface of the face of the ring; the point of reflection is the point of that circle. Afterward, let another needle be used by hand, at the tip of which is a small body; let it be placed on the surface and the axis in such a way that the body and the marked point are on the same line, according to sensory judgment. Let the eye be on the surface of the ring, between its head and the center; it will see the image of the body, and it will see this image, the body itself, and the marked point on the surface of the mirror all on the same straight line. If, however, the straight line is slanted with the small triangle we made, and the eye is in the middle of the ring, it will see the image in front of the mirror, but on the same straight line with the body and the marked point. This reflection will be from the cylindrical sections because the mirror is slanted; and we know [from Book 4, Proposition 21] that an image is not perceived except on the line of reflection. It is clear, therefore, that the location of the image is where the perpendicular intersects the aforesaid line of reflection when the truth is perceived. And even if the certainty of the image is not grasped, the behavior of these images will be the same as those of true images. In the same way, you will be able to see the image in concave conical <note>original: "pyramidalibus"</note> mirrors at the meeting of the perpendicular with the line of reflection. It is clear, therefore, that in all mirrors, images are perceived in the aforesaid place, which is likewise called the "place of the image" <note>original: "imaginis locus"</note>.

*8. The image in any mirror is seen at the meeting of the perpendicular of incidence and the line of reflection. Proposition 37, Book 5.*

Now, we shall declare the cause of why things seen by reflection are perceived in the locations of their images, and why the image is upon the perpendicular drawn from the thing seen to the mirror's surface. When the eye acquires a form through reflection, it acquires it immediately without certainty, and it acquires length through estimation; it will perhaps grasp this length in truth through diligent attention, or perhaps not. We explained this in the second book [Notes 24, 25, 38, 39], and it was said there that the eye...

# ALHAZEN

Sight acquires distance through a <term>syllogism</term> <note>In medieval optics, "syllogismus" refers to an unconscious mental deduction or "calculation" the brain performs to determine distance based on known variables like object size and the visual angle.</note> derived from the size of the body and the specific angle under which that size is perceived. The acquisition of a known visible object is manifest in this way. Even unknown things are perceived in this manner: for they are compared to known things and to familiar sizes or distances. When sight perceives something through reflection, it does not perceive the distance of the image except by estimation; then, with careful attention, it acquires the distance and verifies it through a deduction from the size of the visible object and the angle of the <term>pyramid</term> <note>The "visual pyramid" or cone of light extending from the object to the eye.</note> upon which the form is reflected to the sight. Therefore, when the visible object is among known things, the sight acquires its distance through a distance already known that maintains an angle equal to this one and is similar to this distance. Similarly, when the visible object is unknown, its size is compared to the size of other known visible things, and the distance of its image is acquired through the deduction of the measure of the angle which the image holds at the center of sight at the moment of reflection. And from the place where the form of the visible object is perceived through reflection, the form coming directly to the angle around the eye approaches upon that same pyramid through which the form is reflected to the sight; and that same pyramid will occupy the entire form which was in the location of the image. Sight, therefore, when it acquires a visible object through reflection, acquires it at the location of the image, because the form is perceived at the location of the image through reflection. For this reason, it is similar to a form perceived directly, occupied by that pyramid. And this is the cause why it is perceived in the location of the image.

*9. The image in a plane mirror is seen on the perpendicular of incidence. <note>original Latin: "Imago in speculo plano videtur in perpendiculari incidentiæ." This refers to Proposition 35, Book 5 of the Risner edition.</note>*

[A geometric diagram illustrating the optics of reflection on a plane mirror. It features a vertical line with points 'a' at the top, 'b' at the intersection with the mirror surface, and 'e' at the bottom. A horizontal line representing the mirror contains points 'b', 'c', and 'd'. A line segment 'ac' represents an incident ray from point 'a' to the reflection point 'c'. A line segment 'cf' extends from 'c' to the upper right as the reflected ray. A line segment 'ec' connects the virtual image point 'e' (on the extension of the perpendicular 'ab') to point 'c'. The points 'f', 'c', and 'e' appear to lie on a straight line, representing the observer's line of sight toward the virtual image.]

We shall now say why the image is perceived on the perpendicular. We know [by Book 4, Note 16] that a point perceptible to the sight is not a mathematical abstraction but a sensible thing, and its form is sensible. I say, therefore, that in plane mirrors, since the image does not appear on the surface of the mirror but beyond it, it is more fitting and more reasonable that it should appear upon the perpendicular rather than away from it. For when its distance from the point of reflection of the mirror is assigned on the location of the perpendicular—namely, the part of the line of reflection drawn from the location of the image to the point of reflection—it will be equal to the distance of the visible point from the point of reflection. Because the surface of the mirror is orthogonal to the perpendicular [by the hypothesis], and the line drawn from the point of reflection to the perpendicular is a side common to two triangles, and the angle of the line of approach is equal to the angle of reflection [by Book 4, Note 10, and angle **f c d** equals angle **e c b** by Book 1, Proposition 15: and therefore to angle **a c b**], therefore two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of the other triangle [for the angles at **b** are right angles by the hypothesis and Book 11, Definition 3], and one side is common; therefore [by Book 1, Proposition 26] the remaining sides are equal to the remaining sides. Therefore, if the image appears on the perpendicular, it will be at the same distance from the mirror as the body from which it proceeds; and the image will have the same position with respect to the point of reflection that is in the visible point with respect to that same point; and the position is the same with respect to the sight. Hence, in this position, the truth of both the visible point and the image will appear. But if the image were outside the perpendicular, since it must be on the line of reflection [by Book 4, Note 2], it would either be beyond the perpendicular or closer to it with respect to the sight. If it were beyond, it would indeed be further from the point of reflection and from the sight than the visible point, whence it would hold a smaller angle in the eye than the visible point and occupy a smaller part of the sight; thus, although it is equal in size, it would seem smaller than it. If, however, it were closer than the perpendicular, it would seem larger, as it would be nearer.

*10. The image in convex and concave mirrors—spherical, cylindrical, or conical—is seen on the perpendicular of incidence. <note>original Latin: "Imago in speculis convexis, cauis: spherico, cylindraceo, conico videtur in perpendiculari incidentiæ." Proposition 36, Book 5.</note>*

In a spherical mirror polished on the outside, the image is seen upon the perpendicular. For either the image of the center of sight is seen, or the image of another point. If it is the image of the center of sight: I say that the perpendicular drawn from the eye to the center of the sphere is more worthy for the image of the center of sight to appear upon than any other line. For if the form proceeds directly along this perpendicular all the way to the center of the sphere, it will always preserve the same position with respect to the sight. And thus, to whatever point of the sphere the form is opposed, the perpendicular moved to the center will maintain an identity of position with respect to the sight; and the position of the form will be the same in one perpendicular as in another, since the center of the sphere has the same position with respect to any point of the sphere, and all such perpendiculars are of the same position. If, however, the image were moved away from the perpendicular, its position would change with respect to the sight at every point of the sphere; since it would have a different position outside the perpendicular than in the perpendicular, and the perpendicular would move outside the mirror and not inside; and if it appeared outside the mirror, it would not preserve its position. And it was more fitting that the image should preserve its position rather than change it, so that the sight might perceive the visible thing more certainly. For this reason, the image of the center of sight appears upon the perpendicular. And we cannot assign a certain point on the perpendicular to this image, since no greater merit is found in one point of the perpendicular than in another for this image to appear determinately in it; but we know that in whatever point of this perpendicular it appears, it always appears con-

...is continuous with the eye as it appears: and it always holds the same place and position within the total appearing form. However, the image of any point—other than the center of the gaze—that approaches the mirror moves at a slant: therefore, the similarity of its position relative to the gaze does not last. The <term>perpendicular</term> <note>A line drawn at a 90-degree angle to the surface; in modern physics, this is called the "normal."</note> drawn from the visible point to the mirror falls upon the center of the sphere: and indeed, the image maintains the similarity of its position along this perpendicular. Therefore, there is no point in which the perceived image preserves the similarity of its position except on that perpendicular. And since it is necessary for the image to be perceived on the line of reflection, [by Proposition 21, Book 4] it will be perceived at the intersection of this line with this perpendicular. We have now assigned the cause of this matter. Truly, the state of natural things regards the position of their principles, and the principles of natural things are hidden. The method of proof will be the same for a concave spherical mirror. Similarly in a concave pyramidal mirror, or one polished on the outside <note>original: "extrā polito," referring to a convex mirror.</note>. And universally, the location of the image will be on the perpendicular in any mirror whatsoever: because there is no place outside the perpendicular in which it may observe the similarity of position and identity.

Having explained these things, it remains to declare the location of the image demonstratively in every species of mirror. We say, therefore, that the line through which the form of any point perceived by the eye is reflected in a **plane mirror**, when it has departed from the perpendicular which falls from the center of the gaze to the surface of the plane mirror: will meet with the perpendicular drawn from that point to the surface of the mirror. This point of intersection (which is the location of the image) will be behind the mirror: and its distance from the surface of the mirror will be equal to the distance of the visible point from the surface of the mirror: and the gaze does not acquire the image of the visible point except in 그 place. And for whatever point the gaze acquires in this mirror, only a single image will appear from it.

However, for whatever point the gaze perceives in a **spherical mirror polished on the outside** (convex), when the form departs from the perpendicular drawn from the center of the gaze to the center of the mirror: the line through which the image is reflected to the eye will meet with the line drawn from that point to the center of the mirror. This line is the perpendicular drawn from that point <term>orthogonally</term> <note>At a right angle (90 degrees).</note> upon the line touching the intersection of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror. The position of the point of intersection, which is the location of the image, will be relative to the position of the eye from the surface of the mirror. And perhaps the point of intersection will be behind the mirror, perhaps on the surface of the mirror, or perhaps inside the mirror. The gaze perceives all images behind the mirror, even though their locations are diverse; and it does not perceive the location of any image except by a <term>deductive process</term> <note>original: "syllogisticè," referring to the mind's automatic calculation of depth and space.</note> on the surface of the mirror. And any point perceived in this mirror presents only one image.

In a **cylindrical mirror polished on the outside** and a **pyramidal mirror polished on the outside**, whatever point the eye perceives (when it is outside the perpendicular drawn from the center of the gaze, orthogonal to the surface touching the surface of the mirror): the line through which the form is reflected to the eye will meet with the perpendicular drawn from that point to the straight line touching the common line of the surface of reflection and the mirror. Some locations of the images of these mirrors are behind the surface of the mirror, some are on the surface, and some are in front of it. Yet the gaze acquires all images of these mirrors as if they were behind the surface of the mirror. And whatever point the eye perceives in these mirrors, it produces only one image.

In a **concave spherical mirror**, the lines through which the forms of visible points are reflected: some meet with the perpendiculars drawn from those points to the lines touching the common lines of the mirror's surface and the surface of reflection; some are parallel to these perpendiculars. Of those that meet with the perpendiculars, some have a point of intersection (which is the location of the image) behind the mirror, and some in front of the mirror. Of those in front of the mirror: some are between the eye and the mirror; some are exactly upon the center of the eye; some are beyond the center of the eye. The gaze perceives some of the forms of visible things in these mirrors at the location of the image (the point of intersection), and these are the ones the eye perceives with certainty; some it perceives outside the location of intersection, and this perception is without certainty. Of the things seen in this mirror, some present only one image; some two; some three; some four. It is not possible for one thing to present more.

In a **concave pyramidal mirror** and a **concave cylindrical mirror**, the lines through which forms are reflected to the eye: some meet with the perpendiculars drawn from the visible points to the lines touching the common lines; and some are parallel to the perpendiculars. Of those that meet with the perpendiculars: some have an intersection behind the mirror, some in front. Of those in front: some are between the mirror and the eye; some upon the center of the eye; some beyond the center of the eye. The perception of visible things in this mirror occurs sometimes at the location of the image (the intersection) and sometimes outside the location of intersection. Of those perceived, some present only one image; others two; others three; others four. There is nothing that can present more than four. We shall declare all these things by demonstration.

->11. The visible object and the image are equally distant from the surface of a plane mirror in opposite directions. [Proposition 49, Book 5]<-

Let *a* be the visible point; *b* the center of the gaze; *c d e* the plane mirror; and let *d* be the point of reflection; *c d e* the common line of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror. ### *12. Given the position of the eye and the visible object, to find the point of reflection in a plane mirror. Proposition 46, Book 5.*

If we wish to find the location of reflection by using the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>A line drawn at a 90-degree angle to the surface.</note>: let a segment be extended from the perpendicular beyond the mirror, equal to the part of it that reaches the mirror. That is, let $gc$ be equal to $ac$. Then, let a line be drawn from the center of vision to point $g$, which shall be line $bdg$. I say that $d$ is the point of reflection. For since [by construction and the 2nd axiom] $ac$ and $cd$ are equal to $cg$ and $cd$, and the angle is equal to the angle [angle $acd$ is equal to $gcd$ by the setup and the 10th axiom]. Therefore [by the 4th proposition of Book 1] the triangle is equal to the triangle. Thus, angle $gdc$ is equal to angle $adc$. But $gdc$ is equal to angle $bde$ [by the 15th proposition of Book 1]; it remains, therefore, [by the 1st axiom] that angle $bde$ is equal to angle $ade$. And so [by the 10th note of Book 4] $d$ is the point of reflection; and thus the proposition is clear.

### *13. If a straight line drawn from a single eye is perpendicular to a plane mirror, one point of it, where the eye cuts the surface, will be reflected from the single point of the mirror where it falls, back to that same eye. Proposition 32, Book 5.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing optical reflection on a flat surface. A vertical axis contains points h, a, d, and g. A horizontal line representing the mirror surface contains points e, b, k, and c. Rays are drawn from h, a, and d to point b, and another ray to point c. A line t b is shown as an angular bisector. Numerical annotations 6, 4, 1, 5, and 3 are present at various points in the diagram.</image-desc>

Let $a$ be the center of vision, and let $ag$ be the perpendicular above the plane mirror. Let $d$ mark where this perpendicular intersects the surface of the eye. I say that on this perpendicular, there is no point that can be reflected from this mirror back to the eye, except for $d$. If it were otherwise: let a point be taken beyond the eye on this perpendicular, and let it be $h$. Its form will not reach the mirror along the perpendicular $ah$ because the solid body [of the eye] is in the way; thus its form will not reflect back along the perpendicular. And if it is suggested that it could reflect from another point on the mirror, let that point be $b$. Its form would move toward point $b$ along line $hb$ and reflect along line $ba$. Let angle $hba$ be divided into two equal parts [by the 9th proposition of Book 1] by line $tb$. Therefore, $tb$ would be perpendicular to the surface of the mirror. [For since angle $hbe$ equals angle $abg$ by the setup and the 10th note of Book 4, and $hbt$ equals $abt$ by construction: the whole $tbe$ will equal the whole $tbg$. Therefore, by the 10th definition of Book 1, $tb$ is perpendicular to the common intersection $ge$ of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror. Thus, since the surface of reflection, in which $tb$ lies, is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror by the 13th note of Book 4, $tb$ will be perpendicular to the surface of the mirror by the converse of the 4th definition of Book 1. But by the hypothesis, $tg$ <note>This likely refers to line ag/dg</note> is also perpendicular to the same. Thus, from the same point, one could draw two perpendiculars to the surface of the mirror, which is impossible; for then the three interior angles of a triangle would be greater than two right angles, contrary to the 32nd proposition of Book 1.]

The proof will be the same to show that the form of point $d$ cannot be reflected from any other point of the mirror than point $g$. Therefore, it is not reflected except along the perpendicular $dg$. However, if a point taken on this perpendicular between $g$ and $d$ is said to send its form to the eye by reflection, I disprove this. For it will be either a solid body or a <term>rare</term> <note>original: "rarum," meaning transparent or tenuous, like air or a thin fluid.</note> one. If it is solid, its form will proceed toward the mirror along the perpendicular and return along the same toward itself [by the 11th note of Book 4], and because of its solidity, it cannot pass through to reach the eye. If, however, that point is rare: its form returning from the mirror along the perpendicular will mix with it and cling to it, but will not be reflected to the eye. That the form of any point taken on this perpendicular between $g$ and $d$ cannot be reflected to the eye from any other point of the mirror can be proven in the same manner as above. Similarly, the form of a point taken between $a$ and $d$ is not reflected to the eye via the perpendicular, nor by any other line. For the points interposed between the center of vision and its surface are extremely rare. Hence, their form is neither sent nor reflected in a way that can be perceived. And since any point except $d$ taken on the surface of the eye is positioned before the mirror at an angle that is not a right angle, every point will be seen along the perpendicular drawn from it to the mirror, and its image will appear beyond the mirror at the same distance from the surface as the point itself [by the 11th note]. And since $d$ is seen as continuous with the other points of the eye's surface, and its image is continuous with the other images, the image of $d$ will be seen as far from the surface of the mirror as $d$ itself is distant from it. It is clear, therefore, that the image of any point seen in a mirror will appear on the perpendicular, and the distance of the image and the visible body from the mirror's surface is the same.

# BOOK V OF OPTICS

->**14. From a single point of a plane mirror, one visible point is reflected to a single eye.** <note>original: "45 p 5," referring to Proposition 45 in the 5th book of a related source or earlier edition.</note><-

Furthermore: the form of a visible point in a plane mirror is not reflected to the same eye except from one point only. For let **a** be the center of vision <note>The eye's viewpoint.</note>; **b** the visible point; and **z h** the mirror. If it were argued that the form of **b** is reflected to the eye **a** from two points of the mirror, let one point be **d** and the other **e**. Let a line be drawn from the visible point to the eye, namely **b a**. This line will either be perpendicular to the mirror or it will not. [Indeed, it meets the surface of the mirror. Since it exists in the plane of line **h z** according to note 23 of Book 4, it is necessarily either parallel to it or intersects it.] 

If it is not perpendicular, we know that this line lies in a <term>surface of reflection</term> <note>The imaginary flat plane in which the path of light travels from the object to the mirror and then to the eye.</note> that is <term>orthogonal</term> <note>At a 90-degree right angle.</note> to the surface of the mirror [because it connects the two points **a** and **b**, which, according to note 23 of Book 4, are in the surface of reflection, which is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, per note 13 of Book 4]; and it lies in only one such surface. For if it were in two, it would be common to two orthogonal surfaces; and if a point were taken on it and a line drawn from that point into the other surface, onto the line common to this surface and the surface of the mirror, this line would be orthogonal to the mirror [per Proposition 19, Book 11 of Euclid’s *Elements*]. Similarly, from the same point, if a line were drawn in the other surface to the line common to that surface and the surface of the mirror, this line would also be orthogonal to the mirror. Thus, one could draw two perpendiculars to the surface of the mirror from the same point. [And if the ends of these two perpendiculars were connected by a straight line, they would be perpendicular to that connecting line, per definition 3 of Book 11; thus, in a rectilinear triangle, there would be two right angles, which contradicts Proposition 32, Book 1.] 

Since, therefore, **b a** lies in only one orthogonal surface, and the three points **a**, **b**, **e** are in that same orthogonal surface [per note 23 of Book 4], then **a e** and **e b** will be in that orthogonal surface; likewise [per Proposition 2, Book 11] **e d**, **d b**, and **d a**. Therefore, **e a** and **e b** are in the same surface as **d a** and **d b**. But angle **a e h** is equal to angle **b e d** [per note 10 of Book 4], and angle **a e h** is greater than angle **a d e** [per Proposition 16, Book 1] because it is an exterior angle. Therefore, **b e d** is greater than **a d e**. But **b d z** is equal to **a d e** [per note 10 of Book 4, and by Proposition 16 of Book 1, **b d z** is greater than **b e d**]. Therefore, **a d e** is greater than **b e d**, yet it was just stated that it was smaller. It remains, therefore, that reflection occurs from only one point. 

If, however, **a b** is perpendicular to the mirror: it has already been stated [note 13] that there is only one point on the line drawn orthogonally from the center of vision to the mirror whose form is reflected from the mirror to the eye. And it has already been proven that the image of that point is reflected from only one point. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

<note>The following diagram illustrates Proposition 14. A horizontal line representing the mirror surface is marked **h** and **z**. Above it, the eye is at **a** and the object at **b**. Lines descend to meet the mirror at points **e** and **d**, forming the geometric paths of light used to prove that reflection can only happen at one of these points, not both.</note>

->**15. In a plane mirror, the image of a single point is seen as one, and in one and the same location, by both eyes.** <note>original: "51 p 5"</note><-

Furthermore: when some point is inspected by both eyes, only one and the same image appears to each eye and in the aforementioned location. From this, it is clear that the form of the point is not reflected to both eyes from the same point of the mirror. Because the line of reflection proceeding to one eye maintains an angle with the perpendicular erected above the mirror surface equal to the angle which the line of the form's approach to the mirror maintains with that same perpendicular [per note 10 of Book 4], it would not be possible to take another line in the same surface that makes an equal angle with the perpendicular [otherwise a part would equal the whole, which contradicts Axiom 9]. 

For this reason, no line will be reflected to the other eye from this same point. It is necessary, therefore, for the reflection to happen from different points of the mirror. Let those points be **t** and **z**, let the plane mirror be **q e**, the visible point **a**, the two eyes **b** and **g**, and the perpendicular **a d**. It is evident then [per note 23 of Book 4] that **b t**, **a t**, and **a d**...

Thus, to both eyes, only a single image of point **a** appears, and at the same point on the same perpendicular. This is what was proposed.

*22. If a reflection occurs from the circumference of a circle (which is the common intersection of the plane of reflection and a convex spherical mirror) between the tangent line drawn from the eye to the mirror and a line of reflection whose segment within the circumference is equal to the radius: the image will sometimes be seen inside the mirror, sometimes on its surface, and sometimes outside of it. [A geometric diagram showing a section of a circle representing a convex spherical mirror. Point **d** is at the center.
