[By Proposition 23 of Book 1], let a line be extended making an angle with the perpendicular equal to angle **fng**, and let it be **en**. Since the line **nq** is smaller than **kh** [by Proposition 15 of Book 3], it is also smaller than line **qd** <note>original: "qd"; for **hk** was stipulated to be equal to the <term>radius</term> of the sphere</note>. Thus, [by Proposition 18 of Book 1] angle **qdn** is smaller than angle **dnq**. Therefore, [by Proposition 15 of Book 1] it is smaller than angle **gnf**, and consequently also smaller than angle **enf**. Therefore, lines **en** and **dq** will intersect [at parts **e** and **q**, by Axiom 11].

Let the intersection be at point **e**. It is clear [by Proposition 25 of Book 4] that the line **eqd** is perpendicular to the sphere and cuts line **gnq** (which is the line of reflection) at point **q**, which is a point on the sphere's surface. Therefore, the image of point **e**, when the reflection occurs at point **n**, will appear at point **q** [by Section 3]; and this is on the surface of the sphere. If, however, a point is taken on line **en** beyond **e**, such as **r**, the perpendicular drawn from it to the center of the sphere (which is **rd**) will intersect the line of reflection **gnq** beyond point **q**, which is outside the sphere. Thus, the image of any point on line **en** taken beyond **e** will be outside the surface of the mirror. 

If, however, some point is taken on line **en** closer than point **e**, the perpendicular drawn from it to the mirror will intersect the line of reflection **gnq** inside the sphere, specifically at a point between **n** and **q**. Therefore, the image of any point on line **en** taken between **e** and **n** will appear inside the sphere. Exactly the same proof will hold if any other point on arc **bh** is taken. Thus, for any point on arc **bh**, there is only one image located on the surface of the mirror; for others, some are in the mirror and some are outside. 

What has been demonstrated for arc **zb** can be shown in the same way for arc **za**. The demonstration will be exactly the same for any portion of the sphere's circle that is opposite the eye and divided equally by the perpendicular **gd**. Hence, with the eye remaining still and the perpendicular **gzd** remaining fixed, if the line of sight **gb** is moved parallel to the perpendicular, it will carve out a circular portion of the sphere by its motion, and the image of any point in this portion will appear inside the sphere. If, however, the <term>tangent line</term> <note>original: "linea contingens"</note> **gb** is moved parallel to the perpendicular of the eye, it will carve out a larger portion of the sphere than previously mentioned. From every point of the excess of one portion over the other, an image is reflected whose location will be on the surface of the sphere, while of the others, some will be inside the sphere and some outside. 

We know from this that in this mirror, every image appears on the <term>diameter</term> <note>The line passing through the object and the center of the sphere.</note> of the sphere—either inside the sphere, outside, or on the surface. And every diameter in which an image appears on the surface of the sphere or outside of it is lower than the point of the sphere touched by the tangent line drawn from the center of sight to the furthest point of the visible portion. We also know that every line of reflection intersects the sphere at two points: at the point of reflection and at another. It remains now for us to determine the locations of the images more precisely.

For let point **p** be taken: and let line **h p** be drawn, cutting the sphere at point **b**: and let the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>original: "perpendicularis"; the normal line drawn from the center of the sphere through the point of incidence.</note> **d b m** be drawn: and [by the 23rd proposition of Book 1] let an angle equal to angle **m b h** be made, which shall be **t b m**. It is clear [by the 15th proposition of Book 1 and the 1st axiom] that **t b m** is equal to **p b d**: and it is clear [by the 16th proposition of Book 1] that angle **d p h** is greater than angle **p z f**: because it is external. Therefore, the two other angles of triangle **d p b** are smaller than the two other angles of triangle **z d f** [by the 32nd proposition of Book 1.] But [by the 9th axiom] **p d b** is greater than angle **z d f**: it remains, therefore, that angle **d p b** is smaller than angle **d f z**: but angle **d f z** is equal to angle **z d f**: [as has already been shown by the thesis and the 5th proposition of Book 1:] wherefore angle **d b p** is smaller than angle **z d f**: Therefore it is much smaller than angle **p d b**: thus **t b m** is smaller than **p d b**. Therefore **t b** and **e d** will never meet [on the sides of **t** and **e**:] and so no form from point **b** will be reflected to point **h**, such that **p** becomes the location of the image. Likewise, neither is it the image of any other point. And similarly for any point on line **z d**. It remains, therefore, that the whole line **z d** be empty of image locations.

### 24. *If on the diameter of a convex spherical mirror drawn outside the center of sight, and continued into the visible surface, the boundary of images is marked: the images of the said diameter will be seen between the boundary and the surface of the mirror. [See Proposition 29, Book 6].*

Furthermore: having taken any diameter between the <term>lines of contingency</term> <note>original: "lineas contingentiæ"; tangent lines touching the surface of the sphere.</note> drawn from the sight to the sphere, except for the diameter understood to be from the center of sight to the center of the sphere, and having determined a point in it, which we have called the <term>boundary</term> <note>original: "meta"; the limit or fixed point for image placement.</note> of the locations of images. I say, that only in the points of that diameter which are between the surface of the sphere and the aforesaid boundary are the locations of the images of the points of that diameter. For example, let **b z** and **b e** be the tangent lines: **b** the center of sight: **a** the center of the sphere: **b h a** the visual diameter: **d a** the chosen diameter, whose boundary is **t**: **g** the point on the sphere where the diameter cuts the sphere. I say that the images of the points of the straight line **d a** fall only into the points lying between **g** and **t**. That they do not fall on point **g**, or outside the surface of the sphere, is clear through what was said above [in number 22], that the diameter in which the image location is on the surface of the sphere or outside it is lower than the point of contingency: and since diameter **d a** is between the tangent lines, it will not be the location of an image either on the surface of the sphere or outside it. That the image falls on any point taken between **g** and **t** will be established thus. Let point **f** be taken: and let it be **q**: and let line **b q** be drawn, cutting the sphere at point **p**: and let the perpendicular **a p l** be drawn: and [by the 23rd proposition of Book 1] let angle **d p l** be made equal to angle **l p b**: and let line **b t** be drawn, cutting the sphere at point **f**: and let the perpendicular **a f** be drawn. Therefore triangle **a p b** contains triangle **a f b**: wherefore [by the 21st proposition of Book 1] angle **a f b** is greater than angle **a p b**: it remains, therefore [by the 13th proposition of Book 1] that angle **a f t** is smaller than **a p q**: but angle **a f t** is equal to angle **f a r**, because they correspond to equal sides: [by the hypothesis and the preceding number.] Therefore **a p q** will be greater than angle **f a t**: and therefore also greater than angle **p a q**, [by the 9th axiom.] Wherefore [by the 15th proposition of Book 1 and the 1st axiom] **l p b** is greater than **p a q**. Whence **d p l** is greater than **p a q**: Therefore **p d** and **a q** will meet [by the 11th axiom.] Let **d** be the point of meeting. The form of point **d** will therefore be reflected from point **p** through line **p b**: and the location of its image is **q** [by number 3]. And the proof is the same for any point taken between **g** and **t**. It remains for us to assign the locations of images in the section of the sphere hidden from sight.

...and let **t p** be the line through which the <term>form</term><note>The "form" (forma) in medieval optics refers to the visual information or "species" traveling from an object to the eye.</note> moves toward the mirror. Let the perpendicular **n t u** be drawn; this will necessarily divide the angle **p t a** into two equal parts [as shown in Note 13 of Book 4]. Then, let the perpendicular **n g k** be drawn. By [Proposition 21 of Book 1 <note>References to "p" followed by a number usually denote Euclid's Elements. Here, Euclid’s Book 1, Proposition 21 deals with triangles contained within other triangles.</note>], angle **n t a** will be greater than **n g a**. Therefore, it remains [by Proposition 13 of Book 1] that angle **u t a** is smaller than angle **k g a**. Consequently, angle **p t u** is smaller than angle **b g k** [for angle **k g a** is equal to angle **b g k**, by Note 12 of Book 4]. But [by Proposition 32 of Book 1], the exterior angle **p t u** is equal to the sum of angles **t n p** and **t p n**; likewise, angle **b g k** is equal to the sum of angles **g n b** and **g b n**. Therefore, the two angles **t n p** and **t p n** must be smaller than the two angles **g b n** and **g n b**. However, this is impossible [by Axiom 9], since angle **p n t** contains angle **g n b** as a part of itself, and [by Proposition 16 of Book 1] angle **t p n** is greater than **g b n**. It remains, therefore, that the point **p** cannot be reflected except from the points intermediate between **g** and **l**. Furthermore, all lines drawn from point **a** through these points to the diameter **b n** fall upon points of the sphere that are further from the center of vision than point **g**. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### *31. When the eye and the visible point are at an equal distance from the center of a convex spherical mirror: to find the point of reflection. [Proposition 20 of Book 6].*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 31 showing a circle with center c and point d above it. Lines connect points a and b to a point e on the circumference. A vertical line passes through d, e, and c. Points are labeled a, b, c, d, e.</image-desc>

Furthermore: given a mirror and a given visible point, the point of reflection is to be found. Let **b** be the visible point and **a** be the center of vision <note>The "center of vision" refers to the location of the observer's eye.</note>. Let two lines be drawn from them to the center of the mirror. If those two lines are equal, it will be easy to find: for a circle of the sphere is taken in the plane of those two lines. We know [by Note 29] that the reflection of a single point occurs from only one unique point on that circle. Therefore, let the angle they contain at the center be divided into two equal parts [by Proposition 9 of Book 1], and let a line dividing the angle be drawn outside the sphere. This line will indeed be perpendicular to the line <term>tangent</term> to this circle at the point through which it passes [by Proposition 18 of Book 3]. If two lines are drawn to that point—one from the center of vision and the other from the visible point—they will form, with that perpendicular and the first two lines, two triangles. In these, two sides are equal to two sides and the angle to the angle [and therefore, by Axiom 4 and Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle **a e d** equals angle **b e d**]. And so, the point on the circle through which that perpendicular passes is the point of reflection [because **c e d** bisects the angle formed by the lines of incidence and reflection, as was shown in Note 13 of Book 4]. If, however, the line drawn from the visible point to the center of the sphere is unequal to the line drawn from the center of vision to the same center, we must first set forth certain preliminary propositions, one of which is this:

### *39. To find the point of reflection when the eye and the visible object are at unequal distances from the center of a convex spherical mirror. [Proposition 22 of Book 6].*

Having established the previous points, with a spherical mirror given, the point of reflection can be found. For example: let **a** be the center of vision <note>the eye</note>; **b** the visible point; **g** the center of the sphere. Furthermore: it is impossible for two angles constructed upon point **o** to both be greater than a right angle. If both were greater than a right angle, when an angle equal to angle **skm** is made at the same center, another different angle would be formed at the same center by another line similar to **sk** at **km**. Thus, reflection would occur from point **d** and from another point of that circle, which is impossible, since it has already been proven <margin>Theorem 29</margin> that there is only one point of reflection for one eye, and it has now been shown how it may be found.

**41.** *A visible object reflected from two points of a convex spherical mirror to both eyes has one image.* <margin>34 of Book 6</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circular cross-section of a sphere with center point c. Above the sphere are points e and f. Below the sphere are points a, b, d, g, s, t. On the surface of the circle/sphere are reflection points p, q, u, k. Lines represent light rays or lines of sight reflecting from the surface of the sphere between the observers and the visible points.</image-desc>

Even though there are two points of reflection for two eyes, there will nonetheless be a single sensory image formed by mental synthesis <note>Latin: syllogismo</note>, and one location for that image. We shall prove this when the two lines drawn from the centers of the eyes to the center of the circle are equal. If, therefore, the position of the visible point is the same with respect to both eyes—meaning the lines from the visible point to the centers of the eyes are equal—the proof will be easy. Since the visual diameters <note>The lines of sight</note> mark off the arcs of reflection from the circle, they maintain equal angles with the line drawn from the visible point to the center of the sphere; and the arcs lying between this line and the visual diameters are equal. <gloss>Since, by the premise, each eye is equally distant from both the visible object and the center of the mirror, when the perpendicular of incidence is drawn, two equilateral triangles are formed, which are therefore equiangular by Proposition 8 of Book 1. Thus, equal arcs are subtended by equal angles at the center by Proposition 26 of Book 3.</gloss> And if the points of reflection are taken, according to the proof stated above, the arcs of the circle lying between these points and the point of the circle on the perpendicular line <note>The normal line</note> drawn from the visible point will be equal. <gloss>Because of the equal distance of each eye from the visible object and the center of the mirror, the perpendiculars drawn through the points of reflection enclose equal angles at the center with the perpendicular of incidence, which subtend equal arcs by Proposition 26 of Book 3.</gloss> This will be easily seen by repeating the previous proof; and this remains true whether the points of reflection are in the same plane of reflection or in different ones: those arcs will still be equal, the lines drawn from the centers of the eyes to the points of reflection will be equal, and the lines from the visible point to those same points will be equal. <gloss>Since the angles formed by the visual diameters (which are equal by the premise) and the radii of the mirror have been shown to be equal, the lines of reflection and incidence will be equal to each other by Proposition 4 of Book 1.</gloss> And the lines proceeding from the centers of the eyes to the points of reflection will necessarily intersect <gloss>by Axiom 11: for the angles formed in front of the lines of reflection in both eyes are less than two right angles.</gloss> And the proof is evident that the intersection of both lines of reflection will be upon the same point of the perpendicular drawn from the visible point. <gloss>For the demonstrated equality of the angles of reflection is followed by the equality of the angles of incidence by Theorem 12 of Book 4. The angles enclosed by the lines of incidence, the continuation of the lines of reflection, and the common perpendicular of incidence are equiangular. Therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, as the lines of incidence are, so are the continuations of the lines of reflection; and as the former are equal, so are the latter. Thus, they meet at one point on the perpendicular.</gloss> And at this point, the image will appear to both eyes, and it will be only one image. This is what was proposed.

**42.** *In a convex spherical mirror, the points of the image correspond to the points of the visible object in position and order for both eyes.* <margin>35 of Book 6</margin>

The arrangement of images is just like the arrangement of the visible points. For if a line is taken on the object being seen, from the ends of which two lines are drawn to the center of the sphere, a triangle is formed in which the images of all the points of that line will be contained. And if there is a point on that line that does not have the same position with respect to both eyes, the image of the point further from it will be on a diameter further from its diameter, and closer...

But if a line is taken in which there is a point of the same position, any point of that line will be of the same position with respect to the two eyes according to the aforementioned mode, and it will have a single image on account of the equality of the angles of that line with the visual lines. But if a line is taken which bisects the angle contained by the two lines from the centers of the eyes to the point seen, the position of any point of that line, however far extended, will be the same for both sights as it was for one. And the mode of proof is the same. Besides these two lines, no other can be taken that maintains the same position. Hence, since the point seen is comprehended in the perpendicular [by Proposition 3], its image will fall in different points of that perpendicular, but removed from one another imperceptibly. And the image of any point, by however many eyes it may be seen, always maintains the identity of the part. Whence the unity of the image appears, as was said regarding direct vision [Proposition 27, Book 1], that forms, although they fall in different places, nevertheless on account of their insensible <note>too small to be noticed by the senses</note> distance do not diversify the appearance unless they diversify the part. Similarly here, when the distance of the point from one sight is slightly greater than from the other, the locations of the images will be imperceptibly remote. Whence they appear as one, and from them one compact image is formed, since the locations of the images sometimes do not differ totally, but only partially.

### 43.
If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror is a side of the cylinder or a circle, the locations of both the reflections and the images will behave in the same way as in plane and convex spherical mirrors. [Propositions 42, 43, Book 7].

In external columnar <note>cylindrical</note> mirrors, sometimes the common line of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror is a straight line; sometimes a circle; and sometimes a columnar section <note>a conic section, typically an ellipse, created by an oblique cut of the cylinder</note>. When the common line is a straight line, the location of the image will be on the perpendicular drawn from the point seen to the surface of the mirror, as far distant from the common line as the point seen is from the same. And the proof is the same as that stated for a plane mirror [Proposition 11]. However, when the common line is a circle, the location of the image will sometimes be within the circle, sometimes outside, and sometimes on the circumference itself. The explanation for this matter is entirely the same as for an external spherical mirror [Proposition 22].

### 44.
If the perpendicular of incidence is cut by the lines of reflection within the ellipse (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror) and the tangent at the point of reflection: it will be as the whole perpendicular is to the lower segment, so the upper is to the intermediate. And the lower segment will be greater than the segment of the line of reflection. [Propositions 47, 48, Book 7].

If, however, the common line is a columnar section: I say that some images are within the mirror, some on the surface of the mirror, and some outside the mirror, which will be explained individually. Let **a b c** be the columnar section; let **b** be the point of reflection; **e** the point seen; **d** the center of sight; and [Proposition 12, Book 11] let a perpendicular be drawn from point **b** to the surface tangent to the mirror, which is **g b q**; and [Proposition 11, Book 11] let a perpendicular be drawn from point **e** to the surface tangent to the mirror, which is **e k q**; and let the line tangent to the mirror at point **b** be **t u**, and the line tangent to the mirror at point **k** be **k m**. I say that the two perpendiculars **g b q** and **e k q** will meet. Let lines **e b** and **d b** be drawn, and let line **k b** be drawn. It is clear that **k m** will fall within the figure **e k b**, and line **b t** within the same figure <gloss>because a straight line bisecting the angle of a triangle cuts the base subtended by the angle; otherwise it would not cut the angle</gloss>. Therefore, **b t** will cut **e k**; let it cut it at point **t**. It is clear that angle **g b k** is greater than a right angle, and angle **e k b** is similarly greater than a right angle <gloss>because **g b q** and **e k q** are perpendicular to the lines **t u** and **k m**</gloss>. Wherefore [by Proposition 13, Book 1 and Axiom 11], **g b** and **e k** will meet. Let the intersection be point **q**. Similarly, angle **d b k** is greater than a right angle; therefore **d b** and **e k** will meet. Let the intersection be point **h**. Therefore **h** is the location of the image [by Proposition 4]. I say also that the proportion of **e q** to **q h** is as **e t** to **t h**, and also that **q h** is greater than **h b**. Let **h f** be drawn parallel [by Proposition 3, Book 1] to **e b**. Since, therefore, **t b** bisects angle **e b h**, it will be [by Proposition 3, Book 6] as **e t** is to **t h**, so **e b** is to **b h**. But angle **e b g** is equal to angle **h f b** [by Proposition 29, Book 1]; wherefore **h f** and **h b** are equal. <gloss>For the angle **e b g** was concluded to be equal to angle **h b f**; thus angles **h f b** and **h b f** are equal; wherefore by Proposition 6, Book 1, the sides **h f** and **h b** are equal; therefore by Proposition 7, Book 5, as **e t** is to **t h**, so **e b** is to **h f**</gloss>. But **e b** is to **h f** as **e q** is to **q h** <gloss>by Proposition 4, Book 6: for since **h f** was drawn parallel to **e b**, the triangles **e b q** and **h f q** are equiangular by Propositions 29 and 32, Book 1</gloss>. It will be therefore [by Proposition 11, Book 5] as **e t** is to **t h**, so **e q** is to **q h**. Which is what was proposed. And from this: since the proportion of **e q** to **q h** is as **e b** to **h f** <gloss>and **h f** is equal to **h b**: it will be by Proposition 7, Book 5, as **e q** is to **q h**, so **e b** is to **b h**</gloss> and **e q** is greater than **e b** <gloss>by Proposition 19, Book 1: because angle **e b q** is greater than a right angle</gloss>, **q h** will be [by Proposition 14, Book 5] greater than **h b**. Which is what was proposed. It is clear from this that if a perpendicular to the surface tangent to the section is drawn upon the section **a b c**, it will meet with **g b**. And these things are indeed clear when the point seen is not on the visual perpendicular. For it is clear from the above [Proposition 19] that the form of only one single point approaches the mirror along the perpendicular and is reflected along the same. And it is a point of the perpendicular existing in the surface of the sight; for a point taken beyond the sight cannot be reflected upon this perpendicular, because it cannot approach the mirror...

If, therefore, it were said that from a point other than point **g**, the form **b** could be reflected to **a**: that other point would either be on the line of longitude <note>The "line of longitude" refers to a vertical line or meridian running along the length of the cylinder.</note>, which is **g z**, or on another line. If it is on the line **g z**: let a perpendicular be drawn from it; this will necessarily bisect line **a k** [because it bisects the angle formed by the lines of incidence and reflection, as is clear from book 4, proposition 13] and [by book 1, proposition 28] it will be parallel to line **a m**. The line drawn from point **b** to that point will necessarily meet with **a m** [by the lemma of Proclus to book 1, proposition 29]; and that point and point **m** will be in the same plane. That line will either fall upon point **m** or upon another point. If it falls upon point **m**, it would be possible to draw two straight lines from point **b** to point **m**, which is impossible. [For in this way, two straight lines would enclose a space, contrary to the 12th axiom <note>A fundamental rule of Euclidean geometry stating that two straight lines cannot enclose an area.</note>]. If, however, it falls upon another point of the line **a m**: let a line be drawn from that point to point **z**, and it will be proven that this line forms a straight line with **h z**, just as was proven concerning line **z m**. In this way, it would be possible to draw two straight lines from point **h** passing through point **z** and falling on different points of the line **a m**, which is impossible [and contrary to book 11, proposition 1; and in this way, there would be a common segment for two straight lines, contrary to the definition of a straight line]. It is clear, therefore, that from no point of the line **g z** except **g** can **b** be reflected to **a**. If it is said that it can be reflected from a point taken outside this line: let a line of the mirror’s longitude be drawn through that point [by the 7th theorem of Serenus <note>Serenus of Antinoupolis, a 4th-century mathematician who wrote on the sections of cylinders and cones.</note> on the section of a cylinder]. From the point of the circle **e z i** where this line falls, it will be proven that **h** is reflected to **a** according to the proof stated above. But it has already been proven that **h** is reflected to **a** from point **z**. And thus it is impossible [because in this way, the form of the same visible object would be reflected from two points of the mirror to the same sight, contrary to book 4, proposition 51 and proposition 29]. It remains, therefore, that **b** is reflected to **a** from only a single point of the mirror. Which is what was proposed.

### *48. If the common section <term>common section</term><note>The line of intersection where the plane of reflection meets the surface of the mirror.</note> of the surfaces of reflection and of a convex cylindrical mirror is an ellipse: given the sight and the visible object, to find the point of reflection. Book 7, proposition 29.*

Furthermore: given point **b**, which is reflected to **a**, the point of reflection is to be found; and this will be clear by the reversal of the aforementioned proof. Let a plane be drawn from point **a** parallel to the base of the column <note>In this context, Alhazen uses "column" to mean a cylinder.</note>; this will indeed cut the column into a circle [by the 5th theorem of Serenus on the section of a cylinder], which shall be **e z i**. Let a perpendicular be drawn from point **b** to this plane, which shall be **b h**. Let the point in this plane from which **h** is reflected to **a** be found [as taught in book 4, proposition 31 or 39], which shall be **z**. From point **z**, let a line of longitude be drawn [by the 7th theorem of Serenus on the section of a cylinder], which shall be **z g**. From point **z**, draw the perpendicular **z l**, and from point **a**, draw a line parallel to this, which shall be **a m**. Also, let line **h z** be extended until it meets with it [it will indeed meet by the lemma of Proclus to book 1, proposition 29], and let the intersection be at point **m**. From point **m**, let a line be drawn to **b**, which will necessarily cut line **z g**, since it is in the same plane with it. Since **b h** is parallel to **g z** [by book 11, proposition 6, for each of them is perpendicular to the circle **e z i**], **h z m** will be in their plane [by book 1, proposition 7, because it connects parallels]. Thus **b m** is in the same plane. If it cuts **z g** at point **g**, then **g** will be the point of reflection. If you reverse the aforementioned proof, you will be able to see this.

### *49. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and of a convex conical mirror is the side of the cone: the locations of reflections and images will behave in the same way as in a plane mirror. Book 7, proposition 42.*

In exterior pyramidal <note>Alhazen often uses the term "pyramidal" to describe conical shapes.</note> mirrors, if the common line of the surface of reflection and the mirror is a line of the mirror’s longitude, the location of the image will be as assigned in plane mirrors. And the proof is the same.

### *50. The common section of the surfaces of reflection and of a convex conical mirror is not a circle. Book 7, proposition 12. Also book 4, proposition 41.*

That the common line cannot be a circle is clear from this: that the surface of reflection is orthogonal <note>At a 90-degree angle.</note> to the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection [by book 4, proposition 13]. A circle is necessarily parallel to the base [by the converse of the 4th theorem of Book 1 of the Conics of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga, the famous Greek geometer known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on conic sections.</note>]. Therefore, this plane parallel to the base will not be orthogonal to the tangent surface. [For a plane touching a cone touches it along a "side" <note>original: *latere*, referring to the slant height or meridian line of the cone.</note> by book 4, proposition 35, and is oblique to the base and to the circle parallel to it; because it is the side of an acute-angled triangle made by a plane cutting the cone through the vertex, by the 3rd theorem of Book 1 of the Conics of Apollonius. Therefore, the circle will be outside the surface of reflection, and thus the visible object will not be reflected by it to the sight.]

### *51. If the common section of the surfaces of reflection and of a convex conical mirror is an ellipse: the visible image reflected obliquely will be seen sometimes on the surface of the mirror, sometimes inside, and sometimes outside the mirror. Book 7, proposition 49.*

If, however, the common line is a pyramidal section <note>A conic section, specifically an ellipse.</note>, some images will be on the surface of the mirror, some inside the mirror, and some outside. The method of assignment is the same as it was in the exterior columnar mirror [proposition 44], and the proof is the same. And (as is the case in the exterior columnar mirror) [proposition 44], the form will not be reflected to the eye by the visual perpendicular except for the point of the eye's surface only; and this from only one point of the mirror. The location of its image will be continuous with the locations of other images, as was shown above [proposition 44].

### *52. If reflection occurs from a given point in the common section of the surfaces of reflection and of a convex conical mirror: the sight and the visible object can be so placed that reflection occurs from the same point, as if it were a point on a circle parallel to the base. Book 7, proposition 32.*

It remains to declare in these mirrors that reflection occurs from only one point; which will be clear in this way. Let the sight be **a**, the visible point be **b**, and the point of reflection be **g**. Let a plane be drawn through point **g** parallel to the base [specifically by drawing two perpendiculars cutting each other above the axis: one from the point of reflection by book 1, proposition 12; the other from the point of the axis where the first falls, by book 1, proposition 11. Thus the axis, which by book 11, definition 18, is perpendicular to the base, will be perpendicular to the plane of the drawn perpendiculars by book 11, proposition 4. Therefore, by book 11, proposition 14, the base and this plane will be parallel], which indeed will cut the pyramid into a circle...

### *59. To find the point of reflection when the eye is on this side of a plane drawn through the vertex of a convex conical mirror and parallel to the base, and the visible object is placed beyond the same, or vice versa. (Proposition 40, Part 7)*

[For angle **t e k**, being equal to angle **a e i**, is equal to angle **i e h** by Proposition 15 of Book 1: and therefore by Axiom 1 angle **a e i** is equal to angle **i e b**]. And so the proposition is clear.

It is clear then how to find the point of reflection. And these things which have been said are to be understood regarding a single eye <term>single vision: sight using only one eye</term>: but in double vision <term>binocular vision: sight using both eyes</term> the same thing happens: since the same form and the same location of the form is perceived by both eyes. And (just as was said [Note 41] regarding the exterior spherical mirror) forms perceived by two eyes are seen as one in these mirrors because of their contiguity: and sometimes they are in the same place at once: and sometimes their locations are partially mixed: sometimes they are separated, but only slightly. However, the form that descends through the perpendicular in these mirrors returns according to the same line, as was clear above [Book 4, Note 11]: and that form perceived by one eye upon the perpendicular is perceived by the other eye according to the line of reflection, but the locations of the forms are continuous. Hence the same form appears to the sight.

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s (Ibn al-Haytham’s) foundational study of catoptrics—the science of reflected light. Having previously established the geometry of reflection on flat and conical surfaces, he now moves to the complex behavior of concave spherical mirrors, where images can appear in front of, behind, or even inside the eye itself.</meta>

**60. In a concave spherical mirror, the image is seen sometimes at the point of reflection; sometimes at the eye; sometimes beyond the mirror; sometimes in front of the mirror; and sometimes between the eye and the mirror. <note>original: "11 p 8"</note>**

In concave spherical mirrors, a perpendicular line <note>The "normal" line, drawn at a right angle to the mirror's surface.</note> drawn from the visible point sometimes intersects the line of reflection, and sometimes it is parallel to it. When it intersects, the location of the image <note>original: "locus formae," literally the 'place of the form.'</note> will sometimes be on the mirror, sometimes beyond the mirror, and sometimes in front of it. Furthermore, when the location of the image is in front of the mirror, it will sometimes be between the eye and the mirror, sometimes at the very center of vision, and sometimes in front of the center of vision.

We shall demonstrate these cases. Let **a** be the center of vision <note>The observer's eye.</note> and **d** be the center of the spherical mirror. Let a plane be formed through these points, which will cut the mirror along a circle [according to Theorem 1 of Theodosius’s *Spherics*]. Let this circle be **b f g**. This surface will be the "surface of reflection," since it is perpendicular to any surface touching the circle [by Book 4, Note 13]. Let the line **a d** be drawn. From point **a**, let a line **a e** be drawn to the circle that is longer than **a d**. From point **d**, let a line **d h** be drawn to the circle parallel to **a e**. Let **a d** be extended to points **b** and **i**.

[Indeed, when the eye is inside the circle **h b f g**—or if it is on the circumference or outside—the line **a d** will continue to the circumference in at least one part, and the reasoning for the demonstration remains the same, because **a e** must always be greater than **a d**.]

Now, draw line **d e**. It is clear that angle **a e d** is less than a right angle. [By connecting straight lines **e i** and **e b**, angle **i e b** would be a right angle according to Euclid's *Elements*, Book 3, Proposition 31; therefore, **a e d** is acute.] This is because **e d** is a radius, and any line in a circle forming a triangle with the diameter creates an acute angle [as shown in Euclid Book 3, Prop 31; Book 1, Prop 32; or Axiom 9]. At point **e**, let an angle be made equal to angle **a e d** [by Euclid Book 1, Prop 23], which shall be **d e r**. It is clear that **e r** falls inside the circle. [If it fell outside, it would either touch the circumference and form a right angle with the radius **d e** per Euclid Book 3, Prop 18, or it would cut it and form an obtuse angle. Since both would be larger than the acute angle **a e d**, the requirement of the construction would not be met.]

This line will intersect line **d h** [by Proclus’s Lemma to Euclid Book 1, Prop 29, because it intersects **a e**, which is parallel to it]. Let the point of intersection be **r**. It is also clear that angle **a d e** is greater than angle **d e r**. [Since **a e** is greater than **a d**, then by Euclid Book 1, Prop 18, angle **a d e** is greater than angle **a e d**, which we made equal to **d e r**.] Thus, **e r** will intersect **a b**. [Because angles **a d e** and **e d b** equal two right angles per Euclid Book 1, Prop 13, and since **a d e** is greater than **d e r**, the angles **e d b** and **d e r** together are less than two right angles. Therefore, **e r** and **d b** must meet by Axiom 11.] Let them intersect at point **z**.

Next, from point **a**, let a line **a n** be drawn to the arc **e h**. Draw line **d n**. At point **n**, let an angle be made equal to angle **d n a** by line **m n**, which must necessarily fall inside the circle [for the reason just explained]. It will intersect **d h**. [Since angle **a n d**, contained by radius **d n** and line **a n**, is acute, the equal angle **d n m** is also acute. Furthermore, angle **n d m** is acute as it is part of the acute angle **e d r**. Thus, angles **d n m** and **n d m** are less than two right angles. Therefore, **n m** and **d h** will meet by Axiom 11.] Let them intersect at point **m**. It is also clear that **a n** will meet **d h** outside the circle [per Proclus’s Lemma]. Let the meeting point be **l**.

Also, draw a line from point **a** to arc **e i**, which shall be **a g**. Draw **d g**, and make angle **d g q** equal to angle **a g d**. It is clear that **q g** will intersect **d h** at point **q**. It is also clear that **a g** will meet **d h** on the side of **f**. [That they meet is certain from Proclus’s Lemma; that they meet toward **f** is clear from the previous demonstrations.] Let the meeting point be **o**. That **g q** falls between **d** and **h** is clear: since the arc that **g o** cuts from the circle is greater than arc **g h**. [If line **g h** were drawn, angle **h g d** would correspond to a larger arc than angle **a g d**. Therefore, by Euclid Book 6, Prop 33, angle **h g d** is greater than angle **a g d**. Since **q g d** was made equal to **a g d**, then **h g d** is greater than **q g d**. Thus, the line **q g**, cutting the angle, will intersect the base **h d**.]

Again, from point **a**, let a line **a k** be drawn to the arc **f b**, intersecting **d h** at point **s**. [That it intersects is clear from Proclus’s Lemma.] Let **k s** be greater than **s d**. [If we bisect **d f** and draw **a k** through that point or any point toward **d**, then **s k** will be greater than **f s** by Euclid Book 3, Prop 7, and thus greater than **s d**.] Draw **k d**. It is clear that angle **d k a** is acute [as shown at the start of this section]. Let an equal angle **d k u** be made. It is clear that since angle **k d s** is greater than angle **d k s** [by Euclid Book 1, Prop 18, because **s k** is greater than **s d** by construction], **k u** will intersect **d h**. [Since angles **h d k** and **k d s** equal two right angles, and **k d s** is greater than **d k s**, then **k d s** is also greater than its equal **d k u**. Thus, angles **h d k** and **d k u** are less than two right angles. Therefore, **h d** and **k u** will meet.] Let the meeting point be **u**.

It is clear from the above [and Book 4, Note 12] that:
1. Point **t** moves toward **e** and reflects to **a**. The perpendicular drawn from point **t** is **t d**, which is perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror [per Book 4, Note 25]. It is parallel to the line of reflection **a e** [by construction]. Therefore, it will never meet **e a**. **The image of point t will therefore be seen at the point of reflection e.**
2. Point **z** moves toward **e** and reflects to **a**. The perpendicular drawn from point **z** is **a z**, which meets **a e** at point **a**. **Therefore, the location of the image of point z will be at the eye a.**
3. Point **m** moves toward **n** and reflects to **a**. The perpendicular **m d** meets **a n** at point **l**, which is beyond the mirror. **The location of the image of point m will be l.**
4. The image of point **q** moves toward **g** and reflects to **a**. **Its location will be o, which is beyond the eye.**
5. The image of point **u** moves toward **k** and reflects to **a**. The perpendicular from it is **k d**. **The location of the image is s, between the eye and the mirror.**

It is therefore clear from the preceding that some images appear between the eye and the mirror, some in the eye itself, some in front of the eye, and some beyond the eye. This is what was proposed.

point s] the truth of that image is grasped. When the perpendicular drawn from the visible point is parallel to the line of reflection, the image will appear at the point of reflection [as in e]. Since that point is sensible <note>original: "sensuale," meaning it has physical dimensions rather than being a mathematical point</note> [as is clear from Note 16, Book 4], and taking its middle intellectual point: the image of any part of that sensible point taken beyond the middle will be beyond the mirror, and the image of the part on this side of the middle will be between the eye and the mirror. And since the total form from the further and nearer parts is seen as one and continuous, the form of that sensible point will necessarily be seen in the mirror itself, at the place of reflection. However, in images whose location is at the center of vision, their true form is not grasped; hence error very often occurs in these mirrors. To make this clear: let a piece of wood be erected perpendicularly on the surface of the mirror, less than half the mirror's radius; and let the center of vision be at the top of this wood. If the sight is directed to a point on the mirror whose distance from the wood is greater than the distance of the center of vision from the diameter passing through the wood, it will seem that the image of that wood is beyond the eye, and there will be no certain comprehension of it; indeed, it will appear curved when it is not. In these mirrors, therefore, the truth of the image is not grasped unless its location is beyond the mirror or between the eye and the mirror. But when the center of vision is on the perpendicular passing through the wood, it does not fully grasp the form of that wood.

## 62. When the eye is placed at the center of a hollow spherical mirror, it sees only itself. <note>original: "4 p 8. Idem 44 n 4."</note>

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a spherical mirror. Point 'a' is at the center, representing the eye. Vertical line 'f' stands on the top edge. Radii connect center 'a' to points 'e', 'c', and 'd' on the circumference. Point 'b' is also on the circumference.</image-desc>

If the eye is on the diameter of the sphere and at its center (since any line drawn from it to the mirror is perpendicular to the mirror) [because it is perpendicular to the plane touching the mirror by Theorem 4, Book 1 of *Spherics* or Note 25, Book 4; and for that reason it is reflected back onto itself by Note 11, Book 4], the form of no point will be perceived except the point of the portion of the eye lying between the sides of the visual pyramid <note>A "visual pyramid" is the cone of light rays extending from the eye to the object.</note> which is understood to extend from the center of the mirror. This is because the form of any other point will fall on the mirror at a slanted line and will necessarily be reflected at a slant. Therefore, the line of reflection will not pass through the center, and so it will not reach the center of vision.

## 63. The radius of a hollow spherical mirror in which the eye is located away from the center reflects no point of itself that falls obliquely on the mirror back to the eye; but the other continuous radius does reflect. <note>original: "5 p 8."</note>

If the eye is on the diameter, it will not perceive the form of any other point on the radius in which it is located. This is because the angle formed by two lines—one from a chosen point on the radius and one from the center of vision to the same point on the mirror—will not be divided in half by the perpendicular drawn from that point of the mirror, since that perpendicular tends toward the center of the mirror [by Theorem 4, Book 1 of *Spherics*]. But it will be able to perceive the form of some point on the other radius.

*66. If the eye and the visible object are located on different diameters of a circle (which is the common section of the reflection surfaces and the concave spherical mirror), they reflect to one another in two ways: first, from the arc of the circumference lying between the radii on which they are placed; second, from the arc opposite to that one. However, reflection cannot occur from the remaining two arcs. (Proposition 20 of Book 8).* <note>The "common section" refers to the circle formed where the plane of reflection intersects the sphere of the mirror.</note>

**I**f, however, the visible point $b$ is outside the diameter $dag$, let a diameter be drawn passing through $b$, which shall be $tq$. I say that $b$ can be reflected to the eye $a$ through the arc lying between the diameters on which $a$ and $b$ are located, and similarly through its opposite arc—that is, through arc $td$ and through arc $gq$. It cannot, however, be reflected from any point on arc $gt$ or arc $qd$. For example: let a point be taken on arc $gt$ near $t$, which shall be $k$; let lines $ak$ and $kb$ be drawn until $kb$ falls upon the diameter $dg$ at point $o$. Since $o$ and $a$ are on the same side of the center of the circle (which is $e$), the perpendicular line <term>perpendicular line<gloss>the normal ray drawn from the center of the sphere to the point of reflection</gloss></term> drawn from point $k$ to $e$ will not bisect the angle $oka$. Thus, $b$ will not be reflected to $a$ from point $k$.

*69. <image-desc>A circular geometric diagram labeled with points 'a', 'g', 'm', 'd', 'e', 'z', 't', 'b', 'l', 'p'. Furthermore: of the points perceived in these mirrors, some have their images assigned to four locations, some to three, some to two, and some to one. A point whose image falls in four locations is reflected from four specific points, and not from others or more. A point whose image occupies three locations is reflected from three points of the mirror, and not from more; one with two locations, from two points. However, for a point whose image falls in a single location, it could be that reflection occurs from only one point, or it could be from any point of a specific circle, but not from any other.

For example: let $e$ be the center of sight, $h$ be the visible point on the same diameter, and $d$ be the center of the circle. Let the diameter $zeha$ be drawn. Either $ed$ is equal to $dh$, or it is not. Suppose they are equal. Let the diameter $gdb$ be drawn <term>perpendicularly<gloss>at a 90-degree angle</gloss></term> through point $d$ over $eh$, and let lines $hg$, $ge$, $hb$, and $be$ be drawn. It is clear [by Book 1, Proposition 4] that triangle $hgd$ is equal to triangle $edg$, and equal to triangle $hbd$ and triangle $ebd$. It is clear that, since angle $hge$ is divided into equal parts, $h$ will be reflected from point $g$ to $e$ [by Note 12 of Book 4], and the location of its image is $e$ [by Note 6]. Similarly, $h$ will be reflected from point $b$ to $e$, and the location of its image is $e$. 

Therefore, if the diameter $zeha$ remains stationary and the semicircle $agz$ is moved through the sphere of the mirror—or just the triangle $hge$ is moved—the point $g$ will describe a circle by its motion. Point $h$ will be reflected to $e$ from any point on that circle, and the location of its image will always be point $e$. Thus the proposition is clear. That reflection of point $h$ to $e$ cannot occur from any point other than those on that circle is clear from this: let point $c$ be taken, and let $ec$ and $ch$ be drawn. [By Book 3, Proposition 7], line $ec$ will be greater than line $eg$, and line $hc$ will be less than line $hg$. Therefore, the <term>ratio<gloss>proportional relationship</gloss></term> of $ec$ to $ch$ will not be the same as $ed$ to $dh$. <note>original: "ex thesi" — according to the premise.</note> [For because the premise states point $h$ reflects to $e$ from point $g$, it follows from Note 12 of Book 4 and Book 6, Proposition 3, that $eg$ is to $gh$ as $ed$ is to $dh$. Thus, since $ec$ and $hc$ are unequal to $eg$ and $gh$, they will not be proportional to $ed$ and $dh$.] Therefore [by Book 6, Proposition 3], line $dc$ will not divide angle $ech$ into equal parts. Thus $h$ cannot be reflected to $e$ from point $c$. 

[The same is concluded more briefly by Proposition 4 of the geometry of **Jordanus** <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a prominent 13th-century mathematician.</note>. Therefore $h$ will not be reflected from point $c$ to the eye $e$. That the sides $ec$ and $hc$ are unequal is clear: because by Book 3, Proposition 7, $ec$ is greater than $eg$, which is to say $hg$ (since they were concluded to be equal), and $hg$ is greater than $hc$; thus $ec$ is much greater than $hc$.] The proof will be the same if $c$ is taken between $g$ and $z$.

### 70. When the sight and the visible object are outside the circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) and are located on different diameters: reflection occurs from only one point, and one image is seen. (Proposition 24 of Book 8).

Furthermore: when the visible point and the center of sight are not on the same diameter, and are outside the mirror: the visible point will not be reflected to the center of sight except from only one point of the mirror. For example: let $t$ be the visible point: $h$ the center of sight: $d$ the center of the sphere: and let lines $h$ $d$, $t$ $d$, and $h$ $t$ be drawn. The plane $h$ $d$ $t$ cuts the sphere along a circle: [by Theorem 1 of The Spheres] which we call $e$ $b$ $q$ $g$. It is clear that $t$ will not be reflected to $h$ except from some point of this circle: [because it is the surface of reflection itself.] Therefore, let $h$ $d$ and $t$ $d$ be extended to the circumference of the circle. It is clear that it will not be reflected from arc $q$ $g$, or $b$ $a$ according to the previously described manner [note 66]. It will be reflected either from arc $q$ $b$ or $a$ $g$. Let the angle $t$ $d$ $h$ be bisected [by Proposition 9 of Book 1] by the line $l$ $e$ $d$ $z$: and from point $e$ let a tangent be drawn: [by Proposition 17 of Book 3] which we call $k$ $e$ $f$. If points $t$ and $h$ are upon that tangent: $t$ will not be reflected to $h$ from any point of arc $b$ $g$. For when a line is drawn from point $t$ to any interior point of this arc: the line drawn from point $h$ to that same point will fall upon it from the outside, not the inside. And therefore there will be no reflection [from the concave surface of the mirror.] And that reflection occurs from only one point of arc $a$ $q$ will be clear from this. And so reflection to $h$ will occur from point $z$ [by note 12.] That it cannot occur from another point will be established thus. Let point $o$ be taken: and let lines $t$ $o, h$ $o$ be drawn: and let line $o$ $d$ $m$ through the center $d$ bisect that angle. ### 71. *If a third diameter bisects the angle formed by two diameters at the center of a circle (which is the common intersection of the surfaces of reflection and the concave spherical mirror): and from its endpoint on the circumference subtending said angle, there are perpendiculars to the said diameters: the points on the diameters—both where the perpendiculars fall and within these points at equal distances from the mirror's center—will reflect to one another only from the endpoints of the bisecting diameter; and they will have two images. [Proposition 25 of Book 8].* <note>Alhazen is identifying specific geometric conditions under which exactly two images are formed in a curved mirror.</note>

Furthermore: let $b$ $d$ $q$ and $a$ $d$ $g$ be two diameters of the sphere: and let the diameter $e$ $d$ $z$ bisect the angle $b$ $d$ $g$ into equal parts: and from point $e$ let two perpendiculars be drawn to the two diameters $b$ $d$ and $d$ $g$: [by Proposition 12 of Book 1] which shall be $e$ $t$ and $e$ $h$. It is clear [by Proposition 26 of Book 1] that triangle $e$ $t$ $d$ is equal to triangle $e$ $h$ $d$, and angle $t$ $e$ $d$ to angle $h$ $e$ $d$, and side $t$ $d$ to side $h$ $d$, and side $e$ $t$ to side $e$ $h$: since $e$ $d$ is common to both. Therefore, $t$ will be reflected to $h$ from point $e$. [by Note 12 of Book 4.] In the same way, they reflect from point $z$. [For since angle $b$ $d$ $g$ is bisected by the line $e$ $d$: angle $t$ $d$ $z$ will be equal to angle $h$ $d$ $z$ by Proposition 13 of Book 1, and $t$ $d$ is equal to $h$ $d$ from the previous conclusion, and side $d$ $z$ is common: therefore angle $t$ $z$ $d$ is equal to angle $h$ $z$ $d$ by Proposition 4 of Book 1. Wherefore by Note 12 of Book 4, $t$ and $h$ are reflected to each other from point $z$.] 

And it is clear [by Note 66] that $t$ will not be reflected to $h$ from any point of arc $a$ $b$, or arc $g$ $q$: nor will it be reflected from any other point of arc $a$ $q$ than from point $z$ according to the aforementioned proof [the preceding number]. Truly, that it cannot be reflected from any other point of arc $b$ $g$ than from point $e$ will be shown as follows. Let point $o$ be given: and let lines $o$ $d$, $h$ $o$, $t$ $o$ be drawn: and let a circle be made to the size of line $d$ $e$, passing through the three points $t, d, h$: [it will indeed pass through by the converse of Proposition 31 of Book 3 demonstrated by Theon in the commentaries on the 3rd book of Ptolemy’s Great Construction <note>original: "magnæ constructionis Ptolemæi"—referring to the Almagest.</note>, and by Campanus on Proposition 31 of Book 12:] of which circle line $d$ $e$ will be the diameter: since angle $e$ $t$ $d$, which it subtends, is a right angle. Therefore that circle will pass through point $e$. Since it is common to both circles, and is upon the same diameter: the smaller circle will touch the larger at point $e$: just as Euclid proves [Proposition 13 of Book 3.] Therefore this circle will cut the line $d$ $o$, [otherwise it would touch the larger circle at point $o$: and thus would touch at two points $e$ and $o$ contrary to Proposition 13 of Book 3] let it cut at point $l$: and let lines $t$ $l$ and $h$ $l$ be drawn. 

Now it is clear [from the above] that $t$ $d$ is equal to $h$ $d$ [therefore by Proposition 28 of Book 3 the circumference $t$ $d$ is equal to the circumference $h$ $d$.] Therefore angle $t$ $l$ $d$ is equal to angle $d$ $l$ $h$ [by Proposition 27 of Book 3] because they are over equal arcs. There remains [by Proposition 13 of Book 1] angle $t$ $l$ $o$ equal to angle $h$ $l$ $o$: and angle $l$ $o$ $t$ is equal to angle $l$ $o$ $h$ by hypothesis <note>The law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.</note>: [because they are the angles of incidence and reflection] and $l$ $o$ is a common side: [by Proposition 26 of Book 1] triangle $t$ $l$ $o$ will be equal to triangle $h$ $l$ $o$: and $t$ $o$ will be equal to $h$ $o$: which is impossible: since [by Proposition 7 of Book 3] $h$ $o$ is greater than $h$ $e$, and $t$ $o$ is smaller than $t$ $e$: just as was previously proven, $t$ $e$ is equal to $h$ $e$: [therefore line $h$ $o$ is greater than line $t$ $o$.] It remains, then, that $t$ should not be reflected to $h$ from any other point than from $e$ or $z$. 

Likewise from point $e$ let a line be drawn upon diameter $t$ $d$: which shall be $e$ $m$: and let a part be cut from line $h$ $d$ equal to $m$ $d$: which shall be $n$ $d$: and let $e$ $m$ and $e$ $n$ be drawn. It is clear [by Proposition 16 of Book 1] that angle $e$ $m$ $d$ is greater than a right angle: [because angle $e$ $t$ $d$ is a right angle by construction] let an angle equal to a right angle be cut from it by line $p$ $m$ [by Proposition 23 of Book 1] which will meet with $d$ $e$: [by the lemma of Proclus to Proposition 29 of Book 1] let the meeting be point $p$: and let $n$ $p$ be drawn: and let a circle be made to the size of $p$ $d$, passing through the three points $m, d, n$.

Since angle $p$ $m$ $d$ is a right angle [by construction] $p$ $d$ will be the diameter [by the corollary to Proposition 5 of Book 4] and the circle will pass through $p$, [as has been shown.] It is evident then, that $m$ will be reflected to $n$ from point $e$: [for since by Proposition 4 of Book 1 triangle $d$ $m$ $p$ is equilateral and equiangular with triangle $d$ $n$ $p$: $m$ $p$ will be equal to $n$ $p$, and angle $d$ $p$ $m$ to angle $d$ $p$ $n$: therefore by Proposition 13 of Book 1 and the 3rd axiom, angle $m$ $p$ $e$ is equal to angle $n$ $p$ $e$, and side $p$ $e$ is common: therefore angle $m$ $e$ $p$ is equal to angle $n$ $e$ $p$ by Proposition 4 of Book 1. Wherefore by Note 12 of Book 4, $m$ and $n$ are reflected to each other from point $e$] and similarly from point $z$: and not from any point of arc $a$ $b$, or $g$ $q$: [by Note 66.] And it is clear that reflection does not occur from any other point of arc $a$ $q$ than from point $z$: and that it does not occur from any other point of arc $b$ $g$ than from point $e$ according to the aforementioned manner. For when a point is taken, and lines drawn from points $t, d, h$: and a point is taken in which the final circle will cut the diameter: and from the points of intersection lines are drawn to points $t, h$: the same disproof will follow as before. 

It is clear, therefore, from the foregoing: that if the angle contained by two diameters is divided equally by a third diameter: and from the end of that diameter perpendiculars are drawn to those diameters: the points of the diameters where those perpendiculars fall are reflected to each other from only two points of the mirror. Moreover, for points of the diameters taken within these ends of the perpendiculars (that is, closer toward the center): any of them is reflected from only two points: and one is reflected to that which is at an equal distance from the center: and for all such points there is a double location for the image.

*...the endpoints of the perpendiculars being equidistant from the center of the mirror, they will be reflected from each other from four points on the circumference, and will have four images. [Proposition 26 of Book 8].*

Furthermore: taking two <term>diameters<note>A straight line passing through the center of a circle and touching the edges.</note></term> $b$ $q$ and $a$ $g$, and $e$ $z$ bisecting the angle between them equally: let point $t$ be taken on $b$ $d$ above the point where the <term>perpendicular<note>A line meeting another at a 90-degree angle.</note></term> falls, drawn from point $e$; and on $d$ $g$ let $d$ $h$ be taken equal to $d$ $t$ [by Proposition 3 of Book 1]. Let $t$ $e$ and $h$ $e$ be drawn. Indeed, $t$ will be reflected to $h$ from point $e$, and similarly from point $z$, but not from any other point of arc $a$ $q$, nor from any point of arc $a$ $b$ or $g$ $q$ [by Note 66]. Next, let a perpendicular be drawn from point $t$ onto $t$ $d$ [by Proposition 11 of Book 1]. This will indeed meet with $d$ $e$ outside the circle of the sphere, since the angle $b$ $d$ $e$ is acute [as shown in Note 36]. Therefore, $d$ $e$ and the perpendicular to $t$ $d$ will meet [by Axiom 11], specifically outside the circle $b$ $z$ $g$. Because this perpendicular and the one drawn from point $e$ onto the same semi-diameter $d$ $b$ are parallel [by Proposition 28 of Book 1], they will never meet [by Definition 35 of Book 1]. Therefore, the perpendicular continued from point $t$ will fall outside the circle beyond point $e$. Thus, it will meet with the semi-diameter $e$ $d$ outside the circle $b$ $z$ $g$. Let it meet at point $o$, and let lines $t$ $o$ and $h$ $o$ be drawn. Let a circle be formed passing through the three points $t, d, h$, which will necessarily pass through point $o$ [as demonstrated previously], and $d$ $o$ will be its diameter [by the corollary to Proposition 5 of Book 4]. Let a line tangent to circle $b$ $z$ $g$ be drawn at point $e$ [by Proposition 17 of Book 3], which shall be $k$ $e$. It is clear that the last circle will intersect the first, namely $b$ $z$ $g$, at two points [by Proposition 10 of Book 3]. Let those points be $l$ and $m$, and let lines $t$ $l, h$ $l, t$ $d, m, d, m, h$ $m$ be drawn. Since arc $t$ $d$ is equal to arc $h$ $d$ [by Proposition 28 of Book 3, because lines $d$ $t$ and $d$ $h$ are equal by construction], the angle $t$ $l$ $d$ will be equal to angle $d$ $l$ $h$ [by Proposition 27 of Book 3]. Thus, $t$ will be reflected to $h$ from point $l$ [by Note 12 of Book 4]. Similarly, angle $t$ $m$ $d$ is equal to angle $d$ $m$ $h$ [by Proposition 27 of Book 3]. Thus, $t$ will be reflected to $h$ from point $m$. It is clear, therefore, that $t$ is reflected from four points toward $h$: namely $e, z, l, m$; and its image will be fourfold. And it cannot be reflected to $h$ from any point other than one of these. For let point $f$ be given: let lines $t$ $f, h$ $f, d$ $f$ be drawn, and let $d$ $f$ be extended until it meets the tangent $k$ $e$ [it will meet by Axiom 11 because angle $k$ $e$ $d$ is a right angle by Proposition 18 of Book 3, and $f$ $d$ $e$ is acute, being part of the acute angle $b$ $d$ $e$]. Let the intersection be $k$, and let lines $t$ $k, h$ $k$ be drawn. Therefore, if angle $t$ $f$ $d$ is equal to angle $d$ $f$ $h$ by hypothesis [and Note 12 of Book 4], then [by Proposition 13 of Book 1] angle $t$ $f$ $k$ remains equal to angle $k$ $f$ $h$. But angle $t$ $k$ $f$ is equal to angle $f$ $k$ $h$ [by Proposition 27 of Book 3] because they subtend equal arcs, and $f$ $k$ is common. Thus, the triangles will be equal [by Proposition 26 of Book 1], and so $t$ $k$ would be equal to $k$ $h$, which is impossible. This is because $h$ $k$ is greater than $h$ $o$, and $t$ $k$ is less than $t$ $o$ [by Proposition 7 of Book 3], and $t$ $o$ is equal to $h$ $o$. [For since the line $d$ $t$ is equal to $d$ $h$ by construction, and angle $t$ $d$ $o$ to $h$ $d$ $o$ by the thesis, and side $o$ $d$ is common: therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, side $t$ $o$ is equal to side $h$ $o$; therefore $t$ $k$ is less than $h$ $k$.] It is clear, therefore, that there is no reflection from any points other than these four. Consequently, if two points $t$ and $h$ are taken on different diameters at an equal distance from the center: if they are located at the points on the diameters where the perpendiculars fall (drawn from the end of the bisecting diameter), or if they are between the center and those points (that is, on the near side of the perpendiculars), provided they remain equidistant from the center, then $t$ will be reflected to $h$ from only two points. However, if $t$ and $h$ are located anywhere from the perpendiculars up to the circle itself, $t$ will reflect to $h$ from four points. If they are on the circle or outside it, yet still on the near side of the tangent $k$ $e$, then $t$ will reflect to $h$ from only two points. If they are beyond the tangent, $t$ will reflect to $h$ from only one point. And these things occur while $t$ is at the same distance from the center as point $h$.

# ALHAZEN

Let $rx$ be drawn equal to line $ri$, and let lines $hx$ and $hi$ be drawn. It is clear according to what was said before that from point $m$, no line can be drawn to the side $fl$ that divides it in the same way it divides the line $mck$, except for this single line $mck$. If it were possible, let it be $mpo$. It is clear that $po$ will be smaller than $ck$: which will be evident if line $pq$ is drawn parallel to $ck$. This line will be smaller than $ck$ <note>original: "cū enim triangula k c f, q p f sint æquiangula per 29. 32 p 1: erit per 4 p 6 ut k f ad q f, sic k c ad q p"; Since triangles $kcf$ and $qpf$ are equiangular by Euclid’s Book 1, Propositions 29 and 32, it follows by Book 6, Proposition 4 that the ratio of $kf$ to $qf$ is the same as $kc$ to $qp$.</note> and $kc$ is greater than $qp$ <note>original: "sed k f maior est q f per 9 ax. ergo k c maior est q p"; since $kf$ is greater than $qf$ by Axiom 9 (the whole is greater than the part), then $kc$ must be greater than $qp$.</note> and greater than $po$ <note>original: "quia maior est q p, quę per 19 p 1 maior est o p, cū angulus p o q sit obtusus per 32. 13 p 1"; because $qp$ is greater than $op$, which by Book 1, Proposition 19 is true since angle $poq$ is obtuse by Propositions 32 and 13.</note> and $pl$ is greater than $cl$ <note>by Axiom 9.</note> Therefore, the <term>ratio<note>The quantitative relation between two amounts showing the number of times one value contains or is contained within the other.</note></term> of $po$ to $pl$ will not be as $kc$ is to $cl$. <note>original: "Si enim sit ut k c ad c l, sic o p ad p l: erit per 14 p 5 c l maior l p, contra 9 ax: quia k c maior est o p"; If the ratios were equal, then by Book 5, Proposition 14, $cl$ would be greater than $lp$, which contradicts Axiom 9 because $kc$ is already established as greater than $op$.</note> Therefore, the ratio of $po$ to $pl$ will not be as $hd$ to $dt$ <note>by Book 5, Proposition 11.</note> It remains, therefore, that from point $m$, no other line besides $mck$ can be drawn similar to it. 

But since angle $odi$ is equal to angle $lcm$, and angle $oid$ is equal to angle $clm$ <note>by construction</note>, triangle $clm$ will be <term>similar<note>In geometry, figures are similar if they have the same shape, even if they are different sizes, meaning their corresponding angles are equal and their sides are proportional.</note></term> to triangle $iod$ <note>by Book 1, Proposition 32 and Book 6, Proposition 4, Definition 6.</note> Therefore, angle $iod$ will be equal to angle $lmc$; there remains <note>by Book 1, Proposition 13</note> angle $roh$ equal to angle $kmn$; and the right angle $hro$ will be equal to angle $knm$; there remains <note>by Book 1, Proposition 32</note> angle $nkm$ equal to angle $rho$. Moreover, let line $di$ be drawn until it meets with $hr$ at point $s$ <note>it will meet by Axiom 11 because the angle at $r$ is a right angle, while at $i$ it is acute</note>; angle $sdh$ will be equal to angle $kcf$ <note>by Book 1, Proposition 15 and Axiom 1</note> and triangle $sdh$ will be similar to triangle $ckf$ <note>by Book 1, Proposition 32 and Book 6, Proposition 4, Definition 6.</note> Therefore, the ratio of $sd$ to $dh$ is as $fc$ to $ck$; but <note>by Book 5, Proposition 7</note> $hd$ is to $di$ <note>which is equal to $dz$ itself by Book 1, Definition 15</note> as $kc$ is to $cl$ <note>by construction.</note> Therefore <note>by Book 5, Proposition 22</note> $sd$ is to $di$ as $fc$ is to $cl$; therefore <note>by Book 5, Proposition 18</note> $si$ is to $di$ as $fl$ is to $cl$; but $di$ is to $io$ as $cl$ is to $lm$ because triangle $dio$ is similar to triangle $clm$. Therefore <note>by Book 5, Proposition 22</note> $si$ is to $io$ as $fl$ is to $lm$ <note>and by the corollary of Book 5, Proposition 4, as $io$ is to $si$, so is $lm$ to $fl$.</note> But the ratio of $si$ to $ir$ is as $fl$ is to $ln$, since triangle $sir$ is similar to triangle $fln$ <note>for angle $ris$ is equal to angle $fln$ by construction, and right angle $sri$ to right angle $fnl$; therefore by Book 1, Prop 32 and Book 6, Prop 4, Def 6, the triangles $sir$ and $fln$ are similar.</note> Therefore <note>by Book 5, Proposition 22</note> the ratio of $io$ to $ir$ is as $lm$ is to $ln$ <note>and by the corollary of Book 5, Prop 4, as $ir$ is to $io$, so is $ln$ to $lm$.</note> Therefore, the ratio of $ym$ to $lm$ is as $xo$ to $io$. <note>Because $xi$ is double $ir$, and $yl$ is double $ln$, it will be by Book 5, Prop 15 as $xi$ is to $io$, so $yl$ is to $lm$, and by Book 5, Prop 17, as $xo$ is to $io$, so $ym$ is to $lm$.</note> 

Now, let line $ui$ be drawn from point $i$ parallel to $hx$, and let line $da$ be extended until it meets with $ui$ <note>it will meet by Proclus's lemma to Book 1, Proposition 29</note>; let it meet at point $u$. Triangle $oui$ will be similar to triangle $hox$ <note>by Book 1, Propositions 15, 29, 32 and Book 6, Prop 4, Def 6.</note> Therefore, the ratio of $ho$ to $ou$ will be as $ym$ to $ml$. <note>Because of the demonstrated similarity of triangles $oui$ and $hox$, the ratio of $ho$ to $ou$ is as $xo$ to $io$; and as $xo$ to $io$ is as $ym$ to $ml$ from the previous conclusion; therefore by Book 5, Prop 11, $ho$ is to $ou$ as $ym$ is to $ml$.</note> And so $ho$ is to $ou$ as $hd$ to $dt$ <note>for by construction $hd$ was to $dt$ as $ym$ to $ml$.</note> But since <note>by Book 1, Proposition 4</note> triangle $hri$ is equal to triangle $hrx$ <note>since $hr$ is perpendicular by construction, and $xr$ is equal to $ri$, and side $rh$ is common.</note> Therefore, angle $hxr$ is equal to angle $rih$; and so $rih$ is equal to angle $uio$ <note>because $uio$ is equal to $hxo$ due to the similarity of triangles $uio, hox$.</note> Wherefore <note>by Book 6, Proposition 3</note> the ratio of $ho$ to $ou$ is as $hi$ to $iu$; and so <note>by Book 5, Proposition 11</note> $hi$ is to $iu$ as $hd$ to $dt$. 

In truth, angle $uid$ is greater than angle $dih$ <note>because it was concluded to be equal to angle $oih$</note>; let an equal angle be cut from it, and let it be $pid$; and let line $pt$ be drawn; and let $p$ be a point on the diameter $da$. It is clear that the ratio of $hi$ to $ui$ consists of the ratio of $hi$ to $ip$ and $pi$ to $ui$ <note>because the ratio of the extremes is composed of all the intermediate ratios, as Theon demonstrated in his commentary on Book 6, Definition 5.</note> and <note>by Book 6, Proposition 3</note> the ratio of $hi$ to $ip$ is as $hd$ to $dp$ because $di$ divides the angle $pih$ into equal parts. Therefore, the ratio of $hi$ to $ui$ (which is $hd$ to $dt$) consists of the ratio of $hd$ to $dp$ and $dp$ to $dt$. Therefore, the ratio of $dp$ to $dt$ is as $pi$ to $ui$. In truth, angle $oih$ is half of angle $uih$ <note>from the conclusion</note>; but angle $dih$ is half of angle $pih$; there remains angle $dio$ as half of angle $piu$. But angle $dio$ is half of angle $tdp$ because it is equal to angle $flm$ <note>which was made equal to half of angle $adt$ or $pdt$.</note> Therefore, angle $piu$ is equal to angle $tdp$ and the ratio of $dp$ to $dt$ is as $pi$ to $ui$. Therefore, triangle $uip$ is similar to triangle $tpd$ <note>by Book 6, Proposition 4, Definition 6</note> and angle $upi$ is equal to $tpd$; therefore <note>by Book 1, Proposition 14</note> $tpi$ will be a straight line because angle $dpt$ with angle $tpq$ equals two right angles; and so angle $opi$ with angle $opt$ equals two right angles. <note>The same is evident through the conversion of Book 1, Proposition 15, as demonstrated by Proclus.</note> And so <note>by note 12 of section 4</note> light from $t$ will be reflected to $h$ from point $i$ <note>because line $tpi$ is the <term>line of incidence<note>The path taken by light as it strikes a surface before being reflected.</note></term>, and angles $tid$ and $hid$ are equal by construction.</note> And the proof will be the same, whether $t$ is outside the circle or inside. And similarly if point $h$ is taken outside or inside, as long as they are at unequal distances from the center.

...at unequal distances from the center, are reflected from any point of the periphery contained between the radii beyond which they are located: except for that point in which the intersecting diameter terminates. <note>Refers to Proposition 28 of Book 8 in this specific edition.</note>

Furthermore: having drawn diameters $b q$ and $a g$, and diameter $e z$ bisecting angle $b d g$ into equal parts. I say that whatever point is taken on the arc $a q$, except for point $z$—[for from point $z$, only points on the diameters that are at an equal distance from the center are reflected, as is clear from the previous sections]—infinite pairs of points at unequal distances from the center can be reflected from that point. For example: let point $h$ be taken, and let point $l$ be taken on the radius $g d$; and from the radius $b d$, let $m d$ be cut equal to $l d$ <note>original: "per 3 p 1"; according to Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 3.</note>; and let lines $l m, l h, m h,$ and $d h$ be drawn. Let $f$ be the point where $e z$ divides $l m$; therefore $f l$ will be equal to $f m$ <note>original: "per 4 p 1"; by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 4.</note>. Let $h d$ be drawn until it falls upon $l m$ at point $n$; therefore $l n$ will be less than $m n$. However, since angle $m d f$ is equal to $f d l$ [by the hypothesis] and to angle $q d z$ <note>original: "per 15 p 1"; by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 15, regarding vertical angles.</note>; and angle $m d a$ is equal to angle $l d q$ [by the same reasoning]; and angle $a d h$ is equal to angle $n d l$; then angle $l d h$ will be greater than angle $m d h$. [Because $m d n$ (which is angle $h d q$ by Euclid 1.15) is greater than $n d l$ (which is $a d h$), and $m d a$ is equal to $l d q$, it follows that angle $l d h$ is greater than angle $m d h$.] Therefore $l h$ will be greater than $m h$ <note>original: "per 24 p 1"; by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 24.</note>, since $m d$ and $d h$ are equal to $l d$ and $d h$. Consequently, angle $d h l$ will be smaller than angle $d h m$. For if they were equal, the <term>ratio<note>The proportional relationship between two magnitudes.</note></term> of $l h$ to $h m$ would be as $l n$ to $n m$ <note>original: "per 3 p 6"; by Euclid Book 6, Proposition 3.</note>, which is impossible. [In such a case, the greater line $l h$ would have the same ratio to the smaller $m h$ as the smaller $l n$ has to the larger $n m$.] If, however, it were greater, an equal part would be cut from it, and it would be disproved in the same way. Therefore it is smaller. Let an angle equal to it [$d h l$] be cut from angle $m h d$, which shall be $t h d$. Therefore, point $t$ will be reflected to $l$ from point $h$ <note>original: "per 12 n 4"; referring to a previous rule of reflection.</note>. And line $t d$ is smaller than $l d$ [because it is smaller than $d m$, which by the hypothesis is equal to $d l$]. Similarly, if other points besides $l$ and $m$ are taken on the radii $b d$ and $g d$ at an equal distance from point $d$, it will be proved in the same way that from point $h$ there occurs a reflection of points at unequal distances from the center to each other. Thus, the proof will be similar for infinite points taken on these diameters, and from any point taken on arc $a q$, except for point $z$.

### 75. *If the eye and the visible object are on different diameters of the circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) at unequal distances from the center, and they are reflected to each other from some point of the periphery between the radii beyond which they are located, they will be reflected from only one point.* <note>Proposition 29 of Book 8.</note>

Furthermore: having taken points $t$ and $l$ on the diameters, which are of unequal length from the center, let them be reflected to one another from point $h$. Point $t$ cannot be reflected to $l$ from any other point on the arc $a q$ than point $h$. [For if from another, let it be $k$; and let $t k, l k, d k, l t, t h, l h, n d h$ be drawn; and let $d k$ be extended until it meets $l t$ at point $p$. It will meet it because it bisects angle $t k l$ subtended by the base $t l$.] It is evident that the ratio of $l h$ to $h t$ is as $l n$ to $n t$ <note>original: "per 3 p 6"; by Euclid Book 6, Proposition 3, because by hypothesis $h$ is the point of reflection, and thus by the 4th rule of reflection angle $l h n$ will equal angle $t h n$.</note>. And similarly, since angle $t p k$ is equal to $l k p$ by hypothesis, the ratio of $l k$ to $k t$ will be as $l p$ to $p t$ <note>original: "per 3 p 6".</note>. But $l h$ is greater than $l k$, and $t h$ is less than $t k$ <note>original: "per 7 p 3"; by Euclid Book 3, Proposition 7.</note>; therefore the ratio of $l h$ to $h t$ is greater than the ratio of $l k$ to $t k$ <note>original: "ut patet per 8 p 5"; as is clear by Euclid Book 5, Proposition 8.</note>. Therefore the ratio of $l n$ to $n t$ will be greater than the ratio of $l p$ to $p t$, which is clearly impossible. [For since $l n$ is smaller than $l p$ by Axiom 9 (the whole is greater than the part), and $n t$ is greater than $p t$, the ratio of $l n$ to $n t$ will be smaller than the ratio of $l p$ to $p t$, as is established from Euclid 5.8.] It remains that $t$ cannot be reflected to $l$ from any point on arc $a q$ other than point $h$. Thus, what occurs on arc $a q$ is clear.
