### 78. *If the eye and the visible object are reflected to each other within a circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and of a concave spherical mirror) at unequal distances from the center: the exterior angle formed by the diameters of the eye and the visible object is sometimes greater and sometimes smaller than the angle of incidence and reflection combined. 32 p 8.*

Furthermore, it will be clear from these things that once reflection has occurred to $a$ from point $e$, or from another point at an unequal distance from the center compared to $a$, the diameter in which the reflected point lies makes two angles with diameter $a b g$. One angle faces the angle of reflection, and the other is adjacent to it. This adjacent angle will sometimes be greater than the angle composed of the angle of incidence and reflection combined, and sometimes smaller. For example: let the perpendicular $b f$ be drawn over $e o$ <note>original: "per 12 p 1"; by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 12.</note>. $b a$ will either be perpendicular to $e a$ or not. Let it be perpendicular; therefore, the two angles $f b a$ and $f e a$ will be equal to two right angles <note>By the hypothesis and Euclid Book 1, Proposition 32, regarding the sum of angles in a quadrilateral.</note>. However, once line $b o$ is drawn, the two angles $o b a$ and $o e a$ will be less than two right angles. Therefore <note>original: "per 13 p 1"; by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 13.</note> angle $o b g$ will be greater than angle $o e a$, which is the angle composed of the angle of incidence and reflection. And since triangle $e b f$ is equal to triangle $e b a$ [for since the angles at $a$ and $f$ are right angles by hypothesis and construction, and by Note 12 of Book 4 the angles $f e b$ and $a e b$ are equal, and side $e b$ is common; the triangles $e b f$ and $e b a$ will be equilateral and equal by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 26], then $b f$ will be equal to $b a$. Thus $o b$ is greater than $b a$ [because it is greater than $f b$ by Euclid Book 1, Proposition 19, since it subtends a right angle in triangle $o f b$].

->*84. If two points outside the circle (which is the common section <note>The intersection of the plane where reflection occurs and the surface of the mirror</note> of the surfaces of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) or one inside and the other outside, on different diameters and at unequal distances from the center, are reflected from the periphery <term>periphery: the outer boundary or circumference of the circle</term> contained between the radii outside of which they lie: they will be reflected from only one point. <note>original: 38 p 8</note> Proposition 38, Book 8.*<-

Furthermore: having taken two points on different diameters, which points are of unequal distance from the center: if they are outside the circle and are reflected from some point of the arc opposite the diameters: they will not be reflected from another point of the same arc. For example: let $a$ and $b$ be points on different diameters, outside the circle: $g$ the center: $t$ the point of reflection: and let $b t$, $a t$, and $t g$ be drawn: $b t$ will intersect the arc of the circle: let the point of intersection be $q$: $a t$ will similarly intersect the arc of the circle: let the point of intersection be $m$. Since angle $b t g$ is equal to angle $a t g$: [by note 12 of Book 4: because $t$ is the point of reflection by hypothesis] they will fall upon equal arcs of the circle: [by Book 3, Proposition 26] which will be clear when the radius $t g$ is extended to $p$. Therefore arc $q p$ will be equal to arc $m p$. If, therefore, $b$ is reflected from another point: let it be $h$: and let lines $b h$, $a h$, and $g h$ be drawn. Let $b h$ intersect the circle at point $l$: $a h$ at point $n$: and let $h g$ be extended to $k$. According to the aforementioned proof, $l k$ will be equal to $n k$: but we already have that $q p$ is equal to $p m$: which is impossible [and against Axiom 9]. It remains that $b$ is not reflected to $a$ from point $h$, or from any other point of the arc opposite the diameters, except from $t$. Similarly, if one of the points is on the circle and the other outside: it can be reflected from only one point of the arc to the other.

->*85. If a straight line connecting two points on different diameters of the circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) at unequal distances from the center touches the periphery of said circle, or is outside it: the reflection will occur from only one point. <note>original: 39 p 8</note> Proposition 39, Book 8.*<-

Furthermore: if a line drawn from one of the two points touches the circle, or is entirely outside it: having taken any point in the arc opposite the diameters [in which the given points are located]: one of the lines drawn from either of the two points to that point will be entirely outside the circle: and thus neither point will be reflected to the other from any point of that arc: [$m l$] and from only one point of the mirror [taken on the periphery $d n$ by numbers 73 and the preceding ones].

If, however, the object point and the center of vision <note>The observer's eye.</note> are on the same diameter: reflection will occur from the entire circle, and the location of the image will be the center of vision [as shown in proposition 65]. But if the center of vision is at the center of the mirror: it sees nothing [except itself, as was clear from Book 4, proposition 44, and proposition 62]. If, however, the object point is at the center of the mirror: it will not be seen, because its form reaches the mirror along a <term>perpendicular: a line at a 90-degree angle to the surface</term>, and it cannot be reflected except back along that same perpendicular [by Book 4, proposition 11]. When, however, the center of vision and the object point are on different lines outside the center: those lines, extended to the center, will cut two arcs from the circle of the sphere in different parts. From one point of one arc alone, reflection will occur; from the other, perhaps from four. But if the center of the sphere is on one side, and the center of vision and the object point are on the same side: the arc which the diameters cut will be hidden because of the obstruction of the head. Thus, reflection will then occur from only three points. And if the gaze is directed in this position toward the arc of only one reflection: the other arc of three reflections will be hidden, and a single image will appear. Likewise: if the mirror is complete <note>i.e., a full enclosed sphere.</note>, there will be no perception there; it is necessary, therefore, for there to be a cutout in it. And it will sometimes happen that the arc lying between the diameters is cut away, and then nothing is seen in it. For this reason, it rarely happens that four images are perceived in this mirror. Therefore, if anyone wishes to see this plurality of images: let him position his sight within the mirror and move around it so that the bulk of his head hides only a small part of it, and let his gaze range over the entire surface of the mirror.

*88. In a concave spherical mirror, the image of the same visible object is seen by both eyes sometimes as single, and sometimes as double. (Proposition 59, Book 8 in other editions).*

When something is perceived in this mirror with both eyes: if the line of reflection is parallel to the perpendicular [of incidence], the location of the image will be the point of reflection [by proposition 60]. And since the points of reflection for the two eyes are distant from each other: two images of the same point will appear to the two eyes, and the location of each image is at its own point of reflection. If, however, the line of reflection is not parallel to the perpendicular [of incidence], and the object point is distant from the

### 89. The common intersection of the surfaces of reflection and a hollow cylindrical mirror is sometimes a side of the cylinder; sometimes a circle; sometimes an ellipse. 1 p 9. ###

In concave cylindrical <note>original: "columnaribus"</note> mirrors, sometimes the common line is a straight line: when the surface of reflection passes through the axis [by Definition 21 of Book 11 of Euclid's *Elements*]. Sometimes the common line will be a circle, when that surface is parallel to the bases [by Theorem 5 of Serenus’s *On the Section of a Cylinder*]. Sometimes the common line is a <term>cylindrical section: an ellipse formed by cutting a cylinder at an angle</term>. When it is a straight line: the location of the image and the manner of reflection will be just as in plane mirrors. When it is a circle: it will be the same manner as in concave spherical mirrors.

### 90. If the common intersection of the surfaces of reflection and a hollow cylindrical mirror is an ellipse: the image will be seen sometimes beyond the mirror; sometimes on the surface; sometimes behind the eye; sometimes in the eye; sometimes between the eye and the mirror. 10 p 9. ###

When the common line is indeed a cylindrical section: either the location of the image will be beyond the mirror; or behind the eye; or in the center of vision; or between the mirror and the eye; or in the mirror itself; which will be revealed thus. Let $a b g$ be the section: let a perpendicular be drawn in this section [upon the plane tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection] which shall be $d g$: which is clear from the aforesaid to be the diameter of the circle. [For because the plane tangent to the cylinder touches it along its side <note>a line running the length of the cylinder</note> by 26 n 4: therefore by 3 d 11 the straight line, perpendicular to the tangent plane, will be perpendicular to the side, which is parallel to the axis by 21 d 11. Wherefore by 29 p 1 the perpendicular to the tangent plane is perpendicular to the axis. Indeed, the plane parallel to the base and drawn through the said perpendicular is a circle, having its center on the axis by Theorem 5 of Serenus’s *On the Section of a Cylinder*. Therefore, the straight line perpendicular to the plane tangent to the cylinder at the point of reflection is the diameter of the circle drawn through the point of reflection] and only one such line can exist: since from no other point of the section can a perpendicular be drawn upon the tangent surface. [For since the common intersection of the circle and the ellipse, intersecting each other at the point of reflection, is perpendicular both to the plane tangent to the cylinder at that same point of reflection and to the axis, as has now been shown: therefore straight lines drawn from other points of the section to the axis will be oblique to it; otherwise, by 4 p 11, the axis would be perpendicular to the plane of the ellipse, which contradicts Theorem 9 of Serenus’s *On the Section of a Cylinder*.] 

Let another point be taken, and let it be $b$: and let a perpendicular line be drawn from it in the section upon the line tangent to the section at point $b$: which line, according to the aforesaid, will necessarily meet with the perpendicular $g d$. Let them meet at point $d$: and let $b$ be taken near point $g$, so that angle $b d g$ is acute. Then [by 31 p 1] let a line parallel to $b d$ be drawn from point $g$ in the section: which shall be $g h$: which will indeed fall within the cylindrical section because angle $h g d$ will be acute, since it is equal to $g d b$ [by 29 p 1]. And let a line be drawn from point $g$ between $d$ and $h$: which will necessarily meet with $b d$ [by the <term>Lemma of Proclus: a mathematical aid used by the 5th-century philosopher Proclus to explain Euclid’s parallel postulate</term> to 29 p 1]. Let them meet at point $n$: and between $n$ and $g$ let any point be taken, which shall be $o$: beyond point $n$ let point $t$ be taken. Likewise, from point $g$ let another line $g z$ be drawn above $g h$, yet within the section: which will necessarily meet with $b d$ on the other side [by the Lemma of Proclus to 29 p 1]; let the meeting point be $e$. Let line $g q$ be drawn so that angle $q g d$ is equal to $z g d$ [by 23 p 1], and let angle $l g d$ be made equal to angle $h g d$, and angle $m g d$ equal to angle $n g d$. It is clear [by 12 n 4] that if the eye <note>original: "uisus," meaning the point of sight</note> were at point $z$: point $q$ would be reflected to it from point $g$: and the point of the image is $e$ [by 6 n]. And if the eye were at point $h$: $l$ would be reflected to it from point $g$: and the location of the image would be $g$. If, however, the eye were at point $o$: point $m$ would be reflected to it: and the location of the image would be $n$. If it were at $n$: the location of the image of point $m$ would be in the center of vision, that is, in $n$. If it were at $t$: the location of the image would then be between the eye and the mirror, because it is at $n$. And thus the proposition is clear.

### 92. *If the eye is at the center of the circle of a hollow cylindrical mirror, it will be reflected from the periphery of that same circle, similar to a periphery of a circle drawn through the center of vision; and the image will be seen at the center of vision. 12 p 9.* ###

If, however, the eye is at the center of the circle, a portion of the sight will be reflected—that which is cut by the perpendiculars drawn from the center of vision to the circle [drawn through the center of vision]—from a portion similar to the circle [of the mirror] which those same perpendiculars similarly cut. Because any line drawn from the center of vision to the circle is perpendicular [to the surfaces of the eye and the mirror, by Book 4, Number 25, because it passes through the centers of the eye and the mirror], reflection will occur along the perpendicular [by Book 4, Number 11]. Thus, the location of the image will be the center of vision, which is the center of the circle.

Therefore line $rp$ is perpendicular to one of the four common lines, not to two: for it would be perpendicular to the tangent surface: [by Book 11, Definition 3] and thus it would reach the axis. [For since by Book 11, Definition 21 the cylindrical side is parallel to the axis: and $rp$ is perpendicular to the tangent plane from what was concluded, it is at the same time perpendicular to the side by Book 11, Definition 3: therefore by the lemma of Proclus to Book 1, Proposition 29 (which was shown a little before to be outside the axis), if continued, it will cut the axis: which is absurd.] There are, therefore, different perpendiculars from point $t$ to these four common lines: nor is there but one perpendicular only which passes through $a$. And the perpendicular either is parallel to the line of reflection: or it concurs with it beyond the mirror, or within. If it were parallel: the location of the image will be the point of reflection, as was proved [Number 91]. And since there are four points of reflection: there will be four images. If it concurs, since there are four perpendiculars: there will be four intersections, and four images.

96. *Given the sight and the visible object, to find the point of reflection in a hollow cylindrical mirror. [Book 9, Proposition 16].*

Further: given the visible point and the point of sight: the point of reflection is to be found. For example: let $a$ be the visible point, $b$ the center of sight. Let a surface be made cutting the column parallel to the base [as shown in Number 47] passing through $a$: and [by Theorem 5 of Serenus on the section of a cylinder] it will make a circle. $b$ is either in the surface of this circle or not. If it is: we will find the point of reflection in 그hat circle, just as was said regarding the concave sphere [Number 73]. If it is not: let a perpendicular be drawn [by Book 11, Proposition 11] from point $b$ to the surface of this circle: and let the above-mentioned proof be replicated: and the point of reflection will be found. However, when a double sight is applied <note>Meaning using both eyes.</note>, one image in truth will become two, but contiguous or mixed: whence it will be seen as one.

97. *The common section of the surfaces of reflection and a hollow conical mirror is a side of the cone, or an ellipse. [Book 9, Proposition 2].*

In concave pyramidal <note>In medieval optics, "pyramidal" often refers to the shape of a cone.</note> mirrors, the line common to the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror will either be a line of the length of the mirror: or it will be a <term>conical section: a curve like an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola formed by a plane cutting a cone</term>. If it is a line of length: the locations of the images will be in the mirror itself. If it is a conical section: the locations of the images will sometimes be on this side of the sight: sometimes in the sight: sometimes between the sight and the mirror: and sometimes beyond the mirror, just as was shown in the concave cylindrical mirror.

98. *If the sight is at the common intersection of the axis and a straight line perpendicular to the plane touching the hollow conical mirror: it will be reflected from the whole periphery of the circle (whose center is said common intersection) through perpendicular lines: and the image will be seen in the center of the sight. [Book 9, Proposition 17].*

Further: if on the perpendicular drawn from the center of sight to the surface tangent to the <term>cone<note>original: "pyramidem"; in medieval optics, "pyramid" was frequently used to refer to a cone.</note></term>, a physical point is placed between the eye and the mirror: its form will not be reflected to the eye along that perpendicular, because that point will block the end of that perpendicular, and for this reason, there will be no reflection from it. If, however, there is no point on that perpendicular, the point of the eye itself—and only that point—will indeed be reflected back to the eye along this perpendicular which intersects it. Truly, when the eye is located on this perpendicular and on the axis: a circle will be formed, and a line drawn from the eye to any point on that circle will be perpendicular to the tangent surface. Thus, reflection to the eye can occur from any point on that circle along these perpendiculars. And a reflection of that part of the eye will occur where two perpendiculars intersect it, containing a larger angle within it. If, however, the axis is between the eye and the mirror: reflection will not occur to it along a perpendicular, except for the point of it which the perpendiculars intersect.

From point **t**, let a perpendicular be drawn to line **a b** [by Book 1, Proposition 12 of Euclid], which shall be **t q**; and let it be extended until **q l** is equal to **q t**. For the angles $t z f$ and $f z e$ are equal to the angles $z t n$ and $h t n$ as per Proposition 12 of Book 4 <note>Alhazen frequently cites his own earlier propositions as proofs for his geometric steps.</note>, since by the initial premise, $t$ is the point of reflection: therefore, they are equal to one another. Furthermore, the angles at $s$ are right angles, and $t s$ is a shared side. Thus, according to Proposition 26 of Book 1 <note>original: "per 26 p 1"; referring to Euclid's Elements, which establishes criteria for triangle congruence.</note>, $f s$ is equal to $s z$. But [per Proposition 2 of Book 6] the ratio of $f s$ to $s z$ is as $k i$ to $i z$: therefore $k i$ is equal to $i z$. Since line $p i$ is drawn: and the surface $a t f$ is perpendicular to the surface $z k f$: then [per Definition 4 of Book 11] $p i$ will be perpendicular to $z k$. Consequently [per Proposition 4 of Book 1], angle $p k z$ will be equal to angle $k z p$: but [per Proposition 29 of Book 1] angle $e p o$ is equal to angle $p k z$, and angle $o p z$ is equal to angle $p z k$. Therefore, angle $e p o$ is equal to angle $o p z$. And so $z$ is reflected to $e$ from the point $p$ [per Proposition 12 of Book 4.] This is what was proposed. 

If another point is taken on the circle from which $z$ is reflected to $h$, it will be proven that $z$ is reflected to $e$ from a point on the cone <term>pyramidis<note>While the Latin "pyramis" usually means pyramid, in medieval optics it is frequently used to describe a cone.</note></term> other than $p$. And if $z$ is reflected to $h$ from three points on the circle, $z$ will be reflected to $e$ from three points on the cone; if from four, then four. Indeed, if it is claimed that point $z$ could be reflected to $e$ from more than four points on the cone, it could be shown by reversing the aforementioned proof that point $z$ is reflected to $h$ from more than four points on the circle [which contradicts Proposition 86]. And where it happens that point $z$ is reflected to $h$ from some number of points on the circle, or from only one, it follows that point $z$ is reflected to $e$ from the same number of points on the cone, or from only one, or vice versa. If the contrary were claimed, it could be disproven in the same manner as described above. It is clear, therefore, that some points have only a single image, some have two, some three, and some four; but it is not possible to have more. However, when using both eyes with a mirror, the locations of the same image will differ; this variation does not cause error because it is imperceptible.

### 102. Given the eye and the visible object, to find the point of reflection in a concave mirror. [Proposition 21, Book 9].

The point of reflection from which $z$ is reflected to $e$ is easy to find, once the point on the circle from which $point$ $z$ is reflected to $h$ has been found. The discovery will be made in the manner described above.

# THE OPTICS OF ALHAZEN
## SON OF ALHAYZEN
### BOOK SIX.

*Book six is divided into nine parts. The first part is the title of the book. The second explains that error happens to sight because of reflection. The third concerns errors occurring in flat mirrors. The fourth concerns errors arising in external spherical mirrors. The fifth concerns errors in external cylindrical mirrors. The sixth concerns errors in external conical mirrors. The seventh concerns errors in concave spherical mirrors. The eighth concerns errors in concave cylindrical mirrors. The ninth concerns errors in concave conical mirrors.*

### PREFACE TO THE BOOK. CHAPTER I.

The preceding books have made clear the manner in which forms are acquired in mirrors through sight, the placement of the lines of reflection and approach, the placement of images, and their locations. However, the truth of a form is not always perceived through reflection. For in concave mirrors, the image of a face appears distorted, and its true arrangement is hidden from sight. Thus, it is plain that errors occur in the perception of forms because of reflection. The purpose of the present book is to explain the nature of this error and the cause of its nature, and to discuss the various types of errors according to the different types of mirrors.

### THAT ERROR OCCURS TO SIGHT BECAUSE OF REFLECTION. CHAPTER II.

<margin>1. Reflected sight is similarly deceived as direct sight, but more intensely and more frequently. [Proposition 7, Book 5].</margin>
Book two taught the perception of forms in direct vision, and Book three carefully explained the individual things that induce error in that vision due to a departure from moderation <note>The author uses "temperantia" to refer to the balanced conditions—like distance, light, and size—necessary for accurate vision.</note>. Moreover, the perception of forms occurs through reflection just as it does directly; and those things acquired in direct vision are also acquired in reflection—namely light, color, shape, magnitude, distance, and similar qualities. And just as in direct vision a comparison is made between fixed, known things and others, from which conjecture arises and judgment is formed in the soul, the same happens in reflection. Therefore, whatever conditions depart from moderation and cause error in direct vision will similarly induce error in reflection. And in each case, a greater error occurs in reflection because of the weak light, which the reflection itself weakens. To speak generally, the truth of a form cannot be perceived in reflection as it is in direct vision because of three impediments specific to reflection. The first is that in reflection, the form of the object appears before the eyes as if opposite the sight, when in truth it is not. The second is that the light and color of the visible body are mixed with the color of the mirror, a mixture which the sight perceives rather than the true color or light of the thing seen. The third is that reflection itself, as assigned in the earlier books [Proposition 4, Book 4], weakens light and color. Therefore, the truth of light and color will be more hidden from sight in reflection than in direct vision. Furthermore, previous books have taught that the threshold of moderation for those things that induce error in direct vision depends on the strength of the light and color; for with stronger light or color, the threshold is larger, and with weaker, it is smaller. Since light and color are weakened by reflection, the range of moderation for each factor inducing error will be smaller in reflection than in direct vision; and a diminished range of moderation leads to a plurality of errors. Moreover, certain small details of bodies can be perceived through direct vision,

### ON THE ERROR WHICH OCCURS IN PLANE MIRRORS.
### Chapter III.

<margin>2. In a plane mirror, the image is equal to the visible object. Proposition 32, Book 5.</margin>
In every mirror, an erroneous perception of forms occurs, but the variety of errors follows the variety of mirrors. In plane mirrors, fewer errors occur than in others. For in these, the truth of shape and size is perceived, just as in direct vision <term>directione<note>In this context, "direction" refers to "direct vision," or seeing an object without the intervention of a mirror or lens.</note></term>, as will be shown by proof. Let a plane mirror be proposed: and let line $a\ b$ be in the surface of that mirror, common to the surface of the mirror and the surface orthogonal to the mirror's surface [that is, the surface of reflection, which by Proposition 11, Number 4 is perpendicular to the plane mirror, or to the plane touching a curved mirror at the point of reflection]. Let $l$ and $f$ be two points in that orthogonal surface: $e$ the center of sight <term>centrum uifus<note>The "center of sight" refers to the pupil or the point within the eye where rays are perceived to converge.</note></term>: and from point $l$ let a perpendicular be drawn to the surface of the mirror [by Proposition 11, Book 11] which shall be $l\ h$: and let it be extended so that $h\ g$ is equal to $l\ h$. Similarly, let the perpendicular $f\ z$ be extended so that $d\ z$ is equal to $z\ f$. It is clear from the above [Proposition 2, Book 4] that $l$ is reflected to $e$ from some point of the mirror: and the location of the image is $g$ [by Proposition 2, Number 5] as far distant from the surface of the mirror as $l$ is [by Proposition 11, Number 5]. Similarly, $f$ is reflected to $e$: and the location of the image is $d$ [by Proposition 2, Number 5]. Now, having drawn line $f\ l$: and similarly $g\ d$: whichever point of line $f\ l$ is reflected to $e$, the location of its image is as far distant from the surface of the mirror as the point itself. And thus any point of line $f\ l$ is seen to be as far away as it actually is. Wherefore if line $f\ l$ were straight, line $d\ g$ will be straight: if it were an arc, $d\ g$ will be an arc and of the same curvature. Therefore, line $l\ f$ will appear to be of the same size and the same shape as it truly was. This is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram on the right side of the page illustrating reflection in a plane mirror. A horizontal line 'a-b' represents the mirror surface. Above it, points 'f', 'z', 'l' and 'e' (the eye) are connected by lines representing light rays and perpendiculars to the mirror. Below the mirror, points 'd', 'z', 'g' represent the virtual images. Line 'f-l' and its reflection 'd-g' are shown, proving that in a plane mirror, the image's dimensions and geometry match the object's.</image-desc>

<margin>3. Sight in reflection is chiefly deluded because of the immoderation of light, the diversity of position, and the distance of the sight and the visible object from the mirror. Proposition 7, Book 5.</margin>
However, if in the points of line $f\ l$ there should be a variety of colors minutely varied: perhaps the variation will not be discerned, but a single confusion of color will be presented to the sight. Hence there will be an error in light and color. And this occurs in number <note>meaning "frequently" or "in many instances"</note> because of reflection. For that variety of colors and lights could perhaps be perceived directly, but the color has departed from its proper balance <term>temperantia<note>Original: "temperantia." This refers to the "moderation" or "ideal state" of visual stimuli; reflection weakens the light, pushing it out of the range where the eye can easily distinguish fine details.</note></term> with respect to reflection, though not with respect to direct vision. Similarly, minute particles are hidden or confused in reflection, which could be discerned in direct vision. And because of the weakening of light or color from reflection, an error in distance occurs, which would not happen directly. In position <term>situ<note>Original: "situ." Refers to the spatial arrangement or orientation of the object.</note></term>, an error clearly occurs from reflection alone. For in the image, we perceive as being on the left those things which, in the seen body (if it were in the place of the image), we would see on the right. For when something is placed opposite another, their positions are contrary to each other: for what is right for one will be left for the other. Therefore, what is on the right of the seen object is on the left of the image: and what is left in the image is on the right to the viewer. And generally, in the manner of light, or color, or position, an error always occurs from reflection alone. And in other things that induce error directly, they similarly induce error in reflection—and more easily, since the balance of each is less in reflected sight than in direct. Let one example be proposed for all of these, and the same should be understood for the rest. In direct sight, when the body seen is far from the visual axes, it happens to be seen as two: [as was demonstrated in Proposition 11, Number 3] the same happens in mirrors when the seen object is far from the axes. In mirrors, from a certain distance, a body will be seen as smaller than it is, which perhaps would be seen even smaller than it truly was directly from such a distance, but not quite so small. And this added degree of smallness in mirrors arises because of a lesser balance in length. In shape, an error sometimes occurs in mirrors for the same reasons as in direct sight: but it is greater and more frequent because of the position. If something is placed opposite a mirror from some distance, and its ends are not perceived by the sight, such as a rope or something similar: it will perhaps appear continuous with the mirror. The same happens in direct sight: if some rope is placed opposite a hole and the ends of the rope are not seen, it will not appear as divided if one part is seen but the other is not; perhaps that end will appear continuous. And in every instance where an error occurs directly: it occurs similarly in reflection.

**5. *In a spherical convex mirror, the visible image—whose true magnitude can be perceived by direct vision—is smaller than the object.*** <margin>39 p 6 <note>This refers to Proposition 39 of Book 6 in the medieval edited versions of Alhazen’s Optics.</note></margin>

To prove that the object always appears smaller than it truly is: Let *ab* be the line being viewed; *zx* the mirror; *d* the center <note>the center of the sphere from which the mirror is formed</note>; *e* the point of sight. Let point *a* be reflected to *e* from point *h*, and point *b* from point *n*. The line *ab*, if extended, will either pass through the center of the mirror or it will not. Suppose it does: and let a line tangent to the circle be drawn from point *n* [by Proposition 17, Book 3 of Euclid’s *Elements*], which shall be *nl*; and from point *h* let a tangent be *hm*. It is clear [from Proposition 3, Number 5] that *t* is the location of the image of *a*, and *q* is the location of the image of *b*. I say that the object *ab* is larger than its image *qt*. It is clear from the earlier discussions [18 n 5] that the ratio of *ad* to *dt* is the same as the ratio of *am* to *mt*. Similarly, the ratio of *bd* to *dq* is the same as the ratio of *bl* to *lq*. But [by Axiom 9] *ad* is greater than *db*, and *dt* is smaller than *dq*; therefore, the ratio of *am* to *mt* is greater than the ratio of *bl* to *lq*. [For since among the four lines *ad* is the first and is greater than *bd* the third, and *dt* the second is smaller than *dq* the fourth: the ratio of *ad* to *dt* will be greater than *bd* to *dq*, as is clear from Proposition 8, Book 5; and by Proposition 11, Book 5 the ratio *am* to *mt* is greater than *bl* to *lq*.] Let *am* be divided [by Proposition 12, Book 6] at point *f*, so that the ratio of *fm* to *mt* is as *bl* to *lq*; therefore, the ratio of *bm* to *mt* will be smaller than *bl* to *lq*. Point *k* will necessarily fall between *m* and *q*, because *lq* is smaller than *mq*, and *bl* is larger than *bm*. Since, therefore, *fm* is to *mt* as *bl* is to *lq*, and as *bm* is to *mk*; it follows [by Proposition 19, Book 5] that the ratio of *fb* to *kt* is as *bl* is to *lq*. But *bl* is larger than *lq* [for it was concluded that as *bd* is to *dq*, so *bl* is to *lq*; thus, since *bd* is larger than *dq*, *bl* will be larger than *lq*]; therefore *fb* is larger than *kt*. For this reason, *ab* is larger than *qt*. [Because *ab* is larger than *fb*, which was shown to be larger than *kt*, and *kt* is larger than *qt*. Therefore *ab* is much larger than *qt*.] This is what was proposed. 

But if the line *ab*, when extended, does not reach the center: let a line be drawn from point *a* to the center, which shall be *ad*; let *d* be the center; and from point *b* let the line *bd* be drawn. I say that *ab* is larger than *gp*, because *gp* is either parallel to *ab* or it is not. If it is parallel, it is plain that it is smaller. [For by Propositions 29 and 32 of Book 1, triangles *adb* and *gdp* are equiangular <note>similar triangles</note>; and therefore by Proposition 4 of Book 6, as *ad* is to *dg*, so *ab* is to

In the same way, angle **i g z** will be equal to angle **t g a**. <note>original: "Eodé modo erit angulus i g z æqualis angulo t g a."</note> [For because **m g** is a tangent, and by the construction the ratio of **i m** to **m t** is as **i a** to **a t**, the location of the image of point **i**, reflected from point **g** of the mirror, will be determined by Book 5, Proposition 18. Therefore, if **t g** is continued to **x**, the angles **i g z** and **x g z** will be equal by Book 4, Proposition 12; and by Book 1, Proposition 15, **x g z** and **t g a** are equal; therefore **i g z** and **t g a** are equal.] And since **m g** is perpendicular to **a g z** [by Book 3, Proposition 18], angle **i g m** will be equal to angle **m g t**. [For since the angles **m g z** and **m g a** are right angles and equal by Axiom 10, and **i g z** and **t g a** are concluded to be equal, the remaining angles **i g m** and **t g m** will therefore be equal.]

Furthermore: let line **h p** be drawn from point **h** to line **a b** parallel to **i b** [by Book 1, Proposition 31]; and from point **t**, let **t r** be drawn parallel to **i g** to line **a g**. Angle **i b z** will be equal to angle **h p b** [by Book 1, Proposition 29]. But angle **i b z** is equal to angle **h b a**, as has been said; thus the two angles **h b a** and **h p b** are equal. Therefore, the two sides **h b** and **h p** are equal [by Book 1, Proposition 6]; similarly, **t r** is equal to **t g**. 

However, angle **h p b** is acute, since it is equal to angle **i b z** [which is smaller than the right angle **l b z**]. Therefore, angle **h p a** will be obtuse [by Book 1, Proposition 13], and **a h** will be greater than **h p** [by Book 1, Proposition 19]. Similarly, **t a** will be greater than **t g**. 

Furthermore: since **h p** is parallel to **i b**, the ratio of **i a** to **a h** will be as **a b** to **a p** [by Book 1, Proposition 29 and Book 6, Proposition 4]. Similarly, the ratio of **i a** to **a t** will be as **a g** to **a r**. Thus, the ratio of **a h** to **i a** will be as **a p** to **a b** [by the corollary to Book 5, Proposition 4]. But **i a** is to **a t** as **a b** is to **a r** (since **a b** is equal to **a g**) [by Book 1, Definition 15]. Therefore, the ratio of **a h** to **a t** will be as **a p** to **a r** [by Book 5, Proposition 22]. 

But since angle **h p a** is obtuse [as was shown], the square of **h a** will exceed the sum of the square of **h p** and the square of **a p** by twice the product of **a p** and the line drawn from point **p** to the location of the perpendicular dropped from point **h** [by Book 2, Proposition 12]. <note>This is a geometric statement of the Law of Cosines for obtuse triangles.</note> The perpendicular drawn from point **h** will fall at the midpoint of line **p b**. [It does not fall outside points **p** and **b**, otherwise an acute angle would be greater than a right angle by Book 1, Proposition 16; it falls therefore between points **p** and **b**, and at the midpoint of line **p b** by Book 1, Proposition 26] since **h b** and **h p** are equal. Thus, the square of **h a** will exceed the square of **h p** and the square of **a p** by the product of **a p** and **p b** [by Book 2, Proposition 1]. And so the square of **a h** exceeds the square of **h p** by the product of **a b** and **a p**, since the product of **a p** and **p b** together with the square of **a p** equals the product of **a b** and **a p** [by Book 2, Proposition 3]. 

Similarly, the square of **a t** exceeds the square of **t r** by the product of **a g** and **a r**, or **a b** and **a r**, which is the same [since **a g** and **a b** are equal by Book 1, Definition 15]. Let line **a b** therefore be multiplied by the two lines **a p** and **a r**, and two excesses will result. Therefore, the ratio of one excess to the other is as **a p** to **a r**. [For the same height **a b** multiplying the bases **a p** and **a r** produces two rectangles equal to the two excesses, proportional to the bases by Book 6, Proposition 1.] Therefore, the ratio of the excess of the square of **a h** over the square of **h p** to the excess of the square of **a t** over the square of **t r** is as **a h** to **a t** [for it was shown that **a p** and **a r** are proportional to **a h** and **a t**]. And since **h p** is equal to **h b**, and **t r** to **t g**, the ratio of the excess of the square of **a h** over the square of **h b** to the excess of the square of **a t** over the square of **t g** will be as **a h** to **a t** [by Book 5, Proposition 7]. 

But the product of **e h** and **h d** is equal to the square of the line drawn from point **h** tangent to the circle **d b e** [by Book 3, Proposition 36]; and the [tangent] will be smaller than **h b**. [For because **h b** continued cuts the periphery **d b e**, the rectangle contained under the whole secant and its exterior segment will be equal to the square of the line tangent to the periphery from the same point **h** by Book 3, Proposition 36. Therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 17, as the exterior segment is to the tangent, so the tangent is to the whole secant; but by Book 3, Proposition 8, the exterior segment is less than the tangent; thus the tangent is less than the secant.] Thus the product of **e h** and **h d** is less than the square of **h b**. Let the product of **a h** and **h u** be made equal to the square of **h b** [as was shown in Book 5, Proposition 22]. Therefore **h u** is less than **h a**. [For because the rectangle contained under **h a** and **h u** is equal to the square of **h b**, it will be as **h a** to **h b**, so **h b** is to **h u** by Book 6, Proposition 17. But **h a** is greater than **h b**, as was shown; therefore **h b** is greater than **h u**, so **h a** is much greater than **h u**.] And the square of **a h** is equal to the product of **a h** with **a u** and **h u** [by Book 2, Proposition 2]. Therefore, the product of **a h** and **a u** will be the excess of the square of **h a** over the square of **h b**. 

Therefore, the ratio of **a h** to **a t** is as the ratio of the product of **a h** and **a u** to the excess of the square of **a t** over the square of **t g**. And if two lines **a h** and **a t** are multiplied by **a u**, the ratio of **a h** to **a t** will be as the ratio of the product of **a h** and **a u** to the product of **a t** and **a u** [by Book 6, Proposition 1, because the same height **a u** multiplies the bases **a h** and **h t**]. Therefore, the product of **a t** and **a u** is the excess of the square of **a t** over the square of **t g**; thus the product of **h a** and **h u** will be equal to the square of **h b**, and the product of **a t** and **t u** equal to the square of **t g**. [For because by Book 2, Proposition 2, the square of **a t** is equal to the rectangles contained under **a t** and **t u**, and under **a t** and **a u**; and the rectangle contained under **a t** and **a u** is equal to the excess of the square of **a t** over the square of **t g** by the previous conclusion, the remaining rectangle contained under **a t** and **t u** is therefore equal to the square of **t g**.] 

Furthermore: let arc **b g** be divided into equal parts at point **o** [by Book 3, Proposition 30], and let **a o** be drawn. Let three perpendiculars be drawn to line **h a** [by Book 1, Proposition 12], namely **b f**, **o y**, and **g k**. From point **g**, let a line parallel to **h a** be drawn [by Book 1, Proposition 31], which is **g s**. From point **b**, let a perpendicular be drawn to **a g** [by Book 1, Proposition 11], which is **b c**. If this **b c** were produced to the circle [that is, the periphery of circle **d b e**], line **a g** would divide it into equal parts [by Book 3, Proposition 3], and also the arc of which it is the chord; and thus another arc would be cut equal to arc **b g**, because angle **c b g** would look upon that arc. Thus angle **c b g** is half of the angle at the center looking upon the same arc, according to Euclid [Book 3, Proposition 20]. Therefore, angle **c b g** is half of angle **g a b** [for it is equal to the angle subtending a periphery equal to **b g** itself by Book 3, Proposition 27], which line **a o** divides into equal parts.

<margin>x</margin> Therefore, angle **c b g** is equal to angle **o a g**. Now, the two angles **b s g** and **b c g** are right angles. If, therefore, a circle is understood to pass over **b g** through **s**, it will also pass through **c** [by the converse of Book 3, Proposition 31, demonstrated by Theon in his commentaries on the 3rd book of Ptolemy's *Great Construction*] <note>The *Great Construction* (Magna Constructio) is the Latin name for Ptolemy's *Almagest*.</note> and arc **s c** will be formed, upon which two angles **c b s** and **c g s** fall. Therefore [by Book 3, Proposition 27] these two angles are equal. But angle **g a y** is equal to angle **c g s** [by Book 1, Proposition 29] on account of the 
<margin>1</margin> parallel lines [**g s** and **y a**]; and thus angle **g a y** is equal to angle **c b s**. And, as was said, angle **g b c** is equal to angle **o a g**; angle **o a y** will be equal to angle **g b s**, and triangle **o a y** will be similar to triangle **g b s**. Therefore, the ratio of **g b** to **b s** is as **o a** to **a y**, and the ratio of **g b** to **g s** is as **o a** to **o y**. ### 7. If two visible points are at an equal distance from the center of a convex spherical mirror, but at an unequal distance from the eye: the image and the limit of tangency of the point further from the eye will be further from the center of the mirror. [Proposition 4, Book 6].

Furthermore, in these mirrors, straight lines appear curved, and in most cases, the curvature does not face the mirror but is turned away from it. Similarly, curved lines will appear curved in these mirrors: and if the curvature faces the mirror, it will appear in the opposite orientation. This should be understood not for all cases, but for most. To explain this matter, it is necessary to first set forth certain preliminary points, one of which is: If there are two points at the same distance from the center of the mirror, but at unequal distances from the center of the eye, the image of the point further from the center of the eye will be further from the center of the mirror than the image of the closer point. Also, the limit of tangency of the further point will be further from the center of the mirror than the limit of tangency of the closer point, whether those points are in the same plane as the center of the eye or in different ones. Let **t** and **d** be two points equally distant from the center of the mirror **g**; let **e** be the center of the eye; and let **d** be closer to the eye than **t**. The <term>plane of common section<note>Latin: *superficies communis sectionis*; the flat geometric plane that intersects the mirror, the object, and the eye.</note></term> **d t g** will cut the mirror along a circle [by the 1st theorem of the 1st book on Spheres], which shall be **a b**. Let angle **e g d** be equal to angle **t g z**, and angle **e g t** be equal to angle **t g h**. Take a point on the circle from which **t** is reflected to **z** [by theorem 31 or 39, section 5], which shall be **q**. I say that **t** is not reflected to **h** from any point on the arc **b q**. It is clear that it is not from point **b** [because since that line is perpendicular to the mirror, it would be reflected back onto itself, not toward **h**, by theorem 11, section 4]. If, however, any point is taken on **b q**, a line drawn from point **h** to that point will cut the line **q z**. Therefore, **t** is reflected to that point of intersection from some point taken on **b q**, and it is also reflected to that same point of intersection from point **q**. Therefore, **t** would be reflected to the same point from two different points on that circle, which is impossible in these mirrors, as was shown in the fifth book [theorem 29]. It remains, therefore, that **t** is reflected to **h** from some point on the arc **q a**; let that be **m**. And [by theorem 17, book 3] let a line tangent to the circle be drawn from point **m** to the line **g t**, which shall be **m n**. **n** will be the limit of tangency of **t** with respect to **h** [by theorem 17, section 5]. Let a tangent be drawn from point **q**, which shall be **q o**. This will necessarily fall below **m n**. Furthermore: suppose the line **ab** is divided according to this proportion. If the lines **gz**, **dh**, and **bc** are parallel, and line **ac** is drawn cutting through them, then line **ac** will also be divided according to this same proportion. Since **dh** is parallel to **gz**, the ratio of **az** to **zh** will be the same as the ratio of **ag** to **gd** <note>original: "per 2 p 6"; referring to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 6, Proposition 2, regarding parallel lines in triangles</note>. And since **bc** is parallel to **dh**, the ratio of **ab** to **bd** will be the same as the ratio of **ac** to **ch** <note>original: "per 2 p 6. 18 p 5"; referring to Euclid’s *Elements*</note>. But since (by the initial premise) the ratio of **ab** to **bd** is the same as **ag** to **gd**, it follows that the ratio of **ac** to **ch** is the same as **az** to **zh** <note>original: "per 11 p 5"; Euclid's rule that ratios which are the same as the same ratio are also the same as each other</note>. Thus, the proposition is clear. With these premises established, let us proceed to our main subject.

*11. If a straight line from the center of vision is perpendicular to the surface of incidence: the image of a circumference concentric to the circumference of the circle (which is the common intersection of the surfaces of reflection and of the convex spherical mirror) will appear curved and parallel to that concentric circumference. 46 part 6.*

Let us first demonstrate regarding an arc how its image in these mirrors is curved—the curvature indeed not facing the mirror, but the center. For example: let **ab** be an arc placed opposite a mirror, and let **g** be the center of that arc, as well as the center of the mirror. Let **d** be the center of vision <note>the eye of the observer</note>, and let lines **dg**, **ag**, and **bg** be drawn. Let any point **e** be taken on the arc **ab**, and let line **eg** be drawn. However, let line **dg** not be in the same plane as **abg**. Therefore, line **dg** will either be <term>orthogonal<note>Latin: *orthogonalis*; at a 90-degree right angle.</note></term> to the surface **abg**, or slanted. Suppose it is orthogonal: then the angles **dga**, **dge**, and **dgb** will be equal (because they are right angles) and the sides will be equal to the sides. Therefore, the bases will also be equal. Consequently, all points of the arc **ab** will be the same distance from the center of vision. Thus, the images of all these points will be the same distance from the center. Let **q**, **m**, and **l** be the images of points **a**, **e**, and **b**. Therefore, **gq** will be equal to **gm** and **gl**. Because of this, **qml** will be an arc <note>original: "per 9 p 3"; Euclid’s rule for determining a circle from equal lines from a center</note>, and its convexity will be in respect to the center, not the mirror or the place of reflection. This is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the reflection of a circular arc. It depicts a center point 'g' from which lines radiate through a small arc (marked with points q, m, l) toward a larger outer arc (marked with points a, e, b). Above the arcs, a point 'd' represents the center of vision, with lines connecting to various points on the arcs. Letters such as h, t, z, and n are also present in the layout.</image-desc>

*12. If a straight line from the center of vision is oblique to the surface of incidence: the image of a circumference concentric to the circumference of the circle (which is the common intersection of the surfaces of reflection and of the convex spherical mirror) will appear curved, but not parallel to the concentric circumference. 47 part 6.*

If, however, the line **dg** is not perpendicular to the surface **abg**, a perpendicular line should be drawn from point **d** to this surface. Since that perpendicular is shorter than all other lines drawn from point **d** to this surface, the angle that this perpendicular forms toward **g** will be smaller than any other angle toward point **g** formed by any other line drawn from point **d** to this surface. Furthermore, a line drawn from point **d** to this surface will be longer the further it is from the perpendicular, and it will contain a larger angle toward **g**. 

Therefore, if this perpendicular does not fall upon the arc **aeb**, but to one side, all lines drawn from point **d** to this arc will be slanted to one side; those further away will be longer and contain a larger angle toward **g**. Let this be the case, and let three points be taken on the arc, namely **e**, **c**, and **b**. Let the <term>endpoint of tangency<note>Latin: *finis contingentiae*; the point on the mirror where the line of sight is tangent to the reflection geometry.</note></term> of point **b** be **l**, and let the endpoint of tangency of point **c** be **m**. Since point **c** is closer to **d** than **b** is, **m** will be closer to **g** than **l** is. Thus, segment **cm** is greater than **bl** (because **gc** and **gb** are equal as radii). Let **q** be the image of **c**, and **t** be the image of **b**. Let line **tq** be drawn, and let lines **cb** and **ml** be drawn; when extended, these lines will meet. If a line parallel to **cb** were drawn from point **m**, it would cut from **gb** a line equal to **cm**. But since **cm** is, as shown, greater than **bl**, lines **cb** and **ml** must meet when extended. Let them meet at point **o**. 

And since the proportion is the same (just as **gq** is to **qm**), so **gb** is to **bl**, and **gt** is to **tl**. Therefore, line **qt** will meet with lines **cb** and **ml**. Let the meeting point be **o**. Let the endpoint of tangency for point **e** be **n**. Since point **n** is lower than point **m**, **en** will be greater than **cm**. Therefore, when lines **ec** and **mn** are drawn, they will meet as before. Let them meet at point...

> *13. If the sight is outside the plane of incidence <term>plane of incidence|the flat surface formed by the incoming ray of light and the line perpendicular to the mirror</term>: the image of a circle's periphery that is eccentric <term>eccentric|not sharing the same center</term> to the circle (which is the common intersection of the plane of reflection and the convex spherical mirror) will appear more curved than the image of a concentric periphery. 48 [proposition] of Book 6.*

Furthermore: let a circle be taken whose center is not the center of the mirror, yet let it be in the same plane as the center of the mirror. I say that if an arc is taken in this outer circle on the side of the mirror’s center, closer to it at its middle point, its image will be curved. For given this arc: let a line be drawn from the center of the mirror to the center of the outer circle: and let this line be extended to the given arc: the line drawn from the center of the mirror to this arc, which is part of the diameter of the larger circle, will be shorter than all lines drawn from the same center of the mirror to that arc <note>original: "per 7 p 3"; referring to Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 7</note>. 

And from the center of the mirror, two equal lines can be drawn to the given arc from different sides of this short one <note>original: "per 7 p 3"</note> which indeed will be longer than that short one. And if a circle is made according to one of those, whose center is the center of the mirror: it will pass through the ends of these two lines, an arc exceeding the given arc. And it is clear that the image of this exceeding arc will be a curved line according to the previous statements <note>original: "11. 12 n"; referring to earlier theorems</note>. And the images of the points common to this arc and the given arc are the same: and the middle point of the exceeding arc is farther from the center of the mirror than the point of the given arc which corresponds to it. Therefore its image is closer to the center than the image of the point of the given arc corresponding to it. And thus the image of any point of the outer arc is closer to the center than the image of the point of the given arc which corresponds to it. Therefore the image of the given arc is more curved than the image of the outer arc. Thus the image of the given arc is curved. Which is what was proposed.

An intermediate arc z-m-h is positioned between the top arc and the circle. Various lines connect the center g to points on the arcs.</image-desc>

> *14. If the sight is outside the plane of incidence: the image of a straight line, parallel to a straight line touching the periphery of the circle (which is the common intersection of the plane of reflection and the convex spherical mirror), will appear curved. 49 [proposition] of Book 6.*

Furthermore: that the image of a straight line in these mirrors is curved is proved thus. Let **ab** be the line seen: let **g** be the center of the mirror: let lines **ag** and **bg** be drawn. These are either equal or they are not. If they are equal: let a circle be made, with **g** as the center, according to their size: let it be **aeb**: the line **ab** will indeed fall inside the circle. It is clear from the preceding things <note>original: "11. 12 n"</note> that the image of arc **aeb** will be curved. Therefore let its image be **zth**: let the image of **a** be **z**: the image of **b** be **h**: the image of **e** be **t**: and let **ge** be drawn cutting **ab** at point **f**. It is clear that **e** is on the same line as **f**, farther from the center **g**. Therefore its image will be closer to the center than the image of **f** <note>original: "per 30 n 5"; referring to Book 5, theorem 30</note>. Let it therefore be **m**. It is clear then that line **zmh** is the image of line **ab**: <note>for the images of the common points a and b remain the same</note> and it is a curved line. Which is what was proposed.

### *16. If the point of sight is outside the plane of incidence: the image of an infinite straight line, tangent to the circumference of the circle (the common section of the reflection surfaces and the convex spherical mirror), will appear curved. [Proposition 51, Book 6]*

If the line **ab** touches the mirror: it will either intersect it or be tangent to it. First, let it be tangent: and let **g** be the center of the mirror: and let lines **ag** and **bg** be drawn. The surface **abg** will intersect the mirror along a common circle <note>original: "per 1 th. 1 sphaer."; according to the first theorem of Book 1 of Theodosius’s Spherics</note> which shall be **e h z**. It is clear that line **ab** will be tangent to the mirror in this circle <gloss>for the circumference **ehz** and the straight line **ab** are in the same plane of incidence: and **ab**, being continued, touches the mirror by the premise. Therefore, it touches at the circumference **ehz**.</gloss> Let it be tangent at point **e**. Therefore, let **ab** be extended as far as **e**: and let **d** be the center of sight <term>center of sight|the physical location of the observer's eye</term>. The surface in which lines **dg** and **ag** lie will intersect the mirror along a circle common to the surface of reflection and the mirror <note>according to the same theorem of Spherics</note>: let the arc of that circle be **zp**. Similarly, the line common to the surface of reflection and the mirror, in which **dg** and **bg** lie: and let the arc of that circle be **hp**. It is clear <note>original: "è 29 n 5"; from Theorem 29 of Book 5</note> that **b** is reflected to **d** from some point on arc **hp**. If a tangent is drawn from that point: it will intersect line **bg**, and the point of intersection will be the limit of contingency <note>original: "per 17 n 5"; according to Theorem 17 of Book 5</note>. Let that point be **m**. It is also clear that if a tangent to the arc of the circle is drawn from point **m**: that tangent will fall short of **e**: because **ab** is tangent at point **e**, and point **b** is higher than point **m**. Let it fall, therefore, at point **f**: which tangent, when produced, will intersect line **ae**: let it intersect at point **t**: on the other side it will intersect line **ag**: <note>original: "per 11 ax"; by the 11th axiom</note> let it intersect at point **c**. Let angle **bgs** be made equal to angle **bgd** <note>original: "per 23 p 1"; by Euclid's Elements Book 1, Prop 23</note>: and let **gs** be extended to point **l** to equal the length of line **dg**: therefore <note>original: "per 26 p 3"; by Euclid's Elements Book 3, Prop 26</note> arc **hs** will be equal to arc **hp**. And just as **b** is reflected to **d** from some point on arc **hp**: so **a** will be reflected to **l** from some point on arc **hs**. And the reflection will be from point **f**, just as on arc **hp** there is a reflection from the point from which the tangent is drawn to point **m**. And those two points are of the same distance from point **m**. <gloss>If indeed two straight lines touching the circumference from the same point are connected by two radii: the straight line drawn from the center to that same point will bisect the angle at the center (by the 2nd corollary of Proposition 36, Book 3; Definition 15; and Proposition 8, Book 1): and the circumferences subtended by equal angles at the center, and the straight lines subtending those same circumferences, will be equal (by Propositions 26 and 29, Book 3): therefore the two aforementioned points of reflection will be equally distant from point **m**.</gloss>

20. *If the sight is in the plane of incidence: the image of an infinite straight line—whether it touches the circumference of the circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex spherical mirror) or not, and is slanted toward the side of the sight—will not be seen. If, however, it is said that the point taken on the line is reflected from a point on the arc of the circle which is beneath the line itself, this will also be impossible, because that entire arc is hidden by the line.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of light reflection on a convex mirror. A circle represents the mirror with its center labeled 'g'. A point of sight 'a' is positioned above. Rays labeled 'b' extend from 'a' to the arc and reflect outwards. A central vertical axis connects 'a' and 'g'.</image-desc>

21. *If the sight is in the plane of incidence: the image of an infinite straight line—neither touching nor cutting through the center of the circumference of the circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the convex spherical mirror), and slanted toward the side opposite the sight—will be seen as curved. [Proposition 56, Book 6]*

**B**UT if the line taken does not touch the circle, it can indeed be seen, though only slightly. If the aforementioned slanted line is taken between the line of reflection and the line passing through the point of reflection first taken to the center, this line can indeed be seen. The curvature of the image of this line will be diminished as it approaches closer to the line passing to the center through the point of reflection. If, however, lines are taken between the line passing to the center through the point of reflection, they will indeed be seen, whether their slant is toward the side of the sight or not. The manner of seeing them is similar to the manner of seeing lines between the line of reflection and the line passing to the center.

These things are to be understood regarding lines meeting in the arc of the circle that appears to the sight—that is, in the arc lying between two tangent lines drawn from the center of sight to the circle. However, of lines meeting the circle in the part of the circle hidden from the sight, one will be parallel to the line of reflection, and that one will not be seen. Similarly, a line sharing an endpoint with that parallel line, located below it, will be hidden; but a line sharing an endpoint with the parallel, existing above it, can be seen. 

If a line is taken between parallel lines that does not share an endpoint with any of them: if its slant is toward the side of the sight, it will be seen; if on the other side, sometimes it will be seen and sometimes not. For if a line parallel to the line of reflection is drawn from its endpoint: if the line is below the parallel, it will not be seen; if above it, it can be seen. But if the lines do not meet the circle, they will either intersect the line drawn from the center of sight to the center of the mirror, or they will be parallel to it. If any of them intersects it, that line will either intersect it on the side of the sight (that is, between the sight and the mirror) or beyond the mirror. If beyond, that line will be hidden, but perhaps its endpoints will appear. But if it intersects the visual line on the side of the sight, it will appear similarly. If it is parallel to the visual line, it can be seen.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram illustrating reflections on a convex mirror. It shows a circle with center 'g' and an observation point 'a'. A vertical axis runs from 'a' through 'g'. Multiple lines and segments are labeled with letters (c, d, e, h, f), depicting complex optical paths and intersections related to the curvature of reflected images.</image-desc>

The images of all these lines are curved. When the sight is in the same plane as the center of the mirror and the lines being seen, the clarity of the appearance is diminished. The one that appears most clearly is the one slanted with the greatest slant and facing the sight. In the same way, the images of arcs appearing in these mirrors, when they are in the same plane as the center of the mirror and the sight, are indeed curved, with the curvature facing the mirror. 

These things, however, are to be understood when both eyes <note>original: "duplici uisu"; literally 'double sight,' referring to binocular vision.</note> are in the same plane as the center of the mirror and the thing seen. For if one eye is slightly shifted, the thing seen will be perceived in another way. When the sight is outside the plane of the thing seen and the center of the mirror, the perception of the object itself will be more certain than when it is within that plane.

[Proposition 57, Book 6]

Now, it shall be proved that the image of the object seen is curved when the eye is in the plane of the centers of the mirror and the object. Let *d* be the center of the eye: *g* the center of the mirror: let *h e* be the line being seen, which does not intersect the circle of the mirror, but is parallel to line *d g*, or intersects it on the side of *d*. Let the plane of incidence be that in which the lines *d g* and *h e* lie. Let circle *a b* be the common section of this plane and the mirror. For if *h e* is parallel to *d g*, they will indeed intersect [according to Proclus's lemma on Proposition 29, Book 1]; but if *d g* intersects *h e*, all the more so will *g b* intersect it. That intersection will be either on line *h e* or beyond it. Let it be beyond: let them intersect at point *m*. Let the image of point *m* be *q*: let the end of tangency be *s*: and let line *z q* be drawn, and similarly line *t s*: and let *d g* intersect the circle at *a*: and [through Proposition 17, Book 3] let a tangent *a u* be drawn from point *a*.

Therefore [through Proposition 14, Book 5], *l g* is greater than *r g*. Thus *r* is lower than point *l*. But *z q l* is a straight line; therefore *z q r* is a curved line. And so the image of line *h c* is curved. Therefore, by placing any point of line *h e* in the position of point *m*, and point *e* in the position of point *c*, it will be proven that the image of *h e* is curved. *23. The image of a circumference situated in the same plane as the eye <note>original: "uisu"; the observer's point of sight</note>, when perceived within a convex spherical mirror, appears curved. [Proposition 58 and 62, Part 6]*

But if an arc is presented outside the mirror: it must be proven that its image is curved, just as it was proven when the eye was not in the same plane as the arc and the center of the mirror. And this is the proposition. Therefore, in these mirrors, straight lines appear curved, and similarly, curved lines appear similarly curved. If, however, a curved but long body with little width is presented to the eye in these mirrors: the curvature of that body will appear clearly, since it can be discerned by those things that are above or below the body. For curvature is not clearly discerned, except when it is great, where the ends of the length and width are hidden. Hence, when a body of slight convexity and large size is presented to the eye, its convexity is not clearly discerned, even though its image is convex, since the boundaries of the body do not appear in length or width. Furthermore: all the optical errors occurring in plane mirrors also occur in these: and besides those, it happens that the images of straight lines are curved—an effect which is absent from plane mirrors.

## ON THE ERRORS THAT OCCUR IN CONVEX
## COLUMNAR MIRRORS. Chapter V.

*24. If there are two perpendiculars <note>lines meeting at right angles</note> from two points of a cylindrical ellipse: the first to the axis, forming an acute angle with the straight line drawn from the second point to the same point on the axis; the second to the line tangent to the ellipse at the second point: they will intersect beyond the axis and the said acute angle. [Proposition 114, Part 1; Proposition 44, Part 7]*

Furthermore: in external columnar <note>cylindrical</note> mirrors, the same errors occur as in external spherical mirrors. For straight lines appear curved, and the size of the object appears diminished: but far more strongly in these than in those. For in spherical mirrors a large object will indeed appear smaller, but not much smaller: but in these, even a very large object will appear very small. Similarly, a straight line will appear curved in spherical mirrors, but with slight curvature; in columnar mirrors, it appears with the greatest curvature. Hence the errors of the columnar mirror are multiplied over the errors of the spherical. 

However, in columnar mirrors, reflection sometimes occurs from a straight line—namely, from the <term>line of length</term><note>original: "longitudine speculi"; the vertical meridian or "ruling" of the cylinder</note> of the mirror—sometimes from a circle, and sometimes from a <term>section</term><note>original: "sectione"; likely referring to an elliptical cross-section</note>. When the line being seen is parallel to the length of the mirror, the reflection will occur from the line of length: and the seen line will appear straight, with only slight curvature. These things will indeed be proven; for the proof of which it is necessary to set forth something beforehand, which is as follows. 

Given a columnar section, and a point chosen upon it that is not the point of reflection: if a line is drawn from that point to the perpendicular (which runs from the point of reflection to the axis), and that line forms an acute angle with the perpendicular; and if a line is drawn from the chosen point which is orthogonal <note>perpendicular</note> to the line tangent to that point: this line will intersect with the perpendicular below the axis, and below the intersection of the first line with the perpendicular. 

For example: let *a e b* be a section: *e* the given point: *n* the point being seen: *b* the point of reflection: *b d* the perpendicular: *e d b* an acute angle: *q e l* the tangent. It is clear that the surface *h d g* is orthogonal to the surface of the circle [by Proposition 18, Book 11: because it is drawn through the axis perpendicular to the circle by Definition 21, Book 11]. 

The surface <note>plane</note> tangent to the column at point *b* will be parallel to this surface: since the line of length drawn from point *b* is parallel to the axis [by Definition 21, Book 11]. And the line tangent to the circle at *b* is parallel to *d g* [by Proposition 28, Book 1: for the angles *g d b* are right by construction, as is the angle between the tangent at point *b* and the radius of the circle *d b* by Proposition 18, Book 3]. Therefore, the surface in which lines *l e* and *e t* lie is not parallel to the surface *h d g* [because it is not parallel to the surface tangent to the ellipse at point *b*: since angle *e d b* is acute by the premise]. It will therefore intersect with it. Let it intersect at line *l g*: and let line *t g* be drawn: which will indeed be a tangent, since the surface *l e t* is tangent. 

Now, with line *t d* drawn: angle *g t d* will be a right angle [by Proposition 18, Book 3]: since *t d* is a diameter, [and *t g* touches the circumference at its end *t*]. # OPTICS, BOOK VI.

The angle $gbe$ is a right angle. Therefore, by <note>Euclid's Elements</note> Book 1, Proposition 47, the square of line $go$ is equal to the square of line $bg$ and the square of line $bo$. Similarly, the square of $ge$ is equal to the squares of $gb$ and $be$. And since $be$ and $bo$ are equal [by the previous conclusion] and $gb$ is common to both: $go$ will be equal to $ge$ [because their squares are equal]. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 5, the angle $goe$ is equal to the angle $geo$. Now, if a perpendicular $zgn$ is drawn to the axis, $eo$ will be parallel to it, since $eo$ is parallel to $mbl$ by Book 1, Proposition 30. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 29, the angle $tgn$ is equal to the angle $goe$, and the angle $nge$ is equal to the angle $geo$; for which reason angle $tgn$ is equal to $nge$. Since, however, $tgo$ and $ngz$ are in the same surface <note>plane</note> in which $g$ lies, the points $o, g, t$ will be in the same surface; and thus the lines $ge, og, tg$ are in the same surface by Book 11, Proposition 1. Therefore, $t$ is reflected to $e$ from point $g$. Now, if we take point $h$ on line $th$ at the same distance from point $q$ as point $t$ is, and a line $ho$ is drawn: it will indeed pass through a point on the line of longitude $ag$; let it pass through point $a$. When a perpendicular $da$ is drawn from point $a$ to the axis, and line $ea$ is drawn: it will be possible to prove, as before, that the two angles $abo$ and $abe$ are right angles, the two sides $ao$ and $ae$ are equal, and the two angles $har$ and $ear$ are equal; and thus $h$ will be reflected to $e$ from point $a$. In the same way, for any point taken on line $th$, it can be proven that it will be reflected from some point on the line $ag$. Therefore, the line $th$ is reflected from the <term>line of longitude<gloss>a straight line running along the length of the cylinder's surface, parallel to the axis</gloss></term>, which is $ag$.

28. *If the eye is located at the common intersection of two planes—one containing a straight line and the other the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror—and these planes are perpendicular to each other, the reflection will occur from the circumference of the circle (which is the intersection of the plane of the line and the surface of the mirror), and the image will appear curved.* <note>Reference to Proposition 52, Book 7</note>.

Furthermore: if line $th$ intersects the plane in which the center of the eye and the axis are located, and is perpendicular to it, the eye will either be in that plane of line $th$ (which perpendicularly intersects the plane of the axis and eye) or outside of it. If the eye is in that plane, it is either above line $th$ or below it. If it is above, since that line is a physical object <note>original: "corporalis," implying an opaque line like a rod</note>, it will hide the mirror from the eye; thus there will be no reflection, though perhaps its ends will appear and be reflected from the circle of the cylinder (the intersection of the plane of line $th$ and the cylinder). The image of these ends will be just as it is in exterior spherical mirrors <note>Reference to section 21</note>. Similarly, if the eye is below line $th$, part of the mirror will be hidden by the end where the eye is located. However, part of the visible line is reflected from the circle in exactly the same way as in exterior spherical mirrors.

29. *If the eye, being equidistant from the ends of a straight line, is outside the plane of that line (which is perpendicular to the plane of the axis of the convex cylindrical mirror), the image will appear maximally curved.* <note>Reference to Proposition 53, Book 7</note>.
