# OPTICS, BOOK VI.

By <note>original: "per 18 p 1," referring to Euclid's *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 18</note> Proposition 18 of Book 1, angle $mzd$ is greater than angle $mdz$. Therefore, angle $dzl$ is greater than the two angles $zde$ and $zed$. [For it is established from the two angles $mzl$ and $mzd$, of which the former is greater than angle $zed$, and the latter is greater than angle $zde$.] But angle $dzl$ is equal to angle $nzc$ [by Proposition 15 of Book 1] and angle $ezc$ is equal to the two angles $zde$ and $zed$ [by Proposition 32 of Book 1]. Wherefore angle $nzc$ is greater than angle $ezc$: let it be cut to equality by the line $fz$: which will indeed meet with line $nq$: [by the lemma of Proclus to Proposition 29 of Book 1: because $nq$ and $cd$ are parallel by construction.] Let it meet at point $f$. Since, therefore, angle $fzc$ is equal to angle $cze$: it will be reflected to $e$ from point $z$. [By Theorem 12 of Book 4] it follows that it will be reflected to $e$ from a point on the <term>line of longitude</term> <note>The line running along the length of the cylinder's surface</note>, which passes through $z$ from a point that is beyond $z$. For if it were from a point this side of $z$ (that is, closer to $e$), the line drawn from point $q$ to that point of reflection would cut line $fz$: and thus the point of intersection would be reflected to $e$ from two points: which is impossible [and against Theorem 46 of Book 5]. 

Therefore, let point $k$ be taken beyond point $z$, from which $q$ is reflected to $e$: and let line $ek$ be drawn until it meets with line $nq$ at point $p$ [it will meet by the lemma of Proclus to Proposition 29 of Book 1]. $p$ will be the image of $q$ [by Theorem 4 of Book 5]. But $h$ is reflected to $e$ from the point of the <term>section of the column</term> <note>The cross-section of the cylinder</note> [for $h$ and $e$ are in different planes]. If, therefore, a perpendicular is drawn from point $h$ to the line tangent to the section at some point: that perpendicular will meet with the perpendicular $czd$ beneath the axis [by Theorem 24]. Let them meet at point $u$. Similarly, from point $l$ one must draw a perpendicular to the section, from whose point $t$ is reflected to $e$. And since [from the premise] points $h$ and $t$ are in the same position relative to line $ed$, and the points of the section through which the perpendiculars drawn from them pass are similarly situated. Therefore, those two perpendiculars will meet at the same point on line $ed$. Let them meet, therefore, at point $u$. And because line $eb$ meets with $hu$: let the meeting be at point $r$. Similarly, let $eg$ meet with $tu$ at point $y$: and let line $ry$ be drawn. 

It is clear [by Theorem 4 of Book 5] that $r$ is the image of $h$: and $y$ is the image of $t$: and we have the triangle $ery$: point $z$ is outside the surface of this triangle: and line $ep$ is higher in the surface of this triangle: and thus $p$ is outside. Wherefore line $rpy$ will be curved: and that is the image of line $th$. And indeed, this image has no small amount of curvature. This is what was proposed. It is clear, therefore, that in these mirrors, if a seen straight line is parallel to the line of longitude of the column: its image will be straight, or approaching straightness. If, however, a seen straight line is parallel to the [width of the] column: its image will be curved, with a significant curvature. Furthermore, lines situated between these two—those which more closely approach a position parallel to the column—will have images closer to straightness: and the images of those which are closer to a position parallel to the width will be more curved: and the curvature of the images will be decreased or increased according to the proximity or distance of the lines to either of these positions. And this is what was proposed.

But since angle $f z h$ is acute [by the conclusion], angle $t z f$ will be obtuse [by Book 1, Prop. 13]. Let a line be drawn from point $z$ making an angle with $t z$ equal to angle $o z t$: which line will necessarily cut $f p$ [by Proclus’s lemma to Book 1, Prop. 29: because $z t$ and $f p$ are parallel]. Let it cut at point $p$: and let line $p e$ be drawn. Since $p z$ and $o z$ are therefore in the same surface, and angle $o z t$ is equal to angle $t z p$ [by construction], point $o$ will be reflected to $p$ from point $z$ of the mirror [by Book 4, Number 12]. And because angle $o z t$ is equal to angle $z f p$ [by Book 1, Prop. 29, and $t z p$ is equal to $z p f$ by the same: wherefore $z f p$ and $z p f$ are equal], the sides $z p$ and $z f$ will be equal [by Book 1, Prop. 6]. And because angle $f e z$ is a right angle [since $a e$ is perpendicular to $f e n$], the square of $f z$ is equal to the squares of $e z$ and $e f$: and the square of $p z$ is equal to the squares of $e z$ and $e p$ [by Book 1, Prop. 47]. Therefore $p e$ and $f e$ are equal: [For since $z p$ and $z f$ have already been concluded to be equal, their squares will be equal: thus, by subtracting the common square $z e$, the squares $e p$ and $e f$ remain equal, and therefore their sides $e p$ and $e f$ are equal] and so [by Book 1, Prop. 5] angles $e p f$ and $e f p$ will be equal. Wherefore angles $n e q$ and $q e p$ are equal [for by Book 1, Prop. 29 angles $n e q$ and $e f p$, as well as $p e q$ and $e p f$ are equal: therefore by Axiom 1, $n e q$ and $p e q$ are equal]. And since they are in the same surface, which is $p e n$, point $n$ will be reflected to $p$ from point $e$ [by Book 4, Number 12]. Similarly, if any line is drawn from point $f$ to any point on $z e$, and is extended as far as $o n$: it will be proven regarding the point on line $o n$ upon which it falls, that it will be reflected to $p$ from the point on line $z e$ that the line cuts. And so any point of line $o n$ will be reflected to $p$ from some point on line $e z$.

# ALHAZEN

Line $o z$ cuts the surface tangent to the pyramid <note>In medieval Latin translations of Alhazen, "pyramid" is the standard term for a cone.</note> passing through $a z$. Therefore, line $a z$ lies under the common intersection <note>original: "differentia communi"</note> between the surface $o z h$ and the tangent surface. And this intersection makes a right angle with line $h z$ [by construction]. Therefore, angle $e z h$ is obtuse, and angle $f z h$ is acute [by Book 1, Proposition 13 of Euclid's *Elements*]. Let point $f$ be placed on line $z f$, from which a perpendicular is drawn to line $a e$ and extended straight. It will therefore meet with line $a o$ [by Axiom 11], for angle $a o e$ is acute [by the thesis, and it is a right angle at $e$]. Let them meet at $n$. And let line $e d$ be drawn from $e$ parallel to line $z h$ [by Book 3, Proposition 17]. Thus [by Book 11, Proposition 8], $e d$ will be perpendicular to the surface tangent to the pyramid passing through $a e$. Let a line be drawn from $e$ parallel to line $z m$; let it be $e l$. And let the surface containing lines $l e$ and $e d$ be extended. It will therefore cut the surface of the pyramid and create a section [by Theorem 5 of Book 1 of Apollonius's *Conics*]. For this surface is oblique to the axis $a d$. Therefore, let the section be $d e c$. Since $m z$ is perpendicular to the surface $a z h$ (as was shown previously) [in the preceding number, by the lemma to Theorem 37 of Euclid’s *Optics*], line $l e$ is perpendicular to the surface $a e d$ [by Book 11, Proposition 8]. Therefore, angle $a e l$ is a right angle. Similarly, angle $a e d$ is a right angle [by Book 1, Proposition 29], and $a e n$ is likewise a right angle. Therefore [by Book 11, Proposition 5], lines $l e$, $n e$, and $d e$ are in the same plane. Thus, line $f n$ is in the plane of the section. Let line $f r$ be drawn from $f$ parallel to line $d e$ [by Book 1, Proposition 31]. This line is therefore parallel to line $h z$ [by Book 1, Proposition 30]. And from $z$, in the surface $o z h$, let a line be drawn containing an angle with $z t$ equal to angle $o z t$ [by Book 1, Proposition 23].

Let them meet at $r$. Therefore, the two angles at $r$ and $f$ are equal; for they are equal to the two angles at $z$ [since by Book 1, Proposition 29, angles $o z t$ and $z f r$ are equal; likewise $t z r$ and $z r f$ are equal]. Therefore, the two lines $r z$ and $f z$ are equal [by Book 1, Proposition 6]. And it has been shown that line $f e n$ is in the plane of the section, and line $f r$ is parallel to $e d$; it is therefore in the plane of the section [by Book 1, Definition 35]. Let us connect $r e$; it will then be [by Book 11, Proposition 7] in the plane of the section. Let $d e$ be extended to $k$. It has been shown that $e a$ is perpendicular to the plane of the section; therefore, both angles $a e r$ and $a e f$ are right angles [by Book 11, Definition 3]. Since the two lines $f z$ and $r z$ are equal [by the conclusion], the two lines $r e$ and $f e$ are also equal. [For since angles $a e r$ and $a e f$ are right angles: the squares of $z e$ and $e f$ equal the square of $z f$ by Book 1, Proposition 47; likewise the squares of $z e$ and $e r$ equal the square of $z r$. But since the squares of the equal sides $z f$ and $z r$ are equal, by subtracting the common square of $z e$, the squares of $e f$ and $e r$, and thus the sides $e f$ and $e r$, will be equal.] Therefore [by Book 1, Proposition 5], the two angles $e r f$ and $e f r$ are equal. Thus, the image <note>original: "forma"</note> of $n$ will be reflected to $r$ from $e$ [by Book 4, Number 12: because angles $n e k$ and $r e k$ are equal, since by Book 1, Proposition 29 they equal the equal angles at $f$ and $r$], and the image of $o$ will be reflected to $r$ from $z$. And every line drawn from $f$ to any point on line $o n$ will cut $a e$. It is clear that this line will be equal to the line drawn from $r$ to the same point. For $a e$ is perpendicular to the surface in which lines $r e$ and $f e$ lie—this surface being the plane of the section—and the two lines $r e$ and $f e$ are equal. Therefore, all pairs of lines drawn from $r$ and $f$ to any single point on line $a e$ are equal. It is thus clear that the image of a point on $o n$ will be reflected to $r$ from that point which is cut on $z e$. Similarly, for every point placed on $a n$ beyond $n$, if it is joined with $f$ by a straight line, that line will cut $a e$ beyond $e$. It is clear from this that the image of line $a n$, and whatever is continuous with it, will be reflected to $r$ from the surface of the pyramid $a b g$ along a straight line. The same applies to every line drawn from $a$ that is oblique to the axis. And because triangle $a o h$ is in the same plane [by Book 11, Proposition 2], $n d$ will be in the plane of triangle $a o h$ [by Book 11, Proposition 1]. Thus $c$ is in the plane of triangle $a o h$. The two points $a$ and $u$ are in the plane of this triangle $a o h$, but points $a, u$, and $c$ are also on the surface of the pyramid. Thus, points $a, u$, and $c$ are on a straight line. Therefore, let $a u$ be extended straight to $c$, and let $r z$ be extended straight; it will cut $o h$ [because it cuts angle $z h o$ subtended by the base $h o$, and both $z r$ and $h o$ are in one plane]. Let it cut at point $p$. Thus $p$ is in the plane of triangle $a o h$. Let $a p$ be connected and pass straight through. It will therefore cut $n d$ at $g$ [because it cuts angle $d a n$]. And because $f$ is not in the tangent surface of the pyramid passing through line $a z$ [from what was concluded], angle $f e d$ will be acute. It is therefore clear, as in the previously mentioned figure [Note 30], that angle $d c x$ is obtuse; and that the perpendicular drawn from $c$ upon $c x$ will bisect angle $d c x$ and will meet with $e d$ below $d$. Therefore, let this perpendicular cut $e d$ at $s$. Thus, the perpendicular drawn from $n$ upon the line tangent to the section will cut the section beyond $s$, but further from $d$ than $s$; for these perpendiculars will meet beyond the circumference of the section. Therefore, the perpendicular drawn from point $n$ upon the line tangent to the section will not cut angle $d c x$; it will therefore be further from $n e$ than $n d$ is. Consequently, this perpendicular cuts $a d$ above $d$. Let the perpendicular drawn from $n$ upon the line tangent to the section be line $n q$. It cuts back through $e n$ and cuts the circumference of the section; it is on its surface, and $n q$ is on the surface of the section. Therefore, if $r e$ is extended straight, it will cut $n q$ <note>because, when continued, it cuts angle $n e q$.</note>. Let it cut at $y$; and surface $a n d$ will cut the surface of the section. Likewise, because point $e$ is outside surface $a n d$ (for surface $a n d$ is not the surface of the section <note>in which point $e$ is located</note> because point $a$ is outside the surface of the section, and because $a e$ is perpendicular to the surface of the section and $e$ is on its circumference), therefore $n c d$ is the common intersection <term>common intersection: the line where two surfaces meet</term> of surface $a n d$ and the surface of the section; and $n q$ meets with the section beyond $c$ [as was shown]. Therefore $n q$ is beyond surface $a n d$; thus $y$ is beyond line $a p g$ <note>which is not in surface $a n d$</note>. If, therefore, the eye is at $r$, and the form of some visible object is reflected from the longitudinal line, then $p$ will be the image of $o$ [by Note 4 of Book 5] and $y$ will be the image of $n$; and $a$ will be seen in its own place because it is at the vertex of the pyramid <note>In this context, "pyramid" refers to a cone.</note>. And the image of line $a n$ will be the line passing through points $a, p, y$; but this line is convex because it is beyond line $a p g$. Let this be line $a p y$. And it has already been shown that the forms of all points that are in $a n$ are reflected to $r$ from $a e$. Therefore, the radial lines <term>radial lines: the paths of light rays or visual lines</term> through which those forms are reflected are in the surface of triangle $r a e$. All images of line $a n$ are therefore in this surface. Thus, the convex line $a p y$ is in this surface, and $p$ is closer to $r$ than $y$ is. The convexity of this image will be on the side of the eye, and the convexity will be small; and the diameter of this image will be smaller than the line itself by a modest amount. Therefore, the images of straight lines that are drawn from the vertex of the pyramid obliquely to the axis are perceived by the eye in such a convex mirror. And the forms of these lines are reflected from straight lines extended along the length of the pyramid. And this is what we wished to declare.

### *33. If a straight line is parallel to the width of a convex conical mirror, and the eye is outside the plane parallel to the base through that line, it will be reflected from an ellipse, and the image will appear extremely curved. [Proposition 56, Book 7].*

The forms of lines equidistant to the width <note>meaning parallel to the base or circumference</note> of a convex pyramidal mirror are reflected from convex lines on the surface of the mirror; and the convexity of these lines is clear, as in a convex cylindrical mirror [Note 29]. By that same reasoning, it will similarly be clear that the images of these lines will be excessively convex and manifest to the senses. And the center of vision will be outside the surfaces in which the convexity of the forms of these lines exists. And the diameters of the images of these lines will be much smaller than the lines themselves.

### *34. If a straight line neither falls obliquely to the vertex of a convex conical mirror nor is parallel to its width, it will present an image of varying obliquity to the eye according to its different position. [Proposition 57, Book 7].*

Concerning oblique lines existing between these two modes—those which approach the lines extended along the length of the pyramid in their motion—they have forms that are slightly convex. Those which approach lines equidistant to the width of the pyramid have forms that are clearly convex.

### *35. In a convex conical mirror, the image appears tapered. [Proposition 58, Book 7; Proposition 40, Book 6].*

However, twisted lines <note>original: "lineae tortuosae"</note> that approach the vertex of the pyramid have smaller, narrower, and more convex forms. Those that approach the base of the pyramid have wider forms, because of what was demonstrated regarding convex spherical mirrors: namely, that the smaller the mirror is, the smaller the circles will be that fall upon its surface; and thus the images will be closer to the center and therefore smaller. Similarly, the sections that fall upon a pyramidal mirror which are on the side of the vertex of the pyramid are narrower and smaller; thus the image will be closer to the point in which the perpendiculars meet <note>the perpendiculars passing from the visible line through the lines tangent to the sections, which are common intersections</note>; and therefore these images will be smaller. But the sections on the side of the base of the pyramid are the opposite. Whence it happens that the form perceived in a convex pyramidal mirror is tapered <term>pyramidata: shaped like a pyramid or cone; tapering towards one end</term>: specifically, that which is on the side of the mirror's vertex will be narrower, and that which is on the side of the base will be wider; and the convexity of the width of the form will be manifest.

### *36. The visible image of an object near a convex conical mirror appears larger; that of a distant object appears smaller. [Proposition 59, Book 7].*

It also happens in these mirrors that the more a seen object approaches the mirror, the larger it will appear; and the more remote it is, the smaller it will appear. The deceptions <note>original: "fallaciae," referring to optical illusions or distortions</note> that occur in these mirrors are similar in all dispositions to those that occur in convex cylindrical mirrors, except for the tapering of the form.

# ALHAZEN

*37. The image is shaped in some way by its mirror. <note>original: "38 p 5" — a reference to Proposition 38 in Book 5 of the earlier tradition.</note>*

And in every way, the form of a visible object that is perceived through reflection will always resemble the form of the mirror’s surface from which it is reflected. The reason for this is that the location of the image is always determined by the form of the mirror’s surface and the point where the perpendicular lines meet. Therefore, the surface of the mirror always holds a certain influence <gloss>original: "dignitatem," meaning it plays a primary role</gloss> over the form of the seen object as it is perceived in the mirror. Furthermore, the compound deceptions in this type of mirror are similar to the deceptions found in the previously mentioned mirrors.

### CONCERNING THE ERRORS WHICH OCCUR IN MIRRORS
->spherical concave. Chapter VII.<-

*38. In a concave mirror, distortions occur more frequently and are greater than in flat and convex mirrors. <note>Vitello, in the preface to Book 8.</note>*

In these mirrors, many more errors occur than in all convex and flat mirrors. Indeed, the same errors occur in these as in those—namely, the weakening of light and color, and the variation of position and distance. For the cause of this is reflection alone, not the specific shape of the mirror. However, there also occurs in these mirrors a greater error regarding the variation of size than in convex mirrors. For in convex mirrors, for the most part, an object is perceived as smaller; in concave mirrors, however, it is sometimes perceived as larger, sometimes smaller, and sometimes according to how it truly is. This depends on the variation of the positions of the mirror and the eye, as we shall explain in this chapter. It also happens in these mirrors that a single visible thing is seen as two, or three, or four; this is not the case in flat or convex mirrors. For in those, one visible thing is only ever perceived as one, but in concave mirrors, it is not so. Likewise, the arrangement of the parts of a seen object is perceived in convex and flat mirrors just as it is in reality; in concave mirrors, however, in many positions, it appears otherwise. And these two things—namely, perceiving one thing as one, and perceiving the arrangement of parts as they truly are—do not suffer any deception in spherical convex mirrors. Since deceptions do occur in these spherical concave mirrors, it is clear that nothing is perceived in such mirrors without some distortion, either always or at some time, depending on the change in position. The weakening of light and color, and the variation of position and distance, occur in these mirrors just as in the others, always and in every position. Size, form, and number, however, involve deception in these mirrors in certain positions, as we shall explain. Regarding number, it was explained in the chapter on the image <note>References to Propositions 66, 67, 69, 70, 71, and 72 in Book 5.</note> that one seen object in concave mirrors can have one, two, three, or four images, and that the form of the visible object is always perceived at the location of the image. Indeed, one object seen in spherical concave mirrors is perhaps perceived as one, or perhaps two, or perhaps three, or perhaps four—which does not happen in spherical convex and flat mirrors. Regarding the arrangement of the parts of a visible object, it was said in the chapter on the image <note>Proposition 65 in Book 5.</note> that the form of a single point is reflected from the circumference of a circle, and that visible things whose images appear behind the eye, in front of it, or at the center of the eye appear blurred and uncertain. Whatever is of this nature does not retain the arrangement of its parts as the visible object itself does. This also occurs in these mirrors differently than in convex and flat mirrors. The causes of these things were explained in the chapter on the image. It remains, therefore, to explain that what is perceived in these mirrors is sometimes perceived as larger, sometimes smaller, and sometimes equal; and that in certain positions it will be perceived inverted, and in others upright; and that what is upright in such mirrors will be perceived as concave, convex, or straight; and that the convex and concave will also be perceived differently than they are. These effects also arise from the variation in the arrangement of the parts of the visible object. We shall demonstrate these things in the following manner.

*39. If the eye and the visible object are within a concave spherical mirror, on a straight line with its endpoints at equal distances from the center: the image will be seen beyond the mirror, larger than the object. <note>46 p. 8</note>*

Let us connect $a$ $e$ and $a$ $z$, and let them pass through to $b$ and $g$. Therefore, because $a$ $o$ is equal to $o$ $u$, then $a$ $e$ will be equal to $e$ $b$, and $a$ $z$ will be equal to $z$ $g$. <note>For the diameters of circle $b$ $g$ are bisected at points $e$, $o$, and $z$ by the circumference $e$ $o$ $z$.</note> And because $t$ $e$ is tangent to circle $e$ $z$, $t$ $e$ will be perpendicular to $a$ $b$ <note>By Proposition 18, Book 3 of Euclid.</note>, and similarly $t$ $z$ will be perpendicular to $a$ $g$. ...we have proved [in the previous number] that line f q is greater than line m n. Then, when the sight is placed above point k, and line m n is in some visible object: the sight will perceive a larger form of the visible thing. And thus, if we rotate the entire figure around the line a u while it remains fixed: then point k will describe a circle perpendicular to line a u. And so every point of that circle will have a position, relative to the corresponding line m n, just as the position of k is relative to m n. Therefore, if the sight is at any point on the circumference of this circle, and a line corresponding to line m n is on the surface of some visible object: then the sight will perceive the form of that line as larger. And similarly, if we draw t k as a straight line, and place any point other than k on it, and always draw lines from that point (which acts as point k), the result will be the same as with point k. From these two figures, it is therefore clear that in concave spherical mirrors, many things from many positions are perceived as larger.

### *41. In a concave spherical mirror, the image is sometimes equal to the visible object: that which is between the sight and the mirror is inverted, while that which is behind the sight is upright. 48 p 8.* <note>This refers to Proposition 48 in Book 8 of the broader optical tradition, likely the edition by Risner.</note>

Likewise: let there be a spherical mirror a b around center e: and let us draw a surface passing through e: and let it form circle a b: and let us draw from e the line e z, in whatever manner it may be, up to g: and from g let us draw g d perpendicular to the surface of circle a b: [by Proposition 12 of Book 11] <note>Standard reference to Euclid's Elements.</note> and on it let us mark point d, however it may be: and let us connect d e: and extend it to o: and draw e b so that it forms an obtuse angle <term>obtuse angle<gloss>an angle greater than 90 degrees</gloss></term> with e d: and draw e a so that it forms an angle with e d equal to angle d e b: and connect d a, d b. Thus the surfaces of the two triangles d a e, d b e intersect each other along the line d e: and the two acute angles d b e, d a e will be equal. [By Proposition 4 of Book 1: for the radii e a, e b are equal by Definition 15 of Book 1, and d e is common: and the angles d e a, d e b are equal by construction.] Therefore, let us draw from b a line in the surface of triangle d e b, forming with e b an angle equal to angle d b e. This line will therefore meet with line d e: because angle b e d is obtuse, and the angle at b is acute. [For since angle d e b is obtuse by construction, the remaining angle b e o is acute by Proposition 13 of Book 1, and e b o is acute, because it was made equal to the acute angle d b e. Therefore d e and b o will meet by Axiom 11.] <note>Axiom 11 refers to the parallel postulate or its corollaries regarding intersecting lines.</note> Let them meet at o: and let us also draw from a a line in the surface of triangle d a e, forming with a e an angle equal to angle d a e. It will therefore meet with d e at o: because the two angles a e o, b e o are equal [by construction and Proposition 13 of Book 1] and the angles at a and b are equal [therefore by Proposition 26 of Book 1, b o and a o are equal: and thus they meet at the same point on the extended line d e.]

And let us draw e t so that it forms a right angle with e b: and extend t e from the side of e, and b o from the side of o: and let them meet at h, [they will meet by Axiom 11: because angle h e b is a right angle by construction, and e b o is acute by the conclusion] and e t will be equal to e h [by Proposition 26 of Book 1: for the adjacent right angles at e are equal: likewise a d b by construction: and b e is a common side to both triangles b e t and b e h] and b t equal to b h. And similarly, let us draw e k so that it forms a right angle with e a: and extend it from the side of e: and extend a o, and let them meet at l [they will meet by Axiom 11 as was just shown.] Thus e k will be equal to e l, and k a equal to a l, and t e equal to e h [by Proposition 26 of Book 1, as was evident.] And let us connect t k and l h. They will therefore be equal [for the two sides e l, e h have been concluded to be equal to the two sides e k, e t, and angle l e h is equal to angle k e t by Proposition 15 of Book 1. Therefore by Proposition 4 of Book 1, l h and k t are equal.] If, therefore, the sight is at d, and l h is in some visible object: then the eye at d will perceive l h in mirror a b: and t will be the image of h: and k the image of l [by section 6, note 5.] Thus t k will be the diameter <note>The linear span or width.</note> of the image of l h: and it is equal to it. If, therefore, we rotate the entire figure while l h remains fixed: then d will describe a circle. And if the sight is at any point on that circumference, it will be able to perceive some visible object, equal to line l h: and its image will be equal to it. And similarly, if the sight is at o, and the visible thing is t k: the image will be equal to the visible thing.

But nevertheless, when the visible thing is l h, and the sight is at d, and the image is t k: the image will be inverted <term>inverted<gloss>conversely oriented; upside down or mirrored</gloss></term>: if h is on the right, t will be on the left: and if h is on the left, t will be on the right: and if h is above the line, t will be below the line: and similarly for l. And if the visible thing is t k, and the sight is at o, and the image is l h: the form is upright. For the image l h will be behind the sight, and will be perceived in front of the visible thing, as we explained in the chapter on images in the fifth treatise [section 60]. And the sight will perceive h, which is the image of t, on line h o, and l, which is the image of k, on l o. It is clear, therefore, that in concave mirrors, a visible thing is sometimes perceived as equal to itself.

### ALHAZEN

**44. If the eye is located on this side of the center of a hollow spherical mirror, and the visible object is beyond it: the image, both of the object and of the viewer, will appear inverted and smaller.**

Likewise: let there be a <term>concave mirror<note>A mirror with a surface that curves inward, like the inside of a bowl.</note></term> *a b*, with center *g*. Let it have a flat surface passing through the center, forming circle *a b*. Let us draw a line *g d* in whatever manner; let it pass from part *g* toward *e*, and let the eye be at *e*. Let *t* be on the surface of the eye, and let us draw *t h* perpendicular to line *e d* [by Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 11]. Let *z t* be equal to *t h*. Let the eye at point *e* perceive point *h* from point *a* on the mirror. Let *g h*, extended to *p*, encompass an arc *a p* greater than a quarter of the circle. Thus, the two points *a* and *h* will be on two sides of point *g*. For if they were on the same side, then the line coming from the mirror to *a* would not divide the angle formed by the two radial lines into equal parts [and thus, as shown in Book 5, note 66, no reflection would occur].

Let us draw lines *e a*, *a h*, *g a*, and *g h*. Let *g h* pass straight through to *k*. The two angles at *a* will therefore be equal [by the hypothesis and Book 4, note 12], and *k* will be the image of *h* [by Book 5, note 6]. Let arc *b d* be equal to arc *d a* [it becomes equal by Book 6, Proposition 33, if you set angle *d g b* equal to angle *d g a* by Book 1, Proposition 23]. Let us connect lines *e b*, *b z*, and *b g*. Let us extend *z g* to *l*, and let *z b* cut the diameter *d g* at *f*. The two angles at *b* will therefore be equal. [Because *a g* and *b g* are equal by Book 1, Definition 15, and *g f* is common to both, and angle *a g f* was made equal to angle *b g f*: the base *a f* will equal base *b f*, and angle *f a g* will equal angle *f b g* by Book 1, Proposition 4. For the same reason, *e a g* and *e b g* are equal, because angle *b g e* equals angle *a g e* by Book 1, Proposition 13. Wherefore, since the angles at *a* are equal, the angles at *b* will be equal.] 

The point *z* is perceived by the eye from *b* [by Book 4, note 12], and point *l* will be the image of *z* [by Book 5, note 6]. Let us connect *k l*; therefore *k l* is the diameter of the image of *z h*. Because *t h* is perpendicular to *d e*, and *z t* is equal to *t h*: the two lines *e a* and *a h* will be equal to the two lines *e b* and *b z*. [For since *t h* and *z t* are equal by construction, and *t f* is common, and the angles at *t* are right angles: base *h f* will equal base *z f* by Book 1, Proposition 4. And *a f* was already concluded to be equal to *b f*; thus the whole *a h* equals the whole *b z*, and *a e* and *b e* are concluded to be equal.] 

The two angles at *a* are equal to the two angles at *b*; *h e* will be equal to *z e* [by Book 1, Proposition 4], and line *g h* is equal to line *z h* [by Book 1, Proposition 4: because *z t* and *t h* are equal by construction, *t g* is common, and the angles at *t* are right angles.] Therefore, the two lines *a g* and *g h* are equal to the two lines *b g* and *g z*, and the base *a h* is equal to the base *b z*. Therefore [by Book 1, Proposition 8] angle *a h k* is equal to angle *b z l*, and angle *h a k* is equal to *z b l*. Therefore *h k* is equal to *z l* [by Book 1, Proposition 26: because *z b* was concluded to be equal to *h a*] and line *h g* is equal to *z g* [from the conclusion]. Therefore *g k* is equal to *g l* [by Book 5, Proposition 19]. Therefore *k l* is parallel to *z h* [by Book 1, Proposition 27: for since the angles at the vertex *g* are equal by Book 1, Proposition 15, and as *g z* is to *g k*, so *g z* is to *g h* by Book 5, Proposition 7: angle *z l k* will equal angle *l z h* by Book 6, Proposition 6]. 

Also, angle *h g a* is <term>obtuse<note>An angle greater than 90 degrees.</note></term> [from the hypothesis and Book 6, Proposition 33] and the two angles at *a* are equal: therefore line *g h* is greater than line *g k*. [For because angle *a g h* is obtuse, by Book 1, Proposition 13, angle *a g k* will be <term>acute<note>An angle less than 90 degrees.</note></term>, and *h a g* and *g a k* are equal from the hypothesis because point *a* is the point of reflection. Wherefore by Book 1, Proposition 32, angle *a k g* is greater than angle *a h k*; and by Book 1, Proposition 19, in triangle *a h k*, side *a h* is greater than *a k*. But as *a h* is to *a k*, so *h g* is to *g k* by Book 6, Proposition 3, because the angles at *a* are equal. Thus, since *a h* is greater than *a k*, *h g* will be greater than *g k*.] Similarly, *z g* is greater than *g l*. Therefore line *k l* is smaller than *z h*. [For since triangles *k g l* and *h g z* are equiangular by Book 1, Prop. 15 and Book 6, Prop. 6: it will be, by Book 6, Prop. 4, that as *g k* is to *g h*, so *k l* is to *z h*. And since *g k* is smaller than *g h*, *k l* will be smaller than *z h*.] 

But *k l* is the diameter of the image of *z h*; therefore *z h* appears smaller than it truly is, and line *z h* is the surface of the viewer's face. If we then rotate the circle *a d b* while *e d* remains stationary, a circle will be formed from the two points *a* and *b* on the surface of the mirror. The position of the eye *e*, with respect to any corresponding line *z h* from that circle marked by points *z* and *h*, and from every arc corresponding to arc *a b* from the portion of the mirror divided by the circle marked by points *a* and *b*, is the same as the position that the eye *e* has from line *z h* and arc *a b*. It will be demonstrated similarly if we make line *z h* larger or smaller. 

It is evident from all these things that the diameter of the surface of the viewer's face is perceived in the concave mirror as smaller than it is. It should be known, therefore, that if the eye is at *e*, the viewer will perceive their own form as smaller than it is. And because *k* is the image of *h*, and *l* is the image of *z*, the image will be <term>inverted<note>original: "conuersa". This means the image is flipped both upside down and left-to-right.</note></term>. Thus the eye at *e* will perceive its form such that right is in the left, and up is down, and vice versa. Similarly, if the eye is at any point between which and the mirror’s surface the center of the mirror lies, it will perceive its form inverted. And this is what we intended to show. 

It is clear from these four figures that in a concave mirror, the image is sometimes perceived as larger, sometimes smaller, sometimes equal, and sometimes upright, sometimes inverted. In the chapter on images [Book 5, note 72], we said that in a concave mirror there will sometimes be one image, sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes four; and this same thing happens in these cases mentioned above. Therefore, that which has an image larger than itself might perhaps have others that are smaller and equal; and that which has a smaller image might perhaps have others that are larger and smaller. And that which appears upright might perhaps appear inverted in another image, and vice-versa. It remains, therefore, to describe the forms of those things perceived in these mirrors.

Therefore, the two lines *z h* and *h r* are reflected due to the equal angles [*r h e* and *z h e*, by Book 4, note 12], and *l* will be the image of *r*. I say, therefore, that the form of any point on line *g r* is reflected to the eye at *z* from some specific point on arc *f h*, and from no other. The proof of this is that in the chapter on the image, in the fifth treatise in two figures [note 66], it was stated that the two arcs *a b* and *d o* cannot be such that anything from line *e o* is reflected from them to *z*. I say, then, that this reflection point will not be found except on arc *f h*.

### *46. In a concave spherical mirror, images of lines—whether convex or concave—sometimes appear convex or concave; and they maintain the same slant toward the eye as the line itself has toward the mirror. (Proposition 55, Book 8).*

Let us repeat the figure and construct two arcs on either side of line *g r*, however they may be, namely *g n r* and *g q r*. Let the arc *g n r* not intersect line *g h*, and let us place point *m* anywhere on line *g r*. The form of *m* is reflected to the eye *z* from some point on arc *f h* [according to the preceding section]. Let it be reflected from *t*, and let us connect lines *z t* and *m t*. The two angles *z t e* and *m t n* are equal <note>original: "per thesin" - by the hypothesis or the given geometric setup</note> [and by Book 4, Theorem 12]. Therefore, line *m t* will intersect arc *g n r*; let it intersect at *n*. Let us extend line *t m* past point *m*; it will then intersect *g q r*; let it intersect at point *q*. Let us connect *n e* and extend it straight; it will intersect *z t* below line *k l*; let it intersect it at *i*. Let us connect *q e* and extend it straight; it will intersect *z t* above *k l*; let it intersect it at *p*. Because the two angles at *t* are equal [by the hypothesis and Book 4, Theorem 12], *i* will be the image of *n* [by Book 5, Theorem 6], and the two points *k* and *i* are images of the two points *g* and *r*. Thus, the image of arc *g n r* is the line passing through points *k, i, l*, such as the line *k i l*. But line *k i l* is <term>convex<note>Curving outward, like the exterior of a ball.</note></term> from the perspective of the eye *z*, and arc *g n r* is convex from the perspective of the mirror. Therefore, the eye *z* will perceive the form of the convex line *g n r* as a convex line. And since the two angles at *t* are equal [namely *p t e* and *q t e* by the hypothesis and Book 4, Theorem 12], *p* will also be the image of *q* [by Book 5, Theorem 6], and the line *l p k* will be <term>concave<note>Curving inward, like the interior of a bowl.</note></term> from the perspective of the eye; and it is the image of arc *g q r*, which is concave from the perspective of the mirror's surface. Therefore, the eye *z* will perceive the form of the concave arc *g q r* as a concave line. Thus, in concave mirrors, from certain positions, a convex line is perceived as convex, and a concave one as concave.

### OPTICS, BOOK VI.

*m*, *l*, and *f* will be the images of point *z*. Thus, *z* will be perceived in three places [because it is reflected to the eye *e* from three points *a*, *b*, and *d*]. Likewise, let us draw a line from *e* to the arc *d z*, wherever it may be; let it be *e k*. Let us extend *g k*, and let it intersect the arc *d z* at *k*. Let us connect the line *k z*. Since the arcs *e g* and *g z* are equal [from what was previously concluded], the two angles *e k g* and *g k z* will be equal [by Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 27]. And let us extend *g k* to *r*, and draw lines *e r* and *z r*. Therefore, angle *e r g* is greater than angle *g r z*. For since the lines *a g* and *d g* are equal by Definition 15 of Book 1, the peripheries *a g* and *d g* subtended by them will be equal by Book 3, Proposition 28; and since *e g* was concluded to be equal to *z g*, the remainder *a e* equals the remainder *d z*. Therefore, angle *e r g* is not equal to angle *g r z*, nor is it smaller, as would be shown by the same argument. Therefore, angle *e r g* is greater than angle *g r z*.]

Let angle *g r n* then be equal to angle *e r g* [by Book 1, Proposition 23]. Therefore, the two lines *e r* and *r n* will reflect from each other because of the equal angles [by Book 4, Theorem 12 of this work], and let us extend *e r* to *q*. Let this be *c z p*. Let us set *g* as the center, and at the distance *g n* let us make an arc of a circle *c n p*. It will therefore cut the line *c z p* at two points, let them be *c* and *p*. Let us connect the lines *g c* and *g p*. These will therefore be in a surface perpendicular to the surface *a b d*. Let us extend *g c* and *g p* straight; and centered on *g*, at the distance *g q*, let us make an arc of a circle. It will then cut the two lines *g c* and *g p*; let it cut them at *s* and *o*. Since the surface of circle *a b d* is perpendicular to the surface of the two lines *g c* and *g p*, the two angles *e g s* and *e g o* will be right angles [by Definition 4, Book 11], and *e g* is perpendicular to the surface *g c p*. Therefore [by Book 11, Proposition 18], both surfaces *e g s* and *e g o* are perpendicular to the surface *s g o*. And each of these two surfaces forms a <term>great circle<note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose center is also the center of the sphere, dividing it into two equal hemispheres.</note></term> in the mirror [by Theorem 1 of Book 1 of the Spherics], equal to circle *a b d*.

The point of the circle corresponding to point *r* is that which the surface *e g s* forms. Therefore, two lines meet at it at equal angles between the two points *e* and *c*; and similarly between the two points *e* and *p*. The lines *g c* and *g p* are equal [by Definition 15 of Book 1], and lines *g s* and *g o* are equal; and *q* is the image of *n*, *s* is the image of *c*, and *o* is the image of *p*. Therefore, the image of the arc *c n p*, which is convex toward the mirror, is the arc *s q o*, which is concave toward the eye; and *l* is the image of *z*, and the two points *s* and *o* are the images of *c* and *p*. Therefore, the image of the line *c z p* is the line passing through points *s*, *l*, and *o*; and such a line is concave toward the eye.

### 49. In a concave spherical mirror, the image of a straight line sometimes appears convex. <note>original: "In speculo spherico cauo imago linea recta aliquando uidetur conuexa." This refers to Proposition 57 in some editions.</note>

Having demonstrated these preliminary points, let us redraw the circle and complete the proof, so that the lines are not overcrowded and the letters do not become confusing. Let there be a circle in the second figure, *a b g*, with center *d*. Let us draw the line *d q*, and let *d b* be equal to *d b* in the first figure; let *d o* be equal to *d o* in the first figure; and let *d q* be equal to its counterpart in the first figure, and similarly *d u*. Let us then draw a perpendicular line from *d q* above the surface of the circle <note>following Euclid's Elements, Book 11, Proposition 12</note>, and let *d h* be equal to its counterpart in the first figure. Therefore, the angle *h d q* will be a right angle <note>following Euclid, Book 11, Definition 3</note>. The circle formed by *h d q* within the <term>speculum</term> <note>a mirror, from the Latin 'speculum'</note> will be among those circles from which the forms of points *o* and *u* are reflected. The arc measured by lines *h d* and *d q* will be equal to arc *a g* in the first circle <note>following Euclid, Book 6, Proposition 33, because both subtend a right angle</note>. From two points on this arc, which correspond to the two points *b* and *f*, two points of the line *u p* will be reflected to the two points *n* and *q* equally. Thus, *q* will be the image of *o*, and *n* will be the image of *u*.

Now, let us draw a perpendicular line from *u* on the surface of circle *a b g*, over line *d u* <note>following Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 11</note>; let this be *z u e*. With *d* as the center and the length *d o*, let us describe an arc of a circle. This arc will cut the line *z u e* at two points <note>because point o is higher than point u, based on the first thesis</note>; let it cut at *z* and *e*, and let the arc be *z o e*. Let us connect *d z* and *d e* and extend them outside the circle. From point *d* and with the length *d q*, let us describe arc *t q*; it will cut the two lines *d z* and *d e* at *t* and *k*. Let us connect *t k*; it will cut the line *d q* at *l*.

Since *h d* is perpendicular to the surface of the circle, both angles *h d t* and *h d k* will be right angles <note>Euclid, Book 11, Definition 3</note>. Both surfaces *h d t* and *h d k* will form a circle on the surface of the mirror <note>following the 1st theorem of the Sphere</note>. The arc between the two lines *h d* and *d t* will be equal to the arc between the two lines *h d* and *d q*; the same applies to the arc between lines *h d* and *d k*. Since both lines *d z* and *d e* are equal to line *d o* <note>Euclid, Book 1, Definition 15</note>, these two arcs are such that the two points *z* and *e* will be reflected from them at equal angles <note>as demonstrated in point 66, number 5</note>. The two lines *d t* and *d k* are equal to line *d q* <note>Euclid, Book 1, Definition 15</note>. Therefore, point *t* is the image of *z*, and *k* is the image of *e*.

And because lines *d t*, *d q*, and *d k* are equal, and lines *d z*, *d o*, and *d e* are equal, the ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of *d t* to *d z* is as the ratio of *q d* to *d o*, and as the ratio of *k d* to *d e* <note>Euclid, Book 5, Proposition 7</note>. But the ratio of *q d* to *d o*, as we showed in the first figure of the preceding section, is greater than the ratio of *n d* to *d u*. Therefore, the ratio of *d t* to *d z* is greater than the ratio of *n d* to *d u*, and similarly for *k d* to *d e*. Since the two lines *z d* and *d e* are equal, and the two lines *d t* and *d k* are equal, line *t k* is parallel to *z e* <note>Euclid, Book 6, Proposition 2; for by Book 5, Prop 7, dt is to dz as dk is to de, and by Book 5, Prop 17, as tz is to zd, so ke is to ed</note>. Therefore <note>Euclid, Book 6, Prop 2 and Book 5, Prop 18</note>, both ratios *d t* to *d z* and *k d* to *d e* will be as the ratio *l d* to *d u*. Thus, the ratio *l d* to *d u* is greater than the ratio *n d* to *d u*; therefore, line *l d* is greater than line *n d* <note>Euclid, Book 5, Proposition 10</note>. So *n* lies between *l* and *u*. But *n* is the image of *u*, and the two points *t* and *k* are the images of *z* and *e*. Therefore, the image of the straight line *z u e* is a line passing through the points *t*, *n*, and *k*; and the line that passes through these points is convex. From this it is clear that in concave mirrors, a line sometimes appears convex in certain positions.

### 50. In a concave spherical mirror, the images of lines: whether concave or convex, sometimes appear concave. <note>Proposition 58, part 8.</note>

Likewise: let us place point *m* on line *z u* in whatever manner; and with center *m* and at length *m u*, let us make the arc *r u f*. This arc will therefore cut the arc *u o e* at two points <note>Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 10</note>; let it cut at *r* and *f*. Let us connect lines *d r* and *d f*, and let them extend straight until they meet the arc *t q k* at points *p* and *i*. The surface of the two lines *h d* and *d p* will create a circle in the mirror, from whose circumference lines will be reflected to *r*. Similarly, the surface of the two lines *h d* and *d i* will create a circle in the mirror, from whose circumference lines will be reflected to *f*. Thus *p* is the image of *r*, and *i* is the image of *f*, and *n* is the image of *u*. Therefore, the image of arc *r u f* is the line passing through *i*, *p*, and *n*. But this line will be concave on the side of the eye <note>original: "uisus," referring to the observer's sight</note>, and arc *r u f* is concave on the side of the mirror's surface. Therefore, when the eye is at *h*, and each of the lines *z u e*, *z o e*, and *r u f* is on some visible object, then the straight line *z u e* will be perceived as convex, and the line...

the convex line *z o e* will be perceived as concave, and the concave *r u f* as convex. Therefore, if each of the lines *z u e*, *z o e*, and *r u f* produces a single image, then the shape of those lines will be exactly as we have described; and if they produce other images, they might be similar to the other images or perhaps different. It is clear from these figures, then, that straight lines in concave mirrors are sometimes perceived as straight, sometimes as convex, and sometimes as concave. Similarly, convex lines are sometimes perceived as convex and sometimes as concave; and concave lines are sometimes perceived as convex and sometimes as concave. Therefore, the shapes of visible surfaces are perceived differently than they truly are in such mirrors. For straight lines only exist on flat surfaces; and when a straight line existing on a flat surface is perceived as convex or concave, then the surface on which that line sits will also be perceived as convex or concave. Since the sight perceives convex, concave, and straight lines differently than they truly are, it will also perceive the surfaces in which they reside differently than they truly are. It is therefore clear from what has been said that a deception <note>original: "fallacia"; Alhazen uses this term to describe optical illusions or errors in perception caused by the laws of reflection.</note> occurs in everything perceived in concave mirrors. In some cases, this happens always and in every position; in others, it happens only in certain positions. Composite deceptions occur in these mirrors in the same manner as simple ones. This is what we wished to demonstrate.

### ON THE ERRORS THAT OCCUR 
### in concave cylindrical mirrors.
### Chapter VIII.

In these mirrors, errors occur that are similar to those in concave spherical mirrors. For there are deceptions arising from reflection—namely, the weakening of light and color, and the displacement of position and distance—which occur in all mirrors. There also occurs a variation in size similar to that which occurs in concave spherical mirrors. A single visible object may also appear as one, or two, or three, or four; it may appear upright or inverted according to different positions; and a flat surface may appear concave or convex. We shall therefore show how the size and number of the seen object vary in these mirrors, and how it appears upright or inverted in the same way we demonstrated for concave spherical mirrors.

The line $m\ s$ will be the <term>common section<note>The "common section" (differentia communis) is the line where two planes intersect.</note></term> of these two surfaces. 

Because $a\ k$ lies in the surface passing through the axis (being part of the side of the cylinder) and is perpendicular to $m\ s$ by construction—which is the common section between the surface passing through the axis and the surface of the lines $r\ m$ and $m\ s$—then $a\ k\ n$ will be perpendicular to the surface of the lines $r\ m$ and $m\ s$. However, line $h\ t$ is in a surface perpendicular to the axis that is parallel to the surface from line $r\ y$. Since the two points $h$ and $t$ are the images of $r$ and $y$, and point $s$ is the image of $m$, the image of the line $r\ m\ y$ is the line passing through $h, s, t$. Such a line is <term>arched<note>Original: "arcualis". Alhazen is proving that a straight line in reality appears curved in the reflection.</note></term> because $s$ lies outside the straight path of $h\ t$. 

Let the arched line $h\ s\ t$ pass through these points. Because $h\ t$ was positioned at a distance from the convexity of the column, $h\ t$ will be beyond the surface of the mirror relative to the eye $l$. We have already shown that $s$ is beyond the concavity of the mirror relative to $l$. Thus, the entire line $h\ s\ t$ will be beyond the concavity of the mirror's surface. Since the eye $l$ is within the concavity of the mirror, $l$ is outside the surface in which the line $h\ s\ t$ resides; therefore, the curvature of line $h\ s\ t$ will be clearly visible to the sight. And because $f$ is on the surface of the column, and $t$ is beyond the column within the surface of triangle $l\ h\ t$, the line $l\ f$ will be higher than the surface of triangle $l\ h\ t$. Therefore, the line $l\ s$ will appear higher than the two lines $l\ h$ and $l\ t$ from the perspective of the eye. Thus, $s$ is higher than the two points $h$ and $t$, and the line $h\ s\ t$ will appear concave to the sight.

### 53. *If the sight is in the plane of a straight line that is oblique to the plane of the axis of a hollow cylindrical mirror, the image will appear concave and inverted.* <note>Proposition 28, paragraph 9.</note>

Next, let us cut the column with a surface that is slanted (oblique) relative to its axis; this will create a <term>cylindrical section<note>Original: "sectionem columnarem". Today we call this an ellipse, formed by slicing a cylinder at an angle. Alhazen refers to the Greek mathematician Serenus’s work "On the Section of a Cylinder."</note></term>. Let this section be $a\ b\ g$. In the first figure regarding concave columns, it was demonstrated that in the surface of any section of the column, a perpendicular arises from the point of reflection to the tangent surface, from the ends of which the forms are reflected. 

Let the perpendicular be $g\ a$, and let $b\ e\ k$ be perpendicular to the line tangent to the circumference of the section at $b$, with $b$ being near $g$. Therefore, $b\ k$ will intersect the perpendicular $g\ a$ below the axis and will form an acute angle with it. <note>As shown in note 24: point $b$ is taken so close to $g$ that the line from $b$ and the perpendicular from the point of reflection on the axis form an acute angle.</note> Let them intersect at $e$. The angle $b\ e\ g$ will thus be acute. 

From $g$, we draw a line $g\ d$ parallel to line $b\ k$. The angle $d\ g\ e$ will then be acute, and $g\ d$ will fall within the concavity of the column. We set angle $e\ g\ l$ equal to angle $e\ g\ d$; therefore, $g\ l$ will meet $b\ e$ at point $l$, because the angles at $d, g,$ and $e$ are acute and less than two right angles. Let us mark point $m$ on line $l\ e$; the angle $m\ a\ g$ will be acute, and $a\ m$ will be inside the section. We set angle $g\ a\ d$ equal to angle $g\ a\ m$; thus, $a\ d$ will meet $g\ d$ at $d$, as the two angles at $a$ and $g$ are acute. 

At the intersection $d$, $a\ d$ will cut $b\ k$ (following Proclus's lemma). Let it cut at $t$. When $l\ k$ is part of a visible object and the eye is at $d$, then the form of $l$ will be seen at $g$ (as shown in note 90), because the form of $l$ reflects to $d$ from $g$, and $d\ g$ is parallel to the perpendicular $b\ l\ k$. The form of $m$ will be seen at $t$ because the form of $m$ reflects to $d$ from $a$, and the image is $m$. 

Now, let a surface parallel to the base of the column pass through $d$; it will cut the section $a\ b\ g$ and create a circle $p\ o\ r$ on the surface of the column <note>Referencing Serenus, Theorem 5.</note>. The surface of this circle will intersect $b\ k$, for it intersects $g\ d$, which is parallel to it. Let it intersect $b\ k$ at $k$, and let the center of the circle $p\ o\ r$ be point $h$. We draw $d\ h$ through to $r$, and $k\ h$ through to $p$. The form of $k$ is reflected to $d$ from the circumference of the arc $r\ p$, as is clear from the study of mirror images. Let it reflect from $o$, and connect $k\ o$, $d\ o$, and $h\ o$. The angles at $o$ are equal, and $d\ o$ will intersect $h\ p$ at $n$. Therefore, $n$ is the image of $k$. 

If we connect $k\ d$, then $k\ d$ will be the common section between the circle $r\ p$ and the section $a\ b\ g$. Both points $k$ and $d$ are in both surfaces, and no part of the surface of section $a\ b\ g$ is in the surface of circle $r\ p$ except the line $k\ d$. Therefore, it is outside the circle, and likewise for $b$. These are in the surface of the section, and $n$ is in the surface of the circle $r\ p$. The form $l\ m\ k$ passes through the points $g, t, n$, and the line passing through these points is arched. 

But the surface of the section is slanted relative to the surface of the column; therefore, the axis of the section does not pass through the entire axis of the column, nor is it parallel to the base of the column. It is clear from this figure and the two preceding ones that straight lines parallel to the axis of the column, those parallel to its base, and even those slanted upon its surface, may appear arched, straight, or inverted. Because $t$ is the image of $m$, and $n$ is the image of $k$, the form $m\ k$ will be <term>inverted<note>Original: "conuersa". This describes a reversal of the object's orientation in the reflection.</note></term>. And even if the line were in the surface of a circle parallel to the bases of the column, whose surface passes through the center of the sight...

# BOOK VI OF OPTICS

As was said concerning the images of concave mirrors in the seventh chapter of this treatise: the shape will perhaps be equal and upright; and perhaps it will be inverted. It is clear, therefore, that the shape of those things perceived in concave cylindrical mirrors will perhaps be upright, and perhaps inverted.

*54. If the sight is in the plane of a straight line perpendicular to the plane of the axis of a hollow cylindrical mirror: the image will appear upright and inverted; at other times larger; at other times smaller; at other times equal to the line itself; sometimes simple; sometimes multiple. [See proposition] 29, page 9.*

Again, let us repeat the form of the third figure concerning the <term>fallacies<note>In medieval optics, a "fallacy" or "deception" refers to any instance where the perceived image differs from the physical object in size, shape, position, or number.</note></term> of concave mirrors using the same letters: [41, 42, 43 notes] and let the circle be $b, z, a$ on the surface of the concave cylindrical mirror, and let the sight be at $d$. It will therefore be outside the surface of the circle, and there will be two lines $e\ a$ and $e\ b$ perpendicular to the surfaces tangent to the surface of the cylinder. The surface of the triangle $d\ g\ e$ will be perpendicular to the surface of the circle [per Book 11, Proposition 18] because $g\ d$ is perpendicular to the surface of the circle [as shown in note 41]. Therefore, the surface of triangle $d\ g\ e$ passes through the entire axis, and in neither surface $d\ b\ o$ or $d\ a\ o$ is there any part of the axis of the cylinder, except $e$, which is the center of the circle. Both surfaces $d\ b\ o$ and $d\ a\ o$ create a section in the surface of the cylinder [according to the 9th theorem of Serenus's *On Cylinders* <note>original: "cylindricorum Sereni". Serenus of Antinoöpolis was a 4th-century mathematician whose work on cylindrical sections was a standard reference for medieval scientists.</note>]. Forms are reflected from these sections at two points $a$ and $b$ [as was evident in note 41]. Therefore, form $r$ is reflected to $d$ from $b$, and form $m$ is reflected from $a$. $n\ u$ will be the diameter of the image $m\ r$ [for points $n$ and $u$ are the images of points $r$ and $m$ by note 7, book 5]. This is smaller than $m\ r$ [as demonstrated in note 42]. Similarly, two points $h$ and $l$ are reflected to $d$ from two points $a$ and $b$, and $t\ k$ will be the diameter of the image $l\ h$. $e\ i$ will be equal [as was clear in note 41], and $p\ i$ will be the diameter of the image $f\ q$, and it is larger than that. All these images will be inverted [as shown in note 43]. If the sight is at $o$, and the lines $p\ i, t\ k, n\ u$ are visible, they will be the opposite: then the diameter of image $p\ i$ will be smaller than the object, the diameter of image $n\ u$ will be larger, and diameter $t\ k$ will be equal to it. And all these images will be upright. All these things were shown in the aforementioned chapter. Furthermore, when each extremity of one of these lines has one image, and some point in the middle has several images, then that line will have as many images as the middle point has. If each extremity, or one of them, has several images, and the middle point has one, then the line will have as many images as the extremity has. If each extremity or one of them has many images, and the middle point also has many images, then the line will have as many images according to the greater number. This will be clear, as it was clear regarding the images of concave spherical mirrors. In concave cylindrical mirrors, therefore, deception happens in everything perceived in them, just as it happens in concave spherical mirrors: namely, regarding the shapes of visible forms, their sizes, the number of their images, their uprightness, and their inversion, along with the deceptions specific to reflection. The deceptions in these will be like those in the aforementioned mirrors. This is what we wished to declare in this chapter.

### CHAPTER IX. CONCERNING ERRORS THAT OCCUR IN CONCAVE PYRAMIDAL MIRRORS.

In these mirrors, those deceptions occur which happen in concave cylindrical mirrors. The weakening of color and light, the diversity of position, and distance occur in these as in all mirrors, for the cause of this is reflection itself. A multitude of images also occurs in these mirrors, just as in cylindrical and concave spherical mirrors mentioned in the [second chapter of the fifth book] concerning images.

*55. If straight or curved lines fall obliquely upon the vertex of a hollow conical mirror: they will be reflected from the conical side to a sight positioned between them and the mirror surface. A straight image will appear slightly curved, and a curved image will appear straight. [See proposition] 31, page 9.*

It also happens in these, as in concave cylindrical mirrors, that a straight object may appear convex or concave. The demonstration of this is as follows: straight lines that extend along the length of the mirror, passing through the vertex of the <term>pyramid<note>Alhazen and his translators used "pyramidal mirror" (speculum pyramidale) to refer to what we now call a conical mirror.</note></term>, and those near them, appear convex and perhaps straight. The demonstration of this is like the demonstration for concave cylindrical mirrors. For if we repeat the figure concerning the deceptions of convex pyramidal mirrors [which is note 32], we will find the diameter of the image of a straight line placed in that mirror (which is line $a\ n$ there) inside the concavity of the pyramidal mirror. We will find a point that is below the surface tangent to the pyramid, passing through the line of length from which the form of the straight line is reflected to the sight, which is point $f$ there. If, therefore, that point is the center of the sight, all the points which are in the diame-

*56. If the sight is located at the intersection of the planes of a straight line and the axis of a hollow conical mirror, and these are perpendicular to each other: the image will be seen as upright and inverted; sometimes larger, sometimes equal, and sometimes smaller than the line itself; sometimes appearing as a single image, and sometimes multiple. [See proposition] 34, page 9.*

Likewise, let us repeat the third figure regarding the fallacies of spherical concave mirrors using the same letters [which was note 41]. If, therefore, some point is on the axis of the <term>pyramid<note>original: "pyramidis"; Alhazen frequently uses the term "pyramid" to refer to a cone.</note></term>, and the two lines $a$ and $e\ b$ are perpendicular to the surfaces tangent to the cone—which is possible because they are equal, for they can contain two equal acute angles with the axis—then, when these two lines are perpendicular and the sight is at $d$, the plane in which $g, e, d$ lie will pass through the entire axis and through the center of sight. Both planes $d\ a\ o$ and $d\ b\ o$ will be inclined over the axis of the cone, and their <term>intersections<note>original: "differentię"; in this geometric context, it refers to the line or curve formed where two surfaces meet.</note></term> will be two <term>sections of the cone<note>original: "sectiones pyramidis"; referencing conic sections such as the ellipse or parabola.</note></term> [according to the 5th theorem of the 1st book of Apollonius’s Conics]. The forms of points $h, r, q$ will be reflected to $d$ from $b$, and the forms of points $l, m, f$ will be reflected to $d$ from $a$. When the lines $m\ l\ f$ and $r\ h\ q$ are on some visible surface and the sight is at $d$, then $u\ e$ will be the image of $m\ r$, $t\ k$ will be the image of $l\ h$, and $p\ i$ will be the image of $f\ q$ [as shown in note 54]. Thus, the image $m\ r$ will be smaller than the object itself, the image $f\ q$ will be larger than itself, and the image $l\ h$ will be equal to it. All these images will be <term>inverted<note>original: "conuersæ"; meaning the orientation of the image is flipped relative to the object.</note></term>. If the sight is at $o$, and $n\ u, t\ k, p\ i$ are on the surfaces of visible objects, then their images will be $m\ r, l\ h, f\ q$. Thus, the image $f\ q$ will be smaller than the object, the image $n\ u$ larger, and the image $t\ k$ equal. These images will be <term>upright<note>original: "rectæ"; in this context, meaning the image orientation matches the object.</note></term>. For these images will be beyond the center of sight and are perceived before the eye along the radial lines. Therefore, points $m, l, f$ are perceived on line $a\ o$, and points $r, h, q$ are perceived on $o\ b$; thus the form is reflected upright.

It is clear from what we have said in this chapter that straight lines sometimes appear in these mirrors as convex, sometimes concave, sometimes straight; sometimes larger, smaller, or equal; and sometimes upright or inverted. In the [second chapter of the fifth book] concerning the image, we demonstrated that every visible point in these kinds of mirrors sometimes has one image, sometimes two, three, or four. In everything perceived in these mirrors, therefore, deceptions occur just as they do in concave cylindrical mirrors; and composite deceptions also occur in them, just as in other mirrors. The examples and the demonstration of them are the same as in plane mirrors. This is what we intended to declare in this chapter; now, however, let us finish the sixth treatise.

# THE SON OF ALHAZEN
## THE OPTICS OF ALHAZEN
### BOOK SEVEN.

*The seventh treatise is divided into seven parts. The first part is the introduction. The second shows that light passes through <term>transparent<note>The original text uses the term "diaphana," a traditional word for materials like glass, air, or water that allow light to pass through them.</note></term> bodies along the paths of straight lines, and is refracted when it meets a body whose transparency is different from that of the body in which it already exists. The third part concerns the nature of the refraction of light in transparent bodies. The fourth shows that whatever is perceived by the sight beyond transparent bodies—when their transparency differs from the transparency of the medium where the eye is located—is perceived through refraction, provided the object is at an angle to the <term>perpendiculars<note>Lines at a right angle (90 degrees) to the surface.</note></term> rising from their surface. The fifth part concerns <term>phantasms<note>In this context, "phantasms" refer to optical illusions or images that appear in a different place or shape than the actual object due to the bending of light.</note></term>. The sixth explains how the sight perceives visible objects through refraction. The seventh concerns the errors of sight that occur because of refraction.*

## PREFACE TO THE BOOK. CHAPTER I.

*1. Vision occurs in three ways: directly, by reflection, and by refraction.* <note>In the preface of the 10-book version. The same is stated in Book 4.</note>

It was stated previously in the introduction to the fourth treatise of this book that the sight perceives visible objects in three ways: namely, in a straight line; by reflection from polished bodies; and by <term>refraction<note>From the Latin "refractio," meaning "breaking back." This refers to the bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like water.</note></term> beyond transparent bodies that differ in transparency from the transparency of the air. It was also noted that the sight perceives nothing among visible things except by one of these three modes, and that by any of these modes, the sight perceives visible objects and everything contained within them. These distinctions were explained in the final section of the second treatise. In the preceding treatises, it was explained how the sight perceives visible objects directly and by reflection, and we showed the diversity of how the sight perceives objects in both of those ways. It remains, therefore, to explain how the sight perceives visible objects by refraction beyond transparent bodies. In this treatise, we shall deal solely with refraction: we will demonstrate the form refraction takes, distinguish its modes, categorize its properties, and explain what happens to the sight in this type of vision. First, we will set forth the foundations that confirm everything depending on this matter.

## THAT LIGHT PASSES THROUGH TRANSPARENT BODIES ALONG THE PATHS OF STRAIGHT LINES, AND IS REFRACTED WHEN IT ENCOVINTERS A BODY WHOSE TRANSPARENCY IS DIFFERENT FROM THE TRANSPARENCY OF THE BODY IN WHICH IT EXISTS. CHAPTER II.

*2. Construction of the refraction instrument.* <note>1 p 2.</note>

That light indeed passes into the air and extends along straight lines was shown in the first treatise of this work. Air is one of the transparent bodies; however, light also passes through water, glass, and transparent stones, and extends along straight lines. This is understood through experience. If anyone, therefore, wishes to test this: let him take a round plate of bronze, whose diameter is not less than one <term>cubit<note>An ancient unit of measurement, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note></term>, and let its thickness be somewhat strong. It should have round rims, perpendicular to its surface, and the height of these rims should be no less than the width of two fingers. In the middle of the back of the plate, let there be a small, round, column-shaped body, whose length is not less than the width of three fingers, and let it be perpendicular to the surface of the plate. Let us place this instrument in a <term>lathe<note>A machine tool used for shaping metal or wood by rotating the workpiece against a cutting tool.</note></term> of the kind used by copper-smiths, and let us place one tooth of the lathe in the center of the plate and the other in the center of the end of the body that is on the back of the plate. Let us smooth this instrument by revolving it with true shaving until the roundness of its rims is perfected inside and out, the interior and exterior surfaces are made even and parallel to each other, and the body on the back is also shaved until it is round. When this instrument has been perfected by smoothing: let us mark on its interior surface two diameters intersecting each other perpendicularly, passing through its center. Then, let us mark a point on the base of the rim of the instrument, whose distance from the end of one of the two intersecting diameters is the width of one finger. Then, let us draw from that point a third diameter passing through the center of the plate, which should extend across its entire surface. Then, from the two ends of this diameter, let us draw two lines on the surface of the rim...

### 3. A ray perpendicular to a denser medium penetrates without being refracted. <note>Referencing Proposition 42, part 2; and also 17, note 1.</note>

Therefore, when the experimenter wishes to test the passage of light in water through this instrument: he shall take a vessel with straight edges, such as a copper jar, or a clay pot, or something similar: and let the height of its edges be no less than half a cubit: and let the diameter of its circumference be no less than the diameter of the instrument: and let its edges be leveled until the surface that passes through its edges is a flat surface: and let us place at its bottom an object of various parts or various colors, such as a ring, or painted silver, or let a clear picture be painted on its bottom: then let clear water be poured into the vessel until it is filled: and let him wait until its motion ceases. When its motion has ceased, let the observer stand up, or sit upright, and look into the vessel, and direct his sight to the object at the bottom of the water, or the picture at the bottom of the water, until the line between the sight and the middle of that object or picture is perpendicular to the surface of the water according to the senses, and let him look at the object at the bottom, or the picture: then he will find it exactly as it is, and he will find the arrangement of its parts among themselves in the same way they would be arranged if he were looking at it when the vessel was empty. This having been shown, it is confirmed that what is perceived at the bottom of the water—when he looks at it from the same position as he looked at the object at the bottom of the water, or the picture—is perceived according to the arrangement of its parts. This being confirmed, if anyone wishes to test the passage of light: let him choose a place where the sunlight rises, in which he may place the vessel, and let him observe that the surface of the circumference of the vessel is parallel to the horizon: this can be observed in this way: that the circumference of the surface of the water is parallel to the circumference of the vessel: and if a circle is marked inside the vessel near its circumference, parallel to the circumference of the vessel, it will be better for comparing the circumference of the water's surface to the circumference of the circle. Then the experimenter must place the round instrument inside this vessel, so that the two small rulers placed on the two ends of the larger ruler are placed upon the edge of the vessel on both sides: then half of the instrument, and the ruler extended along the length of the instrument, will be inside the vessel: then water should be added or removed from it until the surface of the water is level with the center of the instrument: and let the water be clear: then let the instrument be rotated around the vessel until that part of its edges which is inside the water is shaded: then let the ruler be held with one hand, and with the other hand let the instrument be rotated upon itself around its center, until the hole that is in the rim of the instrument is opposite the body of the sun, and the sunlight passes through the hole of the instrument's rim, and reaches the other hole of the small plate, and passes through it. Therefore, when the form of the light has passed through the two holes, it will reach the bottom of the water: then the experimenter will observe that the position of the light on the ruler from the second hole is a level position: and with this position preserved, and the light reaching the surface of the water, let the experimenter remove his hands from the instrument, and stand or sit upright, and look to the bottom of the water from the quarter whose edges are cut away, and let him keep the position he had kept when he looked at the object that was at the bottom of the water, so that he is certain that what he sees is as it truly is: then, when he looks at that part of the instrument's rim which is inside the water: he will find the light passing from the two holes...
