...holes <note>The Latin text here reads "raminibus," likely an OCR error for "foraminibus" (holes).</note> upon the surface of the rim of the instrument which is submerged in the water. He will find the light between the two outermost parallel circles of the three marked on the interior part of the rim; or, a small amount will be added to the distance between the circles, and this addition will be equal on both sides of the circles. It follows, therefore, from this positioning, that the point which is in the middle of the light appearing within the water—which is on the interior part of the instrument's rim—is aligned with the middle circle of the three parallel circles marked on the interior of the rim. It will be evident that this light within the water is restricted because the upper rim of the instrument, which surrounds the upper hole, casts a shadow over the interior part of the rim, surrounding the light that is on the interior of the rim. Thus, in that location, there will be no sunlight on the interior part of the rim except for the light that exits through the two holes.

Next, the experimenter should take a small piece of wood, or a needle <term>acus<gloss>a thin, sharp-pointed probe used here as a physical marker to trace the path of light</gloss></term>, and apply it to the outer part of the upper hole in the rim of the instrument, ensuring the needle passes through the center of the hole. Then he should look over the vessel and maintain the position he measured previously; he will then see the shadow of the needle in the center of the light. Next, he should bend the needle, drawing it back until its tip is in the center of the hole, and observe the light within the water and on the surface of the water; he will then find the shadow of the needle's tip in the center of the light that is within the water and in the center of the light on the surface of the water. 

Then he should change the position of the needle, placing its tip again at the center of the hole, and observe the shadow; he will find the shadow of the needle's tip at the center of the light. Then he should lift the needle, and he will find the light returning to its original state within the water and on the surface of the water. Next, he should apply the needle to the side of the hole, placing it as a chord <term>chorda<gloss>a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc—here, the needle is placed off-center across the hole</gloss></term> in the hole, not as a diameter, and observe the light within the water and on the surface of the water; he will then find a shadow in both places that corresponds to that chord. Then he should lift the needle, and the light will return to its place. If he changes the position of the needle to the various sides of the hole, he will find the shadow always on the corresponding side of the light.

It will therefore be demonstrated by this experiment that the light reaching the point in the middle of the light within the water—on the circumference of the middle circle—exited only from the point that is the center of the light on the surface of the water. Furthermore, the light reaching the point at the center of the light on the surface of the water exited only from the point that is the center of the upper hole and passed through the center of the lower hole <note>original: "foraminis inferioris"</note> in the other rims. For if it had not passed through the center of the lower hole, the center of the light on the water's surface would not have been visible when the needle was in the center of the lower hole; rather, nothing of the light on the water's surface would be visible except for some place other than its center. Therefore, the light that reaches the point which is the center of the light on the water's surface, and the light that extends through the air, extends only along straight lines. 

Thus, the light passing through the centers of the two holes extends according to the straightness of the line passing through the centers of the two holes; this is the very light that reaches the center of the light on the water's surface. Therefore, the point in the center of the light on the water's surface lies on the straight line passing through the centers of the two holes. This line is in the plane <note>original: "superficie," here meaning the geometric plane or surface area</note> of the middle circle of the three circles marked on the interior of the instrument's rim. It is the diameter of that circle because this line is parallel to the diameter of the circle on the surface of the plate. Since the point in the center of the light on the water's surface lies on this line, then that point is in the plane of the aforementioned middle circle. Moreover, the point in the center of the light within the water is on the circumference of that middle circle; therefore, both of these points are in the plane of the middle circle. 

If the light on the water's surface is hidden or not clearly visible, then the experimenter should place that smaller ruler into the water, apply its edge to the surface of the plate, and position the surface on which the line is marked so that it follows the surface of the water, moving it until its surface is flush with the water's surface. When the surface of the ruler is level with the water's surface and the ruler stands upright on its edge, then the line on its surface will be in the plane of the middle circle that passes through the centers of the two holes. With this position maintained, the light on the water's surface will appear upon the surface of the ruler, and he will find the center of the light upon the line in the middle of the ruler. 

If the needle is placed over the center of the upper hole, then the line in the middle of the ruler will be shadowed; and if the tip of the needle is placed over the center of the hole, the shadow of the needle's tip will appear in the center of the light on the ruler. If the needle is removed, the light will return as it was. With this ruler, therefore, the light on the water's surface will appear clearly, and it will be manifest that it is upon the line passing through the centers of the two holes; we had already positioned the surface of the water at the center of the plate. 

When the surface of the ruler is flush with the water's surface, the surface of the ruler will pass through the center of the plate; then the distance of the center of the light from the center of the plate will be equal to half the width of the ruler, which is equal to the perpendicular line falling from the center of the hole onto the surface of the plate. Thus, the center of the light on the surface of the ruler will be the center of the middle circle. 

Then the experimenter must remove the thin ruler and place it into the water again, applying the surface of its width to the surface of the plate, and position its acute angle at the center of the light that is within the water—namely, the angle on its upper surface. Then he should move the ruler until its lower sharp edge passes through the center of the plate, and thus its upper sharp edge will pass through the center of the middle circle. Therefore, the point on the upper line of the ruler that is at the water's surface is the center of the middle circle; it is also the center of the light on the water's surface, and its length will be that of the diameter of the middle circle. ### 4. *A ray oblique to a denser medium is refracted toward the perpendicular raised from the point of refraction. <note>original: "Radius medio densiori obliquus, refringitur ad perpendicularem à refractionis puncto excitatam."</note> 43 p 2. The same 17 n 1.*

Next, it will be necessary for the experimenter to place a fixed mark with an engraving upon the center of the light. Then, when the experimenter looks at the point which is in the middle of the light that is within the water, he will find it not equidistant from the two extremities of the plate’s diameter, but outside the two perpendicular lines which are above the extremity of the plate’s diameter that is within the water. And he will find its declination from that line toward the side in which the sun is; and he will find a sensible distance between the point which is the center of the middle light and the point which is the common difference of the line perpendicular to the extremity of the plate’s diameter and the middle point which is the extremity of the diameter of the middle circle passing through the center of the hole. Having declared this, one must put a thin ruler into the water and apply it to the surface of the plate, and place the end of the ruler upon the center of the plate, and move the ruler until its sharp edge is perpendicular to the surface of the water—as far as the senses can tell. Then, therefore, he will find the center of the light which is within the water between the sharp edge of the ruler and the line perpendicular to the diameter of the plate. It will be declared from this, therefore, that this refraction is toward the side of the perpendicular, originating from the place of refraction perpendicular to the surface of the water. When the experimenter is certain of this, he must mark a fixed sign at the extremity of the ruler which is on the circumference of the middle circle (which is the extremity of the perpendicular originating from the center of the middle circle perpendicular to the surface of the water), just as the first one was marked at the center of the light. And it has already been declared that the light which reaches the point that is the center of the light within the water is light extended according to the straightness of the line connecting the two centers of the holes; and this line reaches the center of the middle circle parallel to the surface of the plate, and it is its diameter. If this line were extended in the imagination according to its straightness into the water until it reached the rim of the plate, it would then be parallel to the diameter of the plate and would reach the perpendicular line on the interior part of the plate’s rim. And since the center of the light which is within the water is not on the perpendicular line of the plate’s rim, then the light which extends from the middle of the light on the surface of the water to the middle of the light within the water does not extend according to the straightness of the line passing through the centers of the two holes, but is refracted. However, it has been declared that this light extends straight from the middle of the light on the surface of the water to the middle of the light within the water. Therefore, the refraction of this light occurs at the surface of the water.

### 5. *Rays of incidence and refraction are in one plane. <note>original: "Radij incidentiæ & refractionis sunt in uno plano."</note> 46 p 2.*

It has also been declared that this light passes through the centers of the two holes, and through the middle of the light on the surface of the water (which is the center of the middle circle parallel to the surface of the plate), and through the middle of the light that is within the water (which is on the circumference of the middle circle). From this it is clear that the light reaching the center of the light within the water—while it is extended in the air and after it is refracted within the water—is on the same flat surface, namely, on the surface of the middle circle of the three circles that are on the interior part of the instrument's rim. And this refraction is found when the line passing through the centers of the holes is slanted <note>original: "decliuis"</note> toward the surface of the water, not perpendicular. And this line will never be perpendicular to the surface of the water at the hour of the sun’s passage unless the sun is at the <term>zenith<gloss>the highest point in the sky directly above the observer</gloss></term>; and this happens in some places and not in others, and at certain times and not all. Nor does the sun pass through the zenith of those living in many inhabited places. In those places where it does pass, this experiment will be distinguished at all times; but those over whose zenith the sun passes, if they wish to test this, will avoid the time in which the sun passes directly over their heads.

# OPTICS, BOOK VII.

In the first experiment, the light also passes through the point that is in the middle of the second glass. Then the experimenter should remove the second glass and test the third, and so on for the rest until the last one. It will therefore be clear through this experimentation that the light which passes through the centers of the two apertures, reaching the surface of the ruler, passes through the centers of the surfaces of all the glasses placed upon the surface of the plate. It is clear, therefore, that it lies in the straightness of the line passing through the centers of the two apertures: and the light, which passes through the centers of the two apertures in the experimentation of all the glasses, is extended in the straightness of the line connecting the centers of the two apertures. It is clear, therefore, that the light which passes through the straight line passing through the centers of the two apertures also passes through the centers of the surfaces of the glasses. From this it is evident that light passes into the body of the glass, in which it is extended after it passes through, according to straight lines; and that the light which passes through the centers of the two apertures is extended into the body of the glass according to the straightness of the line along which it was extended in the air before it passed through the glass. And that line along which the light is extended in the air is perpendicular to the surface of the glass opposite the aperture <note>original: "per 8 p 11" — a reference to Proposition 8, Book 11 of Euclid's Elements regarding perpendicular lines</note>. For the line which passes through the centers of the two apertures is parallel to the diameter of the plate, which is perpendicular to the first surface of the glass surfaces: because it is perpendicular to the <term>common intersection line<gloss>The line where two geometric planes meet; original: "differentiam communem"</gloss></term> between the surface of the glass and the surface of the plate.

Likewise, let the experimenter take a hemisphere <note>literally "half of a sphere"</note> of clean, clear glass, such as crystal, whose radius is less than the distance between the tablet and the center of the plate, and let him find the center of its base, upon which he should mark a fine line with ink. Afterward, let him mark off from this line, starting from the center of the base (which is the center of the sphere), a line equal to the diameter of the aperture in the rim of the instrument. This line will therefore be equal to the line between the center of the aperture in the rim of the instrument and the surface of the plate, which is perpendicular to that plate.

<image-desc>A circular diagram on the right side of the page depicting a geometric construction within a circle, likely representing a glass sphere. An interior arc connects points on the circle, illustrating optical refraction or projection geometry.</image-desc>

Next, let us establish a perpendicular line at the end of the marked-off line, and extend it in both directions. Then let us cut the glass along this line using a grinding tool or a lathe until the place of the cut becomes a flat surface, perpendicular to the surface of the base of the semicircle. Let us measure the angle between the two surfaces using a copper <term>right angle<gloss>A square or L-shaped tool used for checking 90-degree angles</gloss></term> until this surface is verified as true. Then the common intersection between this surface and the surface of the base of the sphere will be a straight line; and the line joining the center of the sphere with this line will be perpendicular to the newly created surface. Afterward, a small mark should be made in the middle of this intersection line to denote its center point. When this is completed, let the glass be polished very intensely and placed upon the surface of the plate, with its <term>convexity<gloss>The outward-curving part of the hemisphere; original: "gibbositas"</gloss></term> facing the apertures. Let the cut part of the glass rest on the surface of the plate, and let the straight line (the common intersection of the two flat surfaces of the glass) be placed exactly over the line marked on the plate that cuts the diameter perpendicularly. The center of that line must be placed over the center of the plate.

Once this position is secured, the glass should be firmly attached to the plate. Then let us place a thin ruler on the surface of the instrument, just as we did in the experiment with the cubic glasses. Let the surface of the ruler, on which there is a straight line of width, face the glass and be near it. Then place the instrument in the aforementioned vessel. Let the vessel be placed in the sun, empty without water. Move the instrument until the sunlight passes through the two apertures. Ensure the light from the second aperture is positioned moderately, and let the experimenter look at the ruler. He will find the light that passed through the two apertures upon the surface of the ruler. Then, let him apply a <term>stylus<gloss>A thin, pointed tool used as a marker or pointer</gloss></term> to the upper aperture, placing the tip of the stylus exactly at the center of the hole, and look at the light on the ruler: he will then find the shadow of the stylus tip at the center of the light. Then let him remove the stylus, and the light will return to its place. Next, let him apply the stylus to the second aperture, placing its tip at the second center, and look at the light on the ruler: he will find the shadow of the stylus tip at the center of the light. Afterward, let him place the tip of the stylus at the center of the base of the glass (which is the center of the sphere) and look at the light on the ruler: he will find the shadow of the stylus tip upon the center of the light. Then let him place the stylus in the middle of the light that is on the convex part of the glass opposite the second aperture, which is near it, and look at the light on the ruler: he will find the shadow of the stylus tip at the center of the light.

From this it is clear that the light which passes through the centers of the two apertures also passes through the center of the base of the glass and through the middle of the surface of light on the convex part of the glass. It is manifest, therefore, that the light which passes into the body of the glass is extended according to the straightness of the line passing through the centers of the two apertures; this line is the diameter of the glass sphere. For the perpendicular line extending from the center of the glass base to the plate is equal to the diameter of the aperture. The diameter of the aperture is also equal to the perpendicular line extending from the center of the aperture to the surface of the plate. Therefore, the perpendicular from the center of the glass base to the plate's surface is equal to the perpendicular from the center of the aperture to the plate's surface, and both these perpendiculars fall upon the diameter of the plate. Therefore, if the line passing through the centers of the two apertures is extended straight, it will reach the center of the glass sphere; it will thus be the diameter of this sphere. It is therefore perpendicular to the surface of this sphere <note>original: "ut demonstratū est 25 n 4" — as demonstrated in Proposition 25, Book 4</note>. In the experimentation with cubic glasses, it was shown that light extending into the body of glass follows the straight path it took in the air, provided that path was perpendicular to the glass surface. Since light passes through all transparent things according to straight lines: therefore all lights will be extended in all transparent bodies: because it was declared in the first treatise of this book <note>original: "14. 17. 28 n." In the first treatise, it was declared that all light, whether essential or accidental, strong or weak, is always extended from any point of any body according to a straight line. From all these things, therefore, which we have declared by experience and reason: it is clear that all light in a body that is luminous essentially or accidentally, strongly or weakly, is extended from any point of it through the transparent body touching that body, along every straight line through which it can be extended, whether that touching body be air, or water, or a transparent stone. And if the lights extended through the body touching the light which is its source meet a body of a different transparency from the transparency of the body in which it exists, and they are on lines perpendicular to the surface of the second body: they will be extended straightly into the second body. And if they are on slanted lines to the surface of the second body, they will be refracted in the second body: then in the second body they will be extended in the orientation of straight lines other than the first. And if the light is refracted: then the line along which the light was extended in the first body, and the line along which it was refracted in the second: will be in the same uniform surface <note>original: "ut ostensum est 5 n." Furthermore, their motion in subtle bodies—namely in those that are very transparent—is faster than their motion in those that are grosser than them—namely those that are less transparent. <meta>This page continues the transition from experimental observation to the theoretical and physical explanation of refraction. On the previous page, Alhazen described the behavior of light passing through glass and water. Here, he introduces a mechanical analogy—comparing light to a projectile like an iron ball or a sword—to explain why light bends toward the perpendicular when entering a denser medium.</meta>

### OPTICS, BOOK VII.

there must be some degree of <term>density</term> <note>original: "grossities", referring to the physical thickness or lack of transparency in a material.</note>; for a body of low transparency does not have an end in the imagination, which is the imagination of clear transparency: and all natural bodies reach a limit which they cannot pass. Natural transparent bodies, therefore, cannot escape having some density. Thus, when lights pass through transparent bodies, they pass according to the <term>transparency</term> <note>original: "diaphanitas"</note> that is in them, and are thus hindered by the light according to the density that is in them. Therefore, when light has passed through a transparent body and encounters another body denser than the first, the denser body resists the light more forcefully than the first one did. And every moved object, when it is moved toward any part essentially or accidentally, if it encounters resistance, its motion must necessarily be changed. If the resistance is strong, then that motion will be reflected back to the opposite side; but if it is weak, it will not be reflected to the opposite side, nor will it be able to proceed through that path which it had begun; rather, its motion will be changed. Now, for all things moved naturally that travel in a straight line through some <term>yielding body</term> <note>original: "corpus passibile", a medium that can be penetrated.</note>, the passage along the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>original: "perpendicularis", the line at a 90-degree angle to the surface, known in modern optics as the 'normal'.</note> to the surface of the body in which the passage occurs will be easier.

And this is seen in natural bodies. For if someone were to take a thin board and fix it over a wide opening, and stand opposite the board, and take an iron ball and throw it forcefully at the board, and ensure that the motion of the ball is along the perpendicular to the surface of the board: then the board will give way to the ball or be broken, provided the board is thin and the force with which the sphere is moved is strong. But if he stands at an oblique angle from the position opposite the board, and at that same distance where he was before, and throws the ball at that same board at which he threw it before: then the sphere will slide off the board, if the board is not very thin, and it will not move toward that part toward which it was first moving, but will decline toward some other part. 

And similarly, if he should take a sword and place a piece of wood before him and strike it with the sword so that the sword is perpendicular to the surface of the wood: then the wood will be cut more deeply; but if it is oblique, and he strikes the wood obliquely: then the wood will not be cut, or perhaps it will be cut in part, or perhaps the sword will miss by swerving; and the more oblique the sword is, the less it will act upon the wood. There are many other similar examples from which it is clear that motion along the perpendicular is stronger and easier; and that of oblique motions, the one closer to the perpendicular is easier than the more remote one.

Therefore, if light encounters a transparent body denser than the body in which it exists, it will be hindered by it, so that it will not pass into the part toward which it was moving; but because the body does not resist forcefully, the light will not return to the part from which it was moving. If, then, the motion of light passes along the perpendicular, it will pass straight through because of the strength of motion along the perpendicular; but if its motion is along an oblique line, then it will not be able to pass through [in a straight line] because of the weakness of the motion. It happens, therefore, that it is deflected toward the direction of motion in which it will move more easily than in the direction it was originally moving. But the easiest of motions is along the perpendicular, and what is closer to the perpendicular is easier than what is more remote. And the motion in the body into which it passes, if it is oblique to the surface of that body, is composed of the motion in the direction of the perpendicular passing into the body in which the motion exists, and of the motion in the direction of the line which is perpendicular to the perpendicular passing into it. Therefore, when light is moved in a dense transparent body along an oblique line:

<image-desc>A geometric ray diagram illustrating refraction between two media. A vertical line segment is marked with points 'a' at the top, 'b' in the middle, and 'f' at the bottom. A diagonal line segment labeled 'h' descends from point 'a' to point 'd' on a horizontal interface (marked with points 'e', 'd', 'k'). From point 'd', the line refracts at an angle towards the lower boundary of the medium, marked with points 'q', 'r', and 'g'.</image-desc>

then its passage in that transparent body will be through a motion composed of the two aforementioned motions. And because the density of the body resists it along the <term>direction</term> <note>original: "uerticatio", the line or vector of travel.</note> it intended, and its resistance is not very strong—from which it follows that it would decline toward the part through which it would pass more easily—and since motion along the perpendicular is the easiest of motions: it is therefore necessary that light which extends along an oblique line should move toward the perpendicular emerging from the point where the light meets the surface of the dense transparent body. 

And because its motion is composed of two motions, one of which is along the line perpendicular to the surface of the dense body, and the other along the line perpendicular to this perpendicular; and since the composite motion within it is not entirely abandoned but only hindered: it is necessary that the light decline toward the easier path than the one it was moving toward before, while the composite motion remains within it. But the path easier than the one it was moving toward, while motion remains within it, is that part which is closer to the perpendicular. Hence, if light extending in a transparent body encounters a transparent body denser than the one in which it exists, it will be refracted along a line closer to the perpendicular emerging from the point where it meets the denser body, extending into the denser body along a line other than the line along which it was moving. This, therefore, is the cause of the refraction of light in transparent bodies that are denser than the transparent bodies in which they exist; and for this reason, refraction is properly found in oblique lights. Therefore, when light extends in a transparent body and encounters a transparent body of different transparency from the body in which it exists, and denser, and is oblique to the surface of the transparent body it encounters: it will be refracted

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s investigation into the physical causes of refraction, moving from the mechanical analogy of projectiles (like stones or iron balls) to a geometric proof. He establishes why light bends toward or away from the perpendicular depending on the density of the media, specifically focusing on the relationship between the "surface of refraction" and the interface between two substances like air, water, and glass.</meta>

toward the side of the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>A line drawn at a 90-degree angle to a surface.</note> extended over the surface of the transparent body in the denser medium. However, the cause that produces the refraction of light from a denser body to a thinner body toward the side opposite the perpendicular is this: because when light moves in a transparent body, the body resists it with some repulsion, and a denser body resists it with a greater repulsion—just as a stone, when it moves in air, moves more easily and faster than if it were moved in water, because water resists it with a greater repulsion than air. Therefore, when light passes from a denser body into a thinner one, its motion will be faster. And when the light falls <term>obliquely</term> <note>At an angle, rather than straight down.</note> upon the shared boundary between two transparent bodies, its motion will be along a line existing between the perpendicular issuing from the starting point of its motion and the line perpendicular to that (the horizontal). Therefore, the resistance of the denser body will be from the side toward which this second perpendicular exits. When light leaves a denser body and reaches a thinner one, the resistance of the thinner body offered to the light—being on the side of the second perpendicular—will be less than the first resistance; consequently, the motion of the light toward the side that was being resisted becomes greater. And thus it is for light in a thinner body: it moves toward the side opposite the perpendicular.

## ON THE NATURE OF LIGHT REFRACTION in transparent bodies. Chapter III.

9. *The surface of refraction is perpendicular to the refracting surface.*

In the aforementioned chapter, it was demonstrated that all light which is refracted from one transparent body to another always remains within a single flat surface. Therefore, the straight line through which light travels in the air and the straight line through which it is refracted in the water will always lie in that same plane. According to the inspection of the <term>instrument</term> <note>Alhazen is referring to a specialized bronze disk he designed to measure angles of refraction, often called the "circular instrument."</note> mentioned previously, this surface is the middle circle among the three marked on the inner rim of the instrument. That circle is parallel to the surface of the inner plate, and the surface of the inner plate is parallel to the surface of the back, upon which the square ruler is placed. Therefore, the plane of the middle circle is parallel to the surface of the square ruler. The surface of the square ruler, which is placed upon the back of the plate, is perpendicular to the other surface intersecting it. This ruler surface is placed upon the surface of the two boundaries applied to its ends, which in turn are placed upon the rim of the instrument. Therefore, the plane of the middle circle is perpendicular to the surface passing over the rim of the instrument. During an experiment, this surface passing through the rim of the instrument is parallel to the horizon. Thus, the plane of the middle circle is perpendicular to the surface of the horizon. 

Since it has been demonstrated that the light in the air which is refracted in water is found on the circumference of this middle circle during experimentation, it is clear that light refracted from air to water always stays in the same plane perpendicular to the horizon. Let us also imagine a line from the center of the middle circle to the center of the world; this line will be perpendicular to the surface of the water because it is a <term>diameter of the world</term> <note>original: "diameter mundi". Alhazen assumes the Earth is a sphere and the surface of a liquid like water follows that curvature; thus, a line to the center of the Earth is perfectly vertical/perpendicular to the water's surface.</note>. Since this line lies within the plane of the middle circle, it is in the surface of refraction. Therefore, the surface of refraction is perpendicular to the surface of the water. 

It has already been shown that when light is refracted from air to water, it falls between the first line (the path in the air) and the perpendicular issuing from the center of the circle onto the water's surface. It has also been shown that light reaching a point within the water originates only from light extending from the center of the middle circle. Therefore, light refracted from air to water is refracted in a plane perpendicular to the water's surface. This refraction will be toward the side of the perpendicular at the point of refraction, though it will not actually reach the perpendicular itself. 

The refraction of light from air to glass happens in the same way. In experiments with glass, it was shown that when the line passing through the centers of two holes is oblique to the flat surface of the glass and passes through the center of the glass, the light will be refracted at that center. This refraction occurs in the plane of the middle circle toward the side of the perpendicular. Similarly, when the light is oblique to a *spherical* glass surface, it will be refracted within the glass body at that spherical surface. This refraction also stays in the plane of the middle circle and moves toward the perpendicular issuing from the point of refraction. Since the flat surface of the glass is perpendicular to the plate of the instrument, it is also perpendicular to the plane of the middle circle. Therefore, the plane of the middle circle (the surface of refraction) is perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass.

equal. And the surface of the middle circle also passes through the center of the glass sphere in all glass experiments. Therefore, it is perpendicular to the spherical glass surface. Thus, light which extends through the air and is refracted into the body of the glass during its extension in the air, after it is refracted again in the glass, always remains in a surface perpendicular to the surface of the glass. And its <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another.</note> will always be toward the side of the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>A line standing at a 90-degree angle to the surface.</note> extending from the point of refraction on the glass surface, whether the glass surface is flat or spherical. 

Likewise, it has also been demonstrated that when the line passing through the centers of the two holes is perpendicular to the glass surface and is extended into the body of the glass in a straight line, and the spherical surface is on the side of the holes, and this line (namely, the one passing through the centers of the two holes) is tilted relative to a flat glass surface and passes through the center of the glass, and is refracted in the body of the air touching the flat glass surface and at the center of the glass: then its refraction will be in the surface of the middle circle, and toward the side opposite to that where the perpendicular stands, which issues from the center of the glass upon the flat glass surface. 

It has also been shown that when the line passing through the centers of the two holes is perpendicular to a flat glass surface, and if it is extended into the body of the glass in a straight line, and the flat surface is on the side of the holes, and this line (the one passing through the centers of the two holes) is slanted relative to a spherical glass surface and does not pass through its center, and is refracted at the spherical glass surface into the body of air touching that spherical surface: then its refraction will be in the surface of the middle circle, and toward the side opposite to the perpendicular that issues from the point of refraction upon the surface of the second body. And in these two positions, the surface of the middle circle is also perpendicular to both the flat and spherical glass surfaces. 

Therefore, light which extends through the body of glass and is refracted into the air, while it extends in the glass and is refracted in the air, always remains in a surface perpendicular to the surface of the air; and the refraction will always be toward the side opposite to the perpendicular issuing from the point of refraction on the surface of the air. From all these previously demonstrated points, it is clear that all light refracted from one transparent body to another is always refracted in a surface perpendicular to the surface of the second body. 

If the second body is **denser** <note>original: "grossius"</note> than the first, then its refraction will be toward the side of the perpendicular issuing from the point of refraction on the surface of the second body, but it does not actually reach the perpendicular. And if the second body is **thinner** <note>original: "subtilius"</note> than the first, the refraction will be toward the side opposite the perpendicular issuing from the point of refraction on the surface of the second body, according to the different shapes of the surfaces of the transparent bodies. From these facts, it is also clear that when light is refracted from one transparent body to a second, and from the second to a third, it will also be refracted at the surface of the third if the transparency of the third differs from the transparency of the second. If the third is denser than the second, then the refraction of light will be toward the side of the perpendicular issuing from the point of refraction on the surface of the third; but if the third is thinner than the second, then the refraction of light will be toward the opposite side. This is the same if the light were refracted to a fourth body, a fifth, or even more. We have indeed explained in this chapter how all light is refracted in transparent bodies of varying transparency. The reason why refraction occurs in a surface perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body is this: because the line along which light extends in the first transparent body is refracted toward the side of the perpendicular in this surface—namely, the surface containing both the perpendicular and the first line of light. For the path of the perpendicular is in this surface; therefore, refraction occurs in the surface perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body.

### 10. To explore the magnitudes of the angles of refraction from air to water using a refraction instrument.

The sizes of the angles of refraction vary according to the sizes of the angles formed by the first line (along which light extends in the first body) and the perpendicular issuing from the point of refraction on the surface of the second body, according to the transparency of the second body. For the more the angle contained by the first line and the perpendicular increases, the more the angle of refraction increases; and the more that angle decreases, the more the angle of refraction decreases. However, the angles of refraction do **not maintain the same proportion** <note>Alhazen correctly identifies that refraction is not a simple linear relationship, a precursor to the discovery of the Sine Law.</note> to the angles formed by the first line and the perpendicular; rather, these proportions differ even within the same transparent body. Therefore, when the first line (along which light extends in the first body) forms two unequal angles with the perpendicular at two different times or in two different places, then the ratio of the smaller angle of refraction to the smaller incident angle will be less than the ratio of the larger angle of refraction to the larger incident angle. 

When the experimenter wishes to test these angles, he should mark off from the middle circle, which is on the circumference of the instrument, from the side of the center of the hole located on the circumference, an arc of ten parts out of the 360 parts into which the middle circle is divided. Then, let us draw from the point of difference a straight line perpendicular to the surface of the plate, and let us connect its end on the plate with the center of the plate by a straight line, extending it to the other side. Next, let us also divide on the circumference of the middle circle the arc following the first one, the size of which should be 90 parts; and let us mark a sign at the end of this arc. Therefore, the line issuing from the center of the middle circle to this sign will be perpendicular to the line issuing from the center of the middle circle to the first sign on the circumference <note>Original note: "by book 6, proposition 33: because these two lines encompass a quadrant of the entire periphery"</note> and the remaining arc, which is between the sign and the end of the diameter of the middle circle (which passes through the centers of the two holes), will be 80 parts. Let us also mark a sign at the end of this diameter. Then, let us place the instrument in a vessel and ensure the circumference of the vessel is parallel to the horizon. We should begin the experiment at the hour of sunrise, and pour clear water into the vessel until it reaches the center of the plate. Let us move the instrument until the first line marked on the surface of the plate touches the surface of the water; in this position, the line passing through the center of the middle circle is parallel...

He will also have the ratios of the angles of refraction to the angles formed by the primary lines of light and the perpendicular on the water's surface, which increase by tens. If the experimenter wishes for the angles to increase by five, he may easily do so; and if he wishes for increments smaller than five, he may do so following the aforementioned order.

### 12. To investigate the magnitudes of the angles of refraction from air or water to concave glass, and vice versa, using the instrument of refraction. <note>Refers to Book 7, propositions 8 through 10.</note>

And if anyone wishes to test the quantities of the angles of refraction at the concave surface of the glass: let him take a concave glass with a cylindrical cavity in the amount of a semi-cylinder. Let the shape of the whole glass consist of parallel surfaces; its length should be greater than the diameter of the spherical glass by one <term>barleycorn</term> <note>original: "grano hordei"; a traditional unit of measurement approximately equal to 1/3 of an inch</note>, and its width should be the same. Its thickness should be double the diameter of the hole that is in the rim of the instrument. The concavity should be on one of its sides—specifically, the cylindrical cavity should be on one square surface. Let the length of the cylinder be along the length of the glass, and let the radius of the base of the cylinder be equal to the radius of the spherical glass. The edges of the glass must be perfectly straight lines. This instrument can be well-made using a mold, so that the mold is prepared according to the previously described method, and the glass is melted and poured over the said mold. 

If the experimenter then wishes to test refraction with this instrument: let him mark off an arc from the circumference of the middle circle, the size of which is what he wishes to test. Let him draw a perpendicular from the end of the arc to the surface of the plate, as previously described, and join the end of the perpendicular to the center of the plate with a straight line, extending it to the other side. On this line, on the other side (the side with the two holes), let him mark a line equal to the radius of the base of the cylinder, and from its end, draw a perpendicular to the diameter of the plate, extending it in both directions. 

Then let him place the glass upon the plate, positioning the back of the cavity toward the two holes. He should align the two edges that exceed the diameter of the cylinder with this perpendicular, ensuring that the distances of the two ends of the diameter of the cavity's base from the point where the perpendicular began are equal. Therefore, the center of the base of the cylindrical cavity will be over the point from which the perpendicular began, and over the point whose distance from the center of the plate is equal to the radius of the base of the cavity. 

With this position secured, let him attach the glass firmly. The surface of the middle circle will then cut through the opening of the cylinder and remain parallel to its base, for in this arrangement, the base is on the surface of the plate. And because the edge of the glass is placed upon the line perpendicular to the point on the plate, the diameter of the plate will be perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass—for the flat surfaces of the glass are perpendicular to each other. Therefore, the line passing through the centers of the two holes will be perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass on the convex side [according to proposition 8 of Book 11] because it is parallel to the diameter of the plate; and this flat surface of the glass is on the side of the holes. 

In this position, therefore, the light that extends along the line passing through the centers of the two holes travels straight through the body of the glass until it reaches the concave part of the glass. There, it is refracted at the concave surface, since it does not pass through the center of the circle in the concavity, nor is it perpendicular to the concave surface. Thus, it refracts in the glass's cavity. The <term>common intersection</term> <note>The point or line where two surfaces or paths meet.</note> of this line and the cavity of the glass is the center of the middle circle. Therefore, the light extending along the line through the centers of the two holes refracts at the center of the middle circle. Consequently, the arc between the center of the light and the end of the line passing through the centers of the two holes <term>subtends</term> <note>original: "chordat"; literally 'chords,' meaning the straight line segment connects the endpoints of the arc, defining the angle.</note> the angle of refraction. 

In this way, one can test the quantities of the angles of refraction that occur in the concavity of the glass by adding small increments to the arcs. This refraction is from the concave glass to the air, and the angles obtained by this refraction will be the same as those that occur from air to glass in the concavity of the glass. It was declared a little while ago that the angle of refraction from glass to air, and from air to glass, is the same as the angle contained by the first line along which the light extends and the perpendicular emerging from the point of refraction. In this way, one could obtain the quantities of the angles of refraction from air to water, from air to glass, from glass to air, and from glass to water, from a flat surface, as well as from concave and convex surfaces. With these angles tested and their proportions noted, the experimenter will find two angles, each of which is contained by the primary line along which the light extends and the perpendicular.

He concludes that the principles of refraction—specifically the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction—remain consistent across different media and surface shapes.</summary>

# BOOK VII OF OPTICS

...cular, emerging from the point of refraction upon the surface of the <term>transparent body</term> <note>original: "corpus diaphanum"; any material that allows light to pass through, like glass or water</note>: I say that he will find in those same transparent bodies two different angles. For the angle of refraction from a larger angle [of incidence] will be greater than the two angles of refraction from a smaller angle; and the excess of the angle of refraction over the [other] angle of refraction will be less than the excess of the larger angle, which the first line makes with the perpendicular, over the smaller angle, which the first line makes with the perpendicular. And the ratio of the angle of refraction from the larger angle to that larger angle will be greater than the ratio of the angle of refraction from the smaller angle to that smaller angle. And that which remains of the larger angle after refraction is greater than what remains of the smaller angle after refraction. And the displacement of the angle of refraction, when light passes from a <term>rarer body</term> <note>original: "subtiliore"; a less dense medium like air</note> to a <term>denser one</term> <note>original: "grossius"; a more dense medium like water or glass</note>, will always be less than the angle which the line (along which the light extends to the point of refraction) makes with the perpendicular emerging from the point of refraction. And if the light passes from a denser body to a rarer one, then the angle of refraction will be the mean of the two joined angles. And if you compare the angles of refraction which exist between one of these transparent bodies and another body denser than them, to the angles of refraction which exist between that same rarer transparent body and another body denser than the first dense one: you will find the ratios of the angles of refraction to the angles (which the first line and the perpendicular make) to be greater between the rarer body and the denser body that is more dense, than the ratios of the angles of refraction between the same rarer body and the dense body that is less dense. Since if there are two equal angles, either of which the first line (along which the light extends) makes with the perpendicular emerging from the point of refraction—one being between a rarer body and a denser body, and the other between that same rarer body and a body denser than the first—then the angle of refraction in the denser body will be greater than the angle of refraction in the body that is less dense. And similarly, if the refraction is from a denser body to a rarer one that is even more rare, it will be greater than the angle of refraction from that same denser body to a rarer body that is less rare. These, therefore, are all the things that pertain to the quality of the refraction of light from transparent bodies.

## THAT WHATEVER IS PERCEIVED BEYOND TRANSPARENT bodies, which differ in transparency from the body in which the eye is located, is perceived by refraction when it is oblique to the perpendicular lines upon their surface.

### Chapter 4.

<margin>13. A visible object in a different medium is seen straight if perpendicular, and refracted if oblique. <note>Refers to Book 3, proposition 10.</note></margin>
In the preceding chapter, it was made clear that light passes from glass to air, from air to glass, and from air to water. And since it passes from glass to air and to water, it is established that it passes from water to air—for water is rarer than glass when it is clear—and since it passes from air to glass, it will pass from water to glass, since water is denser than air. Furthermore, it was shown that all <term>accidental and essential</term> <note>“Essential” light comes from a source like the sun; “accidental” light is reflected or borrowed light</note> light, whether strong or weak, passes through these transparent bodies. In these ways, therefore, every luminous body, by whatever light it possesses, sends its light into every transparent body; and if it encounters another transparent body, it will pass into the other body either by refraction or in a straight line. And in the first book <note>Refers to Book 1, sections 14, 18, and 19.</note> it was declared that from any point of any luminous body, light arises along every straight line that can be extended from that point. From this, it is clear that from any point of any transparent body touching a luminous body, light arises along every straight line that can be extended from that point and passes into the transparent body touching that point. And if it encounters another transparent body of a different transparency from that of the body touching it, it will also pass into it either refracted or straight, whether the first body is rarer than the second, or the second rarer than the first. And also in the first book <note>Refers to Book 1, sections 14, 18, 19, and 28.</note> it was declared that from every colored luminous body, color arises along with the light, being mixed with the light; and that when the sense of sight perceives the light, it perceives the form of the color mixed with it. From these things it is clear that colored bodies, which are in water and beyond transparent bodies that differ in transparency from the transparency of air—when there is essential light in them, or accidental light, strong or weak—then the light which is in them arises from every point with the form of the color at that point, and the light mixed with color passes into the body of the water and into every transparent body touching it. The light extends in the body of the water and in every transparent body with the form of the color through straight lines until it reaches the surface of the water or of that transparent body. And when there is air or another transparent body touching the water, then into that transparent body the light will pass with the form mixed with it in the air or in the other transparent body through straight lines. And these second lines, for the most part, will intersect the first lines along which they were extended, and some of them will be in a straight line with the first lines. # ALHAZEN

...[light arrives] <note>The text begins mid-sentence; based on the grammar, it likely completes the thought that light "arrives" or "reaches" a point.</note> with the form of color, which is at that point on the surface of the water or on the surface of that <term>transparent body</term> <note>original: "corpus diaphanum"; any medium that allows light to pass through, such as air, glass, or water</note>. But only one perpendicular line can be drawn from the same point of any surface [by Proposition 13 of Book 11 of Euclid’s *Elements*]. Therefore, from any point of any colored body existing in a transparent medium, there arises a <term>form of light</term> <note>Alhazen uses "form" to describe the physical qualities of light and color as they radiate through space to create an image in the eye</note> along with a form of color throughout the whole of the transparent medium in which it exists, following straight lines; and this form reaches the opposite side of the surface of the transparent medium. One of those lines will be perpendicular to the surface of the transparent medium (or to a surface continuous with it), while the remaining lines will be oblique to the surface of the transparent medium.

But in the preceding chapter [3. 6.8.4.7 n], it was explained that when light extends through a transparent medium and encounters another transparent medium with a different transparency than the first, if the line along which the light extended in the first body is perpendicular to the surface of the second body, then the light will continue to extend in a straight line into the second body. However, if the line along which the light extends is oblique to the surface of the second body, then the light will be refracted.

Thus, from every point of every colored and luminous body existing in a transparent medium, the form of light and color extends throughout the whole transparent medium and reaches the opposite surface of that medium. If there is another medium in contact with the first one that has a different transparency, then the form that reaches the surface of that medium passes into the contacting body itself. All these forms will be refracted, except for the form that is on the perpendicular line, for that one extends in a straight path into the contacting body. And if by chance the perpendicular falls upon a point of a surface continuous with the surface of a body that is not within that transparent medium, then that form will be destroyed <note>i.e., blocked or absorbed</note>, and then all the forms that pass into the contacting body will be refracted.

Therefore, the forms of all visible things—whether in water, in the heavens, or in any transparent bodies in contact with the air that differ from the transparency of the air—extend throughout the opposite air in straight lines. Those lines that are slanted relative to the surface of the air (where it touches the other transparent medium) will have their forms refracted. Those lines that are perpendicular to the surface of the air (where it touches the other transparent medium) will have their forms extended in a straight path.

And since it has already been established that from every point of every colored and luminous body, a form of light and color extends throughout the whole transparent medium, reaches its surface, and is refracted from that surface, it follows that the form extending from a single point to the surface of a transparent medium will be continuous and joined. And since the form is continuous, and the surface of the transparent medium is continuous and joined, and the form is refracted into the other transparent medium, it will therefore be refracted as a continuous whole.

When the refracted form is continuous and encounters a dense body, the form reaches that body through the transparent medium. Thus, the location in the transparent medium through which the form of a point (from the first body) extends and is refracted—since that location is luminous and colored—will send out a form of light and color from every one of its own points along every straight line that can be extended from that point. It follows from this that there are lines refracted toward that location from the lines along which the form of that location extends; and the form of every point of that location was already extending through one of those refracted lines.

Therefore, the form of that location on a dense, colored, and luminous body will be at a place on the surface of the transparent medium where the form of a single point (extended to that place on the surface) is refracted toward that same place on the dense body. From this, it follows that the form of the location on the dense body, which extends to that place in the transparent medium, is refracted along the same lines that extend from a single point to that place in the transparent medium. And when the form of the location in the transparent medium is refracted along those same lines, it will then arrive at that same point.

From this, it is clear that if one imagines a <term>pyramid</term> <note>original: "pyramis"; in historical optics, this refers to the "visual cone" or "cone of light" with its apex at the eye and its base on the object being seen</note> extended from any point in the air along straight lines, and if that pyramid is joined and continuous, and if that pyramid reaches the surface of a transparent medium of a different transparency than the air; and if one imagines every straight line that can be extended from that pyramid to be refracted at the surface of the transparent medium at the point required by its slant—and if any line is perpendicular, it extends straight—then this refracted body also becomes a continuous whole within the transparent medium that differs from the transparency of the air.

When this refracted body reaches a dense body, then that dense body, if it is colored and luminous, will send the form of the light and color within it into this imagined refracted body along every straight line that can be extended in this refracted body from a line extended in the body of the pyramid from a point in the air. For every colored and luminous body properly sends its form from every one of its points along every straight line that can be extended from that point. Therefore, the form of a point of that location on the dense body will be extended through every one of the refracted lines to that location on the dense body.

That form will therefore travel from the dense, colored, luminous body to the place on the surface of the transparent medium where those lines are refracted. And once it reaches that place on the surface of the transparent medium, it will necessarily be refracted along those same lines that extend to that place from a single point in the air. As for the form which is the form of a colored place on a dense body (which is inside a transparent medium of a different transparency than air, and is located on a line among those lines through which the form extends to the <term>center of sight</term> <note>original: "centrum uisus"; the pupil or the functional center of the eye</note>), that form, I say, which extends through that line, will reach the center of sight directly. However, the forms that extend through all the other lines that constitute the pyramid extended from the center of sight will be refracted, not direct. ## 14. The image of a visible object refracted from a denser medium inclines toward the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction; but from a rarer medium, it moves away from it. [4 p 10]

That this is true can be tested experimentally as follows. Let the experimenter take the aforementioned instrument and place it in a vessel. Place the vessel in a well-lit area so that light reaches the interior. Pour water into the vessel until it reaches the center of the <term>plate</term> <note>original: "laminae"; a flat metal or wooden disc used as a measuring scale</note>. Then, reduce the size of the holes with wax so that only a small opening remains in their center. Insert a <term>reed</term> <note>original: "calamum"; used here as a narrow tube or sighting guide</note> into the two holes so that the space between them is fixed. Move the instrument until the diameter of the plate—on whose ends are two perpendicular lines at the rim of the instrument—is perpendicular to the surface of the water. 

Next, take a thin white <term>stylus</term> <note>a pointed rod used as a target for observation</note> and place it in the vessel, positioning its tip at the center point of the middle circle. This point is the intersection of the circumference of the middle circle and the perpendicular line on the rim of the instrument, which marks the end of the diameter passing through the centers of the two holes. The experimenter should then place one eye over the upper hole, close the other, and look at the rim of the instrument submerged in the water; he will then see the tip of the stylus. This experiment will demonstrate that the perception of the stylus tip follows the straight path of a perpendicular line extending from the tip to the surface of the water. <margin>[18. 19 n]</margin> For the line passing through the centers of the two holes (where the center of sight is located) and the stylus tip (along the line of sight through which the eye perceives it) is perpendicular to the water's surface. In the first book [18. 19 n], it was shown that the eye perceives nothing except along the straight lines extending through the center of sight. Thus, the eye perceives the tip of the stylus along the line passing through the centers of the two holes. This line extends directly to the stylus tip and is perpendicular to the water's surface. 

Next, the experimenter must tilt the instrument until the line passing through the centers of the two holes is oblique to the surface of the water. Place the stylus in the water and set its tip on the first point (the end of the diameter of the middle circle passing through the holes). If he looks through the upper hole, he will no longer see the tip of the stylus. He should then move the stylus in the opposite direction from the eye, sliding the tip gently along the circumference of the middle circle while watching the rim of the instrument. When he sees the stylus tip, he should fix it in that place. 

Then, he should ask another person to place a thin wooden rod or needle perpendicularly into the water at the surface, opposite the second hole, so it stands at the center of the middle circle.

...perceives the tip of the stylus in the water from that location—specifically, because he perceives the tip of the stylus when it was between the point where the perpendicular falls and the end of the diameter of the middle circle, which passes through the centers of the two holes. And that <term>form</term> <note>original: "forma"; in medieval optics, this refers to the visual image or species of an object</note> also exited from the water and was refracted in the air; and air is more <term>subtle</term> <note>original: "subtiliar"; meaning less dense or more transparent</note> than water. Next, the experimenter must remove the glass and place it upon the plate outside of its previous position: namely, he should place its convex side facing the two holes, and place its <term>common intersection</term> <note>the line where the flat and curved surfaces meet</note> upon the same line on the surface of the plate where he had placed it in the previous arrangement, and place the middle of that common intersection over the center of the plate. In this way, the line passing through the centers of the two holes will be <term>oblique</term> <note>at an angle other than 90 degrees</note> to the flat surface of the glass, but perpendicular to its convex surface. 

He should then fix the glass in this position, place the instrument into the vessel, and set the tip of the stylus at the end of the diameter of the middle circle, just as he did before. Let him place his eye at the upper hole and look at the rim of the instrument; he will not see the tip of the stylus at that moment. Then, let him move the stylus toward the point where the perpendicular falls; he still will not see the tip of the stylus. Then, let him move it in the opposite direction from where the perpendicular falls, along the circumference of the middle circle, doing so gently; for then he will see the tip of the stylus. 

Thus, when the straight line exiting from the tip of the stylus to the center of the glass is extended straight through the body of the glass, and the perpendicular exiting from the center of the glass is extended along with it, the line passing through the centers of the two holes will be between these two lines. And the form of the stylus tip, which travels along this line when extended toward the center of the glass, will be refracted along the line passing through the centers of the two holes. Therefore, this refraction will be toward the perpendicular exiting from the point of refraction on the surface of the glass. This form exits from the air and is refracted in the glass; and glass is <term>denser</term> <note>original: "grossius"; literally "thicker," referring to optical density</note> than air. 

From all these experiments, it is clear that sight perceives visible objects that are in water, or beyond transparent bodies that differ in transparency from air, according to refraction—except for those objects located on lines perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body in which they exist. It is also clear that the refraction of their forms occurs within surfaces that are perpendicular to the surfaces of the transparent bodies. For everything tested with the aforementioned instrument is found to refract within the plane of the middle circle, which (as has been shown) is perpendicular to the surfaces of the transparent bodies and to the surfaces of the bodies in contact with them. 

From this experimentation, it is also demonstrated that forms perceived by sight through refraction—which pass from a denser transparent body to a more subtle one—are refracted away from the perpendicular exiting from the point of refraction on the surface of the transparent body. Conversely, those passing from a more subtle body to a denser one are refracted toward the aforementioned perpendicular.

### 15. A star is seen by refraction.

Stars are also perceived through refraction; for the body of the heavens is more subtle than the body of the air (that is, it possesses greater transparency). This can be proven through an experiment that shows stars are perceived via refraction; from which it will also be clear that the body of the heavens is more transparent than the body of the air. 

When someone wishes to test this, let him take an <term>armillary instrument</term> <note>an armillary sphere, a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings</note> and place it in an elevated position where the eastern horizon is visible. Let him set up the armillary instrument in its proper manner: namely, by placing the ring that represents the meridian circle within the plane of the local meridian, and let its pole be raised from the earth according to the altitude of the <term>celestial pole</term> <note>the point in the sky around which the stars appear to rotate</note> above the horizon of the place where the instrument is set. 

During the night, let him observe one of the large fixed stars that passes through the <term>zenith</term> <note>original: "uertićem capitis"; the point directly overhead</note> of that location, or near it, and observe it from its rising in the east. Once the star has risen, let him rotate the ring that turns around the equatorial pole until it is aligned with the star, and let the star's position be confirmed by the ring; thus he will have the star’s distance from the celestial pole. Then, let him observe the star until it reaches the meridian circle, and rotate the same ring he moved before until it is aligned with the star; thus he will have the star's distance from the celestial pole when the star is at the zenith. 

When this is done, he will find that the star's distance from the pole at its rising is smaller than its distance from the pole at the hour it is at the zenith. From this, it is clear that sight perceives the stars through refraction, not in a straight line. For a fixed star always moves along the same circle among the circles parallel to the equator and never leaves it (except over a very long period of time). If the star were perceived in a straight line, then the radial lines would extend straight from the eye to the stars, and the forms of the stars would extend through those radial lines until they reached the eye. If the form extended from the star straight to the eye, then the eye would perceive it in its true place; and thus the distance of a fixed star from the pole would be found to be the same throughout the same night. But the star's distance from the pole changes during the same night; therefore, sight does not perceive the star in a straight line. 

In the heavens, there is no dense, polished body—nor is there one in the air—from which forms could be reflected. Since sight perceives the star neither in a straight line nor by reflection, it must be by refraction, as these are the only three ways things are perceived by sight. From the variation in the distance of the same star from the celestial pole during the same night, it is proved beyond doubt that sight perceives the stars through refraction. Therefore, the body in which the fixed stars exist differs in transparency from the air. Furthermore, the transparency of the celestial body can be tested through experiments with the moon. For when you have calculated the position of the moon at a certain hour near its rising, and afterward on a known night and at a known place you verify its position from the celestial pole, then...

It remains, then, to demonstrate that the body of the heavens differs in its <term>rarity</term> <note>original: "subtilitate"; often translated as subtlety or thinness, referring to lower density</note> from the air, and this will be shown by the aforementioned experiment.

### 16. The heavens are rarer than air and fire. <note>original: "Caelum rarius est aere & igne"</note> 50 p 10.

Let the meridian circle at the place of the experiment be circle $a-b-g$; let the zenith be $b$; the pole of the world $d$; and the center of the world $e$. Let us connect $b$ with $e$, and let the position of the eye be $z$. Let the circle parallel to the equinoctial (whose distance from the pole of the world is that in which the star is found at the hour of the first verification of distance) be circle $h-t$; let the position of the star at that hour be $h$. Let the circle parallel to the equinoctial (whose distance from the pole is that in which the star is found at the second hour) be circle $k-b$. This circle will then be the one in which the star rests according to its vertical path. For when a star is at the zenith, or very near it, the eye perceives it directly <margin>by 13 n</margin> because the straight line passing through the eye and the zenith is perpendicular to the concave surface of the celestial sphere and perpendicular to the convex surface of the air. Since it is perpendicular to both bodies, the eye perceives the star on this line directly, whether these two bodies—heaven and air—are of different transparency or the same. Therefore, when the star is at or near the zenith, the eye perceives it in its true circle parallel to the equinoctial, upon which it was moving from the beginning of the night until it reached the meridian. Thus, circle $k-b-g$ is the one in which the star was during the first experiment. Let the vertical circle passing through the star at the hour of the first experiment be circle $b-h-k$; let that circle intersect circle $k-b-g$ at point $k$, and circle $h-t$ at point $h$. And because the distance of the star from the pole was smaller in the first experiment than in the second, circle $h-t$ will be

Since the star is perceived by the eye at the hour of the first experiment at point $h$, and it was then on the surface of the vertical circle $b-h-k$, and the star was at that hour on the circumference $k-b-g$, the star was actually at point $k$ at that hour. Yet it is perceived by the eye at point $h$, and along the straightness of line $z-h$; for the eye perceives nothing except through the direction of the radial lines through which <term>forms</term> <note>the visual images of objects</note> reach the eye. The eye, therefore, perceives the star at point $h$ because the form reaches it along the straight line $h-z$. Since the eye perceives it along $h-z$, and the straight line between the star and the eye is line $k-z$, it is manifest that the eye does not perceive the star at point $k$ directly, but by refraction. 

Let the location of refraction be $m$. Let us connect $k-m$ and extend a straight line from $m$ to $z$. The form of the star reaching $z$, by which the eye perceives the star, extends from the star along line $k-m$ and is refracted along line $m-z$. Forms are not refracted unless they encounter a body of a different transparency from the transparency of the body in which they exist. Therefore, the body in which the star is located—namely, the heaven—is a transparent medium differing in transparency from the air. And since the location of refraction is at the surface passing through two bodies of different transparency, point $m$ is a point on the concavity of the heavens. Let us connect the line between $e$ and $m$; let it be the diameter of the celestial sphere. Line $e-m$ will thus be perpendicular to the concave surface of the heavens touching the air, and to the convex surface of the air <margin>as demonstrated in 25 n 4</margin>. Since the form of the star at point $k$ extends through line $m-k$ and is refracted in the air through line $m-z$, it is clear that this refraction is toward the line in which the perpendicular $e-m$ lies, which passes through the point of refraction and is perpendicular to the surface of the air. Since refraction in the air is toward the side of the perpendicular emerging from the place of refraction, it follows that the body of the air is <term>denser</term> <note>original: "grossius"; literally "thicker" or "grosser"</note> than the body of the heavens. It is therefore clear that what we found through the experiment of the stars demonstratively signifies that the eye only perceives the stars through refraction, that the body of the air is denser than the body of the heavens, and that the body of the heavens is rarer than the body of the air. From all this, it is clear that everything perceived by the eye beyond transparent bodies whose transparency differs from that of the air—if the sight is oblique to the perpendiculars emerging from them onto the surface of the transparent bodies in which they consist—is perceived through refraction.

# BOOK VII OF OPTICS. ON IMAGES. CHAPTER V.
