### 17. *An image (which is the form of a visible object refracted by a different medium) is seen outside the location of the visible object.*

**A**n image is the form of a visible thing that the eye perceives through a <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphanum corpus"; a substance like water or glass that allows light to pass through</note> which differs in its transparency from the transparency of the air, when the line of sight is slanted away from the perpendicular lines extending from that visible object to the surface of that transparent body. For the form that the eye perceives in a transparent body of an object located beyond that body is not the visible object itself. This is because the eye does not perceive the visible object in its true place, nor in its true form, but in another place and in another manner—namely, through <term>refraction</term> <note>original: "refractè"; the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another</note>. Despite this, the eye perceives that object as being directly opposite it; this perceived form is called an "image." 

This can be understood through both reason and experience. By reason, because it is clear from the previous chapter that a visible object in a transparent body of a different transparency than air is perceived by the eye through refraction when the sight is inclined from the perpendicular lines falling from the object onto the surface of the transparent body. And since the eye perceives such an object through refraction, and is not directly in line with it, yet does not "feel" itself perceiving it through refraction, it is clear that it perceives the object outside its actual location. 

Through experience, however, it can be known in this way: if someone takes a vessel with upright, perpendicular sides and places a clearly visible object in its center—such as an <note>original: "obolum aut denarium"; ancient Greek and Roman coins</note>—and stands at a distance until they can just see the object at the bottom of the vessel; then let them move further away until the object gradually disappears from view. At the moment it is hidden, the person should stay in their place and tell another to pour water into the vessel. Without moving their eye or changing their position, as they look at the water in the vessel, they will see the object again after it had been hidden, and they will see it directly in their line of sight. From this, it is clear that the form seen in the water is not in the actual location of the object. For if the form were in the location of the object, the eye would have perceived the object even without the water in the vessel; yet in this second state, the eye perceives the object in front of it, even though the object is not actually in that direct line of sight. In this way, it is demonstrated by both reason and experience that the image of a visible object seen through refraction is not in the actual location of that object.

<margin>Proposition 15, page 10.</margin>

### 18. *An image is seen at the intersection of the lines of refraction and the perpendicular line of incidence.*

**N**ext, I maintain that the image of any point perceived by the eye through refraction is located at the point where the line through which the form reaches the eye intersects with the perpendicular line extending from that visible point to the surface of the transparent body. 

This shall be demonstrated by experience in the following way. Let someone take a wooden circle with a diameter of no less than one cubit <note>roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> and a height of two or three fingers, and make its surface as level as possible. Let them find its center and draw diameters intersecting each other however they wish; let these be marked with an iron tool so they are visible, and fill the lines with a white substance, such as <note>original: "cerusa mixta lacte"; white lead mixed with milk, used as a bright pigment</note>, and let the very center of the center point be black. 

Once this is finished, take a wide vessel, like a basin with raised edges, place it in a well-lit area, and pour clear water into it. The depth of the water should be less than the diameter of the circle but greater than its radius. Measure this with the circle itself until the water rises a few inches above the center of the circle—specifically, so that two or more diameters marked on the vessel are partially covered by water, while the other part remains above the water. Wait until the water is still, then place the wooden circle into the vessel, standing it upright against the edge, with the surface containing the marked lines facing the eye. Then move the circle until one of its diameters is perpendicular to the water's surface. 

Then, lower the gaze and adjust the vessel until the eye is nearly level with the surface of the water, just outside the edge of the vessel, but high enough to see the center of the circle; the experiment is clearest in this position. Having done this, look at the center of the circle and the diameter that is perpendicular to the water's surface; you will find the center of the circle stays perfectly in line with that perpendicular diameter. 

Next, look at a slanted diameter, part of which sticks out above the water. You will find that it appears "bent" where it meets the surface of the water. The part inside the water forms an obtuse angle with the part outside the water; you will find this angle points toward the perpendicular diameter, though the part inside the water still appears straight and continuous. 

From this, it is clear that the form of the point at the center of the circle—the form the eye actually perceives—is not at the physical center of the circle. For if it were at the physical center, it would appear in a straight line with the slanted diameter, as that is its true physical position. Since the eye perceives this point outside the straight line of the slanted diameter, and the angles formed by the parts of the slanted diameter follow the perpendicular diameter, the point that constitutes the "image" of the center is raised from the actual center. And because the eye perceives this point in line with the diameter that is perpendicular to the water’s surface, this image-point must be raised up from the center while remaining on the perpendicular line extending from the center to the water's surface. 

Furthermore, the bending of the slanted diameter at the water’s surface, and the fact that the portion underwater appears straight and continuous, proves that every point on the part of the slanted diameter that is underwater is perceived as being raised from its true location. Finally, the experimenter should rotate the wooden circle until the slanted diameter itself becomes perpendicular to the water's surface, and so on...

And because the sight <note>original: "uifus"; refers to the act of seeing or the visual ray</note> touches the surface of the glass, and one part of the perpendicular diameter is under the glass, another is outside the glass on the side of the center, and another is outside the glass on the side of the diameter's edge: therefore, the part under the glass is perceived by the sight outside the glass through refraction. The part at the edge of the diameter is perceived by the sight outside the glass directly and without refraction. However, the part on the side of the center is perceived by both eyes <note>original: "utroque uisu"</note> through refraction. For the lines that emerge from the center of the sight touching the glass and extend into the body of the glass—when they reach the surface of the glass on the side of the center's edge—will all be slanted relative to the surface of the glass. Therefore, the part of the perpendicular diameter on the side of the center is perceived by the sight touching the glass through refraction. 

Indeed, the lines that go out from the other eye to the upper surface of the glass will be slanted relative to that upper surface; and when they extend to the other surface of the glass on the side of the center, they will also be slanted. Thus, the other eye perceives the part of the perpendicular diameter on the side of the center through two refractions, but the part under the glass through only one refraction; and despite all this, the sight perceives this diameter as a straight line. If the experimenter covers one eye and looks with the eye that is on the side of the glass, he will perceive the perpendicular as straight. And if he raises his eye from the glass and gazes at the perpendicular diameter through the glass, he will perceive it as straight, even though he is perceiving it through refraction. 

The cause of this is that every point on a perpendicular diameter, when perceived through refraction, is seen not in its true place, but nonetheless in a place that is aligned with the perpendicular line that goes out from that point to the surface of the glass. This diameter is itself the perpendicular that goes out from any of its points to the surface of the glass, and no point is perceived through refraction except upon that line. When the sight perceives this diameter as straight, and perceives the form of the center in the alignment of this diameter, the form of the center which the sight perceives through the glass (when the eye touches the glass) is in the alignment of the perpendicular going out from the center to the surface of the glass. 

And when the observer perceives a slanted diameter as bent, he will perceive the part of it that comes out from the center—that is, the part on the side of the center—not in its true place; the point of the center itself is not perceived by the sight except away from its true place. When the angle of the bend is on the side of the circumference, then the point that is the form of the center is below the actual center. From this it is clear that the image <note>original: "imago"; the perceived location of an object after light has been bent</note> of any point perceived by the sight through a <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "corpus diaphanum"</note> that is subtler <note>less dense, like air</note> than the transparent medium where the eye is located, is in the alignment of the line that goes out from that point perpendicular to the surface of the transparent medium where the eye is; and it is further from the surface of that medium than the point itself actually is. 

Every point perceived by the sight is in the alignment of the line through which the form reaches the eye. The image of any point perceived by the sight through a transparent medium subtler than the medium where the eye is, is located at the <term>common difference</term> <note>the line of intersection</note> of the line through which the form reaches the eye and the perpendicular that goes out from the visible point to the surface of the transparent medium where the eye is. From everything declared in this chapter, it is clear that the image of any visible point perceived through a medium of different transparency than the medium where the eye is (when the gaze is slanted relative to the perpendiculars going out from that point to the surface) is at the common difference of the line through which the form reaches the eye and the perpendicular from that point to the surface—whether the medium where the eye is be subtler or denser <note>original: "grossius"; literally "thicker"</note> than the medium where the object is. Why the eye perceives the visible thing in the place of the image, and why the image is at the point of intersection between the line of the form and the perpendicular, will be discussed later.

<margin>
13. 18 p 10.
</margin>
*19. An image is seen both in the line of refraction and in the perpendicular of incidence. 12.*

That the sight perceives the form of a visible point through refraction in the alignment of the line through which the form reaches the eye is manifest; the cause of this has been declared in the preceding treatises. Sight perceives nothing except along the alignment of radial lines, for it is only affected along the paths <note>original: "uerticationibus"</note> of those lines. As for why it perceives the form along the perpendiculars going out from the visible thing to the surface of the transparent medium, it is because—as we declared in the second book—when light extends through a transparent medium, it extends by a very swift motion. In the fourth chapter of this treatise, we declared that the motion of light in a transparent medium along a line slanted to the surface is composed of a motion along the perpendicular going out from the point where the light extends to the surface, and a motion along a line that is perpendicular to that perpendicular <note>i.e., a horizontal or parallel component</note>. The form that extends from a visible point via refraction to the point of refraction (which is the form of the light at the visible point mixed with the form of the color) always extends along a line slanted to the surface of the medium. Therefore, this form extends to the point of refraction by a motion composed of the motion along the perpendicular from the visible point to the surface, and the motion along the line perpendicular to that perpendicular. <meta>This page continues Alhazen’s geometric demonstration of how the "form" (light and color) of an object travels through different media. It focuses on the "location of the image" and how the eye perceives a single point through refraction, even when the light bends.</meta>

ALHAZEN'S [OPTICS]

...the motion of the <term>form<note>original: "formæ"; in medieval optics, this refers to the visual "species" or light/color information traveling from an object to the eye.</note></term>, which moves either along the perpendicular line that stands upon the surface of the <term>transparent body<note>original: "corporis diaphani"; any medium like air, water, or glass that light can pass through.</note></term>, and is then diverted from this perpendicular by another motion; or it moves along a line that exists upon the first perpendicular, and is diverted after its initial motion along that first perpendicular by a combined motion made of the two aforementioned motions. This point is perceived by the sight in the direct path of the line through which the form reaches the eye. Therefore, the form existing at the point of <term>refraction<note>the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another.</note></term> reaches the eye through the motion of the form moving along the line perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body: then it is diverted from this perpendicular by a motion along the straight line through which the form reaches the eye. Furthermore, the form that is on the perpendicular standing upon the surface of the transparent body—and then moves in the direct path of the line through which the form extends to the eye—is the form that extends from the visible point upon the surface of the transparent body until it reaches the point of intersection between this perpendicular and the line through which the form extends to the eye. Therefore, the form of a point which the eye perceives through refraction beyond a transparent body is governed by the motion of the form that reaches the eye from the **location of the image**. The eye perceives this form from the location of the image because it follows the motion of the form that the eye would perceive directly and without refraction: it is the place that is as far from the eye as the point of the image is, and its position relative to the eye is the position of the form at the location of the image. Hence, the eye perceives that point according to refraction at the location of the image. This is the reason why the eye perceives a visible thing beyond a transparent body at the location of the image, and why the image of any point of a visible thing perceived by refraction is at the place where the line through which the form reaches the eye intersects the perpendicular dropped from that point to the surface of the transparent body.

### 20. *A visible object refracted by a medium (which, when cut by a plane, creates a straight or circular common section) has only one image.*

**H**aving clarified this, let us state that every visible thing perceived by the eye beyond some transparent body which differs in transparency from the medium where the eye is located (if the body is one of the common types) has only one image. The common transparent bodies are the heavens, air, water, glass, and transparent stones. The surface of the heavens <note>referring to the celestial spheres of medieval cosmology</note> on the side of the eye is spherical and concave. Thus, every flat surface that cuts it creates a circular line within it, the concavity of which faces the eye. The surface of the air that touches the heavens is spherical and convex. Thus, if it is cut by an equal [flat] surface, a circular line will be formed in it [according to Theorem 1 of Theadosius’s *Spherics*], the convexity of which faces the heavens. The surface of water on the side of the eye is spherical and convex, and if it is cut by a flat surface, a circular line will be formed in it, the convexity of which faces the eye. The shapes of glass and transparent stones are usually round or flat. Thus, if they are cut by flat surfaces, either circles or straight lines are formed in them. We say generally that every point perceived by the eye beyond any transparent body (whose surface facing the eye is a single surface, and if cut by a flat surface, forms a straight or circular line) has only one image; nor does the eye perceive more than one single point.

### 21. *If the common section of the surfaces of refraction and the refractive medium is a straight line: the visible object on the perpendicular drawn from the eye to the refractive medium will be seen directly and as one.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the path of a light ray from an object (b) to an eye (a). A vertical perpendicular line (a-g-c) passes from the eye through the interface (g). A point (p) on the interface shows where a ray from (b) bends to reach (a). A normal line (k-p-l) is drawn through the point of refraction (p).</image-desc>

**L**et the eye be at **a**, and the visible point be **b**. Let the transparent body beyond which **b** is located be that in whose surface **g** lies. Let the transparency of this body be "thicker" <note>i.e., more dense or having a higher refractive index</note> than the transparency of the medium on the side of the eye. Let its surface on the side of the eye be flat, and let us draw a perpendicular line **a g c** from point **a** to that surface. The point **b** will either be on the line **a g c** or outside it. If point **b** is on the line **g c**, then the eye at **a** will perceive **b** directly and without refraction. For when the form of **b** extends through **b g**, it emerges into the medium on the side of **a** in the straight path of **b g**, because **b g** is perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body on the side of the eye. Therefore, the eye at **a** perceives **b** in its actual place and in the straight line **a g b**. We say, then, that point **b** will never be refracted to **a** from outside this line. If it were possible, let the form of **b** be refracted to **a** from point **p**. Let us extend a surface in which the perpendicular **a g b** and point **p** lie; it will create a straight line in the surface of the transparent body; let this be **g p d**. Let us draw a perpendicular from point **p** to the line **d p g**, which is **k p l**. Thus, **k p l** will be perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body (because the plane of refraction **a g p** is perpendicular to the plane of the refractive medium). Let us connect **b p** and extend it to **h**. The angle **k p h** will be the one contained by the line along which the form extends and the perpendicular rising from the point of refraction on the surface of the transparent body. Since the medium on the side of **a** is "subtler" <note>less dense</note> than that on the side of **b**, when the form from **b** reaches **p**, it will be refracted away from the perpendicular **p k**. Therefore, the refracted form will not reach line **a b**; but [by the hypothesis] it is refracted to point **a**, which is impossible. Therefore, the form of **b** will not be refracted to **a** from **p**.

<summary>Alhazen demonstrates that the perceived image of an object through refraction is located at the intersection of the visual ray and the perpendicular from the object to the surface. He also proves geometrically that if an object lies on the perpendicular line relative to the eye, it is seen in its true position without appearing refracted.</summary>

# OPTICS BOOK VII

In a circle: the angle of intersection <note>original: "angulus sectionis"; the angle formed where two lines cross</note> will be equal to the angle at the circumference <note>meaning the inscribed angle, which is half the central angle</note> subtended by the two arcs that those two chords mark off. And if two lines should cut the circle and intersect each other outside the circle: the angle of intersection will be equal to the angle at the circumference subtended by the difference between the larger and the smaller of the two arcs marked off by those two lines. 

For example: in circle $abcd$, let two chords $ac$ and $bd$ intersect at $e$. I say, therefore, that angle $aeb$ is equal to the angle at the circumference which corresponds to the two arcs $ab$ and $cd$: and that angle $bec$ is equal to the angle at the circumference corresponding to the two arcs $dga$ and $bzc$. For let us draw from $b$ a line $bz$ parallel to line $ac$ [by Proposition 31, Book 1 of Euclid's *Elements*]: therefore, arc $cz$ is equal to arc $ab$ [for if the straight line $az$ is drawn: angle $caz$ will equal angle $azb$ by Proposition 29, Book 1; and therefore the circumference $cz$ equals the circumference $ab$ by Proposition 26, Book 3] and arc $cd$ is common: therefore, arc $dz$ is equal to the two arcs $ab$ and $cd$. But arc $dz$ corresponds to angle $dbz$ [by Proposition 8, Definition 3]: therefore, $dz$ corresponds to angles equal to the two arcs $ab$ and $cd$. And [by Proposition 29, Book 1] angle $dbz$ is equal to angle $aeb$: therefore, angle $aeb$ is equal to the angle at the circumference corresponding to the two arcs $ab$ and $cd$. And this is what we wished to show.

Likewise, let us join $dz$: and let us extend $zb$ to $h$: therefore [by Proposition 32, Book 1] angle $hbd$ will be equal to the two angles $bdz$ and $bzd$, and [by Proposition 8, Definition 3] the two angles $bzd$ and $bdz$ are subtended by the two arcs $bgd$ and $bfz$: therefore angle $hbd$ is equal to the angle subtended by arc $dbz$. And arc $ab$ is equal to arc $zc$ [from the previous conclusion]: therefore arc $dbz$ is equal to the two arcs $dga$ and $bzc$. Thus angle $hbd$ is equal to the angle subtended by the two arcs $dga$ and $bzc$: and [by Proposition 29, Book 1] angle $hbe$ is equal to angle $bec$. Therefore, angle $bec$ is equal to the angle at the circumference corresponding to the two arcs $dga$ and $bzc$. And this is what we wished to demonstrate. 

And if the line $hbz$ touches the circle <note>original: "contingat"; is tangent to</note>: then [by Proposition 32, Book 3] angle $ebz$ will be equal to the angle falling in the segment $bad$. Thus arc $bcd$ corresponds to an angle at the circumference equal to angle $ebz$: and [by Proposition 29, Book 1] angle $ebz$ is equal to angle $bea$: therefore angle $bea$ is equal to the angle at the circumference subtended by arc $bcd$. And arc $bc$ is equal to arc $ba$: because the diameter that goes out from $b$ is perpendicular to line $ac$: [for the diameter drawn through point $b$ is perpendicular to the tangent by Proposition 18, Book 3; and so by Proposition 29, Book 1 it is perpendicular to $ac$ itself which is parallel to the tangent] wherefore [by Proposition 3, Book 3] it divides it into two equal parts: therefore arc $ab$ will be equal to arc $bc$: [for if the straight lines $ab$ and $bc$ are drawn, they will be equal by Proposition 4, Book 1; and therefore the circumferences $ab$ and $bc$ subtended by them are equal by Proposition 28, Book 3]. Therefore arc $bcd$ is equal to the two arcs $ab$ and $cd$: therefore angle $bea$ is equal to the angle at the circumference corresponding to the two arcs $ab$ and $cd$. And it will be demonstrated in a similar way that angle $bec$ is equal to the angle at the circumference corresponding to the two arcs $bc$ and $ad$. And this is what we wished to show.

*25. If two straight lines inscribed in a circle, when extended outside, meet: the angle of their meeting is equal to the angle at the periphery which stands upon the arc by which the larger of the included circumferences exceeds the smaller. [Proposition 55, Book 1 of a related text]*

Likewise: let $e$ be outside the circle $abcd$: and let us draw from $e$ two lines cutting the circle $abcd$: and let them be $ead$ and $ebc$. I say, therefore, that angle $ced$ is equal to the angle at the circumference of the circle corresponding to the arc which is the difference <note>original: "excessus"; the leftover amount when one is subtracted from the other</note> of arc $dc$ over arc $ab$. For let us draw a line parallel to line $bc$ [by Proposition 31, Book 1]: therefore [as was shown just before] arc $fc$ will be equal to arc $ab$: therefore arc $df$ will be the difference of arc $dc$ over arc $ab$. But [by Proposition 8, Definition 3] arc $df$ corresponds to angle $daf$: and [by Proposition 29, Book 1] angle $daf$ is equal to angle $ced$: therefore $ced$ is equal to the angle at the circumference $df$. And this is what we wished to show.

Therefore, the form of $b$ will not be refracted to $a$ from point $e$, nor from any other point on the circumference $ced$, nor from any other circle formed on the surface of the transparent body where $b$ is located. Therefore, when $b$ exists on line $cd$, it will not be perceived by the sight through refraction. Thus, only one single point is perceived.

And this is what we intended to prove.

the eye will see only a single image. For then the eye will be at point $b$ and the object seen at $a$. > *29. If the eye is outside the circle (which is the common section of the planes of refraction and the convex spherical denser refractive medium), a straight line in a fixed position can be refracted by a small segment of the periphery: and some point of it [is seen] directly: [while] from the remaining [points] several are seen by refraction: and the location of the whole image is in the eye itself. <note>Proposition 25, Book 10</note>.*

Likewise, let us repeat the figure, placing a point on the circumference $ged$ on the side of $g$, and let it be $e$. From this point let us draw a line parallel to line $ab$ <note>original: "per 31 p 1"; by Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Proposition 31</note> and let it be line $et$. Let us join $ze$ and extend it as far as $h$. Let the ratio of angle $zek$ to double the angle $ket$ be the maximum ratio that the angle through which the form is extended with the perpendicular can have to the angle of refraction which that angle requires, according to the sense of sight. [This can be provided by <note>Propositions 10, 11, and 12 of this book</note>, by which the angles of refraction from a denser medium to a rarer one, and vice versa, are found.] For the angles of refraction which occur between two bodies of different transparency are varied by the light passing through them. The diversity of these, according to the sense, has a limit: if it exceeds this, the sense will not perceive the quantity of refraction, for it will perceive the center of light in the straightness of the line through which the light is extended, namely, when this has been tested by an instrument. And let us set angle $dzt$ equal to angle $ket$ <note>by Euclid 1.23</note>; therefore, angle $zke$ will be double angle $ket$. [For because $et$ and $zb$ are parallel by construction <note>original: "per fabricationem"</note>, angle $kbz$ is equal to angle $ket$ <note>by Euclid 1.29</note>, to which $kzb$ has already been made equal. Therefore, angles $kbz$ and $kzb$ are equal; and since $zke$ is equal to [the sum of] them <note>by Euclid 1.32</note>, it will be double either one of them, and thus double the equal angle $ket$.] And so the ratio of angle $zek$ to angle $zke$ will be the maximum ratio between the angle contained by the first line and the perpendicular exiting from the point of refraction, and the angle of refraction. But line $ek$ will meet with line $ad$ <note>original: "per lemma Procli ad 29 p 1"; according to Proclus’s lemma on Euclid 1.29</note>; let them meet, therefore, at $b$. And let us draw line $ea$ parallel to $tz$; it will meet, therefore (as before), with $zg$ outside the circle on the side of $g$. Let the meeting be at $a$. And let us extend $be$ as far as $l$; therefore <note>by Euclid 1.29</note> angle $lea$ will be equal to angle $zke$; and <note>by Euclid 1.15</note> angle $leh$ will be equal to angle $zek$. Therefore, angle $lea$ will be the angle of refraction required by angle $leh$ (for angle $zek$, which by Euclid 1.15 is equal to angle $leh$, is such by the hypothesis <note>original: "ex thesi"</note>). If, therefore, $b$ is in some eye, and the transparent body whose convex side is toward $a$ is continued from $e$ as far as $b$, and is not divided at the circumference $ged$ on the side of $b$, then the form of $b$ will be extended along line $be$, and refracted along line $ea$, and will be perceived by the eye at $a$ through the direction $ae$. And because angle $aeh$ can be divided by many ratios of those which exist between the angles of refraction and the angles contained by the perpendiculars with the primary lines between two transparent bodies, there will be several points on line $db$ whose forms are extended to arc $eg$ and refracted to $a$ from arc $ge$. When, therefore, the eye is in a transparent medium, and the object seen is in another denser medium, and the surface of the denser medium facing the eye is a convex sphere, and the eye is outside the circle whose convex side faces the eye, and that circle is farther from the eye than the farther of the two points of the intersection made between the perpendicular and the circumference, and the thick transparent body on the side of the eye is continuous as far as the place where the object is, and is not cut off at the circle on the side of the object: then the eye will be able to perceive that object through refraction.

### 30. *If the common section of the surfaces of refraction and of a denser concave refractive medium is a periphery: a visible object on the perpendicular drawn from the eye to the refractive medium will be seen directly and as one.* <note>original: "26 p 10"; likely a cross-reference to another proposition or edition</note>

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram of optical refraction. A vertical axis runs from point 'a' (the eye) at the top to 'z' at the bottom, passing through point 'g' (center of a circle) and point 'b' (the object). A concave arc represents the boundary between media. A ray originates from point 'b', hits the arc at point 'e', and is refracted towards 'a'. The line 'be' is extended to point 't'. Likewise: let $a$ be the eye: and let $b$ be some visible object located beyond a transparent body denser than the one in which the eye is located. Let the surface of the body on the side of the eye be a concave circle, with its concavity facing the eye. I say, therefore, that $b$ will have only one image and only one form at $a$. Let the center of the concavity be $g$: and let us connect $ag$: and extend it straight to $z$. Therefore, $az$ will be perpendicular to the concave surface <note>original: "ut ostensum est 25 n 4"; as shown in Proposition 25 of Book 4</note>: and $b$ will either be on $az$ or outside it. First, let it be on line $az$. Therefore, $a$ perceives $b$ in the straight line $ab$, since $ab$ is perpendicular to the concave surface, and never by refraction <note>original: "per 13 n."</note>. For if it were possible, let the form $b$ be refracted to $a$ from point $e$, and let us connect $be$ and $ge$, and extend $be$ to $t$. Angle $teg$ is therefore the one contained by the line along which the form is extended and the perpendicular emerging from the place of refraction. And because the medium on the side of $a$ is rarer <term>subtilius; refers to a medium with lower optical density, like air compared to glass</term> than the medium on the side of $b$: the refraction will be toward the side opposite to where $eg$ is located <note>original: "per 14 n."</note>. Therefore, the line $et$, when it is refracted, moves away from the line $eg$: and it will not meet the line $ba$ in any way. Thus, form $b$ will not be refracted to $a$: it will therefore not be perceived by refraction, but directly. Consequently, it will have only one form at the eye. And this is what we intended to show.

### 31. *If the common section of the surfaces of refraction and of a denser concave refractive medium is a periphery: a visible object outside the perpendicular drawn from the eye to the refractive medium will be refracted from a single point and will have only one image, positioned differently according to the varying position of the eye or the object.* <note>original: "27 p 10"</note>

Likewise: let us repeat the figure, and let $b$ be outside the line $az$, and let us extend the plane in which $azb$ lies. This plane will be perpendicular to the concave surface <note>original: "per 9 n."</note> and the form $b$ will not be refracted to $a$ except in this plane. For no other equal plane is erected perpendicular to the concave surface passing through $a$ except the one passing through $az$: but through $az$ and through $b$, only one such plane passes. Therefore, the form $b$ will not be refracted to $a$ except in the plane passing through line $az$ and through $b$. Let the common difference <note>the line of intersection</note> between this plane and the concave surface be the arc $hde$, and let the form $b$ be refracted to $a$ from $h$. I say, therefore, that it will not be refracted from any other point. -> 33. *A visible object refracted by a refractive medium of varying shape or transparency, or both at once, has various and monstrous images in various places. <note>Refers to Propositions 29 and 30, section 10</note>* <-

**H**owever, these things we have spoken of are the images of visible objects perceived through simple transparent bodies that are of one substance, and whose shape on the side of the eye is a single shape. But if the transparent body is varied, or of non-uniform transparency, then the images of the visible object vary. And if the surface of the transparent body on the side of the eye is varied, then the locations of the images of the visible object also vary, since the forms of the refractions from the surface of the transparent body also vary. And if someone looks at a small sphere, or some small round body, or a cylinder of glass or crystal, beyond which is some visible object: he will find its image to be different from how the visible object is in itself; and perhaps he will find another image of the visible object, and thus there will be doubt concerning it. But this kind of refraction is not one, but two: for the form of the visible object extends from the object to the sphere or other round cylindrical body, and is refracted from the convex surface of the sphere or cylinder to the interior of the body, and extends within the body until it reaches its [other] surface; and then it is refracted [again] from the sphere or cylinder at the concavity of the air touching the sphere or cylinder. Thus, the perception of such things will be through two different refractions. For this reason, its image will be different from the image of that which is perceived by a single refraction. We shall, however, speak a little about this when we treat the <term>deceptions of sight</term><note>Optical illusions</note> that occur through refraction.

# HOW SIGHT PERCEIVES VISIBLE OBJECTS according to refraction. Chapter VI.

*34. If the eye and the visible object in different media swap their locations: the names of the lines of incidence and refraction are swapped.* <note>original: "9 p 10"; this likely refers to Proposition 9, Book 10 of a related geometric treatise on optics.</note>

In the preceding chapters, we have already demonstrated that when a **form** <note>In medieval optics, a "form" refers to the physical radiation of light and color that travels from an object to the eye.</note> is refracted from one **transparent body** <term>transparent body (corpus diaphanum): a material like air, water, or glass that allows light to pass through it.</term> to another body of different transparency: it travels in a straight line until it reaches the surface of the transparent body in which it is located. Then, it is refracted into that other transparent body along another straight line, which forms an angle with the first line. And when a form travels along this second line, upon which it is refracted in the second body—no matter what other form might be in the second body up to the point of intersection between the two straight lines—it will be refracted back along the first straight line.

It is evident through experience that if someone looks through a transparent body that differs in its transparency from the transparency of the air, they will perceive all those things on the other side that are positioned opposite the sight. If they cover one eye and look with the other, they will still perceive whatever is beyond, whether that body is air, water, or glass. Similarly, if a person places their eye in a body denser than air, such as glass or crystal, they will see everything on the other side that is in the air. If the observer moves their eye to the right or left, or in any direction, and does not move it far from its first position, they will still perceive everything they perceived before, whether the movement of the eye was in air or in glass.

However, we have already demonstrated by experience and proof that the eye perceives nothing of those things beyond transparent bodies (which differ in transparency from air) except through **refraction** <term>refraction (refractio): the bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like water.</term>, with the exception of one single point: the one located on the **perpendicular** <note>The "perpendicular" refers to a line hitting the surface at a 90-degree angle; light traveling this path does not bend.</note> line extending from the center of the eye to the surface of the transparent body. Therefore, every point perceived by the eye beyond a transparent body, except for that aforementioned point, is perceived from a form that extends from that point to the surface of the transparent body beyond which it lies, and is refracted from the surface of that body to the eye.

Since a single eye perceives everything beyond the transparent body, the form of every point existing beyond that transparent body extends in a straight line to the surface of that body and is refracted to that single eye, except for the aforementioned point. And since the forms of all the points in all the visible objects existing beyond the transparent body are refracted at the same time to the center of a single eye, the form of a point existing at the center of that eye (if it were in a visible object) would be refracted to all the points in all the visible objects existing beyond the transparent body opposite the eye, at the same time and in the same way.

The same is true for every point near the point at the center of the eye. For if the eye is moved in any direction, and is not removed far from its location, it will perceive the visible objects. Therefore, the form of any point of any eye, when it is beyond a transparent body, will extend to the surface of the transparent body beyond which it lies, and will be refracted to the whole of what is opposite it within the body of the air. There is no time more appropriate for this than any other; rather, this is a property of the nature of light and color within visible objects: namely, that they always extend from any point of any luminous body along a straight line, and are refracted in every different transparent body, except for the point on the perpendicular.

Every form of any visible point existing in a body different from air will extend within that body in which it exists, and will be refracted into the whole body of the air opposite it, and that form goes out to every point of the air. For this reason, the form of the entire thing seen is joined at every point of the air: and the form of the whole of any object seen existing in a body different from air exists at each and every point of the air opposite that thing seen. That form extends from every point of the thing seen in the body in which it is, is refracted at the surface of that body, and reaches that point of the air.

Therefore, if the eye looks at a transparent body different from air, beyond which there is some visible thing, the eye perceives that thing. For the form of it exists at the point where the center of the eye exists. Because of this, even if the eye perceives a visible thing beyond a transparent body different from air, and then is moved from its place to the right or left—as long as in its motion it remains opposite the transparent body and the thing seen beyond it—it will always perceive that thing. Hence, many observers can perceive one thing in the sky, or in water, at one and the same time.

This also occurs within the same transparent body: namely, that the form for the eye is gathered at every point of the body in which it is. For the form of any point of it extends in a straight line, and between every point of the body in which the eye is and every point of the thing seen, there is a straight line. Therefore, the form of every point of the thing seen extends to every point of the transparent body in which the eye is. The form of every luminous thing is gathered at every point of every body in which it exists, and it is gathered at every point of any transparent body different from the body in which it exists, provided that no obstacle intervenes between the thing seen and that different transparent body. The form of the thing seen, which is at every point of the transparent body in which it extends, reaches that point directly; and its form at every point of a different transparent body reaches that point by refraction; because between every point of the air and any visible thing existing...

# BOOK VII OF OPTICS

...existing in some transparent body different from air: let there be a **refracted pyramid** <note>In medieval optics, a "pyramid" refers to the cone-shaped volume of light rays that has its base at the object and its point (apex) at the eye.</note>, whose apex is a point in the air, and whose base is the object being seen. Its refraction will occur at the surface of the body that differs from the air. Therefore, every visible object in a transparent body different from air, when it is perceived by the sight, is perceived by a "form" extended in a refracted pyramid, joined together at a point existing in the center of the eye. In this way, the sight perceives those things which it sees through refraction.

### 35. The visible image of a refracted object resembles the shape of the refracting medium. <note>original: "46 p 10"</note>

In the chapter concerning the image, we explained that every object is perceived by the sight by means of an image. The location of this image is the point where two lines intersect: the **radial line** (the path through which the form travels to the eye) and the **perpendicular line** (a line standing at a right angle) coming from the point being seen. If, therefore, we imagine that a perpendicular line exits from every point of the visible object to the surface of the transparent body where the object is located, we will create a certain geometric "body" extending from the sight to the surface of the transparent medium. It follows that this geometric body intersects the refracted pyramid, and the surface where it intersects is the image of that visible object.

If the surface of the transparent body containing the object is flat, then the imagined geometric body containing all the perpendicular lines will be equal to the surface. In this case, the image is slightly larger than the actual object seen. 

However, if the body is spherical and its curve (convexity) faces the eye, and its center is positioned over the object, then the imagined body will be pyramidal, with its point at the center of the sphere. The further it extends from the surface of the spherical body, the more it will enlarge. If the intersection occurs between the object and the spherical surface, the image will be larger than the object. But if the intersection occurs beyond the object, the image will be narrower than the object. 

If the object is located beyond the spherical surface, then the imagined body will consist of two opposite pyramids meeting at their points at the center of the sphere. Because the locations where this imagined body and the light-pyramid intersect can vary, the resulting image might be larger, smaller, or equal to the object. 

If the transparent body is spherical and its hollow side (concavity) faces the eye, the imagined body will be a pyramid with its point at the center of the sphere. As this body extends toward the surface of the sphere, it becomes more narrow and compressed; as it extends in the other direction, it enlarges. A small continuous surface will lie between its center and the sphere. If the intersection of this body with the refracted pyramid is closer to the center of the sphere’s hollow than the object itself, the image will be smaller than the object. If it is further from the center, the image will be larger. 

When one object is seen by several viewers at once, all the images they perceive at that time will exist within one imagined construct that is perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body.

### 36. A single image of a refracted object is seen by both eyes. <note>original: "47 p 10"</note>

A single visible object is perceived by a person at one time through both eyes, even through a transparent medium that differs from the air surrounding the eyes; yet, the person still perceives it as one object. For if a person looks at something in the heavens, or in water, or through glass, and covers one eye, they will still perceive it with the other. This proves that a single object beyond a transparent body is perceived by both eyes together and by each eye individually. 

The cause of this, as we stated in the third book, is as follows: at every point of vision where an object is seen directly by both eyes, if two rays from the eyes are joined in a similar position relative to the two **axes of vision** <term>axes of vision (axes uisuum): the central, most direct lines of sight from each eye.</term>, a single thing is perceived. If rays of different positions relative to the axes are gathered, two things are seen. In most cases, the position is similar.

Cases where the positions are different for each eye are very rare, as we said in the third treatise. An object perceived through refraction is seen at the location of the image. The "form" at the image's location is perceived by the eye as if it were a direct sight. The position of this image-form relative to the eye is the same as any other object seen directly. Therefore, the position of these images is mostly similar for both eyes, and at every point of the image, two rays from the two eyes of similar position meet. Thus, one visible object is seen as one by both eyes. 

To make this clearer: every point perceived through refraction is seen at the location of the image, which lies between the intersection of the perpendicular line (coming from the object to the surface) and the radial line (carrying the form to the eye). When a viewer looks at a point with both eyes, the image of that point for both eyes lies on that same perpendicular line. When the form of that point reaches two points on the surfaces of the eyes that are in similar positions relative to the optical axes, the two lines of the forms reach the centers of the two eyes. These lines are either the axes themselves or have a position similar to the axes. The two axes of the eyes always exist in the same plane (surface), and all lines exiting from the centers of the eyes with a similar position to the common axis will be in that same plane. For if something is perceived truly by both eyes at once, the axes meet at a single point of that object. Therefore, they are in the same plane. Likewise, the natural position of the eyes is similar and only changes by accident or force; thus, their axes are in the same plane. For the principle of the...

<meta>This page continues the geometric analysis of binocular vision and introduces the anatomical refraction that occurs within the eye itself, specifically how light interacts with the various layers (tunics) of the eyeball.</meta>

the axis is a single point located in the middle of the concavity of the **common nerve** <note>The optic chiasm, where the optic nerves from both eyes meet.</note>, from which the common axis emerges. Therefore, when both sights <note>The eyes or the visual faculties.</note> are in their natural position, the axes will always be in the same plane, whether they are moving or at rest. If, however, the position of one sight is changed relative to the other due to some impediment, then the visible object will appear double, as we demonstrated in the first book. Thus, for the most part, the two axes exist in the same plane. For this reason, any two rays having a similar position relative to the two axes will be in the same plane. Consequently, the two lines through which the "forms" <note>The visual images or patterns of light.</note> of a single point are extended to two locations of similar position are in the same plane. Since the images of that point, with respect to the two sights, are on those two lines, they are in the same plane. Furthermore, the images of that point lie on the perpendicular lines projecting from that point. Therefore, they are located at the point of intersection between the plane containing the radial lines—which is a single plane—and the perpendicular line. The intersection of a single plane with a single line is a single point. Thus, the images of a single point, with respect to the two sights, when they reach two locations of similar position, are a single point. From this it is clear that the image of the entire visible object, with respect to the two sights, will be one, provided the position of the image is consistent. For this reason, the object is perceived as one by both sights. If, however, the position is slightly different, the object will be seen as one, but not truly, but deceptively. But if the difference in position is great, then the forms of the object will appear as two; however, this happens very rarely. This, then, is the nature of how the sight perceives visible things through refraction.

### 37. Distinct vision occurs through straight lines perpendicular from the visible object to the sight. And all vision occurs through refraction. <note>original: "17. 18 p 3"</note>

Having explained this, let us say universally that everything perceived by the sight is perceived through refraction, whether the sight and the object are in the same transparent medium or in different ones, whether the object is directly opposite the sight or perceived through reflection. For nothing is perceived without refraction occurring at the surface of the sight. This is because the tunics of the eye—which are the **cornea**, the **albuginea** <note>The aqueous humor, or the watery fluid between the cornea and the lens.</note>, and the **glacial** <note>The crystalline lens.</note>—are also transparent and denser than air. It has already been demonstrated that the forms of things in the air and in other transparent bodies extend through those bodies; and if they encounter bodies of a different transparency from the one they are in, they are refracted in that transparent body. Thus, the form of an object in the air always extends through the air. When the air touches the surface of any sight, that form which is in the air is refracted at the surface of the eye, and it is then refracted in every way within the body of the cornea and the albuginea. For refraction properly belongs to the behavior of forms, while receiving forms and refractions is a property of transparent bodies. Therefore, the forms of those things opposite the sight are always refracted in the tunics of the eye. It has already been shown that when forms extend along lines perpendicular to a second body, they pass straight into that second body. Thus, the forms of things opposite the surface of the eye are all refracted in the tunics of the eye; and those which happen to be at the ends of the **radial lines**—which are perpendicular to the surface of the eye—pass through straight, even as the rest of their forms are refracted in the tunics. Many visible objects are opposite the part of the eye's surface that faces the opening of the **uvea** <note>The pupil/iris area.</note>, some of which are at the extremities of the radial lines, and others outside them. All radial lines that are perpendicular to the surfaces of the eye's tunics are contained within a **pyramid** <note>A cone-shaped volume of light rays.</note> whose apex is the center of the eye and whose base is the circumference of the opening of the uvea. The further this pyramid extends and the more distant it is from the eye, the more it widens; all forms of things within this pyramid extend along the straightness of the radial lines and pass straight through the tunics of the eye. This pyramid is called the **radial pyramid**. The lines extending within this pyramid, whose endpoints are at the center of the eye, are called **radial lines**. However, the forms of things outside this pyramid never extend through any of the radial lines; nonetheless, they extend through straight lines between the surface of the eye facing the opening of the uvea. The forms extending through these lines are refracted by the transparency of the eye's tunics. And the form of any point within the radial pyramid extends to the surface of the eye facing the opening of the uvea in a pyramid whose apex is that point and whose base is the surface facing the opening of the uvea. One of the lines imagined in this pyramid is a radial line; all others that are not in this pyramid are not radial, and none of them is perpendicular to the surfaces of the eye's tunics. The form of any point within the radial pyramid extends over every line that can fall into that pyramid whose apex is that point and whose base is the surface of the visible object facing the opening of the uvea. Through one of these lines, the form passes straight through the tunics of the eye; all other forms extended in the rest of the pyramid are refracted in the tunics of the eye and do not pass through in a straight line. Therefore, all things opposite the part of the eye's surface facing the opening of the uvea—whether they are in the air, the heavens, the water, or similar media, or reflected from polished bodies—are refracted in the tunics of the eye when they reach this part of the eye's surface. The forms of those things within the pyramid pass straight through the tunics of the eye, along with the refraction of the forms of those things extending over the pyramid which remain in the whole of this part of the eye's surface. It remains, therefore, to demonstrate that the forms refracted in the tunics of the eye are perceived by the sight and felt by the **sensible virtue** <note>The perceptual power or faculty of the soul/brain.</note>. In the first treatise, we demonstrated that if the sensible organ were to feel every form coming to it from every point of its surface, it would then feel the forms of things mixed together. Thus, the sensible organ...

### OPTICS, BOOK VII

...it <note>Referring to the visual faculty or the crystalline humor.</note> does not perceive forms except from the straightness of the perpendicular lines upon its surface only. Therefore, the forms of visible things pass through, and are not mixed within it. In this treatise, we have shown that refracted forms are never perceived except along the perpendiculars emerging from the visible objects onto the surfaces of the transparent bodies. Therefore, refracted forms in the **tunics of vision** <note>The layers of the eye, such as the cornea and the aqueous humor.</note> are not perceived by the sight except along the perpendiculars emerging from the visible objects onto the surfaces of the tunics of vision; and these perpendicular lines are those emerging from the center of the sight. Thus, all forms refracted in the tunics of vision are perceived by the sight along the straightness of the lines emerging from the center of the sight. 

Therefore, the forms of all visible things—which are opposite that part of the surface of the eye which faces the opening of the **uvea** <note>The pupil, which is the opening in the iris or "uvea" layer.</note> and exist in this part of the surface of the eye—are refracted within the transparency of the tunics of the eye and reach the sensitive member, which is the **glacial humor** <note>The crystalline lens, then believed to be the primary organ of sight.</note>. They are perceived by the visual faculty through straight lines that connect the center of the sight with those visible things. Specifically, the form of any point of any visible object, situated opposite the surface of the eye that faces the opening of the uvea, exists across the whole surface of this part, is refracted by the entire surface, and reaches the glacial humor. Then, that humor perceives the form coming to it, and by its sensitive power, it perceives everything that reaches the glacial humor from the form of a visible point along a single line connecting the center of the sight with that point. In this way, therefore, the sight perceives all visible things. 

In this chapter, we have said that among those things opposite the surface of the eye, some are within the **radial pyramid** <note>The cone of vision whose base is the pupil and whose vertex is the center of the eye.</note> and others are outside it. When I say "surface of the eye," it should be understood from now on as the part opposite the opening of the uvea. Therefore, visible things that are within the radial pyramid are perceived by the sight along the straightness of the radial lines directly, from their forms which extend to the sight along the straightness of these lines. And these lines are the perpendiculars that emerge from the points of the visible objects within the pyramid onto the surfaces of the tunics of the eye. 

However, those things outside the radial pyramid are perceived by the sight from refracted forms, and along the straightness of the lines emerging from the center of the sight that exist outside the radial pyramid. These lines outside the radial pyramid can also be called "radial lines" in a borrowed sense; for they resemble radial lines in that they emerge from the center of the sight. 

It remains, therefore, to demonstrate by experience that the sight perceives those things which are outside the radial pyramid. We say, then, that it is manifest that the **tear ducts** <note>The corners of the eye near the nose.</note> and the areas surrounding the circle <note>The iris.</note> are outside the pyramid whose vertex is the center of the sight and whose base is the circumference of the opening of the uvea (which is the small opening in the middle of the black of the eye). If someone takes a fine, slender **needle** <term>acus <gloss>needle</gloss></term> and places its tip at the far corner of the eye between the eyelids, while the sight remains still, he will see its tip. Similarly, if he places the tip of the needle in the tear duct, or if he moves it into the eye and applies the tip to the side of the black of the eye or near it, he will see the tip of the needle. 

Likewise, all things that are parallel to the surface of the thing seen, from the places surrounding the sight, are outside the radial pyramid. When I say "places surrounding the sight," I mean those from which lines emerging to the middle of the surface of the eye intersect the axis of the radial pyramid. If a man holds up his index finger near his face and close to the eyelid, he will see the finger. Similarly, if he places his finger against the lower eyelid so that the upper surface of that finger is parallel to the surface of the eye (as far as can be sensed), he will see the surface of the finger. But all these locations are outside the radial pyramid, as will be clear. 

For the radial pyramid, which the opening of the uvea contains, is very narrow and extends straight, and its "pyramidality" <note>Its angular width or taper.</note> is not wide. Thus, nothing from it reaches the places surrounding the eye that are close to the body of the eye and parallel to the surface of the eye. Between all the places surrounding the eye and parallel to the surface of the eye, and the surface of the eye itself, there are straight lines; because of their refraction from dense bodies—since the air between them and the surface of the eye is continuous—the form of these visible things reaches the surface of the eye along these lines which are outside the pyramid. Since this form reaches the sight not through radial lines, yet is still perceived by the sight, it is clear that the sight perceives it through refraction. From this experience, it is clear that the sight perceives many things outside the radial pyramid by refraction. 

By **induction** <note>A logical method of moving from specific observations to a general rule.</note> we can also show that the sight perceives those things within the radial pyramid by refraction, even though it perceives them directly, in this manner: Take a thin needle and sit in a place opposite a white wall. Cover one eye and place the needle in front of the other eye. Bring the needle closer until it touches the eyelid, and place the needle directly in front of the middle of the sight, and look at the opposite wall. Then you will see the needle as if it were a transparent body with some slight density. You will see whatever is beyond the needle on the wall, and the needle will appear as a wide body, whose width is many times the actual width of the needle. 

The cause of this was explained in the second treatise: namely, that if a visible thing is very close to the sight, it will appear larger than it is, and the closer it is, the larger it will appear. Its "transparency" appears because the sight perceives whatever is beyond it. The needle is actually a dense, opaque body covering what is beyond it; but because the needle is so close to the eye, it covers a portion of the wall many times its own width. For the base of the pyramid (whose vertex is the center of the sight and whose base is the height of the needle) will be many times the width of the needle. Yet, the sight perceives whatever is beyond the needle, and nothing of the wall is hidden from the sight; rather, it perceives what is beyond it as if through a transparent body. 

When the needle is opposite the middle of the sight, it does not cover the entire surface of the eye because of its thinness, but only a certain part equal to its width. There remains a portion of the eye's surface on the sides of the needle, and its form <note>The light from the wall.</note> moves toward those parts of the surface of the eye that are at the sides of the needle. The form <note>The image of the wall</note> hitting the needle will never reach the eye, nor be perceived by it; but the form that reaches the sides of the surface of the eye is refracted to...

<meta>This page continues the demonstration of how light refracts within the eye itself. Alhazen is using an experiment with a needle to prove that even when the direct, straight-line path to an object is blocked, we can still see it because the light refracts (bends) through the outer layers of the eye. He then transitions into Chapter 7, focusing on how these refractions cause visual "deceptions" or errors.</meta>

...sight, since it does not reach the center of vision in a straight line. Therefore, if the sight did not perceive that part of the wall opposite the needle except by a straight path, then the part of the wall blocked by the needle would be hidden from view. Since it is perceived, and not in a straight line, it is clear that it is perceived through refraction—by the form that is refracted from the sides of the needle at the surface of the eye. 

This is also made manifest if the experimenter replaces the needle with a wider body whose width is greater than the width of the **opening of the uvea** <note>The pupil.</note>. In that case, he will see nothing of the wall at all, nor will he see that body as transparent, but as opaque. Therefore, from the fact that the wall is perceived beyond the needle due to its thinness, but is not perceived beyond a wide body, we know that this perception comes from the form which reaches the needle from the surface of sight and is refracted within the **tunics of vision** <note>The layers of the eye, such as the cornea.</note>. 

And because whatever is perceived by the sight through refraction is seen along the straightness of the perpendiculars, that which the sight perceives, it perceives refractively from the form of what is opposite the needle along the straightness of the lines emerging from the center of vision. These lines are cut by the needle, yet the sight perceives what is beyond the needle even in the straightness of these lines, and perceives the needle itself in their straightness as well. Thus, it perceives the whole form as if through a transparent body in which there is some slight density. 

If the experimenter writes finely on **cotton** <note>original: "bombace"</note> and attaches it to the wall, standing back at a distance where he can still read the writing, and then places a needle in front of the middle of his sight as he did before and looks at the cotton, he will still be able to read the writing. However, he will see it as if through glass or through a transparent body that has some density. If the sight did not perceive the part of the cotton opposite the needle through refraction, then some of the writing would be hidden; for the needle ought to cover much more of the writing than its own width due to the distance of the cotton from the eye. But since no part of the writing is hidden from the sight, it is clear that the eye perceives what is opposite the needle. This cannot happen in a straight line; therefore, it must happen through refraction. 

If the experimenter removes the needle, the refraction that existed before is not destroyed. The refraction did not happen *because* of the needle; rather, the refraction increases because it refracts from the location of the needle. When the experimenter removes the needle, he will perceive what is opposite the sight more clearly. For he will perceive in a straight line that which was covered by the needle, alongside that which he perceives by refraction (just as he perceived it when it was covered). Because of this addition, he perceives it more clearly than before he removed the needle. 

From this experiment, it is clear that whatever is opposite the sight among those things within the **radial pyramid** <note>The cone of light entering the eye from a visible object.</note> is perceived by both refraction and straight lines. From all of this, it is declared that all things perceived by the sight—whether their forms reach the eye straight, reflected, or refracted—are perceived according to a refraction made at the surface of the eye. Some of those things perceived through refraction at the surface of the eye are perceived by refraction and straight lines simultaneously. For this reason, that which is opposite the middle of the sight is clearer than what is around the middle. When the sight perceives a wide object, it perceives the center more clearly than the sides. This was declared in the second treatise, where we showed how this could be tested, and we said the cause of this is the radial lines. This applies to things within the radial pyramid; for others outside it, the cause is refraction. The universal cause for why the center of the field of vision is clearer than the periphery is that the center is perceived by straight and refracted lines together. However, this fact—that *everything* perceived by the sight is perceived through refraction—was said by none of the ancients.

## ON THE DECEPTIONS OF SIGHT WHICH OCCUR from refraction. Chapter VII.

> *38. Refraction weakens the light and color of the visible object; thus, it offers a confused image to the sight.*

The deceptions that occur through refraction are similar to those that occur through reflection. For what is perceived through refraction is not perceived in its true place, since it is perceived in the location of its image; therefore, the position of the perceived form will be different from the position of the visible thing itself. 

Furthermore, refraction weakens the refracted form—specifically, the form of the light and color in the visible thing. This can be understood thus: if you look at something in water, and you are positioned at a great slant from the perpendiculars rising from the object to the surface of the water, and you observe it carefully; then, if you move your eye until you are positioned on a perpendicular line rising from the object to the surface of the water and look again, you will see it more clearly than when you were at a slant. There is no difference between the two positions except that in the first, the form reaching the eye is refracted and very slanted, while in the second, the form emerges straight, or part of it emerges straight and part only slightly slanted and almost straight. From this experiment, it is clear that refraction weakens refracted forms. 

Likewise, things in water or beyond glass and the like, when they are refracted to the sight, carry with them the color of the body in which they exist. Therefore, in those things perceived through refraction beyond transparent bodies, deceptions occur due to refraction that do not occur in things seen in a straight line—namely, the variation of position and distance, and the weakness of light and color. Moreover, they are subject to the same deceptions as things seen in a straight line. For the forms of things perceived by refraction are perceived opposite the sight and in the straightness of the radial lines. Therefore, whatever happens to things seen in the straightness of radial lines happens to these as well. In the third book, we declared all those deceptions and...

### OPTICS, BOOK VII

...the nature and causes of these things, and even the causes of those causes. However, in these instances, deceptions occur more frequently and more rapidly because of the weakness of these forms <note>By "forms," the author refers to the visual information or "images" carried by light.</note>. The particular deceptions that occur because of the shapes of the surfaces of **transparent bodies** <note>original: "corpora diaphana"; these are substances like water or glass that allow light to pass through.</note> are manifold, yet they are rarely encountered by the sight. For those things perceived beyond transparent bodies other than air are the stars and things in water. Those things seen through glass and transparent stones of various shapes are rarely perceived by the sight. This is not the case with these transparent bodies as it is with mirrors; for mirrors are frequently used by people so they may see their own forms in them and are kept in homes. Similarly, when a person looks into any **polished body** <note>original: "corpus tersum"; such as a polished metal plate.</note>, they will see the form of those things opposite to it. Likewise, if one looks at water, they will see their own form in it and see the things opposite it. But it is not so with what is seen through glass and transparent stones, because people rarely look at what is beyond glass and transparent stones. 

Because this is the case, let us discuss the particular deceptions that occur constantly and without difficulty—namely, those that occur in things seen in the heavens and in water—and we shall say a little about those things seen through glass and stones. We say, therefore, that the sight is always deceived regarding things perceived beyond a transparent body different from air, especially concerning their position and distance, their colors and lights, and their size and the shapes of some of them. For things seen in water, and through glass and transparent stones, appear larger; however, the stars and the distances between stars sometimes appear larger and sometimes smaller.

**39. If the common section of the refracting surfaces and the refractive medium is a straight line, and the sight is on the perpendicular drawn from the center of the visible object parallel to the common section: the image will appear larger than the object. [Proposition] 31, p. 10.**

Let the sight be ***a***, and let ***bc*** be beyond a transparent body denser than air <note>original: "grossius aere"; referring to a medium with a higher refractive index.</note>. I say that ***bc*** appears larger than it is. First, let the surface of the transparent body be flat. Let ***a*** be on the perpendicular extending from the middle of ***bc*** to the surface of the body, or outside it. First, let it be on the perpendicular itself: and [by Proposition 12 of Book 1] let that perpendicular be ***amz***. Let us extend the plane in which the lines ***a, z, bc*** lie; and [by Proposition 3 of Book 11] it will form the line ***dme*** on the surface of the transparent body. And [by note 9] the plane containing the two lines ***a, z, bc*** will be perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body. No plane perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body passes through ***a*** and any point of line ***bc*** except the one containing the lines ***a, z, bc***. For no plane perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body passes through ***a*** except that which passes through ***az***; which line is perpendicular to the surface of the body [by note 9 and the conversion of definition 4, Book 11]. Nor does any perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body emerge from ***a*** except line ***az***. Therefore, no plane passes through ***a*** that is perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body except that which passes through line ***az***; and no plane passes through any point of line ***bc*** and through line ***az*** except that plane in which the two lines ***a, z, bc*** lie. Therefore, no plane perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body passes through ***a*** and any point of line ***bc*** except that which contains lines ***a, z, bc***. 

Consequently, the form of any point on line ***bc*** will not be refracted except from line ***de***. And [by Proposition 11 of Book 1] let us draw two perpendiculars from ***b*** and ***c***; they will fall upon line ***de*** at two points, ***d*** and ***e*** [by Proclus's lemma to Proposition 29, Book 1: because ***bc*** and ***de*** are parallel by the hypothesis], namely ***bd*** and ***ce***. Let ***bc*** first be parallel to line ***de***. Let the form of ***b*** be refracted to ***a*** from ***p***, and the form of ***c*** to ***a*** from ***h***. Let us join the lines ***bp, pa, ch, ha***; likewise ***ab, ac***; and let us extend ***ap*** to ***l*** and ***ah*** to ***k***. [For it is clear that ***ap*** and ***ah*** meet with ***bd*** and ***ce*** by Proclus's lemma to Proposition 29, Book 1.] 

Since ***z*** was placed in the middle of line ***bc***, the position of ***b*** relative to ***a*** will be equal to the position of ***c*** relative to ***a***; thus, the distance of ***p*** from ***a*** will be the same as the distance of ***h*** from ***a***. [For since ***az*** bisects ***bc*** and is perpendicular to it by hypothesis, and ***az*** itself is common and equal to itself, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, ***ab*** is equal to ***ac***. Thus, since ***bc*** and ***de*** are parallel by hypothesis, and points ***b*** and ***c*** are equally distant from the sight, the points of refraction ***p*** and ***h*** will be equally distant from the same, because of the uniform diffusion of all points in the same uniform medium. Therefore, ***ap*** is equal to ***ha***.] And thus [by Proposition 15 of Book 1] angle ***dpl*** will be equal to angle ***ehk***, but [by Proposition 29 of Book 1] the two angles ***d*** and ***e*** are right angles. And line ***dp*** is equal to line ***eh***, because ***pm*** is equal to ***mh***. [For because by the construction of the hypothesis and Proposition 24 of Book 1, the whole ***md*** is equal to the whole ***me***; and the angles at ***m*** are right angles by Proposition 29, Book 1; and ***ad, p***, and ***h*** are equal by the conclusion, and side ***am*** is common; by Proposition 26 of Book 1, ***pm*** will equal ***mh***. Therefore, the remainder ***dp*** will equal the remainder ***eh*** by Proposition 19, Book 5.] Therefore [by Proposition 26, Book 1] ***dl*** is equal to ***ek***. Let us join ***lk***: it will therefore [by Proposition 33, Book 1] be equal to line ***bc***. Thus, angle ***cab*** will be smaller than angle ***kal***. [For the straight line ***lk*** cutting the sides ***ab, ac*** makes two exterior angles greater than the opposite interior angle ***kal***.]
