<meta>This page continues the seventh book of Alhazen’s (Ibn al-Haytham’s) work on optics. The previous page introduced how visual deceptions occur when viewing objects through transparent media like water or glass. Here, Alhazen provides a geometric proof to explain why objects viewed through a refractive surface often appear larger than they actually are.</meta>

# ALHAZEN

...at $l$ and $k$ by **Proposition 16 of Book 1** <note>Alhazen frequently cites Euclid's *Elements*; "p 1" refers to Proposition 16 of the first book.</note>: but the exterior angles made by the straight lines $a, b, a, c$ and the secant $k, l$ are equal to the interior angles at $b$ and $c$ of the triangle $abc$ by **Proposition 29 of Book 1**. Therefore, the angles at $b$ and $c$ are greater than the angles at $l$ and $k$. Because of this, by **Proposition 32 of Book 1**, the remaining angle $abc$ is smaller than the remaining angle $lak$: and the line $lk$ is the **diameter of the image** <term>diameter imaginis: the perceived width or span of the object as seen through the refractive medium</term> of $bc$. For every point of the line $bc$ is refracted from some point $ph$. For if the form $b$ is refracted from $p$: then a point that is between $b$ and $z$ is refracted from some point between $p$ and $m$: let us place point $n$ upon the line $bz$. If, therefore, the **form** <note>original: "forma"; in medieval optics, this refers to the visual information or light rays radiating from an object.</note> of $n$ were refracted from some point outside the line $mp$ on the side of $d$: then the line through which the form of $n$ is extended would cut the line $bp$: and thus the form of the point of intersection would be refracted to $a$ from two points [$p$ and $q$], which is impossible, as we stated in the fifth chapter of this book concerning images: (19 n) therefore it is not refracted to $a$ except from some point between $p$ and $m$. And similarly, every point in $zc$ will not be refracted to $a$ except from the line $mh$. 

The line $lk$ is therefore the diameter of the image of the line $bc$: [by 18 n] thus the form $bc$ will be seen in $lk$. Likewise, we have already declared [in the preceding section] that a refracted form is weaker than a direct one: therefore the form $bc$, which is perceived by refraction, is weaker than its form when perceived directly: and on account of the **weakness of the form** <note>The eye perceives faint or less distinct images as being further away, a psychological principle of depth perception used here to explain magnification.</note> of the thing, the sight likens it to the form of a thing seen from a greater distance; for greater distance weakens the form. Also, we have already declared in the second book [38 n] that the sight perceives the image of a visible thing according to the size of the angle, with respect to the distance and position of the visible thing before the sight: and the angle $lak$ is greater than the angle $cab$ [from what was concluded], and the position of $lk$ is like the position of $cb$, and $bc$ is seen in $lk$, and $lk$ is perceived at a seemingly greater distance than the distance of $bc$ because of the weakness of the form. The sight therefore perceives $bc$ by refraction from the comparison of an angle greater than angle $cab$ at a distance greater than the distance of $bc$, and at a position equal to the position of $bc$. Wherefore $bc$ is perceived by refraction as larger: and this is for two reasons, namely the **magnitude of the angle** and the **weakness of the form**. Moreover, the cause of the magnitude of the angle is the proximity of the angle to the sight: and the cause of the proximity of the angle is refraction. Therefore, the cause by which $bc$ is perceived as larger is refraction.

### *43. If the entire image of a visible object refracted by a flat transparent surface appears larger than the object itself: then a part of that image will also appear larger than the corresponding proportional part of the actual object. Proposition 35, Book 10.*

Likewise: let us repeat the first figure of this chapter <note>referring to section 39</note>: and let there be a perpendicular line $amoz$ cutting the line $lk$: therefore $lo$ will be half of $lk$: and point $z$ will be seen at $o$ because it is seen along the perpendicular $zm$: therefore $bc$ will be seen along the line $lk$. Since $bz$ is half of $bc$, and $lo$ is half of $lk$, and $lk$ is seen as larger than $bc$, it follows that $lo$ will be seen as larger than $bz$. Moreover, the cause of the magnitude of $bc$ is refraction: therefore the cause of the magnitude of $bz$ is also refraction. 

Now, the eye $a$ is on the perpendicular $az$, which extends from the end of $bz$ to the surface of the transparent body. This same result follows in the three figures following the first (namely the second, third, and fourth of this chapter): specifically, that the sight perceives the halves of visible objects as larger than they truly are. The eye is positioned on the perpendicular extending from the edge of that half-section to the surface of the transparent body, or onto a surface passing through the edge of that half-section perpendicular to the body's surface. 

For the point that is the middle of the image lies on the perpendicular extending from the middle of the object seen, whether the object is parallel to the surface of the transparent medium or not. Likewise, let $bn$ be a specific part of line $bz$: and let us draw the perpendicular $ng$: the image of $n$ will therefore be on line $ng$ <note>per Proposition 19</note>. Thus $g$ becomes the image of $n$: therefore $g$ will either be on line $lg$ or near it. Because of this, $lg$ will either be equal to line $bn$, or nearly so. 

But in the first figure of this chapter <note>section 39</note>, we showed that $bc$ is perceived as larger than it is. The cause of this is refraction: and the refractions of forms that are further from the perpendicular (dropping from the center of sight to the surface of the transparent body) are greater than the refractions of forms closer to that perpendicular. Therefore, the refraction of form $bn$ to the eye $a$ is greater than the refraction of the part $zn$ to $a$. The cause that makes the image $bz$ appear larger also causes $bn$ to have a greater proportion to it than $bz$ has to $bn$: therefore $lg$ (which is the image of $bn$) is perceived as larger than $bn$.

Likewise, if the eye $a$ did not perceive the image $bn$ as larger than $bn$ itself, it would not perceive the images of the other parts of line $bn$ (those closer to $z$) as larger than those parts. For the forms of those other parts undergo less refraction than the form of $bz$: but refraction is the cause of the image's increased size: therefore $a$ would not perceive $lo$ as larger than $bz$. Consequently, $a$ will perceive $bn$ as larger than it actually is. 

This same effect occurs if $a$ is outside the perpendicular extending from $bz$ to the surface of the transparent body, and the line extending from $a$ to the middle of $bz$ is not perpendicular to $bz$. This follows in the three figures—the second, third, and fourth of this chapter <note>sections 40, 41, and 42</note>. Therefore, everything perceived by sight through a transparent medium denser than air <note>original: "grossius aere"</note> with a flat surface is perceived as larger than it is, whether the eye is on a perpendicular line from the object or not, and regardless of whether the object's diameter is parallel to the surface of the medium.

48. *The image of a visible object refracted from water to air appears larger than the object. 42 p 10.*

And this happens in those things seen in water: for the convex part of the water's surface is spherical toward the eye, and the center of the water's surface is beyond those things that are perceived in the water, and water is denser than air: But that which is seen in water—if the water is clear and shallow—might not be perceived by the sight to be larger in the water than if it were in the air. For its size then does not differ much according to the senses (namely, its size in water versus air): for then that addition in the water will be small, and therefore the sense will not distinguish that addition; however, this can be understood through experience in this way. Take a <term>columnar body</term><note>A cylinder.</note>, whose length is not less than one cubit: and let it be of some thickness: white: for whiteness is more clearly distinguished in water: and let the surface of its base be flat, so that it stands evenly by itself upon the surface of the ground. Having observed this, take a wide vessel, and let its surface be flat, and pour clear water into the vessel to a height less than the length of the columnar body: then place that columnar body into the water, and set it upon its base in the middle of the vessel: there will therefore be some part of this body outside the water: for the height of the water is less—

...nor by the length of this body. For then, when the water has become still, you will see the part of the body that is inside the water to be thicker than that which is outside the water. It is therefore clear from this experience that every visible thing perceived in water is perceived as larger than it is in reality. Likewise, let there be a spherical body whose convex side is toward the eye, and let the thing seen be beyond the center of the spherical surface, and let that body be denser <note>The Latin 'grossius' refers here to optical density—the ability of a material like glass or water to bend light more than air does.</note> than air: But in common visual experiences there is no such thing that is seen beyond a transparent spherical body denser than air, beyond the center of the sphere, while the thing seen is simultaneously inside the spherical body: for this does not happen unless the spherical body is glass or stone, and the entire spherical body is solid, and the visible object is inside it, or if the spherical body is a portion of a sphere larger than a hemisphere and the visible object is placed against its base: but these two positions rarely occur: therefore, things of this kind are not among common visual experiences: thus we ought not to be occupied with those things that happen to such visible objects. But there are some common things which are seen beyond a transparent spherical body denser than air, whose convex side is toward the eye, when the thing seen is beyond a crystalline or glass sphere in the air, not inside the sphere. The positions of such visible objects are many: but these are rarely perceived: and if they are perceived, they are rarely seen. It is therefore not appropriate to distinguish all those positions. Let us be content with one single position, namely where the eye and the thing seen are on the same perpendicular line through the surface of the spherical body.

### *49. If the eye, the center of a dense convex refractive medium, and the visible object placed beyond the refractive medium are on the same straight line: the image will be seen as a ring or bracelet; and larger than the visible object. 43 p 10.*

Let the eye be $a$: and the spherical body $bgzd$: and let its center be $e$: and let us join $ae$, and extend it straight: and let it cut the surface of the sphere at two points $b, d$: and let us extend it on the side of $d$ as far as $h$: and let us extend from the line $hba$ a flat surface cutting the sphere: it will therefore make [by the 1st theorem of the 1st book on spheres] a circle $bgzd$ on the surface of the sphere. Now in the eighth figure in the chapter on the image [29 n] we said that on the line $bd$ there are many points whose forms are refracted to $a$ from the circumference $bgzd$: and that the form of that whole line is refracted to $a$, if $bgzd$ were continuous and not broken at part $b$. Therefore, let $hl$ be refracted to $a$ from the circumference $bgzd$, and let $h$ be refracted to $a$ from $g$: and $l$ to $a$ from $p$: the form of $hl$ will therefore be refracted to $a$ from the arc $gp$: and let us join the lines $gmh, ga, lzp, pa$: $h$ therefore extends through $gh$, and is refracted through $ga$: and $l$ extends through $lp$, and is refracted through $pa$: and let us join the lines $eg, em, ez$: and extend $em$ to $c$: and $ez$ to $f$. Therefore the form which extends through $ag$ is refracted through $gh$ and reaches $h$: and the form which extends through $ap$ is refracted through $pl$ and reaches $l$: this is provided the transparent body is continuous as far as $g$. But if the spherical body is marked at the spherical surface: then the form which extends through $ag$ is refracted through $gm$ toward the perpendicular, which is $eh$: and when the form reaches $m$: it is refracted a second time away from the perpendicular, which is $emc$: let it therefore be refracted to $k$. And likewise the form which extends through $ap$ is refracted through $pz$: and when it has been refracted to $z$, it is refracted a second time away from the perpendicular, which is $ezf$: let the refraction of the form which reaches $z$ be through the line $zo$. Therefore the form $k$ extends through $km$, and is refracted through $mg$: then it is refracted a second time through $ga$. And similarly the form $o$ extends through $oz$, and is refracted through $zp$: then a second time through $pa$. Therefore the form of the whole $ko$ is refracted to $a$ from the arc $gp$. And if the line $ako$ is fixed, and we imagine the figure $agpk$ being rotated around $ako$: then the arc $gp$ will make a circular figure, like a ring <note>original: "armillam," meaning a bracelet or ring.</note>, from the whole of which the form $ko$ will be refracted to $a$: and the image $ko$ will be at the center of sight, which is $a$. Therefore the form $ko$ will be seen on the entire circular surface, which is the place of refraction, which is in the straightness of the radial lines, which is the shape of a ring. Therefore the form $ko$ will appear larger than itself: and the shape of the form will be different from the shape $ko$. This can be tested by experiment as follows. Take a very round crystalline or glass sphere, and take a small body: such as a chickpea or a small piece of wax: for the experiment will be clearer with a small body, and dye it black, and let the shape of the wax be spherical: then place it on the head of a needle, and place the crystalline sphere opposite one of the eyes, and close the other eye, and raise the needle beyond the sphere, and look at the middle of the sphere, and place the wax opposite the middle of the form, so that it is opposite the middle of the sphere: for then you will see a round blackness in the shape of a ring on that surface of the sphere. If you do not see it: move the wax forward and backward until you see the round blackness, then take the wax away, and the blackness will be cut off: then let the wax return to its place, and again you will see that round blackness. From this experience, therefore, it will be clear that if the thing seen is beyond a transparent spherical body denser than air, and the eye, and the thing seen, and the center of the spherical body are in the same straight line: then the eye perceives that thing seen in the shape of a ring.

If, however, *b g z d* were in a cylindrical body, and that body were denser than air: then the form *k o* will be seen at arc *g p* and at an equal and corresponding arc *f i* from arc *b d*. But this form will not be circular, because the figure *a h p g*, when rotated around *a k*, will not pass through that line of the arc *g p* through the entire cylindrical surface. Instead, the form might be refracted from some cylindrical portions, and it will be continuous in one part and similarly in another. For the surface from *l k*, which also passes through the axis of the cylinder, creates a straight line on the surface of the cylinder on the side of *a*, which passes through *b* and extends along the length of the cylinder. The form *k o* is not refracted from that straight line, for *k b* will be perpendicular to that straight line. Therefore, the form will not be round if it is a cylindrical body; rather, there will be two forms, one of which is refracted over the other. Thus, *k o* will appear to be two objects, each of which will be larger than the actual *k o*, and the shape of each will differ from the shape of *k o*. Nevertheless, those two forms will appear at the same point, namely the center of the eye <note>original: "centrum visus" — the point within the eye where the rays of light are perceived to converge.</note>. Among common visible things, however, nothing is perceived by the sight beyond a transparent spherical body denser than air whose concave side is toward the eye. For if it were made of glass or some stone, it would have to be a concave portion of a sphere, and the object seen would have to be inside that sphere, or its surface beyond the concavity would have to be flat with the object seen attached to it. These two setups are either never found or are very rare; therefore, let us not trouble ourselves with such things.

### §1. *A star on the horizon is generally seen larger than in the middle of the sky. <note>original: "54 p 10"</note>*

Likewise, no body is found that is thinner <term>less dense</term> than air whose surface toward the eye is flat or convex. Nothing thinner than air is found beyond which something may be perceived, except for the body of the heavens and fire <note>In the medieval worldview, the "sphere of fire" was thought to exist between the Earth's atmosphere and the celestial spheres.</note>. The surface that distinguishes one part of the air from another is not a sharp division; rather, the closer the air gets to the heavens, the more it is purified until it becomes fire. Its "thinness" <term>rarity</term> therefore changes in an orderly succession, not at a fixed boundary. Consequently, the forms of those things in the heavens, when they extend toward the eye, are not refracted at the concavity of the sphere of fire, since there is no determined concave surface there. Therefore, no body is found thinner than air in which the forms of visible objects extend and are refracted at its surface, except for the celestial body; and the celestial body is a concave sphere from the perspective of the eye. Therefore, all stars in the heavens extend through the celestial body, are refracted at the concavity of the heavens, and extend through the body of fire and the body of air in a straight line until they reach the eye. The center of the concavity of the heavens is the center of the earth.

I say, therefore, that stars are for the most part perceived in their actual locations, and that they are always perceived as having sizes other than their true magnitudes; along with this, the size of each of them varies according to its location. This variation in location is due to the position of the refracted rays, as we said before. The variation in size <term>quantities</term> is due to distance; for because of their distance, they are perceived as smaller than they truly are, as we said in the third treatise—namely, that objects at the greatest distance are perceived as smaller. The variation in size according to the change in location happens because of refraction, the cause of which we have explained here; and in the fourth chapter <note>original: "15 non declaravimus" — this likely refers to a previous section where the author clarifies what had not yet been proven.</note> we did not yet declare that the forms of the stars perceived by the eye are refracted.

I say, therefore, that every star is perceived from every part of the sky through which it moves as being smaller than it truly is, as its distance requires (that is, smaller than if it were seen directly), provided there are no clouds or thick vapors between it and the eye. Every star at the zenith <term>vertex of the head</term> of the observer appears smaller than in any other place in the sky; and the further it moves from the zenith, the larger it appears, so that on the horizon it appears larger than anywhere else. This is common to all stars, whether far or near. Likewise, if there is thick vapor in the air beyond which a star is located, then it will be perceived as larger than if that vapor were not there; and it often happens that thick vapor is on the horizon. Hence, stars are for the most part seen larger on the horizon than in the middle of the sky. This is more apparent in the distances between the stars than in the sizes of the stars themselves; for the size of a single star relative to the eye is small, but the increase in the distance between stars when they are on the horizon is large and obvious to the senses, especially over wide distances, and most of all if there is thick vapor on the horizon.

Let there be a meridian circle on some horizon, *b k*; and let the common intersection between this circle and the concavity of the heavens be the circle *m e z*. [For the radius of the earth has no perceptible ratio to the radius of the heavens, as is taught in astronomy <note>original: "astrologia" — in the medieval period, this term encompassed both what we now call astronomy and astrology.</note>] and the angle of refraction will be a part of it. [For if the angles *a m p* and *g a q* are made equal to angles *z m a* and *h a g* at points *m* and *a* by Proposition 23, Book 1, and the straight lines *a p* and *h p* are connected: the angles *m p h* and *m h p* will be equal by Definition 15, Proposition 5, Book 1. Therefore, the circle containing the triangle *a h d* is larger than the circle containing triangle *a e z*, because angle *a h d* is greater than angle *a z e*, and line *h d* is smaller than *z e*, as has been declared. Therefore, *h d* marks off from the circle containing triangle *a h d* a smaller arc than the arc which *z e* divides from the circle containing *a e z*. Thus, the angle *h a d* is smaller than the angle *z a e*. Let *z a d* be common; therefore, angle *h a z* is smaller than angle *d a e*. Angle *h a z* is that under which the eye at *a* perceives *d e* through refraction, and angle *d a e* is that under which it would perceive *d e* directly, if it could. Therefore, the eye at *a* perceives *d e* through refraction as smaller than it would directly. This demonstration holds if the circle *b d e* were the meridian circle. Thus, when the diameter of a star or the distance between two stars is aligned vertically, it is perceived through refraction as smaller than it would be directly. This is what we intended to show.

### *55. A star appears circular: it appears larger on the horizon than in the middle of the sky; similarly, the distance between two stars so situated. <note>This addresses the famous "Moon Illusion," where celestial bodies look bigger near the ground than high in the air.</note>*

Every star in the sky is perceived as round because its diameters are perceived as equal. Since it is clear that both its vertical and its transverse diameters are perceived as smaller than they would be if seen directly, it follows that every slanted diameter is perceived as equally smaller. Similarly, the distances between stars are perceived in all locations and positions as smaller than if they were seen directly. Furthermore, we have said [in Note 51] that every star is perceived as smaller when at the zenith <note>original: "uertice capitis" — literally "the top of the head," the highest point in the sky.</note> than in any other part of the sky; and the further it is from the zenith, the larger it is perceived to be; it is perceived at its maximum when it is on the horizon. It remains, therefore, to explain the cause of why this happens. I say that we explained this in the second treatise of this book when we dealt with magnitude [in Note 38]: that if the sight perceives the sizes of visible things, it perceives them from the quantity of the angles subtended by the visible objects at the center of the eye, and from the quantity of their distances, and from the comparison of the angles to the distances. We also declared that the sight never perceives the quantities of visible things unless their distances are measured against continuous nearby bodies; and if the sight does not certify the distances of the visible things, it will not certify their quantities. And we declared there also, that if the sight does not certify...

He then introduces the psychological explanation for the "Moon Illusion," noting that stars appear largest at the horizon because the mind uses ground-level distances to judge size.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Alhazen’s investigation into the "Moon Illusion" and the perception of celestial bodies. He transitions from the purely geometric effects of atmospheric refraction to the psychology of visual perception, explaining how the mind estimates size by comparing visual angles with perceived distances.</meta>

# BOOK VII OF OPTICS

...if it has perceived the distance of the object, it can estimate that distance and compare it to the distances of familiar visible things through which such an object is understood, in such a form and shape. It then perceives its magnitude based on the size of the angle that the visible object subtends at the center of sight, relative to the distance it has estimated. However, the distances of the stars do not lie along the same lines as those of nearby objects. For this reason, sight cannot accurately grasp their size nor confirm their true distances. Sight therefore estimates the distances of stars by comparing them to the distances of terrestrial objects, which are perceived at their furthest range, and it estimates their sizes accordingly. 

To our senses, the body of the heavens does not appear spherical, nor does its concave side seem to face the eye. Sight does not perceive the physical body of the sky, nor does it perceive anything about it except for its bluish-gray color <note>original: "colorem glaucum" — referring to the hazy, grayish-blue of the sky</note>. Indeed, its three-dimensional solidity, extension, roundness, and concavity cannot be grasped by sight at all. And if sight cannot confirm the true nature of something, it will liken it to familiar things. Hence, it perceives the sun and moon as flat planes; even convex or concave bodies at a great distance appear flat. Likewise, arcs whose convexity or concavity faces the eye will be perceived as straight lines. For if the eye does not perceive how the center is nearer and the edges are further away in convex shapes—or how the center is further and the edges nearer in concave shapes—it will liken these surfaces to flat planes and these arcs to straight lines. This is because most familiar visible objects are flat and straight. 

Furthermore, when the image of a star reaches the eye, it does not sense that the image has been refracted <note>The eye is unaware that the light has bent as it passed from space into the denser atmosphere.</note>, or that it is being bent through a concave surface, or that the body in which the star resides is more subtle than the air where the eye is located. Instead, the star's image is perceived just like other objects seen through the air in a straight line. The images of visible things do not appear refracted to the eye even when they encounter a medium different from air; the eye senses neither the refraction nor the surface where the bending occurs, unless it is through the natural properties of light and color that extend through transparent bodies. Thus, the images of refracted stars reach the eye just as images of objects in the air do, and they are not perceived as being different from those in the air. 

Sight perceives the color of the sky, yet it cannot confirm its true shape through simple sensation. When sight perceives a color across a certain length and width—beyond just grasping its shape and form—it will perceive it as a flat surface, likening it to familiar surfaces like a wall or similar objects. In this way, it perceives convex and concave surfaces at a great distance as flat. Thus, sight perceives the surface of the earth as entirely flat, not sensing its curvature unless mountains or valleys are present. Likewise, sight perceives the surface of the heavens as a flat plane, and it perceives the stars as it does familiar, separate objects located in wide spaces. 

When the eye perceives familiar objects in a wide space at equal visual angles, and it perceives the differences in their distances, then the object that is further away will be perceived as larger. The size of an object is grasped by comparing the angle it subtends at the center of sight to its perceived distance. Sight perceives the size of a nearby object by comparing the angle it subtends to that nearby distance. This is evident and confirmed by experience: of two visible objects perceived at equal angles but at noticeably different distances, the more remote one will appear larger. 

For example, if a person stands before a wide wall and raises their hand close to their eye, covering one eye and looking with the other, and places the hand between the eye and the wall, the hand will block out a wide section of that wall. They perceive both the hand and the wall at once. The hand is seen through an acute angle; in this state, the width of the wall is perceived as many times larger than the width of the hand. If they then move their hand so that the part of the wall it covered is revealed, and they look at the hand, they will see that the revealed part of the wall is many times larger than the hand—even though the eye perceives the hand and that section of the wall through two equal angles. This proves that sight understands magnitude by comparing the visual angle to the distance. 

Therefore, sight perceives the surface of the sky as a flat plane and does not sense its concavity, yet it perceives the stars as distinct points upon it. It thus perceives stars of equal size as unequal: for it compares the angle subtended by a star near the horizon to a remote distance, while it compares the angle subtended by a star in the mid-heaven <note>original: "medio cœli" — the zenith or highest point of the sky</note> to a closer distance. Similarly, the eye perceives a star that is on or near the horizon as larger than the same star when it is at or near the zenith. Thus, it perceives the same star and the same distance between stars as different sizes in different parts of the sky. 

When the eye compares two angles that are nearly equal in size but correspond to two very different distances, the object that is perceived to be further away is understood to be larger. What confirms this cause is that the angles subtended by the same star at the center of sight from all parts of the sky (even after the lines are refracted) are essentially the same angles as if the star were seen in a straight line. This is because the observer is at the center of the celestial sphere, and the refraction of stellar images does not diminish those angles significantly. Since these differences are not great, the variation is caused by the perceived distance between stars in different parts of the sky...

<meta>non erit</meta>

<summary>Alhazen explains the "Moon Illusion," arguing that because we perceive the sky as a flat ceiling rather than a dome, we imagine stars at the horizon to be further away than those overhead, leading our brains to perceive them as larger despite the visual angle remaining nearly constant.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Book VII of Alhazen’s *Optics*. Following the previous page's discussion on how the mind perceives the sky as a flat plane rather than a sphere, Alhazen here finalizes his explanation of the "Moon Illusion"—why celestial bodies appear larger near the horizon than when they are high in the sky.</meta>

# ALHAZEN

...there will not be a very great difference. And since the difference between these angles is not very great, the magnitude of the star will not be perceived with a very great difference in size; and that which demonstrates the decrease of the angles of refraction relative to the angles contained by straight lines is not of the greatest magnitude. That these angles are quite small is shown by what was said in the previous experiment in the chapter on refraction [15 n.] <note>referring to an earlier section of Book VII</note> in which we demonstrated that the eye perceives a refracted star and sees a fixed star from the pole of the world, and its distance from it in one revolution; for this difference is found to be small. From this, it is clear that the angles of refraction are small. Therefore, because of that small difference between them, the angles by which a star is perceived in different parts of the sky do not vary with a very great difference. Yet the magnitude of a star and the distances between stars differ greatly when they are at the horizon compared to when they are in the middle of the sky <note>original: "medio coeli" — the zenith, or the point directly overhead</note>. Therefore, the cause of the difference in the size of the star and the distance between stars in different parts of the sky is not the difference in the angles of refraction.

We have already demonstrated that sight perceives magnitude by comparing the angles of divergence to the distances. Therefore, if the difference between the angles is slight, but the difference between the distances and reaches is great, then the object will appear larger from a greater distance. The reason, therefore, why the distances of the stars appear larger at the horizon than in the middle of the sky or near it, is this: the sense <note>the faculty of visual perception</note> estimates that they are further away at the horizon than in the middle of the sky. This fact—that the eye perceives stars in different parts of the sky as having different magnitudes—is a perpetual error, because its cause is perpetual. And it is this: sight perceives the surface of the sky as flat, and does not sense its concavity or the equality of its distance from the eye. It is established in the mind that on a flat surface extending in every direction, the distances from the eye vary; and that which is closest is that which is directly over one's head. It therefore perceives that which is at the horizon as being further away than that which is in the middle of the sky.

Since the angles that the same star subtends at the center of sight from all parts of the sky do not vary greatly, and since sight perceives the magnitude of an object by comparing the angle the object subtends to its distance from the eye, it follows that it perceives the size of a star (and the distance between stars) when they are at or near the horizon by comparing the angle to a remote distance. But when they are in the middle of the sky or near it, it compares a nearly identical angle to a closer distance. Between this and the distance of the horizon, there appears to be a very great difference. This is therefore the cause why sight errs in the difference of the magnitude of stars and their distances; and this cause is fixed, perpetual, and unchangeable. 

Sight perceives stars as small because of their great distance; for they subtend small angles at the center of sight. But the sense does not certify the true quantity of the star's distance; rather, it estimates and compares the distances of the stars with the distances of familiar visible things on earth. Thus, it imagines that the distance of a star is like the distance of some extremely remote object on earth. It therefore compares the small angle made by the star at the eye to a distance similar to those on earth, and thus, because of this comparison, perceives the star as small. If sight were certain of the true magnitude of the star's distance, it would perceive the star as massive. It is the same for all extremely distant things on earth: if they are perceived, they seem small because their true distance is not confirmed. We have already demonstrated this perfectly in the third treatise of this book [23 n.].

Just as sight errs in the quantity of a star's distance because it is not certain of it and likens it to distances on earth, so it errs in thinking the distances between stars in different parts of the sky are different when they are actually equal. This is because it likens them to the different distances on earth, about which there is no doubt they are different. And just as the error in the distance and magnitude of a star is perpetual, so the error in the variation of the distances between stars and their magnitudes in different parts of the sky is perpetual. For the forms of those distances do not change for the eye at different times, but are always the same; and sight likens them to the distances of familiar things that are at the greatest distance from the eye upon the surface of the earth.

There is also another cause for things in the heavens appearing larger at the horizon for the most part: namely, the thick vapors <note>atmospheric haze or moisture</note> that are positioned between the eye and the star. When there is vapor at the horizon or near it, and it does not continue all the way to the middle of the sky, it will be a portion of a sphere whose center is the center of the world containing the earth. It is thus cut off toward the middle of the sky, and its surface facing the eye is flat. Because of this, the forms or distances that are beyond that vapor will appear larger than they would without the vapor. In that place in the concavity of the sky where the form of the star is refracted toward the eye, the form exists, and from there it extends in a straight line to the eye, provided there is no thick vapor at the horizon. 

But if there is thick vapor, then this form will extend to the surface of the vapor facing the sky and will exist on that surface. Thus, sight perceives it just as it perceives objects within vapor: namely, that the form extends through the thick vapor in a straight line, then is refracted at the surface of the vapor away from the perpendicular line <note>the normal line</note> projecting from the flat surface of the vapor. This is because the air on the side of the eye is subtler <note>thinner or less dense</note> than that vapor. It follows from this that the form appears larger than if it were seen directly, as we said in the first figure of this chapter [39 n.]; that is, when a subtler body is on the side of the eye and a thicker body is on the side of the object seen, and the surface of the thicker body is flat. The form that reaches the surface of the vapor facing the sky is the "object seen," and the body in which the form extends is the thick vapor, while the air in which the eye resides is subtler than it. 

The principal cause, however, why stars and the distances between them appear larger at the horizon than in the middle of the sky, is the one mentioned before <note>the psychological perception of the sky as a flat plane</note>; it is fixed and perpetual. If it happens that there is also thick vapor, their magnitude increases; but this cause exists in some places always, and in others only sometimes. Therefore, all that we have said in this chapter regarding the things that happen to sight due to refraction are those deceptions that always or mostly occur; and they suffice for what we require concerning deceptions caused by refraction. Now, let us end this treatise, which is the end of the book.

->END OF THE OPTICS OF ALHAZEN, SON OF AL-HAYTHAM.<-

# THE SON OF ALHAZEN
## THE BOOK OF ALHAZEN ON TWILIGHTS
## AND THE HEIGHTS OF CLOUDS.

->Translated by Gerard of Cremona.<-

->*NUMBERS.*<-

> *1. Morning twilight begins, and evening twilight ends, when the sun—before its rising and after its setting—is submerged 19 degrees below the horizon, measured on the circumference of the circle passing through the zenith of the region and the sun’s location.*

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap letter O decorated with botanical and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>In this treatise, I wish to show what twilight is and what cause necessarily makes it appear; from there, I will proceed to identifying the highest point above the earth’s surface reached by the subtle vapors that ascend from it. I say, therefore, that morning twilight and evening twilight are of a similar nature; for one occurs from the approaching light of the sun, and the other from its withdrawal. However, their colors are different due to the different horizons in which the sun appears. For when the sun is on the eastern horizon and not very high, its color to our sight is different from its color when it is at the same height on the western horizon. The same is true of its rays seen in the twilight and the light seen in the ether. The ether itself is colored accordingly, following the sun's position in both directions. For the color in the east is whiteness and brightness, while that in the west tends somewhat toward redness. As to what thing is actually illuminating, how it appears there, and what cause necessarily produces it, we shall first set forth propositions to explain that which we wish to declare. One of these is that the sphere of the world [composed of earth and water] is always entirely bright and luminous from the greater light (the sun), except for the portion covered by the shadow resulting from the earth, in the shape of a pyramid, which is night <note>The "pyramid of night" is a classical and medieval astronomical concept describing the cone-shaped shadow cast by the Earth into space.</note>. In this book, I do not mean that this reception of light happens from the spheres of the stars, but rather that because of the clarity of the air, the subtlety of the ether <term>ether<note>The rarefied, pure substance believed to fill the upper atmosphere and heavens.</note></term>, and its thinness, it does not "catch" any of the sun's light. We see light caught by high bodies (such as the stars), because they are illuminated and bring to us the light they receive, and our sight follows that light in them. And although people may disagree about the nature of stars, they do not disagree regarding their light. However, our sight does not perceive light in the ether unless the bodies there are of a thicker and more intense materiality than the ether in which they exist. This is evident from the fact that some stars hide others from us because they eclipse them, whereas the air hides nothing behind it. Because of this, we see that the whole night maintains a single appearance, in which no part of the ether is illuminated for us—even though we know through our science that a great deal of that ether is luminous and not covered by the earth’s shadow. We see that what is visible to the sun (and not hidden by anything else) looks to our vision exactly like what the earth hides within the pyramid of darkness. This equal appearance to our sight is caused only by what we said regarding the subtlety of the air: it does not transmit its own illumination to us, but transmits its darkness. This state of shadow does not cease to appear the same to us until the brightness of dawn and scattered light begin in the east, starting at the surface of the horizon. The cause of this beginning is nothing but the sun, since the sun is the cause of all illumination. Yet the cause is not the sun itself, nor its rays alone, since we have already stated that its rays pass through the entire ether we see (or most of it), and the state of the ether at that hour is no different from the hour before it. Nevertheless, the rays are "caught" at that time by some body thicker than air; because of its thickness, this body brings to us the ray with which it is clothed. I say that the thing by which the ray is caught at that hour is not the earth, nor the edges of its regions distant from us. For when a viewer is on the level ground of the earth, his sight reaches only about 23 [Italian] miles in every direction. If he happens to be on the highest of mountains (which do not exceed eight miles, according to the wise men who have studied this), his sight then reaches only about 250 miles. This is clear from the shape the earth makes at night; but the height of the viewer’s position from the surface—the distance we mentioned—would hide the sun in a quarter of an hour. Therefore, the sun should rise just a little after morning twilight (by a quarter of an hour at least); however, the actual time between the appearance of twilight and the appearance of the sun is much more than an hour. What we have said here is only an approximation for those not trained in geometry. In truth, sight does not reach a point on earth already illuminated by the sun until the sun itself arrives and its horn <note>original: "cornu" — the very first sliver of the sun's disk to break the horizon.</note> is perceived. Because two lines touching a point on a circle from two different sides, when joined, form a single straight line [p. 14, prop. 1: because a radius of a circle drawn to the point of contact makes right angles with both, p. 18, prop. 3]. Therefore, when an illuminated area appears to us [before sunrise], it is not the earth itself, for the reasons we have stated.

He uses geometric calculations of the earth's curvature and the height of mountains to prove that twilight begins long before the sun's disk could be directly visible.</summary>

# ALHAZEN

...as we said: nor is it the air filling the whole sphere: because, as we pre-supposed, the sun's ray always falls upon all the air or most of it, night and day: and light does not appear within the air itself, because of its own tenuousness <note>The Latin *subtilitatem* here refers to the air being so thin and transparent that it does not scatter light effectively on its own.</note>. And upon the earth there is no body thicker than air, except for the ascending vapors, which are never without illumination from the sun. But then, when the cone of shadow <note>original: *pyramis umbræ*</note> is removed from that part of the sphere of vapors surrounding the earth which our sight reaches, and the body of the sun reaches them, and its rays fall upon them, the ray is held with the vapor and brings the light to us; our sight follows it, and its light is seen by us, just as we see light appear in the clouds from the coloring of the ascending moisture, and like the colors seen in dewdrops, in the form of a portion of a circle <note>A rainbow.</note>, and in other ways. 

Therefore, when we wish to know the maximum height of those vapors from the surface of the earth, four things are first required for that knowledge, none of which can be omitted; and besides these we need no other thing, so that the calculation cannot be done with less, nor is more necessary. These four are: the body of the earth; the body of the sun; the distance of the sun's center from the earth's center in every position; and the degree of the sun's depression below the horizon until morning twilight appears. 

The body of the earth serves as the instrument for all the others: and the size of the great circle containing it—according to what the wise <note>Referencing ancient astronomers like Eratosthenes or Ptolemy.</note> have said and indicated through certain proofs—is 24,000 miles. And they said that by the measure in which the radius <note>original: *medietas diametri* (half-diameter)</note> of the earth is one part, the radius of the sun is five and a half parts: and by that same measure, the distance of the sun's center from the earth's center at the mean distance (not in every position) is about one thousand one hundred and ten parts: and that the depression of the sun below the horizon when twilight begins is 18 degrees: though it is also found at 19: and upon this I shall build our calculation. For when a reporter of a fact provides an additional detail, his word is more worthy to be received when no one else contradicts him; since the reporter with the addition knows what another does not, and achieves what another does not. For he who reports of something that he saw it before another saw it is more worthy to achieve his intent, provided no suspicion is held against him. I will therefore put forward for the matter at hand certain very helpful propositions.

### 2. If a luminous sphere illuminates an equal opaque one: it will illuminate a hemisphere. Vitello Book 2, Proposition 26. <note>Vitello (Witelo) was a 13th-century scholar whose work on optics was heavily based on Alhazen’s research.</note>

I say, therefore, that of any two equal spheres between which there is no other body to hide one from the other: that which, with a turned face, looks at the other from each of them, is exactly half of it. And I mean by the "turned face" of one with respect to the other: that if one of them is luminous and the other receiving light, the half of the light-receiver is illuminated and reflects light. 

An example of this is: let there be two equal spheres **a** and **b**: and I posit that some flat surface passes through the center of each: it will therefore cut the two spheres into two equal circles, and on one surface <note>original: *per th. 1 sphær. Theodosij* — following Theorem 1 of Theodosius’s *Sphaerica*.</note>. Let those two circles be **a g h** and **b d e**: and I will connect **a** with **b**: and I will draw two lines **a g** and **b d** perpendicular to the line **a b**: <note>original: *per 11 p 1* — following Euclid's *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 11.</note> therefore they are parallel <note>original: *per 28 p 1*</note> and I will connect **g** with **d**. And since the two lines **a g** and **b d** are equal (because they are the radii of equal circles) and parallel (as concluded), the two lines **a b** and **g d** will similarly be equal and parallel: <note>original: *per 33 p 1*</note> therefore the two angles at **g** and **d** are right angles: <note>original: *per secundam partem 34 p 1*</note> therefore the line **g d** is tangent to the two circles <note>original: *per consectarium 16 p 3*</note>. 

And when we extend **g a** and **b d** in a straight line to the two circumferences of the two circles, as far as the two points **e** and **z**, and then connect **e** with **z**: the straight line **e z** will be tangent to the two circles (for the same reasons that **d g** was shown to touch them): and each of the two portions **g h e** and **d c z**, of which one faces the other, will be a half-circle <note>original: *per 17 d 1*</note> since the diameter of the circle cuts each of them. And the same happens in all flat surfaces that pass through the two centers of the two spheres. It has now been shown, therefore, that lines going out from one of the two spheres to the other touch both at once and encompass half of each. And that is what we wished to declare.

### 3. If a luminous sphere illuminates a smaller opaque one: it will illuminate more than a hemisphere. Vitello Book 2, Proposition 27.

But we have already drawn it tangent to the larger; therefore, it is tangent to both at once. Similarly, I will draw from point <term>h</term> a line tangent to the two circles on the side of <term>z</term>, which shall be line <term>hzk</term>. 

It follows, then, that the portion of the larger circle <term>a</term> that faces the smaller circle <term>b</term> is <term>dgk</term>: and it is less than half of the circle. This is because angle <term>had</term> is less than a right angle <note>By Euclid I, 32.</note>, since it is in a single triangle, and triangle <term>dah</term> has a right angle at <term>adh</term>. And since line <term>bc</term> is parallel to line <term>ad</term> <margin>from the conclusion</margin>, angle <term>cbh</term> is equal to angle <term>dah</term> <note>By Euclid I, 29.</note>. And I mean by this that no part of one portion is hidden from the other circle: and portion <term>cez</term> is greater than half the circle, and portion <term>dgk</term> is smaller. *4. If two straight lines touch the circumferences of two equal circles: the individual points of the half-circumferences on the convex parts facing each other are visible to one another, but the points of the remaining half-circumferences on the convex parts not facing each other are hidden.*

AND I say, that when there are two equal circles, and two lines are drawn, each of which touches both circles at once according to the form we previously described: then in each of the two portions where one faces the other, there is no place that hides any part of one circle from the other circle; and that in the remaining two portions of the two circles, which do not face each other face-to-face, there is no place that is visible to the other circle. 

As an example of this, let there be two circles <term>abgde</term> and <term>zhtkl</term>: and let two lines <term>bh</term> and <term>dk</term> be drawn tangent to both circles at once. Thus, the two portions <term>bgd</term> and <term>htk</term> are those which face each other face-to-face; the portions <term>bed</term> and <term>hlk</term> are those which do not face each other. The proof of this is: I will connect <term>a</term> with <term>z</term> by the line <term>agz</term>, and I will mark a point <term>m</term> on the arc <term>bgd</term> wherever I wish. 6. *Given the circumference of the greatest circle on Earth as 24,000 Italian miles: the total height of the vapors gathered into clouds from the Earth will be 52,000 paces. Witelo, Book 10, Proposition 60.* <note>Witelo was a 13th-century scholar whose work on optics was heavily based on Alhazen. One "pace" (passus) is five feet; 52,000 paces is roughly 49 miles.</note>

Let us begin now, therefore, from that which we intend concerning the cause of the appearance of twilight, the manner in which it appears to us, and its configuration on the eastern horizon. I shall therefore place a circle marked upon the sphere of the Earth, and over it the flat surface which the Earth hides, passing through the zenith of our heads and through *z*, the center of the Earth, and the circle of the sun *ab*, and the place of sight *a*: and I will cause a line tangent to the circle to pass through point *a* [by Proposition 17 of Book 3] and I will extend its two ends in two directions, upon which let there be *d* and *e*. It is manifest, therefore, that upon everything that falls below the line *dae* toward the side *b*, the sight does not fall, since the Earth hides it from us: because the extension of sight is only upon a straight line [by the first hypothesis of Euclid’s Optics.] And Euclid has indeed already declared [Book 3, Proposition 16] that no line can be drawn from the point of contact between the tangent line and the circle. Sight, therefore, does not fall below the line *dae*, but falls upon that which is elevated above it. And I shall set the form of the <term>pyramid of shadows</term> <note>The conical shadow cast by the Earth into space.</note> resulting from the Earth's shadow, shortly before twilight, when the depression of the sun is more than 19 degrees by one minute, for example, or thereabouts: upon which let there be *g, e, f, c*: for everything that falls within this designated pyramid (whose apex is *f* and whose base is the Earth) is covered from the sun, not visible to it, nor illuminated by it, and is in truth dark: and whatever falls outside of it is visible to the sun, and upon it fall its rays and its light. Nevertheless, that which is of

bodies is very subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" means thin or rare, like the upper atmosphere.</note>, it does not convey to our sight that which it puts on from the ray, because in our vision that which is of the subtle air inside the pyramid is equal to that which is outside it: and the whole ether is seen in the form of light and darkness. And we indeed know that what contains us of the air, and what is near us, is dark, not visible to the sun: and what proceeds in its path upward, or to the right, or to the left, and forward and backward, is luminous, visible to the sun: and both are equally with it to us in the whole comprehension of sight: and nothing appears to our sight before the rising of the sun, and after the setting of the sun, unless it be elevated from the surface of the horizon, and unless it be outside the pyramid of the shadow, and unless it be of the subtle air itself. It is manifest, therefore, that nothing appears to our sight in a state of brightness and illumination, unless by the gathering of three conditions in it: one of which is that it must not be below the line *dae*: since if it is below it, the sphere of the Earth is prohibited between it and the sight: because the sight perceives it as neither luminous nor dark. And the other is that it must not be in the pyramid of the shadow: for if it is in it, it is dark, because it is deprived of the face of the sun and its illumination upon it. And the other is that it be <term>denser</term> <note>original: "spissius," meaning thicker or more opaque.</note> than the subtle air filling the sphere: since we already know that the higher air outside the pyramid falls upon the line *dae*: and with it nothing of light appears to us in it, because of its thinness and subtility, and because we see in this place—and it is a little before twilight—that which we perceive of the sphere, covered, not illuminated, and one part of it is not distinguished from another. And we know that there is not in it a point nor a single place in which these three conditions are gathered. But the point is: where the line *dae* last meets the edge of the pyramid: and we have already placed in it two conditions: since it is not below the line *dae*, nor inside the pyramid: therefore the ray of the sun falls upon it. Its darkness in our eyes then is not made necessary, except by its deprivation of the third condition, which is density. It is now therefore certified that the air where point *e* is, in this place, is subtle, and thick vapors ascending from the earth, which are denser than the air, do not reach it. Then after the sun is slightly elevated, and its depression from the horizon is only 19 degrees, and the form of the pyramid and its figure becomes like that upon which are *i, m, h, k*, and a luminous thing appears on the horizon, and there had not been a luminous thing there before: we know that this is the first of the places and positions in which the three aforesaid conditions are gathered: since a little before that, by an amount that has no quantity, there was nothing of light there: and the first of the places in which it is gathered—that it is not below the line *dae*, nor enters the pyramid of darkness—is point *m*. Therefore point *m* is the first of the places in which the third condition is found, and there is the density of the air there. Therefore point *m* is the furthest extent of the vapors, and their highest ascent: and they are neither shortened from it, nor do they pass beyond it. For if they were shortened from it, point *m* would be in subtle air, and nothing of light would appear to us in it, just as it does not appear in that which is after it, toward part *e*: and if they passed beyond it, point *e* would be illuminated for us before this: since we do not place in that which is between *m* and *e*, in these two places, a perceptible <note>The catchword "sibilem" is the end of the word "sensibilem."</note> thing...

When we then wish to know its distance from the surface of the Earth, we shall connect *k* with *q* by the line *k r q*, and I will connect *k* with *h*. If you then imagine the radii *k l* and *k m* of circle *a b c d* are drawn: the squares of lines *f l* and *f k* will equal the square of the radius *k l* by Prop. 47, Book 1, by which also the squares of lines *h m* and *h k* will equal the square of radius *k m*. Because triangles *f k l* and *h k m* have equal sides, they will be equiangular, and angle *f k l* is equal to angle *h k m* by Prop. 8, Book 1. Again, if you mentally conceive the radii *l c* and *m c* of circle *l m* being drawn: the triangles *l k c* and *m k c* will be equilateral and equiangular, and angle *l k c* will equal angle *m k c*. And since angle *b k c* was 19 degrees (since that is the Sun's depression), there remains angle *h k b* as 71 degrees, 13 minutes, and 56 seconds. But angle *e k b* is 90 degrees, because it is a right angle. Therefore, there remains angle *e k h* of 18 degrees, 46 minutes, and 4 seconds.

And because line *k q* divides it into two equal halves—and this is manifest <margin>Because *e k* and *h k*, as well as *e q* and *h q*, are equal: the former by Def. 15, Book 1, because they are radii of circle *e f g h*; the latter by the second corollary of Prop. 36, Book 3, because they are tangent to the circumference *e f g h* from the same point *q*; and *k q* is common to both. Angle *e k q* will therefore equal angle *h k q* by Prop. 8, Book 1. Wherefore, angle *e k h* is cut in two by the straight line *q k*.</margin>—angle *q k e* is therefore 9 degrees, 23 minutes, and 2 seconds. Therefore, angle *k q e* is the complement of a right angle <margin>by Prop. 32, Book 1: because the angle at *e* is a right angle by Prop. 18, Book 3</margin>, and that is 80 degrees, 36 minutes, and 58 seconds. Therefore, its chord <note>term: <term>chord</term> - a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc. Alhazen is using chord tables, the predecessor to modern trigonometry.</note>, which is line *e k*, is 59 degrees, 11 minutes, and 48 seconds relative to the measure where line *k q* is 60 degrees <margin>As shown in the table of straight lines subtended in a circle.</margin>. However, by the measure where line *k e* is 60 degrees, *q r k* will be 60 degrees, 48 minutes, and five-sixths of one minute. But line *k r* out of those is 60 degrees <note>Because *k r* is the radius of the Earth.</note>; therefore, there remains *r q* of 48 minutes and 50 seconds. In terms of miles (where the circumference of the Earth contains 24,000 miles), this is 51 miles, 47 minutes, 14 seconds, and 6 parts out of 11 seconds-parts.

And that is the final height to which the vapors ascending from the Earth are elevated and reach. And that is what we wished to prove.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the measurement of the height of the atmosphere or vapors. It shows the Earth as a central circle with points e, f, g, h on its perimeter and center k. A larger arc a-b-c-d represents the Sun's orbit. Tangent lines m-h-n and l-f-n delineate the Earth's shadow (pyramis umbræ). A horizontal line p-e-q-o represents the horizon tangent to point e. Point q is the intersection of the shadow boundary and the horizon, representing the highest point of illuminated vapors at twilight. Various other lines connect the center k to points on the circles and the tangent lines to form angles for geometric proof.</image-desc>

->THE END.<-

# FRIEDRICH RISNER’S PREFACE TO VITELLO’S OPTICS

-> TO THE <-

## MOST ILLUSTRIOUS QUEEN Catherine de’ Medici, mother of Charles IX, King of France.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'A' depicting a scholar in academic robes seated at a desk with an open book and various scientific instruments, framed within a classical archway.</image-desc>ALHAZEN <note>original: "Alhazenus." The Latinized name of Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), whose work forms the first half of this volume.</note> has dedicated his optical treasures to you, most illustrious Queen—treasures now explained and clarified by our labors and sleepless nights. Vitello follows Alhazen as his guide; and although Alhazen previously passed him by in silence as if he were unknown <note>Alhazen lived two centuries before Vitello and thus could not have known him; Risner is speaking poetically of their intellectual relationship.</note>, Vitello nevertheless follows him as if moved by an awareness of the excellence that preceded him, confessing himself to be Alhazen’s disciple. Indeed, since Vitello saw that the greatest and most noble part of optics—which he had taken from Alhazen—was already dedicated and devoted to you, by what pretense <note>original: "coloris specie," literally "appearance of color," a rhetorical term for a pretext or excuse.</note> could he offer that same "royal purple" <note>A metaphor comparing the high quality of the scientific work to the imperial purple cloth of royalty.</note> to others, or by what change of atmosphere could he sell it as his own? Certainly, with a noble and generous spirit, he will instead adopt you as his own excellent patroness and place himself under the protection and loyalty of your Royal Majesty. 

Therefore, let us now explain more freely who Vitello <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1280/1314) was a friar and philosopher whose work "Perspectiva" became the standard textbook on light in Western universities for centuries.</note> was, and what he aimed for in such a monumental work. He was of the race of the Sarmatians <note>The "Sarmatians" was a classical name revived by Renaissance humanists to refer to the Polish people.</note> (who are today called Poles). For he says in Book 10, Theorem 74, "specifically in our habitable land of Poland," etc. Therefore, in the title of this optical work, he is surnamed "son of Poles and Thuringians," <note>original: "filius Polonorum & Thuringorum."</note> having been born to a Polish father and a Thuringian <note>Thuringia is a region in central Germany.</note> mother, or perhaps the reverse. Such surnames are common in Arabic inscriptions, such as "Alhazen son of Alhayzen" <note>original: "Alhazenus filius Alhayzeni."</note> and the like. Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), the most influential mathematician and astronomer of the 15th century.</note>, however, in his preface to Alfraganus <note>The 9th-century Arab astronomer Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani.</note>, seems to make him a German; for he says, "Our Vitello the Thuringian," etc. Walther <note>Bernhard Walther (1430–1504), a German astronomer and student of Regiomontanus.</note>, the disciple of Regiomontanus, follows this same opinion when he says in his astronomical observations, "and our Vitello," etc. However, in both cases, they could have been referring to a shared dedication to their craft <note>The "art" of optics/astronomy.</note>, rather than a shared homeland. 

But concerning the time in which Vitello flourished, the matter is more controversial. Tanstetter <note>Georg Tanstetter (1482–1535), an Austrian physician and mathematician who edited an earlier edition of Vitello.</note>, in the letter placed before the previously published edition of Vitello's optics, thinks that Vitello lived six hundred years ago, but he is mistaken in this opinion. For Brother William of <meta>catchword: Moerbeke. Risner is about to refer to William of Moerbeke, the famous translator who was a contemporary and friend of Vitello.</meta>

<summary>In this dedication to Catherine de' Medici, Friedrich Risner introduces the 13th-century scholar Vitello as a devoted student of the Arab scientist Alhazen. Risner argues that Vitello was of mixed Polish and German descent and begins to correct historical misconceptions regarding the era in which Vitello lived.</summary>

# FRIEDRICH RISNER’S PREFACE

Moerbeke <note>original: "Morbeta." Referring to William of Moerbeke (c. 1215–1286), a prolific translator of Greek scientific and philosophical texts into Latin.</note> (to whom Vitello dedicated his optics) lived in the year of Christ 1269, as he himself testifies in his work on *geomancy* <note>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</note> (which we have read in manuscript form), which was collected into eight sections in that same year and dedicated to his nephew, Master Arnolpho. The most learned men and excellent mathematicians, Erasmus Reinhold and Caspar Peucer, have also assigned Vitello to this same period. Therefore, it is established by many testimonies that Vitello lived around the year of Christ 1270, nearly three hundred years ago.

But so much for the date. As for the place where he cultivated these studies, it does not seem to have been Sarmatia <note>An ancient name for the region of Eastern Europe encompassing modern-day Poland, where Vitello was born.</note> at all. There are notes within the optical texts showing that Vitello came to Italy and was aided by the libraries of Italy. Indeed, Vitello himself is a witness to his own life in Book 10, Theorem 42, stating that he was first sparked and inflamed toward the optical arts in Italy at Cubalum <note>The modern town of Gazzo, located between Padua and Vicenza.</note> by the contemplation of very thin and clear water: 

> for by the sight of these forms (he says) and their wonderful transformation, the love of this study first enticed us: <note>original: "harum enim formarum intuitu & mirabili transmutatione primum nos amor huius studij allexit"</note>

And in Book 10, Theorem 67, he writes about a rainbow which he had often seen in the water falling violently from a cliff very near Viterbo, and that many properties and characteristics of the rainbow were noticed and observed by him there: 

> that (he says) was the beginning of our thinking, so that we might apply our study to the task at hand. <note>original: "illud nobis principium cogitationis fuit, ut præsenti negotio studium applicaremus."</note>

But it may seem an even stronger argument that Vitello labored in Italy and Rome, both in other noble liberal studies and in optics, because—as he himself testifies in his preface—he first undertook the writing of his optics at the persuasion and encouragement of William of Moerbeke (who was then serving in Rome as the Pope’s *penitentiary* <note>An official in the Roman Catholic Church responsible for matters regarding the internal forum, such as confessions and dispensations.</note>), to whom he later dedicated the finished work. 

Truly, Vitello may have been a Sarmatian; he may have lived in a time not very devoted to the study of letters, especially such hidden studies; he may have found the libraries of Italy covered in dust and the optical writers buried within them; yet what and how much he achieved by the strength of his intellect, his noble monuments will be an everlasting testimony. This is true not only in his *physiological matters*, which he cites in Book 5, Theorem 18, and Book 10, Theorem 80, but also in his books *On the Order of Beings*, and *On Elemental Conclusions* (which are named in the preface and in Book 1, Theorem 28), and in his books *On the Science of Celestial Motions*,

<summary>Friedrich Risner establishes the 13th-century timeline for the author Vitello, arguing that although he was Polish, his scientific inspiration and patronage (specifically from William of Moerbeke) were centered in Italy.</summary>

-># PREFACE.<-

<note>original: "coelestium"</note> heavenly bodies, which he cites in Book 10, Theorem 53: but most of all in the ten books on optics: which, though he drew them primarily from Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the medieval Arabic polymath often called the "father of modern optics."</note> and then from the sources of Greek authors, he certainly expanded with remarkable additions. He collected all the axioms, hypotheses, and theorems of Alhazen, Euclid, and Ptolemy; this was a task of infinite labor. But from Apollonius, Theodosius, Menelaus, Theon, Pappus, Proclus, and others, he sought out the foundations for many demonstrations with singular judgment. He arranged the entire art wonderfully and completely in a singular and most natural order, according to its classes and species: optics <note>The study of direct vision.</note>, catoptrics <note>The study of reflection by mirrors.</note>, and mesoptics <note>The study of refraction through transparent media.</note>. What more can be said? If he is to be considered the craftsman and author of an art who gave it form and soul, then Vitello may rightfully be held as the author of the optical art.

And let these things indeed be said of Vitello and his optical work. However, as for how much effort, industry, and diligence I myself have put into renewing and restoring it, and how much I have labored in reconstructing and shaping it, I think hardly anyone will imagine, unless they compare the old copy with ours. I shall speak of myself sparingly and briefly. In the version of Vitello published until now, there was absolutely no theorem in whose demonstration letters had not been exchanged in many ways, or substituted one for another. In many demonstrations there were <gloss>gaps</gloss> and no explanations; likewise, many words—indeed even entire clauses, and many of them—were missing. All of these I have restored, aided by ancient manuscript copies which P. Ramus <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), a prominent French humanist and mathematician who was Risner's mentor and patron.</note> had sought out from everywhere; and in the entire work, I corrected and amended 3,645 errors in facts and meanings (for I was able to notice that many), along with other lighter ones, which were innumerable.

But besides the transposed letters in the demonstrations, besides the many words, and besides even the entire omitted sentences, the diagrams—which by themselves, without letters, without words, without written sentences, could demonstrate the matter to an intelligent person—were mostly poorly drawn, not matching the demonstrations. What is even more shameful, they were often fitted not to their own, but to other people's theorems; in some theorems, there were none at all. Therefore, I have reshaped all the diagrams from scratch, and I have acted diligently so that no delay caused by such stumbling blocks might hinder students of optics in the future. Finally, I have indicated the passages of ancient geometers and opticians from which most things were taken; at last, I have strained every nerve so that the fruits of optical matters, however great they may be—which are surely very great (as Alhazen’s preface has already touched upon)—

# TO THE **LOVER** OF
## TRUTH, BROTHER WILLIAM OF
### MOERBEKE, WITELO, SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND
->Poles, <note>original: "Vitello filius Thuringorum et Polonorum"</note> wishes a happy gaze of the eternal light through the unrefracted ray of the mind,<-
->and a clear understanding of the things written below.<-

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial letter "V" depicting a scholar seated at a desk with books, representing the author Witelo or the recipient William of Moerbeke.</image-desc>

THE studious love of universal beings, holding you bound, has joined me to you as one seeking the same thing, so much so that your will is a command to me; may your will also keep me from the passions of those feelings that displease you. Therefore, because to you—as a diligent examiner of all being (while you join the <term>intelligible being</term><note>Meaning reality as it is grasped by the intellect rather than just the senses.</note> proceeding from its first principles to individual sensible beings by way of cause through the act of the mind, and investigate the individual causes of individual things)—it occurred that the influence of divine powers happens to lower corporal <note>physical</note> things through superior corporal powers in a wonderful way. For lower physical things in the order of the parts of the universe do not participate in divine power in an incorporeal way, but participate in that contracted power through the higher things of their own order, as they are able. Just as in the other order of <term>intellectual substances</term><note>Often referring to angels or celestial intelligences in medieval philosophy.</note>, you have perceived with the sharpness of your mind that lower substances are made through the illumination of the higher ones of their own order (derived from the fountain of divine goodness, as the nature of each allows) by way of intelligible influences. Thus, just as all being of things flows from the divine being, and all intelligibility from the divine intelligence, and all life from the divine life: the divine light is the principle, middle, and end of these influences in an intelligible way—as that from which, through which, and to which all things are disposed. But of the corporal influences, <term>sensible light</term><note>Light that can be seen by the eyes.</note> is the medium, wonderfully likening and connecting the lowest bodies (which vary according to their forms and locations) to the higher perpetual bodies which exist in potentiality only according to their location. For light is the diffusion of the highest corporal forms through the nature of physical form, applying itself to the matter of lower bodies, and impressing upon perishable bodies the forms of the divine and indivisible craftsmen <note>the "artificers" or creative principles</note> carried with it in a divisible way; and by its incorporation with them, it always produces new specific or individual forms, in which the divine craftsmanship of both the moved spheres and the moving powers results through the act of light. Because, therefore, the light of physical form has action: it equals itself to the physical dimensions of the bodies into which it flows, and extends itself with the extension of the capable bodies; yet because it always has its fountain (from which it flows) according to the beginning of its power, it takes on the dimension of distance (which is a **straight line**) by accident, and thus fits the name of **ray** to itself. And since a natural straight line is always in some natural surface—and the property of surfaces (which happens to them through the lines that terminate them) is the **angle**—therefore the consideration of the angle belongs to the luminous ray; and the perpendicularity of the rays at **right angles** is the cause. But the slanting of the radiating body over the irradiated body causes **acute and obtuse angles**: and the influences of the lights are varied according to these. When, therefore, the diligence of your skillful genius saw that according to these things, the divine power of celestial influences changed with respect to receptive things, and saw that the things acted upon varied not only according to the active powers, but according to the diversity of the mode of action: it pleased you to be occupied in the hidden investigation of that matter, and to apply your studious soul to its diligent inquiry. And so, searching for the books of the ancients for you on this business, there occurred the boredom of **Arabic wordiness**, the entanglement of **Greek**, and also the scarcity of **Latin writing**, especially because the office of the <term>Roman Penitentiary</term><note>A high-ranking official in the Catholic Church responsible for issues of penance and conscience; William of Moerbeke held this position.</note> committed to you (a part of whose care you carry), believing you should help penitents more by practical intellect than speculative, held you back from a multitude of things to be seen.

<summary>This is the introductory dedication of Witelo's work on optics to William of Moerbeke, explaining how divine influence flows through light into the physical world via geometry (rays and angles).</summary>
