<meta>This page continues the dedication to William of Moerbeke, where Witelo explains why he set aside his broader philosophical work to write this specific treatise on optics at William's request. It then transitions into the formal table of contents/summary for the ten books of the treatise.</meta>

...for you preferred to aid the ailments of languishing souls with a divine antidote <note>Likely referring to William’s theological work or his role as a chaplain and translator for the Pope.</note> rather than simply relieving the ignorance of men. Thinking me to be at leisure, you wished to bind me under the bond of love by which I am joined to you, so that I might take up this burden of labor pleasing to you and apply my mind to these subjects not yet well known to me. But I, who desire to obey all your commands, accepting your wish as a mandate, have set aside for a time a greater project—a chapter concerning the <term>order of beings</term><note>Latin: "de ordine entium." This suggests Witelo was working on a large metaphysical work before shifting to optics.</note> which I had previously undertaken to write—and I have come to write this present work to the best of my ability (though I confess myself unequal to the task). 

Observing also that the same power of <term>form</term><note>In medieval philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that allows it to be perceived.</note> is sent into the opposite sense, and that light is the first of all sensible forms, and because we intend to investigate the <term>efficient causes</term><note>The primary source of change or rest; in this case, what physically causes us to see.</note> of all sensible things—of which sight reveals many differences to us—I decided to investigate the aforementioned matters through the mode of visible entities. This follows the path of many men who treated this science before us, calling it by the name of **OPTICS** <note>original: "PERSPECTIVORVM"</note>. I approve of their naming as it is pleasing, even though the intention of the writer inclines more toward discussing the most hidden mode of action of natural forms, so that the present work may respond to your desires. For that which is acted upon more perceptibly in the sense of sight is by no means avoided in natural things in the absence of that very sense. For the presence of the sense adds nothing to the actions of natural forms. 

Therefore, running through every mode of vision by mathematical or natural demonstration, I shall treat those things concerning the natural actions of forms through the mode of <term>visible passions</term><note>In this context, "passions" refers to how light is acted upon or affected by the objects it hits.</note> according to a triple mode of seeing, to the extent of my ability. For in all those modes of seeing, natural forms diffuse themselves to the sight, and visual rays do not go out to capture the forms of things <note>Witelo is rejecting the "extramission" theory (eyes sending out beams) in favor of the "intromission" theory (objects sending light to the eye).</note>. Hence, if sight is not present for the forms diffused through the natural bodies capable of receiving them, the natural action will not cease because of this; rather, the forms will impress themselves as much as they can upon the underlying bodies unlike themselves. Therefore, you, a man of desires for every scientific good, receive what you ordered to be done; in which, if you find anything unrefined, may you moderate it with your more perceptive genius.

# THE DIVISION OF THE WHOLE WORK INTO TEN
### Books, and what is treated in each.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'P' depicting a landscape or garden scene with figures.</image-desc>

**P**RESENTLY, we have seen fit to distinguish this business into ten partial books. *Wishing to conclude by mathematical demonstration every visible entity, as the "passion" happens to its visibility, and to walk this path as certainly as is possible for us: we have made this book stand by itself, except for those things which depend on the Elements of **Euclid**, and a few things which depend on the **Conic Elements of Apollonius of Perga** <note>A 3rd-century BC Greek geometer known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on curved shapes.</note>, which are only two, and which we have used in this science, as will appear later in the process. 

In the first book of this science, we set forth the **axioms** which are necessary for this science beyond the elements of Euclid; and in this, we declare those two things which were demonstrated by Apollonius. However, many of these things which we set forth in this book are contained in that book which we call the **Elements of Conclusions**, in which we have written down universally all things that have appeared to us, and which have come down to us from men after Euclid, concluded universally for the necessity of particular sciences. 

In the second book, we have treated the mode of the projection of rays through a medium of one **diaphanous** <note>Transparent material, like air or water.</note> substance, or many, upon various figures of bodies; as well as the projection of shadows and the shaping of light falling through windows, as these are the things that are preamble to the sensible action of natural forms, and which happen when the sense is not present. 

In the third book, we have treated the organ of sight and the essential mode of seeing in its own way, as the science of optics allows. 

In the fourth book, we run through the **deceptions** which happen to the sight according to the direct mode of seeing through one medium, whether they be mathematical or natural passions. 

In the fifth book, transferring ourselves to the other mode of seeing which occurs through **reflections** from polished bodies, which we call **mirrors**, we have treated the passions common to every mirror, whether it be plane, spherical, cylindrical or pyramidal, concave or convex. For these are all the mirrors from which...*

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Witelo’s "Perspectiva." Having previously discussed his motivation for writing and the nature of light as a primary form, he now outlines the specific contents of the ten books of the treatise and explains his theory that the laws of optics apply to all natural forces, not just human sight.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<sig>A 2</sig>

*...regular reflection can take place, as we shall declare in its proper place. However, by these <term>mirrors</term><note>Latin: "specula." In this context, Witelo refers to any surface capable of reflecting light, not just glass looking-glasses.</note> we do not mean only bodies polished by artifice, but rather those polished by nature. For when we apply a demonstration to these mirrors, we understand natural bodies of the same shape. For that which occurs by way of example in artificial bodies must necessarily occur with greater certainty in natural bodies. And while we thus discourse through the shapes of mirrors, we declare that celestial and all natural <term>influences</term><note>Latin: "influentias." Medieval science held that stars and planets "flowed" their power down into the earthly realm; Witelo argues this follows the laws of reflection.</note> are reflected from subject bodies to other bodies in a certain mode of reflection. Indeed, the operation of nature lies hidden in these diversities; and from these same agents, according to the mode of this diversity, a diversity of forms arises. This happens to our sight if it should reach the point of reflection—namely, that reflection occurs toward the eyes—since the presence of sight adds nothing to natural things, vision being as it were something subsequent to existing natural forms and bodies.*

*We have proposed the common <term>passions</term><note>Latin: "passiones." In medieval philosophy, these are the "undergoings" or properties and effects that happen to a subject.</note> and all the properties of plane mirrors in the fifth book. In the sixth book, we have demonstrated the effects that happen to sight and to things from reflection made by convex spherical mirrors. In the seventh, we have set forth the properties of effects from convex columnar <note>cylindrical</note> or pyramidal mirrors; and we have joined these two mirrors together because of the similarity of many of their properties. In the eighth, we have treated more at length the reflections that occur from concave spherical mirrors. In the ninth also, we dealt with those that occur from concave columnar or pyramidal mirrors; and in the same book, we have added a treatise on certain irregular mirrors, from whose total surface the reflection of light and power is made to a single point (which we call <term>burning mirrors</term><note>Latin: "specula comburentia." These are parabolic or specially curved mirrors designed to concentrate sunlight to start fires.</note>).*

*In the tenth book of this science, we have dealt with the third mode of seeing, which is through the medium of another <term>transparent body</term><note>Latin: "diaphani." A substance like water, air, or glass that allows light to pass through.</note>, such as when vision occurs through air under water, or under glass. We also deal with the deceptions which happen to the sight from this; for even if sight is not present, the same effects happen to the acting power. And in this tenth treatise, we have also added an effect happening to sight alone from the diversity of media, which is the impression of the "bow of the demon," which is called the <term>iris</term><note>Latin: "iris." While the text uses "arcus demonis," it explicitly identifies it as the rainbow. This may be a regional medieval term or a transcription variant of "arcus dominus" (the Lord's bow).</note>; for the generation of that also has its origin in this present science. And so, having thoroughly treated the general properties of visible questions, we bring the work to an end.*

*It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that there is a triple mode of seeing: one through one medium only, which is direct vision; another through the reflection of visible forms from polished bodies; and another through the refraction of visible forms because of a diversity of media. These three modes of seeing are also signs of a triple action of forms and of all celestial and natural powers. For some act directly upon a susceptible object, and this action is stronger, because it is directly intended by nature and occurs according to straight lines. However, a bodily weakness happens to that power because of a greater distance of the agent from the thing acted upon; for the sun does not heat distant things as much as closer heatable things which are of the same disposition. Another natural action occurs through reflection from other bodies, as the rays of the sun are reflected from the body of the moon; for although, because of the thinness of the lunar body, some of the solar power passes through, most of the rays are reflected downwards, as if from a convex spherical mirror. Therefore, everything we have said regarding the properties of mirrors is applicable to that action, the shape of the body (from which the reflection occurs) likening itself to the shape of a mirror. The third kind of natural action is through several media of different transparencies, which similarly receives a diversity in its mode of acting, which we say happens to the sight. In these natural actions, therefore, sight is a sign, not a cause, unless perhaps there is a deception arising in the sight itself; for even if visual perception does not exist, the modes of all natural actions remain the same. These things having been premised, let us approach our intent. However, we do not wish this to be hidden from the reader: that when we argue from Euclid’s book of Elements, we are content with the naming of the book number and theorem alone; but when we bring forth something from this book of ours, we name both the number and the theorem of this book.*

<meta>This page transitions from the general philosophical introduction to the formal geometric foundation of the treatise. Witelo begins Book 1 by establishing the basic definitions and postulates necessary for his mathematical demonstrations of light and vision, moving from the physical nature of "influences" discussed on the previous page to the abstract geometry of spheres and proportions.</meta>

# WITELO, SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND POLES, FIRST BOOK ON OPTICS.

## DEFINITIONS.

The things which we set forth at the beginning of this first book by way of principles are these:

1. We call a **cathetus** <note>original: "Cathetum." In medieval geometry, this refers to a line dropped perpendicularly onto a surface; in modern optics, we call this the "normal."</note> a line erected perpendicularly over some surface.

2. We call a **pole** every point of a line erected orthogonally from the center over the surface of a circle.

3. We call a line or surface **convex** which has some regular curvature on the outside.

4. We call a line or surface **concave** which has some regular curvature on the inside.

5. We call a line **perpendicular to a convex or concave surface** which is erected over a plane surface that is tangent to the convex or concave surface at the point of its incidence. <note>Witelo is explaining that to find a perpendicular on a curve, you must first imagine a flat plane touching that curve at a single point.</note>

6. Circles are said to be **intersecting each other** when there is some common line between their diameters, with one not containing the other.

7. A **great circle of a sphere** is so called because, passing through the center of the sphere, it divides it into two equal parts.

8. A **lesser circle of a sphere**, however, is so called because it neither passes through the center of the sphere nor divides it into two equal parts.

9. We call spheres **equal** whose diameters are equal.

10. We call spheres or circles containing one another **equidistant** <note>original: "equidistantes." This is the medieval term for "concentric."</note> when lines drawn from the center of the larger, from the convex of the smaller to the concave of the larger, are equal.

11. We call spheres **tangent to each other** which, touching each other externally or internally, do not intersect.

12. We call spheres **intersecting each other** when, the spheres not containing one another, the diameter of one is cut by the other.

13. We call spheres **intersecting each other internally** when the larger part of one is contained in the other.

14. We say a **plane surface is tangent to a sphere** when, although it touches the sphere, it does not cut it when extended in any direction.

15. The **denomination of a proportion** <note>original: "Denominatio proportionis." In medieval mathematics, this refers to the value of a ratio, often expressed as a fraction or integer.</note> of the first to the second is called the quantity which, multiplied by the lesser, produces the greater, or which divides the greater according to the lesser.

16. A **proportion** is said to be **composed** of two proportions when the denomination of that proportion is produced from the multiplication of the denominations of those proportions, one by the other.

---

## POSTULATES.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram located in the right margin, illustrating two intersecting lines. A vertical line connects points 'b' (top) and 'c' (bottom). Two diagonal lines extend from point 'b' down to points 'a' (left) and 'd' (right), forming two symmetrical angles with the central vertical line.</image-desc>

We postulate the following:

1. That **equal angles** established over the same point contain an equal distance of equal lines: for example, if angles *a b c* and *c b d* are equal, and lines *a b* and *b d* are equal, then line *a b* will be as distant from line *b c* as line *b d* is distant from the same line *b c*. <note>This postulate is fundamental to Witelo's later proofs regarding the symmetry of reflection.</note>

2. Likewise, that between any two points a line can be extended, and between any two lines a surface can be extended.

3. Likewise, when two plane surfaces touch each other, they become one surface.

4. Likewise, that two plane surfaces cannot enclose a body. <note>This follows Euclidean logic; it takes at least four planes to enclose a three-dimensional volume, such as a tetrahedron.</note>

5. Likewise, that all these same proportions are composed of similar proportions, and are divided into similar proportions, and have the same denominations.

<summary>Witelo establishes sixteen geometric definitions and five postulates that form the mathematical foundation for his optical theories, focusing on the properties of spheres, perpendiculars, and ratios.</summary>
<keywords>geometry, cathetus, spheres, great circle, proportion, postulates, Witelo, optics, convex, concave</keywords>

<header>T H E O R E M S</header>

### 1. *All parallel lines necessarily lie in the same plane surface.*

->From the 35th definition of Book 1 of the Elements <note>Original: "1 element." refers to Euclid’s *Elements*.</note><-

Let there be two parallel <note>Original: *æquidistantes*, literally "equidistant."</note> lines, *a-b* and *c-d*, arranged in any way: I say that they are in the same plane surface. For let them be joined by the line *b-d*. Since, therefore, the lines *a-b* and *b-d* are joined at an angle: it is clear that they are in the same surface by Proposition 2 of Book 11. Similarly, because the lines *c-d* and *b-d* are joined at an angle, they will be in the same surface. But the line *b-d* is in only one plane surface, because for a part of it to be in the air <note>Original: *in sublimi*, meaning in a different plane or dimension.</note> and a part in the plane is impossible by Proposition 1 of Book 11. It is clear, therefore, that the lines *a-b* and *c-d* necessarily consist in the same plane surface contained between them and between the lines joining the ends of those lines: which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two horizontal parallel lines labeled 'a-c' at the top and 'b-d' at the bottom. A vertical line connects point 'c' to 'd'.</image-desc>

### 2. *A line drawn from a point on one of two parallel lines must necessarily meet the other if it is of indefinite length. Proclus’s Lemma to Proposition 29, Book 1 of the Elements.*

Let there be two parallel lines, *a-b* and *c-d*: one of which, namely *a-b*, is cut by line *b-e* at point *b*. I say that line *b-e* will also cut line *c-d*. For because line *c-d* is assumed to be of indefinite quantity, let line *b-e* be extended toward it: if it meets with *c-d*, the proposition is held. If it does not meet: it is clear by the definition of parallel lines that line *b-e* is parallel to line *c-d*; and because lines *a-b* and *b-e* are both parallel to line *c-d*: by Proposition 30 of Book 1, line *e-b* will be parallel to line *a-b*. But it is clear from the hypothesis that they meet, as at point *b*: therefore line *b-e* is not parallel to line *c-d*: therefore line *b-e* necessarily meets with line *c-d*: which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram with two parallel vertical lines 'a-b' and 'c-d'. A diagonal line originates from point 'b' and extends downward and to the right, intersecting 'a-b' at an angle and continuing towards the line 'c-d', labeled with a 'b' or 'e' at the end.</image-desc>

### 3. *Given three lines, to find a fourth line proportional to any of the three according to the ratio of the other two. From Proposition 12, Book 6 of the Elements.*

Let there be three given lines, which are *a-b*, *c-d*, and *e-f*, for one of which, such as *a-b*, a fourth proportional must be found according to the ratio of the other two, which are *c-d* and *e-f*. Therefore, let two lines equal to the two lines *c-d* and *e-f* be cut from one continuous line, which is *a-e-f* by Proposition 3 of Book 1, and let the third given line, namely *a-b*, be joined at an angle to that line *a-e-f* at point *a*. And from the common point distinguishing the two cut lines (which is point *e*) let line *e-b* be drawn to the end of the third of the given lines, which is *a-b*: and from point *f* let a line be drawn parallel to line *e-b* by Proposition 31 of Book 1, which is *f-g*. Then let line *a-b* be extended continuously and straight until it cuts line *f-g*: it will cut it, moreover, by the previous theorem: let the point of meeting be *g*. I say that by Proposition 2 of Book 6, the ratio of line *a-b* to line *b-g* is the same as that of the given line *a-e* to the given line *e-f*. Similarly, it can be demonstrated for any of the others with respect to the remaining two: thus the proposition is clear.

<image-desc>A diagram illustrating Theorem 3. At the top right are three horizontal lines of different lengths labeled 'a-b', 'c-d', and 'e-f'. Below is a triangle-like construction with vertex 'a'. A line 'a-f-g' extends downward, and another 'a-e-b' extends to the right. Parallel lines connect 'e' to 'b' and 'f' to 'g'.</image-desc>

### 4. *When equal lines are added to two unequal lines of a known ratio: the ratio of the larger to the smaller is decreased. From Proposition 8, Book 5 of the Elements.*

Let there be two unequal lines *a-b* and *c-d* of a known ratio: and let line *a-b* be larger than line *c-d*: and let line *b-e* be added to *a-b*, and line *d-f* to *c-d*: and let lines *b-e* and *d-f* be equal. I say that the ratio of line *a-e* to line *c-f* is less than the ratio of line *a-b* to line *c-d*. For since three lines are given, which are *a-b*, *c-d*, and *b-e*: let a line proportional to line *b-e* be found by the preceding theorem according to the ratio of lines *a-b* and *c-d*, which shall be *d-g*. Because, therefore, line *a-b* is greater than line *c-d*, it is clear that line *b-e* is greater than line *d-g*: therefore line *d-f* is also greater than line *d-g*. Therefore, by Proposition 3 of Book 1, let line *d-f* be cut equal to *d-g*. Since, therefore, the ratio of line *a-b* to line *c-d* is as the ratio of line *b-e* to line *d-g*: by Proposition 15 of Book 5, the ratio of the whole line *a-e* to the total line *c-g* will be as the ratio of line *a-b* to line *c-d*: but by Proposition 8 of Book 5, the ratio of line *a-e* to line...

> ### 5. *When the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then, conversely, the ratio of the second to the first will be as the fourth to the third.*
> ->From Definition 13 and the corollary to Proposition 4 of Book 5 of the *Elements*.<note>The *Elements* refers to Euclid’s foundational work on geometry.</note><-

<image-desc>Four horizontal line segments of decreasing length, stacked vertically and labeled a, b, c, and d from top to bottom.</image-desc>

For let *a* be the first, and *b* the second, and *c* the third, and *d* the fourth: and let the ratio of *a* to *b* be as *c* to *d*. I say that, conversely, the ratio of *b* to *a* will be as *d* to *c*. For since the ratio of *a* to *b* is as *c* to *d*, then by permutation <note>Original: *permutatim*, referring to the alternating of terms in a proportion (if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d).</note> according to Proposition 16 of Book 5, the ratio of *a* to *c* is as *b* to *d*. Therefore, the ratio of *b* to *d* is as *a* to *c*. Thus, again by Proposition 16 of Book 5, by permutation the ratio of *b* to *a* will be as *d* to *c*—that is, the second to the first as the fourth to the third: which is what was proposed.

---

> ### 6. *When, among four quantities, the ratio of the first to the second is greater than that of the third to the fourth, then, conversely, the ratio of the second to the first will be less than that of the fourth to the third.*
> ->Proposition 26 of Book 5 of the *Elements* in Campanus.<note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296) wrote a famous commentary and edition of Euclid's *Elements* used throughout the Middle Ages.</note><-

<image-desc>Five horizontal line segments of varying lengths, stacked vertically and labeled a, b, e, c, and d from top to bottom.</image-desc>

Let the ratio of line *a* to line *b* be greater than the ratio of line *c* to line *d*. I say that, conversely, the ratio of line *b* to line *a* will be less than the ratio of line *d* to line *c*. For let it be according to Theorem 3 of this book, so that the ratio of line *c* to line *d* is the same as the ratio of line *e* to line *b*. Since, therefore, the ratio of line *a* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of line *c* to line *d* by the hypothesis, it is clear that the ratio of line *e* to line *b* is less than the ratio of line *a* to line *b*. Therefore, by Proposition 10 of Book 5, line *a* is greater than line *e*. And because the ratio of line *e* to line *b* is as the ratio of line *c* to line *d*, then by the previous theorem the ratio of line *b* to line *e* will be the same as that of line *d* to line *c*. However, by Proposition 8 of Book 5, the ratio of line *b* to line *a* is less than its ratio to line *e*. Therefore, the ratio of line *b* to line *a* is less than the ratio of line *d* to line *c*: which is what was proposed.

> ### 7. *If, of four proportional quantities, the first is greater than the second, and the third is greater than the fourth, then by conversion the ratio of the first to its excess over the second will be the same as the ratio of the third to its excess over the fourth.*
> ->From Definition 16 and the corollary to Proposition 19 of Book 5.<note>This theorem deals with "conversion of ratio" (eversio), which relates a whole magnitude to its difference with another.</note><-

<image-desc>Two horizontal line segments. The upper segment is labeled with points a, b, and c. The lower segment is labeled with points d, e, and f.</image-desc>

Let there be four proportional lines: *a-c* the first, *b-c* the second, *d-f* the third, and *e-f* the fourth. And let line *a-c* be greater than line *b-c*, and line *d-f* greater than line *e-f*. Also, let line *a-c* exceed line *b-c* by line *a-b*, and let line *d-f* exceed line *e-f* by line *d-e*. I say that the ratio of line *a-c* to line *a-b* will be the same as the ratio of line *d-f* to line *d-e*. For since the ratio of line *a-c* to line *b-c* is as the ratio of line *d-f* to line *e-f*, then by permutation according to Proposition 16 of Book 5, the ratio of line *a-c* to line *d-f* is as the ratio of line *b-c* to line *e-f*. Therefore, by Proposition 19 of Book 5, the ratio of line *a-b* to line *d-e* will be as the ratio of line *a-c* to line *d-f*. Thus, by permutation according to Proposition 16 of Book 5, the ratio of line *a-b* to line *a-c* will be as the ratio of line *d-e* to line *d-f*. Therefore, by Theorem 5 of this book, the ratio of line *a-c* to line *a-b* will be as the ratio of line *d-f* to line *d-e*: which is what was proposed.

---

> ### 8. *If, of four quantities, the first is greater than the second, and the third is greater than the fourth, then the ratio of the first to the fourth will be greater than the ratio of the second to the third.*
> ->A corollary from Proposition 8 of Book 5 of the *Elements*.<note>This theorem establishes how inequalities between magnitudes affect their relative ratios.</note><-

<image-desc>Four horizontal line segments stacked vertically and labeled a, b, c, and d from top to bottom.</image-desc>

Let there be four lines *a, b, c, d*: and let the first, *a*, be greater than the second, *b*; and let the third, *c*, be greater than the fourth, *d*. I say that the ratio of line *a* to line *d* is greater than the ratio of line *b* to line *c*. For because line *c* is greater than line *d* by the hypothesis, it is clear through Proposition 8 of Book 5 that the ratio of line *a* to line *d* is greater than its ratio to line *c*. However, the ratio of line *b* to line *c* is less than the ratio of line *a* to line *c* by the same Proposition 8 of Book 5, since, as was stated, line *a* is greater than line *b*. And since whatever is greater than the greater is also greater than the lesser <note>This is a logical axiom: if x > y and y > z, then x > z.</note>, it is clear that the ratio of line *a* to line *d* is greater than the ratio of line *b* to line *c*: thus the proposition is clear.

### BOOK I.

I say that the ratio of line *a* to *b* is greater than the ratio of *c* to *d*. For since line *a* is greater than line *c*, it is evident through Proposition 8 of Book 5 <note>Witelo is referencing Euclid’s *Elements*. Proposition 8 of Book 5 states that of two unequal magnitudes, the greater has a larger ratio to the same magnitude than the lesser has.</note> that the ratio of line *a* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of line *c* to line *b*. Therefore, the ratio of the first line *a* to the second *b* is greater than the ratio of the third line *c* to the fourth *d*: and this is what was proposed.

**10. *If, among four quantities, the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the ratio of the third to the fourth, then alternately, the ratio of the first to the third will be greater than the ratio of the second to the fourth.***
***From Definition 12, and Propositions 16 and 27 of Book 5 of the Elements in the edition of Campanus.*** <note>Campanus of Novara (1222–1296) produced a highly influential Latin edition of Euclid’s *Elements* that Witelo uses as his primary reference.</note>

Let there be four lines *a, b, c, d*: and let the ratio of *a* to *b* be greater than *c* to *d*. I say that, <term>permutatim<note>In geometry, "permutation" or "alternation" refers to swapping the inner terms of a proportion (if a:b > c:d, then a:c > b:d).</note></term> alternately, the ratio of line *a* to line *c* will be greater than the ratio of line *b* to line *d*. For let there be, by the 3rd proposition of this book, a ratio of line *e* to line *b* that is exactly as line *c* to *d*. Therefore, from the hypothesis and from Proposition 10 of Book 5, line *e* will be less than line *a*. Thus, by Proposition 8 of Book 5, the ratio of line *a* to line *c* is greater than the ratio of line *e* to line *c*. However, from the previous statements and by Proposition 16 of Book 5, the ratio of line *e* to line *c* is as the ratio of line *b* to line *d*. It is clearly evident, therefore, that the ratio of line *a* to line *c* is greater than the ratio of line *b* to line *d*: which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram consisting of five horizontal line segments of varying lengths, vertically stacked and labeled from top to bottom as a, b, e, c, and d.</image-desc>

**11. *When the ratio of the first of four quantities to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, then conjointly, the ratio of the first and second together to the second will be greater than the third and fourth together to the fourth.***
***From Definition 14, and Propositions 18 and 28 of Book 5 of the Elements in the edition of Campanus.***

Let there be four lines *a, b, c, d* where the ratio of *a* to *b* is greater than *c* to *d*. I say that the ratio of the whole line *a-b* to line *b* will be greater than the ratio of the whole line *c-d* to line *d*. For let there be, by the 3rd proposition of this book, a ratio of line *e* to line *b* which is the same as the ratio of line *c* to *d*. Therefore, from the hypothesis, the ratio of line *a* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of line *e* to line *b*. Consequently, by Proposition 10 of Book 5, line *a* is greater than line *e*. The whole line *a-b* is therefore greater than the whole line *e-b*. Thus, by Proposition 8 of Book 5, the ratio of the whole line *a-b* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of the whole line *e-b* to line *b*. By Proposition 18 of Book 5, however, the ratio of line *e-b* to line *b* is the same as the ratio of line *c-d* to line *d*; for it was established in the premises that the ratio of line *e* to line *b* is as line *c* to line *d*. Therefore, the ratio of line *a-b* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of line *c-d* to line *d*: which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram consisting of five horizontal line segments. The first line is composed of two segments labeled a and b, with the transition point marked e. Below it are two separate line segments labeled c and d.</image-desc>

**12. *If the ratio of the first and second quantities together to the second is greater than the third and fourth together to the fourth, then disjointly, the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than the third to the fourth.***
***From Definition 15, and Propositions 17 and 29 of Book 5 of the Elements in the edition of Campanus.***

Let the ratio of the whole line *a-b* to its part, line *b*, be greater than the ratio of the whole line *c-d* to its part *d*. I say that, <term>disiunctim<note>Also known as "division of ratio." This means if (a+b):b > (c+d):d, then a:b > c:d.</note></term> disjointly, the ratio of line *a* to line *b* will be greater than the ratio of line *c* to line *d*. For let there be, by the 3rd proposition of this book, a ratio of line *e-b* to line *b* just like the ratio of line *c-d* to line *d*. Therefore, from the hypothesis, the ratio of line *a-b* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of line *e-b* to the same line *b*. Thus, by Proposition 10 of Book 5, line *a-b* will be greater than line *e-b*. Removing the common line *b* from both, there remains line *a* greater than line *e*. It follows from Proposition 8 of Book 5 that the ratio of line *a* to line *b* is greater than the ratio of line *e* to the same line *b*. But by the premises, the ratio of line *e-b* to line *b* is as the ratio of line *c-d* to line *d*. Therefore, by Proposition 17 of Book 5, the ratio of line *e* to line *b* will be as the ratio of line *c* to line *d*. Thus, the ratio of line *a* to line *b* will be greater than the ratio of line *c* to line *d*: and this is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram showing horizontal line segments. The top segment has points marked A, e, and b. Below it is a segment with points c and d. These represent quantities in the disjunction proof.</image-desc>

**13. *For any three quantities arranged in any order, where the ratio of the middle one to each of the extremes is known: the ratio of the first to the third will be composed of the ratio of the first to the second and the second to the third. From which it is clear that the ratio of the extremes to each other is always composed of the ratio of the intermediates to each other and to those same extremes.***

-># WITELO’S OPTICS<-

...from Theon on the 5th definition of the 6th book of the *Elements* and commentaries on the 1st book of Ptolemy’s *Great Construction* <note>Original: *Magnae Constructionis*, better known today by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*.</note>. Also from the commentaries of Eutocius on the 8th theorem of the 2nd book of Archimedes’ *On the Sphere and Cylinder*.

Let there be three lines apart from the others, which are *a*, *b*, and *g* <note>Witelo uses *g* (gamma) as the third letter of the sequence.</note>, the first of which (*a*) is greater than the middle (*b*), and *b* is greater than the third, which is *g*. Let the ratio of *b* to both extremes be known. I say that the ratio of line *a* to the third line *g* is composed of the ratio of line *a* to line *b*, and the ratio of line *b* to line *g*. Since the ratio of line *a* to line *b* is known, let the quantity *d* be the <term>denomination<note>In medieval mathematics, the "denomination" of a ratio is the number or fraction that expresses its value.</note> of that ratio. Similarly, because the ratio of line *b* to line *g* is known, let the denomination of that ratio be the quantity *e*; and let the quantity *z* be the denomination of the ratio of line *a* to line *g*. I say that *z* is produced by multiplying *e* by *d*. For since, by the 15th definition of this book, line *a* is produced by multiplying the denomination *z* (of the ratio of *a* to *g*) by the line *g* (which is smaller than *a*); and similarly, line *a* is produced by multiplying *d* by line *b*. Therefore, let *z* be the first, *d* the second, line *b* the third, and line *g* the fourth. Since that which is produced from the multiplication of the first and the fourth is equal to that which is produced from the second and the third, it is evident through Proposition 16 of Book 6 <note>Of Euclid’s *Elements*.</note> that the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth. Therefore, the ratio of *z* to *d* is as the ratio of line *b* to line *g*. Thus, the denomination of the ratio of *z* to *d*, by the 5th supposition, is the same as the denomination of the ratio of line *b* to line *g*. But the denomination of the ratio of line *b* to line *g* is the quantity *e*; therefore, the denomination of the ratio of *z* to *d* is the same *e*. Thus, *z* is produced by multiplying *e* by *d*. Because the denomination of the ratio of line *a* to line *g* (which is *z*) is produced by multiplying the denomination of the ratio of *a* to *b* by the denomination of the ratio of *b* to *g*, it is clear by the 16th definition of this book that the ratio of the first line *a* to the third line *g* is composed of the ratio of the first line *a* to the second *b*, and the ratio of the second line *b* to the third *g*: which was the first point to be proved. In the same way, it can be easily demonstrated for any number of intermediate lines placed between any two extremes: for the ratio of the extremes to each other is always composed of all the ratios of the intermediates to each other and to the extremes themselves. This must be demonstrated similarly by the method of division if the middle line happens to be greater than either of the extremes. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing five separate line segments. In the top row, two horizontal lines are labeled 'a' and 'b'. In the middle row, two horizontal lines are labeled 'd' and 'e'. At the bottom, a single horizontal line is labeled 'z'.</image-desc>

> 14. ***If a straight line falls across two straight lines and makes the alternate angles unequal, or the two internal angles less than two right angles, or the external angle unequal to the internal angle: it is necessary that those two lines meet on the side of the smaller angles, but it is impossible for them to meet on the other side. And if the lines meet, it is necessary that the said angles behave in one of the proposed ways. From Propositions 27 and 28 of Book 1 of the Elements. Proclus’ Lemma to Proposition 16 of Book 1 of the Elements.*** <note>This is a variation of Euclid’s famous Fifth Postulate regarding parallel lines.</note>

Let there be two lines *ab* and *cd*, which the line *ef* cuts according to what is proposed. I say that the lines *ab* and *cd* will meet. For if they do not meet, it is clear that they are parallel; therefore, by Proposition 29 of Book 1, the opposite of the hypothesis follows, which is inconsistent. Therefore, they will meet. Indeed, it is necessary that they meet on the side of the smaller angles; for if they should meet on the side of the larger angles, it would follow that the exterior angle of the resulting triangle would be smaller than the interior angle, which is against Propositions 16 and 32 of Book 1. And because, by the preceding proofs, they meet on the side of the smaller angles, if it were granted that they met on the side of the larger angles, it would follow that two straight lines would enclose a surface <note>Meaning they would enclose a space or shape with only two sides.</note>, which is impossible. It is therefore impossible for them to meet on the side of the larger angles: which was the first point to be proved. But also, if it is granted that those lines meet, it is necessary that the angles behave in one of the proposed ways by Proposition 32 of Book 1. Thus, the whole of what was proposed is clear, while always maintaining the hypothesis.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 14 showing two lines, 'a b' and 'c d', which converge toward the right. They are intersected by a transversal line labeled 'e' at the top and 'f' at the bottom.</image-desc>

> 15. ***When lines, intersecting each other between two parallel lines from whose endpoints they are produced, have the parts of the same line on each side of the intersection equal to each other: it is necessary that the lines between which the intersection occurs be equal.***

For example: let it be that two lines *ab* and *cd*, between two parallel lines from whose endpoints they are produced (which are *ad* and *cb*), intersect at point *e* so that line *ae* is equal to line *eb*, and line *ce* is equal to *ed*. I say that line *ad* is equal to line *cb*. For since by Proposition 15 of Book 1 the angle *aed* is equal to angle *ceb*, then by the hypothesis and by Proposition 4 of Book 1, line *ad* will be equal to line *cb*: which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 15 showing two intersecting lines 'a b' and 'c d' meeting at point 'e'. These two segments are bounded by two parallel lines 'a d' and 'c b', forming a bowtie-like shape.</image-desc>

16. *If straight lines are produced through the endpoints of two parallel and unequal lines, it is necessary for them to meet on the side of the smaller line.*

Let there be two lines **ab** and **cd** which are parallel <note>Original: *equidistantes*</note> and unequal: and let line **cd** be smaller than line **ab**: and let lines **ac** and **bd** be produced through their endpoints. I say that those lines **ac** and **bd** will meet beyond line **cd**. For let line **cd** be extended beyond point **d** to point **e**, and let line **ce** be made equal to line **ab** by Proposition 3 of Book 1 <note>Witelo cites Euclid’s *Elements* throughout; "3 p 1" refers to Book 1, Proposition 3.</note>, and let line **be** be drawn. Thus, here line **be** is parallel to line **ac** by Proposition 33 of Book 1: therefore, by Proposition 2 of this book, since line **bd** meets line **be** at point **b**: it is clear that it will meet line **ac**, which is parallel to line **be**: but it is also necessary for them to meet on the side of line **cd**, which is smaller than line **ab**, by Proposition 14 of this book, or by Proposition 2 of Book 6 [of Euclid]: the proposition is therefore clear: for the point of their meeting (which is **f**) will be beyond line **cd**.

17. *Straight lines containing equal angles with a straight line, which they fall upon at a single point, are, when joined together, shorter than all lines drawn from the same endpoints to any other point on the same line that contain unequal angles with that same line.*

Let there be a straight line **abcf**: and let there be two points **g** and **d**, from which two lines **gb** and **db** are produced onto the line **abcf**, containing equal angles, such that angle **abg** is equal to angle **cbd**. I say that if lines drawn from points **d** and **g** to any other point of line **abcf** (let it be **c**) contain unequal angles, such that angle **gca** is smaller than angle **fcd**: then lines **gb** and **db** joined together are shorter than the two lines **gc** and **dc** joined together. For let a perpendicular be drawn from point **g** to line **af** by Proposition 12 of Book 1, which is **gh**: and let line **gh** be produced beyond point **h**: and let **db** be produced until it meets with the produced line **gh**: they will meet, however, by Proposition 14 of this book: let the point of meeting be **k**: and let line **kc** be joined. And since angle **dbc** is equal to angle **gbh** by hypothesis, and to angle **hbk** by Proposition 15 of Book 1: it is clear that angle **hbk** is equal to **gbh**: but angles **ghb** and **khb** are equal: because they are right angles: therefore by Proposition 32 of Book 1, the triangles <note>Original: *trigoni*</note> **ghb** and **khb** are equiangular. Therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, since line **hb** is common and equal to itself, line **gb** will be equal to line **kb**, and line **gh** equal to line **hk**. And by the same reasoning, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, line **gc** will be equal to line **kc**. Because truly, by Proposition 20 of Book 1, line **kd** in triangle **kdc** is shorter than both lines **dc** and **kc** joined together, and line **gb** is equal to line **bk**, and line **gc** is equal to line **kc**: it is clear that both lines **gb** and **db** joined together are shorter than both lines **dc** and **gc** joined together. Likewise, the same must be demonstrated for any lines produced from points **g** and **d** to line **af**: the proposition is therefore clear. <note>This theorem is a fundamental principle of catoptrics (the study of reflection), proving that light reflecting at equal angles follows the shortest possible path.</note>

### *19. When one straight line exists in two plane surfaces, it is necessary that those two surfaces intersect each other along that line. [Euclid, Book 11, Prop 3].*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two rectangles sharing a common central horizontal line. The top rectangle is labeled 'a' and 'b' at the top corners and 'c' and 'd' at the bottom corners. The bottom rectangle shares the side 'c' and 'd' and has its bottom corners labeled 'e' and 'f'.</image-desc>

Let there be two plane surfaces **a b c d** and **c d e f**: in each of which is the line **c d**. I say that those two surfaces intersect each other along the line **c d**. For if those two surfaces were joined continuously at line **c d** as a common boundary in the manner of a single surface: then it is clear that they are parts of one surface, and not two surfaces: which is contrary to the hypothesis. But if the surfaces themselves pass through the given line **c d**, and are not joined at it as a common boundary: it is evident by Proposition 3 of Book 11 [of Euclid] that, since they intersect one another, some line is common to them. Either they intersect along line **c d**, and the proposition is held; or along any other given line: and then, since that line would be common to both proposed surfaces by the aforementioned Proposition 3 of Book 11, and line **c d** is common to the same by hypothesis: it would follow that two plane surfaces would enclose a solid body between those two lines: which is impossible, and against the 4th supposition of this [book]: therefore the proposition is clear.

### *20. From a single point given in the air, only one perpendicular can be drawn to any underlying plane or convex surface. [Euclid, Book 11, Prop 11 & 13].*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a point 'e' at the top of a triangle. A horizontal line 'a-b' represents a plane. A perpendicular line drops from 'e' to point 'f' on the plane. Another line from 'e' goes to point 'g' on the plane. Below the plane, there is a convex arc. Points 'h', 'f', and 'k' are labeled along a line tangent to the arc at point 'f', and points 'l', 'g', and 'm' are labeled on a line tangent to the arc at 'g'.</image-desc>

Let there be a given plane surface **a b c d**, and a point **e** given in the air. I say that from point **e** to the underlying surface, it is possible for only one perpendicular to be drawn. For if it were possible, let two perpendiculars be drawn from point **e** to the given plane surface **a b c d**, which are **e f** and **e g**. Since therefore lines **e f** and **e g** are joined at an angle at point **e**, it is clear by Proposition 2 of Book 11 that those two lines are in the same surface: and since those lines are perpendicular to the surface **a b c d**, the surface in which those lines exist will be erect upon the surface **a b c d**. Therefore, the common section of this surface and the surface **a b c d** is line **f g** by the previous proposition: thus in triangle **e f g** there are two right angles, namely **e f g** and **e g f**, by the definition of a line erect upon a surface (Definition 3 of Book 11): but this is impossible, and against Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>Proposition 32 of Book 1 states that the sum of angles in a triangle is equal to two right angles; thus, a triangle cannot have two right angles.</note>. This is also evident in convex surfaces: because, by the 5th definition of this [book], every line perpendicular to any convex surface is perpendicular to the plane surface tangent to that convex surface at the point of the line's incidence: it is clear because in every convex surface the same impossibility occurs. For if there is a convex spherical surface in which there is an arc **f g**: let a plane surface touch it at point **f**, in which line **h f k** is drawn, and at point **g** a plane surface, in which is line **l g m**. It is evident from the previous points that angles **e f k** and **e g l** are right angles. Also, if chord **f g** is produced: it is clear that angles **e f g** and **e g f** are greater than two right angles, which is impossible. It is therefore not possible for more than one perpendicular to be drawn from one given point to a plane or convex surface. The proposition is therefore clear: since it must be demonstrated in the same way for any other convex surfaces.

I say that line **a e** is the shortest of all the others. For let lines **e f**, **e g**, **e h** be drawn, and let right-angled triangles be constructed. It is thus evident (since by Proposition 32 of Book 1 a right angle is the largest in any triangle...

### *22. If a line is drawn from the highest point of a line standing upright on a surface, to a line that is perpendicular to any line drawn from the point of contact on the underlying surface: then the drawn line must be perpendicular to the one it lies upon. A lemma <note>A preliminary proposition used to prove a later theorem.</note> for the 37th theorem of Euclid's Optics: likewise for the 42nd theorem of the 6th book of Pappus's Mathematical Collection <note>Original: "μαθηματικῶv συναγωγῶv" (Mathēmatikōn Synagōgōn).</note>.*

Let a point be given in the air, which is **a**, from which a line **ab** is erected upon a subject plane surface **bcd** by Proposition 12 of Book 11, meeting the given surface at point **b**: and in surface **bcd** let a line **dc** be drawn as desired, and from point **b** let a perpendicular be drawn to line **dc**, which is **bd**; and let line **ad** be joined. I say that **ad** is perpendicular to line **dc**. For let any point be taken on line **dc**, such as **c**, and let lines **ac** and **bc** be drawn. Therefore, because line **ab** is upright upon surface **bcd**, it is clear by the definition of an upright line (Definition 3 of Book 11), that angle **abc** is a right angle: therefore by Proposition 47 of Book 1 <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the square of line **ac** is equal to the two squares of lines **ab** and **bc**: but also the square of line **bc** is equal to the two squares of **cd** and **bd** by Proposition 47 of Book 1, because line **bd** is perpendicular to line **dc** by hypothesis. The square of line **ac** is therefore equal to the three squares of the three lines **ab**, **bd**, and **cd**: but the square of line **ad** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **ab** and **bd**: therefore the square of line **ac** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **ad** and **dc**. Therefore, by Proposition 48 of Book 1 <note>The converse of the Pythagorean Theorem, used to prove a triangle is right-angled.</note>, triangle **adc** is a right-angled triangle. It is therefore clear that line **ad** is perpendicular to line **dc**: which is what was proposed.

### *23. When a single straight line falls upon two parallel plane surfaces, if it is perpendicular to one of them, it will also be perpendicular to the other. The converse of Proposition 14, Book 11 of the Elements.*

Suppose that one line **ab** falls upon two plane and <term>equidistant</term> <note>Parallel.</note> surfaces, meeting one of them at point **a**, and the other at point **b**. I say that if line **ab** is perpendicular to one of those surfaces, it will also be perpendicular to the other. For let a straight line **ac** be drawn from point **a** in one of those surfaces, and in the other surface let line **bd** be drawn from point **b**. It is therefore evident that lines **ac** and **bd** are parallel: for if extended to infinity they will not meet, because the surfaces in which they lie do not meet. Therefore, if either of the angles **bac** or **abd** is a right angle: it is always clear by Proposition 29 of Book 1 that the other of them will also be a right angle. And since this can be declared in the same way for all lines drawn in the surfaces from points **a** and **b**: it is clear that line **ab** makes right angles with every line meeting it in either of those produced surfaces. Therefore, if line **ab** is perpendicular to one of the surfaces, it is clear that it will be perpendicular to the other of them: and this is what was proposed.

### *25. All perpendicular lines drawn between parallel lines or surfaces are parallel and equal; and if straight lines fall upon parallel lines or surfaces at equal angles, they are equal.*

Let two lines **ab** and **cd** be parallel, between which perpendicular lines are drawn, namely **ef** and **gh**. I say that the lines **ef** and **gh** are parallel and equal. That they are parallel is clear by Proposition 28 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements.</note>; that they are also equal is clear by Proposition 34 of Book 1. The same method is to be demonstrated if the lines **ab** and **cd** are marked on parallel surfaces. But if the lines **ef** and **gh** do not fall perpendicularly, but at equal angles, with lines or surfaces drawn such that angle **ghc** is equal to angle **efd**, the lines **gh** and **ef** will also be equal: for they will meet by Proposition 14 of this book; let the point of meeting be **k**. Because angle **kfh** is equal to angle **khf** by hypothesis, it follows from Proposition 6 of Book 1 that the side **kf** of triangle **kfh** is equal to side **kh**. But by Propositions 29 and 26 of Book 1, the side **ki** of triangle **kil** will be equal to side **kl**: therefore the remaining line **if** is equal to line **lh**: which is what was proposed. In parallel surfaces where lines **ab** and **cd** are marked, the demonstration is the same: therefore that which was proposed is clear.

### *26. To subtend <note>To draw a straight line (a chord) across an angle, connecting two points on the lines that form the angle.</note> a base equal to a given line for any given angle.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an angle abc. A construction is shown to find a base line gf equal to a given line de. An arc is drawn with center f to intersect line ba at g. A second construction involves points h, k, and l. Labels include a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, k, l.</image-desc>

Let the given angle be **abc**, and the given line **de**. From line **bc**, on the side of point **b**, let a line **bf** be marked off, not greater than half of line **de** by Proposition 3 of Book 1. With the fixed foot of the compass placed at point **f**, let a circle be described with a radius equal to the length of **de**. This will necessarily cut side **ba** by Proposition 20 of Book 1, since side **bf** is not greater than half of line **de**. Let it be, then, that it cuts it at point **g**, and let line **gf** be drawn: this will necessarily be equal to line **de** by the definition of a circle (Definition 15 of Book 1 of the *Elements*). Therefore the proposition is clear. The same can also be demonstrated another way. From point **b**, let line **bh** be drawn at an angle, as it happens, upon line **ab**, which by Proposition 3 of Book 1 is made equal to the given line **de**. From point **h**, let a line parallel to line **ab** be drawn by Proposition 31 of Book 1, which by Proposition 2 of this book will necessarily meet with line **bc**. Let the point of meeting be **k**, and from point **k** let a line parallel to line **bh** be drawn, which is **kl**. The resulting figure **bhkl** will be a parallelogram (having parallel sides); therefore by Proposition 34 of Book 1, line **lk** is equal to line **bh**, and thus equal to the given line, which is **de**: thus the proposition is clear.

### *27. Given two unequal angles, to cut off from the larger one an angle equal to the smaller. From Book 1, Proposition 23 of the Elements.*

<image-desc>Two angles positioned side-by-side. The first angle is abc with an interior line bg. The second angle is def. Lines represent the process of cutting an angle equal to the smaller from the larger.</image-desc>

Let the two given angles be **abc** and **def**, where **abc** is the larger and **def** the smaller. It is proposed that an angle equal to angle **def** should be cut off from angle **abc**. This is done by Proposition 23 of Book 1: if upon the endpoint **b** of line **ab**, within angle **abc**, an angle is made equal to angle **def**, which is **abg**. This is what was proposed.

*29. A line dividing the angle of any triangle, if extended, will necessarily cut the base subtended <note>Subtended: the side of a triangle opposite a specific angle.</note> by that angle: and if a line cutting the base is extended to the point where the sides of the triangle meet: it will divide the angle opposite the base.*

Let it be that line **bd** divides the angle **abc** of triangle **abc**. I say that the same line **bd**, when extended, will necessarily cut the base **ac** subtended by that angle. For if it does not cut the base **ac**, it will nevertheless meet the extended line **ac** by Proposition 14 of this book: this is because the angles **bac** and **abf** are less than two right angles by hypothesis and by Proposition 32 of Book 1: let the meeting point therefore be at point **f** beyond point **c**. Therefore, for triangles **abc** and **abf**, angle **bac** is common, and angle **bca** is greater than angle **bfc** by Proposition 16 of Book 1: therefore, by Proposition 32 of Book 1, angle **abf** will be greater than angle **abc**: thus line **bf** does not divide angle **abc**: it must therefore necessarily fall between points **a** and **c**: and thus it will cut the base **ac**: because if it fell on point **a** or point **c**, it would not yet divide angle **abc**: thus the first point proposed is clear. Thus angle **abc** is divided by line **bd**: which is the second of the proposed points.

*30. From the angle of a given triangle, a line is drawn perpendicularly to the base; if the rectangle formed by the parts of the base is greater than the square of the perpendicular: it is necessary that the angle (from which the line is drawn) be obtuse; if less, acute; if equal, right.*

Let there be a given triangle **abc**, from whose angle **bac** a perpendicular line is drawn upon the base **bc**: and let it cut it at point **d**: and let it be **ad**: and let that which is produced from the multiplication of **bd** by **dc** <note>The "rectangle" or product of the two segments of the base.</note> be greater than the square of line **ad**. I say that angle **bac** is obtuse. For it is clear by Proposition 17 of Book 6 <note>Referring to the geometric mean theorem in Euclid.</note> that the ratio of line **bd** to line **ad** is not the same as the ratio of line **ad** to line **dc**. Let it be, therefore, by Proposition 12 of Book 6, that whatever the ratio of line **bd** to line **ad** is, let the same be the ratio of line **ad** to line **ge**: therefore, the product of line **bd** and line **ge** will be equal to the square of line **ad** by Proposition 17 of Book 6: because that which is produced by the multiplication of line **bd** by line **dc** is greater than the square of line **ad**: it is clear that line **ge** is smaller than line **dc** by Proposition 1 of Book 6. Therefore, let a segment equal to line **ge** be cut off from line **dc** by Proposition 3 of Book 1, and let it be **df**, and let line **af** be drawn. Therefore, because that which is produced by the multiplication of line **bd** by line **df** is equal to the square of line **ad**: it is clear by Proposition 17 of Book 6 that the ratio of line **bd** to line **ad** is as the ratio of line **ad** to line **df**: therefore, by the converse of Proposition 8 of Book 6, angle **baf** is a right angle. Therefore angle **bac** is greater than a right angle. In a similar way, it must be demonstrated that if the product of **bd** and **dc** is less than the square of **ad**, then angle **bac** is acute: for the demonstration is done by the same means. It is also clear by the same converse of Proposition 8 of Book 6 that if the product of line **bd** and line **dc** is equal to the square of line **ad**, then angle **bac** is a right angle: thus the proposition is clear.

...let **bc** be perpendicular to **ad**. I say that the proposed isosceles triangle is divided into two similar partial triangles. ### 32. *A line drawn from any point on one side of an extended triangle, cutting the side farther from that point, will necessarily also cut the side closer to it.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of triangle abc with side ab extended to point d. A line de is drawn from d, intersecting side ac at e.</image-desc>

Let there be triangle **abc**, whose side **ab** is extended beyond point **b** to point **d**: and from point **d**, let line **de** be drawn cutting the side of the triangle **ac** at point **e**. I say that **de** will necessarily cut side **bc**. For if it does not cut side **bc**, but only side **ac**, let line **dc** be drawn and extended continuously and straight: thus line **de** will cut line **dc** at some point: since line **dc** goes out from point **d**, from which line **de** also goes out, and it ends at point **c** lying between <note>Or "beyond"</note> point **e**, it will necessarily cut it: let the point of intersection be **f**. It is thus clear that two straight lines, which are **df** and **def**, would enclose a surface: which is impossible <note>A fundamental axiom of Euclidean geometry: two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>. The same also happens if line **de** is drawn outside line **bc** beyond point **a**: which is the proposition.

### 33. *If two straight lines go out from the terminal points of one side of a triangle and meet at one point inside the triangle: the interior angle will be equal to the superior angle plus the two angles contained between the lines drawn to the other two sides of the triangle.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of triangle abc with an interior point d. Lines ad and bd are drawn. Line cd is extended through d to point e outside the triangle.</image-desc>

Let there be triangle **abc**, and from the terminal points of one of its sides **ab**, which are **a** and **b**, let lines be drawn such that they meet inside triangle **abc** at point **d**. I say that angle **adb** is equal to angle **acb**, and in addition to the two angles **cad** and **cbd**. That angle **adb** is greater than angle **acb** is clear by Proposition 21 of Book 1. Let line **cd** be extended beyond point **d** as far as point **e**. Thus, by Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>referring to the Exterior Angle Theorem</note>, angle **eda** is equal to the two angles **dca** and **dac**: and similarly angle **edb** is equal to the two angles **dbc** and **dcb**. Therefore, the whole angle **adb** is equal to angle **acb**, and to angles **dac** and **dbc**: which is the proposition.

### 34. *A line equal and parallel to the base of any triangle, being closer to the top angle, is necessarily subtended by a larger angle.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of triangle abc with a horizontal line de drawn parallel to the base ac. Another transversal line fg intersects the sides of the triangle below de.</image-desc>

Let there be triangle **abc**, with base **ac**: let a line equal and parallel [to the base] be drawn closer to angle **abc**, which is **de**. I say that if lines **bd** and **be** are drawn from point **b**, angle **dbe** is greater than angle **abc**. Since indeed line **de** is equal to line **ac**, it is clear that when so produced, it cuts lines **ab** and **bc**, by the argument of Proposition 16 of this book: which is also clear from others. For every line falling inside a triangle, cutting its sides and being parallel to the base, is smaller than the base by Proposition 29 of Book 1 and Proposition 4 of Book 6. Therefore, let line **de** cut side **ba** at point **f**, and side **bc** at point **g**. Because therefore by Proposition 16 of Book 1 angle **bgf** is greater than angle **beg**: then by Proposition 29 of Book 1 angle **bca** will be greater than angle **bed**: and by the same reasoning angle **bac** is greater than angle **bde**: necessarily therefore by Proposition 32 of Book 1, angle **dbe** (which with its smaller angles equals two right angles) will be greater than angle **abc** (which with its two larger angles equals two right angles): thus the proposition is clear.

Let there be a right-angled triangle **abc**, whose angle **bac** is a right angle: and from point **b** let a straight line **bd** be drawn to side **ac** (which is the base of angle **abc**). I say that the ratio of the further angle **cbd** (from the right angle) to the nearer angle **dba** (to that right angle) is less than the ratio of the further part of the base from the right angle (which is **cd**) to the side **da** which is nearer to the right angle. For since angle **bac** is a right angle, it is clear that angle **bda** is acute by Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>The sum of the angles of a triangle equals two right angles.</note>: therefore, by Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle **bdc** is obtuse: therefore, by Proposition 19 of Book 1, side **bd** is greater than side **ab**, and less than side **bc**. And since the ratio of sector to sector is as the arc **fd** is to the arc **de**, as is clear by the method of demonstration in Proposition 1 of Book 6: since all sectors of the same circle are of the same height, and equal multiples of the arcs make equal multiples of those sectors: the ratio of arc **df** to arc **de** is as angle **dbf** to angle **dbe** by Proposition 33 of Book 6. ### 36. The two extended sides of any triangle form another triangle similar to the first, with the sides transposed in position and orientation.

### 38.
*Of any two right-angled triangles, if the ratio of the hypotenuse <note>original: "latus subtenfum recto angulo", the side subtending the right angle</note> of the one to its smaller side is greater than the ratio of the hypotenuse of the other to its smaller side, then the angle of the lines of the greater ratio will be greater than the angle of the lines of the smaller ratio; and vice versa.*

Let there be two right-angled triangles **abc** and **def**, whose angles **abc** and **def** are right angles: and let side **bc** be smaller than side **ab**, and side **ef** be smaller than side **de**: and let there be a greater ratio of line **ac** to line **bc** than of line **df** to line **fe**. I say that angle **acb** is greater than angle **dfe**. For because the ratio of line **ac** to line **bc** is greater than the ratio of line **df** to line **fe**: but by Proposition 47 of Book 1 <note>The Pythagorean Theorem</note> the square of line **ac** is equal to the squares of the two lines **ab** and **bc**: and the square of line **df** is equal to the squares of the two lines **de** and **fe**: and because by Proposition 20 of Book 6 the ratio of squares is the duplicate ratio of the sides: it is clear that the ratio of the square of **ac** to the square of **cb** is greater than the ratio of the square of **df** to the square of **fe**: therefore, by Proposition 11 of this book <note>Witelo's own previous theorems in Book I</note> there is a greater ratio of both squares of lines **ab** and **bc** to the square of **bc**, than of both squares of lines **de** and **fe** to the square of **fe**: therefore, by Proposition 12 of this book, there is a greater ratio of the square of **ab** to the square of **bc** than of the square of **de** to the square of **fe**: therefore, by Proposition 22 of Book 6, there is a greater ratio of line **ab** to line **bc** than of line **de** to line **ef**. Let it be that the ratio which line **de** has to line **ef** is the same as some line, such as **gh**, has to line **cb** by Proposition 3 of this book: line **gh** will therefore be smaller than line **ab** by Proposition 10 of Book 5. Therefore, let a segment equal to line **gh** be cut from line **ab** by Proposition 3 of Book 1: and let it be **bk**, and let line **ck** be joined: therefore, by Proposition 6 of Book 6, triangles **def** and **kbc** will be equiangular: thus angle **bck** is equal to angle **efd**: but angle **bca** is greater than angle **bck**, the whole being greater than the part. *40. The diagonals of all parallelograms <term>equidistantiū laterū (parallel-sided surfaces)</term> bisect each other; from which it is clear that the point of intersection of the diagonals is the center point of that same surface.*

->[Image: A parallelogram abcd with diagonals ac and bd intersecting at e. Lines fg and hk pass through e, dividing the shape into four smaller sections.]<-

Let there be a parallelogram, whether it is a square or an oblong shape, which is **abcd**, in which the diagonals **ac** and **bd** are drawn, intersecting at point **e**. I say that the diagonals bisect each other, and that point **e** is the center point of the surface **abcd**. For it is clear that triangles **bec** and **aed** are equiangular by Propositions 15 and 29 of Book 1: and angle **ebc** will be equal to angle **eda**, as they are alternate angles. Similarly, angle **ecb** is equal to angle **ead**: therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, the proportion of line **be** to line **ed** will be as line **ce** is to line **ea**, and as line **bc** is to line **ad**. But line **bc** is equal to line **ad** by Proposition 34 of Book 1. Therefore, line **be** is equal to line **ed**, and line **ce** is equal to line **ea**. Those diagonals therefore bisect each other. 

And from this, the corollary is manifest: for point **e** is equidistant from all the outer limits. If, however, any doubt remains, let lines be drawn from point **e** parallel to the sides of the proposed surface by Proposition 31 of Book 1, which shall be **fg** and **hk**. It follows, due to the equality of the parts of the diagonals argued in the manner described above, that line **fe** becomes equal to line **eg**, and line **he** becomes equal to line **ek**. It is thus clear that in every way, point **e** is equidistant from the points of the boundary lines: it is therefore directly opposite them, and thus the middle point between them; which is what was proposed.

### *42. Every angle contained by a diameter and any line on the circumference of a circle is necessarily acute. Alhazen Book 60, number 5.*

### *43. All angles of equal or similar segments of the same circle contained under an arc and a straight line are equal: but it is necessary that the angles of any smaller segment be smaller, and of a larger segment larger. From which it is clear that all angles of semicircles are equal.*

Let there be a circle whose center is **a** and diameter **gf**: and in it let equal arcs be marked, which are **bc** and **de**, with chords **bc** and **de** produced. I say that angles **gbc** and **fde**, contained under the arcs and chords, are equal. For let a line touching the circle <note>a tangent line</note> be drawn from point **b** by Proposition 17 of Book 3, which shall be **bl**, and from point **d** the line **dm**: and let lines **ab**, **ac**, **ad**, **ae** be drawn from the center. By Proposition 5 of Book 1, angles **abc** and **acb** will be equal: and angles **ade** and **aed** will be equal: but triangles **abc** and **ade** are equiangular <note>having the same angles</note> by Proposition 4 of Book 1: for angle **bac** is equal to angle **dae**, by Proposition 27 of Book 3: also angle **abl** is equal to angle **adm**, since each of them is a right angle by Proposition 18 of Book 3: but the <term>angle of contingency (angulus contingentiae)</term> <note>the tiny angle between a curve and its tangent line</note> **lbg** is equal to the angle of contingency **mdf**: since each of them is the smallest of acute angles by Proposition 18 of Book 3. There remains, therefore, angle **gbc** contained by arc **bg** and straight line **bc**, equal to angle **fde**, contained by arc **fd** and straight line **de**: but also angle **gcb** is equal to angle **gbc** for the same reason: similarly also angle **fed** is equal to angle **fde**. Therefore, all these angles are equal. 

Now let there be an arc smaller than arc **bc**, which is cut off from arc **bc**, and let it be arc **no**, and let lines **an**, **ao** be drawn: also let chord **no** be drawn: and let tangents **nq** and **or** be drawn. Because, therefore, the angles at the base of triangle **ano** are equal by Proposition 5 of Book 1, and angle **oan** is smaller than angle **cab** by Proposition 33 of Book 6: then by Proposition 32 of Book 1, any of the angles **ano** and **aon** is greater than any of the angles **abc** and **acb**. Therefore, let angle **ona** be greater than angle **cba**: but the angle of contingency **qng** is equal to the angle of contingency **lbg**: there remains, therefore, angle **gno** smaller than angle **gbc**, since angles **lba** and **qna** are equal: because each is a right angle by Proposition 18 of Book 3. 

Now let there be an arc larger than arc **bc**, which shall be **sc**, and let chord **sc** be drawn: and because angle **cas** is greater than angle **cab** by Proposition 33 of Book 6: it is then clear that angle **asc** is smaller than angle **abc**: and thus it will be concluded as before, that angle **gsc** contained under arc **gs** and chord **sc** is greater than angle **gbc**: therefore it is also greater than angle **gno**. This same thing is clear for any similar arcs of the same circles, since by the definition of similar arcs they receive equal angles by Definition 10 of Book 3. From which the corollary is clear, that all angles of semicircles are equal: for all semicircles are similar: and in the same circle they are similar and equal: this, therefore, was proposed.

### *44. If the same angle stands at the center of one of two equal circles, and at the periphery of the other, the arc corresponding to the angle placed at the periphery will be double the other arc. In unequal circles, however, the proportion of those arcs to their total peripheries is doubled.*

## 52. *If equal arcs lie between two straight lines intersecting a circle, those lines are necessarily parallel; and the same happens if one of them is a secant and the other a tangent.*

Truly, angle **doa** is equal to angle **eoc** by the 27th proposition of the 3rd book, since by the hypothesis arc **da** is equal to arc **ec**. Therefore, angle **dof** will be equal to angle **eof**. Therefore, by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book, angle **dfo** will be equal to angle **efo**. Thus, line **of** is perpendicular to line **de**. Therefore, by the 28th proposition of the 1st book, lines **de** and **ac** will be parallel.

But angle **eoc** is equal to angle **doa** by the 27th proposition of the 3rd book; therefore angle **doe** remains equal to angle **aoc**. Therefore, by the definition of a circle and by the 6th proposition of the 6th book, triangles **doe** and **aoc** are mutually <term>equiangular</term> <note>having the same angles</note>. Therefore, angle **gco** will be equal to angle **odf**. But angle **ogc** is equal to angle **ofd**, because each is a right angle from what was previously stated. Therefore, by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book, triangles **goc** and **dof** are equiangular. Thus, by the 14th proposition of the 1st book, lines **do** and **oc** joined together are one [straight] line, because angles **coh** and **doh** from the premises are equal to two right angles. Therefore, by the 27th proposition of the 1st book, the proposition is clear.

### § 3. *For parallel lines drawn across the surface of a circle, whether both intersect it, or both are tangent to it, or one intersects and the other is tangent, the arcs lying between them are equal.*

Let there be a circle **acbd**, whose center is **e**: and let two parallel lines **fg** at point **d** and **hq** at point **c** be tangent to it: and from the point of contact, which is **d**, let line **de** be drawn to the center **e**. Therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 3, line **de** is perpendicular to the line tangent at that point, which is **fg**. Let line **ce** also be drawn from the point of contact to the center **e**: therefore line **ce** will be perpendicular to the tangent line **hq** at point **c**. Let there also be drawn from the center **e** a line parallel to line **fg** by Proposition 31 of Book 1, which shall be **nm**: this will also be parallel to line **hq** by Proposition 30 of Book 1: therefore by Proposition 29 of Book 1, angle **med** is equal to angle **mec**: therefore by Proposition 14 of Book 1, lines **de** and **ec** joined together form one line: therefore line **dc** is a diameter of the circle, since it passes through the center **e**: thus arc **dac** is a <term>semicircle</term> equal to semicircle **dbc**. 

But if line **ab** intersects the circle parallel to line **hq** which is tangent at point **c**, then again arc **ac** will be equal to arc **cb**. For since the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> **ec** intersects the tangent line, which is **hq**: it is clear by the 2nd proposition of this book, that it will also intersect its parallel, which is line **ab**: let it intersect it at point **o**. And because angle **hce** is a right angle by Proposition 18 of Book 3, it is clear by Proposition 29 of Book 1 that angle **boe** is a right angle: therefore by Proposition 3 of Book 3, line **ab** is divided into equal parts at point **o**. Let lines **ac** and **cb** therefore be drawn: and it is clear by Proposition 4 of Book 1 that those will be equal: therefore by Proposition 28 of Book 3, arc **ac** is equal to arc **bc**. 

But if a line parallel to line **ba** intersects the circle, let it be **kl**: it is clear that the radius **ec**, when extended, will bisect line **kl** by Proposition 29 of Book 1 and Proposition 3 of Book 3: let it therefore bisect it equally and perpendicularly at point **p**: and let lines **pa**, **pb**, **ka**, **lb** be drawn: therefore in triangles **pac** and **pbc** by the previous premise and Proposition 4 of Book 1, side **pa** is equal to side **pb**: and angle **pbc** is equal to angle **apc**: therefore there remains angle **kpa** equal to angle **bpl**: but line **kp** is equal to line **pl**: therefore by Proposition 4 of Book 1, line **ka** will be equal to line **lb**. Therefore by Proposition 28 of Book 3, arc **ka** will be equal to arc **lb**: which was the proposition.
