->### BOOK ONE<-

...are greater than all the angles of the pyramid $abcef$ existing at the base. And in the same way, it can be demonstrated in a pyramid inscribed within pyramid $aghik$. And this is according to what was proposed. But if the line of length, which is $ah$, is extended to point $m$, and the axis $ad$ to point $n$, and a right angle $anm$ is formed, and according to it the pyramid $almop$ is completed upon the axis $an$: the third proposal is clear, namely that the angles of the produced pyramid which are formed at the base will be greater than the angles at the base of the first given pyramid. This is because, from <note>Euclid, Elements,</note> Book 1, Proposition 29, angle $nma$ is equal to angle $dha$, and angle $dha$ is greater than angle $dca$; therefore, angle $nma$ is greater than angle $dca$. Therefore, all the angles at the base of pyramid $almop$ are greater than the angles at the base of pyramid $abcef$, each specifically to its corresponding angle. In the same way, it can be demonstrated even if the pyramid inscribed in pyramid $aghik$ is extended to a base equidistant <note>parallel</note> to the base of the said prior pyramid; for the method is the same. And the final proposal is clear from the aforementioned: specifically, that as much as the angles at the base are increased, the angles at the vertex of the same pyramid are decreased by that same amount. Since any angles of any triangle are equal to two right angles <note>180 degrees</note> by <note>Euclid, Elements,</note> Book 1, Proposition 32, and since the right angle remains constant in all of them, the remaining two angles are worth one right angle; therefore, what is added to one of them must necessarily be subtracted from the other. And this is all that was proposed.

**107. If a round pyramid <note>original: "pyramis rotunda"; this refers to a cone</note> is inscribed in another round pyramid in such a way that while both share the same base, their axes are different: it is necessary that the center of the base and the vertices of both pyramids lie on the same line.**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a cone with vertex 'a' and a circular base 'b c e f'. A vertical axis 'ad' connects the vertex to the center of the base 'd'. An internal vertex 'g' is marked on this axis. The diagram illustrates a smaller cone sharing the same base and axis as the larger one.</image-desc>

Let there be a given pyramid $abcef$, the base of which is the circle $bcef$ and its center is $d$. Let the axis of the pyramid be $ad$, and let it be, for example, a <term>right-angled cone<gloss>orthogonia</gloss></term>. Let there be inscribed within it, by the preceding proposition, a pyramid of a shorter axis upon the same base, in such a way that it is contained within the first. I say that the center of the circle of the base of both pyramids, which is $d$, the vertex of the given pyramid, which is $a$, and the vertex of the inscribed pyramid, which is $g$, will all be on the same line $ad$. This is indeed clear regarding points $a$ and $d$. However, that point $g$ is on the same line is proven thus: If it were not on the same line, then it would deviate toward some part outside that line. Suppose now its deviation is to the right side toward the line $ac$ in the surface of triangle $adc$. Let line $gd$ be produced. Since, therefore, by Proposition 89 of this book, all lines of length <note>slant heights</note> of the same pyramid are equal, it is clear that sides $gb$ and $gc$ are equal. But $bd$ is equal to $cd$, and the axis $gd$ is shared; therefore, by <note>Euclid, Elements,</note> Book 1, Proposition 8, angle $gdc$ is equal to angle $gdb$. Therefore, each is a right angle. However, just as angle $adc$ is a right angle, so too angle $gdc$ would be a right angle. Thus, a right angle would be a part of another right angle <note>which implies the whole is equal to its part</note>; but this is impossible. It is therefore clear that since the same impossibility always occurs wherever point $g$ is marked outside the line $ad$, point $g$ must necessarily be on line $ad$. This is what was proposed. But if the axis produced from point $g$ to the base of the pyramid is said not to fall on point $d$, the center of the circle of the base, another impossibility follows against the hypothesis—namely, that the pyramid would not be inscribed upon that same base, which is contrary to the premises; or it would follow that the lines drawn from the center to the circumference are not equal, all of which is impossible. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

**108. Of two round or sided <note>original: "lateratarum"; referring to pyramids with flat faces</note> pyramids with equal bases and unequal heights, it is necessary that the vertex of the taller one forms a more acute angle.**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram comparing two cones. The left cone is taller (vertex 'a', base 'bc', axis 'ad'). The right cone is shorter (vertex 'f', base 'eg', axis 'fh'). A point 'k' is marked on the axis of the taller cone to show a height equal to the shorter cone.</image-desc>

Of two round or sided pyramids, let $abc$ be the taller, whose axis is $ad$ and vertex $a$; and let pyramid $efg$, whose vertex is $f$ and axis $fh$, be shorter. Let their bases $bc$ and $eg$ be equal, and let axis $fh$ be shorter than axis $ad$. I say that angle $bac$ is smaller than angle $efg$. For let a length equal to axis $fh$ be cut from axis $ad$, which shall be $dk$, and let lines $bk$ and $ck$ be drawn. Thus, pyramid $bck$ will be equal to $efg$. Plane surfaces have formed both pyramids $abc$ and $bkc$ through the axis, and by Proposition 90 of this book, their common sections will be triangles <note>original: "trigoni"</note>. Therefore, let it be that pyramid $abc$ is cut according to triangle $bac$, and pyramid $bkc$ according to triangle $bkc$. Therefore, angle $bkc$ will be greater than angle $bac$ by Proposition 33 of this book. And when other cutting surfaces are drawn, the triangles will always be equal and equiangular to these. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

110. *If a round pyramid <note>cone</note> intersects a sphere, and its conical surface is not intersected by the surface of the sphere: the common section of the surfaces of the sphere and the pyramid will be the circumference of the circle of the pyramid's base.*

For since, by Proposition 69 of this book, a plane surface cuts a sphere according to a circle, and the base of a pyramid is a plane surface because it is a circle: it is clear that that base will intersect the sphere according to a circle. However, the pyramid intersects the surface of the sphere according to its entire base, because its convex conical surface is not intersected by the surface of the sphere, as is clear by the hypothesis. It is thus clear that the common section of the said surfaces will be the circumference of the circle of the base of the pyramid, and that surface contained by the circumference (which is the circle that is the base of the pyramid) will be the common surface; although otherwise the small body (which is a part of the sphere) cut off from the sphere by that surface is a body common to both of the said bodies.

111. *If a pyramid intersects a sphere such that the circle of the base of the pyramid is parallel to a great circle of the sphere in the sphere's surface: it is necessary that the diameter of the sphere erected upon that great circle passes orthogonally through the center of the circle of the pyramid's base. From which it is manifest that the diameter of the sphere and the axis of the pyramid, joined together, are one single line.*

For because by the preceding proposition the circle (which is the base of the pyramid) is common to the sphere just as it is to the pyramid: then by Proposition 68 of this book the proposition is clear. For because the circle (which is the base of the pyramid) is parallel to the great circle of the sphere, and those parallel circles are both on the surface of the sphere: the diameter of the sphere will pass orthogonally through the center of the circle of the pyramid's base, for it passes orthogonally through the centers of both those circles. And since from the endpoint of any line drawn from the center of the common circle to the circumference, there emerge two lines standing orthogonally upon it—namely, the axis of the pyramid, as is clear by Proposition 89 of this book, and the diameter of the sphere, as was premised: it is clear from <note>Euclid, Elements,</note> Book 1, Proposition 14, that those two joined lines are one single line. It is therefore necessary that the diameter of the sphere and the axis of the pyramid be one joined line. And this is what was proposed.

### 113.
> *In a pyramidal section passing through a given point on the surface of a round pyramid <note>a cone</note>, the perpendicular drawn from the given point in the surface of the section to the surface of the pyramid must necessarily meet under the axis of the pyramid with the perpendicular drawn from a point of the same section further from the vertex of the pyramid to the line touching <note>tangent to</note> the section at that point: provided that the line drawn from the lower point forms an acute angle with the perpendicular drawn from the higher point to the axis of the pyramid. Alhazen <note>Book 3, chapter 6, note 30</note>.*

Let there be a pyramid <note>cone</note>, whose vertex is $a$, and its axis is $ack$. Let there be a point $e$ marked on the conical surface of this pyramid, through which a pyramidal section $efz$ passes. In this section, let there be also a point $z$, further from the vertex point $a$ of the pyramid than point $e$ is. Let the line drawn from point $z$ to the axis form an acute angle with the perpendicular drawn from point $e$, which is angle $zed$. I say that if a perpendicular line is drawn from point $z$ to the line touching the acute-angled section <note>original: *oxygoniam*, referring here to an ellipse</note> at that point $z$, and another perpendicular is drawn from point $e$ to the surface tangent to the pyramid at point $e$, those two perpendiculars will meet below the axis $ack$. For let it be that a flat surface cuts the pyramid through point $z$ parallel to the base; according to Proposition 100 of this book, it will cut the pyramid in the shape of a circle. Let that circle be $gbrz$, whose center is $c$. Let the common section of this circle and the acute-angled section be a diameter serving as a chord of the circle $gbrz$ according to Proposition 104 of this book. From the vertex of the pyramid, by Proposition 101 of this book, let lines of the pyramid's length <note>slant height lines</note> be drawn through the points $e$ and $z$ marked on the surface of the pyramid, which shall be lines $az$ and $ae$. Let line $ae$ be extended until it is equal to line $az$. It will indeed reach the circle, because it is a line of length, and because point $e$ is closer to the vertex of the pyramid than point $z$ is. Therefore, let the extended line $ae$ fall on point $o$ of the circle. From the given point (which is $e$), let a perpendicular line be drawn to the surface tangent to the pyramid; this indeed, by Proposition 96 of this book, will meet with the axis of the pyramid, which is $ack$.

Therefore, surface $kzh$ cuts the surface of the section along the line common to both, which is $hz$, by Proposition 19 of this book: and it cuts line $tq$ at point $z$: and surface $hzk$ cuts surface $dzh$ along the line common to both those surfaces, which is line $hzp$. Truly, line $dz$ is in the surface of the section, as was shown above, and is cut by line $kz$ at point $z$: and point $t$ is above surface $kzh$, and point $q$ is below it: and thus surface $kzh$ cuts surface $dzq$ along the common line, which is perpendicular to line $tq$: and it is line $zh$: because that line is in surface $hzk$, and line $tq$ is perpendicular to it, as is clear from what was previously stated. And since surface $hzk$ cuts surface $dzq$, and the inclination of surface $hzk$ from the surface of the section (of which surface $dzq$ is a part) occurs on the side of the radius $zc$: the line which is the common section of those surfaces (which is line $hzp$) will fall between lines $qz$ and $dz$. And so line $zh$, which is drawn from point $z$ perpendicularly to the line touching the acute-angled section <term>oxygoniam<gloss>This term refers to an ellipse, literally an "acute-angled" section of a cone.</gloss></term> $efz$ at that point, will meet with the perpendicular $ed$ under the axis $ack$. This is because the perpendicular $ed$ cuts the axis of the pyramid <note>original: *pyramidis*, referring here to a cone</note>, which is $ack$, at point $d$. That they meet is clear by Proposition 14 of this book. For let line $hz$ be produced beyond point $z$ inside the section to point $p$. Because angle $zde$ is acute, and angle $dzp$ is acute: it is clear that lines $zh$ and $ed$ will meet below point $d$: and let the meeting be point $p$. The proposition is therefore clear.

*116. All acute-angled pyramidal sections broaden toward the base of the pyramid: which does not happen in cylinders.*

This which is proposed occurs because of the sharpness <note>or "tapering"</note> of the pyramidal body and because of the uniformity of cylinders <term>columnarum</term> <note>Vitello uses "columna" to refer to a cylinder</note>. For if, according to the point of the axis of the pyramid where the perpendicular line falls upon the pyramidal section <note>original: "oxygoniae", referring to an elliptical section of an acute cone</note>, a circle is drawn around the pyramid by Proposition 102 of this book, and a cylinder is imagined whose base is that circle: it is clear that the lower part of the pyramid exceeds that cylinder, and the cylinder exceeds the upper part of the pyramid: and thus the lower part of the pyramidal section will contain the lower part of the cylindrical section, and the upper part of the cylindrical section will contain the upper part of the pyramidal section. However, the parts of the cylindrical section are equal because of the uniformity of the body and the angles upon the axis by Proposition 92 of this book. The proposition is therefore clear.

*117. Every plane surface revolved around a fixed axis, until it returns to the place from which it started, describes a surface of a body similar to itself; the common section of the surface of the body and the plane surface cutting that body through the axis is a line similar to the moved line that generated that surface.*

...since the line $a b g d$ is always—wherever the section is revolved—the common intersection <term>communis differentia</term> <note>original: "communis differentia", a technical term for the line where two surfaces meet</note> between the surface continuous with it and the plane cutting surface. *118. Every regular convex or concave surface is either a part of the surface of a sphere, or of a cylinder <term>columnae</term>, or of a round pyramid <note>original: "pyramidis rotundae", which in medieval geometry refers to a cone</note>.*

For every regular line that is uniform in any of its parts is either a circle or a straight line. Now, a circle by its motion creates a sphere, since a sphere is the path of the circumference of a semicircle, as is clear from Principle 11. However, a single straight line by its motion can cause nothing but a pyramid <note>cone</note> when it is the side of a triangle, or a cylinder <note>column</note> when it is the side of a rectangle. For in all other moved figures, with one side remaining fixed, there is an angle causing a diversity of form in the produced surface. Therefore, it does not produce a regular convex or concave surface. It is clear, then, that every regular convex or concave surface is as proposed.

*119. To divide a given line according to any proportion of two given lines. (Proposition 10, Book 6 of the Elements).*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the division of a line according to a given proportion. At the top are two reference segments, c-d and e-f. Below is a construction involving an angle with vertex 'a'. A line 'a-h' is divided into segments 'a-g' and 'g-h' (corresponding to c-d and e-f). Transverse parallel lines connect points 'g' and 'h' to the base line 'a-b' at points 'k' and 'b'.</image-desc>

Let line $a b$ be the given line, which must be divided according to the proportion of two given lines $c d$ and $e f$. From point $a$ of the given line $a b$, let an indefinite line be drawn joined at an angle with line $a b$. Starting from point $a$, let a segment equal to line $c d$ be cut off by Proposition 3, Book 1 <note>referring to Euclid's Elements</note>, which shall be $a g$; and starting from point $g$, let line $g h$ be cut off equal to line $e f$. Let line $b h$ be drawn, and from point $g$ let a line be drawn parallel to line $b h$ by Proposition 31, Book 1. This line, when produced, will cut line $a b$ by Proposition 2 of this book; let it cut it at point $k$. Thus, the proposed undivided line $a b$ will be divided according to the manner of division of the divided line $a h$. For by Proposition 2, Book 6 <note>of the Elements</note>, the proportion of line $a k$ to line $k b$ will be as line $a g$ is to line $g h$. Therefore, it is as line $c d$ is to line $e f$ by Proposition 7, Book 5. And this is the proposition.

*120. When a line is drawn from a given point cutting another line according to a given proportion of the parts of those lines: it is impossible for another line to be drawn from the same point between the same lines which cuts them according to the same proportion from the same ends, while preserving the denomination <note>the order or direction</note> of the proportion.*

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram supporting a proof by contradiction. It features a triangle with vertex 'a' and a base line containing several labeled points. For example: let line $a b$, drawn from a given point $a$, cut line $d e$ at point $c$ according to some given proportion. I say that from point $a$, another line cannot be drawn to line $d e$ which cuts it according to the same given proportion, such that the denomination of the proportion is preserved from the same ends of line $d e$. For if it were possible for another line to be drawn from point $a$ in such a way, let an angle greater than a right angle be made at point $d$, the end of line $d e$, by Proposition 23, Book 1, toward point $b$, the end of line $a b$. Let line $b d$ be produced, and let angle $c d b$ be obtuse. Let line $d b$ be produced continuously toward point $a$, and from point $a$ let a perpendicular line be drawn to line $d b$, which shall be $a f$. Let line $a g$ be drawn cutting line $e d$ at point $h$ according to the proportion previously given, which is line $d c$ to line $c e$. Let line $h i$ be drawn parallel to line $c b$ by Proposition 31, Book 1. Thus, line $h i$ will be greater than line $h g$ by Proposition 19, Book 1. For angle $i g h$ is greater than the right angle $b f a$ by Proposition 16, Book 1; but the right angle $b f a$ is greater than angle $f b a$ by Proposition 32, Book 1. But angle $g i h$ is, by Proposition 29, Book 1, equal to angle $f b a$. Therefore, angle $i g h$ is greater than angle $g i h$. Therefore, by Proposition 19, Book 1, line $i h$ is greater than line $h g$. And let line $h k$ be drawn from point $h$ parallel to line $d b$; therefore, by Proposition 34, Book 1, line $b k$ will be equal to line $i h$. But line $b c$ is greater than line $k b$; therefore, line $c b$ is greater than line $h i$; therefore, $c b$ is greater than line $h g$. But also line $h e$ is greater than line $c e$, since the whole is greater than its part. Therefore, by Proposition 9 of this book, there will be a greater pro-

portion of line $b c$ to line $c e$, than of line $g h$ to line

Therefore, it is not the same proportion, which is contrary to the hypothesis; or it would follow that line $e c$ is greater than line $e h$ per Proposition 14, Book 5, which is entirely impossible. From Proposition 10 of Book 6 of the Elements.* <note>original: "E 10 p 6 element." refers to Euclid’s Elements.</note>

Let line $a b$ be the given line, which we must divide according to the proposed method. Let it therefore be divided according to whatever ratio is desired; let it be divided at point $c$, and let its part $a c$ be greater than part $c b$. Since three lines $a b$, $a c$, and $c b$ are proposed to us, let line $a c$ be divided by Proposition 119 of this book according to the proportion of line $a b$ to line $c b$. Let the division be made at point $d$ so that the <term>proportion</term> <note>meaning the ratio</note> of line $a d$ to line $d c$ is as the whole line $a b$ is to line $c b$. It is therefore clear that line $a b$ is divided in the proposed manner: for the ratio of the whole line $a b$ to one of the outer parts, which is $c b$, is as the remaining outer part, which is $a d$, is to the part that lies between both sections, which is $d c$. It is therefore evident that what was proposed has been done.

### 122. *If a straight line is divided such that the ratio of the whole to one of its outer segments is similar to the ratio of the other outer segment to the segment lying between the sections: if lines are drawn from one end of the given line and from the points of section parallel to each other, and a line is drawn from the other end of the given line intersecting those three parallels, the resulting line will be divided according to the same proportion. Alhazen, Book 6, Number 10.*

From one end of the given line, which is $b$, and from the points of section $g$ and $d$, let lines be drawn parallel to each other by Proposition 31 of Book 1 (of the *Elements*), which are $b c$, $d h$, and $g z$. From the other end of the given line, which is $a$, let a line be drawn intersecting those parallels at points $z$, $h$, and $c$, which is line $a z h c$. I say that line $a c$ will be divided according to this same proportion. For since line $d h$ is parallel to line $g z$ by hypothesis, by Proposition 2 of Book 6, the ratio of line $a z$ to line $z h$ will be as line $a g$ to line $g d$. And since line $b c$ is parallel to line $d h$, by the same Proposition 2 of Book 6 and Proposition 18 of Book 5, the ratio of line $a b$ to line $b d$ will be as line $a c$ to line $c h$. But by hypothesis, the ratio of line $a b$ to line $b d$ was as line $a g$ to line $d g$. Therefore, by Proposition 11 of Book 5, the ratio of line $a c$ to line $c h$ will be as line $a z$ to line $z h$. Thus, the line $a c$, which is drawn from point $a$ at the end of the given line, intersects the drawn parallel lines $b c$, $d h$, and $g z$, and is divided by them according to the proportion of the parts of the division of the given line $a b$. ### 124. *When two lines are joined at an angle and both are divided so that the ratio of each whole line to one of its outer segments is the same as the ratio of the other outer segment to the segment that lies between the two cuts: if lines are drawn from the points of division of one to the points of division of the other—provided they are not parallel to each other or to the base—then these lines must meet at a single point on the extended base. Alhazen, Book 9, Proposition 6.* <note>original: "Alhazen 9 n 6"; refers to the Optics of Ibn al-Haytham.</note>

Let line *ab* be given, divided at points *d* and *g* as proposed—that is, so the ratio of the whole line *ab* to segment *bd* is as line *ag* is to *gd*. Let line *ac* be joined to it at an angle and divided in the same way at points *h* and *z*, so that the ratio of line *ac* to *ch* is as line *az* is to *zh*. If the base *bc* is extended to form triangle *bca*, and *bc* is extended straight out, and lines are drawn from the points of section of one line to the point of section of the other (such as *dh* and *gz*), and all those lines are extended continuously and straight: I say that they will all meet at a single point. 

Since lines *bc* and *dh* are not parallel by our hypothesis, it is clear they must meet; let them meet at point *e*. Line *gz* must also necessarily meet them, since it is not parallel to either. It must meet either at that same point *e*—which gives us our result—or it must meet one of them at some other point. Let that point be *n*, where it meets line *de*. Now, let line *eg* be drawn: this line *eg* will cut line *ac* at a point other than point *z* (because line *gz* cuts line *ac* at point *z*). Let that intersection point be *l*. Therefore, by Euclid 5.11, the ratio of line *al* to *lh* would be as line *az* to *zh*. Consequently, by Euclid 5.18, the ratio of line *ah* to *hz* would be as line *ah* to *hl*. Thus, by Euclid 5.9, line *hz* would be equal to line *hl*—the larger equal to the smaller—which is impossible. The same is also clear by Proposition 120 of this book, since two lines cutting line *ah* were drawn from point *g*. It is clear, then, that line *gz* will not meet lines *bc* and *dh* at any point other than point *e*. This is what was proposed. Similarly, if we assume line *gz* meets line *dh* at point *e*, it can be demonstrated in the same way that line *bc* will meet both of them at point *e*. And if lines *bc* and *gz* meet at point *e*, line *dh* will meet them at that same point *e*. The proposition is therefore clear.

127. **Given two lines: it is possible to join another line to one of them, such that the rectangle formed by the product of the whole line with the added segment and the added segment itself is equal to the square of the other given line. Euclid's Elements, Book 3, Proposition 36.**

For example, let two lines *qe* and *ag* be proposed. I say that it is possible to join another line of whatever quantity to one of them, such as line *qe*, so that the rectangle formed by the product of line *qe* plus the added segment multiplied by that same added segment is equal to the square of line *ag*. Therefore, let the square of line *ag* be formed by Book 1, Proposition 46, and let its square be *ah*: and let the extended line *ag* be cut at point *f* so that line *gf* is equal to line *ag*: and let line *hf* be drawn. It is clear that triangle *ahf* is equal to square *ah*: for parallelogram *ah* is double the triangle *ahg* by Book 1, Proposition 41, and triangle *ahf* is double that same triangle *ahg* by Book 6, Proposition 1. With this triangular area proposed, and the line *qe*, it is possible by Book 6, Proposition 29 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 6, Prop 29: To a given straight line to apply a parallelogram equal to a given rectilinear area and exceeding by a parallelogrammic figure similar to a given one.</note> to construct on the given line *qe* a parallelogram equal to the given three-sided surface *ahf*, which adds onto the completion of the given line *qe* a square area similar to the given square *ah*. Therefore, let it be constructed, and let parallelogram *qm* be equal to triangle *ahf* constructed upon line *qe*, adding upon the completion of given line *qe* the square *em*, which is similar to square *ah*. It is therefore clear that the rectangle formed by the product of the given line *qe* plus the added segment *ez* multiplied by the added line *ez* itself (or its equal line *zm*), is equal to the proposed triangle *ahf*. Therefore, it is also equal to its equivalent, namely the square *ah*. And this is what was proposed: because line *ez* is joined to line *qe* in such a way as was proposed. This same thing can also be demonstrated otherwise. For let a circle be described whose diameter is *qe* and its center *b*, and let a line tangent to the circle be drawn, as it touches at point *g* by Book 3, Proposition 17: and let it be cut to the length of line *ag*: and let it be *ga*: and from its endpoint *a* let a line be drawn through the center *b* cutting the circumference of the circle at points *e* and *q*. Because, therefore, the rectangle formed by the product of line *qa* and line *ae* is equal to the square of line *ag* by Book 3, Proposition 36: it is clear that line *ea* is added to line *qe*, as was proposed.

### 129. Between two straight lines joined at an angle, to draw a straight line from a given point, one of whose parts lying between one of the joined lines and the given point is equal to any given line and additionally to its remaining part lying between the given point and the other joined line. Apollonius's Conics, Book 2, Theorem 4.

For the sake of example, let it be that two straight lines are joined at an angle at one point: let these be *fk* and *tk*, meeting at point *k*, between which is the given point *m*, and let there be the given line *mc*: it is proposed to us that from point *m* a straight line be drawn between lines *fk* and *tk*, cutting them at points *o* and *l* so that its part, which is *lm*, is equal to the given line *mc* and additionally to its remaining part, which is *mo*. However, to demonstrate this through straight or circular lines, much labor and great diversity would fall upon us, and it was not possible for us to complete this through such lines without mechanical motion and imagination, so that while lines *fk* and *tk* are given to us as indefinite, line *lo*, fixed at point *m*, is imagined to move until the sought result occurs for us. Nevertheless, Apollonius of Perga <note>A Greek geometer (c. 262 – c. 190 BC) famous for his work on conic sections.</note> demonstrated this in his book on the elements of conics, book two, proposition four, by the production of a hyperbola <note>original: "sectionis amblygonię" (literally 'obtuse section'). In the terminology of Apollonius and his medieval translators, this refers to a hyperbola.</note> from a given point between two asymptote lines, cutting neither of those lines: whose demonstration, as it depends on many preamble principles of his book, we assume here and use as demonstrated.

*131. Between two intersecting straight lines, to draw a hyperbola from a given point on one side that does not touch those lines, and to designate an opposite hyperbola to the first on the other side of the common intersection of those lines. From this, it is clear that when there are two opposite sections between two lines and the shortest line is drawn from one section to the other, the part of that line lying between one section and the [intersecting] line is equal to the part lying between the other section and the other [intersecting] line. Theorem 48, Book 2 of the Conics of Apollonius.*

What is proposed here was demonstrated by Apollonius in his book on the elements of conics. These are called <term>opposite sections</term> or <term>amblygonia</term> <note>original: "amblygonię siue hyperbolæ". From the Greek "amblygonios" (obtuse-angled), an early term for hyperbolas.</note> when the curvature <note>original: "gibbositas"</note> of one follows the curvature of the other in such a way that those curvatures face each other, and the diameters of both are on a single straight line. For example: let two lines *h l* and *z n* intersect at point *x*. On one side of them—specifically within angle *h x z* or angle *h x n*—from a given point *t*, let an "obtuse-angled" section *t p* be drawn. On the other side—within angle *n x l* or angle *z x l*—let the opposite section *c u* be drawn, so that the diameters of both opposite sections are on a single line *t c*, extended from the vertex of one to the vertex of the other. This line is necessarily the shortest of all lines drawn between those two sections. From these facts, Apollonius declared what is proposed as a corollary: namely, that if line *t c* cuts line *h l* at point *f* and line *z n* at point *q*, then line *t q* will be equal to line *c f*. And if line *t c* passes through point *x*, then line *t x* will be equal to line *x c*. We use this as demonstrated by Apollonius, and because of the symmetry of the section parts with respect to the intersecting lines. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<image-desc>A diagram of two intersecting lines (forming an X) with two hyperbolic curves (t p and c u) positioned in opposite vertical angles. A central axis line connects the vertices t and c, passing through the intersection point x and marking points f and q.</image-desc>

*132. If the immobile foot of a compass is placed at the vertex of one of the conic sections, a circle described with a radius equal to the shortest line drawn between those sections will touch the other section; but if described with a larger radius, it will cut the other section in only two points.*

What is proposed here is easy and requires only a declaration. For let there be, as in the preceding proposition, two opposite conic sections, *t p* and *c u*, between which the shortest line connecting the vertices of both sections is line *t c*. With the foot of the compass placed at one of the points *t* or *c*—say, at point *t*—let a circle be described with the length of diameter *t c*. This circle, therefore, because it does not reach the section *c u* except at point *c*, and because all other lines that can be drawn between these sections are greater than line *t c*, they are consequently greater than the radius of the circle. Therefore, all [other lines] will be cut by the circle, and the circle will not touch the section anywhere except at point *c*. Thus, the first part of the proposition is clear. But if the radius of the circle, line *t c*, is larger than the shortest of the lines drawn between the opposite sections,

### 133. From a given point on the circumference of a circle outside the diameter: it is possible to draw a line through the diameter to the circumference, such that the part of it lying between the diameter and the other part of the circumference is equal to a given line inscribable in the same circle in the manner previously described: but only two such equal lines can be drawn from the same given point in the same circle. Alhazen, Book 4, Section 34. <note>original: "Alhazen 34 n 5"</note>

Let there be a circle *a b g*, whose diameter is *b g*: and let the given point on its circumference be *a*: and let *h z* be the given line smaller than diameter *b g*, which is possible to be inscribed in the circle in the previously described manner. I say that from point *a* it is possible to draw a line passing through the diameter *b g*, whose part lying between the diameter *b g* and the circumference is equal to the given line, which is *h z*. For let lines *b a* and *a g* be drawn in the circle: and upon point *h* of the given line *h z*, let an angle be made equal to angle *a g b*: let this be *m h z*, with line *m h* drawn; and upon the same point *h*, let an angle be made equal to angle *a b g*, which is *l h z*, with line *h l* drawn: and from point *z*, let a line be drawn parallel <note>original: "æquidistans"</note> to line *h m*, which is *z n*: which will indeed cut line *h l*: let it cut it at point *x*: and from point *z* again, let another line be drawn parallel to line *h l*, which is *z t*, cutting line *h m* at point *t*: it will cut it by the second [proposition] of this [book]: and from point *t*, let a conic section be drawn, which is *t p*, as was previously described in Proposition 131 of this [book]. This section does not touch either of the lines *z n* and *h l*, between which it lies. Similarly, let another conic section be made, opposite to this one, between the same lines on the other side, which is *c u*: and among all the lines drawn from point *t* to the section *c u*, let the smallest be line *t c*. Therefore, if this line *t c* is equal to the diameter of the circle *b g*: a circle made according to the semi-diameter *t c* (with the foot of the compass placed at point *t*) is clearly touching the section *c u*. If, however, line *t c* is smaller than the diameter *b g*: a circle made in the aforementioned way according to the size <note>original: "quantitatem"</note> of line *b g* will cut the section *c u* at two points, as is clear from the preceding [proposition].

<image-desc>A circular diagram with horizontal diameter b g. Point a is on the upper circumference. Lines a b and a g connect point a to the diameter's ends. Point d is on the lower circumference, and line a d intersects the diameter at point e. Line d b is also drawn.</image-desc>

Now, let line *t c* first be equal to diameter *b g*. Since line *t c* is drawn to the conic section which lies between lines *h l* and *z n*: line *t c* will necessarily cut both those lines. If it cuts them at point *x* (which is the common point of intersection of those lines), then line *t x* will be equal to line *x c*. But if it cuts them at other points: let it cut line *z n* at point *q*, and line *h l* at point *f*: and let a line be drawn from point *z* by Book 1, Proposition 31 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 31: To draw a straight line through a given point parallel to a given straight line.</note> parallel to line *t c*: which by Proposition 2 of this [book] will cut lines *h m* and *h l*, just as its parallel *t c* does: let it cut them at points *m* and *l*: and let the line itself be *m z l*.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two hyperbolic branches of a conic section between two divergent straight lines acting as asymptotes. Other labeled points include p, r, x, z, n, q, f, and u, marking various intersections and parallel line constructions.</image-desc>

Upon the end *g* of the diameter *g b*, by Book 1, Proposition 23 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 23: To construct a rectilinear angle equal to a given rectilinear angle.</note>, let an angle be made equal to angle *h l m*, which is angle *b g d*: and let two lines *a d* and *d b* be drawn. It is clear then, since angle *g a b* is a right angle by Book 3, Proposition 31 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 3, Proposition 31: An angle in a semicircle is a right angle.</note>, that the other two angles of triangle <note>original: "trianguli"</note> *g a b*, namely *a g b* and *a b g*, are equal to a right angle by Book 1, Proposition 32 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 32: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is equal to two right angles.</note>. Therefore, angle *l h m* (which is equal to those two angles) is a right angle: therefore it is equal to angle *g d b*. But angle *h l m* is equal to angle *d g b*: therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 32, the third angle of one of the triangles <note>original: "trigonorum"</note> *g b d* and *h l m* will be equal to the third angle of the other, namely angle *h m l* to angle *g b d*. ***Given a right-angled triangle, and a given point on one of its sides forming the right angle: it is possible to draw from that point to the other side forming the right angle a line that intersects the hypotenuse <note>Witelo uses "basis" to refer to the hypotenuse of the right triangle.</note> such that the segment of the line between the point of intersection and the side where the given point is not located, has the same ratio to the segment of the hypotenuse between the intersection and the side where the given point is located, as one given line has to another given line.***

Let *a b g* be the given triangle, whose angle *a b g* is right: and on its side *b g* let there be a given point *d*, either inside or outside the triangle: and let there be two given lines, *e* and *z*. I say that from point *d* it is possible to draw a line intersecting the hypotenuse *a g* and meeting side *a b*, such that the part of the intersecting line lying between side *a b* and the hypotenuse *a g* has the same ratio <note>original: "eiusdem proportionis"</note> to the part of the hypotenuse *a g* which is from that line to point *g*, as the given line *e* has to the given line *z*. For let the point *d* first be within the triangle *a b g* itself: and let a line be drawn from it parallel to line *a b* by [Euclid] Book 1, Prop. 31, which is *d m*: and let a circle be made through the three points *g, d, m* by [Euclid] Book 4, Prop. 5: and line *g m* will be the diameter of this circle by [Euclid] Book 3, Prop. 31: for it is subtended by a right angle <note>Since dm is parallel to ab, and ab is perpendicular to bg, angle gdm must be a right angle.</note> according to [Euclid] Book 1, Prop. 29: and let line *a d* be drawn. And because by the same Prop. 29 of Book 1, angle *g m d* is equal to angle *g a b*: it is clear that angle *g m d* will be greater than angle *g a d*, since angle *g a b* is greater than angle *g a d*: therefore, let an angle equal to angle *g a d* be cut from angle *g m d* by Prop. 27 of this book, by drawing line *m n* to the circumference of the circle: and let this be angle *d m n*: and whatever the ratio of line *e* to line *z* is, let the ratio of line *a d* to line *h* be made the same by Prop. 3 of this book: and from point *n*, which is a point on the circumference of the circle, let a line be drawn to the diameter *g m*, which is *n l*, intersecting the circle at point *c*, so that its part lying between the circumference of the circle and the diameter, which is *c l*, is equal to the given line *h* by Prop. 128 or by Prop. 130 of this book: and let line *g c* be drawn: and from point *d* let a line be drawn to point *c*, which, since it falls between two parallel lines, which are *d m* and *b a*, forming an acute angle with one of them, as with *m d*, if it is extended, it will necessarily meet with the other by Prop. 2 of this book: let it therefore meet at point *q*. Therefore, because by [Euclid] Book 3, Prop. 27, angle *g m d* is equal to angle *g c d*, and angle *g m d* is equal to angle *g a b* by Book 1, Prop. 29: it is clear that angle *g c d* is equal to angle *g a b*: therefore by Book 1, Prop. 13, angle *g c q* will be equal to angle *b a l*: but angle *b a l* by Book 1, Prop. 15 is equal to angle *g a q*: therefore angle *g c q* is equal to angle *g a q*. Moreover, let *t* be the point in which line *d q* intersects line *a g*: therefore by Book 1, Prop. 15, angle *g t c* will be equal to angle *a t q*.

Therefore, the line which *a u* cuts from *g d* is *g d*. # THE SECOND BOOK OF THE OPTICS
# OF VITELLO, SON OF THE 
# THURINGIANS AND POLES.

Having set forth the universal mathematical axioms of this science: in this second book (as we promised) we proceed to a treatise on the universal action of perceptible forms. We begin by providing certain natural introductions concerning the manner in which light is projected through a single transparent medium, or through several, onto the various shapes of bodies; and concerning the projection of shadows, and the shaping of light falling through windows. We do this so that we may address those things without which it would be inappropriate to discuss the discourse of visible forms, as will later become clear in the process. Those things which we set forth as being known to the senses are as follows:

## D E F I N I T I O N S .

1. A **luminous body** is any body that is capable of diffusing its own light.
2. A **transparent body** <note>original: "diaphanum"</note> is any body through which light is permitted passage.
3. A **shadowy body** <note>meaning an opaque body</note> is a body through which light is not permitted passage.
4. **Primary light** is that which produces secondary light; for example, light entering a house through a window and illuminating the rest of the house at the spot where it falls is called "primary"; but in the corners of the house, it is called **secondary light** <note>this refers to direct versus ambient or reflected light</note>.
5. **Minimum light** is that which, if it were understood to be divided further, would no longer possess the action of light.
6. A **ray** is a luminous line.
7. A **radial line** is the line through which the diffusion of forms occurs.
8. A **refracted line** is a line whose parts form an angle <note>a "bent" line occurring when light moves from one medium to another, like air to water</note>.
9. A **radial pyramid** is a pyramid whose base is on the surface of the body diffusing its form, and whose vertex is at a point on any other body.
10. A **pyramid of illumination** is that whose vertex is at a point on the luminous body, and whose base is on the surface of the illuminated object.

## P O S T U L A T E S .

We ask that these things be accepted as known to the senses: 
1. That compressed light is stronger than dispersed light. 
2. Likewise, that stronger light illuminates more intensely and diffuses itself further. 
3. Likewise, that a shadow is created in the absence of light. 
4. Likewise, that a shadow vanishes upon the introduction of light. 
5. Likewise, that some shadows are sharpened at their end and terminate at a point. 
6. Likewise, that light is diffused equally toward every difference of position. 
7. Likewise, that light passing through colored things is colored by their colors, as is evident from light passing through glass windows, which is shaped by the colors of those glasses, carrying the forms of those colors with it onto the objects it hits. 
8. Likewise, that nature does nothing in vain, just as it does not fail in necessary things.

## T H E O R E M S

*1. The rays of any light and the multiplications of forms are extended along straight lines. Alhazen 2 n 7.* <note>Reference to the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose work on optics deeply influenced Vitello.</note>

This which is proposed here can be declared not by demonstration, but by means of an instrument. However, the diversity of the ancients used many and various instruments to prove this; we, however, use this one, which we describe below, because we believe it fits this purpose more consistently. Therefore, let a round brass vessel be taken, suitably thick, in the manner of the "mother" <note>the base plate</note> of an astrolabe, the width of whose bottom is one cubit or more, and the height of its rim is equal to the width of two fingers, perpendicular to the base of the vessel. And in the middle of the back of this vessel, let there be some very round columnar body erected perpendicularly, whose length is equal to the width of three fingers, and its width less than one finger. And let this vessel be placed according to its center points on a lathe, and let it be turned until its periphery, inside and out, is truly round, and its flat surfaces are made level, and the columnar body in the middle of the back is made round. Then, let two diameters intersecting each other at right angles be marked on the inner surface of the bottom of this vessel, which shall be *a b* and *c d*. It is clear that these diameters pass through the center of the circle of the bottom, which is *e*. Then, let a point be marked on the base of the rim of this vessel (which is the circle *a c b d*) at a distance of one finger's width from the extremity of one of the extended diameters, such as diameter *a b*.

Then place the base of the small plate upon this line, until the line which is the common difference of the width and depth of the plate ($rts$) is placed under that perpendicular line drawn upon the diameter (which is likewise $rts$). Let the point dividing the line of the plate, which is the common difference of the surfaces of width and depth (which is point $t$), be placed over point $t$ marked on the line $fe$, the semi-diameter of the vessel. Then let the small plate be soldered <note>original: "consolidetur" — meaning to make firm or join permanently</note> to the bottom of the vessel. The aperture $xyz$, which is in the small plate $rus$, will then be directly opposite the aperture $lmn$, which is in the rim of the vessel. The straight line $my$, joining the centers of these apertures, will be in the surface of the middle circle of the three circles previously marked, whose diameter is line $mp$; and line $my$ will be parallel to the diameter of the vessel, $fe$. Next, let a part of the rim of the vessel be cut away between two diameters intersecting each other at right angles; let this be the fourth part <note>a quadrant</note> immediately following the quarter in which the aperture is located (the one to which the plate's aperture is opposite). This corresponds to the arc $ad$ in the circle $acbd$. Let the site of the cut be planed until it becomes one surface with the surface of the base of the vessel. Having drawn a quarter of a circle $ad$, let it be divided into 90 degrees according to the size of the rim's circle, and let the degrees be divided into minutes. To this vessel, thus shaped and figured, we henceforth give the name **instrument**. Then take a quadrangular brass rule <term>rule <gloss>regula</gloss></term>, whose length is one cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note>. Let there be four surfaces containing it, with a width of two fingers, and let its surfaces be leveled until they become equal rectangles. In the midpoint of the length of the rule, and in the middle of one of those surfaces, let a round hole be made, the size of which can accommodate the body <note>the protruding mounting post</note> which is on the back of the instrument. Let the hole be perpendicular to the surface of the rule, passing through to the other side of the opposite surface. Let it be made in such a way that it may be rotated upon the instrument itself, but not with too loose a rotation. Let the instrument be placed upon the rule by inserting the body on its back into the hole of the rule, until the surface of the instrument joins the surface of the rule. The length of the rule will be equal to the diameter...

...of the instrument: let two sighting vanes <note>original: "pinnulæ" — small plates with holes or slits used for aligning the instrument with a light source or star</note> be made, having the same width and thickness as the ruler, but with a length of more than one digit <note>A "digit" or finger-breadth was a standard unit of measure, approximately 0.75 inches</note>. These should be fixed upon the ends of the ruler so that their projection above the ends of the ruler is one digit, or a little more or less; and let those vanes be fixed upon the surface of the ruler that has not been perforated. And because the width of the ruler is two digits, while the height of the body at the back of the instrument is three digits, let that third digit—by which the body projects beyond the ruler—be perforated, just as in an **astrolabe** <note>A complex medieval instrument used for solving problems related to time and the positions of the stars</note>, and let a pin be inserted to hold the ruler to the instrument.

Next, let another bronze ruler be taken, whose width is double its thickness, and let its thickness be equal to the diameter of the hole that is in the rim of the instrument. Its length should be equal to half a cubit <note>roughly 9 inches or 22 cm</note>. Let this ruler be made straight and true, with its surfaces even and parallel. Then, let that ruler be cut obliquely at one of its ends until the end of its length forms an acute angle with the edge of its width, so that it may be moved more easily. On the other end, however, let the edge of its width be perpendicular to the end of its length. Then let the line of its width be divided into two equal parts, and from the point of division let a line be drawn parallel to the lines of its length; this will be perpendicular to the line of width according to Proposition 29 of Book 1 <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements</note>. Therefore, when this ruler is placed upon the surface of the base of the instrument such that its thickness stands orthogonally <note>at a 90-degree angle</note> upon the base, and the surface of its width is applied to the surface of the base of the instrument itself, then its upper surface will be in the plane of the middle circle of the three circles drawn on the rim of the instrument, whose diameter is the line *m p*. This is because the thickness of the ruler is equal to the diameter of the hole, and the diameter of the hole, which is *n l*, is equal to the perpendicular line extending from the center of the hole to the flat surface of the instrument, which is line *m f*, to which the line of the ruler's thickness lies adjacent and equal.

Therefore, when it is desired to demonstrate the proposed conclusion experimentally, let the aforementioned instrument be placed facing the solar body, or any other luminous body, or even a candle. Let the center of the instrument's hole, which is point *m*, be aligned as closely as possible with the luminous body. The luminous ray will pass through the centers of both opposing holes—the one in the rim of the instrument and the other in the perforated plate—which are *x* and *y*. A luminous circle will then be described on the part of the instrument's rim opposite the hole *l m n* directly along the diameter *m p*. The center of that luminous circle will be at point *p*. This can easily be shown if, from point *p* to either side of the circumference of the middle circle (divided into degrees and minutes), the intervening parts of the luminous circle's circumference are counted; for equal numbers will be found on both sides. Therefore, point *p* is the center of that luminous circle. Thus, the line *m p*, along which the ray falls, passing through the center of both holes and through the center of the luminous circle, lies entirely within the flat surface of the middle circle of those three circles and is the diameter of that circle. It is, therefore, a straight line.

And if some body colored with a strong medium color, such as green or red, is placed outside the hole in the rim of the instrument so that the light of the sun or another body passes through it and subsequently falls upon the holes of the instrument and passes through them, then (as was clear from the 7th of the previous suppositions) a circle of light colored with that hue will be described around point *p* on the rim of the instrument. Therefore, color mixed with light diffuses its <term>form</term> <note>original: "formam" — in medieval science, the 'species' or likeness of an object that travels through the air to the eye</note> along straight lines, just as light itself does. It is clear, therefore, that the rays of any lights and the <term>multiplications of forms</term> <note>The process by which light or color propagates through a medium</note> extend along straight lines. And this is what was proposed.

### *2. Unimpeded light must necessarily be carried through a medium proportioned to it in an instant.*

<margin>a</margin>
Let there be a line proportioned to the passage of a very strong light, such as the diameter of the world <note>the universe</note> in the case of sunlight, which shall be line *a b c d*; and let there be a strongly luminous body at point *a*. If it were said that light is carried along line *a b c d* in time, and not in an instant, then in a portion of that time it would be carried along line *a b*, and in a minimum sensible time <note>the smallest duration a human can perceive</note> it would be carried across a minimum sensible part of the line *a b*. For if in a sensible time it were carried through an insensible space, <margin>b</margin> it would happen that a sensible space would be composed of insensible parts, just as a measured time following that space would be composed of sensible times in its parts. It would therefore be carried in a minimum sensible time through a minimum sensible space. But in that same time, the form of a weaker luminous body would be carried through the same space as the stronger one; for there is no sensible space smaller than the minimum sensible space, just as there is no sensible time smaller than the minimum sensible time. Thus, a stronger and weaker light would be of equal power, which is impossible, as it implies a contradiction. <margin>c</margin> It is therefore impossible for light to be diffused through a medium proportioned to it in time; it is therefore necessary that this diffusion occurs in an instant. This is what was proposed. Certain natural arguments of **Aristotle** also serve this purpose, which anyone who wishes may look over, as this one resulting inconsistency is sufficient for us.

<margin>d</margin>
### *3. Every line by which light reaches from a luminous body to an opposite body is a natural sensible line having a certain width, within which a mathematical line is to be imaginably assumed. Alhazen Book 4, Chapter 16.*

For light does not proceed except from a body, because it does not exist except in a body. From this it is clear that in the smallest light that can be taken, there is width; for we call that the "smallest light" which, if divided, no longer has the action of light, because it will not be visible—rather, both parts will be extinguished, as neither part of it will be light, nor will it appear to the sense. There is, therefore, in the radial line according to which the diffusion of light occurs, a certain width, because of which it possesses sensibility. And in the middle of that line is an imaginable mathematical line, to which all other mathematical lines in that natural line will be parallel. And since the smallest light proceeds to the smallest part of a body that light can occupy, it is necessary that its process be according to a mathema-

...mathematical [line], which is in the middle of the sensible line <note>Witelo distinguishes between a "mathematical" line (which has no width) and a "sensible" line (a physical beam of light that we can actually see)</note>, and according to the outer lines parallel to the middle line: nor does the smallest light fall upon a mathematical point of the opposing body, but upon a sensible point corresponding to all the indivisible mathematical points at which the mathematical lines of that sensible line can terminate. For this reason, in demonstrating the properties of light, we shall use the configuration of mathematical lines in our process.

### *4. Transparent bodies are suited for the penetration of light and color without essential change to themselves. Alhazen 1, number 28.* <note>Reference to the "Book of Optics" by the 11th-century scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen</note>

For these bodies <note>term: "corpora diaphana" — transparent or translucent materials like glass, water, or air</note> have the property that they do not prevent the forms of light and color from penetrating them; yet they are not changed by the lights or colors, nor are they altered by them with a permanent alteration. Instead, the diffusion of light and color occurs through them according to straight lines (by the first proposition of this book): some of which are parallel, some intersecting, and some in various positions. The distinction between all these lines is created by the distinct position of the luminous body from which the diffusion of that light or color occurs. Thus, the forms of light and color extended from different bodies into the same transparent medium are each extended according to a straight line and pass through to the opposing bodies. Indeed, a transparent body is not stained by lights or colors, but is only penetrated; for such bodies do not lose their own forms because of lights and colors, nor are they stained by lights and colors with a permanent dye, because the forms of light or color do not remain in them after the light or color has withdrawn from being opposite to them. Therefore, those bodies are not transformed by an essential transformation through lights and colors. This is what was proposed.

### *5. Lights and colors in transparent bodies do not mix with one another, but pass through distinctly. Alhazen 1, number 29.*

To declare this matter by way of experiment: let many candles be placed in some location, distinctly separated from one another; and let them all face one opening passing into a dark place <note>This describes the principle of the *camera obscura*, where light passing through a pinhole projects an image into a darkened room</note>, and let some non-transparent body be placed opposite the opening in the dark place. Thus, the lights of the candles appear upon that body distinctly according to the number of candles, and each of them appears opposite one candle according to a straight line passing through the opening and through the middle of the candle's light. If one candle is covered, only the one light opposite that candle will be extinguished; and when the candle is uncovered, the light returns. It is clear, therefore, that the lights in the middle of the opening—where all or many of them cross at a single point—do not mix at that same point, but remain distinct by their own essences. For this reason, when they extend further, they are then locally distinguished according to the diversity of the places where they fall. And since light passing through colored objects is colored by their colors (as has been assumed), it is clear that if the light penetrates distinctly, the colors carried with the light will also penetrate distinctly. Thus, the proposition is evident.

### *6. The proportion of the power of the whole luminous body to the whole luminous body is the same as the proportion of the power of a specific part to the part of the body proportional to it.*

->[Geometric diagram: four horizontal lines of varying lengths labeled a, b, g, and d]<-

Let there be some luminous body *a b*. I say that the proportion of the power <note>term: "virtus" — here meaning the intensity or active strength of the light</note> of the whole body *a b* to the whole body *a b* is as the proportion of the part of the power which is *a*, to the part of the body which is *a*. For if there is not the same proportion for these, it is either greater or smaller. Let it first be greater: and let the power of the whole body *a b* be designated by the line *g d*; let *g* be the power of the part of the body which is *a*, and *d* be the power of the part of the body which is *b*. Therefore, whatever the proportion of *g* to *a* is, the same is the proportion of *d* to *b*. Thus, by Proposition 18 of Book 5 <note>Reference to Euclid’s *Elements*, a foundational textbook for medieval mathematics</note>, the whole *g d* will be to *a b* as *g* is to *a*. If, therefore, the proportion of *g* to *a* is greater than the proportion of *g d* to *a b*, then the proportion of *g d* to *a b* would also be greater than *g d* to *a b*, which is impossible; for there cannot be two proportions for one thing to another where one is greater than the other. The same impossibility occurs for one who suggests that the proportion of the part of the power *g* to the part of the body *a* is smaller than the power *g d* to the body *a b*. For if the proportion of *g* to *a* is smaller than *g d* to *a b*, and the proportion of *g* to *a* is the same as *d* to *b*, then by Proposition 18 of Book 5, the proportion of the whole power *g d* to the body *a b* will be smaller than the proportion of *g d* to *a b*, which is impossible. Therefore, the proportion of *g* to *a* is as *g d* to *a b*. And this is what was proposed. This is universal, unless perhaps union contributes something to the power; for united power is always stronger than itself when divided. Hence our demonstration holds when the parts are not divided from the whole but act within the whole itself without being actually distinct. For when they are distinct from the whole, they are no longer parts; because the name "part," as the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle</note> says, signifies potentiality, not actuality. A complete discussion of this has been held elsewhere.

### *7. For every luminous body that is unchanging in form and position, its action on another equal and homogeneous body—whether placed directly opposite or through a uniform medium—is always equal and uniform.*

->[Geometric diagram: four horizontal lines labeled a, b-g, c, and d]<-

Let the power of some given luminous body be *a*; let there be an equal and homogeneous body opposite it, *b g*; and let the impression of the power *a* upon the body *b g* be designated by *c*. I say that *a* always impresses the impression *c* upon body *b g*, and that *c* is always equal to itself and uniform. For if it were granted that *a* sometimes impresses impression *c* upon body *b g*, but at other times does not impress *c* but something else greater or smaller than *c*, such as *d*: then since the object-body is homogeneous...

homogeneous and uniform: the diversity of the impression will not arise from the body **b g** receiving it <note>original: "patiente", the body 'suffering' or 'undergoing' the action of the light</note>, but from the power **a** being diversified within itself. Therefore, its action is always equal and uniform upon a body either immediately adjacent to it or opposite it through a uniform medium. And this is what was proposed.

### 8. It is necessary that the terminus of the length of any shadow be a luminous ray.

What is proposed here is sufficiently clear through the previously stated principles. For since, according to the 3rd supposition, a shadow occurs only in the absence of light, and according to the 4th supposition, a shadow vanishes when light is introduced: then it must necessarily be that a shadow is caused in exactly as much space as light is lacking; and where light reaches, there the shadow ceases. Since the terminus of the length of any shadow is a line, it is clear that this line must be luminous. Therefore, that line is a luminous ray according to the 6th definition. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 9. Lines produced from the endpoints of the parallel heights of a higher luminous body and a lower shadowy body that meet at a point are proportional to their heights. From this it is clear that the same height of a shadowy body projects a longer shadow from a lower light than from a higher light.

Let the height of any shadowy body be the line **a b**; and let there be another height parallel to it belonging to a luminous body, which shall be **d e**. Let line **d e** be greater than line **a b**. Let lines **e b** and **d a** be produced, which, when drawn out, will meet at some point **g** according to Theorem 16 of the first book of this work. I say that the proportion of line **g b** to line **g e**, and of line **g a** to line **g d**, will be the same as the proportion of line **a b** to line **d e**. For because line **b a** is parallel to line **d e** by hypothesis, it is evident by Euclid’s *Elements* Book 1, Proposition 29, that angle **g b a** is equal to angle **g e d**, and angle **g a b** is equal to angle **g d e**. Furthermore, angle **b g a** is common to both triangles **d g e** and **a g b**. Therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 4 of the *Elements*, the proportion of line **g b** to line **g e** is as line **b a** is to line **d e**. Then, by Theorem 5 of the first book of this work, the proportion of line **g e** to line **b g** will conversely be as line **e d** is to line **a b**. The proposition is therefore evident, since it can be demonstrated in the same way for lines **g a** and **g d**. And from this it is clear that the same height of a shadowy body projects a longer shadow from a lower light than from a higher light. For suppose that some luminous body is at point **h**; and let the ray **h a** fall upon a point of line **e g**, which shall be **k**. By the previously mentioned method, the proportion of **e k** to **b k** will be as **h e** is to **a b**. But by Book 5, Proposition 8, the proportion of **h e** to **a b** is less than **d e** to **a b**. However, the proportion of **d e** to **a b** is as the proportion of **e g** to **b g**, as was shown. Therefore, by Book 5, Proposition 11, the proportion of **e k** to **b k** is less than **e g** to **b g**. Thus, the shadow **b k** has increased greatly in respect to the shadow **b g**, as is clear by Book 5, Proposition 10 and by Theorem 4 of the first book of this work. And because of this, it happens that lunar shadows are always longer than solar shadows; and so it is for any other luminous bodies, higher or lower. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<note>This diagram illustrates Witelo's proof. Two light sources at different heights (D and H) shine past an object (AB). The higher light (D) creates a shorter shadow (BG), while the lower light (H) creates a longer shadow (BK).</note>

### 10. Every luminous ray extended through a single transparent medium over the top of some shadowy body must be a single straight line.

Let the total arrangement of the immediately preceding section remain, and let point **g** be the end of the shadow. Since, as is clear from Proposition 8 of this book, the terminus of any shadow is a luminous ray, I say that the ray bounding the shadow is a straight line, as line **d a g** is in the proposed figure. For if line **d a g** is not straight, then since line **d a** is straight by Proposition 1 of this book (and thus has no cause for obstruction in its progress) and line **a g** is similarly straight by the same proposition, the lines **d a** and **a g** would then join at an angle at point **a**. Let line **a b** be extended; thus triangle **e d b g** <note>original: "trigonū", a triangle</note> is divided by line **b a** parallel to line **e d**. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 29, triangles **e d g** and **b u g** will be equiangular. Therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 4, the proportion of line **g e** to line **g b** will be as line **e d** to line **b u**. But by the proposition immediately preceding this one, the proportion of line **g e** to line **g b** is as line **d e** to line **b a**. Therefore, by Book 5, Proposition 11, there is the same proportion of line **d e** to both lines **b u** and **b a**, which is contrary to Book 5, Proposition 8 and is impossible; for there is a greater proportion to a smaller thing and a smaller proportion to a larger thing. Or it would follow that a larger line is equal to a smaller line by Book 5, Proposition 9; but this is impossible. It is therefore necessary that the ray **d a g** be a single straight line. Which is what was proposed.

# WITELO’S OPTICS

This, however, occurs on the side opposite the luminous body. Let there be some such shadowy body whose height from the horizon is **a b**, and its vertex <note>the highest point</note> **a**; and let the luminous body be higher than the line **a b**, and let its highest point be **d**. Therefore, the rays falling upon the whole line **a b** are blocked from passing through because of the body's opacity. But let ray **d c** fall just above ray **d a**: this ray, therefore, which is not blocked, passes beyond the body **a b**; in its point of incidence, which is **c**, it brings light. Therefore, the shadow ends there. And the proposition is clear.

*12. Of shadowy bodies of equal heights, that which is closer to a luminous body higher than itself makes a shorter shadow.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the length of shadows. A vertical line on the left represents a light source at point 'g'. Let the highest point of the luminous body be **g**, which is higher than two shadowy <note>opaque</note> bodies. Let its height from the surface of the horizon be line **a g**. Let there be two shadowy bodies of equal height erected upon line **a b**, extended along the surface of the horizon; let these be **d e** and **z h**. Of these, let **d e** be closer to the luminous body **a g**, and **z h** more remote. Let a ray **g e t** be drawn through the vertex of body **d e**, which will be a single line according to the 10th proposition of this book; and through the vertex of body **z h**, let ray **g h b** be drawn. Thus, by the preceding proposition, the shadow of body **d e** will be **d t**, and the shadow of body **z h** will be **z b**. I say that the shadow **d t** is smaller than the shadow **z b**. 

For let a line **h k** be drawn from point **h** parallel to line **e t** by the 31st proposition of the 1st book. It is clear by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book that since line **h k** will intersect with line **a b**, its parallel line **e t** also intersects it. And since lines **h b** and **e t** meet at point **g**, the highest point of the luminous body, point **k** will fall between the two points **t** and **b** (by the 2nd and 14th theorems of the 1st book). Now let line **e h** be connected; by the 33rd proposition of the 1st book and by the hypothesis, it will be equal and parallel to line **d z**. But by the 34th proposition of the 1st book, lines **e h** and **t k** are equal; therefore, lines **t k** and **d z** are equal. When line **z t** is added to both, line **d t** will be equal to line **z k**. Therefore, by the 1st proposition of the 6th book, the shadow **z h k** is equal to the shadow **d e t**, since they are of the same height by hypothesis. But the shadow **z h k** is smaller than the shadow **z h b**, because it is only a part of it. Therefore, the shadow **d e t** is also smaller than the shadow **z h b**. Thus the proposition is clear.

*13. The shadow of a straight line placed perpendicularly opposite a luminous body and fixed into the surface of a dense body is none; when elevated, however, it is linear, but it appears as a point.*

For if, by the 3rd postulate, a shadow exists in the absence of light, then it is clear that if a mathematical line <note>an infinitely thin line</note> of a natural body happens to be offered perpendicularly to a luminous body, only a single radial line will be blocked from passing, along with other radial lines that pass to the surface of that body. None of the other radial lines are blocked by the obstacle of that line; otherwise, it would happen that two or more radial lines would meet at one point with a single perpendicular line placed as an obstacle to them, which is impossible, because indivisible things <note>points</note> do not exceed one another in size. Since a ray is nothing other than a luminous line (as is clear from the 6th definition), it is evident that a ray falls upon the surface of a body as a point, just like a line. Therefore, it is also blocked as a point. But when light is brought in, the shadow vanishes by the 4th postulate. Since only a single ray is blocked, and it falls as a point, it is clear that no shadow remains. 

However, when the line is raised above the surface of a dense <note>opaque</note> body, wherever the dense surface is placed under the line, a shadow is found. And if the descent <note>the projection of the shadow</note> occurs through various points, it is clear that the shadow is projected as a line, because a line can be drawn between any two points. Yet it always appears as a point at its intersection with the surface of the dense body, because only there is it mixed with the shadow of the surface's density. Thus, what was proposed is clear.

*14. The shadow of a plane surface of any shape perpendicular to the surface of a luminous body and fixed in a dense body is none; when elevated, however, it is superficial, but it appears as a straight line.*

This is clear from the preceding proposition; for at any point of a line bounding any given surface placed perpendicularly opposite a luminous body, one can draw a line perpendicularly opposite the luminous body. Therefore, the shadow of any of those lines—when the proposed surface is fixed in a dense body—is none; thus there is no shadow of the whole surface either. But when the opposite surface is raised from that dense body, the shadow of any of those lines is a point (by the preceding proposition); and such points collected together seem to constitute a line. Therefore, the shadow of a surface elevated in such a way appears as a linear shadow. And since circular surfaces, from their diameters or other lines drawn perpendicularly above the luminous body, receive only points of shadows which meet below in a straight line (because they block the passage of a straight line), their shadow becomes a straight line. For shadows are not caused by...

Therefore, whatever the shape of the proposed surface, the appearing shadow will always be superficial <note>meaning two-dimensional or flat on a surface</note>: however, it will appear linear because of the reasons stated previously. The proposition is therefore clear.

*15. For every dense body whose base is equal to or broader than its opposite surface, if it is placed perpendicularly against a surface opposite a luminous body and fixed to that dense body, there is no shadow: however, if it is elevated, the shadow is bodily [volumetric]: yet it appears superficial.*

For example: let there be a round column <note>In medieval geometry, "columna" often refers to a cylinder</note>, or another body whose base is equal to or broader than the surface of that same body opposite the base, provided the surface of the body itself does not end at a single point, as it does in a pyramid <note>cone</note>. If this body is fixed to the surface of some solid body and placed perpendicularly opposite a luminous body: I say that what is proposed is true. For if that body is a round column or another body whose base is equal to the surface of some solid body and facing the luminous body, it is clear that since the light rays from every side reach the base according to the lines of its length: no shadow is formed <note>Because the body is flush against the surface, there is no space for a shadow to be cast behind it on that same surface</note>. And the same is clear if that body is pyramidal: or if the base is larger than the surface opposite it facing the luminous body: for then the light is in no way blocked, which would happen, however, if the surface facing the luminous body were broader than the base of the shadowy body itself: for then, with the passage of light blocked, a shadow would be caused. But whatever the shape of the body may be, if it is elevated from the other body to which it was fixed, a superficial shadow will appear: for the surfaces cutting through the body and falling perpendicularly onto the surface of the luminous body constitute a linear shadow through the previous [propositions]. And because the entire surface of the body opposite the luminous body is exhausted <note>fully covered</note> by such surfaces, and such joined lines constitute a surface: it is evident that the shadow of every body thus arranged appears superficial: however, that shadow will necessarily be bodily [volumetric]: since it will be dimensioned according to the dimensions of the body: which can be declared as before. The proposition is therefore clear.

*16. The longest ray reaching a sphere, or a round column, or a round pyramid, is like a tangent line.*
