Let there be a great circle of a sphere, or a cylinder, or a round pyramid, which is **d g**: whose center is point **a**, and diameter **d g**. And since light diffuses itself to every difference of position <note>in all directions</note>, as is clear through the 6th supposition: let the point of the luminous body be **z**, whose light diffuses over the circle **d g**: and let line **z a** be drawn from the point of the luminous body to the center of the illuminated circle: and let a circle be described according to the diameter **a z**, cutting circle **d g** at points **e** and **b**: and let rays **z e** and **z b** be joined. I say that rays **z e** and **z b** are tangent to the sphere, or to any of the other bodies: and that no longer rays than those can reach those bodies. For let lines **a e** and **a b** be drawn from the center of circle **d g** (which is point **a**) to the points of the sections **b** and **e**. For if it were granted that some longer rays could be drawn from point **z** to those bodies: it is clear through the 8th proposition of Book 3 <note>of Euclid</note> that they would not fall upon the arc **e b**: therefore, when extended, they would cut lines **z e** and **z b** before they reach the arcs **e d** or **b g**: thus two straight lines would enclose a surface: which is impossible. And this is indeed not only demonstrable in bodies to be illuminated, but can also be demonstrated in the same way concerning luminous bodies: because the longest ray falling from them upon object bodies is tangent to those luminous bodies themselves. The proposition is therefore clear.

# WITELO’S OPTICS

Thus, according to Proposition 29 of Book 1 <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements, regarding alternate interior angles of parallel lines</note>, the triangles *u g z* and *d g e* are equiangular <note>having the same angles, or "similar" in modern geometry</note>, because the angle *d g e* is common to both triangles. Therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6 <note>Another reference to Euclid, regarding the proportional sides of similar triangles</note>, the ratio of line *g e* to line *g z* is the same as the ratio of line *d e* to line *u z*. But since line *z g* is longer than line *e g*, it follows that line *u z* is longer than line *d e*. Consequently, the shadow of all bodies (regardless of the ratio of their diameters to the diameter of the luminous body) is always larger than the shading body itself, and they always increase in size the further they extend beyond the shading body—the contrary of which is known to our senses. Hence, it was assumed at the beginning that some shadows narrow at their end and terminate at a point <note>This refers to a conical shadow</note>. Thus, the proposition is clear. And since light proceeds from the luminous body and not only from its center, as we have shown, the corollary is manifest: for light must necessarily proceed from every point on the surface of the luminous body to the bodies being illuminated. For a luminous body is uniform <note>original: "unigeneum"</note> in every one of its points; therefore, by the same logic that light is spread from one point of its surface, it must also be spread from every other point. Thus, the proposition is evident.

**18.** *It is impossible for rays to emerge from the surface of a luminous body only as parallel lines falling upon the body being illuminated.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two circles of different sizes, labeled 'a b' (the larger luminous source) and 'g d' (the smaller opaque object). Parallel and converging lines connect the circles, forming various angles and sections labeled with letters like 'z', 'h', 'u', and 'e'. This illustrates the divergent paths light takes.</image-desc>

If this were claimed to be necessary, then an evident impossibility would follow. For let there be a luminous body with diameter *a b*, and an illuminated body *d g*. Let two longer rays be produced from the luminous body which, by Proposition 16 of this book, will be the two lines touching the edges of the body *g d*; let these be *a g u* and *b d e*, and let them be parallel <note>original: "æquidistantes"</note> by hypothesis. Also, let the illuminated part upon which the light falls be *g z d*, and the part upon which the shadow falls be *g h d*. The shadow is thus contained by the two lines *e d* and *u g*, which are parallel. If, therefore, an equal part of the illuminating body corresponds to every part of the body being illuminated (for only then would the rays fall along parallel lines, according to Proposition 33 of Book 1), it is clear that every shadow would be equal in every part to the body casting the shadow. Therefore, the shadow would neither increase nor decrease, but would extend forever into infinity. This contradicts the initial assumption, as some shadows have a sharp, tapering end. This is therefore impossible, and the opposite must be true. This is what was to be shown.

**19.** *Every point of a luminous body illuminates that part of the opaque body to which it is possible to draw straight lines from that same point. From this it is clear that a single point of a luminous body does not illuminate the entire opaque body.*

Luminous bodies are uniform <note>homogeneous</note> in their parts; therefore, the effect of their parts does not vary, nor is it possible for them to illuminate from one part and not another. However, it is not possible to draw straight lines from a single point of a luminous body to every single point of an opaque body; for this reason, one point does not illuminate everything, but opaque bodies are instead illuminated by various different points of the luminous body. For example, let the luminous body be the circle *a b*, which is touched by the tangent line *d g* at point *a* (according to Proposition 17 of Book 3). Let the illuminated body be the concave arc *e u*, and let the line *d g* intersect it at two points *z* and *h*. I say that it is possible for the entire arc *z h* to be illuminated from point *a* of the luminous body, because, as is clear, it is possible to draw a straight line to point *a* from every point on the arc *z h*. However, it is impossible to draw lines to point *a* from the arc *z e* or from the arc *h u* (by Proposition 16 of Book 3), because it is impossible for any straight line to be intercepted between the tangent line *g d* and the circle itself. Therefore, if any line were drawn from any point on those outer arcs to point *a*, it would necessarily cut through the circle, just as line *u a* cuts the circle *a b* at point *t* before it reaches point *a*. The same is true for all lines produced from any point on the arcs *u h* and *z e* to point *a*; they all cut the circle *a b* at a point other than point *a* before reaching it. Thus, a ray exiting from point *a* does not illuminate both arcs *u h* and *z e*, but only the arc *h z*. Yet nothing prevents those arcs from being illuminated by other points of the luminous circle *a b* from which straight lines can be drawn to them. The same logic applies to any other illuminated bodies: for if concave bodies (which seem most likely to be illuminated from a single point) cannot be fully illuminated from one point of a luminous source, then it is much less possible for straight bodies with several flat surfaces, or spherical bodies, or other convex bodies to be illuminated from a single point of a luminous source. Thus, the proposition and its corollary are clear.

A tangent line 'g d' touches the circle at the top point 'a'. Lines radiate from point 'a' toward the arc; lines aimed at the outer edges of the arc (u and e) are shown passing through the body of the circle at point 't', proving they are blocked by the source's own volume.</image-desc>

**21. It is clear, therefore, from these things, that what is closer to the perpendicular is always more strongly illuminated than what is more remote from the same perpendicular: for more light falls upon it, because it is illuminated by more luminous parts. For what has now been demonstrated in arc *k h* happens similarly in any other of the bodies: we have exemplified this in a concave body because it seems that it ought to be more uniformly illuminated. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

**22. Every opaque body closer to a luminous point is illuminated by that point more strongly than a body at a greater distance.**

Let the luminous body be at point *a*: and let the illuminated body be at line *b g*: and let lines *a b* and *a g* be joined. Thus the power <note>original: "virtus," referring to the physical intensity or influence of the light.</note> of body *a* illuminating body *b g* also illuminates the intermediate air, which is contained in the triangle *a b g*: and let line *d e* be drawn parallel to line *b g* by Proposition 31 of Book 1: and let line *b g* be closer to the luminous body existing at point *a* than body *d e*. ### 23. *A more distant point from a luminous body is struck by rays from more points of the luminous body than a closer point.*

Let there be a circle *abc* of a luminous body, whose center is *d*: and let a perpendicular *dg* be drawn, in which two points are marked: *g* the more distant, and *h* the closer. I say that the more distant point, which is *g*, is struck by rays from more points of the luminous body than point *h* itself. For let the longest rays be drawn from the luminous body to point *g*. And similarly, let the longest rays be drawn from the luminous body to point *h*: these rays will therefore be tangent to the sphere <note>While the diagram is a circle, Witelo treats it as a 3D sphere.</note> according to Proposition 16 of this book. Thus, let the rays falling on point *g* touch at points *a* & *b*, and let the rays falling on point *h* touch the sphere at points *e* & *f*: and it is clear through Proposition 60, Theorem 1 of this work, that the points of tangency *e* & *f* fall within points *a* & *b*. Therefore, because point *h* is irradiated only from the points of arc *ecf* and not from others, while point *g* is irradiated from the points of arc *acb* (which is larger than arc *ecf*), the proposition is clear: since point *g* will be illuminated from the surface of the luminous body which arc *acb* divides equally; and point *h* will be illuminated from the surface of the luminous body which arc *ecf* divides equally. However, on account of the strength of the rays, which follows from their brevity <note>Witelo argues that shorter rays are inherently "stronger" or more "virtuous" because they have traveled less distance.</note>, point *h* will be more strongly illuminated by fewer rays than point *g* by more. For the multiplication of light in the more distant point is from the meeting of many rays falling obliquely and weakly, but in the closer point the light is strengthened by the brevity of the ray, according to which more power is sent from the luminous body.

### 24. *Every luminous body illuminates a smaller space, from which [the light] does not escape, more strongly than a space larger than it.*

What is proposed here is clear enough through an example: for one candle illuminates a small room more strongly than a house or a larger room: yet the same can be demonstrated geometrically. For let there be some point of a luminous body *a*: from which through a large space, in which is line *bg*, rays *ag*, *ab*, *ad* are diffused: and let ray *ad* be perpendicular to line *bg*: therefore the whole space *bg* is illuminated according to these lines falling upon it from point *a*. Let line *ae* be cut off from line *ab* as desired, and let line *af* equal to line *ae* be cut off from line *ag*: and let the produced line *ef* intersect the perpendicular line, which is *ad*, at point *h*. If therefore the space is terminated at line *ehf*, so that the light does not pass beyond, that space will be smaller than the space terminated by line *bdg* according to Book 2, Proposition 6. Moreover, all rays reaching line *bg* will reach line *ef*: therefore the rays are more gathered in space *ef* than in space *bg*: they therefore become stronger, since they are of a more united power: they therefore act more than in space *bg*, in which they are more diffused. Therefore, a smaller space is more illuminated, when the power of the light is terminated at its boundaries, than a space larger than it. And this is what was proposed.

*25. Every axis or diameter of an opaque body that does not perpendicularly face the surface of a spherical luminous body is parallel to some diameter of that luminous body.*

For let the axis or diameter of the opaque body <note>original: "corporis umbrosi," literally "shadowy body," referring to an object that casts a shadow.</note> be line *a b*, which does not perpendicularly face the surface of a spherical luminous body whose center is point *c*. I say that line *a b* is parallel to one of the diameters of body *c*. Let line *a c* be drawn from the endpoint of line *a b* to the center of the luminous body: and at point *c*, the endpoint of line *a c*, let an angle be made equal to angle *b a c* according to Proposition 23 of Book 1 <note>The author is citing Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of the era.</note>, which shall be angle *d c a*, with line *d c* extended in such a way that angles *b a c* and *a c d* become alternate interior angles: therefore, lines *d c* and *a b* are parallel to each other according to Proposition 27 of Book 1. and since line *c d* is drawn from the center of the luminous body: it is clear that it is part of the spherical diameter of that body. Therefore, when the diameter *d c e* is extended, it is clear that it is parallel to line *a b*. And this is what was proposed.

[A geometric diagram showing a circle with center point c. A diameter line d-c-e is drawn. An external line a-b is shown parallel to a portion of the diameter. A line connects points a and c, creating alternate interior angles to demonstrate parallelism.]

*26. When the diameter of a spherical luminous body is equal to the diameter of the body being illuminated: only half of it is illuminated, and the shadow is equal to the object, extended into infinity. Aristarchus of Samos in his book "On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon."* <note>Aristarchus was an ancient Greek astronomer (c. 310–230 BC) who proposed a heliocentric model; his work on the sizes of the sun and moon was foundational for medieval optics.</note>

Let the diameter of the illuminating body be *a g*: the part of which facing the body to be illuminated is *a b g*: let the diameter of the body being illuminated be *d u*, which is equal by hypothesis, and by the previous proposition is parallel to diameter *a g*: and let the illuminated surface be *d e u*. I say that *d e u* is half of the surface of the body being illuminated. For let the rays *a d* and *g u* be drawn. Since therefore diameter *a g* is equal and parallel to diameter *d u* by hypothesis and the previous proposition: it is clear that rays *a d* and *g u* <note>The text says "d u" here, but the context and diagram indicate the ray "g u".</note> are parallel and equal according to Proposition 33 of Book 1: therefore, extended into infinity, they will never meet: thus no part of body *d e u* beyond diameter *d u* is illuminated. Therefore, only half of that body is illuminated: for the shadow is extended into infinity with a diameter equal to the diameter of the body: and it is stretched between lines *d z* and *u h*, and line *z h* is equal to line *d u*. Thus the portion of arc *d f u*, which is half of the total surface of the body *d e u*: and lines *d z* and *u h* contain a shadow equal to the opaque object, which is extended into infinity. Thus the proposition is clear.

[A geometric diagram showing two circles of equal size labeled with points a, b, g (left) and d, e, u, f (right). Parallel tangent lines extend from the first circle to the second and then continue horizontally to the right (labeled z and h), representing a cylindrical shadow of infinite length.]

*27. When the diameter of a spherical luminous body is greater than the diameter of the spherical body being illuminated: more than half is illuminated: and the base of the shadow is smaller than the great circle of the illuminated body, converging to a single point behind the body. Aristarchus of Samos in his book "On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon."*

Let the luminous body be contained by circle *a b*: and let the opaque body to be illuminated be contained by circle *g d*: and let the diameter of circle *a b* be greater than the diameter of circle *g d*: and let the incident rays be *a g* and *b d*: these rays will necessarily meet beyond body *g d*. For if they did not meet, they would then be parallel: it would therefore be necessary for diameters *a b* and *g d* to be equal, which is against the hypothesis: let them therefore meet at point *e*: it is clear then that rays *a g* and *b d* do not pass through the endpoints of the diameter of circle *g d*: for if they did pass through, it is clear that, since those rays touch circle *g d* according to Proposition 16 of this book, the angles *e g d* and *e d g* would be right angles according to Proposition 18 of Book 3. In triangle *g d e* there would then be two right angles, which is impossible and against Proposition 32 of Book 1: it is clear then that rays *a e* and *b e* do not pass through the endpoints of the diameter of circle *g d*, but touch the surface of the body being illuminated beyond them: therefore more than half of the body is illuminated. And because a smaller circle of that spherical body contains the shadow, it is clear that the base of the shadow is smaller than the great circle <note>The "great circle" is the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, sharing the same center and diameter as the sphere itself.</note> of the illuminated body. Which is what was proposed.

[A geometric diagram showing a larger circle (a-b) on the left and a smaller circle (g-d) on the right. Tangent lines from the larger circle converge to a single point e behind the smaller circle, forming a conical shadow.]

*28. When the diameter of a spherical luminous body is smaller than the diameter of the spherical body being illuminated: less than half is illuminated: and the shadow is much larger than the illuminated body, extended into infinity.*

Let the luminous body be that whose great circle is *d g*: and the body to be illuminated be that whose great circle is *a b*: and let the diameter of circle *d g* be smaller than the diameter of circle *a b*: the rays *g a* and *b d* will therefore meet beyond the luminous body *d g* according to the previous proposition.

[A geometric diagram showing a smaller circle (g-d) on the left and a larger circle (a-b) on the right. Tangent lines from the smaller circle diverge as they pass the larger circle, indicating an expanding shadow.]

### 29. *It is necessary that a flat surface erected through the middle of the shadow divides both the opaque body and the luminous body into equal halves.*

Let the luminous body <note>original: "corpus luminosum," a light source like the sun or a candle.</note> be *a b*, whose center is *c*: and let the opaque body <note>original: "corpus umbrosum," literally "shadowy body," an object that blocks light.</note> be *d e*, whose center is *f*: and let there be a point in the middle of the shadow, which shall be *g*: and let line *f g* be connected: line *f g* will therefore fall into the middle of the shadow. Thus, a surface erected through the middle of the shadow will necessarily be erected over the line *g f*: that surface therefore passes through the center of the opaque body and the center of the luminous body: therefore, it must necessarily divide those bodies into equal halves through those things which were shown at the beginning of this [book]. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Lines originate from a vertex point 'e' below the circles, pass through the edges of both circles, and diverge as they extend upwards into the shadow region, representing an expanding shadow cone. A point 'g' is indicated at the top of the central axis.]

### 30. *A flat surface dividing the luminous body and the opaque body into equal halves must be erected through the middle of the shadow. From this it is clear that there are as many shadows of the same opaque body as there are light sources it faces.*

Let there be a body upon which light falls, contained by circle *a b*, whose center is point *g*: and let there be one of the luminous bodies contained by circle *d e*, whose center is *u*: and let there be another luminous body contained by circle *z h*, whose center is *c*: the shadow opposite the luminous body *d e* will therefore be seen, contained by lines *a k* and *b l*, whose midpoint shall be *m*. Therefore, when any surface divides the luminous body and the opaque body into equal halves: it will necessarily pass through line *u g m*: it will therefore cut the shadow itself into equal halves: because being erected perpendicularly, it passes through the center of the body itself, which is point *g*. Likewise, the surface dividing both bodies *z h* and *a b* into equal halves passes through line *c g* drawn through the centers of those bodies: but the same passes through the center of the shadow contained under lines *a n* and *b s* according to its midpoint, which shall be *q*. Therefore, that surface dividing bodies *z h* and *a b* into two halves will also divide the shadow into two equal halves. And since the flat surfaces cutting the opaque and luminous bodies into equal halves are divided on both sides: it is clear that the shadows are also numbered according to them: the proposition is therefore clear. For universally, there will be as many shadows of the same opaque body as there are light sources to which it is opposed.

[A geometric diagram showing a central circle 'a b' (with center 'g') representing an opaque body. The shadow from 'd e' is labeled with points 'k', 'm', and 'l'; the shadow from 'z h' is labeled 'n', 'q', and 's'. Radial lines connect the centers of the light sources through the center 'g' to the middle of the respective shadows.]

### 31. *The shadow of an opaque body further from the light source is less dark; that of a closer one indeed is darker.*

For since, as is clear through Proposition 22 of this book, every opaque body closer to a luminous body is illuminated more strongly than a body further away: it is clear that the shadow of the closer body deprives more light: also the rays bounding it are of stronger light: therefore, the shadow between those rays appears blacker, and casts more shadow <note>original: "magis umbrescit," becomes more shadowy or darker. The author is describing contrast: a brighter light source makes the adjacent shadow appear darker to the eye.</note>: since the rays bounding those shadows are more luminous, because of which the shadows also appear more prominent in their presence. But the shadow of a body further from the luminous body deprives less light: also the rays containing the shadow itself are of weaker light: therefore, the shadow between those rays appears weaker: it therefore casts less shadow. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 32. *Every multiplied shadow is darker.*

For let it be that one opaque body is opposed to several luminous bodies: it is clear then through Proposition 30 of this book, that there will be as many shadows of the same opaque body as there are light sources it faces. If therefore it happens that the shadows intersect: I say that the multiplied <note>original: "multiplicata," referring to the area where two or more shadows overlap.</note> shadow is darker: for each of the shadows takes away some light: therefore, the multiplied shadow will take away more light, which [remains]...

*33. Two bodies, of which one shadows the other according to its middle, must necessarily stand on the same surface erected over the luminous body: and if they stand on the same surface, close to each other, one will shadow the other according to its middle.*

This, as for the first part, is clear through Proposition 30 of this book: for since a flat surface dividing the luminous body <term>luminous body</term><note>The source of light, such as the sun, a flame, or a glowing coal.</note> and the opaque body into equal parts is erected over the surface of the luminous body, and it is erected over the middle of the shadow of the opaque thing: the shadow truly falls upon the light of the shadowed body: therefore it is necessary that that shadowed body be centered in a surface erected over the surface of the luminous body. From this also the second part of the present theorem is clear: because if two bodies near to each other consist in their middle parts on the same surface erected over the surface of the luminous body, one will shadow the other: because the one farther from the light, when it is near to that which is closer to the light, will fall into the shadow of that which is nearer to the light: as when the same ray passing over the top of the nearer body also passes over the top of the farther one, or some point that is higher than it. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*34. The parallelism of radial lines or their convergence is not totally of itself from the nature of the rays, but from the proportion of the diameter of the luminous body to the diameters of the opaque bodies. From which it is clear that light is diffused uniformly through the surrounding air.*

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram featuring a large circle at the top labeled 'a' and 'b' representing a light source. Lines (rays) 'a g' and 'b g' converge at a point 'g', passing around a smaller circle 't i'. Parallel lines 'e u' and 'd z' pass around another circle 'k l' of different size. Various points are labeled with letters including f, d, e, k, l, u, z, t, i, g.</image-desc>

This is clear through Propositions 17 and 18 of this book: and it can be declared by example in this way. Let the luminous body be circle *a b*: and let one of the radial lines <term>radial line</term><note>A line representing the path of a single ray of light.</note> departing from it be line *a g*, and another line *b g*, and let them meet at point *g*: let there also be one line *e u*, and another *d z*: and let *e u* and *d z* be parallel. Let there be one body (whose diameter is smaller than the diameter of the luminous body) upon which the light falls, placed between the two lines *a g* and *b g* which touch it, whose greatest circle is *t i*: and let line *b g* touch it at point *i*, and line *a g* at point *t*: and let another body equal to the luminous body, upon which the light falls, be placed between the two parallel lines *e u* and *d z*, touching that body, whose diameter is *k l*: and let it be touched by line *e u* at point *k*, and by line *d z* at point *l*. Thus, the shadow proceeding from body *t i* is diminished and ends, and is pyramidal <note>original: "pyramidalis," referring to a cone-shaped shadow that tapers to a point.</note> through Proposition 27 of this book, because the rays touching body *t i*, which are *a g* and *b g*, meet at point *g*: the shadow of body *t i* is therefore contained by the two lines *i g* and *t g*, and the surface of body *t i* which is toward the side of *g*. The shadow therefore ends at point *g*. Truly, the shadow of body *k l* extended between the parallel lines *l z* and *k u*, as is clear through Proposition 26 of this book, does not end at any point: since those lines containing the shadow, being extended to infinity, do not meet. But if body *t i*, moved outside the lines *a g* and *b g*, were placed within lines *e u* and *d z*, the lines *e u* and *d z* would meet, and the shadow previously contained by them would vary according to the diversity of the proportion of the diameters of body *t i* and body *k l* to the diameter of the luminous body. And from this it is clear that rays by themselves are neither lines nor regular, nor irregular, nor parallel, nor converging: but "lineation" happens to them in respect to the bodies upon which they fall: and parallelism and convergence happen to them by the proportion of the diameters of the opaque bodies to the diameters of the luminous body. Light is therefore diffused uniformly through all the surrounding air, so that every point of the air, from which it is possible to draw a straight line to any point of the luminous body, is illuminated by the light of the luminous body, as is clear through Proposition 19 of this book. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*35. Rays proceeding from one point of a luminous body, according to the length of the lines, approach closer to sensible parallelism.*

Let it be that from the middle point of the luminous body (which is *a*) the equal rays *a b* and *a g* emerge: let the base *b g* also be joined, and let line *d e* be drawn cutting the triangle *a b g* on this side of the middle of its side *a g* parallel to the base *b g* through [Euclid's Elements] Book 1, Propositions 10 and 31: and let line *a z* be drawn from point *a* perpendicularly over the base *b g* through Book 1, Proposition 12, which shall cut line *d e* at point *u*: and let line *e g* be divided into two equal parts at point *h* through Book 1, Proposition 10, and line *d b* at point *t*: and let line *h t* be drawn: therefore line *h t* will be parallel to the base *g b* through Book 6, Proposition 2: it will therefore cut line *u z* through the 2nd theorem of this book: let the point of intersection be *k*. Let there also be drawn from points *e, d, h, t* perpendicular lines over the base *b g*: which shall be *e l, d m, h n, t s*: the perpendicular *e l* will also cut line *h t*: let the point of intersection be *q*, and the point of intersection of lines *d m* and *h t* be *f*: therefore line *q f* will be equal to line *e d* through Book 1, Proposition 34: it is clear then that line *h t* is greater than line *e d*. Since therefore triangles *a u e* and *e h q* are equiangular through Book 1, Propositions 29 and 32: their sides will be proportional through Book 6, Proposition 4. Since therefore, as was shown above, line *a e* is greater than line *e h*: therefore line *e u* will be greater than line *h q*: but line *h t* is greater than line *e d*, as was previously shown: therefore through the 9th theorem of this book the proportion of line *e u* to line *e d* is greater than

36. *When light falls through a window onto an opposing solid body, the perimeter of the light will be larger than the perimeter of the window.*

Let there be a luminous body whose center is $a$: and a large circle $deg$: and let the diameter of the window be $bc$: and let line $tz$ be on the surface of the solid body opposite the light, upon which the ray falls: let the radial lines touching the periphery of the window also be extended, which are $eb$ and $gc$: these will cut each other in some part of the medium: let the point of common section be $f$: and let these extended lines fall upon the surface of the body opposite the light: and let line $eb$ fall upon point $z$, and line $gc$ upon point $t$. Therefore, because in triangle $ftz$, the side $tz$ is greater than the side $bc$: because triangle $ftz$ is larger than triangle $fcb$. And since rays intersect each other in this way through every point of the periphery of the window: because there is an emission of light from any point of the luminous body into the whole window according to the 20th proposition of this book: it is clear that the perimeter of the light falling on the solid body opposite the window is larger than the perimeter of the window. And this was what was proposed.

37. *When a ray from the center of a luminous body falls perpendicularly to the center of a circular opening, the light on the surface of a dense body parallel to the surface of the opening is truly circular.*

Let the circle of the opening be $abgd$, whose center is $e$: to which the surface of the solid body $fhkl$ is parallel: and let line $ez$ be erected from the center $e$, perpendicularly over the surface of circle $abgd$: therefore, in whatever point of line $ez$ the center of the luminous body may be, I say that the light falling on the surface $fhkl$ is truly circular. For it is clear through the 65th theorem of the 1st book of this work, that all lines $za$, $zb$, $zg$, $zd$ drawn from the pole $z$ to the circumference are equal, and they contain equal angles with line $ez$ according to the 8th proposition of the 1st book <note>Reference to Euclid</note>. Therefore, let line $ze$ be extended beyond point $e$ to the surface parallel to the circle of the opening, which is $fhkl$: and it will fall perpendicularly upon it according to the 14th proposition of the 11th book: let it fall on point $m$: and let line $zb$ be extended to the surface $fhkl$ at point $k$, and line $za$ to point $f$, and line $zd$ to point $h$, and line $zg$ to point $l$: and lines $af$, $bk$, $dh$, $gl$ will be equal according to the 25th theorem of the 1st book of this work on account of the parallelism <note>original: "æquidistantiam"</note> of the surfaces and the equality of the angles: therefore the whole line $zf$ will be equal to the whole line $zh$: and $zk$ equal to line $zl$. Let lines $fm$, $hm$, $km$, $lm$ also be drawn. Therefore, in triangle $fmz$ the base $fm$ will be equal to the base $hm$ of triangle $hmz$ according to the 4th proposition of the 1st book: and in the same way line $km$ will be equal to line $hm$, and line $lm$ equal to line $km$. It is clear therefore, by the 9th proposition of the 3rd book, that the surface $fhkl$ is circular: and it is that upon which the rays of light falling through the window $abgd$ are terminated: since the demonstration is the same for all other lines. Therefore the proposition is clear.

### *38. When a light ray falls obliquely through the center of a circular hole onto a surface placed beneath the opening: the incident light will take the form of a conic section <term>conic section</term><note>original: "sectionis pyramidalis"; Vitello uses the term "pyramidal" to describe what we now call conical. A "pyramidal section" refers to the shape created when a plane intersects a cone of light—in this case, an ellipse.</note>, whose major diameter will be on the surface perpendicular to the surface of the window and to the surface of the underlying body.*

[A geometric diagram depicting a point source of light $f$ projecting through a circular aperture ($a, b, c, d$ with center $e$) onto a lower surface ($h, m, k, l$ with center $g$). A cone of light is formed, and its intersection with the lower plane is shown. Additional circles and lines (including points $p$ and $q$) illustrate the geometry of the projection and its conical sections.]

Let there be a circular hole $abcd$, with center $e$: and let there be a surface $hmkl$ parallel to it: let $f$ be the center of the luminous body <term>luminous body</term><note>The source of light, such as a lamp or the sun.</note>: and let it first be that line $fe$ falls obliquely upon the surface of the circle $abcd$: this line, being extended, will fall upon the surface $hmkl$ in a similarly oblique manner because the surfaces are parallel, as argued in Proposition 23 of Book 1 of this work: let it therefore fall upon point $g$: and let the diameter of the circle, line $aeb$, be drawn: let angle $aef$ be acute: therefore, by Euclid's Elements Book 1, Prop 13, angle $bef$ will be obtuse: let lines $fa$ and $fb$ be drawn. 

And because the square of line $fa$ is less than the two squares of lines $ef$ and $ea$ (by Euclid, Book 2, Prop 13), and the square of line $bf$ is greater than the square of line $fe$ and the square of line $be$ (by Euclid, Book 2, Prop 12): and since the square of line $be$ is equal to the square of line $ae$ (because they are equal radii): and the square of line $fe$ is common to both: it is clear that the square of line $fb$ is greater than the square of line $fa$: therefore line $fb$ is longer than line $fa$. Having extended lines $fa$ and $fb$ to the surface $hmkl$: if line $fa$ falls on point $m$, and line $fb$ on point $l$: line $fl$ will be longer than line $fm$ by the same reasoning as before. Having joined lines $lg$ and $mg$ at point $g$, where the ray passing through the center of the window falls: by Euclid Book 6, Prop 2 and Book 5, Prop 11, the ratio of line $lg$ to line $be$ is as the ratio of line $gf$ to line $ea$: because the ratio of each of those to one another is as line $gf$ to line $fe$: therefore, by Euclid Book 5, Prop 16, the ratio of line $lg$ to line $mg$ is as line $be$ to line $ea$: but line $be$ is equal to line $ea$: therefore line $lg$ is equal to line $gm$. 

Then let diameter $ed$ be drawn perpendicular to diameter $ab$, and let lines $fc$ and $fd$ be connected: let them be extended to surface $hmkl$ at points $h$ and $k$: and let line $hgk$ be drawn. And since the surface in which lines $fe$ and $ab$ lie is the only one perpendicular to the circle of the window (since all other surfaces in which line $fe$ lies fall obliquely to that surface—for so we define line $ab$), therefore surface $afb$ will be perpendicular to the surface of the circle of the window. It is clear, then, because angle $fed$ is equal to angle $fec$: line $fd$ is equal to line $fc$ by Euclid Book 1, Prop 4: therefore, as before, line $hg$ will be equal to $kg$, and line $fh$ equal to line $fk$, and $fg$ is common. And because line $hk$ is perpendicular to line $ml$ and to line $fg$: it is clear by Euclid Book 11, Prop 4, that line $hg$ is perpendicular to the surface in which lines $fg$ and $mg$ lie: therefore by Euclid Book 11, Prop 18, surface $hmkl$ will be perpendicular to surface $fmg$: therefore surface $fmg$ is also perpendicular to surface $hmkl$. 

Imagine then, from point $g$ at the end of the axis (which is $fg$), a circle is drawn around the pyramid of illumination <term>pyramid of illumination</term><note>A cone of light rays originating from a single point.</note> by Proposition 102 of Book 1 of this work: therefore by Propositions 100 and 89 of Book 1, axis $fg$ is perpendicular to that circle, and it is itself oblique to the surface $hmkl$: therefore by Proposition 103 of Book 1, line $hmkl$ will be a conic section, whose major diameter will be in the surface $fml$ perpendicular to surface $hmkl$. The proposition is therefore clear. 

And if the surface of the circular window is the base of the pyramid of illumination, so that the center of the luminous body is the pole of the circle of the window, and the axis is perpendicular to the surface of the window, but the surface of the solid body receiving the light rays is not parallel to the surface of the window: the shape of the light will still be a conic section: which is to be demonstrated in the previously mentioned way: for having drawn a surface parallel to the surface of the window from point $l$ at the end of the longer ray (which is $fl$) by Proposition 102 of Book 1: it is clear by Proposition 100 of Book 1 that the surface will cut the pyramid of illumination into a circle, which we call $lpq$. Therefore, surface $hmkl$ cuts it according to a conic section. The proposition is therefore clear.

### *39. All light falling through angular holes becomes rounded.*

What is proposed here is clear through Proposition 35 of this work. For since all rays proceeding from a single point of a luminous body approach a sensible <term>sensible</term><note>Meaning "perceptible to the senses." Even if rays are not mathematically parallel, they appear so to the eye over long distances.</note> parallelism along their length: it is clear that rays falling into the angles of the holes according to the arrangement of the angular openings apply themselves to the parallelism of the ray falling perpendicularly (or nearly so) to the surface of the hole: they therefore withdraw themselves from the angularity, and thus the light falling on the surface facing the hole begins to be rounded. 

And since, as is clear from Proposition 20 of this work, light is diffused from every point of any luminous body along every line that can be drawn from that point to the opposite surface: for all those rays meet at any point of the medium: it is clear that they intersect each other at any point, and the rays from the lower points of the luminous body intersect other rays from the higher points at the lines of the window and extend further: and thus the light passing through windows of this kind is rounded: which would not happen so much if the rays penetrating the window emerged from only one point of the luminous body. The proposition is therefore clear.

Let the center of the luminous body be $e$: and let the square hole be $abcd$: at whose middle point (which is $f$) there falls

### 41. *When a ray falls obliquely through the middle of a square opening onto the surface of a dense body placed beneath the opening: the incident light will be a figure longer in one dimension with its angles equally curved.*

Let the center of the luminous body be point $e$, as in the preceding: and the periphery of the square opening be $abcd$, through whose middle point (which is [part of line] $ef$) the ray $ef$ falls obliquely: and let the surface of the dense body placed beneath that opening be $ghkl$, upon which the ray similarly falls obliquely. I say that the shape of the light on the underlying surface will be longer in one part <term>longer in one part</term><note>original: "altera parte longior"; a standard geometric term of the era for a rectangle or an oblong shape.</note>. Since those surfaces are not the bases of the pyramids of illumination, but only cut those pyramids obliquely, it is clear by Proposition 99 of Book 1 of this work that both figures $abcd$ and $ghkl$ (whether their surfaces are parallel or not) are figures longer in one part: because those figures which terminate the pyramids at those points where the axis $ef$ falls perpendicularly to the proposed surfaces are both square: but the others falling obliquely to the axis at those points are both longer in one part. Thus the first point is clear. And since, as is clear by Proposition 35 of this book, the longer rays approach a kind of parallelism, it is clear that the angles of that light figure are somewhat curved, just as was explained in the two preceding [propositions]. And this is what was proposed.

### 42. *A perpendicular ray drawn from the center of a luminous body through the middle of a second transparent medium denser than the first, onto the surface of an object, always penetrates without being refracted.*

<margin>Alhazen <note>original: "Alhazen 3 n 7"; refers to Book 3 of the Optics by the 11th-century scholar Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen).</note></margin>
The proof of this proposition rests more upon the experience of instruments than upon any other demonstration. Therefore, when someone wishes to test the manner of the refraction <term>refraction</term><note>original: "fractionis"; the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another.</note> of luminous rays in a second transparent medium denser than the first, such as in water, which is denser than air: let him take a vessel of straight sides of whatever material or shape he wishes, provided the height of the edges is greater than half a cubit <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches (45 cm), so this vessel is over 9 inches deep.</note>, and its diameter or width is not less than the diameter of the instrument we directed to be made in the first [proposition] of this book: and let the edges of that vessel be smoothed until the surface passing through its edges is a flat plane: and let some small visible colored body be placed at the bottom of the vessel, such as a coin or a thing painted with different colors: then let the vessel be filled with clear water. 

When the movement of the water has ceased, if the observer casts his sight perpendicularly over the middle of the coin or painting: he will find the shape and color and their position and the arrangement of parts in the same way they are arranged in themselves, as if they were seen in the air. Let the experimenter then consider that position of his body, whether he is standing or sitting, and his distance from the vessel, and the position of the vessel itself, and all the circumstances of that vision. Let this vessel full of clear water then be placed in a spot where the sun shines, and let the vessel be fixed in such a way that the surface of the circumference of the vessel is parallel to the horizon: this can be determined if the surface of the water is parallel to the rim of the vessel. 

Then let the instrument be placed in this vessel, so that the sighting vanes <term>sighting vanes</term><note>original: "pinnulae"; small plates with holes used to align an instrument with a light source.</note> existing on the ends of the ruler are placed over the edge of the vessel on both sides: then half of the instrument with the entire ruler will be inside the vessel: then let water be removed until the surface of the water cuts the center of the instrument: and let the instrument be rotated around the vessel until the edges above the water shadow those below the water: and then, holding the ruler with one hand, let the instrument be rotated with the other hand around its center until the sunlight passes through the hole $lmn$, which is in the rim of the instrument, and the hole of the square plate, and reaches the surface of the water, because the light passing through a round hole is always widened per Proposition 36 of this book. 

Let the instrument also be stayed in such a way that the light falling upon the plate of the second hole, which is $xyz$, has an equal position: and then the experimenter, having withdrawn his hands from the instrument, should look at the bottom of the water from the side of the quadrant of the instrument whose edge is cut away (which is $ad$), using the same position and manner as he previously looked at the coin: and he will find the light passing from the two holes onto the surface of the other edge, which is inside the water, and the light between the two outer circles of the three parallel marked circles, or exceeding the distance of those circles by a little: and the addition will be equal on the two sides of the circles. From this it is clear that the middle point of this light falls on some point of the circumference of the middle circle of those three circles, such as at point $p$. Then let an iron needle or a small piece of wood applied to the inner part of the hole in the rim of the instrument pass through the middle of the hole diametrically, and then to the one looking as before, the shadow of the needle will be seen in the mid...

When the needle is entirely removed, the light will return. The distance of the center of the light from the center of the instrument will therefore be equal to half the width of the ruler, which is equal to the perpendicular falling from the center of the opening to the surface of the base of the instrument; thus, the center of the light on the surface of the ruler or water will be the center of the middle circle. Therefore, let the ruler be rotated until its sharp edge passes through the center of the instrument, and the lower part of the line dividing its angle equally is at the center of the light which is within the water. The upper edge of the ruler thus passes through the center of the middle circle; therefore, the point of the line on the upper surface of the ruler which is at the surface of the water is the center of the middle circle and of the light on the water's surface; and that line will be the radius of the middle circle. Then, let a long needle be inserted into the water so that its tip is at the point of the ruler’s angle; the shadow of the needle will cut the light that is within the water, and the shadow of the needle's tip will be at the end of the ruler, which is in the center of the light. If the needle's tip is fixed and the needle is moved, the shadow of the needle will change position to different parts of the light, yet the shadow of the tip will not change from the center of the light. When the needle is totally removed, the full light returns. The same thing also happens regardless of which point on the line of the ruler's surface the needle's tip is placed. From this it is clear that light existing at any point of the light within the water proceeds from a similar point in the light on the surface of the water, and that from the central point of the light above the water to the central point of the light within the water, a ray is extended according to the straight line which is the middle of the ruler. From this it is clear that the passage of light through the body of water is according to straight lines, by Book 1, Proposition 11. And this is what we intended to declare experimentally concerning the proposed proposition.

### 44. Through a second transparent medium that is rarer than the first, a ray falling perpendicularly from the center of the luminous body onto the surface of the object penetrates without being refracted.

The proposed theorem can similarly be declared by experimental practice. For let a piece of clear glass or crystal be taken in a cubic shape, with a length double the diameter of the opening on the instrument's rim. Let their flat surfaces be made equal and parallel, and let their sides be straight and highly polished. Then, let a straight line be marked by engraving with hard iron in the middle of the instrument’s base, passing through its center (which is $e$) perpendicularly over its diameter ($fg$), upon the ends of which two perpendiculars, $fh$ and $gk$, are produced on the rim of the instrument. Therefore, let one of these glasses be placed upon the surface of the instrument’s base, and let one of its sides be applied to the perpendicular line $zex$ in such a way that the middle of the side of the glass is truly over point $e$, the center of the instrument. Then, let that glass, placed perfectly upon this cut surface, be positioned on the surface of the instrument's plate so that its convexity <note>original: "gibbositas"; referring to the rounded side of the hemisphere.</note> faces the holes, and let the middle of the line (the common section of the two flat surfaces of the glass) be applied to the center of the plate, and fix the glass upon the plate so it does not fall. Next, let a fine ruler be placed on the surface of the instrument's plate, as in the experiment with the cubic glasses, so that the surface of the ruler containing the straight line of width is on the side of the glass and near it. Then, let the instrument be placed in the aforementioned vessel, and let the vessel be placed in the sun without water. Move the instrument until the sunlight passes through both holes; the light will fall upon the surface of the ruler. Then, let the tip of a needle or an iron stylus be placed over the center of the upper hole; the shadow of the needle's tip will fall upon the center of the light. When the stylus is removed, the light will return to its place. The same thing happens to one placing the tip of a needle over the center of the second hole. Then, let the tip of the needle be placed over the center of the glass sphere; the shadow of the needle's tip will fall upon the center of the light. From this, it is clear that since the light passing through the centers of the two holes also passes through the center of the glass sphere and through the middle of the light's surface on the convex part of the glass. It is also clear from this that light passing into the body of the glass extends according to the straightness of the line passing through the centers of the two holes; and that line is the radius of the sphere. For the perpendicular going from the center of the glass base to the plate is equal to the diameter of the hole and the line going from the center of the hole perpendicularly to the surface of the plate. Since these two perpendiculars fall upon the diameter of the plate, it is clear that the line passing through the centers of the two holes, when extended straight, reaches the center of the glass sphere. Therefore, the diameter of this glass sphere lies on that line. It is thus perpendicular to the surface of this sphere <note>referencing proposition 7 of the 11th book of Euclid</note>. Since the line passes through the center of the sphere, it is clear that it is perpendicular to the convex surface of the sphere, just as was shown above for the cubic glasses. Therefore, let the fine ruler applied to the surface of the plate be removed, and let the instrument be placed a second time in the vessel as before, and moved until the light passes through the two holes. The light will be found on the rim of the instrument, and the center of the light will be found at point $p$, which is the common intersection between the circumference of the middle circle and line $gk$, which is perpendicular on the rim of the instrument. This is at the end of the diameter of the middle circle, which is $mp$, passing through the centers of the two holes $m$ and $y$. From this, it is clear that since light passing into the body of the glass and reaching its center then emerges into the body of the air, it extends according to the line that was extended within the body of the glass. Thus it must necessarily be perpendicular to the surface of the air touching the surface of the glass. Therefore, if water is poured into the vessel, with the glass remaining in its position until the water rises above the center of the glass, the center of the light will still be found at the end of the diameter of the middle circle. And if the glass sphere is moved so that its convexity is situated at the second hole and the flat surface at the center of the instrument (namely point $e$), whether water is poured over it or not, all the same things will happen as in the previous position; for a ray passing through the centers of both holes will always pass through the center of the sphere as well. From all of this, it is clear—

# VITELLO'S OPTICS

Whether the medium is cubic or spherical, it is clear that if the second transparent medium is denser or rarer, as long as the line along which the ray extends is perpendicular to the surface of the second body, the light travels through the second body in a straight line continuing from the first. The point is thus proven: for the body of glass is of a denser transparency than the body of air, and even denser than the body of water.

*45. In a second transparent medium that is rarer than the first, the refraction of rays striking obliquely from the rear surface of the second medium occurs away from the perpendicular rising from the point of refraction on the surface of the second body. Alhazen, Book 7, note 7.* <note>original: "Alhazen 7 n 7"; referring to the "Perspectiva" of the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen.</note>

What is proposed here must be declared through practical experience with an instrument, in conformity with the previous demonstrations. Let the same spherical glass be taken that we used in the preceding, most recent theorem. Let the line that forms the common section of the flat surface of the glass fall obliquely upon the diameter of the plate at any angle of obliquity. It is therefore evident that the line passing through the centers of the two holes is oblique to the flat surface of the glass. 

Therefore, let the glass be firmly joined to the plate of the instrument in this position. Place the instrument in a vessel, and the vessel in the sun, and move the instrument until the light passes through the two holes. The light will fall on the inner rim of the instrument, and the center of the light will be on the circumference of the middle circle, but outside that point $p$, which is the common difference between the circumference of the middle circle and the line standing on the rim of the instrument, which is $gk$. Its deviation will be toward the side where the sun is; it will therefore be toward the side of the perpendicular rising from the place of refraction on the spherical surface of the glass. 

And since this light extends in the air according to the straightness of the line passing through the centers of the two holes (as is clear through this [work]), and this line in this position reaches the center of the sphere on both sides and is oblique to the flat surface of the sphere, it is clear that the endpoint of that light's extension is at the center of the glass. Thus, the light extends into the body of the glass along a straight line from the center of the sphere to the circumference. Since this line is a diameter, it is clear by [Proposition] 72, Theorem 1 of this book <note>original: "72 t 1 huius"</note> that it is perpendicular to the spherical surface of the glass, and therefore also to the concave surface of the air containing the glass sphere. 

Therefore, it is not refracted in the second air, just as it was not in the first; nor is it refracted in the body of the glass, nor in its convex part. It is refracted, therefore, at the center of the glass, because it was oblique to its flat surface, in which the center of the glass is located. It is clear from these experiments what was also declared above: namely, that if light is extended in a subtler <note>less dense</note> body and strikes the surface of a grosser <note>denser</note> body obliquely, it will be refracted by it. Its refraction will be toward the perpendicular on the spherical surface of the grosser body, as was clear from [Proposition] 43 of this book; just as if refraction occurs from air to water, that refraction will be toward the perpendicular rising from the point of refraction on the surface of the water, though the refraction does not actually reach the perpendicular.

But if the glass is positioned conversely—namely, so that its convex spherical surface faces the upper hole, and the midpoint of the line (which is the common difference of the flat surfaces), which is the center of the sphere, is over the center of the instrument—let this line fall obliquely on the diameter of the plate. Let a line be drawn on the surface of the plate from the center of the plate, perpendicular to the line that is the common section of those flat surfaces; this will necessarily be perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass standing upon the surface of the plate.

The deviation of the light will be toward the side opposite to that where the perpendicular rises from the place of refraction on the flat surface of the glass. Thus, the refraction of light occurs at the center of the glass sphere, because the light passing through the centers of both holes becomes oblique to the flat surface of the glass and to the surface of the air touching the glass. 

And if water is poured into the vessel until it rises above the center of the instrument, the center of the light will still fall on the circumference of the middle circle outside the end of its diameter, obliquely toward the side opposite to the side on which the perpendicular falls. And since air is subtler than water, and water subtler than glass, the distance of the center of light from the end of the diameter of the middle circle will be greater in air than in water. 

But if the glass is placed differently on the surface of the plate—namely, so that the line which is the common difference of the two flat surfaces of the glass lies on the line cutting the diameter of the plate perpendicularly, but its midpoint (which is the center of the glass sphere) is not over the center of the plate—and the convex side of the glass is turned toward the holes, and a thin ruler is fixed upright on the surface of the plate at its rim, and its surface containing the line is toward the glass, and the end of the ruler cuts the diameter of the plate perpendicularly: it is clear that the line passing through the centers of the two holes does not pass through the center of the sphere, but through another point on the flat surface of the glass. It will be oblique to the spherical surface by [Proposition] 72, Theorem 1 of this book.

...of the holes is perpendicular to the surface of the flat glass by the 8th theorem of the 11th book <note>Vitello frequently cites Euclid’s *Elements* for geometric proofs; "8 p 11" refers to Book 11, Proposition 8</note>: since that line is parallel to line **f g**, the diameter of the plate, which by hypothesis is perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass. *46. It is necessary that every incident and refracted ray exist within the same plane surface.*

Moreover, what is now proposed can be declared experimentally. For when everything is arranged as in the 43rd theorem of this book, the light incident upon the center of light on the surface of the water, and from the center of the light existing on the surface of the water (which is the center of the middle circle), incident upon the center of light existing within the water (which is on the circumference of the middle circle), passes through the centers of both holes, which are likewise on the surface of the middle circle. It is clear, then, that the line along which the light strikes the surface of the water through the medium of the air, and the line along which it is refracted in the medium of the water, are in the same surface: since both of them are on the surface of the middle circle of the three designated circles. 

Furthermore, this refraction is found in a solar ray when the solar ray, passing through the centers of the holes, is oblique to the surface of the water, not when it is perpendicular. And due to the obliquity of the instrument's position relative to the center of the water's sphere, this radial line will never become perpendicular to the surface of the water unless the sun is perpendicularly at the zenith of the head <note>The "zenith of the head" refers to the point directly overhead in the sky</note>. However, with the sun existing beyond or short of the zenith of the heads, this experimentation is sufficiently evident at any time. Therefore, what was proposed is clear. And we call this surface the "surface of refraction." 

It is therefore clear from all these five preceding propositions that all light passes through any transparent bodies <term>diaphana<gloss>transparent or translucent materials</gloss></term> along straight lines. And as long as the lines are perpendicular to the surfaces of the bodies, no matter how different their transparency may be, the light is always extended along the straightness of that same line and is not refracted. But in a body of different transparency, all light striking the surface of the second body obliquely is refracted along straight lines other than those along which it struck the first body. Nevertheless, these lines will always be in the same plane surface, imagined to cut both of those bodies; and this surface, in the inspection of the instrument, is the middle circle of the three circles marked on the interior part of the instrument's rim, whose diameter is line **m p**. Indeed, when oblique light exits from a thinner <note>original: "subtiliori"; meaning less dense or "rarer"</note> body to a thicker <note>original: "grossius"; meaning denser</note> one, it is refracted toward the perpendicular exiting from the place of refraction, which is perpendicular to the surface of the thicker second body. And when oblique light exits from a thicker body to a thinner one, it is refracted toward the side opposite the perpendicular drawn in the aforementioned manner over the surface of the second body, namely the thinner one.

*47. While a perpendicular ray penetrates every transparent body, a ray incident obliquely in the medium of a second, denser transparent body is refracted toward the perpendicular drawn from the point of incidence upon the surface of the second transparent body; and in the medium of a second, rarer transparent body, it is refracted away from the same.*

That which has been proven thus far through particular experiments with instruments, we intend to support with natural demonstration. For all natural motions that occur along perpendicular lines are stronger, since they are aided by the universal celestial power <note>A common medieval belief that forces from the heavens act most effectively along the shortest, direct path</note> flowing into every subject body along the shortest straight line. The impulses of strikes made perpendicularly are stronger than those made obliquely; and similarly, impacts made perpendicularly are stronger than all oblique impacts; and among all oblique impacts, those that approach closer to perpendicularity are stronger. Since, therefore, the density of any body hinders the passage of light, it is necessary to imagine that light is repelled from its passage...

-># WITELO'S OPTICS<-

...by passing through the resistance of a dense body, and even more through the resistance of a denser body. By this resistance of a passive quality (which is density) to an active quality (which is light), we understand a certain manner of the **motion of light** through the medium of resisting bodies, which are more or less capable of receiving the impression of light. This is not because there is any local movement in the transmutation of light itself—as is clear from the second book of this work—but because light, in the same instant, compresses or diffuses itself more or less according to the diversity of the media. This is what we call here the **motion of light**. Thus, all light passing through a transparent body passes with a very fast and insensible motion; however, the motion is faster through more transparent bodies than through less transparent ones. For every transparent body resists the penetration of light to a greater or lesser degree, depending on how much transparency it participates in; for the thickness <note>The Latin word *grossities* refers to the physical density or "grossness" of the material compared to the "subtlety" of light.</note> of bodies is always resistant to the penetration of light.

Therefore, when light passes through a transparent body obliquely and encounters another denser transparent body, the denser body resists the light more strongly than the rarer body did before. It is necessary, therefore, that the motion of the light be changed because of the resistance of that denser body. If the resistance is strong, then that motion will be refracted toward the opposite side; but because it does not resist with total force <note>i.e., it is not an opaque mirror</note>, the light does not return back toward the direction from which it moved. If, however, the resistance is weak due to the greater rarity of a more transparent body, then the incident light will not be refracted toward the opposite side, nor can it proceed along the line it began, but it will be changed in its position. 

When light falls **perpendicularly** upon any transparent bodies, regardless of their varying transparency, it will not be changed but will penetrate all of them directly. This is because the perpendicular is the strongest of all lines, and those oblique lines closer to the perpendicular are stronger than those further away. Thus, when light falls obliquely on a denser transparent body, it is extended along a straight line approaching the perpendicular that emerges from the point where the light meets the surface of the dense body. This occurs because the easiest of motions is along a perpendicular line. Therefore, if a ray of light falls upon a perpendicular line, it passes straight through because of the strength of the motion on the perpendicular; but if the ray falls obliquely, it cannot pass straight through because of the weakness of motion on oblique lines. It happens, therefore, that it declines toward a path through which the passage is easier than the path it was moving along by the line of incidence. The easiest of motions, and the one most aided by influence, is upon the perpendicular line; for that which is closer to the perpendicular is of easier passage than that which is further from it.

Let it be that from point **a** of a luminous body, several rays fall through the medium **a b** onto the surface of another transparent body, on which there is the line **b c d e**; and let **b f** be the line of depth of that body; and let line **a b** be perpendicular to that surface. It is clear according to the aforementioned reasoning regarding the strength of perpendiculars, and through the instrumental experiments in propositions 42 and 44 of this book, that the ray falling along the perpendicular line **a b** penetrates the entire body **b e f**. However, for the ray falling along line **a c**, if it were to pass directly through the body, then there would be no difference in the transparency of bodies **a b e** and **b e f**, which is contrary to our hypothesis. Therefore, the line **a c** will not be a continuous line due to the difference in resistance.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the principles of refraction. A point 'a' (light source) sits above a horizontal line segment 'b c d e' representing the surface of a medium. A vertical line 'a b' acts as the perpendicular, extending down to point 'f'. Several rays 'a c', 'a d', and 'a e' incline from point 'a' to the surface. At the surface point 'c', a refracted ray continues into the lower medium, bending toward a second perpendicular line 'c g'. But if it was moving freely through a less resistant body along line **a c**, it cannot move along that same line in a body that is more or less resistant. If, therefore, the body **b e f** is denser than body **a b e**, it is clear from the premises that the passage through it is more difficult. If the line **a c** were refracted away from the perpendicular line drawn from point **c** to the surface of the body **b c d e** (which we call line **c g**), its effect would be weakened and it would reach nothing; thus it would have fallen in vain. But **nature does nothing in vain** <note>original: "natura autem frustrà nihil agit" - A fundamental principle in medieval science, suggesting that physical laws always follow the most efficient path.</note>, as was supposed at the beginning. Therefore, line **a c** (as has also been shown experimentally in proposition 43 of this book) is necessarily refracted toward the side of the perpendicular **c g**, so that its action may be strengthened. The same is true for the rays falling along lines **a d** and **a e**.

But if the body whose surface contains line **b c d e** is of a rarer transparency than body **a b e**, the perpendicular ray **a b** still penetrates unrefracted due to the strength of its action. However, the ray passing through the denser body along line **a c** and falling on the surface of the rarer body at point **c** does not find the resistance it had before. And because it is characteristic of "forms" <note>In this context, "form" refers to the active essence or power of the light.</note> to always spread themselves according to the fullness of all capable matter, it is clear that ray **a c** does not proceed along the line **a c**; for if it did, the disposition of the transparent bodies regarding their resistance to receiving light would be uniform, which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore, the ray **a c** is refracted, but not toward the perpendicular **c g**. This is because that refraction does not happen because of the resistance of the matter, but because of the victory of the acting form over matter that is more disposed to it than before. Hence the form spreads itself by its own power from its starting progress along line **a c**, and toward the side opposite the perpendicular **c g** and its parallel **b f**. The same is true of all other oblique rays, such as **a d** and **a e**. The motion of a ray falling obliquely along line **a c** in a second transparent body that is denser (which is **b e f**) is composed of the motion toward the side of the perpendicular **a b** passing through body **b e f**, and of the motion made upon the line **c b**, which is perpendicular to line **c g**. Since the passage of the perpendicular is the strongest and easiest of motions, and the density of the body resists the end of the motion it intended, the line **a c** will necessarily move toward the per-

...toward the perpendicular line $cg$, extending from point $c$, where the ray $ac$ meets the surface of the denser body. And since that motion is resisted because of the thickness of the medium, and also because of the nature of the other motion along line $cb$—which is not entirely lost due to the resistance of the medium but is only impeded—the light will therefore decline toward point $b$, always approaching the perpendicular line $abf$. Let it be so, then, that in a second transparent medium denser than the first, the refraction of ray $ac$ follows the line $cl$, which is closer to the perpendicular $cg$ (extending from point $c$ where it meets the denser body) than the line $ac$ was, along which it struck the surface of that body. If line $ac$ were extended beyond point $c$ to point $h$, it would have been near the same perpendicular extended beyond point $c$ to point $i$, such that the angle $ach$ is greater than angle $lcg$. <note>Witelo is describing the law of refraction: when light enters a denser medium, it bends toward the "normal" (perpendicular) line.</note> It will not, however, meet with the perpendicular $bf$ toward point $f$, but toward point $a$ through $at$; this is because it meets its parallel line $cg$ at point $c$.

But when the ray $ac$ passes from a denser body into a rarer one, then because it encounters less resistance, its motion will be faster and more diffusive of itself. And since the resistance of a denser medium always pushes oblique light so that it gathers toward the perpendicular line produced from the point of incidence upon the surface of that body (which is $cg$), it is clear that in a rarer transparent medium, that resistance will be less than the first. Therefore, the motion of light is made toward the side from which the motion was previously repelled by greater resistance. Thus, light moves in a rarer transparent body more toward the side opposite the perpendicular, such that angle $gck$ becomes greater than angle $ach$. <note>This describes light bending away from the normal when moving from a dense medium (like glass) to a rare one (like air).</note> However, the motion of light $ac$ in refraction from a second body rarer than the first is always between lines $cg$ and $ce$; for since angle $gce$ is a right angle, angle $gck$ can never become a right angle. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 48. *It is not possible for refraction to occur at a single point from all rays incident upon the flat surface of a transparent body.*

For since, as is clear from the previous statements, in every transparent body refraction always occurs either toward the perpendiculars drawn from the points of incidence of the ray upon the surface of the transparent body (from which refraction occurs), or away from those perpendiculars—in whatever way this happens—it is clear that since those perpendiculars upon a flat surface are parallel (by Book 11, Proposition 6), whether refraction occurs toward the perpendiculars or away from them, it is impossible for the refraction of all rays incident upon that flat surface to occur at a single point. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 49. *No refraction changes the position of the parts of a refracted form, but only increases or decreases the shape.*

For since, as is clear by Proposition 47 of this book, every refraction in a second transparent medium occurs away from the perpendicular in a rarer medium, and toward the perpendicular in a denser one, it is evident that the right-hand ray always remains the right, and the left remains the left; and the same applies to other differences of position. Therefore, the positions of the parts of a refracted form are not changed but always remain. However, according to its own manner: when refraction occurs away from the perpendicular, the form is increased through dilation; and when refraction occurs toward the perpendicular, it is decreased, because the angles containing it are narrowed. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 50. *On every similar surface of the same transparent medium, rays incident at equal angles are refracted at equal angles; and if the angles of incidence are greater, the angles of refraction are greater, and if smaller, they are smaller.*

Whether the manner of refraction is considered on the part of the surfaces of the bodies in which refraction occurs—since refraction from a spherical surface is one thing and from a flat surface another—or on the part of the disposition of the transparent media—since refraction from a rarer medium is one thing and from a denser one another, as is clear from several propositions of this book—or if it is considered on the part of the angles of incidence: it is always clear that when the angles of incidence are equal, there is no cause for a difference in the manner of refraction according to the proposed method. Refraction will therefore always occur according to equal angles. And this is the first part of the proposition. 

An example of this is as follows: let there be a spherical transparent body denser than air itself, on the surface of which is circle $abcde$, whose center is $p$. From point $f$ of a luminous body, let radial lines fall, which are $af$, $bf$, $cf$, $df$, $ef$. Let ray $fc$ fall perpendicularly, and the others obliquely. It is clear that all rays incident obliquely on the surface of that transparent body will be refracted by Proposition 47 of this book. For the sake of the example and for brevity of illustration and naming of lines, let all those refracted rays meet at point $g$. Let lines be drawn perpendicularly over the surface of the body, which are $pdq$, $pbr$, $pax$, and $pez$. I say that if the angle of incidence (which is $fdq$) is equal to angle $fbr$, then angle $gdp$ will be equal to angle $gbp$, by the previous [proposition], on account of the uniformity of all the aforementioned...
