...conditions. Similarly, I also say that if angle $fdq$ is greater than angle $fax$, then angle $pdg$ will be greater than angle $pag$. For let there be made at point $a$ (the endpoint of line $xa$) an angle equal to angle $fdq$—by Book 1, Proposition 23 of Euclid’s *Elements*—which shall be angle $hax$. Let the ray $ha$ be refracted at point $a$, and let it meet with line $fg$ at point $k$. By the first part of this proposition, angle $pak$ will be equal to angle $pdg$. However, angle $pak$ is greater than angle $pag$; for it is not equal, because then it would follow from the previous statements that the angles of incidence were equal, which is against our hypothesis, as they are supposed to be unequal. Nor is it smaller, for thus the refraction would become irregular, which is against Propositions 43 and 45 of this book. Therefore, it is greater; and thus angle $pdg$ is greater than $pag$. The same can also be demonstrated more easily: if angle $fez$ is made equal to angle $fax$ by Book 2, Proposition 8, as when the arcs $ac$ and $ce$ are assumed to be equal, then the angles $pag$ and $peg$ will be equal according to the previous premises. Truly, angle $pdg$ is smaller than angle $peg$, which is also evident if the angles of refraction are assumed to be equal. We speak of this matter here only in summary, since we shall pursue it more perfectly in the 10th book of this work, where it has its proper place. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 51. *To know the measurement of a given height by its shadow while the sun is visible. Euclid, Theorem 18 of the Optics.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating a method for measuring height using shadows. It depicts a large right-angled triangle with vertices 'a' (top), 'b' (right angle at bottom-left), and 'd' (acute angle on the far right). Nested within it is a smaller similar right-angled triangle with vertical side 'ez' and base 'zd'. Line 'ab' represents the unknown height, 'bd' is its shadow, and 'ez' is a gnomon or measuring stick of known height.</image-desc>

Let $ab$ be the given height which we propose to measure while the sun is visible. If that height stands upright upon the surface of the horizon, let line $bd$ be drawn on that surface perpendicular to the base of the height $ab$ (which is $b$). Let the solar ray fall through the summit of $ab$ (which is $a$) to the very point $d$; let this ray be $ad$. Therefore, by Proposition 11 of this book, line $bd$ will be the shadow of the height $ab$. Let a rod of known length $ez$ be erected between the shadow $bd$ and the ray $ad$, parallel to the height $ab$, such that $ze$ is a <term>gnomon<note>A rod or stick used in ancient and medieval science to measure heights or the sun's position by the length of its shadow.</note></term> of a known quantity. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 29 of the *Elements*, triangle $dze$ will have the same angles as triangle $abd$. Thus, by Book 6, Proposition 4, or by Proposition 9 of this book, the ratio of $dz$ to $ze$ will be the same as the ratio of $db$ to $ba$. But the ratio of $dz$ to $ze$ is known; for since $ze$ is chosen as a known length, the line of its shadow, $zd$, can also be made known by a simple measurement. Therefore, the ratio of $db$ to $ba$ is known. But $db$ can be made known by measuring it. Therefore, $ab$ will also be known. This is what was proposed, as in the case where line $ab$ is the height of some tower or wall that can be approached to measure the length of the shadows.

# THE THIRD BOOK OF OPTICS 
## BY WITELO, 
## SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND POLES.

In the preceding books, we have set forth the mathematical and natural principles through which, as far as our ability allows, we intend to declare the consequences of our proposal. Wishing to follow the actions of natural forms under a threefold mode of seeing—namely, that which occurs through simple vision, that through reflection, and that through refraction—in this third book, we pursue the mode of simple vision and the specific arrangement of the visual organ <note>The eye.</note>. We assume these things which follow, which have been declared in other places or are known through themselves.

->POSTULATES.<-

1. Vision is not completed until the <term>visible form<note>The "species" or image of the object being looked at.</note></term> reaches the soul. 2. Likewise, only two things are visible by themselves: light and color. Light is seen of itself, and it is the <term>hypostasis<note>original: "hypostasis" — the underlying substance or foundation that gives color its reality.</note></term> of colors. Other things are visible <term>incidentally<note>original: "per accidens" — properties perceived as a result of seeing light and color, rather than being the direct cause of vision themselves.</note></term>, such as distance, size, location, corporeality, shape, continuity, separation or division, number, motion, rest, roughness, smoothness, transparency, density, shadow, darkness, beauty, ugliness, similarity, and difference. For these are grasped not only by sight, but by other senses as well. 3. Likewise, we postulate that strong light hurts the sight if it is gazed upon for a long time. 4. Likewise, that an object of greater size than the eye is seen by the eye. 5. Likewise, that a seen object is perceived according to the position, shape, and order of its parts. 6. Likewise, that the sight sees different visible things at the same time. 7. Likewise, that one thing is seen by both eyes at the same time. 8. Likewise, that color does not move the sight except by the action of light. 9. Likewise, that vision does not occur without contact, just as no natural action does. 10. Likewise, that the visual power is finite and does not extend to infinity.

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

### THEOREMS

**1. If a visible object does not actually participate in light, it is impossible for it to be seen.** <note>original: "Visibili lucem actu non participante: ipsum impossibile est uideri."</note> *Alhazen, Book 1, Note 39.*

For those things which, as has been assumed, are visible by their own nature are light and color. Light, however, is not visible except through itself; and since light is the <term>hypostasis</term><note>The underlying substance or foundation.</note> of colors, it is not possible for colors to be seen without light. Indeed, the form of color is weaker in its nature than the form of light, since color is essentially a kind of light incorporated into mixed bodies. Therefore, the sense of sight does not receive the form of an object’s color unless light is mixed with that form of color. Because of this, the colors of many things are altered in our vision by the changing of the light shining upon them. If color—which is visible in itself—cannot move the sense of sight except through the action of light, it is clear that it is impossible for any visible thing to be seen if it does not actually possess light. Thus, the proposition is evident.

**2. It is necessary that straight lines can be drawn between every point on the surface of a visible object and some point on the surface of the eye for the object to be seen in act. From this it is clear that vision occurs only when the visible object is in opposition to the eye.** *Alhazen, Book 1, Note 21.*

Whether vision occurs because rays go out from the eye to the points of the visible object, or because the forms of the points of the visible object reach the surface of the visual organ via radial lines, it is always necessary that straight lines can be drawn between every point of the visible surface and some point of the surface of the eye so that things may be seen in act. Hence, vision occurs whenever these lines can be produced according to any proposed method, unless the sight is perhaps hindered by the resistance of some other impediment. Therefore, when the eye is <term>opposed</term><note>Positioned directly in front of or facing.</note> to the visible object, it will see it; and when it is moved away from that opposition, it will not perceive it; and when it returns to that opposition, the sensation will return. This is because a line cannot be drawn from the points of visible things to the points of the surface of the eye from any directions other than those directly opposite. Thus, the proposition is evident.

**3. The organ of the visual power must be spherical.** *Alhazen, Book 1, Note 35.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled with a handwritten '6' to the right. It consists of two parallel vertical lines. The left line segment has points 'a' at the top and 'b' at the bottom. The right line segment is longer, marked with 'c' at the top, 'd' in the middle, and 'e' at the bottom. Horizontal lines connect 'a' to 'c' and 'b' to 'd'.</image-desc>

If it were not spherical, I say that vision would be hindered. For instance, if the surface were flat, then the eye would see nothing in a single glance except what was equal to itself in size. Whether rays go out from the eye to the visible object, or forms from the points of the object reach the surface of the visual organ through radial lines, it is clear that perpendicular lines are always the shortest (according to Theorem 21 of Book 1). Thus, the object is closest to the eye along those lines, because objects are seen directly along these perpendiculars and not through oblique lines that might be refracted. This is because, as shown in Theorem 48 of Book 2, refraction of forms toward a single point cannot occur in flat bodies, since in such bodies there is no single point common to all lines. Therefore, a visual organ with a flat surface could only see those things which reach it directly without refraction; and these are the things reaching the eye along perpendicular lines. 

Let the flat surface of the eye contain the line **a b**, and let there be a straight line **c d e** on the flat surface of a visible object that is parallel to the eye and to line **a b**. From point **c**, let a perpendicular line be drawn to the surface of the eye (by Proposition 11 of the *Elements*), falling on point **a**; let this be **c a**. From point **d**, let a perpendicular be drawn to the surface of the eye in the same way, which shall be **d b**. Since lines **a c** and **b d** are parallel and equal (by Theorem 25 of Book 1), then by Proposition 33 of Book 1, line **a b** will be equal to line **c d**. Because line **a b** is equal to line **c d**, but the line **c d e** is larger than line **c d**, it follows that the whole line **c d e** cannot be seen at once. This is because, in this arrangement, the visible object cannot exceed the size of the visual surface. Since this is false and contrary to what is evident to the senses—for it is possible for an object larger than the eye itself to be seen—it is clear that it is impossible for the surface of the visual organ to be flat. Nor can it be of any other shape than spherical, because impossibilities regarding the inequality of vision would always occur. Therefore, the surface of the visual organ must necessarily be spherical, with the convergence of radial lines from a magnitude far greater than the organ itself occurring at its center. Thus, the proposition is evident.

**4. The eye is a spherical organ of the visual power, composed of three humors and four tunics proceeding from the substance of the brain, which intersect each other spherically.** *Alhazen, Book 1, Note 4.*

How the eye becomes the organ of the visual power is a matter we leave to another branch of philosophy. That it is spherical is necessary from the preceding proposition, and also because it is of the nature of water, the property of which is always to be rounded, as has been declared elsewhere. That the eye is composed of three <term>humors</term><note>Clear fluids or semi-fluids within the eye.</note> and four <term>tunics</term><note>Layers or membranes, like the coats of an onion.</note> has been taught by the diligent care of those who perform dissections. The first of these humors is called the **crystalline** or **glacial** humor <note>Now known as the lens.</note>, which is properly the organ of the visual power and is situated in the middle of the eye. It is a small sphere, white and moist, capable of receiving the forms of visible things. In it, the transparency is not very intense, as it has some density; hence its transparency is likened to the transparency of crystal or ice, and for this reason, it is called the crystalline or glacial humor. However, because the transparency of this humor changes in its posterior part toward the brain—the part from which the whole eye receives nourishment—and because this nourishment is not yet fully assimilated in its substantial and accidental forms to the crystalline humor (which is the primary thing intended to be nourished) before it is perfectly united with it, it is necessarily of a different transparency from...

it: and for this reason it is called the second humor: and it is named the <term>vitreous humor</term><note>From the Latin 'vitreus', meaning glassy. Witelo describes it as resembling shards of glass.</note>: because it is likened to broken glass. And because in everything that is nourished, the pure is always separated from the impure: that which is separated from the nourished crystalline humor, as being unsuitable to its purity, flows to the side opposite the nutritional side—that is, to the front of the crystalline humor. And because it is transparent, and in some way resembles the crystalline humor, yet has not yet reached its perfect consistency in density (since it is the surplus nourishment of a denser body), it is clear that it must be a transparent liquid. Hence it is called the <term>albugineous humor</term><note>Meaning 'egg-white like'. This is the aqueous humor in modern terms.</note>, because it is similar to the white of an egg in its thinness, whiteness, and transparency: for it is a white, clear, thin, and transparent humor. Nature’s sagacity appointed this humor to the front part, just as it placed the vitreous humor at the back, for the protection of the crystalline humor, lest it suffer too quickly from external or internal causes and fail in its duty as the organ of sight. A very thin and subtle web contains the first two humors, namely the crystalline and vitreous, separating them from the albugineous and surrounding them both; a part of this same web descending through the middle separates the crystalline from the vitreous: and this web, on account of its thinness, is called the <term>tela aranea</term><note>Literally the 'spider-web' membrane; historically identified as the lens capsule or parts of the ciliary body.</note>. Since the albugineous humor is liquid and cannot hold its shape on its own, it was necessary for it to be held in by something solid for the protection of the eye. Nature therefore surrounded it with a viscous, solid, strong skin, which is not very transparent, so that by its density it might better hold the humor in, and by its warmth it might temper the albugineous humor, preventing the crystalline humor from congealing and becoming unfit to receive visible forms. And because, due to the density and viscosity of this tunic, visible forms could not reach the crystalline humor if it were surrounded everywhere by such a skin, nature cut through this tunic in the front part of the eye, where visible forms are received. A round opening was made, the diameter of which is almost equal to the side of a cube that could be inscribed within that sphere, or to the side of a square inscribed in the great circle of that sphere. This opening is round so that it might be more fit for receiving all forms passing through to the hollow of that same tunic; for this reason, this tunic is called the <term>uvea</term><note>Likened to the skin of a grape (Latin: 'uva').</note>, because it looks like a grape. This tunic is mostly black, though often green and sometimes gray-blue; the body of this tunic is thin and dense, not porous. But so that the albugineous humor does not leak out of the opening of the uvea, and so that the power of sight is not hindered, it was necessary for nature to place a transparent, solid veil over the opening of the uvea, like clear white horn; thus, this tunic is called the <term>cornea</term>. Where this tunic joins with the other parts of the body surrounding the eye, the transparency stops, and the tunic becomes of a different character—more solid than the cornea and not transparent—though it and the cornea together complete a single sphere, which is the sphere of the whole eye. The back part of that sphere, being fleshy rather than transparent, becomes another tunic: and this is called the <term>conjunctiva</term> or <term>consolidativa</term>, because it joins the eye and consolidates it with the neighboring parts of the body.

There will be, therefore, the corneal tunic, the albugineous humor, the <term>glacial humor</term><note>Another term for the crystalline humor or lens.</note>, and the vitreous humor following one another in order: and all these are transparent for the better reception of visible forms. The humors and tunics of the eye proceed from the substance of the brain, because from two parts of the front of the brain grow the two <term>optic nerves</term>—which are hollow and similar, having two tunics arising from the two membranes of the brain. These nerves proceed to the middle of the front of the brain, where they form a single optic nerve <note>This refers to the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet.</note>, which in its progress is again divided into two similar and equal optic nerves. These nerves swap their positions so that the right becomes left and the left right; they proceed to the convexities of the two hollow bones containing the eyes. In the middle of these two hollow bones are two equally perforated holes, called the "holes of rotation" of the hollow nerves. Since those two holes are round, the middle point of either hole is called the center of that hole. Those nerves enter these two holes and emerge into the hollow of the two aforesaid bones, where they dilate and widen. The end of each nerve becomes like an instrument for pouring wine into jars—that is, in the shape of a hollow round pyramid. Each eye is set upon one end of this nerve and is fused with it. Similarly, the tunics of the eyes arise from the tunics of these nerves: for the cornea arises from the outer of the two tunics of the nerve, and the uvea arises from the inner tunic of the two nerves. Within this uvea tunic, the crystalline humor is positioned over the end of the nerve's hollow by means of the vitreous humor; both humors arise from the medullary substance of the brain. Between these humors and the uvea tunic, the <term>tela aranea</term>—which others call the <term>retia</term><note>The retina; 'retia' means net-like.</note> because it is woven like a net—is formed from the very fine threads of the uvea. The humors and tunics of the eye intersect each other spherically: for because the uvea tunic does not form a complete sphere within the eye (since, as mentioned, it has a round opening in front covered by the cornea), the sphere of the cornea necessarily intersects the sphere of the uvea. The common section of their spherical surfaces is the circumference of that opening, which is a circular line according to Theorem 80 of Book 1 of this work. Also, at the front of the crystalline humor, for the better reception of forms, there is a slight flattening of the surface with less curvature than the corneal surface containing it; for the roundness of the surface of the crystalline humor is likened to the flattened surface of a lentil, as is clear to those who study the anatomy of the eye. Its front surface is therefore a portion of a larger sphere than the uvea sphere containing it. This flattening is centered directly opposite the opening in the front of the uvea. Just as the round opening in the front of the uvea is directly opposite the end of the hollow nerve on which the eye is placed, so too in the back part of the uvea's hollow there is a round opening over the end of the nerve. The front opening of the uvea is opposite the opening of the hollow nerve, because the optic nerve intersects the conjunctiva and the uvea, penetrating all the tunics of the eye up to the crystalline sphere. This sphere intersects the pyramid of the nerve, as does the vitreous humor, which is located in the pyramidal hollow of the optic nerve. Thus, the common section of the optic nerve's pyramid and the crystalline sphere is a circle according to Theorem 110 of Book 1. Therefore, the glacial sphere is situated at the end of the hollow of the optic nerve and within the posterior round opening of the uvea. The extremity...

Nature established two eyes for the perfection and completion of the quality of vision. ### 5. It is impossible for sight to be applied to visible things by rays exiting from the eyes. Alhazen, Book 1, Chapter 23, Note 1; also Chapter 23, Note 2.

If indeed any rays exit from the eyes through which the visual faculty is joined to things outside, those rays must be either corporeal <note>physical matter</note> or incorporeal. If they are corporeal, then when the sight sees the stars and the heavens, it would be necessary for a physical substance exiting the eye to fill the entire space of the universe between the eye and the part of the heaven being seen—all without the eye itself shrinking. This is impossible to happen, and certainly impossible to happen so quickly while the size and substance of the eye remain intact. If, however, it is claimed that the rays are incorporeal, since sensation only exists in a physical thing, then the rays themselves would not "feel" the object being seen. Therefore, the physical eye could not perceive anything by means of an unfeeling, incorporeal medium. Such incorporeal things do not return anything to the sight by which the sight could grasp the object, since vision does not occur except through the contact of the sight with the visible form; for without contact, there is no action. Therefore, if the rays proceeding from the eye return nothing to the sight, vision will not happen through them. If they do return something to the sight, these things must be light or colors, which are seen in themselves and which are multiplied through the rays back to the sight. Therefore, rays are not the cause of the connection of sight with visible things; rather, something else that multiplies itself toward the eye is the cause of vision. It is therefore impossible for rays to be the cause of vision in themselves, unless perhaps "rays" are defined as the lines traced by the points of the forms multiplied from the surfaces of visible things to the eye. For, as is clear from Proposition 2 of this book, it must be possible to draw straight lines between any point on the surface of a visible thing and some point on the surface of the eye for the thing to actually be seen. Such rays, however, do not exit from the eyes. The point is therefore proven.

### 6. Vision occurs from the action of the visible form upon the sight, and from the reception of this form by the sight. Alhazen, Book 1, Chapters 2, 3, and 14, Note 1.

That visible forms act upon the sight is clear from the second and third suppositions: for the sight is harmed by strong light, as in the

by the sight of the solar body or another strong light, such as light reflected to the eye from a polished body or from another very white body. In these cases, the vision is weakened to such an extent that it fails in its operation until it is restored by its internal natural power. Furthermore, the vision suffers from sensible forms: for it sometimes retains strong impressions of them within itself. Indeed, after the vision has looked for a long time at a strong light or color, if it then looks at a dark place or a place of weak light, it will perhaps find that visible object which it had previously inspected within itself, along with its light, color, and shape. Sometimes a strong color impressed upon the vision will mix with the colors of things seen in the dark, and those things will appear colored with another mixed color; for example, perhaps a <note>The text likely means "greenness," original: "uiride"</note> makes white things seen afterward in a darker place appear partially green. Even if the eye is closed, the form previously seen will nonetheless occur to the vision. Therefore, visible forms act upon the vision, and the vision is acted upon by them. And because visible things are by their nature light and color, and light is the <term>hypostasis</term><note>original: "hypostasis"; the underlying substance or foundation that gives something its existence.</note> of colors, and light is always diffused spherically in every direction, it is clear that colors are also diffused in this way. Thus, when the vision is set opposite any illuminated or colored thing, the light is multiplied either by itself or with the color of the thing opposite the vision; arriving at the surface of the vision, it acts upon the eye, and the eye is acted upon by it. Therefore, when light and color come together to the surface of the vision and act upon it, and the eye is acted upon by them, the power of the soul—on account of the union of the visible forms with its own organ—becomes "knowing." Then vision occurs because of the presence of the visible forms acting upon the vision. This action and "suffering" <note>In the medieval sense, "passion" or "suffering" refers to the act of being receiving an impression or being changed by an external agent.</note> happen in the manner of other natural actions: for the whole agent acts upon every point of the recipient, even upon the indivisible point, and the whole recipient is acted upon by every point of the agent. Therefore, the forms of light and color that are in any single point of a visible thing reach the entire surface of the eye, and the forms of all points of the surface of a visible thing reach a single point of the surface of the eye; thus action and "suffering" occur between them. However, the action of visible forms upon the vision does not occur unless the visible form is capable of acting and possesses a complete <term>hypostasis</term> through the presence of light, and unless the medium outside the eye and the visible thing is actually luminous, and unless the organ of vision is receptive to the forms through the intervening tunics and <term>diaphanous</term><note>Transparent or translucent.</note> humors of its own specific transparency. For if the part of the <term>cornea</term><note>The clear outer layer of the eye.</note> placed over the opening of the <term>uvea</term><note>The iris/pupil area.</note> (which is first joined to the external air) and the <term>albugineous humor</term><note>The aqueous humor, the watery fluid behind the cornea.</note> filling the opening of the uvea should fail in their proper transparency—perhaps because their specific quality has changed or some other impediment has occurred—or even if the <term>glacial humor</term><note>The crystalline lens.</note> itself were hindered from receiving forms by excessive freezing or some other way, vision does not occur: because the sensible form cannot be imprinted upon the visual organ. Therefore, the visible form coming from the thing seen through a luminous medium to the surface of the vision passes through the transparency of the eye's tunics and reaches the visual power through the opening in the front of the uvea; it reaches the glacial humor and passes through it according to the manner of its transparency. For this reason, nature ordered all the tunics of the eye to be transparent so that they might be acted upon by sensible forms possessing actual light. However, although the vision is acted upon by visible forms, it is not "stained" or permanently dyed by the form of light or color after the presence of the luminous or colored body is removed, just as we have shown universally that this "suffering" happens to every transparent body in Proposition 4, Theorem 2 of this book. And although sometimes, because of the strength of the light and color, some impression or alteration according to those lights and colors occurs in the vision, these do not remain in the vision except for a brief time; therefore, such an alteration is not fixed. Thus, the vision is not dyed with colors and forms of light by a fixed stain, even though the sensible forms act upon the vision. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 7. It is necessary that the center of the sphere of the entire eye, the center of the glacial humor, the center of the external and internal surfaces of the cornea, and the center of the convex surface of the albugineous humor be the same. From this it is clear that the internal surface of the cornea is equidistant from its external surface. Alhazen, Book 1, Chapter 12, Note 1.

Taking up again the figure of the eye which we presented in Proposition 4 of this book: I say that what is proposed here is true, because point **a** is the common center of the proposed spheres. For if it is granted that the center of the sphere of the entire eye (which is point **a**) is not the center of the glacial sphere, it is clear through Proposition 75, Theorem 1 of this book that straight lines perpendicular to the surface of the eye's sphere are not perpendicular to the surface of the glacial sphere, except for that single line which passes through the centers of both. All other lines which are perpendicular to the surface of the vision will be slanted relative to the surface of the glacial humor. If, therefore, the glacial humor perceives the forms of things seen according to the incidence of those lines (which are perpendicular to the surface of the eye but slanted relative to the surface of the glacial humor), then the glacial humor necessarily perceives all forms of visible things as slanted and distorted from their actual position and shape which they have externally on the surfaces of visible things—which contradicts the 5th Supposition set forth at the beginning of this book. And since forms incident upon a second, denser transparent medium along non-perpendicular lines are refracted toward the perpendicular (as is clear through Proposition 47, Theorem 2 of this book), and since the substance of the humors and tunics of the eye is denser than the surrounding air, and since the substances are of different transparency among themselves (as clear through Proposition 4), it is evident that another <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes between different substances.</note> will occur at the surface of the glacial humor than at the surface of the cornea. Therefore, the glacial humor would not distinguish anything in the things seen because of the refraction of forms occurring at its surface. For it is manifest that lines incident obliquely to the surface of the vision are made more oblique at the surface of the glacial humor, since the glacial humor is of a different transparency than the cornea or the albugineous humor; for there is in the glacial humor some transparency because of which it receives forms, and some density which prevents the passage of forms, and for this reason forms are fixed on its surface and body. Thus, the glacial humor would perceive none of the visible forms according to the position and shape they had outside the eye; but this is impossible, for it is clearly evident by the 5th Supposition that the glacial humor perceives the forms of visible things according to the position and shape they have in things outside. It is therefore necessary that the lines which are perpendicular to the surface of the eye are also perpendicular to the surface of the glacial humor: therefore, the surfaces of the eye and the glacial humor [must be concentric]...

It is clear, therefore, by Proposition 73 of Book 1 of this work, that the convex surface of the albugineous humor and the concave surface of the cornea share the same center. Thus, the center of the uvea is more elevated than the centers of all the tunics and humors of the eye which are in the front part of the eye facing the outward air. This is the whole of what was proposed.

### 10. *A straight line produced between the centers of the <term>glacial</term><note>original: "glacialis"; referring to the crystalline lens.</note> and uveal spheres will necessarily reach the center of the circle of consolidation of the glacial and vitreous spheres with the uvea; and it will be perpendicular to the surface of that circle. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 9.*

It was clear from what was stated in Proposition 4 of this book that the glacial sphere intersects the uvea sphere from the inside: therefore, a line passing through the centers of these spheres, according to Proposition 82 of Book 1, will be perpendicular to the center of the circle of their common section. This circle of section is either the circle marking the boundary of the consolidation <note>original: "consolidationis"; the anatomical joining or bonding point of these different eye structures.</note> of these spheres to each other, or it is parallel to it. For the surface that is in the interior part of the glacial humor is opposite the opening in the front part of the uvea; and its position relative to it is a similar position, as was clear in Proposition 4: therefore, the boundary of this surface, which is the circle of section between the two surfaces of the glacial and <term>vitreous</term><note>original: "uitreæ"; the clear gel filling the back of the eye.</note> spheres, is either the circle of consolidation of these spheres with the uvea, or it is parallel to it. 

If, therefore, the circle of section between the two surfaces—namely, the glacial and vitreous spheres—is the circle of consolidation of these with the uvea: then this circle is the circle of section between the surface of the glacial and the uvea: and then, as before, the proposition is clear by Proposition 82 of Book 1. But if the circle of section between the surface of the glacial sphere and the surface of the vitreous sphere is not the circle of consolidation of the crystalline and vitreous spheres with the uvea, but is parallel to the circle of their consolidation with the uvea: then, if the surface of the glacial sphere is imagined to be extended by mathematical reasoning beyond where the natural form of its sphere extends, it will cut the sphere of the uvea at a circle parallel to that circle of section of the glacial and vitreous spheres: because that circle has an equal position from the circumference of the sphere of the uvea. And because that circle is parallel to the circle of consolidation: the circle of section between the surface of the glacial and the surface of the uvea will necessarily be either the circle of consolidation itself, or parallel to it. 

Now, if this circle is the circle of consolidation, it is clear by Proposition 82 of Book 1, because the line passing through the center of the glacial and through the center of the uvea will pass perpendicularly through the center of that circle, because that circle is the circle of section between those two spherical surfaces. But if that circle is parallel to the circle of consolidation, and is parallel to the circle of section between the surface of the glacial and the surface of the uvea: it is therefore, with the circle of section between the surface of the glacial and vitreous, on one spherical surface (which is the surface of the glacial), and is parallel to the circle of said section. But if in any sphere two circles are parallel, a line passing perpendicularly through the center of one will necessarily pass perpendicularly through the center of the other, as is clear by Propositions 68 and 66 of Book 1. 

Therefore, the line which passes through the center of the uvea and through the center of the glacial passes through the center of the circle of consolidation of the glacial and vitreous spheres with the uvea according to all arrangements of the spheres and those circles: therefore, that line is perpendicular to the surface of that circle by Proposition 66 of Book 1. This is what was proposed. Nevertheless, these three circles are necessarily one circle, although even if they were different and parallel circles, the same propositions would apply to all: for the glacial and vitreous humors intersect each other along the same circle, and both of those intersect the uvea and are consolidated with it along the same circle: and that circle is the base of the hollow of the optic nerve: and thus that one circle performs the function of four circles.

### 11. *The vitreous sphere must be eccentric to the glacial sphere; and the center of the vitreous must be closer to the front of the eye. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 10.*

Because the surface of the glacial sphere and the surface of the vitreous sphere are two spherical surfaces intersecting each other: therefore, the center of the front surface with respect to the visible part of the eye is further back in depth than the center of the rear surface, according to Proposition 84 of Book 1. The rear of these two is the surface of the vitreous itself, as was shown before in Proposition 4. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 12. *The line passing through the center of the glacial and uvea spheres must also necessarily pass through the center of the vitreous and the middle of the hollow of the optic nerve. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 5, Section 11.*

Because a straight line passing through the center of the glacial and uvea spheres, when extended to the center of the circle of consolidation of the glacial with the uvea, is perpendicular to the surface of the circle of consolidation of the glacial and vitreous spheres with the uvea, as is clear through Proposition 10 of this book. Now, the circle of intersection of the glacial with the vitreous is either the same as this circle or parallel to it; in whichever of these ways it exists, the aforementioned line will always be perpendicular to the circle of section of the glacial sphere with the vitreous: therefore, it is clear by Proposition 82 of Book 1, that it passes through the center of the vitreous sphere. Because, therefore, this line passes through the center of the vitreous, it is clear by Proposition 82 of Book 1, that it will necessarily pass perpendicularly through the center of the circle of consolidation. It is therefore extended in the middle of the hollow of the optic nerve, upon which the eye is composed: since the circle of consolidation is the base and the extremity of the hollow of the optic nerve, as is clear from Proposition 4 of this book. Because it was shown above in Proposition 9 of this book, that a line produced between the center of the eye and the center of the uvea necessarily penetrates the center of the circle of section of the uvea and the middle of the hollow of the optic nerve,

### 13. *Sight does not perceive visible things unless the intermediate body is <term>transparent</term><note>original: "diaphano"; referring to a medium like air or water that allows light to pass through.</note>. Alhazen Book 1, Chapters 22 and 41.*

For, as is clear from Proposition 6 of this book, vision occurs only from the action of a visible form coming from the thing seen to the sight. However, forms do not extend except through transparent bodies of similar transparency, in which the extension of light and forms occurs according to straight lines, as shown in Proposition 1 of Book 2. Therefore, when no non-transparent intermediate body cuts off the lines produced from the visible things to the sight, then the forms reach the sight and vision is completed. If some non-transparent body intervenes, the multiplication of the form to the sight is hindered. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 14. *Vision does not occur when the visible body is of a similar transparency to the medium. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 42.*

If a visible body is transparent, it is not colored, nor does it possess the form of light, but only of the luminous; therefore, it is not seen. As clear from Proposition 4 of Book 2, light is not fixed in transparent bodies in such a way as to tint them or provide them with the act of visibility. Therefore, when the transparency of the visible body is similar to the transparency of the air, its disposition is like that of air, and it is not apprehended by sight, just as air is not. The same applies to any other medium: for none of these are seen when the transparency of the thing seen is not denser than the transparency of the intermediate body. However, if the body seen is transparent but less so than the medium—like crystal in relation to air—then the thing seen, because it has some color in relation to its density, will be seen through the intermediate air as a colored thing. For when light arises upon it, it will be fixed in it with some stability according to its density, and will pass through it according to its transparency. There will be a form in the air according to the color and light on its surface, and when that form reaches the sight, it will act upon the sight, and the sight will perceive the thing seen. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 15. *It is necessary for there to be a medium distance between the visible object and the surface of the eye. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 37.*

For sight does not apprehend a visible thing unless there is some intermediate light in it, according to Proposition 1 of this book; and this occurs only through an intermediate distance. Therefore, when a visible thing is placed directly upon the sight without a medium, it is not seen. For self-luminous things cannot be applied immediately to the surface of the sight; such things are stars and fire, which cannot be applied directly to the sight, because their application would result in the destruction of the viewer. As for other non-luminous bodies, if they are applied to the sight, they will not be seen without light. Therefore, a medium distance is required between those bodies and the surface of the sight itself, in which the forms of those bodies may diffuse by means of light. Furthermore, if visible bodies were applied directly to the sight, the body of the eye would be prevented from visual operation according to its position. Since vision only occurs through the part opposite the opening of the uvea, as shown in Proposition 4 of this book, if the sight were to perceive a visible thing through immediate contact, it would only perceive it according to the part applied to the opening of the uvea, and would not perceive the rest of the object. Even if we imagine the object moving over the surface of the eye until the sight touches the whole thing, the judgment would not be by sight, but rather by touch. For the visible form (which is the form multiplied outside the sensible object) would not act upon the sight in this way, but rather the object itself. Therefore, vision does not occur unless there is some intermediate distance between the visible thing and the surface of the eye. This is what was proposed.

### 16. *Vision does not occur without pain and a <term>passion</term><note>original: "passione"; in medieval philosophy, a 'passion' is an effect produced in an organ by an external agent.</note> that alters the substance of the eye. From this, it is clear that the sight must be in a suitable state of health to perform vision completely. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 26; also Book 1, Chapter 2.*

Because the glacial <note>The lens.</note> receives the form of light and color, and light and color act upon the glacial, that operation will necessarily not be without pain, although sometimes that pain is not felt, as when it is not very strong. Indeed, strong lights distress the sight and clearly damage it, as is evident in the light of the sun or in light reflected from polished bodies to the eye. And because the operation of all light upon the sight is of the same kind, differing only in degree (more or less), and the greater operation of any light upon the sight is of the nature of pain, it does not vary in this except by degree—to the point that sometimes the pain is hidden from the sense itself. Nevertheless, that passion, however imperceptible, always <term>alters</term><note>original: "abijcit"; literally 'casts out' or 'displaces', meaning it changes the natural state of the organ.</note> the substance of the eye. From this, it is clear that the sight must be in a suitable state of health to perform vision completely, since the comprehension of visible things by the sight is always according to the strength of the sight. The visual sense of the eyes varies according to their vigor and weakness: for moist eyes are more quickly damaged by lights and colors, while dry eyes are less so. These are the things we wished to declare.

# VITELLO’S OPTICS

17. *Distinct vision occurs only along perpendicular lines drawn from the points of the visible object to the surface of the eye. From this it is clear that every visible form is arranged on the surface of the eye in the same order as it is arranged on the surface of the visible object. Alhazen, Book 1, Chapters 15 and 18.*

For although, as shown in Proposition 6 of this book, the entire form of a visible thing acts upon the sight and upon every point of the surface of the eye, nevertheless, by Proposition 20 of Book 1, the form of only one point of the entire surface of the visible object opposite the eye falls perpendicularly upon a single point of the eye's surface. The forms of all the remaining points of the visible object's surface reach that same point of the eye's surface along oblique lines, according to Proposition 13 of Book 1. At any given point on the surface of the eye, the forms of all points on the surfaces of all visible things currently opposite the eye pass through at the same time; for it was assumed in the sixth supposition at the beginning of this book that the sight sees different visible things simultaneously. However, only the form of the point that falls perpendicularly upon that point of the eye's surface passes straight through the <term>transparency</term><note>original: "diaphanitatem"; the quality of allowing light to pass through.</note> of all the <term>tunics</term><note>The various membranes or layers of the eye.</note> of the eye, according to Proposition 47 of Book 1. The forms of all other points are <term>refracted</term><note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium (like air) into another (like the humors of the eye).</note> and pass through the transparency of the eye's tunics along lines that are oblique to the surface of the eye. Furthermore, from any point on the surface of the <term>glacial humor</term><note>original: "glacialis"; the crystalline lens of the eye.</note>, there will be only one perpendicular line to the surface of the eye. Since the center of the glacial sphere and the center of the whole eye are the same (as shown in Proposition 7 of this book), any line that is perpendicular to the surface of one is also perpendicular to the surface of the other, by Proposition 74 of Book 1.

Just as from the same point on the surface of the glacial sphere—according to those who propose that rays exit from the eye—infinite lines go out to the surface of the eye which are oblique to that surface, so too from a point on the glacial surface (from which a perpendicular line goes out to the surface of the eye and passes through the opening of the <term>uvea</term><note>original: "foramen uueæ"; the pupil.</note>), there go out infinite other lines passing into the opening of the uvea and reaching the surface of the eye at an angle. And just as imaginary rays exiting the eyes—when they are imagined to be refracted according to the difference in transparency between the <term>cornea</term><note>The clear front surface of the eye.</note> and the air—reach different places and different points on the surfaces of visible things opposite the eye at one time, and none of those lines meet the point located at the end of the perpendicular; so too, according to us who propose that rays do not exit but that "forms" are diffused toward the eye, the forms of the visible points at the ends of these lines extend along the straightness of these lines. They reach the surface of the eye and are refracted toward that same point on the glacial surface. Only the point at the end of the perpendicular is not refracted, but always extends along the straightness of the perpendicular and passes to that point on the lens.

Therefore, if the lens were to perceive along non-perpendicular lines, then the points on the surfaces of visible objects would never be arranged in the sense of sight in the same order they hold on the surface of the object itself. This is because forms mixed from many different objects and colors would meet at the same point, and nothing could be distinguished among them. But if the lens perceives only according to perpendicular lines, then the points on the surfaces of visible objects will be distinguished within it, and there will be no difference in the position and arrangement of the visible forms on the surface of the lens compared to the visible things outside. Since, according to our fifth supposition, the forms of visible things reach the sight in the same shapes they have in the objects outside, it is clear that vision occurs only along perpendicular lines. For only then is the seen form arranged on the surface of the eye just as it is arranged on the surface of the visible object. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Accordingly, all the lines of diffusion of any seen forms that are perpendicular to the surfaces of the eye's tunics are contained within a <term>pyramid</term><note>Often called the "visual cone" in modern optics.</note> whose vertex is the center of the eye and whose base is the circle of the uveal opening (the pupil), or a part of that circle's surface. The further this pyramid extends and the further it moves from the eye, the more it widens. All the forms of things falling within that pyramid extend in the straightness of the radial lines and pass through the tunics of the eyes without being refracted; and we call this the **radial pyramid**. 

However, the forms of visible things outside this pyramid never fall along any of those perpendicular lines. Instead, it happens that they extend along straight lines between themselves and the surface of the eye opposite the uveal opening, and those forms are refracted by the transparency of the eye's tunics and do not reach the visual power in an orderly way. Hence, there is no distinct vision along those lines. Nevertheless, it happens that those refracted forms are seen in some way, though indistinctly—namely, where they meet the perpendicular lines drawn from the center of the eye outside the radial pyramid. We now define the "surface of the eye" as that part of the eye's surface opposite the opening of the uvea. 

That the sight sometimes perceives things outside the radial pyramid is clear through experiment. For the tip of a needle or a thin stalk placed at the very edge of the eye—such as between the eyelids or in the corner of the eye while the gaze remains fixed—will be seen, even though that tip is outside the radial pyramid. Similarly, if an index finger or another finger is held up in those same spots around the eye outside the radial pyramid (which is very narrow, as its "pyramidality" is not wide, meaning none of it reaches the areas surrounding the eye), the surface of that finger will still be seen. Therefore, the form of these visible things reaches the surface of the eye through oblique lines outside the radial pyramid. It is clear, then, that the forms of things so situated with respect to the radial pyramid reach the surface of the eye after refraction occurs at the surface of the eye from the air (which is a thinner transparent medium) into the tunics of the eye itself. That refraction occurs at the surface of the eye for forms falling upon the sight from everywhere is also clear in the case of those things whose forms would fall within the radial pyramid if they were not blocked. For if a needle or another small, thin object is placed directly opposite the opening of the uvea between the eye and a white wall, the form of the entire wall will still be seen, although in truth the forms...

Therefore, distinct vision occurs only along perpendicular lines drawn from the points of the seen object to the surface of the eye; whereas indistinct vision occurs through non-perpendicular lines. In this way, indistinct vision assists distinct vision.

## 18. *Distinct vision of all visible forms occurs according to a pyramid whose vertex is in the center of the eye and whose base is on the surface of the seen object. From this it is clear that everything seen is seen under an angle. Euclid, Optics, Hypothesis 2; Alhazen, Book 1, Chapter 19, Note 1.*

Since, by Proposition 6 of this book, all vision results from the action of a visible form upon the sight, and any part of a visible form multiplies itself from its point through the external medium to the entire surface of the eye—and the entire surface of the seen object to a single point of the eye—because the <term>tunics</term><note>The various layers or membranes of the eye.</note> of the eye have a different <term>transparency</term><note>original: "diaphanitatem"</note> than the outside air, only those lines of the forms produced from the surface of the visible object to the surface of the eye which penetrate the center of the eye remain unbent. Because these lines are perpendicular to the surface of the eye, they are not refracted in the transparent medium of the <term>cornea</term> itself, as is clear from Proposition 72 of Book 1, Proposition 47 of Book 2, and the preceding proposition. All other lines, however, are refracted because they strike at an angle; hence, vision does not occur according to them.

Furthermore, since the <term>glacialis</term><note>The "icy humor" or crystalline lens, which medieval scholars believed was the primary organ of visual sensation.</note> is properly the organ of sight, and not the surface of the eye (which is part of the sphere of the cornea), it is necessary that the lines through which vision must occur reach the *glacialis*. And because it is impossible for the sight to comprehend a seen object according to its true nature unless it perceives the form of one point of the seen object from only one point of its own surface—since, as was shown in the preceding proposition, every form of a seen object is arranged on the eye's surface just as it is arranged on the object's surface—it is therefore impossible for the *glacialis* to comprehend the seen object according to its true nature unless it perceives the color or form of one point of the seen object coming to it from only one point of the surface of the sight.

Since the center of the eye and the center of the sphere of the *glacialis* are the same point (as shown in Proposition 7 of this book), it is necessary that all lines drawn perpendicularly from the points of visible things onto the transparent surface of the eye meet at the center of the *glacialis*. These lines will indeed be diameters through the surfaces of the eye’s tunics, perpendicular to the tunics themselves. Any such perpendicular will strike the surface of the cornea at one point and the surface of the *glacialis* at one point. Only one perpendicular passes through any given point of the *glacialis* from the center of the cornea through the surface of the cornea positioned above that point of the *glacialis*, which is also perpendicular to the surface of the seen object; for by Proposition 20 of Book 1, only one perpendicular can be drawn from any point to a single surface.

Whence, if the surface of the seen object is parallel to the surface of the sight, that line will be perpendicular to both the surface of the sight and the surface of the seen object by Proposition 23 of Book 1. All other lines are oblique to the surface of the seen object, even though, when extended to the center of the sight, they become perpendicular to the surface of the eye and the surface of the *glacialis* itself. Therefore, the form of any point on the surface of a visible object, moving toward the sight along one perpendicular line drawn from it to the surface of the sight, meets the surface of the sight at a single point, where no other forms of other points of the visible object meet it.

Thus, when lines are drawn from every point of the surface of a visible object to the center of the eye, it is clear that these lines, produced through different points of the eye, will cut the spherical surface of the eye and all meet at the center of the eye. All these lines are contained as if in one continuous body, because they terminate from the nearly continuous points of a single surface of the seen object at a single point, which is the center of the eye. It is clear, then, that all these lines are to be imagined as being within a certain **pyramid** having its vertex at the center of the eye and its base on the surface of the seen object. For the form of every point of the surface of the seen object is extended along the straightness of the line that lies between that point and the vertex of the pyramid (the center of the sight). All the surfaces of the eye’s tunics and humors cut through this pyramid, since the forms penetrate through them. Because the convex surface of the *glacialis* cuts this pyramid nearly parallel to the base, a sort of new pyramid is formed on that surface of the *glacialis*, whose base is on the surface of the *glacialis* and whose vertex is the same as before; the bases of these pyramids are similar, as shown in Propositions 99 and 100 of Book 1. From this it is clear that everything seen is seen under an **angle** contained by the radial lines meeting at the center of the sight. The proposition is thus proven.

Therefore, let the straight line passing through all the centers of the eye's tunics to the place where the hollow nerve (upon which the eye is composed) turns, be called the **axis of the radial pyramid**, because it passes through the center of the sight and the center of the opening in the front of the <term>uvea</term><note>The iris or middle layer of the eye.</note> and through the center of the uvea itself, extending through the middle of the radial pyramid. The other lines of this pyramid shall be called **radial lines**.

## 19. *A visible body must be of some size in relation to the surface of the sight in order for it to be actually seen. Alhazen, Book 1, Chapter 40, Note 1.*

It has already been shown that vision always occurs through a pyramid whose cone is at the center of the eye and whose base is on the surface of the seen object, and that this pyramid marks out a small part on the surface of the sensing member in which the form of the seen object is arranged (as shown in Proposition 17 of this book). In very small things, therefore, the pyramid will be small, and the part marked by it on the convex surface of the *glacialis* (which is the primary sensing member) will be like a point or very small; but the sensing member does not perceive a form except <insert>when</insert><note>original catchword: "quando"</note>

For this reason, they exist according to a certain limit which the sensitive power can reach. Therefore, when the part of the sensing member reached by the form is not of a sensible quantity compared to the entire sensing member, the member does not feel the action by which the form of the visible object acts upon that part, due to its extreme smallness; thus, it does not grasp the form of such a small thing. It is necessary, therefore, that these things be of a certain quantity relative to the surface of the sight. And this is what was proposed.

## 20. *Vision is not completed unless the arrangement of the form received on the glacial surface reaches the common nerve. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 25, Note 1.*

As is clear from Proposition 4 of this book, the sensing and judging visual power for everything visible is established in the meeting of both <term>optic nerves</term><note>The optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet.</note> in the anterior part of the brain. Because of this, there is a <term>unity of the sense of sight</term><note>The phenomenon of "binocular fusion," where two eyes produce a single mental image.</note> in a single viewer; due to this unity, one and the same thing happens to be seen by both eyes at once. It is clear that vision will not be completed unless the visible form is united with the sensing power located in the hollow of the <term>common nerve</term><note>original: "neruum communem"; the optic chiasm.</note>. For it is necessary that the thing to be known is always united with the knower itself. Since, by Proposition 17 of this book, the arrangement of visible forms occurs on the surface of the eye just as they are arranged on the surface of the seen object—and by the premise of this, the seen object is viewed according to the position, shape, and order of its parts—it is therefore necessary for the arrangement of the form to occur in the common nerve itself according to the manner of arrangement in which it was received on the glacial surface; otherwise, vision will not be completed. The proposition is therefore clear.

## 21. *It is necessary that the vitreous humor be of a different transparency than the glacial humor. Alhazen Book 2, Note 2.*

If the <term>transparency</term><note>original: "diaphanitas"; the quality of allowing light to pass through.</note> of these two bodies (namely, the glacial humor and the <term>vitreous humor</term><note>The clear, gel-like substance behind the lens of the eye.</note>) were identical, then (as is clear from Propositions 1, 2, 17, and 72 of Book 1) the visible forms received on the glacial surface, without being <term>refracted</term><note>Bent by passing through different materials.</note>, would converge along radial lines at the center of the eye due to the similarity of transparency, and having intersected there, they would spread out further. However, as shown by the preceding proposition, vision is not completed until the arrangement of the form received on the glacial surface reaches the common nerve. The position of the parts of the form as they exist on the glacial surface cannot reach the common nerve except by its extension in the hollow of the nerve upon which the glacial sphere is composed, because it is otherwise impossible to reach it. Yet the form cannot be extended from the glacial surface to the hollow of the common nerve along a straight-line extension while preserving the positions of its parts as they truly are, unless a medium of a different, clearer transparency meets it before it reaches the center of the eye. If there were no medium of a different transparency, these lines would converge at the center of the eye and become like a single point. And because this center of the eye is located before the place where the optic nerves join, it is clear from Proposition 91 of Book 1 that if those lines were to extend beyond the center of the eye, there would necessarily be an intersection of those lines at the center; after the center, a new pyramid would be created, whose lines of length would be oriented in a manner contrary to the position and site of the first pyramid. Thus, the entire arrangement of the shape of the seen object—as it exists on the surface of the object and on the glacial surface—would be inverted: that which is on the right of the glacial surface would become left to the sense, and vice versa; and the top would become the bottom, and vice versa. Nor would any part of the form reach the common nerve directly except for the single point at the end of the axis of the pyramid. Therefore, all things would be seen in a manner contrary to their natural position, which contradicts our 5th supposition and is manifestly contrary to what occurs in the senses. It is therefore clear that it is necessary for these humors to be of different transparency. This is what was proposed.

## 22. *The surface of the common section of the glacial and vitreous spheres is located in front of the center of the eye; it is necessary for the vitreous humor and the visible spirit to be of nearly the same transparency, and for both to be more transparent than the glacial humor. Alhazen Book 1, Note 30. Also Book 2, Notes 4, 5, 6.*

Since, as shown by Proposition 20 of this book, every form of a seen object reaches the common nerve according to the position, shape, and order of its parts, it is evident (as shown in the preceding) that it is necessary for some refraction to occur before the form reaches the center of the eye. If refraction were to occur after passing the center, the forms would necessarily be inverted, because even then, by Proposition 91 of Book 1, the position of the parts of the form would be changed. Since refraction only occurs toward the <term>perpendicular</term><note>A line standing at a right angle to a surface.</note> or away from the perpendicular (as is clear from Proposition 47 of Book 2), it is evident that it does not change the position of the parts, but only increases or decreases the shape according to Proposition 49 of Book 2. Since the <term>glacialis</term><note>The crystalline lens.</note>, which the forms reach along straight lines, is entirely of one transparency, and refraction only occurs in a medium of a different transparency, it is evident that the refraction of forms can only happen at the vitreous humor, whose body (as shown in the preceding) is of a different transparency than the body of the glacial humor. Therefore, this humor necessarily precedes the center of the eye, so that the forms may be refracted by it before they reach the center of the eye itself—which is the same as the center of the glacial humor according to Proposition 7. Otherwise, a convergence of all radial lines would occur at that center according to Proposition 72 of Book 1, because those lines are all perpendicular to the glacial surface. As those forms proceeded further, an inversion according to position would also happen to them by Proposition 91 of Book 1, as was stated before. And because this is impossible, it is clear that the vitreous humor precedes the center of the glacial humor. Thus, although the glacialis (in which the principle of sense resides) requires radial lines extended in a straight path—because it is impossible for the form of a seen object to be ordered on the surface of the sight due to the size of the seen object, and because...

...the unity of the surface of the body of sight, except through those lines by which the comprehension of the visible thing is completed according to its essence. However, the arrival of forms at the <term>final sensor</term><note>original: "ultimum ſentiens"; refers to the part of the brain or optic chiasm where visual perception is thought to be completed.</note> does not only require the extension of forms along the straightness of those lines. This is because the reception of forms in the sensing member is not entirely similar to the reception of forms in a simple <term>transparent body</term><note>original: "corpore diaphano"; a substance like air or glass that allows light to pass through.</note>. For the sensing member receives these forms because of its transparency, and perceives them because of its sensitive power; and thus it receives forms according to the nature of sensation, whereas other transparent bodies receive forms only to represent them to the sight, but not for the purpose of feeling or sensing them. 

Therefore, the quality of the reception of forms in the <term>vitreous humor</term><note>original: "humore uitreo"; the clear, gel-like substance filling the eyeball behind the lens.</note> along refracted lines is due to the difference in its transparency compared to the body of the <term>glacial humor</term><note>original: "glacialis"; the crystalline lens of the eye, which medieval scholars believed was the primary organ of sight.</note>, and because of the quality of sensitive reception, which is not completed in the glacial humor alone. Furthermore, the subtle body that exists in the cavity of the nerve between the vitreous humor and the <term>common nerve</term><note>original: "neruum cōmunem"; the optic chiasm where the two optic nerves meet.</note>—which body is named the <term>visible spirit</term><note>original: "ſpiritus uiſibilis"; a hypothetical substance or "vapor" thought to carry visual information through the nerves.</note>, since the visible spirits first run through it—must necessarily be transparent. This is because when the forms of visible things arrive in the body of the vitreous humor, the sensation is extended from there into the sensing body stretched within the hollow of the nerve, which continues between the eye and the front of the brain. According to the extension of this sense, the forms are extended, arranged according to their original disposition. 

It is clear, therefore, that the arrangement of the parts of the body sensing the forms, and the arrangement of the sensitive power, is necessarily equal in the vitreous body and in every subtle body extended in the hollow of the nerve. For when a form reaches any point on the vitreous surface, it is extended directly, and its position is not altered within the cavity of the nerve where the sensing body is extended; thus, the forms of all points will maintain a similar arrangement to one another. Therefore, the sensing body within the hollow of the nerve must necessarily be transparent for the reception of visible forms. Its transparency must be nearly the same as the transparency of the vitreous humor, so that the forms do not become distorted or "monstrous" upon reaching the final surface of the vitreous humor adjacent to the body within the nerve cavity. 

Thus, the forms pass through this subtle body by reason of its transparency, and they appear to the sensitive power by reason of that same body's density. Therefore, the final sensor, which is in the common nerve, perceives light from the illumination of this body and color from its coloration, since the forms of these things pass through and are fixed within it. Moreover, the <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another.</note> of forms occurs at the vitreous humor both because of the difference in the quality of sensory reception and because of the difference in transparency between the glacial and vitreous humors. If the transparency of their bodies were identical, the form would be extended into the vitreous body along the straightness of the radial lines; yet because of the different quality of sensation between these two bodies, the form would become either distorted or doubled. 

But when refraction occurs because of the difference in transparency, and the difference in the quality of sense confirms that refraction or bending, then the form—after the bending of refraction—will be a single form, ordered according to the position, shape, and arrangement of its parts, just as the form exists in the object outside. The sensitive power perceives the form of the thing seen from the entire sensing body, extended from the surface of the eye (which first senses and receives the visible forms) all the way to the cavity of the common nerve, which is the final sensing body; for within it, the sensitive power is established. Thus, the vitreous humor and the body in the nerve cavity are of nearly the same transparency, because no further sensible refraction occurs between them; instead, they proceed regularly through the unity of the sensitive power toward the unity of the simple extension of the form after its refraction at the vitreous surface. And since in both these bodies the progression of forms occurs beyond the center of the eye, it is clear that this refraction is made away from the perpendicular line erected from the point of refraction on the glacial surface. Therefore, each of those bodies is more transparent than the body of the glacial humor itself, according to Proposition 45 or 47 of Book 2 of this work. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 23. The surface of the common section of the glacial and vitreous spheres must be flat: or a part of a sphere larger than the glacial sphere, and eccentric to the surface of the eye.

The surface where these spheres—namely the glacial and the vitreous—meet is necessarily flat, or of the nature proposed. This is because it is necessary for the surface of this section to have a consistent arrangement, so that its extremities are positioned at a similar and identical distance from the center of the eye, preventing forms from appearing distorted after refraction. A surface of such consistent arrangement is either flat or spherical. However, this surface cannot be part of a sphere concentric with the eye; for then the radial lines, which are perpendicular to the glacial surface, would also be perpendicular to this surface (according to Proposition 74 of Book 1). In that case, no refraction of forms would occur; instead, they would converge at the center and the forms would become distorted, as shown in the previous argument. 

Therefore, if that surface is part of a sphere, it must be <term>eccentric</term><note>Having a different center than the center of the eye.</note> to the eye. It cannot be part of a sphere smaller than the sphere eccentric to the eye, because, due to the difference of the center, the forms would converge before reaching the center of the eye. (For a smaller sphere has a smaller diameter by its spherical nature). Furthermore, because of the greater transparency of the vitreous sphere over the glacial sphere (as shown previously), the forms would be refracted away from the perpendicular (according to Proposition 47 of Book 2) because of the rarer medium they enter. But if the surface of the common section were a smaller sphere, they would be refracted toward the perpendicular. This would result in distorted forms, as they would proceed toward the perpendicular because of their own perpendicularity to the spherical surface (which always passes through the center per Proposition 72 of Book 1), yet be refracted away from it. 

Therefore, this surface is either flat or spherical—specifically part of a sphere of sufficient size—so that its sphericity matches the arrangement required by the proportion of refraction away from the perpendicular, which occurs due to the nature of the different transparency. Thus, all forms reaching the glacial surface are extended through the glacial body along the straightness of the radial lines until they reach this interface; then they are refracted there along lines of similar arrangement that intersect the radial lines. Thus, a form reaching any point of the glacial surface always...

Among all the lines of the <term>radial pyramid</term><note>The cone-shaped volume of light rays entering the eye from an object, with the vertex at the eye's center.</note>, it is necessary that only the axis passing through the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term><note>The pigmented layer of the eye; here referring to the pupil.</note> be perpendicular to the common surface of the <term>glacial</term><note>The crystalline lens.</note> and <term>vitreous</term> humors, and to the posterior surface of the vitreous. For if this axis were not perpendicular, but slanting upon any of those surfaces, there would occur a diversification in the arrangement of the forms reaching that surface, and the dispositions of those forms would change because of the slant of the axis. For only when the axis is perpendicular to the surface of the glacial humor will the form of the visible object reach the surface of the glacial humor arranged according to the order of the parts of the surface of the visible object; and the form of the point which is at the extremity of the axis on the surface of the visible object will reach the point which is on the axis on the surface of the glacial humor, as is clear from Proposition 17 of this book. And because the surface of the vitreous humor facing the glacial surface—which is the <term>common section</term><note>The boundary where two parts meet.</note> of the glacial and vitreous spheres, as is clear from the previous proposition—is either a flat surface or a spherical one, and its center is not the center of sight: if the radial axis were slanting upon that surface and not perpendicular to it, no plane surface would come from the axis perpendicular to that surface except for one single surface. From this it is clear that the parts of the eye are in no way changed. For the inclination of the pyramidal part of the nerve upon the surface of the **circle of consolidation** <note>The sclero-corneal junction or the ring where the eye's layers join.</note> is always a similar inclination: therefore, the parts of the eye do not change according to their position.
