And since both eyes are of similar disposition in their tunics and parts, and in the shapes of their tunics, and in the position of each of the tunics with respect to the whole eye: it is clear that there is no difference between them regarding what is proposed about the change of position of their parts when the eyes themselves are moved: for the position of both lines passing through the centers of the tunics of sight in each of the eyes is always a similar position in all dispositions of the eyes. Therefore, that which was proposed is clear.

### 26. *When one eye is moved, it is necessary for the other to be moved conformably to it.*

For since the position of the parts of the eye is not changed in either of the eyes, and the motion of one eye is produced by the motion of the optic nerve in the center of the opening of the [orbital] bone, while the motion of the partial nerve proceeds from a point of the **common nerve** <note>The optic chiasm, where the two optic nerves meet and cross.</note>: since that which is moved in parts of others is always moved around something fixed: therefore the motion of the partial nerve begins at a point of the nerve common to both optic nerves of both eyes, in which resides the power of the sensing and moving soul. And since that power is indivisible and uniform, and the principle by which it first moves is a natural body according to its own indivisible natural form: it is evident that by moving one eye it also moves the other: for there is no greater reason why it should move one eye than the other: thus, with one eye moved, both eyes are moved, and one is moved conformably to the other: so that just as the motion of both begins from the same principle, so both motions are terminated at the same end, and as they begin from one indivisible [point], so they are terminated at one divisible [object]. Therefore, what was proposed is evident.

### 27. *With two sights directly opposite one visible object: it is necessary that two pyramids be formed, the common base of which is the surface of the thing seen, and the axis of each passes through the center of the opening of the uvea, and through the center of its own sight.*

For since, as is clear through the 17th proposition of this book, the position of the parts of the surface of the thing seen reaches the surface of each sight, and is formed in it according to perpendicular lines drawn from all points of the surface of the thing seen to the surface of that eye, the convergence of all of which (according to their points of incidence) regards the center of the eye upon whose surface it falls, and finally, after refraction, each of those forms reaches the middle point of the common nerve: the meeting of both those forms thus occurs at the middle point of the common nerve, upon which they fall. Therefore, because the centers of the two sights are two, it is clear that in the vision of the same thing by two eyes, two **visual pyramids** <note>Also called cones of vision; the geometric volume of light connecting the eye to the object.</note> are formed in the proposed manner. For the surface of the thing seen will always be the base of each pyramid proceeding from each of the eyes, because of the multiplication of the form of every point of the surface of the thing seen equally to the sight, and the axis of each of them passes through the centers of the opening of the **uvea** <note>The pupil or the vascular middle layer of the eye.</note> to the center of its own sight. For thus the visible object is directly opposite to one sight, and thus it is directly opposite to the other, by hypothesis: and since both sights are moved equally to see something, through the preceding proposition, it is clear that always in the vision of one thing the middle point of the surface of the sight of the eye is opposed to the middle point of the surface of the thing seen, or near to it: but the middle point of the surface of the sight or the eye is the center of the opening of the uvea through the 4th proposition of this book. Therefore, the form of that middle point of the surface of the thing seen, or of a point near it, reaches the center of its sight through the center of the opening of the uvea. And this is what was proposed.

### 28. *There being two eyes, it happens that only one form of one thing is seen.*

For since, as has been said many times before, the form received on the surface of the **glacial humor** <note>The crystalline lens.</note> passes through the body of the glacial humor, then is extended through the subtle body which is in the optic nerve, and comes to the front of the brain, in which is the **ultimate sensorium** <note>original: *sentiens ultimum*; the final processing power of the soul that perceives the senses.</note>, which is the sensitive power grasping sensible things, of which power the eye is the instrument, receiving the forms of things and returning them to the ultimate sensorium, so that at the nerve common to both eyes—the position of which nerve from the two eyes is a similar position—vision is finally completed: although therefore two forms reach the two eyes from one thing seen: nevertheless, when both those forms reach the common nerve, they meet and become one form, and through the union of these forms the ultimate sensorium perceives the form of the thing seen, and thus it happens that only one form of one thing is seen: unless perhaps by some intervening occasion it happens that the forms accepted by the two eyes are not united, because they do not meet in the union of both optic nerves: for then it happens that two forms are seen, as when the observer changes the position of one eye forward while the other eye remains unmoved. But when the position of the two eyes is natural, then because their position from one thing seen is a similar position, the form from one thing seen reaches two places of similar position, and when the position of one of the eyes is slanted, then the position of the eyes from that thing seen is varied, and thus two forms of that thing seen reach different positions: but this is not in the sight naturally, but only through the violence which the will or natural weakness does to the habit of nature. Therefore, when the position of the eyes is natural, then always it happens that one form of one thing is seen by both sights. Which is what was proposed. Therefore, two forms of the seen point are impressed in the two centers of the two surfaces of both sights, and every other point of the seen form will be impressed in two places of similar position in the two sights:

*29. Every point of a form incident upon the surfaces of the eyes along the radial axes must necessarily reach the center of the opening of rotation of the hollow nerve.*

Since each of the axes passes through the center of the opening of the **uvea** <note>The pupil.</note> to the center of the eye, as is clear from the 27th proposition of this book, it also passes through the center of the sphere of the uvea itself by the 8th proposition of this book. Indeed, every straight line produced between the center of the eye and the uvea, the center of the circle of the section of the uvea, and the middle point of the cavity of the nerve will necessarily penetrate through the 9th proposition. It is clear, therefore—since a perpendicular line always remains unrefracted according to the 47th proposition of the 2nd book—that every point of a form incident upon the surfaces of the eyes along the radial axes must reach the center of rotation of the hollow nerve <note>The point in the orbit where the optic nerve allows the eye to pivot.</note>. From this point, the form is diffused to the middle point of the common nerve. And since the middle point of the common nerve is only one, it is evident that the axes of both eyes always concur at one point of the common nerve. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*30. If two straight lines are produced to the middle of the common nerve from the endpoints of a line drawn between the two centers of the openings of rotation of the hollow nerves: it is necessary that in the resulting triangle, the angles at the base are equal. From this it is clear that those produced lines are equal. Alhazen, Book 3, Proposition 6.*

Let the two centers of the openings of rotation of the hollow nerves be *r* and *t*, and let the line *rt* be drawn between them. Let the middle point of the common nerve be *a*, and let the triangle *rat* be constructed. I say that angle *art* is equal to angle *atr*. Since the position of the two nerves with respect to the cavity of the common nerve is a similar position—because the cavity of one nerve is entirely similar to the cavity of the other by the 4th proposition of this book—it follows that the middle of the cavity of one is similar to the middle of the cavity of the other. Thus, the axis of one nerve is equal to the axis of the other nerve. By the same 4th proposition, the position of the two nerves with respect to the two openings is a similar position, in the middle of which nerves the lines *ra* and *ta* are carried as axes. It is clear, therefore, that the position of the two lines *ra* and *ta* relative to line *rt* is a similar position. This is impossible unless angles *art* and *atr* are equal; for an inequality in these angles would result in an inequality in the position of the middle axis of the hollow nerves themselves, and consequently of the nerves themselves. Therefore, those angles at the base are equal; thus, by the 6th proposition of the 1st book of Euclid, those produced lines are equal, namely line *ar* is equal to line *at*. The proposition is clear.

And although the axes are refracted in the aforementioned way: nevertheless the formation of the **visual pyramids** <term>visual pyramids: the cone-shaped volume of space seen by the eye, with the pupil as the vertex and the object as the base</term> occurs as if the axes reached the vertex whole, nor does any difference happen to the sight from that.

*32. It is necessary that the axes of the visual pyramids of both eyes, passing through the centers of the openings of the **uvea** <term>uvea: here referring to the pupil, the opening in the iris</term>, always be joined at one point of the surface of the thing seen, even when the eyes are moved over the surface of the thing seen. Alhazen, Book 3, note 2.* <note>Reference to the "Book of Optics" by the 11th-century polymath Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen.</note>

For when a viewer looks at some object: then each eye will be in opposition to that seen object according to Proposition 2 of this book, and each of the pupils will be directed to that object in an equal direction, because of the equality of the eyes according to Proposition 4. Let there be two centers of the two eyes, *e* and *g*: and let the middle point of the **common nerve** <term>common nerve: the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet</term> be point *a*: and let the surface of the seen object be *b c d f*, which for the sake of example is equidistant to the line connecting the centers of the eyes, which is *e g*. It is clear, therefore, since from the centers of the eyes perpendicular lines produced onto that surface *b c d f* are equidistant (by Euclid’s Elements, Book 11, Prop. 6); let these be *e q* and *g x*. In this surface *b c d f*, let a point be marked, which is *u*: I say that because of the equality of both eyes in all their arrangements, if one eye were moved to see point *u*, the other would immediately also be moved to see the same point *u*: so that the axes of both visual pyramids passing through the centers of the openings of the uvea are joined at point *u*, with one of them reaching there. 

For if one of those axes fell on point *u*, and the other fell on another point—let that point be *z*—there would be two axes *e u* and *g z*, between whose ends line *z u* is produced. And since the axes thus extended from the two eyes do not meet at any point of line *z u*, just as they do not meet if vision occurs only according to the perpendicular lines *e q* and *g x*: it is clear that none of the points of line *z u* will be seen by both eyes, but only by one. Therefore, one of the eyes would seem to be superfluous, since one eye could imperceptibly run through all the points of line *z u* along its own axis. 

However, nature established two eyes for the perfection of the goodness of vision and its completion, so that their united power might be stronger, as is clear by Proposition 4 of this book. If, therefore, the visual axes do not meet at some single point of line *z u*, it follows either that nature is superfluous, or that it works in the weakest way it can: both of which are impossible. For nature does nothing in vain, nor does it fail in necessary things (as is clear by the 8th supposition of Book 2). This impossibility happens if the axes fall only on different points of the visible surface; but the impossible would never occur if they fall on the same point. It is clear, therefore, since it is always necessary for the axes of the pyramids of both eyes to fall on the same point: because the operation of both eyes is uniform. 

When, therefore, the sight is moved over the object: then each eye will be moved over it, and the axes—gathered at one point of the surface of the thing seen—will both move together to some one point on the surface of that seen object. For both eyes are equal in all their arrangements, and there is one common nerve for both eyes. And since the movement of the eyes proceeds from one power, it is necessary for the moving power to proceed through the unity of the nerve: this power, then, with one eye moved, will move both eyes, as is clear by Proposition 26 of this book. Therefore, the action and reception of the eyes is always equal and similar; and if one eye is moved to see something, immediately the other will be moved to see this same thing with that same movement; and if one eye rests, the other will rest. For it is impossible for one eye to move and the other to rest, unless one were impeded (by Prop. 26). As was also declared in Proposition 18, the surface of the seen object will always be the base of each pyramid proceeding from each of the eyes: because then the position of the point where both axes are joined is a similar position: because it is in opposition to the two centers of both eyes. The proposal is therefore clear: and we shall call the point where both axes meet on the surface of the seen object the **point of union** <note>original: *punctum coniunctionis*</note>.

# VITELLO'S OPTICS

...divides triangle **r t b** into equal parts and its base **r t**, as is clear from the preceding. It is evident, therefore, that the radial axes <term>radial axes: the central lines of vision extending from the center of each eye to the object</term> fall upon the surfaces of the eyes equally and according to equal angles. And if they fall upon the surfaces of the eyes in such a way that they pass through the centers of the eyes, then it is clear that they are perpendicular to the surfaces tangent at points **n** and **q**: they therefore fall upon the surfaces of the eyes equally, striking at right angles. Because of this, in the arrangement, motion, or rest of all eyes, their two axes are always equal, or there is no sensible difference in them that would cause any difference in vision—especially when the thing seen is not very close to the sight, but when its distance from the sight is moderate. For when the seen object is very close to the eye, such that the line between the two centers of the eyes (points **o** and **p**) has a proportion of equality, excess, or only small diminution compared to the radial axis, then the axes will be sensibly unequal and will form unequal angles. Otherwise, they will always be sensibly equal and will constitute sensibly equal angles. Because of the unity of the eyes and the uniform reception of forms, any point is multiplied uniformly to each eye; because of this, all lines equally distant from the axes also make equal angles, and they are all sensibly equal. In the same way, it can also be demonstrated that the angles formed by the axes in the glassy surface <term>glassy surface: the surface of the crystalline lens or the cornea where light bends</term> where refraction occurs are equal. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 36. Of all the oblique lines of the radial pyramid, the refraction of those nearer to the axis occurs at smaller angles; of those further away, at larger angles; and of those at equal distances, at equal angles. <note>original: "Alhazen 9 n 2"; referring to the Optics of Alhazen, Book 2, Note 9</note>

Let there be a radial pyramid <term>radial pyramid: the cone of light rays extending from a single point on an object to the surface of the eye</term> whose vertex is **a** and the diameter of the base (which, by Proposition 18 of this book, is the surface of the seen object) is **b c d e f**. Let the axis be **d a**. Let lines **c a** and **e a** be oblique radial lines closer to the axis **d a**, and let **b a** and **f a** be further away. I say that lines **c a** and **e a** will be refracted at a smaller angle, and lines **b a** and **f a** at a larger angle. 

For let all these lines be understood to meet at point **a**, which is the vertex of the pyramid. Let there be a line on the glassy surface upon which those lines fall, **g h i k l**. This line will therefore be straight or circularly curved by Proposition 23 of this book. Let it first be straight. Let line **b a** fall on that line at point **g**, line **c a** at point **h**, line **d a** (the axis) at point **i**, line **e a** at point **k**, and line **f a** at point **l**. 

Because angle **g i a** is a right angle by the preceding proposition, it is clear by Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>original: "32 p 1"; Euclid's Elements, Book 1</note> that angle **g h a** is obtuse. Therefore, by Proposition 19 of Book 1, line **a g** is greater than line **a h**. And because two lines **a c** and **a b** go out from point **a** to the base of triangle **a g i** (which is **g h i**), angle **a h i** is greater than angle **a g i** by Proposition 16 of Book 1. Since angle **a h i** with angle **c h i** equals two right angles by Proposition 13 of Book 1, and similarly angle **b g h** with angle **a g h** equals two right angles, it is clear that angle **c h i** is smaller than angle **b g i**. Therefore, by Theorem 50 of Book 2 of this work, the angle of refraction of line **c h** is smaller than the angle of refraction of line **g b**. It is therefore clear that line **c h** will be refracted at a smaller angle than line **g b**, and the same applies to lines **e k** and **f l**. And because lines equally distant from the axis **a d** (such as lines **a c** and **a e**) form equal angles on the glassy surface according to the aforementioned method (which are **c h i** and **e k i**), it is clear by Theorem 50 of Book 2 that the angles of refraction are equal. Thus the proposition is clear, because when the line **g h i k l** is a circular line, it must be demonstrated in the same way by Theorem 50 of Book 2.

...the point of conjunction of the axes on the surface of the object seen, let the right axis reaching point **a** and the left reaching point **b** be as follows: let the left also reach point **a**, and so for the other differences of position. Thus, what is "up" relative to point **b** should be "up" relative to point **a**, and what is "down" relative to point **b** becomes "down" relative to point **a**. For in both eyes, a line **i m** is produced—either straight or curved—distinguishing the glassy surface from the glacial surface <note>original: "superficie uitreę à ſuperficie glacialis"; these refer to the boundaries between the vitreous humor and the crystalline lens</note>. Whether this line is straight or curved (one of which is necessary by the 23rd proposition of this book), the angles of incidence will always be equal by the 35th proposition, since the demonstration for them is the same. Furthermore, the angles of refraction are made equal by the preceding proposition. Therefore, because of the conformity of the eyes and the equal distance of points **g** and **c** from point **b** (by hypothesis), it follows that the triangles **y g u** and **x c z** are equiangular. Thus, the angles **g y u** and **c x z** are equal. 

Moreover, since the shapes of the eyes are entirely similar and the transparency is uniform, a uniform refraction of lines **c x** and **g y** will occur at the surface of refraction. Similarly, a uniform refraction of lines **g u** and **c z** will occur according to equal angles. Each of these will therefore be refracted equally from the perpendicular. Let it be, then, that line **c x** is refracted to point **f**, and line **g u** to point **h**, which are the points of the opening where the nerve turns <note>original: "foraminis gyrationis nerui"; the optic disc or where the optic nerve enters the eye</note> around point **r**. Meanwhile, let line **g y** be refracted to point **l**, and line **c z** to point **e**, which is the point of the other opening around point **t**. 

And since all points of the forms are refracted from the perpendicular **n r** according to the shortest straight lines, it is clear that they do not intersect with it. Instead, spreading directly toward the points of the common nerve <term>common nerve: the optic chiasm, where the visual information from both eyes meets</term>, they receive a position and arrangement similar to those they have on the surface of the object seen, which is the base of the pyramid of vision. Therefore, line **x f**, which comes from point **c** of the object seen, is refracted to some point of the nerve other than point **a**, which we shall call **d**. And line **u h**, which comes from point **g** of the object seen, is refracted to another point other than point **a**, which we shall call **k**. 

Since both eyes are of the same disposition, and the distance between the eyes is a small matter (as is clear from the 4th proposition), and the lines produced to such points from both eyes are equal, and the angles of incidence are equal (by the 35th proposition), the angles of refraction are also equal by the preceding proposition. It is clear, then, that line **y l** (which is the form of point **g**) will be refracted to point **k**, where the form of the same point **g** fell coming through line **u h**. Likewise, line **z e** (which is the form of point **c**) will be refracted to point **d**, where the same form of point **c** falls coming through line **x f**. 

The same must be demonstrated for any two points on the surface of the object seen that are equally distant from the point of conjunction, which is **b**. Therefore, all forms of the points of the object seen, surrounding equally the points that strike the surfaces of the eyes according to the radial axes, reach the points surrounding the middle point of the common nerve in a similar manner. The figure and arrangement of the entire surface of the object seen is preserved in its parts, and in its distance from the point on the axis, according to the measure of the distance and inclination of the points whose forms are received there from the point of conjunction on the surface of the object seen, following the arrangement of the angles of refraction at the glassy surface. Thus, the two forms impressed upon two points of similar position on the surfaces of the two eyes reach that same single point in the cavity of the common nerve and are superimposed upon one another at that point, becoming one single form. Lines striking the surfaces of the eyes obliquely, which are refracted at the surface of the eye itself, can also reach the same ordering of the form. Thus, the proposition is clear.

# VITELLO’S OPTICS

...by proposition 30 of Book 1 <note>Unless otherwise noted, these references refer to Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of the time</note>. Since, therefore, by proposition 33 of this book, angle **a f e** is equal to angle **a f g**, it follows that the remainder of the two right angles formed by the axis and line **b c**—which is the intersection of the surface of the object seen and the plane of the axes—will be equal on both sides. Therefore, the visual axes strike the surface of the object seen at equal angles. This is exactly what was proposed, since angle **e f b** is made equal to angle **g f c**.

*39. From the point where the visual axes meet, to draw a line on the surface of the object (if that surface is parallel to the eyes) that is itself parallel to the line connecting the centers of the eyes.*

Let the centers of the two eyes be points **e** and **g**, and let line **e g** be drawn between them. Let the surface of the object being seen be **b c d f**. From a given point **a** on this surface, we must draw a line parallel to line **e g**. Therefore, let line **e g** be divided into two equal parts at point **r** (by proposition 10 of Book 1), and from point **a** to point **r**, let line **a r** be drawn. Then, let lines **e a** and **g a** be drawn; these are the visual axes <note>The "visual axis" is the central, most direct line of sight from the center of the eye to the object</note> meeting at point **a** on the surface of the object. It is clear, then, that since axis **e a** is equal to axis **g a** (by proposition 35 of this book), and line **e r** is equal to line **g r**, and line **r a** is shared by both resulting triangles, then by proposition 8 of Book 1, angle **e r a** is equal to angle **g r a**. Since they are equal and adjacent on a straight line, both are right angles. Thus, line **a r** is perpendicular to line **e g**. Now, from the centers of vision **e** and **g**, let lines be drawn parallel to **r a** (by proposition 31 of Book 1); let these be lines **e z** and **g y**. These lines are equal and parallel to each other (by theorem 25 of Book 1 of this work) and exist in the same plane. Because the intersection of this plane and the object’s surface passes through point **a** and is parallel to line **e g** (by proposition 33 of Book 1), it is clear that line **z a y** is the line we are looking for. Thus, the task is complete.

*40. All lines drawn from both eyes to the same point on a line that forms right angles with both visual axes are necessarily equal in length. Alhazen, Book 3, Proposition 3.* <note>Vitello frequently cites "Alhazen," the Latin name for the 11th-century polymath Ibn al-Haytham, whose *Book of Optics* was the foundation for this field</note>

For example: let the centers of the two eyes be points **e** and **g**, as in the previous proposition. Let the surface of the object be **b c d f**, where the visual axes **e a** and **g a** meet at point **a**. From point **a**, let a single line be extended in both directions, labeled **z a u**, which forms right angles with both axes. Now, let lines **e u**, **g u**, **e z**, and **g z** be drawn from the centers of the eyes. I state that lines **e u** and **g u** are equal to each other, and lines **e z** and **g z** are also equal. Since the visual axes are equal (by proposition 35 of this book), it is clear that axis **e a** is equal to axis **g a**, and angle **e a u** is equal to angle **g a u** (since both are right angles by our premise). Since line **a u** is shared by triangles **e a u** and **g a u**, then by proposition 4 of Book 1, the base **e u** is equal to the base **g u**. Similarly, the base **e z** will be equal to the base **g z**. This holds true for every point along line **z u**. Thus, the proposition is proven.

This can also be demonstrated another way: let a line parallel to line **e g** (the line between the eye centers) be drawn through point **a** on the object’s surface (where the axes meet) following the previous proposition; let this be line **k l**. This line **k l** will lie on the object’s surface. Draw line **z a** perpendicular to line **k l** (by proposition 12 of Book 1). Next, draw a line from point **a** perpendicular to line **e g**, which becomes line **a r**. This line **a r** will divide line **e g** into two equal parts at point **r** (by theorem 31 and proposition 35 of this book, and proposition 5 of Book 1). Because axes **e a** and **g a** are equal, the angles at the base will be equal. Since line **r a** is shared by both triangles **e a r** and **g a r**, and the angles at point **r** are equal right angles, then by proposition 32 of Book 1 and proposition 4 of Book 6, line **e r** is equal to line **r g**. 

Next, draw line **r z**. By proposition 29 of Book 1, line **r a** is perpendicular to line **k a l**. Since (by proposition 34 of this book) lines **e a**, **g a**, and **r a** are in the same plane, and line **z a** is perpendicular to axes **e a** and **g a** by our premise, then by proposition 4 of Book 11, line **z a** is perpendicular to the plane containing the axes. Therefore, it is also perpendicular to line **r a**. Likewise, by proposition 4 of Book 11, line **k a** will be perpendicular to the plane **r z a**. It follows that line **e r** is perpendicular to that same plane **r z a** (by proposition 8 of Book 11). By the definition of a line standing perpendicular to a plane, line **e r** must be perpendicular to line **r z**. Because the two angles **e r z** and **g r z** in the two triangles **e r z** and **g r z** are equal (both being right angles), and line **e r** equals line **r g**, and side **r z** is shared, then by proposition 4 of Book 1, line **e z** is equal to line **g z**. The same logic applies to any other point on line **z u**. Thus, the proposition is clear.

...the same point outside line **u z**, which alone makes right angles with both axes, are always unequal. 
For let two points, **m** and **n**, be marked on line **k l** (which intersects line **u z** in any way) at whatever distance from point **a** is desired. Let lines **e m** and **e n** be drawn. I say that lines **e m** and **g m** are unequal, and lines **e n** and **g n** are unequal. For let a line **r m** be drawn from point **r** to point **m**. Since, therefore, angle **e r a** is a right angle (as was clear in the preceding proposition), it is evident that angle **e r m** is less than a right angle; therefore, angle **g r m** is greater than a right angle, by Proposition 13 of Book 1 <note>Euclid's Elements</note>. Therefore, in triangles **g r m** and **e r m**, side **r m** is shared, and line **e r** is equal to line **g r**, and angle **g r m** is greater than angle **e r m**. Therefore, by Proposition 24 of Book 1, side **g m** will be longer than side **e m**. One must argue similarly regarding all other points outside line **u z**. Thus, the proposition is clear. However, this inequality of those lines is less perceptible when the points of deviation are near the point of intersection.

42. *All lines drawn from the two eyes to points equidistant from the junction of the axes—on a line that forms oblique angles with both axes—are necessarily equal, as are the angles contained by those lines. Alhazen, Book 3, note 3.*

Let the entire arrangement be as above in the two preceding propositions, and let **m** and **n** be points on line **k l** (which forms oblique angles with both axes) that are equally distant from point **a**, which is the point where the axes meet, such that line **m a** is equal to **a n**. I say that the lines drawn from the alternate eyes, such as **e n** and **g m**, as well as **e m** and **g n**, are equal. For since axis **e a** is equal to axis **g a** by proposition 35 of this book, and the angle of incidence of axis **e a** (which is angle **e a m**) is equal to the angle of incidence of axis **g a** (which is angle **g a n**) because angles **r a m** and **r a n** are right angles, the angles **r a e** and **r a g** are also equal (as is clear from the demonstrations in the two preceding propositions). Therefore, the remaining angles **e a m** and **g a n** are equal. But since axes **e a** and **g a** are equal, and line **m a** is equal to line **n a** by hypothesis, line **g n** will be equal to line **e m** by Proposition 4 of Book 1, and angle **g n a** will be equal to angle **e m a**. Therefore, in triangles **e m n** and **g n m**, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, base **e m** is equal to base **g n**. A similar demonstration can be made for all other similar points: for the lines **g b** and **e f**, **g f** and **e b**, **g k** and **e l**, **g l** and **e k**, **g c** and **e d**, and **g d** and **e c**—all of them, as they are named and as they are produced from alternate eyes to points equidistant from point **a**—are necessarily equal. Thus, the proposition is clear for any number of other lines produced in a similar manner.

43. *Certain perception by sight occurs along all lines of the radial pyramid of forms, but more so along lines closer to the axis, and most of all through the axis passing through the center of the opening of the uvea <term>uvea: the pigmented layer of the eye; here referring to the pupil</term>. Alhazen, Book 8, note 2.*

For only the axis extends in a straight line until it reaches the point of rotation <note>original: "locum gyrationis"</note> of the concave nerve <note>the optic nerve</note>, while all other lines are bent <note>refracted</note>, as is clear from proposition 24 of this book. Thus, the form of the visible object placed opposite the middle of the surface of the eye reaches the glacial humor <term>glacialis: the crystalline lens</term> and the vitreous humor <term>uitreus: the clear gel-like substance behind the lens</term> following a straight path all the way to the point of rotation of the concave nerve. However, forms that arrive along other lines are bent. And because the arrangement of bent forms is not the same as the arrangement of forms extended straight—since bending necessarily alters them in some way regarding the certainty of perception—the point of the form reaching the rotation point of the concave nerve, which extends along the straightness of the axis, is more verified than all other points of the forms. And because the bending of lines near the axis is less, and that of more distant lines is greater—because the angles formed by the lines upon which the forms arrive and the perpendiculars produced above the axis in the surface of bending are more acute for lines near the axis and less acute for distant ones (as seen in proposition 36 of this book)—forms whose bending is less are more clearly revealed than those whose bending is greater. Therefore, the point upon the axis reaching the rotation point of the concave nerve is clearer than all other points and perceived with more certainty; and that which is closer to it is clearer than that which is further away. The same is true for the form reaching the common nerve <note>the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet</note>, from which the sensitive power perceives the forms of things. Thus, the proposition is clear.

44. *When the point of intersection lies on the common axis, vision is most certain; it remains certain near that axis, but is less certain further away. Alhazen, Book 10, note 3.*

Let the line connecting the centers of the openings of the uvea be **a b**, and let line **c e** be the common axis. Also, let the point of intersection on line **c e** be **d**, where the axes **a d** and **b d** meet; and let the middle point of the cavity of the common nerve be point **h**. I say that when point **d** exists on line **c e**, vision is then most certain. For the forms of the objects seen reaching the surface of the eye are then more similar, because when the axes fall into the centers of the openings of the uvea (marked by points **a** and **b**), the forms of the points surrounding point **d** fall distinctly and similarly around those centers. And since the common axis, which is **e c**, divides line **a b** into equal parts at point **c** (by proposition 33 of this book and Proposition 29 of Book 1), because the line connecting the centers...

...the openings of the uvea <note>The uvea here refers to the iris; the "openings" are the pupils.</note> is equidistant to the line **r t**, which connects the centers of rotation of the hollow nerves <note>original: "neruorum concauorum." In medieval anatomy, the optic nerves were believed to be hollow tubes that carried "visual spirits."</note>, as is clear from the previous statements and by the 4th proposition of this book. From this, by the 31st and 1st propositions of this book, it is clear that line **h c** divides line **a b** into two equal parts and is perpendicular to it. It is therefore evident by Proposition 4, Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, that the axis **a d** is equal to axis **b d**, and angle **d a c** is equal to angle **d b c**. Furthermore, by the 30th proposition of this book, angles **h a c** and **h b c** are equal. Since the common axis, which is **e c**, reaches point **h** (the center of the concavity of the common nerve <note>The "common nerve" is the optic chiasm, where the two optic nerves meet.</note>), where the forms <note>Images or visual information.</note> from points **a** and **b** are spread, it is evident by Proposition 26, Book 1, that the angles **c h a** and **c h b** are equal.

The same thing occurs at all points where the radial lines fall near the axes **a d** and **b d**, which are essentially equal to the senses <note>i.e., they appear equal to our perception.</note>, as shown by the 40th proposition of this book. These radial lines fall almost equally on identical points of the surface of the common nerve, according to the 37th proposition of this book. Therefore, the forms of points seen in this uniform way are more similar to each other, resulting in a more certain <note>Closer to the truth; more accurate or clear.</note> vision.

However, when the point of conjunction <note>The point where the two eyes focus.</note> is slightly outside the common axis, such as at point **f**—whether that distance is to the left, right, up, down, or in any other direction—the two forms impressed upon the two sights <note>The two eyes.</note> still do not differ much. Thus, at the point of the form where the two axes are fixed (incident upon point **h** at the center of the nerve's concavity), the remaining points of the form of the object seen through radial lines near the axes are united in the concavity of the common nerve around point **h**. This does not happen with the same perfection as the previous arrangement; therefore, the object is still seen with certain vision, but not with the same degree of certainty as before.

But when the point of conjunction is far removed from the common axis **c e**, such as at point **g**, regardless of the difference in position, then the point of the visible object where the two axes meet is still fixed upon point **h**. However, the forms of the remaining points of that visible object, fixed around point **h**, will not receive a disposition similar to the two previous cases. The vision of those points will not be well-verified <note>Accurately perceived.</note> but will remain less certain. Thus, the proposition is clear.

45. *Every visible object at the point of conjunction of the two visual axes is seen more clearly than that seen through rays near the axes; and the degree of certainty decreases according to the distance from the axes. From this it is clear that points on the surface of a visible object equidistant from the point of conjunction are presented similarly to the visual faculty. Alhazen, Book 3, Proposition 15.*

For as shown by the 43rd proposition of this book, a certain comprehension of the visible form is achieved by the sight according to all the lines of any visual pyramid <note>term: visual pyramid (a cone of light rays with the eye as the vertex and the object as the base)</note>; however, it is more certain along lines closer to the axis, and most certain along the axis passing through the center of the pupil. Since the two axes meet at the point of conjunction according to the 32nd proposition of this book, it is evident—since a doubled power is stronger than half of itself—that at the point of conjunction, vision becomes more certain across the whole surface of the visible object (which is the base of both visual pyramids). This follows the proportion of double to double, which is the same as single to single.

However, vision is less certain through radial lines near the axes than through the axes themselves because the forms of those points reaching the sensitive faculty do not arrive directly at the middle of the common nerve. Therefore, the judgment concerning them is not as perfect as it is for the forms arriving through the axes themselves. As those lines move further from the axes, the degree of visual certainty decreases. Because the parts of the object's surface where the axes fall (and the parts nearest to them) are seen more clearly (per Prop 43), the certainty of vision is weakest at the more remote parts of that surface where the extreme lines of the visual pyramid's length fall. In the middle parts, there is a middle state of certainty, depending on whether they are closer to or further from the axes. The proposition is therefore clear. From this, the corollary is evident: for points on the surface of a visible object equidistant from the point of junction, the level of visual certainty is the same on both sides, because their forms are always shaped equally on the surface of the eye and, consequently, on the surface of the common nerve. Thus, all that was proposed is clear.

46. *Every visible object in which the two visual axes or rays near them converge always appears as one. Alhazen, Book 3, Proposition 14.*

Because the forms arriving at the sight through the radial axes fall equally upon both eyes (per Prop 35) and reach the center point of the nerve concavity equally (per Prop 30), both those forms converge at a single point. One form is placed upon the other, and they become a single form. And because all common objects seen by us are always positioned opposite both eyes, and both eyes look at each of those visible objects, the two axes of the two eyes always converge at one point of those objects (per Prop 32). The position of the remaining rays that fall around their common point is a similar position (per Prop 37), especially when they do not differ greatly in distance from the two axes. Because of this, any common visible object appears as one to both eyes. And because, as stated, it is clear by Prop 37 that all forms of points [fall] equally...

[Header: BOOK THREE]

...points surrounding [the center] equally, which fall on the surfaces of the eyes along the radial axes, reach the points surrounding the middle point of the common nerve <note>The "common nerve" refers to the optic chiasm, the X-shaped structure where the optic nerves from each eye meet.</note> in a similar way. However, the radial lines near the visual axes, because they do not fall upon the eyes very obliquely, are therefore not refracted very obliquely, since their refraction occurs at smaller angles according to the 36th proposition of this book. Thus, they reach the hollow of the nerve more directly; they therefore meet around the middle point of the hollow of the nerve and are superimposed upon one another, becoming a single form. And this is what was proposed.

->**47. Every visible object, in which the common axis and one of the visual axes meet, is always perceived as one.**<-

For the common axis <note>The central line of sight projecting between the two eyes.</note> assists the certainty of perception, and a single visual axis imprints only one regularly arranged form upon the middle point of the common nerve. Therefore, only one form is seen, because at that point no refraction of the second form occurs toward any distinct part of the nerve, whether in terms of its position or its distance. The proposition is therefore clear.

->**48. No visible object is seen equally in its entirety at the same time. Euclid in the preface and the 1st theorem of his *Optics*. Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham, the influential Arab polymath whose work *De Aspectibus* served as the foundation for Witelo’s optics.</note> Book 1, chapter 3, note 16.**<-

Whether a visible object exists on the common axis or outside of it, the point of the object upon which the visual axes fall is always seen more clearly than the points upon which the nearby rays fall. Furthermore, those nearby points are seen more clearly than the points upon which the remote rays fall, according to the 45th proposition of this book. It is therefore evident that no visible object is seen equally across its whole surface at once. Only when every point of the object has been scanned by the eye's movement—traversed by all three axes, or at least by the two visual axes—is the whole object seen equally. For at that point, the form of each of its points will be fixed upon the middle point of the hollow of the nerve, and there will always be a new arrangement of the entire form around that point. Consequently, the equality of the parts in relation to one another will be more equally weighed in all their arrangements; thus, the whole object will then be seen equally. 

However, no movement occurs in an instant, but only over time. It is clear, then, that no visible object will be seen equally in its entirety at the same time, though it is certainly possible for the whole to be seen unequally at once. This is because all points of the form opposite the eye, from which straight lines can be drawn to the eye, are multiplied toward the eye simultaneously, even though they are seen differently across different parts according to the variety of their angles. Nevertheless, small bodies and those with narrow diameters are seen more equally than bodies with larger diameters; for parts more remote from the point of junction <note>The focus point.</note> are not as well-certified <note>original: "certificantur," meaning perceived with clarity or certainty.</note> as nearby parts, per the 45th proposition. If the object seen is of a uniform color, less inequality happens within it than if it were of many colors, or if there were lines, or a painting, or other fine details <note>original: "subtiles intentiones," referring to the specific visual characteristics or "intentions" of an object.</note> upon it. In those cases, the form of the outer edges will be more doubtful and not well-certified, for these are perceived through radial lines far from the axis. The proposition is therefore clear.

->**49. It is impossible for many things to be seen equally at the same time.**<-

Sometimes the sight is positioned opposite many visible things of different colors at the same time, and straight lines can be drawn from each of them to the eye through the continuous medium of the air. The forms of light and color that exist in the things seen reach the surface of the eye at the same time, and the form of each of them reaches every part of the eye's surface because of their direct opposition. And although the viewer sees differently colored objects opposite the eye at the same time—meaning there are many different lights and colors on the entire surface of the eye, each filling the surface according to how it falls perpendicularly or obliquely—nevertheless, as is clear from the 17th proposition, distinct vision does not occur except along the perpendicular lines drawn from the points of the object to the surface of the eye. Forms are distinguished according to the distinction of the parts of the eye's surface upon which the perpendiculars fall. 

Even though forms mixed with various lights and colors reach the surface of the eye in this way, the sense of sight still perceives all forms according to their own properties. It is not impossible to see many things at once, but they are seen unequally and indistinctly. For although the glacial humor <note>The crystalline lens of the eye.</note> perceives the form of one thing according to its own being and its shape ordered upon its surface—as is clear from the 17th proposition—it can also perceive the forms of other visible things in that same arrangement. It can perceive the form of any of those things and their positions relative to each other, but not equally. That which it sees through the pyramid <note>The "visual pyramid" or cone of light.</note> whose axis falls through the center of the circle of the uvea <note>The pupil.</note> to the center of the eye is perceived most perfectly. Other things, whose pyramidal axes fall upon other points of the surface of said circle, are seen less perfectly, as is clear from the 43st proposition; for the axes of all those are longer, even if they proceed from the same distance. 

Therefore, when an observer is positioned opposite many visible things and his sight is still, he will find that the object opposite the middle of his eye is clearer than those to the sides, and whatever is closer to the middle will be clearer, and what is more remote will be less clear. This is all evident from the 43rd proposition. It is therefore impossible for many things to be seen equally at the same time, because it is impossible for the axis of a radial pyramid passing through the center of the pupil to fall upon many points, let alone many surfaces, at once, per the 20th proposition of Book 11 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 50. *With various visible objects placed between them, the vision of the more distant ones is sometimes hindered in some part. Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham</note> Book 3, note 3.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating optical perspective, occlusion, and the convergence of visual axes. Two points at the top, labeled 'm' and 'n', represent the eyes or centers of vision. Lines of sight (axes) 'mk' and 'nk' converge at a point 'k' on a horizontal line labeled 'b-k-c'. Below this, another line 'e-f-g-d' is partially intersected by lines extending from 'm' and 'n' through 'b' and 'c' which meet at point 'p'. Further down, a point 'r' is located within an area 'l-o'. A small trapezoidal object 'a' is placed near the top between the primary axes. The diagram uses these points and lines to geometrically demonstrate how foreground objects obscure background ones and how images are formed relative to the 'common nerve'.</image-desc>

For example, let two points *n* and *m* be the centers of the two eyes, and let *r* be a point on a certain visible thing, which is *l o*, further away from both eyes than the visible thing *b k c*. Let both visual axes, which are *m k* and *n k*, meet at point *k*. Let point *r* be positioned such that when the axes *n k* and *m k* are extended to points *q* and *h*, *r* is intercepted between the axes, and no part of it is caught by the interposition of the visible object *b c*. However, let the visible object *e d* be further away than *b c* and closer than point *r*, arranged between the two axes in such a way that the lines *n b* and *m c*, when extended and meeting at point *p*, intercept some part of it, which is *f g*. Furthermore, let the lines *m p* and *n p*, intersecting each other at point *p* and extended, touch the periphery of the body in which point *r* is located at points *l* and *o*. Finally, let *a* be a certain visible object very close to the eye, falling between the axes *m k* and *n k*.

I say that when the sight perceives the forms of the visible objects *b c*, *e d*, and *r* at the same time, the vision of *e d* is sometimes hindered in some part. This is because it is hindered in its part *f g*, which is obscured to the sight by the interposition of the visible object *b c*. It is clear that the form of that part will not reach the eye, nor will it be preserved in the common nerve <note>The optic chiasm, where the visual information from both eyes is combined.</note>. However, the form of the more distant visible object *l o* (containing point *r*), because it falls between the lines *n b* and *m c* (which cross at point *p* and extend beyond to their endpoints *l* and *o*), clearly reaches the eye without being hindered by the visible object *b c*. 

Yet, because the visual axes do not meet at any point on it, its form will appear disordered according to the position of those same parts of the form, which will not be directly superimposed on each other, as was shown in proposition 37 of this book. Therefore, they will be disordered according to their distance from the middle point of the common nerve; this distance will be unequal on either side due to the difference in the incidence of the lines through which the same points of the forms arrive—such as lines *m l* and *n l* with respect to the form of point *l*, and lines *m o* and *n o* with respect to the form of point *o*. Nevertheless, the part of the whole that is perceived to the right or left, upward or downward, regarding the parts of that form, does not change. 

Indeed, since the visible object *b c* is smaller than the visible object *l o* (where point *r* is), when the two axes *m k* and *n k* are joined at point *k* of the visible thing *b c*, then the form of the object *b c* is created in two places in the two eyes in a similar position. But the form of the visible object *l o* will be diversified according to the position of the parts of its form and according to the unequal distance from the middle point of the common nerve. This is because there is a great difference in the angles of refraction <note>Refraction refers to the bending of light as it enters the eye.</note> of its partial forms, just as in their angles of incidence <note>The angle at which light hits the surface of the eye.</note>, as can be seen from proposition 36 of this book. However, there will be no error in the general location, because the forms of the parts will be arranged in their proper order as they are in reality, and the thing will be seen as one. 

This does not happen in the form of the visible object *a*, which is closer to the eye, if it is of small size and there is no sensible difference in the position of those bodies, so that body *a* falls between the axes *m k* and *n k*. Therefore, when both eyes perceive both visible things in which *r* and *d e* are located, and when the two axes are fixed on the visible object *b c*, the forms of those visible things *d e* and *l o* are established in two places in the two eyes according to the areas that are not obscured. They become of similar position in terms of their general direction, but not in their distance from the middle point of the common nerve; nor will all their parts be of similar position in their distance from the two axes, nor will their form be certified <note> "Certified" or "verified" sight refers to a clear, focused, and accurate perception.</note>. 

Regarding the visible object *a*, which is closest to the eyes, because it falls between the axes *m k* and *n k* and the eyes are not fixed upon it, its position relative to both eyes can become diverse in terms of its general direction, so that it is seen neither to the left nor to the right. This is because its form, by itself, is not ordered toward any part of the universe relative to the middle point of the hollow nerve where the visual axes fall. Thus, with the sight remaining fixed and various visible objects placed between them, the vision of the more distant ones is sometimes hindered in some part, as is clear. 

However, when the eyes are moved and the axes are joined at each of the perceived visible objects at once, then the forms of all the visible objects will be perceived simultaneously in both eyes as similar in direction and distance, and the forms of each of the visible objects will be perceived according to their level of certainty. The reason for this entire matter is this: the certainty of vision occurs along the axes, and vision occurs through the multiplication <note>A medieval term for the propagation or "spreading" of light or forms through space.</note> of the visible form into the eye, which is sometimes hindered by an intervening body when the line of the form's multiplication touches another surface of an intermediate body opposite the eye in some way. And this is what we intended to show.

### 51. *All vision occurs either through a simple glance or through diligent intuition. Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham</note> Book 2, note 64.*

We call "simple glance" <note>original: *aspectum simplicem*</note> that first act by which the form of the visible thing is simply received on the surface of the eye. We call "intuition" <note>original: *intuitionem*</note> that act by which the sight seeks a true comprehension of the form of the thing by looking through it diligently, not content with simple reception, but through deep investigation. Thus, the sight through a simple glance perceives the manifest qualities that are in things, but does not verify them;

...through intuition <note>Latin: *intuitionem*; here meaning focused, diligent observation as opposed to a glancing look</note>, however, it considers all the internal properties of the parts that are hidden from a glancing view, and it confirms all the dispositions of that seen form. And because a simple glance can exist without intuition, although intuition cannot exist without a simple glance: it is clear that every act of seeing occurs either through one of these modes or the other. And this is what was proposed.

### §2. While a simple glance is possible through the whole visual pyramid, intuition occurs only through the incidence of the axis of the visual pyramid. Alhazen Book 2, note 65.

Since, as is clear from the previous premise, a simple glance is merely the reception of a sensible form upon the surface of the eye: it is evident that this happens according to the whole **visual pyramid** <note>The cone-shaped volume of light rays stretching from the object to the eye</note>: for any of the perpendiculars or radial lines constituting that pyramid (according to proposition 17 of this book) brings some form of a point from the surface of the visible object, which the eye then sees. Because intuition confirms the truth of the forms perceived, and the confirmation of all visible forms happens more through the **axes** <note>The central, straightest line of the visual pyramid</note> of the visual pyramids than through any other lines of that pyramid (according to proposition 43 of this book): it is clear that intuition occurs only by the falling of that axis upon the object. 

Therefore, when the sight is fixed opposite some visible object of a certain size, and that which is opposite the middle of the eye from that visible object is reached by the visual axis or near it: then that which is on the axis, or which approaches the axis, will be more manifest than the remaining parts of the visible object. If, therefore, the viewer wishes to be certain about the total form of the thing seen, he will move both eyes until the middle of the eye is opposite each of the parts or points of the surface of the visible object facing him. And then, because both radial axes (according to proposition 32 of this book) will fall upon each of the points, a complete intuition of the whole form is achieved in this way. 

For when the sight is directed at the visible object, the sensing faculty perceives the whole form with a general perception (according to proposition 43 of this book), and it perceives the part at the end of the axis with a true perception. Then, when the axes are moved to another point, that same point is perceived more truly; and at the same time, the whole form previously perceived is perceived a second time, including that point where the axes were previously fixed. When the axes are moved to a third point, a third perception of the whole form occurs, along with those points where the axes previously fell. Thus, the perception of the whole form is multiplied according to the number of points upon which the axes fall; however, the point upon which the axes fall will always be perceived more certainly than the other points. 

In this way, the observer, through the movement of the axes, grasps the certainty of every point of the visible object, and furthermore repeats the frequent perception of the whole form according to the number of points the axes strike. It appears to the sight then all that is possible to appear in the form of that visible object, and the form of the visible object will not be certified except after the movement of the eye along its radial axes over all parts or points of the surface of the visible object. For the subtle details <note>Latin: *intentiones subtiles*; the fine qualities or "intentions" of an object like texture or exact shading</note> that are in the thing seen do not appear to the eye except through the movement of the sight, and by the passage of the axis, or the radial lines near it, over every part of the thing seen. Even if the object is extremely small and placed opposite the eye: the eye will not observe it with perfect intuition until, by moving the eye, the radial axis has passed through all the tiny parts or points of that object. Thus, intuition occurs only through the falling of the axis of the radial pyramid, although a simple glance occurs through all the radial lines of the entire visual pyramid. The proposition is therefore clear.

### §3. The radial axis remains fixed in its position throughout the entire movement of the eye: because that movement of the eye is of an imperceptible speed. Alhazen Book 2, note 42.

The movement of the axis over the parts of the visible object does not happen by the rotation of the axis away from the location of the center of the eye itself, but by the movement of the eye as a whole over the parts of the visible object. It is clear (from propositions 25 and 32 of this book) that the line of the axis extends straight to the place of the rotation of the nerve <note>The optic nerve</note> upon which the eye is composed: and that its position within the eye does not change. Rather, when the whole eye moves to face the visible object, and the middle of the eye (where the sense of sight resides) is placed opposite any of the parts of the thing seen, then the axis passes through each of those parts. 

In this manner, the total form of every part of the visible object always extends to the eye according to the straightness of the axis. The rotation of the axis will be unchangeable from its place relative to all the parts and **tunics** <note>The layers or membranes of the eye, such as the cornea or retina</note> of the eye; but the axis will revolve within the hollow of the bone <note>The eye socket</note> with the movement of the entire eye. When the sight wishes to observe a visible thing and begins to look at the edge of the object: the end of the axis will then be upon the edge of the object, and in that arrangement, the larger part of the whole object will be on the part of the eye's surface that is declining or oblique from the axis toward another side. Because its form will be in the middle of the eye and in the place of the axis, the rest of the form will be slanted toward the other side from the axis. 

When the eye, after that arrangement, is moved along some diameter of the visible object, the axis is transferred to the part following that part of the object, and the form of the first part will be declining toward another place opposite to the place where the axis is moving. The form will not cease to decline as long as the axis moves along that diameter, until the axis reaches the end of that diameter of the visible object. Thus, the form of the whole visible object will be in this slanted arrangement relative to the eye and the point opposite the axis, even those parts to which it was previously slanted, as the radial axis falls on other various points, except for the final part and the edge of the visible object, which will remain upon the axis and in the middle of the eye. Throughout this entire movement, the axis will be fixed in its position regarding its uniform passage through all the tunics of the eye. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

### §4. In the movement of intuition, the axis never becomes the base of the angle subtended by the surface of the visible object, nor does it always bisect the angle subtended by any of the diameters of the visible object. Alhazen Book 2, note 43.

Because it has already been shown in the preceding theorem that the axis in the whole movement of the eye for the purpose of intuition...

But this would not be possible unless the axis moved by itself while the whole eye remained at rest. Through this motion, the form of the seen object is moved to the surface of the sight itself, and the part of the surface of the eye where the form was previously being shaped changes; because as the axis moves, the form of the seen object will be on one part of the sight's surface after another. 

For as many times as the sensing power perceives the part of the seen object at the end of the axis, it will simultaneously perceive the entire surface of the seen object and that whole part of the surface of the sight where the form of the entire seen object arrives—which is always changing. Thus, as long as the axis falls on some point of the diameter of the seen object (not at the ends of that diameter), the axis divides the angle which that diameter occupies at the center of the sight. But when it falls on the end of the diameter, the axis itself becomes one of the lines containing that angle. Therefore, it does not always bisect that angle. This is what was proposed.

### § 55. *It is necessary that all vision occurring through a simple glance happens in an instant.*

<image-desc>In the right margin, a vertical line is drawn with specific points labeled from top to bottom as: a, b, 6, c, and d.</image-desc>
<margin>a</margin>
<margin>b</margin>
<margin>6</margin>
<margin>c</margin>
<margin>d</margin>
If simple sight <note>Latin: *aspectu simplici*; a quick glance without focused attention</note> happened in time, no matter how small that time might be, it would be part of a larger span of time. Since vision is not said to happen in time except due to the distance of the visible object from the eye, then clearly time would multiply according to the distance of the object. 

Let a line **a b c d** be drawn, and let the eye be at point **a**, and some visible object at point **b**. Since, as was stated and declared in proposition 6 of this book, the form of point **b** is multiplied <note>The medieval theory that objects "multiply" their image or "species" through the air to reach the observer</note> to the sight, if this happened in any time—even perhaps an imperceptible one—let there be another object at point **c**. Let the distance **a c** be a multiple of the distance **a b**. Therefore, the time in which the form of point **c** reaches sight **a** will be a multiple of the time in which the form of point **b** reaches sight **a**. 

If this time is not yet sensible to us, let there be an object at a further point **d**, more remote from sight **a** than **c** is. Let the distance **a d** be a multiple of distance **c a**; therefore, it will be even more of a multiple of distance **b a**. Thus, the form of point **d** would reach sight **a** in a time that is a multiple of the time it took for the form of point **c** to reach sight **a**. 

But in the passage of the form of point **d** through that space **a d**, no more time is required for the act of seeing than in space **a b**. For when the eyes are opened, distant and near things are seen equally quickly. There is no sensible difference in the time it takes to see a nearby object versus one of the fixed stars, whose distance is roughly the semidiameter of the world <note>The radius of the known universe</note>, which is the greatest of all natural lines. Therefore, it is impossible for vision occurring by a simple glance to happen in time; rather, all such vision must happen in an instant and suddenly. Its beginning does not differ from its end. This is what was proposed.

### § 56. *It is necessary that every act of intuition occurs in time; and the time of intuition for visible properties varies according to the diversity of the properties of the forms being scrutinized.*

> Alhazen 70. 74 n 2.

Since, as was shown in proposition 51 of this book, intuition <note>Focused scrutiny or diligent observation</note> is an act of the visual power by which the sight seeks a true perception of a form by completing it diligently, and the radial axes always move through all points of the surface of the object during this intuition (as declared in proposition 52), and since every sensible motion happens in sensible time (because, as we have declared elsewhere, time is proportional to motion), it is clear that every intuition must happen in sensible time. 

The time for intuition also varies according to the different intentions <note>Latin: *intentiones*; a technical term for the individual qualities or characteristics of an object, such as size, number, or shape</note> of the visible forms one observes. For example: if the sight perceives a long animal with many small feet that is moving, first through a brief intuition it perceives its motion, and through that motion perceives it is an animal. Then, through a brief intuition of the feet, it perceives it has many feet by grasping the distance between them, yet it does not yet know the exact number of those feet. Finally, by scrutinizing more diligently, it will know the number of feet through more intuition and a greater effort of time. 

The perception of its "animal-ness" happens in a short time; the perception of the "multitude of feet" happens in a longer time than that first span in which it was known to be an animal; and the "number of feet" will take a time even longer than either of those. For the sight must observe each of those feet and count them. The amount of time for the intuition of the feet will depend on whether there are many or few. This is also clear from the variety of other visible properties. Therefore, the time for the intuition of visible properties (one of which is number) varies according to the diversity of the properties being scrutinized. The proposition is clear.

### § 57. *The sight cannot grasp the true form of a seen object by a first simple glance, but only after diligent intuition. Alhazen 76 n 2.*

...those features being coarse, presenting themselves at first glance, but some being very subtle, such as tiny lines and colors dispersed minutely, and similar things, which at first glance—which is instantaneous according to theorem 55 of this book—cannot immediately present themselves. Therefore, they need time to be seen; after diligent scrutiny <note>Latin: *intuitum*; here meaning a focused, searching gaze rather than a sudden "hunch."</note>, they will be seen, and not before. ### 58. *Repeated looking fixes and verifies the sensory forms remaining in the soul.*

For when sight comprehends some seen thing, and its form has been verified in the sensing mind, then the form of that seen thing remains in the soul and is fixed in the imagination of the one seeing, as is declared in the natural passions of the soul. And if the comprehension of the seen thing is repeated, then its form will be more fixed in the soul than the form of a thing seen only once. This is because sight rarely comprehends a thing perfectly when seen only once; but always from the repetition of vision, the form reaches the soul anew, and the form previously seen is renewed in the soul. If any of the features of that form have been surrendered to oblivion, they are restored; and if they were not seen before, they are captured. The soul, moreover, remembers the first form through the second form, and when the arrival of the same feature is repeated many times upon the soul, the soul will be more mindful of that feature. Thus, that form will be more fixed in the soul, and also better verified. In the first vision, when the form of the seen thing comes to the soul, perhaps the soul does not comprehend all the features in that form, nor verify them; but when the form returns a second time, the soul comprehends something else from it which it did not comprehend the first time. The more the form is repeated upon the soul, the more there will be revealed from it what did not appear before. When the soul comprehends the more subtle features of forms, the existence of the whole form will be better verified for it. It is clear, therefore, from these things, that repeated looks will be more certain, as is proposed.

<margin>Alhazen Book 2, chapter 18.</margin>
### 59. *Nothing visible is perceived by the sense of sight alone, except for lights and colors.*

For since these things alone are visible in themselves, as was established in the suppositions of this book, it is clear that they are prior to all other visible things. Hence, they are offered to the sight without the others, such as without position, shape, magnitude, and similar things. Other things, however, are not offered to the sight without them, for it is impossible for a visible thing not participating in actual light to be seen, as is clear from theorem 1 of this book. Therefore, concerning light and color, there occurs no other operation of the soul except the sensation of vision itself. For light, which is in an illuminated body, is comprehended by sight according to its being and through itself by the sense itself. But light and color, which are in a colored and illuminated body, are comprehended by sight simultaneously and mixed together. Each of them is comprehended by the sense of sight alone; for primary light is comprehended by sight from the illumination of the sensing body, which is of the substance of the eye, and color from the alteration of the form of that same sensing body and its coloration with the admixture of light, which is the underlying substance <term>hypostasis: the fundamental reality or "foundation" that allows color to be visible.</term> of color. For just as the sensing power comprehends only light upon the arrival of the form of primary light, so upon the arrival of the form of color it comprehends colored light. Therefore, these two are comprehended by the sense of sight alone without other powers and operations of the soul, which does not happen in any of the other invisible properties <note>Witelo means properties that are not visible *in themselves* but are perceived through light/color, like distance or shape.</note>. For those are sensed, as it were, as multiple things by multiple senses; and if some of them are sensed by the sense of sight alone and not by other particular senses, this happens either from some participation in these or the deprivation of them, as is the case in transparency and opacity, darkness and shadow, in which a reasoning process comparing things is necessary, which is not necessary in the comprehension of light and color. Thus the proposition is clear.

<margin>Alhazen Book 2, chapter 10.</margin>
### 60. *Every visible thing is either perceived by sight alone simply, or with reason and discernment.*

As is clear from the preceding, sight alone comprehends light and color simply in themselves. However, there are many other things which are included among the number of visible things, which sight indeed comprehends, though not simply through itself, but with other actions of the soul being added. There are many such visible things whose comprehension is not by the pure sense of sight. For when sight comprehends two individuals of the same species and form at the same time, it then comprehends the individuals, and it comprehends that they are similar. But the similarity of the two forms is not the two forms themselves, nor one of them, nor a third form proper to similarity, but is the agreement of those two forms in something. Therefore, the similarity of two forms will not be comprehended except from the comparison of one of them to the other. Thus, the comprehension of similarity does not happen through sight alone, but from a power of the soul which we call reason <note>Latin: *rationem*; logic or the intellect.</note>, through the act of reasoning <note>Latin: *ratiocinationis*.</note> comparing the different seen forms to one another. And also, when sight sees two white colors, one of which is whiter than the other, it comprehends both...
