However, the distinction between those two whitenesses is not the sense of whiteness itself: for the sense of whiteness arises from the "whitening" of the surface of the eye <note>Medieval optics held that the eye's surface physically took on the color of the object being viewed.</note>, which is caused by both whitenesses. The distinction between those whitenesses, however, occurs because of the difference in the way those two whitenesses act upon the sight itself. Therefore, that distinction is not from the sense alone, but from another power of the soul, which we call the **distinguishing faculty** <note>Latin: *virtus distinctiva*; the mental power that categorizes and separates sensory data.</note>. And it is the same regarding the comparison and distinction of other sensible forms: for none of them are received by sight alone, but by the cooperation of reason and the distinguishing faculty. Sight by itself does not have the power of distinguishing, but the distinguishing faculty of the soul distinguishes all those things by means of sight. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 61. *From the features of individual forms frequently observed, there remains in the soul a fixed and certified universal form, which serves as a principle for the sight to recognize all individuals of the same species. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 4, Section 67, Note 2.* <note>Witelo is citing the "Optics" of Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), his primary source.</note>

For because every individual visible thing has a shape and figure in which all individuals of that species agree—differing only in particular features <term>intentions<gloss>The technical term *intentiones* refers to the specific qualities or "messages" (like size, distance, or texture) that a form conveys to the mind.</gloss></term> grasped by the sense of sight—there will perhaps be in all those individuals a color of one type. This is seen almost universally in individuals of birds, such as the swan, the crow, the magpie, and the jackdaw, and similar ones, in which there is a uniformity of color common to the whole species, at least in most cases (for we have already seen a white crow and a white bear). Therefore, if the shape, figure, color, and all the features from which the form of any individual of a species is composed constitute the universal form of the whole species, and sight grasps that figure, shape, color, and the features of all those things which agree with that species, then the soul will judge that particular thing seen to be an individual of that species. However, it will not, because of this, know one individual as distinct from another individual of the same species until it also grasps the particular features by which individuals differ, and until those have come to rest in the soul and in the imaginative faculty itself. For then, when some previously seen individual occurs to the sight, through the feature of the individuals of that species whose form is present in the soul, the feature of that universal form which belongs to that species will be repeated by the sight, along with the diversity of the particular forms of those individuals. And when that universal form is compared in the soul through the feature of another individual of the same species, it will then be fixed and rest in the soul. Thus, from the diversity of particular forms coming to the sight along with universal forms, the soul will, upon scrutiny, grasp the diversity of individuals of the same species; and through the agreement of visible accidents in different individuals, it will grasp that the form in which all individuals of that species agree is the universal form of them all. Thus, the universal form remains in the soul and in its imaginative faculty; and that form is a principle for the sight to recognize all individuals of the same species, insofar as what is in them is individualized from universal features, and from whatever particular sensible features. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 62. *All true comprehension of visible forms is either through scrutiny alone, or through scrutiny with preceding knowledge. Alhazen Section 69, Note 2.*

Comprehension of visible things by scrutiny alone occurs when foreign visible things are grasped, such as when the sight grasps a seen thing which it has not perceived before, neither in itself nor in its species. Through diligent scrutiny <note>Latin: *intuitio*; a focused, investigative gaze rather than a mere glance.</note>, it acquires all its dispositions and its true form; yet it does not "recognize" its form, because it has not perceived it before or does not recall it. Thus, that form will be grasped by true comprehension through scrutiny alone. However, the other true comprehension of visible forms, distinct from the one made by scrutiny alone, sometimes occurs through scrutiny with preceding knowledge. This happens when the sight grasps the form of some seen thing which it has also grasped before, and the feature of whose form is in the soul either in its entirety or in some part. For then, the sight immediately grasps its form upon looking at that thing; and then, with a brief scrutiny, it grasps its entire form, which is the universal knowledge of its species. It recognizes the universal form which it grasps in that seen thing during the comprehension of the form in the soul by recollecting that specifically seen thing. Then, observing the remaining features which are in that seen thing, it will certify the particular form of it, which is appropriate to that individual sight. And if it is remembering that particular form as previously grasped by sight, then it will recognize that individual form. And because no seen thing is grasped by true comprehension except by one of these modes, the proposition is clear.

### 63. *Visual comprehension through recognition always occurs through some mode of comparative reasoning. Alhazen Section 11, Note 2.*

For recognition <note>Latin: *cognitio*; identifying something as "known."</note> is the comprehension of the similarity of two forms: namely, the form which the sight grasps during the act of recognition (when it feels that it knows the thing it sees) and the form resting in the soul, previously grasped. Hence, visual recognition does not occur except through remembrance; for if no such form were resting in the soul and present to the memory, the sight would not recognize the seen thing. Recognition, therefore, always occurs from the assimilation of a form resting in the soul to a form seen afterward outside, whether the resting form is the form of a species or of an individual to be recognized. The sight therefore grasps many...

...many things through previous cognition: for it knows a man to be a man, a horse to be a horse, and Socrates to be Socrates. It also recognizes animals familiar to it, as well as trees, plants, and stones which it has seen before. It recognizes things similar to them, all familiar <term>intentions</term> <note>Latin: *intentiones*. In medieval optics, "intentions" refer to the non-sensory properties of an object—such as "friendliness," "shape," or "identity"—that the mind perceives beyond just color and light.</note> in visible things, and the sizes of all customary objects which are not known by sight alone according to Proposition 59 of this book. Yet, the sight does not recognize everything it has seen before unless it is remembering a form seen previously. Therefore, visual recognition is not a comprehension by the sense alone, but occurs through reason comparing the form of the present visible object to a form seen previously that is resting within itself. For recognition can never occur except through the comparison of a form resting in the soul to a form seen outside. Thus it is clear that visual comprehension through recognition always occurs through some mode of comparing reason. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 64. *It is necessary that all visual comprehension through recognition occurs in time, but in less time than the time required for comprehension through scrutiny alone. Alhazen, Book 2, Note 71.*

For since, as was set forth in the preceding proposition, all visual recognition occurs through <term>intuition</term> <note>Latin: *intuitio*. In this context, it refers to "diligent scrutiny" or a focused, detailed look, rather than a sudden "hunch."</note> and a form resting in the soul that is remembered and applied to the form now perceived through diligent scrutiny; and since all scrutiny occurs in time according to Proposition 56 of this book, and all remembering of a form seen previously occurs mostly in time (since it happens through the soul's discourse through the forms it holds within its imagination—which, if they occurred immediately to the seeking soul, would not be "recollection" but "continuous memory"); because, therefore, both of these—namely scrutiny and remembering—or at least one of them, occurs in time, it is also clear that all visual comprehension through recognition necessarily occurs in time. 

However, it happens in less time than the time of comprehension through scrutiny alone. This is because the properties existing in the soul of the present memory do not need to have every single property within the forms of recognized things (from which they are truly composed) scrutinized to be known. Instead, it is sufficient for their comprehension to grasp some property unique to them. When, therefore, the distinguishing faculty has grasped some property unique to that form within the form coming to it, it will remember the first form and will know all the forms coming to it. This is because every property appropriate to a specific form acts as a sign for those forms. 

For example, when the sight, looking at Socrates, grasps the outline of a human hand, it immediately understands that it is a man, even before it grasps the outline of his face or other parts. From the comprehension of certain properties that are appropriate to the form of a man, it understands that the same visible object is a man without needing to comprehend the other parts (which it understands only through previous knowledge from forms residing in the soul). By grasping some property unique to that individual—such as the <note>original: "glaucitatem"</note> grayish-blue color of the eyes, the thickness of the mouth, the arch of the eyebrows, or similar features—it understands the properties of that individual as a whole. Similarly, it will recognize a horse by some spot on its forehead or elsewhere on its body. Likewise, a scribe, from the comprehension of certain letters, recognizes all parts of a word or a sentence which he sees frequently and continually. 

And since comprehension acquired only through scrutiny occurs through the consideration of all parts of the seen object and all properties within it, whereas comprehension through recognition occurs through the consideration of only certain properties within that form, it is evident that vision through recognition happens in less time than vision through scrutiny alone. Because of this, the sight comprehends familiar visible things quickly, in a short time that is almost hidden from the senses, and especially those things it has been accustomed to knowing from its earliest beginnings or with which it has remained for a long time. Thus, what was proposed is clear.

### 65. *Vision through previous recognition by means of a brief scrutiny does not produce a certain comprehension of the object’s form. Alhazen, Book 2, Note 75.*

For vision through previous recognition only concerns the totality and universality of the seen object superficially and in bulk, and through certain external signs of that seen object. The distinguishing faculty grasps the particular properties within that seen object according to the way it knew those objects from the first form of that seen object existing in the soul. However, all the particular properties of visible things in corruptible <note>i.e., physical or perishable things</note> objects change with the passage of time. The sight does not grasp the change in the properties of the seen object through the form previously held when the change is not manifest or comprehensible to the sight at first glance. 

Therefore, previous recognition does not produce a true knowledge of the thing. For instance, if a man with a clear face who was known previously later develops a spot or a scar on his face that is not obvious: when that man is seen again after a long time, the viewer will not recognize him according to his own form (which the viewer had previously preserved in memory), nor will the viewer then grasp that spot or scar on his face, except after diligent scrutiny is performed on that spot or scar. Only then will he comprehend the form according to its actual state. 

It is the same if a spot was always on the face of the known person but was not very manifest to the sight. In that case, although the viewer has a "spotless" form of him in his mind, he will not apply it to that spotted face and will not recognize him except after much scrutiny of other particular properties. The same applies to other individual visible things and their various properties. In all of them, vision through previous recognition by means of a brief scrutiny does not produce a certain comprehension of the object's form. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<meta>The catchword "66. Nullius" indicates the start of the next proposition on the following page.</meta>

Witelo notes that while this process is faster than raw observation, it is prone to error if the object has changed over time without the viewer noticing.</summary>

### 66. *The essence <term>quiddity</term> <note>Latin: *quidditas*, from "quid" (what). It refers to the "what-ness" or the fundamental nature that makes a thing what it is.</note> of no entity is visible through itself, but only accidentally, through the mediation of sensible properties <term>intentions</term> <note>Latin: *intentiones*. In medieval science, these are the non-physical qualities—like "friendliness" or "shape"—that the mind extracts from a visual image.</note> which are seen through themselves. Alhazen [Book 2], note 68.*

For since, as was assumed at the beginning of this book, vision is not completed until visible forms reach the soul—all of which belong to the category of accidents <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality like color or size that can change without changing the core nature of a thing. A person might change color due to a sunburn, but they remain the same person (the "substance").</note>, as is clear in their individual listing—it is evident (since the essence of no substance belongs to the category of accidents) that no essence is visible through itself. However, the essence of physical substances is perceived by sight accidentally; that is, through the comprehension of their visible properties, which are seen through themselves. Thus, the essence of a substance is recognized only through the internal cognition of the soul, which occurs by comparing a form perceived later to another form perceived earlier that is resting in the imagination. 

Therefore, the comprehension of the essence of a seen substance—such as a man, a dog, or any other substance—occurs only through recognizing the similarity of the seen object's form to one of the universal forms resting in the soul and fixed in the imagination, which the sight had perceived before. And because the distinguishing faculty <note>Latin: *virtus distinctiva*. This is the mental power that separates, compares, and identifies different sensory inputs.</note> in the soul, through which the soul judges the differences between things (such as a man not being a dog and vice versa), naturally compares these newly seen visible forms to the fixed visible forms in the imagination. Thus, when the sight perceives a thing, the distinguishing faculty immediately seeks its likeness among the forms existing in the imagination; once found, it recognizes the seen object through it and comprehends its essence. If it does not find a similar form among those resting in the soul, it will not recognize the object nor comprehend its essence. 

In this way, no essence of any substance is comprehended by sight except accidentally, as proposed. For if any such essence were perceived through itself by sight, then every essence of any visible substance would be perceivable by sight—just as is the case with light and color— and substances would appear to the senses and the visual operation as indivisible through their essences. This is not true; for it is necessary that a visible body be of a certain size relative to the surface of the eye to be actually seen, as shown in Proposition 19 of this book. The same is clear regarding the essences of all other entities: the essence of any composite is itself composite, and sight cannot perceive its composition through itself. If sight could know an essence as an essence, then sight would know every essence; yet many are invisible since they are only perceivable by the intellect <note>Latin: *per se intelligibiles*. This refers to abstract concepts or spiritual realities that the mind can "see" but the eyes cannot.</note>. Since this is impossible, the proposition is clear.

### 67. *The first thing the distinguishing faculty comprehends from the properties appropriate to a visible form is the essence of light and color. Alhazen [Book 2], note 17.*

For although light and color are visible through themselves and primarily, their essences and essential differences cannot be grasped by the sense of sight alone. The essence of light is not comprehended by sight alone without the cooperation of the soul’s cognitive faculty, since sight recognizes sunlight and distinguishes it from moonlight or firelight through prior knowledge and the form reserved in the soul. Similarly, the essence of color is only grasped by the distinguishing faculty through cognition when the color of the seen thing is among familiar colors. 

That distinguishing cognition occurs by comparing the form of the color now seen to similar color forms perceived earlier. Sight cannot comprehend a red color and the fact that it *is* red unless it recognizes it because its form remained in the soul of the observer from being seen previously. If the sight had never seen red before, it could not recognize it now, but would compare it to known colors close to it, as happens daily with the creation of new color mixtures. Therefore, when the distinguishing faculty comprehends the diversity of light upon seen objects and the diversity of color, it also comprehends the difference between the essence of light and the essence of colors, even though the form perceived by sight is a mixture of the light and color present in the object. 

And since light and color are the primary visible things, by whose participation and help all other things are seen, it is necessary that the first thing the distinguishing faculty comprehends from the properties of a visible form is the essence of light and color. Just as visual comprehension is primarily owed to them, so too the operation of the distinguishing faculty is primarily owed to their essences, as they are the things whose presence first shines in the visual organs (which all approach transparency <note>Latin: *diaphanitatem*. Vitello follows the tradition that the internal parts of the eye must be transparent to receive light and color.</note> to a greater or lesser degree). Thus the proposition is clear.

### 68. *The comprehension of color as color is prior to the comprehension of the essence of that color. From this it is clear that the comprehension of all visible things as they are visible in their genus is prior to the comprehension of their specific essences. Alhazen [Book 2], note 19.*

For sight perceives color and feels *that* it is color before it feels *what kind* of color it is, as is clear with strong colors placed in a poorly lit area. There, the sight perceives colors only indistinctly; they are distinguished later by the arrival of more light or by long gazing. The first thing the sight comprehends from the form of color is the change in the sensing organ and its coloration; for when the form reaches the eye, the eye is colored, and feeling itself colored, it immediately perceives color. Then, from the distinction and comparison of it to colors known to the sight, it comprehends the essence of the color. Therefore, the comprehension of color as color comes before the comprehension of the essence of that color, which occurs not by the sense of sight alone, but through cognition,

recognition, when the same color was previously grasped by sight and its form is preserved in the soul’s memory. And if the sight should grasp a foreign color which it has never seen before, it will then understand *that* it is a color, and yet it will not know *what kind* of color it is; but by comparing it to other colors, it will liken it to the most similar color. It may happen that several people seeing that same color at the same time in the same light will liken it to different colors, as occurs with a color produced from the dissolution of a compound body made of copper and silver. One person might liken it to the greenness associated with copper, while another might liken it to the azure <note>original: *lazulio*; referring to the blue color of lapis lazuli</note> color which comes from silver. It is clear, therefore, through these experiments, that the perception of a color as a general category ("it is a color") comes before the perception of the specific nature <term>quiddity</term> <note>From the Latin *quidditas*, meaning the "what-ness" or the specific defining essence of a thing.</note> of that color.

And since color is the first visible thing after light, it is clear that the perception of all visible things as general "visible objects" comes before the perception of their specific natures. For the sense of sight first perceives "location" as a general category before it perceives any specific type of location; and it perceives "shape" in a general sense before it perceives any specific shape. Even if the specific shape is not clearly resolved by the sight, the general category remains—either the most general category or a secondary one. This is what was proposed.

### 69. The comprehension of different visual properties <term>intentions</term> <note>Latin: *intentiones*. These are the non-physical qualities (like shape, size, or distance) that the mind extracts from a visual image.</note> through reason and discernment happens simultaneously in an instant; however, the comprehension of similar properties happens over time. Alhazen [Book 2], chapters 13, 15, and 71, note 2.

For shape, size, transparency, and many similar things—when they are grasped at first glance (which always happens in an instant of time according to theorem 55 of this book)—are grasped immediately as they present themselves to the sight through reason and discernment. This happens in that same instant because of the speed of reasoning, and all the properties within them are understood. For the power of discernment <note>Latin: *virtus distinctiva*; the mental faculty that distinguishes between different sensory inputs.</note> does not argue through the formal composition and arrangement of propositions like a logical syllogism.

Just as in the intellect—which possesses the disposition of first principles—the actual understanding of universal and self-evident propositions does not require any length of time, nor does the understanding of a universal proposition when its physical particulars are sensed at the same time. Because the human soul is naturally suited to reasoning without difficulty or labor, it draws the conclusion immediately following the premise. Therefore, a person does not even perceive that the comprehension occurring through reason and discernment is actually an act of logic. It is like a small child distinguishing between two beautiful things and choosing the more beautiful one; the child does not perceive that this is done through a process of argument and consideration of the choices. In this same way—as far as is possible—the comprehension of all visual properties through reason and discernment happens in an instant.

For the discernment and argumentation of the power of discernment happen as soon as the forms arrive within the medium of the **common nerve** <note>Latin: *nerui communis*. In medieval anatomy, this referred to the optic chiasm, where the nerves from both eyes meet, allowing for single, unified vision.</note>. Since the entire extended body—from the surface of the eye receiving the forms to the middle of the common nerve—is sentient and transparent, the passage of the "intent" of the forms happens through it in an instant. This is because immediately beyond the substance of the eye is the transparent **visual spirit** <note>Latin: *spiritus uisibilis*. In the 13th century, it was believed that a refined, vapor-like substance carried sensory information through the nerves.</note>, through which the sensitive power is carried to all the transparent humors and membranes of both eyes. All those transparent parts are illuminated by light and colored by a single color or various colors according to the variety of colors in the object being sensed. The body within the hollow of the common nerve is the final point reached by light and color.

Therefore, when a form is extended from the front surface of the sensing organ to the middle of the common nerve, every part of the sensing body feels the form. When it reaches the hollow of the common nerve, it is then grasped by the "ultimate sentient" <note>The final processing part of the brain/soul.</note>, and then the discernment of forms occurs. Yet there is no difference in time between the act of discernment and the act of the first glance. For just as light multiplies itself across the diameter of the world in a single instant because of the transparency of the medium, so too do the sensible forms (as shown in theorem 55) reach through any transparent medium to the middle of the common nerve in an instant. There, through the power of the soul, they are felt, understood, and distinguished. And since the power of the soul is indivisible, all of this happens together in a single instant.

However, when the properties of visible things are very similar—such as the greenness <note>original: *viritas*</note> of rue compared to the greenness of mint—then their discernment does not happen in that same instant in which both greens are grasped by sight. It happens only after a comparison of one to the other is made. Therefore, it happens in another instant, and thus a middle time must necessarily be assumed between the instant of the first simple glance and the instant of discernment by comparison. This is what was proposed.

### 70. It is necessary for the comprehension of the essence <term>quiddity</term> of color to happen over time. From this it is clear that the comprehension of the essence of all similar visible things happens only over time. Alhazen [Book 2], note 20.

For the comprehension of the essence of a color occurs after the comprehension of the color as a general category, as is clear from theorem 68 of this book. And since color as a category cannot be grasped by a simple glance except in an instant (by theorem 55), the comprehension of the essence of any specific color is composed of the perception of color as a category *plus* a subsequent comparative discernment by which the essence of one color is distinguished from the essence of another. Because all mixed colors have an essential agreement in the actual existence of light, and many of them have a very high degree of similarity in how they are mixed, it is clear that the discernment of the specific nature of these colors is completed in a different instant of time than when they were first seen. Between any two distinct instants, there is a span of time. Therefore, because the comprehension of the essence of color happens through the discernment of one color from another, it is clear by the previous theorem that—

...since that distinction is completed in time: therefore, the comprehension of the <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: *quidditatis*; the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</note> necessarily occurs in time. Sight also does not comprehend the essence of a color except through intuition <note>careful, focused observation</note>: for if the color were not on some surface so that the visual axes could be fixed upon it for a perceptible amount of time, the sight would not comprehend the essence of the colors. This is why, in objects moved rapidly, the essence of the color is not distinguished; instead, if there are many colors in a rapidly moving object, they will all appear indistinctly as one mixed color, as is evident in a ball of various colors moved quickly by a strong throw. It is clear, therefore, that the comprehension of the essence of the color itself must happen in time; and from this it is clear that the comprehension of the quantity of all visible forms does not happen except in time. For if sight does not comprehend the essence of color—which is perceived by the sense of sight alone—except in time, it is obvious that it requires even more time for the <term>intentions</term> <note>original: *intentiones*; the specific characteristics or mental images of an object</note> of other visible things, which are perceived mostly through distinction and cognition. Thus, the comprehension of the essences of all visible characteristics happens in time, even though that time may sometimes be very small. And this is what was proposed.

### *71. In individual forms, sight comprehends specific characteristics in less time than individual ones. Alhazen, Book 2, number 72.*

For when the sight perceives a specific individual human, it perceives him to be a human before it perceives his particular form. And perhaps through the characteristics of the human form, or through some features proper to the human form, it perceives him to be a human even if it does not yet perceive the lines of his face—for example, from the uprightness of the body and the arrangement of the body's limbs. However, the individuality of the seen thing will not be perceived except from the comprehension of the particular characteristics proper to that individual, either all or some of them. These cannot be perceived except after the comprehension of the universal characteristics, which belong to the genus or species of that individual, either all or some of them. But the comprehension of a partial form happens in less time than the form of the whole. And since individuality adds something beyond the species <note>being a specific person adds more detail than just being "a human"</note>, it is clear that individuality is like a certain totality in respect to the species. Therefore, the comprehension of the species of a seen thing happens in less time than the comprehension of its individuality. And this is what was proposed.

### *72. The specific and individual characteristics of certain familiar visible things are comprehended in less time than other specific and individual characteristics. Alhazen, Book 2, number 73.*

For some of the species of familiar visible things are not similar to other species, such as the human species, which, because of the uprightness of the body, is not similar to any other animals. Others are similar to different species, such as the species of the horse, which is similar to many animals in its overall form. Therefore, the time in which sight perceives the species of an individual human and perceives him to be a human is less than the time in which it perceives a horse to be a horse, especially when it perceives both of them at a great distance. For sight, perceiving a human individual moving locally, will immediately perceive him to be an animal; from the movement and the uprightness of the body, it will perceive him to be a human. But although it can also perceive through movement that the individual horse is an animal, and through the count of four feet perceive it to be a beast, it will not necessarily perceive it to be a horse for that reason; because the "horse-like" characteristics that are perceptible by sight from a remote distance are present in many quadrupeds that resemble the horse in many essential and accidental characteristics, such as the mule and others. Therefore, if sight does not perceive some characteristic proper to the horse, it will not perceive it to be a horse. Since, therefore, the time in which sight perceives the uprightness of a human body is not the same as the time in which it perceives the form of a horse with the particular characteristics by which a horse is distinguished from other beasts—such as the features of its face, the extension of its neck, the speed of its movement, and the width of its strides—the comprehension of the human species is in less time than the comprehension of the horse species. For although both those times are small, one of them, according to all its conditions, is greater than the other. Similarly, because no other flower resembles the garden rose in its specific form or even in its characteristic redness, sight perceives its species through its "rosy" redness in less time than it perceives the species of rue <note>a perennial herb</note> through its greenness, which many herbs resemble. Generally, the essences of all species that can be confused with others are not so quickly perceived by sight as the essences of all species that resemble few or none. The same is also true of individuals: for an individual that resembles no other is perceived through a brief intuition and through signs; however, that individual which resembles another individual must be perceived through much intuition. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

### *73. The sensitive power perceives the size of the angle which the surface of the visible thing subtends at the center of the eye solely from the comprehension of the part of the surface of the eye in which the form of the visible thing is shaped. Alhazen, Book 2, number 44.*

For although the order of pure mathematics is such that the size of the parts of spherical surfaces subtended by those angles is known through the size of the angles—because just as the center is the principle of the constitution of the whole sphere, so the parts of solid angles which are around the center of the sphere, as...

# THE OPTICS OF VITELLO,
## SON OF THURINGIANS AND POLES,
### BOOK FOUR.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' depicting a scholar seated at a desk, surrounded by scholarly or scientific tools.</image-desc>

WE HAVE TREATED in the preceding third book the properties of the visual organ and the essential ways of seeing. Now, it remains for us to pursue in this fourth book the properties of all visible things. As we stated at the beginning of the third book, these properties are twenty-two in number. Only two of them—namely light and color—are visible <term>per se</term> <note>visible in and of themselves</note>. The others, however, are seen <term>per accidens</term> <note>incidentally; perceived through their relationship to light and color</note>, either because they are perceived by several other senses, or because they are only seen by means of light and color, as is evident in each case. 

And since we have already sufficiently discussed the vision of light and color in the third book, twenty other visible properties now remain to be treated. We shall run through all of these—as well as the impressions and deceptions that happen to visible things and to the intrinsic powers of the soul regarding them—in their proper order using the method of demonstration, as far as nature and our own ability allow. We will first set forth for each of them the manner of its vision, both in itself and in its parts. We will then carefully add the deceptions which occur either to the visual power alone or to the internal powers of the soul (such as those that happen to the powers of distinction and reasoning). The definitions we set forth first are these:

### D E F I N I T I O N S.

1. A form is said to fall **directly** upon the sight when a straight line drawn from it is perpendicular to the surface of the eye and falls upon the very center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> <note>the pupil/iris area</note>.
2. It is said to fall **obliquely** when a straight line drawn in the aforementioned way is not perpendicular.
3. A line is said to be **directly opposite** the sight when the radial axis falls perpendicularly upon it at some point.
4. A line is said to be **oblique** to the sight when the radial axis cannot fall perpendicularly upon any of its points.
5. A surface is said to be **directly opposite** when the radial axis is erected perpendicularly upon it.
6. A surface is said to be **oblique** to the sight when the radial axis falls upon the points of that surface at an angle.
7. The **completion of direction** in the opposition of sight occurs when the perpendicular axis falls upon the middle of the surface or line opposite the eye. The closer the point where the axis falls perpendicularly is to the middle of the surface or line, the greater the "direction" or alignment of that surface or line in opposition.
8. **True comprehension** by sight is that in which there is no sensible difference at all between the perception and the truth of the seen thing, regarding the whole of the thing seen.
9. The **remoteness** of one thing from another is the lack of contact between them.
10. A **cone** is called a pyra- <note>The text cuts off here mid-word; "pyramis rotundus" or "round pyramid."</note>

# POSTULATES.

We grant the following: 1. That things seen under higher rays appear higher, while those under lower rays appear lower; and similarly, things seen under rays further to the right appear further to the right, while those under rays further to the left appear further to the left. 2. Also, that things seen under more angles are perceived more clearly. 3. Also, that all acts of sight of equal disposition are equally fast. 4. Also, that every whole appears larger than its part.

# THEOREMS.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 1, No. 3.</margin>
1. ***Visual deception occurs from an immoderate proportion of the circumstances of visible forms relative to the sight, not only according to the sight itself, but according to the soul's power of distinction.***

From what was declared in the third book, it is clear that eight things are necessary for the perfect operation of sight, which are: Light (by Book 3, Theorem 1); Distance of the visible object from the sight (by Book 3, Theorem 15); Facing position of the sight itself (by Book 3, Theorem 2), or the position relative to the common axis (by Book 3, Theorem 44); Magnitude of the body (by Book 3, Theorem 19); Solidity <note>meaning the opacity or physical density of the object</note> of the body to be seen (by Book 3, Theorem 14); Transparency of the air (by Book 3, Theorem 13); Fitting time for the intuition to be made (by Book 3, Theorem 56); and the Health of the sight (by Book 3, Theorem 16). 

Each of these has a "latitude" <note>a range or span of effectiveness</note> proportioned to the thing seen. For light has a latitude, since excessive light hinders the sight, and weak light does not bring visible things into the act of affecting the sight; hence, tiny bodies or minute <term>visible intentions</term> <note>original: *intentiones uisibiles*; the specific properties of an object like color or shape as perceived by the mind</note> are not seen in weak light. But there is also a latitude in that light which is proportioned to the size of the body. 

The distance of the visible object from the sight (its remoteness) also has a latitude: for a body is fully comprehended from one distance, but not fully from another. Between those distances is a great latitude in which the full comprehension of that body occurs; and the larger the body, the greater the latitude of distance across which it can be seen. Similarly, when there is a great deviation of a body from the direct line of sight, the small particles or marks on it are not comprehended, though they would be seen if the body were only slightly declined; there is also a latitude between those declinations. 

Similarly, a small body placed far from the common axis will appear very elongated and hidden, while the same body placed near the common axis will be seen clearly. It is obvious, then, that the position relative to the common axis has a latitude, since it has a relationship proportioned to the size of the body and its tiny details. 

The size of the body also has a latitude: if the parts of the seen object are not proportional to the total size seen, they will be hidden from the sight; and even if they are proportional to the total size, if the total body is tiny, they still will not be seen. Thus, in small paintings, we do not immediately perceive certain small parts with our sight, even though they are proportional to their whole. Therefore, the latitude of the magnitude of the thing seen must be proportioned to the total body of which that seen size is a part. 

Solidity also has a latitude proportioned to the thing seen. For if the color in some body is very sharp <note>original: *acutus*; meaning vivid or intense</note>, even if the body has little solidity, it can still be seen. This would not happen if the body had greater solidity, for perhaps the color, because of the intense reflection of light (which occurs because of the body's great solidity), would hinder the sight. And if the color is dark, then perhaps a less solid object will appear weaker because of its dark color. 

The transparency of the air also has a latitude: for through flames and smoke, the sight of tiny things does not occur, though perhaps large things can be seen, just as if one saw a sheet of paper through them, but not the writing on it. 

The time fitting for making an intuition also has a latitude: for a body passing suddenly across the sight is not comprehended by the sight, and sometimes the motion of a <term>spinning top</term> <note>original: *trochi*</note> is not seen because it is very fast in a very small amount of time. 

The health of the sight also has a latitude: for in certain illnesses, the tiny details of a body are perceived in a smaller space unless they are hidden, and weaker sights do not see those things which are apparent to stronger sights. Generally, therefore, any of these modes in which the form of the thing seen is not verified as it is in reality is a departure from the "temperance" <note>the balanced or moderate state</note> proportioned to seeing that thing. All these things regard one another according to mutually fitting proportions, and each must have a fitting disposition relative to the other eight—the detailed treatment of which we leave to the consideration of the soul as it looks more closely at these matters.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 2, No. 63.</margin>
2. ***It is impossible for the sight to comprehend one of the visible intentions by itself alone.***

For the sight by itself comprehends the forms of visible things, which are bodily. All bodily forms, however, are composed of many particular visible intentions mentioned before: just as size does not exist without shape, and shape does not exist without position; and all these do not exist without color, and color does not exist without light, and light is not diffused except in a body. Therefore, the sight does not comprehend any of these particular intentions except through the comprehension of visible forms composed of several particular intentions, each of which the sight comprehends simultaneously. And since none of these intentions by itself alone completes any...

<note>original: "intentionum"</note> regarding the forms of physical and sensible objects: it is clear that it is impossible for the sight to perceive any of those characteristics on its own; rather, many of these characteristics are always gathered together in a sensible form. Therefore, the sight always perceives many particular characteristics simultaneously, which are only distinguished with the help of the "power of distinction" <note>the faculty of the soul that judges sensory data</note> through the imagination. And so, finally, the sight perceives any distinct characteristic of those particular things. This is what was proposed.

### 3. Sensible things are not seen under just any angle.

That everything seen is seen under an angle is clear from the corollary of the 18th theorem of Book 2. Also, since by the 19th theorem of Book 3, a visible body must be of a certain size relative to the sight in order to actually be seen, it is clear that it is impossible for any thing to be seen under an "angle of contingency" <note>the infinitesimal angle between a curve and its tangent line</note>, which is indivisible according to Proposition 16 of Euclid's Book 3. For every angle under which vision can occur is divisible by the axis of the radial pyramid <note>the cone of light rays</note> falling perpendicularly upon the surface of the eye itself. This is because all vision occurs through a visual pyramid, the base of which is the surface of the object seen, according to the 18th theorem of Book 3; or at the very least, that angle is contained beneath that axis and another line of the radial length of the pyramid, as declared in the 54th theorem of Book 3. Therefore, the angle is rectilinear <note>made of straight lines</note> and is thus divisible according to Proposition 9 of Euclid's Book 1. And since the largest of the angles under which vision occurs is nearly a right angle, the diameter of the opening of the **uvea** <note>the iris or the pupil through which light passes</note>, which spans that angle at the center of the eye, is nearly equal to the side of a cube that could be inscribed in the sphere of the uvea, or to the side of a square inscribed in the great circle of that sphere, as we showed in the 4th theorem of Book 3. A right angle always spans such a side, according to Proposition 33 of Book 6, because its chord is a quarter of the circle. If, therefore, vision occurred as if the radial lines converged exactly at the center of the uvea, then the maximum angle according to which vision occurs would be nearly a solid right angle, such that the maximum visual pyramid would be right-angled, and the radius of the base of that pyramid would be equal to its axis. However, vision occurs as if the lines converge in the center of the eye, as is clear from the 73rd theorem of Book 3; and the center of the eye is deeper within than the center of the uvea, according to the 8th theorem of Book 3. Therefore, the greatest angle according to which vision occurs is smaller than a right angle, but not by much, because there is no great distance between those centers (namely, of the sphere of the uvea and of the eye). Thus, the axis of the largest visual pyramid is greater than the radius of its base, but not by much. This is also clear by experiment: for if someone stands upright in a flat field and opens their eye as wide as possible, they will see nearly a quarter of a great circle of the celestial sphere passing through the **Zenith** <note>the point directly overhead</note>. Through the division of this angle, vision of its parts occurs, and of all things spanning those angles, until one reaches a minimum angle; if that minimum were divided further, vision would not occur through it. For although every mathematical rectilinear angle is infinitely divisible, in **natural angles** <note>physical angles in the real world</note>—according to whose arrangement the sensory operation occurs—there must be a limit to division. When a thing is smaller than that limit, it will not be sensible; therefore, there will be no sensory vision according to that angle. Since all vision is sensible—being an active process—no vision will occur according to an angle smaller than that. Therefore, sensible things are not seen under just any angle. This must be understood according to radial lines falling perpendicularly to the surfaces of the eyes, not obliquely; for through oblique lines, vision becomes uncertain and the forms of visible things in the sight become confused, as we showed in the 17th theorem of Book 3. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 4. The form of a line placed perpendicularly to the surface of the eye is not seen, because through it only a "punctual distinction" <note>a single point</note> occurs; however, a line facing the eye according to its length is seen according to its own proper form.

<image-desc>Two geometrical diagrams illustrating principles of vision. The first shows a circle labeled 'd' (representing the eye) with a line segment 'a-b' positioned horizontally to its right. The second shows a point 'd' from which two lines radiate to points 'a' and 'c' on a vertical line, forming a triangle. A third line radiates from 'd' to a point 'b' between 'a' and 'c', illustrating visual angles subtended by parts of an object.</image-desc>

Suppose that a line **a b**—which is a sensible line, such as a long body with an imperceptible width, like a hair—falls perpendicularly toward the eye, the center of which is **d**. Although it may be a rounded or faceted column, its base cannot be perceived by the eye. I say that such a body, disposed in such a way, is not seen: for the angle at the center of the eye spanned by the diameter of its base is entirely imperceptible, and according to the previous theorem, vision cannot occur through it. Nevertheless, among other forms being seen, an imperceptible "punctual distinction" <note>a tiny dot or break</note> will occur due to the falling of the form of this kind of body. Because the form of that perpendicularly falling point will mingle with the forms of the surrounding points of other objects, and since it is not of their kind, it will necessarily create some distinction. Thus, the forms of those bodies are actually distinguished, though not very sensibly, and they do not belong to the nature of a single continuous line. However, a line facing the eye according to its length—whether its position is direct or oblique—will always be seen according to its own proper form. This is because its entire length comes to the eye under one angle, and its parts under sensible angles. For instance, if line **a b** is placed facing the eye **d** according to its length and at a suitable distance, then the whole line will be seen under angle **a d c**, and its part **a b** under angle **a d b**, and its part **b c** under angle **b d c**. Whether it is straight, curved, or irregular, some length will always be described across a width on the surface of the eye, according to what is in the eye itself.

*5. Surfaces placed opposite the sight in such a way that, if imagined to be extended, they would cut the eye through its center, appear as only a single line; but those placed opposite the sight according to their width are seen in their proper form.*

For when any surface is placed opposite the sight in the manner proposed, the forms of all its points fall perpendicularly upon the surface of the eye and converge at the center. And since the form of any of those points creates some distinction in the sight (according to the preceding theorem), and all those points falling along the length are joined together on a single line, it is clear that only one line of a surface arranged in this way is seen. However, when that surface is placed with its width opposite the sight, the form of any of its lines is seen according to its own linear form (by the preceding theorem). Therefore, the entire surface is seen according to its proper form, because some length and width will always be seen, whether that surface is flat, concave, or convex; for there is no difference among them regarding this specific property. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

*6. Of bodies placed opposite the sight, only the surfaces are perceived by the sight alone.*

Because bodies are seen by the sight alone according to how their forms present themselves to the eye and are "painted" upon its surface (as is clear from Theorem 17 of Book 3 of this work), the forms of the depth of visible bodies are not presented. Instead, only those parts are seen upon which lines drawn from the center of the sight fall according to length and width (as is clear from Theorem 2 of Book 3 of this work). This is a characteristic of surfaces. Therefore, of bodies placed opposite the sight, only the surfaces are perceived by the sight alone. If a body has only one surface—whether that body is a hollow or convex sphere—only one surface will be seen. If there are several surfaces on one body—as in bodies with all flat surfaces, or round columns, pyramids, and any parts of spheres—nothing will ever be seen except several surfaces, as if it were not a body at all but merely certain surfaces extended in that way, without any inclusion of the body's interior. Therefore, what was proposed is clear. Furthermore, because the property affecting lines in the sight descends into the vision of surfaces, and the property affecting surfaces descends into the vision of bodies, only bodies are seen in and of themselves. This is because only bodies are natural, sensible beings in themselves, while surfaces and lines within them are things we imagine. We must be excused, therefore, if we propose the visual properties of bodies by way of the visual properties of surfaces or lines; for what happens to lines in the sight, we judge to happen only to the length or width of bodies, and what happens to surfaces necessarily happens to the length and width of bodies together. Hence, according to this correspondence, we shall later make use of surfaces or lines.

*7. Of all equal visible things, that which is seen from closer is seen under a larger angle; but that which is further away is seen under a smaller angle. Euclid, Theorem 5 of the Optics.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating visual perspective. A vertex on the left, labeled 'a' (representing the eye), projects an angle defined by two outer rays extending to the right. Between these rays is a vertical segment labeled 'b' at the top and 'c' at the bottom. Further to the right, a second vertical segment of equal height is labeled 'd' at the top and 'e' at the bottom. Inner rays from 'a' pass through the endpoints of the further segment 'd e', showing that it subtends a smaller visual angle than the closer segment 'b c'.</image-desc>

Let there be two equal magnitudes, *b c* and *d e*, and let the center of the sight be *a*. Let *b c* be closer to the sight *a* than *d e* is. I say that *b c* is seen under a larger angle than *d e*. For let the lines *a b* and *a c* be drawn. Since these lines meet at point *a*, it is obvious that they are not parallel by the definition of parallel lines; nor will they meet at any point other than *a*, because then two straight lines would enclose a surface, which is impossible. Therefore, they will never meet anywhere else but at point *a*. If extended beyond points *b* and *c*, they will always move further apart; therefore, they will never touch line *d e*, nor will the vision of any points on line *d e* occur along those lines (by Theorem 2 of Book 3 of this work). If, therefore, the endpoints of line *d e* are to be seen, it must be along lines falling inside the lines *b a* and *c a*, which would be lines *a d* and *a e*. Whether the magnitudes *b c* and *d e* are parallel or not, if a line is drawn from point *d* parallel and equal to *b c* (by Proposition 31 of Book 1), it is clear (by Theorem 34 of Book 1 of this work) that angle *b a c* will be larger than angle *d a e*. Therefore, lines *a d* and *a e* divide the angle *b a c*. Because the partial angle *d a e* is smaller than the total angle *b a c*, what was proposed is clear. The same must be demonstrated if the equal lines *b c* and *c d* share the same endpoint *c*, or if they are tilted toward one another; for then the same result follows as before. However, everything proposed here is more perfectly clear through Theorem 108 of Book 1 of this work: for the axis of the <term>radial pyramid<note>A conceptual cone of light rays with its vertex at the eye and its base on the object being viewed.</note></term> of the more distant object is longer than the axis of the radial pyramid of the closer object; hence the solid angles at the vertices of those pyramids differ. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

## 9. *The distance of a seen object from the sight itself is not perceivable by the sense of sight alone, but by the help of the cognitive and distinguishing power of the soul.*

For the concept of distance between two bodies is the lack of contact because of some space existing between those two bodies. Distance, therefore, is not perceived by itself through sight, but with the help of the <term>distinguishing power<note>The "virtus distinctiva" is the mental faculty that identifies and categorizes sensory data after it has been received by the eyes.</note></term> and cognitive power, which recognizes both ends of the bodies and distinguishes between them. Yet, such perception does not happen over a span of time, but in an instant; for the "sensible intentions" <note>An "intention" in medieval optics is a non-material quality or "species" of an object that the mind perceives.</note> through which distance is understood reside in the soul. And because those intentions have resided in the soul for long periods, due to the great frequency and repetition of those forms occurring many times in the sight, the distinguishing power does not require new temporal comparisons to perceive those intentions. Instead, it perceives the distance immediately, simultaneously with the perception of the object, because of prior knowledge. For because an object placed opposite the sight is seen when the eyes are open, and immediately not seen when the eyes are closed or the object is moved from its position, reason concludes that whatever happens to be in the sight at a certain location, and does not remain after its removal, is not fixed inside the eye. And since its form, through which it is seen, is not inside the sight, it is therefore from the outside—specifically from a body existing outside the sight and not touching the sight. Thus, there is a distance between the sight and that seen object. This reasoning occurs not over time, but instantly, together with the simple act of looking; for from the frequency of seeing, this reasoning settles in the soul as a universal proposition, which the soul does not even notice is resting within itself: namely, that all visible things are outside the eye, and that there is a distance between any seen object and the sight itself. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

<margin>Alhazen 2 4 n 2.</margin>

## 10. *The quantity of distance is perceived by the sight with the help of the distinguishing power, when the distance relates to ordered and continuous bodies.*

The quantity of distance differs from the "concept of distance" in its nature as distance: for the concept of distance creates the lack of contact between any two bodies because of the space between them, but the quantity of distance is the measure of the space existing between those two distant bodies. Therefore, no quantity of distance of any visible thing is perceived by the sense of sight alone, even with the help of the distinguishing power, except for the quantity of distance of those visible things whose distance relates to <term>ordered and continuous bodies<note>Vitello refers to landmarks or intermediate objects like a row of trees or a road that provide a scale for the eye to measure distance.</note></term>, and when the distance is moderate. For then, when the sight perceives ordered and continuous bodies related to the distances of certain objects, and verifies the measurements of those bodies, it consequently also verifies the measure of the distance through the measures of those bodies and the quantities of the spaces between their extremities. For the space between the two extremities of the sight and the body relates to the distance between the sight and that seen object. Thus, when the sight perceives the measure of that space, it also perceives the measure of the object's distance. This happens with certainty through ordered and continuous bodies existing in that space that are truly perceived, and when the distance is moderate. By "ordered and continuous bodies," we mean those arranged in a somewhat straight line at roughly equal distances from one another, such as trees, mountains, or high towers, and similar things. For through the counting of these, when their distance from one another is known in some way, the quantity of distance of that which is removed from the sight along that line becomes known. "Moderate distance" is that in which the quantity of the sensible object is not entirely hidden in relation to the quantity of the total distance. Therefore, the distance from the sight is perceived with true understanding only for those bodies whose distance relates to ordered and continuous bodies, where the quantity and measure of the bodies and the intervening spaces can be perceived by the sight with true understanding, and when the distance is moderate. Hence, if either the perception of continuous and ordered bodies is missing, or the moderateness of the distance is missing, the distance of those bodies will never be perceived with true understanding, but only according to <term>estimation<note>Original: "aestimatio." A judgment based on appearance rather than certain measurement.</note></term>. For instance, a person seeing clouds in a place that is not mountainous will estimate the clouds to be very close to the sky; but if the clouds are seen above the peaks of mountains, or below them, then the sight will know that the clouds are close to the earth. Therefore, when the sight perceives visible things whose quantities of distance are not verified by the sight, the distinguishing power knows the measures of their distance according to estimation, not according to certainty, and it compares their distance to the distance of similar visible things previously perceived by the sight. Thus, when the sight perceives any distant seen object, the distinguishing power immediately perceives its distance and the measure of its distance as best it can, either through certainty or through esti-

...estimation, and immediately the distance of that thing will have an imagined measure in the soul. Indeed, ordered and continuous bodies that relate to the distances of visible things are mostly parts of the earth and familiar visible objects, which are always or more frequently grasped by sight—such as those on the earth's surface, where the body of the earth lies between those objects, just as it also lies between them and the body of the person looking. The body of the earth lying between those objects is measured by the sight through a number of **feet**, since the **foot** is the smallest measure familiar to humans for measuring nearby parts of the earth. Through these nearby parts of the earth, remote parts of the earth are measured by the <term>distinguishing power<note>Original: "uirtus distinctiua." This refers to the faculty of the mind that processes sensory data into logical concepts like size and distance.</note></term> of the soul, because of the frequent grasping of similar parts to that portion of the earth. The measure of these parts rests in the soul, so much so that the soul does not even perceive that the measure of those parts is stored within itself. This measurement reaches the soul because the quantity of the spaces beneath a person’s feet is grasped by the sight; for they are measured, even without conscious intention, by the feet of humans when they frequently walk over those spaces, just as they are also measured by the extension of arms <note>Original: "extentiones brachiorum," likely referring to the cubit or fathom as a standard unit of measure.</note>. The distinguishing power grasps this true measurement and confirms from it the quantities of the parts of the earth continuous with the body of the person seeing. This, resting in the soul, is the principle for measuring all distances according to estimation.

For when the sight always grasps the quantity of the parts of the earth near to it, there remains in the soul also the quantity of the <term>radial lines<note>Original: "lineae radiales." In medieval optics, these were the straight lines of light or "species" connecting the eye to the object.</note></term> stretched from the extremities of those parts of the earth to the eye, and the quantity of that part of the surface of the sensing organ <note>The retina or the crystalline lens, depending on the period's anatomical theory.</note> reached by the form of those parts of the earth, and consequently the quantities of the angles formed at the center of the sight, which those parts of the surface of the eye reflect according to Theorem 73 of Book 3 of this work. Hence, if a standing man looks at the earth before his feet, the length of the radial lines will be the quantity of the line of his height, and if the upper eyelid is lowered over the eye, that angle according to which vision occurs will be almost indivisible (like an **angle of contingency** <note>The infinitesimal angle between a curve and its tangent line.</note>). When he looks further out, the radial lines will be increased (according to Proposition 47 of Book 1 <note>Likely referring to the Pythagorean Theorem in Euclid’s Elements.</note>), and as the upper eyelid is raised, the angle will increase, so that when the quantity of the seen space approaches the quantity of the semi-diameter of the world, the quantity of the angle also reaches nearly a right angle, because that angle will be subtended by a **fourth part of a great circle** <note>90 degrees of the celestial sphere.</note> of the visible celestial sphere itself.

Therefore, when these concepts of lines and angles rest in the soul, they become the principles for grasping the quantities of any distances whatsoever; for equal radial lines and angles are estimated to correspond to equal parts, and the viewer uses them without a conscious intention of comparison. In this, the quantity of the angles and their increase over a longer distance compared to a shorter one helps; and it is similar in the proportion of the length of the radial lines, which the sight perceives by itself with the help of the distinguishing power, recognizing that every whole is greater than its part. In this way, therefore, the sight, with the help of the distinguishing power, grasps the quantity of the distance of things seen according to the lines of their distances from each other and from the sight, just as the sight sometimes grasps through the distinguishing power the quantities of the heights of some bodies elevated above the surface of the earth, such as towers, walls, and mountains, especially when the distance or the height is moderate.

However, when the distance or height is very great, then the small parts at the end of the space are not grasped by the sight, nor are they discerned by the distinguishing power, because a small quantity at a very great distance is hidden from the sight; for it does not make a sensible angle at the center of the sight, which is why the quantity of those things is not certified according to Theorem 3 of this book. Therefore, nothing of the quantities of visible distances is certified except through ordered and continuous bodies at a moderate and equal distance from each other. Also, no distance can be certified unless the sight compares the distance of the seen thing to a distance similar to it among familiar and known distances. A moderate distance, the quantity of which is certified by the sight, is a distance at the end of which no part having a sensible proportion to the whole distance is hidden from the sight, and for which the viewer knows the quantity of the angle according to which he sees a certain distance known to him. Then, according to the excess, or decrease, or equality to that known angle, the distinguishing power judges unknown distances, taking the quantity of the distance itself according to the quantity of the angle. Distance is also certified by the motion of the eye over a body reflecting the distances of the extremities of some surface or space. Generally, the form of the seen object and the form of the distance of the seen object (where the distance is moderate and reflects ordered and continuous bodies) reach the imagination simultaneously upon the intuition of the seen object, and the distinguishing power judges it in the manner described. Thus, the proposition is clear.

...it will necessarily cut the lines **e g** and **e b**, since line **e z**, which is the radius <note>Original: "semidiameter."</note>, is smaller than both of those lines: specifically, line **e b** by the hypothesis, and line **e g** through Proposition 21 of Book 1 <note>Refers to Euclid's *Elements*, Book 1, Prop. 21, regarding lines drawn within a triangle.</note>. Therefore, let it cut line **e g** at point **i**, and line **e b** at point **t**; and let that arc be **i z t**. Because, therefore, triangle **e g z** is greater than sector **e z i**, and triangle **e z d** is smaller than sector **e z t**, then by the 9th theorem of Book 1 of this work, triangle **e g z** has a greater ratio to triangle **e z d** than sector **e z i** has to sector **e z t**. Therefore, by the 11th theorem of Book 1 of this work, the joined ratio of triangle **e g d** to triangle **e z d** will be greater than the ratio of sector **e i t** to sector **e z t**.

But the ratio of triangle **e g d** to triangle **e z d**, through Book 6, Proposition 1 <note>Euclid's theorem that triangles with the same height are in the same ratio as their bases.</note>, is the same as the ratio of line **g d** to line **z d**. However, line **d g** is equal to line **a b** by the hypothesis; therefore, through Book 5, Proposition 7, the ratio of lines **g d** and **a b** to line **d z** is the same. And since, through Book 1, Proposition 29 and by the hypothesis, triangles **a e b** and **e z d** are equiangular—because the angle **a e b** is common to both—it follows from Book 6, Proposition 4 that the ratio of line **a b** to line **d z** is as line **b e** is to line **e d**. Therefore, by Book 5, Proposition 11, the ratio of line **b e** to line **d e** will be greater than the ratio of sector **e i t** to sector **e z t**.

But as sector **e i t** is to sector **e z t**, so is arc **i t** to arc **z t**, which is clear from Book 6, Proposition 1, and we have declared this in the 35th theorem of Book 1 of this work. Moreover, the ratio of arc **i t** to arc **z t** is as the ratio of angle **i e t** to angle **z e t** by Book 6, Proposition 33. Therefore, the ratio of line **b e** to line **d e** is greater than the ratio of angle **i e t** to angle **z e t**. It is clear, then, that the ratio of the greater distance to the lesser distance is greater than the ratio of the greater angle under which vision occurs to the lesser angle. And this is what was proposed. For that which was declared in the case of equidistant [parallel] magnitudes is even more evident in those that are not equidistant, since then the angles of vision are further diminished, as we showed in the 7th [theorem] of this book. Thus the proposition is clear.

12. *Equality of the distance of the endpoints of a line or surface of a visible object from the center of sight is the cause of direct visual perception, just as inequality of the same is the cause of slant <note>Original: "obliquationis," referring to an object being viewed at an angle rather than head-on.</note>. Alhazen Book 4, 5, number 2.*

For equality of the distance of the endpoints of a line or a surface of a visible object causes the equality of the angles of the radial axes themselves falling upon that line or surface at their middle points. For example, if the endpoints of line **a b c**, which are **a** and **c**, are equally distant from the center of sight, which is **d**; and the radial axis **d b** is drawn, along with the radial lines **d a** and **d c**; then it is clear from the hypothesis and by Book 1, Proposition 8, that angles **d b a** and **d b c** are equal. But if the endpoint points **a** and **c** are unequally distant from the center **d**, then lines **d a** and **d c** become unequal; and similarly, angles **d b a** and **d b c** become unequal, and the vision becomes slanted <note>Original: "obliqua."</note>.

->A geometric diagram illustrating vision from a point 'd' (the eye) to a surface 'a c'. A perpendicular axis 'd b' drops to the center of the segment 'a c', with radial lines 'd a' and 'd c' extending to the endpoints. It demonstrates equilateral and scalene triangle configurations for direct and oblique vision.<-

Therefore, if a line or surface of a visible object is directly opposite to the sight, the sight perceives its directness from the sense of equality of the distances of its parts from the visual axis falling perpendicularly to that line or surface. For then, by the definition of a line or surface directly opposite to the eyes, and through the 38th theorem of Book 3 of this work, it is clear that both radial axes <note>Likely referring to the rays forming the visual cone.</note> contain equal angles on either side.

And if the surface of the visible object is slanted, then the sight perceives its slant from the sense of the inequality of the measures of the distances of its endpoints, and also of its angles. Thus, the size of its magnitude begins to be hidden from the <term>distinguishing power<note>Original: "uirtutem diſtinctiuam." The cognitive faculty that judges sensory input.</note></term>. For the distinguishing power understands the slant of the pyramid <note>The "visual pyramid" or cone of light entering the eye.</note> containing the object from the inequality of the distances of the diameters of the endpoints of that slanted space. Therefore, it perceives a decrease in the size of its base because of the slant. The quantity of a magnitude viewed slantedly does not match the quantity of a magnitude viewed directly through simple comparison, except when the comparison is made by the angle alone. But if a comparison is made to both the angle and to the lengths of the radial lines lying between the eye and the endpoints of the visible object, then there will be no doubt regarding the difference in the quantities of magnitude on either side.

For the most remote of the average distances <note>Original: "remotiſsima remotionū mediocrium." This refers to the maximum distance at which an object can still be seen clearly.</note> with respect to an object seen through slant is smaller than the most remote of the average distances with respect to that same object seen through direct orientation. Indeed, an average distance with respect to a visible object is one in which no part of the object having a sensible proportion to the whole object is hidden from sight. Thus, an entire object slanted to the sight is hidden at a distance smaller than that distance in which the object is hidden when seen directly, and its size is diminished at a distance smaller than the distance in which its size is diminished when it is directly opposite the sight. Thus the proposition is clear.

13. *The horizon is seen as if it were the edge of the earth joined together; however, its distance appears greater than the distance to the zenith above the observer's head.*

Because between the horizon (which is the circle bounding the sight at the concave surface of the heaven)
