# VITELLO'S OPTICS

...and between the furthest periphery of the earth, which is the last visible part of the earth, no sensible space is grasped by sight; therefore, the sight cannot discern their certain distance from each other. For, as is clear from Proposition 10 of this book, the quantity of distance is only grasped by sight with the aid of the **distinguishing power** <note>The "distinguishing power" (*virtus distinctiva*) is the mental faculty that processes raw visual data into coherent perceptions.</note> when that distance concerns continuous and ordered bodies. And because between the periphery of the earth and the hollow of the heavens there are no such bodies, the horizon therefore seems to cling to the periphery of the earth.

But the distance of the periphery of the horizon from its center (which is the center of vision) appears sensibly greater than the distance to the zenith above the observer's head, which is the pole of the horizon. Although, according to the truth of the matter, that quantity of distance is either the same or only insensibly greater (which is why in almost all astronomical considerations made through sight, the center of vision is placed at the center of the world), it nevertheless appears sensibly greater to the sight, with the **distinguishing power** judging it so. This happens because of the width of the surface of the earth which is sensed between the eye and the horizon, whereas between the zenith of the head and the earth, nothing is perceived. Since the quantity of distance is known from the sensible distance of intermediate bodies (according to Proposition 10 of this book), it is necessary that where a greater sensible quantity is seen to lie between, a greater distance is judged. Therefore, the distance to the periphery of the horizon seems much greater than the distance to the observer’s zenith; and the same is true for any other part of the visible heaven, because the sight grasps the width of the earth in between. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**14. The location of a visible object is grasped by the sight from its distance, its part of the universe, and the quantity of the distance, with the aid of the distinguishing power. *Alhazen, Book 2, n. 22.***

The concept of distance <note>Original: *intentio remotionis*. In medieval optics, an *intentio* is the mental representation or "notion" of a physical property.</note> is not the same as the quantity of distance. For the concept of distance is the lack of contact between two bodies, and consequently the grasping of a certain layout of things distant from one another; but the grasping of the *quantity* of distance is the grasping of the amount or magnitude of the space lying between those bodies. It is clear, therefore, that the grasping of the location of a visible thing is not the same as the grasping of its distance.

The grasping of the location of a visible thing consists of the grasping of the light and color of the thing, its distance, and the part of the universe in which that visible thing is located relative to the observer, as well as the grasping of the quantity of its distance, when all these things are grasped together through the path of cognition. This is also because, as is clear from Theorem 17 of Book 3 of this work, distinct vision occurs from the arrival of forms according to perpendicular lines falling upon the surface of the eye. When the sight has sensed a form arriving in this way, the **distinguishing power** will estimate the visible thing to be at the extremity of that line, and according to the direction of that line, it will grasp the location of the thing seen. Therefore, the location of a visible thing is grasped by the perceiver from the grasping of the layout of the thing seen during vision, through the direction of the radial line from that place to the eye. Thus, when the form of the visible thing reaches the eye, the sight will sense the part of the sensing organ <note>The "sensing organ" refers here to the surface of the eye or the crystalline lens.</note> which that form has reached, and the **distinguishing power** will immediately grasp the location of the thing seen through the direction of the radial line from that place. And since the concept of distance is already residing in the soul itself, it will grasp the location and the distance simultaneously in the grasping of the form by the sight itself. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**15. Among equal visible objects at unequal distances from the sight, seen with equal attention, the vision of the closer one is more certain. *Euclid, Optics, Theorem 2; Alhazen, Book 2, n. 40.***

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a visual pyramid with its apex at the bottom center, labeled 'b'. Two horizontal parallel line segments represent visible objects: 'gd' (closer to 'b') and 'kl' (further from 'b'). The endpoints are labeled such that 'l' is at the top left, 'k' is at the top right, 'd' is at the middle left, and 'g' is at the middle right. Solid lines connect 'b' to all four endpoints ('l', 'k', 'd', 'g'). Diagonal lines connect 'l' to 'd' and 'k' to 'g'.</image-desc>

Let the center of vision be **b**, and let there be two visible objects **g d** and **k l** at unequal distances from the center of vision **b**. For the sake of example, let them be placed parallel to each other (for if they were touching or intersecting, it is clear that at the point of contact or intersection they are equally distant from point **b**; and for their other points, the demonstration is the same as for these parallel ones, with their parts varying according to their closeness or distance from the sight, regarding the degree of certainty of vision).

Therefore, let **g d** and **k l** be parallel, and let **g d** be closer to the eye. Let the forms of the terminal points reach the eye through lines **d b**, **g b**, **k b**, and **l b**. Triangles **b g d** and **b k l** will be formed. Let lines **l d** and **k g** be drawn, which by Book 1, Proposition 33, will be parallel and equal. Thus, the form of point **l** propagating <note>Original: *multiplicans se*. In medieval science, "multiplication of species" describes how light or forms travel through a medium.</note> itself to the eye **b** will not pass through point **d**, nor will the form of point **k** pass through point **g**; for if they did, line **k g b** would be a single line, and line **l d b** would be a single line; thus lines **k g** and **l d** would meet at point **b**, even though they are parallel, which is impossible.

Furthermore, the propagation of the forms of points **k** and **l** to the eye **b** will not occur outside any point of line **g d**; because then, since in triangle **l k b** the line **d g** falls parallel to line **k l**, it is clear by Book 6, Proposition 2, that line **g d** would be smaller than line **k l**; but it was posited as equal to it. It is clear, therefore, that lines **k b** and **l b** pass through certain points of line **g d**. Thus, some part of line **g d** will be inside the **visual pyramid** <term>visual pyramid: The cone-like volume formed by rays of light traveling from an object to the apex at the pupil of the eye.</term> which is **b k l**.

Under whatever angle **k l** is seen, some part of **g d** is also seen under that same angle, but not vice versa; since, as is clear from Theorem 24 of Book 1, or Theorem 7 of this book, angle **g d b** is greater than angle **k b l**. Therefore, whatever visual power is applied to **k l** is also applied to **g d**, but not vice versa; and this is more strongly evident through Theorem 108 of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, **g d** is seen by more rays and angles than **k l**; thus it is seen more clearly <note>Original: *perspicatius*. Literally "more transparently" or "with greater insight/clarity."</note> according to the supposition set forth at the beginning of this book. Therefore, the vision of it is more certain. And this is the proposition.

# BOOK FOUR.

16. *An error occurs in the **distinguishing power's** <note>The "distinguishing power" (*virtus distinctiva*) is the faculty of the soul or mind that interprets what the eye sees.</note> perception of distance due to the immoderate disposition of the eight circumstances of any visible object. Alhazen [Book 2, Propositions] 23, 34, 45, 52, 58, 64, 66, 69; [Book 3, Proposition] 3.*

For an error in the distance of seen objects happens to the **distinguishing power** in the perception of distance due to the immoderate disposition of light. Indeed, when the distance is moderate but the light is not very certain and is weak—if a group of men or other things are arranged so that one is placed behind the other—then at night or in the twilight, and especially if viewed with only one eye, those men or other things will appear to cling to one another. This is because, due to the weakness of the light, the distance between them is not grasped; and if those men move in the same direction with equal motion, they will always be thought to move together, and the distance between them will not be weighed, but they will be seen as if they were one thing.

Similarly, an error in the distance of seen objects from one another happens to the **distinguishing power** because of excessive distance. For when someone looks at very remote trees, even though they are quite far apart, they will nevertheless appear as if joined or near to each other. In the same way, some stars in the sky are thought to be joined, although in truth they are very far apart; also, because the distance exceeds the moderate range, the **wandering stars** <note>original: *stellae uagantes*; referring to the planets</note> are thought to be carried on the same surface as the fixed stars, even though they are at a great distance from them.

An error in the perception of distance also occurs from an immoderate disposition of **position** <note>original: *situs*; the physical orientation or placement of the object relative to the eye</note> in the opposition of the visible object to the sight. For example, if two bodies are seen, one of which is behind the other so that the front one covers part of the rear one while another part sticks out, and no other visible bodies are between them, and the distance is moderate but not very certain: then the measure of the length from one to the other will not be fully estimated, and perhaps the sight will judge them to be very near to each other. This error is solely from the immoderation of the positional opposition, because if one did not hide part of the other, but both were entirely exposed to the sight so that the difference between them was perceptible, then the distance of one from the other would be discerned. Thus it is clear that this error is due to the immoderation of position; for if the position alone were reduced to a moderate state, such an error would not occur.

An error in the perception of distance also occurs from an immoderate disposition of **size** <note>original: *quantitas*</note>. Hence, if there are two bodies equally distant from the sight according to a moderate distance that is not very certain, and one is much larger than the other, the larger one will be estimated to be closer to the sight because it will be seen more certainly. Thus, because of size, there will be a deception in distance, since one of two equally distant objects appears more distant than the other.

An error of sight in the perception of distance also occurs from the immoderate **solidity** <note>original: *soliditas*; density or lack of transparency</note> of bodies. For if a body is very rare and of minimal solidity, such as pure crystal, and behind it there is a very colorful and bright body, then the crystal is not fully grasped; rather, as if there were nothing in between, the [other] body will be perceived through it. An error occurs in the perception of the crystal because of the [perceived] distance of the crystal from the sight.

An error of sight in the perception of distance also occurs from the immoderate **transparency** <note>original: *diaphanitas*</note> [of the air]. For if the air is cloudy, as often happens in twilight, then some object, such as a tower opposite the sight at a moderate length, will be estimated by the sight to be further away than it is in truth. This is because, due to the density of the air, the amount of ground lying between the sight and the seen object—by which the measure of the tower's distance is taken—is not grasped; and the cause of the error is the immoderation of the air's transparency.

An error of sight in distance also occurs from an immoderate amount of **time**. For if someone looks at something far from a high tower, and it is immediately snatched from view, then the **distinguishing power** will not be able to fully discern the distance of that thing from the tower. It will judge it to be perhaps less remote from the tower, or more, than it was in reality. This is because in such a small amount of time, the quantity of ground lying between the tower and the other seen object is not perceived by the viewer, according to which the measure of their distance from each other is weighed. Nor could the **visual axis** <note>The imaginary line extending from the center of the eye to the object being viewed.</note> traverse the intermediate quantity of ground through diligent looking in such a short time; hence it does not fully grasp it, and thus an error in distance arises from the shortness of time.

An error in distance also occurs from the immoderate **weakness of sight**. For if two bodies are placed before the sight, one of which is further from the sight and of a strong color, and the other, which is closer, is of a weak color: then the weakness of the sight will make the comparison uncertain. And because it is known by those with strong sight, and is clear from the preceding, that a body closer to the sight is of greater certainty, the weak sight will estimate that which is more certain to be closer. Thus, because a stronger color is better perceived by weak sight, it will judge the visible object colored with the stronger color to be closer to itself, even though it is further away in truth; and the error in distance arises from the weakness of sight. Also, because forms are reflected by eyes infected with thick moisture, just like an external rainbow, the weak sight will see a form near to itself, which is actually the form of a remote thing.

So, an error in distance occurs to the perception of the **distinguishing power** from the immoderate disposition of any of the circumstances of a seen thing, of which there are only eight, as was clear through the 1st theorem of this book, the occurrences of which we have run through with these examples and self-evident experiments. The proposition is therefore clear.

17. *The magnitude of a seen object is grasped by sight according to the magnitude of the part of the surface of the eye which the form of the object reaches, and the solid angle formed at the center of sight. Alhazen [Book 2, Proposition] 37.*

For the part of the surface of the eye, which the form of the seen object reaches through the angle of the vertex of the **radial pyramid** <note>The cone of light rays originating from the object and converging at the pupil.</note> (according to which vision of the object occurs by the 18th theorem of Book 2 of this work), is always measured by the angle at the center of sight. For although the sensitive power grasps the quantity of that angle from the perception of the part of the surface of the eye in which the form of the object is shaped, as is clear by the 73rd theorem of Book 3 of this work, the angle is properly the cause of the measurement of that surface; for the proportion of that [angle] is always...

# THE OPTICS OF VITELLO

...part of the eye’s surface to the entire spherical surface of the eye, just as that angle is to eight right **solid angles** <term>solid angle: a three-dimensional version of a standard angle, like the point of a cone</term> according to Theorem 87 of Book 1 of this work. For since the base of the **radial pyramid** <term>radial pyramid: the cone-shaped volume of light rays extending from the object to the center of the eye</term> is always on the surface of the object seen, according to Theorem 18 of Book 3 of this work, that pyramid is nevertheless cut nearly parallel to its base by the surface of the eye itself. Thus, one angle is common to both pyramids—namely, the total radial pyramid and the part of it cut off by the eye's surface. Therefore, the magnitude of the part of the eye's surface reached by the **form** <note>original: *forma*; in medieval optics, this refers to the visual information or "species" of an object traveling through space</note> of the object, and the angle contained by the radial pyramid encompassing that part of the eye's surface, are both the root of the comprehension of the magnitude of the thing seen. 

However, even though both this angle and this part of the eye’s surface vary according to the distance—for the more an object is elongated, the more that angle will be diminished according to Theorem 106 of Book 1 of this work, because the radial pyramid becomes narrower—it is as if one of the radial pyramids (the one for the more remote object) is inscribed within the radial pyramid of the closer object. Therefore, the angle at the center of the eye becomes sharper, and the part of the eye’s surface corresponding to that angle becomes smaller; conversely, the more an object approaches the eye, the more its magnitude is expanded. Nevertheless, the magnitude of the seen object is always perceived by the eye according to the size of the aforementioned part of the eye’s surface and that solid angle formed at the center of the eye. Thus, the proposition is clear.

18. ***All magnitudes perceived by the eye through opposition are the quantities of visible surfaces and parts of those surfaces; likewise of their boundaries and the distinct spaces between visible things. Alhazen, [Book 2, Proposition] 41.***

For the quantity of the entire body of a seen object is not grasped by the eye, since the eye does not perceive the entire surface of a body, but only that which is opposite to it from the body’s surface or surfaces, even if the body is small. This includes everything between which and some part of the eye’s surface straight lines can be drawn, according to Theorem 2 of Book 3 of this work. In this way, the eye perceives only the surface of the object. Even if the eye were to perceive the "bodiliness" (the three-dimensional volume) of the object, it would not grasp its total quantity because of this, but only the **figure of its bodiliness** <note>The visual appearance of depth or shape rather than a mathematical calculation of volume</note>. If the object or the eye should happen to move so that the eye perceives the entire surface of the body, then the **distinguishing power** <note>The mind's faculty for processing visual data</note> would grasp the quantities of its volume through a different operation than what is seen during a single instance of vision. The same is true for the parts of a body. 

Therefore, the quantities that the eye perceives through opposition are nothing other than the quantities of surfaces and the lines bounding those surfaces, or those measuring them according to length or width. And since the eye perceives different bodies by their different surfaces and their boundaries, the distance between those bodies is necessarily perceived through the perception of parts of the eye's surface that are not colored by the color of the seen bodies, but lie between the parts of the eye's surface colored by the colors of those bodies. There are no other magnitudes that can be perceived by the eye; thus, the proposition is clear.

19. ***All things seen under the same angle, whose distance from each other is not perceived, appear equal. Euclid, Optic Hypotheses 7.***

Let the center of the eye be point *a*, and let the object seen be line *bg*. Let the lines along which points *g* and *b* reach the eye be *ga* and *ba*. Line *bg* is therefore seen under angle *gab*. Let there be another object, *de*, falling between those same lines *ga* and *ba*, so that it is seen under the same angle *gab*. I say that lines *gb* and *de* will appear equal if the distances *db* and *eg* are not perceived by the eye. Because the eye at *a* perceives two points, *d* and *b*, upon one line (*ab*), and two points, *e* and *g*, upon one line (*ag*), it does not see any boundary of either of the two quantities *bg* and *de* extending beyond the other; rather, it sees the ends of their extremities as equal. 

And because it does not perceive that the length of lines *db* and *eg* is anything at all, point *d* appears to the eye to be upon point *b*, and point *e* upon point *g*. Truly, of those things where one placed over the other does not exceed the remaining part, nor is exceeded by it, those things are equal to one another. Therefore, the two lines *de* and *bg* appear equal, since according to the judgment of the eye one of them covers the other, and the extremities of one do not surpass the extremities of the other. In this same way, on nights that are somewhat bright—such as when the moon shines from beneath the clouds—or during the twilight hours, if it happens that a man or something else is seen under the same angle as a tall tree or a tower, the man or other thing will perhaps be judged to be the height of that tree or tower. Because of this, much deception occurs in vision. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Point 'a' is the vertex; 'd' and 'b' are on the lower ray; 'e' and 'g' are on the upper ray.</image-desc>

20. ***Everything seen under a larger angle appears larger, and under a smaller angle, smaller: from which it is clear that the same thing seen under a larger angle appears larger than itself seen under a smaller angle: and universally, the proportion of the quantity of the object seen directly or at the same slant follows the proportion of the angle. Euclid, Optic Hypotheses 5 & 6.***

### BOOK FOUR

Let the center of vision be at point **a**, and let the object be seen under the angle **fae**. With lines **af** and **ae** extended, let line **gb** be drawn between them parallel to line **fe**. Therefore, line **gb** will be seen under angle **fae**. It might happen that it appears equal to line **fe** according to the previous proposition <note>original: *per præmiſſam*; Vitello refers to Proposition 20 which discusses the relationship between distance and size</note>, as if the lines **gf** and **be** were not perceived. But if the lines **gf** and **be** are seen, **gb** appears smaller, because in truth—according to Proposition 4 of Book 6 <note>referring to Euclid's *Elements*</note>—line **gb** is smaller than line **fe**, since line **ag** is smaller than line **af** by hypothesis. 

Let a line be drawn from point **e** parallel to line **ag** (by 31 p 1), which intersects the extended line **gb** at point **d**. Thus, by 34 p 1, line **gd** will be equal to line **fe**. Let line **ad** be drawn, intersecting the extended line **ef** at point **h**. Line **hf** will be greater than line **ef**, and angle **fah** is greater than angle **fae** by Theorem 29 of Book 1 of this work. And since angle **fae** is a part of angle **fah**, and line **fh** appears larger than line **ef**, and line **dg** appears larger than line **bg**—because the vision distinguishes the part from the whole—that which is seen under a smaller angle appears smaller. But sometimes, according to the preceding, it appears equal to line **gb**; therefore, line **ef** can appear smaller than line **gd** (which is equal to line **fe**), as is clear from the premises. 

Thus, what is seen under a larger angle appears larger, and what is seen under a smaller angle appears smaller. The cone of the **visual pyramid** <term>visual pyramid: the cone of light rays stretching from the object to the eye</term> **fae**, by which the more remote object **fe** is seen, is smaller and sharper than the cone of the pyramid **gad**. And since the surface of the eye cuts through both these pyramids—since the cone of both is as if at the center of the eye (by Theorem 18 of Book 3)—it is necessary that the base of the pyramid cut off by the eye's surface from pyramid **fae** be smaller than the base of the pyramid cut off from the total pyramid **gad** (by Theorem 109 of Book 1), since those two cut-off pyramids are of equal height. This is because the line drawn from the center of the opening of the **hollow nerve's** <term>hollow nerve: the medieval term for the optic nerve, then believed to be a tube for visual spirits</term> rotation to the outer surface of the eye is the axis of both those cut-off pyramids.

A geometric diagram illustrating optical perspective. Point 'a' represents the center of vision. Rays diverge from 'a' toward the right. Two parallel vertical segments, 'f-e' and 'g-d', represent objects or distances at different depths. Point 'f' is on the ray 'a-g', and 'e' is on the ray 'a-d'. A segment 'g-b' is marked on 'g-d'. A line 'a-d' passes through 'e' and intersects an extension of 'f-e' at point 'h'. A line 'a-k' bisects the angle formed by the rays. The diagram is labeled with letters a, b, d, e, f, g, h, and k.

Therefore, the part of the visual surface shaped there by the form of the seen object **gd** is larger than the part of the same surface shaped by the form of the seen object **fe**. Thus, line **gd** appears larger than line **fe**. And since the **sensitive power** <term>sensitive power: the faculty of the mind that processes sensory data</term> perceives the angle contained by the radial lines at the center according to the size of those parts of the visual surface (by Theorem 73 of Book 1), it is clear that a larger angle corresponds to an object that appears larger, and a smaller angle to one that appears smaller. For the magnitude of the angle under which vision occurs is taken according to how the form of the object is received on the surface of the visual organ, and the judgment of the object's size is made according to this same thing. 

Therefore, every object seen under a larger angle appears larger than itself when seen under a smaller angle. And universally, in objects seen directly, an **increase** <note>original: *excrementum*; used here as a mathematical term for the difference or growth in size</note> in the size of the thing seen follows the increase of the angle; hence, an object seen under a double angle appears double, and under a triple angle triple, and so on according to the proportion of the angles. However, in objects seen obliquely, or in those where one is seen directly and the other obliquely, this is not the case. For if the triangle **aef** were **right-angled** <note>original: *orthogonium*</note> such that its angle **aef** is a right angle, and if angle **fae** is divided equally by a drawn line **ak** intersecting line **fe** at point **k**, line **ef** will not be divided into equal parts at point **k** because of this. For, as is clear by Theorem 35 of Book 1, the proportion of angle **fak** to angle **kae** is smaller than the proportion of line **fk** to line **ke**. Thus, the proportion of seen magnitude to seen magnitude is not always according to the proportion of angle to angle, for such seen things are not seen according to the same disposition and position relative to the vision itself. 

But in uniform visible objects, according to distance, position, and other accidents required for the condition and circumstance of seeing (which are clear from Theorem 1 of this book), the size of the object seen always appears proportional to the proportion of the angle. Hence, even that which is seen under the smallest angle appears smallest, and that which reaches the surface of vision under no angle or an imperceptible one is seen in no way at all, as is clear by Theorem 19 of Book 3. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 21. *Parallel lines seem to meet at their parts further from the vision, yet they will never be seen to meet. Euclid's Optics, Theorem 6.*

What is proposed is universal, regardless of how the vision is positioned relative to those parallel lines: whether the vision is in their plane, or above it, or below it, the same effect always happens to the vision. Let the vision first be in their plane, and let there be two parallel lines **ab** and **gd**. These, by Theorem 1 of Book 1, will necessarily be in the same plane. Let the vision be in their plane at point **e**, or near it. I say that the width of the surface lying between lines **ab** and **gd** will appear unequal, and the part closer to the vision will appear wider than the part further from it; thus, lines **ab** and **gd** will seem to meet. 

For let points be marked parallel and similarly on lines **ab** and **gd**, which are points **z** and **t** on line **ab**, and points **l** and **k** on line **gd**. Let those points and the terminal points be joined by lines **bd**, **zl**, **tk**, **ag**, all of which will be parallel by hypothesis and by Proposition 33 of Book 1. Let lines **eb**, **ez**, **et**, **ea**, **ed**, **el**, **ek**, **eg** be drawn. And since angle **bed** is greater than angle **zel**, as a whole is greater than its part (as is clear by Theorem 34 of Book 1), it is evident by the previous proposition that it will appear larger...

And because the lines of width <note>The "lines of width" refer to the transverse lines connecting the two parallel lines being observed.</note> are diminished in sight in this way, it is clear that the surface lying between the lines will appear smaller: therefore, lines **ab** and **gd** will appear as if to converge; yet they will never be seen as actually meeting, because lines of width are always seen under some angle, the base of which is subtended at the limit of vision, however small it may be; therefore they will never appear to meet. If, however, the lines **lg** and **xe** lie parallel to the sight, which is at **a**, so that the sight is positioned upright above the surface of the horizon, and those lines are on the surface of that horizon, those lines will still appear to almost converge in the parts more remote from the sight. For let a perpendicular line **ab** be dropped from the sight **a** onto the surface of the horizon (by Book 11, Proposition 11 <note>original: "11 p 11"; Vitello frequently cites Euclid’s *Elements*</note>): and let lines **lx**, **kn**, and **tm** be parallel, as before. I say that the surface lying between lines **lg** and **xe** still appears to be of unequal width, and the parts of the lines further from the sight appear to almost converge. For let lines be drawn from point **b** perpendicularly to line **lx**, which is **br**: and lines **br** and **lx** will be in the same plane (by 2 p 11): and let line **br** be extended over line **ge** at point **f**: and let it intersect line **kn** at point **p**, and line **tm** at point **c**: and let lines **la**, **ka**, **ta**, **xa**, **na**, and **ma** be drawn: similarly also let lines **ar**, **ap**, and **ac** be drawn. Therefore, since angle **abr** is a right angle, it is clear that the surface **abc** is upright over the surface **lxeg**, and their common intersection is line **bf** (by Theorem 19 of Book 1 of this work <note>Witello is citing his own earlier propositions in this treatise</note>), because that line **bf** is in both of those surfaces. Therefore, because line **ar** is extended in surface **abc**, and similarly lines **ap** and **ac**: it is clear by definition that angles **arx**, **apn**, and **acm** are right angles: and thus those triangles, which are **abr**, **abp**, and **abc**, are right-angled: but line **pn** is equal to line **rx** by hypothesis and by 34 p 1. Since angle **abr** is indeed a right angle, angle **arb** will be acute (by 32 p 1): therefore, by 13 p 1, angle **arp** is obtuse: line **ap** is therefore larger than line **ar** (by 19 p 1): angle **rax** is therefore (by Theorem 34 of Book 1 of this work) larger than angle **pan**: therefore line **rx** will appear larger than line **pn** (by the preceding theorem): and similarly line **lr** will appear larger than line **kp**, since the demonstration is the same: for line **lr** is equal to line **kp** by the principle: "if from equals [equals are taken]," etc. Therefore, the whole line **lx** will appear larger than the whole line **kn**: and in the same way the whole line **kn** will appear larger than the whole line **tm**. Therefore, the parts of the surface **lxge** more remote from the eye will appear narrower: thus lines **lg** and **xe** will appear as if to converge: yet they will never appear to be meeting, because they will always be seen under some angle. And it must be demonstrated in exactly the same way if the parallel lines are higher than the eye, as when the eye is lower and the parallel lines themselves are on some surface above the eye—as happens in the roofs of houses and similar things when the eye is below. Therefore, the proposition is evident.

**22. When several lines are equally spaced from one another and placed before the sight: the more remote distance appears smaller to the eye. Euclid, Theorem 4 of the Optics.**

<image-desc>A second geometric diagram showing vision angles from a point 'a' to a vertical line, with various points labeled 'r', 'p', 's' and perpendicular lines connecting to a vertical axis.</image-desc>

Let the sight, the center of which is **a**, be positioned upright in the air according to the height of the viewer, as in the previous proposition: also, let lines that are equal, parallel, and separated by an equal distance from one another lie below the eye on the surface of the horizon; let these be **lx**, **kn**, **tm**, and **ge**, placed in this order so that line **lx** is closer to the eye, and the others are more remote from the eye in the order of their names. I say that the distance between lines **kn** and **tm** will appear smaller than the distance between lines **lx** and **kn**. For since those lines (**lx**, **kn**, **tm**, **ge**) are equal and parallel, when their ends are joined by lines **lg** and **xe**, line **lg** will be equal to line **xe** (by 30 and 33 p 1): and let line **ab** be drawn perpendicular to the surface **lxge**, as in the next preceding proof: and once the demonstration is made, as in that one, it will follow that angle **rap** is larger than angle **pac**. Yet this is more easily evident through Theorem 35 of Book 1 of this work: since in the right-angled triangle **abf**, equal parts are cut off from one of the sides containing the right angle, which are **rp**, **pc**, and **cf**: therefore angle **rap** is larger than angle **pac** (by 10 p 5): therefore line **rp** (by the 20th theorem of this book) will appear larger than line **pc**, and line **pc** larger than line **cf**. Therefore, the more remote of these distances (**rp**, **pc**, and **cf**) appears smaller to the eye (by the 20th theorem of this book). And this is what was proposed. And universally, in every disposition of the sight toward given parallel lines, this same thing can be demonstrated, as in the preceding.

23. *Of equal parts of the same visible line [that is] parallel to the line connecting the centers of the openings of rotation of the hollow nerves <note>original: "foraminum gyrationis neruorum concauorum"; this refers to the centers of the pupils or the optic nerves, which were historically believed to be hollow tubes</note>, the one more remote from the sight appears smaller. I say that part **ab** will appear larger than **bg**, and **bg** larger than **gd**, and **gd** larger than **df**. For since the perpendicular **ea** is shorter than all lines that can be drawn from point **e** to line **af**, such as all the lines **eb**, **eg**, **ed**, **ef**—which is clear by Book 1, Proposition 47 <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem in Euclid’s *Elements*</note>—it is therefore manifest that part **ab** is closer to the sight than all those parts which are **bg**, **gd**, and **df**. For let lines be drawn through which the forms <note>In medieval optics, "forms" or "species" were the visual representations of objects traveling to the eye</note> of the points reach the sight, which are **be**, **ge**, **de**, and **fe**: and let line **bz** be drawn parallel to line **ge** (by Book 1, Proposition 31). Because therefore in triangle **aeg**, line **bz** is parallel to side **ge**: it is clear by Book 6, Proposition 2, that the proportion of line **az** to line **ze** is as the proportion of line **ab** to line **bg**: but line **ab** is equal to line **bg** by the hypothesis: therefore line **az** is equal to line **ze**: but by Book 1, Proposition 47, line **zb** is larger than line **za**: therefore line **bz** is larger than line **ze**: therefore angle **zeb** is larger than angle **zbe** by Book 1, Proposition 18: but angle **zbe** is equal to angle **beg** by Book 1, Proposition 29, because they are alternate angles between parallel lines, which are **bz** and **eg**: therefore angle **aeb** is larger than angle **beg**. Therefore, by Proposition 20 of this book, **ab** will appear larger than **bg**: for it will be seen under a larger angle. Similarly also, having drawn a line from point **g** parallel to line **ed**, the demonstration is the same. The same also happens if lines **ae**, **be**, **ge**, **de**, and **fe** are not in one natural plane <note>original: "linea naturali"; refers to a single physical plane or surface</note>, as long as a mathematical line imagined between them remains parallel to line **ge**. And this is what was proposed.

25. *Of equal and parallel magnitudes at unequal distances from the sight, the closer one always appears larger; yet they do not appear [to differ] proportionally to their distances. Euclid, Theorem 8 of the Optics.*

Let there be two visible magnitudes, **ab** and **gd**, at unequal distances from the eye: whose center is **e**, and let **gd** be closer to the sight than **ab**. I say that **gd** will appear larger than **ab**. For let lines **ea**, **eb**, **ed**, and **eg** be drawn: **gd** will be seen under angle **ged**, which is larger than angle **aeb**, as is clear through Theorem 34 of Book 1. It is therefore clear through Proposition 20 of this book <note>Vitello frequently references his own preceding theorems to build his geometric proofs</note>, that line **gd** will appear larger than line **ab**. And this is to be demonstrated in the same way, whether the center of sight and the objects are at the same height or at different ones: such as if the sight is higher than the visible objects, or vice versa. However, these do not appear proportional to their distances—that is to say, the ratio of the larger-appearing **gd** to the smaller-appearing **ab** is not the same as the ratio of the greater distance **be** to the lesser distance **de**. Because, as is clear through Theorem 11 of this book, the ratio of the greater distance **be** to the lesser distance **de** is greater than the ratio of the larger angle **ged** to the smaller angle **aeb**. But in proportion to how much angle **ged** is larger than angle **aeb**, so much does line **gd** appear larger than line **ab**, as we said in Proposition 20 of this book, since those visible objects are arranged uniformly toward the sight. Therefore, lines **gd** and **ab** do not appear proportional to their distances, since the ratio of the distances is greater. And this is what was proposed.

### 26. *Every visible object slanted away from the sight appears smaller than itself [would] if it were directly opposite the eye at its nearest point.*

For let the line connecting the centers of the eyes be **rt**: and let the center of sight be **a**: and let the visible object slanted from the sight be **bc**: and let lines **ab** and **ac** be drawn: and from point **c**, which is the end of the visible object nearest to the eye, let line **cd** be drawn, equal to line **cb**, and parallel to line **rt**, which connects the centers of the eyes—which can be done through Theorem 39 of Book 3. ### 27. *The true size of things is not grasped by sight except with the help of the distinguishing faculty.* <note>original: "uirtutis distinctiuæ"; this refers to the cognitive power of the mind to judge and interpret sensory data, rather than the eye simply acting as a camera</note> *Alhazen 36. 38 n 2.* <note>This refers to the work of Alhazen, or Ibn al-Haytham, the 11th-century scholar whose "Book of Optics" was the primary source for Vitello.</note>

For since, as is clear from the preceding, the angles formed in the center of the sight, and the parts of the surfaces of the sight through which the grasping of the size of the visible object occurs, are always varied according to the approach and removal of the same object, and according to whether it is positioned directly or slanted toward the sight and the radial axes: therefore, the <term>distinguishing faculty</term> <note>the mental ability to judge or differentiate</note> that discerns the true size of a visible object will not consider the angle alone nor the distance alone: because neither of those by themselves is sufficient, but it will consider the angle and the distance together. Therefore, the true sizes of those visible things will not be grasped except through distinction and comparison: and this comparison will happen simultaneously: and it will be of the base of the <term>radial pyramid</term> <note>the cone of light rays extending from the object to the eye</note> (which through Theorem 18 of Book 3 is the surface of the visible object) to the angle of the pyramid, and to the measure of the length of the axis of the pyramid, which is the line of the distance of the visible object from the sight. Indeed, the consideration by the distinguishing faculty of the surface itself is always in the colored part of the surface of the eye, corresponding to the said angle, along with the consideration of the distance of the visible object from the surface of the eye: since the size of that colored part of the surface of the eye is always according to the size of that angle, by Theorem 73 of Book 3. However, in that consideration of the distinguishing faculty, there is no sensible difference between the distance of the visible object from the surface of the eye and its distance from the center of the eye. Therefore, when the sight grasps the lines of the radial pyramid falling perpendicularly upon it: then the distinguishing faculty will imagine the quantity of the extension, according to the quantity of the extension of those lines from the center of the eye to the ends of the visible object: and when, along with this, it has grasped the quantity of the distance of the visible object through Proposition 10 of this book: then it will imagine the quantity of the lengths of those lines and the quantity of the spaces that are between their extremities, which spaces are the diameters of the visible object itself. When, therefore, the distinguishing faculty imagines the size of the angle, and the size of the part of the surface of the eye corresponding to that angle, and the length of the radial lines, and their position relative to one another, and the size of the spaces between their ends: then it grasps the size of the visible object according to its actual being: since then nothing remains ungrasped of those things by which the size of a visible object is understood. This, therefore, is the nature of how the size of seen things is grasped, and it happens mostly through [habit...]

**28. In the vision of magnitude <note>meaning the perceived size of an object</note>, an error occurs in the faculty of distinction <note>the part of the mind that processes visual data</note> from the unbalanced arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible thing.** <note>original: "Alhazen 26.37.47.54.59.64.66.69 n 3." refers to the work of the Arabic scientist Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen, whose optics Vitello expanded upon.</note>

For from an unbalanced arrangement of light—as at night or in the twilight when light is uncertain—if a man is inspected and a grove of trees or a wall is seen at a distance from that man, and the distance between the man and the grove or wall is hidden from the viewer, even though that distance is in truth very great: then the man will seem to be close to the grove or the wall. And if it happens that the same ray reaching the man's head also reaches the top of the grove: then, through Proposition 19 of this book, the man and the grove or wall will appear to be of the same height, because they are seen under the same angle. And perhaps the man will even appear taller than the grove itself, as when a ray passing over the man's head does not reach the height of the grove or wall. A similar thing happened near the city of Wrocław <note>original: "Vratislauiae"</note> at the grove of the village of Borek <note>original: "Boret"</note>: for men were seen there in the twilight appearing taller than that high grove; and a stone next to a piece of wood and a castle in Poland <note>original: "castrum Poloniae"</note> appeared to be the same height as the grove itself. But this happened in the twilight hours when the light is uncertain, and those sights were hallucinated to be phantasms by those seeing them. Nothing of the sort would happen if the light were in a balanced state <note>original: "luce existente in temperamento"</note>, because then the distance of the man from the grove would be discerned, and the height of each would be measured according to its own apparent boundary. 

Similarly, an error in the vision of magnitude happens from the weakness of color: for if a body of strong color is placed in some location, it will not be hidden from sight; but if a body equal to the first is placed in the same spot but with a weak color, that body will not be seen. This error also happens from the identity of colors <note>color camouflage</note> in the intervening medium and in the visible object. Thus, a white body placed in a location where some whiteness is spread over the surface of the ground lying between the eye and the object will not be seen; but if the whiteness of the intervening space is removed, the form of that white body is immediately understood. Therefore, concealment occurs then from the similarity of colors: for if a body equal to it but of another color were placed in that white body's stead, it would be easily seen across the whitened medium. 

An error in the vision of magnitude also arises from an unbalanced length of distance: for then an object will appear much smaller than it truly is, per Theorem 24 of this book. For then even parts of the same object that are disproportionate to their whole are hidden from sight, because they cannot be seen at such a distance, per Theorem 23 of this book. Thus the total appearance of the object becomes smaller, because many parts hidden imperceptibly cause a sensible reduction of the object, which would not happen at a balanced distance. 

Unbalanced proximity also induces an error in the vision of magnitude: for a body brought very close to the eye appears to be of a larger size than it truly is. Because of the size of the angle, the body appears larger, just as previously, because of the smallness of the angle, the object appeared smaller; and these things are clear through Theorem 20 of this book. For according to the larger size of the angle of the visual pyramid, a larger surface of the eye is informed <note>impressed with the image</note>, as is clear through Theorem 87 of Book 1. Hence, the estimation of the size of the visible object is made according to the size of that angle and the elongation of the body, as was stated in the preceding proposition. For the length of the distance of the object does not penetrate to the inner parts of the viewer, since the interior part of the head is not capable of containing the total quantity of the radial lines, nor can it be measured with certainty; and because of this, the size of the object is referred to the capacity of the angle and the known length. 

The true distance of a body is considered along the line proceeding from the center of sight to the surface of the object, in respect to which the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> of the eye begins to be imperceptible; thus it does not cause any sensible error in the estimation of that length. But when a body is brought closer to the eye beyond that distance, then the radius of the eye becomes proportional to the distance of the body in a sensible ratio: for it will be sometimes larger, sometimes equal, and sometimes smaller by a small proportion, such as perhaps half or a third, or something of this sort. Hence, in such proximity of the visible object, the magnitude of the pyramidal angle and the sensible smallness of the estimated length compared to the true length induce a sensible appearance of greatness in the body. 

An error in the vision of magnitude also occurs from a disordered opposition of position: for when someone standing in a high place sees beneath that height several objects equal to each other, which are arranged one after another in order: then, through Proposition 25 of this book, the last one <note>the one furthest back in the row</note>, which is actually closer to the viewer's line of sight <note>in terms of height/angle</note>, will be judged higher than all the others or larger. Just as a watchman standing on the height of some tower, seeing equal men or trees at unequal distances from himself, estimates the one closer to him to be taller. 

An error in magnitude also happens from an unbalanced arrangement of the size of the object: for if two bodies are presented to the sight, one of which is slightly larger than the other—either in length alone, or in width, or in both—they will perhaps be judged equal in every dimension, because the smallness of that excess is not perceived due to its tininess; for it does not exceed the limits of balance in respect to the sight itself. 

An error in the vision of magnitude also occurs from unbalanced solidity: for in an angular crystal, the edges of the angles, because they have little solidity <note>transparency/thinness</note>, are sometimes not seen, whereas the angles of a solid body could be seen. 

An error also occurs from the lack of transparency <note>original: "intemperantia raritatis"</note> in the vision of magnitude: for in cloudy, dark air, as most often happens in the twilight hours, a seen body appears larger than in balanced air, as we shall declare below when we make a treatise on those things seen through a second transparent medium. 

An error in the vision of size also happens from an unbalanced duration of time: for when a burning brand <note>original: "titio," a smoldering piece of wood</note> is moved quickly over some space, the entire space appears ignited: because the quantity of time is not weighed, because

## 29. Vision understands every position <term>situs <note>Refers to the spatial location or orientation of an object relative to the observer.</note></term> through the understanding of the proper distance in the positioned things themselves. <note>original: Alhazen 2.26.</note>

Whether the name "position" refers to the opposition of the whole thing seen, or its parts, to the sight according to its direction or slant; or whether it refers to the arrangement of the surfaces of the thing seen, or its parts, relative to the surface of the eye itself (as when the thing seen has many surfaces appearing to the eye); or whether the name "position" refers to the placement of the lines which belong to those visible surfaces; or whether it refers to the position of the spaces which are between any two visible things understood simultaneously by the eye: always, when position is accepted according to any of these modes, the sight understands each and every one of these as they are arranged in bright or colored bodies, being visible in themselves and established in them. And it always understands any mode of position by understanding the distance from the sight or between the objects themselves, which are due to those wholes or to the positioned parts. Therefore, the proposition is clear, since we shall pursue these modes specifically in the following sections.

## 30. The position of opposition <term>opposition <note>The state of an object being directly in front of and facing the eyes.</note></term> of the thing seen and its parts to the sight is understood by the sense of sight with the aid of the **distinguishing faculty**. <note>original: Alhazen 2.27.</note>

Since the position of anything having a location relative to another is composed of their distance from one another, it is clear that the opposition of the seen thing to the sight—which is indeed a position—is composed of the distance of the seen thing from the sight and from the part of the universe in which the thing is located relative to the sight. Moreover, the comprehension of the distance of the seen thing is achieved by the **distinguishing faculty** <term>uirtus distinctiua <note>The mental power that processes visual sensations into logic and recognition.</note></term> through a concept resting in the soul, as was shown through Propositions 9 and 10 of this book. Therefore, when the distinguishing faculty understands the place of the thing seen and its distance, it will simultaneously understand the opposition of the thing. However, the true place of the thing seen is understood from the position of the sight itself and from the position of the seen thing during the act of vision; for the sight does not understand the seen thing except through opposition.

The distinguishing faculty will therefore distinguish between a place slanted relative to the sight and a place near to it. The distinguishing faculty understands all locations of placed things through the comprehension of distance and the part of the universe toward which that distance lies, as was clear through Proposition 14 of this book; hence it will also understand the place opposite the eye during the comprehension of the thing seen. And since vision of that thing is destroyed when the eye is removed from it, the distinguishing faculty then understands that the thing seen exists only in the part opposite the eye during the vision of that thing. In this way, the locations of visible things are distinguished, because distinct visible things are not distinguished by the sight except by the distinction of different locations on the surface of the sensing organ <note>the eye</note> where the forms of the distinct visible things arrive.

Just as the locations of voices and sounds are understood by the sense of hearing, and thereafter by the distinguishing faculty by means of hearing, so the locations of visible things are understood by the distinguishing faculty by means of sight. For when the form of the seen thing reaches the surface of the eye, the seeing faculty will sense the location on the sensing organ where that form arrived; and from the straightness of the line falling perpendicularly upon that location, the distinguishing faculty will understand the place of the seen thing. And because the concept of distance rests within the soul itself, the soul will therefore understand the place of the seen thing and its distance simultaneously with the comprehension of the form by the sensing eye. Therefore, upon the arrival of the seen form at the eye, the sight understands the light and color of the thing seen, and the part of the eye's surface which is illuminated and colored by that form; and the distinguishing faculty understands the place and the distance of the seen thing, and consequently the opposition of the whole seen thing and all its parts relative to each other within the whole. The comprehension of all these things happens simultaneously. Thus, the position of opposition of the thing seen and its parts to the sight is understood by the sense of sight with the aid of the distinguishing faculty. Which is what was proposed.

## 31. Sight understands the direction and slant <term>obliquatio <note>The angle or tilt of an object's surface relative to the viewer's line of sight.</note></term> of lines, surfaces, and spaces from the comprehension of the difference in the distances of their extremities, with the aid of the **distinguishing faculty**. <note>original: Alhazen 2.28.</note>

When the radial axes cut lines, surfaces, or spaces as if standing perpendicularly upon them, then the sight understands the surface of the thing seen and the equal distances of its extremities on either side of the upright axis; and then it understands that surface to be directly opposite the eye, and the distinguishing faculty will judge that surface to be directly opposite. However, when the sight understands the distance of the extremities of the seen surface to be different—and from the point of the joining of the axes outside the line where the axes fall perpendicularly, it does not find two points of equal distance from the surface of the eye in the whole surface opposite it—then it will understand that surface to be slanted in its opposition, and the distinguishing faculty will judge it to be slanted.

The same applies to the positions of lines and spaces falling between several things seen at once; the sight, with the aid of the distinguishing faculty, will judge their direction and slant. And this equality of direction and difference of slant is often understood by the sensing agent through estimation alone and through signs. For at a very great distance or removal, a surface, line, or space that is slanted will be understood as if it were direct—specifically when the difference between the distances of its extremities is not perfectly understood. Hence, for the sight to understand this well, it is necessary that such visible things...

### *32. The position of the parts and boundaries of a visible surface—or the relative position of its surfaces to one another—and the position of multiple visible things seen at once, is understood by the sight with the help of the distinguishing faculty <term>virtus distinctiva <note>The "distinguishing faculty" refers to the cognitive power of the mind to process raw visual sensations into organized perceptions, such as recognizing borders or depth.</note></term> through the perception of the difference in distance and the arrangement of the forms reaching the eye. <note>original: Alhazen 2.30.</note>*

Because the form of any part of the surface of a visible thing reaches some part of the surface of the eye, just as the form of the whole visible thing does: when the surface of a visible thing has different distinct colors, then the form reaching the eye will also have different colors, and its parts will be distinct according to the distinction of the parts of the visible surface. Thus, the sight perceives each part of the visible form from the sensation of those colors and the light within them; it perceives the locations of the parts of the forms on the surface of the eye from the sensation of the colors and light of those parts. The distinguishing faculty perceives the arrangement of those colors by grasping the diversity of the parts of the form and the differences between those parts; in this way, it understands what is touching and what is separate. The same applies to visible things that are touching or separated. Indeed, the position of the parts of a visible thing relative to each other—regarding their closeness or distance, or the prominence of one over another, or the depth of one beneath another—is understood by the eye through the perception of the degree of distance of the parts, whether greater or lesser. Furthermore, the boundaries of the surface of a visible thing (the lines that limit those surfaces) and their arrangement are understood by the sight through the perception of that part of the eye's surface where the color and light of the visible object arrive, and by the understanding of the boundaries and arrangement of that part, aided by the distinguishing faculty. Since all the things proposed are understood in this manner, what was proposed is evident.

### *33. Every line or surface of a visible thing directly opposite to the eye or eyes is seen more perfectly than one that is slanted; and the imperfection of vision occurs according to the degree of slant. <note>original: Alhazen 3.17.</note>*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the principles of optics and perspective. A point 'a' on the right represents the observer's eye. From 'a', multiple lines of sight radiate towards the left. These lines intersect a vertical line segment containing points 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', and 'f' (where 'd' is directly level with 'a'). An oblique line segment extends from 'f' downwards and outwards, marked with points 'g', 'h', 'i', and 'k'. Horizontal and vertical auxiliary lines (like 'gm' and 'hn') create geometric figures to mathematically compare the size and angle of segments on the direct versus the oblique surface as perceived from point 'a'.</image-desc>

Let the center of the eye be **a**: and let there be, for example, a flat surface of a visible thing directly opposite the sight, in which there is the line **b c d e f**: and let **b c**, **c d**, **d e**, and **e f** be parts of that line, whether equal or unequal. Let there also be a surface slanted to the sight, in which there is the line **f g h i k**: and let it be such that the slanting of that surface begins at point **f**. Let line **a d** be perpendicular to line **b f**: and let lines **a f**, **a e**, **a d**, **a c**, and **a b** be drawn from the center of the eye. Let all these be extended to the slanted surface: let line **a e** fall on point **g**, line **a d** on point **h**, line **a c** on point **i**, and line **a b** on point **k**. And because by Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle **h d f** is a right angle (since angle **a d f** is a right angle by hypothesis), it is clear by Proposition 47 of Book 1 <note>The Pythagorean theorem.</note> that line **f h** is greater than line **f d**. And if from point **g** a line is drawn parallel to line **f d** (by Proposition 31 of Book 1), which we shall call **g m**: then by Propositions 29 and 4 of Book 6, and 47 of Book 1, line **g h** will be greater than line **e d**: and the same will be true for all points given between points **f** and **h**. Likewise, from point **h**, let a line be drawn parallel to line **d c**, which we shall call **h n**. And since by Proposition 32 of Book 1 angle **a c d** is acute, then by Proposition 13 of Book 1 angle **i c d** will be obtuse: therefore by Proposition 29 of Book 1 angle **i n h** is obtuse: therefore by Proposition 19 of Book 1 and Proposition 4 of Book 6, line **h i** is greater than **d c**. The same is done for all points of line **h k**. It is therefore clear that for the same angle formed at the center of the eye, larger parts of a slanted line are always subtended than parts of a line directly opposite the eye. Therefore, the parts of the surface of a visible thing directly opposite the eye or eyes, equally distant from the point of the axis or the point of connection, are presented to the visual power in the same way (by theorem 45 of Book 3 of this work); because of this, that whole surface and all the subtle details within it are seen more perfectly. A surface slanted to the sight, however, acquires an uncertain appearance <note>original: "formam dubitabilem"; a shape that is difficult for the mind to resolve clearly.</note>, whether it is seen by one eye or by both, and whether that form reaches the eye through the axes or outside the axes—even if the distance of that slanted surface is moderate.

Thus, those total surfaces are established upon the visual surfaces as if compressed <note>original: "congregatæ" – literally "gathered together" or "crowded," referring to the way perspective shrinks the perceived area of a slanted object.</note> because of their slant. ### *34. When there is an excessive distance: an object slanted away from the eyes sometimes appears directly opposite. Alhazen [Book 2], [Proposition] 29.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the angle of vision. A right-angled triangle is formed with the vertex 'a' on the far right, representing the center of vision (the eye). A vertical line on the left represents the object 'bc', with 'c' at the top and 'b' at the bottom. A diagonal line 'ac' and a horizontal line 'ab' connect the eye to the ends of the object.</image-desc>

Since the quantity of distance is measured according to the size of the diameters of the thing seen (as is clear from proposition 10 of this book), the "excessiveness" of distance is also measured relative to the diameters of the thing seen. A distance that is not too great for a large visible object is excessive for a smaller one; for the larger and smaller are not perceived by the sight in the same way at the same distance, as is clear from propositions 7 and 20 of this book. Therefore, let the center of sight be **a**, and let the slanted visible object be **b c**, one of whose ends, **b**, is closer to the sight. Let that object be seen under the angle **b a c**. By the argument of propositions 26 and 20 of this book, angle **b a c** will be smaller than if the object **b c** were seen directly from its nearest end to the sight (which is **a**). But by proposition 11 of this book, in all things seen, the ratio of the greater distance to the lesser distance is greater than the ratio of the greater angle to the lesser angle. In an excessive distance, however, the ratio of the distance of one end of the object (such as **c** in this case) to the distance of the other end (such as **b**) is an imperceptible difference—as is the ratio of the longer line **a c** to the shorter line **a b**. Therefore, the difference between the angles themselves is much more imperceptible. Thus, at a very great distance, **b c** will appear as if it were directly opposite the eyes, even though it is slanted. And this is what was proposed.

### *35. Every visible thing existing outside the common axis, but perceived in only one visual axis—either through rays near the axis, or even through rays near both visual axes—appears to be closer to the common axis than its true position.*

For the radial axis, as is clear from proposition 37 of book 3 of this work, always carries the point it strikes to the middle point of the common nerve <note>The optic chiasm, where the visual information from both eyes meets.</note>, where the end of the common axis always resides. When the sight grasps a visible thing as it is, and the form is established in the cavity of the common nerve in one place—continuous with itself according to the continuation of the object—the point of the object that is on the radial axis (even if it is not on the common axis) nonetheless appears in a place closer to the common axis than its true location. Then the remaining points are also seen in a place closer to the common axis than they truly are, because they are continuous with the part near the end of the axis. And if the axes of both eyes concur on some visible thing outside the common axis, that thing will then appear in a place closer to the common axis than its true location. However, this rarely happens, because when the visual axes concur on a visible object, the common axis usually passes through that object. It is rare for the axes of both eyes to meet on an object outside the common axis except through strain or some impediment forcing the sight to do so. Hence, this arrangement is not natural to the eyes; if such an arrangement were very common, it would happen in every act of vision or in most of them, which is not true. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*37. Of surfaces lying below the eye, those farther from the sight appear higher. Euclid, 10th theorem of Optics.*

Let the center of sight *a* be placed in a higher position than the surface of the object seen, in which are lines *b e*, *e d*, *d g*: and let lines *a b*, *a e*, *a d*, *a g* be drawn. For the sake of example, let the position be such that line *a b* is perpendicular to line *b g*, in which lines *b e*, *e d*, *d g* are placed: since in other positions the diversity is greater. I say that line *d g* appears higher than line *d e*, and line *d e* higher than line *b e*. For let a point *z* be taken on line *b e*, from which a line *z i* is drawn perpendicular to line *b e* by Proposition 11 of Book 1. Therefore, since the forms of points *g*, *d*, *e* proceeding to the sight pass through line *z i* before they reach point *a*, the center of sight: let it be that line *g a* cuts line *z i* at point *i*, line *d a* at point *t*, and line *e a* at point *k*. Because point *i* is more elevated than point *t*, and point *t* than point *k*: because line *a t* is greater than line *a i*, and line *a k* is greater than line *a t* by Proposition 19 of Book 1: and on the line where point *i* is, there is also point *g*; and on the line where point *t* is, there is also point *d*; and on the line where point *k* is, there is also point *e*. By the perception of points *d* and *g*, line *d g* is seen; and by points *e* and *d*, line *e d* is seen. It is clear, there-
<margin>b</margin> fore, that line *g d* will appear more elevated than line *d e*: and similarly *d e* will appear more elevated than line *b e*. For whichever point's form, in multiplying itself toward the sight, is more elevated, this appears higher to the sight by the 1st Supposition of this book, because it is offered to the sight in a higher position, and is formed on the surface of the sight according to that manner. The proposition is therefore evident. And it is clear from this that when the sight is greatly exalted <note>original: "exaltato uisu" – when the eyes are positioned very high up.</note>, flat surfaces lying far from the sight will appear concave: for the forms of such points tend toward the sight in the manner of a circumference around the center of sight because of the equality of the visual power. The proposition is therefore evident.

*38. Of surfaces lying above the sight, those farther from the sight appear lower <note>original: "decliuiores" – sloping downward or lower in the field of view.</note>. Euclid, 11th theorem of Optics.*

Let the center of sight be point *a* placed in a lower position than the surface of the object seen, in which are lines *b e*, *e d*, *d g*: and let lines *a b*, *a e*, *a d*, *a g* be drawn as in the preceding, of which *a b* is perpendicular to the surface placed above the sight. ### _39. Of equal magnitudes standing upright beneath the same level of sight, the more remote appear higher. Euclid, 13th theorem of the Optics._ <note>Witelo is referencing Euclid’s "Optica," a foundational Greek text on the geometry of vision.</note>

Let the center of vision be point *i*: and let there be equal magnitudes seen, which are standing upright beneath the level of that sight, which are *a b*, *g d*, and *e z*: and let *a b* be further from the sight, then *g d*, and then *e z*: and let the center of the eye, point *i*, be higher than those magnitudes: and let lines *i a*, *i g*, and *i e* be drawn. I say that of those magnitudes, *a b* appears higher than *g d*, and *g d* higher than *e z*. For since line *i a* is more elevated than line *i g*, and line *i g* more elevated than line *i e*, and on the line where the lines *i a*, *i g*, and *i e* fall are points *a*, *g*, and *e*, and by Proposition 37 of this book, the more remote points appear higher to the sight: and indeed the points *a*, *g*, and *e* are on the magnitudes *a b*, *g d*, and *e z*: therefore the magnitude *a b* appears more elevated than the magnitude *g d*, and magnitude *g d* appears higher than *e z*. This is what was proposed. And because an equal part can be cut off from any longer magnitude to match a shorter one: therefore, this present demonstration holds true for all magnitudes positioned beneath the sight: since the more remote always seem higher than they are in truth.

### _40. Of equal magnitudes standing above the sight, the more remote appear more sloped. Euclid, 14th theorem of the Optics._ <note>Here, "more sloped" (decliuiores) means they appear to descend or hang lower in the field of vision as they recede into the distance.</note>

Let the center of vision be point *i*, as in the preceding; and let there be equal magnitudes, *a b*, *g d*, and *e z*, standing positioned above the sight: and let *a b* be more remote from the sight than the others, and *e z* closer to the sight. Therefore, since—as is clear through Proposition 38 of this book—the form coming through line *i b* falls upon the sight in a more sloped manner than the form coming through line *i d*, and the form reaching the sight through line *i d* falls in a more sloped manner than the form coming through line *i z*: but on the line where the lines *i z*, *i d*, and *i b* fall are points *z*, *d*, and *b*, which points are in the magnitudes *a b*, *g d*, and *e z*. It is clear, therefore, that of these magnitudes, that which is *a b* appears more sloped than *g d*, and *g d* than *e z*. And this is what was proposed. Moreover, it is universal in that way which we described in the preceding.

### 42. *When a taller visible object is seen over the top of a shorter one, if the sight approaches along a line falling perpendicularly to the excess of the taller one, a larger part of the taller one is seen; but if the sight recedes along the same line, a smaller part of the taller one is seen. However, if the sight approaches or recedes along another line, the opposite happens. Euclid, 16th theorem of the Optics.*

Let there be, as in the previous proposition, two unequal magnitudes, which are *a b* and *g d*, of which *a b* is the larger. Let the center of vision be at point *e*, positioned on line *e a*, which falls perpendicularly at point *a*, the higher end of line *a b*. Therefore, both magnitudes *a b* and *g d* will lie beneath the sight, since the vertex of the taller one (which is *a*) is on the perpendicular line drawn from the center of vision to the taller magnitude. For let the magnitudes *a b* and *g d* be erected such that point *a* is higher than point *g*, and let the form of some point on line *a b*, which is *z*, reach the eye *e* by passing over the vertex of line *d g*, which is *g*. Let the line along which that form arrives be line *z e*. Thus, under line *z e*, the line *z a* (part of magnitude *a b*) and the entire magnitude *d g* are seen; and the part of line *a b* that is not seen over vertex *g* remains, which is line *z b*. 

Now let the sight move closer to point *a*, so that it is at point *i* on the same line. It is also clear that in this position, some point of line *a b* lower than point *z* reaches the eye, which is point *t*. Let line *t i* be drawn through the vertex *g* to the eye. Therefore, under line *i t*, the part of magnitude *a b* which is *t a* is seen, as well as the entire magnitude *g d*; and the part of line *a b* that is *t b* remains, seen <note>The Latin 'uisa' suggests 'seen', but contextually it likely means 'remains [unseen] as defined by vertex g'.</note> through vertex *g*. And since line *a t* is larger than line *a z*, which was seen when the eye was further away—it is necessary for line *t a* to become larger than line *z a*—because angle *a i t* is larger than angle *a e z* by the 16th proposition of Book 1. Therefore, that which is seen under angle *a i t* is larger than that which is seen under angle *a e z* by the 20th theorem of this book. Thus, line *a t* will appear larger, and by the 19th proposition of Book 1, it is larger than line *a z*. And when the line in which *e* (the center of vision) is located falls perpendicularly to any point of the excess <note>original: "excessus"; referring to the portion of the taller object that stands higher than the shorter one.</note> of line *a b* over line *g d*, the demonstration is the same. It is clear, therefore, that as the sight approaches, the portion of line *a b* appearing above the other always becomes larger, and as the sight recedes, it becomes smaller. And this is the first part of the proposition. 

However, along another line which is perpendicular to line *a b*, but does not fall on point *a* or any point of the excess, but on some other point of line *a b* lower than the entire excess of line *a b* over line *g d* (such as at point *f*): as the sight approaches or recedes, the opposite happens. For as the sight approaches, less of the total magnitude *a b* is seen over vertex *g*, and as it recedes, more is seen. For when the eye is at point *e*, the form of line *z a* will be multiplied <note>original: "multiplicabitur"; in this context, it means the visual image is conveyed or projected.</note> to the eye; but as the sight approaches to point *i*, and lines *e g z* and *i g t* are drawn, it is clear that those lines will intersect at point *g*, and the form of any of the points of line *z t* will not reach the eye, but only the form of line *t a*, which is necessarily smaller than line *z a*. Therefore, the proposition is clear.
