### 44. In the perception of position, an error occurs in the discerning faculty due to the imbalanced arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible thing. Alhazen 24.35.46.53.58.64.66.69 n 3. <note>Witelo refers to the "eight circumstances"—light, distance, position, size, solidity, transparency, time, and health of the eye—which the scientist Alhazen identified as the necessary conditions for correct vision.</note>

For from an imbalance of light, an error occurs in the discerning faculty in the perception of position: as if in a night that is not dark something slightly deviates from the sight: then a straightness of position will be estimated in it because of the weakness of the light departing from its balanced state. Also, excessive distance induces error in the perception of position: whence a visible thing very far from the sight and slanted to the sight, will seem directly opposite according to the 34th proposition of this book. Imbalance of position also causes error in the perception of position: for when the visual axis <term>visual axis: the central line of sight passing through the middle of the pupil</term> falls on a body at a balanced distance opposite the sight, and another body is taken far removed from the axis, and slanted slightly upon the imaginary line upon which the radial axis falls perpendicularly: then the sight does not comprehend the slant of that body because of the position departing from the balanced state: since there is no full comprehension of bodies placed far from the axis by the 45th theorem of Book 3 of this work: and so because of this error a thing placed obliquely opposite the eyes will be judged to be directly opposite. Imbalance of size also effects an error in the perception of position: since if a mustard seed <note original="granum sinapis">The author uses a mustard seed as a standard example of a tiny object.</note> were slanted from the eyes, it nevertheless seems as if it were directly opposite: because its slant cannot be comprehended because of the smallness of the body: nor indeed is the slant of this seed sensible from the common axis falling orthogonally upon visible things, according to which the obliquity of seen things is discerned with respect to the sight: since the distance between this axis and the edges of the seed is not fully discerned, which is as if the smallest line of all sensible lines. From imbalanced solidity <note>In this context, solidity refers to the density or opacity of an object.</note> an error also occurs to the sight in position: since if the position of a rare body, with respect to the sight, were slanted, its slant will be hidden, and perhaps it will seem to be directly opposite: for one of the extremities of that body will be considered at the same distance as the other, even though they are different: and this happens because of excessive rarity not definitively terminating the operation of the visible things, and inducing uncertainty in the size of the angle under which the vision occurs. Imbalanced transparency also effects an error for the sight in position: for if a seen body is presented to the sight under a small obliquity in dark, dense air, as happens in the twilight hours, the slant will be hidden, which would be evident in clear, bright air: therefore, let there be an error in the position of the opposition of the body to the sight. From an imbalanced amount of time there is also an error to the sight in position: as when something occurs to the sight suddenly, which immediately recedes: for this, perhaps directly opposite the sight, will be considered slanted, or conversely, if it were slanted to the sight, perhaps it will be considered straight. Also from the disposition of the sight in health there is an error to the sight in position: as if from some distance, even if balanced, some body in opposition to the sight is slightly slanted: for then the sight being weak, the slant will not be felt, even though it is a slant according to the truth. Thus, therefore, in the perception of position, an error occurs to the discerning faculty from the imbalanced arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible thing, as was proposed.

...from the circularity of the form described on the surface of the eye; and similarly, the circularity of any of the parts of the surface of the seen object is understood. **46. A rectilinear figure is understood by sight through the perception of its boundaries.**
Since a figure is that which is contained by a boundary or boundaries, and the boundaries of figures are lines, these are perceived by a sight that is not deceived according to their arrangement on the surface of the eye, just as their arrangement exists on the surface of the seen object. It is clear, therefore, that the perception of these lines by the sight is the perception of the figure contained within them, of which those are the boundaries. And this is what was proposed. But in all these things, the sight requires a moderate distance and other proper circumstances due to the sight, lest a deception perhaps occurs within the sight itself.

<margin>Alhazen 35, n. 2. <note>Witelo is referencing the work of the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose "Book of Optics" was a primary source for this text.</note></margin> **47. The flatness of a surface directly opposite the sight at a moderate distance is understood from the perception of the equality of the distance of its parts and the similarity of their arrangement.**

<image-desc>A perspective geometric diagram illustrating a pyramid-like structure. The vertex is labeled 'e' (representing the eye/center of vision). A perpendicular line drops from 'e' to point 'f' at the center of a rectangular base defined by points 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'. Rays connect 'e' to the four corners 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'. Let the flat surface be *a b c d*, and let the center of sight be *e*. From this center, let a perpendicular line *e f* be drawn to the given surface. And since that surface is directly opposite the sight, so that the perpendicular falls upon the middle point of that surface, let lines *e a, e b, e c, e d* also be extended to points *a, b, c, d* which are equally distant from point *f*. Let the lines *f a, f b, f c, f d* be joined; all of these will be equal because of their equal distance from point *f*. Since all those lines *f a, f b, f c, f d*, by the definition of a line erected upon a surface, are perpendicular to line *e f*, it is clear by the 4th proposition of Book 1 <note>original: "4 p 1"; a reference to Euclid's Elements.</note> that the lines *e a, e b, e c, e d* are equal. Therefore, the surface *a b c d* is equally distant from the sight according to those boundaries. Furthermore, if other lines are extended from the center of sight to other points equally distant from point *f*, the equality of all of them to each other is concluded from the preceding arguments. Therefore, the whole surface, according to all its parts equally distant in every direction from point *f*, reaches the sight in a similar manner. Thus, the whole surface will be seen as flat from the perception of the equality of the distance of its parts and the similarity of their arrangement. And this is what was proposed. Even if the radial axes do not fall exactly in the middle, it must nonetheless be demonstrated by the same reasoning; for the boundaries of any parts of the surface will always be straight lines. Therefore, the surface is flat.

<margin>Alhazen 33, n. 2.</margin> **48. The convexity of a surface is understood by sight from the proximity of the middle parts and the equal distance of the outer parts.**

For when a convex surface is placed directly opposite the sight at a moderate distance, then—since every regular convex surface is part of some sphere, round column, or round pyramid according to the 118th theorem of Book 1 of this work—if that surface opposite the sight is part of a spherical surface, and if a straight line is drawn from the center of sight to the center of the sphere, and many other lines besides the center line are extended, it is clear by the 72nd theorem of Book 1 that only that line which passes through the center is perpendicular to the spherical surface. All other lines extended from the center of sight to that spherical surface fall upon that surface obliquely. Therefore, by the 8th proposition of Book 3 <note>Another reference to Euclid.</note>, the part of the perpendicular lying between the center of sight and the spherical surface will be the shortest of all other lines. Therefore, the greatest approximation to the sight occurs along that line. All circles described on the surface of the sphere relative to the point where that perpendicular falls will be closer to the sight at those points, and according to other lines falling obliquely, they will be further from the sight. This is because all lines closer to the perpendicular line in the said manner are smaller than those further away; for by the aforementioned 8th proposition of Book 3, all lines extended from the center of sight to the peripheries of the larger circles are longer than the lines closer to the perpendicular itself. From the understanding, therefore, of the proximity of the middle parts in 그 surface and the distance of the other parts which are at the boundaries, there appears a greater elevation of the middle parts than of the extremes. From this inequality of the elevation of the surface parts, the <term>gibbositas</term> <note>From the Latin "gibbus," meaning a hump or swelling; refers to the outward bulge of a convex shape.</note> is seen, which is the cause of convexity. And since at every point of a spherical surface, great circles passing through the center of that sphere intersect each other, and all lines that approach the shortest line equally on both sides are equal, therefore, at an equal distance from the perpendicular, there is an equality of all lines extended to the sphere's surface from the center of sight. Thus, the curvature of the bulge appears equal according to every difference of position on spherical surfaces, especially when they are directly opposite the eyes. If, however, the convex surface opposite the sight were part of a round columnar or pyramidal surface, then the same demonstration would hold by extending perpendicular lines from the center...

*49. The concavity of a surface is understood by sight from the distance of the middle parts and the equal proximity of the extreme parts. Alhazen, Book 3, Chapter 34, Note 2.*

The proof must be demonstrated by the same means as the preceding one, and similarly run through every surface. For, according to Proposition 8 of Book 3 <note>References are to Euclid’s *Elements*.</note>, a line produced from the center of sight to the center of a sphere or circle is the longest of all because it contains the diameter; and those lines closer to it are longer than the more distant ones, and all lines equally distant from it are equal. Therefore, the boundaries of that surface will appear as arcs, and the entire surface will appear concave. And if those surfaces are slanted to the sight, whether the equality of the boundaries is above, below, to the right, or to the left, it must always be demonstrated by the same principle. The proposition is therefore clear.

*50. When the center of the opening of the uvea and the circumference of a circle exist in the same surface: the circumference appears to approach a certain straightness. Euclid in the preface and the 22nd theorem of the Optics.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating optical perspective on a circular arc. A series of points labeled g, c, i, z, e, d, b are marked along an arc. An external point 'a' (representing the eye/visual center) has lines of sight radiating to each point on the arc. A center point 'k' also has radial lines extending to the same points. Point 'z' is the vertex of the arc directly aligned with points 'k' and 'a'.</image-desc>

Let the center of the <term>opening of the uvea</term> <note>The pupil of the eye.</note> be point *a*, existing in the same surface as the circumference of the seen circle: such that the flat surface of the circle, imagined to be extended, would pass through the center of the sphere of the eye. Let the circumference of that circle be *gb*, and its center *k*; and from the points of that circumference, let many lines be drawn to the sight *a*: which are *ba, da, ea, za, ia, ca, ga*. Along these lines, the forms of those points reach the sight. I say that the arc *bg* appears to the sight as a straight line. For let lines *kb, kd, ke, kz, ki, kc, kg* be drawn from the center of that circle. Since, therefore, line *kb* is seen under angle *kab*, and line *kd* under angle *kad*, which is smaller than angle *kab* (because it is a part of it); therefore, by the 20th proposition of this book, it is clear that line *kb* will appear longer than *kd*, because it is seen under a larger angle. Similarly, line *kd* will appear longer than *ke*, and *ke* longer than *kz*. In the same way, *kg* will appear longer than *kc*, and *kc* longer than *ki*, and *ki* longer than *kz*. Also, point *z* among all the given points, because it falls on the perpendicular *ak*, will appear closer to the center *k* than point *e*, and point *e* closer than point *d*, and point *d* closer than point *b*. In the appearance to the sight, therefore, something of the curvature of arc *zb* is taken away. The same applies to arc *zg*. Therefore, the arc *gb* seems to approach straightness. Since, by Proposition 8 of Book 3, line *az* is the shortest of all, and line *ae* is shorter than line *ad*, and *ad* shorter than *ab*: it is clear that some of the perceived curvature remains in the sight; and thus the entire periphery will not appear as a straight line, but as somewhat approaching straightness. The proposition is therefore clear. This same thing happens to the convex and concave parts of the periphery of a circle positioned opposite the sight. Because if a perpendicular is drawn from point *z* onto line *az*, then there is no great difference to the sight between the arc and the tangent line when the vision occurs over a great distance; but when the sight is close, a greater convexity or concavity is perceived and appears more clearly. But if the center of the eye and the circle are not in the same surface, then the circumference of the circle will appear curved; because then the arrangement of the parts of the circular line reaches the sight according to its own position and proper being, and it is depicted according to its curvature on the surface of the eye, although sometimes the spherical form of that curvature varies in some way.

*51. When the circle and the center of the opening of the uvea are in the same surface: less than a semicircle is seen.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram featuring a circle with a horizontal diameter marked by points 'b' and 'e'. Above the circle, an external point 'a' is shown with two straight lines 'ab' and 'ae' that are tangent to the circle at the endpoints of the diameter. Other points 'c' and 'd' are indicated on the circle's upper arc.</image-desc>

Let the center of the opening of the uvea be point *a*, and let the circle be *bcd*, whose diameter is *be*, existing in the same flat surface. Let the arc *bcd* be seen: I say that less than a semicircle will be seen. For if the arc *bcd* which is seen were a semicircle, it would be necessary for the lines *ab* and *ae* to fall upon the endpoints of the diameter *be*; otherwise, a semicircle will not be seen, because it is only the diameter that divides a circle into equal parts, according to the 17th definition of Book 1. Therefore, the lines *ab* and *ae* will always be tangent to the circle, since they are produced from the endpoints of the diameter. It is clear, therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 3, that each line will contain a right angle with the diameter *be*. Thus, the triangle *abe* would have two right angles plus a third angle; which is contrary to Proposition 32 of Book 1, and impossible. The proposition is therefore clear.

**52.** *When the center of the aperture of the uvea <note>original: "foraminis uueæ"; the uvea refers to the iris, and its aperture is the pupil, which medieval opticians considered the entry point for visual forms</note> is located on the circumference or at the center of a circle, the entire circle is seen.*

Let the center of the aperture of the uvea be point **a** on the circumference of circle **db**: I say that the entire circle **db** will be seen. For there is no point in the entire circle from which a straight line cannot be drawn to any given point on the circumference. And because, as was shown by the 2nd theorem of Book 3 of this work, it is possible to see only that object where straight lines can be drawn between any point on it and some point on the surface of the eye: therefore, the forms of all points of the circle can reach the sight with no external body hindering them. Thus, the entire circle can be seen according to all its points when the center of the aperture of the uvea is placed on the circumference of that circle. And since, with the center of the aperture of the uvea existing at the center of the circle, all lines drawable from the points of the circumference to the center will still reach the sight itself: it is clear, because vision occurs along the lines which are drawn from the points of the circumference to the center of sight, according to the 17th theorem of Book 3 of this work. And this is what was proposed.

**53.** *When the center of the eye is located on a line standing perpendicularly from the center of a circle over the surface of the circle, or at the end of a line slanted toward the surface of the circle that is equal to the radius: all diameters produced in that same circle will appear equal to the sight. Euclid, theorems 35 and 36 of the Optics.*

Let there be a circle **deg**, whose center is point **a**: let line **ab** be erected perpendicularly over the surface of the circle: and let diameters **ez** and **dg** be drawn: and let the center of the eye be placed on line **ab** at point **b**. I say that all diameters drawn across the surface of the circle, such as **ez** and **dg**, will appear equal to one another. For let lines **be**, **bz**, **bd**, and **bg** be drawn from the center of sight. Therefore, since line **az** is equal to line **ag**, and line **ba** is common to both triangles <note>original: "trigonis"</note> **abg** and **abz**, and the angles at the center **a** are also equal because they are right angles: it is clear by Proposition 4 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid’s *Elements*</note> that line **bg** is equal to line **bz**, and angle **abz** is equal to angle **abg**. In the same way, angle **abd** will be equal to angle **abe**, and all angles at the center of sight are equal to each other. Therefore, by the 19th or 20th theorem of this book, all radii <note>original: "semidiametri"</note> appear equal; and indeed the diameters themselves also appear equal, for everything is seen under equal angles, both the whole diameters and their parts. 

Furthermore, all lines parallel to either of the diameters appear smaller than the diameters, and those further away appear smaller than those closer: which is clear if line **fh** is drawn parallel to diameter **dg**, and line **bk** falls upon its midpoint **k**: and let lines **bf**, **bh**, and **ak** be joined. By Proposition 3 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid’s *Elements*</note>, line **ak** will be perpendicular to line **fh**, because coming from the center it divides it into equal parts at point **k**. Thus, because in triangles **bag** and **bkh** the angles **bag** and **bkh** are right angles—**bag** by hypothesis and **bkh** by the 22nd theorem of Book 1 of this work—and line **bk** is greater than line **ba**, and line **ag** is greater than line **kh**: therefore, by the 37th theorem of Book 1 of this work, angle **bhk** is greater than angle **bga**. Similarly, angle **bfh** will be greater than angle **bda**. Therefore, in triangles **dbg** and **fbh**, angle **dbg** will be greater than angle **fbh** by Proposition 32 of Book 1. Thus, diameter **dg** will appear larger than line **fh** by the 20th theorem of this book. The same is also true for all other lines parallel to the diameter, and can be demonstrated in respect to the diameter itself and to each other. Therefore, any smaller line will appear smaller: and so the whole circle will be seen in its own proper shape. And this is the first part of the proposition.

If, however, line **ab** is not perpendicular to the surface of the circle, but stands at a slant, yet is nonetheless equal to the radius of the circle, the diameters **dg** and **ze** will still appear equal when the center of sight is at point **b**. For since, by hypothesis, the radius **za** is equal to line **ab**, and the radius **ae** is equal to the same: it is clear that lines **ab**, **ae**, and **az** are equal. If, therefore, a circle were described around point **a** with the magnitude of radius **ea** on the surface in which lines **ae**, **az**, and **ab** lie: it is clear that it will pass through point **b**. Therefore, by Proposition 31 of Book 3 <note>which states that an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle</note>, angle **ebz** is a right angle. Similarly, it will be shown that angle **gbd** is a right angle. And because all right angles are equal, and objects seen under equal angles appear equal according to the 19th or 20th theorem of this book: it is clear that all diameters of that circle, however many are drawn, will appear equal, just as diameter **ez** appears equal to diameter **gd**. This is the second part of the proposition. Therefore, everything that was proposed is clear.

Euclid, second part of theorems 36 and 38 of the Optics.*

Let there be a circle **bgde**, whose center is **a**: and let the center of sight be **z**: and let line **az** not be erect, but falling obliquely upon—

And every one of these angles closer to angle **ezk** is smaller than one farther away; and two angles approaching angle **ezk** equally from both sides, such as angles **izk** and **pzk**, are equal to each other. Therefore, by theorem 20 of this book, diameter **gd** will appear larger than diameter **it**. And since, as was shown by theorem 39 of Book 1 of this work, angle **ezi** is greater than angle **eza**, while to the middle of both bases of triangles **tei** and **aeb**, which are **it** and **ab**...

### 57. *When the center of vision is located on a line erected over the surface of a square at the point of intersection of the two diagonals: the sides of the square appear equal, and the diagonals appear equal. Euclid, Theorem 59 of the Optics.*

Let there be a square **a b g d**: and let the diagonals **a g** and **b d** be drawn within it: and let their intersection be **e**: let **e z** be raised over the surface of the square by Proposition 12 of Book 11 <note>of Euclid’s Elements, regarding lines perpendicular to a plane</note>: and let the eye be placed at some point on the line **e z**, such as at **z**: and let lines **z a**, **z b**, **z d**, and **z g** be drawn. Therefore, because by theorem 40 of Book 1 of this work, the halves of the diagonals are equal to each other, such as **d e** and **g e**, and line **e z** is common to the two triangles **d z e** and **g z e**, and the angles around **e** are right angles by the definition of a line erected over a surface: by Proposition 4 of Book 1, the base **z g** will be equal to the base **z d**, and angle **e z g** equal to angle **e z d**: therefore, line **d e** will be seen as equal to line **g e** by Proposition 20 of this book. And similarly by the same reasoning, because angle **a z e** is equal to angle **b z e**, the line **a e** will be seen as equal to line **b e**: also the whole line **d b** will appear equal to the whole line **a g**.

<image-desc>A perspective diagram of a square with vertices a, b, g, and d and diagonals intersecting at point e. A vertical line rises from e to a point z, from which lines are drawn to each vertex of the square base, forming a pyramid-like figure.</image-desc>

And since line **g z** is equal to line **b z**, and line **a z** equal to line **d z**, and line **a b** is equal to **g d** itself—since they are sides of the same square—and thus the three sides of one triangle are equal to the three sides of the other: therefore, by Proposition 8 of Book 1, the angles contained by equal sides are equal: thus all the sides of the square itself will appear equal in this way. And this is the proposition: since at every point of line **e z** the demonstration is the same, always concluding by Proposition 20 of this book.

*59. If a straight line falls obliquely from the center of vision to the midpoint of a square surface, and it forms unequal angles with the diagonals—regardless of whether that line is longer or shorter than the semi-diagonal—the diagonals of the square will always appear unequal. (Euclid, Theorem 61 of the Optics).*

Let the arrangement from the previous section remain. Let line **fe** <note>The line of sight from point f to the center of the square e</note> contain unequal angles with the diagonals, so that angle **afe** is unequal to angle **fec**. Let a circle be drawn around the square about center **e**, as before. If line **fe** is longer than the semi-diagonal **ae**, it will be concluded by Proposition 55 of this book that the diameters of the circle (which are the diagonals of the proposed square) appear unequal. If, however, line **fe** is shorter than the semi-diagonal **ae**, then similarly by Proposition 56 of this book, it will be proven that the diagonals of the square appear unequal. Nevertheless, the nature of these inequalities occurs according to the manner proposed there regarding circles, following the difference of the angles falling on either side. Thus, the proposition is clear. And in the same way, it can be easily demonstrated for other figures—such as a rectangle that is longer in one part, or for hexagons, octagons, and universally for all polygons with an even number of angles—that their diagonals sometimes appear equal and sometimes unequal. We have not seen fit to dwell on such matters, because any researcher of this science will easily comprehend this.

*60. When the center of the opening of the uvea <note>term: "uvea" (the pigmented layer of the eye, specifically referring here to the pupil)</note> is positioned at the midpoint of any straight-lined shape, the shape will always appear to the eye in its proper form.*

For example, let the given figure be a square. Let the midpoint be found by Theorem 40 of this book, in which the center of the opening of the uvea is placed—which is to say, the eye is placed directly over that point. And since from that point, equal or proportional lines can be drawn to every point of the sides and angles (just as they are on the surface itself), it is clear that the form of every one of those points will be seen. Because of the equality of the radial lines to those lines on the surface, the shape will be formed on the surface of the eye just as it is externally on the surface of the object being seen. It is clear, therefore, that the total form and shape of that surface will be seen exactly according to its proper configuration, whatever shape it may be. This is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a square abcd in perspective, forming a trapezoidal shape. *61. A square figure, when seen from a distance with only one side directly facing the sight, appears longer in one direction than the other.*

Let there be a square figure **abcd**, with the center of vision at **e**. Let the side of the square, which is **ab**, be placed directly opposite the sight. It is clear, then, that the other sides will be placed obliquely to the sight. But by Proposition 26 of this book, a quantity placed obliquely to the sight appears smaller, because it is seen under a smaller angle. However, the side directly opposite the sight is seen in its proper size relative to the oblique side; for all things directly opposite the eyes are seen under a larger angle than equal things that are placed obliquely to the eyes. Therefore, the entire square figure will appear longer in one part <note>i.e., it will look like a rectangle rather than a square</note>. Indeed, a square surface seen from a distance appears elongated as proposed; but it is also possible for a rectangle to appear square to the sight, such as if its shorter side is placed directly opposite the eye and its longer side obliquely. In that case, because of the arrangement of the slant, it can happen that the longer side appears equal to the shorter one. Many similar things happen from this root principle, such as irregularities in any equilateral and equiangular polygonal shapes. In others, too, a diversity of their true form occurs in vision; we leave all these to the diligence of those inquiring into particulars, for it is sufficient for us to have proposed this principle universally.

### 63. Three-dimensionality is grasped by the sight; in certain bodies by itself, and in others with the help of the faculty of judgment.

Since <term>three-dimensionality</term> <note>original: "corporeitas"; the quality of being a solid, three-dimensional body</note> is the extension of a body according to three dimensions: I say that it is sometimes grasped in certain bodies by the sight on its own. For some bodies are contained by flat surfaces cutting each other at right or oblique angles to one another; and some by concave and convex surfaces; and some by convex and flat surfaces; and some by concave and flat surfaces; and some by various intersecting convex, concave, and flat surfaces; and some are contained by only a single round surface.

Therefore, a body contained by intersecting surfaces, of which one surface is flat: when its surface is opposite the sight in a direct or oblique orientation—provided that the common section <note>The edge where two surfaces meet</note> of the two surfaces is visible, and that both intersecting surfaces meet the sight at the same time—then the extension of the body according to length, width, and depth will be grasped by the sight. In this way, three-dimensionality will be perceived. Also, bodies whose surface is convex (whether it be one or many), when they are placed opposite the sight directly or obliquely, the distances of their parts from the sight will be unequal, and the middle of its convexity will be closer to the extremities of the sight (by Proposition 8 of Book 3); the rest of its parts will be further from the sight. By this perception, the sight senses three-dimensionality, because it perceives the depth of the parts further away from itself relative to the parts closer to it; and with this, it perceives the length and width dimensions of those bodies.

Also, the concavity of a concave body can be perceived by the sight at a moderate distance: for then, because its center is furthest removed from the sight (by Proposition 8 of Book 3, as before), the depth of that body is grasped by the sight due to the greater distance of one part relative to others; consequently, length and width are also evident. But if there are many intersecting surfaces within it, whose common sections offer themselves to the sight, their three-dimensionality is grasped by the sight when the slant of those surfaces is felt. 

In all these cases, however, a moderate distance must be maintained, because at very great distances it is otherwise: for then a body is not grasped by sight alone through the vision of its surface, but with the help of the higher faculty of the soul. For there is a principle resting in the soul from the habit of seeing: and it is such that nothing is seen except a body. Therefore, when the sight sees any visible surface, the <term>judgmental faculty</term> <note>original: "uirtus iudicatiua"; the reasoning part of the mind that interprets sensory input based on experience</note> of the soul immediately concludes that the viewer sees a body, even though the sight does not grasp its extension into the depth. For the sight will grasp width and length on its own through the perception of any surface (by Theorem 17 and Proposition 3 of this book), but it will not always grasp the depth of bodies (which is their third dimension) except with the help of the higher faculty of the soul itself. The proposition is therefore clear.

Therefore (by Proposition 16 of Book 3), those two lines **ze** and **zb** are tangent to the circle **dgeb**...

### 65. To a very distant eye, the convex or concave surface of a sphere appears flat. Euclid’s *Optics*, Theorem 25.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a triangle with its vertex at point 'e' and its base at points 'b' and 'd' on a circular arc. Point 'a' is inside the triangle, and point 'c' is on the arc between 'b' and 'd'. Lines connect 'e' to 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'.</image-desc>

Let there be a sphere whose center is **a**: and in it a <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere itself, dividing it into two equal halves</note> **bcd**: and let the center of sight be **e**: and let lines **ea**, **eb**, **ec**, and **ed** be drawn. It is clear through Proposition 50 of this book that because the form of the arc **bcd** falls upon the sight **e** from a great distance, the incidence of the arc **bcd** approaches straightness: and the same is true of any other arcs upon which the sight falls on the entire given sphere. Therefore, the total portion of the convex surface of the sphere upon which the sight falls appears flat: and just as the arcs of the circles describable on its surface approach the straightness of lines, so the surface of the total sphere approaches flatness. And by the same reasoning, a demonstration can be made regarding the concave surface of that sphere. For since no part of the thing seen appears to be more distant than another, it is necessary for the entire surface of the thing seen to appear as one single arrangement. Thus, when the entire convex or concave body is at a maximal distance from the sight, the sight will not grasp the concavity or convexity, but will grasp it as if it were flat: because the positions of the parts of its surface in relation to one another are not grasped by the sight in any diversity, but they reach the sight according to an equal continuity, and they are figured in the diversity of position on the surface of the eye itself: hence they are judged to be flat, and the total surface of the thing seen will be seen as flat. And for this reason, the shapes of the surfaces of the sun and moon appear flat: for their <term>semidiameters</term> <note>radii</note> in relation to the line of their distance, which is drawn from the center of sight to the centers of the sun and moon themselves, do not have any <term>sensible proportion</term> <note>meaning the ratio is so small it cannot be perceived by the senses</note>: thus it takes nothing away from the length of the line produced from the center of sight tangent to those spheres through the previous proposition. For the longest line reaching the sight from any point of the convex surface of the sphere itself is the line tangent to the great circle of that sphere: and all those lines are equal to each other through Theorem 58 of Book 1 of this work. And since they do not perceptibly exceed the line produced from the center of sight to the surfaces of those spheres: therefore all those lines seem as if equal to the perpendiculars themselves which pass through the centers of those bodies produced from the center of sight, and the intervening arcs approach straightness: hence the total surfaces appear flat. And this same thing happens for the same reason in all other stars, which because of their maximal distance appear as if they were certain surfaces of small circles. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 66. To a single eye viewing an illuminated convex spherical surface, less than a hemisphere always appears; and the part seen is bounded by a circle. Euclid’s *Optics*, Theorem 23.

Thus, let triangle **bgk**, while side **bk** remains fixed, be understood to be rotated around until it returns to the place where it began: and it is clear that since line **bg** is tangent to circle **dg**, it will touch every point of the surface of the sphere through which it is rotated, and line **kg** by its motion will create a section of a circle, and a pyramid <note>a cone</note> will be formed, whose vertex will be point **b**, which is the center of sight, and its base will be the circle made by the motion of line **kg**: therefore the part seen is contained under a circle. **67. As the eye approaches a convex illuminated sphere, less of the sphere's surface is seen; however, it appears as though more is seen.**

Let there be, as in the previous proposition, a sphere whose center is **a**: let the center of sight also be **b**: and let line **ab** be drawn: and let circle **gbd** be described around diameter **ab**: and let line **eaz** be drawn from point **a** perpendicularly over line **ab** through Proposition 11 of Book 1 <note>original: "per 11 p 1", referring to Euclid’s *Elements*</note>. And because lines **ab** and **ez** are in one plane through Proposition 2 of Book 11: let this plane surface be understood to cut the sphere: it will cut the sphere through Theorem 69 of Book 1 of this work according to a circle, which shall be **gezd**: and the points of intersection of the two proposed circles will be **g** and **d**: and let lines **ga**, **da**, **bg**, and **bd** be drawn: and it is clear, in the manner of the next preceding proposition, that lines **bg** and **bd** are tangent to the sphere, and the part of the sphere **gd** is seen by the eye located at point **b**. 

Therefore, let the eye approach the sphere and be placed at point **c**: and let **ca** be drawn, around which, as a diameter, circle **akcl** is described: and let lines **ck**, **cl**, **ak**, and **al** be drawn: therefore, through the previous proposition, the part of the sphere which is **kl** will be seen by the eye located at point **c**, which is smaller than the part of the sphere **gd** seen by the eye located at point **b**: because the arc falling between the points of tangency of lines **ck** and **cl**, which through Proposition 64 of this book are tangent to the sphere, is smaller than arc **gd**, which falls between the points of tangency of lines **bg** and **bd**: which is clear through Theorem 60 of Book 1 of this work. It is evident, therefore, that as the eye approaches the sphere itself, less of the sphere's surface is seen. 

However, because (as is clear through Theorem 60 of Book 1 of this work) lines **gb** and **ck** converge if they are extended toward point **g**: it is evident through Proposition 16 of Book 1 that angle **kca** is greater than angle **gba**: similarly, angle **acl** is greater than angle **abd**: therefore, the whole angle **kcl** is greater than the whole angle **gbd**. Therefore, the part of the sphere in which arc **kl** exists will be seen under a larger angle than the part of the sphere in which arc **gd** exists. Therefore, through Proposition 20 of this book, the part of the sphere **kl** appears larger to the sight than the part **gd**. And this is what was proposed.

**68. If the line connecting the centers of both eyes is equal to the diameter of an illuminated convex sphere, then a hemisphere is what is seen by both eyes.**

Let the center of the given sphere be **a**: and let its <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on a sphere's surface that has the same diameter as the sphere, such as the equator on a globe.</note> be that whose diameter is **bg**: which, by hypothesis, is equal to the distance between the eyes—that is, the line connecting the centers of both sights, which are **e** and **d**. Let also perpendiculars **bd** and **ge** be drawn from points **b** and **g**, which are made equal through Proposition 3 of Book 1: and let line **ed** be joined: which through Proposition 33 of Book 1 and by hypothesis will be equal and parallel to line **gb**. Let also a perpendicular be drawn from point **a**, the center of the sphere, over line **gb** through Proposition 11 of Book 1: which, when extended to line **de**, cuts it at point **z**. 

It is evident, therefore, through Proposition 29 of Book 1, that line **az** is perpendicular over line **ed**, and through Proposition 28 of Book 1, line **az** will be parallel to line **ge**: therefore, through Proposition 33 of Book 1, it is clear that line **ed** is divided into equal parts at point **z**, because, as is clear from the hypothesis, the eyes are at points **d** and **e**: I say that it is a hemisphere that is seen. For, while line **az** remains fixed, let the parallelogram **abzd** be rotated until it returns to the place where it began: therefore, the moved line **ab** will describe a circle equal to circle **gb**, of which it is the radius: moreover, the great circle of the given sphere is circle **gd** <note>likely a typo in the original for **gb**</note>: therefore, by the movement of line **ab**, a great circle is described: and this divides the sphere into two equal halves. Thus the proposition is clear.

**69. If the line connecting the centers of both eyes is greater than the diameter of an illuminated convex sphere, then more than a hemisphere is seen by both eyes.**

Let the given sphere be that whose center is **a**: and let its great circle be **ed**: and let the centers of both eyes be **b** and **g**: and let the line **bg**, when drawn, be greater than the diameter of the given sphere and its great circle. I say that with both sights, more than a hemisphere will be seen. ### 70. *If the line connecting the centers of both eyes is smaller than the diameter of a convex sphere, less than a hemisphere is seen. Euclid, Theorem 28 of the Optics.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a sphere with center a and diameter f h. Below the sphere are two points, d and e, representing the eyes, connected by a line. Tangent lines b d and g e extend from the sphere's surface through the eye points to converge at a single vertex z further below. Points b and g are on the circle's circumference.</image-desc>

Let there be a given sphere whose center is **a**, and let the diameter of its great circle be **fh**. Let the centers of the eyes be **d** and **e**, and let line **de** be drawn connecting the centers of the eyes, being smaller than diameter **fh**. Let lines be drawn tangent to that circle, which shall be **db** and **eg**. I say that what is seen is less than a hemisphere. For let lines **bd** and **ge** be extended. And since line **de** is smaller than diameter **fh**, it is clear through Theorem 16 of Book 1 of this work that lines **bd** and **ge** will meet beyond both eyes: let the point of meeting, therefore, be point **z**. It is clear through Theorem 58 of Book 1 of this work that since two lines tangent to one circle are drawn from point **z**, which are **zb** and **zg**, the arc **big** is smaller than a semicircle: therefore, less than a semicircle **bg** is seen by eyes **d** and **e**. Therefore, as before, less than a hemisphere will be seen by eyes **d** and **e**. And this is what was proposed.

### 71. *When the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> <note>The "uvea" was historically understood as the middle layer of the eye; its "opening" refers to the pupil.</note> is located on the surface of an illuminated concave sphere, the entire interior surface of the sphere is visible. Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 44.*

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a concave sphere. A point a is located at the top of the interior circumference. Two lines or arcs extend from point a to points b and g on the lower sides of the circle, illustrating the field of view within the concave space.</image-desc>

Let the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> be point **a**, and let there be a given sphere whose great circle is **bag** passing through center **a**. It is clear, therefore, through Proposition 52 of this book, that with the sight so arranged, the entire circle **bag** can be seen. And because many great circles of a sphere intersect at the poles of the sphere, and every point of a sphere is a pole of the sphere, it is clear that all the great circles of the given sphere (which can be imagined through all points of the sphere's surface) will intersect each other at point **a**. Therefore, point **a**, which is the center of the opening of the uvea itself, will be in every one of those great circles. Moreover, all those great circles of the sphere exhaust the entire surface of the sphere, because there is no point on the sphere's surface through which some great circle does not pass. Therefore, with the sight so arranged, the entire concave surface of the sphere will be seen. And this is what was proposed.

### 72. *When the center of the opening of the uvea is inside the surface of an illuminated concave sphere, or outside of it, a circular portion of the sphere will be seen upon which equal lines drawn from the center of sight fall; sometimes a hemisphere will be seen, sometimes a larger portion, and sometimes a smaller portion. Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 44.*

<image-desc>A circular diagram with center point e. A second point a is located inside the circle, positioned slightly above the center e. Points b, c, and d are marked along the circumference of the circle.</image-desc>

Let the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> be point **a**, and let there be a concave sphere whose great circle is **bcd**, and let the center of the sphere be point **e**. If, therefore, the center of sight is at point **e**, the center of the sphere (which is also the center of the great circle **bcd** by the definition of a great circle), then it is manifest through Proposition 52 of this book that the entire circle **bcd** will be seen. But also through the same Proposition 52, all other circles of the underlying hemisphere parallel to circle **bcd** will be seen, since the center of sight will be the pole of all of them. Also, all straight lines drawn from the pole to the periphery of its circle are equal through Theorem 65 of Book 1 of this work. And since all these circles exhaust the entire hemisphere, it is clear that in this position of sight, the entire hemisphere will be seen. But if point **a**, the center of the opening of the uvea, is below the center of the sphere (which is point **e**), then through the same reasoning, less than a hemisphere will be seen. If it is above center **e**, whether it be inside the sphere or outside, then similarly through Theorem 2 of Book 3 of this work, all circles to whose circumferences straight lines can be extended will be seen; therefore, more than a hemisphere will be seen. And if a line drawn from the center of sight to the surface of the sphere falls obliquely upon the surface of that sphere, then it is clear that it also falls obliquely upon the surfaces of many circles; and it can happen that the entire figure of the sphere appears unequal, with certain peripheries of its circles tending toward the shape of a <term>columnar section</term> <note>original: "sectionis columnaris"; this refers to a conic section, likely an ellipse, where a circle viewed at an angle appears elongated.</note> through Propositions 55 and 56 of this book. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 73. *As the eye approaches a concave hemisphere, less of the sphere's surface will be seen; however, it appears that more is seen.*

This can be demonstrated just as Proposition 67 of this book was demonstrated regarding a convex sphere; for the method of demonstration is the same in every respect. Thus, a concave sphere should be figured here as the convex one was there, and the total configuration should be arranged under the same letters, and the conclusion reached through the same steps. These things are said concerning the vision of spheres when their surfaces opposite the sight are entirely luminous by themselves or illuminated from elsewhere. For if this is not the case, although the visibility of the mentioned modes remains in the surfaces of the spheres, they will not actually be seen except by the intervention of light, as is clear from Theorem 3 of this book. Furthermore, according to the diversity of luminosity in the parts of the spherical surface that are seen, new perceptions <note>Latin: *passiones*, often meaning "affects" or "phenomena" in a medieval optical context</note> are generated in the eyes, such as those we now intend to explain.

### 74. *When the diameter of the seen illuminated sphere is greater than the distance between the eyes, and the diameter of the illuminating sphere is equal to or greater than it, and the circle of the base of the vision pyramid is parallel to the circle of the base of the illumination pyramid or touches it internally: the entire base of the vision pyramid appears illuminated to the sight; however, at a greater distance, it appears almost flat.*

This is clear through Theorem 26 or 27 of Book 2 of this work, since given the size of the diameters of these bodies as proposed: then the base of the illumination pyramid <note>The "pyramid" refers to a cone-shaped volume of light or sight lines</note> is either a great circle of the illuminated sphere or parallel to it. The circle which is the base of the vision pyramid, as is clear through Proposition 70 of this book, is always smaller than the great circle of the seen sphere, because, as is clear from the hypothesis, the diameter of the seen sphere is greater than the distance between the eyes. If, therefore, the circumference of the smaller circle is parallel to the circumference of the larger circle, then through Theorem 68 of Book 1, the centers of those two circles lie on the same diameter of the sphere, and the entire base of the vision pyramid is visible to the eyes because it is entirely illuminated. Moreover, the surface appears flat through Proposition 65 of this book. And this is what was proposed. But even if the centers of these circles are shifted until the point of contact of the circumferences, as long as one circle does not cut the other, the entire base of the vision pyramid always appears illuminated. The light on the surface of the seen sphere always appears circular, and the entire base of the pyramid is illuminated; however, the base of the vision pyramid becomes darker toward that part where the contact of those circles occurs, through Theorem 21 of Book 3. Thus the proposition is clear. And what has been shown here regarding two eyes is even more clearly evident if vision occurs with only one eye, through Proposition 66 of this book.

### 75. *If the diameter of the illuminated sphere is greater than the distance between the eyes, and the diameter of the illuminating sphere is equal to or greater than it, and the base of the vision pyramid intersects the base of the illumination pyramid so that both centers of the bases are below the surface of the common section: that common section will be a part of an irregular spherical surface; and the surface will appear flat and protuberant, as if contained by two curved lines of unequal size and curvature.*

Imagine the centers of the bases (which by the preceding proposition are arranged to be on the same diameter of the seen sphere) to be moved so far apart from each other that the circles of the bases intersect to any degree, provided they remain outside both bases below the surface that is common to both those bases. Then that common section will be part of a spherical surface of irregular shape. This is because, as is clear through Theorem 26 or 27 of Book 2, and from Proposition 70 of this book, and as was shown in the next preceding one, the arc of the circle of the illumination pyramid's base is larger than the arc of the circle of the vision pyramid's base. If a middle point were taken on that surface, lines drawn from that point to the peripheries of the arcs would be unequal. Moreover, that surface appears to be flat through Proposition 65 of this book, and it will be protuberant <note>Latin: *gibberosa*, meaning hunchbacked or unevenly curved</note>, as it is contained by the two aforementioned curved lines of unequal size and curvature: because the arc of the circle of the vision pyramid is more curved and a larger portion of its circumference than the arc of the circle of the illumination pyramid's base is a portion of its circumference. This happens because of the inequality of the circles. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 76. *When the base of the vision pyramid of a sphere intersects the base of the illumination pyramid such that their axes contain a right angle: their common section is a quarter of the spherical surface; however, at a greater distance, it appears as a flat surface contained by one straight line and a semicircle.*

That the illumination of any sphere occurs according to a pyramid whose base on the surface of the illuminated sphere is a circle is clear through Theorems 26, 27, and 28 of Book 2. That the base of the vision pyramid of every sphere is also a circle is clear through Propositions 66, 68, 69, and 70 of this book. And since the axes of these pyramids, when extended as per the hypothesis, contain a right angle to each other: then it is clear through Proposition 33 of Book 6 <note>Referring to Euclid's *Elements*</note>, that by drawing a circle from the intersection point of those axes according to the quantity of the semi-diameter of the seen sphere, a quarter of the circle will lie between the axes. And since each of the axes is perpendicular to the surface of the illuminated sphere seen, it is evident through Theorem 111 of Book 1 that each axis will pass through the center of that sphere. Therefore, the point of intersection of the axes is in the center of that sphere, and only that point, which is the center of the sphere, will be common to both axes. Thus, a quarter of a great circle of the sphere will lie between the axes, equidistant from the two points of the two intersections of the circles of the illumination pyramid's base and the vision pyramid's base; the common...

Indeed, the axis of the pyramid of vision <note>The cone of sight lines extending from the eye to the object.</note> falls upon the surface of the circle of the base of the pyramid of illumination <note>The cone of light rays falling upon the object from a light source.</note>, because of its perpendicular position over the axis of that pyramid, as is clear from Proposition 4 of Book 11 of Euclid's *Elements*. ### 77. *When the base of the vision pyramid of a sphere intersects the base of the illumination pyramid, their common section (which neither axis hits) is a portion less than a fourth part of the spherical surface; it appears, however, as a flat surface contained by two arcs of the base circumferences that are nearly equal.*

As was sent forward in the previous proposition, every illumination of a sphere occurs according to a pyramid whose base is a circle, as is clear from several propositions in the second book of this work. Similarly, the base of the pyramid of vision is a circle according to Proposition 66 of this book. It is clear that if these circles, which are the bases of the pyramids, do not intersect—for instance, because they are situated in nearly opposite parts of the sphere's surface (where one part is illuminated and another is seen)—then the incidence of light hitting the sphere's surface will not be perceived by the sight at all. For example, if you place a wooden or wax globe (whose diameter is greater than the distance between the eyes) directly between the eyes and a light, then if the globe is rotated so that the light falling on the spherical surface of the globe becomes somewhat visible, then the illuminated part of the globe's surface, which the circumference of the base of the vision pyramid receives, will be seen. And since that seen part, as it is illuminated, is bounded by the circumference of the base of the illumination pyramid, it is clear that the seen portion of the sphere is less than a fourth part of the sphere's surface. 

Since neither axis of the pyramids hits the surface of the common section, as is clear from the hypothesis, it is evident through Proposition 33 of Book 6 that because the arc dividing that surface—equidistant from the two points of intersection of the circles of the said bases, dividing the whole sphere and that common section surface into equal parts—is less than a quarter of a circle. Since the angle subtended by it is less than a right angle, it is clear that the arc is less than a quarter of a circle; and the seen surface itself appears flat according to Proposition 65 of this book. And because none of those circles or arcs is directly opposite the eyes, each of them is seen in its own curvature, since the form of the points of each of those arcs reaches the sight according to its own position. Therefore, that portion of the common section of the bases of the said pyramids appears as if contained by two equal arcs because the inequality is imperceptible, especially when the vision occurs from a more remote distance according to Proposition 50 of this book. 

It is certain, however, through Theorem 27 of Book 2 and through Proposition 70 of this book, that the arc of the base of the illumination pyramid is part of a larger circle than the arc of the base of the vision pyramid; this is because the diameter of the sphere of the illuminating body <note>such as the Sun</note> is larger than the diameter of the illuminated sphere <note>such as the Moon</note>, and the distance between the eyes is smaller than that. Thus the proposition is clear. From these four theorems, it is clear why the shape of the moon becomes razor-crescent <note>original: *nouacularis*, from *novacula* meaning "razor." This refers to the thin, sharp-pointed crescent moon.</note> when receding from conjunction. 

At the time of conjunction, the moon is not seen unless a solar eclipse occurs, so that the sun's rays—penetrating the transparency of the moon's body because of the difference in density of the lunar body compared to the transparency of the parts of its neighboring sphere, and reaching the sight—make the spherical body of the moon visible; then the moon is seen distinctly according to its shape, but deprived of its own light. In other conjunctions, however, because the rays falling perpendicularly on the lunar body reach the sight either very obliquely or not at all, the body of the moon is not seen, because the base of the vision pyramid falls on the part opposite the base of the illumination pyramid, and neither of those bases intersects the other. 

But when the moon recedes from the sun, these bases begin to intersect each other; then their common section (which is a portion of the surface of the moon's spherical body) is seen. Because of the great distance, that portion of the sphere appears like a flat surface contained by two curved lines according to its convex and concave sides. These appear equal because of the distance, but they are not actually equal: the one on the convex side (the arc of the circle of the illumination pyramid's base) is always part of a larger circle than the one on the concave side (the arc of the circle of the vision pyramid's base). And since the axis of the illumination pyramid is always perpendicular to the body of the sun, as is clear from Theorem 111 of Book 1, the convex side of the moon is always turned toward <note>original: *aversum*, usually "turned away," but here likely a scribe's error for *adversum* (turned toward) or referring to the orientation of the light's boundary.</note> the sun, and the horns always seem to look toward <note>or "regard"</note> the sun. Hence their position always varies according to the position of the sun and according to the latitude of the moon's motion. 

This shape lasts in the moon until the axes of the pyramids intersect each other at right angles (according to Proposition 76 of this book); then the moon will be seen in quadrature <note>The "half-moon" phase, 90 degrees from the sun.</note>, because the fourth part of its sphere lying between the peripheries of the said bases will be seen. In both the first and second quadrature, the arc of illumination, because it is directly opposite the eyes, will appear as a straight line, while the arc of the illumination pyramid remains curved. Once this position changes, the centers of the bases of both pyramids are within the surface of the common section; the moon will then appear gibbous <note>original: *gibberosa*, meaning "humpbacked" or the phase between half and full.</note> and as a flat surface according to Proposition 65 of this book. This will last until the circles of the bases touch each other internally, at which point the moon appears full. And when the centers of the circles of the said bases are placed one over the other, so that both are in a single line—as when those circles become equidistant on the same surface of the moon's sphere (as shown by Theorem 68 of Book 1)—then there will be the true filling of the moon, and the light is carried around equally on every side. Thereafter, as the moon moves toward the hollow of the circles of those bases, it always appears full, though the light is somewhat darkened

### 78. *A round column or convex cylinder viewed with one eye: less than half of the curved surface is seen. Euclid, Theorem 29 of the Optics.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an eye (d) observing a cylinder. The cylinder is illustrated by two circular bases. Lines of sight (d-g and d-b) are tangent to the upper circle at points g and b. The center of the upper circle is marked a, and its diameter is marked by points f and h. From the tangency points g and b, vertical lines extend down to points z and e on the lower circular base, outlining the visible portion of the cylinder's curved surface.</image-desc>

Let there be a round column <term>columna rotunda</term> <note>Witelo uses the term "column" for a cylinder.</note> whose base is the circle **g b**, its diameter **f h**, and its center **a**. Let the center of the eye be point **d** on the plane of that circle. Let line **d a** be drawn, connecting the center of sight with the center of the base circle of the column. Let lines **d b** and **d g** be drawn, which touch the circle **g b** <note>Lines d b and d g are tangents.</note> according to Proposition 17 of Book 3 of the *Elements*. From points **g** and **b**, let two lines of the column’s length <note>Vertical lines or "generators" along the side of the cylinder.</note> be drawn according to Theorem 101 of Book 1 of this work, which shall be **b e** and **g z**. These lines will be perpendicular to the base **g b** according to Theorem 92 of Book 1. Let one flat surface pass through lines **b e** and **b d**, and another flat surface through lines **g d** and **g z**. Neither of these surfaces cuts through the column, since lines **d b** and **d g** are tangent to the base circle, and lines **b e** and **g z** are lines of length on the surface of the column that do not cut into it; therefore, those surfaces are tangent to the column itself. Since both of these tangent surfaces pass through the center of sight, and their common intersection is a straight line (by Proposition 3 of Book 11), the intersection occurs at a certain line passing through the center of sight parallel to the axis of the column. Only that which is intercepted between these surfaces on the surface of the column is seen. Because the lines of length **b e** and **g z** are parallel (by Proposition 6 of Book 11), it is clear by Proposition 33 of Book 1 that the chords of the base arcs falling between them (which are **g b** and **z e**) are equal; therefore, by Proposition 28 of Book 3, the arcs corresponding to those chords will be equal. Thus, the portions of the circles of the bases intercepted between these lines of the column's length (**b e** and **g z**), and all circles parallel to the bases, are equal to the portion of circle **g b**. This portion is less than a semicircle according to Proposition 51 of this book; therefore, all portions of the other circles are also less than their semicircles. Consequently, less than half of the column will be seen. This is what was proposed. The same would also happen in multi-sided columns <note>Prisms.</note>, except that the angles sometimes hinder and sometimes aid the quantity of vision; we omit the manner of their vision due to the infinite number of variations, since, once the present foundation is established, a diligent investigator will conclude many specific details.

80. **As the eye approaches a convex cylinder, less of the curved surface is seen; however, it appears as if more is being seen. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 30.**

Let the base of the cylinder be circle *b g*, with center *a* and diameter *f h*. Let the center of the eye be at point *e*. Let line *e a* be drawn between those centers, and let lines *e b* and *e g* be drawn tangent to the circle <note>Following the method in Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 17.</note>. From points *b* and *g*, let lines of the cylinder’s length be drawn—*b i* and *g z*—according to Theorem 101 of Book 1. Thus, as shown in the previous proofs, when the eye is at point *e*, the surface of the cylinder *i b g z* is seen, which is less than half the cylinder according to Proposition 78 of this book. Now, let the eye approach the column and be at point *t*. Let lines tangent to the base of the column be drawn, *t k* and *t l*, and from points *k* and *l*, let the lines of the cylinder’s length be drawn, *l n* and *k m*. Therefore, when the eye is at point *t*, the visible surface of the cylinder is *l n k m*, which is smaller than the surface *i b g z* seen from point *e*. The proof of this is similar to the proof given in Proposition 67 of this book. Thus, as the eye approaches the cylinder, less of its surface is seen; yet it appears as if more is seen, because according to Theorem 60 of Book 1 and Proposition 21 of Book 1, angle *l t k* is larger than angle *b e g*, for lines *t k* and *e g* converge toward point *g*. Thus, the proposition is clear by Proposition 20 of this book.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a perspective view of a cylinder from a single eye point 'e' on its central axis. Lines representing the visual rays form a "pyramid of vision" that meets the base, marking points of visibility along the height and curved surface of the cylinder.</image-desc>

81. **When the axis of only one eye falls upon the center of the base of a round or many-sided column, or if the distance between the eyes is equal to or smaller than the diameter of the cylinder's base directly facing the sight, only the base is seen. If the distance is larger than the base, the entire cylinder will be seen, except for the far base.**

When vision occurs with only one eye, and the visual axis falls on the center of the circular base of a round or many-sided column, then—because all lines of length are perpendicular to the base <note>as shown in Book 1, Theorem 92</note>—the form of any point on those lines will not be seen, except for the common point where the line of length meets the edge of the base surface. Therefore, only the base will be seen. The same is true if vision occurs with both eyes, provided the distance between the eyes (the line connecting the centers of the eyes) is equal to or smaller than the diameter of the base. For then, as is clear from Proposition 4 of this book, none of the lines of the column’s length will reach both eyes, except (as previously shown) the point that is the common intersection of one of those lines and the edge of the base itself. 

However, if the distance between the eyes is greater than the diameter of the base, then all the lines of the column’s length will reach both eyes. The entire visible convexity of the column will be seen, as well as the upper base closer to the eyes; the lower base, however, is not seen, because no point of it reaches the eye except its edge where it meets the lines of the column’s length. If vision occurs with only one eye and the axis falls outside the center of the base, some part of the lines of length of the entire column will be seen, since then the edge of the base cuts through the pyramid of vision <note>The cone-shaped field of light rays entering the eye.</note>. Thus, what was proposed is clear. Furthermore, it is possible that when the sight falls obliquely upon the base of a column, the entire column—even if it is regular—may appear longer on one side, and the entire column may appear to be an irregular shape, according to Propositions 55 or 56 of this book. This is a point worthy of note.

# WITELO’S OPTICS

82. **When the visual axis of only one eye falls upon the center of a columnar section (which forms the base of a round columnar segment), that entire base and a part of the vertical lines of the segment are seen.**

Suppose a round column is cut in such a way that its axis is not standing perpendicular to its base. It is then clear from the 103rd theorem of Book 1 of this work that this base is a section called a "columnar section" or an acute-angled section <note>original: "sectio oxygonia"; this refers to an ellipse formed by cutting a cylinder at an angle.</note>. This cut-off part of the column is called an *absis* <note>original: "absis"; a segment or arch-like portion.</note>. I say that if the visual axis hits the center of that base, the part of the lines of length <note>These are the vertical lines running along the height of the column.</note> of the segment—specifically those on the more slanted side that are closer—will be seen even with a single eye. The reason for this is the obliquity of the base, which is seen under a smaller angle according to Theorem 26 of this book. Because of this, the forms of the points on the lines of length adjacent to the more remote part are also seen, as the remaining angles reach the eye. This would not happen if the base could be placed directly opposite the eye; however, that is impossible without also seeing the lines of length of the segment. Thus, the proposition is evident.

83. **When the center of the pupil <note>original: "foraminis uueae"; literally the opening of the uvea.</note> is located within the illuminated concave surface of any column, the entire concavity of the column is always seen; in other views of parts of concave columns, the same thing occurs as with the concavity of spheres.**

When the eye is arranged in the proposed manner with respect to any concave column, the forms of all points on the lines of length that are cut by the surface of the pupil then all reach the eye. This is because they reach the center of that opening along straight lines. Only one line hits the surface of the eye directly at that center, while others hit it at various points on the circle of the pupil. Therefore, they will all be seen according to Theorem 2 of Book 3. And since the forms of all other lines of length and all points of the bases reach the eye either directly or obliquely, it is clear that the entire concavity of the column is seen in every point of its surface. However, an irregularity in the perceived shape might occur because of the slant of some of its parts relative to the eye, according to Theorems 55 or 56. In other views of parts of concave columns, the same thing happens as in concave spheres: when the eye is placed at the midpoint of the rectangle bounding a semi-cylinder, it will be seen in its entirety according to Theorem 60. Moreover, every point of the concave surface and the bases meets the eyes. As the eye moves away from that point, a portion of the column either smaller or larger than a semi-cylinder will always be seen. Thus, the proposition is clear.

84. **When the base of a round pyramid <note>A "round pyramid" is what we call a cone.</note> is in the same plane as the center of one eye, less than half of the convex surface of the pyramid is seen. Euclid, Theorem 31 of the *Optics*.**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the optics of a cone. The cone's vertex is labeled 'a' at the top. Its circular base is drawn in perspective as an ellipse with a horizontal diameter marked 'f', 'k' (center), and 'h'. Points 'b' and 'g' are marked on the front curve of the base. Below the base, point 'd' represents the viewer's eye. Lines from 'd' are tangent to the base at 'b' and 'g'. The visible surface of the cone from point 'd' is bounded by the lines 'a-b' and 'a-g'.</image-desc>

Let there be a round pyramid whose base is circle *b g*, with diameter *f h* and center *k*. Let the vertex of that pyramid be point *a*, and let the center of vision be *d*. Let lines *d b* and *d g* be drawn tangent to circle *b g* according to Theorem 17 of Book 3 of Euclid’s *Elements*. Therefore, by Theorem 58 of Book 1 of this work, arc *b g* is less than a semicircle. Let the lines of length *a b* and *a g* also be drawn from vertex *a* according to Theorem 101 of Book 1. It is thus clear, in the same manner as we demonstrated with columns, that only the surface intercepted by lines *a b* and *a g* is seen. And since these lines cut off similar parts from all circles parallel to the base of the pyramid and contain them within themselves—and since by Theorem 58 of Book 1 arc *b g* is less than a semicircle—the arcs of all other circles will necessarily be smaller than their respective semicircles. Therefore, the visible portion will be less than a half-cone <note>original: "hemiconium".</note>. For just as the entire convex surface of the pyramid corresponds to the entire base, so does the proportional part of the entire convex surface correspond to the proportional part of the base relative to the whole base. This is because the lines of length produced from the vertex to the edge of the base divide the conical surface just as the lines produced from the ends of those lines to the center of the pyramid's base divide the base itself. This can also be proved by the argument in Euclid, Book 12, Proposition 5. Thus, the proposition is clear.

85. **When the centers of both eyes are in the same plane as the base of a cone, if the line connecting the centers of the eyes is equal to the diameter of the base, a half-cone will be seen; if it is larger, more; if it is smaller, less.**

The arrangement for the cone is the same as that for the column in Theorem 79 of this book, with this one addition: that the centers of vision are only in the same plane as the base of the pyramid and are not elevated along a line parallel to the axis of the cone, as can happen with a column. For if the eye is raised along a line parallel to the axis of a column, the same thing happens as when it is in the base, because in a column it is sufficient even if they are in a plane parallel to the base. It is clear, therefore, what is proposed here, and the method of demonstration is the same. Thus, it would be a waste of parchment <note>original: "frustra est membranas denuò occupare"; a common medieval expression for avoiding redundant writing.</note> to cover it again.

86. **As the center of vision in the plane of the base of a cone approaches, less of the conical surface is seen, though it appears that more is seen. Euclid, Theorem 32 of the *Optics*.**

Let circle *a b* be the base of the cone, with center *l*, and let point *g* be the vertex of the cone. Let the center of the eye be *d*. Let there be drawn...
