**87. When lines are drawn from the center of vision tangent to the base of a cone, and lines of the cone's length are drawn from the points of contact: if the eye approaches the cone along the line produced by the intersection of the surfaces through these same lines and through the center of the eye, then the same portion of the conical surface will be seen as before, and it will appear to be of the same size.**
<note>Reference: Euclid, *Optics*, Theorem 33.</note>

Suppose there is a cone whose base is the circle *bzg* and its vertex is point *a*. Let the axis be *ah*, and let the center of the eye be *d*. Through Proposition 17 of Book 3 <note>References to "p" and "th" usually cite Euclid’s *Elements* or Witelo’s own earlier books.</note>, let lines *dz* and *dg* be drawn from the center of vision *d* tangent to the circle *bzg*. Since this is established by our hypothesis, it is clear by Proposition 16 of Book 3 and Proposition 2 of Book 11 that the center of vision is in the same plane as the base of the visible cone. 

Let two lines of length be drawn from the points of contact *z* and *g* through the cone's vertex point *a*, which are *za* and *ga*; this is done according to Theorem 101 of Book 1 of this work. From the center of vision at point *d* to the vertex point *a*, let line *da* be drawn. Let two surfaces <note>In this context, "surfaces" refers to geometric planes.</note> be drawn: one through lines *dg* and *ga*, and the other through lines *dz* and *za*. Since these surfaces meet at the center of vision *d* and at the vertex of the cone *a*, their common section <note>The line where the two planes intersect.</note> will be the line *ad*, according to Proposition 1 of Book 11 and Theorem 19 of Book 1 of this work.

I say that if the eye approaches the cone along the line *da*, no larger portion of the conical surface will be seen now than was seen before when the eye was at point *d*.

For example, let the eye approach the cone until it reaches point *e* on line *da*. Let lines be drawn from point *e* parallel to lines *dg* and *dz* toward the visible surface of the cone. These lines will necessarily be tangent to some circle of the cone that is parallel to the base *bzg*. Therefore, they must fall on certain points of the lines *az* and *ag*, because those lines cut the base of the cone and all circles parallel to it proportionally. This is because the vision is bounded along those lines, and the vision of those circles is bounded by those tangent surfaces. 

If it were argued that those tangent lines drawn from point *e* fall outside lines *az* and *ag*, several impossibilities would follow. Since the lines drawn from point *e* to lines *az* and *ag* bound the vision, and those tangents also bound the vision, it would follow either:
1. That the radial lines are refracted within a single transparent medium (which contradicts Theorem 44 and following of Book 2 of this work);
2. Or that the radial lines are curved (which contradicts Theorem 1 of Book 2);
3. Or that two straight lines enclose a surface (which is impossible in geometry).

Therefore, the said tangent lines drawn from point *e* to the conical surface must fall on lines *az* and *ag*. Let them fall on two points, *i* and *c*, forming lines *ei* and *ec*. Because angle *cei* is equal to angle *gdz* (by Proposition 10 of Book 11), just as the angles formed by lines *ci* and *gz* are related—since all those angles are formed by parallel lines joined at an angle—it is clear through Theorem 10 of this book that the proposition is true. And because wherever the eye is placed along line *da*, the angles at the eye remain equal (by Proposition 10 of Book 11), the claim is proven. This can be demonstrated in the same way for both eyes.

<note>Reference: Euclid, *Optics*, Theorem 34.</note>

From point *t*, which is below point *a* (the vertex of the cone), let a line be drawn parallel to line *ab* (by Book 1, Proposition 31), which, when extended toward line *bl*, intersects it at point *p*. Therefore, that which is seen from point *t* is greater than that seen from point *k*, but it appears to be less. And this is what was proposed. This same point can also be demonstrated in its own way regarding both eyes. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 89. If a line is drawn from the center of vision to the vertex of a cone and is perpendicular to the axis, half of the conical surface is seen. 
<note>Reference: Alhazen, Book 4, Section 36, Number 4.</note>

For example, let there be a pyramid <term>pyramid: used here by Vitello to refer to a cone</term> *acn*, whose axis is *ad* and vertex is *a*. It is clear from Theorem 89 of Book 1 of this work that point *d* is the center of the circle forming the base of the cone. Let the center of vision be *b*, and let line *ba* be drawn making the angle *bad* a right angle. I say that half of the conical surface *acn* will be seen.

Suppose a certain plane cuts the cone *acn* parallel to the base *cn*. This plane, by Theorem 100 of Book 1, will cut the cone into a circle, which we shall call *fg*. Its center, point *l*, will be at some point on the axis *ad*. Let a flat surface <note>a plane</note> cut the pyramid through the axis *ad* and through the center of vision *b*. That surface will then cut the circle *fg*. The line common to this surface and the circle *fg* will be perpendicular to the axis, because the axis is upright <note>perpendicular</note> to the surface of the circle, and it will pass through the center of the circle. Let that line be *kl*. By Book 1, Proposition 28, it will be parallel to line *ba* and is in the same plane with it. 

Also, let the diameter *flg* be drawn through the center of the circle perpendicular to line *kl*. From the ends of this diameter, let two lines tangent to the circle be drawn (by Book 3, Proposition 17), which shall be *fe* and *gh*. From these same points *f* and *g* <note>The text says g and h, but the logic follows points f and g on the circle</note>, let two lines of length <term>lines of length: the straight lines running from the vertex to the base along the surface of the cone</term> be drawn to the vertex of the cone (by Book 1, Theorem 101), which shall be *fa* and *ga*. Therefore, it is clear that two flat surfaces—one containing lines *fe* and *fa*, and the other containing lines *gh* and *ga*—will be tangent to the pyramid along the lines of length *fa* and *ga* (by Book 1, Theorem 95). 

And since line *kl* is parallel to line *ba* and to the lines tangent to the circle (*fe* and *gh*), as is clear from Book 3, Proposition 16 and Book 1, Proposition 28, it follows by Book 11, Proposition 9 that lines *fe* and *gh* are parallel to line *ba*. Therefore, each of them is in the same plane with that line (by Book 1, Theorem 1). Thus, those two surfaces must necessarily intersect each other along line *ba* (by Book 1, Theorem 19). Therefore, each of the surfaces tangent to the proposed pyramid at the ends of the diameter of one of its circles passes through the center of vision. Consequently, whatever of the conical surface falls between those surfaces is visible to the eye. This is exactly half of the pyramid, because half of the circle lies between those tangent lines. Therefore, in this position, half of the conical surface is seen. This is what was proposed.

### 91. *When the line of longitude of a cone, extended beyond the vertex, meets the center of vision, nothing of the entire conical surface will be hidden from view except that single line of longitude. Alhazen, Book 4, Number 38.*

Let there be a pyramid <note>original: "pyramis," here referring to a cone</note>, whose vertex is point *b*: and let the line of longitude be *cb*: and let the center of vision be point *a*: and let line *cb* extended beyond point *b* meet with the center of vision at point *a*. I say that no part of this entire conical surface will be hidden from the sight, except a certain mathematical line <note>original: "lineam intellectualem," literally an intellectual line, meaning a line with length but no width</note>, which is the line of longitude *bc* itself. For every surface in which there is a line drawn from the center of vision to any point of the axis will cut the pyramid, except only that surface in which is the line *abc*: for this touches the pyramid along line *bc* by Theorem 95 of Book 1 of this work. And since that which is contained under the surface touching the pyramid and passing through the center of vision is visible to the sight by Theorem 17 of Book 3 of this work: for the forms of all points of that conical surface are depicted on the surface of the eye: it is therefore clear that the entire conical surface is seen, except for the single mathematical line, which is *bc*. For given any point of the pyramidal surface outside line *bc*: I say that it will be seen. For let that point be *h*: and let line *ah* be drawn to it from the center of vision *a*: and from that same point, by Theorem 101 of Book 1 of this work, let the line of longitude be drawn, which is *hb*: and there will be a triangle *hba*, which will necessarily be in some surface cutting the pyramid, passing through the center of vision *a*: but of the lines of that surface, only two fall on the conical surface of the pyramid, namely the line of longitude *bh*, and the line opposite to line *bh* on the other part of the pyramid: since, as is clear by Theorem 90 of Book 1 of this work, the common section of a plane surface cutting the cone through the axis and the conical surface is a triangle contained by two lines of longitude of the pyramid and the diameter of the base: but line *ah* cuts line *bh* at point *h*, and line *cb* cuts the same *bh* at point *b* by Theorem 91 of Book 1 of this work: therefore no line from the vertex of the pyramid will meet line *ah* except at point *a*: nor will lines drawn from the vertex *b* fall upon any middle point of line *ah*: therefore point *h* will not be hidden by any other point from reaching the center of vision *a*. Therefore point *h* is visible to the eye, since no solid body is interposed between it and the eye. The same proof also holds for any other given point of the surface of the pyramid: but on line *bc*, which is perpendicular to the surface of the eye <note>original: "superficiem uisus"</note> by Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work, it is possible for only a single point to be seen, as was shown in Theorem 4 of this book: all other points of line *bc* are necessarily hidden. Therefore the proposition is clear. It is thus clear from these things, since in this position none of the surfaces touching the pyramid reach the center of vision, except that which touches the pyramid in the line of longitude *bc* passing through the center of vision: and all other surfaces touching the cone cut the line extended from the center to the pyramid itself between the vertex of the cone and the center of vision.

### 92. *When the axis of the pyramid meets the center of vision toward the vertex: the entire conical surface is seen with one eye. Alhazen, Book 4, Number 39.*

I say that in this position of the eye the entire conical surface of the pyramid is visible to one eye: for no point of the conical surface of the entire pyramid is hidden from view. # VITELLO'S OPTICS

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the upper right margin depicting a pyramid or cone with its apex at the top. A line from an external point 'a' extends towards the pyramid, intersecting its surface. Points 'k', 'b', 'l', 'c', and 'd' are marked, illustrating the geometric argument regarding lines of sight and the pyramid's surface.</image-desc>

By Theorem 10 of Book 1 of this work, let the line of longitude <note>original: "linea longitudinis"; a line running straight from the vertex to the base along the surface</note> of the pyramid be *lb*: this forms the triangle *lba*, which must necessarily be in the surface cutting the pyramid, because the line *ac* drawn from the center of vision enters into the pyramid itself, cutting it, and this line is in the said surface by Proposition 1 of Book 11 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, since the line *ab* is in the surface. Indeed, the line *al* cuts the line *bl* at point *l*. Among the lines of the surface in which the two lines *al* and *bl* are found, there are only two lines on the surface of the pyramid: namely, the line of longitude which is *bl*, and another line of longitude opposite to it, which we shall call *bk*, as is clear from Theorem 90 of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, this line *bk*, extended beyond point *b*, since it is in the same surface as lines *ab* and *bl*, will necessarily bisect the angle *abl*. Thus, by Theorem 29 of Book 1 of this work, it will also cut the base *al*; let it cut it at point *d*. And because the line *al* cuts the two lines *kb* and *lb*, which are the only lines from the cutting surface that are on the surface of the pyramid (for line *al* cuts line *kb* outside the pyramid at point *d*, and line *lb* on the surface of the pyramid at point *l*), it follows that the line *ak* extended to infinity will not meet any of those lines. Therefore, no solid point, such as *k*, will be interposed between the eye and point *l*; nor will any other points of the pyramid itself be interposed, since none of them fall on that surface. Therefore, the given point *l* will not be hidden from the eye located at point *a*, since no solid body happens to be interposed between it and the center of vision. The same demonstration applies to any given point on the entire surface of the pyramid. Thus, the proposition is clear. It is evident from these things that in this position, no surface tangent to the pyramid passes through the center of vision, but any of them will cut the line from the center of vision through the vertex entering the cone between the center of vision and the pyramid—namely, at the vertex of its axis—as is clear to the observer.

93. *All lines or surfaces produced from the center of vision between the lines or surfaces that touch a cylinder or a round pyramid and bound the visible surface will necessarily intersect the cylinder or pyramid.*

For example, let there be two lines of longitude of the cylinder or pyramid bounding the visible surface, which are *ab* and *cd*. I say that if a line *ef* is drawn from the center of vision (which is *e*) between those lines *ab* and *cd*, then the line *ef* will intersect the proposed cylinder or pyramid. For let a plane surface pass through the cylinder or pyramid, cutting it at point *f* parallel to the base; by Theorem 100 of Book 1 of this work, the common section <note>the line where two surfaces meet</note> will be a circle, which we shall call *gfh*. This circle cuts the lines of longitude of the cylinder or pyramid—namely, line *ab* at point *g*, and line *cd* at point *h*. Let two lines tangent to that circle be drawn from point *e* by Proposition 17 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid</note>, which are *eg* and *eh*. It is clear, however, by Theorem 57 of Book 1 of this work, that since line *ef* exists in the same surface as those lines, it cuts the circle *gfh*; therefore, it will cut the cylinder or pyramid which is cut by that same circle. The same also occurs if one chooses to demonstrate this through a longitudinal section, and it leads to the same result. The proposition is therefore clear.

Therefore, let the common section of that surface and the visible convex surface of the cylinder be the line of longitude *mo*. Imagine a plane surface tangent to the cylinder along the line of longitude *mo* by Theorem 95 of Book 1 of this work; therefore, that tangent surface and the surface cutting through the axis will be perpendicular to each other by Theorem 97 of Book 1. If, therefore, a point *p* is marked on the line *mo*, and a line *tps* is drawn in the tangent surface, then it is clear that the line *tps* will touch a certain circle of the cylinder's surface parallel to the bases, which we shall call *bq*; let its center be *u*. They cut that line which is tangent to the circle, which is *p s*, at points *t* and *s*. Let line *a p* be drawn; when extended, as is clear from Proposition 18 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, it will reach the axis at point *u*, the center of the circle. Let lines *b u* and *q u*, the radii of circle *b q*, be drawn within the column. Thus, triangles *a b u* and *a q u* are equilateral <note>meaning their corresponding sides are equal</note>; therefore, by Proposition 8 of Book 1, they are equiangular. Thus, angle *u a b* is equal to angle *u a q*. But in triangle *a t p*, angle *a p t* is equal to angle *a p s* of triangle *a p s* by the definition of a line erected upon a surface. Therefore, by Proposition 32 of Book 1, angle *a t p* is equal to angle *a s p*; therefore, by Proposition 6 of Book 1, line *a t* is equal to line *a s*. 

And because lines *a b* and *a q* are equal, as shown above, if lines *a t* and *a s* are subtracted from them respectively, the remaining line *t q* will be equal to line *s b*. But line *t q* is equal to line *t p* by Theorem 58 of Book 1 of this work, since two lines tangent to the circle have been drawn from point *t*, which are lines *t q* and *t p*; likewise, line *s b* is equal to line *s p*. Since, therefore, by Proposition 13 <note>the text likely refers to the congruence of triangles</note>, triangles *b s p* and *q t p* are equal, the chord *b p* will be equal to chord *p q* by Proposition 4 of Book 1. Therefore, by Proposition 28 of Book 3, arc *p b* will be equal to arc *p q*. 

And since the same occurs in the bases of the column and in any other circles parallel to the bases, the first proposition is clear: namely, that a flat surface cutting the column through its axis and passing through the center of vision cuts the visible surface into two equal parts. And since all other surfaces declining from the axis fall obliquely upon the surface tangent to the column at the midline of the visible surface of the column itself (which is line *m o*), it is clear that none of them cut that visible surface into equal parts. 

But also, the surface that cuts the visible part of the column’s surface into equal parts necessarily passes through the axis. For let the arrangement be as before, and let all the previous lines be drawn. Therefore, the line *m o*, upon which that surface falls, will divide the visible surface into equal parts, and it is the common section of the cutting and tangent surfaces. Thus, by Theorem 61 of Book 1 of this work, line *p t* will be equal to line *p s*. But line *p t* is equal to line *t q* by Theorem 58 of Book 1 of this work, and likewise line *p s* is equal to line *s b*. It remains, therefore, that line *a t* is equal to line *a s*. And since in those triangles *a p s* and *a p t*, line *a p* is common to both, then by Proposition 8 of Book 1, angle *a p t* will be equal to angle *a p s*. Each of those angles is therefore a right angle, and line *a p* is perpendicular to line *t p s*. Therefore, since line *a p* contains equal angles with line *m o*, it is clear by definition since the surface is tangent to the column at line *m o*. Therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 11, the surface in which line *a p* is cutting the column is erected <note>perpendicular</note> upon the surface itself tangent to the column along line *m o*. Therefore, by Theorem 97 of Book 1 of this work, it is clear that it passes through the axis of that column. And it is to be demonstrated in exactly the same way for round pyramids. And this was what was proposed.

### 95. **Rectangular magnitudes seen from a greater distance appear circular. Euclid, Theorem 9 of the Optics.**

<image-desc>A smaller diagram on the right side showing a square with vertices 'b', 'g', 'z', and 'd'. From a point 'a' below, a visual axis line 'a-z' is drawn. A circle is sketched within the square to demonstrate how corners of a square (like a tower) appear rounded when viewed from a great distance.</image-desc>

Let there be a rectangular magnitude seen from a great distance, which is *b g d z*. Since every visible thing has a length of distance at which vision no longer occurs, as is clear from Theorem 8 of this work, and an angular body is smaller around its corners than around its other parts, it is necessary for the body to fail the sight first around the corner *g* rather than around the more remote points *d* and *z*. A similar thing will happen at each of the other corners. Therefore, the entire periphery of the body, as far as the prominence of the corners is concerned, will not appear because of its distance from the eye. 

Thus, a rectangular body appears to the eye to be of a circular shape; for example, a square tower will look round. Therefore, when the sight perceives a square or a polygon from a distance, it will perceive it as round if it has equal diameters; or it will perceive it as an oblong, rounded shape if it has unequal diameters, such as a shape longer on one side. For the most part, there are quadrangular towers which, when seen from a distance, appear as rounded shapes. For the excess of the rays proceeding from the corners of a square surface to the eye over the length of the rays proceeding from the flat sides is not proportional to the distance of the whole body from the eye by any sensible ratio. Hence, because the excess is imperceptible, all rays are estimated to be equal. This usually happens even more in other polygonal figures; for acute-angled <note>original: "oxygona"</note> bodies seen from some great distance most often appear round, and this is to be demonstrated in almost the same way as the premises. And this is the proposal.

97. *In the vision of a shape, an error occurs in the discerning power from the immoderate arrangement of the eight circumstances of any seen thing. Alhazen 2.36.47.54.59.64.66.69 n 3.* <note>The "eight circumstances" are a standard medieval list: distance, position, light, size, solidity, transparency, duration of time, and the health of the eye</note>

From an immoderate arrangement of light, an equilateral polygonal shape will appear circular or spherical at night: because the light is too weak to reveal the angles: and even a sphere seen under very weak light is judged to be a flat surface, because due to the weakness of light, the protrusion of parts on the surface of the sphere itself is hidden from sight. Also, from an immoderate length of distance, a square shape will sometimes appear round and spherical: and even a square shape sometimes appears to the sight longer on one side, as is clear through proposition 59 of this book: when, also due to excessive distance, the slant of one side of the square is not perceived, then because of that distance the square is seen as longer on one side, as is clear through proposition 62 of this book. An error also happens to the vision of a shape from an immoderation of length: for a shape of many equal sides directly opposite the sight appears circular and round at a great distance, because its angles are imperceptible to the sight, which is clear through proposition 95 of this book: and a curved line is judged straight by proposition 50: and a spherical shape appears flat by proposition 65. From a disorder of position, an error also happens in the vision of a shape. For if a circular body, such as a small dish <term>scutella</term> <note>A shallow bowl or platter</note>, is moved away from the central axis and tilted slightly over the line where the axis falls perpendicularly, its diameters will appear unequal through proposition 96 of this book: and a circular shape, through propositions 55 and 56, will appear as an acute-angled section or a columnar shape: and similarly, because of the equality of the opposition of one of the sides to the sight, a square shape will be judged longer on one side through proposition 61. From an immoderation of size or magnitude, an error also happens to the vision of shapes. For when the seen surface is very small, if there are angles in it, they will be hidden from the sight: wherefore perhaps its angular form will be judged round, spherical, or columnar. And if there are any protrusions on its surface, they will escape the sight, and their surface will be judged flat, as these things can be seen in the "atoms of the sun" <note>Probably referring to dust motes dancing in a beam of sunlight</note>, whose certain shape is not grasped, since their angles are hidden from the sight from even a small distance, as is clear through proposition 8 of this book. From immoderate solidity, an error also happens to the vision of shapes. For if a body in which there are angles is less solid, those angles will perhaps be hidden from the viewer, and the angular form will be thought spherical, and perhaps the sphericity of those bodies will appear flat. Immoderate transparency also induces error in the vision of shapes: since when the air is cloudy and dark, as in twilight, if there are angles in that body, it will perhaps appear spherical: and if there is sphericity in it, it will perhaps appear flat: because the medium is not so arranged that a complete vision can occur through it, for which light is required, as is clear through theorem 1 of book 2. Shortness of time also brings error to the sight in the vision of shapes: for a small bump on a thing seen suddenly escapes the sight, and is judged as flatness: and if things of an angular shape are seen suddenly, they will perhaps appear spherical. Weakness of sight also causes error in the vision of shapes: for a small bump and multiple angles escape a weak sight: and spherical things are seen as flat, and angular things as spherical: thus, therefore, the proposal is clear in all the circumstances of visible things. And this was what was proposed.

98. *In the vision of three-dimensionality <term>corporeitas</term>, the errors happening to the discerning power from the immoderate arrangement of the eight circumstances of any seen thing are the same as those that happen in position and shape. Alhazen 2.5 n 3.*

For three-dimensional bodies, as is clear in proposition 63 of this book, are grasped by the sight from the grasping of the shapes which the surfaces containing the body make: therefore the cause of error is the same on both sides: and every error which can happen to the sight in the failure to grasp true three-dimensionality, or in an erroneous grasping, happens from an error arising concerning the types of shapes: as when a convex or concave spherical surface is judged flat through proposition 65 of this book: because in bodies at a very great distance from the sight, the sight does not grasp three-dimensionality when it does not grasp the slant of the surfaces. And all this happens because of a deception concerning shapes: for the sight does not then grasp the position of the parts of those surfaces in relation to each other, which position creates the shape: hence when a shape is grasped with certainty, three-dimensionality is grasped with certainty: and when a shape is grasped indistinctly, three-dimensionality is also grasped indistinctly. And this happens in all the ways in which error happens in the visions of shapes. And because position is the cause of shapes, therefore also the errors happen...

# BOOK FOUR

...belonging to position also happen to corporeality <note>This refers to "three-dimensionality" or the physical volume of an object</note>: for because corporeality is included under shape and position, an error in perceiving corporeality carries within itself an error in both position and shape.

## 99. The distinction of visible things is perceived by sight through the distinction of the forms of those visible things impressed on different parts of the surface of the eye. Alhazen [Book 2], 46, n 2.

The distinction that exists between any two bodies arises either from light, or from color having the property of light, or from darkness: for these are the principles of the distinction of forms on the surface of sight, since these reach a part of the surface of the eye by their own power. Sometimes the light, color, or darkness are in the forms themselves which are being distinguished; but sometimes the light, color, or darkness that distinguishes the seen things are in the medium bodies <note>The "medium" refers to the substance between the eye and the object, usually air</note> that separate the bodies according to their position. In this case, if the eye does not sense that the light, color, or darkness at the point of distinction is not part of the body continued on either side, then it will not perceive the distinction between the two bodies. Furthermore, distinction of visible things sometimes occurs because it is impossible for multiple visible things to be seen equally, according to theorem 49 of Book 3 of this work. For either the surface of each of those bodies is slanted relative to the surface of the eye at the point of distinction, and the slant is unequal; or the form of one is slanted while the form of the other is directly opposite the eye—the latter being clearer to the sight than the one slanted away. According to this, the sight perceives the distinction of visible forms, whether the space between them is wide or narrow, provided it is sensible <note>Meaning "perceivable by the senses"</note> relative to the distance of the seen bodies and their size. For perhaps sometimes the distinction between forms is only the thickness of a single hair, and such a tiny distance does not produce a perceptible gap in the eye. Thus, the proposition is clear.

## 100. The continuity of visible things is perceived by sight from the absence of distance. Alhazen [Book 2], 47, n 2.

When the eye does not sense any distance within a body, it perceives it as continuous. If there is a hidden distance in the body not grasped by the eye, the sight will perceive that body as continuous, and it will distinguish between "continuation" <note>Being a single piece</note> and "contiguity" <note>Two things merely touching</note> based on the perception of the joining of the two boundaries of the bodies. If, therefore, the perceiver does not sense that each of the two touching bodies is different and distinct from the other, then they will not sense the contiguity, but will judge there to be perfect continuity between those seen things and a perfect unity of the whole seen surface. Thus, the proposition is clear.

## 101. Number is perceived by sight through the fact that one visible thing is perceived as distinct from another. Alhazen [Book 2], 48, n 2.

When the eye perceives many distinct visible things at the same moment, and perceives their distinction, it understands that each of them is divided from the other. It therefore perceives a multitude; then the distinguishing power <note>The "virtus distinctiva" was considered the mental faculty that processed raw visual data into concepts</note> perceives the number from that multitude—whether it is even or odd, the half of an even number, and each individual unit. In this way, it perceives the number of all seen things, both mathematical and natural. Thus, the proposition is clear.

## 102. Every form falling obliquely upon the eyes always appears beyond the location of a form falling directly. From this it is clear that forms falling more obliquely upon both eyes according to an equality of angles are most distant from each other.

What is proposed here is quite clear. For when a radial line <note>A ray of light</note> falls obliquely on the surface of the eye, it is refracted from the surface of the eye according to theorem 47 of Book 2 of this work, and it reaches the concavity of the nerve <note>The "concavum nerui" refers to the optic nerve or the back of the eye where the Greeks and Medievals believed the visual spirit resided</note> more obliquely. Since the size of the angle of refraction is formed according to the angle of incidence, as per theorem 36 of Book 3, it is evident that because of the slant of its incidence and the sharpness of the angle, the line falling obliquely makes its angle of refraction acute. Thus, the line of refraction intersects the line falling directly (which is refracted equally from the surface of the eye), and so the slanted form is seen beyond the form seen directly. And if both forms fall obliquely in the same manner of slant—so that the angles of incidence and refraction are equal on both sides—then the form falling on the right eye, crossing the line through which a direct ray would have reached the center point of the nerve's concavity, becomes "left" from that point; and the form falling obliquely on the left eye becomes "right" relative to that same center point. Thus it sometimes happens that those forms appear very far apart. And since each of them is offered to the sensitive power—because the form is painted on the surface of the sensing organ in two places according to the number of eyes it hits and from whose surfaces it is refracted, based on the lights and colors in the external form—the form falling directly is ordered toward a single place in all its parts, as is clear from theorem 37 of Book 3. Therefore, a form falling obliquely always appears beyond the place of a form falling directly. Thus the proposition and its corollary are clear.

# VITELLO’S OPTICS

**103. *Every visible object that is positioned directly opposite the center of one eye, but is oblique relative to the other eye, is always seen as two objects. Alhazen, Book 3, [Chapter 13], Note 3.***

<image-desc>Geometric diagram illustrating proposition 103. Two circles at the bottom, labeled 'a' and 'b', represent eyes. A horizontal line 'e f' is situated above them. Radial lines extend from the centers of the circles 'a' and 'b' to points on the line 'e f'. The line from 'a' is perpendicular to 'e f' at point 'e'.</image-desc>

For the form of a point that falls directly upon the center of one of the eyes reaches the center point of the <term>concavity of the nerve</term> <note>The "common nerve" or optic chiasm, where the visual information from both eyes was thought to combine</note>, as is clear from Theorem 29 of Book 3 of this work, because the form of that point falls upon the eye along the <term>axis</term> <note>The central, most powerful ray</note> of the visual pyramid. However, the form of a point falling <term>obliquely</term> <note>At an angle, rather than straight on</note> upon the center of the surface of the other eye reaches a point other than the center point of the concavity of that nerve, according to the slant of the point on the surface of the eye. Thus, those forms do not converge in that same center point of the concavity of the nerve. 

For example, let the centers of the two eyes be *a* and *b*. Let the line *e f* be a certain visible object directly opposite the center of eye *a*, but let this same line *e f* be obliquely opposite the eye whose center is point *b*. Therefore, because the form of line *e f* reaches the center of the concavity of the common nerve directly (through Theorem 29 of Book 3), it is clear that its form is arranged around that center point of the nerve's concavity according to the positions of all its parts (through Theorem 37 of Book 3). But because the form of the same line *e f* falls entirely obliquely upon the surface of eye *b*, it is clear from the proofs in Theorem 37 of Book 3 that its form does not reach the center point of the nerve's concavity, but rather some other point of it. Therefore, it will not be superimposed upon the first form, but will remain distinct from it. Consequently, two forms will appear, because the form of the visible object is presented to the "sensing power" <note>The faculty of the mind that interprets visual data</note> in two different places of the sensing organ; thus, the mind judges them to be two, and not one. The proposition is therefore clear.

**104. *Every form of a seen object positioned between the radial axes meets both eyes obliquely; hence it is always seen as two. Alhazen, Book 3, [Chapter 11], Note 3.***

<image-desc>Geometric diagram illustrating proposition 104. Two circles labeled 'a' and 'b' represent the eyes at the base. A vertical axis 'd c' rises between them. Two converging radial lines from 'a' and 'b' meet at point 'c'. A point 'e' is marked between these radial lines.</image-desc>

For example, let the centers of the two eyes be *a* and *b*, and let the visual axes converge at point *c*. Let the <term>common axis</term> <note>An imaginary central line between the two eyes</note> be *d c*, and let the object seen be *e*. I say that the form of the seen object *e* always meets both eyes obliquely, and thus it will always appear to be two. That it always falls obliquely on both eyes is clear: for when a line *e a* is drawn from point *e* perpendicularly to the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> <note>original: "uueæ oculi"; here referring to the pupil</note> of the eye whose center is point *a* (as per Theorem 24 of Book 3), and when line *e b* is drawn perpendicularly to the center of the opening of the uvea of the eye whose center is point *b*, it is clear by Proposition 13 of Book 11 [of Euclid] that other perpendiculars cannot be drawn from any point of the surface of the seen object *e* to the said centers of the openings. Therefore, all lines produced from the surface of body *e* to the surface of the eyes are oblique (by Theorem 24 of Book 3). Thus, they will not converge in the center point of the nerve's concavity due to refraction, but beyond it, and will be greatly distant from each other (by Theorem 102 of this book). They will therefore always appear as two, according to the preceding theorem. 

Whenever the axes of the two visual pyramids converge at some point of a seen object, and two other oblique rays encompass another visible thing closer to the two eyes or further away between the axes, then its position relative to the two eyes will be different in terms of direction. For that object will be to the right of one visual axis and to the left of the other. Also, the rays coming from the object seen in this way to one eye will be to the right of the axis, and those coming to the other eye will be to the left of its axis. Thus its position for the two eyes will be different in direction, and the form of one seen object falls on the two eyes in two differently positioned places, reaching different locations in the concavity of the common nerve on two sides of its center point. The parts of that form are not superimposed on each other; therefore, there will be two forms. And so, the form of an object arranged in such a way relative to sight always appears as two forms, and the object itself is always seen as two. This is the proposition.

**105. *Regarding straight lines near the eyes, situated in the plane of the common axis and perpendicular to the triangle of the visual axes upon which the point of junction falls: only that point of junction will be seen as one; all other points of the said line will be seen as two, declining equally from the point of junction, as if two lines were intersecting each other at the point of junction.***

Let the center of the left eye be point *a* and the right eye be point *b*. Let there be a straight line *h z* which is extended between both eyes in line with the middle point of the nose in such a way that the visual axes converge at a certain designated point on it, which is *q*. Therefore, *q* will be the point of junction <note>The point of focus or convergence</note> of both visual axes. And since this point is on the line *h z*, which is כך extended between both radial axes, it is clear that the line is in the plane in which the common axis lies, standing perpendicular to the base of triangle *b q a* (by Theorem 33 of Book 3). I say, therefore, that wherever the point of junction *q* of the line *h z* falls obliquely upon the eyes—that is, with the two axes *b q* and *a q* (or either of them) not containing right angles with the line *h z*—only point *q* will be seen as one, as it truly is. This is because only its form reaches the center point of the nerve's concavity through both radial axes; and thus one form is seen for one thing...

...of one, as can be seen through Theorems 46 and 47 of Book 3 of this work: but all the other points of the line *h z* seem to decline from the point of conjunction, as if two lines intersect at the point of conjunction, which is *q*. This is because various rays coming from those points to both <term>eyes</term> <note>original: "uisus"</note> are oriented to the left and to the right. 

For all rays exiting from other points of the line *h q* to the right eye on the side of axis *h q*, become "left" relative to axis *a q*; and those reaching the left eye from the side of axis *h q*, become "right" relative to axis *b q*. For they reach the surface of the eye from one side of the radius of the <term>pupil</term> <note>original: "foraminis uueæ" – literally the 'opening of the uvea,' which we now call the pupil</note>, which looks toward the common axis from the center of the <term>uvea</term> <note>The uvea is the pigmented layer of the eye, including the iris</note>. And the rays reaching the right eye from points of line *q z* likewise become "left" of axis *a q*, and those reaching the left eye become "right." Both sets of rays reach the surface of the eye from the side of the radius which, together with the previous radius, completes the entire diameter of that opening of the uvea. 

And since both eyes are equal in all their dispositions, according to Theorem 4 of Book 3 of this work, it is clear that the angles of both axes and those radii are equal around the center of each circle of the pupil. The angles *c q z* and *d q z* are also equal for the same reasons. Therefore, having drawn line *c z d* from point *z* parallel to line *a b* (according to Proposition 31 of Book 1), and extending line *a q* to point *d* and line *b q* to point *c*, it is clear that the vision of those forms occurs along those lines. 

Since the angles according to which the <term>slanting of vision</term> <note>original: "obliquatio uisionis"</note> occurs—which are *c q z* and *d q z*—are equal, then by Propositions 13, 15, and 14 of Book 1, the visual lines (for example, lines *b q* and *q c*) are joined as a single line; and it is the same for lines *a q* and *q d*. However, one radial line is seen as two lines because of the difference in how the form of that point falls upon both eyes. This slanting occurs in the manner of two lines intersecting each other around point *q*. For the form falling upon the eyes according to the radial axes reaches the middle point of the <term>concavity of the nerve</term> <note>The optic chiasm, where the visual nerves from both eyes meet</note>, and the forms falling obliquely are shaped by intersecting themselves around that point. 

The distances of any two radial lines (coming from any point on line *h z* to both axes) will always be in two different directions. Because of this, the two forms of any such point will fall upon two points of the concavity of the common nerve on two sides of the middle point, as we have shown in the preceding sections. Thus the proposition is clear. It is also clear that if the point of conjunction is changed, the size of the intersected lines changes; however, the parts of the lines on both sides of the intersection are always equal. According to their proximity to the eyes, the middle angles (such as *a q b* and *c q d*) become larger, and according to their distance from the eye, they become smaller, until <term>visual pyramids</term> <note>The cone of light or "pyramid" of rays stretching from the object to the eye</note> are described around the radial axes, the base of which is the entire surface of the seen object. 

Experimental proof of these things happens if, with the eyes arranged in the manner described, one of them is closed and the other kept open, switching back and forth in this way as much as you please.

**106. *If a line is drawn from the point of conjunction between two perpendiculars produced from the ends of the line connecting the centers of the eyes, and if that line is equal and parallel to the first: the form of any point on that produced line or of an object existing upon it, and the form of an object existing upon either of the perpendiculars at a point near the aforesaid line, will be seen as only one; however, an object existing on the same perpendicular far from the produced line will always be seen as two.***

Let the centers of the two eyes be *a* and *b*. Therefore, the line connecting the centers is *a b*. From its ends, let perpendiculars *a c* and *b d* be erected (by Proposition 11 of Book 1). Let the point of conjunction be *q*. The visual axes will therefore be *a q* and *b q*. From point *q*, let line *k q t* be drawn parallel to line *a b* (by Proposition 31 of Book 1). 

I say that the form of any point of line *k t*, or of an object existing upon it, will always be seen as one; and if a visible object is placed on either of the perpendiculars *a c* and *b d* at a point near line *k t* (such as at point *r*), its form will still be seen as one. But if it is at a very remote point, such as at point *f*, then one object existing there will be seen as two. 

For let lines *b k*, *b r*, and *b f* be drawn from point *b*. It is clear then (by Propositions 47 and 19 of the Elements) that line *b k* is greater than line *b t*. But line *k q* is equal to line *q t* by hypothesis. Therefore (by Theorem 35 of Book 1 of this work), angle *t b q* is greater than angle *q b k*; for in the right-angled triangle, which is *t b k*, line *b q* is produced from angle *t b k*. Therefore, the ratio of angle *q b k* to angle *t b q* is less than the ratio of the part of the base, which is *q k*, to the part of the base, which is *q t*. But those parts of the base are equal to each other; therefore angle *t b q* is greater than angle *q b k* (by Proposition 10 of Book 5). But (by Proposition 4 of Book 1), angle *t b q* is equal to angle *k a q*. Therefore, angle *k a q* is greater than angle *k b q*. ...as stated in the first book of this work, the distance of line *ak* from axis *aq* is greater than the distance of line *bk* from axis *bq*. However, the difference between these two distances is slight, because the difference between the two angles *kaq* and *kbq* is slight. Thus, the form of point *k* will not be much skewed from the visual axes, which are *bq* and *aq*. Therefore, only one form of that point *k* will be seen, because its form does not stray far from the middle point of the nerve's concavity <note>The "nerve concavity" refers to the point in the optic nerve where visual information is centered; Vitello is essentially describing the fovea or the center of the visual field</note>. And since, when some body exists at point *r*, it is clear that the rays exiting toward it are *br* and *ar*; and because the two angles *raq* and *rbq* do not differ much, as angle *kbr* (which is the difference between those angles) does not have a perceptible size when point *r* is very near point *k*, the form of point *r* will still only appear as one. 

If, however, some body whose form is offered to the sight exists at some point on a line perpendicular to the surface of the eye (which is *ac*), far removed from point *k*—such as point *f*—then, because angles *fbq* and *faq* differ by the greatest diversity (since angle *fbk*, which is the difference between those angles, is of a perceptible size), the body at point *f* will appear as two when the two axes meet at point *q*. For the form of point *f* falls obliquely on the surface of eye *b*, and thus does not reach the middle point of the nerve's concavity (as is clear by Theorem 102 of this book), but appears beyond it; thus the form of that point *f* is doubled <note>original: "numeratur," literally "is numbered" or "is counted as more than one"</note>. 

From this it is clear that the object of sight, in which the two axes meet, is always seen as one (as was also clear by Theorem 46 of Book 3), and that any object of sight in which rays of similar position meet—between which there is no great distance from both axes—is also seen as one. However, that object of sight in which rays meet that are far distant from the axes is seen as two: because it falls directly to one eye and very obliquely to the other; or if it falls obliquely to both eyes, one of those obliquities is significantly greater than the other. Such a thing, therefore, appears as two according to Theorem 104 of this book. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 107. When the point of conjunction falls on the vertex of a triangle whose base is equal to the line connecting the centers of the eyes, and whose base ends are applied to the centers of both sights: each of the two sides of the triangle represents two forms to the sight.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating binocular vision. Two circles at the bottom, labeled 'a' (right) and 'b' (left), represent the eyes. Lines extend from these circles to a common point 'q' at the apex of a triangle. Another point 'f' is marked within the triangle to the left of the central axis 'hq'. The triangle's base corresponds to the distance between the eyes.</image-desc>

Let the centers of both eyes be *a* and *b*, and let triangle *abq* be applied to the sights as proposed. Or, let it be such that the base *ab* of triangle *abq* is lower than the centers of the eyes, and let the visual axes fall on point *q*, which is the point of conjunction; and let the common axis be *hq*. I say that each of the sides of the triangle, which are *aq* and *bq*, will present two forms to the viewer. For since each of the forms of lines *aq* and *bq* offers itself to each eye both directly and obliquely—as the right line, which is *aq*, offers itself directly to the right eye (*a*), because all rays exiting from any of its points fall into the center of the opening of the <term>uvea</term> <note>original: "foraminis uueæ" – we now call this the pupil</note> according to Theorem 24 of Book 3; and the left line, which is *bq*, falls obliquely on the right eye (*a*). Conversely, line *bq* falls directly on the left eye (*b*), and line *aq* falls obliquely on the same left eye (*b*), as all these things are clear through Theorem 24 of Book 3. 

Thus, the form falling obliquely on the right eye deviates beyond the left side (of which it is the form) and is to the left of the axis; and the form falling obliquely on the left eye deviates toward the right side (of which it is the form) and is to the right of the axis. All points of the sides of the triangle will therefore be doubled in the appearance of the eyes, except for point *q* alone, which is the point of conjunction. The reason for this appearance is the same as that declared in the preceding theorem. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 100. *In the vision of division, continuity, and number, an error occurs in the distinguishing faculty due to the immoderate disposition of the eight circumstances of any seen object.* <note>The "eight circumstances" in medieval optics were: distance, position, light, size, solidity, color, time, and movement.</note>

For an error in the vision of the aforementioned things happens from the weakness of light: because if a table is seen at night in which there are extensions of dark lines, the one seeing them will perhaps think they are divisions or cracks; and thus what is continuous will be thought to be divided, and parts of the same continuous thing will be thought to be many as if they were divided, even though the table is continuous and only one. Similarly, when the sight is in strong reflected light, if bodies separated by a small distance are presented to the sight, they will appear continuous and as one, because of the reflection of light created by those bodies, which does not allow their distance to be discerned. Error in the vision of the aforementioned things also occurs from immoderate distance. For when some wall is seen from afar, if there is a dark color on part of it, it will perhaps be thought that a division of that wall has been made according to the space of that color. Similarly also, if a multitude of plants grows near that wall, as ivy is accustomed to grow in such places, the wall will perhaps seem divided according to the space of the ivy. And similarly, when the sun's light shines upon a white wall, if some strong shadow divides the light of the wall, the wall will be judged to be divided. And so in all these ways, and also in many other ways, it can happen that what is continuous is judged to be divided, and consequently, one thing is judged to be many. But also, sometimes things that are truly divided are judged to be continuous, and many things are judged to be one. For bodies seen from afar that are similar in color and close to one another are believed to be continuous; because of this, the boards of a wall or a bench sometimes appear continuous when they are divided from one another by a small gap. And thus, things that are divided are judged to be continuous because of their distance from the sight, and many are judged to be one. Error in the vision of the aforementioned things also arises from an irregular position of opposition: for if there is a great tilting away from the sight of some body in which there are sensible black or very dark points, those will be thought to be certain divisions; and between the parts bordering those points, division and plurality will be judged, even though there is a union of continuity in them. And if there are sensible dark lines in this body, its continuous parts will be judged as divided when they are continuous, and many when they are one. The same is true from the tilting of the position of several walls relative to the sight, one of which is arranged behind the other at a small distance from it, so that they can be seen in one glance; perhaps the space that is between those walls will be hidden from the viewer, and they will be thought continuous and as one, though they are distinct and many. How one may err in number because of position is sufficiently clear through the previous proposition. Error in the vision of the aforementioned things also happens from immoderate size: for if a hair is sticking to a glass vessel, the glass will appear cracked; this happens because the smallness of the hair is not perceived as a body. For if a reed or another sensible body were lying upon the glass vessel, the glass would not be perceived as cracked because of it. Similarly, error also happens in continuity: for if sheets of thin parchment are of equal height, so that they are placed on the same flat surface and well pressed together, and the viewer is unaware that they are sheets, he will judge them to be continuous, and their surface to be one. The cause of this error is the smallness of the amount of space and air where those sheets touch each other, and thus number also induces error. Error in the vision of the aforementioned things also happens from an immoderation of solidity: for in a body of great rarity <note>In this context, "rarity" refers to transparency or low density</note>, such as in pure crystal, if there were a black line on some part of its surface, it would appear

And if two such bodies are only slightly distant from each other, they will be considered continuous and as one. From an immoderate degree of thinness <note>original: "intemperantia etiam raritatis"</note>, the same error occurs in the vision of the aforementioned things as happens from a lack of solidity, though it is increased because of the excessive thinness. Error also occurs in the vision of the aforementioned things due to a shortage of time. For if a body on which a black line is drawn is suddenly diverted from the sight, that line will be thought to be a division of parts: and if contiguous or very close bodies are suddenly seen, they will be estimated as continuous, just as happens in the boards of benches when inspected suddenly; thus an error occurs in continuity and number. From an immoderate weakness of sight, error also occurs in the vision of the aforementioned things, occurring according to the modes of brief time: for what happens to a healthy sight in a short duration happens to a weak sight over a longer time, and perhaps constantly during the duration of the sight’s weakness. Also, a person who squints <term>strabo|a person with strabismus or crossed eyes</term> or someone with weakness in one eye sometimes judges one thing to be two: for then the thing seen has a diversity of position with respect to those two eyes, which diversity causes one thing to appear as two, even through two healthy eyes of equal arrangement, as has been sufficiently demonstrated from the preceding points. The proposition is therefore clear.

*110. Motion is perceived by the sight from the perception of the moved object according to its different positions at different instants, between which a sensible time occurs. Alhazen 4, n. 49.*

Since "to be moved" is to be in a different state now than before, it is evident that the ease of this perception of motion arises from the comparison of the moved object seen to another visible object that is resting and not moved. For when the position of one mobile object is perceived with respect to another visible object, then the diversity of its position is also perceived with respect to that visible object, and then motion is perceived. Therefore, motion is always perceived by the sight either from the perception of the diversity and change of position of the moved object seen with respect to another visible object—which is further from or closer to the sight, while the sight itself remains in its place—or motion is perceived by observing the position of some part or parts of the moved object seen with respect to that visible object which is not moved according to its whole self: and in this way, the sight perceives circular motion. It also happens similarly that motion is perceived by the sight if the moved object seen is compared to many immovable visible objects. For when the sight is at rest and the object seen is moved toward the sight itself or away from it, then the sight, sensing the different location of the moved body, will sense the motion: for the mobile object will then either move further away or approach the sight through motion. And because, as is clear from the 9th theorem of this book, distance or approach is sensed by the sight, it is evident that motion is then sensed. But if the mobile object moves only circularly around the sight, then—since the visual surface of the eye is not entirely spherical, as is clear from the 4th theorem of the 3rd book, because only the surface of the <term>uvea|the pigmented, middle layer of the eye, which medieval opticians believed was the primary seat of visual power</term> is visual, and not the other parts of the surface of the eye—as some object is moved around the sight, the position of the part opposite the sight must necessarily change. When that part of the moved object seen has been changed, the sight will sense its change: and thus, with the sight remaining in its place, the sight will sense the motion of the object seen. And even if the sight itself is moved, it will nonetheless perceive motion according to any of these modes, as when the sight senses the diversity of the position of the moved object seen, sensing that the diversity is not due to the motion of the sight itself. Yet when both the sight itself and the object seen are both moved, the sight still discerns the motion: because it distinguishes between the diversity of sight that happens to the moved object seen due to the motion of the object itself, or due to the motion of the sight itself. This is because when the sight is moved, the forms of existing objects that are not moved are also sensed, nor does the sight always judge a seen object to be moving because of its own motion, unless perhaps the form of the moved object seen reaches the sight. And since all motion is in time, the sight does not perceive motion except in time: for the diversity of the position of the parts of the seen object cannot be perceived except in at least two instants: and because a medium time falls between any two instants, it is clear that a medium time falls between those two instants: and since the visual power is a sensitive power, it is necessary that the time perceived by it be sensible <note>original: "sensibile"; meaning a duration long enough to be consciously noticed by the senses</note>. And this is what was proposed.

*111. The quality of motion is perceived by the sight from the perception of the space over which the object itself is moved. Alhazen 50, n. 2.*

Whether the motion is upward or downward, or even upon the surface of the horizon or parallel to it, or even if the motion is not straight but is winding or circular: the quality of motion is always perceived by the sight from the perception of the space over which the moved object itself is moved. For the quality of straight motion is perceived from the perception of the space over which the seen object is moved according to its whole self in a straight motion, and then the sight certifies the quality of the motion through the certification of the shape of the straight space over which the motion occurs on the surface of the horizon, or on a surface parallel to it, or on a line perpendicular or oblique to the surface of the horizon. Similarly also, the quality of other motions, such as winding and circular, is perceived by the sight from the perception of the winding or circular space on the surface of the horizon, or parallel to it, or upright upon it: for the sight will perceive motion composed of circular and straight elements from the perception of the winding space over which the motion occurs. The sight also perceives the diversity and equality of motions according to velocity and slowness from the perception of the spaces over which the moved visible objects move, and the knowledge of the time in which those motions occur. For when the sight senses that one space traversed by one mobile object in some time is greater than another space traversed by another mobile object in the same time: or when the sight senses the equality of two spaces with an inequality of the times of the two motions:

112. *Rest is perceived by the sight from the perception of the thing seen remaining in the same place and position for a sensible amount of time. Alhazen, Book 2, number 52.*

For when the sight perceives the object seen in the same place, and according to the same position at two different moments between which a sensible amount of time falls: then it will understand that the object was not moved during that time, by the 110th proposition of this book: because if that object was moved during that time, its position changed: it will therefore perceive that object as resting. However, the position of a resting object is perceived as unchanged with respect to another object or other objects seen, and also with respect to the sight itself. Therefore, according to this manner, the perception of the rest of seen bodies by the sight occurs. And this is what was proposed.

113. *There is a place in which, with the eye remaining still and the object seen being moved, the object always appears equal. Euclid, Theorem 44 of the Optics.*

Since, therefore, the equal lines **b g** and **d g** are seen under equal angles, which are **d a g** and **b a g**, from here and there: it is clear that those equal lines appear equal to the sight by the 20th proposition of this book. Therefore, the proposition is clear. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

**116. A quantity falling obliquely on a flat surface in which the center of vision is located, if moved uniformly along the periphery of a circle whose center is the center of vision, will always appear equal. However, if that quantity is equal to the radius of that circle and moves along the periphery of that circle while maintaining its original orientation (parallelism), it will sometimes appear equal, sometimes smaller, and sometimes larger to the sight. Euclid, Theorem 43 of the *Optics*.**

Let there be a circle $ad$, whose center is point $e$: and on its periphery let point $d$ be taken: let there also be a line $dz$ falling obliquely upon the surface of the circle: and let the center of the eye be at point $e$, the center of the circle. I say that if the line $dz$ is moved uniformly along the periphery of the circle so that it always maintains an equal angle with the radii of that circle, it will always appear equal. This can be proven by Book 1, Proposition 4, as in the preceding case: for the angle $dez$ is always equal to itself: therefore the object always appears equal by the 20th proposition of this book. And this is the first part of the proposition. 

Again, let the center of vision be at point $e$, the center of circle $ad$, upon whose surface the line $dz$ falls obliquely, and let $dz$ be equal to the radius $de$. Let it be moved along the periphery of that circle while remaining parallel to its first position, and for the sake of example, let the angle $zde$ be acute. I say that sometimes the moved line $dz$ will appear equal to its own true quantity (namely, the radius of the circle), sometimes larger, and sometimes smaller. For let a line $eg$ be drawn from the center of the circle $e$ parallel to line $dz$ by Book 1, Proposition 31, and let it be made equal to it by Book 1, Proposition 3. Also, from point $g$, let a perpendicular $gi$ be drawn to the surface of the circle by Book 11, Proposition 11. Draw the line $ei$ from the center of the circle and extend it to the periphery of the circle at point $a$. From point $a$, draw a line $ab$ parallel to line $eg$ by Book 1, Proposition 31, and let it be cut to be equal to line $dz$ by Book 1, Proposition 3. Line $ab$ will also be parallel to line $dz$ by Book 1, Proposition 9, or Book 11, Proposition 9.

Every angle closer to it is smaller than one further away, and two angles approaching it equally from either side are equal to each other. 

I say, therefore, that line $ab$ will appear the smallest of all lines equal to line $dz$ as they are moved along the periphery of the circle. For let lines $gz$, $gb$, $eb$, $ez$, and $ed$ be drawn. Since the angle $gea$ is acute, as clear from the premises (due to the obliquity of line $ge$ over the surface of circle $ad$), the angle $ged$ will therefore be obtuse by Book 1, Proposition 13. But since line $ez$ is the diagonal of parallelogram $edzg$, it is evident that angle $dez$ is half of angle $ged$ by Book 1, Proposition 4; and similarly, angle $bea$ is half of angle $gea$. Therefore, angle $dez$ is larger than angle $bea$. Thus, by the 20th proposition of this book, the quantity of line $ba$ will appear smaller than the quantity of line $zd$. 

And by the premises, since angle $gea$ is the smallest of all angles contained between line $ge$ and any line produced on the surface of circle $ad$, it is evident that half of angle $gea$ will be smaller than half of any of the other angles. Therefore, the quantity of line $ab$ will appear the smallest of all others equal to it. And since angle $zed$ is the largest of all those other angles, the quantity $zd$ will appear the largest. Those in the middle will appear in a middle way, and quantities on the circle's periphery equally distant from both quantities $ab$ and $dz$ will appear equal to each other. And this is what was proposed.

Therefore, let a circle be circumscribed around it by Book 3, Proposition 22 and Book 4, Proposition 9; and let the circumscribed segment of the circle be $bdza$. Let line $bz$ be drawn, cutting arc $ea$ at point $t$. It will cut it because, as is clear from the premises, point $z$ falls between points $e$ and $g$. Let line $ta$ be drawn. By Book 1, Proposition 16, the exterior angle $atb$ will be greater than the interior angle $azb$. But angle $atb$ is equal to angle $aeb$ by Book 3, Proposition 27, since they fall on the same arc, which is $ba$, of the smaller circle segment $bea$. Therefore, angle $aeb$ is greater than angle $azb$. But angle $azb$ is equal to angle $adb$ by the same Proposition 27 of Book 3, since both those angles fall on the same arc, which is $ab$ of the larger circle $bdza$. Therefore, angle $aeb$ is greater than angle $adb$. When the center of sight is at point $d$, line $ab$ is seen under angle $adb$; but when it is at point $e$, it is seen under angle $aeb$. Therefore, it will appear larger at point $e$ than at point $d$ by the 20th proposition of this book. Thus, when the eye is moved along the points of line $ed$, the magnitude $ba$ will always appear unequal, because it is always smaller than itself; and the more it approaches point $d$, the smaller it will appear; and

Thus the proposition is clear.

**119. While the seen object remains fixed, but the sight is moved along a line parallel to the seen object: its size at some times appears equal, and at other times unequal.** Euclid 47th theorem of Optics.

Let the seen magnitude, which remains fixed and unmoved, be $ab$: and let it be divided into equal parts at point $e$: and let line $ez$ be erected perpendicularly over it by Book 1, Proposition 11 <note>constructing a perpendicular line</note>: and let the center of the eye be at point $z$: and let lines $za$ and $zb$ be drawn, so that triangle $azb$ is completed: and let a segment of a circle $azb$ be described around triangle $azb$ by Book 4, Proposition 5 <note>circumscribing a circle about a given triangle</note>: and let line $zd$ be drawn parallel to line $ab$ by Book 1, Proposition 31 <note>drawing a line parallel to a given line through a given point</note>: and let the center of the eye be moved to point $d$: and let lines $da$ and $db$ be drawn: and to the point where line $db$ cuts the circle, which is $l$, let line $al$ be drawn. 

It is clear then by Book 1, Proposition 16 that angle $alb$ is larger than angle $adb$: but by Book 3, Proposition 27, angle $azb$ is equal to $alb$: therefore angle $azb$ is larger than angle $adb$: thus the magnitude $ab$ will appear larger with the center of the eye being at point $z$ than at point $d$, as is clear by the 20th proposition of this book. And if line $zg$ is equal to line $zd$, line $ab$ will appear equal at points $d$ and $g$: for this is concluded by Propositions 34 and 4 of Book 1, with lines $gb$ and $ga$ drawn: for angle $bga$ is equal to angle $bda$: and this is similarly clear in other points equally distant from points $d$ and $g$: therefore by the 20th proposition of this book, at such points line $ba$ will always appear equal to itself.

Since therefore angle $zeb$ is a right angle, it is clear by Book 1, Proposition 32 <note>the sum of angles in a triangle is two right angles</note> that angle $zbe$ is acute: therefore by Book 1, Proposition 13 <note>angles on a straight line</note> angle $qbz$ will be obtuse: therefore by Book 1, Proposition 29 <note>parallel lines and their angles</note> angle $hzb$ is obtuse: therefore by Book 1, Proposition 16 angle $ghb$ is obtuse: thus line $bg$ is larger than line $bh$ by Book 1, Proposition 19 <note>the greater side of a triangle subtends the greater angle</note>. For angle $bza$ becomes the greatest of all those angles, and those closer to it become larger than those further away, and those equally distant from it become equal. And according to the sizes of those angles, the size of the visible object changes according to the 20th [proposition] of this book.

### 120. *There are locations where, if the eye is moved, equal magnitudes that commonly occupy certain places in a straight line appear sometimes equal and sometimes unequal.*

Magnitudes are commonly said to "occupy their places" when one is joined to another in such a way that nothing falls between them, neither along a straight line equally joined to both magnitudes, nor along a line falling angularly upon either of those magnitudes. Let the center of the eye be at point $d$, and let the equal visible magnitudes be $ab$ and $bg$, commonly occupying place $b$. And from point $b$, let a perpendicular line $bz$ be drawn over both those magnitudes. Let the eye be placed in such a position that line $zb$, extended beyond point $b$, meets the point where the center of sight is located. And since, at whatever point on line $dz$ the center of sight is placed, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, the angles $bdg$ and $bda$ at the center of sight will always be equal: it is therefore manifest by the 20th [proposition] of this book that from any point on line $dz$ where the center of sight $d$ is placed, the magnitudes $bg$ and $ab$ will always appear equal. Now let the eye be moved, and let it be outside the line $dz$ at point $e$. I say that the magnitudes $ab$ and $bg$ will appear unequal. For let lines $ea, eb, eg$ be extended, and let a circle $aedg$ be described around triangle $aeg$ by Proposition 5 of Book 4, and let the straight line $bi$ be added to line $eb$, reaching the circumference on the side opposite point $e$. Because arc $az$ is equal to arc $zg$ by Proposition 33 of Book 6 because of the right angles at point $b$, whether the point is the center of the described circle or not; for always from the hypothesis, and by Proposition 3 of Book 3 and Proposition 4 of Book 1 and Proposition 28 of Book 3, arc $ai$ will be larger than arc $ig$. It is also clear by Proposition 33 of Book 6 that angle $aei$ is larger than angle $ieg$. But magnitude $ab$ is seen under angle $aei$ by an eye located centrally at point $e$, and magnitude $bg$ is seen under angle $ieg$. Therefore $ab$ appears larger than $bg$ when the eye is so positioned, as is clear by the 20th [proposition] of this book. It is also clear by the 118th [proposition] of this book that if the eye is moved along line $ei$ falling obliquely on those magnitudes, the visible magnitudes $ab$ and $bg$ always appear unequal; and the closer they are to point $b$, the larger they appear by Proposition 16 of Book 1 and the 20th [proposition] of this book, since an exterior angle is always larger than the interior angle opposite it. If, therefore, the center of sight is understood to move along the circumference of the circle, the magnitudes $ab$ and $bg$ always appear unequal; and if the eye is placed outside the circle and not in line with $dz$, the magnitudes $ab$ and $bg$ still appear unequal. This is what was proposed.

### 122. *There is a place in which unequal magnitudes commonly occupying certain locations obliquely sometimes appear unequal, and sometimes equal. Euclid, Theorem 49 of the Optics.*

Let it be, as in the preceding, that the center of vision is at point $z$; and let there be two magnitudes of which the larger is $bg$ and the smaller is $gd$, joined according to the angle $dgb$, which is divided into equal parts by Proposition 9 of Book 1 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Prop. 9: To bisect a given rectilinear angle.</note> by drawing line $gz$. I say that with the eye existing upon any point of line $zg$, the magnitudes $bg$ and $gd$ will always be seen as unequal, and $bg$ will be larger. For with lines $bz$ and $dz$ drawn, the angles at point $z$ are made unequal, and the larger angle is the one which the larger base subtends by Proposition 25 of Book 1 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Prop. 25: If two triangles have two sides equal respectively, but one has a larger base, it will also have a larger angle opposite the base.</note>. Since

->[Image: A geometric diagram featuring two arcs of different curvatures intersecting at point $z$. These arcs are built over segments $b-g$ and $g-d$ which meet at an angle at $g$. Straight lines connect point $z$ to the endpoints $b, g,$ and $d$.]<-

if it were granted that those angles were equal, the triangles $bzg$ and $gzd$ would be equiangular and equilateral <note>original: "equianguli & æquilateri"</note>, which is contrary to the hypothesis. It is therefore evident that those angles will be unequal; thus, by Proposition 20 of this book, those magnitudes will be seen as unequal, and $gb$ itself will appear larger because it will be seen under a larger angle. But also, sometimes those magnitudes are seen as equal. For let there be described, as in the premise, around the larger line $bg$ a portion larger than a semicircle, which shall be $bzg$; and let lines $bz$ and $gz$ be drawn; and let there be circumscribed around the smaller line $gd$ a portion similar to the portion $bzg$—that is, containing an angle equal to angle $bzg$; let the common point of these intersections also be point $z$; and let lines $zb, zg,$ and $zd$ be drawn. Therefore, because angle $dzg$ is equal to angle $bzg$ (since they fall into similar portions), with the center of the eye placed at point $z$, which is the common point of the intersection of those portions, the magnitudes $bg$ and $gd$ appear equal. Which is what was proposed.

### 123. *There are places in which, with the center of vision positioned, equal magnitudes erected upon a subject plane surface sometimes appear equal and sometimes unequal. Euclid, Theorem 48 of the Optics.*
