124. *There are places where, when the center of vision is positioned, the equal sides of a rectangle in the same plane sometimes appear equal and sometimes unequal.*

Let there be a rectangle $abgd$, whose two sides $ab$ and $gd$ are equal. I say there are places where, when the center of vision is positioned, those two sides will appear equal. Let a circle be circumscribed around that rectangle by Theorem 40 of Book 1 of this work and Proposition 9 of Book 3 <note>Euclid, Elements, Book 3, Prop. 9: Finding the center of a circle.</note>. On any point of either of the arcs (which are $bd$ and $ag$), let the center of vision be placed. For example, let it be placed at the midpoint of arc $bd$, which is $o$, and let lines $oa, og, ob, od$ be joined. Since the sides $ab$ and $gd$ are equal, the arcs $ab$ and $dg$ will be equal by Proposition 28 of Book 3. Therefore, by Proposition 27 of Book 3, the angles $aob$ and $god$ will be equal. Thus, by Proposition 20 of this book, sides $ab$ and $dg$ appear equal when the vision is at point $o$. This must be demonstrated similarly for any point on both arcs $bd$ and $ag$; for whenever the center of vision is at any of those points, the magnitudes $ab$ and $gd$ appear equal. Similarly, if line $bd$ is divided into equal parts at point $f$ by Proposition 10 of Book 1, and the center of vision is placed at point $f$, then again by Proposition 4 of Book 1 and Proposition 20 of this book, lines $ab$ and $gd$ will appear equal. And if a perpendicular line $fz$ is drawn from point $f$ to line $bd$ by Proposition 11 of Book 1, cutting the circumference <term>peripheria</term> <note>The outer boundary or "periphery" of the circle.</note> of the circle at point $o$, then according to the previous points, at whatever point on line $fz$ the center of vision is placed, those lines $ab$ and $dg$ will always appear equal by Proposition 4 of Book 1 and Proposition 20 of this book. 

But if the center of the eye is outside the circle $abgd$, such as at point $e$—which, for the sake of the example, is closer to line $dg$ than to $ba$—I say that line $ab$ will appear larger than line $gd$. Let the lines $ae, ge, be, de$ be extended, and let line $ea$ cut the circumference of the circle at point $t$, and line $eg$ at point $r$; let lines $bt$ and $dr$ be joined. Since, as was clear above, lines $ab$ and $gd$ are equal by hypothesis, arc $ab$ will be equal to arc $gd$ by Proposition 28 of Book 3. Therefore, by Proposition 27 of Book 3, angles $atb$ and $grd$ are equal because of the equality of the two arcs. Thus, by Proposition 13 of Book 1, angles $bte$ and $dre$ are equal. Because arc $bt$ is larger than arc $dr$ due to the greater proximity of point $e$ to line $dg$, side $bt$ will be larger than side $rd$ by Proposition 29 of Book 3. However, line $et$ is smaller than line $re$, which is clear from Proposition 17 of Book 6 and Proposition 36 of Book 3, having first drawn from point $e$ a line $eq$ tangent to the circle at point $q$ by Proposition 17 of Book 3. Then, since line $ae$ is larger than line $eg$ by hypothesis, it is also clear by Propositions 8 and 10 of Book 5 that line $er$ is larger than line $et$. 125. *There are locations where, when the eye is placed there, unequal magnitudes joined together appear equal to each other. Euclid’s Optics, Theorem 50.*

Of two given magnitudes, let *bg* be the larger and *dg* the smaller. Around each, let a semicircle be described: around line *dg*, the semicircle *dzg*; and around line *bg*, the semicircle *gkb*. Let a third semicircle be described around the whole line *db*, which shall be *dab*. When lines *da* and *ba* are drawn, it is clear that when extended, they intersect the smaller semicircles. Therefore, let line *ab* intersect semicircle *gkb* at point *k*, and let line *da* intersect semicircle *dzg* at point *z*. Let lines *zg* and *kg* be drawn. 

It is clear by Proposition 31 of Book 3 that angles *dzg*, *gkb*, and *dab* are all equal, because they are right angles <note>In geometry, any angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (90 degrees).</note>. Therefore, as the center of the eye is moved through points *k*, *a*, and *z*, line *bg* will appear equal to line *gd*, and line *db* will appear equal to one of the others, and line *dg* will appear equal to both lines *dg* and *bg*. The same happens as the center of the eye is moved through any points of the shapes of the semicircles. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Thus, when the vision is at the point of their common intersection, which is point *h*, then by the same gaze, line *ab* will appear as if it were double line *bg*. 

In the same way, the appearance of equal things is diversified by dividing the angle by any other number. For this is a general principle: given a magnitude and an angle, one can divide the angle according to some proportion by Proposition 27 of Book 1 of this work, and describe a segment of a circle around the magnitude containing an angle equal to one of those divisions. Whenever the center of vision is placed at that angle, the apparent size of the magnitude will seem to vary according to it. This, then, is the proposition. However, the length of the distance extended along a straight line from the point where the lines containing that angle meet has a significant effect; for in all things seen from an unequal distance, the ratio of the greater distance to the lesser is greater than the ratio of the angle to the angle, as is clear from Proposition 11 of this book. The same also happens if angle *akb* is divided according to another proportion, and an angle equal to it is constructed in a segment of a circle over line *bg*; the proof is the same. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 127. There are locations where, by positioning the sight, the same magnitude appears sometimes in its full size, sometimes as half, sometimes as a quarter, or according to any given proportion.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram with horizontal chord a-b. Point g is the center. Points e and d are on the upper arc. Lines connect g-a, g-b (forming a central triangle), and e-a, e-b (forming an inscribed triangle).</image-desc>

Let *ab* be the magnitude being seen. I say that it (when the center of vision is moved to different points) sometimes appears in its own proper quantity, and sometimes in any other proportion. Let a circle *aeb* be described around line *ab*, such that line *ab* is not the diameter of that circle; this can be done by taking a line larger than line *ab* as the diameter of the circle. Let the center of that circle be point *g*, and let lines *ag, bg, ae, be* be drawn. It is clear then, by Proposition 20 of Book 3 <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 3, Prop. 20: The angle at the center of a circle is double the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.</note>, that angle *agb* is double angle *aeb*. Therefore, when the center of the eye is at the center of the circle *g*, line *ab* will appear twice as large as it appears when the center of the eye is on the arc *aeb*, according to Proposition 20 of this book. This is because all angles contained under the lines drawn from those points on the arc to points *a* and *b* are equal by Proposition 21 of Book 3; and the angle at the center *g* is double any of them by Proposition 20 of Book 3. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 128. As the eye moves closer to the object being seen, the size of the seen thing will appear to increase. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 55.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a triangle with base b-g. A vertical line drops from the center of the base to a point z. Point d lies on this vertical line between the base and z. We understand here that the approach is along a straight line perpendicular to the magnitude being seen. Therefore, let lines *bd* and *gd* be drawn. Since, by Proposition 21 of Book 1 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Prop. 21: If two lines are drawn from the ends of one side of a triangle to a point inside, they will contain a larger angle than the original sides.</note>, angle *bdg* is larger than angle *bzg*, and an object seen under a larger angle appears larger by Proposition 20 of this book, the size of line *bg* will appear increased when the eye is at *d* compared to when the center of vision was at point *z*. This is the proposition.

### 129. Increased magnitudes will appear to approach the eye. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 58.

*130. All magnitudes lying in the same plane, whose extremities are not in a direct line with their middle, sometimes produce a concave total figure, and sometimes a convex one. Euclid’s Optics, Theorem 59.*

<image-desc>Two geometric diagrams illustrating visual perception of curvature. Both feature an observer at point k at the bottom. On the left, visual rays extend to points g, b, and d forming a concave arc where b is further from k. On the right, the arc g-b-d is convex with b closer to k than the endpoints g and d.</image-desc>

For example, let magnitude *g b d* be seen lying in some plane: and let its middle point, which is *b*, not be in a direct line with the two extremities, but outside them: and let the eye be at point *k*: and let lines *k g*, *k b*, and *k d* be drawn. Thus, the total figure *g b d* will appear concave if its middle point is farther from the sight. But let the middle point of the seen object, which is *b*, approach the sight and become closer to the eye: I say that the entire magnitude will appear convex. For the sight sees the middle and extreme points simultaneously, whose forms are described on the surface of the sight according to their position and distance: and there occurs a passion <note>In medieval science, a "passion" refers to an effect or impression received by a sense organ.</note> in the sight, which occurs from concave and convex surfaces. Therefore, those things appear concave or convex according to the diversity of the position of their middle point. And this is what was proposed.

*131. Of all objects moving at equal speed along the same line, located beyond the point where the visual axes meet closest to the sight, those that are further away appear to move more slowly.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a visual field originating from point a at the bottom. Several diverging lines extend upwards, intersected by lines representing paths of motion labeled with points b, c, d, g, and s.</image-desc>

Let there be two moving objects *b* and *c* moving at equal speed: and let the center of vision be *a*: and let the moving objects *b* and *c* be on the line *a g*: and let *b* be further from the sight than *c*. Because line *a b* is greater than line *a c*, it is clear by Proposition 7 of this book <note>Witelo’s Prop. 7: Objects further away are seen under a smaller angle.</note> that vision occurs under a smaller angle along line *a b* than along line *a c*. Therefore, the vision occurring at point *b* will be less certain than that occurring at point *c*: and similarly, by the same Proposition 7, the space that the moving object *b* traverses in a certain time is seen under a smaller angle than the space that moving object *c* traverses in the same time. Therefore, the motion of moving object *b* is not understood as perfectly as the motion of moving object *c*: thus, *b* will seem to move more slowly, because object *b* is seen under a smaller angle than object *c*. And similarly, the space that object *b* traverses will be seen under a smaller angle than the space through which object *c* passes in the same time. Therefore, the space through which object *b* has moved will appear smaller than the space traversed by object *c*, according to Proposition 20 of this book. And if both these moving objects are on a line oblique to the sight outside the axis, such as line *a d*: then both will appear to move less than their true motions: but *b*, which is further from the sight, will still seem to move less than *c* itself. But if both are on one visual axis, and one of them is within the meeting of the axes closest to the sight, that closer one will be seen entirely obliquely, as has been clear through many of the preceding propositions: whence it will be estimated to move more slowly, even though it is closer to the sight. Thus the proposition is clear.

*132. Of all objects moving at equal speed upon parallel lines that are not close to the sight, those further away appear to move more slowly. Euclid’s Optics, Theorem 56.*

<image-desc>A geometric perspective diagram. An observer is at point z at the bottom apex. Two horizontal parallel lines, a-d (further away) and b-e (closer), are shown within the triangular visual field defined by rays from z.</image-desc>

Let there be two moving objects *a* and *b* moving at equal speed over two parallel and equal lines, which are *a d* and *b e*, of which *a d* is further from the sight: and let the center of vision be point *z*: from which let lines *z a*, *z b*, *z d*, *z e* be drawn. I say that moving object *a*, which is further from the sight, will appear to become slower than moving object *b*, which is closer: because by Propositions 7 and 20 of this book, line *a d* will appear smaller than line *b e*, even though they are equal. Therefore, moving object *a*, which cuts off equal parts of line *a d* in equal time, appears to move more slowly than moving object *b*, which in the same time, proportional to the division of line *a d*, appears to cut off larger parts of line *b e*, although, as is clear from the hypothesis, those parts are equal on both sides. Therefore, moving object *b* appears to move faster than moving object *a*, which is further from the sight. For when moving object *b* reaches point *e*: then moving object *a* reaches point *d*, which appears to be behind point *e*: and so moving object *a* appears to be placed behind moving object *b*: because line *b e* appears

133. *With the eye remaining fixed and the <term>visual axis</term> <note>The central line of sight extending directly from the pupil to the object.</note> shifted equally, those more distant visible objects which are equally far from the original position of the axis seem to lag behind. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 57.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a vertex e at the bottom from which two rays extend upwards and outwards. On the left ray are points a and b; on the right ray are points d and g. A line segment connects a and d, and another connects b and g.</image-desc>

Let there be two visible objects, *a* and *g*, existing on two equal lines, which are *ab* and *gd*. Let the center of vision be *e*, and let it be that the visual axis passes from point *d* to point *b*. Point *b* will therefore be farther from the sight than point *d*. It is clear, then, through Theorem 7 of this book, that since line *ab* is farther from the sight, it is seen under a smaller angle than its equal, *gd*, which is closer to the sight. Therefore, angle *deg* is larger than angle *bea*. Consequently, by Theorem 20 of this book, line *gd* appears larger than line *ab*. Thus, while the eye remains fixed at point *e* and the visual axis moves through the entire space in which the visible objects *a* and *g* are located, the axis—on account of the smallness of angle *bea* compared to angle *deg*—passes across visible object *a* more quickly than across visible object *g*. Therefore, visible object *a* seems to fall behind visible object *g*, because object *g* will be seen behind it. Which is what was proposed.

134. *Among objects moving at equal speed along a line to which they stand perpendicularly—that line being parallel to a line drawn from the eye—the object that is farther from the center of vision seems to lead, while the closer one seems to follow. However, when the crossing is made to the other side of the line drawn from the eye, the more distant object seems to follow, while the closer one seems to lead. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 52.*

<image-desc>A complex perspective diagram illustrating moving objects relative to a center of vision m at the bottom. Three horizontal parallel lines are shown at different distances from m. Rays from m pass through points on these lines, labeled with various letters: k, a, d, z, b, g on the lower part; f, e, l on the middle line; and s, t, p, r, n, x on the upper line. Points q and k appear at the far left and right ends of the motion paths.</image-desc>

Let there be three objects moved at an equal velocity: *bg*, *dz*, and *ka*, positioned upon a line *ga* so that they stand perpendicularly at points *g*, *z*, and *a*. Let moving object *bg* be more remote from the center of vision, which is point *m*, and let moving object *ak* be closer to the sight. Let a line *ml* be drawn from the eye at point *m* (by the first book, Proposition 31) parallel to line *ga*. Let lines *mg*, *mz*, and *ma* be drawn, and let lines *ka*, *dz*, and *bg* be extended to line *ml*. Let line *ka* meet line *ml* at point *f*, line *dz* at point *e*, and line *bg* at point *l*. Since lines *ga* and *ml* are parallel, it is clear by Theorem 21 of this book that they seem to converge toward the side of *l*. Therefore, *g* will appear closer to point *l* than *z* is to point *e*, or *a* is to point *f*. Thus, *bg* appears to be leading, *dz* follows it, and *ka* is the last of them. 

Now, let line *ga* be extended beyond point *a* to point *q*, and let line *qm* be joined. Because, by the first book, Proposition 16, angle *maq* is greater than angle *mza*, and angle *mza* is greater than angle *mgz*, it is clear that line *mg* seems to approach closer to point *g* than line *mz* does to point *z*, or line *ma* to point *a*, since exterior angles are larger than interior ones. Thus, the moving object *bg*, which is more remote, will seem to lead the moving objects *dz* and *ka* (as the objects *ka*, *dz*, and *bg* approach the line *ml* at equal velocity along the straight line *ga*). However, object *ka*, which is the last one, seems to follow because it appears to be further removed from line *ml*. This will continue until line *ga* is superimposed upon line *ml*. At that point, along the straight line *ml*, object *ka* appears closer to the sight than the others, and larger by Theorems 7 and 20 of this book. 

However, once the crossing is made beyond line *ml*—so that the objects which were previously to the right of the sight become to the left, or vice versa—then the more remote object will seem to follow, and the closer one to lead, for the same reason we stated before. To make this clear by example: let moving object *bg*, which is farther from the center of vision *m*, having crossed line *ml*, arrive at the position of line *nx*; let *dz* arrive at line *pr*; and let *ka*, which is closer to the sight, arrive at line *st*. Let lines *mn*, *mp*, and *ms* be drawn from the center of vision to points *n*, *p*, and *s*. Moving object *nx* will then seem to follow the other two objects because, as previously stated, line *nx* approaches closer to point *l* than line *pr* does to point *e*, or line *st* to point *f*. Therefore, object *bg*, which was previously leading, will seem to follow when it reaches line *nx*; and line *ak*, which was previously following, will seem to lead when it is on line *st*. And so, with the position of these moving objects changed, the motion will appear different. Which is what was proposed.

135. *When several objects move at unequal speeds in the same direction as the observer, those moving at the same speed as the eye seem to be at rest; those moving more slowly seem to move in the opposite direction; and those moving faster seem to move ahead. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 53.*

# BOOK FOUR

Let there be three moving objects **b**, **c**, and **d**, and let the center of the eye be point **a**. Let **b** be the slowest among these, **c** be as fast as the sight, and **d** be faster than **c**. Let all move toward the same part of the universe. From the center of the sight, let lines **ab**, **ac**, and **ad** be drawn. Therefore, when the eye **a** is moved, the moving object **c**, which is as fast as the eye, is moved equally with the eye. It does not, therefore, change its position with respect to the eye; thus, by Theorem 112 of this book, it will appear to be at rest. However, because moving object **b** is the slowest, it is clear that it is passed by the motion of the sight because of the faster motion of the sight itself. And because moving object **c** appears to be at rest, and moving object **b** is always removed further and further from moving object **c** due to the excess of speed of moving object **c** over moving object **b**, moving object **b** therefore appears to move in the opposite direction. But moving object **d**, because it is the fastest, precedes moving object **c** and the sight itself, and it always becomes more distant from the sight. It therefore appears to move forward. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a point 'a' at the bottom representing the eye, with rays extending upwards to two labeled points 'c' and 'b'.</image-desc>

136. *If some moving objects are seen moving at the same speed, and something else appears unmoved: that object will appear to move in the direction opposite to the other moving objects. Euclid, Optics, Theorem 54.*

Let there be two moving objects **b** and **d**, which move at equal speed toward any one direction; and let **c** be something that is not moved. Let the center of sight be **a**, and let lines **ab**, **ac**, and **ad** be drawn from the center of sight. Therefore, because moving object **b** moves toward some endpoint, it is clear that it becomes closer to that point than the body **c**, which does not move. But moving object **d** is also moved at the same speed as moving object **b**. Therefore, moving objects **b** and **d** do not seem to change their position relative to each other; however, the body **c** changes its position with respect to both of those moving objects. Therefore, **c** appears to move in the direction opposite to them, which is clear through Theorem 110 of this book. And this is what was proposed. From this, it is apparent why, when clouds are moved quickly, the seen moon appears to move in the opposite direction. For because the parts of the clouds are moved at an equal speed, like **b** and **d**, but the moon's own motion is not perceived by the sight in a short time because of its distance, the moon (like the object **c**) therefore appears to move in the opposite direction.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram similar to the first, with point 'a' at the bottom and three rays extending upwards to points labeled 'c', 'd', and 'b'.</image-desc>

137. *Points marked on a thing moved circularly appear as circles; and lines appear as rounded surfaces.*

When such moving objects marked in this way are moved circularly, any one of their points describes a circle by its motion. Because any given point is not fixed in the same place during <term>sensible time</term> <note>A duration of time long enough for the human senses to perceive.</note>, but in a small amount of time it revolves around the entire circumference upon which it is rolled, the form of the marked point then reaches the surface of the sight in the manner of the circumference of a circle. Indeed, because circular motion is entirely one, not dividing time, the sight cannot grasp the form of the marked point except according to the circumference of the circle; for in the smallest time, it perceives the color of that point as it revolves. And if there are several points marked in order, one below the other, several circles will appear contained alternately and in order. This is seen in the play of children with <term>spinning tops</term> <note>original: "trochis"; refers to a hoop or a top spun on flat surfaces.</note> driven circularly over flat surfaces; for when the top is revolved with a strong motion and someone looks at it, if there is one point marked on it, a circle will be seen. If there are several points distant from each other, several equidistant circles will be seen around the same center, and the sight will see the difference of the colors of any of those circles. And if several points of different colors are placed close to each other, the sight will grasp all the colors of those points as if they were one color, different from all the colors that are in those points, as if it were a color composed of all the colors of those points; it will not grasp the lines nor the diversity of colors. And if the motion is very strong, the sight will grasp that moved body as if it were at rest and circularly shaped, because no point of that body is fixed in a place during sensible time, but in the smallest time the entire circumference upon which it revolves is turned. Similarly, a moved line will appear, according to the length of the line, as the width of a certain rounded surface described upon the surface of the sight itself. And if that line was colored, then because of the speed of the motion, the motion makes the entire rounded surface appear colored. And this is what was proposed.

138. *In the vision of motion and rest, error happens to the <term>power of discernment</term> <note>original: "virtuti distinctive"; the faculty of the mind that distinguishes and judges sensory input.</note> from the immoderate arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible thing. Alhazen 28.39.49.55.60.65.67.70 n 3.*

Error happens in the vision of motion and rest due to immoderate light. For if at night the sight perceives a man before some grove, perhaps the distance of the man to the grove will be hidden from it. If, therefore, the viewer moves toward the man being seen, the closer he approaches him, the more certainly he will see that distance. Thus, while previously the man appeared together with the grove, the more he approaches him, the more the man appears removed from the grove. And since the grove certainly remains unmoved to him, he will judge the man to be walking in the direction opposite to the grove, even though the truth is that the man being seen is unmoved and at rest. Also, if a man seen at night is not fully perceived and moves slightly, his motion will not be discerned, and he will appear at rest. These errors would not happen in <term>temperate light</term> <note>Balanced or adequate lighting conditions.</note>.

# WITELO'S OPTICS

An error also occurs in the vision of motion and rest due to excessive <note>original: "intemperata," meaning a distance beyond the moderate range where the eye functions accurately</note> distance. For if someone moves toward the direction in which they see the moon, the sun, or some star, and after much movement they still see the moon ahead of them, distant by no less than at the start of their journey, they judge that the moon itself is moving in the same direction with them and receding from them, and that for this reason the distance remains the same. This also happens when the moon is actually hurrying in the opposite direction. This error occurs because it is known to man that in these lower natures <note>Meaning the terrestrial realm below the moon</note>, when there are two existing bodies, one of which moves in some direction, if the identity of their relative positions remains the same, then it is necessary that the other body has also moved in the same direction with equal motion. However, this should not be judged so in the case of the moon or stars, because the magnitude of the path a person travels by their own motion is not proportional to the magnitude of the body of the moon or another star. Therefore, the difference between the final proximity to the star and the first proximity is not sensible <note>perceptible to the senses</note> in respect to the total distance. 

The same error also happens in the motion of clouds: for the motion of the moon is believed to be very fast because the parts of the clouds through which the moon is seen are suddenly changed, and the moon is seen to be positioned now with these parts of the clouds, now with those. Because the moon is a body more luminous to the sight than the clouds, the moon is judged to move with a motion by which, in truth, it does not move. Similarly, an error occurs regarding rest: for something seen from a great distance, moving with a motion that is not fast, appears to be at rest; because of this, we believe the planets to be unmoved, although they move swiftly. For the paths they travel in a small amount of time are not perceptible to the sight from such a great distance; hence, while their position remains identical in respect to the viewer, they are thought to be at rest. 

Similarly, this error occurs if a seen body moves toward or away from the sight along the same visual line or axis. For then, unless its motion is very strong, it will be thought unmoved, because it is not perceived whether the parts or the whole are in a different state now than before; for the path it travels is imperceptible from such a great distance. 

An error also occurs to the discerning power <note>original: "uirtuti distictiuę," the faculty of the soul that judges sensory input</note> in the vision of the aforementioned things due to the excessive obliquity of the position. Thus, when someone is navigating quickly on a river and looks obliquely at the trees on the riverbank, they will judge the trees far from the visual axis to be moving, while those trees upon which the visual axis falls will seem to be at rest. Similarly, a moving wheel, such as a mill wheel, appears to be at rest when seen obliquely. This error is due solely to the slant of the object's position relative to the sight, since such a wheel is seen to move when viewed directly. 

An error also occurs in the vision of the aforementioned due to excessive size. For if two things move, one of which is a little faster than the other, the viewer will think their motion is equal, since the excess of one motion over the other is insensible to the sight; similarly, the quantity of the excess of the path which the other traverses is imperceptible to the sight. Hence, the equality of motions and paths is judged. Similarly, a small moving thing will perhaps be judged not to move, even if its distance from the sight is moderate. 

An error also occurs in these matters due to excessive rarity <note>meaning lack of clarity or transparency in the medium</note>. For if two bodies move in cloudy, dark air, one of which moves a little faster than the other, their motions will perhaps be judged equal, since because of the lack of transparency of the air, the excess of the motion of one over the other cannot be discerned; nor is the excess of the path traversed by one over the path traversed by the other then perceived by the sight. Similarly, in such air at a medium distance (though not small), if someone sees flowing water, they will either judge it unmoved, or if its flow is strong, it will be judged to move less than it actually does. 

The greatest error in the vision of motion and rest (which are measured by time) also happens from an excessive disposition of time. For when one of two moving objects moves a little faster than the other, the motions grasped in a brief time will be judged equal, because their excess is not so suddenly perceivable. If something moves slowly, it will not seem to move when inspected in a brief time, because the path through which it moves in a small time is imperceptible to the sight due to its smallness. But also a thing moving very fast in a circle and remaining in the same place, like a <term>spinning top</term> <note>original: "trochus," a child's toy top</note>, is not judged to move; for the location of the top is not changed, and the parts return very quickly to their prior position. 

An error also happens to the vision of the aforementioned due to an imbalance in the state of the sight itself. For when someone has been spun around many times and then stops, they then think that the nearby walls are moving. This is because the visual spirits <note>In medieval physiology, "spiritus uisibiles" were subtle fluids in the nerves that carried visual information to the brain</note> moved within are running about from the motion made by the body itself; when the exterior body rests, the spirits moved inside do not rest immediately, because being lighter than the coarse body, they are more mobile than it, and a smaller power of the soul moves them. These spirits, being in motion, represent moving forms to the discerning power. Therefore, all things whose forms are offered to the power of the soul by the moving spirits seem to move, even after the rest of the viewer himself. 

The case is similar in other moved things: for a <term>spinning top</term> moves for a long time after the rest of the hand that moved it, and does not rest until the <note>original: "uirtus influxa," a reference to "impressed force" or impetus, a precursor to the concept of momentum</note> impressed force within it ceases to move it. There is also a certain infirmity of the body and eyes in which all things seem to revolve. If a body of similar parts is also turned slowly, as happens in some clock wheels, then a weak sight will not perceive its motion, nor will even a healthy sight perceive the motion of a small duration of time. But if it is a body of dissimilar parts, as in mill wheels, then perhaps even a weak sight will grasp the motion, unless the revolution of the wheel is very fast; for because of the speed of the motion, the dissimilarity of the parts of the wheel perhaps cannot be grasped. Therefore, that which was proposed is clear.

### 139. Roughness is understood by the sight from the perception of light incident upon the surface of a rough body, through which the diversity of the positions of the parts of the surface of the body is understood.

Since roughness is a diversity of the positions of the parts of the surface of a body, it is clear from Theorem 11 of Book 2 of this work that the protruding parts create shadows when light falls upon the surface of that body. Therefore, the protruding parts will be manifest and exposed to the light, and shadows reach into the deep parts, mixing with the light falling on those parts. Therefore, the form of light on the surface of that body will be diversified...

...which does not happen on a flat surface: for its parts are of a similar position, and the form of light becomes uniform in all its parts. The sense of sight, therefore, recognizes that the form of light on rough and flat surfaces is different, due to the frequent experience of seeing both rough and flat surfaces; and according to this, it judges the roughness or flatness of the surface in any rough bodies. But if the parts of a rough surface are very prominent, sight can also perceive the prominence of those parts by perceiving the distance that exists between the parts. Thus, from the perception of the diversity of the positions of the parts of a rough surface, it will also perceive its roughness. Light will also be of the greatest diversity in that roughness, since it is distinctly mixed with larger shadows; and from the diversity of the form of light, the distance of the parts and the diversity of their positions will be seen, and from this, the roughness of the body will be visible. But if the prominences of the parts of the surface of the seen object are very small, sight will not perceive that roughness of the body except with a very close inspection. Thus, roughness is perceived by sight through the diversity of light falling on the surfaces of rough bodies, and consequently through the perception of the diversity of the positions of the parts of the body's surface. The proposition is therefore clear.

---

*140. Smoothness or flatness is perceived by sight through the perception of light falling upon the surface of a smooth body, and also through the complete uniformity of its parts. Alhazen, Book 2, chapter 34.*

Because smoothness is the equality of the position of the parts of a surface, it is clear that the parts of a smooth body are of a similar position. Therefore, the light falling on those bodies becomes uniform and unmixed with any shadows. For this reason, the shine or polish of a body—which is a kind of smoothness or flatness—is perceived by sight from the sparkling of light on the surface of that body, and from the position according to which the light is reflected to the eye or to another object. Sight also sometimes perceives flatness through diligent inspection, by which it perceives the equality of the parts of the seen surface; sometimes it also perceives flatness itself by placing the eye on one part of that seen surface. When the forms of the extreme parts of that surface, which are further from the eye, reach the eye along straight lines projected across that surface, then sight perceives the flatness of the surface in this way. The proposition is therefore clear.

---

*141. In the vision of roughness and smoothness, an error occurs in the faculty of discrimination due to the immoderate arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible thing. Alhazen, Book 3, chapters 29, 40, 50, 56, 61, 65, 68, 71.*

An error occurs in the vision of roughness and smoothness due to the weakness of light: for at night, a seen roughness might perhaps be judged as smoothness or vice versa, according to the quality of the object seen. Also, when light is reflected from washed black hair, that hair is estimated to be perfectly smooth, although in truth it is rough because there is an innumerable diversity and distance within it. Excessive distance also causes an error in the vision of roughness and smoothness; thus, in the painted hair or fur of some depicted image, roughness is estimated because of the distance, because the senses are accustomed to perceiving roughness in real hair. The same thing happens in the wrinkles of painted clothes, which because of distance seem to be folded, although they are established on a single flat surface. Similarly, if a body in which there is slight roughness is placed before the eye from a great distance, it will be thought smooth; because from such a distance the diversity of parts or the projection of shadows from the high parts onto the low parts cannot be discerned, and so smoothness is judged in it.

An error also occurs in the vision of roughness and smoothness due to immoderate position. For if light reflects obliquely from the painted hair of a depicted image, such that the eye is not in the place of reflection, the roughness of the hair will be perceived, even though there is only smoothness there <note>Meaning the physical surface of the painting is smooth, but the lack of direct reflection allows the painted "rough" texture to be seen</note>; this would not happen to an eye directly receiving the reflected light, because then the true smoothness would appear. Also, when a body with slight roughness is tilted away from the visual axis, it will appear smooth; but if it were placed directly before the eye, its roughness would present itself to the sight.

An error also occurs in the vision of these things due to immoderate size: for when a very small thing is encountered by the eye, smoothness will perhaps be seen where there is roughness, or vice versa; for the prominence of some parts over others is not perceived because of the extreme smallness of the body. An error also occurs in the vision of these things due to immoderate solidity <note>Density or lack of transparency</note>. For if there is a slight roughness in a very rare <note>Thin or low-density</note> body, it will perhaps be thought smooth; and if the whole is smooth, but a rough body or one of different colors is seen through it, this body which is rare and smooth will be estimated to be rough, and there will be an error in roughness and smoothness.

An error also occurs in the vision of these things due to immoderate transparency <term>raritas</term> <note>Vitello uses 'raritas' here to mean the clarity or thinness of the medium, like air</note>: because in dark, cloudy air, a rough body will appear smooth because the causes of the roughness are hidden, and a polished object, when reflection from it is not discerned, will perhaps be estimated as rough. An error also occurs in the vision of these things due to the smallness of time: for when something rough is seen suddenly, it will be estimated as smooth, and if something smooth is seen suddenly, the smoothness or roughness cannot be discerned; thus an error occurs under doubt. An error also occurs in the vision of these things due to weakness of sight: because weak sight will perhaps consider a slightly rough body to be smooth, or vice versa, if there is a dissimilarity in the forms of the rough and smooth body. The proposition is therefore clear.

# VITELLO’S OPTICS

<meta>catchword: For it is</meta>

As we have previously stated, those transparent bodies are the ones through which sight can pass to see other objects. Thus, a transparent body is not seen by itself (as is clear from Proposition 14, Book 3 of this work <note>original: "14 t3 huius"</note>) unless it possesses some thickness <term>thickness: *spissitudo*, referring to the physical density or lack of perfect transparency</term> relative to the transparency of the air between it and the eye—such as crystal, beryl, and similar transparent things. However, even the transparency of these objects is not grasped by sight except through the perception of the form of a body existing beyond them or surrounding them, whose light or color reaches the eye through those transparent media. Therefore, when the sense of sight recognizes that the form of light or color it perceives belongs only to the body existing beyond the transparent body, it then senses the transparency of that body. But if the transparent body is only weakly transparent—for instance, if it has a greater density than other transparent things—and the objects existing beyond it have weak light or color, then its transparency is hardly perceived by sight unless it is placed in strong light. In that case, its transparency can be better understood. Furthermore, because of the close application of very dense bodies to such transparent bodies, the sight’s perception of them is entirely blocked in the area where they touch; this is evident in the case of jasper set in gold. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 5, chapter 6, number 2.</margin>
### 143. *Density or thickness is perceived by sight through the absence of transparency.*

When the sense of sight perceives a body and does not sense any transparency within it, it immediately concludes that the body is dense. This is because the visual operation terminates immediately at that body, nothing penetrates through it, and the sight cannot be extended to see the forms of other bodies beyond it. Then, the sight judges it to be thick or dense and composed of compact parts. Thus, thickness or density is perceived by sight through the deprivation of transparency. This is what was proposed.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 3, chapters 30, 41, 50, 56, 61, 65, 68, 71, number 3.</margin>
### 144. *In the vision of rarity and solidity, an error occurs in the power of discernment due to the immoderate arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible object.*

<note>The 'eight circumstances' are the environmental conditions Vitello (following Alhazen) deemed necessary for accurate vision: distance, position, light, size, solidity, transparency, time, and the health of the eye.</note>

For example, due to the weakness of light (as at night), the rarity <term>rarity: *raritas*, meaning the opposite of density; a quality of being thin, porous, or transparent</term> of a very rare body will appear to be less than it is. Because the form of a solid body beyond it is not fully perceived, it will be thought that a lack of rarity is blocking the passage of forms, and even a moderately rare body will then be judged as solid. An error in the vision of the aforementioned properties also occurs due to immoderate distance. For when a needle or some other very thin object is held close to the eye, although it appears larger to the sight than it actually is, it does not hide any part of the opposite wall or other body from view. Therefore, because rarity is not perceived except when other bodies are seen behind rare ones (as is clear from Proposition 142 of this book), transparency will be thought to exist in the needle or other body since the whole wall is seen behind it. This happens because such a small distance is immoderate relative to the needle's ability to hide things. Similarly, if someone looks from a great distance at a rare body behind which there is no colored or dark body, that rare body will not be considered rare, but solid; for no other body is perceived behind it, which is the defining property of rare bodies.

Error in the vision of the aforesaid also happens from an immoderate arrangement of positions. For if light falls at an angle into a glass full of wine, and the passage of light through the glass is hidden from sight, and there is a great deflection of that light from the incident rays, and it is also hidden from the viewer that there is wine in the glass vessel, then the viewer will judge the wine to be a solid body—that is, the wine together with the glass vessel. This error would not happen if the light passed directly through the glass vessel placed straight ahead.

Error also occurs in the vision of these things from immoderate size. For if someone looks at a body with very polished parts so that light can be reflected from it, and it is similar to a pearl, the sight will judge it to be rare even though it is dense. Similarly, when a very small rare body is seen, it will be likened to a solid because no solid body is perceived behind it.

Error also occurs in the vision of the aforesaid from immoderate solidity. For if a body that is not very rare and is strongly colored is placed behind a very rare body, then the first will appear not very rare, but its rarity will be likened to the rarity of the body behind it. For example, glass placed over other glass does not appear as rare as it does when seen by itself; thus an error in rarity occurs. However, if a solid body is placed very close behind a rare body, the first will be judged solid, and an error in solidity occurs. Also, if a very rare glass vessel contains wine, since no light or other body is perceived behind it, the wine itself together with the glass vessel might be judged as a single solid body.

The same error also happens in the vision of the aforesaid from a lack of rarity <note>In this context, Vitello likely means a lack of transparency in the surrounding medium.</note>. In cloudy, dark air, a rare body will appear less rare and will perhaps be thought solid; thus an error occurs in both solidity and rarity. Error also happens from a shortness of time. For when light falls at an angle on a body of low rarity, and that body also passes quickly before the sight, since the deflection of the light is not perceived, it might be thought that the body is extremely rare. If it were looked at for a longer time, the sight would perceive that the deflection of light was the cause of the appearance of greater rarity in the body. Furthermore, if someone looks at a rare body only for an instant and does not discern the passage of light through it, they will think it is solid.

Weakness of sight also brings error to the vision of these things. For when there is little solidity in a rare body, that solidity will be judged by a weak sight to be greater than it truly is. And when there is a strong color in a rare body, or behind it, or if there is only a little rarity, that body will be thought solid by a weak sight. Thus, what was proposed is clear universally in all these cases.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 2, chapter 57, number 2.</margin>
### 145. *Shadow is perceived by sight through the deprivation of some light while another light is present.*

<summary>This page analyzes how the human eye and mind distinguish between transparent, dense, and rare objects, noting that transparency is often perceived indirectly by seeing objects behind the medium. Vitello details various optical illusions (errors of the "eight circumstances") where conditions like poor light, extreme distance, or short duration lead the viewer to misidentify a material's density or rarity.</summary>
<keywords>transparency, density, rarity, optical illusions, eight circumstances, Vitello, Alhazen, medieval optics, visual perception, shadow</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of transparency and density. Having established how we perceive objects through transparent media, the author now transitions into the perception of shadows and darkness, explaining how the eye distinguishes between the absence of light and the physical properties of dark objects.</meta>

-># BOOK FOUR<-

For a shadow is the deprivation of a certain action <note>original: "actus"; in medieval physics, the "action" of light refers to its active presence or effect on a space</note>, occurring when the presence of one light exists while another light is absent in a shaded place. Therefore, when the sense of sight perceives a body near a shadow that has greater illumination and stronger light than the body existing in the shaded place, it then perceives the "shadowing" of that place and the deprivation of the light that falls upon the bodies neighboring it. Thus, when sight perceives some light in a place that lacks primary sunlight (which is projected according to the direct path of the rays), it nevertheless perceives secondary light, which is created by the diffusion of the primary light. For example, when a sunbeam enters a house through a single window, it illuminates the entire house by its diffusion. In this case, the sight—existing outside the path of the beam—perceives the shadowing of the place and the deprivation of the primary sunlight found in the beam, or from some other strong light. Sometimes the sight immediately perceives a shaded body; at other times, it only does so through careful intuition. Occasionally, it will see a "multiplied" shadow according to the deprivation of various lights, while some light always remains, from whose presence <note>original: "actualitate"</note> the sight can exercise its action toward other things. Generally, therefore, shadows can be seen according to all the modes of shadows that we have previously discussed. And this is the proposition.

*146. Darkness is understood by the sight from the total deprivation of light. Alhazen, Book 58, number 2.* <note>The author refers to the *Optics* of Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), the foundational authority for this work.</note>

When the sight perceives a place and no light within it, it then senses its darkness, even if that darkness is perhaps caused by shadows—as in a gloomy dungeon during the day, where darkness is seen because of the shadows of thick walls. Likewise, the night is dark because of the shadow of the earth. Therefore, darkness is a "large shadow" whose boundary is not felt to reach any bright object; similarly, a shadow is a "small darkness" having some action of light and bounded by something bright. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*147. In the vision of shadow and darkness, error happens to the distinguishing power <term>distinguishing power: *virtus distinctiva*, the cognitive faculty that processes visual information</term> from the immoderate arrangement of the eight circumstances of any seen thing. Alhazen, 31, 42, 50, 56, 62, 65, 68, 71, number 3.* <note>The "eight circumstances" are the physical conditions of sight: distance, position, light, size, solidity, transparency, duration, and the health of the eye.</note>

Error occurs in the vision of shadow and darkness due to the immoderate arrangement of light. For if there are dark parts on a white wall and the light of a candle falls upon it, it can happen that the person seeing that darkness will judge it to be a shadow, and perhaps it will seem that the apparent shadow proceeds from a neighboring wall. And if there is a very intense blackness in a part of the wall, it might be judged as the emptiness of a hole providing a path for the emerging darkness. If the entire surface of the wall is blackened with intense blackness, perhaps the whole wall will be judged as a certain darkness of shadows, as happens with a wall covered in the soot of smoke when seen under weak light.

Error also occurs in the vision of shadow and darkness due to excessive distance. For if a white body is placed opposite the sight at a very great distance, and there is some dark part on it while sunlight descends upon that body, a shadow will appear in the dark part of the body. If another body is then seen next to that first one, it will be judged that the appearing shadow is projected from that other body onto the first. Thus, because of the excess of distance, an error occurs in the vision of the shadow. Likewise, if a white body is seen from afar in which there are many black parts, they will perhaps be judged as darkness in that area; for it will be believed that the white body is perforated according to its black parts, through which the darkness existing behind the white body emerges. This, however, would not happen at a moderate distance.

Error also occurs in the vision of the aforementioned things due to an unorganized position of opposition, just as it does from immoderate distance. For if a body is far away and has a dark part, it will perhaps be thought a shadow; and if some body is placed near that first one, the shadow will be judged to be projected from that second body onto the first. If there is a very black part in that body, it will perhaps be judged as the perforation of a hole in that place through which the darkness existing behind the white body emerges. This would not happen with a body approaching the direct line of sight.

Error also occurs in the vision of the aforementioned things due to the smallness of the quantity of the thing seen. For if there is a distinction of points that are not very black on a white wall placed opposite the sight, and sunlight falls directly or nearly so upon the wall, each of those points will be judged by the viewer to be an individual hole in which there is a shadow, since the light does not penetrate them—just as usually happens when light falls upon the surface of many holes. Thus, an error of shadow occurs from the smallness of the points. If those points are of the greatest blackness, they will then be judged as small holes through which darkness passes; and thus, the smallness of those points alone is the cause of the appearance of darkness.

Error also occurs in the vision of shadow and darkness due to immoderate solidity—namely, due to a lack of solidity. For when sunlight descends into a house through a hole and falls upon a glass window, if that house is shadowy, a shadow will appear upon that window, even though in truth light has fallen upon it. This light would be perceived if the body of the window were solid <note>original: "solidum"; here meaning opaque or dense enough to reflect light rather than let it pass through</note>, since then the light would not penetrate, and thus light appears upon a solid body. Therefore, an error occurs regarding the shadow because of the lack of solidity. Similarly, an error occurs in the vision of darkness or obscurity from the lack of solidity: for when sunlight does not descend directly into the water of a river or the sea (as happens in the morning and evening hours), if there is great clarity in the water, it will appear dark; and the clearer it is, the darker it will appear. This happens because the upper part of the water projects a shadow upon the next lower part of the water, and that next part upon the other next lower part, and thus through each part, the upper always projects a shadow upon the lower all the way to the bottom of the water. Although the shadow of each individual part is small in itself, many shadows joined together create one very large shadow, just as is clearly seen to happen in the color of wine. For in a small quantity of wine, the color is weak, but in a large quantity of wine, although all the wine is homo-

homogeneous in substance and color, that same color becomes stronger. However, the reason why shadows in the sea—with their upper parts lying over the lower parts—appear as darkness amidst the clarity of the sea is this: the intense clarity of the water is a sign of intense <term>rarity</term><note>In medieval science, "rarity" refers to low density or high transparency, the opposite of "density" or "solidity."</note>, which allows for a greater penetration of visible forms. From this comes a greater diffusion of the forms of many parts of the sea that create a shadow; the perception of these aggregated shadows creates the appearance of darkness. But if the sea is turbulent, because of its diminished rarity [transparency], only a few forms of the parts will penetrate to reach the sight, and only a small part of the water will be grasped. Although this part creates a shadow, since the part itself is small, the shadow will be faint, and the color of that part will overpower the shadow. For in turbid water, the specific color of the parts of the water appears, whereas in clear water, none appears. Thus, because of the more apparent turbid color and because of the faintness of the visible part of the shadow, "darkness" is not perceived in the water. Therefore, when the water is turbid, it will appear colored, and when it is clear, it will appear dark. However, when a ray of the sun falls directly upon the surface of the sea, since the passage is open to it because of the water's rarity, all appearance of darkness and shadow is cast away.

Thus, both shadow and darkness are caused by a lack of solidity: because light cannot pass through a perfectly solid body, while through a body of perfect rarity [transparency], light passes without shadow. An error in the vision of the aforementioned things also happens due to an "immoderate rarity" <note>An excess of transparency that confuses the eye's ability to gauge depth or substance.</note>. If a white body containing small, round black particles is seen through cloudy or dark air (as at twilight), and the light of a fire falls upon that body in such a way that the overall state of the air is not changed, then shadows will appear in those spots. Or, perhaps, they will be thought of as holes providing a path for the darkness behind that body to reach the sight. Thus, an error in the vision of shadow and obscurity happens because of the immoderate rarity of the body.

An error in the vision of these things also happens due to a shortness of time. For if there are darkish parts on a white wall, and the light of a fire falls upon that wall, those black parts, seen suddenly, will be thought to be shadows. If, however, the blackness of those parts is intense, they will be judged to be holes full of darkness. Error also happens to the vision of these things due to the weakness of the sight. For on a white wall, darkish spots appear as shadows to a weak sight when light falls upon them; and if they are very black, they will appear to be holes through which darkness from the places behind that white wall reaches the sight. Therefore, in all the eight aforementioned circumstances of visible things, what was proposed is clear.

148. *Beauty is perceived by the sight either from the simple comprehension of visible forms that please the soul, or from the conjunction of several visible <term>intentions</term> <note>original: "intentionum"; in this context, "intentions" are the individual qualities or characteristics of an object that the mind perceives, such as size, shape, or color.</note> that have a proper proportion to one another in the form being seen. Alhazen Book 4, proposition 59, note 2.*

For that "pleasing of the soul" which is called beauty sometimes arises from the simple comprehension of visible forms, as is clear by running through all the species of visible things. To speak by way of example so that other things may be understood through it: **light**, which is the first visible thing, creates beauty; hence the sun, moon, and stars appear beautiful because of light alone. **Color** also creates beauty, such as the color green or rose, and other sparkling colors that diffuse the form of their own specific light to the sight. 

**Distance** and **proximity** also create beauty in the sight: for in some beautiful forms there are small, ugly spots or wrinkles that are displeasing to the seeing soul, but which remain hidden to the sight due to distance, and thus the form pleasing to the soul reaches the sight because of that distance. In many beautiful forms, there are also small, subtle "intentions" that contribute to the beauty of the forms, such as graceful linework and a lovely arrangement of parts, which only appear in proximity to the sight and make the form appear beautiful. 

**Magnitude** [size] also creates beauty in the sight: for this reason, the moon appears more beautiful than other stars because it is seen as larger, and larger stars are more beautiful than smaller ones, as is most evident in stars of the first or second magnitude. **Position** [site] also creates beauty in the sight: for many beautiful intentions do not appear beautiful except through the arrangement of their parts and positions. Thus, writing and painting, and all arranged and varied visible intentions, do not appear beautiful except through a position suitable to them. For even if the shapes of letters are all well-disposed and beautiful in themselves, if one of them is large and another small, the sight will not judge the writing composed of them to be beautiful. 

**Shape** [figure] also creates beauty: hence well-shaped artificial objects appear beautiful, and even more so the works of nature. Thus, when human eyes are almond-shaped <note>original: "amygdalaris"</note> and elongated, they appear beautiful, but round eyes appear utterly deformed. **Corporeity** [three-dimensionality] also creates beauty in sight: hence a spherical body, a round column, and a well-squared body appear beautiful. 

**Continuity** also creates beauty in the sight: hence continuous green spaces and thick green plants please the sight, because things that possess continuity are more beautiful than the same things when scattered. **Division** also creates beauty: hence stars that are separate and distinct are more beautiful than stars placed too close to one another (like the stars of the Galaxy [the Milky Way]), and distinct candles are more beautiful than a single large, gathered fire. **Number** also creates beauty: for this reason, areas of the sky with many distinct stars are more beautiful than areas with few stars, and many candles are more beautiful than few. 

**Motion** and **rest** also create beauty in the sight: for the movement of a person in speech and their gestures creates beauty; for this reason, a certain "gravity" [seriousness] in speaking appears beautiful, as does a silence that orderly distinguishes words. **Roughness** also creates beauty: for the shagginess of certain woven cloths <note>original: "pannorum catenatorum"</note> and others pleases the sight. **Smoothness** also creates beauty for the sight: because the smoothness of silk cloths—and even more so when they are polished...

whether they involve a polished surface <note>original: "tersionem"</note>, it pleases the soul and is beautiful to the sight. **Transparency** <note>original: "diaphanitas"</note> also allows beauty to appear, because through it sparkling things are seen at night—as is evident in a clear sky, through which stars are seen at night, a phenomenon that does not occur in air thickened by vapors. **Density** <note>original: "spissitudo"</note> also creates beauty: for light, color, shape, line, and every visible beauty are grasped by the sight because of the boundaries of the bodies in which they exist, and these boundaries are caused by density. Even **shadow** makes beauty appear: for in many visible forms there are subtle blemishes that make them ugly when they are in the light, but which remain hidden to the sight in shadow or weak light. **Twisting** or curvature, such as is found in the feathers of birds like peacocks and others, also makes beauty appear to the sight because of the shadow; when shadow mixes with light, it creates various colors that would not otherwise appear in total darkness or weak light. **Darkness** itself allows beauty to appear to the sight, for stars are not seen except in the dark. **Similarity** <note>referring here to symmetry and proportion</note> also creates beauty: for the members of the same animal—for instance, Socrates—do not appear beautiful unless they are similar to one another. Thus, eyes where one is round and the other oblong are not beautiful, nor if one is larger than the other, or one black and the other green, or if one cheek is sunken and the other protruding; for the whole face will not be beautiful when its matching parts are not similar. **Diversity** also creates beauty: for the diverse parts of the universe adorn and make the universe beautiful, just as the diverse parts of animals make the animals beautiful. The same hand is adorned by the diversity of the fingers; indeed, all beauty of the limbs arises from the diversity of the shapes of their parts.

Thus, beauty is grasped by the sight from a simple perception of visible forms that please the soul. However, any one of these visible <term>intentions</term><note>In medieval philosophy, an "intention" (intentio) is a formal property or quality of an object—like color or shape—as it is perceived by the mind.</note> does not create beauty in every form in which that property meets the sight; for every shape does not create beauty in every kind of form, and the same is true for all other specific visible properties. Beauty in the sight arises from the joining together of many properties of visible forms, and not only from the properties themselves; for example, sparkling colors and a painting are more beautiful when they are proportionately arranged than colors and paintings lacking such an orderly arrangement. It is the same with the human face: the roundness of a face combined with a delicate and subtle color is more beautiful than one without the other, and a moderately small mouth with proportionally slender lips is more beautiful than a small mouth with thick lips. Therefore, in many visible forms, the conjunction found in diverse forms creates a mode of beauty that one of those properties could not create on its own. Indeed, the proper **proportionality** of parts suited to some natural or artificial form creates more beauty through the conjunction of sensible properties than any single property does. For all beauties created by sensible properties through their conjunction consist in the proportionality appropriate to the forms which they complete under that mode of conjunction.

When, therefore, the sight perceives some visible thing in which there is a specific property that creates beauty by itself, the form of that property passes after the initial gaze to the <term>sensing power</term>, and the <term>distinguishing power</term><note>original: "uirtus distinctiua"; the cognitive faculty that analyzes and judges sensory data.</note> grasps the beauty of the visible thing containing that property. Thus, the conjunction of different properties causes beauty when that conjunction reaches the sensing power; then the distinguishing power compares those properties to one another, and grasps the beauty of the composite visible thing from the conjunction of the properties within it. These are the ways in which the beauty of all sensible forms is received by the sight. In most of these cases, however, **custom** <note>original: "consuetudo"</note> creates beauty. Thus, every nation of men approves of the form of its own custom, regarding that which it judges by itself as the pinnacle of beauty. A <term>Moor</term><note>A person from North Africa.</note> approves of different colors and proportions of the human body and paintings than a <term>Dane</term><note>A person from Scandinavia.</note>; and between these extremes, a **German**—and those near to them—approves of middle colors, tall statures, and specific manners. Just as each person has their own custom, so too does a specific judgment of beauty happen to each. Let this be said, therefore, in a topical and figurative manner. And what was proposed is now clear.

### 149. *Ugliness is grasped by the sight when sensible properties, neither by themselves nor by their conjunction with one another, cause any beauty. Alhazen 60 n 2.*

The **ugliness** <note>original: "turpitudo"</note> of forms is the deprivation of beauty in them. It has already been stated that properties do not create beauty in all forms, but only in some. Therefore, forms in which specific properties do not create any beauty—neither by themselves nor by their conjunction—such as those in which there is no customary proportionality between their parts, lack all beauty and are thus ugly. If it should happen that beautiful and ugly properties are gathered in the same form, then the sight perceives beauty from the beautiful part and ugliness from the ugly part, with the help of the distinguishing power when it gazes upon the properties in that form. It is therefore clear how ugliness is grasped by the sight; but even in this, custom helps greatly, because of which it sometimes happens that one person sees as ugly what appears beautiful to another.

<meta>This page continues Vitello’s discussion of how the beauty and deformity of objects are judged by the sight. He explores how various environmental and physical factors—the "eight circumstances" of vision—can lead the observer to misjudge an object's true appearance, specifically focusing on how fine details are lost under imperfect conditions.</meta>

# VITELLO'S OPTICS

If there are subtle paintings <note>original: "picturæ"; in this context, it refers to fine decorative details or artistic features</note> in a visible object that decorate it more perfectly, since these are hidden from the sight at night, the object appears deformed. Excessive distance is also a cause of error in the vision of the things mentioned above. For when an object is viewed from a distance, if there are small spots on it that make it ugly, it happens that they are hidden by the distance, and the object will be judged beautiful. Conversely, if a beautiful object with minute decorations is seen from a great distance, it will be judged deformed, because the **distinguishing power** <term>distinguishing power: the cognitive faculty, or "virtus distinctiua," that processes visual data to make judgments</term> judges things according to how they appear.

Errors in the vision of the aforementioned things also occur due to an improper arrangement of the position relative to the observer. For when a distant body is far from the **visual axis** <term>visual axis: the direct line of sight from the center of the eye to the object</term>, and it has small spots that make it ugly, those spots will sometimes be hidden because of the slant relative to the visual axis. Because of this, a freckled face seen from an angle appears beautiful. This is also why when the moon is viewed at an angle, its dark spots are hidden and it then appears more beautiful. However, if an object has subtle paintings that decorate it, those paintings will be hidden if slanted toward the sight, and its beauty will be judged as deformity.

Error also occurs in the vision of these things because of smallness of size, since due to their smallness alone, certain minute things that make visible objects ugly or beautiful are not seen. Error also occurs due to a lack of **solidity** <note>original: "soliditas"; here meaning opacity or physical substance</note>. For if a very thin glass vessel has small parts or measurements that give it beauty, and turbid, ugly, or dreg-filled wine is poured into it, those causes of beauty will be hidden and the vessel will be judged deformed. Conversely, if such a vessel is made ugly by certain particles, and clear, bright wine of a beautiful and pleasing color is poured into it, those causes of ugliness will be hidden and the vessel will appear beautiful.

Error also occurs in the vision of these things from an excess of **rarity** <note>original: "raritas"; referring to the thinness or clarity of the medium, like air</note>, as when beauty or deformity is not seen due to dark, cloudy air. Error also occurs from a shortness of time, because the minute causes of beauty or deformity cannot be grasped in a brief moment. This happens when someone looking through a hole sees a face; at that time, they sometimes judge a deformed face to be beautiful, and sometimes the reverse. The same thing happens when objects move suddenly while the eye remains stationary. Error also occurs from a weakness of sight; for a weak sight does not see the minute things that are the cause of beauty or deformity, and thus it judges each of them in the opposite way. Thus, the proposition is clear.

***

*151. Similarity is grasped by the sight from the agreement of the forms perceived in relation to one another. Alhazen, Book 2, Proposition 61.*

Similarity is the equality of two forms or two **intentions** <term>intentions: the underlying qualities or mental impressions of a thing, such as its shape or color, as understood by the mind</term> in a thing in which they are alike. Therefore, when the sight perceives two similar forms or two similar intentions at once, it will grasp their similarity by perceiving each of those two forms and their intentions and by comparing one to the other. Thus, the sight grasps similarity in similar forms and intentions by perceiving each form and intention according to its own being, and by perceiving them in relation to one another.

***

*152. Diversity is grasped by the sight from the absence of similarity in the perceived sensible forms. Alhazen, Book 2, Proposition 62.*

Since diversity, as it is understood here, is nothing other than the difference between the sensible forms perceived by the sight, this diversity is grasped by the sight in different forms by perceiving each of those different forms, comparing one to the other, and perceiving the absence of similarity in them. Therefore, diversity is grasped by the sense of sight by perceiving each of the forms and intentions on its own, by comparing them to each other, and by the sensation of the absence of similarity by the perceiver themselves.

***

*153. In the vision of similarity and diversity, error occurs to the distinguishing power due to the improper arrangement of the eight circumstances of any visible thing. Alhazen, Book 3, Propositions 33, 44, 51, 57, 63, 65, 68, 71.*

Due to a lack of light, error occurs in the vision of the similarity and diversity of bodies of the same kind of color or shape, in which partial diversity is marked by hidden signs; for then those signs are not seen in weak light, and thus an all-encompassing similarity will be judged between those bodies. And if some bodies share a similarity only because of certain minute signs common to them, then because of the weakness of light those causes of similarity are not perceived, and a total diversity will be judged, which would not happen in proper light.

Error also occurs in the vision of these things due to excessive distance, as is clear in the previous examples. For minute causes of similarity or dissimilarity are not seen from a great distance (according to Proposition 8 of this book). Likewise, error occurs from an excessive slanting of the position, which does not allow small things to be grasped by the sight (according to Proposition 26 of this book). Error also occurs in the vision of these things because of the smallness of the causes of similarity or dissimilarity; because of this, even if other factors are properly arranged for the sight, such things are not seen. Error also occurs due to a lack of solidity. For if two very thin vessels agree in kind, shape, and transparency, but differ in the arrangement of some of their parts, then when both are filled with wine of the same color and clarity, the causes of their diversity will be hidden and they will be considered entirely similar.

And if they differ in species, shape, and density <note>original: "raritate"; here referring to the physical makeup or transparency of an object</note>, but agree only in some partial features, then they will be thought entirely similar when viewed through a similar medium. This error happens because of a lack of solidity in the objects themselves; since they are transparent <note>original: "pervia"</note>, the things seen through them take away the causes of perceived similarity or dissimilarity.
