*154. An error of the **distinguishing power** <term>distinguishing power: the "virtus distinctiva," the cognitive faculty that processes and judges visual information</term> sometimes occurs from the combination of several causes, none of which is sufficient by itself to cause an error. Alhazen 72, book 3.*

For sometimes two imbalances <note>original: "intemperantiæ"; referring to a deviation from the ideal range of the eight circumstances</note> of the eight visual circumstances concur in one visible thing and produce an error in sight, even though neither of them would be sufficient by itself to cause an error. For if something is moved from a great distance with a slow motion, it will suddenly appear to the sight as if not moving; yet that motion could be perceived at a moderate distance even with a sudden glance, or it could even be perceived at that remote distance through diligent observation over a suitable amount of time. But when those two causes of error occur together, then the distinguishing power will err, and the thing will appear unmoved. Sometimes, however, many imbalances concur to cause a single error, whereas none of them would cause it on their own. For if, from a great distance under weak light and in a small amount of time, a body of diverse colors moved with a slow motion is presented to a weak sight, then it will perhaps appear to be at rest. Yet its motion could perhaps be perceived if any one of those causes were absent. And perhaps sometimes the imbalances of all the circumstances of visible bodies concur to cause one error, or sometimes several of them, according to various combinations which relate more to experience than to reason in all their diversity; therefore, it is enough to have given these examples.

*155. An error occurs to the sight by way of **knowledge** <term>way of knowledge: "via scientiæ," the process where the mind identifies an object by matching it to a "form" or concept stored in memory</term> through the improper application of a form that is in the soul to a certain seen thing, during an imbalance of any of the eight circumstances of the seen thing. Alhazen 21, book 3.*

When a thing appears to the sight as something else, or as a different species than it is in reality, then an error occurs in the sight by way of knowledge. This is because a form resting in the soul is improperly applied to another thing to which it does not belong; and this happens because of an imbalance of any of the eight circumstances of visible things. For most errors in the recognition of things happen because of a lack of light, as is evidently clear in itself. An excessive weakness of light brings error to the seen form; thus error occurs in the twilight <note>original: "crepusculis"</note> regarding all seen things. This is also why "night-lights" <note>original: "noctiluca"; likely referring to bioluminescent organisms like glow-worms or certain fungi</note> are seen to shine in the dark, though their true form is not light, nor even a sparkling color; none of which would happen in temperate light. Because of the excessive distance of a visible object from the sight, a known person is sometimes thought to be a stranger, and vice versa; or even one known person for another, such as Socrates for Plato, or the reverse. Sometimes someone seeing a horse thinks they are seeing a donkey. Universally, an error of knowledge occurs either from species to species, or from individual to individual of the same species, or from an individual of one species to an individual of another—as when Peter's horse is judged to be Martin's mule. And sometimes a person seeing a fire far away in the air thinks they see a star; for if all these things were near, they would be seen without error. The position of the object <note>original: "Situs etiam oppositionis"</note> also induces error; for sometimes Peter, when far from the visual axis, will be thought to be Martin, and sometimes a seen horse will be thought to be a donkey, but if they are placed directly opposite the sight, the error will cease entirely. Size existing outside of the temperate range also causes error to the sight and to knowledge, as when a mustard seed is believed to be a nasturtium seed. Solidity is also a cause of this error; thus a crystal, because it has little solidity, is believed to have the color of a ruby when such a color is placed beneath it and the sight is on the opposite side. Greatly diminished transparency <note>original: "diaphanitas"</note> is also a cause of this error; for when colored glass is placed between the sight and a colored object, the color of the opposite body will be judged to be a mixture of its own color and the color of the glass. And if a very thin cloth <note>original: "pannus multùm rarus"</note> is placed between the eyes and the seen things, the color of the body will appear mixed—not because the parts of the object's color passing through the holes of the cloth actually mix with the colors of the threads, but because the points of the object's color and the threads are situated near each other on the surface of the sight without a sensible distance between them. Thus those different colors appear to be joined point-by-point to one another, which is why a single color mixed from both appears to the sight. From this it happens that when the color of some body is seen through a woolen cloth, it will appear as a mixture of colors mostly matching the color of the threads, because the holes of a woolen cloth are narrow and covered by many colored hairs. Also, when performers <note>original: "ioculatores"; entertainers, magicians, or puppeteers</note> make painted wooden images move behind cloths surrounding them, the likenesses of those images will appear to the person looking through a fine linen cloth (as is usually done) to be birds or other animals fitting those shapes. This is due to a lack of transparency in the medium, because in the open air something else would be seen. The imbalance of time is also a cause of this error. For if someone looks through a hole at some body passing by with a rapid motion, and does not fully grasp the form of the body—or if someone suddenly sees something that immediately recedes from the sight—they will err regarding the individual identity of that form. Thus there may be an error in the species, or in the individual, or in both; for they might perhaps judge a horse to have been a mule, or Peter to have been Martin, or the horse

...that Peter's mule was actually Martin's. Weakness of sight is also a cause of this error: for sight damaged by a strong color upon which a strong light falls judges every color seen to be of that color, or of another color mixed from those two. Furthermore, because of an illness of the eyes, a horse sometimes appears to be a donkey, and Socrates seems to be Plato. Similarly, in other visible things, the sight will err solely because of an imbalance <note>original: "intemperantiam"; referring to a deviation from the ideal state</note> of its own steady disposition, even when no other impediment is present. Thus, errors in knowledge happen to the sight according to the individual imbalances of the eight circumstances of the thing seen, as is evident. We did not think it necessary to dwell much on these and similar matters, because what we have said suffices as the root of all such things. And this is the intended point.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 2, Chapter 3.</margin>

### 156. An error in sight alone sometimes occurs because of an imbalance in any of the eight circumstances of things properly seen through it.

Since light and color are the proper objects of sight—as is clear from the third principle of this book—it is evident that an error cannot happen to the sight alone except regarding light and color. An error happens to the sight in these things because of an imbalance in their intensity: for example, a strong light does not allow other visible things to be seen, and a strong color makes all other things appear similar in color to itself, even though their own colors are different. The same occurs with the weakness of light and color. For if a body in which there is a great variety of colors, such as a garment of diverse colors, meets the sight under very weak light, it will appear to be of a single color. And if the color itself is very weak, it will not be seen even in temperate light; thus, light outside its balanced state causes a deception of the sight at both extremes.

Distance also induces error in the sight: because of disproportionate distance, a thing made of many tiny scattered colors will appear to be of one color. The position of the object relative to the eye also causes the sense to err: for when a body is seen at a sharp angle <note>original: "multum obliquatum"</note>, its tiny parts are hidden from the sight because of its slanted position. If there is a variety of colors in those small parts, it will appear as one color in the whole body; but if the body returns to a direct position, the variety of those colors will appear, unless perhaps the distance of the parts of the colored body from the visual axis is too great. 

Magnitude <note>size</note> also induces error in the sight: because even when light, distance, and position are suitable for vision, the colors of very small parts of a body of diverse colors escape the sight, and the thing is seen as a single color; this would not happen if the smallness of the parts did not exceed the balanced range. Solidity <note>or density</note> is also a cause of visual deception if it is too reduced: thus, a crystal appears colored with the color of the object placed beneath it because of the low level of its own solidity; this would not happen if the crystal were more solid <note>meaning more opaque or dense</note>. 

Error also happens to the sight from transparency <term>diaphanitas: the quality of allowing light to pass through</term>: because if a flame is placed between the sight and the thing seen, even if that thing has a strong color, the body will appear dark solely because of the lack of transparency in the medium. Time is also a cause of error: for if the sight is directed suddenly toward a body of diverse colors, that body will appear to be of one color until it is discerned through careful gazing. 

Weakness of the sight also causes error in the vision of the aforementioned things: for when a strong light acts upon the eye, the sight is immediately harmed, and when turned toward the color of some body, it perceives that color as dark until the injury fades after some time. Similarly, when there is an illness in the eyes, the variety of colors will be hidden from the sight; thus, an error occurs in such things solely from the quality of the sight deviating from its balanced state. It is clear, therefore, that it is possible for deception to occur in the sight alone according to all the circumstances of visible things. And this was the proposition.

### 157. A bright thing mixed with black, or seen through a black medium, presents a crimson color to the sight.

The proof of this comes from natural sensory experiences: for we see that in well-polished, bright mirrors, a bright object is presented to the sight in its own brightness. But if the mirror is not bright, then the form of the bright object, mixed with the black color of the mirror, is presented to the sight—not with the intensity of its brightness, but as if somewhat blackened—and thus it appears red or crimson <note>original: "puniceus"; a reddish-purple color</note>. 

For it is a universal rule, as was assumed at the beginning of this second book, that the colors of strongly colored things and the light of the medium are carried to the sight mixed with color. For instance, if something is seen through colored glass, the color of the object seen is presented to the sight as a mixture of its own color and the color of the glass; one can clearly see many experiences of this. It also happens to those with moist eyes that the form of a bright white object, passing through the infected humors and tunics of the eye to the center of the eye, is changed by the judgment of the sight into a middle color, and a phantom of crimson color appears to the eye. 

We also see that the flame of green wood approaches a red or crimson color: because the fire, being bright and white, appears crimson through the black smoke due to the thickness of the material and the watery moisture mixed into that smoke. Through a mist or black smoke, the sun also appears not bright but crimson, when such smoke or mist happens to be placed between the sun and the eyes; and this same thing can be observed in other stars. Likewise, the circles <note>halos</note> seen around candles appear purple because of the thickness and blackness of the air: since the thickened air is somewhat blocked by the nature of the bright light, and because of the mixing of shadow, it seems to be mingled with blackness, or another middle color according to the arrangement of the light and the mixed shadow. A diligent inquirer can apply many more experiences to declare this more fully. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 158. It is evident that the sight becomes much weaker when extended far away.

For the sight does not see things placed far away in the same way as things existing nearby. If a porous body <note>original: "foraminosum"</note> with small holes is seen from a distance, the whole appears continuous; thus if someone...

If someone sees a dewy vapor <note>original: "uaporem roridum"; likely referring to mist or fog</note> from a distance, the sight will judge the whole thing to be one continuous body. Furthermore, the sight judges straight things to be curved, and round things to be square from a distance, just as was declared in the previous theorems of this book. And if the sight looks for a long time at a colored cloth in which there is a tiny scattering of different colors—where the distance of the parts is out of proportion <note>original: "intemperata"; imbalanced or lacking the right conditions</note> for the sight itself—that cloth will appear to be of only one color. This is because the distance is beyond the balanced limit in respect to the individual colors, even if all other conditions remain within the proper balance for the sight. Therefore, because the sight, when stretched, does not perceive the visible circumstances of the thing, it is clear that it is weakened by its own extension toward the visible object, or by the distance of the visible object from itself. And this is what was proposed.

*159. The appearance of blackness in a thing that is not black arises from a failure of sight.*

*Experience similarly proves what is proposed here, with the help of the preceding point. For since it is evident that sight becomes much weaker when stretched afar, as was previously stated, it happens that those things seen at a distance all appear darker because of this weakening. In the same way, distant bodies appear smaller and flatter than they actually are, because the protrusions of their parts—the roughness and swellings that create texture in them—are not seen. Similarly, things seen in mirrors appear darker to the observer because their distance is increased by reflection. For the more the distance from the surface of the mirror is increased due to the remoteness of even a white object (the mirror remaining unmoved), the more that white color approaches blackness in the sight. This is also why clouds appearing in water look darker than they do in their actual place, even with the observer in the same position, because the reflection made in the water increases the distance. It makes no difference whether an object appears to the sight from a great distance or if the sight completes its vision of the object through a great distance; the judgment of the visual power is always made according to the form received in the organ of sight. Nor will this escape the observer: when a bright cloud is near the sun, it will appear only white to someone looking at it; but if it is reflected by water, and the sight sees it in the water, then that white cloud will present some color from the intermediate colors <note>The "middle colors" between white and black in medieval color theory</note> to the sight, such as scarlet, purple, green, and azure. Thus, just as the sight sees a black color as being darker through reflection, so it sees a white color as less white because of reflection. Therefore, the sight sees a cloud that is actually white as black in its color because of the greater distance created by reflection; it appears similar to a privation or negation <note>original: "privationi & negationi"; philosophical terms for the absence of light or color</note> because of the weakness of the stretched sight. And since the coloration of the cloud results from the impression of light from some luminous body, it can be concluded from the previous points that in every body where light or color is impressed by a luminous body, it will share the same cause and effect. And this is what was proposed.*

HAVING cleared away, to some extent, those things which were seen to be necessary for simple and direct vision and those errors that happen to it, it now remains for us to proceed appropriately to that mode of vision which occurs by reflection <term>reflexionem: the bouncing of light off a surface</term> from polished bodies, which we call mirrors <term>specula: any reflective surface, whether a manufactured mirror or still water</term>. We shall treat more exquisitely every mode of reflection from any kind of mirror. First, therefore, in this present fifth book of this science, we shall set forth those things which we consider common to all mirrors; and then we shall add the properties <note>original: "passiones"; the effects or "undergoings" of the light</note> that happen to things and to the sight from plane mirrors <term>speculis planis: mirrors with a flat surface</term> alone. The form of these mirrors is simpler than the forms of all other mirrors, which is why the properties of plane mirrors are common to certain other mirrors, as will be clear in the following books, for which we reserve the specific properties of other mirrors. However, as we said at the beginning of this science, we do not mean in this treatise only those bodies shaped and polished by artifice, but also natural bodies themselves, from whose surfaces the same reflection occurs as happens from the surfaces of artificial bodies. Nor do we mean that this reflection happens only to the sight of animals; even when eyes are not present, the reflection of forms occurs. It happens to the sight only if it is positioned in the places of the reflected forms. This is clearly evident from the fact that reflection does not occur at every location for every sight from every mirror. There is, however, a certain property in the reception of these reflected forms in the sight, and especially in those modes of reflection in which...

### VITELLO'S OPTICS

*...in which there may be some deception in sight. Because of this, the same form is reflected from the surfaces of mirrors which also meets the sight directly in the mode of simple vision. Nevertheless, in reflection produced by the surfaces of any mirrors, the truth of the form cannot be grasped as it is grasped in simple direct vision. For in reflections made by any mirrors, the form of the object appears for the most part before the eyes, as if positioned opposite to the sight itself, even though in truth it is not positioned opposite them. Furthermore, the light and color of the seen body are always mixed with the color of the mirror from which the reflection occurs; the sight perceives this mixture in reflections, and not the true light or the true color of the seen object. Also, every reflection, as we shall declare more perfectly below, weakens light and color; hence in every reflection, the truth of light and color is hidden from the sight more than in direct simple vision. Those things which we set forth concerning this mode of vision, which occurs through reflection from any mirrors, and especially from flat mirrors, are these:*

## DEFINITIONS.

1. **Polishing of bodies** is the continuity of the parts of the surface of a polished body without any perceptible pores or division. 2. A **Mirror** is said to be any body polished by the work of art or nature. 3. The **Line of incidence** is that line according to which the form of the object falls upon the surface of the mirror. 4. The **Line of reflection** is that line according to which the form, having been struck back because of the solidity of the mirror (which it cannot penetrate), is reflected to the sight. 5. The **Point of incidence** is that point in which the line of incidence falls upon the surface of the mirror; and it is the same as the point of reflection, since the reflection of forms to the sight always happens from the point of incidence. 6. A **Perpendicular** above the surface of the mirror from which the reflection occurs is a line erected orthogonally from the point of incidence above the surface of that mirror from which the reflection occurs, if that surface is flat. But if that surface is convex or concave, then the perpendicular above it is said to be that which is perpendicular to the flat surface that is tangent to that convex or concave surface at the point of incidence. 7. The **Plane of reflection** <note>original: "superficies reflexionis"</note> is the surface containing the line of incidence and reflection, and the perpendicular produced from the point of contact above the surface of the mirror itself, or above the tangent surface itself. 8. The **Cathetus of incidence** <note>term: cathetus | in medieval geometry, this refers to a perpendicular line dropped from a point (like the object being viewed) to a surface or a line.</note> is a line perpendicularly erected above the flat surface of the mirror, or above the straight line tangent to the common section of the plane of reflection and the surface of a convex or concave mirror, drawn from the point where the incidence begins, such as from the center of the sight or from any other point whose form is reflected from the mirror to the sight. 9. The **Cathetus of reflection** is the line erected above that same surface or line from the point at which the line of reflection terminates, such as from the sight or from another point where the reflection ends. 10. The **Plane of incidence** is the surface contained by the line of the object seen and by the cathethi of incidence of the endpoints of that line. 11. The **Angle of incidence** is the angle which the line of incidence contains within the plane of reflection, along with the line that is the common section of the plane of reflection and the surface of the mirror itself, or the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection. 12. The **Angle of reflection** is the angle which the line of reflection contains within the plane of reflection with the said common section. 13. An **Image** is the form grasped in the mirror. 14. The **Location of the image** is called the place of the vision of that form, namely, the place in which the form is seen.

## POSTULATES.

We assume the following: 1. That the endpoints of an object, whether moved far away or brought close to the mirror, are sometimes seen. 2. Also, that the uniform positioning of a point of a seen object with respect to the surface of any mirror from which its form is reflected occurs only according to its cathetus of incidence.

# BOOK FIVE

## THEOREMS

### 1. *The surfaces of polished, smooth bodies, of whatever shape they may be, reflect light, colors, and the forms of opposite things from any of their points along the straightness of lines. Euclid, 2nd hypothesis of Catoptrics; Ptolemy, Book 1 and Book 3, Theorem 1 of Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Note 2.* <note>original: "Euclides 2 hypothe. catoptr. Ptolemæus 1 & 3 the. 1 catoptr. Alhazen 2 n 4." Vitello is synthesizing the three greatest authorities on optics: the Greek tradition of Euclid and Ptolemy and the Arabic tradition of Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham).</note>

For as was made clear through the 1st theorem of the 2nd book of this work, the form of light from a luminous body is always diffused according to a straight line into every body opposite to it, and similarly the colored form of a body possessing the action of light. Therefore, when these strike any smooth, polished body: because in such a body the passage of light or color is not open due to the density of such a body and its lack of transparency <note>original: "priuationem diaphanitatis"</note>, and since they have flat surfaces in which there is no roughness, a reflection of light, color, and forms always occurs from them. Because of this, when a mirror is placed opposite a strong light striking it obliquely, a reflection of light and color clearly occurs upon a neighboring wall, if the color was joined with the light; and the reflected light striking the wall will be seen with the color. When the mirror is moved, the reflected ray will move, changing its place; and when the mirror is taken away, the reflected light is removed. 

If a hand or another clean or polished body is led along a straight line from the place where the luminous ray strikes to the surface of the body from which the reflection occurs, it will be evident that the reflection was made according to the straightness of lines. This is because to the experimenter returning along a straight line to the body from which the reflection occurs, the reflection of the light always happens to be seen. Therefore, in every polished surface of whatever shape, reflection occurs from any of its points according to the straightness of lines: for light from any point of a luminous body falls upon any point of a polished body. 

Hence, as was shown in the 20th theorem of the 2nd book of this work, a <term>pyramid<gloss>a cone-shaped beam of light with its tip at a single point</gloss></term> is formed upon any point of the polished body, whose vertex is at the point of the polished body and whose base is on the surface of the luminous body; and from any point of the luminous body, a pyramid proceeds whose vertex is at the point of the luminous body and whose base is on the surface of the polished body. And if light proceeds from the luminous body to the polished body along parallel lines, those lines, containing a sort of column, are terminated at the bases of the aforementioned pyramids. However, through whatever lines light strikes a polished body, it is reflected according to the property of those lines, whether they are perpendicular or oblique: therefore, the proposition is clear. Furthermore, reflection of light occurs from polished bodies, but not from unpolished, rough bodies: because in those there are pores and pits which the light enters, and it returns into itself mixed with the shadow of those bodies; hence no perceptible reflection occurs from them.

### 2. *From every colored body in the presence of light, color is sent to an opposite polished body mixed with light: and sometimes it is reflected from it totally, and sometimes partially, just as light itself is. Ptolemy, Book 3, Theorem 1 of Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Note 3.*

What is proposed here is declared by experiment. For let it be that within a house with only one window, the light of the sun descends upon a body strongly colored with a powerful color: and let a silver mirror be placed in opposition to it, and again, let a concave vessel in the manner of a cup <note>original: "scyphi"</note> be placed against the mirror, which is white on the inside, or in which a white body is placed, and let it be fitted such that the reflected light strikes upon that white body. Thus, the color of that body upon which the light first descended will appear upon the face of the white body. Color, therefore, is reflected mixed with light: therefore, it also strikes the polished body mixed with light. 

If this polished body is dense and hard, the color with the light is totally reflected from it, so that it does not color the polished body itself. But if the polished body is thin and actually clear, such as water and glass and similar things, then the colors and lights are reflected from it and also penetrate into it. This is clear through the fact that the form of reflection from these bodies is of weaker light and color than from other bodies denser than they are; and also around some point under these bodies, or within them, the forms of light and color striking the upper surface of these bodies are seen. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

### 3. *Every reflection weakens lights and colors: and universally all forms. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 4.*

For since continuous light is stronger than light dispersed <note>original: "disgregata"</note> (by the 1st petition of the 2nd book of this work), and as much as light is elongated further from its source, so much more is it weakened (by the 22nd theorem of the 2nd book), it is clear that when light proceeds from some point of a luminous body to the surface of a polished body in the manner of a pyramid, the further it is elongated from that point, the greater is its weakening, both because of the distance from the source of light and because of the dispersion. 

Indeed, light reflected from some polished body is weakened more, both because of the distance from the place of reflection and dispersion, and because of the reflection itself. Also, lights striking polished bodies along parallel lines are weaker than lights striking obliquely, because they are less gathered together. Likewise, the reflection of colors, although it occurs from every polished body just as light does (as is clear by the 1st theorem of this book), is nevertheless not very perceptible because of the weakening that occurs from reflection, and because of the mixing of the color of the mirror itself which conforms to the reflected colors—unless perhaps the reflection occurs from a silver mirror. For in an iron mirror, the color appears weaker, because the color of the iron mixed with the reflected light and the reflected color itself weakens that reflected color. Therefore, all reflections of colors can best be experienced in a house with a single opening, opposite which opening a white wall is placed. For then, with a silver mirror placed in the sun's ray, and some colored thing placed between the mirror and the wall, the reflection of the color to the white wall will be perceptible. The same also happens...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physical properties of reflection, specifically how the process of reflecting off a surface diminishes the intensity of light and color compared to its source, while establishing the geometric efficiency of nature's paths.</meta>

# WITELO'S OPTICS

It happens that if a colored transparent <note>original: "diaphanum"</note> body is placed in the ray of incidence of the mirror itself, through which the ray passes and falls upon the mirror—for instance, if colored glass is placed before a window, or if it is arranged in a similar way, as will be seen by one experimenting. Thus, when a strong light falls upon a silver mirror and is reflected onto a white wall, the light on the wall will be seen to be notably weaker than that on the mirror. Reflection, therefore, weakens light. In the same way, a reflected color is weaker than the color from which the reflection arises. It is clear, then, that reflection weakens both light and color, but colors more so than light. For colors fall in a weaker manner than light; hence they are more easily weakened in reflection. For a weak color, when it reaches the mirror, is mixed with the color of the mirror and is changed because of that admixture; for this reason, the reflected color appears weak and dusky. Generally, reflected forms are weaker than they are in the place from which they are reflected. Thus it is evident that every reflection is a cause of weakness. For this is also perceptibly clear in light: although direct light and reflected light may be at an equal distance from their source, nevertheless the reflected light is weaker. For if a mirror smaller than the opening is placed in the air in the path of a sunbeam entering a house through a single window, so that the remaining light from the opening—which does not fall on the mirror—falls upon the ground onto a white object; and if the light reflected from the mirror falls similarly upon a white object raised from the ground; and if care is taken that the distance of the raised object and the one lying on the ground from the center of the window opening is the same: then a lesser light will be seen upon the raised white object to which the reflection occurs than upon the object lying on the ground. Of this diminished intensity, reflection alone is the cause. The same can easily be demonstrated in the reflection of colors, and in the same manner. The proposition is therefore clear.

#### 4. *Every reflected light, although it is weaker than the primary light, is nevertheless stronger than secondary light, when both are at an equal distance from their origin; and the same is true for color. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 5.* <note>original: "Alhazen 5 n 4." In medieval optics, "primary light" is direct light from a source, while "secondary light" is the ambient or accidental light that illuminates a room outside of the direct beam.</note>

Indeed, when reflected light falls upon some body, if another similar body is placed outside the path of reflection, and it is at the same distance from the mirror as the first: a secondary light will be seen upon that second body which is lesser than the light on the body placed in the path of reflection. For suppose a mirror is placed on the ground directly in line with a window through which a ray enters a house, receiving the whole light of the ray falling through that window (which light we called "primary light" earlier at the beginning of the second book of this science): then it will be made clear that the light will be stronger upon a body placed in the path of reflection than upon another similar body placed outside that path at the same distance from the mirror. The same happens if the surface of the mirror does not receive the ray directly, but obliquely. The same is also clear in colors: since when a reflection of color is made from a silver mirror, a white body placed in the path of reflection receives a great deal of color; but another equally white body existing outside the path of reflection, and at the same distance from the mirror, appears indeed colored, but much more weakly than the body placed in the path of reflection. And if the mirror were made of iron, perhaps a moderate color would be seen on the body in the path of reflection, but outside the path of reflection on an equally white body, almost no color will appear. The proposition is therefore clear.

#### 5. *Nature acts in all things according to the shortest lines. Euclid in the preface to his Optics; Ptolemy, Book 1, Theorem 1 of Catoptrics.* <note>original: "Euclides in præfatione opticorum. Ptolemæus 1 th. 1 catoptr." This refers to the principle of economy in nature, often called the "Principle of Least Path."</note>

This is universally evident in all the works of nature. For all natural motions occur in this way: heavy things descend perpendicularly to the surface of the horizon. Also, arrows shot violently from bows are carried by the shortest line according to the angle of their release; for motion is swiftest along the shortest line from one point to another. And because, as was assumed at the beginning of the second book of this science, nature does nothing in vain, nor fails in necessary things: it is clear that it necessarily acts according to the shortest lines. For if it could complete the intended operation through motion or action along the line *a b*, and yet acted through
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line with points a and c at the ends and a point b positioned slightly above the midpoint. The points a, b, and c are connected to form a triangle.</image-desc>
the line *a b c*: every action it performs on the line *b c* is in vain, since it attained its end at point *b*; therefore it does not act according to any point on the line *b c*. And this same thing can be shown through many natural examples. Hence even animals, whose mover is the soul, are moved toward a goal according to the shortest line, as is clear in the straightness of the threads of spiders, from which they weave their webs; which webs, although they are sometimes found to be circular, are nevertheless woven from straight threads in both the warp and the structure because of the shortness of the line. The same is also clear in dogs, which, ignoring two sides of a triangle, run along the third, as if naturally informed they knew that two sides of a triangle are greater than the third—a thing which geometers teach to men in the 20th proposition of the 1st book <note>original: "20 p 1." This refers to Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 20, the triangle inequality theorem.</note>. The proposition is therefore clear, as far as was possible for us.

#### 6. *Every reflection of light and color occurs according to sensible lines having width. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 16.* <note>original: "Alhazen 16 n 4." Witelo distinguishes between the "mathematical line" (a theoretical line with no width) and the "sensible line" (the actual physical beam of light we see).</note>

For the incidence of light occurs according to such lines, even the smallest light upon a polished body, as is clear through the 3rd theorem of the 2nd book of this work. Therefore, the width of the line of reflection is equal to the width of the line of incidence: and the mathematical line, which is the middle line of the entire line of reflection, has the same position in the place of reflection as the mathematical line which is the middle of the sensible line of incidence in the place of incidence. Similarly, any of the other mathematical lines within the sensible line of reflection retains the same position as its counterpart in the sensible line of incidence; and for this reason, it is not inappropriate to use mathematical lines instead of sensible ones in treatises on reflections. The proposition is therefore clear.

# BOOK FIVE

### 7. ***In reflections made by any mirrors, deception occurs because of the immoderation of light; or because of a difference in position; or because of the distance of the point whose form is reflected; or even because of the distance of the center of the sight itself from the surface of any of the mirrors. Alhazen Book 3, number 6.***

Generally, in whatever ways the sight happens to be deceived regarding the "intentions" <note>The term "intentions" (intentiones) refers to the perceived qualities of an object, such as shape, size, or color.</note> of visible things through simple, direct vision, it also happens that the sight is deceived in vision that occurs through reflection. This is because this vision is also a type of seeing in which the form of light and colors, and other visible intentions, are presented to the discriminative faculty <note>The "virtus distinctiva" or discriminative faculty is the cognitive power that interprets visual data.</note>. And this, as was shown in Theorem 1 of Book 4 of this work and in many of its other theorems, happens in eight modes. However, this occurs most frequently and clearly in mirrors: either because of the weakness of the light; or because of a difference in position, due to which the lines of reflection happen to be moved away from the visual axes; or because of the distance of the point of the thing seen, whose form is reflected from the surface of the mirror; or even because of the distance of the center of the eye itself, to which the distant reflection is made from the surface of the mirror. In the other five modes, although error is similarly caused in the vision of forms reflected from any mirrors to the sight, that error is not so perceptible as in these proposed modes; nevertheless, there is no total excuse from them. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 8. ***The mirrors from which regular reflection occurs are only seven.***

Since regular reflection cannot occur except from regular bodies, and regular bodies can only be bodies of mostly plane surfaces or of a single concave or convex surface. As is evident to the senses, although the types of plane bodies may vary according to their shapes and the number of their angles, yet as far as the nature of reflection is concerned, there is an identity of the plane surface in all of them; for no variation is found in them regarding this. As is clear from Theorem 118 of Book 1 of this work, every regular convex or concave surface is either part of the surface of a sphere, or of a column <note>A cylinder.</note>, or of a round pyramid <note>A cone.</note>. Thus, there are seven mirrors in total: one of which is plane (of whatever shape); three are convex (spherical, cylindrical, and conical); and three are concave (spherical, cylindrical, and conical). It is not possible for there to be more mirrors from which regular reflection may occur. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 9. ***We establish an instrument in which the modes of all reflections from any regular mirrors are demonstrated by means of tools. Alhazen Book 7, number 4.***

Let there be taken a bronze semicircle of suitable thickness, such as half a barley grain <note>A traditional small unit of measurement.</note> or thereabouts, and of suitable size. Let this be **a b c**, its diameter **a c**, and its center **d**. Let the line **d b** be drawn perpendicular to the diameter **a c** by the 11th proposition of Book 1 <note>References are to Euclid's Elements.</note>; therefore **d b** is the radius of the circle dividing the semicircle into equal parts by the 33rd proposition of Book 6. Let a sixth part of it be cut off from the line **d b** at the top by the 9th proposition of Book 6, which shall be **b e**; and according to the quantity of the line **e d**, let a semicircle be made from center **d**, which shall be **f e g**. Then let the arc **b e** be divided into as many parts as desired, according to points **h, i, k**; and let the arc **b a** be divided into the same number of parts according to points **l, m, n**, so that arc **l b** is equal to arc **b h**, and arc **m l** to arc **h i**, and arc **n m** to arc **i k**, by the 23rd proposition of Book 1 and the 26th proposition of Book 3, with lines **d h, d i, d k, d l, d m, d n** being drawn.

In this way, line **b p**, and consequently the entire ruler, will be divided into four equal parts. Let all the other six rulers be divided and marked in this same manner; and thus, what was proposed has been done.

10. **In plane mirrors, the reflection of an obliquely incident ray occurs on the opposite side; and it is experimentally proven that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Euclid, Theorem 1 of the *Catoptrics*; Ptolemy, Theorem 4, Book 1 of the *Catoptrics*; Alhazen, Book 4, number 10.**

Therefore, let a plane mirror of circular shape be made of pure iron, whose diameter, by the previously mentioned method, is three digits. Let the aforementioned ruler be hollowed out around center **z** (which is the midpoint of the ruler) in a circle the size of the mirror's diameter. Let it be recessed to the thickness of the mirror itself, and let it be fitted so that the surface of the mirror and the ruler become one single surface, and so that the center of the mirror's circularity is placed directly over point **z**. Thus, line **c q**, which divides the wider surface of the ruler into two equal parts, will also divide the surface of the mirror into two equal parts; let the experimenter’s diligence ensure this.

Now, let this ruler be inserted into the wooden ring until center **d** (the pointer of the brass plate) falls upon the mirror. Then, let that ruler with the mirror be supported in the square hollow by some device so that it does not wobble but stands firm. Next, let all the holes of the instrument be well blocked, except for one that inclines obliquely over the surface of the ruler. For example, let it be the hole corresponding to line **d h** in the brass circle **a b c**. Let this open hole be exposed to a sunbeam—it is best if the sunbeam enters through a window of a house. The ray incident upon the plane mirror will then be seen to reflect to the other hole corresponding to line **d h** <note>The author likely means the hole symmetrical to d h on the opposite side of the normal line.</note> in the brass circle **a b c**. If that hole at point **h** is opened, and the previously covered hole at point **l** is blocked, the ray will again be reflected into that covered hole.

Angle **b d l** is equal to angle **b d h**, as is clear from the hypothesis in the previous section. Therefore, angle **l d a** is equal to angle **h d c**, since the whole angle **b d a** is equal to the whole angle **b d c**, as each is a right angle. If a hollow iron column (which we mentioned before) is placed in the open hole, the light will descend through the hollow of the column to the mirror and reflect into the hole maintaining an equal angle as before. If the column is moved to the second hole, the ray will reflect to the first. However, the light descending through the column will always be weaker than the light descending through the hole without the column.

The method of experimenting is the same if one of the holes is blocked with wax and a small hole is made in its center with an iron stylus; for then the light will reflect into a similar small space around the center of the other hole, which faces the first at an equal angle. Even if the hollow of the iron column is blocked, provided a hole is made in the center of its base, the light will descend along the axis of the column and reflect to the center of the other hole—the equality of angles always being observed in all cases. If the instrument is adjusted so that light enters through two holes, it will similarly reflect through two other holes similar to them; for the deviation of the lines of reflection is always equal to the deviation of the lines of incidence. And since line **b x p** (which is the median line of the ruler's length) is orthogonal to the lower width line of the ruler parallel to line **c q**, and since that is the common section of the ruler's surface and the surface of the base...

Thus, lines **l d** and **d h** are parallel to two lines imagined to be drawn from the point of the ruler, which is **z**, to the center of the two holes touching points **l** and **h**, according to Proposition 33 of Book 1. Therefore, by Proposition 10 of Book 11 <note>Another reference to Euclid's Elements regarding angles formed by parallel lines in different planes.</note>, the angles contained by those lines in parallel surfaces are equal. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 11. *It is demonstrated by means of an instrument that in plane mirrors, a ray falling perpendicularly is reflected back upon itself. Euclid, 2nd theorem of Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Chapter 11.*

With all the settings of the instrument remaining as before, and with the ruler in which the plane mirror is situated erected upon the bottom of the square hollow (which is in the wooden table that serves as the base of the instrument), let all the holes be blocked except for the middle one, to which the semi-diameter **d b** of circle **a b c** corresponds. Let a columnar stick be made to the size of the hole, whose end is sharpened so that only a point remains, which is the end of its axis. This is inserted through the hole to the mirror, and the point where it falls should be marked with ink. Then, after removing the stick, let the open hole be presented to a ray of light; the ray will fall upon the marked point and create a circle around it. Let a point be marked at the edge of this circular light, and let a circle be made according to the size of the line lying between the marked points. This circle will be larger than the circle of the hole, according to Theorem 36 of Book 2 of this work, since the progression of light entering through a hole is always in the form of a pyramid <note>In medieval optics, a "pyramid" (pyramis) of light refers to what we would now call a cone or a beam of light spreading from a point or aperture.</note>. In none of the other holes, nor in any part of the ring's hollow, will reflected light be seen. It is clear, therefore, that light descending through the axis is reflected back through the same axis, and the entire reflection of the incident light is ordered according to that reflection. Although the circular light around the inner base of the hole may appear larger than the incident light or ray, and although that light appears larger than the circle of the inner light itself, and it is clear that this light appears through reflection—this does not happen because of the reflection of the perpendicularly incident ray, which is the axis of that luminous pyramid. Rather, it happens because of the reflection of other rays of the pyramid falling obliquely, which are reflected to opposite parts according to the manner of their obliquity, and not back into themselves. This is evident if both bases of the hole are blocked with wax, with a small hole made according to the axis; for then, with the sun's ray descending only by way of the axis, the circular reflected light will not appear around the inner base of the hole. It is clear, therefore, that the circular light did not proceed from the reflected light of the axis, but from the reflection of light falling obliquely upon the mirror itself. But if the ruler, in which the said plane mirror is placed, is tilted somewhat backward, then it is clear that the ray falling through the middle hole does not fall perpendicularly upon the surface of the mirror, and the reflected light will be seen remote from the middle hole according to the degree of the mirror's tilt. Nevertheless, the center of the light will always fall upon a line drawn on the hollow surface of the ring, perpendicular to the surface of the brass circle **a b c**, and descending through the center of the base of the middle hole; for this always intersects the circular reflected light and divides its circle in the middle. And if the ruler is tilted to the right or left side, the ray will always be made oblique according to this; but when the ruler returns to its upright position, the reflection of the light will return to the inner base of the hole, as before. Thus, the proposition is clear: in plane mirrors, a ray falling perpendicularly is always reflected back upon itself; but in rays falling obliquely, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, as is clear from the preceding.

### *13. In spherical concave mirrors, with the incident and reflected ray, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Euclid, Theorem 1 of the Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Note 12.*

Let a spherical mirror be made as above; and according to the convex portion of that circle, let it be ground and polished very smoothly on the inside. The equality of the angles of incidence and reflection will be declared as before, both in rays falling obliquely and in the ray falling perpendicularly. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### *14. In columnar <note>original: "columnaribus"; referring to cylindrical mirrors.</note> convex mirrors, with the incident and reflected ray, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Euclid, Theorem 11 of the Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Note 12.*

For let a round column <note>a cylinder</note> be taken, which is three fingers in height, and whose base circle diameter is six fingers. Let a portion of the circle of that column's base be cut away, as before in the spherical mirrors. Let a portion of a column be made from pure iron, whose base is that portion of the circle, and its height three fingers. According to the concavity of that portion, let the convexity of the piece be formed. Let all its lines of length be perpendicular to both bases; and the versed sine of the base will be less than half of one finger. Therefore, let this mirror, polished to the highest degree on its convex side, be attached to one of the rulers similar to the previous ones, so that its midpoint falls upon the midpoint of the ruler (which is **z**), and so that the line of length dividing its convex surface into equal parts is on the surface of the ruler. Let it be applied to the ruler according to its line of length, which is **b p**. This can be done if the arc of each base is divided into equal parts, and the marked midpoints are applied to line **b p**. Therefore, let the ruler with the mirror be placed into the instrument as before, and let the operation be similar to the previous one. The equality of the angles of incidence and reflection will be demonstrated as above. Nor is there any difference in these mirrors from the behavior of plane mirrors, except in this: that if the ray falls through the middle hole and this ruler is slanted toward the right or left side, the light will appear to be reflected back through that same middle hole, and the center of the light upon the center of the hole—whereas in other mirrors, such light is slanted away. For in cylindrical mirrors, a ray incident perpendicularly to one line of length is incident perpendicularly to each of the others opposite to it. Because of this, a uniformity of reflection occurs in all of them, and the perpendicular ray is always reflected back upon itself. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### *15. In pyramidal <note>conical</note> convex mirrors, with the incident and reflected ray, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Euclid, Theorem 1 of the Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Note 12.*

Let a pyramidal mirror be made of pure iron, whose base is equal to the base of the cylindrical mirror; therefore the chord of that base will be three fingers, and the versed sine less than half of one finger. However, let the line of length of the mirror be four and a half fingers. Let this mirror, polished to the highest degree on the outside, be attached to one of the similar rulers, hollowed out in such a way that its midpoint is upon point **z** (the midpoint of the ruler), and so that its point <note>the apex of the cone</note> is at the end of line **b p**. Let the line dividing the pyramidal portion into equal parts (namely, the line drawn from the vertex of the pyramid to the midpoint of the base's arc) be on the surface of the ruler. With the ruler and mirror placed in the instrument, let the operation be done as before. Everything that happened in the convex cylindrical mirrors will happen here. Therefore, in these as well, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the perpendicular ray is always reflected back upon itself, as was clear in the preceding cases. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

Let a concave cylindrical iron mirror be made, whose concavity is entirely equal to the previous cylindri...

### 17. *In concave conical mirrors, with the incident and reflected ray, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Euclid, Theorem 1 of the Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 4, Number 12.* <note>original: "Euclides 1 the. catoptr. Alhazen 12 n 4." Vitello is citing his primary sources: Euclid's work on mirrors and the "Perspectives" of the Arabic scholar Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen).</note>

Let a concave conical <term>pyramidal: in medieval optics, this term usually refers to a cone-shaped mirror.</term> iron mirror be made, whose concavity is entirely equal to the convexity of the previously mentioned convex conical mirror: and let it be polished on the inside: and let it be applied to one of the similar rulers in such a way that its midpoint is over point **z**, and its apex is directly on line **b p**, and the chord of the arc of its base is on the surface of the ruler. Since, however, the line of length of the portion of the conical mirror is four and a half fingers, there remains a finger and a half of the length of the ruler in both the concave and the convex mirror. When the ruler with the mirror has also been placed into the instrument, let the operation be performed as before: and all those things will happen which happened in the convex conical mirrors in the reflection of rays incident obliquely at equal angles: and in the reflection of perpendicular rays back upon themselves. Therefore, the proposition is clear. It is evident, then, from the premises, that in every reflection from any regular mirrors (such as these seven mirrors) <note>Vitello identifies seven types of mirrors: plane, convex/concave spherical, convex/concave cylindrical, and convex/concave conical.</note>, a ray incident perpendicularly along a straight line is always reflected perpendicularly along the same straight line: and that a ray incident obliquely along a straight line is reflected along another oblique line, yet in such a way that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Therefore, having found this through the rational experience of the senses, we shall henceforth use it as a universal principle in all these mirrors: and although this has been declared experimentally as a principle of this science, it can nevertheless also be reached through some mode of demonstration; wherefore we shall attempt to demonstrate it as diligently as we can: for which reason we have thought it necessary to set forth the two following theorems.

### 18. *Every object seen through any mirror is perceived by the sight along the shortest lines. Ptolemy, Theorem 4, Book 1 of the Catoptrics.* <note>Ptolemy’s "Catoptrics" is actually a work now attributed to Hero of Alexandria, which Vitello knew under Ptolemy's name.</note>

Let there be a mirror, on whose surface is a line, either straight or curved, which is **a c b**: let the point of the seen object be **d**: and let the center of the eye be **f**: and let point **d** be seen reflected from point **c** of the mirror. I say that lines **f c** and **d c** are shorter than all lines drawn from points **d** and **f** to any other points of the mirror.

For let lines **e d** and **e f** be drawn from another point of the mirror's surface (which is **e**), which are neither shorter than lines **c d** and **c f**, nor equal to them, but longer. Because, therefore—as is clear from Proposition 5 of this book—nature in all things acts according to the shortest lines: <note>original: "natura in omnibus agit secundū lineas breuiores." This is the classic principle that nature does nothing in vain and always takes the most efficient path.</note> and the multiplication of forms <note>A "form" or "species" refers to the visual information or light radiating from an object.</note> toward the surfaces of mirrors is natural: since it happens by the work of nature, just as does every other diffusion of forms, as we have shown in *Natural Philosophy* in the chapter on natural action: and similarly the reflection of forms from the surfaces of mirrors to the sight is purely natural, since it happens by the work of nature, and is completed through the action of the soul, just as is every other vision, as is clear through the whole fourth book of this our science: moreover, the soul is as the nature of animals. It is clear, therefore, that this diffusion of form and reflection and perception, which happens according to it, is truly natural: it will therefore happen according to the shortest lines: which is the proposition: for it would be in vain to happen according to longer lines, when it can happen better and more certainly according to shorter lines.

### 19. *The lines of incidence and reflection, containing equal angles with the perpendicular drawn from the point of their meeting upon the surface of a plane or convex mirror, are shorter than all lines produced from the same endpoints upon the same surface of the mirror containing unequal angles with the perpendiculars drawn from the points of their meeting.*

What is proposed here can be easily demonstrated through Theorems 17 and 18 of Book 1 of this work: but because the same is demonstrable in another way, let there be any seen object in which there is a point **c**: and let there be a plane mirror, on whose surface the line **h d e** is formed: now, for the sake of example, let the given mirror be plane: therefore the line **h d e** will be a straight line: also let the lines containing equal angles with the line **h d e** be **c d** and **d f**. Either, then, the center of the eye will be in the same line parallel to line **h d e** in which point **c** of the seen object is, or not. Because, therefore, angle **c d h** is equal to angle **f d e**, when those equal angles are subtracted from two right angles (which are **g d h** and **g d e**), the remaining angles will be equal: therefore angle **c d g** is equal to angle **g d f**. And since in both triangles **c d g** and **f d g** the angles which are at point **g** are right angles: it is clear by Book 1, Proposition 32, that angles **d c g** and **d f g** are equal. Therefore triangles **c d g** and **f d g** are equiangular: thus the sides opposite the equal angles are proportional according to Book 6, Proposition 4: and since side **d g** is equal to itself, side **f d** will be equal to side **c d**; and lines **f e** and **c e** having been drawn over point **e**

# WITELO'S OPTICS

...by all lines produced from the same endpoints over the same line to another single point. And this we have proposed through Proposition 17 of Book 1 of this work regarding straight lines, and through Proposition 18 of the same first book regarding convex lines.

<margin>Euclid, Theorem 1 of *Catoptrics*; Ptolemy, Theorems 4 and 5 of Book 1 of *Catoptrics*; Alhazen, Book 4, [propositions] 10, 18.</margin>
**20. In every reflection made by any mirror, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection; from which it is clear that the inequality of the lengths of the lines does not change the nature of the reflection.**

For since, as is clear from Proposition 18 of this book, every object seen through any mirror—whether flat, convex, or concave—is perceived along the shortest lines: and the lines produced from the same points (namely, from the point of the object seen and the center of the eye) to the surface of any mirror are shortest when they contain equal angles, both with the lines tangent to the surfaces of the mirrors and with the perpendiculars produced from the point of their intersection upon the surfaces of the mirrors, as is clear from the previous proposition: and the angle made by the line produced from the point of the object seen is the **angle of incidence** <term>angle of incidence: the angle between the incoming ray and the mirror's surface or its perpendicular</term>, and the angle made by the line produced from that point to the center of the eye is the **angle of reflection** <term>angle of reflection: the angle between the reflected ray and the surface</term>: it is therefore clear that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, regardless of whether the reflection occurs from a flat or convex mirror.

But this is also clear in any concave mirror. For let there be a convex mirror in which there is a circle **e b d**: which circle **a b c** touches externally at point **b**: and let a line **f b g** be drawn touching both circles at point **b**: and let the point of the object seen be **h**, whose **form** <term>form: in medieval optics, "forma" refers to the visual information or "species" radiating from an object</term> is reflected from point **b** of the convex mirror to the eye located at point **k**: and by the previous proposition, angle **h b a** will be equal to angle **k b g**: but also angle **a b f** is equal to angle **c b g** by Proposition 16 of Book 3 <note>original: "16 p 3" — Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 16, regarding the "horn angle" or angle of contingency between a circle and its tangent.</note>, since they are angles of contingency: therefore, there remains angle **h b f**, which is the angle of incidence in the concave mirror **a b c**, equal to angle **k b c**, which is the angle of reflection. Thus the proposition is clear. For this demonstration can be adapted universally to all concave mirrors.

Furthermore, this is also reasonable. For if the line of incidence—for example, **a b**—were to penetrate through point **b** to point **e** along the straight line **e b d** extended into the surface of a flat mirror (or a line tangent to the convex or concave surface of some mirror) without reflection: it is evident by Proposition 15 of Book 1 <note>original: "15 p 1" — Euclid’s Elements, regarding vertical/opposite angles.</note> that the angle of incidence **a b c** would be equal to the angle **e b d**. Therefore, if a reflection occurs along line **b f**: it is more fitting that it occurs according to an angle equal to that opposite one rather than according to any other angle, so that angle **f b d** becomes equal to angle **e b d**, and thus to angle **a b c**. For if, while points **c** and **d** remain unmoved, the line **c d** is imagined to be revolved: then line **e b**, because of the equality of angles **e b d** and **d b f**, will fall upon line **b f**: and this seems to be what the name "reflection" implies. Thus the proposition is clear.

From this, the corollary is also clear: because the inequality of the lines does not change the size of the angles, it therefore does not change the nature of the reflection. Thus, points on the same line that are further from the point of reflection can be reflected to the eye just as points on the same line that are closer to the point of reflection. For universally, all points on the same line can be reflected according to an equal angle. And this was what was proposed.

**21. For every form incident along a line perpendicular to the surface of any mirror, the reflection occurs back along that same line.**

For example, let the form of point **a** be incident to the surface of mirror **b d c** along line **a d**, which is perpendicular to the surface **b d c**: I say that the reflection of the form of point **a** will be along that same line **d a**. For granted that the reflection were to occur along another line: then, since the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection (as is clear from the previous proposition), and in this case the angle of incidence is a right angle: and since there are infinite right angles arranged around point **d**, there would be no reason for the form to decline toward one point of the surface **b c** more than toward another: for line **a d**, which is the line of incidence, is related equally to point **b**, to point **c**, and to all other points of the surface **b c**. Thus there would be infinite reflections to infinite points of the surface **b c**: because for whatever reason it would reflect to one position, it would by that same reason reflect to another and to all: which is impossible <note>original: "inconveniens" — literally "inconvenient," but used here in the logical sense of a reduction to absurdity.</note>. Therefore, it must necessarily be granted that the reflection occurs back over the one and same line **a d** along which the incidence occurred. Therefore, perpendiculars either do not reflect, or they return into themselves, and the action of such forms is strengthened. However, if it were said that the perpendicular...

**22. Between the points of the form of any surface incident upon a mirror and the surface of the mirror opposite it, it is necessary that infinite pyramids <term>pyramids: Witelo uses this term for what we would call cones of light or "pencils" of rays</term> be shaped, having cones and bases mutually on both sides.**

For it was declared through the first [proposition] of this book <note>Proposition 1 establishes that light and color travel in straight lines</note> that from any point of an opposite body, light or color proceeds to any point of a mirror: for all lines drawn from any point of a body fall upon a single point of the mirror: and the form of one point of the body falls upon all the points of the surface of the entire mirror: because there is a diffusion of forms to every difference of position. Therefore, the entire form of the body will be in every single point of the mirror: and the form of any point of the body will be in the entire surface of the mirror. Therefore, as many points as there are in the surface of the mirror, there are just as many pyramids terminated at the entire surface of the form of the body, which surface becomes the base of all those pyramids: and as many points as there are in the total surface of the body whose form falls upon the mirror, there are just as many pyramids terminated at the entire surface of the mirror, which is the base of all those pyramids. And all these pyramids are continuous because of the continuity of the points existing in the said surfaces potentially, though not in act: and the axis of any of these pyramids will be the point through which it falls upon the mirror, the middle point of the entire form falling upon the mirror: since from that [point] all other surrounding points fall at an equal distance, equally surrounding the middle point of the form. Therefore the proposition is clear.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 4, [proposition] 20.</margin>
**23. It is impossible for images to be seen in any mirrors whatsoever because of the reflection of visual rays <term>visual rays: a theory (extramission) suggesting the eye sends out feelers to "see" objects</term> from the mirrors to the things seen: but only because of the reflection of forms from the mirrors to the sight.**

For if visual rays were reflected from the mirror to the things whose images the sight perceives, and they carried back those forms from the mirrors to the sight: then any image would be seen in the place of its own object, of which it is an image: which is contrary to the senses. And because, as was shown before through the second [proposition] of this book, color is sent to an opposite body from every colored body when light is present, mixed with light, and is sometimes totally and sometimes partially reflected from it: then if visual rays falling upon mirrors were reflected from them to the things themselves and carried the forms back with them, it would happen that two images of every single thing would be seen, one of which the reflected visual ray itself would offer to the sight, and the other which the ray of the form of the thing itself falling upon the mirror (in which the forms of things are impressed and reflected from the mirror to the sight) would offer: all of which is impossible to the senses.

# WITELO’S OPTICS

...by Proposition 15 of Book 1 <note>Witelo frequently cites Euclid’s Elements; Book 1, Prop 15 concerns vertically opposite angles</note>: therefore angle *r a u* is equal to angle *g a b*, and angle *l b z* is equal to angle *g b a*: therefore, by Proposition 20 of this book, two rays *g a* and *g b* will be reflected from two points *a* and *b* to two points *u* and *z*. If, therefore, the center of vision <note>The 'center of vision' refers to the observer's eye</note>, which is *g*, approaches the surface of the mirror and the line *a b*, such as if it arrives at point *f*: then, because the angle of incidence, which is *f a t*, is smaller than the angle of incidence *g a t*, by Proposition 20 of this book the angle of reflection *q a r* will be smaller than the angle of the previous reflection *u a r*: and angle *q a r* will be larger than angle *u a g*, and line *q i* larger than line *u i*. Therefore, as the eye approaches the surface of the mirror, the edges of the previously seen object (which are *u* and *z*) will not be seen according to the edges of the mirror (which are *a* and *b*). 

But even with the eye remaining at point *g*, and the line *u z* approaching the mirror as far as point *x* (which is a point on line *i h*), the edges of line *u z* (which are *u* and *z*) will not be seen, but only some specific points of it, where the visual ray *g a* reflected from the mirror's surface cuts *u z*; let these be points *m* and *n*. For line *n m* will be smaller than line *u z*: which is evident by Proposition 34 of Book 1 <note>Euclid's theorem on parallelograms</note>, by drawing parallel and perpendicular lines, which are *n o* and *m p*. And if line *u z* is moved further away from the surface of the mirror, no point of it will be seen according to the rays *a u* and *b z*: because other visual rays from the extreme points of the mirror itself (*a* and *b*) are not reflected to any point of line *u z*, but beyond them: which is clear by Proposition 34 of Book 1, by joining the parallel lines *u u* and *z z*. Therefore, in such a setup regarding the mirror, none of the points of line *u z* would be seen: which is contrary to experience and the senses. For it happens that the extremes of an object, whether near or far, are sometimes seen in the mirror, as was assumed at the beginning of this book. And just as this is clear in flat mirrors, it is also clear in any other mirrors: since the demonstration for all of them is the same. Therefore, the proposition is clear, or at least the opposite of it cannot be concluded from these facts.

**24. Reflection alone, which returns to the eye, brings about the comprehension of visible forms in a mirror; hence, the eye is necessarily informed according to the arrangement of the lines of reflection. Alhazen [Book] 4, [proposition] 21.**

That rays do not go out from the eye and, returning to the sight, bring back the forms of visible things with them, has been shown by the preceding [proposition]. However, that a sensible form does not "inform" <note>In medieval philosophy, to 'inform' means to give a specific nature or shape to matter; Witelo is arguing that the image is not physically 'painted' onto the mirror</note> the mirror itself, like a natural form informs its own matter, is clear from this: that forms are not seen in mirrors in every possible position. For anyone looking who moves toward a fixed mirror sees a form that they did not see before; and moving away from the place where the form was previously seen in the fixed mirror, they no longer see it. Also, by looking at one part of a mirror, one does not necessarily see a part of the forms appearing in the mirror; rather, in the same point of a mirror, different observers can see different and distinct forms. These forms, as complete acts, cannot "inform" the same part of the mirror at the same time. Furthermore, the form of an object is seen in mirrors which cannot be multiplied in a straight line to the eye; many other things also happen, the reason for which will be explained later, but they demonstrate a great impossibility [for other theories]. It is clear, therefore, that forms do not proceed from the mirror as if existing within it and multiplying themselves toward the eye, but rather as falling upon the mirrors from formed objects and being reflected from the mirrors to the eye. Therefore, the eye is necessarily informed according to the arrangement of the lines of reflection: since the eye truly sees no other thing except that whose form it perceives reflected from the mirror. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**25. In every reflection made from any mirror, it is necessary that the surface of reflection be perpendicular to the surface of that mirror, or to the surface touching that mirror at the point of reflection. Alhazen [Book] 4, [proposition] 13.**

Since if light or a form falls upon any mirror according to a perpendicular line, it is reflected back along the same line by Proposition 21 of this book: it is clear that the incidence and reflection then occur along the same line; and it is necessary that the surface of reflection be erected <note>i.e., perpendicular</note> over the surface of the mirror by Proposition 18 of Book 11. If, however, light or a form falls upon the surface of any mirror along oblique lines, then the angle of incidence, which the line of incidence makes with the perpendicular, is always equal to the angle of reflection, which the line of reflection contains with the same perpendicular, as is clear by Proposition 20 of this book. Therefore, both of them are in the same surface with the perpendicular line by Proposition 2 of Book 11: therefore, both are in the same surface which is, as is clear by definition, the surface of reflection. Therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 11, that surface is erected over the surface of the mirror, or over the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection. 

This is clearly shown by the example of the surface of the circle cutting the ring <term>ring: Latin 'armilla', a part of an optical instrument</term> of the instrument in [Proposition] 9 of this book, parallel to its bases through all the centers of the holes, and parallel to the surface of the bronze circle, which is *a b c*. For when a ray falls through the middle hole and the mirror is tilted according to the rule, the demonstration is the same as for rays falling obliquely: for then the ray is always reflected to the longitudinal line of the ring, which then is not parallel to the line *b z p*, which is the longitudinal line of the rule. And since reflection then occurs from point *z*, where the axis of the round column falls, or the ray perpendicular over line *c q* (which is the common intersection of the surface of the rule and the surface of the circle passing through the centers of the holes), and the line *d b* (the radius of circle *a b c*) is parallel to this axis: they are therefore in the same surface by the 1st theorem of Book 1 of this work. But line *d b* is perpendicular to the line of the width of the rule, which is the common intersection of the surface of the rule and the circle *a b c*: therefore, by the definition of a surface erected over a surface, the surface in which the axis of the iron column (or the incident ray) and the line *d b* are located is erected over the surface of the rule or the mirror. In this surface is the perpendicular line, which is the line of the height of the ring, passing through point *b* and through the center of the middle hole, along which line the reflection of the light of the axis of the radial pyramid <term>radial pyramid: a cone of light rays</term> occurs. Therefore, the proposition is clear also in each of the mirrors: since this demonstration extends to every mirror, as was clear from the preceding.

<summary>Witelo uses geometric proofs to demonstrate that visual perception in mirrors is caused solely by the reflection of light rays rather than the eye emitting its own rays. He also establishes the law that the plane containing the incident and reflected rays is always perpendicular to the mirror's surface.</summary>
