# BOOK FIVE

*26. In every reflection from any mirror surface, a straight line bisecting the angle formed by the lines of incidence and reflection is necessarily perpendicular to the line that is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror, or to the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of incidence; from this it is clear that this line is perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror at that point.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram labeled with points a, f, c, g, b, h, d, and e. It depicts a ray originating at a (the object), reflecting at b (the mirror surface), and continuing to c (the eye). For let it be that the form of point *a* <note>The "form" refers to the visual image or light ray</note> falls upon the surface of some mirror at point *b*, and is reflected to point *c*. Therefore, the line of incidence is line *ab*, and the line of reflection is line *bc*; these are in one surface standing perpendicular to the mirror's surface according to the previous proposition. Let there also be some plane surface tangent to the mirror at point *b*, and let the common section of this tangent surface and the surface of reflection be line *dbe*. Furthermore, let line *bf* bisect angle *abc* into equal parts. I say that line *fb* is necessarily perpendicular to line *dbe*. Because angle *dba* is equal to angle *ebc* by the 20th proposition of this book <note>Prop. 20 states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection</note>—for the angle of incidence *dba* is equal to the angle of reflection *ebc*—and because angle *abf* is equal to angle *fbc* by hypothesis <note>The hypothesis here is that line bf bisects the angle</note>, it is clear that the whole angle *fbd* is equal to the whole angle *fbe*. Therefore, line *fb* is perpendicular to line *de* by the definition of a perpendicular line. 

This holds if line *dbe* is a straight line; but if it is curved, let a straight line *gh* be tangent to it at point *b* according to Euclid's *Elements* Book 3, Proposition 17. And because the angles of contingency <term>angles of contingency (anguli contingentiae): the tiny, non-rectilinear angles formed between a curve and its tangent line</term> *gbd* and *hbe* are equal, it remains that angles *fbg* and *fbh* are equal; thus line *fb* will likewise be perpendicular to line *gh* and to line *de*. Since, therefore, line *fb* is drawn in the surface of reflection (which by the previous proposition stands perpendicular to the mirror surface or the tangent surface at the point of incidence) and since it is perpendicular to their common section, it is clear that line *fb* stands perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror at that point; for it contains equal angles with all lines produced in that surface. And since the proof can be made in the same way for sections <note>Cross-sections of different mirror shapes like spherical or cylindrical</note>, the proposition is clear.

*27. In every surface of reflection from any mirrors, it is necessary that the center of sight, the point of the seen form, the point of reflection, and the endpoint of the perpendicular and of both normals [catheti] consist together; from this it is clear that the perpendicular line drawn from the point of reflection is common to all surfaces of reflection incident at that point. Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 23.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing three vertical lines e-a, d-c, and f-b descending to a horizontal surface a-c-b. Ray lines connect f to c and e to c, illustrating the path of reflection relative to the perpendicular d-c.</image-desc>

It was shown by Proposition 25 of this book that in every reflection made from any mirror, the surface of reflection—in which are the lines of reflection, incidence, and the perpendicular drawn to the mirror surface from the point of reflection—is always perpendicular to the surface of the mirror from which the reflection occurs. Since the line of incidence begins from the point of the perceived form and ends at the point of reflection, and the line of reflection begins at the point of reflection and ends at the center of the eye, it is clear that these three points are in the same surface. 

But since the perpendicular is erect above the mirror surface, upon which the surface of reflection is also erect by Prop. 25, the entire perpendicular must be in that surface. For since the perpendicular intersects the lines of incidence and reflection at the point of reflection, and since by definition it is in the same surface with them, then by Euclid's *Elements* Book 11, Proposition 1, the upper end of the perpendicular will necessarily be in the same surface with the aforementioned points. If that perpendicular were to end at some other point outside the surface of reflection, it is clear that the perpendicular would be in another surface, which contradicts the definition of a surface of reflection; and also, if it were in another surface, a right angle would be smaller than a right angle, which is impossible. For a line produced from the point of reflection within the surface of reflection, standing perpendicular to the mirror surface, forms a right angle with a line produced from the same point in the mirror surface, and the [actual] perpendicular does the same. If those two lines ended at different points, one right angle would be greater than another right angle. 

In the same way, the proposition is clear concerning the <term>catheti (catheti): lines dropped perpendicularly from the object or the eye to the mirror's surface</term>. And since all surfaces of reflection that pass through the same point of reflection and any point of a perceived form always pass through the same endpoint of the perpendicular—even if they end at different centers of sight—and since all are erect above the mirror surface or the tangent surface, it is clear that they all intersect at the perpendicular. Therefore, the perpendicular is common to all of them. But this should also be declared with a figure. Let a perpendicular *cd* also be drawn above the mirror surface *bca* from point *c*, according to Euclid 11.12. Let it also be understood that a perpendicular *ea* is drawn from point *e* to the surface *bca* (or its continuation) according to Euclid 11.11; line *ea* will be parallel to line *dc* according to Euclid 11.6, because both are orthogonal to the same...

### 28. *It is necessary that every point of reflection of the form of a point falling obliquely upon a mirror consists between the cathetus of incidence and the cathetus of reflection on the surface of the mirror.*

Let the cathetus of incidence be $da$, and the cathetus of reflection be $eb$. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 29. *It is impossible for two points of the same visible object to be reflected from the same point of any mirror to the same center of vision; or for the form of one point to be reflected to the same eye from two points of plane or convex mirrors. Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 5.*

For it is clear through the 13th proposition of the 11th book of Euclid that if some point of a form falls perpendicularly on the mirror surface, it is impossible for another line from another point of the same object (or another) to be drawn perpendicularly to the same surface at that same point. That a perpendicular is reflected back upon itself is clear through the 21st proposition of this book; therefore, it is impossible for two points of the same visible form to be reflected perpendicularly from the same point of the mirror to the same center of vision. But neither is it possible for this to happen when the line of incidence is oblique. For every point of any form falls upon the mirror and is reflected to the vision according to the shortest lines, through the 18th proposition of this book; and all such reflection to the vision and the comprehension of the forms themselves happens according to the arrangement of the reflected lines, through the 24th proposition of this book. For if the lines of incidence of the forms of different points do not vary the points of reflection, but instead fall upon the same point: it is clear that either some entire form, or several points of that form, can fall upon one point and be reflected into one point, which is the center of the sight: and the entire form will appear as a single point. For example, if from two points of a form falling on the mirror, which are **a** and **b**, two lines **ac** and **bc** fall upon the same point of the mirror, which is **c**: and from that point they are reflected to the same center of sight, which is **d**: it follows that if from one point of reflection **c**, different forms of points **a** and **b** reach the center of sight **d**, then two straight lines, which are **cd**, would enclose a surface: <note>In Euclidean geometry, two straight lines cannot enclose a space; this is used here as a logical proof by contradiction.</note> which is impossible. 30. **It is not possible for the form of one point of a visible thing to be reflected from one point of the surface of any mirror to two eyes. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 4.**

For since the line of reflection proceeding to one eye maintains an angle with the perpendicular erected from the point of reflection upon the mirror's surface equal to the angle which the line of incidence maintains with the same perpendicular (as is clear through the 20th [theorem] of this book): it is evident that another line cannot be taken in the same surface that would make an equal angle with the drawn perpendicular. Thus, the form of the same point will not be reflected from this point to another eye. It is necessary, therefore, that reflection to different eyes occurs from different points of any mirror. And since there are only two eyes, it is necessary at the minimum that the reflection of the form of one point of the visible thing to both eyes occurs from two points of the surface of any mirror. Thus, the proposition is clear.

31. **From one point of reflection of any mirror, it is possible for the forms of several points to be reflected to different eyes: and from different points, one [form may be reflected]. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 4.**

For although, as is clear through the 29th [theorem] of this book, the reflection of only one incident point is possible from only one point of the mirror at the same time to one center of sight: it is nevertheless possible for the reflection of the forms of different incident points to occur simultaneously to different eyes from one point of the mirror. This is because those points fall according to different angles and are reflected according to different angles: therefore, the reflected lines terminate at different points, in which different eyes falling [upon those lines] will perceive the points of different forms reflected from one point of the mirror to the different eyes. And if one eye is moved and varies its position while the mirror remains immobile: then also, according to the diversity of its position, points of different forms will be reflected to it from the same point of the mirror; yet the <term>pyramid</term> <note>original: "pyramis"; in medieval optics, this refers to the cone of light rays extending from an object to the eye.</note> of the remaining forms will always be completed. But also, one moving eye, or different eyes, will see the same form reflected from different points of the mirror: because any point of the incident form falling upon the total surface of the mirror is reflected toward some opposite part, and according to the manner proposed in the 22nd and 24th [theorems] of this book, it is clear that the pyramids of the forms are varied. And because the different axes of the pyramids (which are of the same form) fall upon different eyes, it happens that one form is seen by different eyes reflected from different points of the mirror's surface. And the same thing happens even to the same eye when moved, while the mirror remains immobile. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<meta>This page continues the geometric proofs regarding the behavior of light and reflection in various types of mirrors. Witelo is specifically examining why certain points on a perpendicular line relative to the eye cannot be seen through reflection, reinforcing the idea that the geometry of the eye and the laws of reflection (angles of incidence and reflection) restrict what can be perceived.</meta>

# THE OPTICS OF WITELO

...of any plane or convex mirror, and let there now be, for the sake of example, the line **bg** of a given plane mirror. Let there also be a perpendicular line **ag** drawn from point **a** above the line **bg**. Furthermore, let the line **ag** intersect the convex spherical surface of the eye at point **d**. I say that in the entire perpendicular **ag**, however far it is extended, there is no point which is reflected from this mirror to the center of sight **a**, except for point **d** alone. For if some other point of the said perpendicular besides point **d** were reflected to the sight, that point would either be beyond the center of sight **a**, or below the sight. If it is beyond the sight, let that point be **h**. It is then clear that its form will not reach the mirror along the perpendicular **ha**, because of the interposition of a solid body <note>Witelo is referring to the viewer's own head or body blocking the path of light.</note> which is beyond the sight in the viewer's head. Therefore, the form of point **h** will not be reflected upon the perpendicular **hg**. 

But if it is claimed that the form of point **h** could be reflected to the sight **a** from some other point of the mirror besides point **g**, let that point be **b**. Let there be a line of incidence **hb** and a line of reflection **ha**. If the angle **hba** is divided into equal parts by the line **bt** drawn to the perpendicular **hg** (by the aid of the 9th proposition of Book 1), then, by the 26th proposition of this book, the line **bt** will be perpendicular to the line **bg**. But the line **gt** is also perpendicular to that same line **hg**. Therefore, from the same point **t**, it would be possible to draw two perpendicular lines to the line **bg** and to the surface of the mirror itself, which is impossible. For it would follow that two angles of the triangle **abg** would be right angles, namely angles **tgb** and **tbg**, and multiple perpendicular lines would be drawn from the same point to the same surface, which is contrary to the 20th theorem of Book 1 of this work. 

Therefore, no form of the points on line **hd** can be reflected to the sight, except for point **d** alone, since the same must be demonstrated for all other points in the same way. Nor can it be said that any form of any point taken between points **a** and **d** is reflected to the sight, except through the perpendicular line **da**. This is because points placed between the center of sight and its surface are very thin <note>original: "rari" – referring to the transparent humors of the eye like the aqueous or vitreous humor</note>; hence, the form of any of them is not sent into the sight, nor is it reflected from any mirror so as to be perceived. Furthermore, the form of none of the points on line **dg** can be reflected to the sight **a** from point **g** of the mirror, such as the form of point **f**. For if that point **d** were a solid body, it is clear that it would hinder the reflection to the sight along the line **dg**, because due to its solidity, the form of point **f** could not pass through and reach the sight. If it were thin <note>transparent</note>, the reflected form from the mirror would still be mixed with it and cling to it, and would not reach the sight. 

Nor can the form of any of those points be reflected from another point of the mirror other than point **g**, such as from point **k**. For once lines **fk** and **ak** are drawn, and angle **akf** is divided into equal parts by line **kl**, the same impossibility follows as before: namely, that lines **lk** and **lg** would be perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, or to the surface tangent to the mirror, which is contrary to the 20th theorem of Book 1. Thus, of all the points on line **hg**, none is reflected to the sight **a** except point **d** alone. And since any point of the entire visible object in which line **hg** exists (except for point **d**) is impressed upon the surface of the sight and faces the mirror at something other than a right angle—because all points surrounding point **d** meet in the center of sight **a** and form the cone of a pyramid <note>a "visual pyramid" or "visual cone" is the standard medieval way of describing how light from an object tapers into the eye.</note> whose base is on the surface of the mirror around the axis **ag**—the forms of all those points will be seen along the perpendiculars drawn from them to the surface of the mirror. Thus the proposition is clear. 

In convex mirrors, the line **hg** is always perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, and no other perpendicular can be drawn from any of its points to the mirror's surface, according to the 20th theorem of Book 1. However, let these things that have been set forth be understood for only one eye in all plane and convex mirrors, as the proposition proposes. For the form of the same point of a visible thing reflected to both eyes, if it falls perpendicularly on one of the eyes, it can fall obliquely on the other eye according to a line of reflection proceeding obliquely from the surface of the mirror to the center of sight. Thus the same point of a visible thing will be seen by two eyes according to a different mode of its reflection. However, in any concave mirrors, it is otherwise.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a vertical line labeled with points h, t, a, d, g from top to bottom. A horizontal line extends from the bottom point g to the right, ending at point e. Point k is marked on the horizontal line between g and e. A point f is marked between d and g on the vertical line. Lines connect point a to g and k, and point h to b (a point to the left of g) and k. Arcs indicate angles and points of intersection.</image-desc>

**33. It is impossible for a form falling obliquely upon a mirror to be reflected back along its line of incidence, or toward the side of its smaller angle.**

<margin>Euclid, Theorem 3 of the *Catoptrics*</margin>

Suppose that the form of point **c** falls obliquely on mirror **ab** at point **d**, such that angle **cdb** is greater than angle **cda**. I say that the form of point **c** will not be reflected back into itself along line **cd** because of the inequality of the angles; for the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection by the 20th proposition of this book. Nor will it be reflected toward the side of its smaller angle, which is **cda**. For let it be reflected along line **de** dividing angle **cda**. Then angle **cdb** would be equal to angle **eda**. But angle **cdb** is greater than angle **dac** <note>likely intended as angle **cda** based on context</note> by the hypothesis. Therefore, angle **eda** would be greater than angle **cda**, a part being greater than its whole, which is impossible. Therefore, the reflection will always occur according to the larger angle, which in this proposition is angle **cdb**. And this is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line labeled a, d, b. A point c is positioned above point d. Lines extend from c to d, and from d to another point e above the line a b, representing angles of incidence and reflection. The lines show how reflection must move away from the smaller angle.</image-desc>

<summary>Witelo proves that in plane and convex mirrors, only one specific point on a perpendicular line from the eye can be reflected directly back to the center of sight, and demonstrates that light must reflect at an angle equal to its incidence, never back along an oblique path.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the geometric demonstrations of Book 5 of Witelo's Optics. Having previously discussed why certain points on a perpendicular line cannot be seen via reflection, Witelo now moves to the spatial arrangement of reflected images. He establishes that the middle points of an object always appear between its edges in a mirror and introduces the "cathetus of incidence"— the perpendicular line used to locate where an image appears to the viewer.</meta>

BOOK FIVE.

# 34. **In every mirror, the reflection of the forms of the middle points of any seen object occurs between the reflection points of the forms of the extreme points of that same seen object.**

Suppose an object $a b c$ is seen by reflection from any mirror. Let its extreme points be $a$ and $c$, and let $b$ be some point in the middle of the line $abc$. Let the surface of that mirror—whether it be plane, convex, or concave—contain the line $d e f$, which is the common section of the mirror and the surface of reflection. Let the center of sight be point $g$. Let the form of point $a$ reflect to the sight $g$ from point $d$ on the mirror, the form of point $c$ reflect from point $f$, and the form of point $b$ (the middle point) reflect to the sight from point $e$ on the mirror. I say that point $e$ necessarily falls between points $d$ and $f$, which are the points of reflection for the forms of the extreme points $a$ and $c$. For if point $e$ were to fall outside points $d$ and $f$, then line $be$ (which is the line of incidence for the form of point $b$) would intersect one of the lines $ad$ or $cf$. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing three points (a, b, c) representing an object. Lines of incidence travel from these points to a mirror surface at points d, e, and f. From there, they reflect to a single point g, representing the eye. The diagram shows that for the middle point b to reach the eye g, its point of contact on the mirror e must lie between the contact points of the outer edges d and f. An intersection point h illustrates the logical impossibility of the lines crossing otherwise.</image-desc>

Whichever line it intersects, let that point of intersection be $h$. It is thus clear that the form of point $h$ would be reflected to the sight $g$ from two different points on the mirror: either $e$ and $f$, or $e$ and $d$. This is clearly impossible in plane and convex mirrors according to the 29th proposition of this book <note>original: "29 huius"</note>. In concave mirrors, the number of reflection points would be doubled beyond what is appropriate for those mirrors; furthermore, no form in any mirror would correspond to its other points. Thus, the object would be seen in a way that distorts its own parts, which is entirely impossible. Therefore, the proposition is evident.

# 35. **When the shape of the surface of the incident body and the mirror are similar, and they exist in similar positions, there will be in every mirror a complete representation of the body’s form and shape. *Alhazen, Book 2, chapter 4, note 22.***

When the shape of the mirror and the body are the same and their orientation is the same—for instance, if both surfaces are flat and parallel <note>original: "æquidistent"</note>—then the form of the first point of the surface of the seen body falls upon the first point of the mirror, the second point upon the second, and so on for all other corresponding points. Thus, the total shape of the surface of the seen body is created on the surface of the mirror, which does not happen in a mirror of a different shape. Similarly, if any part of a mirror is taken whose shape is similar to the shape of the body and positioned parallel to it, there will always be a complete representation of the body's shape within it. Since there are infinite such parts of a mirror, it is clear that there will be infinite forms of the body falling upon the mirror, which are always reflected to different points from which different viewers <note>original: "uisus diuersi"</note> perceive the form of the body in the same mirror. This occurs in all mirrors, but is most evident in plane ones. Since any point of a flat surface falling upon another flat surface results in the surrounding parts having a similar arrangement and position, a similar reflection happens from all points simultaneously and in the same manner; thus, the completion of the body's form and shape occurs in the mirror. This is what was proposed.

# 36. **In any mirror, every point seen is perceived upon its cathetus of incidence. *Euclid, Theorems of Catoptrics 16, 17, 18; Alhazen, Book 5, note 9.***

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a vertical line a-g, where a is the object and g is the point where the perpendicular meets the mirror surface. A line of incidence goes from a to point d on the mirror, and a line of reflection goes from d to the eye at b. The image is perceived as being located somewhere along the vertical line a-g.</image-desc>

Let there be any mirror; for the sake of example, let it be a plane mirror $gd$. Let the point being seen be $a$, and the center of the eye be $b$. Let the <term>cathetus</term> <note>From the Greek 'kathetos,' meaning a perpendicular line. In optics, this is the straight line drawn from the object perpendicular to the mirror's surface.</note> of incidence be drawn from the point of the seen object $a$, which is $ag$. I say that the image of point $a$ is always seen on the line $ag$. For it was assumed at the beginning of this book, in the second supposition, that the uniform positioning of a point of a seen object relative to the surface of any mirror from which its form is reflected occurs only along the cathetus of its incidence. The form seen in the mirror is the image of the thing seen, as is clear by definition; it is therefore necessary that the image be seen according to the uniform positioning of the point of the seen object relative to the mirror. Otherwise, that form would not be seen as an image. Therefore, it will necessarily be seen on the cathetus of its own incidence. This is what was proposed, and it is to be demonstrated in the same way for other types of mirrors.

# 37. **The location of the image of a seen object in any mirror must be at the point where the line of reflection meets the cathetus of incidence. *Alhazen, Book 5, notes 2, 4, 6, 7, 8.***

An example of this is: if a <term>right-angled pyramid</term> <note>original: "pyramis orthogonia"</note> is erected perpendicularly upon the surface of any mirror, then another continuous pyramid will appear to the sight, joined to the external pyramid like a rhombus. The vertices of these pyramids will appear to be at a uniform distance from the surface of the mirror. And if a straight line is imagined to be drawn from the vertex of one pyramid to the vertex of the other, it is clear that this line will be perpendicular to the base of the seen pyramid, and thus perpendicular to the surface of the mirror—since the surface of the mirror and the base of the seen pyramid are the same (as in plane mirrors), or the base of the seen pyramid

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof from page 207, moving from the relative positioning of reflected points to the specific location where a reflected image is perceived. Witelo is explaining that an image is always seen at the intersection of the line of sight and the perpendicular line (cathetus) dropped from the object to the mirror surface.</meta>

[Page 208]

...is equidistant to the surface tangent to the mirror, as in convex mirrors, where the surface of the mirror itself is tangent to the base of the visual pyramid <note>The "visual pyramid" or "cone of vision" is the 3D volume of light traveling from an object to the eye or mirror.</note>, or it is equidistant to a surface tangent to the mirror's surface, as in concave mirrors, where the base of the pyramid erected upon the mirror is equidistant to a plane surface tangent to the mirror. Therefore, the vertex of the pyramid will always be seen on a perpendicular line drawn from it to the mirror. Similarly, if a line is drawn from any point of the pyramid parallel to its axis, it will always fall upon a corresponding point in another [imaginary] pyramid. This produced line—according to Proposition 8 of Book 11 <note original="8 p 11">Likely referring to Euclid’s Elements</note>—will always be orthogonal to the bases of said pyramids and to the surface of the mirror, or to the surface tangent to the mirror. Therefore, the image of any point of a pyramid thus placed opposite a mirror falls on the perpendicular line understood to be drawn from that point to the mirror's surface.

But whatever point of a body is placed opposite a mirror, it is necessary to imagine an orthogonal pyramid equidistant to the tangent surface—as is clear from Proposition 22 of this book—the vertex of which is the point being seen, and the base of which is the mirror's surface or a surface continuous with it. It is appropriate to imagine another pyramid opposite that one, completing a sort of rhombus <note>A diamond shape formed by two cones/pyramids joined at their bases.</note>, where the base of both is either the same, or the base of one is parallel to the other; the line drawn from the vertex of one to the vertex of the other will be perpendicular to the mirror's surface. 

And because the image of any point opposite a mirror falls on the perpendicular line drawn from that point to the mirror’s surface (or its extension), it is clear that the location of the image is on that perpendicular line, as was also clear from the preceding proposition. But since in any mirror the perception of forms does not happen except through lines of reflection—as is clear from Proposition 24 of this book—it is also evident that the image of any seen point falls on the line of reflection. And because every such line is straight, the image of any point of a reflected form falls exactly on the point where the perpendicular line and the line of reflection intersect. 

Sometimes, therefore, it is seen in front of the mirror's surface, such as when the intersection of these lines—namely the line of reflection and the <term>cathetus of incidence<gloss>the perpendicular line dropped from the object point to the mirror surface</gloss></term>—cannot occur except below the mirror's surface. However, the extended line of reflection meets the cathetus of incidence. For the line of reflection meets the perpendicular line drawn from the point of reflection upon the mirror's surface itself, as is clear from what has been said. In plane mirrors, that perpendicular is parallel to the cathetus of incidence according to Proposition 6 of Book 11, for both are perpendicular to the mirror's surface. It is therefore manifest through Theorem 2 of Book 1 of this work that in those mirrors, the line of reflection meets the cathetus of incidence. 

In other [curved] mirrors this is even more manifest, since in most of them the cathetus of incidence meets the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection to the mirror’s surface. This will be demonstrated for each individual type of mirror in what follows. It is at the meeting point of these lines that the image is seen. Therefore, the location of the image is there, as was proposed. 

This is necessary because, since the medium between the seen point and the mirror's surface is not a vacuum, there is a reflection of the form of the intervening medium to the eye, just as there is of the point of the body at which the sight is directed. There is no difference between the reflection of the form of the medium and the reflection of the form of the intended point, except as between a single whole continuous body and a small part of it that one intends to see. For example, if one intends to see the eye of a needle in a mirror, and its form is multiplied to the sight, the entire form of the needle is nonetheless arranged in the mirror. 

And since forms falling upon the eyes and upon any regular mirrors retain the essential order of their parts and shapes (as is clear from Proposition 34 of this book), it is therefore necessary for the points of forms incident to mirrors to sometimes be seen at a certain distance. This happens when the points of the object are outside [the mirror], and when the line of reflection and the cathetus meet below the mirror's surface or between the eye and the mirror, and not on the mirror's surface itself or behind the viewer. In all these cases, the universal cause is the same as previously stated, differing only according to the various modes of reflection. 

It happens to things—according to how their forms are spread through the medium to the mirror's surface—that they differ in their specific forms. However, nothing is sensibly carried to the mirror except light, color, shape, and the like, which do not create the specific difference in things (such as between wood and stone). Nevertheless, the <term>discriminative faculty<gloss>the power of the mind to distinguish between objects</gloss></term> perceives the specific difference through knowledge of these "accidents" <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are properties like color or size that aren't the essential nature of a thing.</note>—namely, by applying those accidents to their proper subjects, which appear to the eyes directly looking at them under such accidents. 

Just as the forms of the parts of a single continuous natural body are carried to the mirror's surface, and the total form and shape are preserved, it necessarily happens that the parts further from the mirror's surface appear further away, so that the form and shape of the seen things are not confused. Thus it necessarily happens with things seen through the air: just as the form of the air is pre-arranged in its place, so the forms of all its points are seen in respect to the form of the object seen through the air. Otherwise, the shape and form of the things multiplied to the mirror's surface would be confused. And this, it seems to me, is the true cause of this matter, which others have sought through many long-winded wanderings. 

Therefore, a thing is necessarily seen on the perpendicular because (as is clear from Theorem 21 of Book 1) this is its shortest distance from the mirror's surface from which reflection to the sight occurs. According to this line, a uniform arrangement of the seen thing is made with respect to the mirror; it is from this that the form of the thing takes the name "image," as we said in the previous section. Although the form of a thing may be reflected to the eye along another line, the judgment of the visual faculty nonetheless follows the shortest line along which the seen form falls upon the surface of the mirror itself, for the sake of the proper arrangement of forms on the mirror's surface and in the eye, and for the more certain knowledge of its own proper size. For since it is necessary for the image to be on the line of reflection, if it were seen closer to the eye than the cathetus, it would appear larger; if beyond the cathetus, it would appear smaller, as if seen from further away. But on the cathetus—as much as the shape of the mirror and the distance of the eye permit—it is seen according to its own proper size. It is therefore necessary for it to be seen at the point where the line of reflection meets the cathetus of incidence. For when the sight [perceives] through reflection...

Having established on the previous page that the location of an image is determined by the intersection of the line of sight and the perpendicular line from the object, he now moves to the physical properties of mirrors—such as their shape, their construction, and the way they are polished—and how these factors influence the appearance of the reflected image.</meta>

<note>S 3</note>
<note>catchword: some</note>

...perceives forms, he does not notice that this perception occurs through reflection. As we said above in the introduction to this science, reflection does not happen because of any property of sight; for even if sight is removed, reflection still occurs from mirrors. This is because a physical form falls upon the surfaces of mirrors no less than on other objects, but because it encounters resistance to passing through due to the solidity of the mirror-like body, it is reflected from them. If it happens that a viewer's eye is in the location where the reflected lines gather, the sight will perceive those forms at the heads of those lines. Every form reflected from any mirror appears in that mirror as if it were not coming from outside, but as if it were a natural form of the mirror itself—even though it is not part of the mirror's essence. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 38. *The form of every seen thing perceived through reflection from the surface of some mirror must necessarily be assimilated, in some way, to the shape of that mirror's surface.* <note>Reference to Alhazen, Book 3, Section 37, Note 6.</note>

Since, as is clear from the previous proposition, the location of the image of any point of a seen form is at the meeting point of the line of reflection and the <term>cathetus of incidence</term> <note>The "cathetus of incidence" is the perpendicular line drawn from the object point to the mirror's surface.</note>, the meeting of these lines is diversified according to the shape of the surfaces of the mirrors from which the reflection occurs. Because of the arrangement of that shape, there is a diversity in the meeting of the cathetus of incidence and the perpendicular line drawn from the point of the incident form to the surface of the mirror (or to the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection). The meeting of these perpendiculars varies the meeting point of the lines of reflection with the cathetus of incidence, which is where the image is located, as was declared in the previous proposition. Thus, the surface of the mirror from which reflection occurs has a certain "power" in the formation of the seen images reflected from them. However, this assimilation to the mirror's shape does not always happen according to the entire arrangement of the forms, except when the locations of the images fall on the very surfaces of the mirrors, rather than inside or outside them. Yet even then, they are assimilated in some way to the forms or shapes of the mirrors; for in pyramidal mirrors, the forms appear somewhat pyramidal, and the same occurs in other mirrors. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 39. *When the surface of any mirror is divided, it happens that the form of a single point of the seen object is multiplied by the number of those parts.*

What is proposed here is true when, through the division of the surface of some perceptible mirror, there occurs a diversity in the order and position of the partial surfaces, both in themselves and in respect to the sight. This occurs most frequently in <term>leaded glass mirrors</term> <note original="speculis uitreis plumbatis">Early mirrors were often made of glass backed with lead or tin; if the glass cracked or the backing was uneven, the reflection would split into multiple images.</note>, which easily lose their surface unity through division. This does not happen as easily in other mirrors. Therefore, when the surfaces of other mirrors lose their unity of surface in terms of position and order due to a division made in them, the form of one point of the seen object is multiplied by the number of those parts. For then, different catheti of incidence are created for the form of that same point relative to those different partial surfaces; similarly, there are different points of reflection and different lines of reflection to the center of the same eye. And because the location of any image is always at the point where the line of reflection meets the cathetus of incidence (as is clear from Proposition 37 of this book), it is clear that the images of the same point are numbered according to the number of these lines and their intersections. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 40. *On every mirror surface, the reflection of forms occurs in length and width according to the manner of its polishing.*

What is proposed here is clearly seen by example in any mirrors polished by craftsmanship. For if they are polished lengthwise—as happens with the surfaces of swords—then the face of the viewer will appear elongated relative to its own true arrangement. If some surfaces are polished according to their width, then the image of the viewer’s face will appear wider than its true property according to that arrangement. Sometimes the image will appear slanted because of the slant of the polishing. In all these cases, the cause is the greater union of the surfaces of the polished bodies themselves, from which (and from whose parts) the reflection flows together into a union of reflected forms which reach the sight accordingly. For, as we said in the definitions at the beginning of this book, <note>Referring to Book 1, Definition 1.</note> polishing is the continuity of the parts of a polished body's surface without perceptible pores or divisions. Thus, when those pores are smoothed down in a certain direction, it is necessary that the forms falling upon those many points flow together and unite into a single form according to that direction. In this way, the form seen through reflection is increased and appears larger. However, in other directions, it must necessarily be seen in its own proper arrangement, or close to it. Thus, a certain "monstrosity" <note original="monstruositas">In this context, Witelo uses "monstrosity" to mean a visual distortion or an unnatural, deformed appearance.</note> occurs in the images of forms seen this way, because their reflection is unequal on this side and that, and becomes irregular. Therefore, so that reflection from artificially polished bodies may be regular and match the arrangement of the reflected forms, it is necessary that their surfaces be polished in a circular manner—not in length, width, or slanted—lest the proper arrangement of the forms be deformed by those methods. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 41. *In every mirror, it happens that the same image is sometimes seen as two by two eyes.*

The occurrence of this event happens to the sight in the vision of a single image reflected from any mirror, just as the same error happens to it in the simple vision of objects when the same causes (or some of them) coincide, as we declared in theorems 103, 104, 105, 106, and 107 of Book 4. For instance, this happens when the form of the same thing reflected from the same mirror is presented directly to one eye and obliquely to the other, or when the reflected form, positioned between the radial axes, meets both eyes obliquely. For in whatever ways it happens that the form of the same thing is seen as two, in those same ways it is possible for the image of that form to be seen as two, if according to the manner of its vision...

<meta>This page continues Book 5 of Witelo's Optics, specifically discussing the properties of reflection in plane mirrors. Having established the general principles of how forms are reflected in the previous section, he now addresses why images appear to move when the object moves and begins a series of geometric proofs regarding the paths of light.</meta>

VITELLO'S OPTICS

...reflected by some mirror. And for that reason, one should not dwell on such matters differently than what was said regarding simple vision <note>Vitello refers to his earlier discussion on direct vision (non-reflected) in Book 4, where he explains why we see a single image despite having two eyes.</note>: for that does not happen because of a diversity in the points of reflection of the form of the same point to both eyes; since that diversity is either non-existent or is not perceptible. Hence, it introduces no perceptible error to the eyes, but both eyes, following that [reflection], successfully reach the vision of the unity of the same form, as will be declared later; therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 42. *The image of a moved object seen in any mirror is seen to move.*

The cause of this is nothing other than the uniformity of reflection from any point of the mirror over which the motion occurs. And because all points of the seen object are reflected from different points [of the mirror] than before, a new image of the entire seen object is produced, according to how the points from which the reflection is made are changed by its motion. Thus, the form seems to move, although in truth it does not move, but rather a new image is generated as the position of the seen object is changed. This, however, happens because of the continuity of the points of reflection on the surface of mirrors. Therefore, the proposition is clear. Having thus set forth these common properties of all mirrors, it remains for us to turn our pen to the specific properties of plane mirrors.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two similar right-angled triangles adc and bec sharing a vertex at point c on a horizontal line de. Vertical segments ad and be represent catheti (perpendiculars), while lines ac and bc represent incident and reflected rays meeting the mirror surface at c. Point a is labeled at the top left, d at bottom left, c in the center, e at bottom right, and b at top right.</image-desc>

### 43. *In every reflection made by plane mirrors, the lines of incidence and reflection are proportional to the <term>catheti</term> dropped from the points of their endpoints, and to the bases themselves interspersed on the surface of the mirrors. Euclid, 3rd hypothesis of the Catoptrics.* <note>A "cathetus" is a perpendicular line. Here, it refers to the height of the object and the observer's eye above the mirror surface.</note>

Let there be a plane mirror, in the surface of which is the line $d c e$: and let the line of incidence be $a c$: and the line of reflection be $c b$: and let the catheti of incidence $a d$ and of reflection $b e$ be drawn. I say that the ratio of $a d$ to $b e$ is the same as $a c$ to $b c$ and $d c$ to $c e$. Since in triangle $a d c$ the right angle, which is $a d c$, is equal to the angle $b e c$, which is also right: and angle $a c d$, which is the angle of incidence, is (by the 20th [proposition] of this [book]) equal to angle $b c e$, which is the angle of reflection: then necessarily angle $d a c$ of triangle $a d c$ will be equal to angle $c b e$ of triangle $b e c$ (by Book 1, Proposition 32 of Euclid's *Elements*): therefore (by Book 6, Proposition 4) the sides of those triangles facing the equal angles are proportional: therefore, the ratio of line $a d$ to line $b e$ is the same as the ratio of line $a c$ to $b c$, and line $d c$ to $e c$. And since the same resulting proportion always remains from the equality of the angles: therefore, the proposition is clear.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the reflection of a point source a in a plane mirror. A horizontal line bd represents the mirror. A vertical line through b connects point a above the mirror to point e below it, such that ab equals be. An incident ray ac meets the mirror at c, and the reflected ray is shown as the extension of line ec toward point f. This demonstrates the construction of a virtual image.</image-desc>

### 44. *To find the location where the eye must be placed for reflection to occur from a point of a seen object incident on the surface of a plane mirror.*

Let $a$ be the point whose form is incident on a plane mirror: and let line $b c d$ be the common section of the <term>surface of reflection</term> <note>The "surface of reflection" is the imaginary flat plane that contains both the incident ray and the reflected ray.</note> and the mirror, drawn in the surface of the mirror: and let point $a$ be incident on the mirror at point $c$: and let the line of incidence be $a c$: and from point $a$ let line $a b$ be drawn perpendicular to line $b c d$ (by Book 1, Proposition 12 [of Euclid]): and let it be extended to point $e$, until (by Book 1, Proposition 3) line $b e$ is made equal to $a b$: and let line $e c$ be connected: which is extended beyond $c$ to point $f$. I say that with the eye existing at any point on line $c f$, reflection will always occur to it, and it will see the form of point $a$. For let line $a c$ be joined: and angle $a b c$ will be equal to angle $c b e$, because, as is clear from the premises, both those angles are right. Since therefore (by Book 1, Proposition 4), as from the hypothesis line $b e$ is equal to $a b$, and the side $b c$ is common, the triangles $a b c$ and $c b e$ are equiangular; angle $a c b$ will be equal to angle $b c e$: but (by Book 1, Proposition 15) angle $f c d$ is equal to angle $b c e$: therefore angle $f c d$ is equal to angle $a c b$: therefore (by the 20th [proposition] of this [book]), since line $a c$ is the line of incidence, $c f$ will be the line of reflection. Therefore, with the eye placed on that line, reflection will occur to the eye. Which is the proposition.

### 45. *The form of a point is not reflected from a plane mirror to the same eye, except from one point only. Alhazen Book 4, [Theorem] 5.*

Let the center of the eye be $a$: and the seen point $b$: and let $z h$ be the surface of the plane mirror. I say that the form of point $b$ is reflected to the eye $a$ from only one point of the surface $z h$. For if it were possible for it to be reflected from two points, let those two points be $d$ and $e$: and let a line be drawn from the center of the eye, point $a$, to the seen point $b$: which let be $a b$. Thus the line $a b$, extended beyond either of the points $b$ or $a$, either intersects the surface of the mirror or is parallel to it. If it intersects, whether it is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror from which the reflection occurs or not, it will always necessarily be in only one surface of reflection. For if it is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror: then it is clear that it is in one surface of reflection (by the 27th [proposition] of this [book]): since it is reflected back onto itself (by the 21st [proposition] of this [book]). If, however, line $a b$ is not perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, since it is a straight line extended between two endpoints which (by the 25th [proposition] of this [book]) are both necessarily in one surface of reflection erected [perpendicularly] over the surface of the mirror, the line $a b$ will also be in only one such surface: since if it were in two such surfaces, then it would be the common section of those two surfaces orthogonal to the surface of the mirror (by the 19th theorem of Book 1 of this [work]): whence, taking a point in it...

...from point $e$, and a line drawn from that point in one of the surfaces upon the line common to this surface and the surface of the mirror, this line will be perpendicular to the surface of the mirror by the definition of a surface erected upon another surface. Similarly, from the same point, let a line be drawn in the other surface upon the line common to it and the surface of the mirror; this line will again be orthogonal <term>orthogonal</term> <note>A technical term meaning "at a right angle" or perpendicular.</note> to the surface of the mirror. It would then follow that from the same point, two perpendicular lines could be drawn to the same surface of the mirror, which is impossible and contrary to the 20th theorem of the first book of this work. Therefore, the line $ba$ will exist in only one surface of reflection, erected upon the surface of the plane mirror. Furthermore, the three points $a$, $e$, and $b$ will be in the same surface of reflection according to the first proposition of the 11th book [of Euclid]; and the lines $ae$ and $eb$ will be in that surface of reflection in which the line $ab$ is, by the 25th theorem of this book; and similarly for the lines $ed$, $db$, and $da$.

Wherefore, the lines $ea$ and $eb$ will be in the same surface as lines $da$ and $db$ by the second proposition of the 11th book. But angle $aeh$ is greater than angle $ade$ by the 16th proposition of the 1st book, for an exterior angle is greater than an interior one. However, by the 20th theorem of this book, the angle of incidence, which is $aeh$, is equal to the angle of reflection, which is $bed$; and angle $ade$ is equal to angle $bdz$. Therefore, angle $deb$ is greater than angle $ade$, and thus also greater than its equal, namely angle $bdz$. But this is against the 16th proposition of the 1st book, for the exterior angle $bdz$ is greater than the interior angle $bed$. Consequently, angle $adh$ is also greater than angle $bed$, and thus the same angle would be both greater than and less than the same angle, which is impossible. Therefore, the reflection of the form of point $b$ to the eye $a$ occurs from only a single point of the plane mirror.

If, however, the line $ab$ is perpendicular to the surface of the plane mirror, it is clear by the 22nd theorem of this book that only one point is reflected along it to the eye, and from only one point of the mirror. But if line $ab$ does not intersect any of the lines extended on the surface of the mirror, but is parallel to one of them, then by the 9th proposition of the 11th book, it will be parallel to any line parallel to that line produced on the mirror’s surface. Let it then be parallel to line $hz$. By the 1st theorem of the first book of this work, lines $ab$ and $hz$ will be in the same surface. Let the deduction be made as before, showing that an interior angle would be greater than an exterior one, which is impossible. Therefore, the premise from which this followed is also impossible. Thus, what was proposed is clear.

46. *In plane mirrors, to find the point of reflection for a given seen point and a given center of vision.*
Alhazen, Book 5, [Proposition] 12.

Let there be a plane mirror, on whose surface is line $ag$; let the center of vision be $b$, and let the point of the thing seen be $d$. Let the <term>catheti</term> <note>From the Greek 'kathetos,' these are lines dropped perfectly perpendicular to a surface.</note> $ad$ and $gb$ be drawn perpendicularly to the surface of the mirror by the 11th proposition of the 11th book. Let line $ag$ be divided at point $h$ so that the ratio of line $ah$ to line $hg$ is the same as the ratio of line $ad$ to line $gb$, according to the 119th theorem of the first book of this work. I say, therefore, that the form of point $d$ will be reflected to the eye $b$ from point $h$ of the mirror.

For let lines $dh$ and $bh$ be drawn. It is clear by the 6th proposition of the 6th book and from the hypothesis that triangle $dha$ is equiangular to triangle $hgb$. For angle $had$ is equal to angle $hgb$, because both are right angles, and the ratio of line $ad$ to line $gb$ is as line $ah$ to line $hg$. Therefore, angle $ahd$ is equal to angle $ghb$. Thus, from the point of the mirror which is $h$, the form of point $d$ will be reflected to the eye $b$ by the 20th theorem of this book, for the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. If, however, point $h$ is blocked by something placed over it, such as wax or pitch or something similar, no image of point $d$ will be seen by the eye positioned in the prescribed manner. This is because it is impossible for reflection to occur from any other point, as established by the preceding theorem; for from any other point, the ratio would vary, and the angles of incidence and reflection would become unequal. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 48. *In plane mirrors, to find the location of the image of a point reflected to the center of sight.*

Let there be a plane mirror, on the surface of which is line $abc$. Let it also be that the form of the point of the seen object, which is $d$, is reflected to the center of sight, which is $e$, from point $b$ of the mirror. Let the line of incidence be drawn, which is $db$, and the line of reflection, which is $be$. I say that it is possible to find the location of the image <term>locum imaginis</term> in which the form of point $d$ is seen. Since, by the 27th theorem of this book, points $d$, $b$, and $e$ are in the same surface, it is clear by the 1st and 2nd propositions of the 11th book [of Euclid] that line $abc$ is in the same surface as lines $db$ and $be$. Therefore, imagine line $abc$ being extended continuously until a perpendicular line $ec$ is produced from point $e$ upon it (by the 12th proposition of the 1st book), and from point $d$ a line $da$ parallel to it (by the 31st proposition of the 1st book). Now, because line $eb$ meets line $ec$ at point $e$, it is clear by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book of this work that it will also meet the extended line $da$. Let the point of intersection be $f$. I say, by the 37th theorem of this book, that point $f$ is the location of the image of the form of point $d$. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 49. *The distance of the location of the image from the surface of a plane mirror below the mirror is the same as the distance of the seen point from that same surface existing above the plane mirror.*
->Euclid, 19th theorem of the Catoptrics; Alhazen, Book 5, note 11.<-

Let the point of the seen object be $a$, and let the center of sight be $b$. Let $cde$ be the common line of the surface of reflection and the surface of the plane mirror. Let $d$ be the point of reflection. From point $d$, let line $df$ be drawn perpendicular to line $cde$ (by the 11th proposition of the 1st book), or over the entire surface of the plane mirror (by the 12th proposition of the 11th book). From point $a$, let a perpendicular be drawn to the surface of the mirror (by the 11th proposition of the 11th book), which shall be $ac$, and let it be extended beyond the mirror. Let the line of incidence be $ad$, and the line of reflection be $bd$. It is clear by the 27th theorem of this book that lines $ad$, $fd$, and $bd$ are in the surface of reflection. Since line $fd$ is parallel to line $ac$ (by the 28th proposition of the 1st book or the 6th proposition of the 11th book), and line $bd$ meets line $fd$ at point $d$, it is clear by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book of this work that line $bd$ if extended will meet line $ac$ if extended. Let them meet at point $g$. I say that line $gc$ is equal to line $ac$. 

Because angle $bde$ is equal to angle $adc$ by the 20th theorem of this book (for they are the angles of incidence and reflection), and angle $bde$ is equal to angle $cdg$ by the 15th proposition of the 1st book (since they are vertically opposite angles), therefore angle $adc$ is equal to angle $cdg$. Since angle $acd$ is equal to angle $dcg$ (for both are right angles), then by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book, angle $cad$ of triangle $cad$ will be equal to angle $cgd$ of triangle $cgd$. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of the 6th book, the sides containing equal angles will be proportional. But side $cd$ is equal to itself; therefore the remaining sides corresponding to the equal angles will be equal to each other, such as $ac$ to $cg$, and $ad$ to $dg$. Since the location of the image is at point $g$ by the 37th theorem of this book, and line $cg$ is equal to $ac$, the proposition is clear. Thus, if a line $cg$ equal to line $ac$ is imagined to be cut off from the perpendicular beyond the surface of the mirror, the location of the image will always be at point $g$, as far distant from the surface of the plane mirror below the mirror as the point of the object being seen—whose form is visible in the mirror—is distant from that same surface above the mirror. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 51. In a plane mirror, when one point is perceived by both eyes, the location of the image will be the same for both sights; from which it is clear that only one image meets both eyes. Alhazen, Book 5, Proposition 15.

Let there be two sights (eyes) *b* and *g*, and let *a* be the point of the thing seen. Let line *q d z e* be a line drawn on the surface of the plane mirror, and let line *ad* be the perpendicular drawn from point *a* to the surface of the mirror. Because, according to the 30th theorem of this book, reflection cannot occur from a single point of the mirror to both eyes, but must occur from at least two points, let those two points be *t* and *z*. Let lines *bt*, *at*, *az*, and *zg* be drawn. 

It is clear from the 25th theorem of this book that lines *bt*, *at*, and *ad* are in the same plane of reflection, which stands perpendicular to the surface of the mirror. Line *dt* is the common section <note>The "common section" is the line where two planes intersect.</note> of the plane of reflection (which is *adtb*) and the surface of the mirror itself. Likewise, line *dz* is the common section of the plane of reflection (which is *adzg*) and the mirror surface, according to the 19th theorem of the 1st book. 

If both lines of reflection, *bt* and *gz*, are in the same plane standing perpendicular to the mirror surface, it is clear that line *tdz* will be a single straight line. This is because the common section of the mirror surface and any plane standing perpendicular to it is a single straight line (by Proposition 3 of Book 11). Then the perpendicular *ad*, which is between those two lines of reflection *tb* and *gz*, will either be in the same plane as them or outside them in another plane. Whichever the case may be, the line of reflection *bt*, when extended, will always cut from the perpendicular *ad* (extended beyond the mirror) a segment equal to *ad* itself, according to the 49th theorem of this book. Let this point be *h*. This is because lines *bt* and *ad* are always in some single plane, as previously stated. 

Similarly, by the 49th theorem, the line *gz* when extended will cut from the extended perpendicular a segment equal to line *ad*; therefore, it will intersect it at the same point *h*. Thus, the image of point *a*—at the same point *h* on the perpendicular—will be perceived by both eyes, and the location of the image will be the same. Therefore, there will be only one image, and it will be seen in one and the same place by both eyes, just as it would be perceived by only one eye.

52. *In plane mirrors, the shape of the thing seen and the arrangement of its parts according to the quantity of length and width are not changed. From this it is clear that the image of any object seen in a plane mirror is equal to the form of the object outside.* Euclid 19th theorem of the *Catoptrics*. Alhazen Book 2, note 6.

Let there be a plane mirror, in which the common section of the surface of that mirror and the surface of reflection is the line *a b*. Let the two endpoints of some object seen be *f* and *l*. Let a cathetus be erected perpendicularly over the surface of the mirror from point *l*, which is *l h*; and from point *f* let there be a cathetus *f z*. Then *z* and *h* will be two points on the surface of reflection by the 27th theorem of this book. Let these be extended below the mirror in such a way that the line *h g* is equal to *l h*, and the line *z d* is equal to *f z*. Let the center of sight also be *e*. Let a <unclear>perpendicular</unclear> <note>original: "p p n p i c u l a r i s"; likely an OCR error for "perpendicularis."</note> cathetus be drawn from point *e* over the mirror, which is *e b*. It is therefore clear from the 28th theorem of this book that the form of point *l* is reflected to the sight *e* from some point of the mirror on line *h b*; and the location of its image, by the 49th theorem of this book, is point *g*, being as far distant from the surface of the mirror beyond the mirror as the point *l* is above the mirror. Similarly, the form of point *f* is reflected to the sight *e* from some point on line *z b*; and the location of the image is point *d*. Having drawn line *f l* and line *d g*, it is clear that because whatever point of line *f l* is reflected to the sight *e*, the location of its image is similarly as far distant from the surface of the mirror beyond the mirror as that point is above the mirror. Therefore, every point of line *f l* is seen to be as far distant below the mirror as that point itself is above the surface of the mirror. If, therefore, line *f l* is straight, line *d g* will be straight; if line *f l* is an arc of a circle, line *d g* will also be an arc of a circle, and always of the same curvature and disposition. Therefore, line *f l* will always appear of the same size and shape as it is outside the mirror. And this is what was proposed. It must be assumed, however, that such a plane mirror is uniformly polished: because if the polish deviates too much in length or width, the form will also deviate according to the same by the 40th theorem of this book; nor will there be a proper order of the form in length and width.

Lines indicate rays from the object points f and l reflecting off the mirror toward an observation point e to the right.</image-desc>

53. *Heights and depths seen in plane mirrors appear reversed when they stand perpendicularly to the surfaces of the mirrors. Euclid 7th theorem of the Catoptrics.*

Let the form of point *a* fall along line *a h* and be reflected along line *h d*; and let the form of point *b* fall along line *b g* and be reflected along line *g d*; and let the form of point *c* fall along line *c f* and be reflected along line *f d*. I say that the height *e a* will appear reversed. For having extended the line *e a*, which is perpendicular over the line *e i*, below the mirror, and having extended all the lines of reflection to 

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram showing the reflection of a vertical height marked with points a, b, c, e. their meeting point where line *a e* is extended beyond point *e*: let line *d h* fall on point *m*, line *d g* on point *l*, and line *d f* on point *k*. It is clear by the previous theorem that line *k e* is equal to line *e c*, *l e* to *e b*, and *m e* is equal to *e a*. Therefore, the points of the height *e a* that are closer to the surface of the mirror existing above will appear closer to the same below the mirror, and points further from the surface of the mirror above will appear further below the mirror. Therefore, the height will appear reversed <note>This "reversal" refers to vertical inversion, where the top of an object (like a person standing by a pond) appears furthest down in the reflection.</note> under the mirror: for what is higher in height will appear lower, because it is seen at a greater distance from the sight; and what is lower in height will appear higher, because it is seen closer to the sight. And the same thing is to be demonstrated if line *a b c* were a line of the depth of some object. Thus the proposition is clear.

Let there be a line $k q a g$: and let the center of sight be point $b$: and let the form of point $d$ fall upon the mirror according to line $d a$, and be reflected according to line $a b$ to the center of sight: and let the form of point $e$ fall according to line $e g$, and be reflected to the sight according to line $g b$: and let the <term>cathetus</term> <note>A line dropped perpendicularly from the object point to the surface of the mirror.</note> $d k$ be drawn perpendicularly, and the line of reflection, which is $b a$, until they meet at point $m$: and let the cathetus $e q$ be drawn perpendicularly, until it meets with line $b g$ at point $l$: and by the 49th theorem of this book, line $d k$ will be equal to line $k m$, and line $e q$ equal to line $q l$. And since the length $d e$ is positioned obliquely to the surface of the mirror, (for indeed point $e$ is farther from the mirror than point $d$) the line $e q$ will be longer than line $d k$: therefore line $q l$ is also longer than line $k m$. Therefore, the point of that oblique magnitude which is farther above the surface of the mirror is likewise seen from a farther distance below the surface of the mirror: and that which is higher and closer to the mirror is also seen to be in a closer place below the mirror. Therefore, such magnitudes are seen just as they are arranged. And this is what was proposed.

### 55. **In plane mirrors, right things appear left, and left things right.** Euclid, Theorem 19 of the *Catoptrics*.

Let the plane mirror be $g s t$: and let the thing seen be $d b$: let the lines of incidence also be $d g$ and $b s$: and let the center of sight be $p$: let the lines of reflection also be $p g$ and $p s$: and let it be that the line of reflection, which is $p g$, meets with the cathetus of incidence, which is $d h$, at point $f$: and let the line of reflection, which is $p s$, meet with the cathetus $b t$ at point $e$: and let the line $f e$ be produced, which, by the 52nd theorem of this book, is the image of the thing seen, $d b$: therefore right things will appear left, and left things right. For since, by the 33rd theorem of this book, reflection always occurs at an angle greater than the angle of incidence <note>This refers to the internal angle formed with the surface or the relative geometry described in Witelo's specific proofs.</note>, and thus toward the part opposite to the part of incidence: it is clear that the right side of the thing seen will always be seen under the line of reflection that is further to the left, and the left side under the line of reflection that is further to the right: for that line of reflection, which is more to the right, will fall upon the right part of the image, and the left will fall upon the left. Thus, the right of the object appears under the left of the image, and vice versa: since the image of the thing is seen to relate to the object just as a man standing with his face upright toward another person: for then the left part is opposed to the right, and the right to the left: because whenever one man is opposed to another, their relative positions are contrary to each other: for at the same difference of position, the right of one is the left of the other, and vice versa: and thus what is the right of the thing seen becomes the left of its image: and what is the left of the thing seen will be the right in the image according to the sight. The proposition is therefore clear.

Incident rays from d and b hit the mirror and reflect toward the eye at point p. Perpendicular lines from the object points d and b extend behind the mirror to points f and e, respectively, forming the inverted image f-e. Other labels include h, c, and n.</image-desc>

### 56. **It is possible for a plane mirror to be so positioned that a viewer, without seeing their own image, may see the image of another thing that is not seen.** Ptolemy, Chapter 9 of the 2nd book of the *Catoptrics*.

Let $a b$ be a piece of wood fixed perpendicularly to the horizon, or to a surface equidistant to it, or however else arranged, which is $b g$: and let there be a plane mirror, in which is the line $d b$: and let it be square. And because the wood $a b$ is erected perpendicularly over the surface $g b$, let the line $g b$ be drawn as it happens: it is therefore clear that angle $a b g$ is a right angle: therefore let that right angle be divided into three equal parts by the 28th theorem of the 1st book <note>Witelo refers to Euclid's Elements, Book I, for many of these basic geometric constructions.</note>: and let the mirror $d b$ be inclined from the wood $a b$ in such a way that the angle $d b a$ is one-third of a right angle, which is $a b g$: therefore the angle $d b g$ will be two-thirds of a right angle. In this consists the excellence of the mechanical operation and the more useful effect: however, whatever other part of the right angle is cut off, the demonstration reaches the same result, as is clear. Let, therefore, the angle $a d b$ be one-third of a right angle: and let the line of the mirror, which is $b d$, be extended beyond point $d$ continuously and straight as far as a point, which is $e$. And since line $g b$ is perpendicular to line $a b$, while it also contains an acute angle with the line of the mirror, which is $d b$: then from point $g$, which is on a surface orthogonally erected over the surface of the mirror, let a perpendicular line be drawn over the line $b e$ by Prop. 12 of Book 1, which is $g e$: therefore angle $b e g$ will be a right angle. Let the location of the sight itself be point $g$, from which the line $g d$ is drawn to point $d$: also from point $d$, let a line be produced falling upon line $b g$, which meets at point $z$, so that angle $z d g$ is equal to angle $e g d$ established upon the end of line $g d$ by Prop. 23 of Book 1: therefore line $z d$ will be parallel to line $g e$ by Prop. 27 of Book 1: therefore by Prop. 8 of Book 1: line $z d$ will be erected perpendicularly over the surface of the mirror, and perpendicular over the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror, which is $b d$: therefore angle $z d b$ is a right angle equal to angle $g e d$ from the premises, and also by Prop. 29 of Book 1. Also from point $z$, let line $z h$ be drawn perpendicular over the surface $g b$ by Prop. 11 of Book 11: and upon point $d$, the end of line $z d$, let there be established...
