### VITELLIO'S OPTICS

Let an angle equal to angle $gdz$ be constructed, which shall be angle $zdi$. And since by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book of this work <note>original: "p 2 th. 1 huius"</note> line $di$ will intersect with line $zh$: because line $di$ produced beyond point $d$ will intersect with line $ab$, as is clear from the previous statements and by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work: let the intersection of lines $di$ and $zh$ therefore be at point $i$. From point $i$, let a line be drawn parallel to line $bd$ by [Euclid's Elements] Book 1, Proposition 31, which shall be line $it$. From point $b$, let a perpendicular be drawn above the surface of the mirror by [Euclid's Elements] Book 11, Proposition 12, which shall be $bq$. By Book 1, Proposition 28, line $bq$ will be parallel to line $ge$. Therefore, by Book 11, Proposition 8, line $bq$, just like line $ge$, is erected perpendicularly above the surface of the mirror, which is $db$. Above point $b$ at the end of line $qb$, let an angle be constructed equal to angle $gbq$, which shall be $qbt$. Therefore, line $bt$ will intersect with the line drawn parallel to line $db$ from point $i$, which is line $it$, by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book of this work. Let the intersection be point $t$, and let the board <note>original: "tabula"; here meaning a painted panel or flat surface</note> $it$ be completed.

Accordingly, let whatever image is desired be painted on the board in which line $it$ is located. Let the board of the painted image be placed in the location of line $it$, with the middle of the board's line corresponding to line $zi$. Let the surface $gb$ be perforated along the line $zb$, so that the form of the painting can reach the mirror $db$. 

Thus, when the center of sight is at point $g$, the person looking will see the form of the image painted on board $it$, but they will not see their own proper image. This is the demonstration of that fact: Since angle $geb$ is a right angle, it is clear by Book 1, Proposition 16 that angle $gdb$ is obtuse. Similarly, for all points of the form or of the face itself falling upon the mirror $db$, the angles are obtuse by the same Proposition 16. Since the angles of incidence are always equal to the angles of reflection by the 20th theorem of this book <note>The fundamental law of reflection</note>, it is clear by Book 1, Proposition 13 that there will never be a reflection of the form of the viewer themselves to the center of sight, but always to points that are below the sight, as is clear by the 33rd theorem of this book. Therefore, a person whose center of sight exists at point $g$ will never see their own image in a plane mirror arranged in such a position.

And if the sight is moved further from the mirror at any point beyond point $g$, such as to point $f$, it is clear that angle $feb$ is greater than a right angle. Moreover, angle $fdb$ is greater than angle $feb$ by Book 1, Proposition 16. Therefore, reflection will never occur to point $f$, but always to another point below the line. Similarly, if the sight approaches the mirror at any point on line $gz$, except for point $z$ itself, the viewer will never see the image of themselves. For only the perpendicular, which is line $zd$, as is clear from the previous statements, is reflected back upon itself by the 21st theorem of this book. Thus, with the center of sight positioned at point $z$, the person looking will see the form of their own eye reflected by a plane mirror so disposed, but not any other part of the face, because only the perpendicular, which is a single line, is reflected back upon itself; and thus the reflection of only that point occurs, and not of other points.

If, therefore, the sight approaches the mirror from point $g$ toward point $k$, falling between points $g$ and $z$: if a line $kd$ is drawn from point $k$ to point $d$: it is clear by the 14th theorem of Book 1 and from the previous statements that lines $dk$ and $eg$ will intersect beyond line $gk$. For only line $dz$ is parallel to line $eg$. Angle $ged$ is a right angle, and angle $zdb$ is a right angle; therefore angle $kdb$ is obtuse. Reflection will therefore occur to another point below point $k$. However, from point $z$, as was said before, reflection will occur back to point $z$ itself, because line $zd$ is parallel to line $ge$ and is perpendicular to line $db$ by Book 1, Proposition 29, and by the hypothesis. Similarly, with the sight placed at any point on line $zb$ (since a perpendicular can be drawn from any of those points to the surface of the mirror, or to line $db$), any of those lines is reflected back upon itself by the 21st theorem of this book. Thus it is clear that with the sight positioned on line $gz$, the person looking will not see the image of themselves, because, as was said, only the perpendicular at a single point is reflected to the sight, and not other points of the form.

But because angle $idz$ is equal to angle $zdg$, and line $zd$ is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror $db$, therefore by the 20th theorem of this book, the form of point $i$ is reflected from point $d$ of the mirror to the sight existing at point $g$. And because angle $tbq$ is equal to angle $gbq$, as is clear from the previous statements, and line $bq$ is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, it is clear by the 20th theorem of this book that the form of point $t$ is reflected from point $b$ of the mirror to the sight at point $g$. Therefore, by the 34th theorem of this book, the form of the entire line $it$ is reflected from mirror $db$ to the sight at point $g$.

The painted board $it$ itself will not be seen [directly], because it is below the surface upon which the mirror and the sight stand. It is possible here that a wall be built upon the ground along the length of line $zb$ to the height of the viewers, which is made concave on the inside and open at the top toward the mirror. In that wall, the painted board, which is $it$, may be placed parallel to the mirror $bd$. Let the sight be at a distance from the mirror according to the position of point $g$, and let it be prevented by some means from being able to approach closer. Then all the forms of the points of the painted image will fall upon the sight. Let it therefore be so arranged by ingenuity <note>original: "p ingeniū" (per ingenium)</note> that the painted board is in no way seen directly. Let the mirror be positioned toward the light so that the air around it is luminous, and let the painted board likewise have light; for otherwise, lying hidden in shadows, it could not be seen. For by means of light, it multiplies its form through the medium, reaches the mirror, and is reflected to the sight. Thus the proposition is clear.

57. It is possible for a single flat mirror to be positioned in its own room in such a way that those things occurring in another house, or in the streets and squares, may be seen within it.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled with points a, b, g, d, e, h, and f, illustrating the optical paths and reflection angles within a rectangular space representing a room (camera).</image-desc>

<margin>
6

Let there be a certain place in the observer's room where, when the eye is positioned there, it is desired to see through a flat mirror everything that is happening elsewhere. Let this place in the room, where the center of vision is located, be marked by point **a**. Let the place where there is a desire to see what is happening be marked by point **b**. Let there be a chink or a window in the observer's room opposite place **b**, which shall be **g**. Let line **bg** be drawn and extended continuously and straight inside the room to some point, which shall be **d**. All of this can be accomplished using an **astrolabe** <note>A multi-purpose astronomical instrument used here for sighting and measuring angles.</note> or a **quadrant**, or another instrument for the **verification of sightlines** <term>instrumentum certificationis visuum</term> <note>original: "instrumentum certificationis uifuum"; likely a sighting tube or surveying tool to ensure the line of sight is perfectly straight.</note>. Indeed, once point **b** has been sighted, let the sight be rotated while the instrument remains fixed, so that the sight falls through the same unmoved **sighting-vanes** <note>original: "pinnulas"; the small plates with holes used to align an instrument's aim.</note> onto point **d** in the room.

Therefore, let lines **da** and **ga** be drawn. Let line **ga** be divided at point **e** according to the 119th theorem of the 1st book of this work, so that the ratio of line **ae** to line **eg** is the same as the ratio of line **ad** to line **dg**. Both of these ratios are known through the measurements taken by the instrument. Let line **ed** be drawn; therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 3 [of Euclid's *Elements*], line **de** will bisect angle **adg** into equal parts. Now, let a mirror be placed standing perpendicularly above line **de** at point **d**, according to the converse of Book 1, Proposition 11. Let the line of this mirror be **fh**. Thus, from point **d** on the mirror, the form of point **g** is reflected to the eye at **a**, according to the 20th theorem of this book. Consequently, the form of point **b** is also reflected by the same logic, for distance along the same line does not change the nature of reflection. Therefore, the eye, existing at its center at point **a** in the room, will see everything that exists and everything that is done in place **b**, whether it be another house, a street, or a square. And this is what was proposed.

58. It is possible for a mirror composed of several flat mirrors to be constructed, in which several images of the observer alone are seen in the manner of **dances** <note>original: "chorearum"; referring to a circle of dancers (a ring dance or carole) where the viewer sees multiple versions of themselves surrounding them.</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an arc divided into segments labeled a, b, g, d, e, z. Lines radiate from a central point h to these segments, and another set of parallel lines labeled i, k, l, m, n, x is positioned above the arc to represent mirrors and their reflections.</image-desc>

Let an arc of a circle **az** be taken, the center of which is **h**. Since the arc **az** is taken as indefinite, let it be divided (for the sake of example) into five equal parts, or as many as one wishes, so that arc **ab** is equal to arcs **bg**, **gd**, **de**, and **ez**. Let the chords **ab**, **bg**, **gd**, **de**, and **ez** be drawn, all of which will be equal by Book 3, Proposition 29 [of Euclid's *Elements*]. From the center **h**, let lines **ha**, **hb**, **hg**, **hd**, **he**, and **hz** be drawn. Once the arcs above the chords **ab**, **bg**, and the others are removed, let flat, quadrangular, parallelogram mirrors be erected so that their sides **ai**, **bk**, **gl**, **dm**, **en**, and **zx** are parallel to each other. Let the mirrors be continuous with one another in such a way that their sides **bk**, **gl**, **dm**, and **en** are shared. Furthermore, let the mirrors be joined together so that the angles contained by lines **ai** and **ik**, **bk** and **kl**, **gl** and **lm**, **dm** and **mn**, and **en** and **nx** are equal to the angles contained by lines **ha** and **ab**, **hb** and **bg**, **hg** and **gd**, **hd** and **de**, and **ez**.

Let the surfaces standing on lines **ab**, **bg**, **gd**, **de**, and **ez** be turned downward, and placed below the other surfaces raised above, in which are the lines **ik**, **kl**, **lm**, **mn**, and **nx**. Let these upper surfaces be parallel to the lower ones. All these mirrors, arranged in this way, will have a uniform appearance to the eye located at center **h**. Since lines **ha**, **hb**, **hg**, **hd**, **he**, and **hz** are drawn from the center **h** to points common to the chords and arcs, it is clear by Book 3, Proposition 18 [of Euclid's *Elements*] that all are perpendicular to the lines touching the circle **az** at those points. Therefore, by the 21st theorem of this book, all those lines are reflected back upon themselves. The distinction of images will therefore follow those lines.

Furthermore, the perpendiculars <term>catheti</term> <note>The "cathetus" is a technical term in optics for the line drawn from a point of an object perpendicular to the reflecting surface.</note> drawn from point **h** to the surfaces of the flat mirrors are equal in number to the surfaces of the mirrors, according to the 20th theorem of the 1st book of this work. Around all of these, there is a uniform reflection to the eye. Therefore, the images will be numbered according to the number of mirrors, and the locations of the images will be numbered by that same count. This is because the perpendiculars produced from point **h** do not meet beyond the mirrors, since they all converge at point **h**. The location of each image is at the intersection of the **perpendicular** <gloss>catheti</gloss> and the line of reflection, by the 37th theorem of this book.

And since these mirrors uniformly face the eye at point **h**, it is clear that for the same reason a reflection occurs from one of them to the eye, a reflection occurs from any of the others. Thus, the lines of reflection are numbered according to the number of perpendiculars. Consequently, many images will be seen, arranged with one another in the number and order of the mirrors. Because the mirrors face the eye as their center, in the manner of a circular arc, the images of the observer will face the observer in the manner of **dances** <note>original: "chorearum"; a circle of reflections.</note>. This is what was proposed. Through this mirror, by varying the position, many arrangements of images can be elicited; we believe this should be left to the skill of the experimenter—for instance, if mirror **ab** is positioned according to the base **ai** parallel to the surface of the horizon, or varied in other different ways as one pleases.

**61.** *It is possible for the image of the same point to be seen through however many plane mirrors one wishes, arranged relative to one another according to the layout of an equilateral and equiangular polygon.* Euclid, Theorem 14 of the *Catoptrics*; Ptolemy, Theorem 8 of Book 2 of the *Catoptrics*.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating reflection in a series of plane mirrors arranged as the sides of a polygon. A pentagon is inscribed within a circle. The center of the circle is marked 'c'. Vertices are labeled 'a', 'e', 'd', 'g', 'b'. Lines represent visual paths or rays reflecting between the vertices. Point 'a' represents the center of vision, and 'b' represents the object being viewed. Additional perpendicular lines and points 'f', 'h', and 's' represent mirror orientations and further reflection points.</image-desc>

Let the center of vision be point **a**: and let the point of the object seen be **b**: and let line **ab** be drawn: and according to the quantity of line **ab**, let an equilateral and equiangular polygon <note>A regular polygon, such as a regular pentagon or hexagon.</note> be described, with as many sides as it seems fit to arrange. Let there be now, for the sake of example, a pentagonal polygon **aedgb**: let a circle be circumscribed around it by Proposition 14 of Book 4 [of Euclid]: and let lines be drawn to the center of the circle, which is **c**, from the angles of the polygon, which are **ac**, **ec**, **dc**, **gc**, **bc**: it is clear, therefore, that all those lines are equal by the definition of a circle: therefore all angles at the bases are equal by Propositions 5 and 8 of Book 1: and at the meeting of any of the said sides let a plane mirror be placed, except at points **a** and **b**, such as at points **e**, **d**, **g**: or if it were a polygon of more sides, let more be placed: and let them all be erected orthogonally <note>At a 90-degree right angle.</note> upon the lines drawn to the center of the circle, as are these lines **de** and **ge**: which is done by Proposition 11 of Book 11: so that mirror **fh** stands perpendicularly upon line **gc**: let the point of the object seen be at one angle, and let the center of vision be at another angle very near to it, as are here points **a** and **b**. Therefore, because angle **cgf** is equal to angle **hgc**, because both are right angles by Proposition 18 of Book 3: but also angle **cgb** is equal to angle **cgd**, as is clear by the premise and by Proposition 8 of Book 1: therefore angle **bgf** is equal to angle **dgh**. Therefore the form of point **b** is reflected from point **g** of mirror **fh** to point **f** of the nearest mirror, which is at point **d**: for all reflection occurs through equal angles, as is clear by Theorem 20 of this book. And since all those angles are equal to each other, similar to the two preceding angles: it is clear that reflection occurs from point **d** to point **e**, and from point **e** to point **a**, which is the center of vision. Thus the sight existing at point **a**, and looking only at the mirror of which point **e** is a part, will see form **b** (which would not be reflected immediately to itself from point **e** of the mirror) reflected by means of mirrors **g** and **d**. This is what was proposed. But if the center of vision were at point **c**, which is the center of the circle whose periphery all the mirrors placed at the angles of the polygons touch: it is clear that the form of point **c** is reflected from all points back into itself: since all the lines, which are **ca**, **cb**, **cg**, **cd**, **ce** are perpendicular upon the surfaces of the mirrors: they are therefore reflected into themselves back to point **c** by Theorem 21 of this book. Therefore the proposition is clear. And if many mirrors are arranged in this way, the same demonstration and the same method of circumscribing a circle to another polygon applies as it did to the pentagon. Therefore, through these two theorems it is clear that the image of a thing that is not [directly] seen can be seen in a mirror: as if the thing is so placed in relation to the first mirror that the sight cannot reach it directly: this, however, easily occurs to one who thinks about it.

Therefore the form of point **b** will be seen by the sight existing at point **a**, even though the object in which point **b** exists is not visible by itself. And so, universally, no matter how many even or odd mirrors are placed, according to this, the arrangement of images varies according to right and left. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Nor do we think these things require any demonstration other than those which have been set forth previously regarding simple plane mirrors; and we consider that these matters should be entrusted to the practice of craftsmen. For even these things which we have set forth regard the suitability of mechanical work more than the firmness of demonstration; for this was a diligent invention of the ancients, to which he who has diligently examined the things we have written by the necessity of demonstration in this book can add or take away.

65. *It is impossible to kindle fire with a single plane mirror held opposite the sun; however, it is possible with many.*

This is evident because fire is only kindled through the gathering of many rays. However, the lines of reflection produced from different points of plane mirrors do not converge, as was demonstrated in Theorem 47 of this book. Therefore, those reflected rays do not meet at any single point to generate fire in any combustible material. Thus, the first part of the proposition is clear. Now, however, Anthemius <note>Anthemius of Tralles (c. 474 – c. 534 AD) was a famous Greek geometer and architect of the Hagia Sophia, known for his work on "burning mirrors."</note> stated, led by I know not what experience, that a mere twenty-four reflected rays meeting in a single point of flammable material would ignite a fire in it. He joined seven hexagonal plane mirrors in a stable, fixed arrangement—specifically, six outer ones around one placed in the middle. These mirrors were joined at every angle of the hexagon; this was done because hexagonal shapes fill a flat surface perfectly, as three angles of a hexagon are equal to four right angles <note>In geometry, a regular hexagon has interior angles of 120 degrees. Three of these meet to form 360 degrees, or four 90-degree right angles, allowing them to tile a floor without gaps.</note>. And Anthemius said that fire could be kindled in this way at any distance. But if he joined them to complete a single flat surface, he could not achieve his goal any differently than with a single plane mirror, as can be seen from what was said before. This is because, as stated, three hexagonal surfaces fill a single point; since any angle of a hexagon is worth two-thirds of two right angles <note>original: "duas tertias duorum rectorum," i.e., 2/3 of 180 degrees = 120 degrees.</note>, and three angles of a hexagon are worth four right angles, three such angles meeting leave no vacuum. There is, therefore, nothing that distinguishes the point of their meeting from the nature of a single flat surface. But if those same hexagons are inclined toward each other in such a way that they can be enclosed within a sphere, then all the rays falling perpendicularly onto those surfaces from a single point will reflect toward the center of that sphere, and the strength of the heat will be increased. Thus, such a mirror could be better composed of triangles <note>original: "trigonis."</note> than hexagons, because the rays would be as numerous as the surfaces, and the power of the heat would increase. These things, however, because they are easy, we have not thought to pursue further, leaving them to the industrious soul of the craftsman.

# THE OPTICS OF WITELO, SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND POLES, BOOK SIX.

<image-desc>An ornamental historiated woodcut initial 'L' depicting a seated male figure, likely a scholar or author, holding a book or object within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>

*Having run through the properties <note>original: "passiones," literally "passions" or "undergoings," here meaning the mathematical properties or physical effects.</note> of plane mirrors as broadly as we could, it now remains for us to turn to the specific properties of other mirrors. And because convex mirrors are simpler than concave ones—since some of the properties of convex mirrors descend into the concave ones, as in those whose properties vary in many different ways—it is appropriate that we first place the treatise on convex mirrors before the others. But among convex mirrors (some of which are spherical, some columnar <note>i.e., cylindrical.</note>, and some pyramidal), the spherical mirrors are simpler than the others. Indeed, the properties and causes of reflections of convex spherical mirrors descend into columnar and pyramidal convex mirrors when reflection happens to occur from some points of their circles, just as the properties of plane mirrors descend into the same columnar and pyramidal mirrors when a reflection to the eye occurs from any point along one of the lines of their length. Therefore, after the treatise on plane mirrors, it seemed worthy to proceed with convex spherical mirrors, as they are simpler than all the others and the concave mirrors. These, then, are the principles we set forth to pursue the specific properties of spherical mirrors:*

->DEFINITIONS.<-

1. We call a convex or concave spherical mirror "larger" if the diameter of its sphere is larger, and "smaller" if it is smaller. 2. We call the diameter of the spherical mirror the diameter of the sphere of which the mirror is a portion. 3. We call the center of the mirror the center of the sphere of which the mirror is a portion. 4. We call the "visual diameter" the line passing from the center of the eye through the center of the spherical mirror; this is also called the <term>cathetus of reflection</term><note>A "cathetus" is a line perpendicular to a surface. In this context, it is the normal line used to calculate angles of incidence and reflection.</note>. 5. We say a straight line is "parallel" to a convex spherical mirror when it is parallel to a line tangent to the midpoint of an arc of a great circle of that mirror. 6. The "end of contingency" is called the point where one of the perpendiculars <note>original: "cathetorum."</note> cuts the line tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection. 7. We call the "limit of image locations" <note>original: "metam locorum imaginum."</note> the point or line beyond which images are no longer seen.

# THEOREMS

> 1. *It is necessary that the intersection of the surface of reflection and the surface of a convex spherical mirror be a great circle <note>A "great circle" is a circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same diameter as the sphere itself, like the equator on a globe, dividing it into two equal halves.</note> or an arc of a great circle of that sphere; from which it is clear that every surface of reflection divides the sphere of the mirror into two equal halves.*

As is clear from the beginning of Book 5, Definition 7, the "surface of reflection" is defined as the plane containing the line of incidence, the line of reflection, and the perpendicular line drawn from the point of contact to the surface of the spherical mirror. Since all these are straight lines, it is clear that the surface of reflection is a flat plane. Every convex spherical mirror is either a whole sphere or part of a sphere, as shown in Theorem 8 of Book 5. Therefore, by Theorem 69 of Book 1, if the surface of reflection cuts the mirror, their common intersection is a great circle, an arc of a circle, or part of a circle. And since perpendiculars to the tangent surfaces of spheres necessarily pass through the center of the sphere—as can be shown by Theorem 72 of Book 1 and by the definition of a line perpendicular to a spherical surface at the beginning of this book—it is clear that every surface of reflection passes through the center of the mirror. Thus, that intersection is a great circle or an arc of a great circle of that mirror's sphere by the definition of a great circle. This is what was proposed. The corollary is also clear: because every surface of reflection passes through the center of the mirror, it obviously divides the sphere of the mirror into equal halves. And this was the second point to be shown.

> 2. *A tangent line drawn from the center of vision to the surface of a convex spherical mirror, when moved uniformly around a fixed visual diameter, determines a portion of the mirror's surface from whose points the reflection of forms to the eye will occur. Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 25.*

Let the center of vision be point **a**, and let the intersection of the surface of reflection and the surface of the convex spherical mirror be the circle **b c d k**, whose center is **e**. From point **a**, by Proposition 17 of Book 3 <note>Vitello refers here to Euclid’s *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of the time.</note>, let a tangent line **a d** be drawn to the circle at point **d**. Let the visual diameter be **a e**, which cuts the circumference of circle **b c d** at point **c**. I say that if the diameter **a e** remains fixed while the tangent line **a d** is imagined to move uniformly around the circumference of the mirror—always maintaining the same angle **e a d** until it returns to where it started—that by its motion relative to point **d**, it will describe a circle. This circle defines the portion of the convex spherical mirror from which the reflection of all forms to the eye (located at point **a**) occurs, separating it from the other part of the mirror's surface from which no reflection happens. Let line **a d** be extended beyond the point of contact **d** to point **f**, and let line **e d** be drawn and extended beyond the mirror through point **d** to point **g**.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrates a convex spherical mirror as a circle with center 'e' and surface points 'b', 'c', 'd', 'k'. Above the circle is the center of vision, point 'a'. A vertical line 'ae' (the visual diameter) connects the viewpoint to the center, passing through point 'c' on the mirror's surface. Two lines, 'ad' and 'ak', originate from point 'a' and are tangent to the circle at points 'd' and 'k'. The tangent 'ad' is extended further down to point 'f'. A normal line from the center 'e' through point 'd' is extended outwards to point 'g'. An additional line 'ah' is drawn from the viewpoint to a point 'h' on the mirror's lower arc, passing through points 'm' and 'l' on the aforementioned extended lines to provide a proof by contradiction.</image-desc>

Therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 3 [of Euclid], all angles at point **d** will be right angles. Thus, all points located on line **d f** will be seen directly, because line **a f**, remaining as one, is not reflected from point **d**. However, because this same line touches the mirror, points on line **d f** begin to participate somewhat in the nature of reflection; hence they will be seen reflected from point **d** along line **d a** to the eye at **a**, according to Theorem 20 of Book 5, since the angle of incidence (**f d g**) is equal to the angle of reflection (**g d a**). I also say that no reflection to the eye **a** can occur from any point on the arc **d k b**. If this were possible, let it be that from point **h** on arc **d k b**, some point is reflected to the eye at point **a**. Let the line of reflection to the eye be **h a**. This line cannot pass through the solid body of the mirror (that is, by cutting through arc **b c d**), so it must pass outside the circle. Since the "angle of contact" <note>The infinitesimal angle between a curve and its tangent line.</note> **h d f** is indivisible by Proposition 16 of Book 3 [of Euclid], it is clear that the line of reflection **h a** will not pass through point **d**. It must therefore cut line **d g**; let it cut it at point **l**. And because the line of reflection **h a** does not cut the angle **h d f**, it is evident that since it does not cut arc **h d**, it must cut line **d f**; let it cut it at point **m**. If the line **h m** then reaches point **a** from point **m**, it is clear that two straight lines (**m l a** and **m d a**) would enclose a surface, which is impossible <note>A fundamental axiom of Euclidean geometry is that two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>. Or it may be deduced thus: in triangle **d l m**, angle **m d l** is a right angle; therefore, angle **d l m** is acute by Proposition 32 of Book 1; therefore, by Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle **a l d** is obtuse. But angle **a d l** is a right angle, because angle **a d e** is a right angle. Therefore, by Theorem 14 of Book 1, since line **e g** falls upon both lines **a d** and **h a** and creates angles arranged in the aforementioned way, it is clear that lines **h l a** and **a d** will meet on the side where the angles are smaller. Thus, no form will be reflected from point **h** to point **a**, which contradicts what was given. The proposition is therefore clear, since the same deduction can be made for any given point on arc **d k b**.

### 3. *When a convex spherical mirror is placed before the sight, such that the sight is not on the surface of that mirror or on a surface continuous with it: the common intersection of the base of the cone of vision and the surface of the mirror will be a circle smaller than the great circle that divides the sphere of the mirror into equal halves.*

<margin>Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 24.</margin>
When a spherical mirror is placed before the sight such that the eye is not touching the surface or any surface connected to it: I say that the part of the mirror perceived by the sight will be a part of the sphere enclosed by a circle, which is formed by the movement of the tangent ray as it touches the sphere's surface. Because, as is clear from Theorem 16 of Book 2 of this work, the longest ray reaching the surface of the sphere acts like a tangent line touching the mirror. If one imagines that ray moving in a circle while maintaining contact with the sphere until it returns to the first point from which it began its motion, it is evident from the previous theorem that the point of contact on the sphere's surface will describe a circle. This circle will be a "minor circle" <note>In geometry, a "minor circle" is any circle on a sphere that does not pass through the sphere's center, meaning it does not divide the sphere into two equal halves.</note> compared to the "great circle" of that sphere. For if we imagine planes intersecting through the diameter of the sphere and passing through the poles of the aforementioned circle—dividing the sphere into equal parts—it is clear that all those circles have tangent lines that form the edges of the cone of vision. Therefore, by Theorem 58 of Book 1 of this work, any of the arcs lying between the sphere's surface and these flat planes cutting the sphere will be smaller than a semicircle of a great circle.

For example, by Theorem 69 of Book 1, let there be a circle which is the common intersection of the sphere's surface and a flat plane passing through the eye **a** (located outside the sphere) and through the center of the sphere, which we call **b**. Let this be circle **csd**, with its center at **b**. Let the "pole" <note>The "pole" here refers to the central point on the sphere's surface directly in front of the observer.</note> of the imagined circle, where the base of the cone of vision cuts the mirror's surface, be point **s**. Let the radius **bs** be extended to the eye **a**, forming line **bsa**. From point **a** (the center of vision), let a tangent line **ac** be drawn to the circle, and from the point of contact **c**, let line **cb** be drawn to the center **b**. I say that the arc **cs** is less than a quarter of a great circle. For the angle **bca** is a right angle <note>original: "rectus"</note> by Book 3, Proposition 18 [of Euclid’s *Elements*]; therefore, angle **cba** must be acute, because there cannot be two right angles in the same triangle **abc** by Book 1, Proposition 32. Since arc **cs** corresponds to this angle at the center, it is clear by Book 6, Proposition 33 that the arc itself is less than a quarter of the circle. And because the same is true for all points of the imagined circles, it is manifest that any of the arcs of those circles is smaller than a quarter of a great circle. Therefore, the circle bounding the vision is smaller than the great circle of the proposed sphere. This is what was proposed. This demonstration holds for a single eye, or for both eyes, provided that the diameter of the spherical mirror is larger than the distance between the eyes; for if they were equal, the great circle of the sphere would be the circle of the intersection, and exactly half the sphere would be seen. If, however, the distance between the eyes were larger than the mirror's diameter, more than half the sphere would be seen, and the intersection would be a minor circle, as demonstrated in Book 4 of this work.

->[Image: A geometrical diagram showing a sphere with center 'b' and an observer at point 'a'. Tangent lines 'ac' and 'ae' touch the sphere, and a horizontal chord 'ce' marks the boundary of the visible area.]<-

### 4. *In convex spherical mirrors, as the sight moves closer to the mirror, the size of the circles bounding the vision decreases; as the sight moves away, it increases.*

Let there be a convex spherical mirror with center **b**, and let the center of vision be **a**. Let the circle bounding the vision on the mirror's surface be **eghe**. I say that as the sight moves closer to or further from the mirror, the size of those circles changes: it decreases as one moves closer and increases as one moves away. For let the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror be circle **cdef**, whose arc **cde** stands upright over circle **eghe** (which contains the visible part of the mirror). Let the midpoint of arc **cde** be point **d**, and let lines **ac**, **adb**, **cb**, and **ae** be drawn. By Book 3, Proposition 18, angle **acb** will be a right angle. Now, let the sight move closer along line **ab** to point **k**. If the vision were still bounded by the same circle **eghe** as before, line **kc** would be drawn. And since, by Theorem 16 of Book 2, the longest ray from the sight to the sphere is like a tangent line, it is clear by Book 3, Proposition 18 that angle **kcb** is a right angle. But angle **acb** was also a right angle. Thus, a smaller right angle would be equal to a larger right angle, which is impossible. Therefore, when the sight is at point **k**, the vision will not be bounded by circle **eghe**, but by some circle smaller than **eghe**. Since from point **k** two other lines are drawn touching the same circle between the two tangent lines **ac** and **ae** drawn from point **a**, it is clear by Theorem 60 of Book 1 that the points of contact for the inner lines will fall inside the points of contact for the outer lines. Therefore, the lines that are closer will encompass a smaller arc of the circle than those further away. Thus, the proposition is clear.

->[Image: A diagram illustrating two points of vision, 'a' and 'k', on a single axis pointing toward a sphere. Tangent lines from the closer point 'k' hit the sphere at points 'g' and 'h', while tangents from the further point 'a' hit at 'c' and 'e', showing the larger area visible from further away.]<-

# WITELO’S OPTICS

### 5. *From any point on the surface of a convex spherical mirror opposite the eye, reflection can occur to the eye. Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 25.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circular section representing a spherical mirror. Point b is the center. Various lines represent light paths and normals. Labeled points include a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, k, m, r, s. A tangent line h-k touches the circle at point d. Lines from points a and e (outside the circle) meet at point d on the circle's surface.</image-desc>

Let the arrangement be the same as in the 3rd proposition of this book: I say that from any point of the part of the mirror opposite the eye, such as from any point on arc *cs* and all arcs similar to it, reflection can occur to the eye. For let any point on arc *cs* be marked as *d*, and let the radius *db* be drawn. It is clear by Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work that the line *db* is perpendicular to the flat surface <note>The tangent plane.</note> touching the mirror at point *d*. Therefore, when the "form" <note>The "form" (forma) refers to the visual species or light ray emanating from an object.</note> of a point of the visible object falls upon point *d*, it is clear by Theorem 27 of Book 5 of this work that the line of reflection will be in the same plane as the radius *db* and the perpendicular line *ab* <term>cathetus</term> <note>A cathetus is a line falling perpendicularly onto a surface; here, it is the line from the eye to the center of the mirror.</note> falling orthogonally upon the surface of the mirror, because it passes through its center *b*. 

And let a line touching the circle *cds* be drawn through point *d* by [Euclid's Elements] Book 3, Proposition 17, which shall be line *hdk*. Therefore, by Book 3, Proposition 18, the angle *bdk* will be a right angle; thus, the angle *adb* of the triangle *dba* will be obtuse. If, therefore, line *bd* is extended outside the sphere to point *f*, the angle *fda* will be acute by Book 1, Proposition 13; this is because angle *bda* is obtuse, as is clear from what was previously stated by Book 1, Proposition 13. This is also clear because, since line *ad* falls within the line *ac* which touches the mirror, it is evident by Theorem 57 of Book 1 that the extended line *ad* will cut the sphere of the mirror. Furthermore, the surface touching the sphere at point *d*, in which the lines *hk* and *dg* lie, will be more slanted than line *ad*, and it will intersect line *ab*. 

And because the radius *bd* is perpendicular to the surface *hkdg* touching the mirror at point *d*, the angles *fdk* and *fdh* will be right angles. Consequently, angle *bdk* will also be a right angle, angle *bda* will be greater than a right angle, and angle *fda* will be less than a right angle. Therefore, if an acute angle equal to angle *fda* is cut away from the right angle *fdh* by Theorem 27 of Book 1, let it be *mdf*; the lines containing these angles will be in the same plane. Therefore, a point of the visible object existing on line *md*, falling upon the surface of the mirror at point *d*, will be reflected to the eye through line *da* by Theorem 11 or 20 of Book 5; for the lines *md* and *ad* contain equal angles with the perpendicular *bf*. These lines of incidence and reflection, as was shown by Theorem 25 of Book 5, will be in the same plane, which will be the plane of reflection standing perpendicular to the surface touching the sphere of the mirror at point *d*. 

The same can be demonstrated in the same way for any point on arc *cs*, and for any arc similar to it—that is, for the entire portion of the mirror opposite the eye—since it can be demonstrated in the same way for any given point. It is therefore clear that from any point of the surface of a convex spherical mirror opposite the eye, reflection can occur to the eye, just as was proposed.

### 6. *In every plane of reflection from convex spherical mirrors, it is necessary for the center of sight, the center of the mirror, the point of reflection, and the reflected point to lie: from which it is clear that the line produced from the center of sight to the center of the mirror is common to all planes of the sections that cut such mirrors according to different points. Alhazen, Book 4, Propositions 23 and 25.*

This is clear through Theorem 25 of this 5th book. For in every plane of reflection, the lines of incidence and the line of reflection are necessarily present; moreover, these lines contain three points: the reflected point <note>The object being seen.</note>, the point of reflection <note>The point on the mirror surface.</note>, and the center of sight <note>The eye.</note>. And because each of those planes is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror from which reflection occurs, the lines produced within it that are perpendicular to the surface of the mirror will pass through the center of the mirror by Theorem 72 of Book 1. It is therefore manifest that each of those planes passes through the center of the sphere. 

In each plane of reflection, therefore, are the four aforementioned points: the center of sight, the center of the mirror, the point of reflection, and the reflected point. From these facts it is clear that, since the common intersection of intersecting flat planes is a straight line (as shown by Book 11, Proposition 3), the common intersection of these planes will necessarily be the line produced from the center of sight to the center of the mirror. This is because, while the other two points <note>The object point and the reflection point.</note> vary according to the number of planes of reflection, these two points—namely the center of sight and the center of the mirror—always remain in such planes. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 7. *Every line of reflection (except for tangent lines) cuts the circle (which is the common intersection of the plane of reflection and the surface of the convex spherical mirror) in only two points: namely, in the point of reflection and in another point on the portion of the mirror's surface that is not visible.*

Let the common intersection of the surface of the convex spherical mirror and the plane of reflection be the circle *abcd*, whose center is point *g*. Let the center of sight be *e*, from which the lines touching that circle are drawn, namely *ea* and *ec*. It is clear then, by the 2nd proposition of this book, that reflection to the eye occurs from the entire arc *abc*. Suppose, therefore, that from point *b* (which is between points *a* and *c*) reflection occurs to the eye *e*, and let the line of reflection be *be*. I say that the line *eb*, when extended beyond point *b*, will cut the circle *abc* at some point on the arc of the mirror that is not visible, which we shall call *d*. For let the visual diameter *efgh* be drawn, dividing the circle into two equal semicircles, which are *fch* and *fah*. It was shown, however, by Theorem 57 of Book 1...

...since from one point to a given semicircle only one tangent line can be drawn: and it is granted there that every line drawn from the same point below the tangent line cuts the semicircle at one point above the point of tangency and at another below it. ### 8. In every reflection from convex spherical mirrors, the line drawn from the center of the mirror to the point of reflection divides the angle formed by the lines of incidence and reflection into two equal parts. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 13.

Let the center of vision be *a*: and let the point of the object seen by reflection from the proposed mirror be *b*: and let the common section <note>The intersection of the plane of reflection and the sphere.</note> of the surface of reflection and the mirror be the circle *cde*: whose center is *f*: and let the "form" <note>original: "forma"; refers to the visual species or light ray.</note> of point *b* be reflected to the eye *a* from point *d* of the mirror: and let line *df* be drawn. I say that line *df*, extended outside the circle to point *g*, divides the angle *adb* into equal parts: so that angle *adg* is equal to angle *gdb*. For let a line be drawn touching the circle *cde* at point *d* by Proposition 17 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, which is *hk*: <margin>therefore by Proposition 18 of Book 3, the angles *fdk* and *fdh*</margin> will be right angles: therefore by Proposition 11 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid</note>, angles *gdk* and *gdh* are right angles and equal: but since angle *bdk* is the angle of incidence, it is equal (by Theorem 26 of Book 5 of this work) to angle *adh*, which is the angle of reflection: therefore, there remains angle *adg* equal to angle *gdb*. Therefore, the line *fd* extended from the center of the mirror to the point of reflection, which is *d*, divides angle *adb* into equal parts. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with center z. Point a is an external object point and point b is the eye. A line a-z is drawn as the cathetus of incidence. A line of reflection d-b is shown. The line b-d is extended inside the circle to meet the cathetus a-z at point e.</image-desc>

### 9. In convex spherical mirrors, it is necessary for every line of reflection to meet the cathetus of incidence drawn from the same point to the center of the mirror. Alhazen, Book 5, Note 8.

Let the common section of the surface of reflection and the convex spherical mirror be circle *gd*: whose center is *z*: and let the center of vision be point *b*: and let the point of the object seen be *a*: and let the form of point *a* be reflected to the center of vision *b* from point *d* of the mirror: and let the line of reflection be *db*: let the line of incidence also be *ad*. Therefore, let a line be drawn from the given point *a* to the center of the mirror *z*, which is the <term>cathetus</term> *az* <note>A cathetus is a line falling perpendicularly onto a surface; in this context, the normal line from the object to the center of the sphere.</note>, cutting the surface of the mirror at point *g*: and let line *dz* be joined: and let *bd* be extended inside the mirror until it meets <margin>with line *az* (moreover, it will meet it by Theorem 29 of Book 1 of this work: for since the extended line *bd* made angle *adz*, as is clear from the preceding and by Proposition 15 of Book 1: it will therefore also cut the base *az*)</margin> let the point of intersection be *e*: now line *az* is the cathetus of incidence of point *a*, as is clear from the definition of a cathetus, and by Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work. Thus, the proposition is clear, since the line of reflection meets the cathetus of incidence. Moreover, what we have demonstrated here regarding the intersection of the line of reflection <note>The text says "incidence" but the context of the proof describes the reflection line meeting the cathetus.</note> with the cathetus of incidence, we have added because of Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work: for it is necessary for vision to occur according to both of those lines: since according to the line of reflection the form is reflected to the eye, and according to the cathetus of incidence the object "looks at" the mirror itself, from whose surface the form of the visible object is reflected to the eye.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with center d. A vertical line g-k-z-d passes through the center. Point g is the center of vision, k is on a smaller concentric circle (representing the eye's surface), and z is on the mirror's surface. A secondary point a is marked on the mirror's circumference with lines suggesting a different reflection path.</image-desc>

### 10. When the center of vision is placed on the cathetus of incidence falling upon a convex spherical mirror: reflection will occur from only one point of the mirror: and the image will be seen on the surface of the mirror, specifically at the point of reflection itself: unless perhaps it is drawn to another location for the image because of its continuity with other points of the visible form. Alhazen, Book 5, Note 19.

It was shown through Theorem 32 of Book 5 of this work that every perpendicular is reflected back upon itself: now, however, we shall show what is proposed here. ...the line *gd*, whose <term>form<note>original: "forma". **11. The location of the visible image in convex spherical mirrors must be at the intersection of the line of reflection with the <term>cathetus of incidence<note>original: "catheto incidentiæ". This is the perpendicular line drawn from the object point through the center of the mirror's curvature.</note></term>: from which it is clear that in every reflection made by these mirrors, the image of the whole visible object is always contained within some line produced between the locations of the images of its extreme points: it is also clear that in these mirrors it is possible for the location of the image to be found. Euclid, 17th theorem of the *Catoptrics*; Alhazen, Book 3, Chapter 16, number 5.**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating reflection on a convex spherical surface. It shows an arc of a circle labeled 'z g q' with a tangent line 'e g p' touching at point 'g'. A vertical normal line 'h g n' passes through the center 'n'. Line 'a n' represents the cathetus of incidence from point 'a'. Line 'b g' is the line of reflection from point 'b' (the eye), which is extended to intersect the cathetus at point 'd'.</image-desc>

That the line of reflection meets with the cathetus of incidence is clear through the 9th proposition of this book: and the same can be demonstrated in another way. For let the point of the object seen be *a*: the center of the eye *b*: the point of reflection *g*: the center of the mirror *n*. It is clear then, by the 25th theorem of the 5th book of this work, that the line of incidence *ag* and the line of reflection *gb* are in the same surface <note>meaning the same plane</note> erected perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror at point *g*. Therefore, let the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror be the circle *zgq*: and let the common line of the surface touching the mirror at point *g* and the surface of reflection be the line *egp*: and let line *hg* be drawn perpendicular to line *egp* by the 11th proposition of the 1st book of Euclid’s *Elements*. And it is clear by the 19th proposition of the 3rd book of the *Elements* that line *hg* when produced will reach the center of the circle *zgq*: which, since it is a great circle, as is clear from the 1st proposition of this book: it is evident that its center is the center of the mirror itself. Therefore, the line *hg*, produced beyond point *g*, passes through the center of the mirror, which is *n*: for otherwise, a line drawn from the center of the mirror to point *g* would also be perpendicular to line *pge*, and line *hg* produced is perpendicular to the same: it would then be possible to draw two perpendicular lines from the same point to the same point on a single line: which is impossible. Therefore, line *hg* will reach point *n*. Let line *an* then be drawn from the visible point to the center of the mirror: and line *an* will be, by the 72nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, perpendicular to the surface of the mirror: and therefore also to the surface touching the mirror at that point through which it passes. And because line *bg* falls between the two lines *hg* and *pg* which contain a right angle: it is clear that it does not touch the circle *zgq*: therefore, when produced, it cuts the circle: it will therefore meet with line *an*: let them meet at point *d*. Since, therefore, as is clear by the 6th proposition of this book, point *a*, whose form is reflected from the mirror point *g*, and the center of the mirror, which is *n*, are necessarily in the same surface: therefore, by the 1st proposition of the 11th book of the *Elements*, line *an* will be in the same surface as line *bg*. It is clear then by the 37th theorem of the 5th book of this work that point *d* will be the location of the image: since it is the common point of the line of reflection, in which the form must necessarily exist, and of line *an*, which is the cathetus of incidence of the form of point *a*, along which—as the shorter line—the form is necessarily seen. Thus the main proposition is clear through the 37th theorem of the 5th book. And by this the corollary is clear, that in every reflection made from convex spherical mirrors, the image of the whole visible object is always contained in some line produced between the locations of the images of its extreme points: since the catheti of incidence of the middle points always fall between the catheti of incidence of the extreme points: for the catheti of incidence produced from any of those extreme points to the center of the mirror cannot cut any cathetus of incidence of the middle points. It is also clear that in these mirrors it is possible for the image location of any point of the visible object to be found: for when a straight line is produced from any point seen by reflection to the center of the mirror, and the line of reflection is produced to the meeting point with it: the point of the common section of those lines will always be the location of the image. And this was what was proposed.

### 13. *In every convex spherical mirror, the straight line lying between the center of the mirror and the location of the image is greater than the straight line lying between the location of the image and the point of reflection. Alhazen 17 n 5.*

Let the arrangement be as in the preceding: I say that line *nd* is greater than line *dg*. For let line *age* cut line *an* at point *e*: it is clear that point *e* is called the <term>limit of contingency<note>original: "finis contingentiæ". In this context, it refers to the point where the line of sight or reflection meets the axis/cathetus relative to the tangent of the mirror.</note></term>, as is clear from the definitions at the beginning of this 6th book. And because, by the preceding proposition, the ratio of line *an* to line *nd* is as line *ae* to *ed*: and the ratio of line *ae* to *ed* by the 3rd proposition of Book 6 is as the ratio of line *ag* to *gd*: since, as was previously shown, line *eg* divides the angle *agd* into equal parts: therefore the ratio of line *an* to *nd* is as line *ag* to line *gd* through the 11th proposition of Book 5: therefore by the 16th proposition of Book 5, by permutation, the ratio of line *an* to *ag* is as line *nd* to *dg*: but by the 19th proposition of Book 1, line *an* is greater than *ag*: because angle *agn* is obtuse, since it is greater than the right angle *nge*: therefore line *nd* is greater than line *dg*. And because by the 11th proposition of this book, point *d* is the location of the image: it is clear that line *nd* lying between the center of the mirror and the location of the image is greater than line *dg* lying between the location of the image and the point of reflection, which is *g*. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 14. *When a line is drawn from the cathetus of incidence to the center of the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the convex spherical mirror), and a line is also drawn tangent to the same circle at the point of reflection: the part of the cathetus lying between the limit of contingency and the circumference of the circle is smaller than the radius of the same circle. Let the arrangement remain exactly as above. And because point *e* is the limit of contingency: let line *an* intersect the circumference of the circle at point *f*. I say that line *ef* is smaller than the radius of the circle, which is *fn*. For since, as is clear from the premises in the nearby theorem, the ratio of line *ag* to *gd* is as the ratio of line *ae* to *ed*: and the ratio of line *an* to *dn* is as line *ad* to *dg* <note>The text likely implies the proportional relationship established in the previous proofs</note>: therefore by the 11th proposition of Book 5, the ratio of line *an* to *dn* will be as line *ae* to *ed*: therefore by the 16th proposition of Book 5, by permutation, the ratio of line *an* to *ae* will be as *dn* to *de*: but line *an* is greater than line *ae*, since the whole is greater than its part: therefore line *dn* is greater than line *de*: thus line *dn* will be much greater than line *fe*, which is a part of *de*: much more so, therefore, will line *nf* <note>the radius</note> be greater than line *fe*. Which is what was proposed.

Let the center of vision be *b*, and let the point of the object seen be *e*. Let the common section of the surface of reflection and the convex spherical mirror be the circle *ag*. Let the point *e* fall upon different points of the mirror on the circle *ag*, which are *a* and *g*. I say that the two lines of reflection *ba* and *bg* are not parallel; however, they will not meet in the single center of vision. For given that they meet at point *b*: let a chord of the arc *ag* be drawn within the circle, which is the straight line *ag*. Let it be extended outside the circle as far as point *f* on the side of *a*, and on the side of *g* as far as point *n*. And because, by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work, angle *egn* is equal to angle *bga*; but angle *egn* is greater than angle *eag* by the 16th proposition of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>: therefore angle *bga* is greater than angle *eag*. But angle *baf* is greater than angle *bga* by the 16th proposition of Book 1: therefore angle *baf* is greater than angle *eag*. Therefore the form of point *e* is not reflected to the eye existing at point *b* from the point *a* of the mirror, by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work. And yet, because angle *baf* is not equal to angle *bga*, but smaller: therefore because by the 16th proposition of Book 1 angle *egn* is greater than angle *eag*: therefore by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work, and from the hypothesis, angle *bga* will be greater than angle *baf*. It is clear then, by the 14th theorem of Book 1 of this work, that the two lines *ba* and *bg* are not parallel; but as is evident from the premises, they will never meet at point *b*, in which is the center of vision. Thus the proposition is clear. And through this it is evident that a single eye cannot see the <term>phantom</term><note>Latin: *idolum*. In medieval optics, this refers to the reflected form or image perceived by the observer.</note> of the same form reflected from different points of such mirrors. Which was to be shown.

### 16. *From the surface of a convex spherical mirror, the form of any point can only be reflected to a single eye from a single point; and only one image occurs to the eye. Alhazen 29 n 5.*

Since it is clear through the 10th proposition of this book that a form falling perpendicularly on a mirror of this kind—with the center of vision existing on that perpendicular—is reflected to the eye from only one point: we need now only demonstrate the proposition for lines falling obliquely on these convex spherical mirrors. Therefore, let the point of the object be *b*, and the center of vision be *a*; and let point *a* not be on the perpendicular drawn from the object to the center of the mirror, which is *n*. I say that the form of point *b* is reflected to the center of vision *a* from only one point of the mirror, and only one image occurs to the eye. For it is clear by the 5th theorem of this book that for a visible object in which point *b* is located, placed in a suitable way opposite the mirror, the form of point *b* can be reflected to the eye *a* from some point of the mirror's surface. Let that point of reflection be *g*. Let the lines *bg* and *ag* be drawn, and let the <term>normal line</term><note>Latin: *kathetus*. A line dropped perpendicularly to a surface; in this context, the line passing from the object through the mirror's center.</note> of incidence be drawn, which is *bn*, cutting the surface of the mirror at point *l*. Let *an* be the visual diameter, cutting the surface of the mirror at point *r*. Also, let points *d* and *e* be the boundaries of the portion of the mirror surface opposite the eye. Let the line of reflection *ag* be extended; this line, extended beyond point *g*, will cut the perpendicular *bn* by the 9th theorem of this book. Let it therefore cut it at point *q*, which point *q*, as is clear through the 11th theorem of this work, is the location of the image. Thus it is clear by the 6th theorem of this book that points *a*, *n*, and *b* are in the same surface <note>plane</note> orthogonal to the surface of the mirror. And because of the surfaces erected upon the sphere of the mirror in which points *b* and *n* are located, none can be extended to point *a*, which is the center of vision, except only one: since point *a* is indivisible, it cannot be common to surfaces that do not intersect around it or the line in which it exists. Then it is clear that points *a* and *b* are in only one surface erected upon the sphere of the mirror, and not in many. Therefore the reflection of point *b* to the eye *a* will not occur except in the circle of the sphere which is the common section of the surface of the mirror and the surface *anb*. Therefore, let this circle be *dge*. I say that from no point of this circle *dge*, except only from the point which is proposed to be *g*, will the reflection of the form of point *b* to the center of vision *a* occur. For if it were possible for reflection to occur from another point of the circle *dge* other than point *g*: let that given point be *l*, in which the normal of incidence *bn* cuts the surface of the mirror. Since therefore line *bn* is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, and line *al* is not perpendicular to it (because it does not pass through the center of the mirror, which is *n*): and a form coming along a perpendicular line must necessarily be reflected along the same perpendicular, since the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection: it is clear that the form of point *b* is not reflected to the eye *a* from point *l*. It is also clear that it will not be reflected from any point of the arc...

...the arc *l e*: for this is impossible. This is because to whatever point of that arc a line is drawn from point *b*, it will maintain an obtuse angle on the side of *e* with the line tangent to the circle at that point. This is because the angle contained by the diameter of the circle and the line tangent to the circle at that point is a right angle, according to Proposition 18 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. Since that radius, when extended, does not reach point *b* (since the radius *n l* reaches there), the angle contained by the line drawn from point *b* and that tangent line on the side of point *b* must necessarily be obtuse. 

Furthermore, the line drawn from point *a* will maintain an acute angle toward *l* with that tangent line at the given point. For a line coming from the center of the mirror to that point of tangency will maintain a right angle with the line tangent to the circle at that point, according to Proposition 18 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. However, a line coming from point *a* will maintain an angle smaller than a right angle with the same tangent on the side of point *l*. This tangent cannot be drawn from point *a*, which is evident from Theorem 57 of Book 1 of this work, since the lines *a e* and *a d* are tangents to the surface of the mirror by hypothesis. This is because lines *a e* and *a d* contain the arc of the circle *d g e* visible to the eye, which, according to Theorem 2 of this book, is determined from the surface of the mirror not visible to the eye by the tangent lines. Therefore, if a reflection were to occur from that point, then by Theorem 20 of Book 5 of this work, it would follow that an acute angle was equal to an obtuse angle—which is impossible. Therefore, no reflection will occur from any point of the arc *l e*.

But also, in this arrangement, no reflection can occur from any point of the arc *g l*. For suppose, if it were possible, that it occurred from point *z*. Let the line *a z o* be drawn, intersecting the <term>cathetus incidentiæ</term> <note>The "cathetus of incidence" is the normal line or perpendicular line drawn from the object point to the mirror's surface.</note>, which is *b n*, at point *o*. Let a line tangent to the circle at point *z* be drawn; this tangent must necessarily fall between the lines *b g* and *b l*, since point *z* is between points *g* and *l*. Therefore, let that tangent be line *z m*, and let *g f* be the line tangent to the circle at point *g*. Let line *z m* intersect the normal of incidence at point *m*, and line *g f* at point *f*. It is clear, then, by Theorem 12 of this book, that the ratio of line *b n* to line *n q* is the same as the ratio of line *b f* to line *f q*. Similarly, the ratio of line *b n* to *n o* will be as the ratio of line *b m* to *m o*. But because line *o n* is greater than line *q n* (since the whole is greater than its part), the ratio of line *b n* to *n q* will be greater than the ratio to line *n o*, according to Proposition 8 of Book 5 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. Therefore, the ratio of line *b f* to *f q* is greater than the ratio of line *b m* to *m o*. This is impossible and contradicts Theorem 9 of Book 1 of this work, since line *b f* is smaller than line *b m*, and *f q* is greater than *m o*. It remains, therefore, that reflection does not occur from point *z*. 

Neither does it occur from any other point of the arc *g l*, because for any point other than *z*, the same deduction can be made in the aforementioned manner. Similarly, reflection will not occur from any point of the arc *g d*. For if it were to occur from some point, let that be *t*. Let line *b t* be drawn, and line *a t h* intersecting the normal *b n* at point *h*. Let the tangent to the circle at point *t* be drawn, which shall be *t p*, intersecting the normal *b n* at point *p*. Then, by Theorem 12 of this book, the ratio of line *b n* to *n h* will be as the ratio of line *b p* to *p h*, and the ratio of line *b n* to *n q* is as the ratio of line *b f* to *f q*. But the ratio of line *b n* to *n h* is greater than the ratio of line *b n* to *n q* by Proposition 8 of Book 5 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. Therefore, the ratio of line *b p* to *p h* is greater than the ratio of line *b f* to *f q*. This is impossible and contradicts Theorem 9 of Book 1 of this work; for the ratio of a greater value to a smaller is greater than the ratio of a smaller value to a greater, by the same Theorem 9 of Book 1 of this work. Indeed, line *b f* is greater than *b p*, and *p h* is greater than *f q*. 

It is clear, therefore, that the form of point *b* will be reflected to the eye *a* from no point of the arc *g d*. Thus, any point of a visible form is reflected to the eye from only one single point of a spherical convex mirror. There will, therefore, be only one line of reflection for any visible point. But there is also only one <term>cathetus incidentiæ</term> <note>The normal line</note> by Theorem 20 of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, there is only a single point in which those straight lines intersect each other, which is the **location of the image**, as is clear by Theorem 11 of this book. Thus, for one point, there is one unique image. And this is what was proposed.

...the premise: but it is necessary that it be reflected from some point of the arc *gl* between points *g* and *l*. For if it were granted that the reflection of the form of point *p* to the eye occurred from some point of the arc *gd*, let that point be *t*. Let *pt* be the line of incidence of the form of point *p*. Let the perpendicular line *ntu* be drawn to point *t*. Therefore, by Proposition 8 of this book, this line necessarily divides the angle *pta* into equal parts. Let the perpendicular *ngk* also be drawn to point *g*. It is clear, then, by Proposition 21 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid’s Elements</note>, that angle *nta* is greater than angle *nga*. Therefore, angle *uta* (which, by Proposition 11 of Book 1, is the remainder of two right angles after subtracting angle *nta*) is smaller than angle *kga*, which is the remainder of two right angles after subtracting angle *nga*. But angle *kga*, by Proposition 8 of this book, is equal to angle *bgk*. Therefore, angle *uta* is smaller than angle *bgk*. Consequently, angle *ptu* (which is equal to angle *uta* by Proposition 8 of this book) is smaller than angle *bgk*. However, angle *ptu* is equal to the sum of angles *pnt* and *tpn* by Proposition 32 of Book 1, and angle *bgk* is equal to the sum of angles *gbn* and *gnb* by the same Proposition 32 of Book 1. Therefore, the two angles *tnp* and *tpn* will be smaller than the two angles *gbn* and *gnb*. This is impossible, since angle *pnt* contains angle *bng* as a part of itself, and angle *tpn* is greater than angle *gbn* by Proposition 16 of Book 1. It is clear, therefore, that point *p* is not reflected except from some point of the arc *gl* lying between points *g* and *l*. And since, among the points *g* and *l*, point *g* is closer to point *a* (which is the center of sight), it is evident that every point of arc *gl* other than point *g* is further from the center of sight *a* than point *g*, which is the point of reflection for the form of point *b*. Therefore, the point of reflection for the form of a point closer to the center of the mirror is further from the center of sight than the point of reflection for the form of a point further from the center of the mirror. This is what was proposed.

**18. The forms of all points at an equal distance from the center of a convex spherical mirror are reflected to the eye according to equal angles contained at the center of the mirror between the perpendiculars of incidence and the visual diameters.**

Let the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the convex spherical mirror be the circle *abc*, the center of which is point *d*. It is clear by Proposition 1 of this book that point *d* is the center of the mirror. Let there be two points, *e* and *f*, at an equal distance from the center of the mirror, *d*; therefore, the lines *ed* and *fd* are equal. I say that it is necessary for the forms of those points to be reflected to the eye at equal angles. For example, if the form of point *e* is reflected to the eye located at point *g* from point *h* of the mirror, and the form of point *f*—which, by the preceding proposition, cannot be reflected to the eye *g* from point *h*—is reflected to the eye located at point *k* from point *l*. Let the lines *gd* and *kd* be drawn. I say that angle *edg* is equal to angle *fdk*. For let the <term>perpendicular of incidence: cathetus incidentiae, the line from the object point through the mirror's center</term> *ed* intersect the circle at point *a*, and the perpendicular *fd* at point *b*. Let the <term>visual diameter: diameter visualis, the line from the center of the eye through the mirror's center</term> *gd* intersect the circle at point *c*, and the diameter *kd* at point *m*. Because the lines *ed* and *fd* are equal, it is clear by the preceding proposition that the points of reflection, *h* and *l*, are at an equal distance from the eyes to which they are reflected. Just as point *h* (the point of reflection) is distant from point *c* (where the visual diameter *gd* intersects the circle), so too is point *l* (the point of reflection) distant from point *m* (where the visual diameter *kd* intersects the circle). This is because the point of reflection for the form of a point less distant from the center of the mirror is, by the preceding proposition, further from the center of sight, and the point of reflection for a more distant point is closer. Therefore, in those cases where the distance is equal, there will be equality of distance from the eyes to which they are reflected. Nor is there any difference in this whether the points are on different perpendiculars of incidence or on one; for the condition and ratio of reflection for points equally distant from the center of the same mirror is always the same. Therefore, arc *hc* is equal to arc *lm*, and by the same reasoning, arc *ah* is equal to arc *bl*. Therefore, since by Proposition 33 of Book 6 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note> the periphery of a circle (just as, by Theorem 87 of Book 1 of this work, the entire surface of the mirror) relates equally to the center, and points *e* and *f* are at an equal distance from that same center, the whole arc *ac* is equal to the whole arc *bm*. Thus, by Proposition 27 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, angle *edg* is equal to angle *fdk*. This is what was proposed.

It is clear from the hypothesis that angle *edg* is greater than angle *fdg*, as the whole is greater than its part. Therefore, let an angle equal to angle *edg* be constructed at point *d* at the end of line *fd* by Proposition 23 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, and let this be angle *fdh*. **20.** *To find the point of reflection when the point of the object seen and the center of sight are at an equal distance from the surface of a convex spherical mirror. Alhazen <note>original: Alhazen 38 5</note>.*

Let *b* be the point of the object seen, and let *a* be the center of sight. Let also the center of the given convex spherical mirror be *c*, and let the circle (which is the common section of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror) be *efg*. Let the <term>catheti<note>Latin: *catheti*. In medieval optics, these are the perpendicular lines or axes passing from a point through the center of the mirror's sphere.</note></term> *bc* and *ac* be drawn, intersecting the circle at points *f* and *g*. Since, therefore, on account of the equality of the height of the point of the object seen with the center of sight, these two lines *bc* and *ac* are equal, it is manifest—through those things which were shown in the demonstration of Proposition 17 of this book—that reflection will necessarily occur from some point of the arc *fg* lying between the catheti of incidence and reflection. Therefore, by Proposition 9 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, let the angle *acb* be bisected into equal parts by the line *cd*, intersecting the arc *fg* at point *e*. It is also clear by Proposition 26 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid</note> that the arc *fe* is equal to arc *eg*. Line *cd* will be perpendicular to the line tangent to the circle at point *e* by Proposition 18 of Book 3. Therefore, let two lines *ae* and *be* be drawn to point *e*. The two triangles *aec* and *bec* will be equiangular and equilateral by Proposition 4 of Book 1 and from the hypothesis. Therefore, angle *aed* will be equal to angle *deb*. Thus, by Proposition 8 of this book, point *e*, which is the midpoint of arc *fg*, is the point of reflection of the form of point *b* to the sight at *a*. And this is what was proposed. 

If, however, the lines *bc* and *ac* were unequal, let an equality be made on the longer one; for example, if line *bc* is longer than *ac*, since *fe* is equal to *cg* <note>original: *cg*, though *cg* and *cf* are radii</note> because they are radii of the same circle, let line *bf* be cut to the equality of line *ag* at point *h*, such that *fh* is equal to *ag*. It is clear, then, by the previous statements, that the form of point *h* is reflected to the sight *a* from point *e*. But points closer to the center *c*—because by Proposition 17 of this book they are in their point of reflection at a greater distance from the point that is the center of sight—cannot fall on point *e*. It is clear that they are reflected from points on the arc *ef*, and according to their distance from the center of the circle *c*, the proximity of their points of reflection to the center of sight will be according to their points of reflection. But more remote points, such as those above point *h* (namely points *m* and *b*), will be closer to the center of sight than point *e* according to their points of reflection; they will therefore fall on arc *eg*, and according to their proximity to the center of the circle *c*, there will be a greater distance of the points of reflection from the center of sight *b* <note>original: *b*, likely meaning the eye at *a* or the general axis</note>. While this may provide knowledge in a general way, it must nevertheless be examined more diligently according to the reflection of individual points from individual points of the mirror's surface.

**21.** *If the angle contained under the line of incidence—drawn obliquely from the point of the object seen to some point on the surface of a convex spherical mirror—and the line drawn from the center of the mirror to that same point is not greater than a right angle, it is impossible for a perfect reflection to occur to any sight from that point. Alhazen <note>original: Alhazen 40 n 5</note>.*

Let *a* be the center of sight and *b* the point of the object seen. Let also point *g* be the center of the convex spherical mirror, and let the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror be a circle, whose center will be point *g* by Proposition 1 of this book.
