For if angle *bdg* is not greater than a right angle, it is either a right angle or less than a right angle. If it is said to be a right angle, then by Proposition 16 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid</note>, line *bd* is tangent to the circle at point *d*. But by Theorem 20 of Book 5 of this work, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection; therefore, angle *adg* will also be a right angle and tangent to the circle at point *d*. Thus, by Proposition 14 of Book 1, the two lines *bd* and *da* joined at point *d* are a single line. Therefore, reflection does not occur according to the perfect nature of the reflection of the form of point *b* to the sight existing at point *a*, but it is simply a case of vision along the line *adb*, which is contrary to the hypothesis, since point *d* was assumed to be the point of reflection. If, however, angle *bdg* is said to be less than a right angle, then from point *d* let a line be drawn tangent to the circle at point *d* by Proposition 17 of Book 3; which should be extended...

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof for Proposition 22 in Book VI. The previous page established the ratios between specific lines in the construction of the reflection. The current text completes the demonstration that reflection in a convex mirror requires specific angular conditions to avoid a contradiction of Proposition 16, which states that a single point cannot be reflected from two different points on the mirror to the same eye.</meta>

...*o k*: it was previously shown that the ratio of line *z q* to *q d* is as the ratio of line *o f* to *f k*: therefore, by Theorem 5 of Book 1 of this work, the converse ratio of line *q d* to *z q* will be as *f k* to *o f*. Therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 5 <note>of Euclid’s *Elements*</note>, the ratio of the whole line *z d* to *z q* is as the whole line *o k* to *o f*. Then, by Proposition 22 of Book 5, *z b* will be to *z q* as *s o* is to *o f*. Thus, by Proposition 6 of Book 6, the triangles *z q b* and *o f s* are equiangular. Therefore, angle *z b q* is equal to angle *o s f*. The remaining angle *q b d* is thus equal to angle *f s k*. But angle *f k s* was made equal to angle *b d q*, and angle *p k f* is equal to angle *q d g*. Therefore, the whole angle *s k p* is equal to the whole angle *b d g*. Thus, by Proposition 31 of Book 1 and Proposition 4 of Book 6, triangle *b d g* is similar to triangle *s p k*, and the whole triangle *b d x* is similar to the total triangle *c k s*. Therefore, the ratio of line *s p* to *p k* is as *b g* to *g d*.

Having established the point above the center, since point *u* will be the point of reflection. And because, as is clear through Proposition 16 of Book 1 and from what was said before, the prior angle *s p k* is greater than the present angle *s p k* because it is an exterior angle, it is evident that reflection would occur from two points of the mirror, which are *d* and *u*. This contradicts Proposition 16 of this work. Therefore, the angle *s p k* can never be anything other than greater than a right angle if the discovery of the point of reflection is to be made according to it; because with the point of the seen object and the center of sight arranged in such a disposition, reflection is not possible.

Likewise, it is impossible for two angles established upon line *m o* to both be greater than a right angle. For if both such angles were greater than a right angle, when an angle equal to angle *s k m* is made at the center *g* of the proposed circle, another angle different from it would be formed at the same center. Another line similar to the prior line *s k* would produce this upon *k m*. In this way, the reflection of the form of the same point to the same eye would occur from point *d* and from another point of that circle, which is against Proposition 16 of this work. It is necessary, therefore, that only one of those angles be greater than a right angle, not both greater or both less than a right angle. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 23. On a single perpendicular line of incidence of a convex spherical mirror surface, or on different ones similarly situated with respect to the eye to which the reflection occurs, given two points whose forms are reflectible from the mirror's surface to the eye: the location of the image of the point closer to the center of the mirror will be further from the center, and the image of the point further from the center will be closer to the center.

Let circle *a b c* (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the convex spherical mirror) have center *d*. Let the center of sight <note>the eye</note> be *e*, and let the <term>cathetus incidentiæ</term> <note>the perpendicular line of incidence drawn from the object through the center of the mirror</note> be *d f g*. On this line are two points, *f* and *g*, whose forms are reflectible to the eye. Let point *f* be closer to the center *d* and point *g* be further away. Let that same perpendicular line intersect the circle *a b c* at point *c*.

I say that the location of the image of the form of point *f* is further from the center of the mirror (*d*) than the location of the image of the form of point *g*. Since, as is clear by the hypothesis, each of the forms of these points is reflected from some point of the mirror to the eye, and since those points are positioned on the same perpendicular line of incidence, it is clear by Proposition 6 of this book that the center of sight *e* is in the same surface of reflection as both of those points. Therefore, the reflection of each of those points to the eye *e* will occur from some point of the circle *a b c*. Let it be that the form of point *g* reflects from point *a*, and the form of point *f* from point *b*. Then, by Proposition 17 of this book, point *b* will be further from the center of sight *e* than point *a*.

Now, let the visual diameter *e d* be drawn, and let the lines of incidence *g a* and *f b* be drawn, along with the lines of reflection *a e* and *b e*. These lines, when extended inside the circle, will intersect the perpendicular *d f g* by Proposition 9 of this book. And since they concur with the visual diameter *e d*, let line *a e* intersect the perpendicular *g d* at point *h*, and line *b e* at point *k*. Therefore, point *h* will be the location of the image of the form of point *g*, and point *k* the location of the image of the form of point *f*, according to Proposition 11 of this book.

Truly, point *h* is closer to center *d* than point *k* by Theorem 29 of Book 1 of this work. Because line *h e* cuts the angle *d e k*, it is clear that it will also cut the base subtended to it, which is *d k*. Therefore, point *h* is closer to the center of the mirror *d* than point *k*. And since, as is clear according to this method, all lines drawn from the center of sight *e* through any points of the arc *a c* between points *a* and *c* to the perpendicular *d g* fall upon points of the radius *d c* further from the center than point *h*, the proposition is clear. From this it is also evident that the closer the points of line *e g* are to center *d*, the further the locations of their images are from the center of the mirror *d*. And since all perpendiculars of incidence meet at the center of the mirror, it is clear that for points on different perpendiculars similarly situated with respect to the eye, the demonstration is the same as for points on the same perpendicular. For every point marked on one similar perpendicular, a similar point at the same distance from the center of the mirror corresponds on the other perpendicular; and the locations of the images for any of those points (because they regard the eye in a similar way) are ordered similarly with respect to the center of the mirror. Thus, the proposition is clear.

# VITELLO'S OPTICS

*24. If, from any point on a convex spherical mirror, a line of reflection is extended to cut the circle (which is the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror) in such a way that the portion of the extended line within the circle is equal to the radius of the circle: the location of the seen image will always be inside the convex mirror. <note>Original: Alhazen Book 5, Proposition 20.</note>*

Let the center of sight <note>the eye</note> be point **g**, and let the center of the convex spherical mirror be point **d**. Let the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror be circle **abk**. From the center of sight, point **g**, let two tangent lines be drawn to circle **abk** according to Proposition 17 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid’s *Elements*</note>, which shall be **ga** and **gb**. By Proposition 2 of this book, the portion **ab** of the circle will be visible to the eye, and its center is point **d**. However, since the eye and the mirrors change position, let a configuration of the eye to the mirror be made such that a line drawn from point **g** (the center of sight) cutting circle **abk** has a part inside the circle—which is the chord of the circle's arc, namely **hk**—that is equal to the radius of that circle. Let that line be **ghk**, whose part **hk** inside the circle is equal to the radius **dk**. This is possible to construct if, according to Proposition 1 of Book 4 <note>of Euclid</note>, a line **hk** equal to the radius of the circle is inscribed in circle **abk**, and the center of sight is placed on that line **kh** extended outside the circle. I say that the location of the image reflected from point **h** is always inside the convex surface of the mirror. 

For let a perpendicular line **hm** be drawn from point **h** upon the line tangent to the circle at point **h**. Therefore, this line, when extended into the circle, passes through the center **d** according to Proposition 19 of Book 3 <note>of Euclid</note>. I say that when the form of any visible thing is reflected from point **h**, the location of its image will always be inside the convex mirror. For let a line be drawn from point **h** establishing an angle at point **h** (the endpoint of line **hm**) equal to angle **ghm** according to Proposition 23 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid</note>; let this be angle **phm**, with line **hp** being extended. Therefore, by Theorem 20 of Book 5 <note>of this work</note>, the points of this line **hp** will be reflected to the eye **g** from point **h** of the mirror, and the points of no other line can be reflected from point **h** to the eye. 

Let some point of it be taken, which shall be **p**, and let a line be drawn from it to the center of the mirror, which is **pd**. Also, by Proposition 1 of this book and by Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work, line **pd** will be perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror at the point where the line **pd** itself cuts the circumference of circle **abk**. Let line **dk** also be joined. And because the angle of incidence **phm** is equal to the angle of reflection **mgh**, as is clear from the premises—and indeed angle **ghm**, by Proposition 15 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid</note>, is equal to angle **khd**—therefore angle **phm** is equal to angle **khd**. But angle **khd** is equal to angle **hdk** by Proposition 5 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid</note>, because side **hk** is by hypothesis equal to the radius **dk**. Therefore, angle **phm** is equal to angle **hdk**. 

Because line **md** falling upon lines **hp** and **dk** makes the exterior angle **mhp** equal to the interior angle **mdk**, line **hp** is therefore parallel to line **dk** by Proposition 28 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid</note>. Thus, lines **hp** and **dk**, if extended to infinity, will never meet. And line **pd**, which is the <term>cathetus of incidence</term> <note>the perpendicular line from the object to the mirror's center</note> for the form of point **p**, or any other line drawn from any point of line **hp** to the center **d**, will always intersect the line **hk** (which lies between the parallel lines **kd** and **hp**) between points **h** and **k**, as is clear from Theorem 29 of Book 1 of this work. For all those <term>catheti</term> <note>perpendiculars</note> divide angle **hdk**; therefore, they will also cut the base **hk**, for any of those catheti of incidence is always drawn to the center of the mirror, which is point **d**. 

Therefore, whatever point is taken on line **ph**, the line drawn from that point to point **d** will always intersect the line of reflection, which is **ghk**, inside the convex mirror. Since the cathetus of incidence extended to the center of the mirror is always perpendicular to the surface of the mirror where the reflection occurs, as in **pd**, the image of any point of line **ph** will, by Proposition 11 of this book, appear inside the convex mirror. And this is what was proposed.

At point **i**, let an angle be made equal to angle **tig** according to Proposition 23 of Book 1 [of Euclid’s *Elements*], which shall be angle **pit**. It is therefore clear that only the points of line **pi** are reflected from point **i** to the center of sight **g**, according to Theorem 20 of Book 5 of this work <note>referring to Alhazen’s *Optics*</note>. It is also clear by Proposition 15 of Book 3 [of Euclid] that line **is** is longer than line **hk**; therefore, line **is** is greater than the radius **sd**. In triangle **sid**, therefore, angle **sdi** is greater than angle **sid** by Proposition 18 of Book 1 [of Euclid]. Consequently, by Proposition 15 of Book 1, angle **sdi** is greater than angle **tig**. Thus, angle **sdi** is greater than angle **tip**, which from the premises is equal to angle **tig**. Therefore, by Theorem 14 of Book 1 of this work, lines **pi** and **ds** are not parallel. Even if extended to infinity on the side of their points **p** and **s**, they will never meet; however, they will meet if extended from their points **i** and **d**. From whatever point on line **pi** a cathetus of incidence <note>the perpendicular line falling from the object point to the mirror's surface</note> is drawn to the center **d**, it will intersect line **gis** (which is the line of reflection) within the convexity of the mirror. And every line drawn from any point on line **pi** to point **d** will be perpendicular to the surface of the mirror according to Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work; therefore, it is itself the cathetus of incidence, just as line **pd** is now. Since the location of the image is at the intersection of the cathetus of incidence and the line of reflection according to Theorem 11 of this book, it is clear that the image location of any point on line **pi** will always be within the convexity of the mirror. And since the same demonstration holds for any given point on arc **hz**, it is manifest that the proper location of all images of arc **hz** will be inside the mirror. This is what was proposed.

26. *From any point on the arc of the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the spherical convex mirror) lying between the point where the line of reflection—whose part inside the circle is equal to the radius of the circle—intersects the circle, and the nearest point where a line drawn from the center of sight touches the circle, let a reflection occur: the location of the seen image will sometimes be inside the mirror, sometimes on the convex surface of the mirror, and sometimes outside the mirror. <note>Original: Alhazen Book 5, Proposition 22.</note>*

Let the total arrangement of the figure remain as it was in the preceding theorem and in Theorem 24 of this book; specifically, that the line of reflection, which is **ghk**, intersects the circle **abk** (whose center is point **d**) in such a way that its part inside the circle, which is **hk**, is equal to the radius **dz**. Let lines **ga** and **gb** be tangents to circle **abk** at points **a** and **b**, and let point **b** be closer to point **h**. I say that from whatever point on arc **hb** a reflection occurs, the location of the seen image will sometimes be inside the mirror, sometimes on the surface of the mirror, and sometimes outside the mirror. For let some point **n** be taken on arc **hb** from which a reflection occurs to the eye **g**. Let that point of reflection be **n**, and let the line of reflection be drawn intersecting the circle, which, when extended through the circle, is **gnq**. From the center **d**, let radius **dq** be drawn, and to the point of reflection let the perpendicular **dnf** be drawn. Let it be extended, as in the previous cases, so that line **ne** forms an angle with the cathetus **dnf** equal to angle **fng**, which shall be angle **fne**. Since line **nq**, by Proposition 15 of Book 3 [of Euclid], is shorter than line **hk**, it is clear that line **nq** is shorter than the radius **qd**. Because line **hk** is equal to radius **qd** by hypothesis, line **qn** will be shorter than line **qd**. Therefore, the angle **qdn** of triangle **qdn** is smaller than angle **dnq** by Proposition 18 of Book 1 [of Euclid]. Thus, by Proposition 15 of the same book, angle **qdn** is smaller than angle **gnf**, and therefore also smaller than its equal, angle **enf**. Consequently, lines **dq** and **ne** will meet on the side of the smaller angles by Theorem 14 of Book 1 of this work; let their intersection be at point **e**. It is clear, as in the previous cases, that line **eqd** is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror according to Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, line **ed** is the cathetus of incidence of the form of point **e**, and it intersects line **gnq** (the line of reflection) at point **q**, which is a point on the surface of the mirror. Thus, the image of point **e**, when the reflection is made from point **n** on arc **hb**, will be seen at point **q**, which is on the convex surface of the mirror. And since the line of reflection, which is **gq**, [intersects] the periphery of arc **bk** at only one point...

->### VITELLO'S OPTICS<-

And since it intersects, as is clear by the 17th [theorem] of this book: it is evident that it does not happen that the image of the form of any point on the line is seen in the very surface of the mirror, except only at that one point where the <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "cathetus"; a perpendicular line drawn from the object point to the center of the mirror</note> drawn to it intersects the line of reflection in the mirror's surface, as is the cathetus of point **e** in this proposal. 

If, however, on line **en** a point **r** is taken beyond **e**, and the cathetus of incidence drawn from that point **r** to the center of the mirror (which is **rd**) intersects the line of reflection (which is **gnq** extended beyond point **q**) at point **l**: then the intersection will be outside the surface of the mirror. Therefore, the image of any point on line **ne** taken beyond point **e** will be seen outside the surface of the mirror according to the distance of the incident point; and always, as is clear by the 11th [theorem] of this book, the location of the image will be at the point of intersection of the cathetus and reflection lines: just as the location of the image for the form of point **r** is now at point **l**, which is the common intersection of the aforementioned lines. 

If, however, some point **c** is taken on line **en** between points **n** and **e**, the cathetus drawn from it to the center of the mirror will intersect the line of reflection **gnq** inside the mirror: for it will intersect it at some point among those between points **n** and **q**. Therefore, the image of any point on line **en** taken between points **e** and **n** will be seen inside the mirror. And similarly, the same thing can be demonstrated in the same way for various points of the lines of incidence at any other point on arc **bh**, and this is what was proposed. 

Just as we demonstrated regarding arc **zb** in the previous three theorems, so too can it be demonstrated by applying the diagram to arc **za**, since there is complete symmetry on both sides: and the same is true for all circles of a convex spherical mirror similar to circle **abk**. For if the perpendicular **gzd** remains fixed, and the line **gh** is imagined to move according to the equality of angle **dgh** until it returns to its starting place, then the moved line **gh** will cut out a portion of the surface from the entire convex surface of the mirror by its motion: and the image of the form of any point reflected from any of the points of this portion will always be seen inside the mirror. 

If, however, while diameter **gzd** remains fixed, the line tangent to the circle **abk** (which is **gb**) is moved until it returns to the place from which it started, it will cut a larger portion out of the sphere: and when a reflection of the form of any point is made from any points of the surface of the mirror described by arc **hb**, or from points of arcs similar to it: then, with the cathetus of incidence intersecting the line of reflection on the surface of the mirror itself, the location of the image of that point's form will always be on the surface of the mirror. But for other points existing on that same line, the location of the image for some is inside the mirror, and for others outside the mirror, according to how the cathetus lines drawn from those points to the center of the mirror intersect the lines of their reflections. 

And since the position of the center of sight, or the surface of the mirror, or even the object seen can be varied in many ways, we leave this to the experimenter. Convex spherical mirrors are in common use among the people of our habitable world—since the glass pieces used for viewing are blown out by the breath of craftsmen in a spreading spherical way <note>This is a fascinating historical note on 13th-century glassblowing: mirrors were often made from blown glass spheres that were then coated with lead or tin.</note>. Any portion [of a mirror] can be positioned such that sometimes the image of the point seen appears inside the mirror (that is, beyond its surface), sometimes on the surface of the mirror itself, and sometimes outside the surface of the mirror, such that the surface of the mirror is not between the image being seen and the eye of the viewer, but is seen to the side externally: and this has already happened many times to those who experiment. Hence it is clear through these things that a convex spherical mirror, the center of sight, and the object seen could be positioned so that the image appears outside the mirror in the air; we leave this to the skill of the investigator.

27. **Every diameter of a convex spherical mirror upon which the location of the image falls, whether on the surface of the mirror itself or outside the mirror, is necessarily joined to the portion of the sphere of the mirror not visible to the eye. From this it is clear that this diameter is lower than any of the tangent lines drawn from the center of sight to the surface of the mirror.**

What is proposed here is clear from the previous statements, using the diagram from the preceding section. And since, as is clear, reflection can occur from any point of arc **ab**: and every line of reflection is also drawn from the center of sight below the line drawn from the center of sight tangent to the circle, it is clear by Theorem 57 of Book 1 of this work that it intersects the circle. Whenever the location of the image is on the mirror's surface or outside it, it is clear that this cannot happen on the diameters of the mirror joined to arc **ab**: for the location of the image cannot be on the surface of the mirror in those diameters, since the catheti of incidence and the lines of reflection of those points cannot meet at those points. Nor can the location of reflection be on those diameters outside the surfaces of the mirrors, since the lines of reflections will not meet on that side outside the mirror. Therefore, all diameters of any convex spherical mirror in which the locations of images are on the mirror's surface or outside the mirror are necessarily joined to the portion of the mirror not visible to the eye. And since the visible and non-visible portions of the mirror are determined by tangent lines drawn from the center of sight to the surface of the mirror (as is clear by the 2nd [theorem] of this book), therefore the proposed corollary is manifest. For any of the diameters in which the location of the image is on the surface of the mirror itself or outside the mirror must be lower than any of the tangent lines drawn from the center of sight to the surface of the mirror. And this was what was proposed. However, the diameter in which the image location appears inside the mirror can be either higher or lower than that tangent line, as is clear from what has been demonstrated in the previous sections. It remains, however, for us to determine the locations of images more precisely in what follows.

28. **If a line of reflection is drawn to the diameter of a convex spherical mirror such that it intersects the mirror, and the part of the drawn line lying between the surface of the mirror and the diameter is equal to the part of the diameter lying between the point of intersection and the center of the mirror: the location of any image is not in that part of the diameter, but that part is the limit of images, just as it is at that point of intersection.** <note>original: "Alhazen 23 n 5"; referring to Book 5, Proposition 23 of Alhazen’s Optics.</note>

-># BOOK SIX<-

Because **b f e g** [are points on the mirror surface]: let point **h** be the center of sight <note>The location of the observer's eye</note>, and let point **d** be the center of the sphere of the mirror. Let **d e** be the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> of the mirror, which is necessarily perpendicular to the surface of the mirror according to the 72nd theorem of the first book of this work. Let line **z h** be the line of reflection, cutting the convex surface of the mirror at point **f**, and meeting the radius **e d** at point **z**. Furthermore, let line **z f** be equal to line **z d**, which is possible to construct by the 136th theorem of the first book. I declare that on the line segment **z d**, there is no location for any image. For point **z** cannot be the location of any image except perhaps for points on the extended line **e d**; this is because, as shown in the 11th theorem of this book, the location of the image of any point’s form is always on its <term>cathetus of incidence</term> <note>The perpendicular line drawn from the object point to the center of the mirror</note>. a perpendicular from the center **d** through point **f**, which, when extended outside the circle, is **d f n**. Upon this perpendicular, let an angle be formed at point **f** equal to angle **n f h** (by the 23rd proposition of the 1st book of Euclid), which shall be angle **q f n**. Therefore, by the 15th proposition of Euclid's 1st book, angle **q f n** is equal to angle **z f d**. But since lines **z d** and **z f** are equal by our hypothesis, then by the 5th proposition of the 1st book, angle **z d f** is equal to angle **z f d**. Therefore, angle **q f n** is also equal to angle **z d f**. Consequently, by the 28th proposition of the 1st book, lines **z d** and **q f** are parallel to each other; thus, even if extended to infinity, they will never meet. Therefore, the form of no point on line **e d**, no matter how far extended, will move toward point **f** along the line of incidence **q f**. But there can be no location for an image at point **z** unless a form moves to point **f** along line **q f**; otherwise, line **f h** would not be the line of reflection, at whose intersection with the diameter **d e** point **z** is located. Therefore, point **z** is not the location of an image for any points on line **e d**, nor for any other image of any point's form outside line **d e**. The same demonstration holds true no matter which diameter **e d** is chosen. 

Furthermore, no other point on line **z d** besides **z** can be the location of an image. Suppose that point **p** could be the location of an image: let line **h p** be drawn, cutting the convex surface of the mirror at point **b**, and let the perpendicular **d b m** be drawn. As before, let an angle equal to angle **m b h** be made at point **b**, which shall be **t b m**. It is evident then, as before, that angle **t b m** is equal to angle **p b d**. But angle **d p b**, by the 16th proposition of the 1st book, is greater than angle **p z h**, since it is an exterior angle to triangle **p z h**. Therefore, the other two angles of triangle **p d b** are smaller than the other two angles of triangle **d z f**. However, angle **p d b** is greater than angle **z d f**, because the whole is greater than its part; this is also clear by the 29th theorem of the first book of this work. It follows, therefore, that angle **d b p** is smaller than angle **d f z**. But angle **d f z** is equal to angle **z d f**, as was previously shown; therefore, angle **d b p** is smaller than angle **z d f**. It is thus much smaller than angle **p d b**. Consequently, angle **t b m** is smaller than angle **p d b**. Therefore, lines **t b** and **e d**, by the 14th theorem of the first book of this work, will never meet on the side from which reflection could occur. Thus, no form incident at point **b** will be reflected to the sight **h** such that the location of the image is at point **p**. Similarly, the image of no other point will present itself to the sight on any point of line **z d**. 

Therefore, the entire line **z d** will always be empty of images; a location for images will never exist upon it. The same can be demonstrated for any other diameter of the proposed mirror, provided the hypothesis is maintained. It is also clear from the premises that line **z d** is the **limit of images** <note>original: "meta imaginum"</note>. If line **f z** were greater than line **z d**, no image would ever appear; because angle **z d f** (by the 18th proposition of the 1st book) would be greater than angle **d f z**, and thus greater than angle **n f h** (by the 15th proposition), and thus greater than angle **q f n** (by the 8th theorem of this book). Lines **e d** and **q f** (by the 14th theorem of the 1st book) would then not meet toward the direction of points **e** and **q**, but toward the direction of points **d** and **f**. Thus, no image could appear at point **z**, nor at any point on line **z f**. 

However, if line **f z** is smaller than line **z d**, then following the previous method, angle **z d f** will be smaller than angle **q f n**. Therefore, by the 14th theorem of the 1st book, lines **e d** and **q f** will meet toward the direction of points **e** and **q**; from that point, a reflection of one of the points on line **e d** can occur toward the sight. The location of the image will be at point **z** (by the 11th theorem of this book). Line **z d** will be a location of an image at every one of its points until the line of incidence relative to the diameter receives the proposed division. It is clear, therefore, that when line **z f** is equal to line **z d**, line **z d** is the limit of images, beyond which none are seen, and within which every image is seen. Similarly, point **z** is the limit of images. Since, as is clear from the premises, every line of incidence drawn from any point of the mirror to the sight **h** between points **z** and **d** is greater than the line which is cut off from line **z d** by it—because that line is greater than line **z f** (by the 15th proposition of the 3rd book), it is also greater than line **z d** by hypothesis, as is clear regarding line **b p**, which is greater than line **p d** or line **z d**. And every line drawn between points **z** and **e** to the sight **h**, lying between the circumference of the circle and the diameter, is smaller than line **f z**, and thus smaller than line **z d**. Therefore, it is also smaller than the line which it cuts off from the radius **d e**. Thus, as is clear from the premises, the locations for images are on line **z e**, except at point **z**; however, on line **z d**, there are no locations for images. Thus it is clear that point **z** is the limit of images. It makes no difference whether point **z** falls inside the circle, outside it, or on the very surface of the mirror; for whenever it happens that line **z d** is equal to the part of the reflection line lying between the point of reflection and point **z**, point **z** will always be the limit of images, and the same applies to the whole line **z d**. The proposition is therefore proven.

I say, therefore, that at any point taken between **e** and **i** is the location of an image: and points **e** and **i** are the limits of the images <note>original: "metae imaginum"; the boundaries defining where a virtual image can possibly appear to the eye</note>. And since line **h y** falls outside the mirror: the form <note>In medieval optics, a "form" (forma) refers to the visual information or species traveling from the object to the eye</note> of point **y** will move along line **y h** toward the mirror: it will also be reflected from the point on the mirror, which is **h**, to the sight existing at point **a**: and its image will appear at point **f**, at the intersection of the cathetus of incidence <term>cathetus of incidence: a line drawn from the object point perpendicular to the mirror's surface</term>, which is **b f**, with the line of reflection, which is **a h**, outside the surface of the mirror. 

And in the same way, it must be demonstrated for all points of the line. For the images of the forms of all those points are seen outside the mirror, except for **l** alone, where the diameter **b l** cuts the surface of the mirror: because at that point the location of the image is on the surface of the mirror: for this reason, that the line of reflection, which is **a l**, intersects with the cathetus of incidence, which is **b y**, on its surface: and there will be a point whose form's image is seen at point **l**, reflected from point **r**, standing on the diameter **b y** extended beyond point **l**, as is clear by the 27th theorem of this book: but, as is clear by the 30th theorem of this book, all forms of points falling on the diameter **b y**, beyond the point reflected from point **r**, are reflected from some point of the arc **r u**, and the locations of the images of all those points are on line **a l**: because, as is clear from the preceding, point **i** is the limit of images, beyond which point no image ever appears when the sight is at point **a**, and the mirror is arranged thus, as is clear from the hypothesis. It is clear, therefore, that at any point of the line **i l** taken between points **e** and **i**, is the location of the image of the form of some point of the diameter **b e** extended beyond point **e**. Therefore, some images on the diameter **e b** are assigned locations inside the mirror, some outside the mirror, and one alone on the surface of the mirror, namely at point **l**. And in the same way, on any point of the arc **o g**, it can be demonstrated by the diameters passing through the given points of arc **o g** and cutting the surface of the mirror, just as the necessity of the demonstrations requires.

32. *If the cathetus of incidence falls upon any point of the circular arc (which is the common intersection of the plane of reflection and the convex spherical mirror) lying between the point where the line of reflection (a part of which is inside the circle) is equal to the radius of the circle, in the non-visible portion, and the point distant from the point of contact by a quarter of that same circle: the location of the image will always be outside the mirror. Alhazen 27 n 5.* <note>Reference to Book 5, Proposition 27 of Alhazen's *Optics*</note>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating optical reflection principles on a convex spherical mirror. A circle representing the mirror's cross-section has its center at 'b'. Point 'a' is located above the circle, representing the observer's position. Multiple lines are drawn from 'a' to the circle and through it, illustrating incident rays, reflected rays, and their extensions. A tangent line 'ap' touches the circle at point 'g'. Let all things be arranged as in the preceding diagram **b**, so that line **a m o** cuts the circle of the mirror such that line **m o** is equal to the radius <note>original: "semidiametro"</note> of the mirror: and let it be, as in the 30th theorem of this book, that angle **h b g** is a right angle: and let line **a g p** be tangent to the mirror at point **g**. I say that for the catheti of incidence meeting the arc **o h**, the location of the image will always be outside the mirror. For let a diameter **b q** be drawn through some point of the arc **o h**: let it meet the tangent **a g p** at point **p**: and let line **a u q** be drawn from the center of vision, cutting the mirror above in the portion visible to the sight at point **u**. And because, as was clear before, line **m o** is equal to line **b q**, and line **u q** is greater than line **m o** by the 15th proposition of the 3rd book [of Euclid]: therefore line **u q** is greater than line **q b**. Also, a line drawn from the circumference to the diameter **b p**, which is equal to the part of the diameter **p b** lying between itself and the center of the mirror, will not fall between points **q** and **b**. For if this were possible, then, as before, line **u q** would be smaller than line **q b**: since if that line were to fall on point **q**, its part inside the circumference would be greater than line **u q** by the 15th proposition of the 3rd book: it remains, therefore, that the equal line falls between **p** and **q**. That it does not fall on point **p** is clear from this, that angle **p g b** is a right angle: therefore, by the 19th proposition of the 1st book, in triangle **p b g**, side **p b** is greater than side **p g**. Thus, let the line so drawn fall on this side of **p**: and let the point where it falls be **s**: therefore, by the 28th theorem of this book, point **s** will be the limit of the image locations: and any point between points **p** and **s** will be a location of images: and the demonstration is the same as in the above, namely the 30th and 31st theorems of this book: and in any point of arc **h o** there is the same demonstration. From these preceding propositions, it is clear that the images of the diameters of arc **h o** are all outside the surface of the mirror: but of the images of diameter **f y**, as in the 31st theorem of this book, only one is on the surface of the mirror, such as that which is at point **l**: others are indeed inside the surface of the mirror, such as those which fall on the part of the diameter which is **i l**: while all others are outside the mirror, such as those which fall on line **l e**. Also, of all the images of the diameters of arc **o g**, some are inside the surface of the mirror: some outside of it: some on the convex surface of the mirror itself, as was concluded there in the preceding. Thus, what was proposed is clear.

33. *Into the arc of the circle (the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the surface of the convex spherical mirror) lying between the point where the visual diameter and the point distant from the point of contact...*

-># BOOK SIX<-

*...passing through the fourth part of the circle and cutting the circle below, the perpendicular of incidence cannot fall in such a way that any image location occurs there. Alhazen, Book 5, number 28.*

With all other things arranged as in the figure immediately above: I say that in the arc **h z**, no diameter <note>In this context, a "diameter" refers to the "perpendicular of incidence," a line extending from an object point through the center of the spherical mirror</note> can fall in which a location for any image might exist. For since the tangent line, which is **a g p**, is parallel to the diameter **b h** (by the 28th proposition of the 1st book [of Euclid]), it is then clear that toward point **p**, no diameter falling into arc **z h** meets with the tangent line **a p**. Furthermore, from whatever point on such diameters a line is drawn to the convex surface of the mirror, it falls upon the non-visible portion of that mirror—namely, onto the portion of the circle **g z c**. None of these lines fall onto the portion of the circle **g d c** that faces the eye, unless they cut through the sphere of the mirror itself. Therefore, no "form" <note>The "form" (forma) is the medieval term for the visual information or "species" traveling from an object to the eye</note> of any point on such diameters will reach the visible portion of the mirror or the eye. 

All these things which have been declared regarding the semicircle **d g z** and its arcs in the preceding six theorems can similarly be demonstrated in the arcs of the semicircle **d e z**, just as they were in the arcs of the semicircle **d g z**. For by taking similar arrangements of the arcs on both sides and making similar extensions of the lines, the same effects will occur in all cases, and the method of demonstration is the same. Similarly, what is now declared regarding circle **c d g z** can be shown in every one of the circles that are the common sections of the surfaces of reflection and the convex surfaces of the spherical mirror. Hence, all the effects proven according to any points of the circle **d g z c** happen in complete circles throughout the entire surface of the mirror—just as if point **g**, or another designated point, were moved across the surface of the sphere and described a circle. 

The effects of the arcs of circle **d g z c**, however, occur across a certain wide surface contained beneath the boundaries of parallel circles throughout the whole sphere of the mirror—just as if some arc parallel to the pole, moved by the mirror, were to mark out a surface, as is clear to one who considers it. If, therefore, line **b h** is moved while angle **h b z** remains the same, it will mark out a portion of the sphere by its motion according to point **z**, in whose diameters there will be no location for an image. And if line **b h** remains unmoved while arc **o h** is moved, a portion of the sphere will be described in which all images existing in diameter **b o** (or another extended diameter) are outside the mirror. But when arc **o g** is moved, it creates a portion of the mirror where some images of the diameters are on the surface of the mirror, some are outside, and some are inside the mirror. However, the sight does not always grasp which images are on the surface or which are outside; nor is it certain in the perception of these things, except insofar as it senses that they are beyond the visible portion of the sphere. Thus, from the preceding six theorems, it is clear that in the proposed mirrors, the locations of images are determined according to how the images of these mirrors are presented to a single eye.

**34. When the form of a single point reaches both eyes from two points of reflection on the surface of a convex spherical mirror: there is only one image location, and only a single image is seen. Alhazen, Book 5, number 41.**

Let the centers of the two eyes be **a** and **b**, and let the point being seen be **c**. Let **d** be the center of the great circle which cuts both circles that are the common sections of the two surfaces of reflection and the mirror from whose points reflection occurs. Let the portion visible to the eye be **e f**. Let the point of reflection of the form of point **c** to eye **a** be point **g**, and let the point of reflection of the form of point **c** to eye **b** be point **h**. Let the perpendicular of incidence <term>cathetus incidentiae: a line drawn from the object point to the center of the mirror's curvature</term> be drawn from point **c** to the center of the mirror, which is **c d**, cutting the circle at point **o**. Let the line of reflection **a g**, when extended, cut that same perpendicular **c d** at point **k**, and let line **b h** cut it at point **i**. 

First, let both eyes be equally distant from the center of the mirror **d** and from the point of the object being seen, **c**. I say that for both eyes **a** and **b**, although there are two points of reflection (**g** and **h**) for the form of the seen point **c**, only one image is seen because there is only a single image location. For let lines **a d** and **b d** be drawn from the centers of both eyes to the center of the sphere, cutting the mirror at points **l** and **m**. It is clear that these lines are equal; for with the eyes being equally distant from the center of the mirror **d**, it is clear that line **a b** (connecting the centers of the eyes) with both lines **a d** and **b d** contains equal angles by the argument of the 20th theorem of the 3rd book of this work; therefore, by the 6th proposition of the 1st book [of Euclid], lines **a d** and **b d** are equal. If, therefore, the position of point **c** with respect to each eye **a** and **b** is the same, so that line **a c** is equal to line **b c**, then it is clear by the 8th proposition of the 1st book that each of the visual diameters (namely **a d** and **b d**) contains equal angles with the perpendicular **c d**. Therefore, by the 26th proposition of the 3rd book, the mirror arcs **l o** and **m o** are equal. Because the visual diameters **a d** and **b d** cut the arcs from the circles common to the surfaces of the mirror and reflection, and contain equal angles with the perpendicular **c d** at the center **d**, it is clear by the 26th proposition of the 3rd book that those arcs [contain] lines **c d** and **b d** on one side, and on the other, lines **c d**...

Light reflects off the convex mirror surface (arc e-f) at two distinct points, g and h. These reflected rays are extended back (virtual rays) to intersect the central perpendicular line c-d at the same point k. This explains why we see one image instead of two.</image-desc>

-># VITELLO’S OPTICS<-

...and the distances to the two intervening points of reflection, which are **h** and **g**, and the point **o**, are equal by the 26th proposition of the 1st book <note>Vitello refers here to Euclid’s *Elements*, the foundation of medieval geometry.</note>: since the perpendiculars drawn from the center to the points of reflection, which are **d g** and **d h**, contain equal angles with the line **c d**. And because the arcs **h o** and **g o** are equal, and the radii **d h** and **d g** are equal, the lines of reflection—which are **h b** and **g a**—will also be equal by the 4th proposition of the 1st book. This is because they are incident upon the eyes, which are equally distant from the center of the mirror and at equal angles. Similarly, the lines **g c** and **h c** will be equal. The lines **b h** and **a g** must necessarily intersect each other: since the angles are less than two right angles, it is clear by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work that the lines **b h** and **a g** must meet at some point. 

Because the angles of reflection for both eyes are equal—due to the equal distance of both eyes from the point being seen and from the center of the mirror—the angles **c g a** and **c h b** are also equal to each other. It is therefore clear by the 13th and 32nd propositions of the 1st book that the triangle **g c k** is equiangular to the triangle **h c i**, and the line **c h** is equal to the line **c g**. Therefore, by the 4th proposition of the 6th book, the line **h i** is equal to the line **g k**, and the line **c k** is equal to the line **c i**. Thus, points **k** and **i** are actually one and the same point. 

Therefore, the intersection of both lines of reflection, **a g** and **b h**, will occur upon the same point of the cathetus <term>The "cathetus" is the perpendicular line of incidence, drawn from the object through the center of the mirror.</term> with the cathetus of incidence, which is **c d**. At this point, the image will appear to both eyes. Thus, only one single image will be seen, because there is one and the same location for the image. Even if the eyes are not equally distant from the mirror or the object, a single image will still be seen. Although the image of a point for each eye might fall on different points of the perpendicular, this is nevertheless imperceptible <note>Vitello argues that while the math says the two eyes might see the image in slightly different spots, the human eye cannot distinguish such a tiny difference.</note>, because the distance between those points is too small to be noticed. 

The image of any point, regardless of which eye sees it, always maintains the same arrangement of its parts, and because of this, the image appears as a unity. The distance of the seen point from one eye may be slightly greater than from the other, and because of this, the locations of the images are imperceptibly removed from one another; they appear as one because a single "compacted" image is formed from them. This happens because the locations of the image are not totally distant from each other, even if they differ slightly in their parts. Thus, the proposition is clear. However, it can sometimes happen that if the reflected form <note>The "form" (original: *forma*) is the visual information or "species" traveling from the object.</note> falls very obliquely upon one eye, that one form may appear as two because of that obliquity. This occurs when the centers of both eyes are in the same plane of reflection; then the aforementioned angles at the center of the mirror become unequal, and two forms happen to be seen, just as we discussed regarding the "vision of numbers" in the fourth book of this work. But this happens only rarely, and we have said something about this in the 7th theorem of the 5th book.

*35. In a convex spherical mirror, the arrangement of the points of the images for both eyes is the same as the arrangement of the points of the object being seen. Alhazen, Book 5, number 42. Also Book 6, number 4.*

Let two perpendiculars (catheti) be drawn from the endpoints of a line in the object to the center of the mirror. It is clear then that there will be a triangle in which all the images of all the points of that line are contained. If there is a point on that line that does not hold the same position relative to both eyes, the image of the point further from it will be on a diameter further from its diameter, and the image of the closer point on a closer diameter. This is because the image of any point of a seen object will always be seen at the intersection of the line of reflection and the cathetus of incidence drawn from that point to the center of the mirror, as is clear from the 11th theorem of this book. Thus, the position of the parts in the images will be preserved just as the position was in the points seen. If a line is chosen where every point has the same relative position, every point of that line will hold the same position relative to the eyes. If a line is taken that bisects the angle formed by two lines drawn from the centers of the eyes to the seen point, the position of every point on that line, however far extended, is perceived similarly by both eyes as if by one. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*36. In certain positions, it is possible for an object to appear to multiple eyes as a single thing having one image in convex spherical mirrors.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram illustrating Proposition 36. A large circle represents a convex spherical mirror with center point d. At the top of the vertical axis is point c (the object). Let the common section of the surface of reflection and the convex spherical mirror be the circle **a b**, the center of which is **d**. Let point **c** be the point of the object being seen. Let the line **c d** be drawn from the seen point to the center **d**, cutting the circumference of the mirror at point **o**. Let arc **a o** be equal to arc **o b**, and let lines **c a** and **c b** be drawn, which will be equal by the 8th proposition of the 3rd book and by our hypothesis. From point **a**, let the tangent line **f a e** be drawn by the 17th proposition of the 3rd book, and from point **b**, the line **p b q**; then let line **a b** be drawn. 

It is clear then by the 5th proposition of the 1st book that the angles **c a b** and **c b a** are equal. Furthermore, the angles **o a b** and **o b a** (contained by the curved and straight lines) are equal by the 43rd theorem of the 1st book of this work. The angles of contingency <note>original: *anguli contingentiae*; these are the "horn-like" angles between a tangent and the circumference of a circle.</note> **o a e** and **o b p** are also equal by the 16th proposition of the 3rd book. Therefore, there remains the angle **c a e** equal to the angle **c b p**. Thus, upon point **a**, the end of line **c a**, let an angle be constructed equal to angle **c a e** by the 23rd proposition of the 1st book, which shall be **g a c**; and upon point **b**, the end of line **c b**, let an angle be constructed equal to angle **p b c**, which shall be **h b c**. Angle **h b c** will be equal to angle **g a c**. 

With the eyes placed at points **g** and **h**, it is clear by the 20th theorem of the 1st book of this work that the form of point **c** is reflected to both eyes at points **g** and **h**: specifically, to point **g** from point **a**, and to point **h** from point **b**. Let line **g a** also be extended beyond point **a** to the line **c d**, which will meet it according to the 14th theorem of this book, because angles **g a c** and **a c d** are less than two... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, continuing the proof on the next page.</note>

-># BOOK SIX<-

...two right angles: they meet in such a way, namely at point **k**: and the line **l i b** is extended to line **e d**: which will similarly meet by the previous [proposition], and at the same point **k**. Because, as is clear from the preceding statements, line **a c** is equal to line **c b**, and **a d** is equal to **b d** because they are radii, and line **c d** is common to both triangles **a c d** and **b c d**: the angles **a c d** and **d c b** will be equal by Proposition 8 of Book 1 <note>The author cites Euclid’s *Elements* throughout to prove his geometric points.</note>, and angle **g a c**, as is clear from the preceding, is equal to angle **h b c**: but angle **p b c** was also shown to be equal to angle **e a c**: therefore angle **h b q** is equal to angle **g a f** by Proposition 13 of Book 1: but angle **e a k** is equal to angle **g a f**, and angle **p b k** is equal to angle **h b q** by Proposition 15 of Book 1: therefore angle **e a k** is equal to angle **p b k**: thus the total angle **c a k** will be equal to the total angle **c b k**: therefore by Proposition 32 of Book 1, triangles **c a k** and **c b k** are equiangular: therefore by Proposition 4 of Book 6, since **a c** is equal to **b c**, the side **a k** will be equal to side **b k**: they will therefore meet in a single point **k**: since the side **c k** is in both triangles and is equal to itself. But point **k** is the location of the image of point **c**: therefore the location of the image will be the same for both eyes. Thus, whether they are looking at their own face, or see other things reflected from the location of point **c** by points **a** and **b** to the eyes existing at points **g** and **h**, the same thing happens in both cases. The same also happens in the entire circle passing through points **b** and **a**: since at any point of that circle, with the eyes arranged in the manner previously described, the proof is the same. The proposition is therefore clear. But if the angles of reflection are different: then one thing will be seen in different places by the different eyes, and it will produce multiple images. And this must be noted, and was sufficiently clear from the preceding: because those lines of reflection meet at different points on the diameter of the mirror: and for this reason, they establish different locations for the images, as is clear from the 11th proposition of this book. The proposition is therefore clear.

**37.** *In convex spherical mirrors, the distance of the image from the surface of the mirror is less than the distance of the object itself outside. Euclid, 20th theorem of Catoptrics.* <note>Euclid’s *Catoptrics* was the standard classical text on the study of mirrors.</note>

Let the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the convex spherical mirror) be **q h k r**: its center is **z**: and let the line being seen, falling obliquely on the mirror, be **e f**: and let the center of the eye be **b**: and let point **e** be reflected from point **h** of the mirror to the eye **b**, and point **f** from point **q**: and let lines **e h**, **h b**, **f q**, **q b** be drawn: and let the <term>catheti<note>From the Latin *cathetus*, referring to a perpendicular line drawn from a point to a surface or another line.</note></term> **e z** and **f z** be drawn perpendicular to the surface of the mirror: and let line **e z** intersect the circle of the mirror at point **r**: and **f z** at point **k**: and **b h** extended inside the mirror, let it intersect **e z** at point **a**: and let **b q** intersect **f z** at point **g**: and let line **a g** be drawn: which by the 11th proposition of this book will be the image of line **e f**: and let a line touching the circle be drawn from point **h** by Proposition 17 of Book 3, which shall be **h t**: and this line, extended, shall intersect line **e z** at point **t**: and point **t** will be the end of the tangency of line **h t**: and let line **t h** extended beyond **h** intersect line **b g** at point **l**: and from point **t** let a perpendicular be drawn to line **e z** by Proposition 11 of Book 1, which when extended shall intersect line **h** at point **d**, and let it be **t d**. Therefore, because angle **b h l** is equal to angle **e h t** by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work: but also angle **t h a** is equal to angle **b h l** by Proposition 15 of Book 1: therefore angle **e h t** is equal to angle **t h a**: therefore by Proposition 3 of Book 6, the ratio of line **e h** to **h a** is as the ratio of line **e t** to line **t a**: but line **e h** is greater than line **h a**: therefore line **e t** is also greater than **t a**. However, it is clear that line **e h** is greater than line **h a**. For since angle **e t d** is a right angle: angle **e t h** will be greater than a right angle: therefore by Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle **e t h** is greater than angle **a t h**: but also angle **e t h** is greater than angle **e h t** by Proposition 32 of Book 1: but angle **e h t** is equal to angle **a h t**, as is clear from the preceding. Since therefore all the angles of triangle **e t h** taken together are equal to all the angles of triangle **a t h** taken together by Proposition 32 of Book 1: there remains therefore angle **t a h** of triangle **t h a** as being greater than angle **t e h** of triangle **h e t**. In triangle **a e h**, therefore, angle **e a h** is greater than angle **a e h**: therefore in triangle **e a h**, side **e h** is greater than side **h a** by Proposition 19 of Book 1: therefore line **e t** is greater than line **t a**: therefore, by much more, line **e r** is greater than line **r a**: but line **r a** is the distance of the image of point **a** from the surface of the mirror inside the mirror: and line **e r** is the distance of the point being seen, which is **e**, from the surface of the mirror outside the mirror. And if from point **q** a line is drawn touching the circle, which when extended to the <term>cathetus</term> **f z** intersects it at point **m**: and from point **m** a perpendicular is drawn to **f z**, which when extended to **f q** is **m n**: it will similarly be clear that line **f k** is greater than line **k g**. This is therefore the proposition: because if lines are drawn from the middle points of line **e f**, just as from the endpoints, the same will be clear in all their images, which by the 11th proposition of this book all fall on line **a g**. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

Various labels like 'e, f, t, a, r, h, k, g, b, z, d, m, n' mark key points, angles, and intersection points.</image-desc>

...the extended line will be equal to line **i g**. And let line **a y** be extended outside the mirror as far as point **p**: there remains, therefore, angle **i g r** equal to angle **i y p**. Truly, since line **t s** is equal to line **r o**, as was shown above, and **t y** is equal to **t g**: there remains line **g o** equal to line **y s**. Therefore, the two sides **a y** and **y s** are equal to the two sides **a g** and **g o**, and the base **a s** is equal to the base **a o**: therefore, by the 8th proposition of the 1st book <note>Vitello refers here to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 8, which deals with the equality of triangles (SSS congruence).</note>, the angles contained by the equal sides of triangles **a y s** and **a g o** are equal: thus angle **a y s** is equal to angle **a g o**. Consequently, by the 13th proposition of the 1st book, there remains angle **s y p** equal to angle **o g r**: therefore the two angles **i g r** and **o g r** are equal to the two angles **i y p** and **s y p**.

Truly, the line **a s** cuts the convex surface of the mirror: let the point of intersection be **e**: therefore, the three points **e**, **y**, and **d** are on the convex surface of the mirror. Thus, the lines drawn from the center of the mirror (which is **a**) to those three points are equal. Because the triangle **t a s** is entirely in the same surface according to the 2nd proposition of the 11th book, it is clear that these three points **d**, **y**, and **e**, which are on the sides of that triangle, are in the same surface. Therefore, the line **e y d** is, by the 9th proposition of the 3rd book, an arc of a "great circle" <term>great circle: a circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere and shares its center</term> of the mirror's sphere, whose center **a** is the center of the mirror. Moreover, in the surface of reflection, there is the common intersection of the surface of the mirror and the reflection **t s p** according to the 1st proposition of this book: therefore, the form of point **i** is reflected to the eye located at point **s** from the mirror's point **y**, and the location of the image is point **t**. 

Similarly, by dividing angle **n a s** into equal parts by the line **a x** drawn over **q s** to point **x**, and extended outside the mirror's surface to point **æ**, it will be demonstrated in the previously mentioned manner that line **q x** will be equal to line **q m**, line **a x** equal to line **a m**, and line **x s** equal to line **m z**. The two angles **n x æ** and **s x æ** will be equal to the two angles **n m u** and **z m u**. Thus, the form of point **n** will be reflected to the eye located at point **s** from the mirror's point **x**, and the location of the image is point **q**. Just as before, the forms of the two points **n** and **i** are reflected from the two mirror points **x** and **y** to the eye at point **s**: and line **t q** will be the image of line **i n**, and line **t q** is equal to line **i n**. The proposition is therefore clear, as before.

Likewise, if a perpendicular is drawn from point **i** onto line **n a**, it will fall between points **n** and **q**, not outside point **n**. This is because, since by the 42nd theorem of this 1st book angle **i n a** is acute, if it fell outside point **n**, an exterior angle would be made acute to a right angle, and thus larger by the 16th proposition of the 1st book, which is impossible. Therefore, that perpendicular falls short of point **n**: it will thus make a right angle upon line **n q**, which line **i n** will face. Therefore, by the 19th proposition of the 1st book, line **i n** will be greater than that perpendicular: thus that perpendicular will be smaller than line **t q**, which is equal to line **i n**. 

Accordingly, the point of line **n q** where that perpendicular falls (let it be **k**) is reflected to the eye at point **s** from some point of the mirror; the location of its image will be on line **n a** by the 11th proposition of this book. It will be further from the center of the mirror (**a**) and beyond point **q** than point **q** itself is, as is clear by the 17th proposition of this book. For the more distant the points are whose forms are reflected from spherical convex mirrors, the more the locations of the images approach the center of the mirror. But point **i** of that perpendicular is reflected to the eye from the mirror's point **y**, and the location of its image is point **t**. Truly, whatever line is drawn from point **t** to any point of line **n q** beyond **q**, closer to point **n** (such as line **t k**), since it is opposite an obtuse angle, it will be greater than line **t q** by the 19th proposition of the 1st book. Therefore, it will also be greater than line **i n**, which is greater than that perpendicular whose image meets the eye. It is clear, therefore, that the image of that perpendicular will be greater than the perpendicular itself. 

The same thing happens regardless of what line is drawn from point **i** to line **n q** between that perpendicular **i k** and line **i n**; for line **i n** will always be greater than that line by the 47th or 19th proposition of the 1st book. The image of that line will always be greater than line **q t**, and so its image will always be greater than the line itself. This is what was proposed. 

However, these things can be made more clear. Because the form of point **n** is reflected to the eye at point **s** from the mirror's point **m**, and the location of the image is point **q**, it is clear that the line of reflection, which is **z m q**, cuts the circle. Let the point of intersection be **z**. It is clear, then, that a tangent drawn from point **z** to the circle (which is the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror) cannot fall on point **m**; because by the 21st proposition of this book, angle **a m z** must be greater than a right angle, which would contradict the 18th proposition of the 3rd book if line **z m** were tangent to the circle. Nor can it fall on point **z**, because there it cuts and does not touch. Therefore, it will fall on some point of the arc **m e**, and being extended to line **n a**, it will fall higher than point **q**. The point where it falls is called the "endpoint of contingency" <term>endpoint of contingency: the mathematical limit on the mirror's surface beyond which an object's reflection cannot be seen from a specific viewpoint</term>, let it be **n** <note>The author uses 'n' here for the limit point, though 'n' was used earlier for an object point; medieval geometry often reused letters in different contexts of a proof.</note>. This is the "limit of images" (*meta imaginum*), as is clear from the 7th definition of this book. Points existing below that point, which is the limit of images, cannot be reflected to the eye, whereas those higher than it can be reflected. 

Therefore, if the perpendicular drawn from point **i** to line **n q** falls higher than point **n** (the limit of images), that point of line **n q** where the perpendicular falls can be reflected to the eye; and, as was stated, the image of the perpendicular will be larger than the perpendicular itself. But if the perpendicular falls on point **n** itself (the limit of images) or lower than it, then the form of the point where the perpendicular falls will not be reflected; thus there will be no image of the perpendicular. Nevertheless, when the endpoint of contingency is lower than line **i n** and closer to the center, there will be infinite points between the point which is the endpoint of contingency and point **n**, any of which is reflected to the eye. The image of each will be on line **n q**, and for any line drawn from point **i** to any of those points, the image will be greater than the line of which it is the image. Thus, the proposition, sought through long windings, is clearly established.

### 41. *In the same convex spherical mirror, while the center of vision remains unmoved: the image of an object brought closer to the surface of the mirror appears larger, and when moved further away along the same line, it appears smaller.*

For since, as is clear by the 11th proposition of this book, the images of the points of the seen object are seen on the perpendiculars <term>cathetis</term> <note>original: *cathetis*; these are the normal lines perpendicular to the mirror's surface at the point where light hits it.</note> of their incidence, and the images of the seen things are between the perpendiculars of the incidence of their boundaries: indeed, the perpendiculars of the boundary points of an object moved away from the mirror's surface contain a smaller angle, and those of an object brought closer a larger angle, by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work: for a line equal and parallel to the base of a triangle is subtended by a larger angle when it is nearer to the top angle. And since when an object is moved in space, its image is changed in every mirror, as is clear by the 42nd theorem of the 5th book of this work: it is clear that the image of a distant object becomes smaller: whence it also appears smaller: and that of an object near the surface of the mirror becomes larger: whence it also appears larger: because according to the premises in the immediately preceding section, it is seen under a larger angle contained in the center of vision under the lines of reflection of those boundary points of that object, as can be clear by the 34th theorem of the 1st book, and by the 23rd proposition of this book. The proposition is therefore clear. And through these things and through the premise, it can be clear that if there is a ratio of the distance of the seen object from the surface of the larger mirror to the distance from the surface of the smaller mirror, just like the difference of the images, which arise in those mirrors exceeding each other according to the ratio of the diameters of the mirrors: it is possible for an equal image of the same object to be seen in a larger mirror further away from the seen object, and in a smaller mirror closer to the same object, which otherwise would appear larger in the larger mirror and smaller in the smaller mirror, as is clear by the premise. And this is worthy of note.

### 42. *In a convex spherical mirror, the right parts of the seen object appear on the left, and the left on the right. Euclid, 20th theorem of the Catoptrics.*

This requires no other demonstration than that which declares a similar occurrence in plane mirrors: hence it is to be demonstrated in the same way: nor is it necessary to dwell on it otherwise.

45. *For two points of a seen object equally distant from the center of a spherical convex mirror, and unequally distant from the center of sight in the same or different surfaces: the image and the limit of tangency of the point further from the center of sight will be further from the center of the mirror than the image and the limit of tangency of the closer point. ### 46. The image of an arc concentric to a convex spherical mirror (with the visual diameter being perpendicular to the surface of incidence) appears curved, and is always equidistant to the arc of which it is the image. <note>original: Alhaz. 11 n 6; referring to Alhazen's Book 7, Proposition 11.</note>

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram showing an arc ab positioned in front of a convex spherical mirror htz with center g. Lines connect the arc to the center g and to a point d (the eye). The diagram demonstrates how the object arc ab is reflected as a corresponding concentric arc qml within the mirror, showing the preservation of the curve.
</image-desc>

Let **a b** be an arc opposite a convex spherical mirror: in which the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is the circle **h t z**: and let **g** be the center of that arc **a b**, and likewise the center of the mirror: since by hypothesis the arc seen and the mirror are concentric: and let **d** be the center of vision: and let lines **d g**, **a g**, and **b g** be drawn: and let point **e** be taken anywhere on arc **a b**, and let line **e g** be drawn: and thus the surface **a g b** will be the surface of incidence, in which line **e g** will lie: and line **d g** is the visual diameter, which by hypothesis is perpendicular to the surface **a g b**: therefore, by the definition of lines perpendicular to a surface, the angles **d g a**, **d g b**, and **d g e** are right angles and all equal: but also the sides are equal to the sides, since **d g** is equal to itself, and the other sides are equal by the definition of a circle: therefore, by the 4th proposition of the 1st book, the bases of those triangles are equal. All points of the arc **a b** are therefore at the same distance from the center of vision: wherefore the images of all those points will be at the same distance from the center of the mirror by the corollary of the previous proposition. And let **q m l** be the image of arc **a b**: line **g q** will therefore be equal to lines **g m** and **g l**: wherefore, by the 9th proposition of the 3rd book, line **q m l** will be the arc of a circle whose center will be point **g**: its convexity will therefore be with respect to the center **g**, not with respect to the convex surface of the mirror or the place of reflection. And since the curvature of arc **a b** faces the convexity of the mirror's surface, as it is concentric to it by hypothesis, it is clear that the same arc is concentric to its image: therefore, by the 73rd theorem of the 1st book, it is clear that the image is equidistant to the arc seen: since it is always in the surface of incidence: for the image of any point is always on the cathetus of its incidence by the 11th proposition of this book: and all those catheti are in the surface of incidence. Thus, the proposition is clear.

# BOOK SIX

**47. The image of an arc concentric with a convex spherical mirror (when the visual diameter falls obliquely on the surface of incidence) appears curved, and not equidistant to the arc of which it is an image, unless the perpendicular line drawn from the eye falls upon some point of the observed arc. Alhazen, Book 6, Proposition 12.** <note>original: "Alhazen 12 n 6." Witelo is citing the "De Aspectibus" by the Arabic scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen.</note>

Let everything be arranged as in the preceding theorem, except that the visual diameter, which is line **dg**, is not upright but falls obliquely on the surface **abg**. I say that the image of arc **ab** appears curved. For let a perpendicular be drawn from point **d** to this surface by the 11th proposition of the 11th book. Since that perpendicular is shorter than all other lines drawn from point **d** to this surface by the 21st theorem of the 1st book of this work, the right angle which this perpendicular contains toward point **g** will be smaller than any imaginary angle toward point **g** contained by another line drawn from point **d** to that surface by the 16th proposition of the 1st book. Furthermore, a line drawn from point **d** to that surface will be longer the farther it is from the perpendicular, and it will contain a larger angle toward **g**, because it contains a smaller angle toward the perpendicular by the 21st proposition of the 1st book. 

If, therefore, this perpendicular does not fall on the arc **aeb**, but beyond it, then all lines drawn from point **d** to this arc will be slanted in one direction, and those farther away will be longer and contain a larger angle toward point **g** than those closer to the perpendicular. If, then, three points are taken on the arc **ab**, which are **e**, **c**, and **b**, and the limit of tangency <note>The "limit of tangency" refers to the point where the line of sight is tangent to the mirror's surface during reflection.</note> for point **b** is **l**, and the limit of tangency for point **c** is **m**: it is clear by the 45th proposition of this book that because point **c** is closer to the eye **d** than point **b**, point **m** will be closer to the center **g** than point **l**. However, lines **gb** and **gc** are equal by hypothesis and the definition of a circle. Therefore, line **cm** is longer than **bl**. 

Now, let **q** be the image of point **c**, and **f** be the image of point **b**. Let line **qt** be drawn, and let lines **cb** and **ml** be drawn, which will certainly meet if extended. Therefore, lines **cb** and **ml** meet at point **o**. And since by the 12th proposition of this book the ratio of line **gc** to **gq** is as the ratio of line **cm** to **mq**, it will be, by the 16th proposition of the 5th book, alternately the ratio of **gc** to **cm** is as **gq** to **mq**. Similarly, it will be **gb** to **bl** as **gf** to **fl**. Therefore, by the 124th theorem of the 1st book of this work, since the lines **gc** and **gb** joined at an angle are divided proportionally, and from the points of the sections lines are drawn that meet (namely **co** and **mo**), it is clear that line **qt** will meet with lines **cb** and **ml**, and their meeting point will be at point **o**. 

Furthermore, let the limit of tangency for point **e** be **n**. And since point **n**, by the 45th proposition of this book, is lower than point **m**, it will be, as before, that line **en** is longer than line **cm**. Therefore, having extended lines **ec** and **nm**, it is clear, as before, that they will meet;

Let the straight line being seen be **ab**, and let the center of the convex spherical mirror be **g**. Let the center of vision be **d**, located outside the surface. ### 50. For a straight line not parallel to the mirror, which if extended would not touch or cut the surface of the convex spherical mirror (when the eye is not in the surface of incidence), the image appears curved. Alhazen, Book 6, Proposition 15.

Let everything be arranged as in the preceding, except that line **ab** is not parallel to the mirror, nor does it touch or cut the mirror, but is merely oblique to it. It is clear then that the extended lines **gb** and **ga** are unequal. This can also be easily shown through the midpoints of arc **ae** and line **ab**. The proposition is therefore clear; and line **ab** being cut from any of its parts, the demonstration is always the same as before.
