### 52. *The image of a straight line which, when extended, would intersect the circle (which is the common section of the surface of incidence and the surface of a convex spherical mirror) but not through the center—while the sight is not located in the surface of incidence—appears curved. Alhazen, Book 6, Theorem 17.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with center G. A series of lines extend from points A and B towards the circular surface, reflecting towards a point D (representing the eye). Various points on the circle and lines are labeled with letters including E, H, Z, F, and X.</image-desc>

Keeping the previous arrangement, let line **a b**, when extended, intersect circle **e h z** (which is the common section of the surface of incidence and the mirror) at point **e**. Let the point of reflection for the form <note>In medieval science, "form" (forma) refers to the visual appearance or "species" of an object as it travels to the eye.</note> of point **b** to the point of sight **l** be point **f**. Let **m** be the endpoint of the tangency of the line that is tangent to circle **e h z** at point **f** and extended to line **b g**. Therefore, **b** will be reflected to **d** from some point on arc **h p**, just as was established in the preceding proposition. Furthermore, the arc from that point of reflection to point **h** is either equal to, greater than, or less than arc **h e**. If it is equal, since by the previous arguments that arc is equal to arc **h f**—because tangent lines extended from point **m** reach equal arcs according to the 59th theorem of Book 1 of this work <note>Witelo frequently cites his own first book, which serves as a mathematical and geometric primer for his optical theories.</note>. Therefore, let **q** be the point on the circle where the tangent drawn from point **m** falls on the side of **e**. Thus, line **a e** passes through point **q**; and so line **q** <note>The text likely implies the tangent line through q.</note> intersects line **a e** across point **e**, since both points **e** and **q** are on the circumference of the circle and are the same point. If, however, that arc is smaller than arc **h e**, the line **q m** will intersect line **a e** beyond point **q**, so that it intersects it at point **t**, forming a triangle by drawing line **e q**. If, however, that arc is greater than arc **h e**, line **m q** will intersect line **a e** before point **q**. Whichever of these occurs, the proof of the preceding proposition is repeated, and it will be proved in exactly the same way that the image of line **a b** is curved. Which is what was proposed.

### 53. *The image of a straight line which, when extended, passes through the center of the circle (which is the common section of the surface of incidence and a convex spherical mirror)—whether the center of sight is in that same surface or outside it, provided it is not on that line—always appears straight. Alhazen, Book 6, Theorem 18.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with center G. A line containing points A and B passes directly through the center G. A point D, representing the eye, is located off this axis, with lines of sight drawn to the points on the line A-B.</image-desc>

Let everything be arranged as in the preceding sections, except that up to now we have spoken of the properties of these lines when the sight is not in the surface of incidence; now we assume the sight is sometimes in the surface of incidence, located at point **d** as before. Let line **g d** be drawn, and let line **a b**, when extended, meet circle **e h z** while passing through its center **g**. It is clear, therefore, that the angle of those lines **a g** and **d g** falls upon **g**, the center of the mirror; and the image of line **a b** will be seen as a single straight line. Indeed, the image of any point on that line **a b**, since it is arranged on the cathetus <term>cathetus|the perpendicular line drawn from a point to the surface of a mirror; the image always appears somewhere along this line</term> of its incidence, will appear on line **a b** itself when extended to the center **g**, according to the 11th theorem of this book. Therefore, the image of that entire line will be straight, just as line **a b** itself, when extended, is a straight line. Thus the proposition is clear.

Alhazen, Book 6, Theorem 19.*

If this is the case, the image of this slanted line **a b** will not be seen except according to that single point **b**. ### 55. *In a straight line inclined away from the center of the circle (which is the common section of the surface of incidence and the spherical convex mirror), with the center of sight located in the same surface of incidence—such that the inclination of the line is toward the side of the sight—whether it touches the surface of the mirror or not, the image of no point is seen. Alhazen, Book 6, Proposition 20.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a convex mirror segment (arc) with center point g. Line segments d-h and d-g extend from a point d (vision). A line a-b represents the object. Point h is on the mirror's surface.</image-desc>

Let the arrangement be as above, and let line **a b** be taken as inclined as proposed. Let its inclination be on the side of the sight **d**. I say that no point of that line will be seen. For suppose that some point of that line could be reflected from some point of the arc lying between the line of reflection (not blocked by the body of the line lying between the sight and the mirror) and the line **d g** drawn from the center of sight to the center of the mirror. Let line **a b** be drawn from that point to the chosen point on the arc; this line will therefore intersect the line of reflection, and the point of intersection would be reflected to the sight from two points of the mirror, which is impossible. 

If, however, it is said that a point chosen on line **a b** is reflected from a point of the circle's arc which is beneath that line **a b**, this will be impossible because that entire arc is hidden by the line interposed between the sight and the mirror, which cuts off all the lines of reflection of its points. Furthermore, according to this arrangement, the sight is on the side of the smaller angle of the oblique line incident to the mirror, but reflection only occurs on the side of the larger angle, as is clear from the 33rd theorem of the 5th book of this work. It is therefore not possible for any of the points of that line to be reflected to the sight so situated. Therefore, the image of no point of that line **a b** is seen. This is what was proposed.

### 56. *In an oblique straight line not touching the surface of a convex spherical mirror, with the sight existing in the surface of incidence such that the slant of the line is toward the side away from the sight, a small amount of the image is seen, and the image will always be curved. Tangent line l-c-m is shown at the point of reflection.</image-desc>

For let line **d b** be drawn over the surface of the mirror, falling upon point **c** of circle **e h z** (which is the common section of the surface of incidence and the surface of the mirror). From point **c**, let a line tangent to the circle be drawn (by Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 17), which shall be **l c m**. Upon the endpoint **c** of line **m c**, let an angle be made equal to angle **d c l** by line **c f** intersecting line **a b** at point **f**. It is therefore clear that the form of point **f** is reflected to the sight **d** from point **c** (by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work), and the location of the image will be on line **f g**. Similarly, the form of point **b**, since it has no obstacle, will be reflected to the sight from some point of the mirror, and the location of its image will be on line **b g** (by the 11th proposition of this book). Because of the interposition of the solid line **f b**, other points of line **a b** cannot be reflected to the sight, except for the points of line **b f**. The images of all these points fall on the line drawn between the intersection points of the lines of reflection for points **b** and **f** and the catheti **b g** and **f g**. Since this is a very small area, it is clear that only a small part of the image of line **a b** is seen. This is what was proposed. ### 57. *When the sight exists in the surface of incidence of a straight line which does not meet the surface of a spherical convex mirror, but is parallel to the line lying between the center of the mirror and the sight, or meets it outside the mirror on the side of the sight: the image will appear curved.*

58. *Every arc of a circle, in whose surface of incidence the center of sight is located, always appears as a curved image within a convex spherical mirror.*
<margin>*Alhazen book 4, chapter 3, number 6.* <note>Vitello frequently cites "Alhazen" (Ibn al-Haytham), whose work *Perspectiva* was the foundation for this text.</note></margin>

Let the arc of sight be **a b**: and let the center of the mirror be point **g**: and the center of sight be point **d**: and let this center of sight be in the surface of incidence, which is **a b g**. I say that the image of arc **a b** always appears curved when it is seen perceptibly within the mirror. For let the <term>chord</term> <note>A straight line connecting the two endpoints of an arc.</note> **a b** be drawn: and it is clear from the preceding propositions that the image of the chord **a b**, according to its every position with respect to the mirror, always appears curved; except only then, when it is on the cathetus of incidence of one of its extremities: as when it is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, passing through its center: for then its image appears straight, as is evident through the 53rd [proposition] of this book.

However, it is impossible for the arc **a b** to be on the cathetus of incidence of its own extremities, since every one of its points has a different cathetus of incidence. Therefore, the image of an arc arranged in such a way will never be seen as a straight line: because the locations of the images of the various points are always on different catheti. Indeed, the curvature of the images can easily be concluded according to the method which we used previously for straight lines: and the 45th [proposition] of this book will assist in this. The proposal is therefore clear.

### 60. Of curved images, that of the same seen arc farther from the center of a convex spherical mirror appears more curved.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a convex mirror segment and its center point g. Two arcs are shown: one representing an object 'a e b' and another representing its image. Rays (catheti) are drawn from the center g through the endpoints and midpoint of the object arc.</image-desc>

Let *a b* be the seen arc, whose midpoint is *e*: and let the image of this arc be curved: and let its <term>chord</term> <note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on the arc.</note> be the straight line *a b*: and let the center of the mirror be *g*. I say that as the line *a b* approaches the mirror, its image becomes of lesser curvature, and as it recedes, it becomes of greater curvature. For let the <term>catheti</term> <note>Lines drawn from the object points through the center of the spherical mirror.</note> *a g* and *b g* be drawn, in which the locations of the images of points *a* and *b* will be, through the 11th [proposition] of this book. Therefore, because as the straight line *a b* approaches the surface of the mirror, angle *a g b* becomes larger, and as it recedes, angle *a g b* becomes smaller through the 34th theorem of the 1st book of this work: but the image of point *e* when further elongated from the center of the mirror becomes closer to the center of the mirror, and the image of the same point when approaching the mirror becomes further from the center through the 23rd theorem of this book: and the outermost points of that image are always on the catheti *a g* and *a b*: it is clear, therefore, that the image of arc *a b* when further from the center of the mirror is more compressed, and when closer it is more expanded: and according to this, the manner of its curvature is varied in the proposed way. Since the image of that which is farther from the center of the mirror becomes more curved, and of that which is closer becomes less curved: because it always becomes part of a larger circle when approaching the center of the mirror, and becomes part of a smaller circle when receding from the center: and the size of said images varies according to the amount of that approach and recession. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 61. Every image meeting the sight on the surface of a convex spherical mirror always appears convex. <note>original: "Euclides 23. th. catoptr."; Euclid, Theorem 23 of the Catoptrics.</note>

Let there be a convex spherical mirror *a g*: and let the center of sight be *e*: and let there be a straight or curved seen line, which is *d k*: in which points *b* and *i* are marked, and let it be that the locations of the images of these points are on the surface of the mirror itself, with the <term>lines of incidence</term> <note>The path the light takes from the object to the mirror.</note> being those which are *d a*, *b c*, *i z*, and *k g*: and the <term>lines of reflection</term> <note>The path the light takes from the mirror to the eye.</note> being *a e*, *c e*, *z e*, and *g e*. If, therefore, any of those lines of reflection is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror: it is clear through the 72nd theorem of the 1st book of this work that it will pass through the center of the mirror: therefore by <margin>the 8th [proposition] of the 3rd [book of Euclid] or by the 21st theorem of the 1st book of this work</margin> that line will be the shortest of all those lines of reflection, and those closer to it are shorter than those further away. It is clear, therefore, that the image appears curved: because some part of it is closer to the sight, and some further away. The same thing also happens if none of those lines of reflection is perpendicular to the mirror's surface: because when a perpendicular line is drawn from point *e* to the surface of the mirror through the 11th [proposition] of the 11th [book of Euclid]: it is clear that all lines of reflection closer to that perpendicular are shorter than those further away: and thus likewise the image of a straight or curved line, which is *d k*, meeting the sight on the surface of the mirror, always appears curved. And since it is to be demonstrated in the same way for any image appearing on the surface of the mirror: the proposition is therefore clear.

### 62. The image of a curved line whose concavity faces the surface of a convex spherical mirror sometimes appears straight. <note>original: "Alhazen 23 n 6"; Referring to the work of the physicist Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen, Book 6, section 23.</note>

For let its straight chord be drawn, which is *a c*: and it is clear through several of the preceding propositions of this book that in some position the image of that straight line appears curved with a curvature facing the center of the mirror. Therefore, because the ends of the curved line *a b c*, which are *a* and *c*, are seen at the ends of the image of the straight line *a c*: let it be imagined that a chord is stretched within the mirror under that curved image of the straight line *a c*. If, therefore, this should happen, which is possible, that the curvature of the arc itself (which is *a b*) be similar to the curvature of the image of its chord, so that its <term>versed sines</term> <note>A trigonometric term referring to the distance from the center of an arc to the center of its chord.</note> on both sides are simi-

->**BOOK SIX**<-

...visible: it is clear by the 2nd and 45th propositions of this book that the image of the curved line, which is *a b c*, will be a straight line, stretched like a <term>chord</term> <note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on an arc.</note> across the curved image itself. Therefore, the image of the curved line *a b c* will appear as a straight line. This is what was proposed. This is also clear in another way: for since, as was said in the next preceding proposition, every image meeting the sight on the surface of a convex spherical mirror always appears convex, facing the center of the mirror with its concavity, and the image of the same arc falling within the mirror faces the center of the mirror with its concave side. Since, in reflections of this kind, one does not move from one extreme to the other without a middle point, and the surfaces of the parts of the same image are continuous: it is clear that in some position, that image must have a straight arrangement. And because all the locations of the images of the points of that arc fall into a single straight line—though it would be long and useless to seek out the exact position of the sight, the object seen, and the mirror—the way to seek it will nevertheless be simple and clear from the preceding premises to anyone who wishes to do so. In this way, therefore, it happens that a circle sometimes appears like a semicircle and a diameter, and from a portion of a circle, a reversed portion is formed, so that the image of a straight line becomes curved, and that of a curved line becomes straight. And sometimes both appear curved in the same direction, if the curvature of the arc to the sight is less than the curvature of the image of its chord; and sometimes they appear in different directions, like the surface enclosed by the intersection of two unequal circles. There is a great diversity among these images, which we leave to be investigated by the diligent skill of the reader based on the principles established above. Thus, in these mirrors, the image of a straight line appears curved, and the image of a curved line always appears curved, though sometimes it appears straight to the sight. And what we have shown regarding lines also happens in the case of plane, concave, and convex surfaces through the lines that exist on those surfaces; the result is exactly the same for the lines of their length and width. If, however, a long curved body with a small width is presented to the sight in these mirrors, the curvature of that body will appear clearly, since it can be discerned by those things that are above, around, or below the body. For a curvature that is not great is not well discerned when the extremities of its length and width are hidden; hence, in a body of slight convexity and great size, its convexity is not well discerned, even though its image is convex, since the boundaries of the body in length or width do not appear—boundaries which help significantly in the perception of convexity.

### 63. *From the surface of a convex spherical mirror composed of different spherical surfaces, the reflected forms of a monstrous image are seen.*

Because the centers of different spherical surfaces are different, and the location of the image of any point in convex spherical mirrors is (by the 11th proposition of this book) on the <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "catheto"; the perpendicular line from the object point to the center of the sphere.</note> of its incidence, drawn from the seen point to the center of the mirror; and because these centers are varied in irregular mirrors of this kind, it is clear that the forms of different points are drawn out in different directions. And since reflection occurs from the whole surface, and the reflected points are varied according to their locations rather than the same arrangement, it is clear that the whole image, which is gathered and united from the locations of such points, receives a disordered arrangement of its parts. Therefore, the image in such mirrors appears <term>monstrous</term> <note>In this context, "monstrous" (monstruosa) refers to a distorted or unnaturally deformed image rather than something frightening.</note>: there is a uniform extension of some of its parts according to the uniform extension of those surfaces, while other parts are deformed by others. Hence, some parts of the image are pulled in length, some in width, and some crosswise, according as some parts of the mirror's surface face different centers of different spheres. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 64. *It is possible for the image of the same point to be seen through as many convex spherical mirrors as one might wish. Euclid, Theorem 15 of the Catoptrics.*

Let the arrangement be made here that was described in the 61st theorem of Book 5 regarding plane mirrors: let *a* be the center of sight and *b* the seen point. For example’s sake, let an equilateral and equiangular polygon be described, which shall be *a b g d e*. At points *g*, *d*, and *e*, let there be convex spherical mirrors touching the points of equal angles. Let tangent lines be imagined touching the mirrors at those same points—for example, at point *g*, the line *l k*. Since the angle *b g k* is equal to the angle *d g l*, it is clear by the 20th theorem of Book 5 that the form of point *b* will be reflected from point *g* to point *d*; and by the same reasoning from point *d* to point *e*, and from point *e* to point *a*. This, then, is what was proposed.

Lines connect these points in sequence from 'b' to 'g' to 'd' to 'e' to 'a'. Tangent lines are drawn at vertices 'g', 'd', and 'e', labeled with 'l', 'k', and 'h' to show the surfaces of reflection. The entire construction is enclosed within a circular boundary.</image-desc>

### 65. *It is impossible to ignite a fire from the surface of a single convex spherical mirror; however, it is possible from a combination of several.*

Since, as was shown in the 15th proposition of this book, the lines of reflection of the form of the same point from different points of the same convex spherical mirror are not parallel, nor do they converge in the center of a single sight; therefore, neither solar rays nor any others incident upon the surface of this mirror can ever converge at any single point, but rather are dispersed in the medium itself. Thus, those rays, even when gathered, can never in any way ignite a body, no matter how combustible it may be, as they are reflected from the surface of a single mirror. However, by a combination of several mirrors, something of this kind could be achieved, so that from one point of each of those mirrors, one ray would be reflected to a single point, converging with the rays of the other mirrors. In this way, the action of the rays at that point would be strengthened, and the number of rays and the union or gathering of power would correspond to the number of mirrors. Such a combination of mirrors, however, would be more difficult than useful; therefore, we do not believe it worthy to insist on such a work. Thus, the proposition is clear.

# THE SEVENTH BOOK OF THE OPTICS
## OF VITELLO, SON OF THE
### THURINGIANS AND POLES.

<note>Decorative historiated initial 'O' containing a woodcut scene of a figure sitting in a landscape with trees.</note> The sequence of the real order reminds us that, having traversed as best we could the specific properties of plane and convex spherical mirrors, we should now turn our attention to the properties of cylindrical <note>original: "columnariu̅"</note> and pyramidal mirrors. For some of the properties of these mirrors are established from or composed of the properties of the mirrors previously discussed, just as the shapes of these mirrors are in some way composed of the shapes of those preceding mirrors. For a cylindrical mirror, being a part of a round column (as we declared in the 8th, 14th, and 15th theorems of our fifth book), is clearly formed—according to what was set forth in the first book of this science and in the principles of the 11th book of Euclid—by the passage of a rectangle <note>original: "quadrilateri rectanguli"</note> which, with one of its sides fixed, is rotated with the others moved around until it returns to the place from which it began its motion. A pyramidal mirror <note>In medieval geometry, "pyramidal" often referred to cones as well as pyramids.</note> is likewise caused by the motion of a right-angled triangle, one of whose sides containing the right angle is fixed, and the other two are rotated in the manner previously described until they are led back to the place from which they began to move. Therefore, because both of these mirrors have their origin in the motion of straight lines, it is clear that they do not escape the specific properties of straight lines. However, insofar as those lines cause circular shapes when they are rotated in a circle, these mirrors commonly follow circular properties—that is, spherical ones, whose origin is the circle. This appears most evidently in cylindrical mirrors, as we shall manifest in the progress of this work. But the properties specific to these mirrors, such as those which happen according to acute-angled sections <term>ellipses</term> <note>original: "oxygonias sectiones." Vitello uses the ancient term for ellipses, which are formed by cutting a cylinder or cone at an angle.</note>, which belong only to these mirrors (whether they be convex or concave), happen in them from a certain common nature of straight lines and motion. Therefore, these mirrors receive a later order than plane and convex spherical mirrors. We shall proceed with these convex cylindrical and pyramidal mirrors before any concave or spherical ones, because of the simplicity of the properties of convex mirrors compared to concave ones, and because the former descend into the latter. Those things which we set forth first are these:

->DEFINITIONS.<-

1. We call a convex or concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror "greater" if it is part of a larger column or pyramid, and "lesser" if it is part of a smaller one.
2. We call the "axis of a cylindrical or pyramidal mirror" the axis of that column or pyramid of which the mirror is a part.
3. We call the "bases of the proposed mirrors" the bases of their respective columns or pyramids.
4. We call the "visual diameter" the line drawn from the center of sight perpendicular to the surface of the mirror and extended to the axis; and this same line is called the "vertical line <term>cathetus</term> of reflection."
5. The "vertical line <term>cathetus</term> of incidence" is called, as before, the perpendicular line drawn from the point of the thing seen to the line which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror: namely, onto the straight line which is the line of the mirror's length, or onto the circle, or onto the acute-angled section <note>ellipse</note>, according to which of these lines the reflection proceeds from.
6. The "limit of tangency" is called the point in which one of the vertical lines <term>catheti</term> cuts the line touching the mirror at the point of reflection according to a circle or an acute-angled section.
7. We call the "boundary of places" <note>original: "metam locorum"</note>, as in spherical mirrors, the point or line beyond which images are not seen.

->THEOREMS.<-

1. *When a convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirror is placed opposite the sight and erected perpendicularly, so that the sight is not on the surface of the mirror or continuous with it: a straight line drawn from the center of sight [meets] with the axis of the mirror in the*

# BOOK SEVEN.

*With the vertex holding an acute angle: reflection to the eye occurs only from the part of the mirror's surface lying between the tangent surfaces drawn from the center of sight to the surface of the mirror. Alhazen, Book 4, [proposition] 35.*

This, which is proposed here, applies universally to a convex cylindrical <note>original: "columnari"</note> mirror, whether the visual line falls upon it at a right angle or an acute angle: for as was shown through the 78th theorem of our 4th book, always less than half of the cylindrical surface is visible to the eye, and reflection to the eye occurs only from that part. Furthermore, this surface of the cylindrical mirror is contained by two surfaces produced from the center of sight, touching the cylinder along the lines of longitude <note>Lines running the length of the cylinder</note>. And since the method of demonstrating this property is the same in both of the opposing mirrors—though more difficult in the pyramidal ones—it is sufficient, for the sake of example, for the proposition to be demonstrated in pyramidal <note>In this context, "pyramidal" refers to a cone. Conical mirrors were a standard part of catoptrics (the study of reflection).</note> mirrors. Let there be, therefore, a convex pyramidal mirror, whose axis is *a d*, and its vertex *a*: let the diameter of the base be *c h*, and the center of the base *d*. Let this pyramid be standing upright upon the surface of the horizon, so that it is not tilted; and let the center of sight be *b*. Let the line *b a*, produced from the center of sight to the vertex of the mirror, meet the axis of the given pyramid, forming an acute angle with it, which is *d a b*. I say that reflection to the eye occurs only from that part of the conical surface of this pyramid which lies between the tangent surfaces drawn from the center of sight to the surface. For let us imagine a surface proceeding from the center of sight which cuts the pyramid orthogonally <note>at a right angle</note> through the axis: and it is clear through the 100th theorem of our 1st book that the common section of that surface and the surface of the pyramid will be a circle parallel to the base of the pyramid. Let that circle be *f g*: and from the center of sight let two lines, *b f* and *b g*, be drawn touching that circle, according to [Euclid] Book 3, proposition 17. Through the 101st theorem of our 1st book, let two lines of longitude of the pyramid be drawn from points *f* and *g*, which are *e f a* and *n g a*. It is therefore clear that the surface in which the lines *e f a* and the line *b f* lie will touch the pyramid. For if it were said that it cuts the pyramid and does not touch it, it is clear that the line *b f*, which is in that surface, would cut the circle *f g* and not touch it; but it was drawn as a tangent: therefore, for it to cut is impossible. That surface will therefore touch the pyramid. And it must be shown similarly for the surface in which the lines *n g a* and *b g* lie, that it also touches the pyramid. Therefore, the surface of the pyramid lying between these two tangent surfaces will be visible to the eye, and reflection to the eye will occur only from this part: because, as shown in the 16th theorem of our 2nd book, the longest radius reaching the circle of a round cylinder or pyramid is like a tangent line. The proposition is therefore clear, since it is to be demonstrated similarly in a cylindrical mirror.

*2. If from the center of the eye to the lines which are the boundaries of the surfaces of convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirrors appearing to the sight, two surfaces of reflection are produced: it is necessary that the mirror be touched by both of them. Alhazen, Book 4, [proposition] 26.*

For example, let there be a convex cylindrical mirror, which is *d f e g*, and let there be two lines of longitude, which are *d e* and *f g*: and let those lines be the boundaries of the surface of the cylinder mirror appearing to the sight, as is clear from the premise and by the 78th theorem of our 4th book. Let the center of sight be *a*: and with the lines *a d, a f, a g, a e* produced, there will be the triangular surfaces *a d e* and *a f g*. I say that those surfaces will touch the cylinder. For if it were said that one of them cuts the cylinder, such as surface *a d e*, it is clear that that section will be upon the line of longitude *d e*, in which that surface falls: and the procedure would be similar if surface *a f g* were to cut the cylinder, and the section were upon line *f g*. Let it be, then, that a plane surface passing through the center of sight cuts the cylinder parallel to the bases; and by the 100th theorem of our 1st book, the common section of that surface and the mirror will be a circle, which becomes *b c*: this therefore passes through the two lines of longitude *d e* and *f g*. Let the lines *a b* and *a c* be drawn to this circle. Since these are in those surfaces cutting the surface of the cylinder, they will cut the circle *b c*: therefore, less of arc *b c* would be seen than that which is contained under the lines touching the circle *b c* drawn from the center of sight, namely point *a*, which is contrary to what was declared in the 51st theorem of our 4th book; and it must be declared similarly regarding the bases of the cylinder. Therefore, those surfaces would not be produced to the boundaries of the surface of the cylinder appearing to the sight, but falling short of them: which is contrary to the hypothesis. The same is also to be demonstrated regarding pyramidal mirrors: and the same impossibility follows as before, through the 84th theorem of our 4th book: which is contrary to the hypothesis. The proposition is therefore clear.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a vertical cylinder with lines of longitude d-e and f-g. Point 'a' represents the viewer's eye, with lines of sight forming triangles a-d-e and a-f-g that are tangent to the sides of the cylinder. A circular cross-section b-c illustrates the arc of the cylinder visible to the viewer.</image-desc>

*3. The common section of all surfaces produced from the sight, tangent to a convex cylindrical mirror, is a line passing through the center of sight parallel to the axis of that mirror. Alhazen, Book 4, [proposition] 26.*

What is proposed here is evident. For let the axis of the convex cylindrical mirror <note>original: "speculi columnaris conuexi"</note> be *h k i*: and the upper base of the cylinder be circle *f d*, whose center is *h*: and the lower base be circle *g e*, whose center is *i*: and let the common section of some surface of reflection and the surface of the cylindrical mirror be the circle *b l*, whose center is *k*. Since, therefore, the axis *h i*, which is perpendicular <note>original: "orthogonalis"</note> to the bases (as is clear through the 92nd theorem of the 1st book of this work), it is also perpendicular to the circle *b l* through the 100th and 23rd theorems of the 1st book: and by the same reasoning, the lines of the cylinder’s length <note>term: "lineae longitudinis" (lines of longitude), which are straight lines running along the height of the cylinder.</note> *d e* and *f g* are perpendicular to the circle *b l*. Therefore, the surfaces touching <note>original: "contingentes"; tangent surfaces.</note> the cylinder along those lines *d e* and *f g* will be erected over the circle *b l* through [Euclid's Elements] Book 11, Proposition 18: and therefore also over the surface of reflection, which cuts the cylinder along that circle *b l*. Therefore, by Book 11, Proposition 19, the common section of those surfaces touching the cylinder will be perpendicular to that surface of reflection. Therefore, by Book 11, Proposition 6, the common section of those surfaces will be parallel to the axis of the cylinder, which is erected perpendicularly over that same surface. Moreover, those surfaces intersect each other at the center of sight: since the center of sight exists in all of them, as is clear from the hypothesis regarding the plane surfaces touching the proposed mirror, and regarding the surface of reflection from the 27th theorem of the 5th book of this work. Thus, what was proposed is clear.

### 4. To whatever point marked on the visible surface of a convex cylindrical or conical <note>original: "pyramidalis"; in medieval optics, "pyramidal" often refers to cones as well as pyramids.</note> mirror a straight line is drawn from the center of sight: that line, when extended, will necessarily cut the mirror. Alhazen, Book 4, Number 27.

Let the arrangement be in every way as the preceding: and let point *q* be marked in the portion of the mirror visible to the sight, which is *e d f g*: and let the line *a q* be produced. I say that line *a q*, when extended, will necessarily cut the mirror. For let a line of the cylinder's length be produced from point *q*, which shall be *q m*, according to the 101st theorem of the 1st book of this work: this line will therefore be parallel to both lines of length *d e* and *f g* through the 92nd theorem of the 1st book, and [Euclid] Book 11, Prop 6, and Book 1, Prop 30. Let it also be that some surface of reflection cuts the cylinder beyond point *q* according to the circle *b l* through the 100th theorem of the 1st book. The line *q m* will therefore necessarily pass through the circle of the section, which is *b l*, cutting it at a point: let that point be *p*: and let the line *a p* be drawn. This line, because it falls between the lines drawn from the center of sight *a* to the circle *b l* which touch it (which are *a b* and *a l*), will clearly cut the circle. Therefore also the surface extended from the center of sight to the surface of the mirror, in which are the lines *a p* and *a q*, will cut the mirror: because that surface will cut the surface of the cylindrical mirror along the line of length, which is *m q*. It is clear, therefore, that line *a q*, when extended, will cut the mirror: and the same is clear in the same way for any other given point. In convex conical <note>original: "pyramidalibus"</note> mirrors, it is to be demonstrated in the same way, by drawing a line from the vertex of the cone to any point given on the surface of that mirror. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 5. Every plane surface touching the mirror along any line of length on the surface of a convex cylindrical or conical mirror visible to the eye, cuts the surfaces produced from the sight which touch the boundaries of the visible portion: and all those surfaces are extended between the eye and the surface of the mirror. Alhazen, Book 4, Number 27.

Let the previous arrangement remain: and let some plane surface touch the visible surface of the mirror along the line of length, which is *m o*, through the 95th theorem of the 1st book: and let the surface of reflection be drawn, which is *a b l*: and in it, let the line touching the circle *b l* at point *p* be drawn, which is *s p t*. It is clear, therefore, that line *s p t* will cut lines *a b* and *a l*. For let line *p l* be drawn. Since, therefore, line *s p t* cuts angle *a p l*, it is clear through the 29th theorem of the 1st book that it will cut line *a l*. Similarly, line *p b* being drawn, it is clear that line *s p* will cut line *a b*: it is clear, therefore, that lines *a l* and *p t* will meet. But line *p t* is in the surface touching the cylinder along the line of length *m o*: while line *a l* is in the surface touching the cylinder along the line of length *d e*, which is the boundary of the visible portion. Thus the first part of the proposition is clear. But also all such surfaces, such as the surface in which line *s t* lies, are extended between the eye and the surface of the mirror. And concerning the surface of the mirror, it is clear, since those surfaces are tangent to the surface of the mirror itself and do not cut it: but it is also clear regarding the center of sight. For let point *n* be the nearest markable point below point *b*, on the arc *l b*: and imagine some surface touching the surface of the cylinder on the line of length in which point *n* lies: this will therefore necessarily cut the surface of reflection, which is *a b l*: since it is perpendicular to it by Book 11, Proposition 18. Therefore, let the common section of the surface of reflection *a b l* and the said surface be the straight line *n r*. It is clear, therefore, through the premises, that line *n r* touches the circle *b n* at point *n*: but point *n* is lower <note>original: "demissius"; further down the arc.</note> than point *b*:

6. *Every surface of reflection in which there is a line tangent to the base of a convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirror and a line of longitude <note>term: "linea longitudinis" (line of longitude); in geometry, this refers to a straight line drawn along the surface of a cylinder or cone from top to bottom.</note> of the same mirror: it is necessary that it is tangent to the same mirror along its line of longitude.*

This is clear by the method of the 2nd theorem of this book, since the demonstration of this and that are the same. For, using the preceding figure, let the surface of reflection be *g a f*, in which let line *z f* be tangent to the column <note>The author uses "column" (columna) and "cylinder" interchangeably.</note> or pyramid at point *f*, and let the line of longitude of the column or pyramid be *g f*. I say that this surface of reflection will be tangent to the column or pyramid. For if it were granted that this surface cuts the column or pyramid of the mirror, then line *z f* would cut the base of that mirror, which is contrary to the hypothesis. The proposition is therefore evident.

7. *When a convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirror is placed opposite the sight, so that the center of sight is not on the surface of the column or pyramid, and the point of the object being seen is with the sight in the same surface that cuts the mirror through its axis: the common section <note>term: "communis fectio" (common section); the line or shape formed where two surfaces intersect.</note> of the surface of reflection and the visible surface of the mirror will be the line of longitude of the mirror; and if that common section is a line of longitude, the surface of reflection cuts the mirror through the axis. Alhazen, Book 4, [Proposition] 29.*

<image-desc>Geometrical diagram of a cylinder (speculum columnare) illustrating catoptric principles. The cylinder is labeled with an axis h-i and surface points f, g, d. Lines of reflection and tangency are drawn from a point f to the axis and through the cylinder's volume.</image-desc>

Let there be a convex cylindrical mirror whose axis is *h i*, and whose surface visible to the sight is *e d f g*. Let *a* be the center of sight and *b* the point being seen. Let the surface of reflection (in which, by the 27th theorem of the 5th book, points *a* and *b* must necessarily lie) cut the mirror itself through the axis *h i*. I say that the common section of that surface of reflection and the surface *e d f g* is a line of longitude of the mirror. For since, by the 93rd theorem of the 1st book, the common section of that plane surface and the surface of the whole cylindrical mirror is a rectangle contained by two lines of longitude and two diameters of the bases of the column, and since the surface of reflection passes through the center of sight (to which the visible surface is directly opposed in the mirror, per the 1st theorem), it is clear that the common section of those two surfaces will be one line of longitude. This line is one side of that rectangle which forms the common section of that plane surface and the surface of the entire column. Similarly, it is also clear through the 90th theorem of the 1st book regarding a pyramidal mirror, because the common section of the surface of reflection and the conical surface of the mirror visible to the eye is one side of that triangle (which is the common section of this plane surface and the entire surface of the pyramid mirror itself), which is one of the lines of longitude of the pyramid. The proposition is therefore clear.

8. *Of all plane surfaces tangent to the surface of a convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirror, only one is perpendicular <note>original: "erecta" (erect or upright).</note> to the surface of reflection that cuts the mirror through its axis; specifically, that which is tangent to the mirror along the common section of that surface and the mirror—namely, the line of longitude that divides the visible surface of the mirror into two equal parts.*

Let the center of sight be point *a*, and let the common section of the surface of reflection (which cuts the mirror through the axis) and the mirror be the line of longitude *m o*, which divides the surface *e d f g* into equal parts. Let any number of plane surfaces be tangent to the surface of the mirror. I say that only that one which is tangent to the mirror along the line of longitude *m o* is perpendicular to that surface of reflection, and all others are slanted <note>original: "obliquatæ"</note> relative to it. For, as is clear through the 92nd theorem of the 1st book, the line *m o* contains right angles with the semi-diameters of the bases of the column, and similarly with the semi-diameters of all circles parallel to those bases cutting the column (as is clear through the 100th and 23rd theorems of the 1st book). It is also evident through the 96th theorem of the 1st book that all perpendiculars which can be drawn within the column to the surface tangent to the mirror necessarily pass through the axis of the mirror. ...surface cutting the mirror through the axis. Therefore, by definition, that tangent surface is upright <note>meaning perpendicular</note> upon that surface of reflection. All other surfaces, therefore, which are tangent to the said surface of the mirror along other lines of longitude, are oblique to that surface of reflection. For otherwise, since those tangent surfaces necessarily intersect one another: if from some point on the line (which, by the 11th proposition of the 3rd book of Euclid, is the common section of those surfaces) two lines were drawn in those tangent surfaces to the surface of reflection, the ends of which were joined by a third line in the surface of reflection itself: two right angles would be created for that triangle, which is impossible. Therefore, none of the other surfaces tangent to the mirror is upright upon that surface of reflection, except for the single one tangent to the mirror at that common section. And in the same way, the demonstration can be formed for pyramidal mirrors. The proposition is therefore clear.

9. *When a convex cylindrical mirror is placed opposite the sight, such that the sight is not on the surface of the cylinder itself, and the point of the object being seen is in the same surface with the sight and parallel to the bases of the cylinder: the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror will be a circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 30.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a cylindrical mirror. The cylinder is defined by a vertical axis h-i and circular bases at the top (f-d) and bottom (g-e). To the left are two points: 'a' representing the eye (center of vision) and 'b' representing the object. A horizontal plane of reflection passes through 'a' and 'b', cutting the cylinder at a circular cross-section marked 'z c'. Vertical lines 'd-c-e' and 'f-z-g' show the lines of longitude on the cylinder's surface.</image-desc>

Let there be a convex cylindrical mirror whose axis is *h i*, the upper base is circle *f d*, and the lower base is circle *g e*. Let the center of sight be point *a*, and the point of the object seen be *b*. Let the mirror be placed directly opposite the sight, as proposed. I say that the surface of reflection (which is *a b c z*) will cut the surface of the proposed mirror in such a way that the common section, *c z*, will be a circle parallel to the bases of the mirror. This is clear from the hypothesis and through the 100th theorem of the 1st book of this work; or also in this way: Let two lines be drawn from the sight tangent to the mirror, which are *a z* and *a c*. Let *z* and *c* be the points of tangency opposite each other in the same surface. From each of those points, let lines be drawn along the length of the column, which are *d c e* and *f z g*. And since line *d c* is equal to line *f z*, and line *c e* is equal to line *z g* by the hypothesis and by the 25th theorem of the 1st book of this work—because the bases of the mirror and the surface of reflection are parallel—it is evident that line *z c* (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror) will be parallel to the arcs of the bases, which are *d f* and *g e*. For if the straight lines *d f*, *c z*, and *g e* are drawn, those straight lines will be parallel by the 33rd proposition of the 1st book of Euclid. Therefore, these curves, which are in the same surfaces, will also be parallel; and they are circular because they are parallel within the same cylindrical surface. The proposition is therefore clear.

10. *When a convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirror is placed opposite the sight, such that the sight is not on the surface of the cylinder or pyramid, and the surface of reflection falls obliquely to the axis of the mirror: the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror will be an ellipse <note>original: "oxygonia sectio" (literally, an acute-angled section, the classical name for an ellipse)</note>. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 31.*

<image-desc>A second geometric diagram showing a cylindrical mirror with axis h-i. In this case, the plane containing the eye (a) and the object (b) is tilted at an angle, intersecting the cylinder obliquely. This results in the intersection 'c z' forming an oval or elliptical shape rather than a perfect circle.</image-desc>

Let there be, as in the previous cases, a convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirror whose axis is line *h i*. Let its surface visible to the sight be *e d f g*, and let the center of sight be point *a* and the point of the object seen be *b*. Let the surface of reflection cut the mirror obliquely across the axis—that is, not parallel to the bases of the column. I say that the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror visible to the sight is part of an ellipse <note>original: "oxygonia sectio"</note>. Since it is clear through the 103rd theorem of the 1st book of this work that it is impossible for the common section of any surface cutting a cylinder or pyramid across the axis (and not parallel to the bases) to be a circle, or even a line of longitude by the 7th theorem of this book—since such a flat surface does not cut the pyramid or cylinder along the axis of length—it is clear that the common section of the surface of reflection (which is flat) and the part of the surface of the pyramidal or cylindrical mirror opposite the sight cannot be an arc of a circle, nor a line of longitude. It will therefore be part of an ellipse; for we have called the entire such section of the whole pyramidal or cylindrical surface and a flat surface cutting the pyramid or column an "oxygonian section" <note>term: "oxygonia sectio"; Vitello follows the ancient terminology of Apollonius where ellipses were defined by the angle of the cone's vertex.</note> in the 98th theorem of the 1st book of this work. The proposition is therefore clear.

11. *When the common section of the surface of reflection and a cylindrical mirror is a circle: all flat surfaces tangent to the mirror are upright <note>perpendicular</note> upon the surface of reflection.*

# BOOK SEVEN

Let the arrangement remain as it was set forth in the 9th proposition of this book. And because, by the 95th theorem of the 1st book, all plane surfaces touching the column <note>a cylinder</note> touch it along a line of longitude, it is clear by the 92nd theorem of the 1st book—since all lines of longitude contain right angles with the semi-diameters of the bases—that all are erected upon those bases. Therefore, by the 100th and 23rd theorems of the 1st book, all those lines are erected upon the circle parallel to the bases of the column. This, however, is the circle which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror, according to the 9th proposition of this book. Therefore, by the definition of surfaces erected upon surfaces, all those surfaces touching the column are erected upon the aforementioned surface of reflection. Which is what was proposed.

*12. It is impossible for the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex pyramidal mirror to be a circle. Alhazen, Book 4, Note 41. Also Book 5, Note 50.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a pyramid labeled 'a b c'. The apex is at the top labeled 'a'. The base 'b c' is at the bottom, with its center labeled 'd'. An axis line 'ad' runs vertically from the apex to the center of the base. Inside the pyramid, two horizontal line segments are drawn, suggesting cross-sections. Points 'k' and 'n' are marked on the central axis. Point 'g' is on the left surface of the pyramid, with point 'h' opposite it on the right. A line 'gm' extends from the surface at 'g' inwards through point 'n'. Outside the pyramid to the left, points 'e' (representing the eye) and 'f' (representing an object) are positioned. Lines connect 'f' to 'g' and 'g' to 'e'.</image-desc>

Let there be a convex pyramidal mirror <note>a cone-shaped mirror</note> **a b c**, whose vertex is **a** and the diameter of the base is **b c**. Let the axis of the mirror be the line **a d**; therefore, by the 89th theorem of the 1st book, point **d** is the center of the base. Let the center of sight <note>the eye</note> be **e**, and let the point of the thing seen be **f**. I say that the form of point **f** cannot be reflected to the sight **e** from any point of the proposed mirror in such a way that the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is a circle.

For if this were possible, let the form of point **f** be reflected to the sight **e** from point **g** of the mirror; and let circle **g h** be the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror, the center of which is **k**. By the 100th theorem of the 1st book, circle **g h** will be parallel to the base **b c**. Therefore, from point **g** outside the mirror, let line **g m** be drawn perpendicularly upon the surface touching the pyramid at point **g**, by the 12th proposition of the 11th book <note>of Euclid’s Elements</note>. Truly, because the surface of the base is not orthogonal <note>perpendicular</note> to the surface touching the pyramid at point **g**—since every surface touching a pyramid along a line of longitude is a tangent (as is clear by the 95th theorem of the 1st book), and the line of longitude stands obliquely above the surface of the base—it is evident that the surface of the circle **h g**, being parallel to the base, is not orthogonal to the surface touching the mirror at point **g**. Therefore, when the perpendicular line **g m** is extended inside the pyramid, it is clear that it will not reach the center of the circle, which is **k**, but will fall below it at another point of the axis, which we call point **n**. Line **g n** will contain an acute angle with the axis toward the vertex point—namely, angle **g n a**—which is necessarily acute by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book, because angle **g k n** is a right angle by the 29th proposition of the 1st book, since angle **a d c** is a right angle. And since, as is clear by the 27th theorem of the 5th book, it is necessary for point **m**—which is the end of the line perpendicular to the surface of the mirror (the perpendicular being line **n g m**)—to consist within the surface of reflection, then line **h k g** is not in that surface. It is clear, therefore, that the reflection of the form of point **f** to the sight **e** will not occur from point **g** of the mirror as if from a point of a circle. For if a reflection were to occur from point **g** as from a point of circle **g h**, it would be necessary for the surface of circle **g h** to be perpendicular to the plane surface touching the mirror at point **g**, and for the perpendicular **m g** to be extended to the center of the circle **k**, which is impossible by the preceding arguments. The proposition is therefore clear.

*13. When a convex pyramidal mirror is placed opposite the sight, so that the sight is not on the surface of the pyramid or continuous with it, and the point of the thing seen is with the center of sight in the same surface parallel to the base of the pyramid: it is impossible for reflection to occur to the sight.*

For with such an arrangement of the center of sight and the point of the thing seen with respect to the convex pyramidal mirror, as is proposed: it is clear by the 100th theorem of the 1st book that since the surface of reflection is a plane surface, the common section of itself and the conic surface of the mirror is a circle. The proposition is therefore clear by the preceding <note>Proposition 12</note>. For it was shown therein to be impossible for the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex pyramidal mirror to be a circle. Because if that common section were a circle, it would be parallel to the base of the mirror by the 100th theorem of the 1st book, and the surface of that circle would be in the surface of reflection. And because the axis **a d** is perpendicular to that circle by the 23rd theorem of the 1st book, the lines of longitude of the pyramid will be inclined over that circle, containing acute angles with the diameters of the base; and thus those lines would be oblique to the surface of reflection. Therefore, in that surface, a perpendicular could not be drawn to the line of longitude. But by the 27th theorem of the 5th book, a perpendicular drawn upon the surface touching the mirror at the point of reflection is in the surface of reflection and is perpendicular to the line of longitude, since any surface touching the pyramid touches it along a line of longitude. Therefore, in this situation, a reflection of any point of the seen object will never occur to the sight when the surface of reflection touches the pyramidal mirror as a pyramid. If, however, the surface in which the line touching the circle of the mirror lies should cut the surface of the mirror at some point of that circle, then it is possible for a reflection to occur from these mirrors and from that point of the circle—not as from pyramidal mirrors, but insofar as their convex surface shares characteristics with spherical or convex cylindrical mirrors, the properties of which we have declared in the preceding sections; nor then does this property belong to the specific nature of pyramidal mirrors. The proposition is therefore clear.

<meta>This page continues the geometric study of reflection in Book 7 of Vitello’s Optics, moving from the general properties of curved mirrors to specific cases involving pyramidal (conical) and columnar (cylindrical) mirrors. It focuses on the "lines of longitude"—straight lines running along the length of the mirror's surface—and how they relate to the observer's point of view.</meta>

# VITELLO'S OPTICS

14. *Of the surfaces of reflection (the common section of which with the surface of a pyramidal mirror is a straight line), it is possible for sometimes only one, and sometimes very many, to be applied to the same point of sight, depending on the various positions of the eye.*

For in whatever way the sight is arranged so that less than half of the conical surface of the pyramid is seen (according to the 84th theorem of the 4th book of this work), then only a single surface of reflection passes through the eye such that its common section with the surface of the pyramid is a line of longitude <note>A "line of longitude" refers to a straight line drawn from the apex of a cone or along the length of a cylinder; in modern geometry, this is called a "generatrix."</note>. This is because only one such surface will then pass through the axis of the pyramid. Indeed, it was shown by the 7th theorem of this book that in every surface of reflection formed by pyramidal mirrors (whenever the common section of the reflection surface and the mirror is a line of longitude), it is necessary for the axis of the mirror to be within that surface. However, when the sight is so positioned that the entire pyramid is seen (according to the 92nd theorem of the 4th book), not only many, but even infinite surfaces of reflection (whose common section is a line of longitude) can be applied to the eye, as is proposed. This is because the center of sight is then common to all the lines of longitude of the entire mirror, and all relate equally to the eye. For when the visual ray is continuous with the axis of the pyramid, the whole pyramid is seen by the 92nd theorem of the 4th book. Therefore, in any surface of reflection, the entire axis and the line perpendicular to the mirror's surface (passing to the axis from the point of reflection) will exist. The section of any such surface of reflection and the pyramidal surface of the mirror will be a line of longitude in this position, since any surface in which the entire axis exists shares a common line of longitude of that pyramid with the surface of the pyramid (by the 90th theorem of the 1st book). Thus, the proposition is clear.

15. *Every surface of reflection (whose common section with the surface of a convex columnar or pyramidal mirror is a line of longitude of the mirror) divides the apparent surface of the mirror into two equal parts.*

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram illustrating proposition 15. It shows a circular cross-section of a cylinder with various internal lines and points. A point 'a' (representing the eye or viewpoint) is positioned outside the circle to the right. Lines connect point 'a' to points 'b' and 'l' on the circle's circumference. A vertical chord labeled 'm o' passes through the circle, with point 'p' marked on it. The diagram includes a central point 'x' and tangent lines 's' and 't' meeting at 'p'. Letters 'f', 'h', 'd' are at the top and 'e', 'g' are at the bottom of the apparent surface area.</image-desc>

Let there be a convex columnar <note>A "columnar mirror" is a cylinder.</note> mirror, whose apparent surface to the eye is **e d f g**, and its axis is **h i**; and let the center of sight be **a**, as previously established. It is clear by the 7th theorem of this book that a surface of reflection cutting a columnar or pyramidal mirror in such a way cuts it along the length of the axis **h i**. Let the line of longitude, along which that surface of reflection cuts the mirror, be line **m o**. I say that line **m o** divides the surface of the mirror **e d f g** visible to the eye into equal parts. It is clear by the 25th theorem of the 5th book that this surface of reflection is orthogonal <note>perpendicular</note> to the surface touching the column at line **m o**. If, therefore, a point **p** is marked on line **m o**, and line **a p** is drawn, and from point **p** a line **t p s** is drawn in the surface touching the mirror such that line **s p t** touches a certain circle of the column parallel to the bases (which is circle **b l**), then line **a p** will be perpendicular to line **r p s**, because it is drawn in a surface erected above that surface. Therefore, by the 19th proposition of the 3rd book, line **a p** extended passes through the center of circle **b l**, which is **x**. Let lines **a b** and **a l** be drawn, which are equal by the 58th theorem of the 1st book; let the semi-diameters **x b** and **x l** also be joined. The triangles **a b x** and **a l x** will therefore be equiangular by the 8th proposition of the 1st book, and angle **p a l** will be equal to angle **p a b**. Therefore, by the 58th theorem of the 1st book, line **a p** divides the arc **l p b** into equal parts at point **p**. But arc **l p b** is parallel to the bases of the column. Also, the straight lines terminating the surface of the mirror visible to the eye are parallel to line **m o**, which is clear by the 92nd theorem of the 1st book and by the 28th proposition of the 1st book. Thus, line **m o** will divide the bases of the column into equal parts; moreover, line **m o** is in the surface of reflection. It is clear, then, that this surface of reflection divides the surface of the mirror appearing to the eye into equal parts. And since in a pyramidal mirror, whether there be one or many such surfaces of reflection (as shown by the previous proposition), the demonstration is always the same. Thus, the proposition is clear.

16. *Of all the surfaces of reflection formed from the same convex columnar mirror to the same point of sight, there is only one whose common section with the surface of the mirror is a line of longitude of that mirror.*

Because the common section of the surface of reflection and the proposed mirror is never a line of longitude of the mirror unless the surface of reflection cuts the column through the axis (according to the 7th theorem of this book), in this position the surface of reflection (which is **a h i**) cuts the surface **e d f g**...

<summary>This page demonstrates that reflection surfaces passing through the axis of a conical or cylindrical mirror bisect the visible portion of the mirror. It also establishes that, for a fixed viewpoint, there is generally only one reflection surface that aligns perfectly with the mirror's length (line of longitude).</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN

[appearing] to the sight into two equal parts, as is clear from the premise of this [book], and the surface passing through the axis **hi** is unique: it is clear that the common section of this [surface] alone and the surface of the mirror is the line of longitude of the mirror. If, however, it is claimed that there is another surface of reflection whose common section with the surface of the mirror is also the line of longitude of the mirror: then, by the 7th theorem of this book, that surface cuts the mirror along the axis **hi**. Therefore, let a line be drawn in that surface from the center of sight to the axis **hi**, which shall be **ak**: and let the line **apk** be drawn in the proposed surface of reflection, which cuts the visible surface of the mirror into two equal parts. It is then evident that these two straight lines would enclose a surface, which is impossible <note>In Euclidean geometry, two straight lines cannot enclose a space or surface.</note>. The proposition is therefore clear. For only a single surface can be imagined in which the axis of the column, the center of sight, and the point of the object seen all exist, and no more.

17. *Of all the surfaces of reflection from the same convex columnar mirror to the same point of sight, there is only one whose common section with the surface of the mirror is a circle parallel to the bases of the column.* <term>Alhazen, Book 4, Chapter 7, Note 30.</term>

Let the arrangement be as above, such that the common section of the surface of reflection and the convex columnar mirror is a circle. Because in every such surface of reflection, the line erected perpendicularly over the surface touching the mirror at the point of reflection is the diameter of the circle parallel to the bases of the column: and there can only be one circle on the surface of the column parallel to the bases that is in the same surface as the center of sight: it is evident that of all surfaces of reflection from the same convex columnar mirror to the same sight, there is only one whose common section with the mirror is a circle parallel to the bases of the column. For if it were said that there are several: let the common section of one of those surfaces and the surface of the mirror be a circular line, which is **b p t**: and let the other be **x y z**: also, let the points where the centers of those circles meet the axis of the column be **k** and **r**: and let the lines **a k** and **a r** be drawn from the center of sight to those points. It is evident then, because the bases are parallel to these [circles], that in the triangle **akr** the two angles at the base **kr** are right angles: for the line **kr**, being part of the line **hi** (the axis of the column), is just as the straight line **hi** is to the bases of the column by the 92nd theorem of Book 1 of this work: so it is also [perpendicular] to the surfaces of the circles parallel to those bases by the 23rd theorem of Book 1. Therefore, it is also perpendicular to the diameters of those circles: but those diameters are in the lines **ak** and **ar**. Therefore, the line **kr** is perpendicular to both lines **ak** and **ar**: which is impossible <note>A triangle cannot have two right angles at its base, as the angles of a triangle must total 180 degrees.</note>. The proposition is therefore clear.

18. *Of the surfaces of reflection (whose common section with the surface of a convex columnar or pyramidal mirror is an acute-angled section), it is possible for many to be applied from the same visible portion of the mirror to the same point of sight.* <term>Alhazen, Book 4, Note 31.</term>

Let the figure be arranged as above in the 15th theorem of this book: and let the common section of the surface of reflection passing through the axis **hi** be the line **mo**: and let the common section of the surface of reflection parallel to the axes of the column be the circle **b p l**. It is clear from what has been established that reflection can occur to the sight **a** from all points of the columnar surface **mpb** and **mpl**, according to the parts of the columnar section. For since an object point can fall upon any of those points: it is clear that reflection to the sight can occur from any of those points by the 1st theorem of this book. It is therefore manifest that the parts of those columnar or pyramidal sections can be infinite, any of which cuts the column or pyramid of the mirror according to the same perpendicular line over the axis, as is clear by the 104th theorem of Book 1. The proposition is therefore clear.

19. *When the line of longitude is the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex columnar or pyramidal mirror: from whichever point of that line reflection to the sight occurs, it always remains in the same surface.* <term>Alhazen, Book 4, Note 32 & 42.</term>

Having designated, as in the previous 15th theorem of this book, a surface of reflection such as is proposed, which cuts the surface of the mirror along the line **mo**. I say that from whichever point of that line reflection to the sight occurs: all lines of reflection will always be in the same surface **a m o**. For since the axis **h i** is in the surface **a m o** by the 7th theorem of this book: and the unique surface touching the mirror at that line **m o** is erected over the surface of reflection...

This is because, by the 18th [proposition] of the 3rd book <note>original: "per 18 p 3"; referring to Euclid’s Elements, which states a radius is perpendicular to a tangent line at the point of contact</note>, that line drawn from the point of contact to the center of the circle is perpendicular to the line touching the circle drawn in the surface tangent to the column. Therefore, surface **mohi** is erected above the surface touching the mirror along line **mo**. But the center of sight is in a surface at a right angle to that same surface: because the center of sight, the line **mo**, and the axis of the mirror **hi** are all in one surface, as is clear from what was said before. However, there is only one surface at a right angle to that tangent surface along the line **mo**: because if the opposite were true, it would happen that two lines would stand perpendicularly on one point to one surface, which is impossible by the 13th [proposition] of the 11th book <note>original: "per 13 p 11"; Euclid’s Elements</note>. Therefore, all reflections made from points on line **mo** are in one and the same surface. Which is what was to be shown.

***20. When the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex columnar mirror is a circle: from whatever point of that circle a reflection occurs, it will always be in the same surface.*** <term>Alhazen, Book 4, Note 32.</term>

Therefore, any such perpendicular extended outwards above the surface tangent to the column will lie entirely within the same surface, according to the 1st [proposition] of the 11th book <note>original: "per 1 p 11"</note>. However, that surface drawn outside the column is the surface of reflection. Since every such perpendicular is in the surface of that circle, and the point of sight, which is **a**, is likewise in the same surface: it follows that in this surface alone will the reflection of any point of the object seen occur, whether from any point of that whole circle or from its visible portion. Which is what was to be shown.

***21. Every perpendicular erected from the point of reflection on the convex surface of a columnar mirror, when extended inside the mirror, is the diameter of a circle parallel to the bases of the column: and vice versa.*** <term>Alhazen, Book 4, Note 34.</term>

Let the arrangement of the figure be as before: and let the point of reflection be **p**, whether the common section of the reflection surface and the mirror is a line of longitude, a circle, or a columnar section <note>Likely referring to an elliptical cross-section</note>. And from point **p**, let a perpendicular line be drawn to the surface touching the mirror at that same point **p**; let this be **pq**. I say that if line **pq** is understood to be extended inside the mirror, it will fall on point **k**, which is the center of circle **bpl**, and it will be the diameter of that circle. For if it is claimed otherwise: since it is established by the 18th [proposition] of the 3rd book that the diameter **kp** is perpendicular to the line **st** touching the circle **bpl** at point **p**, and consequently to the surface touching the column at that point (in which line **st** lies, by the 6th [theorem] of this book); and since line **qp** is also perpendicular to the same line and surface touching the mirror at the same point: it is clear that these two perpendiculars **qp** and **kp** would be joined at point **p** as a single line, according to the 14th [proposition] of the 1st book <note>original: "per 14 p 1"</note>. For both those lines emerge from a single point **p** of line **sp**, and each of them contains a right angle with the same. To claim the opposite would also mean that from the same point **p** of the tangent surface, two perpendiculars are erected above that surface, which is against the 13th [proposition] of the 11th book. For if diameter **kp** is extended outside the mirror and does not reach point **q**: let it be that it reaches point **z** outside the mirror above the tangent surface. It would then happen that both **pz** and the perpendicular **qp** are perpendiculars produced to the same point **p** on the same surface: which is impossible. Thus the first part of the proposition is clear. The converse is also clear in the same manner.

If, however, the common section of the surface of reflection and the <term>columnar mirror<gloss>a cylindrical mirror</gloss></term> is a circle, as is clear by the 9th [theorem] of this book: then reflection will occur from only one point of that circle, just as was shown for convex spherical mirrors by the 16th theorem of the 6th book. But if that common section is <term>elliptical<gloss>literally "oxygonia" or an acute-angled section, which refers to an ellipse formed by a plane cutting a cylinder</gloss></term>, as is clear by the 10th [theorem] of this book: then this proposal must be specifically demonstrated for the mirrors in question. Let the arrangement of the figure be as in the next preceding [proposition]: and let the part of the cylindrical section be the line which is **pu**. I say that from only one point of the line **pu** will reflection occur to the sight in that surface. For given any other point, it is clear that the perpendicular erected from that point of reflection over the surface of the column is orthogonal to the line of the column’s length passing through that point: therefore it will also be perpendicular to the axis by the 29th [proposition] of the 1st [book of Euclid’s Elements]: and that perpendicular will be the diameter of the circle parallel to the bases of the mirror by the preceding [proposition]. And the surface of reflection and that circle intersect each other, and their common line is the diameter of that circle by the 104th theorem of the 1st book: and that diameter is perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror at that point: and the surface of reflection also cuts that line of the column’s length upon which the contact occurs: and it is inclined upon it: therefore that surface of reflection will also be inclined upon the axis. But in a plane surface inclined over some line (as is specifically clear concerning the elliptical section by the 112th theorem of the 1st book) one cannot understand more than one line falling orthogonally into that line or into the axis itself: since the line terminating that surface intersects the line upon which the surface is inclined at only one point: therefore reflection will occur from only one point of that section. For if reflection were granted to occur from two points of that section to the same sight: it would follow that in the same surface of that reflection there would be two lines of that surface orthogonal to the axis of the column: which cannot be, since that surface is inclined over the axis itself. For the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection falls into the circle parallel to the bases of the column at a point on the axis: and it is the common section of the circle's surface and this surface of reflection by the 104th theorem of the 1st book. If, therefore, reflection also occurred from another point: then likewise the perpendicular drawn from that point of reflection would be, by the next proposition, the diameter of another circle parallel to that first circle, and it would fall on a point of the axis where the surface of reflection does not fall. In all these surfaces of reflection, therefore, reflection occurs from only one point of the common line in the same surface with respect to the same sight: although with respect to two sights, reflection can occur from two points of the mirror’s surface, such as from the two ends of the diameter of the circle which is perpendicular to the section itself: yet only if that diameter is equal to or less than the distance between the eyes, and not otherwise: but for one sight this cannot happen: since from one [eye] one always sees less than half of the cylindrical mirror by the 78th theorem of the 4th book. The proposition is therefore clear: which we shall finally pursue more particularly, showing that in these mirrors, whatever line is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror, reflection to the sight will occur from only one point of the entire mirror.

Therefore, the surface **bfa**, which is the <term>plane of reflection<gloss>the surface containing the incident and reflected rays</gloss></term>, transversally cuts the axis **de**: since the visible line is higher or lower than the center of vision by the hypothesis.
