The same is true for point **c**, and any middle point of the line **bc**. Therefore, although all points of the line **bc** are reflected to the center of vision **a** from the <term>longitudinal line<gloss>the vertical line along the length of the cylinder</gloss></term> of the mirror: nevertheless, the reflection of any point to the sight will occur according to an elliptical section. Similarly, it must be demonstrated if the <term>plane of incidence<gloss>the surface containing the incoming light ray and the perpendicular to the mirror</gloss></term> of the line **bc** orthogonally cuts the axis of the mirror and the surface **ade**: for then the common section of the plane of incidence of line **bc** and the surface of the mirror will be a circle parallel to the base of the mirror, according to the 100th theorem of the 1st book. Whence if reflection to the sight occurs, it will happen from the arc of a circle parallel to the base of the mirror: yet any plane of reflection passing through the center of vision will cut the axis of the mirror obliquely according to some point of that arc. Thus, although all points of line **bc** are reflected to the sight **a** from the arc of the mirror’s circle: nevertheless, the reflection of any point of that line happens according to an elliptical section. If, however, any of the points of line **bc** were in the same plane as the center of vision, parallel to the base and cutting the mirror: the reflection of that [point] alone would occur according to a circle, whereas the reflection of all other points would occur according to elliptical sections: and thus the points of that line will present different <note>original: "passiones," referring here to the physical impressions or perceptions</note> effects to the sight. The proposition is therefore clear.

> *24. In every plane of reflection from convex cylindrical or pyramidal mirrors, it is necessary that the center of vision, the point seen, the point of reflection, and the point on the axis upon which the perpendicular falls (drawn from the point of reflection to the surface of the mirror) all lie within the same plane. Alhazen Book 4, [Propositions] 23, 34.*

That the center of vision, the point of reflection, and the reflected point are in the plane of reflection is clear through the 27th theorem of the 5th book. For in every plane of reflection, there are necessarily the lines of incidence and reflection, which contain the three aforesaid points. And if the plane of reflection cuts the mirror along the line of its length: it is evident through the 7th [theorem] of this book that the entire axis and the point upon which the perpendicular falls (drawn from the point of reflection) are in this plane. If, however, the common section of the plane of reflection and the mirror is a circle: it is evident because the center of that circle—which is a point on the axis at which all perpendiculars produced from the point of reflection of the whole circle meet, according to the 21st [theorem] of this book—is in the plane of reflection: since then the entire circle is in the plane of reflection. But if the common section of the plane of reflection and the mirror is an elliptical section: it is evident through the 10th [theorem] of this book because this section is inclined upon the axis of the column, intersecting the axis at the point where the perpendicular falls, which is produced from the point of reflection to the surface tangent to the column at the point of the section. The proposition is therefore clear according to every variation of the said sections.

> *25. On the visible surface of a portion of a convex cylindrical mirror, whether the common section of the plane of reflection and the mirror is a longitudinal line, a circle, or an elliptical section: reflection can occur to the sight from any point. Alhazen Book 4, [Proposition] 28.*

Let the boundaries of the visible portion of the column be marked as before: and let that portion be **defg**: and let **p** be a given point on that visible surface: and let **x** be the point of the thing seen. I say that from point **p**, a reflection of the form of point **x** can occur to the center of vision, which is **a**. For let it be first that the plane of reflection (in which are the point of sight, which is **x**, and the center of vision **a**, and the point from which reflection occurs, which is **p**) cuts the column of the mirror along the axis **hki**: therefore, by the 7th [theorem] of this book, the common section of that plane and the mirror will be the line of the column's length, which is **mpn**. Let the line **xp** be drawn: and from point **p** let a perpendicular line be erected over the line **mn** by the 11th [proposition] of the 1st [book of Euclid], which is **pz**: and upon point **p**, the end of line **zp**, let an angle be made equal to angle **xpz**, which is **zpq**. If the center of vision, which is **a**, were on the line **pq**, it is clear by the 20th theorem of the 5th book—since the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection—that the reflection of the form of point **x** will occur from point **p** to the sight **a** existing on line **pq**. But if the plane of reflection cuts the column of the mirror parallel to the bases: it is evident that the common section will be a circle by the 9th [theorem] of this book: and again, reflection will occur from point **p** to the sight. For let a circle parallel to the bases of the column be drawn through the 102nd theorem of the 1st book, passing through point **p**, which is **bpl**: the center of which is **k**: if the point seen is in that surface extended outside the mirror, and line **xp** is drawn, which if produced passes through the center of the circle **k**: it is evident, since the axis of the column **hki** is orthogonal to the surface of that circle, just as it is to the bases of the column by the 100th and 21st theorems of the 1st book, that the axis **hki** itself will also be orthogonal to line **xp**: therefore the line of the column's length (which is **mp**) will also be orthogonal to line **xp** by the 29th [proposition] of the 1st [book of Euclid]. Therefore, by the 21st theorem of the 5th book, line **xp** will be reflected back onto itself, and the form of point **x** will meet the sight existing on that line. If, however, line **xp** produced does not pass through the center of the circle **k**, but is oblique to it: then let the semi-diameter **kp** be joined, which, as is clear from the premises, will be orthogonal to the axis **hi**: therefore line **kp** will be perpendicular to the line of length **mp** by the 29th [proposition] of the 1st [book of Euclid]: therefore **kp** will be perpendicular to the surface tangent to the column along the line of length **mp**: in which surface let a line tangent to the circle **bpl** be drawn at point **p**, which is **spt**: and let line **kp** be extended perpendicularly over that surface to point **u**: and let the center of vision **a**, as before, be on line **qp** in the same plane as the circle. And since line **st** is in that surface tangent to the circle, angle **kpt** will be a right angle: therefore angle **spa** is also a right angle by the 15th [proposition] of the 1st [book of Euclid]. It is clear then that angle **aps** is less than a right angle: therefore it is acute:

26. *When the common section of the plane of reflection and a convex cylindrical mirror is a longitudinal line of the mirror: the reflection of the form of the same visible point from the entire surface of the mirror to one sight occurs at only one point. ### 28. When the <term>intersection<gloss>the line or curve where two surfaces meet</gloss></term> of the plane of reflection and the convex cylindrical mirror is an <term>acute-angled section<gloss>an "oxygonia," which in this context refers to a conic section like an ellipse or hyperbola formed by cutting the cylinder at an angle</gloss></term>: the form of the same point of the visible object will be reflected to the eye from only one point of the entire surface of the mirror. <note>original: Alhazen 47 n 5. This refers to the work of the Arabic scientist Alhazen, Witelo's primary source.</note>

Let the surface of reflection be **a b g**: whose common section with the surface of the cylindrical mirror is an acute-angled section, passing through point **g** on the surface of the mirror: and let **b** be the point of the visible object: and **a** the center of vision: and **g** the point of reflection. I say that the form of point **b** is not reflected to the center of vision **a** from any point of the entire surface of the mirror except from point **g**. For let a surface be drawn from point **a** parallel to the bases of the cylinder, cutting the mirror according to a circle, which is **e z i**: which is done in this way. For with a line drawn from point **a** perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder through the 12th [proposition] of the 1st [book]: this line will be a perpendicular erected upon the surface of the cylinder: because it will be perpendicular to the <term>line of longitude<gloss>a straight vertical line running down the length of the cylinder</gloss></term> of the cylinder, which it meets through the 29th [proposition] of the 1st [book]. Likewise, let another line containing a right angle with the axis be drawn from the same point of the axis, which is **q**, which is line **q e**. Therefore, by the 18th [proposition] of the 11th [book], it is clear that the flat surface imagined to pass through those lines **a q** and **q e** will be orthogonally erected upon the surface of the mirror. And since by the 4th [proposition] of the 11th [book] the axis of the mirror is erected upon that surface, it is clear by the 14th [proposition] of the 11th [book] and the 92nd theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work] that that surface is parallel to the bases of the mirror: therefore by the 100th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work], since it cuts the surface of the cylinder parallel to the bases: it is clear that it cuts according to a circle, which is **e z i**, the center of which will be point **q**. And in the same way from point **g**, let a surface parallel to the bases of the mirror be drawn, which cuts the mirror according to circle **s g p**: whose center is **t**: and in that circle let a line be drawn from the axis to point **g**, which is **t g**: and this, by the 21st [proposition] of this [book], will be perpendicular to the surface <term>tangent<gloss>touching the cylinder along a line without crossing into its interior</gloss></term> to the cylinder along the line of longitude in which point **g** is located. Also, let the produced line **t g** meet with line **a b** at point **k**: it will meet it by the 29th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]: therefore, because it divides angle **a g b**, and points **g**, **a**, **b** are in the same plane of reflection by the 24th [proposition] of this [work]. Let also a line of longitude of the mirror be drawn from point **g** by the 101st theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work], which is **g z**, falling between the two sections parallel to the bases of the mirror just drawn: and by the 25th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work], the part of the axis **t q** will be equal to line **g z**: and from point **b** of the visible object, let a line be drawn perpendicular to the surface cutting the mirror according to circle **e z i** by the 11th [proposition] of the 11th [book]: which is **b h**: and let two lines **a z** and **h z** be drawn: and let line **z q** be drawn from point **z** in that surface to the axis of the mirror: and this line **z q** will be perpendicular to axis **q t** by the 21st [proposition] of this [book], just as the surface **e z i** in which it is drawn: and by the same 21st [proposition] of this [book], line **z q** will be perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror at point **z**. Because, therefore, line **q z** drawn outside the surface of the mirror necessarily divides angle **h z a**, because it is produced orthogonally from the meeting of lines **h z** and **a z** upon the tangent surface, which surface lines **a z** and **h z** fall upon obliquely: it is clear by the 29th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work] that the produced line **z q** will meet with line **a k**, which is <term>subtended<gloss>opposite to and defining the limits of an angle</gloss></term> by angle **a z h**: let it meet, therefore, at point **l**. I say that the form of point **h** of line **b h** is reflected to the eye **a** from point **z** of the mirror. For let a line parallel to line **k g** be drawn from point **a**, which is **a m**: this certainly, by the 2nd theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work], will meet with line **b g**, with which its parallel meets: for lines **a b**, **b g**, **k g** are all in the same plane of reflection: let the point of meeting of lines **b g** and **a m** be point **m**. It is also clear by the 6th [proposition] of the 11th [book] that line **g z** is parallel to line **b h**, since each of them is orthogonal to surface **e z i** parallel to the bases of the cylinder: therefore by the 7th [proposition] of the 11th [book], line **b g m** is in the same surface, since it cuts those two parallel lines. Therefore, in the plane of reflection (which is **a b g**) there are...

Likewise, because line **a m** is parallel to line **k g**, and line **z l** is parallel to line **k g** through the 33rd proposition of the 1st [book of Euclid’s *Elements*]: for lines **g z** and **t q** are equal and parallel, as is clear from the previous statements, and line **t g** is extended to point **k**, and line **q z** to point **l**; therefore, by the 30th proposition of the 1st [book], line **l z** will be parallel to line **a m**. Therefore, by the 2nd theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work], lines **l z** and **a m** are in the same surface; and line **h a** is in the same [surface] by the 7th proposition of the 11th [book]. Therefore, the three points **m**, **z**, **h** are in the same surface in which lines **l z**, **a m**, and **h a** are located, which is the surface **h l z m**. But it has already been shown above that they are in the surface **m b h**; therefore, they are on the line common to those two surfaces; thus, by the 3rd proposition of the 11th [book], line **h z n** is a straight line. 

Since, therefore, point **g** is the point of reflection by hypothesis, by the 20th theorem of the 5th [book] of this [work], the angle **a g k** will be equal to angle **k g b**; but angle **k g b**, by the 29th proposition of the 1st [book], is equal to angle **a m g**, since it is an exterior angle to it and line **k g** is parallel to line **a m**; and also angle **a g k** is equal to angle **m a g** by the same 29th proposition of the 1st [book], because it is an <term>alternate angle<gloss>angles on opposite sides of a line crossing two parallel lines</gloss></term>; therefore, angles **a m g** and **m a g** are equal; thus, by the 6th proposition of the 1st [book], the two lines **a g** and **m g** are equal. 

Because, indeed, line **g z** is erected upon the surface **a h z**, as is clear from the previous statements, line **g z** will be <term>orthogonal<gloss>at a 90-degree angle</gloss></term> to any line of the surface **a h z** drawn from point **z**; therefore, it will be perpendicular to line **z m**; angle **m z g** will therefore be a right angle; also, by the 47th proposition of the 1st [book] <note>This is the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the square of line **m g** will be equal to the two squares of lines **m z** and **g z**; and similarly, the square of line **a g** is equal to the squares of lines **a z** and **g z**. But the square of line **m g** is equal to the square of line **a g**, since lines **m g** and **a g** are equal; therefore, subtracting the common square from both sides, which is the square of line **g z**, there remains the square of line **m z** equal to the square of line **a z**. Line **m z** is therefore equal to line **a z**. Therefore, by the 5th proposition of the 1st [book], angle **a m z** is equal to angle **z a m**. But by the 29th proposition of the 1st [book], the exterior angle **l z h** is equal to the interior angle **a m z**, and angle **z a m** is equal to angle **l z a** by the same 29th proposition of the 1st [book], because those angles are alternate; therefore, angle **a z l** is equal to angle **l z h**.

The form, therefore, of point **h** falling upon the mirror at point **z** is reflected to the center of vision from the point of the mirror which is **z**, as is clear by the 20th theorem of the 5th [book] of this [work]. If, however, it is claimed that the form of point **h** can be reflected to the sight **a** from a point other than point **g**, that other point will either be on the line of longitude, which is **g z**, or on another. If it is on line **g z**, let a line be drawn from the given point of line **g z**, which is **d**, perpendicular to line **g z**; let this be line **o d f** produced to both sides, and let lines **a d** and **b d** be joined. Therefore, line **o d f**, by the 29th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work], will necessarily cut line **a b**, and it will be parallel to line **a m** by the 28th proposition of the 1st [book]; and the line drawn from point **b** to that point **d** will necessarily meet with line **a m** by the 2nd theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]. Point **d** and point **m** will be in the same surface, since lines **d f** and **a m**, being parallel, are in the same surface by the 1st theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]. Therefore, line **b d** will either fall upon point **m** or upon another point of line **a m**. If it falls upon point **m**, it would mean drawing two straight lines from point **b** to point **m**, namely line **b g m** and line **b d m**, which is impossible, since then two straight lines would enclose a surface <note>A fundamental axiom of Euclidean geometry is that two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>. 

If, however, line **b d** falls upon a point of line **a m** other than point **m**, let that point be **n**; and let line **n z** be drawn from point **n** to point **z**. It can be proved that this line **n z** with line **h z** forms a straight line, just as was previously proved for line **m z**. For since points **n**, **z**, **h** are in two plane surfaces, they are in their common section; therefore, by the 3rd proposition of the 11th [book], line **h z n** will be a straight line; and so from point **h** it would be possible to draw two straight lines passing through point **z** and falling on different points of line **a m**, which is impossible by the 1st proposition of the 11th [book]. It is clear, therefore, that the form of point **h** can be reflected to the sight **a** from no point on line **g z** except for point **g** alone. 

If it is said that the form of point **h** could be reflected to the sight from a point taken on the surface of the mirror outside this line: let a line of longitude of the mirror be drawn through that point of the mirror by the 101st theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]; and from the point of the circle **e z i** where this line falls, it will be proven that the form of point **h** is reflected to the sight **a** according to the aforementioned proof. But it has already been proven that the form of point **h** is reflected to the sight **a** from point **z** of the mirror; and thus there would be a reflection of the form of the same point **h** to the same sight **a** from two points of one circle, which is against the 16th theorem of the 6th [book] of this [work], and impossible. It remains, therefore, that the form of point **h** is reflected to the sight **a** from only the proposed point of the mirror. 

Indeed, it is clear that if the common section of the surface of reflection and the cylindrical mirror were an <term>oxygonia fectio<gloss>an acute-angled section, or ellipse</gloss></term>, then reflection would not occur except from only one point. Because, as is clear by the 24th [proposition] of this [book], in every surface of reflection made from these mirrors, it is necessary that there be a point on the axis upon which the perpendicular falls, drawn from the point of reflection, which is orthogonal to the line of longitude of the mirror passing through that point; and therefore also [perpendicular] to the axis of the mirror by the 28th proposition of the 1st [book], since the line of longitude of the cylinder and the axis are always parallel by the 92nd theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]. Furthermore, that perpendicular is common to the acute-angled section from whose point reflection occurs, and to a certain circle parallel to the bases of the mirror by the 104th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]; it is therefore the <term>semidiameter<gloss>radius</gloss></term> of that circle. 

The surface of reflection and that circle intersect each other on that perpendicular radius of the circle upon the periphery of the circle by the 21st [proposition] of this [work]; and the surface of reflection, in which that acute-angled section is located, is inclined over the surface of the circle and over that radius, which is the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection. Upon any surface inclined over the axis of the cylinder, only one line can be understood falling perpendicularly upon the axis by the 112th theorem of the 1st [book] of this [work]. If, indeed, reflection were to occur from two points from the same acute-angled section, it would be necessary that two perpendiculars to the axis of the mirror could be drawn in that surface of the section, which is impossible, since one sight always sees less than half of the cylinder. And similarly, it is clear by the 79th theorem of the 4th [book] of this [work] that two sights see less than half of the cylinder when the diameter of the base of the cylinder is greater than the distance between the eyes; this, however, is more clearly declared in the 22nd [proposition] of this [work]. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<keywords>cylindrical mirrors, catoptrics, Witelo, Euclidean geometry, laws of reflection, ellipse, axial perpendiculars, optical uniqueness</keywords>

--- Page 597 ---
<meta>This page continues the geometric proof from page 281, which discusses finding the point of reflection on a cylindrical mirror when the intersection of the plane and the cylinder forms an ellipse (an acute-angled section). It concludes this discussion and moves into Proposition 30, regarding the reflection of a line parallel to the mirror's axis.</meta>

-># WITELO'S OPTICS<-

<margin>Alhazen [Book 4, Chapter 5], Note 48.</margin>
I have corrected [the proof]: to find the point of reflection for a given visible point to a given center of vision.

When the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the proposed mirror is the <term>line of longitude<gloss>a vertical line running along the surface of a cylinder, parallel to its central axis</gloss></term> of the mirror, the point of reflection can be easily found, as was shown for plane mirrors in the 46th theorem of Book 5 of this work. If, however, that common intersection is a circle, then the point of reflection can be easily found, as was shown for convex spherical mirrors in the 20th or 22nd theorems of Book 6 of this work. But if that common intersection is an <term>acute-angled section<gloss>an ellipse, formed by cutting a cylinder at an angle</gloss></term>, such as is proposed here: let **b** be the given point of the thing seen, which is reflected from some point of the acute-angled section to the center of vision **a**. I say that it is possible to find the point of reflection. For let a surface be drawn from point **a**, as in the preceding proposition, parallel to the bases of the column <note>the "column" refers to the cylinder of the mirror</note>: this will cut the column along a circle, which we shall call **e z i**. From point **b**, draw a perpendicular line to this surface according to the 11th proposition of the 11th Book [of Euclid's *Elements*], which shall be **b h**. Through the 20th or 22nd theorem of Book 6 of this work, as was shown for convex spherical mirrors, let a point be found in this surface from which the form of point **h** is reflected to the eye **a**, which shall be point **z**. From point **z**, through the 101st theorem of Book 1 of this work, let a line of longitude be drawn, which shall be **z g**. Draw line **h a**, and from point **z** draw a perpendicular to line **h a** through the 12th proposition of Book 1, which shall be **z l**. To this, draw a parallel line from point **a** through the 31st proposition of Book 1, which shall be **a m**. Let line **h z** be extended until it meets line **a m**, and let the meeting point be **m**. From point **m**, draw a line to point **b**, which will necessarily cut line **z g**, since it is in the same surface with it. Because line **b h** is parallel to line **g z** through the 6th proposition of Book 11 (since both lines **b h** and **g z** are perpendicular to the same surface **e z i** parallel to the bases of the column), line **h m** will therefore be in their surface through the 7th proposition of Book 11. Thus, line **m b** will be in the same surface. If it cuts line **z g** at point **g**, it is clear from those things set forth in the preceding proposition that point **g** will be the point of reflection of the form of point **b** to the eye **a**. All these things and many others are evident through what was said in the preceding demonstration. And this is what was proposed: because in this manner, the point of reflection for any given point to a given eye can be found.

<margin>Alhazen [Book 6], Note 26.</margin>
### 30. For a straight line parallel to the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror, when the eye is not in the same surface, reflection occurs from the line of longitude of the mirror to the eye.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the reflection of a line on a convex cylindrical mirror. A vertical cylinder is shown with its central axis labeled z-l-k. A vertical line t-q-h is drawn parallel to this axis. An observer's eye is located at point e. The diagram includes an elliptical cross-section b-f representing the cylinder's curve. Various construction lines connect points t, q, e, h, z, l, k, b, f, m, a, g, o, and d to demonstrate the geometric paths and normals involved in the reflection.</image-desc>

Let the axis of the convex cylindrical mirror be line **z k**, and let the line being seen be parallel to the axis, which is **t h**; and let the center of vision **e** be outside the surface **t h z k**. I say that the form of line **t h** is reflected to the eye **e** from the line of longitude of the mirror, which is the common intersection of the surface **t h z k** and the surface of the mirror. Because the eye **e** is not in the surface **t h z k**, let a surface passing through the eye itself cut the column of the mirror parallel to the bases; this surface will cut the column according to a circle by the 100th theorem of Book 1 of this work, which circle shall be **b f**. It is clear then, since line **h t** by hypothesis is parallel to axis **z k**, that some point of it is reflected to the eye **e** from some point of circle **b f**. Let this be from point **b**. Let the point of line **t h** which is reflected to the eye **e** from point **b** of the mirror be **q**. Draw lines **q b**, **e b**, and **q e**. Through the 101st theorem of Book 1 of this work, draw the line of longitude of the column from point **b**, which shall be **a b g**. Draw a perpendicular from point **b** falling upon the axis **z k** at point **l**, which, when extended to line **q e**, will cut it by the 2nd theorem of Book 1 of this work, since those two lines are parallel, as is clear from the premises. And since surface **e q b** is the surface of reflection, it is clear that point **b** with line **e q** is in the same surface. Therefore, let line **b l** extended cut line **q e** at point **m**, and let it be line **m l**. Draw from point **e** a line parallel to line **m l** through the 31st proposition of Book 1, which shall be **e o**. Extend line **q b** beyond point **b**; because it meets line **m l**, it is clear by the 2nd theorem of Book 1 that it will meet its parallel, which is line **e o**. Let the point of meeting be **o**. It is clear by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work that the <term>angle of incidence<gloss>the angle at which light hits the mirror</gloss></term>, which is **q b g**, is equal to the <term>angle of reflection<gloss>the angle at which light bounces off the mirror</gloss></term>, which is **e b a**. But angles **m b g** and **m b a** are equal because they are right angles; therefore, there remains angle **q b m** equal to the remaining angle, which is **e b m**. But by the 29th proposition of Book 1, angle **q b m** is equal to angle **b o e**, because an exterior angle is equal to the interior [opposite] angle; and also angle **m b e** is equal to angle **b e o** because it is an alternate angle; therefore, angle **b o e** is equal to angle **b e o**. Therefore, by the 6th proposition of Book 1, in triangle **b e o**, side **b e** is equal to side **b o**. Now take another point on line **t h**, which is point **t**, and draw line **t o**. Since line **t h** is parallel to the line of longitude of the mirror (which is **a g**) by the 30th proposition of Book 1, because both of them are parallel to axis **z k**, it is clear by the 1st theorem of Book 1 of this work that lines **t h** and **a g** are in the same surface, since line **t h** and axis **z k** are also in the same surface. Therefore, by the 7th proposition of Book 11, line **q b o** cutting those parallel lines **t h** and **a g** is in the same surface with them; and similarly line **t o** is in the same surface with them by the 11th proposition of Book 11, for points **t** and **o** are in the said surface. Therefore, line **t o** will cut line **a g**. Let the point of intersection be **g**, and draw lines **e g** and **e t**. Since **a g**, which is the line of longitude of the mirror, is perpendicular to the surface of circle **b f** by the 8th proposition of Book 11 (because axis **z k**, to which line **a g** is parallel, is perpendicular to the same circular surface by the 23rd theorem of Book 1 of this work, as it is perpendicular to the base of the column by the 92nd theorem of Book 1)...

-># BOOK SEVEN<-

The surface of circle **b e f** is part of the surface **e o b f**: for this surface cuts the <term>column<gloss>a cylinder</gloss></term> parallel to the base, as is clear from what was previously stated. Therefore, by the definition of a line erected upon a surface, angle **g b o** is a right angle, and angle **g b e** is a right angle. Thus, by <note>original: "47 p 1"; Euclid's *Elements*, Book 1, Proposition 47, known as the Pythagorean Theorem</note> the square of line **g o** is equal to both squares of lines **g b** and **b o**; and the square of line **g e** is equal to both squares of lines **g b** and **b e**. And since it has been shown that lines **b e** and **b o** are equal, their squares will also be equal, and the square of **g b** is common to both. Therefore, the square of line **g e** will be equal to the square of line **g o**. Thus, by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 6</note> in triangle **e g o**, line **g e** is equal to line **g o**. Consequently, by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 5</note> angle **g e o** will be equal to angle **g o e**.

Now, from point **g**, let a perpendicular be drawn to the axis of the mirror, which is **z k**, by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 12</note>; let this be line **g z**. Let this be extended beyond point **g** to line **t e**, becoming **z g n**. Line **z n** will be parallel to line **l m** by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 28</note>, since lines **z n** and **m l** are both perpendicular to the axis **z k**. But line **e o** is also parallel to line **m l**, as is clear from the previous statements. Therefore, line **z n** is parallel to line **e o** by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 30</note>. It follows by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 29</note> that the exterior angle **t g n** is equal to the interior angle **g o e**, and the angle **n g e** is equal to angle **g e o** because they are alternate angles. But angle **g e o** was shown to be equal to angle **g o e**; therefore, angle **t g n** is equal to angle **n g e**.

Since line **t g o** and line **n g z** are in the same surface in which point **g** lies, points **o**, **g**, and **t** will be in the same surface. Therefore, lines **e g**, **o g**, and **t g** are in the same surface by <note>Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 1</note>. The image of point **t** is therefore reflected to the eye **e** from the point of the mirror **g**, as is clear by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work, because of the equality of angles **t g n** and **n g e**.

Now, if we take point **h** on line **t h** at the same distance from point **q** and from the center of vision **e** as point **t**, and line **h o** is drawn, this will pass through the line of longitude of the mirror, which is **a g**. Let the point of intersection be **a**. When a line perpendicular to the axis **z k** is drawn from point **a** (let this be **a d**), and it is extended to line **h e** (let it be **d r**), and line **e a** is drawn, it will be clear, as before, that the two angles **a b e** and **a b o** are right angles, and the sides **a e** and **a o** are equal. Thus, as before, the two angles **h a r** and **e a r** will be equal. The image of point **h**, as shown above, is therefore reflected to the eye **e** from point **a** of the mirror. Similarly, for any point taken on line **t h**, it can be proven that the point is reflected to **e** from some point on the line of longitude of the mirror, which is **a g**. Therefore, the entire line **t h** is reflected from a single line of longitude of the mirror, **a g**, to the eye **e**, which is what was proposed.

It should be noted, however, that in this arrangement of the figure, point **g** on line **t h** is the midpoint of that line, and it is in the same surface as the center of vision **e**. Because of this, points **t** and **h** are equally distant from the eye, as are the points of reflection **g** and **a**. From this, it is clear that lines **g b** and **b a** are equal, and the whole arrangement of the figure follows from those points. But if the eye is lower than the entire line **t h**, it should be noted that the reflection occurs from the line **a g** as it cuts through several <term>acute-angled sections<gloss>ellipses formed by the intersection of a plane and a cylinder or cone</gloss></term>, as is clear by the 23rd theorem of this book; otherwise, a reflection must sometimes occur from some point of a circle.

### 31. When the line of longitude is the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex conical mirror: reflection can occur from any point of the mirror's surface visible to the eye.

<margin>
Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham</note>, Book 4, Proposition 40, Note 4.
</margin>

Let the convex <term>pyramidal mirror<gloss>a conical mirror</gloss></term> be **b x p**, with its vertex at **b** and the diameter of the base **x p**. Let the center of the base be **q**; therefore, line **b q** will be the axis of the mirror itself. Let there also be any given point on its visible surface, point **g**; let the center of vision be **a**, and the point of the thing seen be **n**. I say that the image of point **n** can be reflected from point **g** to the eye **a**, if it is in a position suitable for reflection.

By the 102nd theorem of Book 1 of this work, let a circle be drawn through point **g** parallel to the base **x p** of the mirror's pyramid. Let its center be **d** and its diameter **g c**. The radius **g d** will necessarily be perpendicular to the axis **b q** by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 29</note>, because the radius of the mirror's base **x q** is perpendicular to the same axis **b q**, just as the other radius of the base existing in the same surface is parallel to the diameter **g c**. For the axis **b q** is perpendicular to the surfaces of both circles **x p** and **g e** by the 23rd theorem of Book 1 of this work. Let line **g b** be drawn from the given point **g** to the vertex of the pyramid **b**. It is therefore clear by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 32</note> that angle **g b d** is acute, since angle **b d g** is a right angle.

In the surface of triangle **g b d**, let there be a line of reflection, which is **a g** by the 7th theorem of this book, and by hypothesis, the lines of reflection **a g**, the line of longitude **b g**, and the axis **b d q** will be in the same surface. And since angle **b g d** is acute, let a right angle **b g r** be made by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 23</note>, with line **g r** extended to the axis. Line **r g** will be perpendicular to the line of longitude **b g** by <note>Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 2</note>. From point **g**, let a line be drawn <term>tangent<gloss>touching at a single point</gloss></term> to the circle by <note>Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 17</note>, which shall be line **l g s**. By <note>Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 18</note>, line **l g s** will be perpendicular to the diameter **g c**. Let another diameter of the circle **f k** be drawn perpendicular to diameter **g c** through point **d** by <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 11</note>. As before, diameter **f k** will be perpendicular to the axis **b q**. Therefore, by <note>Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 4</note>, diameter **f k** is perpendicular to the surface in which lines **g c** and **b q** lie. Diameter **f k** will be parallel to the line tangent to the circle, **l g s**, by <note>Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 18</note> and <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 28</note>. Therefore, by <note>Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 8</note>, the line tangent to circle **g c**, which is **s g l**, is perpendicular to the surface containing diameter **g c** and axis **b q**. Thus, by the definition of an erected line, angle **l g r** is a right angle. If, therefore, we imagine a surface tangent to the pyramid in which the line **l g s** is tangent to circle **b c**, it is clear that line **r g** is perpendicular to that surface.

And the same must be demonstrated for any other given point on the surface of the mirror. Thus the proposition is clear.

32. *Given a point on a convex conical mirror from which the reflection of a given point of a visible object to a given center of sight occurs, whether from a point of an <term>oxygonian section<gloss>an ellipse; literally an "acute-angled section" in classical geometry</gloss></term> or from a <term>line of longitude<gloss>the slant height; a straight line from the vertex to the base along the surface</gloss></term> of the mirror: it is possible to find the locations where, once the center of sight and the point of the visible object are placed, a reflection to the sight occurs from that same given point of the mirror, insofar as it is a point on a circle parallel to the base.* <note>original: "Alhazen 52 n 5"; referring to the Optics of Ibn al-Haytham</note>

Let **a** be the center of sight: **b** the point of the visible object: and let **g** be the point of reflection on the surface of the convex conical mirror, whose vertex is **e**. I say that it is possible to find what is proposed. For let there be drawn, as we taught in the 28th theorem of this book, a surface through point **g** parallel to the base, cutting the pyramid along a circle parallel to the base by the 100th theorem of the 1st book of this work, which shall be **p g**: let its center be **t**: and let lines **a g**, **b g**, **a b** be drawn: and from point **g** let line **g t** be drawn to the center of the circle: and from the vertex of the pyramid, which is point **e**, let the axis **e t** be drawn. And since the surface of reflection is always erected upon the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection, as is clear by the 8th theorem or the 25th theorem of the 5th book: let a line be drawn in the surface of reflection perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of reflection **g**, which shall be **h g**: and it is clear by the 26th theorem of the 5th book that this line divides angle **a g b** into equal parts: therefore, when extended, it will cut line **a b** by the 29th theorem of the 1st book: let it therefore cut it at point **z**. Also, from point **e**, the vertex of the pyramid, let the line of longitude of the mirror be drawn, which is **e g**: and let a line be drawn parallel to this line **e g** from point **a**, the center of sight, which will necessarily cut the surface of circle **p g**: let it therefore cut it at point **n**: and let it be **a n**. Similarly, from point **b**, let a line be drawn parallel to the same line **e g**, which shall be **b m**, cutting the surface of circle **g p** at point **m**. Since, therefore, both lines **a n** and **b m** are parallel to the same line of longitude of the mirror, which is **e g**: it is clear by the <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 30</note> that they are parallel to each other, namely lines **a n** and **b m**. Therefore, from point **n**, let a line be drawn by the <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 31</note> parallel to the semi-diameter of the circle, which is **g t**, and let that be **n f**: which is parallel to line **n f** <note>The text repeats "n f" here, likely indicating a parallel construction involving point m</note>: and let lines **n g**, **m g**, **n m** be drawn. It is thus clear by the 29th theorem of the 1st book that line **t g** extended will cut line **n m**: because it bisects angle **m g n**: for it is drawn transversely in the same surface: and also lines **n f** and **g t** are parallel: but line **n m** cuts line **n f**: therefore it will also cut line **g t** by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book: let it cut it at point **q**. It is also clear by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book that line **m g** extended will cut line **n f**, since it cuts line **g t** which is parallel to **n f**: let the point of intersection be **f**: and from point **a** let a line be drawn parallel to the line perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror at point **g**, which is line **h z**: and let that parallel be line **a l**. It is therefore clear by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book that line **b g** will meet with line **a l**: because it cuts its parallel line **h z**: let the point of meeting be **l**. Also draw the line which is the common section of the surface tangent to the mirror at point **g** and the surface of circle **p g**, which shall be line **g o**. It is clear that line **g o** will be perpendicular to the semi-diameter of the circle, which is **g t**, by the <note>Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 18</note>: because line **g o** is tangent to circle **p g**: since it is drawn in the flat surface tangent to the mirror at point **g**. ->### BOOK SEVEN<-

[the line] itself will cut line **al** parallel to line **gh**: therefore, let the point of intersection be **d**: and line **gd** will be perpendicular to line **al** by the <note>original: "29 p 1"; the 29th proposition of the 1st book of Euclid's *Elements*</note>: for line **gd** is perpendicular to line **gh**. Since line **hg** is perpendicular to the surface tangent to the circle at point **g**, it will necessarily be perpendicular to line **gd** produced from the same point in that surface, by the definition of a line erected upon a surface. Moreover, it is clear from what was previously said that since line **nf** is parallel to the radius of the circle **pg** (which is **gt**), and similarly line **al** is parallel to line **gh**, then by the <note>original: "15 p 11"; Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 15</note> the surface in which lines **nf** and **al** lie is parallel to the surface **gth**. These lines **nf** and **al**, if extended beyond points **l** and **f**, will necessarily meet by the <note>original: "14 th. huius"; the 14th theorem of this book of Witelo's *Optics*</note>, because angles **fna** and **laf**, as is evident, are less than two right angles. But line **eg** is also parallel to line **bm**, as is clear from the premises: therefore, by the <note>original: "1 th. 1 huius"; the 1st theorem of the 1st book of this work</note> they are in the same surface cutting the two aforementioned parallel surfaces—one of them along line **eg**, and the other along line **fl**. Therefore, by the <note>original: "16 p 11"; Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 16</note> their common sections will be parallel; thus line **fl** will be parallel to line **eg**. But line **an** is parallel to line **eg**, as is clear from the premises: therefore, by the <note>original: "30 p 1"; Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 30</note> line **fl** will be parallel to line **an**. 

Truly, the surface tangent to the mirror at point **g** cuts those same parallel surfaces, which are **gth** and **nfal**: one of them along line **eg**, according to which it is tangent to the mirror, and the other along line **od**. Therefore, by the <note>original: "16 p 11"</note> line **od** is parallel to line **eg**: thus by the <note>original: "30 p 1"</note> line **od** will be parallel to lines **an** and **lf**, which are parallel to line **eg**. And because lines **nf** and **al**, between which lines **an**, **od**, and **fl** are drawn, are in the same surface by the <note>original: "2 p 11"; Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 2</note>, it is clear that lines **an**, **od**, and **fl** are in the same surface. 

Therefore, let line [**fi**] be drawn from point **f** parallel to line **la** by the <note>original: "31 p 1"; Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 31</note> cutting line **od** at point **k**, and line **an** at point **i**: and line **fi** will be equal to line **la** by the <note>original: "34 p 1"; Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 34</note>: and similarly line **fk** will be equal to line **ld**, and **ki** equal to **da**. However, by the <note>original: "2 p 6"; Euclid, Book 6, Proposition 2</note> the proportion of **ik** to **kf** is as **no** to **of**: therefore, by the <note>original: "7 p 5"; Euclid, Book 5, Proposition 7</note> the proportion of line **ad** to line **dl** will be as line **no** to line **of**. 

And since from the premises angle **bgz** is equal to angle **agz** (because line **gz** divides angle **agb** equally by the <note>original: "26 th. 5 huius"; the 26th theorem of the 5th book of this work</note>), but angle **bgz** is equal to angle **gla** by the <note>original: "29 p 1"</note> (for an exterior angle is equal to an interior one) and lines **hz** and **al** are parallel; similarly, angle **zga** by the same <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 29</note> is equal to angle **gal** because they are alternate angles; therefore angle **gla** is equal to angle **gal**. Thus, by the <note>original: "6 p 1"; Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 6</note> lines **ga** and **gl** are equal: and line **gd** is perpendicular to line **al**, as is clear from the premises. Therefore [triangle] **agl** is divided into two equiangular and similar <term>trigones<gloss>triangles</gloss></term> by the <note>original: "31 th. 1 huius"; 31st theorem of the 1st book of this work</note>. Therefore, the proportion of line **ad** to line **dl** is as line **ga** to line **gl**: but line **ag**, as is clear from the premises, is equal to line **gl**: therefore line **ad** is equal to line **dl**. Consequently, line **no** is also equal to line **of**: and line **go** is, by the <note>original: "29 p 1"</note>, perpendicular to line **nf**: since line **go** is perpendicular to line **gt** as is clear from the premises by the <note>original: "18 p 3"; Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 18</note>, and lines **gt** and **nf** are parallel, as was previously stated. 

Since therefore angle **gof** is equal to angle **gon**, and line **of** equal to line **on**, and line **go** is common: then by the <note>original: "4 p 1"; Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 4</note> angle **ofg** will be equal to angle **ong**. But angle **qgm** is equal to angle **ofg** by the <note>original: "29 p 1"</note>, since it is exterior to it, and angle **qgn** is equal to angle **ong**, since it is alternate to it, and lines **tq** and **nf** are parallel as is clear from the premises. Therefore, angle **qgm** will be equal to angle **qgn**. Thus, by the <note>original: "20 th. 5 huius"; the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work</note>, from point **g** of circle **pg**, the form of point **m** can be reflected to the eye located at point **n**. This does not mean, however, that reflection occurs from these convex <term>pyramidal specula<gloss>conical mirrors</gloss></term> according to the whole circle, but rather that point **g** is part of the circle which is a section of the sphere or column imagined within the conical mirror. Because the surface tangent to circle **pg** is erected over the surface of reflection, it must necessarily cut the <term>pyramid<gloss>cone</gloss></term> of the mirror in its wider part (such as toward the base) according to the parallelism of the axis of the mirror's cone. Thus the surface of reflection (in which are the center of vision, the point of the object, and circle **pg**) is erected over that tangent surface: and points **n** and **m** face each other in the surface of that circle according to equal angles contained with its diameter. 

Therefore, with the center of vision placed at point **n** and the point of the visible object at point **m**, or vice versa, the form will always be reflected to the center of vision, provided the body of the conical mirror does not present an impediment—as if perhaps lines **an** and **bm** fall in that very circle of the base, and because of the body of the mirror's cone, nothing can be reflected from point **g** to the eye. And this is what was proposed.

### 33. *When the common section of the surface of reflection and the convex conical mirror is a line of the mirror's length, the reflection of the form of one point of a visible object to the eye occurs from only one point of the mirror's surface. Alhazen 53 n 5.*

Let the arrangement be exactly as in the next preceding [proposition]: and let the form of point **b** be reflected to the eye located at point **a**, from point **g** of a convex conical mirror, such that the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is the line of the mirror's length, which is **eg**. I say that the form of point **b** is reflected to the eye **a** from only the point of the mirror's surface which is **g**. 

For if it were said that it could be reflected from another point of the mirror's surface, then that other point would either be on the line of the mirror's length, which is **eg**, or not. If it were on the line of the mirror's length, **eg**, let that point be **x**: and from it let a perpendicular be drawn to the surface tangent to the mirror at that point by the <note>original: "12 p 11"; Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 12</note>. Let this perpendicular therefore be **xz**: and line **xz** will be parallel to line **zg** by the <note>original: "6 p 11"; Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 6</note>, which was previously drawn perpendicular to the same surface, since points **g** and **x** are on the same line of length along which that surface is tangent to the cone. 

And because line **hz** and **al** are parallel, as is clear from what was said in the premises, then by the <note>original: "30 p 1"</note> that perpendicular **xz** will be parallel to line **al**. And because line **xz**, just like line **zh**, is in the surface of reflection (which by the <note>original: "8 huius uel 25 th. 5 huius"; the 8th of this book or the 25th theorem of the 5th book</note> is erected over the surface tangent to the mirror at line **eg**), then by the <note>original: "1 th. 1 huius"</note> line **al** is in the surface of reflection of this perpendicular line **xz**, and it will similarly be in the surface of reflection of the perpendicular line **zg**. Therefore those two surfaces of reflection cut each other along line **al** by the <note>original: "19 th. 1 huius"</note>: but they also cut each other at point...

Therefore, let the axis of the mirror be line **fn**, and let the center of sight be point **a**. I say that when the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is an <term>oxygonia section</term> <note>original: "sectione oxygonia." From the Greek for "acute-angled," this refers to an ellipse formed by cutting a cone at an angle.</note>, which we will call **bi**, it is possible for a reflection of some visible point to occur from any given point on the mirror to point **a**, which is the center of sight. 

For let point **b** be a given point on the surface of the mirror, about which it is doubted whether a reflection of some point of a visible object can occur from it to the center of sight **a**. Therefore, through point **b**, let the line of longitude of the pyramidal mirror <note>The author uses "pyramid" to refer to what we now call a cone.</note> be drawn (following the 101st theorem of Book 1 of this work), which shall be **bf**. Let a perpendicular line be drawn from point **b** to that line of longitude outside the mirror, which shall be **bg**. At the endpoint **b** of line **bg**, let an angle be made (by the 23rd proposition of Book 1 [of Euclid’s Elements]) equal to angle **abg**, which shall be **gbp**, with line **bp** drawn in the same surface of reflection. It is clear (by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work) that every point of a visible object existing on line **bp** will be reflected to the sight at point **a**. However, the reflection to the sight at point **a** will occur from only point **b**, or perhaps only from two points. 

It is evident (by the 96th theorem of Book 1 of this work) that if the perpendicular **gb** is extended inside the pyramid, it will meet the axis **fn**; let the point of intersection be **c**. It is then clear that angle **gcf**, being in the surface of the section toward the vertex of the pyramid, is acute (by the 32nd proposition of Book 1 [of Euclid]), since in triangle **bcf**, angle **cbf** is a right angle. Therefore, let a circle be drawn around the pyramidal mirror from the point of reflection **b** (by the 102nd theorem of Book 1 of this work); let its diameter be **bd** and its center **e**, cutting the axis **fn** at point **e**. Since that circle is parallel to the base of the mirror (by the 100th theorem of Book 1), it is clear that the perpendicular **gc**, which holds an acute angle with the axis **fn**, will be inclined toward the surface of that circle. If a line parallel to line **gc** were drawn from point **n** (the center of the base of the mirror), it is clear that it is inclined toward the base of the pyramid, as line **nq**. 

Now, draw line **cd** from point **e** on the axis to the circumference of the circle. Since angle **bec** is equal to angle **dec** (because both are right angles—for all angles contained between the radii of the circle and the axis **fe** are equal), and the lines from the center to the circumference are equal, and line **ec** is shared by both, it is clear (by the 4th proposition of Book 1 [of Euclid]) that side **bc** is equal to side **cd**. All angles of the resulting triangles are equal, and the same is true for all lines drawn from point **c** to the circumference of circle **bd** (by the 65th theorem of Book 1), because point **c** is the "pole" of circle **bd**. 

Thus, a new <term>imagined pyramid</term> <note>original: "pyramis intellecta." This is a theoretical geometric construction used to prove the properties of the physical mirror.</note> is formed, whose base is circle **bd**, vertex is **c**, and axis is **ce**. The surface of reflection, which cuts the mirror along an acute-angled section, will either touch this [imagined] pyramid **cbd** or cut through it. 

If it touches it, I say that reflection according to that same surface will occur from only point **b**, which is the point of reflection. It is clear that the surface of reflection touches the pyramid along a line of longitude of that pyramid (by the 95th theorem of Book 1); this will be line **bc**, in which point **b** is located, from which line **bc** is drawn perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, along with the line of reflection **ba**. From point **f**, which is the vertex of the mirror’s pyramid, let several lines be drawn to the acute-angled section (the common section of the reflection surface and the mirror), which is **fks**. All those lines will fall into the surface of circle **bd** (the base of the imagined pyramid) before they reach the section itself, except for one alone: line **fb**, which falls exactly on the point of reflection **b**. 

Therefore, reflection to the sight will occur from only point **b**. For if it were granted that reflection to sight **a** occurred from another point of the said acute-angled section, such as point **i**, then the line drawn from that point **i** to point **c** (the vertex of the imagined pyramid), which is **ic**, would be—as before—perpendicular to the surface of the mirror (by the 96th theorem of Book 1). Since that perpendicular must necessarily be in the surface of reflection in which the section lies, it must fall on point **c**. Thus, it would be perpendicular to the line of longitude of the mirror’s pyramid passing through point **i**, which is **fil**. Let the point where line **fi** cuts circle **db** be point **r**. It is clear from the previous arguments (and the 96th theorem of Book 1) that line **cr**, drawn from the vertex of the imagined pyramid to that line of longitude, must be perpendicular to it, just as line **cb** is perpendicular to the line of longitude of the mirror **fb**. Since the angles of all lines of longitude with the radius of the base and with the axis at the vertex are equal (by the 89th theorem of Book 1), there would then be two right angles in triangle **cir**. This is impossible and contrary to the 32nd proposition of Book 1 [of Euclid]. Therefore, reflection will not occur from any other point of the acute-angled section **bi** than from point **b** when the surface of reflection touches pyramid **cbd**.

But if the surface of reflection cuts the pyramid **cbd**, it is clear (by the 104th theorem of Book 1) that it will cut circle **bd** (the base of the same pyramid) at exactly two points. I say, therefore, that in only these two points can reflection to the sight occur from the whole given acute-angled section. Since from both of these points a line drawn to point **c** (the vertex of pyramid **cbd**) is perpendicular to the line of longitude of the mirror passing through that point, reflection can occur from those two points to the sight **a**, as demonstrated in the manner above. If other points of that acute-angled section were proposed as points of reflection, then a line drawn from a given point (call it **h**) to point **c** would always maintain a right angle with the line of longitude of the mirror passing through that point; this would result in an exterior angle being equal to the opposite interior angle (contrary to Euclid 1.16) or two angles of a triangle being right angles (contrary to Euclid 1.32). For the line from point **c** to the common section of that same line of longitude and the circle...

### 35.
**Given a convex conical mirror, and with the center of sight and the point of the visible object both existing between the surface parallel to the base (which touches the mirror at the vertex) and the base itself: it is possible to find the point of reflection. Alhazen 5, 4, n 5.** <note>Witelo credits the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose work on optics was the primary source for this text.</note>

Let **a** be the point of the visible object and **b** be the center of sight. Both of these are below that surface **mng**—that is, between it and the base of the mirror. Let a surface be drawn from point **a** (the object) cutting through the pyramid parallel to the base, as before. From the vertex of the mirror (point **g**), let a line be drawn to point **b** (the center of sight), which shall be **gb**. This line, when extended, will fall upon the surface drawn from point **a** parallel to the base of the pyramid. Since line **gb** is drawn between parallel surfaces and passes from the vertex through the axis of both those surfaces, let the point where this line **gb** falls be point **h**. Therefore, following the method of demonstration used in the 32nd theorem of this book, it can be proven that the form of point **a** will be reflected to a sight existing at point **h** from some point on the circle created by the intersecting surface drawn through points **a** and **h**. ### 42. *When the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex cylindrical or conical mirror is a line of length: the locations of the images and their distance from the eyes will be the same as in plane mirrors.* Alhazen 43, Book 5. <note>Witelo cites the work of the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose "Optics" was a primary source.</note>

When the cause in different subjects is made universal <note>original: "univocatur"; meaning the underlying physical principle is identical</note>, the effect <note>original: "passio"; the resulting phenomenon</note> will also be made universal. For this reason, we do not repeat here those things which were said concerning plane mirrors in the fifth book of this science. Because in both cases—namely in plane mirrors and the mirrors now proposed—the lines of incidence and reflection fall upon and are reflected from straight lines; in both cases, the location of the image will be on the <term>cathetus<note>The "cathetus of incidence" is a line drawn from the object point perpendicular to the mirror's surface.</note></term> drawn from the visible point to the surface of the mirror, as far distant from the surface of the mirror as the point of the visible object is distant from that same surface of the mirror. This is because the image of a visible object is always seen at the intersection of the line of reflection with the cathetus of incidence in all these mirrors, as is clear by Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 43. *When the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex cylindrical mirror is a circle: the points of reflection and locations of images will be the same as in convex spherical mirrors.* Alhazen 43, Book 5.

For sometimes the location of the image will be within the convex cylindrical mirror; sometimes on the surface of the mirror; and sometimes outside the mirror, according to the manner in which the cathetus of incidence and the line of reflection concur at different points. For the cause and demonstration of this, let one return to those things demonstrated in the sixth book of this science concerning convex spherical mirrors; for the reasoning is entirely the same on both sides. This is because the limits of the tangencies, the boundaries of the images and their locations, and the same proportions of the lines are found in those mirrors as in these. The proposition is therefore clear through those; nor did it seem worthy to us to dwell longer on these matters.

### *45. A perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection of a pyramidal section onto the surface of a convex pyramidal mirror must necessarily meet the cathetus of incidence <term>cathetus of incidence: a line drawn from the object point perpendicular to the mirror's surface</term> at a point further from the vertex of the mirror than the point of reflection, falling below the axis of the mirror; provided, however, that the line drawn from the point of the cathetus of incidence to the perpendicular contains an acute angle over the axis. Alhazen, Book 6, Proposition 30.*

This proposition is also clear by Theorem 113 of Book 1 of this work; however, so that it may be more easily applied to pyramidal mirrors: let there be a convex pyramidal mirror *a b g*, whose vertex is *a* and axis is *a k*. Let an acute-angled section <note>original: "sectio oxygonia." This refers to an ellipse formed by the intersection of a plane and a cone.</note> fall upon it, from whose circumference the forms of observed points are reflected to the eye; let this section be *e f z*. Also, let the point of reflection be *e*, and let line *e d* extending from point *e* (which is the point of reflection) be perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror. This line, when extended in the surface of the section, will indeed meet with axis *a k* by Theorem 14 of Book 1 of this work, for angle *e a k* is acute and angle *a e d* is a right angle. Let them meet, therefore, at point *d*. Let there be a cathetus of incidence of the form of some point reflected from point *e z* of the mirror, which shall be *h z*. I say that the cathetus *h z* will meet with the perpendicular *e d* beyond point *d* below the axis of the mirror. For let line *t z q* be drawn, which touches the section *e f z* at point *z*, provided that point *z* is further from point *a* (the vertex of the mirror) than point *e* is. Also, let the drawn line *z d* contain an acute angle with the perpendicular *e d* over the axis of the mirror where point *d* falls. Let a surface parallel to the base of the mirror also pass over point *z*, which by cutting the mirror forms circle *r z g* by Theorem 100 of Book 1 of this work. This circle, therefore, cuts the section *e f z* in only two places by Theorem 104 of Book 1 of this work, because the circle is perpendicular to axis *a d* and the section is oblique to the same axis. Let lines *a z* and *a e* be drawn. Also, let line *a e*—which by hypothesis is shorter than line *a z* because point *z* is further from the vertex of the pyramid than point *e*—be extended beyond point *e* until it meets the circumference of circle *r z g*. Let the point of meeting be *o*. Therefore, point *o* is further from point *a* (the vertex of the mirror) than point *e* is, and line *a o* will be equal to line *a z* by Theorem 89 of Book 1 of this work, because both are drawn from the vertex of the pyramid to the circumference of the circle. When, therefore, a perpendicular is drawn from point *o* to the surface tangent to the mirror along line *a o*, that line will meet axis *a k* beyond point *d* (where the perpendicular *e d* was previously given to fall) by Theorem 2 of Book 1 of this work; for that line will be parallel to line *e d* by Proposition 6 of Book 11. ### 50. If a straight line is parallel to the axis of a convex columnar mirror, and the center of sight exists in the same surface, it is possible for reflection to occur from the entire line of the mirror's length to the sight: and its image will be seen as straight, equal to the thing seen. Alhazen [Book 6], 25 n 6.

Let there be a columnar <note>Cylindrical.</note> mirror, as in Proposition 30 of this book: let a straight line, which is $t h$, be parallel to its axis $z k$: therefore by Proposition 30 of Book 1 and by theorem 92 of Book 1 of this work, line $t h$ will be parallel to the <term>line of length</term> <note>The "line of length" (linea longitudinis) refers to a meridian or vertical line on the cylinder's surface.</note> of the columnar mirror, which, existing in the same surface $t h z k$, shall be line $a g$. I say that if the sight (the center of which is $e$) were in the same surface $t h z k$ with line $t h$, and with axis $z k$: it is possible that all points of line $t h$ are reflected to the sight $e$: since by Proposition 30 of this book it is possible that the points of reflection of all points of line $t h$ are in the line of the length of the column, which is $g a$: because that line is common to the surface of reflection (in which are the sight $e$, the axis $z k$, and the line $t h$) and the surface of the column, as is clear by theorem 93 of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, the image of the form of line $t h$ will be seen as straight: because any perpendicular drawn from a point of line $t h$ will be in the same surface with the sight and the axis: and the locations of the images of the points of line $t h$ will be proven to be arranged according to a straight line, just as was proven concerning straight lines seen in plane mirrors by theorem 52 of Book 5 of this work. The proposition is therefore clear.

*52. When the surface of a straight line being seen cuts the surface containing the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror at a right angle, and the center of vision exists in both surfaces: the reflection will occur from the circumference of the circle (which is the common intersection of the said surfaces and the mirror), and the image of the straight line seen will be curved.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a vertical cylinder with an axis labeled d at the top and f at the bottom. A horizontal cross-section circle is drawn through points b and g. Point e (the eye/vision) is to the left, and a vertical line representing the object with endpoints t and h is to the right. Various lines of sight and reflection connect point e to points b and g on the cylinder, and from there to points t and h. Other labels include points a and z on the cylinder's circumference.</image-desc>

Let line $t h$ be on a flat surface cutting the surface containing the center of vision $e$ and the axis of the given cylindrical mirror $d f$ at a right angle. Let point $e$ be in the same surface as line $t h$; therefore, point $e$ will be on the line where those two surfaces intersect, which is necessary by Theorem 19 of Book 1 of this work, and by Book 1, Proposition 11. I say that the forms of the entire line $t h$ will be reflected to the sight from the circumference of the circle $g b$ (which is the common intersection of the surface $t h e$ and the surface of the mirror's column). For either the center of vision ($e$) will be behind the line $t h$, and then—since that line is a physical object and not transparent—its density will hide the mirror from the sight; in this case, no reflection occurs unless perhaps only the forms of the tips of the line, $t$ and $h$, appear and are reflected to the sight from the circle of the mirror $b g$. The image of the forms of these tips will tend toward curvature, just as was shown in Theorem 56 of Book 6 regarding convex spherical mirrors. 

However, if the line $t h$ is transparent with a thick transparency, like crystal, this will be discussed differently in the tenth book of this science <note>Vitello refers here to his future volume on refraction, where light passes through dense media like glass or crystal.</note>. But if the sight is below the line $t h$ (that is, between the line itself and the mirror), whether the line is transparent or not, then part of the line $t h$ will be hidden because the head containing the eye is in the way. However, that part of line $t h$ which can be seen despite the interference of the head will be reflected from the circle $b g$ to the sight in exactly the same way we showed in the appropriate place regarding convex spherical mirrors. Therefore, the image of a straight line $t h$ seen in this way is always curved. If the center of vision $e$ is outside the boundaries of line $t h$ in the same surface as before, and the form of line $t h$ is reflected to the sight, the entire image of line $t h$ will appear curved, as is evident from what has been said. And this is the proposal.

*53. When a straight line is seen in a surface cutting the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror at a right angle, and the center of vision is not in that same surface, and a reflection is made to a sight equidistant from the ends of that line: its image is seen with the greatest curvature.*

Which is what was proposed.

*54. A visible straight line not parallel to the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror, the surface of which cuts the axis obliquely: the image appears curved with varying curvature according to the diversity of its position.*

Since it is clear by Proposition 51 of this book that a straight line parallel to the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror has an image that is not straight but curved, albeit of slight curvature—while the image of a line (whose surface cuts the axis of the mirror orthogonally, with the eye not existing in the same surface as the visible line) always appears curved by the nearest preceding proposition—it is clear by the same reasoning that lines situated between these two, which more closely approach the position of a line parallel to the <term>longitudinal line of the column<note>A line running along the length of the cylinder.</note></term>, will have images more closely approaching straightness. Truly, those lines which more closely approach the lines whose surfaces cut the axis orthogonally approach more closely to curvature in their images; and the curvature of the images is increased or decreased according to the approach or withdrawal of the lines to either of these positions. And this is what was proposed.
