It was shown in the preceding points that the form of point *o* is reflected to the eye located at point *r* from point *z* of the mirror, and the form of point *n* is reflected from point *e* of the mirror. In that case, point *p* will be the location of the image of the form of point *o* according to Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work; for point *p* itself is the common intersection of the line of reflection, which is *zr*, and the cathetus of incidence <term>cathetus of incidence: the perpendicular line dropped from a point of the object to the surface of the mirror or its tangent plane.</term> of the form of point *o*, which is line *oh*. Furthermore, point *y* is the location of the image of the form of point *n*. The form of point *a*, however, will be seen in its own proper place, because it is at the vertex of the pyramid <note>In this context, "pyramid" refers to a cone, and "pyramidal mirror" refers to a conical mirror.</note>; thus, the image of line *aon* will be a line passing through points *a*, *p*, and *y*. 

But this line is convex, because point *y* is beyond line *apg*; let that image-line therefore be curved, which is line *apy*. It has now been established that the forms of all points of line *an* are reflected to the eye located at point *r* from the longitudinal line of the mirror, which is *ae*. Therefore, the lines of reflection through which those forms are reflected are all in the plane of triangle *rae*. Consequently, all images of the points of line *an* are in this plane; therefore, line *apy*, which is convex, is in this plane. Point *p*, which is the location of the image of the form of point *o*, is closer to the center of sight (point *r*) than point *y*, which is the location of the image of the form of point *n*. Because of this, the convexity of this image will face the center of sight, and the convexity will be slight. The diameter of this image (which diameter is line *ay*) will be smaller than line *an*, of which it is the image; however, the excess of that difference will be of a modest quantity. Therefore, the images of lines drawn from the vertices of convex conical mirrors obliquely to the axis of the mirror are perceived by the sight in such mirrors according to the line of their reflected length, and they appear convex. And this is what was proposed.

**56.** *Every form of a straight line parallel to the width of a convex conical mirror, with the eye being outside its surface (cutting the mirror parallel to its base), is reflected to the eye according to acute-angled sections, and its image is seen as a curve of maximum curvature, whose convexity is toward the eye. Alhazen, Book 6, Prop. 33.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating optical reflection on a conical surface. A cone (pyramid) with vertex 'a' and base 'bc' is shown. A horizontal line 'ef' representing a seen object passes in front of the cone. Point 'd' is the observer's eye. Lines of sight and reflection are drawn from 'd' to the cone and through line 'ef', showing how the points on the line are mapped onto the curved surface through "oxygonias" (acute-angled) conic sections.</image-desc>

Let there be a convex conical mirror whose vertex is *a* and whose base diameter is *bc*; its width <note>The "width" (latitudo) here refers to the cross-section of the cone.</note> is therefore triangle *abc*. Let the center of sight be *d*, and let the straight line being viewed be *ef*, parallel to the surface of triangle *abc*. Let the center of sight *d* be outside the plane in which line *ef* exists, such that the mirror would be cut by that plane parallel to its base. I say that the form of line *ef* is reflected to the eye *d* according to acute-angled sections <note>original: "oxygonias sectiones" — these are the conic sections, specifically ellipses, formed when a plane intersects the cone at an angle.</note> cutting the surface of the mirror. For it cannot be reflected along a longitudinal line of the mirror, since it would then be necessary for it to meet the axis of the mirror toward the vertex (by Theorem 41 of this book) and fall obliquely upon it, the opposite of which is stated in the hypothesis. Nor does reflection occur from the surface of these mirrors according to a circle (by Theorem 12 of this book). 

It is therefore necessary that the reflection of these lines to the eye must occur according to acute-angled sections. And since the catheti of incidence, which are perpendicular to those acute-angled sections (because they are perpendicular to the lines tangent to those sections), meet with the lines of reflection not in the same line parallel to the line being viewed, but in different lines, the images of such lines arranged in this way relative to the surfaces of these mirrors appear curved—just as we showed for cylindrical mirrors in Theorem 53 of this book. Moreover, the images of these lines are very curved, so much so that their curvature is manifest to the sense of sight; and the center of those images is outside the surfaces in which the convexity of the forms of these lines exists. The diameters of the images of these lines become much smaller than the lines themselves, which happens because of the increase in their curvature. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**57.** *For straight lines incident on the surfaces of convex conical mirrors neither meeting the vertex of the axis nor parallel to the width of the mirror, but incident obliquely between these, the images are curved, with varying curvature according to the manner in which they share more in the extreme positions. Alhazen, Book 6, Prop. 34.*

What is proposed here has a sufficiently evident cause. For straight lines applied to these mirrors neither along a longitudinal line (as in Theorems 41 and 55 of this book) nor parallel to the width of the mirror (as in the previous theorem), but in a middle way, share the modes of curvature according to whether they more closely approach one position or the other. Hence, those that approach closer in their position to the longitudinal lines of the mirror have less convex forms, while those that approach closer to lines parallel to the width of the mirrors have more manifestly convex forms—yet they are distorted. For those that approach nearer to the vertex of the mirror have narrower and more convex forms, while those that approach nearer to the base of the mirror have wider forms; nevertheless, the convexity of all those images will be manifest. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**58.** *Every form of an object seen in convex conical mirrors appears conical, similar to the shape of the mirror. Alhazen, Book 6, Prop. 35.*

What is proposed here is clear through Theorem 40 of Book 6 of this work; for it was demonstrated there regarding spherical convex mirrors that the smaller that mirror is, the smaller will be the circles falling on its surface; and thus the images will be closer to the center, and therefore they will be smaller. Similarly also—

# WITELO’S OPTICS

# BOOK SEVEN

...sections falling on any conical mirror <note>original: *speculo pyramidalis*. Witelo uses "pyramidal" to refer to what we call "conical" shapes.</note>: those that are closer to the vertex <note>the apex or tip of the cone</note> are smaller and narrower; and thus the location of the image will be closer to the point in which the perpendiculars—drawn over the surfaces tangent to the mirrors at the points of reflection of the acute-angled sections <term>acute-angled sections: these are elliptical sections formed when a plane intersects the cone at an angle</term> from whose points reflection occurs to the eye—meet with the axis of the mirror. Therefore, those images will be smaller. However, the acute-angled sections that are closer to the base have a contrary disposition to the others above, since they are wider, as is clear through Theorem 116 of Book 1 of this work. Hence, the locations of the images become more remote from the point in which the aforesaid perpendiculars meet, drawn over the surfaces tangent to the mirrors at the points of reflection; therefore, the images become larger. And because of this, it happens that the images of forms seen in convex conical mirrors become tapered <note>literally "pyramidal"</note>, similar to the conical shape of the mirrors. For whatever part of the forms was closer to the vertex of the mirror will be narrower, and what was closer to the base will be wider. Indeed, the forms of a seen object, which are perceived through reflection made by any mirror, will altogether be assimilated to the surface of the mirror from which that form is reflected, as is clear through Theorem 38 of Book 5 of this work. Furthermore, all the other illusions <note>original: *fallaciæ*, referring to optical distortions or "deceptions" of the eye</note> that happen to the sight from convex cylindrical mirrors also happen from these convex conical mirrors; hence, one should not linger here on the repetition of such things. Conversely, whatever illusions happen in these conical mirrors also happen in the cylindrical ones, except for the tapering of the images; this is because the acute-angled sections of cylindrical mirrors, which are of the same declination over the axis of the cylinder, are all equal. Every part of such a section looking toward the top of the mirror is similar to an equal part looking toward the base of the mirror in the same position, which is not the case in the acute-angled sections of cones; for these, as shown by Theorem 116 of Book 1, all widen toward the base of the cone, according to how the circles cutting them parallel to the bases are larger, whereas all such circles in cylinders are equal. Thus, the proposition is clear.

->59. *In larger convex cylindrical or conical mirrors, larger images <note>original: *idola*, here meaning the visual species or phantom image</note> are seen; and the image of a closer seen object appears larger. Alhazen Book 3, chapter 6.*<-

The proposed properties and others, which are mostly common to these cylindrical and conical mirrors and to convex spherical mirrors, mean that the method of demonstrating these properties, as well as others held in common, is the same on both sides. But if in these proposed mirrors an acute-angled section is made by the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror—which does not happen in spherical mirrors, since in those there are only circles—then it must be demonstrated here in those sections (as it was there in circles) from those things which we have set forth previously in this our book; and the proposition will be clear to a diligent mind.

# THE OPTICS OF WITELO, 
## SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND 
### POLES, BOOK EIGHT.

HAVING EXPLAINED to some extent the properties <note>original: "passionibus"; literally "passions" or "affections," referring here to the physical characteristics and behaviors of light reflection</note> of plane and regular convex mirrors, such as spherical, columnar, and pyramidal mirrors: it remains now for us to write something concerning the properties of **concave mirrors**, as they are those in which a greater diversity of reflections results, along with a wonderful diffusion of natural forms and a multifaceted deception of the viewing eyes. 

Indeed, regular concave mirrors (as we declared in Theorem 8 of Book 5 of this work) are only three: namely, spherical, columnar, and pyramidal. Among these, we shall first treat spherical concave mirrors in the present book, as they are those whose properties—being simpler than the others—descend into the remaining concave mirrors. And since we premised the principles common to these concave spherical mirrors and convex spherical mirrors at the beginning of Book 6 of this work: therefore, we do not repeat them here, as they are assumed from what was previously stated; however, we have seen fit to explain those things that are proper to these mirrors specifically.

### DEFINITION.

We call an **inverted image** <note>original: "imaginem conuersam"</note> that which varies the total position of the seen object: such as if the head of the viewer, which is above, appears below: and according to this, the entire position of the parts of the image is varied with respect to the position of the parts of the seen object.

### THEOREMS

1. *When a concave spherical mirror is placed opposite the sight: the common section of the base of the pyramid of vision and the concave surface of the mirror will be a circle of the sphere, sometimes a great circle, sometimes smaller than that.*

For sometimes the entire concave surface of the sphere is seen, sometimes a larger part, and sometimes a smaller part, as is clear through Theorem 72 of Book 4 of this work. Therefore, according to this, that common section of the base of the **pyramid of vision** <term>pyramid of vision: the cone-shaped volume of space through which an eye perceives an object, with the eye at the apex</term> and the surface of the mirror varies. Since, however, the surface of the base of the pyramid is a plane surface, and the surface of concave mirrors is spherical: it is clear through Theorem 10 of Book 1 of this work that their common section is always a circle. Here, then, it is sometimes a **great circle** <note>a circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere itself, dividing it into two equal halves</note>, as when it passes through the center of the mirror: and sometimes smaller than a great circle, as when it does not pass through the center of the mirror but falls outside it. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

2. *It is necessary that the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of a concave spherical mirror be a great circle or an arc of a great circle of its sphere: from which it is clear that every surface of reflection cuts the sphere of a concave mirror into equal parts.*

There is no other demonstration of this proposed theorem than that which was made above in Theorem 6 of this work <note>referring to Book 6</note>: where the same

And because the concavity of a sphere relates to the center in the same way as its convexity, and the **surface of reflection** <term>surface of reflection: the imaginary flat plane containing both the incoming ray of light and the reflected ray</term> is always a flat surface standing upright (perpendicular) over the surface of the mirror according to Theorem 25 of Book 5 of this work: the proposition is clear, since the method of proof here will be the same as above. And since this diameter is common to both the surface of reflection and the sphere itself, the proposition is evident.

**3. In every surface of reflection from spherical concave mirrors, it is necessary that the center of sight, the center of the mirror, the point of reflection, the point being seen, and the endpoint of the visual diameter (drawn from the center of sight through the center of the sphere to the sphere's surface) all sit upon the same plane.**

Since the surface of reflection contains the line of incidence and reflection, it is clear that it contains the point of the thing seen (whose form is reflected), the point of reflection (from which it is reflected), and the center of sight (to which it is reflected). And since the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the surface of the concave spherical mirror is a great circle (according to the previous theorem), it is clear that the center of the mirror is in any such surface of reflection. This is because every one of them passes through the center of the sphere of the mirror itself, since each of those surfaces stands upright over the flat surface touching the mirror at the point of reflection (per Theorem 25, Book 5). Furthermore, according to Proposition 1 of Book 11 <note>original: "per 1 p 11", referring to Euclid's Elements</note>, if a visual diameter is extended through the center of sight and the center of the sphere, the endpoint of that diameter must necessarily be in the same surface as its other two points. Therefore, the aforementioned five points are necessarily in every surface of reflection created by the proposed mirrors. And this is the proposition.

<margin>Euclid, Theorem 24 of the *Catoptrics*. Ptolemy, Theorem 1, Book 2 of the *Catoptrics*. Alhazen, Note 44, Book 4; also Note 62, Book 5.</margin>

**4. If the center of sight or the point of the thing being seen exists at the center of a spherical concave mirror, the reflection from any point will return back into itself. From this, it is clear that in this position, the sight will perceive nothing but itself, and that a point of an object existing at the center of the mirror is not reflected in any other way to the sight.**

Let there be a spherical concave mirror whose center is *a*; and let one of its great circles be marked as *b c d e*; and let the center of sight be at the center of the mirror, which is point *a*. I say that from whatever point a reflection is made to the eye, the ray must always be reflected back into itself. For given that a reflection occurs from point *b* to the center of the mirror *a* (where the eye is located), it is clear by Theorem 72 of Book 1 that the line *b a* (which is the line of reflection) is perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror at point *b*. But every perpendicular line always reflects back onto itself, according to Theorem 21 of Book 5. If, therefore, line *b a* is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, it is clear that the incoming line was also perpendicular and identical to line *b a*. For if the opposite were assumed, it would follow that the **angle of incidence** would be unequal to the **angle of reflection**, which is contrary to Theorem 20 of Book 5 and is impossible. Thus, line *a b* reflects into itself, just as it was made as line *b a*. And since in this position of the eye, all lines falling upon the surface of the mirror are its radii, it is clear that all angles of incidence are equal to one another according to Theorem 43 of Book 1, because they are "angles of semicircles" <note>In medieval geometry, this refers to the angle formed between a diameter and the circumference of a circle.</note>. They are therefore necessarily reflected into themselves. Consequently, the form of the observing eye will be seen as a single form across the entire surface, and it will appear at the surface of the mirror; no other form will be seen reflected to the eye at that time. From this, it is clear that when the sight is at the center *a*, it will see itself perpendicularly from every point of the given mirror, and it will see nothing else by reflection from the mirror's surface, because it is impossible to draw more than one perpendicular line from a single point of the mirror to the center (as shown in Theorem 20, Book 1). Similarly, a point of a seen object existing at the center of sight is not reflected to the eye [elsewhere], but only into itself, since all incident lines are perpendicular to the surface of the mirror; whence

And these things have been said, provided that the physical density of the head <note>The author is being practical: for an eye to be at the exact center of a sphere, the observer's head would usually block the light. He is speaking mathematically here, assuming the "sight" is a single point that doesn't obstruct anything.</note> does not present an impediment to the sight. If, therefore, the center of human sight is positioned on the diameter of the sphere of a concave mirror, and specifically at its center (since any line drawn from the sight to the surface of the mirror is perpendicular to it) then, as demonstrated before, the sight will perceive itself. The form of any other point of the mirror will not be perceived, except for the points on the portion of the circle lying between the lines of the **visual pyramid** <term>visual pyramid: the cone-shaped field of vision extending from the eye to the object being seen</term>, which is understood to extend from the center of the mirror. This is because the form of any other point will fall into the mirror upon a line slanting from the sight, and will necessarily be reflected along that same slanted line. Therefore, the line of reflection will not pass through the center of the mirror, and thus it will not reach the center of sight. Thus the proposition is clear.

**5. When the center of sight is located on a radius of a concave spherical mirror, but away from the center of the sphere: it is impossible for the form of any points on that same radius to be reflected to the sight if they strike the mirror obliquely; however, points on the opposite radius can be reflected.**

This proposition is clearly demonstrated. For if the center of sight is on a certain radius of the proposed mirror, but not at its center: the sight will not perceive the form of any point on that same radius if it hits the mirror at an angle (obliquely). This is because the angle formed by two lines—one drawn from a point on that radius and the other from the center of sight to the same spot on the mirror—cannot be divided in half by a perpendicular line drawn from that spot on the mirror. This is because that perpendicular line must always point toward the center of the mirror. 

However, the sight *can* perceive the form of a point located on the *other* radius (the one that joins with the first to complete the full diameter). In this case, when the point strikes the mirror obliquely, the angle between the **line of incidence** <term>line of incidence: the path the light takes from the object to the mirror</term> and the **line of reflection** <term>line of reflection: the path the light takes from the mirror to the eye</term> can be divided into two equal parts by a line drawn from the point of reflection to the center of the mirror. This is the fundamental law of reflection for all mirrors: the perpendicular line drawn from the point of reflection always bisects the angle formed by the incoming and outgoing light (according to Theorem 26 of Book 5 of this work). Therefore, that point can be seen in the mirror. There is only one such point on any given diameter that can be reflected from a specific circle of the mirror to the eye. Because the center of the mirror and the center of the eye are fixed, only one point from a single circle of the mirror will reflect to the eye; however, different circles of the mirror can reflect different points of the diameter. Thus the proposition is clear.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 4, Chapter 5, Note 4.</margin>
**6. When the sight is positioned away from the center of a concave spherical mirror: a reflection of some other point's form can occur to the sight from any point on the mirror, except only from that point where the visual diameter strikes.**

Let the intersection of the surface of reflection and the surface of the concave spherical mirror be a **great circle** <term>great circle: the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, sharing the same center and diameter as the sphere itself</term> (according to Theorem 2 of this book), which we shall call *g d c*. Let its center be *b*, and the center of sight be *a*. Let the **visual diameter** <term>visual diameter: the straight line passing from the eye through the center of the mirror</term> be drawn from the center of sight through the center of the mirror *b*; let this be *a b d*, hitting the surface of the mirror at point *d*. I say that from any point on this mirror, a reflection of the form of another visible point to the sight *a* can occur, except from point *d* alone. 

For let there be another point on the mirror, *g*. Let the radius *b g* be drawn to it, and let the line of reflection be *g a*. Now let a **tangent line** <term>tangent line: a straight line that touches a curve at exactly one point without crossing it</term> *f g l* be drawn touching the great circle of the mirror at point *g*. It is clear from Euclid's *Elements* (Book 3, Prop. 18) that the angles *b g f* and *b g l* are right angles. It is also clear from Theorem 42 of Book 1 of this work that the angle *b g a* will be **acute** <note>original: "acutus"</note>. This is because the line *a g* will fall between the diameter and the tangent line *f g l* (which is outside the mirror), regardless of where the center of sight is placed, whether inside or outside the circle *g c d*. Let us also construct (by Euclid's *Elements* Book 1, Prop. 23) an angle *h g l* on the line *l g* at point *g* that is equal to angle *f g a*. Therefore, the angle *h g b* will be equal to angle *b g a*.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram depicting reflection in a concave spherical mirror. A circle is labeled with points g, c, d. Point b is the center of the circle. Point a is an internal point representing the center of sight. A line (diameter) passes through a and b to meet the circumference at point d. Another point g on the circumference has a radius b-g and a line g-a (the reflected ray). A tangent f-g-l passes through g. And since the **angle of contingency** <term>angle of contingency: the infinitely small "angle" between a curve and its tangent line</term> is the smallest of all angles (according to Euclid's *Elements* Book 3, Prop. 16), it is clear that if any acute straight-lined angle is subtracted from the right angle *b g l*, the line forming that angle will always fall *inside* the circle *g c d*, because only the angle of contingency stays outside the circle. Therefore, if we place any visible point on the line *h g*, a reflection of that point's form will always reach the sight at *a*. 

The same can be proven for any other point on the mirror besides point *d*. However, a reflection also happens at point *d*. Since the line *a d* is perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror at point *d*, it is clear that the line *a d* reflects back upon itself (according to Theorem 21 of Book 5 of this work). Thus, if something opaque is placed between the eye at *a* and the mirror at *d*, the reflection is blocked. But if nothing is in the way, the eye will see only the form of its own surface reflected from that point, and nothing else. And this is the intended proposition.

VITELLO'S OPTICS

# 7. *In concave spherical mirrors, if the center of sight is placed on or outside the circumference: the eye is not seen, unless the light is reflected along the diameter of the mirror. Euclid, Theorem 25 of the Catoptrics.*

Let the great circle of a concave spherical mirror be $a$, $b$, $g$. Let the center of sight be at point $b$ on the circumference of the mirror, and let lines $b a$ and $b g$ be drawn, but not through the center. Since the angle of the larger portion of the circle is greater (as shown in Theorem 43 of Book 1 of this work <note>original: "43 th. 1 huius"; Vitello frequently cites his own earlier mathematical proofs</note>), and the angle of reflection must always be equal to the angle of incidence (as shown in Theorem 20 of Book 5), it is clear that reflection will not occur along the line $a b$. Instead, it will be directed toward the side of the larger angle. The same is true for point $g$: reflection will not occur along the line $b g$, but toward the side of the larger angle, according to Theorem 33 of Book 5. 

For if the form <note>In medieval optics, a "form" or "species" is the visual image or information traveling from an object to the eye.</note> of point $b$ were reflected back to itself from points $a$ and $g$, then the angles of the circular portions at point $a$ and point $g$ would have to be equal. This is impossible and contradicts Theorem 43 of Book 1. However, the incoming sight can be reflected back onto itself along the diameter of any great circle of the entire concave spherical mirror. This is because the angles of all semicircles of the same circle are equal, according to the same Theorem 43 of Book 1. But in that case, no reflection will occur except for the single point of the mirror's surface that falls directly along the diameter, such as along line $b c$. This point is not actually perceived because it is **indivisible** <note>The author follows Euclidean geometry, where a "point" has no width or height. To be visible, an object must occupy enough space to create a "visual angle" at the eye.</note>. Everything that is seen must be divisible because it is seen under an angle, according to Theorem 18 of Book 3. Other points falling obliquely are reflected toward the side of the larger angle and do not reach the sight—except for those whose lines of reflection happen to strike the surface of the eye. In those cases, the parts of the thing seen are perceived with their positions reversed. Anything not reflected in this way is not seen. Therefore, in these concave spherical mirrors, if the center of sight is placed on the circumference, the eye is not seen unless it is reflected along the diameter. The same thing happens if the eye is placed outside the circumference of the proposed mirror, and it is demonstrated in the same way, since the inequality of the lines does not change the nature of reflection, according to Theorem 20 of Book 5. Thus the proposition is clear.

# 8. *If the sight is positioned on the other side of the extended diameter outside the circle of a concave spherical mirror—whether on a transverse diameter, or beyond it, or on this side of it—none of the things arranged in 그 part can possibly be seen. Euclid, Theorem 26 of the Catoptrics.*

Let the common section of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror be the circle $a g d$. Let its center be $z$, and let the radius $z g$ be extended outside the mirror to point $h$. Let another diameter $a z d$ be drawn through center $z$ and points $p, i, h$, perpendicular to the line $h g$. Let the center of sight be at point $b$ on the other side of the diameter $h g$. From point $b$, draw a line parallel to line $h g$ (according to Book 1, Proposition 31), which shall be line $b e$, meeting the surface of the mirror at point $e$. I say that none of the visible things placed on that side of the diameter $h g$ and line $b e$ (the side where the eye is located) can be seen. 

Suppose, if it were possible, that point $q$ located on that side could be seen by the eye at point $b$ through reflection. Let the form of point $q$ fall upon the mirror at point $e$, making the line of incidence $q e$. From point $e$, draw a line tangent to the circle (according to Book 2, Proposition 17), which shall be $p e o$, and draw line $e z$. If the form of point $q$ were reflected from point $e$ to the eye at $b$, it is clear from Theorem 20 of Book 5 that angle $q e o$ would be equal to angle $b e p$. But angle $b e p$ is greater than a right angle, because angle $z e p$ is a right angle (according to Book 3, Proposition 18). Therefore, angle $q e o$ would also be greater than a right angle, which contradicts Book 1, Proposition 13 <note>Proposition 13 states that angles on a straight line must sum to two right angles; an angle of reflection cannot physically "exceed" the boundary of the reflecting surface's tangent.</note>. 

It is therefore clear that the form of point $q$ is not reflected from point $e$ to the sight at $b$. Nor can it be reflected from any other point on the arc $e d$, for the same impossibility would result. However, if an angle equal to angle $b e z$ is constructed upon the end of line $z e$ (according to Book 1, Proposition 23), it would be possible for the forms of points on the extended line $r e$ to be reflected from point $e$ to the eye at $b$. The same result is clear if the sight is placed at point $m$ on this side of diameter $a d$ (with line $t k$ extended), or if it is placed at point $m$ beyond diameter $a d$ (with line $m n$ drawn), after connecting lines $z k$ and $z n$ and following the same deduction as before. Thus the proposition is clear.

**11. The location of the images of forms reflected from concave spherical mirrors is sometimes at the very point of reflection; sometimes beyond the mirror; sometimes between the eye and the mirror; sometimes on the surface of the eye itself; and sometimes behind the eye. <note>original: "Alhazen 60 n 5." This refers to Book 6, Proposition 5 of the "Optics" by the mathematician Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen.</note>**

When the form of a point of an object seen is viewed along the <term>cathetus of its incidence</term> <note>The cathetus is a line perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of reflection. In medieval optics, the image was believed to always lie on this perpendicular line.</note>, then the image is necessarily seen on the surface of the mirror itself, specifically at the point of its reflection. But when the forms fall obliquely onto the surfaces of the proposed mirrors, the locations of the images vary, as is proposed. This is what was proposed. And if the center of the eye is outside the circle of the mirror or on its circumference, the same thing happens and is to be demonstrated in the same way, since line $a e$ is always longer than line $a d$; and everything occurs as before. Thus, what was proposed is evident.

**12. The perception of images reflected from concave spherical mirrors varies according to the specific difference of their locations. <note>original: "Alhazen 61 n 5." Referring to Alhazen’s Book 6, Proposition 5.</note>**

Let the arrangement from the previous figure remain entirely the same. When the location of the image is beyond the mirror, as at point $l$, or between the eye and the mirror, as at point $s$, then—because the eye always perceives forms more perfectly when they are positioned in front of it—the truth of that image is grasped. However, when the location of the image is at the point of reflection (as when the perpendicular drawn from the point of the object being seen is parallel to the line of reflection), the location of the image is then at point $e$. Because point $e$, by the 3rd theorem of the 2nd book, is a <term>natural point</term> <note>original: "punctus naturalis." In medieval physics, a "natural point" is not a dimensionless geometric point, but the smallest physically perceptible unit of matter or space.</note>—which is divisible and sensible, capable of holding the image of a sensible object—it will have its own dimensions. Taking an "intellectual" <note>purely geometric</note> point in its middle, the image of any part of that sensible point that is beyond the chosen middle point will appear beyond the mirror, and the image of the other part, which is closer than the middle point, will appear between the eye and the mirror. Since the total form, following its parts further from or closer to the eye, always appears as one continuous thing, the form of that sensible point nearest the intellectual point will necessarily be seen on the surface of the mirror itself, at the point of reflection. Other parts of the sensible form surrounding that point will be seen to deviate from that point in the manner described: some toward the eye and within the mirror, others beyond the mirror. 

But in images whose location is point $a$ (the center of the eye), their true form is not grasped; hence, visual error occurs more frequently in forms seen this way. For greater evidence of this, so that not only demonstration but also experience may teach what we have set forth: let a wooden or iron rod be erected perpendicularly on the surface of a concave spherical mirror, and let it be shorter than half the radius of the mirror. Let the center of the eye be placed near the top of this rod, and let a visual ray be directed to a point on the mirror whose distance from the rod is greater than the distance of the center of the eye from the diameter passing through the rod. The image of that rod will then appear behind the eye, nor will there be a certain perception of its form; indeed, it will appear somewhat curved, even though the rod is straight. From this, it is clear that in these mirrors, the truth of the image is not grasped unless its location is beyond the mirror or between the eye and the mirror. These things can be made clear through experience by varying the position of the rod and the eye in different ways; it also happens that when the center of the eye is on the perpendicular line passing through the wood, it will not fully perceive the form of that wood. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Referring to Alhazen’s Book 6, Proposition 11 (in some editions).</note>**

*14. In concave spherical mirrors, it is sometimes possible for reflection to occur along the entire circumference of a single circle. Alhazen Book 5, number 65.*

Let there be a great circle of a concave spherical mirror, which is $abgd$: whose diameter is $bed$, and center $e$. Let two points be fixed upon the diameter $bed$ on either side of the center $e$: let these be $h$ and $z$, at an equal distance from the center $e$; therefore lines $he$ and $ze$ will be equal. Let the diameter $gea$ also be drawn through the center by the 11th proposition of Book 1, perpendicular to the diameter $bd$: and let lines $ha$ and $za$ be joined. Since in triangles $hea$ and $zea$ the two sides $he$ and $ze$ are equal by hypothesis, and line $ea$ is common, and the angles $hea$ and $zea$ of both triangles are equal because they are right angles: it is clear by the 4th proposition of Book 1 that angle $hae$ is equal to angle $zae$. Therefore, by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work, the points $h$ and $z$ are reflected to each other from the point of the mirror, which is $a$. The same is also clear if lines $hg$ and $zg$ are drawn: because the mutual reflection of those points will occur from point $g$. If, therefore, with diameter $bd$ fixed, we imagine the triangle $ahz$ to be rotated around diameter $bd$, while the line of the triangle (which is $hz$) remains fixed: then point $a$ by its motion reaches point $g$, and from there returns to its first place, and by its motion describes a circle in the concavity of the mirror, from whose total circumference the mutual reflection of the forms of points $h$ and $z$ to one another will occur. This is because to whatever point of that circle lines are drawn from points $h$ and $z$, if a radius is always drawn from the center to that point, the angles at the point of that circle will be equal: and so from that point reflection occurs by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work. If, therefore, the center of the eye is at point $h$, the form of point $z$ will be reflected to it from the entire circumference of that circle. However, if points $h$ and $z$ are at unequal distances from the center $e$, reflection will not occur from that circle, but perhaps it will occur from another circle, which the point of reflection describes by its motion. Thus the proposition is clear.

Lines connect h and z to points a and g on the circumference, forming a diamond-like shape within the circle.</image-desc>

16. *With two points existing on one diameter of a concave spherical mirror at unequal distances from the center of the mirror, if the proportion of the excess of the distances to the smaller distance is the same as the proportion of the part of the diameter lying between both points to the part lying between the point closer to the center and the mirror: it is impossible for mutual reflection of those points to occur from the circle of that diameter.*

Let the great circle <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same center and radius as the sphere itself.</note> of the concave spherical mirror be *a b g d*: its center *e*: and the diameter *b d*: and let two points *z* and *h* be established upon that diameter *b d*: of which point *z* is further from the center *e*, and point *h* is closer: therefore line *z e* will be greater than line *h e*: and let their excess be line *z t*. I say that if the proportion of line *z t* to line *t e*, or to line *h e*, is as the proportion of line *z h* to line *h b*; then it is impossible for reflection to occur from any of the points of the circle *a b g d*. It is clear from the preceding proposition that reflection cannot occur from any of the points of the semicircle *a d g*: but neither can it from any of the points of the semicircle *a b g*. For let it be granted, if it were possible, that it occurs from point *l* of arc *a b*: and let line *l b* be drawn, and let a line parallel to it be drawn from the center of the mirror through <unclear>point l</unclear>, which shall be line *m e n*: and let lines *l z*, *l e*, and *l h* be drawn: therefore, by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, line *l z* will intersect line *n m*: let the point of intersection be *m*. Let line *l h* also be extended beyond point *h*, which similarly, by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book, will intersect line *m n*: let the point of intersection be *n*. Therefore, because by hypothesis the proportion of line *z t* to line *t e* is as the proportion of line *z h* to line *b h*: then by the 18th proposition of the 5th book, by composition, the proportion of line *z e* to line *t e*, or by the 7th proposition of the 5th book to line *h e*, will be as the proportion of line *z b* to line *b h*: therefore, by the 16th proposition of the 5th book, the proportion of line *z e* to line *z b* will be, alternately, as the proportion of line *h e* to line *b h*. But because lines *b l* and *n e* are parallel: it is clear by the 15th and 29th propositions of the 1st book that triangles *b l h* and *n h e* are equiangular <note>original: "æquiangula"; triangles with the same angles.</note>: therefore, by the 4th proposition of the 6th book, the proportion of line *e n* to line *b l* is as the proportion of line *e h* to line *b h*. Similarly, triangles *b l z* and *e m z* are equiangular by the 29th proposition of the 1st book, because lines *b l* and *e m* are parallel: therefore the proportion of line *e m* to line *b l* will be as the proportion of line *z e* to line *z b*: but the proportion of line *e h* to line *h b* is the same as that of line *z e* to line *z b*: therefore the proportion of line *e n* to line *b l* is the same as that of line *e m* to the same line *b l*. Therefore, because the proportion of lines *n e* and *m e* to line *b l* is the same: then by the 9th proposition of the 5th book, lines *n e* and *m e* are equal. Since, therefore, angle *n l m* is divided into equal parts by line *l e*, as is clear by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work: (for the reflection of points *h* and *z* occurs from point *l*) the proportion of line *l n* to line *l m* will be, by the 3rd proposition of the 6th book, as the proportion of line *n e* to line *e m*: thus line *l n* is equal to line *l m*: but line *l e* is common to both triangles *l e n* and *l e m*: therefore, by the 8th proposition of the 1st book, angles *l e m* and *l e n* are equal: they are therefore right angles by the definition of right angles: therefore, by the 29th proposition of the 1st book, angle *b l e* will be a right angle: therefore line *b l* touches the circle <note>i.e., it is a tangent.</note>, and falls outside the circle by the 16th proposition of the 3rd book: which is impossible: for it was drawn as a line cutting the circle by the 2nd proposition of the 3rd book. Therefore, reflection will not occur from point *l*. Furthermore, a greater impossibility follows if the proportion of line *z t* to line *t e* is made as the proportion of line *z h* to some line smaller than line *h b*. Therefore, the proposition is clear: since the same deduction must be made for any given point.

<margin>18. When the forms of two points existing on the same diameter of a concave spherical mirror are reflected to each other from some point of the mirror, it is impossible for them to be reflected from any other point of that same quadrant of the circle.</margin>

Let the arrangement be as in the preceding figures: let the form of point *h* be reflected to point *z* from point *l* of the mirror. I say that it is impossible for the reflection of the forms of those points to occur to each other from any other point of that same quadrant of the circle, which is *b a*, other than from point *l*. For let it be, if possible, that it occurs from point *s* of the same quadrant: and let the lines *z l*, *h l*, *z s*, *h s*, *e l*, *e s* be drawn. Since the angle *z l h* is divided into equal parts by the line *e l*, it is clear by the 3rd proposition of the 6th book <note>original: "3 p 6"; the Angle Bisector Theorem, stating the ratio of the sides is equal to the ratio of the segments of the base</note> that the ratio of line *z l* to line *l h* is as the ratio of line *z e* to line *e h*. Similarly, because angle *z s h* is divided into equal parts by line *e s*, by the 3rd proposition of the 6th book, the ratio of line *z s* to line *s h* will be as the ratio of line *z e* to line *e h*. Therefore, by the 11th proposition of the 5th book, the ratio of line *z s* to line *s h* will be as the ratio of line *z l* to line *l h*. Then, by the 16th proposition of the 5th book, by permutation, the ratio of line *z s* to line *z l* will be as the ratio of line *s h* to line *l h*. But line *z s* is shorter than line *z l* by the 7th proposition of the 3rd book; therefore, line *s h* is shorter than line *l h*. This contradicts the same 7th proposition of the 3rd book, because line *s h* is closer to the center of the mirror (which is *e*) than line *h l*. And since the same deduction can be made for any point on the arc *a b*, it is clear that reflection cannot occur from any point of the quadrant of the circle other than from point *l*. Similarly, it must be demonstrated in the quadrant of the circle which is *b g*, if reflection were to occur from any point of it. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<margin>19. When the center of a concave spherical mirror lies outside the line connecting the center of vision and the point of the object seen, these being in different diameters and equally distant from the center of the mirror: reflection to the sight occurs from only one point of the semicircle in whose radii those points do not lie.</margin>

at the point of the semicircle *a b g*, which is *b*. For let lines *d z*, *d h*, *z b*, and *b h* be drawn. And because, by the 3rd proposition of the 3rd book <note>original: "3 p 3"; Euclid’s theorem regarding lines bisecting chords</note>, line *b d* bisects line *h z* equally, it is clear that the two sides *b e* and *e h* are equal to the two sides *b e* and *z e*, and the angles *b e h* and *b e z* are equal because they are right angles. Therefore, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work, the reflection of the form of point *h* occurs from point *b* of the mirror to the center of vision, which is *z*. I say, therefore, that this reflection cannot occur from any other point of the mirror. For if it were granted that it occurs from point *t*, let lines *z t* and *t h* be drawn, and from the center *d* let line *d t* be drawn to the point of reflection *t*; let this line, when extended to line *z h*, intersect it at point *k*. Since, therefore, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work, line *k t* bisects angle *z t h* equally, it is clear by the 3rd proposition of the 6th book <note>original: "3 p 6"; the Angle Bisector Theorem</note> that the ratio of line *z t* to line *t h* is the same as the ratio of line *z k* to line *k h*. But line *z k* is smaller than line *z e*; therefore, it is also smaller than line *k h*. Thus, line *z t* will be smaller than line *t h*. But by the 7th proposition of the 3rd book <note>Euclid's theorem on lines drawn from a point to a circle's circumference</note>, line *z t* is greater than line *z b*, and line *h b* is greater than line *h t*; therefore, line *z b* will be smaller than line *h b*, which is contrary to the premises and contrary to the 4th proposition of the 1st book <note>The Side-Angle-Side congruence theorem</note>. Therefore, the form of point *h* will not be reflected to the center of vision at point *z* from point *t* of the mirror. Similarly, this must also be demonstrated for any other point of the semicircle *a b g*. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**20. When the center of vision and the point of the object being seen are located on different diameters of the great circle of a concave spherical mirror: it is possible for reflection to occur from some point of the arcs lying between the diameters of the circle passing through those points, but not from any point of the other arcs. Alhazen [Book 4], 66, number 5.**

Let the circle (which is the intersection of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) be *d g t q*. Let *a* be the center of vision <note>The position of the observer's eye</note> inside the concave spherical mirror, let *e* be the center of the mirror, and let *b* be the point of the object being seen. Let the diameter *d a g* be drawn through the center of vision *a*, and let the diameter *t q* be drawn as it happens. I say that if the point *b* of the object seen is on the radius <term>semidiameter|The distance from the center to the edge; a radius</term> *e t*, reflection of its form can occur to the eye at *a* from some point of the semicircle *d t g*, and from some point of the semicircle opposite to it, which is *d q g*. For let the line of incidence <note>The path the light travels from the object to the mirror</note> *b m* be drawn from point *b* of the object to some point *m* of the semicircle *g t d* (specifically on the quadrant arc *t d*). Let lines *b a* and *m a* be drawn, and let the radius *e m* be drawn. Because *e m* bisects the base *a b* of triangle *a m b*, it therefore bisects the angle *b m a* by the 29th theorem of the 1st book of this work. Therefore, let the radius *m e* be extended toward the part of the circumference opposite point *m*, to a point *h* on the arc *g q*. Let lines *b h* and *a h* be drawn; line *a h* will also intersect the diameter *t q*. Let it intersect it at point *c*, and line *h b* will intersect the same diameter *t q* at point *b*. <note>The text likely means point 'b' or another point on that diameter; the diagram clarifies the intersection</note> Points *b* and *c* are also on different sides of the center *e*. Therefore, line *e h* will bisect angle *a h b* by the 29th theorem of the 1st book of this work, since it bisects the base *b c* subtended <note>stretched underneath or across</note> by it. 

I say, therefore, that the form of point *b* can be reflected to the eye *a* from some point of the arc lying between the radii *e t* and *e d* (in which points *a* and *b* are located), which is arc *t d*. Likewise, it can be reflected from some point of the arc opposite that arc, lying between the other radii sharing those boundaries, which are *e g* and *e q*—namely, from some point of the arc *q g*. Furthermore, I say that reflection cannot occur from any point of arc *g t*. For if this were said to be possible, let some point *k* of arc *g t* be taken, closer to point *t*. Let lines *a k* and *k b* be drawn, and let line *k b* be extended until it falls upon diameter *d g* at point *o*. It will fall there by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work, because angle *b e d* is a right angle and angle *k b t* is acute, and all those lines are in the same surface <note>The same geometric plane</note>. Since, therefore, points *o* and *a* are on the same side of the center of the circle *e*, it is clear that the perpendicular drawn from point *k* to the center *e* does not bisect angle *o k a*. Thus, the form of point *b* cannot be reflected to the eye *a* from point *k* of the mirror. Similarly, if another point *f* is taken such that line *b f* is parallel to diameter *d g*, or such that angle *f b t* becomes obtuse, it will always be clear that the perpendicular *e f* does not bisect angle *b f a* by the 29th theorem of the 1st book of this work, because it will fall outside the base *a b* of triangle *a b f*. Therefore, the form of point *b* cannot be reflected to the eye *a* from point *f* of the mirror, nor consequently from any point of the arc opposite arc *g t*, which is arc *d q*. The same thing must also be demonstrated if point *b* of the object seen is on the surface of the mirror or outside the mirror, provided that point *a* (the center of vision) is inside the mirror; the method of proof will be the same. Likewise, if point *a*, the center of vision, is on the surface...

Even if the center of vision *a* is outside the mirror, and the point of the seen object *b* is inside the mirror, the same proposition is evident. For let lines be drawn from point *a* (the center of vision) tangent to the circle *g t d* according to the 17th proposition of the 3rd book <note>original: "17 p 3"; Euclid’s theorem on drawing a tangent to a circle from a point</note>, which are lines *a h* and *a z*. It is clear from the previous statements that the form of point *b* is reflected to the eye *a* from some point on the arc *t d*. Therefore, it must be from some point on the arc *t z*, because it is impossible for it to be reflected from any point on the arc *z d*. This is because that arc falls below the point of tangency, and also because of the inequality of the angles; for according to the 18th proposition of the 3rd book <note>original: "18 p 3"; Euclid’s theorem that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius</note>, angle *e z a* is a right angle, and angle *b z e*, by the 42nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, is less than a right angle. However, no reflection will occur from arc *t g* or *d q* due to the reasons mentioned above. Likewise, if point *b* is moved to another diameter, which is the same diameter *t q*, the same result will occur as before. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*21. When the center of vision and the point of the object seen are on different diameters of a large circle of a concave spherical mirror: if a line is drawn from the center of vision parallel to the diameter in which the object point lies, cutting the circle, then all locations of the images of points reflected from the arc of the mirror lying between the end of the object's diameter and that parallel line will be outside the mirror. The locations of images reflected from the remaining arc lying between the diameters will be behind the eye. For the opposite arc, the locations of the images will be between the center of vision and the mirror. Alhazen <note>original: "Alhazen 67 n 5"; referring to Book 5, note 67 of Alhazen’s Optics</note>.*

Let the arrangement be as before, and let a line be drawn from point *a* parallel to the semi-diameter *t e*, which shall be *a p*. I say that the locations of the images reflected from points on the arc *t p* will be outside the mirror, while the locations of the images from arc *q g* will be between the center of vision and the surface of the mirror. For given that the form of point *b* (located on semi-diameter *t e*) is reflected to the eye *a* (located on semi-diameter *d e*) from some point on arc *p t*, which we call *m*: it is clear by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work that lines *a m* and *b e* will meet beyond points *m* and *b* outside the mirror. Let the point of intersection be *l*, which, by the 37th theorem of the 5th book of this work, will be the location of the image of the form of point *b*. But if reflection occurs from point *n* of arc *d p*, it is clear by the same 14th theorem of the 1st book that lines *a n* and *b e* will meet beyond points *a* and *e*. Let the intersection be at point *s*; point *s* will be the location of the image of point *b* behind the eye. However, if the form of point *b* is reflected to the eye *a* from some point on arc *q g*—since it was shown in the preceding sections that this is possible—let that reflection occur from a point on arc *q g*, which we call *u*. It is clear, then, that the line *b e* when extended divides the angle *a e u*. Therefore, by the 29th theorem of the 1st book <note>Euclid’s theorem on parallel lines and alternate interior angles</note>, it is clear that it intersects the base *a u*; let it intersect it at point *x*. Thus, line *a u*, which is the <term>line of reflection<note>The path the light takes from the mirror to the eye.</note></term>, and the <term>cathetus of incidence<note>original: "cathetus incidentiae"; a line drawn perpendicular to the mirror's surface from the object, used to find the image location.</note></term> of the form of point *b*, which is *b e*, intersect each other at point *x*. Therefore, by the 37th theorem of the 5th book, point *x* is the location of the image of point *b*, and it lies between the eye and the mirror. According to these principles, the locations of images vary, as was also explained in the 11th theorem of this book. It is never possible for the location of the image to be at the center of vision, except when the object point and the center of vision are on the same diameter. For then, whenever reflection is possible, it is always clear that the line of reflection and the cathetus of incidence meet at the center of vision, since only that point is common to both those lines. Thus, what was proposed is clear. The proposition is always to be demonstrated in the same way, whether the center of vision *a* is inside the mirror, on its surface, or outside the mirror—provided that the line drawn from point *a* parallel to the diameter containing the object point intersects the circle of the mirror and is not tangent to it. Indeed, a form reflected from point *p* along line *p a* (if the point whose form is reflected is on the semi-diameter *t e*, to which line *a p* is parallel) can be seen on the mirror surface itself, as we showed in the 11th and 12th theorems of this book.

*22. Any point on the diameter of a large circle of a concave spherical mirror can be a location for images, no matter how far it is extended. Alhazen 68 n 5.*

Let *a g* be the diameter of the circle of a concave spherical mirror, which is *a r m g*, whose center is *d*. Let it be extended outside the circle, and let point *z* be marked on it. It is clear then, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book, that the form of point *l* is reflected to the eye located at point *e* from point *t* of the mirror. 23. ***When the center of vision and the point of the object being seen exist on the same diameter of a great circle: for points reflected from concave spherical mirrors, where the location of the image is the center of vision, it is possible for reflection to occur to the eye from only one point of the semicircle; or only from any point of one other specific circle.*** <note>Vitello is citing Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), Book 5, 69th proposition.</note>

Let *g z b a* be the circle of a concave spherical mirror, whose center is *d*. Let two diameters, *z a* and *g b*, intersect each other orthogonally (at right angles). Let point *e*, which is the <term>center of vision</term> <note>the position of the observer's eye</note>, be on diameter *z a*; and let *h*, the point of the object being seen, be on the same diameter *z a*. This is because wherever the eye and the object are located on a single diameter of that circle, the said diameters can always be drawn so that they intersect orthogonally, with diameter *z a* passing through points *e* and *h*. 

Now, either line *e d* (lying between the eye and the center of the mirror) is equal to line *d h*, or it is not. If they are equal, so that those points are equidistant from the center of the mirror: let lines *h g*, *h b*, *e g*, and *e b* be drawn. It is then clear by the 4th proposition of the 1st book <note>original: "4 p 1"; Euclid's Side-Angle-Side theorem</note> that triangle *h g d* is equal to triangle *g d e*, and equal to triangle *h d b* and triangle *e d b*, and their angles corresponding to equal sides are equal. Since angle *h g d* is equal to angle *d g e*, it is clear that angle *h g e* is divided into two equal parts by line *g d*. Therefore, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book, the form of point *h* can be reflected from point *g* of the mirror to the eye at point *e*. By the 37th theorem of the 5th book, the location of the image will be point *e*, which is the center of vision. Similarly, the form of point *h* can be reflected from point *b* of the mirror to the eye at point *e*, and again the location of the image will be point *e* for the same reasons as before. 

If, therefore, diameter *z a* remains unmoved while the semicircle *z g a* is imagined to move through the sphere of the mirror—or even if only triangle *h g e* moves while side *e h* remains fixed—it is clear that point *g* describes a circle by its motion. From any point on that circle, the form of point *h* can be reflected to the eye *e*, and the location of the image will always be point *e*, which is the center of vision.

Furthermore, it is manifest that the form of point *h* cannot be reflected to the eye *e* from any point of the mirror other than a point on that circle. For if it were reflected from another circle than the one caused by the motion of point *g* or point *b*, then it would have to be reflected from another point of that semicircle *a g z*. Let us suppose it is reflected from a point of that semicircle called *c*, which would be outside that imagined circle on the surface of the mirror. Let lines *h c* and *e c* be drawn. Line *e c* will be greater than line *e g* by the 7th proposition of the 3rd book <note>original: "7 p 3"; Euclid's theorem on lines drawn from a point to a circumference</note>, and line *h c* will be smaller than *h g* by the same proposition. Therefore, the ratio of line *e c* to line *h c* will not be the same as the ratio of line *e d* to line *b d*, which are equal. Thus, by the 3rd proposition of the 6th book <note>original: "3 p 6"; the Angle Bisector Theorem</note>, angle *e c h* is not divided into two equal parts by line *d c*. Consequently, the form of point *h* is not reflected to the eye *e* from point *c* of the mirror. The same deduction follows if point *c* is taken between points *g* and *z* on the arc *z g*. It is therefore clear that when the eye *e* and the object point *h* are on the same diameter and equidistant from the center of the mirror, the reflection of the object's form to the eye always happens in the manner proposed.

Therefore, the ratio of line *e q* to line *q g* is as the ratio of line *q g* to line *q h*. Furthermore, angle *g q h* is common to both of the triangles *e q g* and *h q g*. Just as these things have been demonstrated concerning mathematical points and circles, they are also to be understood regarding the middle points of <term>natural images</term> <note>In medieval optics, a "natural image" refers to the physical light and form of an actual object, as opposed to an abstract geometric point.</note> that are reflected. For the form of point *h* is seen as continuous with the forms of other points, and it is to be understood as the middle point in the whole reflected natural image. The middle point of that entire form will be at point *e*, which is the center of vision, and the whole form will be reflected from a circular area of the mirror having a perceptible width, the mathematical center of which is the aforementioned circle; points *e* and *h* are the <term>poles</term> <note>The fixed points around which the circle is generated.</note> of that circle. 

However, when line *ed* is greater than line *dh*, it could be so much greater that the form of point *h* is not reflected to the vision *e* from the point of the mirror *g*, as we showed in the 17th theorem of this book. For unless the ratio of the excess of line *ed* over line *dh* to line *dh* is greater than the ratio of line *eh* to line *ah*, the form of point *h* cannot be reflected to the vision *e* by the 16th theorem of this book. And the ratio of line *ea* to line *ah* will be greater than the ratio of line *ed* to line *dh*; otherwise, the form of point *h* could not be reflected to the vision at point *e*. Because if it were granted that it could be reflected, let it be reflected from point *g*. 

I say, therefore, that it necessarily follows that the ratio of line *ea* to line *ah* is greater than the ratio of line *ed* to line *dh*. For by the 42nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, the angle *hdg* will be acute; and by the same 42nd theorem of the 1st book, angle *dgh* will be less than a right angle. Therefore, let a line *gf* be drawn from point *g* tangent to the circle *agzb*. This line will necessarily meet with line *eh* by the 14th theorem of the 1st book, since angle *hdg* is acute and angle *dgf* is a right angle by the 18th proposition of the 3rd book. Let the point of meeting be *f*. Therefore, by the 13th theorem of this book, the ratio of the <term>perpendicular of incidence</term> <note>original: "catheti incidentiæ" — the vertical line dropped from the object to the reflecting surface.</note>, which is *hd*, to the line *de* (drawn from the center of the mirror to the location of the image), will be as the ratio of line *hf* (drawn from the point of the object seen to the end of the tangent) to line *fe* (drawn from the end of the tangent to the location of the image). 

Therefore, by the 5th theorem of the 1st book, the converse is true: the ratio of line *ef* to line *fh* is as the ratio of line *ed* to line *dh*. But the ratio of line *ea* to line *ah* is greater than the ratio of line *ef* to line *fh* by the 4th theorem of the 1st book; since an equal line (which is *fa*) added to both sides diminishes the ratio, therefore the ratio of line *ea* to line *ah* is greater than the ratio of line *ed* to line *dh*. If, therefore, the form of point *h* is reflected to the vision *e*, it is necessary that the ratio of line *ea* to line *ah* be greater than the ratio of line *ed* to line *dh*. This being so, it must be demonstrated in this arrangement of the center of vision and the point of the object seen, just as before. Thus, all things that were proposed are evident, since the center of vision and the point of the object seen were on the same diameter of the proposed circle of the mirror. Thus the proposition is clear.

24. ***When the point of the object being seen and the center of vision exist outside a concave spherical mirror, and not on the same diameter of the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror), it is not possible for reflection to occur to the eye except from only one point; and there will be only one location for the image.*** <note>Vitello is citing Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), Book 7, Section 5 (or proposition 70).</note>

Let *t* be the point of the object seen, and *h* the center of vision, and let *d* be the center of the mirror. Let lines *hd*, *td*, and *ht* be drawn. Therefore, the surface of reflection, which by the 3rd theorem of this book is the surface *hdt*, intersects the surface of the mirror by the 2nd theorem of this book along a circle, which we shall call *ebqg*. It is thus evident that the form of point *t* is not reflected to the vision *h* except from some point of this circle; for no reflection occurs outside the surface of reflection. Therefore, let angle *tdh* be divided into two equal parts by the 9th proposition of the 1st book <note>Vitello refers to Euclid’s Elements for these geometric constructions.</note>; let line *dl* divide it, intersecting the periphery of the circle at point *e* and line *ht* at point *l*. If, therefore, points *t* and *h* were upon that tangent line, wherever they might stand, it is clear that it is not possible for the form of point *t* to be reflected to the eye *h* from any point on the arc *bg*. For if a line is drawn from point *t* to any interior point of this arc, the line drawn from point *h* to that same point would fall upon the same arc from the outside and not the inside, since the point is outside the mirror. Thus, there would be no reflection from the interior part of the concavity of the mirror, as the body of the mirror itself would block it. However, reflection is possible from arc *aq*, because it is possible for lines drawn from point *t* and point *h* to fall upon the concavity of that arc. 

Therefore, let line *ld* be extended until it intersects arc *aq*, and let the point of intersection be *z*. I say that the form of point *t* will be reflected from point *z* to *h*, the center of vision. For let lines *tz* and *hz* be drawn, and let line *hz* intersect the perpendicular of incidence <term>cathetus: a line drawn perpendicular to the reflecting surface, used here to determine the geometry of the reflection</term>, which is *tdq*, at point *p*. Since angle *tdh* is divided into equal parts, it is clear that angle *tdz* is equal to angle *hdz* by the 13th proposition of the 1st book. Therefore, lines *td* and *hd* are either equal or they are not. If they are equal, and line *dz* is common to both, then by the 4th proposition of the 1st book, triangle *tzd* will be equal to triangle *hzd*, and angle *tzh* is divided into equal parts by line *dz*. Therefore, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work, the form of point *t* will be reflected to the eye at point *h* from point *z* of the mirror. 

But it is not possible for the form of point *t* to be reflected to *h* from any other point on arc *aq*. For suppose, if it were possible, that it is reflected from point *o*, and let lines *to* and *ho* be drawn. Let line *odm*, drawn through the center of the mirror, also divide angle *toh* into equal parts and intersect line *ht* at point *m*. It is clear, then, by the 8th proposition of the 3rd book, that line *tz* is shorter than line *to*, and line *ho* is shorter than line *hz*. Furthermore, by the 3rd proposition of the 6th book (since angle *tzh* is divided equally), the ratio of line *tz* to line *hz* is as the ratio of line *tl* to line *hl*. The ratio of line *to* to line *ho*, by the same 3rd proposition of the 6th book, is as the ratio of line *tm* to line *mh*. But by the 9th theorem of the 1st book of this work, the ratio of line *hz* to *tz* is greater than the ratio of line *ho* to *to*. Therefore, by the 11th proposition of the 5th book, the ratio of line *hl* to *lt* is greater than the ratio of line *hm* (which is greater than *hl*) to line *mt* (which is smaller than *lt*). This is impossible. For the ratio of a smaller quantity to a larger one is always less than the ratio of a larger one to a smaller one, which is easily shown by the 9th theorem of the 1st book. Therefore, the reflection of the form of point *t* to the eye *h* will not occur from point *o* of the mirror. Similarly, it must be demonstrated that it occurs from no other point except point *z* alone, which is what was proposed. 

But if lines *td* and *hd* are unequal, let the longer be made equal to the shorter by the 3rd proposition of the 1st book, and let the demonstration be organized as before. And since the form of any point of a seen object existing on the same line is always reflected from the same point of any mirror to the eye existing at any point on that same line (since the inequality of the lines does not change the nature of the reflection, as is clear from the 20th theorem of the 5th book; for the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection), it is clear that whichever of those lines is larger than the other, reflection will not be hindered on this account. Thus, reflection will occur from only one point of the mirror, and this can be declared by the diligence of the investigator following the previously established method. And because in such an arrangement of the center of vision and the point of the seen object, reflection occurs from only one point of the mirror to the eye, it is clear that there is only one line of reflection, which is *hz*. Therefore, there is only one location of the image, namely point *p*, where the line of reflection (which is *hz*) intersects the perpendicular of incidence (which is *tdq*). Thus, the proposition is clear.

Because if point *k*, which is a point on the tangent line, falls outside the periphery of the circle *mdto*, by joining the lines from the intersection points of line *ek* to the periphery of the smaller circle, it will be deduced in the manner described previously. For if a circle were created having its center on line *dz* in the manner of circle *tdho* having its center on line *do*: it is clear by the method of Proposition 24 of this book, having drawn line *th*, that the lines drawn from points *t* and *h* to point *z* (the endpoint of diameter *dz*), if they were extended to the other side beyond points *t* and *h*, would cut off equal intercepted arcs between one of them and diameter *edz*, which are *pe* and *se*. Therefore, they create equal angles with the diameter at point *z*, and reflection is possible, which occurs from point *z*. But to other points of the neighboring arcs, the lines extended from points *t* and *h* always cut off unequal arcs; because of this, they create unequal angles upon the circumference of the larger circle. By the method we used in Proposition 24 of this book, an impossibility follows against the 9th theorem of the 1st book of this work <note>original: "9 th. 1 huius"</note>, as is manifest through the preceding arguments. Therefore the proposition is clear: since reflection only occurs from four points when the arrangement is such, and there are only four locations of images. This is what was proposed.

**28. If another diameter bisects the angle contained by two diameters of a great circle of a concave spherical mirror: from every point of the arc lying between the first semidiameters <note>The "semidiameter" is what we today call the radius of the circle.</note> in which the reflected points do not lie (except for the point where the bisecting diameter falls), infinite pairs of points at unequal distances from the center of the circle are reflected.**

->[A circular geometric diagram labeled with points b, g, a, q, d, e, z, h, l, m, f, n, t, p, r, i. It illustrates reflection geometry in a concave spherical mirror, showing light paths between points l and m reflecting at point h on the arc. Diameter ez bisects angle bdg.]<-

Let the arrangement of the figure be as in the preceding: and let two diameters, which are $bq$ and $ag$, intersect the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the concave spherical mirror) at center $d$. Let diameter $ez$ bisect angle $bdg$. I say that whatever point is taken on arc $aq$, except for point $z$, from that point infinite pairs of points at unequal distances from the center can be reflected. For let point $h$ be taken on arc $aq$: and let point $l$ be taken on semidiameter $dg$: and from semidiameter $bd$ let line $md$ be cut equal to line $ld$: and let lines $lm, lh, mh, dh$ be drawn. Diameter $ez$ will intersect line $ml$ by the 29th theorem of the 1st [book] of this work, because it bisects angle $bdg$, which line $lm$ subtends. Let the point of intersection, therefore, be $f$. By Proposition 4 of Book 1 <note>This refers to Euclid's *Elements*, a foundational text for Vitello.</note> and from the hypothesis, line $mf$ will be equal to line $fl$. Let line $hd$ also be extended until it falls upon line $ml$; it will fall by the 29th theorem of the 1st [book] of this work. Let the point of intersection be $n$. Line $ln$ will be smaller than line $nm$: because line $dn$ bisects angle $fdl$, since angle $hdz$ (which by Proposition 15 of Book 1 is equal to angle $ndf$) is smaller than angle $adz$. But since angle $fdm$ is equal to angle $fdl$ by hypothesis, and to angle $qdz$ by Proposition 15 of Book 1, and angle $mda$ is equal to angle $ldq$: and angle $adh$ is equal to angle $ndl$: indeed angle $mdn$ is greater than angle $ndl$, and angle $hdq$ is greater than angle $adh$: therefore the whole angle $ldh$ is greater than the whole angle $mdh$. Therefore, by Proposition 24 of Book 1, line $lh$ is greater than line $hm$, since line $md$ is equal to line $dl$, and line $dh$ is common to both triangles $mdh$ and $ldh$. Thus, angle $dhl$ will be smaller than angle $dhm$. If it were granted that they are equal, then the ratio of line $lh$ to line $mh$ would be as the ratio of line $ln$ to line $nm$ by Proposition 3 of Book 6: which is impossible by Proposition 8 of Book 5. If, however, it is granted that angle $dhl$ is greater than angle $dhm$: then by the 27th theorem of the 1st [book] of this work, let an angle equal to angle $dhm$ be cut from angle $dhl$: and an impossibility follows, as before, by extending that cutting line to line $ln$ by the 29th theorem of the 1st [book] of this work. Therefore, angle $dhl$ is smaller than angle $dhm$. Therefore, let an angle equal to angle $dhl$ be cut from angle $mhd$, which becomes angle $thd$. Therefore, the form <note>The "form" (*forma*) refers to the visual species or the light reflecting from the object.</note> of point $t$, by the 20th theorem of the 5th [book] of this work, will be reflected to the eye existing at point $l$ from the point of the mirror which is $h$. And line $td$ is smaller than line $ld$, since it is smaller than line $dm$. Similarly, if other points than $l$ and $m$ are taken on semidiameters $bg$ and $gd$, equidistant from points $l$ and $m$, it will be similarly proved that from point $h$ there is a reflection of points at unequal distances from the center to one another. And so for infinite points taken on these diameters, the proof will always be similar. And from whatever point of arc $aq$, other than from point $z$, the demonstration is the same. But from point $z$, reflection is not possible because of the inequality of angles $tzd$ and $dzl$: which is clear by Proposition 4 of Book 1, by reflecting <note>Original: *relecta* (perhaps a typo for *reflecta* or *relecta* in the sense of 'laid out')</note> line $ld$ at point $p$ to the equality of line $dt$ by Proposition 3 of Book 1, and joining line $pz$. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

**29.
