# BOOK EIGHT.

Therefore, as is clear from the hypothesis, the form of point $t$ is reflected to the eye located at point $l$ from point $h$ of the mirror: this is evident by the 20th theorem of the 1st book of this work <note>Vitello’s first book serves as a mathematical primer for the rest of his treatise.</note> because the angle $thl$ is bisected by the line $ndh$. Therefore, by the 3rd proposition of the 5th book <note>Vitello frequently references Euclid's *Elements*.</note> it is clear that the ratio of line $lh$ to line $th$ is the same as the ratio of line $ln$ to line $nt$. And similarly, since angle $tkp$ is equal to angle $lkp$ by hypothesis: it will be, by the same 3rd proposition of the 6th book, that the ratio of line $lk$ to line $tk$ is as the ratio of line $lp$ to $pt$: but line $lh$ is greater than line $lk$ by the 7th proposition of the 3rd book, and line $th$ is smaller than line $tk$: therefore, by the 9th theorem of the 1st book of this work, the ratio of line $lh$ to line $th$ is greater than the ratio of line $lk$ to line $tk$: therefore the ratio of line $ln$ to line $nt$ will be greater than the ratio of line $lp$ to $pt$: which is impossible, and contrary to that same 9th theorem of the 1st book. Indeed, for any other given point of the said arc $hq$, the same impossibility occurs. It is clear, therefore, that it is impossible for the form of point $t$ to be reflected to the center of sight $l$ from any point of arc $aq$ other than point $h$. Therefore, it is not possible for any of the points equally distant from point $t$ and from point $l$ to be reflected from any point of arc $aq$ other than point $h$. And this is what was proposed. Thus, from these two theorems, the universal property is clear which applies to visible objects and to the sight so arranged with respect to the center of the mirror from all points of arc $aq$: since from no point of the other arcs is reflection possible for points so arranged, as is also clear by the 27th [proposition] of this book.

**30. With the center of sight within the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) and located on its diameter: from any point of that semicircle, the forms of points at equal or unequal distances from the center of the mirror are reflected to the sight along with the center of sight itself.**

->Alhazen, Book 76, note 5.<-

Let $a$ be the center of sight <term>center of sight: the point representing the observer's eye</term>: and let the center of the concave spherical mirror be $b$: and let $a$ be inside the mirror: and let a diameter be drawn, which is $dabg$: and imagine a plane surface in which points $a$ and $b$ are extended in any way: this therefore, by the 69th theorem of the 1st book of this work, will cut the sphere of the mirror along a circle, which is $dlg$. I say that from any point of either of these semicircles, the forms of points at unequal distances from the center of the mirror (relative to point $a$ itself) are reflected to the sight $a$. For let point $e$ be taken on the circumference of one of those semicircles: and let lines $ea$ and $eb$ be drawn. It is clear then that angle $aeb$ will be acute by the 42nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, because it falls within an arc smaller than a semicircle. Therefore, at point $e$, the endpoint of line $be$, let an angle be made equal to angle $aeb$ by the 23rd proposition of the 1st book, which shall be $peb$: and let line $pe$ be extended as far as you please. It is clear then, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work, that any point on that line is reflected to the sight $a$ from the point of the mirror which is $e$. Also, by drawing a perpendicular from the center of the mirror, which is $b$, to line $pe$ by the 12th proposition of the 1st book: either that perpendicular will be equal to line $ba$ (which is the distance from the center of sight to the center of the mirror), or greater, or smaller. If it were equal: then, since all lines drawn from center $b$ to line $pe$ (except for that perpendicular) are greater than that perpendicular by the 19th proposition of the 1st book (because they are opposite the right angle in that triangle): it is clear that all lines will be greater than line $ba$: and so every point of line $pe$, except for the single point where the perpendicular drawn from center $b$ falls upon line $pe$, will be at an unequal distance from center $b$ compared to point $a$, the center of sight. If, however, the perpendicular were greater than line $ba$: then it is clear from the preceding that all points of line $pe$ will be further from center $b$ than point $a$ is. But if that perpendicular were smaller than line $ba$: then it is possible for two lines to be drawn from point $b$ on different sides of the perpendicular equal to line $ba$: which is done by subtending those angles, right-angled on both sides of the lines, equal to line $ab$ by the 26th theorem of the 1st book of this work: and all other lines drawn from center $b$ to line $pe$ are either smaller or greater than line $ba$. It is clear then, by the 28th [proposition] of this book, that from point $e$ all points of line $pe$ are reflected to $a$, the center of sight, whose distance from the center of the mirror is unequal to the distance of the center of sight (which is $a$) from the same center of the mirror. But, as is clear from the premises, among these are points equally distant from the center of the mirror along with point $a$. Moreover, by taking any point in that whole semicircle in which point $e$ was taken, the proof is always to be demonstrated in the same way. The demonstration can also be formed in the same way in the other semicircle of circle $dlg$. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

<meta>This page continues the geometric proofs of Book 8 of Vitello's *Optics*, specifically building upon the work of the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham). This section focuses on the specific conditions under which light reflects within a concave spherical mirror depending on whether the observer's eye is inside or outside the sphere's curvature.</meta>

# VITELLO’S OPTICS

31. When the center of sight is outside the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror), if two lines are drawn from the sight touching the circle as tangents, along with a diameter of the circle: from any point on the arc lying between the far end of the diameter and the point of tangency (excepting those specific points), a reflection can occur to the eye from points that are at unequal distances from the center of the circle compared to the center of sight. <note>original: "Alhazen 77 n 5"</note>

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram showing a circle with center b. A point h lies outside to the right on a horizontal diameter line dg. From h, two tangent lines are drawn to points q and t on the circle. Another point f is marked on the arc between q and t.</image-desc>

The demonstration of this is evident from what has been previously stated. For let the center of sight **h** be outside the circle **d t g q**, the center of which is **b**: and let the diameter **h d b g** be drawn. It is clear through the 6th proposition of this book that no reflection occurs to the eye from point **g**. Let two lines be drawn from point **h** (the center of sight) touching the circle **d t g q** (following the 17th proposition of the 3rd book of Euclid's *Elements*), and let these be lines **h t** and **h q**. It is clear from what was said in the 24th proposition of this book that no reflection occurs to a sight at point **h** from the arc **q d t** <note>This arc is the part of the mirror facing away from the eye.</note>. Furthermore, no reflection to the eye at point **h** can occur from either of the points of tangency, **q** and **t**, because the angle of contact <term>angulus contingentiae; the "horn angle" between a tangent and the curve of a circle</term> is indivisible. Since lines **q h** and **t h** are tangents to the circle, and as is clear through the 42nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, every angle contained under the end of a chord and a diameter is acute, whereas angle **b q h** is a right angle. Therefore, no reflection of any form will occur from those points to the eye at point **h**. However, from the remaining points of arc **q g t**, except for point **g**, reflection can occur, as shown by repeating the demonstrations of the 6th and 24th propositions of this book. Thus the proposition is clear, the previous hypothesis being preserved.

32. When the center of sight is inside the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror), and a reflection is made from some point on the circumference of a point among those points unequally distant from the center of the mirror compared to the center of sight: the diameter of the circle in which the reflected point lies, together with the diameter in which the center of sight lies, sometimes makes an angle external to the angle of reflection that is greater, and sometimes smaller, than the angle composed of the angles of incidence and reflection. <note>original: "Alhazen 78 n 5"</note>

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram showing a circle with center b. A point a is located inside the circle on a horizontal line segment marked with points d, a, b, and g. Above the circle, a horizontal line segment contains points f, o, n, and p. Point e lies on the upper arc of the circle. Multiple lines radiate from centers b and e to the points on the upper line.</image-desc>

Maintaining the previous arrangement from the 30th proposition of this book, let line **b f** be drawn from the center of the mirror, **b**, perpendicular to line **e p**. Either line **b a** is perpendicular to line **e a**, or it is not. Let it first be perpendicular: then the two angles **f b a** and **f e a** will be equal to two right angles by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book of Euclid, because in the quadrilateral **f b a e**, the other two angles are right angles by hypothesis. Therefore, let line **b o** be drawn to line **e f**: and the two angles **o b a** and **o e a** will be less than two right angles, because angle **b o e** is obtuse and angle **b a e** is a right angle. Therefore, angle **o b g** (which, by the 13th proposition of the 1st book, equals two right angles when added to angle **o b a**) will be greater than angle **o e a**, which is the angle composed of the angle of reflection and incidence. And since triangle **e b f** is equal to triangle **e b a**—because angle **b f e** is equal to angle **b a e** (since both are right angles) and angle **b e f** is equal to angle **b e a** by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work—then by the 26th proposition of the 1st book of Euclid, angle **e b a** will be equal to angle **e b f**, for **b e** is a common side to both of those triangles. Furthermore, by the 4th proposition of the 6th book, side **f b** will be equal to side **b a**, since they correspond to equal angles. But side **o b**, by the 19th proposition of the 1st book, is greater than side **b f**, and therefore it is also greater than side **b a**. Now, if line **b n** is drawn to some point on line **f p**, then by the previous arguments, the two angles **n b a** and **n e a** will be greater than two right angles; but by the 13th proposition of the 1st book, the two angles **n b a** and **n b g** equal two right angles. Therefore, angle **n b g** is smaller than angle **n e a**. And since line **n b** is greater than line **b f** by the 19th proposition of the 1st book, it will be greater than line **b a**. Thus, the form of point **n** is reflected to the eye at point **a** from the point of the mirror **e**, and it is at an unequal distance from the center of the mirror **b** than is the center of sight **a**. And the diameter **b n**, in which the point of the thing seen (**n**) lies, makes with the diameter **a b g** (where the center of sight **a** lies) an angle **n b g** that is smaller than angle **n e a**, which is the angle composed of the angles of incidence and reflection. However, diameter **o b** with diameter **a b g** contains an angle **o b g** greater than angle **o e a**. Thus the proposition is clear. If, however, line **b a** is not perpendicular to line **e a**, then by the 12th proposition of the 1st book, let a perpendicular **b k** be drawn from point **b** to the extended line **e a**. Whether this falls beyond line **a b** or toward point **e**, the proof remains the same. For let line **b f** be perpendicular to line **e p**, and let line **f** <note>This likely refers to a segment of the line</note> be equal to line **a k**, and let line **t b** be drawn. It is clear then that in triangle **k e b**, angle **e k b** is a right angle, equal to an...

**34. When the center of vision and the point of the object seen are on different diameters of a circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror), and are at unequal distances from the center of the mirror: if reflection occurs from two points of the arc lying between the diameter in which the center of vision is and the other in which the point of the object seen is: both angles consisting of the angle of incidence and reflection will not be smaller than the angle, external to the angle falling on the same arc, contained by the said diameters. Alhazen, Book 5, Number 80.**

Let the center of vision be **b**, as in the previous proposition: and the point of the object seen be **a**: let the center of the concave spherical mirror be **g**: and let a diameter be drawn through points **b** and **g**, which shall be **z d**: and let a plane surface cut the mirror along diameter **z d**: and (by Theorem 69 of Book 1 of this work) the common section will be a circle, which shall be **e d h z**: and let diameter **e h** be drawn, in which the point of the object seen, **a**, is located: and let line **b g**, which is the distance of the center of vision from the center of the mirror, be greater than line **a g**. I say that if the form of point **a** is reflected to the eye located at point **b** from two points of arc **e z**, both angles consisting of the angles of incidence and reflection will not be smaller than angle **a g d**. For let there be two points from which the reflection of the form of point **a** to the eye at point **b** occurs, which are points **t** and **q**: and let lines **b t**, **g t**, **a t**, **b q**, **g q**, and **a q** be drawn. If, therefore, angle **b t a** (consisting of the angle of incidence, which is **a t g**, and the angle of reflection, which is **g t b**) is smaller than angle **a g d**, which is the angle external to the angle falling on arc **e z**: and it is angle **a g d** itself falling on arc **e d**. I say that angle **a q b**, which consists of the angle of incidence **a q g** and the angle of reflection **g q b**, will not be smaller than angle **a g d**.

For granted that that circle passed through center **g**, it would follow by Proposition 22 of Book 3 that angle **a g b** with angle **a t b** would be equal to two right angles: because those two angles would be positioned opposite each other in a quadrilateral inscribed in that smaller circle: but those two angles are smaller than two right angles, as is clear from the hypothesis, since angle **b t a** is smaller than angle **a g d**, which by Proposition 13 of Book 1 along with angle **a g b** equals two right angles. Therefore, that smaller circle will not pass through the center of the larger circle, which is **g**. ### *35. In concave spherical mirrors, it is possible to find two points, existing on different diameters and at unequal distances from the center of the mirror, which are reflected to one another from two points of the mirror—namely the arc lying between the semi-diameters in which those points consist. Alhazen, Book 5, Proposition 81.*

Let there be a circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the concave spherical mirror) whose center is **d**: and let two diameters be taken in it, which are **g a** and **b h**, intersecting each other at center **d**: I say that it is possible for what is proposed to be done. For let angle **g d b** be bisected by the semi-diameter **d e**: and on the semi-diameter **b d** let point **m** be taken beyond point **n**, upon which falls the perpendicular drawn from point **e** to diameter **b d**: and let line **n d** on diameter **d g** be taken equal to line **m d**: and by Book 4, Proposition 5 <note>Euclid's Elements: To circumscribe a circle about a given triangle.</note>, let a circle be made passing through the three points **m**, **d**, **n**: this will therefore necessarily pass beyond point **e**. For if it were granted that the circle passes through point **e**, let lines **m e** and **n e** be drawn: and a quadrilateral **d m e n** will be formed within the circle: therefore by Book 3, Proposition 22 <note>The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to two right angles (180 degrees).</note> the two opposite angles of the quadrilateral itself, such as those at points **m** and **n**, are equal to two right angles: which is impossible: because both angles **e m d** and **e n d** are acute, less than two right angles <note>In this context, "less than two right angles" means their sum is less than 180 degrees; specifically, each is acute (less than 90).</note>: because lines **e m** and **e n** fall beyond the perpendiculars drawn from point **e** onto the semi-diameters **b d** and **g d**. A similar deduction will also be made if the circle passes on this side of point **e**: for then the angles of that quadrilateral falling upon points **m** and **n** will again be less than two right angles. Therefore, circle **d m n** passes outside point **e**: it will therefore intersect the proposed circle of the mirror itself at two points by Book 3, Proposition 10: let those two points be **t** and **l**: and let lines **n t**, **m t**, **n l**, **d l**, **m l** be drawn: and let line **m n** be drawn intersecting line **t d** at point **f**, and line **e d** at point **p**. Since therefore angle **l m t** is equal to the two angles **m q t** and **m t q** by Book 1, Proposition 32 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Proposition 32 states that the exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note>, and angle **l n t** is equal to angle **l m t** by Book 3, Proposition 27 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 27: Angles standing on the same arc are equal to one another.</note>, for they are established upon the same arc, which is **l t**; and since angle **i n z**, from the premises, is equal to angle **m t q**, then angle **i n t** will be equal to angle **m q t**. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 32, triangle **m t q** is equiangular <note>The author uses "equiangulus," meaning the triangles have the same angles and are therefore similar.</note> to triangle **i n t**, since angle **o t n** is equal to angle **m q t**. Similarly, triangle **i n z** is, by Book 1, Proposition 32, equiangular to triangle **t n z**, since angle **t z n** is common to both those triangles, and angle **i n t** is equal to angle **o t n**. Therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 4 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 6, Proposition 4: In equiangular triangles, the sides about the equal angles are proportional.</note>, the ratio of line **n t** to line **t q** is as the ratio of line **n i** to line **m q**. Therefore, by Book 3, Proposition 27, angle **i n t d** is equal to angle **d t n**. But angle **q t m** is equal to angle **o t n** from the premises; thus angle **q t f** is made equal to angle **f t r**, because it consists of equal angles. Therefore angle **q t f** is acute, and line **k f** is perpendicular to line **t d**. Angle **t f k** is also a right angle; therefore, by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work, line **k f** if produced will meet with line **t q**. Let the point of meeting be **s**; and the line produced from point **t** as far as point **s**, which is the point of meeting, of which line **t q** is a part, is equal to line **t r**. For since the angles of those triangles at point **f** are right angles, and at point **t** they are equal from the premises, it is clear by Book 1, Proposition 32 that those triangles **t f s** and **t f r** are equiangular, and line **t f** is common. Therefore the remaining sides, which are **t s** and **t r**, are equal by Book 1, Proposition 26. But line **t s** is greater than line **t q**, and line **t z** is greater than line **t r**; therefore line **t q** is less than line **t z**. Thus, by Book 5, Proposition 8 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 5, Proposition 8: Of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has.</note>, the ratio of line **n t** to line **t q** is greater than the ratio of line **n t** to line **t z**. Therefore the ratio of line **n i** to **m q** is greater than the ratio of line **i n** to line **n z**; wherefore, by Book 5, Proposition 10, line **m q** is less than line **n z**. Let a line equal to line **m q** be cut from line **n z**, which shall be **n x**, and let line **d x** be drawn. And since by Book 3, Proposition 22 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 3, Proposition 22: The opposite angles of quadrilaterals inscribed in circles are equal to two right angles (180 degrees).</note>, angle **l n d** with angle **l m d** equals two right angles, and angle **q m d** with angle **l m d** by Book 1, Proposition 13 equals two right angles, angle **l n d** will be equal to angle **q m d**. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 4, triangle **x n d** is equal to triangle **d m q**, and line **d x** is equal to line **d q**, and angle **x d n** is equal to angle **q d m**, and angle **d x n** is equal to angle **d q m**. But angle **d x z** is greater than a right angle, since it is greater than angle **d n x** by Book 1, Proposition 16; and angle **d n x** is greater than a right angle by Book 3, Proposition 31, because it falls into a segment smaller than a semicircle, which is **d n l**; and this is also clear by Book 3, Proposition 22. For since angle **l m d** is acute, because angle **e m d** is acute from the premises, it is clear that angle **d n l** is obtuse. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 19, line **d z** is greater than line **d x**; therefore line **z d** is greater than line **q d**. Thus the form of point **q** can be reflected to point **z** from two points of the mirror, which are **t** and **l**; and points **q** and **z** are at unequal distances from the center and on different diameters. This is clear because angle **x d n** is equal to angle **q d m**; therefore, when the common angle **x d m** is added, angle **n d m** will be equal to angle **q d x**. But angle **n d m** is less than two right angles; therefore angle **q d x** is also less; therefore, even more so, angle **q d z** is less than two right angles. Therefore the two points **q** and **z** are not on the same diameter, but on different ones. And this is what was proposed.

### 36. Regarding concave spherical mirrors, for two points at unequal distances from the center and located on different diameters, which reflect to one another from two points of the arc lying between those semidiameters on which those points are located: it is impossible for them to be reflected to one another from any other point of that arc. Alhazen [Book 5], 82, number 3. <note>original: "Alhazen 82. n. 3." — Reference to the fundamental optical work by the 11th-century polymath Ibn al-Haytham.</note>

Let the circle of the concave spherical mirror be **a g b**, whose center is **d**. Let there be two points **k** and **o** reflected to one another from two points of the arc **b g**. Let point **k** be further from the center of the mirror, which is **d**, than point **o**. Let lines **g d a** and **b d m** be the two diameters on which those points **k** and **o** are located. Let point **k** be on the semidiameter **g d**, and point **o** on the semidiameter **b d**. Let the forms of these points be reflected to one another from two points of the arc **g b**, as shown by the preceding proposition; and let there be one point of the arc **b g** from which reflection occurs. It is evident then, from Proposition 34 of this book, that neither of the two angles consisting of the angles of incidence and reflection will be less than angle **o d a**; nor is any of those angles equal to angle **o d a**, as is clear from those things demonstrated in Proposition 33 of this book. Therefore, one of them will be greater than angle **o d a**. Let the angle which is at point **t** be greater than angle **o d a**. Let lines **o t**, **d t**, and **k t** be drawn. From angle **o t k**, by the 27th theorem of the 1st book of this work, let an angle equal to angle **o d a** be cut, which shall be **o t f**, with line **t f** drawn to the diameter **g d**. Let angle **f t k** be divided into equal parts by Book 1, Proposition 9, with line **t e** drawn to line **k f**. From point **k**, let a line parallel to line **t f** be drawn by Book 1, Proposition 31, which shall be **k z**. And since line **t f**, being parallel to line **k z**, meets with line **t e** at point **t**, it is clear that line **k z** will meet with line **t e** produced by the 2nd theorem of the 1st book of this work. Therefore, let line **k z** meet with line **t e** at point **z**. Let line **o k** be drawn, and by Book 1, Proposition 9, let angle **o d k** be divided into equal parts by line **d u**, intersecting line **k o** at point **p**. Since line **k d** is greater than line **o d**, as is clear from the hypothesis, and because by Book 6, Proposition 3, the ratio of line **k d** to line **d o** is as the ratio of line **k p** to line **p o**, line **k p** will be greater than line **p o**. Likewise, let line **d t** intersect line **k o** at point **n**. It is evident that line **d p u** falls between the two points **k** and **n**, but not between the two points **n** and **o**. For since angle **k p d** equals the two angles **p o d** and **p d o**, and angle **o p d** equals the two angles **p d k** and **p k d** by Book 1, Proposition 32; and angle **p d o** is equal to angle **p d k**, and angle **k o d** is greater than angle **o k d** by Book 1, Proposition 19; then angle **k p d** is greater than angle **o p d**. Therefore angle **k p d** is greater than a right angle by Book 1, Proposition 13, and angle **o p d** is acute. And angle **k n d** is also acute, which is clear if a circle is made passing through the three points **o**, **t**, **k** by Book 4, Proposition 5; for this will pass below point **d**, which is the center...

If, however, a line is drawn from that point of division of arc ***o k*** to the midpoint of line ***o k*** (which is the chord of that arc ***o k***), that line will be perpendicular to line ***o k*** by Book 1, Proposition 8 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Prop. 8 refers to the side-side-side congruence of triangles, used here to bisect a chord with a perpendicular.</note>. That perpendicular will fall between points ***p*** and ***k***, since line ***k p*** is greater than line ***p o*** from what was previously stated. The angle at point ***n*** on the side of that perpendicular will be acute; therefore, it will also be acute on the side of ***p***. The angle at point ***p*** on the side of ***o*** will also be acute, as was shown above. 

If, therefore, it is granted that point ***p*** falls between the two points ***n*** and ***o***, it will be impossible for that perpendicular to fall between points ***n*** and ***p***, because then it would intersect line ***d p*** and form a triangle in which one angle would be right and another obtuse. Since this is impossible <note>A triangle cannot have both a right angle and an obtuse angle, as the sum of all angles must be 180 degrees (two right angles).</note>, it is necessary that angle ***k n d*** be acute. Therefore, by Book 1, Proposition 13 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Prop. 13: If a straight line stands on a straight line, it makes either two right angles or angles whose sum is equal to two right angles.</note>, angle ***o n d*** is obtuse. Consequently, point ***p*** does not fall between points ***n*** and ***o***. 

Since angle ***o n d*** is obtuse, and as is clear from the premises, angle ***d p k*** is also obtuse, it would follow that in triangle ***d n p*** there are two obtuse angles. Since this is impossible by Book 1, Proposition 32 <note>The sum of the angles of a triangle is 180 degrees; thus, it cannot contain two angles of 90 degrees or more.</note>, it is evident that point ***p*** does not fall between points ***n*** and ***o***. Nor does it fall on point ***n***, as is obvious. Therefore, it falls between points ***k*** and ***n***. 

Because, as shown previously, angle ***k t d*** is half of angle ***k t o***, and angle ***k t e*** is half of angle ***k t f***, and angle ***k t o*** is greater than angle ***f t o*** within angle ***k t f***, it remains that angle ***e t d*** is half of angle ***f t o***. But angle ***f t o*** is equal to angle ***o d a***; therefore, angle ***e t d*** is half of angle ***o d a***. However, angle ***o d a*** plus angle ***o d f*** equals two right angles by Book 1, Proposition 13, and the three angles of triangle ***e t d*** equal two right angles by Book 1, Proposition 32. Thus, the three angles of triangle ***e t d*** are equal to the two angles ***o d a*** and ***o d f***. Therefore, by subtracting angle ***e d t*** (which is common to both) and subtracting angle ***e t d*** (which is half of angle ***o d a***), it remains that angle ***t e d*** is equal to half of angle ***o d a*** plus the whole of angle ***o d n***. 

But angle ***o d p***, which is half of angle ***o d k*** plus half of angle ***o d a***, is a right angle. Moreover, angle ***o d p*** is greater than angle ***o d n***, which is clear by Theorem 29 of Book 1 of this work <note>Witelo is referencing an earlier theorem in his own first book of Optics.</note>. Since, as is clear from the premises, point ***n*** of line ***d n*** falls between points ***p*** and ***o***, then angle ***o d p*** plus half of angle ***o d a*** is greater than angle ***t e d*** plus half of angle ***o d a***. It is clear then, since angle ***o d k*** plus half of angle ***o d a*** is a right angle, that angle ***t e d*** is acute. Wherefore, by Book 1, Proposition 15 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Prop. 15: If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another.</note>, its vertically opposite angle, which is angle ***k e z***, is acute. 

Therefore, if by Book 1, Proposition 12 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Prop. 12: To draw a straight line perpendicular to a given infinite straight line from a given point not on it.</note>, a perpendicular is drawn from point ***k*** to line ***t z***, it will fall between points ***e*** and ***z***, because as clear from the premises, line ***k e*** is not perpendicular to line ***t e z***. If, however, it were said that the perpendicular falls beyond point ***e*** onto line ***t e***, then since angle ***t e k*** is obtuse by the premises and Book 1, Proposition 12, it would result in a triangle having two angles—one right and one obtuse—which is impossible by Book 1, Proposition 32. Thus, that perpendicular will fall between points ***e*** and ***z***; let this be line ***k q***. 

With this maintained, we now interpose a necessary point: namely, that line ***k t*** relates to line ***t f*** as line ***k d*** relates to line ***d o***. For line ***t o*** is either parallel <note>original: "equidistans"</note> to line ***k d*** or concurrent with it. Let it first be parallel; then by Book 1, Proposition 29 <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Prop. 29: A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal.</note>, angle ***o d a*** will be equal to angle ***t o d***. Therefore, angle ***t o d*** is equal to angle ***o t f***, since, as is clear from the premises, angles

If, however, lines ***o d*** and ***t f*** meet, they will form a triangle, two sides of which will be equal by Book 1, Proposition 6 <note>original: "6 p 1"; Euclid’s Elements 1.6 states that if two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite them are also equal.</note>: because its two angles, which are ***f t o*** and ***d o t***, are equal. Since line ***f d*** cuts those two equal sides parallel to the base ***d o***: therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 2 and Book 5, Proposition 18 <note>original: "2 p 6 & 18 p 5"; these propositions deal with ratios in triangles with parallel lines and the addition of ratios.</note>, the ratio of one of those sides to line ***d o*** will be as the other is to line ***f t***: therefore line ***t f*** is equal to line ***o d*** by Book 5, Proposition 9 <note>Euclid 5.9: Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal to one another.</note>. > **38. With two points existing on different diameters of a concave spherical mirror circle, both outside the circle, or one inside the circle and the other outside it, and at unequal distances from the center, facing the arc of the mirror from which reflection occurs: if they are reflected from any point of the arc opposite those diameters, it is not possible for them to be reflected from any other point of the same arc. Alhazen [Book 5, Prop.] 84.**

Let there be two points ***a*** and ***b*** on different diameters outside the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the concave spherical mirror) whose center is ***g***: and let those diameters be ***a e*** and ***b d***: and let the point of reflection be ***t***: and let lines ***b t***, ***a t***, and ***g t*** be drawn. Line ***b t*** will thus intersect the arc of the circle: let the point of intersection be ***q***: and line ***a t*** will also intersect the periphery of the same circle: let the point of intersection be ***m***. And since angle ***b t g*** is equal to angle ***a t g***: it is clear by Proposition 26 of Book 3 <note>original: "26 p 3"</note> that they fall upon equal arcs. Therefore, let diameter ***t g*** be produced to the other part of the circumference at point ***p***: and arc ***q p*** will be equal to arc ***m p***. If, therefore, the form of point ***b*** is reflected to the sight existing at point ***a*** from some other point of the same arc: let that other point be ***h***: and let lines ***a h***, ***b h***, and ***g h*** be drawn: and let line ***b h*** intersect the circle at point ***l***, and line ***a h*** at point ***n***: and let radius <term>semidiameter</term> ***h g*** be produced to a point on the circumference, which shall be ***k***. Indeed, whatever other point of that arc ***d t e*** is given, the same impossibility occurs. It remains, therefore, that the form of point ***b*** is not reflected to the sight ***a*** from point ***h***, or from any other point of the arc ***d t e*** opposite the diameters in which points ***a*** and ***b*** are located, except from point ***t***. The same impossibility also occurs, and is to be deduced in the same way, if one of the given points is in the circle, and the other indeed outside the circle. The proposal is therefore clear.

**40.** *When two points exist on different diameters of the circle of a concave spherical mirror, at unequal distances from the center: if the line connecting those points, when extended, intersects the circle, it is possible for one of those points to be reflected to the other from only one point of the mirror, or from two, or from three, or from four: and the locations of the images are counted according to these.* Alhazen [Book 4], Proposition 86, number 5.

For then it is manifestly clear that circle *a b g* will not cut the circle of the mirror along arc *l m*: because that arc lies between lines *a g* and *b g*, and arc *b g a* falls outside those lines at other points of the periphery of the mirror circle itself, since both points *a* and *b* are outside the circle of the mirror. 

If, however, point *b* is on the periphery of the mirror circle or within it, while point *a* is positioned outside: it is then clear that arc *l m* will not be cut at two points, but arc *b g* will pass through some point of arc *l m*, which is *t*. Therefore, the angle made upon arc *l m* will be greater than angle *b g d*: because, once lines *l t*, *b t*, and *a t* are drawn, it is clear according to the premises of Proposition 22 of Book 3 <note>original: "22 p 3"</note> that angle *l t b* is equal to angle *b g d*: but angle *a t b* is greater than that one. It is therefore clear by Proposition 34 of this book that in this arrangement, reflection of the forms of those points to each other will occur from a single point, or from two points of arc *l m*. 

If, however, the two points *a* and *b* are within the circle of the mirror, and circle *a b g* cuts the circle of the mirror: then it is clear that circle *a b g* will cut arc *l m* at two points: because the two diameters of the larger circle, which are *g l* and *g m*, cut circle *a b g* at points *a* and *b*, and passing through they cut off arc *l m* from the circle of the mirror. Let circle *a b g*, therefore, cut arc *l m* at two points, which are *t* and *h*: and there will remain from that same arc *l m* two arcs on different parts of it, which are arcs *l t* and *h m*. Every angle established upon the arc of the mirror circle, which is *t h*, will be greater than angle *b g d*: which is clear if angle *a e b* is made on the periphery of the mirror; for that is greater than angle *b g d*. For if line *b e* is extended to the periphery of circle *a b g* at point *f*, and line *a f* is joined, then by Proposition 22 of Book 3 and Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle *a f b* will be equal to angle *b g d*: but by Proposition 21 or Proposition 16 of Book 1, angle *a e b* is greater than angle *a f b*: and therefore also [greater than] angle *b g d*. And the same must be demonstrated for any other point of arc *t e h*. From this arc *t e h*, therefore, as is clear by Proposition 34 of this book, reflection could occur, perhaps from only one point, and perhaps from two. 

But if reflection occurs from the two arcs *l t* and *h m*, which remain above arc *t e h* from arc *l m* and from different parts of the circle *a b g* itself: then according to the premises, all angles consisting upon those arcs contained under the lines produced from points *a* and *b* will be smaller than angle *b g d*. For let angle *b k a* be made upon a point of arc *l t*. And since arc *a t* of circle *a b g* is within the mirror circle under arc *l t*, let line *b k* cut arc *a t* at point *o*: and let line *a o* be drawn. It is therefore clear by Proposition 22 of Book 3 and Proposition 13 of Book 1 that angle *a o b* is equal to angle *b g d*: but angle *a o b* is greater than angle *a k b* by Proposition 16 of Book 1: it is clear, therefore, that angle *a k b* is smaller than angle *b g d*. And the same must be demonstrated for any point of arcs *l t* and *h m*. Therefore, by Proposition 34 of this book, reflection will occur from only one point of those arcs. Thus, in this position, reflection will occur from two points of arc *l m* lying between the diameters, or perhaps from three: and it is clear by Propositions 27 and 29 of this book that reflection will occur from only one point of arc *n d*: and so in this position, reflection will sometimes occur from three points of the mirror, and sometimes from four points. 

If, however, one of the points *a* or *b* is on the periphery of the circle, and the other is within the circle, and circle *a b g* cuts the circle of the mirror: then it will cut arc *l m* at only one point, which is *t*: because point *a* or *b* will be in the place of the other point *l* or *m*. For existing in one of the diameters *n m* or *l d*, and on the circle's periphery itself, it will be at the point which is the common section of those lines. And thus, with point *b* existing at point *m*, and point *a* within the mirror: only one arc of the whole arc *l m* will remain, which is *l t*. It is clear, therefore, according to the premises—with lines *a f* and *b f* drawn, as before, upon the arc of circle *a b g*, and lines *a e* and *b e* upon some point of arc *l m*, which is *e*—that by Proposition 21 of Book 1 all angles consisting upon arc *t b* are greater than angle *b g d*: therefore by Proposition 34 of this book, reflection can occur from two points of that arc, or from one. But all angles of arc *l t* will be smaller than angle *b g d*, as was shown before: and so by Proposition 34 of this book, from only one point of arc *l t* [reflection will occur]

**41.** *If two points exist on different diameters of a concave spherical mirror and are equally distant from the center, and if the line connecting those points cuts the circle: it is possible for one of those points to be reflected to the other from only one point of the mirror, or from two, or from four; but it is impossible for it to be from three. The locations of the images are numbered according to these points.* <note>Reference to Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 87, section 5.</note>

Let there be, as in the previous theorem, two points *a* and *b* on different diameters of a concave spherical mirror circle, which are *l d* and *m n*, such that point *a* is on diameter *l d* and point *b* is on diameter *m n*. Let points *a* and *b* be equally distant from the center of the mirror, and let line *a b* be drawn from one of those points to the other following the circle (which is the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror) whose center is *g*. I say that what is proposed is true. Indeed, that mutual reflection of those points toward one another sometimes happens from only one point of the mirror is clear from Proposition 19 of this book; and the same can also be shown by the method of Proposition 24 of this book. For the inequality of the lines in that position does not change the nature of reflection, as was declared in the 20th Theorem of Book 5 of this work. However, sometimes mutual reflection of these points *a* and *b* occurs from only two points; [but] it is impossible for the forms of points equally distant from the center of the mirror to be reflected toward one another from [exactly three points of] these mirrors. For if this mutual reflection should occur from any two points of one arc, then if the arc lying between those points is divided into equal parts and lines are drawn to that [midpoint], it is clear by Proposition 27 of Book 3 <note>Likely referring to Euclid’s Elements.</note> and because of the equality of the sides *g a* and *g b*, that the angles formed at that point are equal. Therefore, reflection will occur from that point by the 20th Theorem of Book 5 of this work; and reflection will also occur from some point of the arc opposite to that arc. It is therefore clear that reflection will occur from four points of the mirror, and not from three. And since, as is clear from the preceding theorem and from many propositions of this book, reflection of any two points toward one another never happens from three points of the mirror unless it happens from two points of one arc and from some point of the opposite arc lying between those diameters: it is therefore clear that in this arrangement, reflection will always occur from four points of the proposed mirror, and never from three. And this was what was proposed. Since we have arranged these two preceding theorems in the manner of an epilogue <note>A concluding summary of previously proven geometric principles.</note> to many of the preceding theorems, we believe they should be committed to memory.

**42.** *If the form of one end of a line is reflected from one point of an arc of a concave spherical mirror, and the form of the other end of the same line is reflected from another point of the same arc: it is necessary that all middle points of the observed line be reflected from the middle points of that arc. From this it is clear that the locations of the images of the middle points fall between the images of the endpoints.* <note>Reference to Alhazen, Book 4, Proposition 45, section 6.</note>

And from this it is clear that both the lines of reflection of the intermediate points, and the <term>perpendiculars of their incidences</term> <note>original: "catheti suarum incidentiarum." In optics, the "cathetus" is the normal line from the object to the mirror surface, or its extension through the center.</note>, meet between the locations of the images of the endpoint points. And because the common intersection of these lines is the location of the image by Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work, it is therefore clear that the locations of the images of the intermediate points fall between the locations of the images of the endpoint points. And this is what was proposed. The same thing happens even if the object seen or the center of sight are placed outside those diameters of the mirror, since other diameters can always be drawn through those points. Thus, the proposition is clear.

Thus, let line $ch$ be drawn: therefore angle $chd$ and angle $cmd$ are equal to two right angles by Book 3, Proposition 22: but angle $bmd$ with angle $bme$ equals two right angles by Book 1, Proposition 14: it remains, therefore, that angle $chd$ be equal to angle $bme$: but angle $zhd$ adds angle $chz$ to angle $chd$, which by Book 3, Proposition 27 is equal to angle $cdz$: and angle $cdz$ is a multiple of angle $zda$ by Book 6, Proposition 33: since, as shown above, arc $cz$ is a multiple of arc $zh$: therefore angle $chz$ is a multiple of angle $edg$: therefore angle $dhz$ exceeds angle $chd$ by a multiple of angle $edg$. And because arc $fmd$ is equal to arc $zhd$ by the 64th theorem of the first book of this work, arc $fzd$ remains equal to arc $zfd$: therefore by Book 3, Proposition 27, angle $fmd$ will be equal to angle $zdh$: but angle $chd$ is equal to $bme$: therefore angle $fmd$ exceeds angle $bme$ by a multiple of angle $egd$: but angle $omd$ is equal to angle $bme$ by Book 1, Proposition 15: therefore angle $fmd$ exceeds angle $omd$ by a multiple of angle $edg$. And because angle $gom$ is worth angle $omd$ and angle $odm$ by Book 1, Proposition 32: it is clear that angle $fmd$ exceeds angle $mog$ by a multiple of angle $edg$: but angle $fmd$ by Book 1, Proposition 32 exceeds angle $mud$ by the single angle $edg$: therefore angle $mud$ is greater than angle $mog$: therefore angle $mou$ is greater than angle $muo$ by Book 1, Proposition 13 taken twice: therefore by Book 1, Proposition 19, line $mu$ is greater than line $mo$. And because arc $hd$ is equal to arc $md$ by the preceding, the two angles $hfd$ and $mfd$ will be equal by Book 3, Proposition 27. Therefore, the forms of the points of the two lines $hf$ and $fu$ are reflected to each other: and similarly the forms of the points of lines $hb$ and $bo$ are reflected to each other: since by the preceding, angle $dbh$ is equal to angle $dbm$ by Book 1, Proposition 4 and by the previous hypotheses. Therefore, the two points which are $o$ and $u$ are reflected to the eye existing at point $h$ from the two points of the mirror which are $b$ and $f$. Therefore, by the 37th theorem of the fifth book of this work, point $q$ is the image of point $o$, and point $n$ is the image of point $u$. Let a line be drawn from point $m$ parallel to line $hq$ by Book 1, Proposition 31: which shall be line $ms$: and a line parallel to line $hn$, which shall be $mp$. Therefore, because angle $hnd$ is greater than angle $hqd$ by Book 1, Proposition 16, angle $mpo$, which by Book 1, Proposition 29 is equal to angle $hnd$, will be greater than angle $mso$, which by Book 1, Proposition 29 is equal to $hqd$: therefore point $p$ will be between the two points $s$ and $u$ by the converse of Book 1, Proposition 21. And because angle $hdn$ is a right angle: by Book 1, Proposition 32, angle $hnd$ will be acute: therefore angle $mpd$ is acute: therefore angle $mps$ is obtuse by Book 1, Proposition 13: therefore line $ms$ is greater than line $mp$ by Book 1, Proposition 19. But from the preceding, line $mu$ is greater than line $mo$: therefore by the 9th theorem of the first book of this work, the ratio of line $ms$ to line $mo$ is greater than the ratio of line $mp$ to line $mu$: but the ratio of line $ms$ to line $mo$ is as the ratio of line $qb$ to $bo$ by Book 6, Proposition 4: for triangles $qbo$ and $smo$ are equiangular by Book 1, Proposition 29: since line $ms$ is parallel to line $qb$, and angle $qob$ is common to both those triangles. And similarly the ratio of line $pm$ to line $mu$ is as the ratio of line $nf$ to line $fu$: by the same reasons as before, and by Book 5, Proposition 11, the ratio of line $qb$ to line $bo$ will be greater than the ratio of line $nf$ to line $fu$: but the ratio of line $qb$ to line $bo$ is as line $qd$ to line $do$: and the ratio of line $nf$ to $fu$ is as line $nd$ to $du$ by those things shown in the 13th [theorem] of this [book], the declaration of which, since it is manifest, we omit here on account of the multitude of diagrams. It is clear, therefore, that the ratio of line $qd$ to line $do$ is greater than the ratio of line $nd$ to line $du$. And this is what was proposed.

**45. In concave spherical mirrors, when the image occurs between the eye and the mirror: sometimes the distance of the image from the eye will be less than that of the object itself: however, from the surface of the mirror it will sometimes be less, sometimes greater, and sometimes equal.**

Let there be a great circle $abg$ in a concave spherical mirror, whose center is $d$: and let the radius be $db$: and let the center of vision <note>The observer's eye.</note> be at point $e$: and let the line of the object seen be $ztm$: which is reflected to the eye from point $b$ on the mirror. Let the line of incidence be $zb$, and the line of reflection $be$. I say that what is proposed is true. For let a line be drawn through the center $d$ to the line of reflection $eb$, which shall be $tdh$: and let it be perpendicular to the radius $db$. Similarly, from the point of the object, which is $z$, let line $zd$ be drawn: which, extended beyond point $d$ to the line of reflection $eb$, cuts it at point $k$: and similarly from the object point $m$, let line $md$ be drawn: which, extended to the line of reflection $eb$, cuts it at point $l$. Therefore, by Theorem 37 of the third book of this work, point $k$ is the location of the image of the form of point $z$: and point $h$ is the location of the image of point $t$: and point $l$ is the location of the image of point $m$. And it is clear because points $k$ and $h$ fall between points $e$ and $b$: and it is clear that since the locations of the images are closer to the eye (which is at point $e$), the distance of those images from the eye will be much less than that of the object itself. For since line $db$ always bisects the angle of every reflection <note>The law of reflection: the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence bisects the angle between the incident and reflected rays.</note>: it is clear that the center of vision and the point of the object are always placed on opposite sides of the center. Let line $ez$ also be drawn: and in triangle $kez$, angle $ekz$ will sometimes be greater than angle $kze$: therefore by Book 1, Proposition 19, line $ez$ (which is the distance of the object from the center of vision) will then be greater than line $ek$, which is the distance of image $k$ from the center of vision: but the locations of images $h$ and $l$ are less distant from the eye. Because in triangles $bdt$ and $bdh$, the two angles $bdt$ and $bdh$ are equal: because they are right angles by hypothesis: and the two angles $hbd$ and $tbd$ are equal by Theorem 20 of Book 5 of this work, since they are the angles of incidence and reflection: by Book 1, Proposition 32 those triangles will be equiangular: therefore by Book 6, Proposition 4, since line $bd$ is equal to itself, line $bt$ will be equal to line $bh$.

Therefore the image and the object seen will be equidistant from the surface of the mirror. But line $bk$ is shorter than line $bh$, and line $bz$ is longer than line $bt$: therefore line $bz$ will be longer than line $bk$: then the location of the image and the image itself will be closer to the surface of the mirror than the object of which it is the image. And because line $bm$ is shorter than line $bl$: and point $l$ is the location of the image of point $m$: it is clear that the object seen is closer to the mirror than its image. Thus the proposition is clear. And from this it is clear that for objects that are further removed from mirrors, and whose forms are reflected to the eye such that the locations of the images are between the eye and the surface of the mirror: their images become closer to the surface of the mirror and further from the center of vision. Also, for objects that are closer to mirrors, and whose forms are reflected to the eye, and the locations of the images are between the mirror and the eye, the images are further removed from the surface of the mirror and become closer to the eye.

And since by Proposition 29 of Book 1, angle $abm$ is equal to angle $kab$: therefore it is also equal to angle $kba$: because lines $ak$ and $bm$ are parallel, and these are <term>alternate angles</term> <note>Angles on opposite sides of a line crossing two parallel lines.</note>. And similarly, angle $agn$ is equal to angle $kag$ for the same reason: since lines $ak$ and $gn$ are also parallel: therefore it is also equal to angle $kga$.

And since angles $kag$ and $kab$ are equal, as shown before: angle $abm$ will therefore be equal to angle $agn$, and line $bm$ by hypothesis is equal to line $gn$: therefore by Proposition 4 of Book 1, line $am$ is equal to line $an$: therefore, as in the premise, line $af$ will be equal to line $aq$: therefore by Proposition 2 of Book 6, line $qf$ is parallel to line $mn$: and line $fq$ is greater than line $mn$. Since, therefore, the eye <note>original: "uisus"</note> is at point $k$ or above point $k$ on line $tk$: and line $mn$ is in some visible object lower than the eye itself: then the form of point $m$ falls upon the mirror according to line $mb$, and is reflected from point $b$ of the mirror to the eye according to line $bk$ in the surface of the circle passing through points $b, a, k$: and the form of point $n$ falls upon the mirror according to line $ng$, and is reflected from point $g$ of the mirror to the eye according to line $gk$ in the surface of the circle passing through points $g, a, k$: and by Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work, the image of point $m$ will be point $f$: and the image of point $n$ will be point $q$: and line $qf$ will be the diameter of the image of line $mn$: and line $fq$ will be greater than line $mn$. Therefore, the image of the seen object will appear larger than the object itself, and beyond the mirror. In this position of the eye and the visible object, the proposition is clear.

If, therefore, the whole figure is rotated around line $au$, while line $au$ itself remains immobile: then point $k$ will describe by its motion a certain circle, over which line $au$ is erected, passing to each side of the surface of that circle: and every point of that circle will have a position relative to a line equivalent to line $mn$. If, therefore, the eye is at any point on the circumference of this circle, and a line equivalent to line $mn$ is on the surface of some seen object, facing the center of vision according to that position, just as the seen object (in which line $mn$ is) faced the eye existing at point $k$: then the eye will perceive the form of that line to be larger than its own proper size. And similarly, if line $tk$ is extended continuously and straight: and another point besides point $k$ is marked on it, such as point $p$: and lines are drawn to that point $p$ just as they were previously drawn to point $k$: the same result will occur as happened before at point $k$. Thus, as is clear through the present theorem and through the one immediately preceding, it is often seen in concave spherical mirrors that the image of the seen object is larger than the seen object itself: which is to be noted.

# WITELO'S OPTICS
### BOOK EIGHT

...line $zl$, just as the ratio of line $zb$ is to line $ha$: but line $zb$ is equal to line $ha$, as is evident from the previous points: therefore line $hk$ is equal to line $zl$. But line $hg$ is also equal to line $zg$, as was shown above: therefore the remainder will be equal to the remainder: thus line $gk$ is equal to line $gl$. Since, therefore, the two lines $zg$ and $hg$ are equal to each other, and the two lines $gk$ and $kl$ <note>The OCR likely intended $gl$ here based on the geometry</note> are equal to each other: it is clear by Proposition 7 of Book 5 <note>Propositions cited throughout refer to Euclid's *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of the time.</note> that the ratio of line $zg$ to line $gl$ is as the ratio of line $hg$ to line $gk$: but angles $zgh$ and $kgl$ are equal by Proposition 15 of Book 1: therefore by Proposition 6 of Book 6 the <term>triangles<note>original: "trigona"</note></term> $zgh$ and $kgl$ will be equiangular. Therefore, angle $zhk$ is equal to angle $lkh$: thus by Proposition 27 of Book 1, the lines $zh$ and $kl$ are parallel; which can also be shown by Theorem 14 of Book 1 of this work. Likewise, angle $hga$, as is clear from the premises, is obtuse: therefore by Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle $agk$ is acute. Indeed, the two angles $hag$ and $gak$ are equal: there remains, therefore, by Proposition 32 of Book 1, that angle $akg$ is greater than angle $ahg$. Thus, by Proposition 19 of Book 1, in triangle $ahk$, side $ah$ is greater than side $ak$, and the two angles at $a$ are equal: therefore by Proposition 3 of Book 6, line $hg$ is greater than line $gk$: and similarly line $zg$ is greater than line $gl$. Therefore line $zh$ is greater than line $kl$ by Proposition 4 of Book 6: but line $kl$ is the diameter of the image of line $zh$: therefore, the line $zh$ will be seen as smaller than it truly is. 

If, therefore, we were to rotate the circle $abd$, while line $ed$ remains fixed: a circle would be described on the surface of the mirror by the two points $a$ and $b$: and just as the eye existing at point $e$ relates to the visible thing in which line $zh$ lies, so it will relate to any corresponding line falling within that circle, which the points $z$ and $h$ mark, reflected from an arc corresponding to arc $ab$, from that portion of the mirror divided by the circle marked by the two points $a$ and $b$. And it can be declared similarly if line $zh$ is placed larger or smaller than it has been placed now. For universally in this position, the diameter of the image or of the face of the beholder is perceived in a concave spherical mirror as smaller than it is: but the image also appears inverted. For if the eye is at point $e$, then the beholder will perceive his own form in such a mirror as smaller than it is. And because point $k$ is the image of point $h$, and point $l$ is the image of point $z$: the image will be inverted: because the right part will appear left, and the left right: and similarly the upper part will appear lower, and the lower upper. And in the same way, the eye will perceive its own form: because that which is on the right, it will perceive on the left, and vice versa: and what is below, it will perceive above, and vice versa. Likewise also, if the eye is at any point between which and the surface of the mirror the center of the mirror is located: it will always perceive its form as inverted. And this is what was proposed. 

From these four preceding theorems, it is clear that in concave spherical mirrors, the image of a visible thing is sometimes larger, sometimes smaller, and sometimes equal to the visible thing: and sometimes it has a position conforming to the visible thing itself, and sometimes inverted. And since, as we showed through Proposition 40 of this book, sometimes one image of one thing is seen, sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes four: therefore, that which has one image larger than itself may perhaps have others smaller or equal; and that which has one image smaller than itself may perhaps have others larger or equal; and that which has one equal, may perhaps have others larger or smaller. And that which has one image whose position is direct <note>i.e., upright</note> relative to the visible thing, may perhaps be seen under other images having an inverted position contrary to the visible thing. And all these things can be made clear from the premises, based on the diversity of the position of the visible thing and of the eye itself with respect to the points of reflection. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 52. When incident lines intersect each other in concave spherical mirrors: heights and depths erected above the surface of the mirror existing on this side of the point of intersection [appear] reversed: but those which are on the same lines beyond the intersection appear just as they are. Euclid, Theorem 11 of the *Catoptrics*.

...moreover, by the 37th theorem of Book 5 of this work <note>Witelo's own fifth book, which establishes the fundamental laws of reflection</note>, since the location of the image of the form of point $h$ will be at point $l$, and the location of the image of the form of point $n$ will be at point $p$, the line $lp$ will therefore be the image of the entire line $hn$. However, the image $lp$ has a reversed position with respect to the position of line $hn$: because point $h$ is higher than point $n$, and point $l$, which is the image of point $h$, is lower than point $p$, which is the image of point $n$. And this is what was proposed concerning heights. Concerning depths, indeed, the same is evident: for if lines $hn$ and $de$ are assumed to be certain depths, then the demonstration is the same. For the depth $hn$ appears reversed, and the depth $de$ appears just as it is arranged. This, therefore, is what was proposed. If, however, both lines $de$ and $hn$ were on any one side of the intersection of the lines of incidence, there would be a consistent orientation of their images, as is clear from the previous points.

<margin>53.</margin> *When the lines of incidence <note>The paths light travels from the object to the mirror</note> intersect one another in concave spherical mirrors: those objects of oblique length existing on this side of the point of intersection appear as they are; however, the images of those which are beyond the intersection on the same lines are seen reversed. Euclid, Theorem 12 of the Catoptrics <note>original: "catoptricorum"</note>.*

Let there be a concave spherical mirror $ag$, the center of which is $m$, and let the center of sight be $b$. Let line $de$ be oblique <note>slanted</note> upon the surface of the mirror. Let the form of point $d$ be reflected to the sight $b$ from the point of the mirror which is $a$, and the form of point $e$ from point $g$. Let the lines of incidence (which are $da$ and $eg$) intersect each other at point $i$. Let there be a line $kc$ on this side of point $i$, falling obliquely to the surface of the mirror, whose point $k$ is reflected from point $g$ of the mirror, and point $c$ from point $a$ of the mirror. Therefore, let line $dm$ be drawn from point $d$ to the center of the mirror; this line (on account of the obliquity of line $ba$ upon the surface of the mirror, since line $dm$ is perpendicular to that same surface of the mirror by the 72nd theorem of Book 1 of this work, because it passes through the center of the mirror, which is $m$) will concur with line $ba$, which falls obliquely on the surface of the mirror, as can be seen by the 14th theorem of Book 1. Let the meeting point be $l$. Similarly, line $em$ will also concur with line $bg$; let the point of meeting be $n$. It is clear, therefore, by the 37th theorem of Book 5 of this work, that the image of the form of point $d$ is at point $l$, and the image of the form of point $e$ is at point $n$. Let line $nl$ be drawn, which will be the image of the entire line $de$. The image $nl$ also holds itself in reverse to the position of line $de$: because point $n$, which is the image of the lower point $e$, is higher than point $l$, which is the image of the higher point $d$. Let line $mk$ also be extended until it concurs with the extended line $bg$; it will concur, however, on account of the obliquity of line $bg$ upon the surface of the mirror and on account of the perpendicularity of line $mk$. Let the meeting point be $f$. Let line $mc$ be extended until it concurs with the extended line $ba$, and let the meeting point be $s$. Let line $fs$ be joined; line $fs$ will therefore be the image of line $kc$. And just as point $k$ is higher than point $c$, so point $f$ will be higher than point $s$. Thus, the image $fs$ has a consistent position with the visible object itself, which is $kc$, meeting the mirror on this side of the point of intersection of the lines of incidence, which is $i$. The proposition is therefore clear.

*55. In concave spherical mirrors, the sight perceives, from certain positions, the image of a convex line as convex, and a concave line as concave: and of a line whose convexity faces the mirror, the image will be convex facing the sight: and of a line whose concavity faces the mirror, the image will be concave facing the sight. Alhazen 46 [Book] 6.*

# BOOK EIGHT.

...of the concave part of the mirror. Therefore, the sight <note>original: "uisus", referring to the eye or the observer's point of view</note> existing at point **z** will perceive the form of the concave arc **g q r** as a concave line. And this is what was proposed.

§ 6. *In concave spherical mirrors, the sight, from certain positions, will perceive four curved images of a straight line; of a curved line whose convexity is toward the mirror, it perceives a curved image; and the concavity of all these images faces the sight.* Alhazen 4, theorem 47, note 6. <note>Vitello is citing the work of the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose "Perspectiva" was the foundation for medieval European optics.</note>

Let there be a concave spherical mirror, in which there is a great circle <term>great circle: a circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same center and radius as the sphere itself</term> **a b d**: whose center is **g**: and let a radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> **g b** be drawn from the center **g**, however it may fall: let it be divided into unequal parts at point **t** such that line **g t** is greater than half of line **b g**: and from point **t**, let line **t z** be drawn perpendicularly over line **g b** by the 11th proposition of the 1st book <note>Vitello refers to Euclid's *Elements* for his geometric proofs</note>: and let line **z t** be extended beyond point **t** to point **e**: and let lines **z t** and **e t** both be equal to line **t g** by the 3rd proposition of the 1st book: and let lines **g e** and **g z** be drawn: and let a circle be circumscribed <term>circumscribed: drawn around the outside of a shape so that it touches all the vertices</term> around triangle **e g z** by the 5th proposition of the 4th book: and the center of that circle will be point **t** by the 9th proposition of the 3rd book. And because line **t g** is greater than line **t b**: it is clear that this circle will cut circle **a b d**: it will therefore cut it at two points by the 10th proposition of the 3rd book: let those two points be **a** and **d**. Let lines **g a**, **g d**, **e a**, **b**, **e**, **d**, **z a**, **z b**, **z d** also be drawn. Because, therefore, the two lines **e t** and **z t** are equal, and the angles at point **t** are right angles, and line **t g** is common: by the 4th proposition of the 1st book, the two lines **e g** and **z g** will be equal: and similarly by the same 4th proposition of the 1st book, the two lines **e b** and **z b** are equal: therefore by the 28th proposition of the 3rd book, the two arcs **e g** and **g z** are equal: therefore by the 27th proposition of the 3rd book, angle **e a g** is equal to angle **g a z**: and angle **e d g** is equal to angle **g d z**: and angle **e b g** is equal to angle **g b z**: since all those angles fall upon the same arcs. Therefore, the form of point **z** is reflected to point **e** from points **a**, **d**, and **b** of the mirror, or vice versa, by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work. And because line **g t** is greater than line **t b**: and the two lines **e b** and **z e** are equal to each other, and the two lines **e g** and **z g** are equal to each other by the 4th proposition of the 11th book <note>likely a scribal error for the 1st book</note>: it is clear by the 47th proposition of the 1st book <note>the Pythagorean Theorem</note> that line **g e** is greater than line **b e**. For the square of line **g e** is equal to both squares of lines **g t** and **t e**, and the square of line **e b** is equal to both squares of lines **e t** and **t b**: therefore, when the common square of line **t e** is removed, the square of line **g e** remains greater than the square of line **e b**: since line **g t** is greater than line **t b**. Therefore line **g e** is greater than line **e b** in triangle **g e b**, and, as is evident by the 18th proposition of the 1st book, angle **g b e** is greater than angle **e g b**: but angle **e g b** is half of a right angle by the 5th and 32nd propositions of the 1st book: therefore the two angles, **b g e** and **e b g**, taken together, are greater than a right angle: therefore angle **b e g** is less than a right angle by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book: but angle **e g z** is a right angle by the 31st proposition of the 3rd book: and therefore since angles **e g t** and **t g z** are two halves of one right angle: therefore by the 14th theorem of the 1st book of this work, the two lines **e b** and **g z**, when extended, will meet outside the circle: let their meeting point be **l**. And because line **e d** is inside triangle **l e g**: it is clear that when extended it will meet with line **g l** by the 29th theorem of the 1st book of this work: it will meet, therefore, at point **m**. These arcs lie between the radii of the mirror, where the center of vision (at point **h**) and the points being reflected (**e** and **z**) are located. By the 17th proposition of the 5th book, the proportion of line **t z** to **z d** is as **k e** to **d e**. Therefore, by the 2nd proposition of the 6th book, line **t k** is parallel <note>original: "equidistans"</note> to line **e z**. However, if the eyes are moved from this position, multiple images may appear. And this is what was proposed. Nevertheless, whenever something is perceived in these mirrors by double vision, if the line of reflection is parallel to the perpendicular of incidence <note>original: "catheto incidentiæ", the line from the object point perpendicular to the mirror surface, which in a sphere passes through the center</note>: the location of the image will be the point of reflection itself, according to Theorem 11 of this book: and since the points of reflection are distant from one another with respect to both eyes, two images of the same point will appear to the eyes, and the location of each image is at the point of its own reflection. But if the line of reflection is not parallel to the perpendicular of incidence, and the object point is just as far from one eye as from the other—or if there is a slight difference in distance—if the image location is on the surface of the eye itself: two images will still be seen. Otherwise, however, for the most part, the image location with respect to both eyes will be the same, or only slightly distant; hence either only one image will be seen, or it will appear almost as one.

**60. If both eyes are placed on one diameter of a concave spherical mirror at equal distances from the center of the mirror, neither eye will be seen. Euclid, Theorem 27 of the Catoptrics <note>Catoptrics is the study of mirrors and reflection</note>.**

Let there be a concave spherical mirror **a t g d**, whose center is **z**, and diameter is **a d**: and let two eyes **b** and **e** be positioned on the diameter **a d**, equidistant from the center **z**. I say that neither of the eyes will be seen. For let the radius **z g** be drawn perpendicular to the diameter **a d**: and let lines **b g** and **e g** be drawn. Because in triangles **e z g** and **b z g**, side **e z** is equal to side **z b** by hypothesis, and side **z g** is common: and the angles **e z g** and **b z g** are equal because they are both right angles: then by Proposition 4 of Book 1, angle **b g z** will be equal to angle **e g z**. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle (representing a concave mirror) with points a, t, g, d on the circumference. A diameter line passes through the center z, containing points b and e (representing eyes) equidistant from z. A perpendicular radius z g meets the mirror at g. Lines are drawn from b and e to g, and from b and e to another point t on the arc. A line t z bisects angle b t e. The diagram illustrates reflections in a spherical concave mirror.</image-desc>

Therefore, the form of point **b** will be reflected to point **e** from point **g** of the mirror, and vice versa, by Theorem 20 of Book 5. But it is also not possible for the form of point **b** to be reflected to point **e** from any other point of the mirror. For suppose it were possible that the form of point **b** is reflected to point **e** from another point of the mirror, which we call **t**: and let lines **b t**, **t e**, and **t z** be drawn: then line **t z** divides angle **b t e** into two equal parts by Theorem 20 of Book 5: therefore, by Proposition 3 of Book 6, the ratio of line **b t** to line **t e** is as the ratio of line **b z** to line **e z**: but line **b t** is greater than line **b g** by Proposition 7 of Book 3: and line **b g** is equal to line **e g**, as shown above: and line **e g** is greater than line **t e** by Proposition 7 of Book 3: therefore, line **b t** will be greater than line **e t**: therefore, line **b z** will be greater than line **e z**: which is contrary to the hypothesis and impossible. And the same can be demonstrated for any point of the semicircle **a g d**. Therefore, the form of point **b** is not reflected to point **e** from any point of the mirror other than point **g**. Therefore, eye **b** will not see eye **e**: because the line of reflection, which is **b g**, does not meet with the perpendicular **e z** (drawn from point **e** through the center of the mirror **z**) except at point **b**: and the line of reflection, which is **e g**, does not meet with the perpendicular **b z**, except at point **e**. Thus, the location of the image of **e** is point **b**: but **b** is similar to **e** itself in form, and **e** to **b**. Therefore, no distance is perceived that would cause a difference between those views. Consequently, one eye will not perceive the form of the other as existing within itself, but will judge that it sees its own form. Thus, one eye so positioned will not see the other eye; and this is what was proposed. However, other parts of the body surrounding the center of vision can be seen: those whose perpendiculars of incidence meet with their lines of reflection, whether that meeting point is on the surface of the eye or at any other points: and regarding this, many variations occur to the eyes.

**61. If both eyes are placed on a line drawn parallel to the diameter from the midpoint of the radius, perpendicular to the diameter of a concave spherical mirror, and equidistant from the center of the mirror: only one image of the eye will appear at the point of reflection. Euclid, Theorem 28 of the Catoptrics.**
