# VITELLO'S OPTICS

Let there be a concave spherical mirror **a g d**; its center is **k**, and its diameter is **a d**. Let the radius **k g** be drawn perpendicular to the diameter **a d**, and from the midpoint of the radius **k g**, let a line be drawn parallel to the diameter **a d**. On this line, let both eyes be placed, equidistant from the center **k**. I say that only one image of both eyes will be seen, specifically at a single point of reflection. For let it be that from point **p** (which is the midpoint of line **k g** by Proposition 10 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>), a line is drawn parallel to diameter **a d** by Proposition 31 of Book 1, which shall be **e z**. Let both eyes, **b** and **t**, be placed on that perpendicular line **e z**, equidistant from the center **k** and from the line **k g**. Therefore, lines **b p** and **t p** will be equal. Let lines **b g**, **t g**, **b k**, and **t k** be drawn. Therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, since line **p g** is common to both triangles **b p g** and **t p g**, and since angles **b p g** and **t p g** are right angles, angle **b g p** will be equal to angle **t g p**. Therefore, the form of point **b** will be reflected to point **t** from point **g** of the mirror, and vice versa. And because line **k p** is equal to line **p g** (since point **p** is the midpoint of line **k g**), and lines **b p** and **t p** are equal, and angle **k p t** is also equal to angle **b p g** by Proposition 15 of Book 1, then by Proposition 4 of Book 1, angle **t k p** is equal to angle **b g p**. Thus, by Proposition 27 of Book 1, line **t k** is parallel to line **b g**. But line **t k** is the <term>cathetus</term> <note>original: "cathetus"; in optics, this is the line passing from the object through the center of curvature to the mirror's surface</note> of point **t**, 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle (the concave mirror) with points a, g, d on its perimeter and center k. A vertical radius connects k to g, and a horizontal diameter connects a to d. A horizontal line segment e-z passes through a point p on the radius k-g. Two points b and t (representing the eyes) are marked on e-z. Various lines connect b, t, g, k, and p, illustrating how light reflects from the mirror surface at point g.</image-desc>

and line **b g** is the line of reflection; therefore, they will never meet. Thus, by Theorem 11 of this book, the form of point **t** (which is one of the eyes) will not be seen by the other eye, which is **b**, nor vice versa by the same reasoning, except at point **g**, which is the point of reflection. For line **b g**, which is the line of reflection of the form of point **t** to the sight **b**, does not intersect with the cathetus of incidence of the form of point **t**, which is line **t k**. Each of the eyes will therefore see the other at only one point of reflection. Thus, the image of both eyes will be only one, and so only one eye will appear. And since the rest of the viewer's face is presented to both sights behind the eyes (because the lines of reflection meet the catheti of incidence at that part, as is clear to the observer—for if lines **b k** and **t g** fell between the intersecting lines, then they themselves would intersect, which is impossible since they are parallel; those lines will therefore intersect behind both sights), then by Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work, the face of the viewer will then appear one-eyed, in the manner of a painting of a Cyclops <note>Vitello is describing an optical illusion where the two reflected eyes merge into a single central eye, resembling the mythical one-eyed giant</note>, and the eye will be protruding beyond the face, since it is seen only at the point of reflection by Theorem 11 of this book. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 62.
**If a line is drawn parallel to the diameter from a point closer to the diameter of a concave spherical mirror than the midpoint of the radius drawn perpendicularly to that diameter, and the eyes are placed on that line equidistant from the center of the mirror, they will appear behind themselves: the right part on the right, and the left on the left; the image will be larger than the face, and the image will be further from the sight than the viewer's face is from the surface of the mirror.** Euclid, Theorem 29 of the *Catoptrics*.

Let the radius **k g** be drawn perpendicular to diameter **a d**, and let the midpoint of this radius **k g** be **p**. Let the centers of both eyes be points **b** and **t**. Therefore, from point **g**, the sights will be reflected toward each other by Theorem 20 of Book 5 of this work. But line **n g** is greater than line **n k**. Therefore, by Proposition 3 of Book 1, let line **n g** be cut at point **q** so as to be equal to line **n k**, and let line **b q** be drawn. Line **t k** is the cathetus of point **t**, and line **g b** is the line of reflection. Therefore, the form of point **g** will be seen behind sight **b**. *63. If a line parallel to the diameter is produced from a point further from the diameter of a concave spherical mirror than the midpoint of the radius, and if the eyes are placed on that line equidistant from the center of the mirror, right things appear left, and left things appear right; and the image of the viewer is larger than the face; and the distance of the image from the mirror will be greater than the distance of the viewer’s face. Euclid, in the second part of Theorem 28 of the Catoptrics.* <note>original: "Euclides altera parte 28 th. catoptr."</note>

Let there be a concave spherical mirror, the common section of whose surface and the surface of reflection is the circle **a k f**: its center is **z**: and its diameter is **a f**: and from the center **z** let a perpendicular be drawn to the diameter **a f**, which is the radius **z k**: let this be divided into equal parts at point **e**: and from point **e** let a line **c d** be drawn parallel to the diameter **a f**: let line **e k** also be divided into equal parts at point **n**: and from point **n** of line **e k** let a line **l m** be drawn parallel to line **a f**: let the eyes be placed on this line **l m** equidistant from the center **z**: I say that what is proposed is true. For let the eyes **b** and **g** be arranged on line **l m**, as proposed: therefore, as in the previous proposition, angles **b k n** and **g k n** will be equal by Proposition 4 of Book 1: therefore the eyes **b** and **g** will be reflected to each other mutually from point **k**. Let lines **b e** and **g e** also be drawn: and by Proposition 4 of Book 1, angle **b e n** will be equal to angle **b k n**: but angle **b e n**, by Proposition 16 of Book 1, is greater than angle **b z e**: therefore angle **b k z** is greater than angle **b z k**: and therefore it is also greater than angle **k z g**: therefore, by Theorem 14 of Book 1 of this work, lines **b k** and **z g** will converge: let the point of intersection be **q**: and likewise, by the same theorem, lines **g k** and **z b** will converge: let the point of intersection be **p**. Since, therefore, line **g k** is the line of reflection of the form of point **b** from point **k** of the mirror, and line **z b** is the perpendicular of incidence <note><term>cathetus incidentiæ</term>: a line perpendicular to the mirror's surface at the point of reflection, used to determine where an image appears to be located.</note>: therefore, by Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work, point **p** will be the image <note>original: "imago"</note> of the form of point **b**: and similarly, point **q** will be the image of the form of point **g**. Let line **p q** therefore be drawn: and this will be the image of line **b g**. Therefore, the right will be seen as left, and the left as right, because of the intersection of the lines of reflection **b q** and **g p**, as is clear from Proposition 53 of this book. Likewise, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, line **z b** is equal to line **z g**: therefore, by Proposition 5 of Book 1, angle **z b n** is equal to angle **z g n**, and angle **p b g** is equal to angle **q g b**: but angle **n b k** is equal to angle **n g k**: therefore angle **k b p** remains equal to angle **k g q**: but angle **b k p** is equal to angle **g k q** by Proposition 15 of Book 1: therefore, by Proposition 32 of Book 1, triangles **b k p** and **g k q** are equiangular: therefore angles **b p k** and **g q k** are equal. And since angles **p b g** and **q g b**, as is clear from what has been said, are equal,

Since lines **b q** and **g p** are equal, and lines **b k** and **g k** are equal: line **k q** will be equal to line **k p**, and angles **p k o** and **q k o** are equal by Proposition 15 of Book 1 and by the preceding arguments: therefore line **p o** will be equal to line **q o**. If, therefore, line **p o** is greater than line **b n**: it is clear that line **o k** is greater than line **k n**: and line **o k** is the distance of the image behind the mirror, and line **n k** is the distance of the reflected object from the surface of the mirror. Thus the proposition is evident.

### VITELLO'S OPTICS

...proportionally according to an equal distance from the diameter and the center of the mirror: right things appear left, and left things right: and the image appears smaller than the face and appears between the sights and the surface of the mirror.

Let the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the concave sphere be circle **d b k**: whose center is **o** and diameter **d k**: and let diameter **b o a** be produced outside the mirror perpendicularly to diameter **d k**: and let the two eyes be at points **e** and **c** of line **c e**, which is perpendicular to line **b a**: and let both eyes be equally distant from that diameter **b a** and from point **a**: therefore line **e a** will be equal to line **a c**: and let lines **e b** and **c b** be drawn: therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, angle **e b a** will be equal to angle **a b c**: therefore, by the 20th theorem of Book 1 of this work, both sights **e** and **c** are reflected to each other from point **b**. Therefore, let a line be produced from point **e** to the center **o**: this produced line will meet with line **c b** by the 29th theorem of Book 1 of this work: let the intersection be point **f**: and similarly, let a line be drawn from point **c** through the center **o** meeting with line **e b** at point **g**. Therefore, by the 37th theorem of Book 5 of this work, the image of the form of point **e** appears at point **f**: and the image of the form of point **c** appears at point **g**: thus right would appear left, and left would appear right. But also, by Proposition 5 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, angle **b e c** is equal to angle **b c e**: since lines **b e** and **b c** are equal. But since in the two triangles **e a o** and **c a o**, the two sides **e a** and **c a** are equal, and side **a o** is common, and the angles **c a o** and **e a o** are equal because they are right angles: by Proposition 4 of Book 1, angle **f e a** will be equal to angle **g c a**: therefore triangles **e f c** and **c e g** are equiangular by the preceding and Proposition 32 of Book 1: therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, the ratio of line **e g** to line **e f**, and of line **e f** to line **c g**, is as the ratio of line **e c** to itself: therefore lines **e g** and **c f** are equal, and lines **e f** and **c g** are equal. But the total line **b e** is equal to the total line **b c**: therefore there remains line **b g** equal to line **b f**: therefore, by Proposition 5 of Book 1, angle **b g f** is equal to angle **b f g**: but those angles with angle **g b f** equal two right angles by Proposition 32 of Book 1: therefore those two angles are equal to the two angles **b e c**, **b c e**: therefore those triangles **e b c** and **g b f** are equiangular: therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, whatever the ratio of line **b g** to line **b e**, the same is the ratio of line **g f** to line **e c**: but line **b g** is smaller than line **b e**: therefore line **g f** is smaller than line **e c**. The image of the viewer's face is therefore smaller than the face seen. Moreover, it appears between the eyes and the surface of the mirror: since line **g f** (which is the diameter of the image) falls between line **e c**, in which both sights are located, and the surface of the mirror. Thus the proposition is clear.

***65. Images of things appearing behind concave spherical mirrors, when the objects of which they are images are moved, are seen to move in the same direction.***

Let there be a circle **a g b** in a concave spherical mirror: whose center is **d**: and let the center of vision be point **e**: and let there be two points of the thing seen on either side of point **e**: which shall be **z** and **h**: and let two <term>catheti of incidence<note original="catheti incidentiæ">Lines drawn from the object perpendicular to the mirror's surface, used to determine the location of a reflected image.</note></term> be drawn, which shall be **d z c** and **d h k**: and let the form of point **z** be reflected to the sight **e** from point **a** of the mirror: and the form of point **h** from point **b** of the mirror: and let the lines of reflection be drawn, which shall be **a e** and **b e**: and let line **a e** meet with the <term>cathetus</term> **d z** at point **c**, and line **e b** with the <term>cathetus</term> **d h** at point **k**: points **c** and **k** will therefore be the locations of the images behind the mirror by the 37th theorem of Book 5 of this work: so that point **c** is the location of the image of the form of point **z**, and point **k** is the location of the image of the form of point **h**: and the locations of the images will be in those parts in which the things themselves, of which they are images, are perceived. Thus, let the point of the thing seen, which is **h**, be moved to point **l**: and let it be reflected to the sight **e** from point **g**: and let the <term>cathetus</term> **d l** be drawn meeting with the line of reflection, which is **g** <note>likely meaning line g-e</note>, at point **m**: and the location of the image of the form of point **h** will be at point **m**, having moved to it from point **k**, which location **m** will be in that direction toward which the object itself (whose image is at point **m**) was moved. If the points of the thing seen were **h** and **l**, and they are above the sight: the locations of the images, which are **k** and **m**, will be above the sight: and they will appear above the things whose forms they are. And if points **h** and **l** were to the right of the sight itself: the locations of their images, which are **k** and **m**, will also be to the right: but they will not be thought to be the right side, as was clear above by the 51st theorem of this book: because, due to the reversal, right things appear left, and left things right. Thus the proposition is clear.

### BOOK EIGHT. V.

66. **Images of objects appearing between concave spherical mirrors and the sights, when the objects are moved, are seen to move in the opposite direction.**

Let the circle of a concave spherical mirror be **a b g**: let its center be point **d**: and let the center of the sight <note>The observer's eye or point of view</note> **e** be closer than the center of the mirror, which is **d**: and on the sides of the observer let there be two points of the object seen: let these be **z** and **h**: let them be reflected to the sight from two points **a** and **b**: let the lines of reflection be **e a** for point **z**, and **e b** for point **h**: and let the <term>catheti of incidence<note>In medieval optics, the 'cathetus' is a perpendicular line drawn from the object through the center of the mirror's curvature to determine the image location.</note></term> **z d c** and **h d k** be drawn, intersecting the lines of reflection at points **c** and **k**: therefore, by the 37th theorem of Book 5 of this work, points **c** and **k** will be the locations of the images: **c** for point **z**, and **k** for point **h**. Thus, the forms of those points will be seen in different parts than where the objects themselves are, according to the 49th theorem of this book. Now, if point **h** of the object seen is moved to point **i**: and it is reflected from point **g** of the mirror to the sight **e**: and let the line of reflection be drawn, which is **e g**: and the cathetus **l d m**, intersecting the line of reflection, which is **e g**, at point **m**: then by the 37th theorem of Book 5 of this work, point **m** will be the location of the image of the form of point **l**. Therefore, the image of point **h**, which is **k**, will have moved to a different side than that to which the real object moved. And if points **h** and **i** were moved upward above the sight: then their images, which are **k** and **m**, will be seen to move downward. And if points **h** and **i** were moved to the right side of the sight: the forms of the images will be seen to move to the left: and thus the images always move in the opposite direction to the objects. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

Point e represents the eye or center of sight. Lines connect objects z, h, and i through the center d to points c, k, and m on the reflection lines, illustrating how image positions shift relative to object movement.]<-

67. **By means of concave spherical mirrors, as many as one wishes, it is possible for the image of the same point to be seen. Euclid, 15th theorem of the Catoptrics; Ptolemy, 8th theorem of Book 2 of the Catoptrics.**

Let the arrangement be made as it was for plane and convex spherical mirrors: let the center of sight be **a**: and let the point of the object seen be **b**: and according to the distance of the center of sight (which is **a**) from the point of the object seen (which is **b**), let an equilateral and equiangular polygon be described, with as many angles as one pleases: let it be, for the sake of example, a pentagon: let this be **a b g d e**: and let a circle be circumscribed around that pentagonal polygon by the 12th proposition of Book 4 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>: and upon the angles of that pentagon, let concave spherical mirrors be placed orthogonally <note>at right angles</note> upon lines drawn from the center of the circumscribing circle to the circumference according to their midpoints, which mirrors are parts of the same sphere and equal portions. It is clear, therefore, since the flat surface of the pentagon **a b g d e** will intersect any of the mirrors along a circle by the 69th theorem of Book 1 of this work. Thus, let one arc of one of those circles be **z g e**: and let the tangent lines be drawn to any of those arcs at points **g**, **d**, **e**: and let the line **l k** touch arc **z g c** at point **g**. Therefore, because by the 43rd theorem of Book 1 of this work the angle of the portion, which is **b g z**, is equal to the angle **d g ç** <note>The ç likely represents a vertex or a point on the tangent</note>: and the angles of contingency <note>The angle between a tangent and a curve</note>, which are **k g z** and **l g e**, are also equal: it is evident then, by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work, that a reflection of the form of point **b** occurs from point **g** of the mirror to the point of the other mirror, which is **d**. And similarly, by the same demonstration, a reflection will occur from point **d** to the point of the other mirror, which is **e**, and from point **e** to the center of sight, which is **a**. Thus the proposition is clear. And so, however many angles the polygon has, let that many mirrors be taken, and that which was stated will always happen.

->[A circular diagram illustrating multiple reflections within a system of concave mirrors. A regular pentagon is inscribed within a circle, with vertices labeled a, b, g, d, e. Vertex a is at the bottom. Small arcs representing concave mirrors are placed at vertices g, d, and e. Geometric lines show the path of a light ray reflecting from point b through mirrors at g and d to reach point e and finally the center of sight at a.]<-

Let there be a concave spherical mirror placed opposite the sun: in which let the circle **k a b g x** be marked, whose center is **c**: and let it be that the flat surface intersecting the mirror along this circle also intersects the body of the sun through its center: therefore, by the 69th theorem of Book 1 of this work, the common section of that flat surface and the sun will be a great circle, which is **d e z**: and from some point of that solar circle, such as from point **d**, let a line be drawn, along which a ray proceeding to the center of the mirror, which is **c**, falls upon a point of the mirror, which is **g**: and from a point of the sun's circle, which is **e**, a ray proceeding to the center of the mirror, which is **c**, falls upon point **b** of the mirror: and from a point of the sun, which is **z**, an incident ray passing through the center of the mirror **c**, falls upon point **a** of the mirror. Moreover, at any of those points, some <term>combustible body<note>An object capable of catching fire, such as dry wood or tinder.</note></term> will be set on fire by the reflected rays. Thus, the proposition is clear. It would also be possible, through the diligence of a craftsman, for a mirror to be composed of several such mirrors, which would be of greater effectiveness for burning; however, we leave this to the industry of the researcher, as it is enough for us...

### BOOK NINE OF THE OPTICS OF WITELO, SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND POLES.

In the preceding book we have discussed, to the best of our ability, the properties <term>passiones</term> <note>Witelo uses the Latin term *passiones* (passions) to refer to the physical properties, behaviors, or phenomena of light as they "suffer" or undergo changes through reflection.</note> of concave spherical mirrors; it now remains for us to demonstrate some properties of concave cylindrical <note>original: *columnarium*</note> and pyramidal mirrors. For in these mirrors, the properties of almost all the previously mentioned mirrors converge: those of flat mirrors, since in these, reflection occurs from the longitudinal line of the mirror. Many properties <term>passiones</term> of convex cylindrical and pyramidal mirrors also descend to these concave mirrors, because their generation is similar according to their shapes, from which a certain similarity of properties arises in both; except that here and there, according to the nature of the convex and the concave, those properties are in a certain way arranged in a contrary manner according to their position. From this it happens that sometimes the reflected line in convex mirrors becomes the location of the image in concave ones, and vice versa; and for these same reasons, the principles in these and those mirrors must be adopted consistently (following the figures previously laid out). 

Thus, having treated the properties of all regular mirrors as far as our strength and experience allowed, we turn our attention to certain mirrors of irregular and composite shapes. We see that the diligence and care of the ancient mathematicians <note>Witelo refers here to "geometers," though in the 13th century, geometry and mathematics were inextricably linked to physics and optics.</note> was greatly occupied with **burning mirrors** <term>specula comburentia</term> <note>Mirrors designed to concentrate sunlight to a single point to generate intense heat or fire, a topic of great fascination in the Middle Ages.</note> (from whose total surface the reflection of light and incident forms occurs toward a single physical or mathematical point). This is a matter that applies the great precision of the science of geometry to natural things, accelerating the action of natural forms in the production of marvelous effects. Consequently, we have dedicated our care to this task in this book, as to a subject toward which all that we have previously stated about the nature of any mirrors is, in some way, directed as if toward the most noble end. 

From the preceding books, however, it is clear enough that the shape of such burning mirrors is not possible on a flat surface (as is clear from Theorem 65 of Book 5 of this work); nor is it possible from any convex surface—whether that convex surface be spherical (as is clear from Theorem 65 of Book 6), or cylindrical or pyramidal (as is clear from Theorem 59 of Book 7)—for any rays to be gathered into a single mathematical or even physical point. Even from concave spherical mirrors, reflection does not occur toward a single mathematical point on the axis, except from the circumference of only one circle, and from the whole surface of one hemisphere toward the entire semi-diameter or axis of the mirror, as was shown in Theorem 68 of Book 8. The reflection of all rays falling parallel to the axis of the mirror's surface does not occur at a single point. Nor is it possible from any surface of concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirrors, as we shall demonstrate later in this present book. It remains, therefore, that we search with diligent demonstration for other surfaces suitable for our purpose; for that which we previously said would be possible through the composition of several regular mirrors for this effect does not reach the certainty of a single surface (from which reflection occurs in its entirety to one point). It does not achieve their convenience, nor does the excellence of human ingenuity and the utility of shapes shine forth as much in them. Thus, in these cylindrical and pyramidal mirrors, and in any other irregular ones, and even in those burning mirrors themselves

For these mirrors, we assume the principles that were set forth in the preceding books, as is evident in the 5th, 6th, and especially the 7th and 8th books of this science. # THEOREMS

1. **In concave cylindrical mirrors, the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is sometimes a line along the length of the mirror; sometimes a circle; and sometimes an acute-angled section <term>oxygonia sectio</term> <note>In this context, an "acute-angled section" refers to an ellipse formed by cutting a cylinder at an angle.</note>.** <margin>Alhazen Book 5, Number 89.</margin>

What is proposed here is evident from what was set forth in the 7th book of this work regarding convex cylindrical mirrors. And because a concave cylindrical mirror participates no less in the form and property of a cylinder than a convex one, it is clear that the proposed property <term>passio</term> must be demonstrated for concave cylindrical mirrors in entirely the same way as for convex cylindrical ones. The proposition is therefore clear; for it is not necessary to dwell further on such matters. When that common section is a line along the length of the mirror, the modes of reflection and the locations of the images will be just as they are in flat mirrors. However, when that common section is a circle, the modes of reflection and locations of reflection will be just as they are in concave spherical mirrors. The locations of the images will be sometimes beyond the mirror, sometimes on the surface of the mirror itself, sometimes between the eye and the mirror, and sometimes on the surface of the eye itself. The method of demonstrating all of these is the same as that which was made clear for those concave spherical mirrors in the 11th theorem of Book 8 of this work.

2. **In concave pyramidal [conical] mirrors, it is possible for the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror to be a line along the length of the mirror or an acute-angled section; but it is impossible for it to be a circle.** <margin>Alhazen Book 5, Number 97.</margin>

The properties proposed regarding the present mirrors are demonstrable in entirely the same way as they were shown for convex pyramidal mirrors through various propositions in Book 7 of this work. The proposition is therefore clear. And when the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is a line of length, the modes of reflection and locations of images will be those which were also shown for flat mirrors in the 49th theorem of Book 5 of this work.

3. **In every surface of reflection from concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirrors, it is necessary for the center of vision, the point of the object seen, the point of reflection, and the point on the axis (upon which falls the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection to the surface touching the mirror at the point of reflection) to consist [together in that same plane].** <margin>Alhazen Book 4, Number 46.</margin>

Let there be a concave cylindrical mirror whose axis is line $a-b$. Let the center of vision be point $t$, and the point of the object seen be point $d$. Let the form of the point of the object seen, which is $d$, be reflected to the eye $t$ from point $e$ on the mirror. At point $e$, let a flat surface touch the surface of the mirror; upon this surface, let a perpendicular line be drawn from point $e$ (according to the 12th proposition of Book 11 [of Euclid's *Elements*]), which intersects the line $a-b$, the axis of the mirror, at point $f$; and let this be line $e-f$. I say that the points $t, d, e,$ and $f$ will always necessarily be in the same surface [plane] of reflection. For either this surface of reflection will be parallel to the bases of the cylinder, or it will not. If it is, it is clear from the 100th theorem of Book 1 of this work that the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror will be a circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder; and the line drawn from the point of reflection, which is $e$, passing through the center of that circle, is perpendicular to the surface of the cylinder, as is clear from the 96th and 100th theorems of Book 1 of this work. And if the center of vision, $t$, and the point of the object seen, $d$, are on that line, the reflection of the forms of the points seen occurs only according to that line (by the 21st theorem of Book 5 of this work); and those four points ($t, d, e, f$) will all be in the surface of reflection. But if the center of vision or the point of the object seen is not on this perpendicular line, the line $e-f$ drawn perpendicularly from point $e$ will nonetheless always fall on the axis $a-b$ (by the 96th theorem of Book 1); and the line of reflection will contain an acute angle with that perpendicular. This is because it falls between the perpendicular $e-f$ and the line that touches the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror) at point $e$. And since this line of reflection always falls within the mirror—because, according to its path which strikes the mirror, it necessarily falls between the flat surfaces drawn through the center of vision that touch the visible portion of the mirror—and since (by the 26th theorem of Book 5) the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, it is clear that if one of those points is in the surface of reflection, then the other is as well. For since angle $def$ will be equal to angle $fet$, these angles fall on opposite sides of the perpendicular line $ef$ within the mirror. Therefore, all points $t, d, e, f$ will fall in the same surface. And it is to be demonstrated in the same way, from whatever point of the circle (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror) the reflection occurs; for those four points will always be in the surface of reflection. But if the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror is a line of length of the mirror; then again, from whatever point of that line the reflection occurs, it is always...

### 4. When the center of sight is inside a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror: reflection to the sight occurs from any point on the mirror. <margin>Alhazen Book 4, Number 49.</margin>

Let there be a concave cylindrical mirror whose axis is $a b$; and let the center of sight be $t$, and let point $t$ be inside the mirror: I say that reflection to the sight occurs from every point of the mirror's surface. For whether the common section of the surface of reflection and this mirror is a longitudinal line of the mirror's cylinder—as when the surface of reflection cuts the surface of the mirror according to the length of the axis, as is clear by the 93rd theorem of Book 1—or whether it is a circle parallel to the bases of the mirror's cylinder, or whether it is an acute-angled section: it is always clear by the preceding theorem that the point of reflection and the center of the circle (or the point on the axis upon which the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection to the surface of the mirror falls) are in the same surface. It is therefore always possible for reflection to the sight to occur from that point: because in the concavity of such mirrors there is no dense body <note>An opaque object.</note> resisting the multiplication of forms <note>The travel of light rays.</note> through the medium. Therefore, the reflection of forms to the sight occurs from any point of the surface of such mirrors. The same is also clear in concave pyramidal mirrors. For since the center of sight is always inside such mirrors, it does not matter from which point of the mirror's surface the reflection occurs: because it will always be possible for the form to reach the sight, unless perhaps the density of the back of the head <note>The viewer's own head blocking the light.</note> in certain positions hinders the reflection. The proposition is therefore clear, by reusing the diagram of the preceding theorem and placing point $t$ inside the surface of the mirror on line $t e$. For whatever point in both mirrors is given: let that point be $e$; and let a perpendicular be drawn from it to the plane surface touching the mirror at that point, according to the 12th proposition of Book 11 <note>Likely Euclid's Elements.</note>. And since that perpendicular falls on the axis of the mirror by the 96th theorem of Book 1: let it fall on point $f$: and upon point $e$ at the end of line $e f$, let an angle be made equal to angle $t e f$ (which is $f e d$) according to the 23rd proposition of Book 1. It is clear, therefore, that the form of point $d$ will be reflected to the sight existing at point $t$ at the point $e$, according to the 20th theorem of Book 5. And this is what was proposed.

### 5. When the center of sight is outside an incomplete concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror, reflection to the sight occurs from the majority of the mirror's surface. <margin>Alhazen Book 4, Number 49.</margin>

Let there be a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror whose axis is $a b$, and let the center of sight be point $t$, and let it be outside the mirror: I say that reflection to the sight occurs from the larger part of the concave surface of the mirror. For imagine tangent surfaces produced from the sight to the cylinder or pyramid; it is clear by the 1st theorem of Book 7 of this work that only the part of the mirror's surface lying between those tangent surfaces is that from which reflection to the sight occurs when the mirror is convex. However, that part is the smaller part of the mirror's surface, as is clear regarding cylindrical mirrors through the 78th theorem of Book 4, and regarding pyramidal mirrors through the 84th theorem of Book 4: therefore, when that part is removed, the larger part of the mirror's surface remains. Moreover, reflection to the sight occurs from that entire surface: since every line drawn below the lines tangent to the mirror in any of those surfaces, when produced, cuts the surface of the mirror according to the 4th theorem of Book 7; therefore, reflection to the sight can occur along that line. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 6. In an entire concave pyramidal mirror, when it is opposite the sight from the direction of its base, the form of no point will be seen unless it exists within the mirror. <margin>Alhazen Book 4, Number 50.</margin>

But if the center of sight $c$ is below any of the longitudinal lines of the mirror: then the proposition is still clear. It is therefore necessary that the points of the object seen—whose forms are reflected to the eye from any points on the entire surface of the mirror—must always be within the mirror itself. Thus, the proposition is clear. If, however, some portion is removed from such a mirror along its length, then external things located outside the mirror can be perceived: for a free entrance will be open to the lines of incidence of external forms, which will then be reflected to the eye. A similar thing happens if the pyramid of the mirror is cut in the manner of a ring along some circle parallel to the base, or even along an acute-angled section <term>sectio oxygonia</term> <note>An ellipse formed by cutting a cone or cylinder at an angle.</note>, such that the vertex of the mirror’s pyramid is removed. For then the lines of incidence will have free entry. Nevertheless, more forms will be reflected to the eye if the center of sight is on the side of the mirror's concave surface than if it were on the side of its base, because a wider path then lies open to the incoming lines.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 4.</margin>
### 7. From any point on a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror, it is impossible for the form of more than one point to be reflected to the same eye.

Suppose, as in the previous case, a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror whose axis is $a b$. From its point $e$, let the form of point $d$ be reflected to the eye $c$. I say that it is impossible for the form of any point other than $d$ to be reflected to the eye at point $c$ from that same point $e$. For let a perpendicular line be drawn from the point of reflection $e$ to the surface touching the mirror at point $e$; this line will cut the axis of the mirror according to the 96th theorem of Book 1 of this work. Let it, therefore, cut at point $f$. It is clear then, through the 3rd theorem of this book, that points $c, d, e, f$ are in the same surface. And since only one single straight line can be drawn from the center of sight $c$ to the point of reflection $e$, it is clear that the angle $c e f$ cannot be varied. Therefore, neither can angle $d e f$, which is equal to angle $c e f$ by the 20th theorem of Book 5. Thus, the line $e d$ is the only line from which the form of some point can be reflected to the eye $c$. But by hypothesis, the form of point $d$ is reflected to the eye; therefore, the form of no other point will be reflected to it. For when any line of incidence reaches a point on a body, the form of another point cannot fall upon the mirror through that same line, because a point higher up hides the one behind it and does not allow its form to pass through. Thus the proposition is clear: because in these mirrors, once a reflection of the form of one point has occurred from any given point, the form of another point cannot be reflected from that same point of the mirror to the same eye. However, from two different eyes, the forms of two points can be perceived in the same point of the mirror, just as from several eyes several forms of different points can be seen. This is because, as is clear from the 18th theorem of Book 7, infinite surfaces can be taken intersecting over the perpendicular $e f$, in any of which two equal acute angles can be taken on either side of the perpendicular $e f$. Although what is proposed here was sufficiently clear through the 29th theorem of Book 5, we have declared it again here because the opposite seemed more likely to be true in the case of these specific mirrors.

### 8. When the longitudinal line of a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror is the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror: there is only one point of reflection, only one point of the object is seen by one center of sight, and a single image is seen.

It is not necessary to dwell on the demonstration of this proposition any differently than how the same was shown in plane mirrors: that reflection occurs from only one point and only one image meets the eye, as is clear through the 46th and 48th theorems of Book 5. For the straight line is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror on both sides; therefore, there is only one point of reflection. Thus, only a single image will be seen, always appearing beneath the surface of the mirror, as in plane mirrors. And by the 49th theorem of Book 5, the distance of the image beneath the mirror will be equal to the distance of the object above the mirror. Thus, the proposition is clear.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 4, No. 48. Also Book 5, No. 93.</margin>
### 9. When the common section of the surface of reflection and a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror is an acute-angled section: the form of the same point of the object can be reflected from several points of that section to the same center of sight.

Let there be a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror whose axis is $a b$, and let the center of sight be $c$, and let the point of the object be $d$, as is clear in the figure for theorem 6 of this book. If, therefore, the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is an acute-angled section <gloss>an ellipse</gloss>: I say that the form of point $d$ can be reflected to the center of sight $c$ from several points of that section. For we have already shown above, in the 22nd theorem of Book 7, that in convex cylindrical mirrors the reflection of the form of the same point to the same eye occurs from only one point of the acute-angled section. We also said that if the diameter of the cylinder were equal to the distance between the eyes, then reflection could occur from two points of the acute-angled section; otherwise, the points of reflection facing each other would be hidden from the eye—namely, those through which the circle of the cylinder passes, drawn through the point of reflection parallel to the bases. Thus, when one of those points is seen, the other point will be hidden because of the appearance of a smaller portion of the cylinder itself. However, in these concave cylindrical mirrors, a larger portion of the cylinder appears to the eye, as is clear through the 5th theorem of this book. Thus, both points—which are the ends of the diameter of the circle parallel to the bases of the cylinder—can be perceived by a single eye. The same thing must be declared in exactly the same way regarding concave pyramidal mirrors: for more than half of its surface meets a single eye, and two points opposite each other across the diameter of a circle parallel to the base of the pyramid can be seen. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 10. When the intersection of the surface of reflection and a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror is an acute-angled section, the location of the image will be sometimes beyond the mirror, sometimes before the eye, sometimes at the center of sight, sometimes on the surface of the mirror, and sometimes between the eye and the mirror. <note>original: Alhazen 90 n 5; referring to Book 5, Proposition 90 of Alhazen’s Optics.</note>

Let there be a concave cylindrical mirror, part of whose axis is $dk$. Let the intersection of its cylindrical surface and the surface of reflection be an acute-angled section <term>oxygonia</term> <note>This refers to an ellipse, specifically one created by cutting the cylinder or cone at an acute angle.</note>, which is $abg$. I say that everything proposed here is possible. Let a perpendicular line be drawn in this section to the surface touching the mirror at the point of reflection, which is $dg$. Therefore, by the 112th and 104th theorems of Book 1 of this work, this will be the radius of a certain circle cutting the column of the mirror at that point parallel to the bases. It will cut the axis of the mirror, which is $kd$; let it cut the axis at point $d$. This perpendicular line will be the only one, since from no other point of the section $abg$ can a perpendicular line be drawn to the surface touching the mirror at the point of reflection except from that one point of reflection. This is because all other lines drawn from any points of the section $abg$ to the axis $dh$ are oblique to the surface touching the mirror, as is clear through the aforementioned propositions.

Now, let another point of the section $abg$ be taken, which is $b$. Let a perpendicular line be drawn from that point $b$ to the straight line touching the section $abg$ at point $b$. This line, by the 114th theorem of Book 1, will necessarily meet with the perpendicular $gd$. For example, let the meeting point be at $d$; if they meet below point $d$, the proof is the same. Let point $b$ be taken on the section $abg$ near point $g$ such that angle $bdg$ is acute. Then, from point $g$, draw a line in the surface of the section $abg$ parallel to line $bd$ (by Euclid, Book 1, Prop. 31), which is $gh$. This line will fall within the pyramidal section because, since angle $gdb$ is acute by hypothesis, its alternate angle (which is angle $hgd$) will be similarly acute (by Euclid, Book 1, Prop. 29), since lines $bd$ and $gh$ are parallel to each other.

Also, between points $d$ and $h$, let a line be drawn from point $g$ in the surface of the section, which, by the 2nd theorem of Book 1, will necessarily meet with line $bd$, since it meets with line $hg$ which is parallel to line $bd$. Let the meeting point be $n$. Thus, line $gn$ falls between lines $gh$ and $bn$. On this line $gn$, let any point be taken, $o$, between the two points $g$ and $n$, and beyond point $n$ let point $t$ be taken on line $gn$. Furthermore, from point $g$, draw another line within the section $abg$ but outside both lines $gh$ and $bd$; let this be $gz$. Because this line $gz$ meets with line $hg$ at point $g$, it will necessarily meet with line $bd$ extended beyond point $b$ (by the 2nd theorem of Book 1). Let the meeting point be $e$. At the end of line $gd$, let an angle be made equal to angle $zgd$ (by Euclid, Book 1, Prop. 23), which is angle $dgq$. Let point $q$ fall on line $bd$. Similarly, let angle $lgd$ be made equal to angle $hgd$, and let angle $mgd$ be made equal to angle $ngd$. Let all the points $q, l,$ and $m$ be on line $bd$.

It is clear through the 20th theorem of Book 5 that if the center of sight is at point $z$, the form of point $q$ will be reflected to it from the mirror at point $g$. By the 37th theorem of Book 5, the location of the image will be point $e$. If the center of sight is at point $h$, the form of point $l$ will be reflected to it from point $g$. And since the cathetus <term>cathetus incidentiæ</term> <note>The normal line or the line falling perpendicular to the reflecting surface from the point of the object.</note> of incidence, which is $ld$, is parallel to the line of reflection $gh$, it is clear that lines $ld$ and $gh$ will never meet. Therefore, the location of the image will be as described in the 12th theorem of Book 8. If the center of sight is at point $o$, the form of point $m$ will be reflected to it from the point of the mirror $g$, and the location of the image will be point $n$. If the center of sight is at point $n$, the location of the image of the form of point $m$ will be in the center of sight itself, which is at point $n$. But if the center of sight is at point $t$, the location of the image of the form of point $m$ will again be at point $n$, which will then be between the eye and the surface of the mirror. Thus, the proposition is clear, for in concave pyramidal mirrors the proof can be easily adapted according to the premises, with the help of the 113th theorem of this work. This is what was proposed.

### 11. When the center of sight and the point of the object are on the same perpendicular line to the surface of a concave cylindrical or pyramidal mirror: sometimes reflection occurs from one point of the mirror, and sometimes from two; and the location of the image will always be the center of sight. <note>original: Alhazen 91 n 5; referring to Alhazen’s Book 5, Prop 91.</note>

Let line $ef$ be extended to the other side of the mirror at point $g$. I say that sometimes from one point of the mirror, such as point $e$, and sometimes from two, such as points $e$ and $g$, the form of point $d$ can be reflected...

Therefore, the perpendicular *ef* divides the angle *dec* into equal parts; and the perpendicular *fg*, drawn from the point of reflection to the center of that circle, divides the angle *dge* into equal parts. And since the perpendicular of incidence <term>cathetus incidentiae</term> <note>The line from the object point perpendicular to the mirror's surface.</note>, which is *df*, does not meet with the line of reflection *ec* or *gc* except at the center of sight, which is *c*: it is clear through the 37th theorem of the 5th book of this work that the center of sight is the location of the image of the form of point *d*. But other points of the perpendicular line, which is *cdh*, are not reflected to the sight *c* from point *h* of the mirror, except only that point which is on the surface of the eye itself, as was shown above; for this reason, it is not reflected except through the same perpendicular. However, when the common section of any of those perpendicular surfaces upon the mirror's surface at point *e* and the surface of the mirror is an acute-angled section <term>oxygonia</term> <note>This refers to an ellipse, created by cutting the cylinder at an angle.</note>: the points of the line of reflection cannot be reflected to the sight from any other points of the section; since (as is clear through the 112th theorem of the 1st book) two perpendicular lines on the surface of the mirror in the plane of the section cannot intersect each other, just as in the surface of a circle parallel to the bases of the mirror two such diameters intersect at the center *f*, as has already been shown, which are *ph* and *eg*. For the diameter of the section (which is *ph*) is not perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror at point *h*, but falls obliquely upon it, whereas the diameter *eg* is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror; and this happens because of the slant of the acute-angled section relative to the axis of the mirror's column. Therefore, the form of point *d* will not be reflected to the sight *c* through the line *cdh*. It is clear, then, that reflection of the form of point *d* to the sight *c* will occur from those two points; and the location of the image in both cases will be the center of sight, which is *c*. But if points *d* and *c* were on the perpendicular *ef*: then reflection will not occur from any point of the acute-angled section except only from point *e*: since a form falling upon the surface of the mirror along a perpendicular line is reflected along the same perpendicular; and in an acute-angled section there is only one line perpendicular to the surface touching the mirror. Wherefore, as was said before, reflection occurs through that line alone for only the point of the perpendicular line which is on the surface of the eye; and as before, the location of the image will be at the center of sight. By the same reasoning, the same proposition is clear in concave pyramidal <note>conical</note> mirrors. For once a straight line perpendicular to the surface touching the pyramidal mirror has been drawn from the center of sight to that surface: if a physical point is taken on that perpendicular between the sight and the mirror, it is clear that its form will not be reflected to the sight along that perpendicular; for that point will hide the endpoint of the perpendicular, and it will not be reflected from it. However, if no physical point is on that perpendicular: only the form of the point on the surface of the eye which the perpendicular itself cuts from that surface will be reflected to the eye along this perpendicular. *12. When the center of sight is located at the center of the base of a concave cylindrical mirror, or at the center of a circle parallel to the base, a reflection of the form of the eye itself will occur from an arc of the mirror's circle similar to the great circle arc on the surface of the eye; and the location of the image will be the center of sight. Alhazen Book 5, Note 92.*

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram of a cylinder shown in perspective. A central axis is labeled 'a b'. A horizontal diameter line 'b' connects to a point on the circumference labeled '6'.</image-desc>

Suppose there is a concave cylindrical mirror whose axis is *a b*, and let the center of sight be at point *b*. According to the 92nd theorem of the 1st book of this work, point *b* is the center of the circle forming the base of the mirror. I maintain that the form of the eye itself will be reflected back to the sight from an arc of the circle at the base of the mirror. This arc is similar to the arc of the "great circle" <note>In spherical geometry, a great circle is the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, like the equator on a globe.</note> of the entire sphere of the eye that passes through the center of the pupil <note>original: "foramen uuææ"; literally the "opening of the grape-like layer," a medieval term for the pupil</note> and the center of the eye. This is the arc that lies between the outermost perpendicular lines drawn from the center of sight, passing through the edges of the pupil to the circumference of the mirror's circle. Imagine those lines traveling from the center of the eye, through the pupil, and across the entire arc of a great circle of the eye's sphere, bisecting the portion of the eye's sphere that corresponds to the pupil. All those lines will be perpendicular to the surface of the eye's sphere according to the 72nd theorem of the 1st book, because they are drawn from the center. Furthermore, these same lines, when extended to the circumference of the base circle of the mirror, are perpendicular to the surface of the mirror for the same reason: they originate from the center of that circle, which is *b*. Therefore, these lines are perpendicular to both surfaces. Thus, by the 21st theorem of the 5th book, they reflect back upon themselves. Consequently, the forms of the points on the surface of the eye falling on those perpendiculars are reflected back to the sight along those same lines. And since the circle of the eye's sphere and the circle of the mirror's base (having the same center) are parallel circles, it is clear by the definition of similar arcs that the arcs lying between any two of their radii are similar. Therefore, the arc of the mirror's circle from

*13. In concave cylindrical mirrors, if two points are taken on the axis of the mirror, it is possible for one to be reflected to the other from an entire circle of the mirror; and the location of the image will be a certain circle outside the surface of the mirror. Alhazen Book 5, Note 94.*

let there be a line *k h p*: and let lines *t l, m h, l h,* and *m* be drawn. And because the axis of the mirror, which is *e z*, is erected upon the surface of the circle *l m* according to Theorem 92 of Book 1 of this work: it is clear that the angles *t l q* and *t q m* and *h q l* and *h q m* are right angles. But line *t q* is equal to line *q h* by hypothesis: and lines *q m* and *q l* are equal by the definition of a circle. Therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 1 <note>original: "4 p. 1"; referring to Euclid's Elements, which proves triangle congruence by Side-Angle-Side</note>, the four triangles—*t q m, h q m, t q l,* and *h q l*—have equal angles. Thus, angle *t l q* is equal to angle *q l h*, and angle *t m q* is equal to angle *q m h*.

If, therefore, the center of sight is at point *t*, and the point of some object being seen is *h*: the form of point *h* will be reflected to the eye at point *t* from the point of the mirror which is *l*, and similarly from point *m*. If, then, the triangle *t l h* is imagined to move—while side *t h* (which is part of the mirror's axis) remains fixed—until it returns to the place where its motion began, then point *l* will describe a circle by its motion. The two angles *t l q* and *q l h* will always remain equal, and throughout this motion, the form of point *h* will always be reflected to the eye at point *t*.

Because the diameter *p h* is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, it is clear that it is the perpendicular of incidence <term>cathetus incidentiae: the straight line falling from the object to the reflecting surface at a right angle</term> for the form of point *h*. Let this same perpendicular *p h k* be extended beyond point *k* outside the surface of the mirror until it meets the line of reflection, *t l*, when extended. They will meet according to Theorem 14 of Book 1 of this work: since angle *t h k* is a right angle, angle *h t l* must be acute. Let the meeting point be *f*. Similarly, when the perpendicular *h p* is extended beyond point *p*, it will meet the line of reflection *t m*. Let that meeting point be *r*.

By Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work, points *f* and *r* will be the locations of the images of the form of point *h*. As triangle *t l h* moves, triangle *t f h* will move along with it. In this motion, point *f* will describe a circle outside the cylinder of the mirror; and that entire circle will be the location of the image. The same method of proof will hold for any two points chosen on the axis of the mirror. It will be necessary, however, in this case, for the sight to be positioned so that its center is directly on the axis of the mirror, and the point of the object seen is at some center of a circle of the mirror, or its base, or a circle parallel to it; otherwise, the location of the image will not meet the eye outside the mirror. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 14. *When the common section of the reflection surface and the concave cylindrical mirror is a circle: sometimes one, sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes four points of reflection will exist, and no more; and the locations of the images are numbered according to these. Alhazen, Book 5, number 95.*

Let there be a concave cylindrical mirror whose axis is *a b*. Let the common section <note>The "common section" refers to the line formed where the plane of reflection intersects the mirror's surface.</note> of the surface of reflection and the mirror be the circle *e d f*, the center of which is *b*. Let the center of sight be *g* and the point of the object seen be *h*, both of which are within that circle, at equal or unequal distances from the center *b*, and both on one side of center *b*. I say that what is proposed is true.

Let the diameters *g b* and *h b* be drawn and extended to the circumference of the circle. It is clear through Theorem 40 of Book 8 of this work that it is sometimes possible for the form of point *h* to be reflected to the eye at point *g* from only one point of the circle *c d e f*; sometimes from two; sometimes from three; and sometimes from four; but never from more. And since in this proposal the reflection occurs from the circle of the mirror, there is no difference in that regard; thus the first part of the proposition is clear. It is also clear, as shown in Theorem 11 of Book 8, that whether the perpendiculars of incidence meet the lines of reflection or are parallel to them, the images are numbered according to the number of the lines of reflection. This is everything that was proposed.

### 15. *In concave cylindrical mirrors, when the common section of the reflection surface and the mirror is an acute-angled section: for certain forms of points of the object seen, reflection to the sight occurs from only one point of the mirror; for some from two, some from three, and some from four; and no more. The locations of the images are numbered according to these. Alhazen, Book 5, number 95.*

Let there be a concave cylindrical mirror whose axis is the line *x h*. Let the point of the object seen, falling obliquely upon the mirror so that it is not on any of the lines perpendicular to the surface of the mirror, be point *a*; let it be such that the common section of the reflection surface and the mirror is an acute-angled section <note>original: "oxygonia"; in this context, it refers to an elliptical section created by a plane cutting the cylinder at an angle.</note>. I say that it is possible for reflection to occur to the eye from one, two, three, or four points of some acute-angled section: and sometimes a single image appears, sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes four, but no more images, because only that many points of reflection are possible.

Imagine a flat surface passing through point *a* parallel to the bases of the proposed mirror. The common section of this surface and the mirror's surface will be a circle according to Theorem 100 of Book 1, and the center of this circle is *h*. Let another point, *b*, be taken on the surface of that circle, at a different distance from center *h* than point *a*. Let lines *a h* and *b h* be drawn from points *a* and *b* to the center of the circle *h*. Let the diameters of that circle be completed by extending these same lines to the circumference of the circle on both sides.

It is clear from what was said in the preceding theorem and in Theorem 40 of Book 8 that from one point of the arc lying between the two radii *a h* and *b h*, the form of point *a* can be reflected to the eye at point *b*; or perhaps from two or three, but not more. From the arc opposite to that one (namely, from the arc that falls between those same radii extended to the other part of the circle's circumference), reflection of the form of point *a* to the eye *b* can only occur from a single point. Suppose, then, that the form of point *a* is reflected to the eye *b* from three points of the proposed mirror's arc, namely one

And angle *i q a* is equal to angle *q a n*, because they are alternate angles: therefore, angle *i q t* will be equal to angle *i q a*. In the same way, it must be demonstrated that the form of point *a* is reflected to the eye at point *t* from the other two points of the mirror similar to point *q*, which are points *l* and *m*. Thus, the reflection of the form of point *a* to the eye at point *t* will occur from three points of the concave cylindrical mirror, which are *q, l, m*, and all on the same side of the cylinder. Nor is it possible for such a reflection to occur from more points of the mirror on that side. Therefore, the reflection of the form of point *a* to the eye existing at point *t* will not occur except from three points of the concave cylindrical mirror: which are *q, l,* and *m* on one side of the mirror itself. Thus, if the other part of the cylindrical mirror were cut away, it is clear that reflection would only occur from three points of the mirror; but if the whole mirror were complete, it is possible for reflection to occur from four points. For it has already been shown by Theorem 27 of Book 8 of this work that from the arc of the circle whose center is *h*, opposite to arc *g d e*, the form of point *a* can be reflected to the eye existing at point *b* from only one point. 

Let that point be *z*: and let the radius *h z* be drawn: and from point *a*, let a line parallel to it be drawn according to Proposition 31 of Book 1 <note>original: "31 p 1", referring to Euclid's Elements, Book 1</note>: let this be *a s*: and let the line of reflection be drawn, which is *b z* meeting with line *a s* at point *s*: it will meet, however, by Theorem 2 of Book 1 of this work: since it meets with line *h z* which is parallel to *a s*: and from point *z*, let line *z o* be raised perpendicularly above the surface of the circle whose center is *h*, according to Proposition 12 of Book 11 <note>original: "12 p 11", referring to Euclid's Elements, Book 11, dealing with solid geometry</note>: this line will therefore be parallel to line *b t* by Proposition 6 of Book 11. Therefore, let line *t s* be drawn, which, as we have declared previously in other cases, will cut line *z o*: since they are in the same surface: let the point of intersection be *o*: and it will be clear according to the modes previously set forth, that the form of point *s* is reflected to the eye existing at point *t* from the point of the mirror which is *o*: nor will reflection be possible from any point of the mirror's surface on that side, except from point *o*. 

For if it were granted that this were possible from some other point: it would follow, as we deduced before, that similarly the form of point *a* could be reflected to the eye existing at point *b* from another point of that arc of the circle (whose center is *h*) other than point *z*, which is impossible, and contrary to Theorem 29 of Book 8 of this work. If, therefore, the form of point *a* is reflected from one point of the circle (whose center is *h*) to the eye existing at point *b*: the same form of point *a* will be reflected from the same side of the concave cylindrical mirror to the eye existing at point *t* from only one point of the mirror: and if reflection of the form of point *a* to *b* occurs from two points of the mirror: then *a* will also be reflected to *t* from two points of the mirror. But if one of these reflections occurs from three points: the other will also occur from three: and from that part of the circle where it is not possible for more reflections to occur. Just as the reflection of the form of point *a* to point *b* occurs from only one point of the opposite arc in the circle: so also from that side of the mirror, the reflection of the form of point *a* to the eye existing at point *t* occurs from only one point. 

Likewise, line *t b* is parallel to the axis *x h*: they are therefore in the same surface by Theorem 1 of Book 1 of this work, which is the surface *t b h u*: for no other plane surface can be taken in which those lines *t b* and *h x* exist, by Proposition 1 of Book 11. Likewise, no plane surface can be taken in which point *a* and axis *x h* exist, except for the surface *a u h*, which by Proposition 18 of Book 11 is raised perpendicularly above the surface of the circle whose center is point *h*: since by Theorem 92 of Book 1 of this work, the axis *h u* is perpendicular to it. Therefore, point *t* is not in the same surface with point *a* raised above the surface of the said circle: but neither are those points *t* and *a* in the same circle: nor are they on the axis of the mirror: since line *b t* is parallel to the axis of the mirror, which is *x h*. Therefore, the surface in which the form of point *a* is reflected to the eye existing at point *t* is an <term>acute-angled section</term> <note>original: "oxygonia sectio." This is the classical term for an ellipse, which forms when a cylinder is cut at an angle.</note>. 

However, let line *t a* be produced on both sides beyond points *t* and *a*, so that it becomes line *p r*: since there are four surfaces of reflection: because reflection occurs from four points, which are *q, l, m, o*, and in each of those four surfaces it is necessary for two points to exist, which are *a* and *t*: it is clear that line *p r* is common to those four surfaces by Proposition 1 of Book 11: since on line *p r* are the center of sight, which is point *t*: and the point of the object seen, which is point *a*: which must be in every surface of reflection made by these mirrors, as is clear by Book 3 of this work. Each of those surfaces, however, cuts the mirror upon the surface tangent to the mirror at the point of its reflection: and for each of these surfaces of reflection and the surface tangent to the mirror at 그 point, the common section is a straight line by Proposition 3 of Book 11. And just as the points of reflection are not the same: so also the common lines of those sections are not the same: therefore line *p r* is perpendicular to only one of those four common lines, not to two. For if it were perpendicular to two of those lines: it would be perpendicular to two surfaces tangent to the mirror at the points of those lines: therefore line *p r* would necessarily pass through the axis: yet it was shown before that line *t a* (which is part of line *t p r*) falls short of the axis of the mirror, which is *x h*. 

Necessarily, therefore, different perpendicular lines must be drawn to those four common lines from the point of the object seen, which is *a*: these will be four <term>perpendiculars of incidence</term> <note>original: "catheti incidentiae," the lines dropped from the object point perpendicular to the reflective surface</note> perpendicular to the acute-angled sections <note>ellipses</note>, which are common to those surfaces of reflections and the mirror. Each of these perpendiculars will either be parallel to the line of reflection: or it will meet with it, whether inside the mirror or outside. If it is parallel: the location of the image will be the point of reflection itself, as was shown above in Book 11 of this work. And since there are four such perpendiculars: there will be four locations of images, and four images: because there are four locations of reflections. But if all those four perpendiculars meet with the lines of their reflections: there will again be four images: because there are four intersections of those lines. Thus, therefore, the locations of images are numbered according to the number of points of reflection. And this is what was proposed.

In all these reflections, the location of the image will always be in the center of sight: since reflection does not occur except according to perpendicular lines. point *b*, by its motion, will describe a circle on the concave surface of the mirror; and from any point on the circumference of that circle, the form of point *t* will be reflected to the sight located at point *h*. Similarly, point *l*, by its motion, will describe a circle outside the mirror, and the location of the image of the form of point *t* will lie on the entire circumference of that circle. This is because, along the entire circumference of that circle, the <term>perpendiculars of incidence<note>Latin: "catheti incidentiæ." These are the lines drawn perpendicular to the reflecting surface from the point of the object.</note></term> of the form of point *t* and the lines of reflection of the form of point *t* to the sight *h* will intersect. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**79. In concave pyramidal mirrors, when the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is an <term>acute-angled section<note>Latin: "sectio oxygonia." In this context, it refers to an ellipse created by the intersection of a plane and the cone.</note></term>, and the center of sight and the point of the object seen exist in the same surface of the mirror's base (or one parallel to it), and neither is on the axis of the mirror: for certain points of the object seen, there is reflection from only one point of the mirror; for others, from two; for others, from three; for others, from four; but never from more. The number of images is counted according to these reflection points. Alhazen, Book 5, Proposition 100.**

Let there be a concave pyramidal mirror *a g u*, whose axis is *a d* and vertex is *a*. Let point *e* be the center of sight, and let point *z* be the object seen, falling obliquely on the mirror. This point is not on any of the lines perpendicular to the surface of sight, nor on the axis of the mirror (which is *a d*), nor does reflection occur from any of the longitudinal lines <note>The straight lines running from the vertex to the base of the cone.</note> of the mirror. However, let the reflection of the form of point *z* to the sight *e* occur from some point on the surface of the proposed mirror. Therefore, the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror will necessarily be an acute-angled section, according to Theorem 2 of this book. Let points *e* and *z* be in the same surface of the circle of the mirror's base, or one parallel to it. I say that it is possible for the reflection to the sight to occur from only one point of the mirror, or two, or three, or four, and no more. Consequently, sometimes a single image will appear, sometimes two, sometimes three, and sometimes four; it is not possible to see more images, because only that many points of reflection are possible.

Imagine, then, a flat surface passing through point *z* parallel to the base of the mirror. By Theorem 100 of Book 1 of this work, this surface will cut the mirror into a circle. The center of sight (which is point *e*, as stated in the hypothesis) will be in the surface of that circle, whose center is *t*. Let line *e z* be drawn, and let it be extended to cut that circle. It is clear from what was demonstrated regarding concave spherical mirrors in Theorem 40 of Book 8 of this work that, in such a setup, the form of point *z* is reflected to the sight at point *e* from the circumference of that circle on one side (namely, from the arc lying between the radii on which points *z* and *e* stand) from one, two, or three points of the mirror. From the other side (namely, the arc between the remaining radii where points *z* and *e* do not stand), reflection occurs from only one point.

Let the point of intersection be *q*. Through Theorem 101 of Book 1, let a line of the mirror’s length be drawn, which is *a h*. From point *q*, let a line be drawn falling perpendicularly upon line *a h* according to Book 1, Proposition 12 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>; let this be *q m*, intersecting line *a h* at point *n*. When extended beyond point *q*, let it intersect the axis of the mirror (*a d*) at point *d*. Let lines *z m* and *e m* be drawn. From point *z* (the object), let a line be drawn in the surface of that circle parallel to line *q h*; let this be *z l*.

Since line *e h* meets line *q h* at point *h*, it is clear from Theorem 2 of Book 1 of this work that line *e h*, when extended beyond point *h*, will meet line *z l*. Let the meeting point be *l*. From point *h*, let a perpendicular line be drawn to line *l z*, which is *h p*. Then, in the surface *e m z*, let a line be drawn from point *z* parallel to line *q m*; let this be line *z o*. Since line *e m* meets line *m q*, it is clear from Theorem 2 of Book 1 that it will also meet line *z o*, which is parallel to it. Let the meeting point be *o*, and let line *l o* be drawn. If, in this arrangement, reflection occurs from two points of the circle, there will also be reflection from two points of the mirror, as demonstrated by the same logic. If reflection occurs from three points of the circle, it will also occur from three points of the mirror; and if from four points of one, then from four points of the other. And just as reflection occurs from one point on another part of the circle, so too will it occur from one point of the mirror on that same part. Thus, the proposition is clear.

For always, as is clear from the preceding, from however many points of the circle the image of point $z$ is reflected to point $h$: from just as many points of the mirror will that same image of point $z$ be reflected to point $e$: and vice versa: and for anyone saying the contrary, an impossibility follows in the manner predicted. It is therefore clear that of the points of an object seen in mirrors, some have a single image: some two: some three: some four: and that it is not possible for more images to be produced in <term>columnar<note>Meaning cylindrical.</note></term> or <term>pyramidal<note>Meaning conical.</note></term> concave mirrors: just as it is not possible in spherical concave mirrors: which is to be noted.
