**21.** *Given the center of vision and the point of an object seen in concave <term>pyramidal mirrors<note>Latin: "speculis pyramidalibus." In this period, "pyramidal" was frequently used to describe what we now call conical mirrors.</note></term>, to find the point of reflection. <note>original: "Alhazen 102 n 5," referring to Book 5, Proposition 102 of Alhazen’s "Optics."</note>*

Let there be a concave conical mirror whose axis is line $ad$. Let the point of the object being seen be $z$, and let the center of vision (the eye) be point $e$, both being in given locations. I say that it is possible to find the point of reflection. Indeed, if the object point $z$ and the center of sight $e$ are in a single flat surface cutting through the mirror's axis, then it is clear by the 90th theorem of Book 1 of this work that because the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is the longitudinal line of the mirror’s cone, the point of reflection can be found just as it is in flat mirrors by the 46th theorem of Book 5. 

However, if points $z$ and $e$ <margin>The OCR text reads "z and b," but the context suggests "z and e" for the object and eye.</margin> are not in that specific plane, imagine a surface passing through point $z$ that cuts the mirror parallel to its base; therefore, by the 100th theorem of Book 1, the intersection of that surface and the mirror will be a circle. The center of vision, point $e$, will either be in the plane of that circle or it will not. In whatever way it is positioned, it is impossible—as shown in the 12th theorem of Book 7—for the intersection of the surface of reflection and this mirror to be a circle. Therefore, that intersection will always be <term>oxygonia<note>Latin: "oxygonia," from the Greek for "acute-angled." In the context of conic sections, this refers to an ellipse or an acute-angled intersection of a plane and a cone.</note></term>. By repeating the demonstration of the 19th theorem of this book or the one immediately preceding it, the discovery of the point of reflection will be easily revealed. For the form of point $z$ will be reflected to the sight existing at point $h$ <note>The text shifts to 'h' here, likely referring to the eye's position in a specific geometric configuration.</note> from some point on the circumference of the circle whose center is $q$. It may reflect from two, three, or four points; however many there are, the point of reflection corresponding to that point on the circle will always be found in the manner described previously. This is done by finding the point of reflection of those points on the periphery of the circle through what we have explained in the various propositions of Book 8. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**22.** *In concave <term>columnar<note>Cylindrical.</note></term> or conical mirrors, an image appears almost as a single image to both eyes.*

In these mirrors, the points of reflection for the form of the same object point to the different eyes of the same viewer do not have a great difference in distance, owing to the closeness of the eyes to each other. Thus, even if the image of a single point's form occurs somewhat doubled to both eyes, those images are nonetheless contiguous and blended; hence they appear as if a single image. Because the difference in the locations of those images is imperceptible, it does not create any noticeable distance in the sight, nor does it cause any error. Therefore, the image is seen as one. Similarly, in the manner we showed in the 59th theorem of Book 8, it is possible for a single image to sometimes appear in these mirrors (as in others) to the distant and distinct eyes of different viewers. Because the position is identical, we have decided not to dwell on it here. Thus, the proposition is clear.

**23.** *For a straight line parallel to the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror (with the center of vision being in the same surface or another), the reflection occurs from the longitudinal line of the mirror to the eye.*

Let the axis of the concave cylindrical mirror be line $zk$, and let the seen line parallel to the axis be $tqh$. Let the center of vision be point $e$. I say that the form of line $tqh$ is reflected to the eye $e$ from the <term>longitudinal line<note>A line running the length of the cylinder's surface.</note></term> of the mirror $abg$, which is the intersection of the surface $thzk$ and the surface of the mirror. 

<image-desc>A technical diagram of light reflecting inside a concave cylinder. A vertical line t-q-h represents an object being reflected. Point 'e' is the eye. The lines show how light travels from points t, q, and h to points g, b, and a on the mirror's surface, then to the eye 'e'. Auxiliary lines and points (o, z, k, d, f) establish the geometric proof using angles of incidence and perpendiculars.</image-desc>

And this indeed can be demonstrated in every way as in the 30th theorem of Book 7, provided the center of vision (point $e$) is not in the surface $thzk$. If, however, the center of vision is in that same surface, the same proposition will be demonstrated as in the 51st theorem of Book 7. The form of point $t$ will reflect from point $g$ of the mirror; the form of point $q$ from point $b$; and the form of point $h$ from point $a$. Thus, the angle $tgn$ will be equal to angle $nge$; angle $qbm$ equal to angle $mbe$; and angle $har$ equal to angle $rae$. It is also clear from the 30th theorem of Book 7 that lines $ek, ha, qb,$ and $tg$ meet at point $o$. It is also clear there that line $abg$ is a straight line extended along the length of the mirror, and that lines $gz, bl,$ and $ad$ are perpendicular to the surface tangent to the mirror along the line $abg$. Furthermore, line $abg$ is perpendicular to the surface containing triangle $ebo$, and line $tq$ is equal to line $qh$, and line $ab$ is equal to line $bg$. It is therefore evident—since the demonstration is the same for both these and those mirrors—that the form of line $tqh$ is reflected from these mirrors from their longitudinal line. The proposition is thus clear; for whether the longitudinal line $abg$ is on the convex or concave side of the mirror, there is no difference in the outcome for this purpose.

**24.** *The image of a line parallel to the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror (the center of vision being in the same surface) will appear straight, equal, and conforming to the object seen.*

Suppose the arrangement is the same as in the preceding section. Let the form of line $tqh$ be reflected from the surface of the mirror along the longitudinal line $ag$, and let the center of sight $e$ be in the surface $thzk$. I say that the image of line $tqh$ will appear...

...will appear straight, and equal to the line $tqh$ itself. For any perpendicular drawn from any point of the line $tqh$ will always be in the same surface as the center of vision and the axis: and it will be proven that the locations of the images of the points of line $tqh$ are situated according to a straight line, just as was shown regarding straight lines seen in plane mirrors through the 52nd theorem of Book 5 of this work. As if some straight line of the object seen were imagined to be placed in these mirrors at the location of the image, and the vision were positioned proportionally to it, just as it is now positioned to line $th$: the location of the image of that line will be line $th$, and it will appear straight and equal to the object seen. Likewise, that which is higher on the line of the object seen will be higher in the image; and what is lower in the object seen will be lower in the image. Thus, the image will conform to the object seen. But the width of such objects seen will be greater than the width of their images: because images are compressed according to their width due to the points of reflection, which are narrowed, and the points of width are reversed: because the left of the object is the right of the image, and the right of the object is the left of the image. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

## 23. **A straight line parallel to the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror (the center of vision not being in the same surface), the image will sometimes appear straight and larger than the object seen: sometimes concave: sometimes convex: sometimes single: sometimes multiple. <note>original: "Alhazen 51 n 6"</note>**

Let the arrangement of the preceding [theorem] remain, except that the center of vision (which is $e$) is not in the surface $thzk$: I say that it will be as proposed. **26. When a surface containing a seen straight or curved line intersects the surface in which the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror lies at a right angle, and the center of vision exists in both surfaces: reflection will occur from the circumference of the circle (which is the intersection of said surface and the mirror); and the image of the seen line will sometimes be straight, or sometimes convex.**

Having also established the figure from Theorem 52 of Book 7, let the demonstration be completed as in that proposition: the image of the straight line $th$ will be curved. If, therefore, the same mirror which was taken as convex there is now assumed to be concave—and a curved line is understood to be placed in the location of the image, along whose outer endpoints a straight line is also drawn in the surface of the seen object, and the center of vision is arranged proportionally around that line in the same surface—then the location of the image of the seen curved or straight line will be the straight line $th$. The proposition is therefore clear: and perhaps the line of the image will be equal to the straight one or perhaps convex, just as was shown in Theorem 57 of Book 8 of this work; and it is to be deduced here in the same manner.

## **28. If a straight line seen in the surface of incidence obliquely cuts the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror, with the center of vision being in that same surface: the image is seen as concave with respect to the sight and reversed in position. Alhazen, Book 6, Number 53.**

Let there be a concave cylindrical mirror, which is cut by a surface oblique to the axis; the common section of that surface and the mirror's surface will therefore be an <term>oxygonian section<gloss>an ellipse, literally an "acute-angled section" of a cone or cylinder</gloss></term> according to Theorem 103 of Book 1 of this work. Let that section be $abg$. It was shown in Theorem 11 of this book that sometimes, in the surface of an ellipse, there will be a line perpendicular to the surface tangent to the cylindrical mirror starting from the point of reflection; from the two boundaries of this line—namely, from the two common sections of itself and the surface of the mirror—the reflection of forms to the eye occurs. Therefore, let there be such a perpendicular in section $abg$, which shall be $ga$. Let line $bek$ be perpendicular to the line tangent to the periphery of the section at point $b$. Let point $b$ be near point $g$, so that a line drawn from point $b$, together with the perpendicular line drawn to the surface of the mirror from the point of reflection (which is $g$), contains an acute angle over the axis of the mirror. It is clear, then, by Theorem 44 of Book 7 of this work, that line $bek$ will cut the perpendicular line $ga$ below the axis of the mirror, and will contain an acute angle with it. Let the intersection of those lines be at point $e$. The angle $beg$ will therefore be acute, as is clear by Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid</note>. Let point $k$ fall on the periphery of the section; and from point $g$, let a line $gd$ be drawn parallel to line $bk$ by Proposition 31 of Book 1. Angle $dge$ will then be equal to angle $beg$ by Proposition 29 of Book 1; therefore, both are acute. Consequently, line $gd$ will be within the concavity of the mirror, since a line drawn from point $g$ (the endpoint of the perpendicular $ag$) outside the section would be tangent to the section and contain a right angle with line $ag$, or it would not be tangent and would contain an obtuse angle.

This surface will intersect the cylinder of the mirror along a circle, according to Theorem 100 of Book 1 of this work; let this circle be $p o r$. And since the center of sight $d$ is in the surface of the section $a b g$, it is clear that the circle $p o r$ will intersect the <term>acute section<gloss>original: "sectionem oxygoniam"; an elliptical section formed by cutting a cylinder at an angle</gloss></term> $a b g$ at two points, by Theorem 104 of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, the surface of that circle will intersect line $b k$, since it intersects line $g d$ which is parallel to line $b k$ (for it is drawn through point $d$). Let it, therefore, intersect line $b k$ at point $k$; and let the center of circle $p o r$ be point $h$. Let line $k h$ be drawn, which, passing through the circle, intersects its circumference at point $p$; and let line $d h$ be drawn, which, extended to the circumference of the circle, meets it at point $r$.

The form of point $k$ is reflected to the sight at point $d$ from some point on the arc $r p$, as is clear from Theorem 27 of Book 8 of this work, where this was shown regarding the reflection of a visible form to the sight from some point on the circumference of a circle in such a position. Let that reflection occur from a point of the mirror—specifically on arc $p r$—which we shall call point $o$. Let lines $k o$, $d o$, and $h o$ be drawn; therefore, angle $k o h$ is equal to angle $h o d$ by Theorem 20 of Book 5 of this work. And since the line of reflection, which is $d o$, intersects the radius $h p$ (because line $d h r$ passes through the center of the circle, and line $d o$ is drawn on this side of it with respect to point $o$), it therefore intersects the radius $h p$; let it intersect it at point $n$. Now, line $k h p$ is the <term>cathetus of incidence<gloss>the perpendicular line from the object to the mirror surface used to locate the image</gloss></term> of the form of point $k$; therefore, by Theorem 37 of Book 5 of this work, point $n$ is the location of the image of the form of point $k$.

Then, let line $k d$ be drawn, which, by Theorem 19 of Book 1 of this work, will be the <term>common section<gloss>the line where two surfaces meet</gloss></term> of the surface of circle $p o r$ and the section $a b g$, or part of that common section. For the two points $k$ and $d$ are in both of those surfaces, and nothing of the surface of the acute section (which is $a b g$) is in the surface of circle $p o r$ except line $k d$, or the line of which $k d$ is a part. Therefore, point $g$ is outside the circle, and similarly point $b$; and they are in the surface of the section. Point $n$ is in the surface of circle $r o$, and the image of the form of line $l m k$ passes through points $g, t, n$. However, the line passing through these points is curved, because the surface of the section is inclined upon the surface of the column by Theorem 103 of Book 1 of this work. Thus, the longer diameter of the section itself does not pass through the entire axis of the column, nor is the surface of the section parallel to the base of the column. Therefore, the line $t n g$, which is the image of the straight line $k m l$ (whose surface cuts the axis of the mirror obliquely), is curved with maximum curvature, and its concavity faces the sight located at point $d$.

And because point $t$ is the image of the form of point $m$, point $n$ is the image of the form of point $k$, and point $g$ is the image of the form of point $l$, it is clear that the image of line $l m k$ is inverted, so that the highest point of the image relative to the sight (which is $g$) corresponds to the lowest point of the line being seen (which is $l$), and the lowest point of the image (which is $n$) corresponds to the highest point of the line being seen (which is $k$). Thus, the arrangement of the parts of the image does not conform to the arrangement of the parts of the object seen, but is reversed and distorted. The proposition is therefore proven. It is thus clear from this proposition and the two preceding ones that straight lines parallel to the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror, those parallel to its base, and even those that are oblique to its surface, will sometimes appear curved and concave, sometimes straight and conforming in their arrangement to the parts of the object seen, and sometimes distorted, having a reversed arrangement of their parts relative to the sight and the parts of the object seen.

Alhazen [Book] 5, [Proposition] 4, [Number] 6.**

The <term>cathetus<gloss>original: "cathetus"; a perpendicular line dropped from a point to the surface of the mirror, used to locate where an image appears</gloss></term> of incidence for the form of point $r$ is the line $r e n$, which cuts line $b d$ (the line of reflection) at point $n$. Likewise, the cathetus of incidence for the form of point $m$ is line $m e u$, cutting the line of reflection $a d$ at point $u$. It is clear that points $n$ and $u$ are the locations of the images for the forms of points $r$ and $m$. Thus, line $n u$ will be the diameter of the image of line $m r$; and it is smaller than line $m r$, as was shown in Theorem 49 of Book 8 of this work. Similarly, the forms of the two points $h$ and $l$ will be reflected to the sight at point $d$ from two points of the mirror, $a$ and $b$. Following the method described previously, line $t k$ will be the diameter of the image of line $l h$; and according to the premises in Theorem 48 of Book 8 of this work, the diameter of the image $t k$ will be equal to the diameter of the object seen, which is line $l h$. Likewise, line $p i$ will be the diameter of the image of line $f q$, and it is larger than the diameter of the object seen, which is line $f q$. All these images will be <term>inverted<gloss>original: "conuersae"; meaning the orientation is flipped relative to the object</gloss></term>, as shown in Theorem 50 of Book 8. 

However, if the <term>center of sight<gloss>the observer's eye</gloss></term> were at point $o$, and the forms of the lines $p i$, $t k$, and $n u$ were reflected to the sight at point $o$ from the points of the mirror $a$ and $b$, then the opposite would occur. For the diameter of the image of line $p i$ (which is line $f q$) would be smaller than the diameter $t k$ of the object seen. Line $l h$ would be the diameter of the image of line $t k$ and equal to it, while line $m r$ would be the diameter of the image of line $n u$ and larger than it. All the images of these straight lines would be upright, but <term>reversed<gloss>original: "conuersae secundum situm"; the image is not upside down, but its left and right sides are swapped</gloss></term> according to the position and order of the parts that the objects themselves have. For the right side of the object becomes the left of the image, and the left of the object becomes the right of the image; the same applies to the parts that are top and bottom. 

Furthermore, since each of the ends of these lines has a single image, yet some other point in the middle might have several images, then the form of that line will have as many images as its middle point does. All those images will join together at the endpoint of that image, and that single line will be the diameter of all those images. If both ends of the line (or just one of them) have multiple images, but the middle point has only one, then again, the whole line will have as many images as both its endpoints, or at least as many as its one endpoint. And if both ends (or one) have multiple images, and the middle point also has many images, then the entire line will have images according to the highest number. This will be evident just as it was shown above regarding images in concave spherical mirrors. 

Indeed, in concave <term>columnar<gloss>cylindrical</gloss></term> mirrors, <term>optical illusions<gloss>original: "fallacia"; errors in perception where the image does not match the physical reality of the object</gloss></term> occur in all things perceived in them, just as they do in concave spherical mirrors: specifically regarding the shapes of visible forms, their sizes, the number of their images, their conformity to the objects of which they are images, and the deformity of their positions due to the inversion of partial forms, along with all the illusions associated with inversion. All the illusions in these mirrors are the same as in the aforementioned concave spherical mirrors. Therefore, what was proposed is evident.

### 30. *A visible straight line, not parallel to the axis of a concave cylindrical mirror, where the surface of incidence cuts the axis obliquely and the center of sight is not in that same surface, appears as a curved image, of varying curvature according to the variety of its position; and it is inverted.*

Let the total arrangement for this proposed theorem be the same as in Theorem 28 of this book; everything proposed there will appear in these concave cylindrical mirrors. Thus, assuming that some straight line is not parallel to the axis of the concave cylindrical mirror, and its <term>surface of incidence<gloss>the plane in which the light travels from the object to the mirror and then to the eye</gloss></term> cuts that axis obliquely: if the center of sight is in that surface, then it is clear from Theorem 28 of this book that the image of that line appears curved with respect to the sight and inverted according to the position of the visible object itself. 

But if the center of sight were outside that surface on a line erected perpendicularly above that surface from point $d$ (where the center of sight was located there), then if lines are drawn along the length of the mirror from points $a, g, o$ (from which reflection occurs), according to Theorem 101 of Book 1, and the points of reflection for the forms of points $m, b, k$ are found, it will be clear—following the method of several previous theorems—that the forms of points $k, m, b$ will be reflected to the sight according to a disposition different from their actual position. According to this, the curvature of the images and the inversion of the figure will be arranged. If the center of sight were not on a line perpendicularly erected over that surface from point $d$, then let a perpendicular be drawn from the center of sight to that surface (according to Proposition 11 of Book 11 <note>original: "11 p 11"; likely referring to Euclid's Elements</note>). Once the points of reflection for the forms of points $b, m, k$ are found, the proposition will be clear as before. And this is what was proposed.

Therefore, the image of the entire curved line $a p y$ will be the straight line $a o n$, because the same demonstration applies to the other points. If some visible object is placed in the location of the straight line $a y$, which is the diameter of that curved image line $a p y$, then the two endpoints of the line $a y$ (which are $a$ and $y$) will have their image locations at points $a$ and $n$, as before. However, the locations for the image of the middle point corresponding to point $p$ (which falls on the extended line $z p$) and for the other middle points will differ. Depending on the variation in how the catheti of incidence of the forms of those points intersect with their lines of reflection—along which they are reflected from points on the line of length $a z e$ of the proposed concave mirror to the eye at point $f$—the image locations for those points will vary, appearing either beyond line $a o n$ or in front of it. Sometimes they will face the concavity and sometimes the convexity relative to the center of sight. Nevertheless, that curvature will be slight, because there is only a small deviation of those aforementioned image locations relative to the line $a o n$. It is therefore evident from the premises that if a straight line, which is the diameter of the curved image $a p y$, were part of some visible object and the center of sight were at point $f$, then the image of the straight line arranged in the aforementioned manner would perhaps appear convex, or perhaps concave. This is what was proposed.

### 32. *If a seen straight line's surface of incidence cuts the axis of a concave pyramidal mirror at a right angle, and the center of sight is not in that same surface, the image will appear concave, with a remarkable concavity facing the sight.*

The image location for point $m$, however, will be point $s$, which is outside the straight path of line $t h$. Thus, the image of line $r m y$ lies on a certain line passing through points $h, s$, and $t$; but such a line is curved. Therefore, for a straight line which...

### 33. *When a straight line is seen not parallel to the axis of a concave pyramidal mirror, and its surface of incidence cuts the axis of the mirror obliquely, the image appears curved, with varying curvature according to the difference of its position.*

For since, as was shown in Theorem 31 of this book, the form of a straight line incident to the vertex of this mirror obliquely to the axis represents a curved image to the eye where the reflection occurs; and it is clear through the previous theorem that a straight line, whose surface of incidence cuts the axis of the mirror orthogonally <gloss>at a right angle</gloss>, is seen with a remarkable concavity facing the eye. If, therefore, a straight line is positioned between these arrangements so that its surface of incidence, as proposed here, cuts the axis of the mirror obliquely: it is clear that the image of that line will vary according to the modes of different curvature. These happen on one side or the other for lines situated according to both previously mentioned modes, the demonstration of which is consistent with the preceding ones. Therefore, the proposition is clear; for we do not think it worthy to dwell on such matters, which clearly receive the substance of their certainty from previously demonstrated conclusions; hence we leave such things to the inquiring mind <note>Witelo often uses this phrasing to encourage the reader to work out the geometry themselves based on the principles already established.</note>.

### 34. *The image of a straight line existing in a surface cutting through the axis of a pyramidal mirror, with the center of sight being in the common section of that same surface and the surface cutting the mirror through its axis, will be seen as straight: sometimes larger, sometimes equal, sometimes smaller than the thing seen: but always having a reversed position: and sometimes one, sometimes several images will meet the sight.* <note>Referencing Alhazen, Book 5, Chapter 56, Note 6.</note>

### 35. *It is possible for a mirror to be made composed of convex and concave surfaces, in which right appears right and left appears left, and many diversities of images occur. Euclid, Theorem 30 of the Catoptrics; Problems, Theorem 3 of the second Catoptrics.*

Let a circle be taken of the size one wishes to build such a mirror, which shall be $a\ b\ g$. Let the side of an inscribable pentagon be inscribed in that same circle <note>Using the method from Euclid's *Elements*, Book 4, Proposition 11</note>, which is $a\ b$; and similarly, let the side of a hexagon be inscribed in the same circle <note>Using the method from Euclid's *Elements*, Book 4, Proposition 15</note>, which is $b\ g$. By that same proposition, line $b\ g$ will be equal to the <term>semidiameter: the radius, or half the width of the circle</term>. Let a segment $a\ e\ b$ be cut from that circle, whose arc $a\ b$ <note>according to Book 3, Proposition 28 of the *Elements*</note> is equal to a fifth part of the circle's circumference. Similarly, let segment $g\ z\ b$ be cut from the same circle, whose arc $b\ g$ is equal to a sixth part of the circle. Let regular templates be made to the size of those two segments: one made according to the size of segment $a\ e\ b$, which is concave, like the figure we have described, $z\ h\ f\ k\ m\ l$; the other made to the size of segment $g\ z\ b$, which is convex, like figure $x\ o\ p$. Let a rectangular piece of iron be taken, whose length is greater than both chords $a\ b$ and $b\ g$, and whose width is greater than chord $b\ g$. Let the iron be bent so that its length follows the convexity of segment $a\ e\ b$, so that the concave surface $k\ f\ t$ is applied to it from the outside; and its width follows the remaining length of the concavity of segment $g\ z\ b$, so that the convexity of surface $x\ o\ p$ is applied to it from the inside. Let it be made such that the convex shape does not hinder the concave shape, but let each be impressed upon the same surface of the mirror. Let the mirror be polished on both sides; for this reason, the plate to be mirrored must be suitably thick, so that it can be polished on both sides while preserving the shape. If this mirror is placed on a rotating base prepared for this purpose and rotated so that now the convex and now the concave surface faces the viewer, then right will appear as right and left as left; and at a di-

### 36. *It is difficult to ignite a fire from concave columnar or pyramidal mirrors.*

For if in concave <term>columnar mirrors</term><note>cylindrical mirrors</note> the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is a line of longitude <note>a straight vertical line running along the side of the cylinder</note>, it is not necessary for fire to be lit by them, just as it is not from plane mirrors, even if all the surfaces of reflection intersect each other at the axis of the column. Indeed, rays falling parallel to the surface of the mirror will certainly be reflected parallel; those that are perpendicular to themselves will cut the axis at the diverse points of the columnar mirror where they fell upon it. Thus, they will never concur <note>meet or focus</note> at a single point, but will be spread out along the entire line of the axis.

Non-perpendicular rays, however—namely those falling obliquely upon the surface of the mirror—are reflected to another part in the same surface from the said perpendicular, according to the angles they make with the perpendicular drawn from the axis to the line of longitude (which is the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface touching the column). It is clear, therefore, that just as they fall parallel to each other, so they are reflected nearly parallel to each other, and they concur not in a point, but in a line, through proposition 29. 

If it is said that some surfaces of reflection do not intersect at the axis of the column, but are parallel (which is impossible, as is clear through theorem 7 of book 7 of this work), it is nevertheless evident that the reflected rays in them will never concur. If, however, the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the column is a circle, then it is clear that the rays passing through its center (since all are perpendicular to the surfaces touching at the points of their incidence, as shown by theorem 21 of book 7) are all reflected back onto themselves. They will concur at the center of that circle, whether it be the base of the mirror's column or a circle parallel to the base. 

This center, however, will always be on the axis, and there are as many centers of such circles on the axis as there are circles in the column. Therefore, the rays of the entire surface of the columnar mirror do not reflect to one point, but to the entire line of the axis. But if the reflected rays do not pass through the center of the circle according to the circle, then a diversity of reflection toward the semi-diameter <note>radius</note> of the circle will occur according to the diversity of the angles of incidence. The concurrence of rays will not happen at the center of the circle, but along the whole radius; thus fire can only be ignited with difficulty, just as was said before regarding the concave spherical mirror in theorem 68 of book 8. 

If the common section of the said two surfaces is a <term>columnar section</term><note>an elliptical or curved cut through the cylinder</note>, then very few rays will concur. It is clear, therefore, that it is not possible for all the rays of the surface of a concave columnar mirror to be gathered into one place or even into one line; for this reason, few of the ancients used such a mirror for combustions. 

Likewise, it is not necessary for gathered light from <term>pyramidal mirrors</term><note>conical mirrors</note> to kindle fire, although the imagination of many is inclined toward this. The cause of this is that in such mirrors, the common section of the surface of reflection and the surface of the mirror cannot be any circle, neither the base nor one parallel to the base, because of what was said before, and as is clear through theorem 2 of this book. In no event, therefore, can the rays concur at the center from the periphery of a circle, as happens to some extent in a columnar mirror. 

If the common section of the said surfaces is the line of longitude of the mirror, then, since the surface touching the mirror touches it at the line of longitude, it will happen in these mirrors just as was said before regarding plane and columnar mirrors. For whatever angles the incident rays make with the line of longitude, they will make the same reflected angles with the same line; thus the incident rays are parallel and are reflected parallel. They will not concur, therefore, even if they are in the same surface of reflection; and if they are in different surfaces, it is clear they will not concur except at the axis, because the surfaces of reflection intersect each other upon the axis of the pyramid. Then the concurrence of rays will happen in a line, not in a point. 

If the common section of the said surfaces is a pyramidal section, still not all or even many rays of the same surface or of different surfaces will concur in any way. In no way, therefore, can all the rays incident on a pyramidal mirror, or many of them, or even a few, concur at one point so that they are able to ignite something resistant to ignition; nor will a plurality of joined mirrors bring anything significant relative to the extra labor involved. Thus, what was proposed is clear.

Then, in the middle of its width, let a groove be carved along a straight line and smoothed out, and let it be arranged such that a <term>sliding carriage<note>original: "nauicula"; literally "little boat," used here to describe a component that slides smoothly within a track</note></term> can run within it in the manner of a turner's device. In this carriage, let an iron hook be fixed. Let this ruler, thus hollowed and arranged, be positioned so that its hollowed surface stands upright above the surface of the horizon, and the lines of the depth of its hollow are perpendicular to the surface of the horizon. Let the line which the hook of the moving carriage describes by its motion be equal to the semi-diameter of the proposed circle, which is $e\ d$, so that point $e$ falls on the inner surface of the iron hook itself, which is moved by the motion of the carriage to which it is attached.

Next, let another wooden or bronze ruler be taken, similarly rectangular like the first and with flat surfaces. Let this ruler likewise be finely hollowed in its wider surface along straight lines, and let the surfaces of the hollow be smoothed so that another thin ruler or a cord can be moved through that hollow without hindrance. Let the hollow of that ruler be double the line $e\ d$—that is, let it be equal to the diameter of the circle, which is $a\ c$. Let this ruler be fitted to the first ruler such that its non-hollowed surface is parallel to the horizon, and its hollowed surface faces the hollow of the first ruler. Let it be arranged perpendicularly over the first, so that the angle $d\ e\ c$ is a right angle; and let the midpoint of the length of its hollow correspond to point $e$, which is the point of the hook of the carriage itself. Let all these things be in the same surface parallel to the surface of the horizon.

Also, let a third bronze ruler be made, long with flat rectangular surfaces and straight lines, which shall be $e\ f\ g$. Let its part $e\ f$ be equal to the semi-diameter of the circle, which is $e\ c$. Let it be so arranged that it is attached to the hook of the carriage at point $e$ by means of some ring or hole, so that it can move through the hollow of the line $a\ c$. Let there be a knob at point $f$, the diameter of which is greater than the diameter of the hollow of ruler $a\ c$. Also, let the remaining part of the line $e\ f\ g$, which is $f\ g$, be of any length desired; and at point $g$, let a sharp nail be applied at the very tip, of such a size that when line $e\ f\ g$ is moved, it can reach the floor or another surface placed beneath it.

Now, with all these things thus arranged, let the ruler $e\ f\ g$ be inserted into the hook of the carriage according to the hole at point $e$, and let the carriage be pulled smoothly by a <term>screw<note>original: "cochleam"; likely a worm gear or lead screw used to ensure precise, steady movement</note></term> or in another way, as shall seem fit, provided the pull is smooth and even. The ruler $e\ f\ g$ will follow the pull of the carriage, and point $f$ will run along the surface of ruler $a\ c$; thus the center of the circle, whose diameter is line $e\ f$, will constantly change. 

Therefore, when point $e$ reaches point $d$, then point $f$ will be at the midpoint of line $a\ c$, which is the center of the previously mentioned circle. Of all the points of reflection of light or of any forms from the quarter of the circle which is $c\ b$, the meeting of the rays or the diffused power will be at the center of the circle, which is $e$; since all the points of burning <note>original: "combustionum"; referring to the focal points where heat concentrates enough to ignite materials</note> meeting on the axis $e\ b$ are brought back to point $e$, which is the center of the circle, as if from all the rays falling on the circle of the mirror parallel to the diameter $a\ c$. 

Similarly, if you wish, let it be done in the other quarter of the circle by moving the carriage smoothly, bringing point $f$ back to point $a$. For then point $g$ of the line $f\ g$ will, by its motion, describe a certain line, which will be traced on the floor by the nail attached to it; and we call this line the <term>eccentric line<note>original: "lineam eccentrem"; a curve generated by the intersection of multiple circular paths</note></term>, since it is the intersection of infinite circles. For every point of that line (except for the endpoints corresponding to points $a$ and $c$ of the diameter $a\ c$, and any two points equally distant from the midpoint of the whole eccentric line) corresponds to a different center, just as any two points equally distant from the midpoint look toward the same center; they are points of one circle intersecting another circle. We shall use this line, therefore, for the construction of the proposed mirror, hollowing out some mirror surface according to it, as will be said below by way of demonstration and craftsmanship. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 38. It is possible for fire to be ignited from the intersection of several concave pyramidal mirrors.

What we propose here was the first thing that occurred to us when we were seeking knowledge of these matters, and it was in the discovery of this thing that our mind first found rest. For even if rays cannot easily be gathered at a single mathematical point, they can be gathered at a single "natural point" <note>Witelo distinguishes between a dimensionless "mathematical point" and a "natural point," which we would call the focal spot—the smallest area where the light concentrates</note> having a small and almost imperceptible width from the rays of an entire surface; and the things which occurred to us later are even more effective. However, we have decided that none of these should be omitted, so that the minds of those who come after us may grow to even greater heights.

In the present demonstration, we have decided to mix in the mechanical work itself to some extent, yet omitting nothing of the substance of the proof. Let any pyramid be taken, therefore, which shall be $a\ b\ c\ d$, whose vertex is point $a$; and let the lines of the length of that pyramid be $a\ b$ and $a\ c$, and let its axis be line $a\ d$. Let this axis be, for example, 18 parts, according to which the diameter of the circle of its base, which is $f\ b\ e\ c$, is 6 parts. Then, by theorem 89 of book 1 of this work, point $d$ will be the center of the circle which is the base of the pyramid itself. Let a line equal to its semi-diameter be inscribed in the circle of the base according to Proposition 1 of Book 4 <note>Euclid, Elements IV.1</note>, which shall be $f\ e$; and let there be some diameter in the circle parallel to the inscribed line. Since line $f\ e$ is divided into equal parts according to Proposition 10 of Book 1 <note>Euclid, Elements I.10</note>, let a perpendicular be drawn from the point of division (which is $g$) to that line according to Proposition 11 of Book 1 <note>Euclid, Elements I.11</note>. This will also pass through the center of the circle by Proposition 1 of Book 3 <note>Euclid, Elements III.1</note>. Let that line be extended to both sides of the circumference, and let it be $b\ c$. 

Then, let a perpendicular be drawn from the center of the base circle, which is $d$, to the diameter $b\ c$; let this be $d\ h$, and let it be extended to the other side of the circle. This will become the diameter $h\ k$, parallel to line $e\ f$ by Proposition 28 of Book 1 <note>Euclid, Elements I.28</note>. Let two lines of the length of the pyramid be drawn from points $h$ and $k$ to the vertex, which shall be $h\ a$ and $k\ a$. Also, let a line parallel to line $k\ a$ be drawn from point $e$, and from point $f$ a line parallel to line $h\ a$ by Proposition 31 of Book 1 <note>Euclid, Elements I.31</note>. Let the extended lines meet at point $x$; they will meet for this reason: because their parallels, which are $k\ a$ and $h\ a$, meet at point $a$. Therefore, between the two lines $e\ x$ and $f\ x$, a flat surface is continued and terminated at line $f\ e$...

Triangle $x\ f\ e$, because its sides are parallel to the sides of the large triangle in the pyramid ($a\ h\ k$), will itself be parallel to that large triangle. Just as triangle $a\ h\ k$ divides the pyramid into equal parts—since it is bounded by two longitudinal lines and the diameter of the base—so too triangle $x\ f\ e$ cuts off a certain portion of the pyramid. Therefore, let this portion be cut away from the whole pyramid; let it be $l\ f\ b\ e\ g$. Let straight lines $l\ e$ and $l\ f$ be drawn. By Theorem 89 of Book 1 of this work, the lines $l\ f$ and $l\ e$ will be equal parts of a single <term>conic section<note>In this context, Witelo is describing the curved edge of a slice taken through the pyramid.</note></term>, which is $e\ l\ f$, divided equally at its highest point, $l$. 

However, line $l\ b$, which is part of the longitudinal line of the pyramid, will be shorter than either line $l\ e$ or $l\ f$. Line $b\ g$ will be the line of depth of this portion; line $f\ e$ the line of width; and line $l\ g$ the upright side of the portion, which is parallel to line $d\ a$, the axis of the pyramid. It is therefore useful for those focused on mechanical work <note>original: "operi mechanico consulentes"</note> that we seek knowledge of all these lines, assuming those things which have been proven regarding chords and arcs.

It is clear from the preceding that line $f\ e$, which is inscribed in the circle, is equal to its semi-diameter and is 60 parts (in a system where the diameter of the circle is 120). Therefore, the arc $f\ e$ is likewise 60 parts (where the whole circle is 360). Let lines $b\ f$ and $b\ e$ also be drawn. Since the diameter $b\ c$ divides the chord $f\ e$ equally and at right angles, it is evident by <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Proposition 4</note> that the straight lines $f\ b$ and $b\ e$ are equal. Therefore, arcs $f\ b$ and $b\ e$ are equal by <note>Euclid, Book 3, Proposition 28</note>. Thus, arc $f\ e$ is bisected at point $b$. Arc $f\ b$ is therefore 30 parts; the chord $f\ b$ is 31 parts, 3 minutes, and 30 seconds. 

But since line $f\ g$ is half of line $f\ e$ (which was 60), it is clear that line $f\ g$ is 30. Let line $f\ b$ and line $f\ g$ be squared according to <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 46</note>. Because the square of line $f\ b$ in triangle $f\ b\ g$ subtends the right angle, it is clear by the <term>Pythagorean theorem<note>original: "47 p 1" referring to Euclid, Book 1, Prop 47</note></term> that the square of line $f\ b$ is equal to both the squares of lines $f\ g$ and $b\ g$ together. Thus, when the square of $f\ g$ is subtracted from the square of $f\ b$, the square of $b\ g$ remains. Let the square root of that remainder be extracted; that is the length of line $b\ g$. According to the scale where line $f\ g$ is 30 parts, $b\ g$ will be 8 parts, 2 minutes, and 29 seconds. 

However, in a scale where the diameter $b\ c$ is 6 parts and the semi-diameter is 3 parts, and line $f\ g$ is 8 parts and 30 minutes, line $b\ g$ will be 24 minutes and 6 seconds. A diligent investigator searching for the unknown fourth value from three known ones can easily find this with the help of <note>Euclid, Book 7, Proposition 19</note>. 

Since line $g\ l$ is erected parallel to the axis of the pyramid ($d\ a$), it is clear from <note>Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 29</note> that triangles $d\ a\ b$ and $g\ l\ b$ have equal angles. Therefore, by <note>Euclid, Book 6, Proposition 4</note>, the ratio of line $d\ a$ to line $g\ l$ is as the ratio of line $d\ b$ to line $g\ b$. By permutation <note>Euclid, Book 5, Proposition 16</note>, the ratio of $d\ a$ to $d\ b$ is as $l\ g$ to $g\ b$. But line $d\ a$ is six times line $d\ b$ by hypothesis; therefore, line $l\ g$ will be six times line $b\ g$. It is thus clear that line $l\ g$ will be 2 parts, 24 minutes, and 36 seconds, in the scale where line $d\ a$ is 18 parts.

But because in triangle $l\ b\ g$ the angle $l\ g\ b$ is a right angle—since the side $g\ l$, like line $d\ a$, is erected perpendicularly upon the surface of the circle of the pyramid’s base—it is clear that the square of line $l\ b$ equals the squares of both lines $l\ g$ and $b\ g$. Let the squares be added and the square root of the sum be extracted; that is the length of line $l\ b$, which (using the scale where the base semi-diameter is 3 parts) will be 2 parts, 26 minutes, and 35 seconds. 

And because line $l\ g$ is erected upon the surface of the pyramid’s base, it is clear by the definition of a line perpendicular to a surface that it forms right angles with lines $g\ f$ and $g\ e$, as it does with all lines drawn in said surface. Therefore, the square of the straight line $e\ l$ (which is opposite the right angle in the right-angled triangle $e\ g\ l$) equals the square of line $l\ g$ and line $g\ e$. Having joined those squares, let the root of the sum be extracted; it is clear that the straight line $l\ e$ is 2 parts, 50 minutes, and 19 seconds. By the same logic, since the square of line $f\ l$ equals the square of line $f\ g$ (which is equal to $g\ e$) and the square of $l\ g$, it is clear that $l\ f$ is equal to $e\ l$. Thus, line $f\ l$ is 2 parts, 50 minutes, and 19 seconds. 

We now have the measurements of all the lines of the assumed pyramidal portion necessary for the present work. Although it is difficult to actually obtain a pyramid suitable for the purpose (since it would have to be entirely hollowed out of a solid, polishable body for the making of a mirror, as was said before, and cutting a section from that would be difficult), it is sufficient to hold the mathematical pyramid in the imagination. 

When, therefore, one wishes to proceed to the work of the mirror: let a concave portion of a pyramid be made from a polishable white body, such as silver or good iron, such that the base of that section is a portion of the circle that forms the base of the imagined pyramid. Let its chord be half the diameter of the imagined circle, which is line $f\ e$; it will be 2 parts. The <term>sagitta<note>original: "sinus uersus"; the "versed sine" or "arrow," representing the depth of the arc.</note></term>, which is $g\ b$, should be 24 minutes and 6 seconds according to that quantity, which is the line of depth for the chosen section. Perhaps, when it is drawn out, it resembles an arrow <note>original: "fagittæ" (sagittae)</note>, just as those lines resemble a chord and an arc. The straight lines $e\ l$ and $f\ l$ shall be equal, each being 2 parts, 50 minutes, and 19 seconds; and line $l\ b$ shall be 2 parts, 26 minutes, and 35 seconds. If all these are well-measured, it is clear that one has a portion of a pyramid whose base circle diameter is

It is clear from Proposition 2 of this book that in a concave pyramidal mirror, reflection occurs along the lines of the pyramid's length, such that the angle formed by the incident ray with the line of the mirror’s length is equal to the angle of reflection—that is, the angle formed by the reflected ray with that same line of length. Therefore, the angle of incidence, which is $hts$, will be equal to the angle of reflection; but angle $hts$ is equal to angle $qbt$ by [Euclid’s Elements] Book 1, Proposition 29, and angle $qbt$ is equal to angle $qtb$ by Book 1, Proposition 5, because sides $qb$ and $qt$ are equal by the definition of a circle. Therefore, the angle of reflection will be equal to angle $qbt$. Consequently, the line of reflection will be equal to line $qb$ by Book 1, Proposition 6; thus, the reflection occurs along line $qt$. Therefore, a ray incident at point $b$ and reflected from point $t$ will meet at point $q$, because it is impossible to draw from point $t$ another line equal to line $qb$ that forms an angle with line $bt$ equal to angle $qbt$. Similarly, the angle of incidence, which is $kds$, is equal to the angle of reflection; and this is also equal to angle $qbd$, following the previously mentioned method of deduction from Book 1, Proposition 29. Therefore, angle $qbd$ and the angle of reflection of the incident ray $kd$ are equal, and thus the reflection occurs along line $qd$. The same must be demonstrated for the others.

It is therefore clear that all rays incident at the points of the sections made by the sides of the triangles extended from point $b$ toward the axis $qs$ are reflected to a single point, which is the center of the chosen circle. And because those sections can be made almost infinite from a single line so arranged in a sector, the aggregations of rays at a single mathematical point become almost infinite. This having been demonstrated, it is clear that all rays incident at points $b, t, d, e, f, l$ are reflected to a single point, which is $q$. And if the protruding small portions are removed, the boundaries $td$ and $ef$ will regulate the intervening lines so that the reflection made from them will not be far from the point of reflection, which is $q$. There will be an aggregation of all rays incident on the total line $bl$ to a single natural, sensible point in the vicinity of point $q$. Therefore, this line $bl$, by its motion, will produce the surface of the previously assumed section of the <term>pyramid<note>Again, referring to a cone.</note></term> by polishing and carving; from the whole of this surface, reflection will occur to a single natural point, as will be taught below. The proposition is therefore clear: for these triangles, by their motion, create intersecting pyramids.

*39. If a straight line touches a parabolic section, and from the point of contact a straight line is drawn perpendicularly over the extended diameter of the section to the point of meeting with the tangent: the part of the diameter lying between the perpendicular and the periphery of the section will be equal to the part lying between the section and the tangent.*

Let there be a parabolic section—the name of which we previously explained in the first book in the commentary on Proposition 98—which shall be $lag$, whose <term>latus rectum<note>The "upright side" or parameter of a conic section that defines its proportions.</note></term> is $lg$ and its <term>diameter<note>In this context, the diameter refers to the axis of symmetry of the parabola.</note></term> is $ad$. Let a straight line, which is $hbk$, touch this section at point $b$. Let the diameter $da$, extended outside the section, meet with the tangent line $hbk$ at point $h$. From the point of contact $b$, let a line be drawn by Book 1, Proposition 12, perpendicular to the diameter $ad$, cutting it at point $z$; let this be $bz$. I say that line $za$—the part of the diameter lying between the perpendicular point of the section $bz$ and the periphery of the section $lag$—is equal to line $ah$, the extended part of the diameter lying between point $h$ (the meeting point of the diameter and the tangent line $hbk$) and point $a$ (the end of the diameter falling on the periphery of the section itself). And this is universal, even if the straight line touches the section at point $g$. This was demonstrated by Apollonius of Perga in his book *On Conic Elements* <note>original: "De Conicis elementis"</note>, and we shall use it here as demonstrated.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a parabola with its vertex at point 'a'. A vertical axis extends upwards from 'd' through 'z' and 'a' to a point 'h' outside the curve. A tangent line 'hbk' touches the curve at point 'b'. A horizontal line 'bz' represents the perpendicular from the tangent point to the axis. The curve is labeled with points 'l', 'f', 'e', and 'g' denoting its shape.</image-desc>

*40. Every square of a perpendicular line drawn from any point of a parabolic section to the diameter of the section is equal to the rectangle contained by the part of the diameter lying between that perpendicular and the periphery of the section, and by the latus rectum of that section.*

For example: let there be, as in the previous case, a parabolic section $lag$ whose latus rectum is $lg$ and whose diameter is $ad$. From some point of the section, $b$, let a perpendicular $bz$ be drawn to the diameter $ad$. I say that the square of the perpendicular line $bz$ is equal to the rectangle formed by the multiplication of line $za$ (the part of the diameter $ad$ lying between the perpendicular $bz$ and the periphery) and line $lg$ (the latus rectum of the section). Therefore, by Book 6, Proposition 17, the proportion of line $lg$ to line $zb$ is as $zb$ is to line $za$. This was likewise demonstrated by Apollonius of Perga in his book *On Conic Elements*, and we shall use it as demonstrated. These two theorems, along with other theorems of Apollonius, we did not include at the beginning of this book because we only require them to explain the following theorem, and in none of the other theorems of this entire book.

For the angle $b-e-h$ cannot escape one of three conditions. It will either be acute, right, or obtuse. First, let it be acute: and from point $b$, let a perpendicular $b-z$ be drawn to the diameter $a-d$ according to Proposition 12 of Book 1: point $z$ will fall between the two points $a$ and $e$ according to Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>This identifies the relative positions of the points on the axis based on the steepness of the curve.</note>: and let the diameter $a-d$ be extended beyond point $a$ until, by Theorem 2 of Proposition 1 of this book, it meets the line tangent to the section, $k-b-h$: let the intersection be at point $h$: angle $a-h-b$ will then be acute: therefore, the perpendicular $b-z$ falls between points $h$ and $e$, and by Proposition 39 of this book, line $a-z$ will be equal to line $a-h$. Because line $a-e$ is divided at point $z$, and a segment equal to one part of the dividing segments ($a-h$) is added to it: therefore, by Proposition 8 of Book 2, the square of line $e-h$ is equal to four times the rectangle formed by line $e-a$ and line $h-a$ (or line $a-z$), plus the square of line $z-e$: but line $e-a$ is a fourth part of line $l-g$ by hypothesis: therefore, by Proposition 1 of Book 2 or Proposition 1 of Book 6, that which is produced by multiplying line $a-z$ by line $a-e$ four times is equal to that which is produced by multiplying line $a-z$ by line $l-g$ once. Therefore, the product of line $a-z$ and line $l-g$, together with the square of line $z-e$, is equal to the square of line $e-h$: but it is clear from the preceding proposition that the product of line $a-z$ and line $l-g$ is equal to the square of line $b-z$: since line $b-z$ is perpendicular to the diameter $a-d$: the two squares $b-z$ and $z-e$ are, by Proposition 47 of Book 1 <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, equal to the square of line $b-e$: therefore the squares of lines $e-h$ and $e-b$ are equal: thus line $e-b$ is equal to line $e-h$: therefore, by Proposition 5 of Book 1, in triangle $e-b-h$, angle $e-h-b$ is equal to angle $e-b-h$: but lines $t-b$ and $d-a$ are parallel: therefore, by Proposition 29 of Book 1, the exterior angle $t-b-k$ is equal to the interior angle $d-h-b$: thus angle $e-b-h$ is equal to angle $t-b-k$. The same must also be demonstrated for any line parallel to the diameter $a-d$ and line $b-e$ joined to point $e$, whenever that line forms an acute angle with the diameter $a-d$ at point $e$. Thus the proposition is clear according to this method. But if the angle $b-e-h$ were a right angle, the proposition is still clear, that angle $t-b-k$ is equal to angle $e-b-h$. For since angle $b-e-h$ is a right angle: it is clear that line $b-e$ is perpendicular to the diameter $a-d$: therefore line $e-a$, by Proposition 39 of this book, is equal to line $a-h$: but line $e-a$ is by hypothesis a fourth part of line $l-g$: therefore line $h-e$, which is double line $a-e$, is half of line $l-g$: therefore by Proposition 4 of Book 2, the square of line $e-h$ is a fourth part of the square of line $l-g$. Likewise, the product of line $e-a$ and line $l-g$ is equal to a fourth part of the square of line $l-g$ by Proposition 1 of Book 6: since line $e-a$ is by hypothesis a fourth part of line $l-g$.

43. *With a concave mirror of parabolic section placed opposite the sun, such that its axis is directed toward the solar body: all rays falling on the mirror parallel to the axis are reflected to a single point on the axis, distant from the surface of the mirror by a fourth part of the latus rectum of the parabolic section that forms the mirror's surface. From which it is clear that it is possible for fire to be ignited from the surface of such mirrors.*

Let there be a concave mirror with the concavity of a parabolic section: let its vertex <note>The "tip" or highest point of the curve.</note> be point $a$: and let its base be circle $q e z$: and its axis $a d$: and let the distance of the point on the axis (which is $h$) from the point of the mirror's vertex (which is $a$) be equal to a fourth part of line $q z$, namely the latus rectum of the parabolic section $a g q$, which by its motion around axis $a d$ creates the surface of that concave mirror: let this be placed opposite the sun according to its axis $a d$. For let the center of the solar body be $k$: and let the mirror be positioned such that its axis $a d$, thus extended, reaches the center of the sun at point $k$. I say that all solar rays falling parallel to the ray $k a$ upon the surface of the proposed mirror are reflected to point $h$ of line $a d$, which is the axis of the mirror. Since indeed all rays exiting from any point of the solar body upon any point of the mirror's surface proceed according to straight lines, as is clear through Theorem 1 of Book 2 of this work: then it is evident that line $k a$ is a straight line. Therefore, let point $g$ be marked anywhere on the circumference of any parabolic section of the mirror itself (which is $g a z q$): and from point $g$ of the mirror through Proposition 1, let line $g t$ be drawn to some point of the solar body (which is $t$), parallel to ray $a k$, which falls upon the surface of the mirror along axis $a d$. It is necessary, however, that every line produced from any point of the mirror parallel to ray $a k$ falls upon the surface of the solar body: since there is little or no proportion <note>Meaning the mirror is so small compared to the sun that the rays are essentially parallel.</note> between the surface of the mirror and the solar surface: let therefore point $t$, which is the end of line $g t$, be on the surface of the solar body itself. Therefore, all lines that can be drawn from the surface of the mirror parallel to its axis $a d$ fall upon the solar body, and the incidence upon the mirror's surface occurs according to those lines, with respect to the ray that falls along the axis of all parallels: this is true of all rays falling upon any point of the entire mirror's surface: since through Proposition 31 of Book 1, we know how to draw a parallel line to any given line, such as axis $a d$ in this case, from any point given near or far. I say, therefore, that all those rays are reflected from the total surface of the mirror to one point of the mirror's axis, which is point $h$. For all those rays are straight lines: it is clear through the premise that with the lines drawn from all points of their incidence to point $h$ they contain [equal] angles...

<meta>This page concludes the mathematical proof regarding the focus of a parabolic mirror and transitions into a practical manual for craftsmen on how to physically construct these "burning mirrors." From this, it is clear that all rays incident upon the periphery of the section, parallel to the ray incident along the line which is the diameter of that section, are reflected to a point on the diameter. This point $h$ cuts off from the vertex <note>original: "capite," literally 'head'</note> of the diameter, on the side of the section’s curve, a part equal to the fourth part of the <term>latus rectum</term> <note>The 'latus rectum' is a geometric parameter that defines the width of a parabola. And since all those lines intersect at point $h$, it is clear that point $h$ is the meeting place of all those rays. In that point, therefore, all the power <note>original: "uirtus"; the active energy or potency of the light.</note> of all the rays falling upon the total surface of the mirror is gathered. And since every small ray carries with it something of the active power of the solar body, it is clear that at that point the entire power is converging—specifically, from all rays incident to the surface of the mirror parallel to the axis $a d$. From this, it is clear that by placing some combustible material at point $h$, it is possible for fire to be ignited. This is the best and strongest shape of all figures for gathering solar rays into a single point, because from its entire surface, and from every point of it, the solar rays are gathered into one point. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 44. To artificially construct a mirror according to the shape of a parabolic section, or an eccentric line, or the intersection of a pyramid [a conic section], or any other given regular or irregular line.

The line which we call the periphery of the section must be found by the industry of the craftsman. This has been discovered by us through many artificial attempts, yet it is easily imagined: for as we said in Theorem 98 of Book 1 of this work, it is the line which is the common section of the conical surface of any pyramid—most ideally a right-angled one—and a surface cutting the pyramid through the diameter of the base parallel to any line of the length of that pyramid. Specifically, it is the one whose common surface with the axis of the pyramid stands upright over the flat surface cutting the pyramid in the said manner. Let such a parabolic section, thus artificially discovered, be $a e g$. Let a sheet of good iron or steel be taken, of whatever measure and size is pleasing, which shall be $a b g d$. Let the parabolic section be drawn upon it, equal and similar to section $a e g$. Let the sheet be cut according to that section $a e g$, or according to some part of it—whether it pleases you to use the part near the vertex, which is $a$, or from the side of one of its ends, which is $g$, or from the side of its other end, which is opposite point $g$ on its latus rectum. Indeed, there is a great difference in the projection of the rays according to the diversity of those parts of the section. Once the sheet $a b d g$ is cut according to the form and figure of section $a e g$, let the edge of the sheet which follows the shape of the section be sharpened with a good sharpening, so that it is able to scrape <note>original: "radere"; the tool acts as a template-scraper to shape the mirror's interior.</note> the entire surface over which it is moved.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a parabolic curve within a rectangular frame. The vertex of the parabola is at point 'a' (top left). The curve extends to point 'g' on the right. The base of the rectangular frame is marked by points 'b' (left corner) and 'd' (right corner), with 'e' marking the center point on the base line. A vertical dashed line connects 'a' to 'e'.</image-desc>

Next, let another sheet be taken of strong steel of some suitable thickness, which is again cut according to the shape of the previously selected part of that section. Let that surface, similar to the parabola, be cut with many closely-spaced grooves in the manner of a file, so that iron can be filed by it. Then, let a metal body be prepared suitable for that figure, the surface of which we propose to hollow out and polish in the manner of a mirror—whether it be according to the shape of the part of the section adjacent to the vertex of the parabola, or the ends. For in these, there is much diversity in the form or figure of the mirror. The form of a concave mirror shaped according to the parts adjacent to the vertex of the section, equally distant on either side from the vertex point, is of a nearly annular <note>ring-shaped</note> figure; and the form of a concave mirror shaped according to the parts adjacent to the ends of the section is of a nearly oval figure—that is, in the manner of the length of an egg. Therefore, let the mirror of whatever figure it ought to be be filed by a file similar to it in shape, in such a way that the surface of the file, which is made for filing, meets the entire surface of that mirror. If, then, the mirror is filed according to an oval shape, let it be fixed in a set place so that its concave surface, as far as the line of its base periphery, is in the periphery of that circle of the base; or if it is of an annular figure, at the periphery of the circle parallel to the base. And in the place of the axis, let the sheet of the file be fixed with its scraping surface smoothed, and let it be moved to hollow out the mirror. Let it be turned <note>original: "tornetur"; this suggests the use of a lathe or a rotating jig to ensure perfectly symmetrical carving.</note> just as other instruments are turned, until the periphery of the sharp sheet meets the entire surface of the mirror and every roughness of it is hollowed out. Let it also be smoothed as much as possible; the surface of that mirror will then have the shape of a parabolic section across its whole self, and reflection will occur from all points of its surface into a single point. Let the ingenious artisan do the same in any other lines, such as in those lines which...

# BOOK TEN OF THE OPTICS 
## BY WITELO, SON OF THE THURINGIANS AND POLES <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1280) was a friar and scholar of mixed German and Polish heritage; his name is often Latinized as Vitello.</note>

Above, we have treated two modes of vision: namely, that which occurs directly through a single transparent <term>medium</term> <note>A substance, like air or water, through which light travels.</note>, and that which occurs through reflection from polished bodies. It now remains for us to pursue the third mode of seeing, which occurs through **refraction**, caused by several transparent bodies placed between the eye and the object being seen; for according to this mode, the action of natural forms and the manner of their action is varied in different ways. For the powers <note>original: "virtutes"; the inherent active energy of light or heat.</note> of natural forms, when gathered through refraction, act more strongly and impress more of the form's action upon susceptible bodies. This is why fire is kindled from the rays of the sun under a spherical transparent body that is denser than air or water, such as under ice or crystal. Generally, however, the gathering of the power of the rays of stars or other forms at or around the same natural point results in a stronger action; whereas the dispersion of the powers of natural forms weakens their natural actions, for a scattered power acts more feebly and to a lesser extent. 

In all these matters, however, as we have said regarding the other modes of seeing above, visual cognition is a **sign**, not a **cause**. For it is not because the sight sees in such a way that it happens thus in the forms of the acting things; rather, it is because natural forms act in such a way that the sight perceives them acting so—except perhaps in certain deceptions which happen to the sight through itself. Every effect <note>original: "passio"; here meaning an impression or physical effect received by a body.</note> occurring to nature or to sight according to the modes of any refraction always happens because of the diversity of the **transparency** <note>original: "diaphanitas"; the quality of allowing light to pass through.</note> of the intermediate bodies between the agent and the recipient, or between the eye and the thing seen. 

The transparent bodies familiar to us are air—which is of a rarer transparency than all other transparent bodies except for the body of the heavens, which is rarer than air, as we shall demonstrate later in our progress. Here, however, and in the whole following treatise, we include **fire** under the name of "air." Although there is a specific formal difference between these two and a differing rarity in the dispositions of their matter, no sensible diversity occurs from this difference in the refraction of forms. This is because the fire that is here below with us exists in thick earthly, watery, or airy matter, and accordingly follows the effects of other bodies; whereas fire in its own sphere <note>According to medieval cosmology, the "sphere of fire" was located just below the moon and above the air.</note> is contiguous with the air according to its formal distinction and is continuous with it in its nature of transparency. It does not possess a distinct surface from the air in which a sensible refraction might possibly occur. For the closer the air is to the heavens, the rarer its transparency becomes; the same is true of fire, such that the bottom of the fire and the top of the air have almost one and the same transparency, in which sensible refraction cannot occur. Thus, the concave surface of the fire is not of a different and sensibly determined transparency from the convex surface of the air; therefore, no refraction occurs between them. And so, in this treatise, we imply fire under the name of air. There is, however, some diversity of refractions in denser and rarer air, whenever that diversity of density becomes sensible: as most often...

Here, Witelo categorizes various transparent media—air, water, and stones—and provides the foundational definitions and postulates for the geometric study of refracted light.</meta>

happens in condensed air near the earth: and especially in evening and morning twilights. But there is another transparent <term>medium</term> <note>A substance through which light travels.</note> different from these, namely water, which also contains within itself a variety of refraction according to its rarity and density, as is found in its kind; yet it is called by a single name. For there are hot sulfurous waters and salty waters, like those of the sea, which are of a thicker transparency than other cold, clear, and fresh waters. Other transparent bodies familiar to us are certain stones, such as crystal, beryl, and similar ones, as well as types of glass. It is also said of certain living bodies that they are transparent, such as those which take on the colors of the bodies they rest upon; we do not pursue the <term>affections</term> <note>The physical properties or "passions" acting upon a body.</note> of these living bodies, however, because they are of irregular shape. Therefore, the surface of the heavens which meets the sight is a concave sphere: which, if it is cut by any flat surface, the common section of those surfaces will be a circular line, the concavity of which is on the side of the eye, as is clear through the 69th theorem of the first book of this work. And the surface of the air which touches it is a convex sphere: which, if it is cut by a flat surface, the common section will be a circular line, the convexity of which is on the side of the heavens. But the surface of water, from the perspective of the sight standing above the water, is a convex sphere: which, if it is cut by a flat surface, the common section will be a circular line, the convexity of which is on the side of that sight. The shapes of glass and transparent stones, however, are round, or flat, or irregular; wherefore, if they are cut by flat surfaces, the common sections in them will be either circles, or straight lines, or irregular lines. According to the diversity of these lines and surfaces, the diversity of the "affections" that meet the eyes is varied.

### DEFINITIONS.

<margin>1.</margin> The **line of incidence** is the name given to the line along which a form is directly spread through the medium of a single transparent body. And the same is called the line of extension of the form. <margin>2.</margin> **Refraction** is the name given to the bending of that same line to contain an angle: as when the lines, through which a single form of a seen thing reaches the eye, do not proceed straight, but are broken at the surface of another transparent body. <margin>3.</margin> The **point of refraction** is the point on the surface of the transparent body from which the refraction of the line of incidence (or the line of extension of the form) toward the eye occurs. <margin>4.</margin> The **line of refraction** is the name given to the line extended from the point of refraction to the center of the eye. <margin>5.</margin> The **perpendicular line** is here called the line which is erected from the point of refraction upon the surface of the body from which the refraction occurs. <margin>6.</margin> The **cathetus of incidence** <note>original: "cathetus incidentiae"; a cathetus is a line falling perpendicularly to a surface.</note> is the name given to the line drawn perpendicularly from the point of the seen object to the surface of the body in which the object is seen, and from which the refraction occurs. <margin>7.</margin> The **surface of refraction** is the name given to the surface in which the lines of incidence and refraction are contained. <margin>8.</margin> The **angle of incidence** is the name given to the smaller angle which the line of incidence makes with the perpendicular line drawn from the point of refraction upon the surface of the body from which that refraction occurs. <margin>9.</margin> The **refracted angle** is the name given to the smaller angle which the refracted line makes with the said perpendicular. <margin>10.</margin> The **angle of refraction** is the name given to the angle which the line of refraction makes with the line of incidence (extended continuously through the transparent body from whose surface the refraction occurs). <margin>11.</margin> To be **seen directly** is defined just as it was in the 1st definition of the 4th book of this work: when the form of the seen object reaches the eye without refraction. <margin>12.</margin> To be **seen obliquely** is said when the form of the seen object reaches the eye through refraction. <margin>13.</margin> A **refracted image** is the name given to the form of the seen object reaching the eye obliquely. <margin>14.</margin> The **place of the refracted image** is the name given to the place where the refracted image appears to the eyes.

### POSTULATES.

We also assume these things: 1. That the light of the Sun is seen in some way in the morning and evening twilights. 2. Also, that the rainbow is seen according to a round shape and various colors.
