# BOOK TEN

# THEOREMS

1. In every plane of refraction, there must necessarily be: the point from which the form is refracted; the point of refraction itself; the center of vision; and the perpendicular line drawn from the point of refraction to the surface where the refraction occurs. From this it is clear that for any single refraction, there is only one unique plane of refraction.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram illustrating the theorem of refraction. A horizontal line segment labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' represents the surface of a second transparent medium. A vertical line 'f-b-g' intersects this surface perpendicularly at point 'b'. A light ray originates from point 'd' in the lower right, passes through point 'b' on the surface, and is refracted towards the center of vision at point 'e' in the upper left. Point 'g' is shown as the straight-line extension of ray 'd-b' below the interface.</image-desc>

Let there be a surface of a second <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphani"</note>—either denser or rarer than the first medium—on which there is a line **a b c**. Let the point from which the <term>form</term> <note>In medieval optics, the "form" or "species" is the visual information traveling from an object to the eye.</note> is refracted be point **d**; let the center of vision be **e**; and let the refraction occur at point **b** on the surface of the second medium. From point **b**, let a perpendicular line **b f** be drawn to the surface **a b c**. I say that points **d**, **e**, **b**, and line **b f** are always in the same plane of refraction. For, as is clear from the definition set forth in the beginning of this book, and by the 46th theorem of Book 2 of this work, the incident radial line (which is **d b**) and the refracted line (which is **b e**) are in the same plane of refraction. Therefore, point **d** (from which the form falls and is refracted), the point of refraction (that is, the point where the bending happens, which is **b**), and the center of vision (which is **e**) are in the same plane <note>Witelo cites Euclid's *Elements*, Book 11, Proposition 1, which states that all parts of a single straight line are in the same plane.</note>. Furthermore, by the second proposition of Book 11 of Euclid, the line **b f**, which is perpendicular to the surface **a b c**, is in the same plane as line **b c**, and therefore also with lines **d b** and **b e**, since line **b f** is perpendicular to line **a b c** and shares the same plane with it. Similarly, if line **d b** is extended beyond point **b** to point **g**, it remains in the same plane. Thus, points **d**, **b**, **e** and line **b f** are in the same plane. For every refraction occurs either toward that perpendicular **b f** or away from it, and always in the same plane in which the incident form was traveling. Since every refraction occurs at every difference of position (for by whatever reason it happens on one side, it would happen by the same reason on any other), the determination of refraction to a specific position is made only by the sight: because in whatever plane the center of the eye is located, it is only in that plane that the refraction is perceived to occur. The proposition is therefore clear. And from this it is evident that since all these points—**d**, **e**, **b** and line **b f**—constitute the plane of refraction, if any of these are missing, the plane of refraction does not exist; and that for a single refraction there is only one unique plane of refraction, because it is possible for all these points to meet in only one such plane and not in several. And this is what was proposed.

2. It is necessary that every plane of refraction be perpendicular to the surface of the body where the refraction occurs (whether that surface is flat, convex, or concave). <note>Citing Alhazen, Book 7, Section 9.</note>

What is proposed here is clear from the previous theorem. Since in every plane of refraction there are necessarily: the point whose form is refracted, the point on the body's surface where refraction occurs, the center of vision, and the perpendicular line drawn from the point of refraction to the surface of that body; therefore, by the 18th proposition of Book 11 of Euclid, it is clear that every plane of refraction is perpendicular to the surface of the body where the refraction occurs. For if that surface is flat, then the proposition is evidently clear by that same 18th proposition of Book 11, as was previously stated. If, however, that surface is a convex or concave sphere, then it is clear by the 72nd theorem of Book 1 of this work, since a perpendicular line drawn from the point of refraction to the surface of the body always passes through the center of that body, and it is perpendicular to the surface tangent to that body at the point of refraction. Therefore, again by the 18th proposition of Book 11, the plane of refraction stands upright upon that tangent surface, and thus also upon the surface of the body itself. The same must also be demonstrated whether the shape of the body from which refraction occurs is cylindrical <note>original: "columnaris"</note>, pyramidal, or of any other shape whatsoever; for the plane of refraction will always be upright upon the surface of the body. And if it happens that the surface of the body where refraction occurs is parallel to the horizon, then the perpendicular line drawn from the point of refraction to the body's surface is also perpendicular to the surface of the horizon (by the 23rd theorem of Book 1); therefore, by the 18th proposition of Book 11, the plane of refraction is perpendicular and stands upright upon the surface of the horizon. Moreover, this is clear through the demonstration made with the instrument which we described in the first theorem of Book 2. For since the incident radial line and the refracted line from the surface of one transparent body to another are always in one flat plane (as shown by theorem 46 of Book 2)—which is the middle circle of those three circles marked on the inner part of the instrument's rim, parallel to the surface of the instrument's inner plate—and that plate's surface is parallel to the back of the instrument, which rests upon the surface of the cubit-long ruler holding the instrument. Thus, the plane of the middle circle is parallel to the surface of the long rectangular ruler placed behind the plate (by theorem 24 of Book 1). But that surface is perpendicular to the surfaces of the sides of the ruler's length, which are standing 
upright <column-break/>
upon the rims of the instrument. Thus, the plane of the middle circle is, by the converse of the 14th proposition of Book 11, perpendicular to the surfaces of the ruler's length, standing 
upright

upright over the edges of the instrument: but those two surfaces of the ruler are parallel to the horizon during the time of the experiment, by means of the instrument being placed in a vessel, as is the custom. Therefore, the surface of the middle circle is perpendicular to the surface of the horizon. And since the surface of the middle circle is the surface of refraction, the proposition is clear. The same can also be shown by an imaginary line drawn from the center of the middle circle to the center of the world <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the "center of the world" is the center of the Earth, which provides the absolute reference for "down" and thus for perpendicularity.</note>. For this line, since it is a radius of the world, is perpendicular to the surface of the water that is in the vessel: moreover, that line lies within the surface of the middle circle, which is the surface of refraction. For when light is refracted from air to water: the line of refraction will fall between the first line through which it is extended in the air—which is its line of incidence—and the perpendicular coming out from the center of the middle circle to the surface of the water: and the center of the light within the water always proceeds from the center of the middle circle. It is clear, therefore, that light which is refracted from air into water is refracted in a surface perpendicular to the surface of the water: and therefore also to the surface of the horizon. The same also happens when refraction occurs from air to glass. It is evident, then, whether the surface of the body from which refraction occurs is flat, convex, or concave, that the surface of refraction is always upright upon it. And this is what was proposed.

<margin>Alhazen Book 7, Chapter 13.</margin>

### *3. When the center of vision is located beyond the medium of a second transparent body: all forms incident obliquely to the surface of the second transparent body, with respect to the eye, meet the eye as refracted; but those incident perpendicularly are seen directly.*

For since light passes through <term>transparent bodies</term> <note>original: "corpora diaphana"</note> upon which it falls, it does so either directly—as when the incident ray is perpendicular to the surface of the body opposite it—or obliquely—as when the ray falls at an angle. From a single point of a luminous body, light is diffused along every line that can be drawn from that point, as is clear from Theorem 20 of Book 2 of this work: and because the <term>form</term> <note>original: "forma." In medieval optics, this refers to the visual information or "species" of an object's color and light.</note> of color always diffuses itself along with the light: it is clear that for any point of any colored or bright luminous body existing in some transparent body, the form of its light and color is extended throughout the nearest transparent body and reaches the surface of the transparent body opposite it. 

And if there should be another transparent body touching that second transparent body, which is of a different transparency <note>Meaning a different optical density or refractive index.</note> from the first: then the diffused form penetrates it, and all the radial lines by which the light or color falls obliquely on those transparent bodies will be refracted, except for the line incident perpendicularly. For that line alone is extended in a straight path into the transparent body nearest to it, and into the other transparent body touching that nearest transparent body: provided that it falls perpendicularly upon both. And if by chance any of the radial lines should fall perpendicularly upon a point of a surface continuous with the surface of the nearest transparent body, yet there is no transparent body for that second surface: or if there is a transparent body, its surface is not parallel to the surface of the prior transparent body: then from the point of incidence of the radial line upon the surface of the second body, another perpendicular can be drawn. Therefore, that form which fell upon the surface of the prior body according to the perpendicular will then be displaced: since it is impossible for two perpendicular lines to be drawn from one point to one surface, by Proposition 13 of Book 11 <note>Another reference to Euclid's *Elements* regarding the uniqueness of a perpendicular line.</note>. 

All forms of that point, therefore, passing into the transparent body touching the body nearest to that point, will be refracted. And since light and color are extended from every point of any luminous or colored body, penetrating the whole transparent body placed before it, and are refracted from the surface of another body of different transparency succeeding it (by Theorem 47 of Book 2 of this work): it is clear that the form of light and color will be one continuous, joined form: and it is refracted as a whole, continuous and joined, the surface of the transparent body being continuous; and thus the refracted form will be continuous. If, therefore, a body of denser transparency than the first transparent medium should meet that form: then the continuous form will reach that body more gathered and united. Likewise, if a rarer transparent body is met: then every point of the transparent body through which the form of the point (which is in the first luminous or colored body) is extended, will transmit the form of light and color to any point of that second or third transparent body along every straight line that can be extended from that point. 

If, therefore, one were to imagine rectilinear <term>pyramids</term> <note>original: "pyramides." These are the "visual cones" or "cones of light" that have their base at the object and their apex at the eye.</note> coming out from every point of the air reaching the surface of the body of another transparency: and if on the surface of this second transparent body the obliquely incident lines are imagined to be refracted (with the perpendicular line, which is the axis of that imagined pyramid, passing through without refraction), then a single continuous body is still produced in refraction, just as the form of the body incident on the surface of that second transparent body is one. If, therefore, in the place of the imagined pyramid there is established in reality a sensible pyramid in the air, whose body is densely colored or luminous: the light or color of that pyramid will be mixed with the light or color of the body from which refraction occurs. Their multiplication will occur through every straight line that can be extended from that point which it strikes: and the form of the point incident on any point of the dense body will be extended through any of the refracted lines to that point of the body in which refraction occurs, corresponding to it. 

And if the eye is on the other side of that transparent medium: then those forms reach the eye: but the perpendicular (because it is not refracted) reaches the center of the eye perpendicularly: and the forms incident along oblique lines reach the eye refracted and obliquely. Since, therefore, the lines along which the form is refracted diffuse themselves in the air through every intervening body when they are joined at a single point of the air—because there is much intersection of them due to the equal diffusion of those forms to every difference of position—then if the center of vision is placed at that point, the vision will perceive that object according to refraction (except for the single point incident perpendicularly).

*4. Every form seen through refraction—if the refraction occurs from a second transparent medium denser than the first toward the eye—appears to be toward the side of the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction to the surface where the refraction occurs. If, however, it occurs from a rarer transparent medium, it appears to be toward the side opposite that perpendicular. Alhazen <note>original: "Alhazen 14 n 7." Witelo is referencing the "Optics" (De Aspectibus) of the 11th-century polymath Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen.</note> Book 4, Number 7.*

What is proposed here can be demonstrated with an instrument, so that the proof is expressed sensibly with the help of the device. Therefore, let the aforementioned instrument be taken, which we used in the preceding parts: whose diameter, which we marked there with the letters **f, g**, we now call **b q g**, so that point **q** is the center of the plate of the instrument’s base. This instrument is placed in a vessel situated parallel to the surface of the horizon, and water is poured in up to the center of the plate, which is **q**: let the apertures of the instrument also be blocked with wax or in some other way, so that a small part remains of the apertures around their middle, which should be equal in both apertures: and this can be measured by a small cylinder of equal size inserted into those apertures. Then the instrument is moved until the diameter **b q g** is perpendicular to the surface of the water. Let a thin white stylus <note>A pointer or rod used to mark positions in the water.</note> also be placed into the vessel, so that its end falls on point **z**, which is the end of the diameter of the middle circle, which is **k f z**: and let one eye be placed over the upper aperture at point **k**, and the other be closed: for then the end of the stylus will be seen according to the straightness of the perpendicular emerging from the end of the stylus to the surface of the water: for the center of sight and the end of the stylus are then on the line **k f z** perpendicular to the surface of the water, along which the vision occurs. For the line **k f z** is perpendicular to the surface of the water by Book 11, Proposition 8 <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements.</note>: because it is parallel to the line **b q g**, which by hypothesis is perpendicular to that same surface of the water.

Then the instrument is tilted until the line **b q g** is oblique to the surface of the water: and let the eye be placed over the upper aperture: and the end of the stylus will not be seen. Therefore, move the end of the stylus along the circumference of the middle circle little by little toward the side opposite the eye, until that end is seen, and let it be fixed at that point of the middle circle where it appears. If, then, some small dense body is placed on the surface of the water at the center of the middle circle, which is **f**: then that end of the stylus will not be seen: but when that small body is removed, the end of the stylus will be seen. If the distance of the end of the stylus from point **z** is considered in the number of degrees of the middle circle, a sensible distance will be found. But the point **z**, which is the end of the diameter of the middle circle passing through the center of the two apertures, can be found in this way:

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an optical instrument used for measuring refraction. It consists of a large circle with several intersecting lines and labeled points. namely, that the wider end of a thin ruler is placed over the center of the plate, and its midline is extended according to the diameter of the plate: for then the sharp point of the ruler falls upon point **z**, as was previously set forth in the second proposition of this book. If, having taken a glass <note>original: "vitrum"</note> that is part of some sphere, as was assumed in some of those propositions—a glass of which one surface is flat and the other a convex sphere—and that glass is applied to the plate so that its flat surface is on the side of the apertures, and the line **q** (which is the <term>common difference<gloss>the line of intersection where two surfaces meet</gloss></term> of its flat surfaces) is upon the line **o d**, cutting the radius **b q** of the plate perpendicularly: thus the diameter **k f z** will be perpendicular to the flat surfaces of the glass and to the convex ones. 

Next, the instrument is placed in water, and the end of the stylus is placed on point **z**, and the center of sight on the upper aperture: and the end of the stylus will be seen, which could not be seen at any other point of the middle circle. From this it is clear that when the end of the stylus is on a line perpendicular to the surface of the body from which refraction occurs (as the line **k f z** is now perpendicular to the surface of the glass), its form is seen not through refraction, but directly. From this it is clear that a form falling perpendicularly is not refracted. 

But if the convex part of the glass is placed on the side of the second apertures, and the common difference of the two flat surfaces of the glass is placed on the first position, namely the line **o d**: since then also the line **k f z** is perpendicular to both surfaces of the glass: the end of the stylus at point **z** will be seen then, as before. But if, with the glass removed from the surface of the instrument's plate at the center of the plate, which is **q**, a radius **q r** is drawn on the surface of the plate, forming an obtuse angle with the radius **b q**: then a radius **q u** is drawn, forming a right angle with line **q r**: and it is extended to the other edge of the instrument: therefore the angle **b q u** will be acute, and the radius **b q** will be oblique to the line **q u**. 

Then the line that is the common difference of the flat surfaces of the glass is placed over the line **q u**, and let the flat surface of the glass be on the side of the apertures, and let the middle of the common difference of the flat surfaces of that glass be over the center **q**. Thus the center of the glass will then be over the center of the middle circle, as has been shown before in other places, and the line **k f** passes through the center of the glass and is oblique to its flat surface: since the diameter **b q**, being parallel to that line which is **k f**, falls obliquely upon the line **q u**: and since the line **k f** passes through the center of the glass: it is clear that it is perpendicular to the convex surface of the glass. Then from point **r** a perpendicular is drawn to the line **q r**...

...perpendicular to the edge of the instrument as far as the circumference of the middle circle, which we shall call **f e**. Let both of these lines, **q r** and **f e**, be made black so that they may be more easily observed by the eye. Now, imagine a line **e f** being drawn; according to Theorem 72 of the first book of this work <note>Witelo frequently cross-references his first book, which contains the geometric foundations for his optical theorems.</note>, this line will be perpendicular to the convex surface of the glass because it passes through its center. It is also perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass because it is equidistant to line **q r**, which is itself perpendicular to line **q u**, upon which the common section of the flat surfaces of the glass is placed. Therefore, point **e** is a point on the middle circle where the perpendicular—extending from the center of the glass to its flat surface—falls.

Let the instrument, thus arranged, be placed in the vessel, and let the tip of the white stylus be placed, as before, at point **z**. If the eye is placed over the upper aperture at point **k**, the tip of the stylus will not be seen. Now, if the stylus is moved along the circumference of the middle circle away from point **e**, the tip will still not be visible. However, if it is moved gradually toward point **e**, the tip of the stylus will become visible. If, at that moment, point **f** (which is the center of the middle circle) is covered by some small object, the tip of the stylus will disappear; but when that object is removed, the tip of the stylus will be seen again.

From this, it is clear that the perception of the form of the stylus tip (which we call **a**) occurs according to a refraction made at the center of the glass. The refracted form lies in the plane of the middle circle, which is perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass. The location of the form of the stylus tip **a** will be found between points **e** and **z**. Since the refraction occurs at the center of the glass, the line drawn from the center of the glass to the edge of the glass—which lies between lines **f z** and **f e**, and which we call **a f**—is clearly perpendicular to the convex surface of the glass. Its form reaches the eye through line **k f**, passing through the centers of both apertures. This line is further from the perpendicular drawn to the flat surface of the glass (which is line **f e**, equidistant to line **q r**) than the line along which the form of point **a** falls upon the glass.

Thus, when the form of point **a** falls upon the glass along line **a f**, it passes through the entire body of the glass perpendicularly. Because line **q f** passes through the center of the glass, it is perpendicular to the surface of the glass. When it has passed through the body of the glass and reaches the air (a medium of rarer transparency than the body of the glass) and reaches the center of the eye, it is evident that it has been refracted from its original path along line **a f** and has reached the path of line **z f k**. Since line **z f** is further from the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction to the flat surface of the glass (line **e f**) than line **a f** is—because point **a** falls on the surface of the middle circle between points **e** and **z**—it is clear that this refraction occurs toward the side opposite the perpendicular **e f**, which is drawn from the point of refraction to the surface of the air touching the flat surface of the glass. Indeed, line **f z**, passing through the centers of both apertures, is further from that perpendicular **e f** than the line extending from the tip of the stylus to the center of the glass (**a f**). If line **a f** were extended continuously and directly, it would fall between the extended perpendicular **e f** and line **f k**. Therefore, because it reaches point **k** (where it is seen), it is clear that refraction occurs toward the side opposite the perpendicular **f e**.

And since this form is refracted from glass into air, which is thinner than glass, it is clear that refraction occurs in a similar way from water into air, since air is also thinner than water. But if the convex side of the glass is placed on the side of the apertures, and the common boundary of its flat surfaces is placed on line **q u**, and the middle point of that common boundary is placed over the center of the plate (which is **q**), it is clear that line **k f** will be slanted relative to the flat surface of the glass and perpendicular to its convex surface. Line **r q** will be perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass because it is perpendicular to line **u q**. Line **e f** will be perpendicular to the convex surface of the glass (by Theorem 72 of Book 1) and also to its flat surface (by Proposition 8 of Book 11 <note>This refers to Euclid's Elements, Book 11, which deals with solid geometry.</note>) because lines **e f** and **r q** are equidistant.

Let the tip of the white stylus, **a**, be placed at point **z** as before, and let the eye be placed over the upper aperture of the instrument at point **k**; the tip of the stylus **a** will not be seen. If the stylus is moved toward point **e** along the circumference of the middle circle, the tip will still not be seen. However, if it is moved in the opposite direction from point **e**, the tip of the stylus will then be seen. Line **f z** will then fall between the straight line **a f** (extending from the stylus tip to the center of the glass, along which the form of point **a** is extended) and the perpendicular **f e**. The form of point **a** at the stylus tip will be refracted from the center of the glass to the eye along line **f k** passing through the centers of both apertures, because line **a f** strikes the flat surface of the glass (where refraction occurs) at an angle. That refraction will also be toward the side of the perpendicular line **f e** extending from the place of refraction to the flat surface of the glass. This form exits from the air and is refracted into the glass, which is denser <term>grossius (denser): in medieval optics, "grossness" referred to the physical or optical density of a medium.</term> than air.

Thus, forms that are refracted from a denser body to a rarer one decline toward the side opposite the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction to the surface of the transparent body where the refraction occurs. Conversely, forms refracted from a rarer body to a denser one decline toward the side where the perpendicular is drawn. And this is what was proposed.

### 5. To demonstrate experimentally the quantities of the angles of refraction from air to water. *Alhazen 10 n 7.* <note>original: "Alhazen 10 n 7." Referring to the Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, Book 7, though the numbering in medieval Latin translations often varied.</note>

The difference in the angles of refraction depends on the size of the angles of incidence contained between the line of incidence (or the extension of the ray in the first medium) and the perpendicular extending from the point of refraction to the surface of the second medium. For the angles of refraction increase and decrease according to the arrangement of those angles of incidence in different media and positions. And because refraction from a rarer transparent body to a denser body occurs toward the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction to the surface of the second body, and from a denser transparent body to a rarer one, refraction occurs toward the side...

### 6. To demonstrate experimentally the sizes of the angles of refraction from air or water to flat or convex glass, and vice versa. Alhazen [Book 7], [Proposition] 11. <note>The reference to Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham) acknowledges the source of these experimental methods in the "Perspectiva" or "Kitab al-Manazir."</note>

Let the arc of the middle circle of the instrument be divided in the same manner as in the previous [proposition]: let arc **k n** be 10 parts, and let line **n l** be drawn perpendicular to the surface of the plate; let line **l q** also be joined. Let a piece of glass shaped into a cube be placed upon the surface of the plate itself, so that the common section of the two flat surfaces—which is a straight line (as is clear from Book 11, Proposition 3 of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid's geometry.</note>)—is placed upon line **l q** in such a way that its midpoint is placed upon the line marked on the surface of the plate perpendicular to line **l q**. This line is parallel to line **s f** drawn on the surface of the middle circle. Let the midpoint of that line of glass be above point **q**, the center of the plate. Let the flat surface of the glass be positioned on the side of the apertures, and let the glass be fitted well to the plate. Let the instrument, placed in a vessel, be moved until light passes through both apertures; let a mark be made upon the center of the light. Let the sizes of the angles of refraction from air to glass be considered by the sizes of the arcs, as in the preceding [proposition]. 

But if anyone wishes to investigate the angles of refraction from glass to air or water, let him take a piece of glass that is part of a sphere—as we ourselves used above in the second proposition of this science <note>referring to Book 2</note> and in the fourth theorem of this [book]—and let the convex side of the glass be placed on the side of the centers of the two apertures. Let the midpoint of the line, which is the common boundary of the flat surfaces, be placed over the center of the plate, so that the common boundary lies upon line **l q**. Then the light which passes through the centers of the two apertures arrives directly at the center of the glass and is refracted there from glass to air. Afterward, let the arcs be divided successively as in the previous [proposition], and let the position of the glass be changed so that the common section of the flat surfaces of the glass lies upon line **p q**. Again, let the midpoint of that line of glass be over point **q**, the center of the plate. 

After making further divisions of the middle circle and drawing lines as before, and moving the glass according to them, the specific angles of refraction will be obtained, as well as their proportion to the angle of incidence. The angle of incidence is contained by the diameter passing through the centers of the apertures and the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction to the flat surface touching the convex surface of the glass. In these arrangements of the glass relative to the plate of the instrument, the center of the glass sphere will always be at point **f**. By the 72nd theorem of the first book, line **s f** will be similar to it—perpendicular to the convex surface of the glass and to its flat surface, from some point of which refraction occurs. This is because any of those lines is perpendicular to the lines parallel to lines **l q** and **p q**, and to any others like them. 

As before, by repeating the operation with the end of the rod, the whole mode of refraction will be known, as well as the angles of refraction from the glass to the center of sight located at point **k**, the center of the upper aperture. In these two positions, whether the refraction is from air to glass or from glass to air, the sizes of the angles of refraction from air to glass and from glass to air will always be found equal, provided that the angle formed by the line of light and the perpendicular when passing from air to glass is equal to the angle formed when refracting from glass to air, as is clear to one working with the instrument.

proceeding from the center of the middle circle, which is **f**, above the center of the plate, which is **q**: but line **o q** is equal to the radius <note>original: "semidiametro"</note> of the base of the column by hypothesis. Therefore, by Proposition 33 of Book 1 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>, the line which proceeds from the center of the middle circle (**f**) to the center of the semicircle—which is formed on the surface of the concave column parallel to the base—is equal to the radius of the base of the concavity of the concave column. Thus, the center of the middle circle, **f**, is on the circumference of the semicircle made in the glass column. Center **f** is therefore in the concave surface of the column. And because the flat end of the glass is placed over the perpendicular line drawn from point **o** above the diameter of the plate **b q**, it is clear that the diameter of the plate, **q b**, is perpendicular to the flat surface of the glass, because the flat surfaces are erected perpendicularly to one another.

Therefore, line **k f z**, passing through the centers of both holes, will be perpendicular to the flat surface on the convex side of the glass, according to Proposition 8 of Book 11 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. This is because that line **k f z** is parallel to the diameter of the plate **b q g**, which is perpendicular to that surface, as is clear from what was said before; and this flat surface of the glass is on the side of the holes. In this position, therefore, the light which extends through the line passing through the centers of the two holes extends in a straight line through the body of the glass until it reaches the concavity of the glass; it is then refracted at the concave surface of the glass. For since it does not pass through the center of the circle located in the concave surface of the glass, it is clear by Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work that it is not perpendicular to the concave surface of the glass. It will therefore be refracted at the concave surface of the glass. The common section of that line and the concavity of the glass is the center of the middle circle; and at this point, the refraction from air to glass occurs.

Thus, the arc falling between the center of the light and point **z** (which is the end of the diameter passing through the centers of both holes) is subtended by the angle of refraction. Similarly, it is also clear in the refraction of any other arcs from point **k**; and the quantity of all angles of refraction from the concave surface of the glass can be shown. If the glass is so arranged that the common section of its flat surfaces is placed upon line **o e**, and the convexity of the glass faces the centers of the holes: then because the line **k f z** passing through the glass reaches the concavity of the glass unrefracted (since it is perpendicular to its flat surface, but oblique to its concave surface, and therefore also to the convex surface of the air touching the glass), it will be refracted from the concave surface of the glass. This refraction is from the glass concavity to the air. The angles formed from air to glass in the concavity of the glass are the same as these, since the angles of refraction from glass to air and from air to glass are always the same, because the angle contained by the line along which the light first extends and the perpendicular proceeding from the place of refraction is the same angle. In the same way, the angles of refraction from water to glass and from glass to water can be known on the concave surface of the glass, or on any other surface whatsoever. If the tip of a stylus is moved from point **z** on the periphery of the middle circle as before, then once the position of the glass is arranged according to the requirements of that refraction, the knowledge of the angles of this refraction will be revealed to the sight as before. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 8. The angles of all refractions are revealed by tables. *Alhazen, Book 7, Section 12.*

Having taken measurements with instruments as accurately as we could, regarding the angles of all refractions between any known transparent media <note>original: "diaphano"</note> (such as from air to water and glass, and from water to glass; and conversely from water and glass to air, and from glass to water), we found that the angles of refraction are always the same from any rare transparent medium to a medium denser than it, and from that same dense medium to the same rare one. According to this, we have made these tables, the form of which follows. We first set forth the angles of incidence.

# BOOK TEN

first: then we add other angles according to the patterns of their circles, which we place at the heads of their lines. Therefore, according to these tables found experimentally through the aforementioned instrument, a diligent investigator can know all the angles of refraction from media of any different transparency <note>original: "diaphanitatis"</note>. And it is clear from them that the angles of incidence of the form of the same point closer to the ray—incident perpendicularly from the point of the thing seen to the surface of the transparent body (from which the refraction occurs)—are smaller; and those further from it are larger. For when a larger angle is taken from its right angle, that which remains becomes smaller than another angle when a smaller angle is taken from a right angle.

In the same transparent medium that is denser than the first, the angle of refraction from a larger angle of incidence will be larger than the angle of refraction from a smaller angle of incidence. Furthermore, the excess of the larger angle of refraction over the smaller angle of refraction will be less than the excess of the larger angle of incidence over the smaller. And the ratio <note>original: "proportio"</note> of the angle of refraction from a larger angle of incidence to that larger angle will be greater than the ratio of the angle of refraction from a smaller angle of incidence to that smaller one. And the "refracted angle"—namely, that which the larger angle of incidence adds over its angle of refraction <note>This refers to the angle of deviation, or the amount the light is bent from its original straight path.</note>—is larger than the "refracted angle" which the smaller angle of incidence adds over its angle of refraction.

Therefore, in a medium of a second transparent body denser than the first, the angle of refraction <note>the angle relative to the normal</note> will always be smaller than the angle of incidence; and the ratio of these refracted angles to equal angles of incidence varies according to the difference in density of those media. For when refraction occurs from the same air into water and into glass at an equal angle of incidence, the refracted angles become more acute in glass than in water; and thus the angles vary according to the difference in transparency.

If, however, the medium of the second transparent body is rarer <note>less dense</note>: then the angle of refraction will always be larger than the angle of incidence. The relationship of these angles to other angles will be the reverse of the aforementioned angles, as if the aforementioned tables were arranged in reverse order. And the ratio of these refracted angles and of the refraction—according to the greater or lesser rarity of the transparency of the second medium relative to the same angle of incidence—varies. For when refraction occurs from glass into water or into air: then the angles which are formed in air are larger than the angles formed in water; and according to this, the ratio of the angles of refraction to the angles of incidence varies. These, therefore, are the things that happen to lights and colors, and universally to all forms in their diffusion through transparent bodies, and in the refraction that happens in all of them, both in themselves and in respect to the sight. Thus, what was sought is clear.

<margin>9. With the center of vision and the point of the object seen through refraction in different transparent media swapping their proper locations, the same line swaps the names of incidence and refraction. Alhazen, Book 7, Proposition 34.</margin>

It has already become sufficiently clear from the preceding propositions of this tenth treatise that forms seen through refraction extend directly along a straight line until they reach the surface of the other transparent body in which the eye is located; then they are refracted in that other transparent body along another straight line which forms an angle with the line of incidence. Therefore, let the center of vision be **a**, and the point of the object seen be **b**. Let the surface of the body in which point **b** is located be surface **c d e**, and let the form of point **b** be refracted to the eye existing

at point **a** from the surface of the body **c d e** at point **d**. Let the line of incidence be **b d**, and the line of refraction be **d a**. I say that if the center of vision and the point of the object swap locations, so that the center of vision is placed at point **b** and the point of the object at point **a**, then refraction will still occur at the same point of the body, which is **d**. Line **a d** will then be the line of incidence, and line **d b** will be the line of refraction; and thus only the names of the lines are swapped, while the lines themselves and the angle remain the same.

This, moreover, is clear through experience. For when someone existing in the air looks at a body contained within another body that is transparent—differing in its transparency from the transparency of the air—then the sight will perceive all things that are beyond that body, whatever is opposed to the sight. And if they cover one of their eyes and look with the remaining one, they will see those same things as before, whether

beyond that transparent body <note>original: "corpus diaphanum"</note> which is positioned opposite the sight at that time; and that refraction would happen in the same way. The same is true for any point near that point where the center of vision is located. For if the center of vision remains at the same point but the eye moves to any different position, it will perceive all those visible things. Therefore, when the **form** <note>In medieval optics, the "form" or "species" refers to the visual information or light rays carrying the appearance of an object.</note> of any point of any visible thing is beyond some transparent body, it extends to the surface of the transparent body beyond which it is located, and it is refracted toward the whole of that which is opposite it in the air or another transparent medium.

That form will exist at every point of that second transparent body. Because of this, the form of the entire visible object is joined at every point of the air or other transparent body. Indeed, the form of any point of a visible object spreads itself along a straight line to every single point of the transparent body. Hence, if there were as many centers of vision in the air as there are points of air, every one of those eyes would see the total form of the visible object which is under the other transparent medium. For the form of the visible thing will always be at the point where the center of vision is located. Thus, even if the sight moves from place to place over the same transparent medium, it always sees the same form as long as that form can reach the sight along straight lines.

Similarly, many observers perceive one thing in the sky or in the water at one and the same time. Therefore, the form of any point of a visible thing extends to every point of the transparent body in which that visible thing exists; and the forms of all points of a visible thing are gathered at every point of any transparent body in which it exists, and at every point of a transparent body different from the one in which the visible thing exists. For between any point of the air and any visible thing existing in some transparent body different from air, a **pyramid** <note>The "visual pyramid" or cone of light, where the base is the object and the vertex is the eye.</note> is formed, the vertex of which is at some point in the air and the base is on the surface of the visible object. There are as many pyramids as there are points in the air or other transparent medium in which the diffusion of forms occurs.

Because the whole medium is full of the forms of things, and the angles of refraction produced from air to water are the same as the angles of refraction produced from water to air (as is clear from the previously mentioned tables), these same angles are always contained by the same lines. It is clear, therefore, that if the location of the center of vision and the point of the visible thing are swapped from one transparent medium to another, there is always a universal diffusion of forms. However, every form is not perceived by every sight at every point, but only at that point from which the refracted line is directed to that sight. It is clear, then, that those lines remain the same in substance, with only the names being swapped from one side to the other: so that what was previously the line of incidence or extension of the form itself later becomes the line of refraction, and vice versa. The proposition is therefore proven.

### **10. *Every refraction represents the form of light and color, which are in the thing seen, more weakly to the sight.***

<margin>Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham</note> Book 3, Chapter 8, Number 7.</margin>
This is clear through experience. For when something is seen in the middle of a second transparent medium—for example, through air into water—and the sight is positioned very obliquely <note>At a sharp angle.</note> from the perpendicular lines coming from the points of the visible object to the surface of the water, and then the sight is moved until it is placed on some perpendicular line coming from the visible object to the surface of the water, then the light and color of the visible thing become more manifest than they were when they were viewed obliquely.

For then, the figure coming to the sight along oblique lines is refracted and much distorted; however, on the perpendicular line, the whole form comes out straight, and certain parts of it arrive obliquely or nearly straight, depending on whether they are more or less distant from the perpendicular. It is clear from this that refraction weakens the light and colors in refracted forms, which the forms of visible things carry with them to the sight through any transparent body. There is no other difference in the existence of those forms, nor for the sight, except for the obliquity inducing refraction and the perpendicularity assisting the directness of vision; according to these, the sight judges the forms of light and color to be weak or strong. 

Thus, in bodies seen through a second transparent medium, a deception occurs because of refraction which would not happen if they were seen directly. This is because, as is clear from Theorem 33 of Book 4 of this work, every line or surface of a visible thing positioned directly opposite the eyes is seen more perfectly than one that is slanted; and the imperfection of vision corresponds to the amount of slanting. The proposition is therefore proven.

### **11. *The refracted image of a visible thing never appears to the sight in the actual location of the thing seen, but always outside its place.***

<margin>Euclid, 7th hypothesis of Catoptrics. Alhazen Book 1, Chapter 7, Number 17.</margin>
What is proposed here is clear through both reason and experience. The reason is this: the form perceived by the sight in a transparent body other than air is not the visible thing itself, since the sight does not perceive the thing then in its true form or shape, but in other dispositions and in another manner. For it perceives the refracted image in its opposite position, even though the thing is not directly opposite the sight. And because it perceives the thing through refraction—because the sight is slanted from the perpendicular lines coming from the visible thing to the surface of the transparent body—it therefore perceives it as being outside its place, not in its place.

The same is also clear through experience. Let a vessel be taken having rims standing upright above its base; in the middle of the bottom of the vessel, let a silver **denarius** <note>A common Roman/medieval silver coin.</note> be placed. Let the experimenter move away until he can see that coin at the bottom of the vessel; then let him move further away little by little until he can no longer see it. At the very moment it is hidden, let him stand in his place with his sight unmoved, and let him order water to be poured into the vessel so that the coin does not change its position. He will then see the coin in that opposite position, even though it is not truly in that opposite position. From this, it is clear that the form which the experimenter sees in the water is not in the place of the thing seen. For if the form...

### *12. Every form of a point seen through refraction is perceived along the straightness of the line through which the form is extended from the point of refraction to the eye. Alhazen 19 n 7.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a vertical line representing a visual path. The line contains three labeled points: 'd' at the top (the center of vision), 'b' in the middle (the point of refraction on a surface), and 'a' at the bottom (the object point). A horizontal line passes through point 'b' representing the surface of the medium.</image-desc>

For let there be a point seen through refraction, which is **a**: let its **form** <note>In medieval science, the "form" (forma) or "species" is the visual information or light that travels from an object to the eye.</note> be refracted to the eye from some point of the surface of another **transparent body** <note>original: "corporis alterius diaphani"</note>, which is **b**: and let the center of vision be **d**: I say that the form of point **a** is perceived by the eye according to the straightness of line **d b**. This, moreover, must be demonstrated by means of an instrument. Therefore, let the first instrument be taken, and let it be placed in a vessel filled with water, as before: and let some object to be seen through refraction be marked on the rim <note>original: "ora"</note> of the instrument opposite the eye: and let the experimenter look through both holes, so that he sees it through refraction: then let the second hole of the instrument be closed: and then the thing seen will not be perceived: and if the first hole is closed, similarly nothing will be seen: because the straight line imaginarily going out from the center of vision to the place of refraction has been cut off. For the form of the point seen through refraction is extended in the transparent body in which the object is located, and it is refracted in the transparent body which is between it and the center of vision, and it reaches the eye through a straight line going out from the center of vision to the point of refraction: and the eye perceives nothing except along the straightness of the **radial lines** <note>original: "linearum radialium"</note>, through which the visible form moves to the eye. And if the operation is performed by placing some glass between the eye and the thing seen, as above: by working in entirely the same way, the same will be evident. And this is what was proposed. For the eye perceives nothing except along the straightness of the radial lines: for it is not affected except by things positioned opposite to it, whose forms multiply themselves toward the eye according to straight lines, as was evident from theorem 2 of Book 3 of this work, and through many similar points. Therefore, what was proposed is clear.

### *13. Every form seen through refraction is perceived on the perpendicular line drawn from the point of the thing seen to the surface of the body from which the refraction occurs. Alhazen 19 n 7.*

What is proposed here is clear for this reason: because light is extended in a transparent body with the swiftest passage, understanding that speed in the manner previously explained: and it has already been made clear from those things which were said in theorem 47 of Book 2 of this work, that the passage of light in a transparent body along a line sloping <note>original: "decliuem"</note> over the surface of that body is composed of motion along a perpendicular line, going out from the point from which the light is extended over the surface of that transparent body, and of motion along a line which is perpendicular to this perpendicular line. But the form, which is extended from the point of the thing seen through refraction to the point of refraction itself—which is the form of the light existing in the point of the thing seen mixed with the form of the color—is always extended along a line sloping over the surface of the transparent body. This form, therefore, is extended to the place of its refraction by a motion composed of motion along the perpendicular, going out from the point seen itself over the surface of the transparent body, and of motion along a line which is perpendicular to this perpendicular. Therefore, the motion of the form, which moves toward the eye, is either along the perpendicular drawn from that point whose form it is over the surface of the transparent body—although afterwards it was moved away from this perpendicular by another motion—or its motion is along the perpendicular drawn over that prior perpendicular, and it was moved after its motion over the first perpendicular drawn from the point of the thing whose form is moved over the surface of the transparent body: and let this translation be because of the composition of the two aforementioned motions. Therefore, the form exiting from the place of refraction reaches the eye itself through the motion of the form which moves along the perpendicular drawn from the point of the thing seen over the surface of the transparent body: then it was moved away from this perpendicular through motion along the straightness of the line through which the form [reaches] the eye. It is also clear what was proposed through this: because if the point of the surface of the transparent body, which the perpendicular drawn from the point of the thing seen happens to strike, is hidden from the eye—for instance, because of the interposition of some opaque body—the vision of that point of the thing seen will not occur. Therefore, the form of the thing seen is perceived on the perpendicular drawn from the point of the thing seen over the surface of the body from which the refraction occurs. Thus the proposition is clear, which we shall also study to declare more clearly later by means of an instrument.

### *14. Of all the forms of the points of a thing seen that are more distant from the perpendicular line drawn from the center of vision to the surface of the transparent body from which the refraction occurs, the refraction is greater than that of points less distant from it.*

Let the center of vision be **a**: and let the line seen through refraction be **b c d e**: and let the common section of the surface of refraction and the body from whose surface refraction occurs be line **f g h i**: and let the perpendicular drawn from the center of vision over the surface of that body be line **a f**: which strikes point **b** of the thing seen: and let it be **a f b**:

It begins an analysis of how the angle of refraction increases as an object moves further from the central visual axis.</summary>

It establishes that the degree of refraction increases as an object moves further from the perpendicular line of sight and begins to define the "locus" or perceived location of a refracted image.</meta>

# WITELO'S OPTICS

...and let point **d** be more distant from point **b** and the perpendicular **a f b** than point **c**, and let point **e** be more distant than point **d**. I say that the refraction of point **e** will be greater than that of point **d**, and the refraction of point **d** will be greater than that of point **c**. For since the **form** <note>The "form" (forma) refers to the visual species or light rays emanating from an object.</note> of point **a** is on the perpendicular line itself, it is clear from the 2nd theorem of this book that it is not refracted. However, it is clear from the 4th theorem of this book that the forms of the other points, which are **c**, **d**, and **e**, are refracted. And since, as is clear through the 49th theorem of the 2nd book of this work, no refraction changes the arrangement of the parts of a refracted form, but only increases or diminishes its shape, it is clear that of necessity the diversity of the forms of the points of the thing seen is refracted from different points of the surface of that thing seen. Thus, the form of a point more remote from the eye is refracted from a point on the surface more remote from the center of vision; otherwise, there would be a displacement of the seen forms through refraction.

Therefore, let it be that the form of point **c** is refracted from point **g**, the form of point **d** from point **h**, and the form of point **e** from point **i**. Let line **g l** be drawn from point **g**, line **h m** from point **h**, and line **i n** from point **i**, which are **perpendicular** <note>original: "perpendiculares"</note> to the surface of the **transparent body** <note>original: "corporis diaphani"</note> according to Proposition 12 of Book 11 <note>of Euclid's Elements</note>. Let the lines of incidence of the forms be extended beyond the surface of the body: line **c g** to point **o**, line **d h** to point **p**, and line **e i** to point **q**. Let the refracted lines be joined from points **g**, **h**, and **i** to the eye, which are **g a**, **h a**, and **i a**. Since, therefore, in triangle **a f i**, lines **a g** and **a h** are drawn, it is clear by Proposition 21 of Book 1 that angle **a g f** is greater than angle **a h f**. Because angles **l g f** and **m h f** are right angles and equal, it remains that angle **a g l** is smaller than angle **a h m**. But angles **o g l** and **p h m** are equal; for any line of incidence contains equal angles with its perpendicular because of the equal distance of points **b**, **c**, **d**, and **e** from one another and from the transparent surface where refraction occurs. Therefore, angle **p h a** is greater than angle **o g a**, and angle **q i a** is greater than angle **p h a**. Moreover, the disposition of the **medium** <note>The substance, such as water or air, through which light travels.</note> in which the refraction of the forms of points **c** and **d** occurs from points **g** and **h** is the same. It is therefore clear that a greater refraction occurs from point **h**, which is more remote from the eye **a**, than from point **g**, which is closer to the eye than point **h**. Similarly, it is clear in the same way regarding point **i** with respect to point **h**; for according to the premises, angle **a i q** is greater than angle **a h p**. Therefore, the refraction of point **i** is greater than that of point **h**, and thus also greater than that of point **g**. It is therefore clear universally what was proposed. For in all points and surfaces from which refraction occurs, the demonstration is the same.

> ### *15. The location of the refracted image of any point of an object seen through refraction lies at the intersection of the line of refraction (through which the form reaches the eye) and the cathetus of incidence (projected from that point of the object perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body touching the eye). From this it is clear that the location of the image of a point existing in a second transparent medium denser than the first appears closer to the eye; but in a rarer medium, it is further away. Alhazen 18 n 7.*

I say that the location of the refracted image is at the point which is the intersection of the perpendicular line **a c** and the extension of line **d b**. This is indeed clear. For since, by the 12th theorem of this book, the form of the perpendicular—which is **a c**—[reaches the eye], it therefore meets at their common intersection, which is point **x**.

# BOOK TEN

Suppose there are objects on the bottom of a vessel; let the water rise several inches <note>original: "aliquot digitos," literally "several fingers," a standard unit of measurement roughly equal to an inch.</note> above point **e**, the center of the circle at the base of a column. Wait until the water in the vessel becomes still. Then, move the column until diameter **g h** of the base is perpendicular to the surface of the water. Let the observer’s gaze be tilted outside the rim of the vessel, coming so close to the plane of the water’s surface that point **e** (the center of the circle) and diameter **g h** can be seen. The center of the circle **e** will be found to be in direct alignment with that diameter.

Next, let the eye look at diameter **i k**, which is slanted relative to the water’s surface. It will be seen to bend and "break" <note>original: "frangi," the root of the word "refraction."</note> at the surface of the water. The part of the diameter inside the water and the part outside the water will form an obtuse angle relative to the eye. Meanwhile, the diameter **g h** remains a single straight line, both inside and outside the water, without any refraction or the formation of an angle. 

From this, it is clear that the form of the central point **e** perceived by the eye is not located at the actual center of the circular base. If it were, it would also appear in alignment with the slanted diameter **i k**, because that is its true physical position. Therefore, since the eye perceives that point outside the alignment of the slanted diameter **i k**, and the angle formed by the parts of diameter **i k** follows the perpendicular **g h**, it is evident that the point where the image of center **e** is seen is elevated from the actual center of the column's base. And because the eye perceives this point in alignment with diameter **g h**, it is clear that the form of center **e** is elevated from its true location along the path of the perpendicular diameter **g h**. It is also clear from the bending of the slanted diameter **i k** at the water's surface—and from the straightness and continuity of its part within the water—that every point of the part of diameter **i k** that is underwater is elevated from its true place.

Next, let the circular base of the column be rotated until diameter **i k** becomes perpendicular to the water's surface. Then diameter **g h** will be slanted relative to the water's surface, and the form

Other points labeled around the circle and lines include h, m, q, c, k, i, and p.</image-desc>

of center **e** will be seen in alignment with diameter **i k**, and out of alignment with diameter **g h**. This is because diameter **g h** will appear to break and bend at the water's surface. The angle of this bending will be obtuse, facing the eye and the diameter **i k** which is perpendicular to the water's surface. 

The same thing will happen if many diameters are marked on the surface of the column's base: the form of center **e** will always be seen in alignment with whichever diameter is perpendicular, and any slanted diameter will appear to bend at the water's surface, forming an obtuse angle with its underwater portion—though the underwater portion itself will always appear continuous and straight. 

From this, it is clear that the form of a point **a** seen in a body of greater density <note>term: "diaphanitatis grossioris" (denser transparency). This refers to the optical density of materials like water or glass compared to air.</note> than air appears elevated from its true place along the perpendicular line extending from that point to the surface of the transparent body, provided that the line **d b** (connecting the center of sight **d** with the point of refraction **b**) is not perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body. 

And because (as has been shown both through instruments and through reasoning in Proposition 11 of this book) every point is perceived by the eye as being directly opposite the eye and in alignment with the line through which the form extends to the eye, the points that the eye perceives through refraction must necessarily be seen at the intersection of the perpendicular **a e** and the line **d a** extended to the perpendicular. Therefore, the point where those two lines intersect is the location of the refracted image. 

Even if the refraction of the form of the seen point occurs from a rarer <note>term: "subtiliori" (thinner/finer). In optics, this refers to a less dense medium like air.</note> transparent body to a denser one, the same result occurs as in the previous cases. The location of the refracted image will still be at the intersection of the line of refraction (through which the form reaches the eye) and the perpendicular line drawn from the point of the thing seen to the surface of the body where the refraction occurs. 

To demonstrate this, let a piece of glass be taken with flat and parallel surfaces, with a length of eight inches and a width and thickness that are equal, each being four inches. Then, on the base of the wooden column mentioned earlier, let a line of ten inches be inscribed (following Proposition 1 of Book 4); let this line be **l m**. Half of line **l m** will be five inches. Let it be divided into two equal parts at point **n**. From the center of the base, **e**, let line **e n** be drawn, and let that line be extended on both sides to the edge <note>original: "peripheriam" (periphery/circumference).</note> so that it becomes the diameter **o n e p**. Thus, according to Proposition 3 of Book 3, line **e n** will be perpendicular to line **l m**. Draw line **e l**, and complete the diameter **l q**. Let these two diameters, **o p** and **l q**, be carved deep with a knife; let the hollow of diameter **p o** be filled with white color, and the hollow of diameter **l q** with another color. 

Then, place the glass on the base of the column in such a way that one end of its length is placed over half of line **l m** (which is **n l**). Since the glass is eight inches long and line **l n** is five inches, the length of the glass exceeds the length of line **l n** by three inches. Let three inches of the glass be marked off, two of which will be on the side of the slanted diameter **l q** outside the circle; one inch of the glass's length will remain beyond the perpendicular diameter **p o** (which is perpendicular to line **l m**). Let the body of the glass be on the side of center **e**—that is, between line **l m** and center **e**—and let the glass be attached to the board with glue. Thus, the perpendicular **p o** will be upright relative to the ends of the glass (which are two parallel surfaces), and diameter **l q** will be slanted relative to those two surfaces.

### WITELO’S OPTICS

Indeed, let the sight be positioned in the part where the glass and the circle are located. Let the portion of the glass surface opposite the sight be covered with a linen or cotton cloth <note>original: "panno linteo uel bombace," referring to common 13th-century materials used for damping light or creating a backdrop.</note>, applied to the surface of the column in such a way that nothing is seen except the single slanted diameter **l q** through one eye touching the glass; whereas the white perpendicular diameter **p o** is seen by both eyes. With the sight and instrument así arranged, the center of the circle **e** will be found in the straight line of the white diameter **p o**, which stands erect upon the surface of the glass. The slanted diameter, which is **l q**, will be found to be bent at the surface of the glass on the side of the center **e**, and the angle of this bending will fall toward the circumference; yet the sight will perceive that part of the diameter **l q** which is beneath the glass in a straight line. 

And since the sight touches the surface of the glass, and some part of the perpendicular diameter (which is **p o**) is beneath the glass, and another part is outside the glass toward the center **e**, and another part is outside the glass toward the end of the diameter—such as the part **o a**—that part which is beneath the glass is perceived by the eye existing outside the glass according to refraction. The part **o n**, which is toward the end of the diameter, is perceived by the eye outside the glass directly and without refraction. However, the part toward the center is perceived by both eyes through refraction. For the lines proceeding from the center of the sight touching the glass, and extending into the body of the glass until they reach the surface of the glass on the side of the center, all become slanted upon the surface of the glass. Therefore, that part of the perpendicular diameter **p o** which is toward the center is perceived by the eye touching the glass through refraction. 

The lines proceeding from the other eye to the upper surface of the glass will be slanted upon that upper surface. When they are extended to the other surface of the glass (the one on the side of center **e**), they will also be slanted upon it, as is clear from the 23rd theorem of Book 1 of this work; for those surfaces of the glass are parallel by hypothesis. Therefore, that sight will also perceive the part of diameter **p o** that is toward center **e** by two refractions <note>A "double refraction" occurs here because the light passes through two parallel surfaces of a glass block.</note>: the part beneath the glass by a single refraction, and the upper part of **p o** it will perceive without refraction. Nevertheless, both eyes perceive this diameter **p o** as a straight line. 

And if the experimenter, having covered one eye, looks only through the eye placed upon the glass, he will perceive the perpendicular **p o** as a straight line; and if he raises his eye from the surface of the glass and looks at the diameter **p o** beyond the glass, he will still perceive it as a straight line, even though he perceives it through refraction. This is because any point on diameter **p o**, even if it is not perceived by the eye in its true place, is nonetheless perceived along the straight line of the perpendicular that proceeds from that point to the surface of the glass. This is the line **p o** itself, according to the 20th theorem of Book 1 of this work; for from a single point, only one perpendicular can be drawn to any surface. Since this line **p o** proceeds perpendicularly from every one of its points to the surface of the glass, all refraction of its points occurs along that same line. 

Thus, the form of center **e**, when the eye touches the glass, is perceived in the straight line of diameter **p o** proceeding perpendicularly from center **e** to the surface of the glass. The part of the slanted diameter **l q** existing outside the glass toward center **e** is perceived not in its true place. This is because the point of center **e** is not perceived by the eye except in a place other than its own; and when the angle of bending is toward the circumference, then the form of center **e** is seen beneath the center of the base of the column. 

Because the form of any point perceived by the eye in a second transparent medium <term>diaphani (transparent medium): a substance like water, air, or glass that allows light to pass through.</term> that is rarer than the medium in which the eye is located is in the straight line of the perpendicular produced from that point to the surface of the transparent body touching the eye, and it is further from the surface of that medium than the point itself whose form is seen; and since every point perceived by the eye (according to theorem 12 of this book) is in the straight line along which the form reaches the eye, it is clear that the form of any point in any such situated transparent media is perceived at the point which is the "common section" <note>original: "communis fectio," meaning the intersection point.</note> of the line through which the form reaches the eye and the perpendicular line proceeding from the point of the object to the surface of the transparent body touching the eye. 

The corollary is clear from what has been said: for the location of the form of a point of an object seen through refraction, when that refraction occurs in a second medium denser than the first, the location of the image <term>locus imaginis: the perceived position of an object, as opposed to its physical location.</term> approaches the eye itself, as is clear in the first experiment concerning center **e** when it is seen under water. But when the refraction occurs from the surface of another medium rarer than the first medium touching the eye, then the location of the image is moved further from the eye, as is clear in the second experiment concerning center **e** seen under the glass brought near the eyes; its form is diffused through a medium rarer than glass (which is air) to the surface of the glass, and is refracted through the glass to the eye. This is also clear by example in the first figure of the present proposition: for point **x** is closer to the eye existing at point **d** than point **z**. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 16. *The location of the image of a point of an object seen through refraction, existing in a second transparent medium, is sometimes in that second transparent body itself; sometimes on its surface, as at the point of refraction itself; sometimes between the eye and that transparent body; sometimes behind the eye; and sometimes on the surface of the eye itself.*

For it has been shown by the preceding proposition that the location of the refracted image of any point of an object seen through refraction is at the intersection of the line through which the form reaches the eye and the perpendicular line proceeding from that point of the object to the surface of the transparent body touching the eye. Since these lines must necessarily either meet or be parallel: it is clear that if they meet, wherever those lines intersect—whether this be within the transparent body where the object point is, or outside that body between the eye and the surface of that body, or in the center of the eye, or behind the eye—there will always be the location of the image of the form of the point of the object seen. But if that line through which the form reaches the eye is parallel to the perpendicular, then there will be no specific certainty regarding its location.
