Thus the proposition is clear: for those perpendiculars vary according to the diversity of the surfaces of the bodies from which the refraction occurs.

## 17. *In the refraction of forms from the surfaces of bodies of a different transparency to the sight, there is always a deception in location.*

For since according to all lines through which a form is extended to the sight, refraction always occurs at the surface of a body of different transparency, so that the line through which the form is extended in the medium of one transparent body contains an angle with that line through which the form reaches the sight in the second transparent body. However, only the perpendicular drawn from the seen point upon the surface of the transparent body is not refracted. And the location of every refracted image is at the common section <note>The intersection point.</note> of the second line, through which the refracted form is extended to the sight, and the perpendicular line exiting from the point of the seen object upon the surface of the transparent body touching the sight, according to the 15th theorem of this book. This intersection, moreover, is always outside the true location of the seen point, since only the line of incidence meets with that perpendicular at the very point of the seen object from which both those lines are produced. It is clear, therefore, that the sight never sees the form of a seen object through refraction except in a different place and location than the seen object itself is. Thus, the position of the form grasped by the sight will be different from the position of the seen object. And it is the same regarding distance; for these are aspects of "location." Indeed, the point of the common section of the said lines creating the "location of the image" <note>original: "locus imaginis," a central concept in medieval optics referring to the perceived rather than actual position of an object.</note> raises itself by approaching the sight in refraction from a denser transparent medium to a finer <term>less dense</term> one, and in refraction from a rarer medium to a denser one, it lowers itself, moving away from the center of sight, as was clear through the corollary of the 15th theorem of this book. It is clear, therefore, that the location of the image always varies; and according to this, the sight is deceived regarding the location of the image, perceiving a different place and a different situation of the seen object according to that. The proposition is therefore clear.

## 18. *Every form of a seen object perceived through refraction is grasped as if the object of 그 form were established in the location of the image. Alhazen 19, book 7.*

For just as was said in the 12th theorem of this book, a form existing at the point of refraction reaches the sight itself through the motion of the form, which is moved along the perpendicular line to the surface of the transparent body drawn from the point of the seen object; then it is transferred from this perpendicular through motion in the straightness of the line through which the form reaches the sight. Therefore, the form which is upon the line falling perpendicularly to the surface of the transparent body, and then moves in the straightness of the line through which the form is extended to the sight, is the form which is extended from the seen point in the straightness of the perpendicular exiting from it upon the surface of the transparent body, until it reaches the point of intersection between this perpendicular and the line through which the form is extended to the sight. Thus, the form which the sight perceives as refracted beyond the transparent body is through the motion of the form which reaches the sight from the location of the image. Moreover, the sight perceives this form in the location of the image just like other things which it perceives in their own place without refraction through a medium of a single transparency and directly. Therefore, the object appears to be as distant from the center of sight as the point of the image is distant from the same center of sight; since the position of the image location in respect to the sight is the position of the form which is in the location of the image. Hence, because of refraction, the form of the seen object is perceived in the location of the image. The proposition is therefore clear.

## 19. *When the common section of the surface of refraction and the surface of the transparent body from which refraction occurs is a straight line, and the point of the seen object is on the perpendicular drawn from the center of sight upon the surface of the transparent body of whatever kind, no refraction will occur from any point of 그 surface; and only one image will meet the sight. Alhazen 21, book 7.*

Let the center of sight be point **a**, and the point of the seen object be **b**. And let the point of the seen object, which is **b**, be on the line **g c**. It is clear, therefore, through the 3rd theorem of this book, that the sight **a** will perceive the form of point **b** directly without any refraction. For since the form of point **b** is extended in a straight line through line **b g** to the surface of the transparent body which is touching the sight at point **a**; and because line **b g** is perpendicular upon the surface of the transparent body touching the sight; therefore, the sight **a** will perceive point **b** in its own place according to the straightness of line **a g b**. It is therefore not possible for point **b** to be refracted to the sight **a** from outside the line **b g a**. But if it were granted that this is possible: let there be another point of refraction on the surface of that transparent medium (in which point of refraction **g** is), which let be **p**, outside the line **a g b**; and let the form of point **b** be refracted to the center of sight **a** from point **p**. Let us imagine, therefore, the surface of refraction, in which the perpendicular line **a g b** lies, to pass through point **p**. Therefore, the angle **k p h** will be contained by the line **p h**, through which the form is extended, and by the perpendicular line **k p**, coming out from the point of refraction, which is **p**, upon the surface of the transparent body. Therefore, whatever the second transparent medium may be, whether rarer or denser than the first transparent medium, as long as the point of the object seen is so disposed, refraction to the sight will occur from no point of that transparent surface: but the thing will be seen on the perpendicular line itself drawn from the center of the sight to the point of the object seen, cutting the surface of the second transparent body in only one point **g**. Therefore, the form of that point is perceived from only one point of the surface of that transparent body: it has, therefore, only a single non-refracted image. Which is what was proposed.

### 20. *When the common section of the surface of refraction and the surface of the transparent body from which the refraction occurs is a straight line, and the seen point exists outside the perpendicular drawn from the center of vision upon the surface of a transparent body denser than the transparent body touching the sight: refraction will occur from only one point: and a single image will be seen. Alhazen, Book 2, Chapter 7.* <note>Witelo credits the 11th-century polymath Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham), whose work "Optics" was the foundation for this text.</note>

Let the arrangement remain as it was in the closely preceding case: and let point **b** be outside the perpendicular line drawn from the center of vision **a** upon the surface of the second transparent medium, which is **a g c**. Let a plane surface also be extended through the line **a g c** and through point **b**: this, then, will be perpendicular to the surface of the second transparent body through the 18th proposition of the 11th book <note>Euclid's *Elements*.</note>: and it will cut the surface of the transparent body along a straight line through the 3rd proposition of the 11th book: let this be **g d**. Therefore, the form of point **b** will not be refracted to the sight **a** (through the 2nd theorem of this book) except from some point of the surface in which line **g d** is: for a perpendicular surface does not pass through two points **a** and **b** upon the surface of the second transparent body, except only the surface passing through the perpendicular **a c**: but through the perpendicular **a c** and through point **b**, no plane surface passes except one alone. Therefore, the form of point **b** is refracted to point **a**, the center of vision, from some point of the line **g d**: let this be **e**: and let two lines **b e** and **e a** be drawn: and from point **e**, let a perpendicular line be drawn upon the surface **g e d** through the 12th proposition of the 11th book: let this be **h e z**: which, through the 1st theorem of this book, will be in that surface of refraction: therefore, line **h e z** will be perpendicular to the two surfaces of those two transparent bodies: because it is drawn perpendicularly in a surface standing upright over both those surfaces. Therefore, let line **b e** be extended continuously and straight: and let it be line **b e p**: line **e p** will therefore fall between the two lines **e h** and **e a** through the 4th theorem of this book. For the transparent body which is on the side of the center of vision **a** is rarer than the transparent body which is on the side of **b**: therefore, by that same 4th theorem, the form of point **b**, which is extended through line **b e**, when it reaches the given point of refraction **e**, will be refracted toward the side opposite to the side of the perpendicular, which is **z e h**: therefore, line **e p** will be between the two lines **e h** and **e a**.

Therefore, angle **p e a** is greater than angle **l o a** by Theorem 8 of this book. For it was shown in the corollary that follows the tables placed there (the truth of which is clear from the preceding experiment) that the angles of refraction in a denser transparent medium—by which the angles of incidence differ from the refracted angles contained under the perpendicular line drawn from the point of refraction upon the surface of the transparent medium and from the lines refracted to the sight—are greater in larger angles of incidence and smaller in smaller ones. Therefore, angle **a e h** is smaller than angle **a o f**, which is impossible. ->*23. When the common section of the surface of refraction and the surface of the transparent body from which refraction occurs is a circle, and the point being seen lies outside the perpendicular drawn from the center of sight over the convex surface of a transparent body denser than the transparent body touching the sight: refraction will occur from only one point, and a single image will be seen; the location of the image, however, will vary according to the different locations of the point being seen or the center of sight. Let it also be that lines **z e** and **b m**, since they are in the same surface of circle **c d e**, intersect each other at a point, which we shall call **g**. Let line **b e** be extended outside the circle to point **h**, line **b m** to point **n**, line **z e** to point **p**, and line **z m** to point **l**. 

Therefore, angle **h e p** will be equal to the angle of incidence through Proposition 15 of Book 1 <note>This refers to Euclid's Elements; the angle of incidence is defined here by vertical angles</note>, since each of them is contained under line **e b**, through which the form is extended, and under the perpendicular **e p**, emerging from the location of refraction (which is **e**) over the surface of the body from which refraction occurs. Angle **h e a** will be the angle of refraction. Likewise, angle **l m n** will be equal to the angle of incidence through Proposition 15 of Book 1, contained under line **n m** (through which the form is extended) and under the perpendicular **l m** emerging from the location of refraction, which is **m**; and angle **n m a** is the angle of refraction. 

Therefore, angle **h e p** will either be equal to angle **n m l**, or greater, or smaller. If it is equal, then through Theorem 8 of this book, the angle of refraction **h e a** will be equal to angle **n m a**, which is similarly the angle of refraction. And since each of these with its fellow <note>The supplementary angle</note> equals two right angles through Proposition 13 of Book 1, then angle **a m b** would be equal to angle **a e b**. But if line **a b** were produced, this would be impossible and contrary to Proposition 21 of Book 1. 

If, however, angle **h e p** is smaller than angle **l m n**, then angle **h e a** will be smaller than angle **n m a** through Theorem 8 of this book. Therefore, through Proposition 13 of Book 1, angle **a m b** will be smaller than angle **a e b**, which again is contrary to Proposition 21 of Book 1 and impossible. 

But if angle **h e p** is greater than angle **l m n**: let line **e b** be extended in the direction of point **b** to a point on the circumference, which we shall call **f**, and let line **m b** be extended beyond point **b** to a point on the circumference, which we shall call **o**. Therefore, angle **e b m** will be, through Theorem 54 of Book 1 of this work, equal to the angle which is at the circumference falling on an arc equal to the two arcs **e m** and **f o**. And since angle **h e p** is by hypothesis greater than angle **n m l**, then angle **z e b** will be greater than angle **n m l** through Proposition 15 of Book 1; therefore it is also greater than angle **b m z** by that same Proposition 15. Since therefore angle **z e b** is greater than angle **b m z**, the excess of angle **m z e** over angle **e b m** will be equal to the excess of angle **z e b** over angle **b m z**, through Proposition 32 of Book 1. 

For since in the triangles **e b g** and **m g z** the angles of intersection at point **g** are equal (as is clear through Proposition 15 of Book 1), and since any of the remaining two angles together with their third equals two right angles, it is clear that the two remaining angles of one triangle are equal to the two remaining angles of the other triangle. In as much, therefore, as angle **z e b** is greater than angle **b m z**, in so much is angle **m z e** greater than angle **e b m**. 

However, the arc corresponding to angle **m z e**, if it were at the circumference, would be double the arc **m e** through Proposition 20 of Book 3 and Proposition 33 of Book 6. If, therefore, angle **m z e** were greater than angle **m b e**, then the doubled arc **m e** would be greater than the two arcs **m e** and **f o**, and the excess of the doubled arc **m e** over the two arcs **m e** and **f o** would be equal to the excess of arc **m e** over arc **f o**—since arc **m e** is common to both, and once it is removed, the same excess remains. Even if the geometric proportion is varied, the arithmetic proportion <note>The difference between the values</note> is not varied. Therefore, the excess of angle **m z e** over angle **e b m** is that which corresponds at the circumference to the excess of arc **m e** over arc **f o**. But the excess of arc **m e** over arc **f o** is less than the two arcs **m e** and **f o**, since it is a part of arc **m e**. Therefore the excess of angle **m z e** over angle **m b e** is smaller than angle **m b e** through Proposition 33 of Book 6, and as is clear from what was previously stated. Thus, the excess of angle **z e b** over angle **z m b** is smaller than angle **m b e**. Therefore, as was shown above through Proposition 15 of Book 1, the excess of angle **h e p** over angle **n m l** is smaller than angle **m b e**. Therefore the excess of the angle of refraction, which is **h e a**, over the angle of refraction, which is **n m a**, is much smaller than angle **m b e** through Theorem 8 of this book; but the excess—

### WITELO’S OPTICS

...the maximum proportion that the angle of incidence—formed by the line along which the form of a point of the object is extended to the surface of the body from which it is refracted, and the line drawn perpendicular to the surface of that body from the point of refraction—can have to the angle of refraction required by that angle of incidence as far as the sense [of sight] is concerned. (For the angles of refraction that occur between two bodies of different transparency <note>original: "diaphanitatis"</note> vary according to the light passing through those bodies; the diversity of these, as far as the sense is concerned, has a limit. If the angle exceeds this limit, then the sense will not grasp the quantity of refraction, for it will directly perceive the center of the light passing through those two bodies in the straightness of the line along which it is extended; and this can be more fully tested using the instrument we employed above.) <note>Witelo refers to his own invention, a graduated bronze cylinder used to measure angles of refraction.</note>

And since, as is clear from the preceding, angle **e z d** is greater than angle **k e t**: let angle **d z t** therefore be set equal to angle **k e t** by the 27th theorem of the first book of this work. <note>Witelo's first book acts as a mathematical primer for the rest of the treatise.</note> Because line **e k** meets with line **e t**, it is clear by the 2nd theorem of the first book of this work that because it meets with line **a d** (which is parallel to it), it follows that they meet at point **b**. Similarly, line **z t** will meet with line **e t**: let it meet at point **t**. And because lines **e b** and **z e** are between two parallel lines and on the same surface, it is clear that they intersect each other: let the point of intersection be **k**. By the 32nd proposition of Book 1, angle **z k e** will be equal to the two angles **k z b** and **k b z**. But angle **k b z** is, by the 29th proposition of Book 1, equal to angle **k e t**. Therefore, angle **z k e** is equal to double the angle **k e t**. Thus, by the 7th proposition of Book 5, the ratio of angle **z e k** to angle **z k e** will be the maximum proportion possible to find between the angle of incidence (contained by the line along which the form is extended and the perpendicular emerging from the place of refraction) and the angle of refraction required by that angle of incidence.

Likewise, from point **e**, let a line be drawn parallel to line **t z** by the 31st proposition of Book 1, which by the 2nd theorem of the first book of this work will meet with line **z g** toward point **g**: let the point of meeting therefore be **a**. And let line **b e** be extended outside the circle **g e d** to point **l**. Therefore, angle **l e a** will be equal to angle **z k e** by the 29th proposition of Book 1, and angle **l e h** is equal to angle **z k e** by the 15th proposition of Book 1. It follows, as is clear from the preceding, that angle **l e a** is that angle of refraction required by angle **l e h**, since by the 15th proposition of Book 1, angle **l e h** is equal to angle **z e k**, which was chosen as proposed.

If, therefore, the center of sight is at point **a** (specifically a point in the air), and a transparent medium <term>diaphanum<gloss>a transparent substance, like glass or water</gloss></term> denser than air (whose convex side is toward the eye **a**) is continued all the way to point **b**, and is not distinct at the circle **g d e** on the side of **b**—so that the difference of another transparent medium does not hinder the nature of refraction—then the form of point **b** is extended along line **b e**, is refracted along line **e a**, and is perceived by the eye at point **a** through line **e a**.

And since the angle of refraction **a e l** can be divided into many portions of those that can exist between the angles of refraction and incidence (which the said perpendiculars contain with the lines along which the forms fall upon the transparent bodies from whose surface they are refracted), there will be many points on line **d b** whose forms are extended to the arc **g e** and are refracted from it to the eye **a**. Thus, the forms of the entire line **d b**, in which all those points reside, are refracted to the eye **a** from the arc **g e**.

If, therefore, the line **a g b** is shaped, and the triangle **a e b** is rotated around the fixed line **a b**, and the part of the surface of the transparent body facing the object seen is spherical, then point **e** (which is the point of refraction) will, by its motion on the convex spherical surface of the body, mark a circle on the side of the eye **a**, from which the entire form of point **b** will be refracted to the eye **a**. But the location of the image in the entire periphery of the circle of refraction will be one and the same. For, as is clear from the 15th proposition of this book, the location of the image is the center of sight, where the line of extension of the form (which is **e a**) and the perpendicular **b z a** meet. Similarly, the forms of all points on line **d b** except for point **d** are refracted from some point of arc **e g**, as previously stated; and the location of the image for all those points will always be in the center of sight. Thus, the entire image of that visible object is a single unity.

The form of this visible object is therefore perceived by the eye as a circular form at the circle of refraction, and its unique upper point near point **d** is seen in the straightness of the perpendicular passing through the center of sight and the object seen. Therefore, when the center of sight is in one transparent medium and the object seen is in another denser medium, and the surface of the denser transparent body facing the eye is convex and spherical, and the eye is outside the circle (whose convex side faces the eye), and that circle is farther from the eye than the most distant point of the form being refracted (which in this case is point **b**), and is distant from the two points of the section made between the perpendiculars and the circumference—and when the denser transparent body on the side of the object is entirely continuous to the place where the object is, and the medium is not interrupted at any point—then the eye will perceive the form of that visible object both truly and by refraction. <note>Witelo means the eye sees a clear, single image despite the light bending.</note> The location of the image of that visible object will be in the center of sight, but it will be seen on the surface of the eye. This is what was proposed.

However, if it should happen that the perpendicular drawn from the object seen to the surface of the body from which refraction occurs is parallel to one of those lines through which the form reaches the eye, and not to another, it will be possible for the form of the object to be seen partly on the surface of the body from which refraction occurs, and partly...

### 26. *When the common section of the surface of refraction and the surface of the transparent body from which the refraction occurs is a circle, and the point of the object being seen lies on the perpendicular line drawn from the center of vision through the concave surface of the transparent body facing the eye: the form of the object seen will meet the eye directly, no refraction will occur from any point, and only one image will be seen. Alhazen, Book 7, Number 30.*

Let **a** be the center of vision; and let **b** be the point of the object seen beyond the transparent body, which, for the sake of example, is denser than the one in which the center of vision **a** is located. Let the surface of the denser body facing the eye be a concave sphere, the center of which is **g**. I say that when points **a** and **b** exist on a single perpendicular line above the surface of that concave body, then the point of the object **b** will have only one image and only one form at the center of vision **a**. For let the line **a g** be drawn and extended straight to point **z**. Therefore, by the 72nd theorem of the first book of this work, line **a z** will be perpendicular to the concave surface of the transparent body. Let point **b** also be on line **a z**. Thus, the eye at **a** will grasp the form of point **b** along the straightness of line **a b**, because line **a b** is perpendicular to the concave surface of that body, which is a denser transparent medium; nor can it grasp a refracted form from any other point.

If the opposite were claimed to be possible, let it be that the form of point **b** is refracted to the eye **a** from point **e** on the body. Let lines **b e** and **g e** be drawn; line **g e** will be perpendicular to the surface of the body from which the refraction occurs. Let line **b e** be extended to point **t**. Therefore, angle **t e g** is the angle of incidence <note>the angle at which light hits the surface</note> contained by the line along which the form is extended and the perpendicular line coming out from the place of refraction on the surface of the body. And because the body on the side of the eye **a** is finer <note>less dense</note> than the one on the side of the object where point **b** is located, it is clear by the 4th theorem of this book that the refraction will be toward the side opposite to that where the perpendicular **e g** is located; and line **e t** does not meet with line **b a** in any way. Therefore, the form of point **b** is not refracted to the eye **a**. Thus, the eye will not grasp it by refraction, but only directly. Therefore, point **b** will have nothing but a single form and a single image at the eye **a**. If, however, the body in which the object is seen were rarer than the body where the center of vision is located, the demonstration remains the same; for even then, the refraction will not reach the center of vision. Thus, the proposition is clear.

If the eye **a** is on line **k d**, then it will either be at the center **g**, or on one of the two lines **g k** or **g d**. If the eye **a** is at the center **g**, then the form of point **b** will not be refracted to the eye **a** according to the immediately preceding proposition; for the lines connecting the spherical transparent body with the center **g** are, by the 72nd theorem of Book 1, perpendicular to the surface of the body on the side of the eye. -># VITELO'S OPTICS<-

...standing at point **a** from the same point, as is clear from the 9th proposition of this book: but it has already been declared in the preceding proposition that this is impossible. For the form extended along line **bh** and refracted along line **ba** <note>original: "refracta per lineam ba"; the ray path from the object to the eye</note>, cannot be refracted to the sight at point **b** <note>The text likely means point **a**, following the usual geometric notation for the eye in these proofs</note> from any other point of the circle **hdk** except from point **h**; nor from any other point on the surface of the transparent body, because that circle alone falls within the surface of refraction. ### 29. *When the concave surface of a transparent body denser than air is placed opposite the sight: it is possible for a straight line to be positioned such that one of its points is seen directly, and various points of the same line are seen by refraction: and the entire form of that line is refracted from a portion of the surface of that body: and the location of its image is at the center of the sight.* <margin>Alhazen [Book 7] 29, note 7.</margin>

Let there be, according to the manner of the 25th proposition of this book, a common section <note>The line where two surfaces intersect</note> of the surface of refraction and of a concave spherical body denser than air (such as glass or crystal), which is circle **ged**, whose center is point **z**: and let radius **ze** be drawn: upon whose endpoint, point **e**, by the 23rd proposition of the 1st book, let angle **zek** be made equal to the maximum angle of incidence <term>angle of incidence: the angle at which light hits a surface</term>, which the line of extension of the form of a point of an object existing under that transparent medium contains toward the sight existing outside that transparent medium in air or another rarer medium, with the perpendicular line drawn from point **e** onto the surface of that body from which the refraction occurs: and let angle **ket** be made, by the same 23rd proposition of the 1st book, equal to half of the maximum angle of refraction <term>angle of refraction: the angle at which light bends when passing from one medium to another</term> that can occur between any those given transparent bodies, such as, for example, between concave glass and air (this is indeed possible, since all these angles are known from the 8th proposition of this book). And from point **z**, the center of the concave body (like glass or crystal), let a line be drawn parallel to line **et** by the 31st proposition of the 1st book, which, when extended on both sides to the circumference, shall be **gzd**: and let line **ez** be extended from point **e** outside that body as far as point **h**. And thus, the entire configuration and demonstration of the 25th proposition being completed: it is clear that with the concave surface of a transparent body denser than air placed opposite the sight, it is possible for a straight line to be positioned so that one of its points is seen directly, and different points of that same line are seen by refraction. The entire form of that line is refracted from one portion of the surface of that concave body of glass or crystal, bounded by a "not-great" circle <note>A circle on a sphere that does not share the same center as the sphere itself; also called a small circle</note> of that sphere: and point **d** is seen along the perpendicular **ad** without refraction, while the forms of all other points on line **db** are refracted. The perpendiculars of all those points meet on line **ba**, concurring with the lines through which the forms come to the sight at the very center of vision, point **a**. Therefore, the proposition is clear by the 15th theorem of this book. 

From the preceding eight theorems, the conditions occurring to the sight because of the medium of a second transparent body are clear, in which the thing is seen, the shape of which is spherical, whether it be convex or concave. And when the body of the second transparent medium has a cylindrical <term>columnar: shaped like a column or cylinder</term> or pyramidal shape, the common section of the surface of refraction is a straight line: then a completely uniform effect happens to the sight through those, just as occurs through other transparent bodies with flat surfaces, whose common section with the surface of refraction is also a straight line, and must be demonstrated in the same way. But when that common section is a circle: then the same things occur in transparent cylindrical bodies as occur in concave or convex spherical bodies; except for this, that refraction to the sight cannot occur from the circumference of a single circle of the surface of the second transparent body in such bodies, as we showed happens from convex spherical bodies in the 23rd proposition of this book. 

In concave or convex transparent pyramidal bodies, the common section of the surface of refraction and the surface of that body cannot be a circle, as was shown regarding the surfaces of reflections by the 12th theorem of the 7th book and the 2nd theorem of the 9th book of this work: since all surfaces of refraction are also perpendicular to the surfaces of the bodies from which the refraction occurs, as is clear from the 2nd proposition of this book; hence these conditions do not pertain to them. If the common section of the surface of the transparent body should be an acute-angled section <term>oxygonia: an ellipse or acute-angled conic section</term>: refraction will occur from only one point, as we have just shown in the case of convex or concave circles. And the image of the form of the object seen will sometimes be seen inside the transparent body; sometimes between the sight and the transparent body; sometimes on the surface of the transparent body itself; and sometimes at the surface of the sight itself, as it happens that the perpendicular line drawn from the point of the object seen to the surface of the transparent body meets or is parallel to the line of extension of that form through which the form reaches the sight. For this reason, we did not think it necessary to dwell further on such matters.

### 30. *With the surfaces of transparent bodies of various shapes placed opposite the sight, or to those...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of optical refraction from Book 10, moving from the study of single refractive surfaces to more complex cases involving composite shapes and varying densities. It builds on the principles established in the previous propositions regarding how the geometry of a transparent medium alters the perception of an object's size and shape.</meta>

-># BOOK TEN<-

*In bodies of diverse transparency: the locations of the images of forms seen through those bodies are varied; and monstrous <note>The author uses "monstrous" (Latin: monstruosæ) to describe shapes that appear distorted, unnatural, or deformed compared to their true appearance.</note> forms and images numbered by the number of refraction points appear to the sight. Alhazen [Book 7] 33, note 7.*

Based on what has been previously stated, it is clear that in transparent <term>diaphanous: materials that allow light to pass through, like glass or water</term> bodies that are of a single shape and substance, only one image of all the objects appears to the sight, whose forms are multiplied through those transparent bodies to the eye. If, however, the transparent body through which vision occurs has a surface composed of different shapes—for instance, perhaps from a flat and a spherical surface, or from a spherical and a columnar <note>original: "columnari"; refers to a cylindrical shape</note> surface—then the situation changes. Since the surface opposite the eye is diverse, being composed of different shapes, and the nature of the perpendiculars and lines of extension of the forms is varied according to the diversity of the shapes of those surfaces, it is clear from the 15th proposition of this book that the locations of the images of the seen forms vary.

And perhaps there will be different points of refraction for the form of the same point of the object seen by the same eye, as well as different lines of extension of the forms and different perpendiculars <term>perpendiculars: in optics, these are the "normals" or imaginary lines at a right angle to the surface, used to calculate the angle of refraction</term>. Because of this, several images of the same seen object will appear, refracted from the surfaces of such bodies. Hence, if someone looks at a visible object existing beyond a transparent body whose surface opposite the eye is a composite shape made of the surface of a large and a small sphere—as often happens in crystals or other transparent stones and glass—it is clear that the centers of those spheres are different (by the 8th theorem of the 1st book). For those spheres intersect one another. Therefore, the perpendiculars drawn from a single point of the object to the surface of that body will have great diversity. 

And if the shape of the surface of those bodies is composed of a spherical and a columnar surface, it is clear that there is even greater diversity in both the points of refraction and the perpendiculars drawn. Thus, the arrangement of images through these transparent bodies will be deformed; and perhaps that form will appear monstrous, due to the flowing together of different images into the constitution of a single form, since the points of refraction are near each other, and the intersections of the perpendiculars and the lines of extension of the forms are also near each other. If, however, the points of refraction or the aforementioned sections are sensibly distant from each other, then several images of the same seen object are observed, because their refraction is not unified, nor do they join, but they remain distinct. For the form of the seen object is extended from itself to the spherical or columnar surfaces (or whatever other shape the transparent body has) and is refracted from them at the hollow of the air touching that transparent body. Thus, the comprehension of the forms of the same object occurs from different refractions; hence, distinct images are created, numbered according to the number of refraction points. 

The same thing also happens if a transparent body, even if uniform in its surface, has varying transparency—that is, if it is denser in one part and rarer <note>original: "ratius"; meaning less dense or thinner</note> in another. For then, according to one part of itself, refraction occurs toward the perpendicular, and in another part, toward the opposite side. Thus, again, either the forms become monstrous, or perhaps otherwise diverse and differing in number. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

*31. When the common section of the surface of refraction and the surface of the body from which refraction occurs is a straight line; and the eye also exists on a perpendicular emerging from the midpoint of the viewed line onto the flat surface of the transparent body from which the form of that line is refracted to the sight; if the viewed line is parallel to the surface of the transparent body (whether it be denser or rarer than the first medium): the image of the refracted object seen is perceived as larger than the object itself. Alhazen [Book 7] 39, note 7.*

Let point **a** be the center of sight; and let the line being seen, which is **bc**, be in the middle of a second transparent medium. Let its midpoint be **z**. Let the common section of the surface of refraction and the flat surface of the transparent body be line **de**. Let a perpendicular line be drawn from point **z** (the midpoint of line **bc**) to line **de** (by the 12th proposition of the 1st book), which shall be **zm**; and let it be extended beyond point **m**. Line **zm** will therefore be erected perpendicularly upon the flat surface in which line **de** lies. This is because the surface of refraction, in which line **zm** is produced and in which line **ed** lies, is erected upon that surface of the transparent body (by the 2nd theorem of this book). Let line **bc** be parallel to line **de**. 

With the center of sight **a** existing on line **zm**, I say that line **bc** is seen as larger than it truly is. For no surface that is erected upon the surface of the transparent body passes through the center of sight **a** and through any point of line **bc** (except point **z**), other than the surface of refraction alone, in which lines **az** and **bc** are located. For no surface erected upon the surface of the transparent body passes through **a** except that which passes through line **az** (which is the line perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body); nor does any perpendicular emerge from point **a** to the surface of the transparent body except line **az** (by the 20th theorem of this book). Therefore, no surface perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body passes through point **a** except that which passes through line **az**. And no surface passes through any point of line **bc** other than point **z**, and through line **az**, except that surface in which the two lines **az** and **bc** lie. 

Therefore, no surface perpendicular to the surface of the transparent body passes through the sight **a** and through any point of line **bc** (except point **z**) other than that in which lines **az** and **bc** lie. Consequently, the form of none of the points on line **bc** is refracted except from some point on line **de**. Therefore, let two perpendiculars be drawn (by the 31st proposition of the 1st book) from the aforementioned points **b** and **c** to line **de**, which, as is clear from the premises, necessarily fall upon it; let these be lines **bd** and **ce**. And since lines **bc** and **de** are parallel by hypothesis, and lines **bd** and **ce** are parallel (by the 28th proposition of the 1st book), it is clear that each of those lines **bd** and **ce** is parallel to line **az** (by the same 28th proposition of the 1st book). And it is clear that the form of point **b** will not be refracted...

It is then clear that line **nq** will cut line **bp**: let the point of intersection be **s**. Thus, the form of point **n** would reach sight **a** from two points of refraction, namely **p** and **q**: which is contrary to the 20th or 21st theorem of this book, and is impossible. Therefore, the form of point **n** will not be refracted to sight **a** except from some point of line **pm** which is between points **p** and **m**. The same is also true for every point of line **zc** which is between points **z** and **c**: for none of them is refracted to sight **a** except from some point of line **hm** which is between points **h** and **m**. And because on line **lk** all the perpendiculars drawn from the points of lines **b** and **c** intersect with the extended lines of refraction: it is clear that line **lk** is the diameter of the image of line **bc**. Therefore, the form of line **bc** is seen in line **lk** as larger than line **bc** actually is, according to the 20th theorem of the 4th book of this work. For it is seen under a larger angle: because angle **kal** is larger than angle **bac** by the 34th theorem of the 1st book of this work: which is what was proposed. And this kind of deception <note>Witelo uses "deceptio" (deception) to refer to optical illusions where the mind misinterprets the size or distance of an object due to the physical properties of light.</note> happens to the sight because of the weakness of the refracted form, as is clear from the 10th theorem of this book: because of which the sight likens it to the form of a thing seen from a greater distance; for a greater distance weakens the form. Thus, the sight perceives the form of line **bc** refractively by comparing the angle **kal** (which is larger than angle **bac**) at a distance greater than the actual distance of line **bc**, in a position equal to the position of **bc**. In this way, the quantity of line **bc** is perceived refractively as larger because of the magnitude of the angle created by its proximity to the sight, and because of the weakness of the form caused by refraction. And so, universally, the reason why line **bc** appears larger is the refraction of its form in the second transparent medium toward the eye: and the demonstration is always the same, whether the refraction occurs at the surface of a second transparent medium that is denser or rarer than the first in which line **bc** is located; for there is no difference in that regard. However, it might be possible to find transparent bodies placed in such a way that a flat surface could be in a rarer body touching the eye itself: just as happens when a flat piece of glass touches the eye, so that the center of the pupil <note>original: "foraminis uveae"; literally the "opening of the uvea," referring to the pupil.</note> is positioned on the flat surface of the glass.

And this is what was proposed; nor should the difference in the position of different transparent media be considered a concern here.

Therefore, line **lg**, which is the image of line **bn**, is perceived as larger than line **bn** itself. *36. When the common section of the surface of refraction and a spherical transparent body denser than air (from which refraction occurs) is a circle, and the center of sight is in the same surface outside the circle on a line perpendicular to the surface of that body, and the thing seen exists between the center of the body and the eye, such that the ends of the thing seen are equidistant from the center of the body: the image will appear larger than the thing seen. <image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the refraction of an object through a spherical surface. Let there be a spherical surface of a transparent body denser than air; let its convex side be toward the eye, whose center is **a**: and let the thing seen be **bc**: and let the center of the spherical body be point **d**: which is beyond the line **bc** with respect to the eye **a**: and let point **z** be the midpoint of line **bc**: and let lines **db**, **dz**, **dc** be drawn: and let them be extended until they meet with the surface of the spherical transparent body: line **db** at point **e**: and line **dz** at point **m**: and line **dc** at point **n**: and let the eye **a** be on line **zm**, which is perpendicular to the surface of that transparent body by the 72nd theorem of Book 1 of this work. Therefore, **amz** will be a straight line. And since line **bz** is equal to line **zc**, and because points **b** and **c** (which are the ends of the thing seen) are equidistant from the center **d** by hypothesis: line **db** will also be equal to line **dc**: therefore, triangles **bdz** and **cdz** will be equilateral <note>original: "æquilatera"; in this context meaning congruent, as they share the same side lengths</note>: since line **zd** is common to both those triangles: therefore, by the 8th proposition of Book 1 <note>original: "8 p 1"; Euclid’s Elements, proving congruence by three sides</note>, the angles at point **d** will be equal, which are angles **zdb** and **zdc**: and similarly, the angles at point **z** will be equal: they are therefore right angles: thus, by definition, the line **az** is perpendicular to line **bc**. ### 40. *The image of a refracted line seen passing through the center of a spherical transparent body denser than air, when the line is not on the perpendicular drawn from the center of sight to the surface of that body, always appears larger than the line itself.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the refraction of light through a spherical diaphanous body. It shows a circle with its center labeled 'd'. Above the circle is a point 'a', representing the center of vision. A horizontal line 'b-c' passes through the center 'd', with a point 'z' between 'b' and 'd'. Several lines originate from point 'a', passing through the surface of the circle. Internal points and line segments are labeled 'k', 'o', 'l', and 'm' to demonstrate how an image (the arc k-l) appears larger than the object line (b-c) due to refraction.</image-desc>

Let **a** be the center of sight outside a transparent body thicker than air, whose center is **d**. Let the seen line be **bc**, passing through the center **d**, provided that the center of sight is not on that line **bc** however far it is extended. I say that its image always appears larger than the line itself. Since the <term>perpendiculars</term> <note>lines meeting a surface at a right angle</note> to the surface of the body drawn from any points on line **bc** all contain line **bc**, and since the sight exists in the air, refraction always occurs toward the side opposite the perpendicular drawn from the point of refraction to the surface of the body, as is clear from the 4th theorem of this book. Therefore, according to the previous demonstrations, it is clear that the lines extending the forms of the endpoints of line **bc** (which are **b** and **c**), produced inside the transparent body from whose surface the refraction occurs, will intersect the perpendiculars of points **b** and **c**. Consequently, the image of line **bc** will always appear larger than the line itself; in truth, the line then becomes a part of its own image. Thus, the proposition is proven. 

This method of demonstrating could also be expanded to other positions of the seen line, which could be beyond the center of the transparent body denser than air, while the sight is outside that body in the air, and the convexity of the body faces the eye. For even then, the image sometimes appears larger than the object seen in the manner described in other positions before the center, such as when the seen line is close to the center of the transparent body. 

However, if the seen line **bc** is perpendicular to the line **adz** (drawn from the center of sight through the center of the body), and the lines extending the forms of the endpoints of line **bc** cut the surface of the spherical transparent body and intersect the perpendicular lines drawn from points **b** and **c** to the surface of the transparent body inside the body, then the image will appear smaller than the object seen. 

But if the lines extending the forms of points **b** and **c** are <term>tangents</term> <note>touching at a single point without intersecting</note> to the circle of the transparent body at the ends of the perpendiculars drawn from points **c** and **b** to the surface of the body, or intersect the circle at those same ends, then the image will always be equal to the object seen, by the 15th proposition of Book 1 and the 26th and 28th of Book 3 <note>of Euclid</note>; and the image of line **bc** will appear like a certain chord of the arc of that circle. 

And if it should happen that the lines extending the forms touch the circle of the transparent body at two points in the middle of that arc—as if the eye were very close to the surface of the transparent body—then those lines will meet with the perpendiculars outside the surface of the body; and the image of line **bc** will appear larger than the line itself, and extended outside the surface of the body according to its endpoints. 

Finally, if the seen line **bc** is outside the transparent body, either touching it or at a distance from it, but not being part of line **ad**, then its image will appear smaller than the object seen when it occurs between the transparent body itself, or beyond it, between the object seen and the surface of the body. But in commonly seen objects, there is nothing of this sort, unless perhaps it is some transparent body of glass or stone, and the whole body is solid and the seen object is inside it; or if the seen object is beyond a crystalline or glass sphere. We leave the demonstration of the diversity of these positions from the aforementioned principles to the skill of the investigator.

### 41. *In all refractions made from the spherical surfaces of transparent bodies to the eye, where the image appears larger than the object seen, any part of the image will appear larger than the corresponding proportional part of the object seen. Alhazen Book 7, chapter 47, note 7.*

Let the arrangement be as it was in the 35th theorem of this book. Let line **dm** intersect line **kl** (which is the diameter of the image) at point **o**. Thus, line **ko** will be the image of line **bz**, because point **z** is seen along the perpendicular **az** according to the 5th theorem of this book. The angle **kao** will be larger than angle **baz**, and the position of line **ko** with respect to the eye **a** is similar to the position of line **bz** with respect to the same eye. Both those lines are equally distant from the center of sight—or if there is any difference in this, it will not be perceptible to the eye. Thus, the image **ko** appears larger than line **bz**. Their points **z** and **o** fall on line **za**, which is drawn from the center of sight, and of which line **zm** is a part, exiting from the end of line **bz** perpendicularly to the surface of the transparent body, falling on point **m**. 

Now, if another part of line **bz** is taken, let it be **bf**, and let the location of the image of the form of point **f** be at point **r** on line **ko**. Then line **kr** will be the image of line **bf**. As shown above, it is clear that line **kr** will appear larger than line **bf**, because more refraction occurs to line **bf** than to line **fz** through the 14th theorem of this book; therefore...

Therefore, the enlargement of the image is owed to it compared to the line **fz**. If, however, the point **a** (the center of vision) is outside the surface in which all the perpendiculars lie—those extending from the points of line **bc** to the surface of the <term>transparent body</term> <note>original: "corpus diaphanum"; any clear substance like glass or water</note> where refraction occurs (for line **az**, which extends from point **a** perpendicularly to the midpoint of line **bc**, which is **z**, is not for that reason perpendicular to the surface of the body in which line **bc** lies)—the same result will be clear. For since lines **bc** and **kl** are erected above the line **azd**, and line **ko** is the image of line **bz**, and line **lo** is the image of line **zc**, the angle which line **ko** subtends at the center of vision **a** (which is angle **kaz**) is larger than angle **baz**, which line **bz** subtends at the center of vision **a**. Therefore, through the 20th theorem of the 4th book of this work, line **ko** will appear larger than line **bz**; and similarly, line **kr** will appear larger than line **bf**. All these points are clear from what was set forth in the 33rd theorem of this book. Thus, whether the surfaces of the transparent bodies facing the eye are flat or spherically convex, it happens that the image of the thing seen appears larger than the thing itself. There is, however, a difference: in transparent bodies with flat surfaces, the excess in size of the image over the thing seen exists only in the appearance to the eye, due to the larger angles under which both the image and the object are seen; for otherwise, the images are in truth equal to the objects themselves. But in refraction caused by convex spherical bodies, the image is in truth larger than the object itself; and it also appears larger to the eye due to the larger angles, since in this position the image subtends a larger angle at the center of vision than the object itself does. In both cases, the parts of the images are larger than the parts of the objects proportional to them. Thus, the proposition is proven.

### 42. *Every object seen in water is perceived as larger than it truly is.*

<margin>Alhazen Book 7, Number 48.</margin>
What is proposed here is sufficiently clear from the preceding proofs; however, it was also decided to demonstrate this experimentally and to provide a specific example of the universal cause. Therefore, let a columnar body one <term>cubit</term> <note>a traditional unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips</note> in length and of some thickness be taken; let it be white, so that it can be more clearly distinguished in the water. Let its base surfaces be flat, so that it can stand evenly by itself on the surface of the horizon, the ground, or a vessel. Then, clear water should be poured into a vessel with a flat base, such that the water does not submerge the entire length of the object; let the object be stood upright on its base in the middle of the vessel in the water. Some part of it will therefore remain outside the water, because the depth of the water is less than the length of the object. When the water has settled, the part of the object inside the water will appear thicker than the part outside the water. Thus, the proposition is clear through experiment. But the same is also clear in another way. For since the convexity of the water's surface is of a spherical shape and faces the eye—and the center of the water's surface, which is the center of the universe (as we have shown elsewhere), is always beyond all those visible things perceived in water—and since water is denser than air: whether the edge of the object seen is at an equal or unequal distance from the center of the water; and whether the eye is on one of the perpendicular lines extending from any point of the object to the surface of the water, or all are outside those perpendiculars; it is always necessary, as is clear from the six preceding propositions, for the form of the object seen to appear larger than the object itself while it is inside the body of water. But perhaps if the water is very clear and shallow—such as the waters we have seen in a subterranean place in a mountain cave between the cities of Padua and Vicenza (a place called <term>Cubalus</term> <note>Likely the Grotta del Covolo di Butistone</note>), which were as bright as air—then perhaps the image of the object seen under such water might not be perceived as larger than if it were seen in air. This is because there is then no difference in the size of these things to the senses, as the density of the water adds very little to the density of the air; therefore, the sense does not distinguish the addition in size. Nevertheless, in truth, the image always becomes larger than the object itself, even if this sometimes escapes the senses. Thus, the proposition is clear; yet it is more evident in denser waters, such as hot sulfurous ones, in the viewing of which and the marvelous transformation of forms the love of this study first enticed us.

### 43. *When an object is seen through a spherical transparent body denser than air, such that the center of vision, the object, and the center of the spherical body are on the same straight line: the image of the object is perceived in a ring-like shape, much larger than the object seen.*

And if line **ako** were fixed, and we imagined the figure **kagp** revolved around the fixed line **ako**, then the arc **gp** would describe a circular figure, like a small ring <note>original: "armillam"</note>, from whose entire surface the form of line **ko** would be refracted to the sight **a**. The center of sight **a** will be the location of the image according to the 15th theorem of this book. The form of line **ko**, therefore, will be seen on the entire circular surface which is the place of refraction, and it is ring-shaped on the surface of the sphere. Thus, the form of line **ko** will appear much larger than itself, and the shape of the form will be different from the shape of **ko**. 

This, moreover, can be declared by experiment in this way. Let a crystalline or glass sphere of perfect roundness be taken, and let a small body be taken, such as black spherical wax, which is placed on the head of a needle. Let the crystalline sphere be placed opposite one of the eyes, and let the other be closed. Let the needle be raised beyond the sphere, and let the middle of the sphere be looked at. Let the wax be opposite the middle of the sphere in a straight line; a round blackness in the shape of a ring will be seen on the surface of the sphere. But if such a figure is not seen, let the wax be moved back and forth until such roundness is seen; and then let the wax be removed, and the blackness will recede. If someone brings the wax back to its prior place and position, the round, ring-like blackness will immediately return. But in these matters there is much diversity, which we leave to the study of the inquirer.

### 45. *When the center of sight is located on the diameter of a concave spherical transparent body denser than air, and the object being seen faces the convex side of that body: the image will sometimes appear smaller than the object seen, and sometimes larger, as when it is a ring-like figure.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram on the right side of the page illustrating optical refraction. It shows a circular arc representing a spherical surface. A vertical axis contains points labeled 'e', 'd' (center of the circle), and 'f'. Point 'a' represents the center of vision. Lines radiate from 'a' through the arc toward points 'b' and 'c' located at the top. The diagram maps the relationship between the object (b c) and its projected image through the lens or sphere.</image-desc>

Let the center of sight be **a**; let the line seen be **b c**; and let there be a concave spherical body of a denser <term>transparency</term> <note>original: "diaphanitatis"; referring to the material's ability to transmit light</note> than air, the center of which is **d**, and the diameter is **e d f**. Let line **b c** be outside the convex part of that body, and let the center of sight **a** be on its diameter within the concave body. I say that the image of the object seen, line **b c**, will always be smaller than the object itself. For if the center of sight **a** were at the center of the body, point **d**, it is evident through Theorem 72 of Book 1 of this work that since all the lines of extension of the forms from the points of line **b c** to the sight **a** will be perpendicular to the surface of the body (because they pass through its center), the location of the image, according to Theorem 15 of this book, will be the arc of refraction itself, and the image will appear curved and smaller than the object seen. 

But if the center of sight **a** were at any point on the radius **e d** closer to the object, or at any point on the radius **d f** further away, the lines of extension of the forms to the sight will still always intersect the <term>perpendiculars</term> <note>lines drawn at a 90-degree angle to the surface</note> drawn from the points of the object to the surface of the transparent body (from which refraction occurs) at the points of refraction themselves. That is, at the points of the arc from which refraction occurs, or around those points inside or outside the transparent body. Therefore, the image will sometimes appear curved, sometimes straight, and sometimes irregular, but always smaller than the object seen; because, as is clear, the chord or any other diameter of the image is smaller than the object seen, and every line falling between the center of sight point **a** and line **b c** is smaller than line **b c** when it falls between lines **a b** and **a c**, as can be seen from Proposition 29 of Book 1, or Proposition 4 of Book 6. 

Thus, in such an arrangement, the image is always smaller than the object itself; yet its image will sometimes be larger, as when it is of a ring-like <term>armillary</term> <note>original: "armillaris"; shaped like a bracelet or a series of rings</note> figure. For if line **b c** is positioned on the diameter **f d e**, then the refraction of the forms of points **b** and **c** will occur from any two points on one arc of the circle of the body, and the refraction of the middle points of line **b c** will occur from the middle points of that arc. And if, while line **a b c** remains fixed, one imagines that figure being rotated until it returns to the place where the motion began, a certain ring-shaped surface will be described by the arc of refraction across the entire spherical surface of the body, from which total refraction to the sight will occur. The location of the image will be in the center of sight, which, by applying the seen form to the surface of refraction itself, judges the object to be of a ring-shaped figure, as we have more fully declared in Theorem 43 of this book. The proposition is therefore clear. However, in the visible things familiar to us, nothing is perceived by the sight beyond a spherical transparent body denser than air whose concavity is on the side of the eye, unless perhaps the body is made artificially from glass, or crystal, or ice, or something similar to them. Nevertheless, the refraction that occurs to the sight from the concave surface of the heavens is similar to this, except that according to that, there is no refraction except of spherical forms, the nature and manner of which we have intended to pursue below.

### 46. *The image of the form of any object seen is shaped differently according to the shape of the surface of the body from which refraction to the sight occurs. Alhazen, Book 7, Number 35.*

For since the location of a refracted image is always at the intersection of the <term>cathetus of incidence</term> <note>original: "catheti incidentiae"; the perpendicular line dropped from the point of the object to the surface</note>—which is drawn perpendicularly from the point of the object seen to the surface of the transparent body in which the object is located—and the line through which the form reaches the sight, as is clear from Theorem 15 of this book. If, therefore, we imagine that from every point of the object seen a cathetus of incidence goes out, which is perpendicular to the surface of the body in which the object is located, then we will have a certain columnar or solid figure extending from the surface of the entire object seen to the surface of the transparent body. This figure intersects the <term>radial pyramid</term> <note>original: "pyramidem radialem"; the cone of light rays with its tip at the eye</note> according to which the refracted vision occurs (the vertex of which is at the center of sight); and the intersection of these two solid figures—namely the columnar and the pyramidal—is the location of the image of the form of the object seen. 

If, therefore, the surface of the body from which the refraction of the form of the object occurs is flat, then the imagined body containing all the perpendiculars will be similarly of a flat surface; wherefore that image will be equal to, or slightly larger than, the form of the object seen; nevertheless, it will always appear much larger than the object. But if the body from which refraction occurs is spherical, and its convex part is on the side of the sight, and the object seen is at the center of that transparent body, or between that center and the sight, then the image of the object seen will be of a pyramidal figure, since all the perpendiculars which are catheti of incidence meet at the center of the transparent body through Theorem 72 of Book 1. And this image is amplified the more it is extended toward the convex surface of the transparent body; and wherever the location of the image is between the object seen and the spherical surface of the body, the image will always be larger than the object seen. If, however, the location of the image is beyond the object seen, then the image will be narrower than the object. But if the object seen is beyond...

For in this way, they are intersected differently by the lines of the extension of the forms, and the image is varied in many forms, as is clear through the 15th and 16th theorems of this book. The cause of all these things is sufficiently clear from what has been said before. What was proposed is therefore evident.

### 47. *A single refracted image appears to both eyes of the same viewer.*

Since the refracted form of the same object—refracted from any surface of a transparent body in which that object is located—offers itself to both eyes of the same viewer, there is no difference in the viewer's sight regarding the act of seeing from simple vision, which we treated in the third and fourth books of this science. There, we said that an object is seen according to a pyramid <note>In medieval optics, a "pyramid" often refers to a cone of light rays</note> whose vertex is in the center of sight and whose base is on the surface of the object. We showed that even then, a single form is seen by both eyes. Therefore, we assume the same here for refracted forms as for forms seen directly. For if a person perceives something visible in the sky, or in water, or under glass or crystal with both eyes, and then closes one eye, they will nonetheless perceive that visible object. Therefore, the same form is perceived by both eyes together and by one eye alone. This is what was proposed; for we see nothing in such matters worthy of further delay.

### 48. *With a spherical crystal placed opposite the sun, it is possible for fire to be ignited in a combustible thing placed behind it.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the refraction of solar rays through a spherical crystal lens. A point 'a' at the top represents the sun. These rays are shown refracting inward as they enter the sphere and then exiting at points 'e' and 'f', eventually converging at a single point on the central axis 'a-b' below the sphere. Let the center of the sun be point **a**; let the crystal be placed opposite it, with its center **b**; and let a plane surface passing through both centers, **a** and **b**, cut the spherical crystal along a circle (according to the 69th theorem of Book 1), which shall be **c d e f g**. I say that if some combustible material is placed behind this crystal—so that the crystal is between the sun and the combustible thing, such as tinder <note>original: "stupam," flax-tow or kindling</note> or something similar—it is possible for fire to be ignited in that body. For imagine a ray, **a b**, spreading from the center of the sun **a** to the center of the crystal **b**. Since this ray is perpendicular to the body of the sun and the body of the crystal (by the 72nd theorem of Book 1), because it passes through the centers of both, it is clear (by the 47th theorem of Book 2) that it is not refracted but passes through the body of the crystal unrefracted. However, all the sun's rays falling on the spherical surface of the crystal parallel to the ray **a b** clearly strike it obliquely. Therefore, it is clear by the 47th theorem of Book 2 that all those rays are refracted toward the perpendicular **a b**; for each of those rays is refracted toward the perpendicular from the point of refraction to the surface of the crystal. All these perpendiculars meet with the diameter **a b** at the center of the crystal sphere. Moreover, the refraction happens toward those perpendiculars because the body of the crystal is denser than the body of air through which the rays pass before striking the crystal. And since, at an equal distance from the ray **a b**, other rays proceeding from the body of the sun strike the body of the crystal at equal angles (by the 43rd theorem of Book 1), it is clear (by the 8th theorem of this book) that they are refracted at equal angles. Imagine, therefore, the ray **a b** to be extended beyond the body of the crystal; it is clear that from every circle of the crystal opposite the entire surface of the sun, rays are refracted to a single point on the perpendicu-

For all the angles of refraction from the air to the upper surface of a single circle of the crystal (the <term>pole</term> <note>The central point or axis of the circular surface</note> of which is the point where line a b intersects the surface of the crystal) are equal; and the angles of refraction of those rays from the surface of the crystal back into the air are also equal. ### 49. *It is demonstrated instrumentally that the stars of heaven and the moon are perceived by the eyes through refraction. Alhazen, Book 7, Proposition 15.*

An <term>armillary instrument</term> <note>An astronomical device made of graduated metal rings representing the great circles of the celestial sphere</note> should be placed in an elevated location from which the eastern part of the horizon is visible, such that the ring representing the <term>meridian circle</term> <note>The circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith</note> is positioned exactly on the surface of the meridian. Its pole should be raised from the earth's surface according to the elevation of the world’s pole above the horizon of that inhabited place. At night, one of the large fixed stars should be observed; when it reaches the meridian circle, it should pass through the center of the experimenter's head or near it. Let it be considered at its rising while it is being elevated above the surface of the horizon. Then, the revolving ring should be turned around the pole of the world (which is the equinoctial pole) until it becomes equidistant from the <term>great circle</term> of heaven passing through the equinoctial poles and through the center of that star's body. Let the location of the star be confirmed from the ring so that the star's distance from the pole of the world is obtained. Next, let the star be observed until it comes to the meridian circle; let the mobile ring be moved until it is equidistant from the star's circle as before, and let it be on the surface of the meridian circle. Then, the star's distance from the pole of the world will be obtained again when the star is at the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer</note> or near it. It will be found that the distance of the star from the pole at the time of its rising and elevation is less than its distance from that same pole when it is at or near the zenith. It is clear from this that the sight perceives the forms of rising stars through refraction and not in a straight line; for any of the fixed stars always moves through the same circle among the circles equidistant from the equator, unless perhaps its position changes slightly over a very long time due to latitudinal motion, about which we shall speak more fully elsewhere. If, therefore, the sight perceived the stars directly and not through refraction, then the sight would perceive any star in its true place, and at every hour of the night, that star would appear to be at the same distance from the pole; the opposite of this happens to the sight through the instrument. The same thing happens with the moon. For if someone calculates the moon's position at an hour near its rising using <term>astronomical tables</term> <note>Reference charts used by medieval astronomers to predict the positions of celestial bodies</note>, and knows its latitude and distance from the pole, and then calculates it again for midnight, and knows its latitude and distance from the pole: if the moon's location is then found using the armillary rings at the time of its rising, there will be no discrepancy between the calculation from the tables and the experiment with the instrument. However, when finding the moon's location with the rings while it is on the meridian circle, the distance of the moon from the zenith found by the instrument will be greater when the moon's latitude is southern, and smaller when it is northern, than the true distance from the zenith found by the table calculations. It is clear, therefore, that the light of the moon does not reach the eye in a straight line but is refracted in some medium of a second transparency; for unless it were refracted, its distance from the zenith measured by the instrument and by the tables would be the same, as happens when it is on the horizon; but now it differs. The proposition is therefore evident: that all stars are seen through refraction.

### 50. *The transparency of the celestial body is rarer than the transparency of air and fire. Alhazen, Book 7, Proposition 16.*

With the armillary instrument arranged as above, the distance of one of the stars from the zenith must be found. Let the meridian circle at the place of experimentation be a b g, and let the zenith point be b, the pole of the world be point d, and the center of the world be point e. Let the radius of the meridian circle be drawn, which is e b, passing through the center of the experimenter's sight at point z. Let circle h t be equidistant from the equinoctial circle and its pole d; the pole of that circle h t will be point d according to the 68th theorem of the first book of this work, because of the equidistance of those circles. Let the distance of circle h t from point d (the pole) be that at which the star is found at the hour of the first confirmation of distance, which is at the point of its rising; let the location of the star at that hour be point h. Let there be another circle, k b g, equidistant from the equinoctial circle and also from circle h t; let its distance from the pole d be that at which the star is found at the second hour of consideration, when the star is near the zenith on the meridian circle a b g. Circle k b g will be equidistant from the pole d and very close to the zenith, or passing through point b, which is the zenith. That circle k b g, therefore, is where the slant of refraction ceases. For when the star is at the zenith at point b, or very close to it, then the sight perceives its form directly.
