...of the sphere of air through the 72nd theorem of the first book of this work: since it passes through the center of both of those spheres. Therefore, the sight, on account of the perpendicularity of the line z b over the spheres of air and heaven, will perceive a star existing on this line directly, whether the body of heaven and air are of the same <term>transparency</term> <note>The quality of allowing light to pass through; here used to compare the "thickness" of the sky and the air</note> or different: since, as was shown above by the 3rd theorem of this book, a perpendicular radial line is not refracted when entering a second transparent medium. Thus, the form of the star appearing at point b reaches the sight without any refraction through the intermediary bodies of the heavens, fire, and air (which in this context are treated as uniform, although fire is more transparent than air; and nothing from the celestial lights reaches us or our sight except through the intermediate spheres of fire and air, which in this respect act as a single sphere). Therefore, the sight will perceive a star existing at the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer</note> or near it in its true circle parallel to the equinoctial circle [the celestial equator], upon which it moved from the beginning of the night until it reached the meridian circle.

In the circle k b g, therefore, was the star in the first experimentation according to truth. Let the circle of altitude passing through the star in the first hour of experimentation be circle b h k: and let this circle intersect circle k b g at both points: namely at point k, which is in the east, and at point g directly opposite to it: and let it cut circle h t at point h, where the body of the star is seen to be at the time of the first observation. And because the distance of the star from the pole of the world according to the sight was smaller in the first experimentation than in the second: it is clear that circle h t is closer to the pole d than circle k b g: thus point h of the circle of altitude (which is b h k) is closer to the zenith b itself than point k. Let two lines h z and k z be drawn to the center of sight z.

Because, therefore, the star is perceived by the sight in the first hour of experimentation at a point of circle h t, and at that time it was on the surface of circle b h k—and yet the star was in that hour, according to truth, on the circumference of circle k b g—it is necessarily required that the star in that hour was, according to truth, at the point common to those two circles, k b g and b h k, which is point k above the earth. However, it is perceived by the sight at point h through line z h, because the form of the star reaches the sight in the straight line h z, while the line which is between the star and the sight according to truth is line k z. It is clear, therefore, that the sight does not perceive the star which is at point k directly; it perceives it, therefore, by refraction. 

And because refraction cannot occur within the celestial body itself due to the homogeneity of its transparency, it must occur at some point in the body adjacent to it. Let the place of refraction made in the medium of the second transparent body (which is air or fire) be point m: and let line k m be drawn: and let a straight line be extended from point m to point z, the center of sight. Therefore, because the form of the star extends from the star through line k m, and is refracted to the sight through line k m z—and since forms are only refracted when they encounter a body of different transparency, as we showed in the second book of this work and in the preceding propositions of this book—it follows that the celestial body in which the star is located is of a different transparency from the transparency of air or fire. 

And because the place of refraction is at the surface passing between two bodies differing in transparency, as is clear from theorem 4: point m is therefore in the <term>concavity of the heavens</term> <note>The inner boundary of the celestial sphere where it meets the atmosphere</note>. And if line e m is produced, this will be in truth the radius of the sphere of heaven, the concavity of which touches the convexity of the fire itself. It is therefore perpendicular to the concave surface of the heaven (which touches the air or fire) and to the convex surface of the air or fire. And because the form of the star, extended in the celestial body through line k m, is refracted in the air toward the sight through line m z, the line k m, if extended beyond point m, would cut line z m and move away from point e, the center of the world. Therefore, because it falls obliquely on the concave surface of the heaven itself, it is clear that this refraction is toward the side where the perpendicular e m is, which passes through the point of refraction perpendicularly over the convex surface of the air. And since in neither the heaven nor the air is there any dense, polished body from which reflection can occur (as from a mirror), it is clear that this variation happens because of the refraction of the form in the medium of the second transparent body. Therefore, the body of air is denser than the body of heaven, as is clear from theorem 4 of this book. And this is what was proposed.

### 51. The diameters of all stars and the lines determining the distances of any two stars existing at or around the zenith are perceived as smaller through refraction than if they were seen directly. *Alhazen, book 7, number 52.*

In the same way, it can be shown that $gz$ is perpendicular to the surface of the heaven, falling on point $z$. Therefore, point $m$ will be between the two lines $tb$ and $tk$. For if point $m$ were beyond line $tk$, then the perpendicular going out from point $g$ to point $m$ would also be beyond point $k$; and thus, when the form of point $k$ was refracted to the sight from point $m$, it would be refracted toward the side of the perpendicular $mg$ and would not reach the perpendicular $ge$; therefore, it would not reach the sight at $t$. It is clear, then, that point $m$ is between the two lines $tk$ and $tlb$; and in the same way, it can be declared that point $z$ is between the two lines $tb$ and $tl$. Let line $tm$ be extended to point $q$ of the meridian circle, and line $tz$ to point $r$ of the same meridian circle. Thus, arc $qk$ will be equal to arc $lr$, and angle $qtr$ will be smaller than angle $ktl$, because it is a part of it. But angle $qtr$ is the angle through which the sight at $t$ perceives arc $kl$ by refraction, and angle $ktl$ is the angle through which the sight at $t$ would perceive arc $kl$ directly—if it could perceive it directly. But the distance of arc $kl$ from the sight is very great; for which reason its quantity is not perceived with certainty.

Thus, the sight accepts the distance of arc $kl$ through estimation, not through certainty; but the estimation of the sight when it perceives something by refraction does not differ from its estimation when it perceives something directly, except in this alone: that it thinks it perceives directly when it is actually perceiving by refraction. Therefore, the sight at $t$ perceives arc $kl$ by refraction from a smaller angle than that angle by which it perceives it directly, and according to a comparison to that same distance to which it would compare it if it were perceiving it directly. But the sight at $t$ perceives magnitude from the quantity of the angle with respect to the distance of point $t$ (which is the center of the sight) from the surface of the thing seen, according to the 27th theorem of the 4th book of this work. Therefore, it perceives the quantity of arc $kl$ by refraction as smaller than if it perceived it directly.

And if the figure in which points $k, l, t, b$ are located is imagined to be rotated while line $tb$ remains immobile, a circle will be described intersecting the meridian circle at two points; the pole of this circle will be point $b$, the <term>zenith</term> <note>the point directly overhead</note> of the head. All angles at the sight $t$ contained by two lines similar to lines $tk$ and $tl$ will be equal to one another, each to its counterpart. Therefore, the sight at $t$ will perceive the form of arc $kl$ by refraction in every position with respect to the meridian circle, when it is at the summit of the head, as smaller than if it perceived it directly. And if line $tb$ bisects arc $kl$ into two equal parts, then the two points $q$ and $r$ will be between the two points $k$ and $l$. Angle $qtr$ will be smaller than angle $ktl$, and every angle equal to angle $qtr$ starting from point $t$ and cutting through a star will be smaller. The line going out from the center of the sight $t$ in the surface of that circle will cut the major circle of that star, and its quantity is perceived as smaller than it truly is; and thus the whole star will be seen as smaller than it is.

Therefore, every star is seen as smaller when it is at the zenith of the head than if it were seen directly. And it is the same for every distance between any two stars when the zenith is between the two extremities of that distance; for it will be perceived in all its positions as smaller than if it were perceived directly without refraction. Thus, every star located at the summit of the observer's head is seen as smaller than in any other place in the heaven; and the more it is removed from the summit of the head, the larger it always appears; thus, at the horizon, it appears larger than in any other place. This is common to all stars—namely, planets and fixed stars—that at the zenith or near it they are always smaller. This similarly appears in the lines determining the distances of stars: that is, in the distances of the stars themselves, such as the spaces of the sky that are between the stars, even more so than in the quantities of the stars themselves. For the quantity of a star, as far as the sight is concerned, is a small thing, and the increase of its quantity is a small thing, but the diversity and increase of distances is more easily perceived. The proposition is therefore clear.

### 53. *The diameters of stars or the lines determining the distance of stars, when positioned in some altitude circle erect above the horizon, appear smaller through refraction than if they were seen directly.*

Let the arrangement remain as above: and let the diameter of some star or the distance of any two stars be line $d e$, which is erect in some circle of altitude passing through the zenith of the head, which is point $b$; let this circle of altitude be $b d e$. Let the common section of the surface of circle $b d e$ and the surface of the concavity of the lowest celestial sphere be circle $g h z$ by the 69th theorem of the 1st book. Let lines $a d$ and $a e$ be drawn, and let the form of point $d$ be refracted to the sight at $a$ from point $h$, and the form of point $e$ from point $z$. Let lines $d h$ be joined and extended beyond point $h$ to point $n$, and $e z$ extended beyond point $z$ to point $o$. It is therefore clear, as in the previous theorem, that point $h$ is higher than line $a d$, and that point $z$ is higher than line $a e$. Thus, let lines $a h, h d, a z, z e, m h,$ and $m z$ be drawn. Let line $m h$ be extended beyond point $h$ to the circle of altitude at point $t$, and line $m z$ beyond point $z$ to point $k$. Therefore, the refracted angle created by the refraction of the form of point $e$ to the sight at $a$ (which is angle $a z m$) will be very small (since line $a m$, which is the semi-diameter of the earth, is of no sensible quantity compared to such a great distance, as we have declared elsewhere in the <term>science of celestial motions</term> <note>meaning astronomy/astrophysics</note>), and its angle of refraction will be small, following the manner of that angle $a z m$. Since air is denser than the celestial body, as is clear by the 50th theorem of this book, it is evident by the 4th theorem that refraction occurs toward the perpendicular, which is $z m$. Therefore, by the 8th theorem, angle $e z k$ will be acute, and similarly angle $d h t$ will be acute. Therefore, each of the angles $a h d$ and $a z e$ will be obtuse by the 13th proposition of Book 1. Thus, point $z$ will either be on the surface of the horizon or higher. If it is on the surface of the horizon, it will be at the extremity of a perpendicular emerging from the center of sight, which is $a$, upon line $b a$ standing perpendicularly to the surface of the horizon, which perpendicular is imagined to be drawn on the surface of the horizon; or if it is higher than the horizon, it will be higher than that perpendicular line; and point $h$ will always be higher than point $z$. In triangle $hmp$, therefore, the two angles $mhp$ and $mph$ are equal according to Proposition 5 of Book 1 <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements, which Witelo uses as his mathematical foundation.</note>. But in triangle $hap$, the side $ap$ is greater than side $ah$ because it is greater than side $aq$ according to Proposition 7 of Book 3. Therefore, according to Proposition 19 of Book 1, angle $ahp$ is greater than angle $hpa$. There remains, therefore, angle $apm$ which is greater than angle $ahm$. However, by Proposition 4 of Book 1, angle $apm$ is equal to angle $azm$; thus, angle $ahm$ is smaller than angle $azm$.

Therefore, line $ht$ is equal to line $zk$, since they are the remainders of equal lines after equal parts have been taken away. Therefore, line $hd$ marks off a smaller arc from the larger circle (containing triangle $ahd$) than the similar arc which line $ze$ cuts from the smaller circle (containing triangle $aez$). Consequently, angle $had$ is smaller than angle $zae$. Let angle $zad$ be common to both angles; then angle $haz$ will be smaller than angle $dae$. Angle $haz$ is the angle by which the sight at $a$ perceives line $de$ through refraction, and angle $dae$ is the angle by which the form of line $de$ would be perceived directly (if such a thing were possible). Thus, the sight at $a$ perceives line $de$ through refraction as smaller than it would directly, according to Theorem 20 of Book 4, because it perceives it under a larger angle directly than through refraction. The proposition is therefore clear.

### § 4. All stars appear round: they appear larger on the horizon than in the middle of the sky, unless the opposite occasionally happens due to vapors coming between the sights and the stars. *Alhazen, Book 7, Section 55.* <note>Refers to the "Optics" of Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen.</note>

All stars are perceived as round, because both of their diameters—namely, their length and width—are perceived as equally smaller than if they were perceived directly. Thus, any of their inclined diameters is perceived as equally smaller through refraction than if it were seen directly. Therefore, a star is perceived as round in any position. Furthermore, all stars are perceived as smaller through refraction than if they were seen directly, because their diameters are perceived as smaller, as is clear from the preceding propositions.

This holds true regarding the refraction that occurs in the middle of the second transparent medium <note>original: "diaphani"; refers to the atmosphere</note>, which is the air—a medium denser than the heavens according to Proposition 50 of this book. Thus, at the concave surface of the heavens, refraction occurs toward the perpendicular line extending from the point of refraction upon that surface; this is toward the line that is the semidiameter of the world, according to Proposition 4 of this book. 

The variation in refraction, however, which occurs according to the distance of the stars from the pole of the world, is found to be small, because those angles of refraction are small. Hence, the perceived size of the stars does not change significantly because of them. But the magnitude of the stars and the size of the distance between them differ greatly when they are at the horizon compared to when they are near the zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note> or in the middle of the sky, due to the sensible difference in their refraction. 

This is a "perpetual error" <note>An optical illusion that is constant and predictable</note> because its cause is perpetual: namely, the greater rarity of the celestial body compared to the rarity of the air. It happens, however, that stars sometimes appear larger at one time than another, such as when a thick vapor <note>e.g., fog, mist, or heavy humidity</note> is between the sight and the stars. In that case, because of the refraction of the lines extending the forms of the stars in that vapor—refraction which occurs away from the perpendicular—the form meets the eye in a more dispersed manner and the forms of the stars are seen under larger angles. 

This is just like what happens with a penny <note>original: "denario"; a Roman silver coin</note> seen under water, which appears larger than if it were seen in the air. This kind of perceived size of the stars happens most of all when the stars are at the horizon or near it. Thus, the two refractions following the first one (which occurs at the concave surface of the heaven itself and happens in every sighting of a star) create new changes in how the stars are seen. For when that thick vapor is at or near the horizon and does not continue all the way to the middle of the sky, it will be a portion of a certain sphere concentric to the world, and its surface facing the sight will be flat. Because of this, the forms or distances of the stars located beyond that vapor will appear larger than if they were seen without that vapor. For in that location of the heaven's concavity where the star's form is refracted to the sight, the form of the star exists and extends from there to the sight, provided no thick vapor intervenes. But if a thick vapor [is placed] between the sights and the stars...

# BOOK TEN.

If vapor comes between the stars and the eye, then the form of the star is extended to the uppermost surface of the vapor and is refracted there toward the perpendicular. Then it is extended to the lowest surface of the vapor and is refracted from there into the pure air containing the sight. This second refraction occurs away from the perpendicular that emerges from the point of refraction on the flat surface of the vapor. In this way, the size of a star and the distance between stars appear larger than if they were seen only after the refraction that occurs at the concave boundary of the heavens and the uppermost element <note>Refers to the sphere of fire or the upper atmosphere.</note>, with no refraction occurring at the surface where the vapor meets the air below it—the air being a rarer medium containing the sight itself, situated beneath the denser body of vapor.

However, the reason why—even when all intervening vapor is excluded—the size of a star and the distances between stars appear larger at the horizon than in the middle of the sky or near it, is greatly aided by the **estimation of the viewer**. This is because the viewer estimates that the stars are further from the sight at the horizon than in the middle of the sky. The viewer perceives the part of the sky that is near the **zenith** <note>The point directly overhead.</note> to be closer than the part at the horizon, as we demonstrated in Proposition 13 of Book 4 of this work.

Therefore, the sight perceives the size of a star and the size of the distance between stars when they are at or near the horizon by comparing the angle under which the vision occurs to that far distance. But when they are in the middle of the sky or near it, the sight perceives their size by comparing an angle that is equal (or nearly equal) to the first one to a closer distance—and there is a perceived maximum difference between this distance and the distance of the horizon. Thus, the mind judges the size of the stars in the same way it judges the size of blurred visible objects. For things that are seen at a greater distance under the same angle as other closer things are judged by viewers to be larger, as we showed in Book 4.

This cause of the stars' appearance is perpetual and unchanging, common to all viewers. The same thing happens to viewers in the perception of the distances between the stars themselves; for the forms of these distances do not vary in the sight at different times, but are always the same. The sight compares these distances to the distances of familiar things that are very far from the eye upon the surface of the earth. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 55. Twinkling always happens to all fixed stars because of the divergence of the form in the location of the image, occurring from the motion of the underlying body.

As is clear from the preceding five theorems, the location of the image of any star's form will be in the convex of the air or fire beneath the concave of the lowest heaven which contains the fire. Any of these elements is mobile by its own nature in a straight motion—namely, upward because of the lightness within them—and is also moved accidentally in a circular motion along with the daily motion of the heaven. Because of this, the form of the stars falling upon them must necessarily diverge and be distracted, just as the form itself seems to change location somewhat because of the motion of the body in which it is seen. 

There is no difference in this whether the light of the stars is spread by itself, or whether this happens because of the reflection of solar light from the stars. For light spread by itself from a luminous body, as well as light spread from other bodies (when seen through refraction), always becomes weaker according to Proposition 10 of this book. Therefore, when the image is located in a body moving with various motions, or one strong motion, that weakened form must necessarily appear diverged and distracted because of the motion of the underlying body in which it is seen; thus, in these cases, the reflection of light is not the cause.

A similar thing happens in fast-running water: the forms of stars reflected from its surface appear to twinkle more than when seen refracted through the air in the place of their image. Because of the motion of the water, the reflected form is distracted and the location of the reflected image is changed; because of this, the forms of the stars seem to move more, and therefore they appear to twinkle more intensely. Similarly, the forms of stars in the location of their image twinkle more during windy times because of the greater motion of the medium.

In the **planets** <note>In medieval astronomy, planets were "wandering stars" (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) as opposed to the "fixed stars."</note>, however, twinkling does not always happen. Although they might twinkle more [in certain conditions] and have the same image location, and their forms are weakened by refraction, they do not suffer much weakness because of their proximity to us viewers; for the refraction in them is smaller according to Proposition 14 of this book. Therefore, their forms reach the sight strongly. Thus, they penetrate the location of their image steadily and without any divergence, even though the underlying body moves—unless perhaps a body thicker than air is interposed between the sight and the forms of the planets, such as thick water vapor. In that case, because of the unsteady motion of that vapor (especially when agitated by winds), the forms of the planets reach the sight as if twinkling.

For this same reason, we sometimes see the sun itself twinkling in the morning when it is visible at its rising, according to the resolution of the **visual spirits** <note>original: "spirituum visibilium". In medieval science, visual spirits were a subtle fluid or pneuma that traveled from the brain to the eyes to enable sight.</note>. Because of the resolution and motion of these spirits, the sun always seems to twinkle for a while when looked at, and its form seems to move. This is because the form is received in the moving spirits which, because of the overwhelming power of the light, are thinned out beyond their natural consistency when they are at the point of being exhausted by the act of seeing. Thus they move with a motion that is unnatural and unusual to them, becoming the cause of the motion of the seen form; and then the form of the seen thing appears to twinkle. 

This also happens when a strong reflection of light from polished bodies hits the sight; for then, because of the disproportion of that light to the visual spirits, a motion of those spirits occurs, and the forms of those bodies appear twinkling and moved because they are received in a disturbed body <note>Referring to the physical state of the eye.</note>. Thus, twinkling always happens to all fixed stars because the cause is perpetual: namely, the divergence of their form in the location of the image, happening from the motion of the underlying body. In planets, however, twinkling happens only rarely, because its cause occurs only rarely. In the forms of other bodies whose excellence <note>i.e., extreme brightness.</note> corrupts the sense, it is not properly "twinkling," whether that corruption happens through the simple emission of light or through reflection from polished bodies; for that twinkling does not happen to the sense when it is in its proper disposition, but when it is at the point of its own breakdown. For if everything seems to move for those who have the form of a moved thing in their eyes, or who are themselves moving, because of the motion of the spirits running about without the guidance of the soul, we do not say for that reason that the forms of all things twinkle. The proposition is therefore clear. And because, according to the aforementioned modes of refraction, the impressions of the lowest and high...

# VITELLO'S OPTICS

...we have finished discussing [these matters]: it remains for us to briefly treat the refractions that occur in intermediate bodies, such as those encountered in the middle of vapors.

### 56. *It is impossible for light to become more perceptible in a non-luminous body than in the surrounding medium, unless the rays of the luminous body are gathered together.*

The point proposed here is evident: because when light is spread through some part of a medium, the extension of the ray will be uniform along a straight line (according to Book 2, Theorem 1 of this work). Therefore, if the rays are not gathered together <note>original: "aggregatis"; refers to the concentration or convergence of light rays into a smaller area</note> in some body that the rays of light encounter, the light will not be more perceptible in that body than it was in any other part of the medium through which it was carried in a straight line. Indeed, if light is spread equally through one body and another, it will not be felt more in one than in the other (provided all other visual circumstances and distances are equal), unless some change occurs in the light itself. But if a change occurs in the rays of light with respect to different bodies (as shown in Book 5, Theorem 4), then in that body where the rays are more scattered, less light appears. Therefore, if more light appears in a certain body, it is necessary that the rays are more concentrated in that body. It is clear, then, that if the rays of a luminous body are not gathered together in a non-luminous body more than in the medium, it is impossible for the light to become more perceptible in that body than it is in the middle of a single <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphani"; a substance like air, water, or glass that allows light to pass through</note>. From this it follows that if rays are gathered more in some body than in the medium, the light will appear more perceptible in that body than in the medium, and the light will seem to intensify according to the amount the rays are gathered.

### 57. *It is evident that the rays of a luminous body are gathered together through reflection or refraction.*

This is clear from the following. When a ray is rebounded or reflected from a body, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (by Book 5, Theorem 20), and the incident and reflected rays are in the same plane (by Book 5, Theorem 27). Therefore, in that same plane, two rays incident at equal angles are reflected and united so that they become one. Thus they are gathered together because two occupy one place—or more truly, they become one. For example, let there be a single plane of reflection, *a b c*, and let two rays from different parts of the diameter of a luminous body fall upon it (namely from *a* and *c*) to a single point of the body from which reflection occurs (let this be point *b*), and let the angles of incidence be equal. If a line is drawn from point *b* in said plane to each side—which is the intersection of the plane of reflection and the surface of the reflecting body (let this be *d b e*)—then the angle of incidence *a b d* will be equal to the angle of reflection *c b e* (by Book 5, Theorem 20). But the reflection of ray *c b* also occurs according to the angle of incidence *c b e*. Therefore, the reflected ray *b a* and the incident ray *b [c]* are made into one ray, and the reflected ray *b c* and the incident ray *a b* are made into one. This is how it is for all other rays that fall according to a pyramid <note>Vitello uses "pyramid" to describe what we would call a "cone" of light rays</note> whose point is at some spot on the reflecting body and whose base is on the luminous body.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the law of reflection. A horizontal line segment represents a reflective surface, with its endpoints labeled 'd' (left) and 'e' (right). A central point on this line is labeled 'b'. Two rays descend from above, originating at points 'a' (top left) and 'c' (top right), both converging at point 'b'. A small 'v' or angle mark is located at the vertex at point 'b'.</image-desc>

It is clear, then, that at the very least all those rays are doubled upon themselves. Since these rays are infinite (being existing only in potential within a continuum), and there are as many such pyramids as there are points on the reflecting body, it is clear that they are gathered by reflection. But it can also be shown through practical experience that light is gathered by refraction in the middle of a second transparent medium. For it has been shown that in the middle of a second transparent medium denser than air, there is always a gathering of rays on the side opposite the surface of incidence—indeed, they converge at a single point where they generate light and heat. Furthermore, they can even cause fire in a flammable body where they remain, as is clear from Book 10, Theorem 48 of this work. Refraction, therefore, generates light because it unites the rays. Even at the surface where refraction occurs, the incident ray and the refracted ray (which would have been a single line if they continued through a single medium) form an angle of refraction within the depths of the denser transparent body. According to Book 2, Theorem 46, these rays are in one plane called the "plane of refraction," which is always perpendicular to the surface of the body where refraction happens (by Theorem 2). Thus, all such rays, falling upon themselves in this way, are brought closer and gathered when they are refracted, with the angle of refraction varying relative to the angle of incidence depending on the nature of the second medium. For in a thicker or denser medium, a ray that is not perpendicular is weakened more; thus it is refracted more strongly toward the perpendicular and falls at a closer point on the axis. The angle thus becomes sharper than its angle of incidence, compared to what it would be if the ray had entered a thinner medium at that same point. Because of this—since the angle formed by all refracted rays with the line that is the intersection of the plane of refraction and the surface of the body is smaller in denser transparent bodies than in less dense ones—it is clear that rays are gathered more in denser bodies (by Book 2, Theorem 8). Sometimes this gathering of rays occurs because of the reflection of light to a single mathematical or physical point, as we showed in the ninth book of this science regarding <term>burning mirrors</term> <note>mirrors designed to focus sunlight to a single point to start fires</note>, and in other books where such things were discussed. This gathering also happens sometimes through refraction, since rays incident at equal angles are refracted at equal angles (by Book 2, Theorem 8) and sometimes converge at a single point (by Book 10, Theorem 48). In such cases, the reflected and refracted rays always double themselves in some part of the medium, thereby creating a greater light. When the rays are gathered by refraction, as is clear from what has been said, then light is generated for a viewer located at the place where they are gathered. And since in a body...

# BOOK TEN

In transparent <note>original: "diaphanis"; referring to materials like glass, water, or crystal that allow light to pass through</note> bodies having smooth surfaces, which are denser than air, the light falling upon them is reflected because of the smoothness of the surface, as we showed through Theorem 5 of Book 1. It is then clear that light is gathered together because of this reflection. Furthermore, because there is a refraction <note>original: "refractio"; the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another of different density</note> of light toward the perpendicular line inside these bodies—due to the different density of the transparent medium, as seen in Theorem 4 of this book—the visibility of the light is strengthened at the boundary of every refracting surface. This happens because the rays are brought close to each other due to the acute angle of refraction. 

Therefore, when the surfaces of such bodies are smooth, such as those polished by nature, then even though refraction occurs within them, reflection of the rays also occurs from their surface, albeit weakly. Because of these two concurrent causes, light is gathered on the surface of such bodies, and the bodies appear very luminous; indeed, the denser they are, the more luminous they appear. There are no other ways for rays to be gathered except through reflection and refraction; for if any other modes appear, they are fundamentally reduced to these primary two. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### *58. Without the opposition of a body denser than the medium through which the rays of a luminous body are currently passing, it is impossible for reflection, refraction, or greater visibility of those rays to occur.*

This is evident from the following: since the rays of any radiant body are always luminous and uniform in themselves, if the medium through which they are carried is uniform, they will never be reflected or refracted. Instead, they will always be carried in a continuous and straight line, as shown by Theorem 2 of Book 1. Nor will the light be gathered together (on account of their dispersion) in a way that overcomes the light received in the eye of the viewer from the equal diffusion of light. No reflection will occur toward the sight, nor refraction toward the side opposite the axis of the visual pyramid, nor will the light or the visibility of the light be made greater. The proposition is therefore clear: without the opposition of a body denser than the first medium through which the ray of a luminous body is carried, it is not possible for reflection or refraction of those rays to occur, since every reflection or refraction always happens because of such bodies, as has been maintained from the preceding points.

There remains, therefore, angle $h k b$ as 71 degrees, 13 minutes, and 56 seconds. But angle $e k b$ is 90 degrees, since it is a right angle. There remains, therefore, angle $e k h$ as 18 degrees, 46 minutes, and 4 seconds. And since line $q e$ is equal to line $q h$ through Theorem 38 of Book 1 of this work (since they are drawn from a single point touching the same circle), the angle $q k e$ will be equal to angle $q k h$ through [Proposition] 8 of Book 1. Therefore, angle $q k e$ will be 9 degrees, 23 minutes, and 2 seconds.

And since angle $q e k$ is a right angle through [Proposition] 18 of Book 3, angle $k q e$ will be the complement of one right angle through [Proposition] 32 of Book 1—that is, 80 degrees, 36 minutes, and 58 seconds, where four right angles equal 360 degrees. And according to a system where two right angles equal 360 degrees, angle $k q e$ will be 161 degrees, 13 minutes, and 56 seconds. With a circle circumscribed around the triangle $q e k$, the arc subtended by line $k e$ will be 161 degrees, 13 minutes, and 56 seconds. Therefore, its chord <term>chord: a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc</term>, which is line $k e$, will be 118 parts, 23 minutes, 20 seconds, and 18 thirds, according to the measurement where the diameter $q k$ is 120 parts. And according to the measurement where the diameter $q k$ is 60, the chord $k e$ will be 59 parts, 11 minutes, 40 seconds, and 9 thirds. Therefore, according to the measurement where line $k e$ is 60, line $k q$ will be 60 parts, 48 minutes, and 50 seconds.

Taking away from line $k q$ the 60 parts which is the length of line $k r$, the semi-diameter of the earth, there remains line $r q$ (which is the height of the elevated vapors) as 48 minutes and 50 seconds, according to that measurement where the diameter of the earth is 120 parts. And since, according to cosmographers, the greatest circle of the earth is known in miles, the quantity of the diameter is therefore known. Thus, line $r q$ is also known. And this is what was proposed. According to the computation of Abbomadi <note>original: "Abbomadi"; likely referring to the mathematician Al-Mahani or a related Arabic source used by Alhazen</note> based on miles (by which the circumference of the earth is 24,000 miles), line $r q$ is 51 miles, 47 minutes, 14 seconds, and approximately 31 thirds. Therefore, the highest point to which vapors are elevated according to their consistency is less than 52,000 paces <note>approximately 52 miles</note>, as can be clear to one who investigates.

### 61. It is manifest that the reflection of rays from a luminous body occurs from water, dense air, and dewy vapor.

This is discovered by the senses in polished bodies (such as mirrors and the like), and we have pursued this with great diligence in several of the preceding books of this science. In water exposed to the sun, the same is clear: because a ray is seen in the part opposite the sun, especially if the opposite place is dark; this happens through reflection. The same occurs in somewhat denser air, such as when it is thickened and consistent like a cloud; for then a reflection of light occurs from it, as appears in the evening and morning twilights. It is also attested by the fact that in rainy weather, the sun's rays are often dispersed in the air and barely reach the earth thinly because of the moisture and thickness of the air placed against the sun. 

This is also clear because in air of moderate density in winter, especially when the south wind <note>original: "austro"</note> is blowing, light is frequently seen to be reflected around lamps in a circular form. This happens especially to "moist eyes" <note>original: "visibus humidis"; a medieval medical concept suggesting eyes with excess humors are more prone to seeing reflections or halos</note>, to which the reflection of light and forms occurs easily, since the visual power is weakened due to the weakness of the organ. Thus, it cannot penetrate the moderate density of the air, but the form of the seen object is reflected to it from the moderately dense air, just as light is reflected to strong eyes only from some solid object lacking transparency. 

Hence, someone with weakened sight who does not see sharply, perhaps due to ophthalmia or something else, sometimes sees his own image in the thick air before him, as if in a mirror, standing opposite him and walking with him when he walks, and looking back at him. Thus, an acquaintance of mine, after staying awake for many nights, when he was riding in a daze the following night, saw his own form—that is, another man riding with him—

saw, while crossing a certain body of water where the air was thick, that when he stopped, another figure stopped as well, performing all his actions. When that acquaintance of mine reached clear air, his companion disappeared, for it was nothing but his own form <note>This is a description of a "specter of the Brocken" or a similar mirage effect where a person's shadow is cast onto mist</note>. Thus, an error occurs to a weak sight. This is not surprising, for this sometimes happens even to healthy eyes due to thick air at a great distance. Just as with the help of mirrors (as we showed in Theorem 60 of this Book 7), it could happen that someone sees their own image, or another, not in the mirror but outside the mirror in the air, in the place of the image, which could be deliberately shifted to a specific location. Also, in **dewy vapor** <term>dewy vapor: *vapor roridus*, referring to mist, fog, or air saturated with water droplets</term>, a reverberation of light occurs when the aqueous vapor begins to dissolve into drops; for each of its parts becomes like a mirror, and because of this, light is reflected from it. This is apparent in water scattered drop by drop, since light is reflected from it even to the opposite side, although it is colored after the reflection. Thus, the proposition is clear.

*62. It is evident that refraction occurs toward the perpendicular from the surface of water, dense air, dewy vapor, and similar media.*

What is proposed to be declared here is clear through [Theorem] 4 of this book, but it is also proven by experiments, and this is universal. When the form of a thing or a ray proceeds through a rarer <note>original: "rarius"; meaning less dense</note> medium to a denser transparent medium, then refraction always occurs toward the **perpendicular** <term>perpendicular: the "normal" line, an imaginary line at a right angle to the surface</term> in the second transparent medium. For example, if water in a vessel is exposed to the sun, the rays will be seen to gather at the bottom of the vessel. Also, when the sun shines through dense air placed between the sight and the sun, the light is sometimes gathered and greater heat reaches us, although a large part of the light is reflected upwards to the nearby clouds. This happens most often in the time preceding rain; hence, after such heat disproportionate to the season and unusual light, rain very often falls. From this it is clear that, because a cloud is resolved into dewy vapor, refraction of rays occurs in that dewy vapor, and the rays of the sun reach us gathered by refraction. It is therefore clear that in water, dense air, and dewy vapor—when the form or light is in a rarer transparent medium and falls upon those denser transparent media—the transparent medium in which the sight is located differs greatly from the transparent medium by which refraction occurs; then a sensible refraction toward the perpendicular will happen. But if the form or light is in a denser transparent medium, or is seen through a denser medium, then refraction will occur **away from the perpendicular**. Because of this, all such things appear larger than their true size to the sight, as is clear through [Theorem] 42 of this book. For this reason, it happens that the tops of things seen in the sea appear refracted, because their form is dispersed away from the perpendicular in the second, thinner medium—namely, in the air—and their forms are seen at the intersection of the line of refraction with the perpendicular drawn from the object seen to the surface of the water, as is clear through Theorem 15 of this book. Also, a coin placed in a vessel under water is seen at a distance at which the sight could not see the coin directly without the water, due to the height of the vessel's rim; and then it even appears larger, since it is seen under a larger angle. In dense air also, such as when the **East winds** <note>original: "euri"; the SE or East wind, often associated with dampness</note> blow and the air is humid and thickened, the sizes of all things appear larger. The sun also, and all the rising and setting stars, appear larger than when they are in the middle of the sky, due to the gloom and the air thickened by the vapors of the earth placed between them and the eyes, as is clear through [Theorem] 54 of this book. This is a temporary cause; but there is another perpetual one, which we mentioned in the same place. From this it also follows that if clear glass or crystal is placed at the location of an image, or between the image and the sight, so that the image reflected from a mirror to a certain place in the air is seen through the glass, then the image will appear larger. According to how the transparent media are multiplied from denser to rarer, the form approaches the eyes so that it is finally seen through the air; the reason for this is clear from several preceding theorems of this book. Therefore, in all these intermediate bodies so disposed, refraction occurs away from the perpendicular drawn from the center of the thing seen to the surface of the transparent body containing the thing itself or the refracted form. In these ways, therefore, refraction occurs to the sight in the proposed bodies or those similar to them. Among these, however, it occurs most in water; but it occurs even more in dewy vapor beginning to become water than in the air. Nor is this surprising, because dewy vapor (which occurs at the time of the transformation of clouds from continuous vapor into water scattered drop by drop) is thicker than air; hence the refraction made in it is felt more. However, the figure of the thing seen, whose form is refracted, cannot reach the sight distinctly because of the multitude of refractions. Instead, only some form of the thing reaches the sight; just as it is also clear that in mirrors of small parts, or of broken surfaces raised one above the other—even if the protrusions are slight—provided that the surfaces of these mirrors are not in the same straight or curved line, then the proper size or figure of the thing does not appear, but only the color of the thing seen appears, whose form is reflected by them. By this it is clearly evident that the form of a luminous body, which is reflected to the sight by water or thick air as a whole (that is, as to figure and light or color), is reflected by dewy vapor without a certain figure or size, but only with its color or light. And so, when the reflection of solar or stellar light to the sight occurs from dewy vapor, the proper figures of the reflected forms are not seen, but only the forms of the reflected light. Thus the proposition is clear.

*63. It is possible for the irradiation of any spherical luminous body... to occur according to a round pyramid, whose base is in the irradiated body, and whose vertex is in the center of the luminous body. From this it is clear that all irradiation of this kind occurs according to equal angles of incidence.* <note>The "round pyramid" described here is what modern geometry calls a cone.</note>

Let there be a spherical luminous body, in which there is a great circle *b c d*; and let its center be the point...

# BOOK TEN

Even if it happens that there is a flat surface, let it be *s* at point *c*; and let the surface of the body to be illuminated by a spherical body be surface *g*, which is, by hypothesis, parallel to surface *s-p*; and let the line *a-c-g* be drawn from the center of the spherical body perpendicular to the surface of said body. I say that it is possible for the radiation of that body to be formed according to a **round pyramid** <term>round pyramid: what we would today call a cone</term>, whose base is on the surface of body *g*, and whose vertex is at point *a*, the center of the luminous body. For if the perpendicular *a-g* does not fall in the center or in the middle of surface *g*, let a line *a-f* be drawn to the shorter edge of that surface *g*. At its endpoint at point *a*, let an angle be constructed (according to Proposition 23 of Book 1 <note>original: "ex 23 p 1"; referring to Euclid’s *Elements*</note>) equal to angle *g-a-f*, which shall be *g-a-h*. Let line *a-h* be extended to surface *g*, and let lines *g-f* and *g-h* be drawn on surface *g*. And since the angles *a-g-f* and *a-g-h* of the two triangles *a-g-f* and *a-g-h*, which are at the base, are equal by the definition of a line erected upon a surface, and angles *g-a-f* and *g-a-h* are equal, and side *a-g* is common to both: it is clear from Proposition 26 of Book 1 <note>Euclid's *Elements*</note> that side *a-f* will be equal to side *a-h*, and *f-g* equal to *g-h*. Similarly, by making another angle equal to angles *g-a-f* and *g-a-h* of triangles *a-g-f* and *a-g-h*, let it be *g-a-k*. When lines *a-k* and *g-k* are drawn, it will be, as in the preceding steps, that line *a-k* is equal to line *a-f* or *a-h*, and line *g-k* will be equal to line *g-f* or *g-h*. Therefore, since three equal lines depart from point *g* and lie on the same surface, it is clear from Proposition 9 of Book 3 <note>Euclid's *Elements*</note> that the line *f-h-k*, produced from point *g* according to the quantity of line *g-f*, is circular.

->![A geometric diagram illustrating the optics of light radiation from a spherical body. At the top, a circle representing a light source has its center labeled 'a' and points 'b' and 'd' on its circumference. A horizontal line 's-p' is positioned below it, with point 'c' at the intersection of a vertical perpendicular line from 'a'. Further down, a surface 'g' receives the radiation. Because, therefore, the radiation occurs according to these lines—namely *a-f*, *a-h*, *a-k*—and according to all other drawable lines containing angles equal to the angles of the aforementioned triangles at point *a* with line *a-g* (such as line *a-l* and others), it is clear from the definition of a **round pyramid** that the radiation occurs in the shape of a cone. For it is formed according to a figure that can be described by a right-angled triangle *a-g-f* with side *a-g* remaining fixed, while sides *a-f* and *g-f* are revolved back to the place from which they began to move. And from the premises, it is clear that the radiation of this always occurs according to equal **angles of incidence** <term>angles of incidence: the angle at which a ray of light strikes a surface</term>. Thus, the proposition is clear. If it is said that radiation also occurs outside this pyramid, this is true; but because the nature of light is to always diffuse equally (as is clear from Theorem 20 of Book 2 of this work), then radiation will occur toward every part of surface *g* according to a pyramid or according to a part of a pyramid received within it (with the other part of the pyramid extended toward the surface of a body that cannot be illuminated). Hence, if the illuminated part outside the designated pyramid is small, no sensible radiation will occur in it because of the "fewness" of the rays. But if it is large, since many rays meet in it at equal angles, then the radiation will be sensible because of the convergence of many rays and the equality of the angles. And thus, because of the "single-naturedness" <note>original: "unigenitatem"; referring to the uniform properties of light</note> of light, it is possible for radiation to occur according to a circular line, which is the boundary of the base of the pyramid or part of the base. In the same way, it is to be demonstrated if surface *g* is parallel to surface *s-p* touching the luminous body at points *b* and *d*, or at other marked points.

Generally, for bodies that receive a sensible splendor from any luminous body, it is necessary that their aspect toward the luminous body be as the theorem supposes: namely, parallelism to the flat surface touching the luminous body at the point where the perpendicular drawn from the center of the luminous body to the surface of the body to be illuminated cuts the surface of the luminous body. A sign of this is the radiation of the moon, which is never illuminated except on the part opposite the sun; and always half of it—namely, that which looks toward the sun—is necessarily illuminated because of the nature of the aforementioned aspect. The radiation of the sun in no way reaches the other part, unless perhaps by refraction. And since pyramids having their vertex in the center of the luminous body are applied to infinite bases in the body to be irradiated, with one base inscribed within another, therefore the entire surface of the irradiated body looking toward the luminous body is illuminated in many forms, and the radiation is increased. This is because such a body must be denser than the medium through which the light comes to it; for such a body must have some degree of density. Hence, if light met no resistance, it would pass through and would not illuminate the body by its passage; otherwise, reflection or refraction would not occur in it (according to Theorem 58 of this work). And since rays are gathered by reflection, and similarly by refraction (from Theorem 57 of this work), then (by Theorem 56) if the rays were not gathered, no more sensible radiation would occur than in the medium itself. But since radiation is assumed in the theorem, it is clear that the body to be irradiated must be denser than the body <note>the medium, like air</note> near the luminous body. This can be declared by example through what we showed in Theorem 37 of Book 2 of this work. For if a sunbeam penetrates through a round hole, it is immediately applied to the base in the opposite body, and the light is shaped into the form of a pyramid. This is a sign, therefore, that the same thing happens in every ray of a luminous body; since they are of a homogeneous nature, the nature is the same in the whole and in the part. And at the least, if it is not always necessary for this to happen, it is nevertheless possible for it to happen, as proposed. Thus, the intent is clear.

*64. If the refraction or reflection of light from any surface occurs toward the same center of sight: it is necessary that the outer boundary of that surface of light falls upon the sight in a circular fashion according to a **round pyramid** <term>round pyramid: what we would today call a cone</term>. From this it is clear that the center of the radiating body, the center of sight, and the center of the circle forming the base of the pyramid of refracted or reflected radiation must all lie on the same straight line.*

Suppose that some illuminated body is positioned between the sight and the radiating luminous body: and let that middle body be **transparent** <term>transparent: "diaphanum" in Latin; a material that allows light to pass through</term>, so that the refracted rays are able to gather at the center of the sight; for otherwise, the radiation would not be seen. Also, let the center of the radiating body be *a*: and let the surface of the illuminated body be *f h i k*: let the perpendicular line drawn from the center of the luminous body to that surface be *a g*: and let lines *a f*, *a h*, *a i*, *a k* be drawn: as well as lines *g f*, *g h*, *g i*, *g k*: and let the center of sight be *b*: and let lines *b f*, *b h*, *b i*, *b k*, and *b g* be drawn. 

Since, as is clear from the hypothesis, the light of the radiating body is seen at point *b* through refraction: and according to the 3rd proposition of this book <note>original: "3 huius"</note> the perpendicular ray is not refracted, but passes through at right angles, just as it fell upon lines *f g*, *h g*, *i g*, *k g*, many refracted rays (which fall obliquely upon that surface by hypothesis) meet at one point, such as the center of the eye. By the same logic that one refracted ray reaches the center of the sight, all rays falling upon the surface of the body *f h i k* along a circle (whose center is point *g*) will reach the center of sight after being refracted, as was shown in the 48th proposition of this book: for those angles of incidence are all equal, as is clear from the previous proposition: therefore, all the angles of refraction will also be equal according to the 8th proposition of this book. 

In the center of a single sight, therefore, no outer rays meet except those which are refracted according to equal angles. Let it be, then, that this refraction occurs according to certain outer angles, which are *b f g*, *b h g*, *b k g*, and *b i g*: these angles will therefore be equal. But the angles at point *g* beneath line *b g* and beneath lines *f g*, *h g*, *k g*, and *i g* are also equal, because they are right angles. Therefore, the triangles *b g f*, *b g h*, *b g k*, and *b g i* are equiangular according to Proposition 32 of Book 1 <note>Referring to Euclid’s *Elements*</note>: therefore, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, their sides are proportional. But side *b g* is equal to itself, since it is common to all those triangles: therefore the sides *b f*, *b h*, *b k*, and *b i* are equal to one another, and the sides *g f*, *g h*, *g k*, and *g i* are equal to one another. 

Therefore, by Proposition 9 of Book 3, the line *h f i k* is the **circumference** <term>circumference: "peripheria" in Latin</term> of a circle whose center is point *g*: and it is thus described on the surface of the eye. A refracted pyramid is thus formed, whose vertex is at point *b* (the center of sight), and its base is on the illuminated surface: and there is another pyramid of illumination, whose vertex is at point *a* (the center of the light), and its base is also the circle *f h i k*. It is clear, then, that the lines *g f*, *g h*, *g i*, and *g k* of these two pyramids are in the same surface as before: since the rays are refracted by the same lines upon which they fell. There is, therefore, one common surface bounding these two pyramids, which is the circle *f h i k*: and it is the base of both of those pyramids. This is also clear from Proposition 5 of Book 11: because those lines make right angles with line *b a* at a single point, which is *g*. For angle *f g b* is equal to angle *f g a*: since each of them is a right angle, based on the assumption that angle *a g f* is a right angle. And the surface in which the lines *f g*, *h g*, *i g*, and *k g* lie will be **perpendicular** <term>perpendicular: "orthogonalis" in Latin</term> to all the surfaces of refraction. Thus, one of the points proposed is clear.

However, if the center of sight is positioned between the illuminated body and the radiating body: then, with the same arrangement remaining (except that point *b* is placed between points *a* and *g*), the proposition is clear from this: that then the illuminated body is seen only through the **reflection** of the light received from the luminous body. And the angle of incidence will always be equal to the angle of reflection by the 20th theorem of the 5th book of this work: because the exterior angle to angle *a g f* in triangle *a g f* of the pyramid of illumination will be equal to angle *b f g*, which is at the base of triangle *b f g* of the pyramid of reflection. Nor will the vision of the radiation be possible except at a point on the axis of the pyramid of illumination, where the reflected rays from the entire surface of the illuminated body meet according to equal angles. And all the angles of the triangles of the pyramid of reflection that are at the base will be equal to each other by the 20th theorem of the 5th book: since the exterior angles of the pyramid of radiation, which are the angles of incidence, are all equal to each other. 

Thus, all rays reflected to the sight, which are in the same surface, will be equal according to Proposition 6 of Book 1. And since the lines *f g*, *h g*, *i g*, and *k g* are equal: it is clear by Proposition 9 of Book 3 that line *f h i k* is the circumference of a circle: which follows the proposal. And since line *b g*, which is perpendicular to that surface, is common to all those triangles, and the angle of each of the triangles at the base is equal to its corresponding angle by Proposition 4 of Book 1—since the lines *f g*, *h g*, *i g*, and *k g* are equal to one another, as declared before, and the reflection to the sight occurs from them—it is clear by the 106th theorem of the 1st book of this work that there will be, through the rays reflected from them, a pyramid inscribed within a pyramid on the same base, but of a different height. This is because point *b*, which is the center of sight, is placed between the radiating body and the illuminated body: and that base will be common to two pyramids, namely the pyramid of radiation and the pyramid of reflection, being perpendicular to all surfaces of reflection. Therefore, what was proposed in the corollary is clear by the 107th theorem of the 1st book. It has also seemed to some that for the purpose of the things seen, the circulation...

# BOOK TEN

...to unite the circulation of the opening of the **uvea** <note>original: "uueæ"; referring here to the pupil of the eye</note>, as if the rays fall only upon the periphery of the opening: and thus they are rounded on the surface of the sight. Even if this is sometimes possible, it is not universally necessary: because to whatever part of the surface of the sight the rays fall according to equal angles, it will always necessarily happen that the shape is seen as circular. From these points, therefore, it is clearly evident that even if the entire surface of some body—whether irregular or regular, rectilinear or circular—is irradiated: nevertheless, only its irradiated part will appear circular when it is seen through reflection or refraction. This is because, for the sight to judge it as irradiated, many rays must be gathered at the center of the eye: however, none converge except those which, falling upon the surface of the irradiated body and reflected to the center of the eye, all constitute equal angles. Such rays fall according to a circle: for they form a **pyramid** <term>pyramid: in medieval optics, "pyramis" typically refers to what we now call a cone of light</term>, as is clear from what has been said, and they are necessarily reflected or refracted according to that same circle.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the paths of light rays. It shows a tall pyramid or cone with its apex at point 'a'. A central vertical axis descends from 'a' through point 'b' to point 'g', which is the center of a circular base. Several rays radiate from 'a' towards the base, passing through points 'd' and 'e' on a horizontal plane or circle. The base of the cone is represented by a circle with diameter 'k l'. Intersecting lines and points 'f' and 'h' are also marked, showing the angular relationships described in the text regarding light reflection and refraction.</image-desc>

Therefore, the surface of that body will always appear circularly irradiated: nor will the sight see that irradiation unless it is positioned at the point of convergence of the lines reflected in such a manner. And because of this, different circles will appear to different eyes on the same surface of an irradiated body: because the same lines do not converge at different points, but in only one: and larger circles will appear to those further away: namely, those for which the rays fell at larger angles and are reflected or refracted at larger angles: and these are the outer ones on the periphery of the base.

Thus, the inner pyramid—namely, of reflection or refraction—is inscribed within another pyramid of reflection or refraction that surrounds it more narrowly on the outside: and a center of sight closer to the irradiated surface will see a smaller circle than a more distant sight: since the rays in the smaller circle fall according to smaller angles, and are reflected according to smaller angles by the 20th theorem of Book 5 of this work, or are refracted according to smaller angles by the 8th theorem of this book. It is clear, moreover, by the 106th theorem of Book 1, that as the angle of refraction or reflection is decreased further, the angle contained within the sight is increased accordingly. And because the angle of refraction or reflection is always acute and divisible by straight lines, for this reason the angle in the eye is always acute, nor can it grow to a right angle so as to make a quarter part of the circle's height correspond to itself: since among the angles causing the pyramid, that angle in the eye and the angle of reflection or refraction equal one right angle: since the angle at the axis is always a right angle by the 89th theorem of Book 1 of this work. From the preceding, a very beautiful corollary is also clear with the help of the 12th theorem of this book. For since in a right-angled pyramid the center of the base circle and the cone's vertex are always on the same line (as on the axis), in the present case *a* and *g* will be on the axis *ag*: but by the same reasoning *b* and *g* will be on the same line: indeed, lines *bg* and *ga* joined together are one line: because the line *fg* coming from their endpoint makes right angles with both of them. In whatever way the sight is related to the irradiated body, provided that reflection or refraction occurs toward it: the proposition is clear, since the center of the radiating body and the center of the eye and the center of the circular base of each pyramid—namely, of irradiation and of vision—are always on the same line, that is, the axis of the pyramid of irradiation: nor is it possible for the irradiation to be seen otherwise.

*§ 5. Likewise it is necessary that it be seen from the reflection and refraction of rays of a luminous body.*

**In being about to speak** of the **rainbow** <term>rainbow: "iris" in Latin</term>, we intend to speak principally of that which, intersecting the horizon, extends to different parts of the world: although we shall not make it our primary intention to speak of others which appear similar to that rainbow. That the rainbow is produced from a multitude of light from a luminous body received in the sight is evident to the senses: but that (without the gathering of rays from a luminous body) light could become more perceptible in a non-luminous body than in the **medium** <term>medium: the substance light travels through, like air or water</term> through which the light was previously carried, was shown to be impossible by the 56th theorem of this book. From this it is clear that light is invigorated by the gathering of rays from a luminous body, so that it becomes more perceptible in some body than in the medium. That this gathering of rays from a luminous body occurs through reflection or through refraction, which happens in a body of a denser **transparent** <term>transparent: "diaphani" in Latin</term> nature than the medium through which it was previously carried, was declared by the 57th theorem of this book. It is therefore generally clear that the greater perceptibility of light is caused by reflection or by refraction in all visible things. That the rainbow specifically is produced from reflection is clear from this: because its perceptible light reaches the sight, as was assumed in the 2nd petition of this book. It was also shown by the 20th theorem of Book 5 that everything seen through reflection is seen in such a way that the angle at which the form falls upon a mirror or other polished body is equal to the angle at which that form is reflected to the sight: which is also clear by the 26th theorem of Book 5, drawing a perpendicular from the point of incidence upon the surface of the polished body, to which the angles of reflection are referred: for the incident ray and the reflected ray contain equal angles with that same perpendicular. Since, therefore, the form of the rainbow is produced in the sight: it is clear that the rainbow is caused by the reflection of the rays of a luminous body to the sight. That the rainbow [is also caused] through refraction...

# THE OPTICS OF WITELO

...also occurs [the aggregation] of the rays of the luminous body: it is clear from this that the **rainbow** <note>original: "iris"</note> is not generated unless it is in some transparent material existing in the middle, which hinders the passage of light. It has also already been stated in the fourth book of this work that in transparent bodies denser than the first transparent medium, even if reflection occurs from their surface, refraction always occurs toward the perpendicular; and thus the light falling obliquely on the surfaces of such bodies is extended as if divided into two opposite parts along one line. Therefore, through refraction in such bodies, an aggregation of light occurs which is offered to the sight, just like any other visible thing. And just as a white cloud and the light reflected from the surface of those bodies to the sight helps to make an act of greater sensitivity in the sight, so we see that a more sensible reflection occurs from white bodies, which have more light, than from bodies colored with a medium color. 

This is also evident through the deepening of light in the generation of the rainbow. For while those things that have only the reflection of light are irradiated only on the surface, the matter of the rainbow is found to be irradiated deep within. Because of this (as discovered by **Philip, the companion of Plato** <note>Likely Philip of Opus, a student of Plato associated with early astronomical and meteorological observations</note>, and as happens daily to those walking near a rainbow, and as we ourselves have learned by experiment), the rainbow changes according to the movement of the viewer. For it follows the one fleeing from it, and stays ahead of the one who moves toward it. And if anyone moves to the right or left side, the rainbow will be seen to move to that same side. 

But things seen only according to reflection flee the one fleeing, and meet the one approaching; for such things are always seen at the intersection of the line of reflection proceeding to the sight with the perpendicular drawn from the point of the thing seen onto the surface of the body from which the reflection of the seen form occurs, as is clear from the 37th theorem of the fifth book. Therefore, the rainbow is seen not only through reflection, but also through the refraction of light within the body from which it is reflected. Although for one approaching the rainbow, or moving far from it, the reflection of light to the sight occurs from different surfaces of the bodies obstructing the light: because the fleeing of the rainbow from the one approaching it, and its following of the one fleeing from it, happens because of different reflections which occur to the sight from different parts of the rainbow's matter. This is specifically according to how the sight changes the points in which all rays from the angles of the base of one **pyramid** <term>pyramid: in medieval optics, this refers to a cone-shaped volume of light</term> converge in the center of the eye itself. 

And because such bases are infinite, and the points in which their reflected rays are collected on the axis are infinite, it is also clear that through manifold reflection, infinite rainbows are seen according to the infinity of points on the axis meeting the one approaching or receding along the line of the same axis. Or even for one going to the side, it changes according to the movement of the axis from the center of the luminous body through another point of its surface than that through which the first axis emerged. For a new pyramid and a new base are created for the sight changing to the sides in this way; and there is another point on the surface of the luminous body through which comes the ray perpendicular to the surface of the rainbow's matter, which (with the center of the eye falling upon it) becomes the axis of each pyramid. In this way, infinite rainbows are seen for whatever difference of position the viewer moves—provided he does not move directly against the luminous body. Even if this were true and could happen by the nature of reflection alone, the refraction of the rays of the luminous body always increases the light so that it may be seen more clearly by the sight. 

For it is clear that the refraction of the rays of the luminous body aggregates light so that it becomes more visible; because of that refraction of rays around the same part of the medium, the ray is doubled. Similarly, the reflection of those rays aggregates light and brings it back sensibly to the sight. Indeed, a rainbow does not occur except from aggregated light, nor does it occur from that light unless it meets the sight. Therefore, the refraction of the rays of the luminous body and the reflection of the same are necessary for the generation of the rainbow. And this is what we wished to investigate in the present theorem.

### 66. It is necessary for the rainbow to be generated in dewy vapor.

What is proposed here is clear. Since a rainbow does not occur without light—indeed, a multitude of light—and light is not aggregated except from the reflection or refraction of the rays of a luminous body (as is clear from the 57th theorem of this book), and these do not occur unless a body denser than pure air is placed in the way of the light (per the 56th theorem), it follows that in the place of the rainbow's generation, there will be no generation without an irradiable body from whose surface the reflection and refraction of incident light can occur. 

It is impossible for any flat solid to be there. But neither can it be water; for water would run down suddenly to the lowest possible place, while the rainbow remains for some time—not as the same thing, but always different because of the continuous descent of the **dewfall** <note>original: "rorationis"; the falling of mist or droplets</note>. Nor could the continuous shape of a rainbow be generated in water, because the entire light would be reflected from the surface of the water due to the continuity of the water itself. For the rainbow that occurs in water scattered by **oars** <note>The author uses the example of light hitting the spray created by a rower</note> occurs because of the dispersion of the water; for then the sailor uses the oar like a hand to spray the water, and because of this, when water is scattered in this way, the colors of the rainbow appear in it. 

It is also not possible for the rainbow to be generated in "thick air"; for the impression of light in air would not produce the colors of the rainbow, but would create a certain whiteness, as appears in the early morning dawn and also at the end of evening twilight, and universally in all similar cases. Nor can it be a continuous vapor, whether it is raised for the generation of a cloud or condensed into a cloud. For let it be granted that it is possible for a rainbow to be generated from a continuous vapor. Let a radiant body (whose center is *a*) be placed in the circle of the horizon; and let a surface erected orthogonally over the surface of the horizon through the center of that body cut it; and let the line *h g* be drawn in that intersecting surface through the center of the luminous body. Thus, a continuous irradiable vapor is either parallel to this intersecting surface or it is not. If it is parallel, let there be a line in its surface *b c d* parallel to line *h g*; and let rays *a b*, *a c*, *a d* fall upon it. Let line *a b* be perpendicular to the surface of the vapor, which will be reflected back upon itself (by the 21st theorem of the 5th book); and lines *a c* and *a d* will also be reflected because they are not perpendicular. Since, however, angle *a c b* is acute (by the 32nd proposition of the 1st book), since angle *a b c* is a right angle: it is clear (by the 13th proposition of the 1st book) that angle *d c a* is obtuse: per-

### BOOK TEN

Therefore, a perpendicular line drawn from point **c** will not intersect with the axis **ab**; consequently, the reflected ray will not either. Since the center of sight must necessarily be located on line **ab** (as established in Theorem 64 of this book), which lies on the surface of the **horizon** <term>horizon: the circle that bounds what an observer can see</term>, and the center of sight is the center of the horizon (point **f**), it is clear that light reflected in this way will never reach the eye—unless perhaps that reflected ray, striking the surface of another flat body, were reflected back to the sight. Therefore, if the vapor is arranged in such a way, a rainbow will not be seen. Furthermore, if the surface of the continuous vapor is not parallel to the surface cutting through the luminous body <note>the sun</note> but instead intersects it: if those surfaces meet below the horizon, the same impossible result occurs, and it is deduced in the same way. For even if it were possible for some rays to be reflected to the eye below the horizon, the sight would not judge them as a perceived experience; for things that are below the horizon are not seen, since the horizon is the circle that terminates the sight. And since the surface of the horizon is oblique to the surface of the vapor, it is clear that a ray falling perpendicularly from the center of the luminous body onto the vapor's surface falls below the horizon. All rays that do not fall perpendicularly onto the surface of the vapor beyond the surface of the horizon are reflected toward the side opposite the center of sight located at the center of the horizon. Thus, the rainbow will not be seen when the center of sight and the surface of that vapor are arranged toward each other in such a way.
