But if those two surfaces—one of the vapor and the other cutting the luminous body—meet not below the horizon but above it, then again it is not possible for the light to be reflected to the sight for the reasons previously stated. For the angle **acd**, being exterior to the angle **abc** in the right-angled triangle **abc**, will always be greater than a right angle (according to Proposition 16 of Book 1 <note>Witelo is citing Euclid’s Elements</note>). Therefore, the reflection will never reach the eye, which is at the center of the horizon. But even granted that in some of the aforementioned arrangements a reflection to the eye could occur (which is nonetheless impossible), a rainbow would still not be seen because of the continuity of the vapor. There would be a massive generation of light across the vapor's surface, creating a continuous light which, when reflected to the eye, would weaken the sight and would not allow it to look into the depths of the vapor. Common people call such light a **watery sun** <note>original: "sol aqueus"; a pale, blurred appearance of the sun through mist</note>, and it lacks any distinction of colors. Furthermore, if the said surfaces met above the horizon, then the rainbow would appear deflected from the **zenith** <term>zenith: the point in the sky directly above the observer</term> perceptibly according to the bulge of the circle by which it is seen; all of which is contrary to the senses and does not appear to the sight. Therefore, it is not suitable for a rainbow to be caused in such vapor.

<image-desc>Geometrical diagram showing a ray m-d entering a circle centered at f. A horizontal line g-h passes through the center. The diagram illustrates refraction or reflection within a spherical medium, with points labeled m, f, a, d, g, h.</image-desc>

However, between continuous watery vapor and rain falling from the clouds, there is a certain medium called **dewy vapor** <term>dewy vapor: Latin "uapor roridus," a mist consisting of tiny, distinct water droplets</term>. This occurs when the condensing cold begins to reduce the watery vapor into its proper form, namely water. For then the thin parts of the vapor are condensed, and a distance is created between the parts of the vapor, which begin to round themselves out. Yet, due to the weakness of the cooling agent, they are not yet reduced to their proper form, which would cause them to move downward <note>i.e., they are not yet heavy enough to fall as rain</note>. These particles of vapor then act as certain tiny mirrors in which only the color of the radiant body appears, without its size or shape, as we stated in Theorem 62 of this book. If, therefore, any of the rays falling upon these small bodies that are beginning to round out is refracted toward the back of the body toward the perpendicular line (drawn from the point of incidence upon the surface of that body according to Theorem 4), and since by Theorem 72 of Book 1 that perpendicular passes through the center of that spherical body, it is clear that the refracted ray will fall obliquely upon the surface of that body opposite the luminous body. Light will then aggregate in the depth of the entire mass of these small bodies because of the refraction occurring in each of them, just as we see in a round crystal. For beyond its rear surface, there is an aggregation of rays in the air at a single point, as is clear from Theorem 48. In each of these small bodies (whether they are larger than the drops generated from them later by the way of condensation, as is sometimes possible, or whether a drop is formed by the aggregation of many small bodies—for in this regard, as far as the generation of the rainbow is concerned, there is no difference), infinite rays always fall. These rays are also reflected from the surface of those small bodies according to their angles of incidence, which they make with lines touching the major circles of said small bodies at the point of their incidence. These angles are diverse, and because of this, the angles of reflection are made diverse, as is clear throughout the entire sixth book of this science. The rays making angles with the lines touching the aforementioned small bodies, and with lines marked on the surface cutting the luminous body, meet above the hori-

VITELLO’S OPTICS

...front, and intersecting the axis of the **pyramid of illumination** <term>pyramid of illumination: the cone-shaped volume of light spreading out from a light source like the sun</term> further beyond point **b**, more distant from the luminous body (as at point **m**), because such angles inside the pyramid are obtuse. Therefore, by Theorem 33 of Book 5 of this work, those rays incident in such a way are reflected to the sight; and at the point where many such rays meet on the axis, between the luminous body and the eye placed in the vapor, light is seen. 

And since there are certain small bodies into which, as has been said, rays from the center of the luminous body fall at equal angles: such rays are indeed infinite, scattered from every part of the cloud. For since the entire consistency of the vapor is full of such small bodies, there are infinite such rays on the surface of the cloud or dewy vapor that meets or even runs parallel to the surface cutting through the luminous body, according to how it regards the consistency of the vapor. In their irradiation, a pyramid is formed whose vertex is at the center of the luminous body, and whose base is in the consistency of the dewy vapor; the lines of length of that pyramid terminate at different parts of various small bodies. When these are reflected to the eye at similar angles to their incidence, they create another pyramid whose vertex is at the center of the sight, and whose base is the same as the base of the first pyramid. This base is a circle, as was shown universally in Theorem 64 of this book. That reflected light will appear continuous due to the proximity of the parts of the vapor and the fact that their distance is imperceptible to the eye; for the sight, extended from them, is deceived because of its own weakness. On account of this, the eye receives the light reflected collectively from all those small bodies without recognizing or perceiving the distance between the parts, and judges them as one.

It is clear, therefore, from the foregoing, that although the entire consistency of the vapor is radiant, and perhaps the entire irradiated surface is many-sided, it nevertheless always appears circular. The reason for this is that nothing is seen except what is reflected from it at equal angles toward a single point on the axis of the radial pyramid. When the angles at the base are equal, the sides containing those equal angles are equal (by Proposition 6 of Book 1 of Euclid’s *Elements*); therefore, by Theorem 65 of Book 1 of this work, the center of the sight is the **pole** <term>pole: the central point from which all points on a circle's circumference are equidistant</term>, and the surface where those equal lines terminate is a circle. Thus, the rainbow appears circular. 

For the sake of example, the same thing can be declared another way: namely, by drawing three or more lines from the points of reflection perpendicularly over a line falling perpendicularly to the total consistency of the vapor from the center of the luminous body. For those lines will be in the same surface (from Proposition 5 of Book 11), and they were equal (from Propositions 32 and 26 of Book 1); therefore, at the point of their meeting on the axis is the center of the circle (from Proposition 9 of Book 3). And because the rays of the whole base are not reflected at equal angles, the entire radiant circle is not seen, even though light exists everywhere in the entire consistency of the cloud. For rays that are reflected at greater angles than the angles of the rays reflected to the eye are reflected beyond the point of sight to another place on the axis; rays that are reflected at smaller angles than those which reach the eye meet at another place on the axis below the center of sight. Thus, neither are seen, unless perhaps by other eyes located at the places of their meeting. 

Because of this, it happens that when a person moves forward or backward, a different rainbow is seen; for the sight of the one proceeding or receding always falls upon the points where different rays aggregate. This also happens in different men who are positioned more or less distant from the center of the sun according to the different distance of the **zenith** <term>zenith: the point in the sky directly above an observer</term> of their head, even if they are under the same meridian or another circle of altitude. The rainbow therefore appears circular and concave for these reasons: because neither the outer nor the inner rays falling on the surface of the entire dewy consistency meet at the same point at the eye; hence, the sight judges the other parts of the vapor to be deprived of light. 

A sign of this is what happens on the flat surface of water, in which the form of the sun, moon, or stars exists at every point; yet it is only seen at one point or location from which a reflection to the eye is possible. When the observer moves further, the form of the luminous body is seen again in another place from which reflection to the eye is possible. The same is seen regarding a candle or any distinct light on a new knife or polished iron or other surface: because while the object remains immobile, the seen form changes as the eye moves, according to the way it is possible for it to be reflected to the eye; and at any other point, it is not seen. 

Another sign of this is that if someone is standing in a ray of sunlight, and another person outside the ray scatters water from their mouth or by some other artifice like a spray <note>original: "roratim"</note> into the ray, the sight of the one in the ray perhaps will see nothing but a white color. Yet the one scattering the water, who is opposite the vapor, sees the light and the colors of the rainbow—though they are confused, unless the arrangement of the dewy particles is such that a definite reflection to the eye can occur in the middle of the ray. 

It is clear from the foregoing that the rainbow is generated in dewy vapor. A sign of this is that the rainbow lasts only a short time: because such vapor, being made of heavy matter already approaching the form of a heavy thing, cannot remain above the surface of the horizon unless it moves toward the center of heavy things, which is the center of the world, as much as is possible for it. Because of this, after the appearance of the rainbow, when the matter is condensed by the operation of an active agent and is reduced to a form capable of movement, rain occurs. From each of the small bodies previously separated in the vapor, a descending water drop is made through the condensation of the matter. Another sign is what was said before: when water is scattered like vapor by the mouth, hand, or an oar—as with sailors—the rainbow and the colors of the rainbow appear in the solar ray, and different onlookers see it because the incident rays are reflected in different ways by the droplets. Therefore, the proposition is clear: the rainbow is generated in dewy vapor. If it is said that the parts of the small bodies in the matter of the rainbow are not all perfectly spherical, the objection carries no weight; for the exact same thing happens in non-spherical bodies as has been said of spherical ones: for a rainbow will never occur unless many gathered rays are reflected uniformly to the eye.

### 67. Every rainbow is three-colored.

This theorem is proposed having been doubted by the ancients because of its difficulty. For the shape and size of the rainbow were clear to many mathematicians, and these things were assumed by the investigators of natural philosophy; however, the color we see has not yet been adequately treated by anyone, except through the distinction of the matter of the rainbow according to the nature of the burnt, the undigested, and the opaque <note>These terms refer to Aristotelian theories of "pepsis" or the "cooking" of vapors to produce color</note>. Whether this can preserve and be consistent with the motion and possibility of natural things, we have thought should be left to the intellect of those who wrote such things.

### BOOK TEN

The colors of the rainbow, according to the truth—which has revealed itself to us after many thoughts and experiences—can be explained in this way. Since the entire **dewy vapor** <term>dewy vapor: the mist or cloud of droplets that forms the "matter" of the rainbow</term> (which is the substance of the rainbow) is irradiated both on its surface and in its depth, and its depth is substantial, it is clear that in its aspect toward the sun, it contains a light that is quite frequent and unmixed. However, this light is still mixed with the color of the vapor itself, which is black <note>original: "niger"; in medieval optics, "black" or "darkness" was often used to describe the absence of light or the inherent color of dense, watery matter</note>, as is evident in watery vapors (for they are all dark). Now, it is the nature of light to mix itself with the colors of the things from which it is reflected. This was established at the beginning of Book 2 in the 7th postulate: light passing through colored things is colored by their colors. This is plain to the senses; hence reflected light also carries with it the color of the object from which it is reflected to the sight, as is seen in a ray passing through colored glass. Therefore, since light is by its nature brilliant, and in the generation of the rainbow it is received into dark, watery vapor, it must necessarily present a **crimson** <term>crimson: "puniceus" in the original, referring to the reddish-purple outermost band of the rainbow</term> color to the sight, according to Theorem 157 of Book 4. Consequently, that part of the rainbow appears crimson to the eye because of the strength of the vision and the great reflection of the strongest rays from a nearby location, due to the proximity of the luminous body from which the impression of reflected light is made along a shorter line. And since the entire cloud is luminous, and light is always reflected at equal angles from different surfaces within the depths of the cloud—surfaces that are equidistant to the base of the first **pyramid of illumination** <term>pyramid of illumination: the cone of light spreading from the sun</term>—it is reflected to the same sight through the surface of the previous pyramid closer to the eye. For, as is clear from Theorem 68 of Book 1, equidistant circles on the same axis have their own poles, and the same point is the pole of different circles.

It is clear, then, that even the light within the depth of the cloud is seen. However, because that light is **refracted light** <term>refracted light: light that has bent as it passed into the water droplets, losing intensity</term>, it is weak and much mixed with the dark color of the cloud. And because it is seen through a **visual pyramid** inscribed from the same vertex (namely, the center of the eye) within the first visual pyramid—according to which the closer rays, appearing crimson, are reflected to the eye—it is clear from Theorem 106 of Book 1 that the angles formed at the base of the inscribed pyramid will be larger than the angles formed at the base of the first pyramid. Therefore, light from that location is reflected to the eye in rays at a larger angle; hence the rays are less unified with the light and are presented more weakly to the sight. Also, the angles they make at the center of the sight are smaller, as shown by the same Theorem 106 of Book 1, than the angles made by the rays of the first pyramid at the center of the sight. Thus, the light in the body of the cloud is seen under a smaller angle than that on the surface; and what is seen under a smaller angle appears smaller and less distinct, as per Theorem 20 of Book 4. This is evident to anyone experimenting with the light of a star or a candle: for what first appeared brilliant with an open eye begins to lose its brilliance and turn dark when the eye is partially closed. Likewise, because such light is seen from a greater distance, it appears weaker; for the distance or protrusion of the visible object from the sight is a cause of visual weakness, as shown by Theorem 158 of Book 4. Furthermore, because the vapor further from the luminous body is thicker, darker, and more watery, the darkness of the vapor incorporated into the light darkens it further, presenting it to the sight as more obscured. 

These factors indeed have some causality in the colors of the rainbow. But the **total cause** <note>Witelo is looking for a single, universal explanation for all rainbow colors</note> universal to all these colors is the **mixing of shadows with the brilliance of light**. Since the dewy vapor is the matter of the rainbow, from whose small bodies light is reflected to the sight, and since (by Theorem 11 of Book 2) all dense bodies cast a shadow on the side opposite the luminous body, it is clear that the rays reflected from the surfaces of more distant particles mix with the darkness of the shadows of the particles in front of them. Thus, mixed with the black color of the shadows, they reach the eye as reflected light. Depending on whether they are mixed more or less with the darkness of the shadows, they diversify the act of their luminosity into various colors. A sign of this is found in colors similar to the rainbow seen at the edges of windows when the sight is partially obstructed by a hand or another shadowy object. Another sign is the blackness of the sea, which occurs in deep, clear waters into which light sinks, due to the multiplication of shadows; whereas in turbulent sea waters, which light does not penetrate to create shadows, the sea appears not black but **green**. Also, when the eyelids are lowered, the colors of the rainbow are seen by the eye in respect to light, coming from the shadows of the eyelashes. Every particular instance in which the colors of the rainbow appear can be traced back to this cause of shadows as a kind of universal principle, as is seen in the necks of ducks and peacocks, which are colored in various ways according to their different positions. For the **waviness** <term>waviness: "crispitudo," referring to the texture or structure of the feathers</term> of their feathers casts shadows here and there, which, mixed with light, create different colors in different places. Nor could our intellect investigate any other causes for the aforementioned phenomena. Since there are only 22 **visible properties** <note>a reference to the standard list of "common sensibles" in medieval Aristotelian science, such as light, color, size, shape, etc.</note>, none of the others besides shadow and light seem to be the cause of these colors appearing to the sight. Hence, we estimate this to be the proximate cause of the rainbow's colors. Yet we have seen no one whose intellect has directed them to speak intelligibly on this matter; rather, while the cause of this thing is easy, everyone else seems to have given difficult explanations. We, however, shall be content with this cause as universal and convertible, setting down the other factors mentioned earlier as supports to this cause. 

Therefore, with all or many of these causes concurring sensibly at the intersection of the pyramids of reflection with equidistant bases, the judgment of the sight fails. The light—more mixed with the darkness of the vapor, less refracted, reflected at a larger angle, seen at a smaller angle, positioned at a greater distance from itself, radiated in thicker matter, and mixed with more shadows—is judged by the sight to recede further from white than the crimson color. Thus, that reflected light appears **leek-green** <gloss>original: prasinus</gloss> to the observer. And after this green color, when the reflection of more pyramids has occurred...

He argues that the specific color perceived depends on the angle of reflection, the distance from the eye, and the degree of shadow-mixing.</summary>

In reflection, when the stated conditions vary significantly from the prior conditions, the light seems to approach black more closely, and the color **azure** or **deep blue** <note>original: "alurgus siue lazulius"</note> appears to the sight. This color is more thoroughly mixed with the blackness of the vapor and with more shadows than the **leek-green** <note>original: "prasinus"</note> color. Finally, when these conditions begin to vary noticeably at the edges of the bases of the many visual pyramids associated with this azure color, and when the light is no longer reflected to a sight so disposed, it becomes black, which no longer appears mixed with light. 

A sign of the aforementioned is this: when someone, after looking at the sun or some other gleaming body, closes their eyes suddenly and tightly—first with the eyelid covering the eye—that which they previously saw as gleaming now appears white to the sight; then **crimson** <note>original: "puniceum"</note>; then green; then purple; and finally, the form of the light, falling away into a black color, is extinguished. Thus, as the motion is created in the sight by the white itself being gradually extinguished, the resolution always moves toward a color closer to black. 

It is clear, therefore, from the premises, that the **rainbow is tricolored**. The highest of these colors is crimson; the green color is contained below the crimson, because the color of the edges of the green bases is carried to the sight below the color of the edges of the crimson bases. Similarly, the azure color is contained below the green for the same reason; and thus one colored arc is seen below another continuous colored arc. The **yellow** <note>original: "xanthus"</note> color, however, which is seen between the green and the crimson, is not a distinct color from the others in the rainbow, but occurs to our sight from the mixing of green and red. 

For the crimson color appears white to the sight when next to the green, just as the purple color appears white when next to black; green is also mixed with white. Because of this, the yellow color—being closer to black than the crimson—is seen between the crimson and the green. Hence, when a rainbow is formed in a very black cloud, the uppermost color is not crimson, but appears yellow, due to the heavy mixing of the vapor’s blackness with the light. When the cloud dissipates, what previously appeared crimson finally appears white. The green also seems to tend toward a yellow color, and the azure toward green. 

Indeed, a certain man of experience once saw a **totally white rainbow**. This happens because of the thinness of the matter and the brightness of the light, combined with an optimal disposition of the sight itself and a proportionate distance to the object seen. Or perhaps it occurs because of a very great thickness and density of the vapor, into which the light could not penetrate deeply; instead, reflection occurred from the surface of the vapor. Because of this, the light had not received color from the color of the body mixed with it, nor was it mixed with the blackness of the shadows. Thus, the reflection creating the rainbow was reflected in the form of light without any admixture of blackness and shadows. 

A sign of the varying appearance of colors can be seen in the weaving of **purple fabrics**, in which colors placed next to others create a great difference and mixture in the sight. For the same purple does not look the same when placed next to white as it does next to black or any other color. Because of this, due to a certain brightness that a color receives from a neighboring color, other fantasies of color arise in our vision. This also happens to those working by lamplight, who are deceived in colors because of the admixture of impure light; they happen to err and take some colors for others, as a variation of color is generated by the mingling of impure light. 

Thus, it can be reasonably said that the middle colors of the rainbow are generated from the middle pyramids according to the stated circumstances and the mixing of various shadows with the light. Following the ancients, we have determined the number of rainbow colors to be three; for they extend the names of the colors so far that a middle color takes the name of the extreme color with which it shares more of its nature. Thus, it is necessarily proved that the rainbow has only three colors, and painters cannot fully imitate such colors. 

Regarding the colors that appear in a rainbow generated in water vapor scattered by the mouth or by some other subtle device, by hand, or by an oar, the entire cause has been stated. For when light falls upon such small droplets and is reflected by them to the eye—whether placed in a ray or in a window through which the ray falls, with the back of the head turned directly toward the center of the sun—then the light reflected from closer is of such brightness that the light reflected from further away becomes more and more darkened by the mixing of shadows from the higher droplets closer to the eyes and the luminous body, according to the modes previously described. When the sight is so positioned, the rainbow will appear rounded for the reasons previously given. However, if the sight is positioned differently toward the ray, the colors of the rainbow will appear disordered due to irregular reflection to the eye. Since that reflection does not occur according to equal angles, it does not achieve the round shape of the rainbow. According to how the light touches the dewy droplets, the light induces various colors in the sight through whatever reflection is perceived. But the further the rays are from the beginning of their gathering at the window, the more opaque the colors become due to the mixing of more shadows into the reflected light itself.

We ourselves discovered on summer days, around the evening hour or a little before, near **Viterbo** <note>A city in Italy where Witelo likely performed his research</note> at a precipice by the bath (which is called the *scopuli*), that water was falling with great force. Going down to see what might happen there with the sun opposite it, we saw a **permanent rainbow** existing while the sun was at the proper aspect for it. We noted many of the properties of the rainbow. Therefore, because the things previously written about the rainbow did not seem sufficient to us in all respects (except for what **Aristotle** had written in an involved manner), that was the starting point of our thinking, leading us to apply our study to the present business. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### **68. A halo is formed by the refraction of the light of the sun, moon, or first-magnitude stars from humid vapor in a circular shape toward the sight.**

The impression (which in Greek is called *halōs* <note>original: αλως</note> and in Arabic *alileti*) is called a **halo** <note>original: "corona"</note> in Latin. This impression occurs in the sight from the incorporation of light into some consistency of vapor. For since, as is clear from Theorem 56 of this book, it is impossible for light to be made sensible when the rays of a luminous body are not gathered in a non-luminous body more than in the medium, it is clear that for the generation of a halo it is necessary for some vapor to be interposed between the luminous body and the eyes. Therefore, when some continuous humid vapor is interposed between the eyes and a luminous body that is unable to quickly dissolve or disperse that vapor, then a refraction of light occurs toward the eye in a circle, according to Theorem 64 of this book. For the light falling upon that vapor through fire and air at equal angles is refracted to the sight at equal angles, according to Theorem 8 of this book. Thus it appears...

He then begins explaining the "halo" (corona) as a phenomenon of refraction through humid vapor.</summary>

Therefore, the light appears circular because of the equal refraction of the gathered light toward the eye; for, due to the refraction of light (as is clear from theorem 57 of this book), the rays are gathered in the depths of the vapor. For when radial lines are refracted at angles, the light is, as it were, doubled for the sight, and it reaches the eye more intensely. And if perhaps that vapor is dewy <note>original: "roridus"</note>, divided into tiny particles, then more refractions occur, and the light is increased. 

And since the same ray falling upon the surface of the vapor is refracted in the body of the vapor toward the perpendicular (from the point of its incidence upon the surface of the body from which it is refracted), and the shadow is stretched out according to the extension of the line of incidence (by theorem 11 of Book 2); and since the incident ray and the refracted ray are not one single line but contain an angle; it is therefore clear that the refracted ray "flees" <note>moves away from</note> the shadow cast by the body upon which it fell. This shadow, however, is small, because for the most part a **halo** <term>corona: a circular ring of light around the sun or moon</term> is seen in thin, lightly condensed vapor. 

Nevertheless, because a new refraction occurs behind the consistency of that vapor in the air between the vapor and the eye (which occurs away from the perpendicular by theorem 4 of this book), it is clear that the refracted light reaching the center of the eye is not mixed with the blackness of shadows, but is free from them. Because of this, it always appears **white**, or perhaps colored throughout with a slight and indistinct **reddish** color. 

The **rainbow** <term>Iris</term>, however, occurs through the reflection of rays penetrating the cast shadows; therefore, those rays reach the sight under the influence of color, and the distinction of colors occurs according to the degree of diversity between the light and the shadows. Thus, a halo is sometimes seen from the refraction of solar light, but this happens rarely because of the strength and intensity of that light, which suddenly dissolves the vapor (which is the material of the halo). However, this often happens from the light of the moon and stars of the first magnitude <note>the brightest class of stars in ancient astronomy</note>, whose light cannot dissolve that consistency of vapor. A halo does not occur from smaller stars because of the weakness of their light, which cannot produce such an effect. 

Sometimes a halo is also seen around the light of candles in thick air, mostly when the **East wind** <note>original: "euro"</note> is blowing; and then, sometimes because of the density of the air casting the shadow of the upper parts upon the lower, a **purple** color is presented to the sight from such refracted or reflected light. Thus, the proposition is clear.

### 69. *It is not possible for a rainbow in the southern part of the world to be seen by northern observers.*

What is clear through theorem 107 of Book 1 regarding purely mathematical pyramids <term>visual pyramids: the cone of light entering the eye</term> inscribed within one another is also clear through theorem 64 of this book regarding reflected pyramids, which cause the same effects and follow the nature of mathematical pyramids. For it is always necessary that the center of the sight be between the center of the luminous body and the center of the rainbow for that impression to be seen which we properly name a **rainbow**; although other impressions, imitating the colors of the rainbow, can sometimes be seen through other modes, as will be clear below. 

That a southern rainbow cannot be seen by northern eyes is clear enough from what we have said regarding the generation of the colors of the rainbow, which are caused by the reflection of light and the mixing of shadows with that light. This can also be shown by the fact that the material of the rainbow is easily dissolved into water or refined into clear air when it is near the luminous body. Reflections cannot occur from the surface of such air; and even if they did occur, they would tend toward the side where the sun is and would not reach the eye. Also, because the colors of the rainbow, which occur due to the weakening of reflected light, cannot be caused in such a place; for since there is always more light around the luminous body, the reflected rays are not weakened but are made more visible. 

In such places, however, once the refraction of rays toward the eye has occurred through vapor or dense air, some gathered light can be seen in the condensed vapor or air, as we said in the previous section regarding the generation of the **halo**, which sometimes occurs from the refraction of the sun's light—though rarely, due to the strength of that light. It is often generated, however, from the light of the moon and stars of the first and primary magnitude. 

Therefore, when a rainbow is to be generated, it is necessary that the rays be reflected to the eye and that there be no other light shining behind the dewy vapor (which is the material of the rainbow by theorem 66 of this book). Whence it is also possible for a thick halo appearing to the sight—specifically in thick and dense material caused by a strong light—that some colors of the rainbow may appear within it, with the sight positioned between the luminous body and the vapor. For then all the conditions and causes of the colors of the rainbow will coincide in such a place, and the material is present. Thus, a rainbow could appear in this way. 

Perhaps it happens that the material in which the rainbow is seen reflected by more southern people from dewy vapor appears as a halo to more northern people from the same vapor (so that the same vapor appears to both inhabitants at the same time and according to the same circle of altitude); and the same will be true in any circle of altitude in the predicted manner for any viewers so positioned. 

From these things which have been said, it can also be clear that sometimes, from strong solar rays reflected from a solid watery cloud to a place where there is dewy vapor, colors of the rainbow can be generated from some side of the sun in full circles or incomplete portions of circles. This happens when a solid watery cloud is diametrically opposite the body of the sun, and the ray falling upon it is reflected, and the dewy cloud stands in the way of the reflected ray, in which the refraction and reflection of rays reaching the eye occurs. Then the colors of the rainbow appear straight to the sight, as when the vapor is not directly opposite the eye; and such colors are in thin, mixed watery vapor. Sometimes, however, they appear circular and become like rainbows. For such a rainbow to be seen, it is necessary that the cloud (to which the reflection of the sun's rays occurs toward the opposite vapor), and the dewy vapor (to which and from which the reflection of light to the eye occurs), and the eye (at which the reflection occurs) all consist in the same straight line; and that the surface of the cloud from which the reflection occurs, and the surface of the vapor from which and to which the reflection occurs, when extended above the horizon, meet as if in the upper hemisphere. Otherwise...

However, by this meeting of surfaces, we mean the meeting of the tangent lines of the particles of dewy vapor at the very point of reflection. We ourselves saw at **Padua**, while the sun was already declining toward evening, not just one or even two such rainbows, but four at the same time. These rainbows were not at a distance of 10 degrees from the sun; they were all complete circles, located on different surfaces, and some were almost touching each other on the outside. 

Furthermore, those rainbows which are formed from the rays of a luminous body—not reflected from another cloud to the vapor, but reflected from the vapor itself to the sight—cannot possibly occur except when the luminous body is in opposition to the vapor, with the viewer in the middle. For this reason, in our habitable world, a rainbow cannot be seen toward the south, because the vapor is not interposed there between the sight and the luminous body. For the paths of the **planets** <term>original: "stellarum erraticarum," literally wandering stars; the sun, moon, and five known planets</term> are limited according to the region where the edge of the **zodiac** ends, which cannot occur in our northern habitable zone. And this is what was proposed.

### 70. Rainbows are generated only from solar and lunar rays.

This is because only the rays of these two bodies are perceptibly extended according to the diameter of the world: those of the sun, because it is the largest body in quantity of all luminous bodies and of the purest substance; those of the moon, because it is closer to the earth, whence its rays are presented perceptibly to the sight. The sight is excused from the perceptibility of light from other bodies because of the smallness of those bodies compared to the sun, and their great distance from us compared to the moon. 

That a rainbow is formed by the sun is known to the senses. It is also possible for a rainbow to be formed from the rays of the moon, and this has often been seen, especially among those further north, to whom the material is often presented. Hence, nocturnal observers in **Germany** <note>original: "Alemania"</note> saw a lunar rainbow twice in one year; and perhaps it would be seen more often, depending on how the agent and the material present themselves. Among southern peoples, however, it is seen more rarely, because the material does not present itself as often, even if the agent is always disposed to the diffusion of light, as in every full moon or around it. Thus, **Aristotle** did not observe a lunar rainbow occurring in his place of residence except twice in 50 years. 

Furthermore, several lunar rainbows occur in the twilight when the moon is full or **gibbous** <term>gibbous: more than half but not fully illuminated</term> and large, positioned near the east above the horizon in such a way that the rays of the sun are not seen. They also occur at night, yet always in opposition to the moon. The lunar rainbow has the same form and matter as the solar rainbow, and likewise the same distinction of colors. However, these colors are **whiter** than the colors of the solar rainbow. The reason for this is that the appearance of the lunar rainbow occurs against a black cloud and at night; thus, with the blackness doubled (that of the night and that of the cloud), the white light produced from the moon’s rays appears more white. And because **crimson** <note>original: "puniceum"</note> is a weakly white color, the crimson will then appear more white in comparison to the greater blackness. The same is true for each of the other colors; for each of those colors appears whiter. Thus the entire lunar rainbow appears whiter than the solar rainbow. For the shadows falling upon the rays of the moon are not as black as the shadows of the sun, and the causes for this are various, as has been said. For the light of the moon is paler than the light of the sun; hence the colors formed from its mixture are stained and do not reach the peak of their own proper form. This is similar to how, because of the paleness of candlelight, many colors vary and some are taken for others by the sense. Thus it is clear from which bodies' rays rainbows are generated: since they come only from the rays of the sun and moon, and not from the rays of any other stars whatever; which is what was proposed.

### 71. It is not possible for more than two rainbows, differing in the placement of colors, to be seen.

For example: since there are only three colors of the rainbow (as is clear through theorem 67 of this book), it is not possible for the colors of the rainbow to be diversified in position, except according to the extreme colors, namely **crimson** <note>original: "punicei"</note> and **indigo** <note>original: "alurgum," a sea-purple or deep blue-violet</note>; because the middle color always remains in a middle causality between them. Because of this, it is clear that more than two rainbows differing in the placement of colors cannot occur, because the middle color cannot have a cause for generation while the other colors remain in their proper form, even if they are transposed in position. 

As for the fact that sometimes several rainbows with the same placement of colors are seen, one under another, such as first **red**, then **green**, and then **indigo**, and again **red**, again **green**, and finally **indigo**: this happens because of the diversity of the matter in different surfaces, one of which is in front of the other, and which happen to be seen under a single angle. Hence they appear as if they were held together or contiguous. But if there is a diversity in the angle—as when a line exiting from the sight and passing through the **hump** <note>original: "gibbum," the peak or apex of the arc</note> of one rainbow (the lower one) does not pass through the hump of the upper one—then they will be seen following one another, and between the **indigo** of the upper one and the **crimson** of the lower one, there will be a notable difference, namely a **white** one; since from that part of the cloud, whether further or nearer...

However, rainbows of this kind are always on different surfaces, and are caused by one **pyramid** <term>pyramid: in medieval optics, this refers to a cone of light rays</term> of reflected light: and because of this, they share a single center, as it were, which is the center of the pyramid of irradiation, and their peripheries appear equidistant to the sight. And it is possible (though it does not often happen) that several such rainbows—namely, one within another—are presented to the sight. This can be proved by two people splashing water in a ray of light, specifically with one person positioned below the other: for then a rainbow beneath a rainbow can be seen. However, it is impossible for this to occur on the same surface—namely, that several rainbows with the same color arrangement appear—since reflection occurs only from that part of the surface where the rays fall according to equal angles, and not from other parts of the same surface higher or lower than the aforementioned periphery, as is clear from theorem 66 of this book. Moreover, the colors of the outer rainbow always appear weaker than the colors of the inner rainbow: because they are formed by rays farther from the perpendicular and more distant from the sight: hence the light reflected through them is seen as weaker, compared to that which is caused by the inner rays.

### 72. In the outer rainbow, sometimes the colors are seen reversed and weaker than those of the inner rainbow.

We say the colors of the rainbow are **reversed** <note>original: "contrapositos," meaning mirrored or in opposite order</note> when, just as the color of the inner rainbow is **crimson** <note>original: "puniceus," a deep reddish-purple</note> on its outer circumference, the color of the outer rainbow is **crimson** on its *inner* periphery; the middle color of both rainbows is **leek-green** <note>original: "prasinus"</note>; and the innermost color of the inner rainbow is **sea-purple** <note>original: "alurgus," a deep blue or violet</note>, just as the outermost color of the outer rainbow is. With two rainbows arranged this way, all the colors of the outer rainbow are weaker than the colors of the inner rainbow. A cause of this could be found if all those colors

Thus, it is the **nadir** <term>nadir: the point directly opposite the sun in the sky</term> of the sun, and it moves always according to the sun's motion. In its movement, it describes a circle similar to the circle of the sun's motion—specifically, parallel to it—which the sun describes above the horizon in its daily motion: for the said center, which is the center of the base of the pyramid of illumination below the horizon, describes such a path. And just as when the sun is at the eastern point of the horizon, the center is in the western part of the horizon; so when the sun is at the western point of the horizon, that center is in the eastern part. And since the lines drawn from the center of the sun to the circumference of the base of the pyramid of illumination are equal by theorem 89 of Book 1: it is clear that the surface of the base of the aforementioned pyramid intersects the horizon in such a way that it, along with the surface cutting the sun and standing perpendicularly to the horizon, will meet below the horizon: therefore it makes an obtuse angle above the horizon with respect to the sight. Nor is this surprising, since the horizon passes through one of the poles of the base circle—as through the center of sight, which is the pole of that circle by theorem 65 of Book 1—it is clear that it does not pass through the other pole of that circle. Therefore, in whatever part of the vapor the outer rainbow is formed, that part which is on the higher part of the rainbow's circle is further removed from the sight. If rays happen to be reflected from it to the sight, the higher ones must appear darker to the observer compared to those rays reflected from the lower parts of the same surface, as is clear from theorems 158 and 159 of Book 4. And thus, it is necessary for the lower periphery of the upper rainbow, which is closer to the sight, to show **crimson** colors, the middle to show **leek-green**, and the uppermost to show **sea-purple**. The extent of the distance in the magnitude of elongation outweighs the quantity of the angles of reflection and the quantity of the angle of vision. For this reason, the colors of the upper rainbow are sometimes seen reversed compared to the colors of the inner rainbow, in which the upper periphery always appears crimson. For when reflection occurs to the sight from that part of the surface in a way disproportionate to the reflections of the distance, then the lower rays of the same surface cannot be reflected to the sight at the same distance, because their proximity exceeds the required distance: they are closer than the distance proportioned for reflection to such a sight. Therefore, what can appear irradiated to the sight from the nearby vapor appears crimson due to proximity and other causes mentioned earlier in theorem 67 of this book. according to what was previously stated. Thus, a certain convexity is formed in the irradiated vapor <note>original: "vapore irradiato"</note> with respect to the sight. And for this reason, perhaps, it has been said by some that the cloud in which the rainbow is generated is concave; however, it is not necessary to ascribe the things that are seen to the concavity of a cloud: because the vapor (as far as its total consistency is concerned) is a whole, filled with distinct tiny particles—just as atoms are seen to fill the entire path of a sunbeam—and such vapor is thicker on the side away from the sun than on the front side facing the sun. But if the center of the sun were placed on the horizon line <note>original: "peripheria horizontis"</note>, so that the base of the pyramid of illumination <term>pyramid of illumination: a cone-shaped volume of light rays extending from the sun</term> stood perpendicularly to the horizon, the outer rays reflected to the sight would still be longer than those reflected from the inner peripheries, according to theorem 19 of this book: for in the same triangle ending at the eye, they are opposite the larger angle. Thus it is clear that, wherever the body of the sun is positioned, it is possible for the colors of the outer rainbow to appear reversed compared to the colors of the inner rainbow.

All the colors of the secondary rainbow are necessarily weaker than the colors of the primary rainbow: since they are formed by rays further from the perpendicular and reflected toward the eye at larger angles; because of this, these rays are less concentrated with the incident rays, and therefore they produce less light and color. We use what we have just set forth as a guiding principle to explain our proposal (even if it is not the absolute cause). For it is manifest that those rays—since they are outside the periphery proportioned for reflection to that sight, specifically beyond the red <note>original: "puniceam," a reddish-purple color often used for the outer band of the rainbow</note> band of the inner rainbow—will not be reflected to the sight with light unless they are prepared for reflection by the rays reflected from the inner primary rainbow, and unless their light is brought into a state of visibility through the gathering of the light of those rays with the rays reflected to the eye.

A sign of this is the whiteness <note>original: "albedo"</note> that appears in a circle in the cloud between the upper red periphery of the lower rainbow and the lower red periphery of the upper rainbow: because this whiteness is caused by light illuminating the cloud that is not reflected to the eye. For among the rays capable of being reflected from the same surface that can be reflected to the eye in any one arranged place, those are the ones reflected from the outermost periphery of the lower rainbow; none of the higher rays will be reflected to that sight, but the white cloud, resulting from the mixture of non-reflected light seen by simple vision <term>simple vision: direct sight without reflection or refraction</term>, will meet that sight.

Indeed, even if many rays from the red periphery of the lower rainbow—besides those reflected to the sight—spread out to neighboring parts of the misty vapor, the light from their fall cannot be reflected to that sight from the neighboring vapor. This is because those rays fall onto the surface of the vapor at an angle that is still disproportionate to the eye, so the distance is not suitable for reflection. This begins at the start of the red periphery, where the rays fall upon the cloud according to the sharpest angles in that pyramid; but other rays, following these rays in the red periphery of the lower rainbow, fall at larger angles with respect to the eye (since they are on a deeper surface from the eye) and are reflected to that surface of the vapor where the lower red periphery of the upper rainbow is located. There, gathered together with the rays falling on that part of the vapor from the sun, they make that part of the surface visible due to the accumulation of greater light, with the rays reflected to the eye which previously could not be perceived as reflected due to the weakness of the light.

And since the rays reflected upward from the lower part to other parts of the misty vapor (whether the vapor where the reflection occurs is in the same surface as the first rainbow or in another surface) form angles with the rays reflected from the same periphery to the eye in the generation of the primary rainbow—as explained in theorem 66 of this book—triangles are formed. The angles of these triangles are at the center of the eye, and the bases are the lines lying between the red periphery of the lower rainbow and the red of the upper one. And because there is no sensible reflection to the eye from those bases, their entire surface appears white, with no light being reflected from it to the eye.

In a similar way, reflection occurs from the other colors of the lower rainbow to the upper rainbow. And since the angles of incidence of the rays causing those parts of the rainbow are larger, as shown above by theorem 106 of Book 1, therefore by theorem 20 of Book 5, the angles of reflection are also larger. Therefore, those rays reach higher into the vapor, producing colors similar to themselves; for those rays, due to the mixing of the shadows of other particles, participate in color, which is transmitted to the opposite mixed body along with light, according to theorem 2 of Book 5.

And just as it was shown by theorem 55 of Book 5 that because of reflection, right-hand things appear on the left and left-hand things on the right, so it also happens in this reflection that the colors of these rainbows appear reversed. The colors of the secondary rainbow also appear weaker than those of the primary (lower) rainbow: because rays falling on the cloud far from the axis of the pyramid of irradiation are weak and imperceptible to the eye due to the great distance, as shown by theorem 158 of Book 4; also, rays reflected from the refracted rays of the primary rainbow are weak, as shown by theorem 3 of Book 5 and theorem 10 of this book. It follows necessarily, therefore, that their reflection to the eye is weak; thus all the colors of the secondary rainbow are weak and are mixed more with the blackness of shadows. Therefore, the colors of the secondary rainbow necessarily appear weaker than the colors of the primary rainbow; nor does any further reflection occur from them to the higher parts of the misty vapor, because of the weakness of those rays.

And perhaps for this reason Aristotle said that no more than two rainbows can be seen: because there are only two that are formally distinguished by the placement of their colors, even though more may sometimes be seen, as explained in the preceding section. Thus the proposal is clear.

### 73. *It is necessary that every sensible arc of the rainbow be divided into two equal parts by its circle of altitude. From this it is manifest that every observer sees his own private rainbow.*

Since, as is clear from the preceding, the surface of the horizon intersects the surface of the circle of the rainbow, then their common section is a straight line, according to Book 11, Proposition 3. But because the circle of altitude <term>circle of altitude: a vertical circle passing through the zenith and a point on the celestial sphere</term> of the rainbow always passes through the zenith of the head—since the center of the eye is the pole of the rainbow (as clear from theorem 64 of this book and explained in what came before)—the center of that circle of altitude is the center of the world and of the horizon.

Therefore, it passes through the poles of the horizon: for the zenith of the head <note>The "zenith of the head" is the point directly above the observer.</note> is the pole of that same horizon. Truly, the line drawn from the pole to the center of the horizon is perpendicular to the surface of the horizon, according to the beginning of the first book of this work. Therefore, by Proposition 18 of Book 11 <note>Witelo frequently references Euclid’s "Elements" using this notation.</note>, that circle of the rainbow’s altitude is perpendicular to the surface of the horizon; and it passes through its center: for since they are both great circles of the world's sphere, it is clear they share the same center, which is the center of the world. That circle of altitude, therefore, cuts the horizon into equal parts and at right angles. Similarly, since the same circle of altitude passes through the center of the sight <note>The observer's eye.</note>, through the center of the rainbow’s circle, and through the center of the sun (for these three are on the same line according to Theorem 64 of this book), it also passes through the poles of the rainbow’s circle; and according to what was said before, it cuts it into equal parts and at right angles. But if the circle of altitude cuts both the horizon and the rainbow's circle into equal parts and at right angles, it will also cut their intersection into equal parts and at right angles, according to Proposition 19 of Book 11. Let that common intersection be line **a b**, which the extended circle of altitude divides into equal parts at point **c**. Let line **c d** be drawn upward in the surface of the circle of altitude from point **c**: this is the common intersection of the surfaces of that circle and the rainbow; and this line **c d** will be perpendicu-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram positioned on the right side of the text block. It shows a circle with a vertical diameter labeled 'd' at the top. lar to line **a b** according to Proposition 19 of Book 11: because the circle of altitude is perpendicular to the surface of each of those two circles whose common intersection is line **a b**. Let point **d** be the common intersection of the circumferences of the circle of altitude and the rainbow. Therefore, angle **d c a** is a right angle, and similarly angle **d c b**. Let lines **a d** and **b d** be drawn opposite those angles; it is clear from Proposition 4 of Book 1 and from what was said before that they are equal. Therefore, by Proposition 28 of Book 3, the arc of the rainbow **a d** is equal to the arc **b d**. Thus, the part of the rainbow's circumference that is above the horizon (since that part alone is visible) is divided into equal parts by the circle of altitude. This is what was proposed. From this, a very beautiful corollary is evident: namely, that **each person seeing a rainbow sees their own unique one** <note>This is a fundamental concept in medieval optics: the rainbow is not a physical object in one place, but a geometric relationship between the sun, the drops, and a specific observer's eye.</note>. This is because when an observer moves from place to place, the zenith of their head always changes. It is clear that different people have different zeniths and different horizons; nor is it possible for any two people to have the same horizon, since the eye of the observer is always the center of their horizon. If, therefore, the difference between people is only according to distance in latitude, then the rays reflected from the body of the cloud will meet at their eyes differently according to different points of gathering. The person farther from the dewy vapor will see a larger rainbow, and the closer one a smaller one, if the rainbows appear on the same surface. If they appear on different parallel surfaces, then the rainbow can be seen as equal circles; and the rainbow will follow the one who flees and flee from the one who follows, as we said in Theorem 65 of this book. They share the same circle of altitude, but it is not oriented in the same way. But if the difference between people is only according to longitude, then there will be different circles of altitude, and each of those circles (according to what was said) divides the arc of the rainbow above the horizon into two equal parts; therefore, since the dividing lines are different, the arcs divided are also different. Each person, therefore, will see their own rainbow. If both the latitude and longitude of the observers differ, then it is clear from the above that they will in no way see the same rainbow. Thus, what we intended is clear. A proof of this is: if someone standing in a sunbeam with their back to the sun sprays water from their mouth <note>original: "aquam ore spargat"</note>, they will see with both eyes the colors of the rainbow in front of their forehead, and the arc will be equally distant from each eye. But if they spray water a second time and close their right eye or cover it with their hand, they will see the arc equally distant from the center of the left eye, and the arc of the rainbow will seem to cut across the right eye; and it will be the reverse if they close the left eye: for then they will again see the arc equally distant from the center of the right eye, cutting across the left eye. From this, it can be clearly seen that the color of the rainbow is an **affection of the sight** <term>affection of the sight: "passio visus," meaning the rainbow is an optical phenomenon occurring in the eye/perception rather than a solid physical object</term>; that the rainbow changes according to the movement of the observers; that its material is dewy vapor; and that the distinction of colors does not arise from the quality of the material, but from the reflection of light to the sight, to which color essentially comes from the mixing of the blackness of shadows.

Therefore, let the circle of the rainbow be drawn around over the surface of the horizon, intersecting it, which (as is clear from what was previously stated) will pass through point **m** of the circle of altitude: let it be, therefore, that the circle of the rainbow itself intersects the horizon at point **n**. Lines **k m** and **h m** will therefore touch the two circles at point **m**, namely according to their common intersection. Therefore, whatever the proportion of line **c d** to line **h k**, the same will be that of the known line **b c** to some other by Theorem 3 of Book 1 of this work. ...according to the things previously noted. Therefore, let a line be joined from point to point **m** in the surface of the <term>circle of altitude</term> <note>A vertical circle passing through the zenith, used to measure the height of celestial bodies.</note>, which shall be **p m**: and it will necessarily be that as the ratio of line **c d** is to **h k**, or line **b c** to **k p**, the same will be the ratio of line **a b** to line **p m**. 

But if it is said that this is not possible: then whatever the ratio of line **c d** is to **h k**, or **b c** to **k p**, the same will be the ratio of **a b** to some other line either greater or smaller than line **p m**, by Theorem 3 of Book 1 of this work. Suppose now that the ratio of line **a b** is to some smaller line **p q**, which we will call **p r**. Therefore, as the ratio of line **c d** is to line **h k**, or **b c** to line **k p**, so is **a b** to line **p r**. But since the ratio of line **c d** to line **h k** is the same as **b c** to line **k p**, then by Proposition 16 of Book 5 <note>Reference to Euclid’s Elements regarding proportional magnitudes.</note>, as the ratio of line **c d** is to **b c**, so is **h k** to **k p**. And as the ratio of line **b c** is to **k p**, so is line **a b** to line **p r**. Therefore, again by Proposition 16 of Book 5, as the ratio of line **b c** is to **a b**, so is line **k p** to **p r**. 

Thus the lines **c d**, **b c**, and **a b** will be proportional to lines **h k**, **k p**, and **p r**. But since the ratio of line **a b** to **b c** is the same as line **b d** to **a b**, it will also be so in their proportional counterparts: just as line **r p** relates to **p k**, so the whole **p h** will relate to line **p r** when combined. Let lines **h r** and **k r** be drawn; two triangles will be formed, **h r p** and **k r p**, which share the angle **r p h**. The sides containing said angle are proportional with respect to the different triangles: for the ratio of line **p r** (a side of the larger triangle) to line **p k** (a side of the smaller triangle) is the same as the ratio of line **h p** (a side of the larger triangle) to line **p r** (a side of the smaller triangle **p r k**). Therefore, by Proposition 6 of Book 6, those triangles are <term>equiangular</term> <note>Having the same angles; similar triangles.</note>. 

Thus, by Proposition 4 of Book 6, their sides opposite equal angles are proportional. Therefore, the ratio of line **h p** to line **p r**, and line **p r** to line **p k**, is as line **h r** to line **k r**. But whatever ratio line **h p** has to line **p r**, line **b d** has to line **a b**; and whatever **b d** has to **a b**, **a b** has to **b c**; and whatever **a b** has to **b c**, line **h m** has to **k m** by the hypothesis. Therefore, by Proposition 11 of Book 5, it is clear that whatever ratio line **h r** has to line **k r**, line **h m** has to line **k m**. However, this is impossible and contradicts Theorem 56 of Book 1 of this work: since in any semicircle, if two lines are drawn to any point of the circumference—namely one from the end of the diameter and another from the center, as are lines **h m** and **k m** in this case—it is impossible to draw two other lines from the same points to any other point of the circumference that are proportional to the first two. 

It is therefore impossible for line **a b** to have the same ratio to any line smaller than line **p m** as line **b d** has to line **h p**, or **c d** to **h k**, or **b c** to **k p**. But neither can line **a b** have that ratio to any line greater than line **p m**, because the reasoning is the same and leads to the same impossibility. Therefore, whatever the ratio of **c d** to line **h k**, or line **b c** to **k p**, the same will be the ratio of line **a b** to **p m**. And it follows, by repeating the prior demonstration that led to an impossibility, that as the ratio of line **h p** is to **p m**, and line **m p** to **p k**, the same is the ratio of line **h m** to **k m**. 

Accordingly, with several semicircles of altitude drawn around center **k** beneath the horizon, proportional lines to the aforementioned lines **h m** and **k m** are drawn according to the method of Theorem 56 of Book 1. If, therefore, line **m p** is standing perpendicularly upon diameter **h g**, then with center **p** and radius **p m**, a circle is described. But if line **p m** is not perpendicular to diameter **h g**, then with point **p** acting as a <term>pole</term> <note>A fixed point around which a line or circle rotates.</note> by Theorem 65 of Book 1 (since that point will be equally distant from all points marked in those semicircles similar to point **m**), a circle is drawn according to the distance of line **p m**. This circle will reach all said points of the semicircles of altitude where the aforementioned proportional lines fall, which are the angles of reflection causing the rainbow. For if it were said that it does not reach them, there would occur a contradiction to Theorem 56 of Book 1, which is impossible. 

It can also happen that the semicircle **h m g** is half of the horizon, and once the division is made at point **m**, that same semicircle is understood to be rotated around. For it makes no difference whether one describes various semicircles or rotates one. Point **m**, when rotated, will describe the circle of the rainbow, which is **n m**, around the center or pole **p** at the distance of line **p m**. And the angles of the lines drawn from the end of the diameter (point **h**) and from the center **k** to the circle **n m** will all be equal in any <term>surface of reflection</term> <note>The plane in which the path of light and the observer's eye lie during reflection.</note>. This is because triangle **h m k**, throughout the entire rotation, causes triangles similar to itself in every surface of reflection; and similarly, triangle **h m p** by its motion will describe similar triangles, and triangle **k m p** will likewise describe similar triangles. 

If, therefore, line **m p** is not perpendicular to diameter **h g**, let a perpendicular be drawn from point **m** by Proposition 12 of Book 1 onto diameter **h g**. That perpendicular will fall, by Theorem 29 of Book 1, between points **k** and **p**, or between points **p** and **g**, because line **m p** forms an acute angle with diameter **h g** on some side, as is clear from the premises. And similarly for line **m k**, because the rainbow does not appear except beyond the middle of the horizon’s diameter, as was shown before. Let that perpendicular fall on point **o**. Similarly, to that same point of the diameter, perpendicular lines will necessarily fall from all the angles of the other semicircles; or the angle **k o m**, by its motion in all surfaces of reflection, will cause equal angles. Therefore, point **o** is the center of the circle of reflection made to the sight. Since the center of the rainbow is on the diameter of the horizon, half of it will be above the horizon (which is **n m**) and half below the horizon, because then the common section of the surfaces of the horizon and the rainbow is the diameter of the rainbow. The same would happen if line **m p** were perpendicular to the diameter. <note>original: "Et hic est modus, quo Aristoteles propositũ cõclusit."</note> And this is the method by which Aristotle concluded the proposition. Nevertheless, the specific knowledge of these lines did not seem necessary to us, because the same thing can be declared in the same way without them.

### 75. When the center of a luminous body exists in any circle of altitude above the horizon, the center of the rainbow circle is depressed below the horizon according to its elevation; and a portion of the rainbow smaller than a semicircle is seen.

Let it be according to the previous arrangement: let the horizon be circle **h m g**, whose diameter is line **m h** and center **k**. Let the circle of altitude passing through the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point directly above the observer.</note> of the head and through the center of the luminous body be **l m n h**. Let the center of the sun be elevated above the horizon in the circle of altitude at point **n**. Therefore, that line produced from point **n** through the center **k** will necessarily fall on some point of the circle of altitude, which let be **l**: and the semicircle of altitude raised above the circle of the horizon, which is **h n m**, will be equal to the semicircle **n m l**: since they are halves of the same circle. Therefore, having removed the common arc, which is **n m**, the arc **h n** will be equal to the arc **m l**. But point **l** is the location of the center of the circle of irradiation: and point **n** is the location of the center of the sun. It is clear, therefore, that by as much as the center of the sun is raised above the horizon, by that same amount the center of the circle of the base of the pyramid of irradiation is depressed below the horizon. And this is the first point proposed. 

Moreover, when both of the centers are on the circle of the horizon, a semicircle of the rainbow is seen, as was shown in the preceding theorem: therefore, when the center of the sun is raised and the center of the [rainbow] circle is depressed, less than a semicircle will be seen. And this is what was proposed in the second place. What we have now said in explaining the proposition while the sun is in the east is the same if it were in the western part of the horizon, or in whatever part of the horizon it may be: as it is for those whose latitude is 66 degrees and 9 minutes <note>This refers to the Arctic Circle; Witelo is noting that at high latitudes, the sun's behavior on the horizon changes, but the optical laws remain universal.</note>: for to them the sun is on the meridian at the point of the winter tropic on the horizon. And thus, according to different regions, the proposed theorem is always universal.

### 76. *It is manifest that a complete circle of a rainbow can never be seen.*

For since if the sun is on the horizon, only a semicircle is seen, as is clear from the 74th theorem of this book; and if it be above the horizon in any circle of altitude, it is clear through the premise that by as much as the center of the sun or moon is raised above the horizon, by so much is the center of the rainbow depressed below the horizon. Whence, at that time, a part of the rainbow smaller than a semicircle is always seen above the horizon, just as is clear in other <term>parallels</term> <note>Parallel circles on a sphere.</note> in the sphere, through whose center the horizon does not pass. For these are cut into unequal portions below the horizon and above the horizon. It is clear, therefore, since the luminous body at the time of the vision of the rainbow is either on the horizon or above the horizon, that a complete circle of a rainbow can never be seen: unless perhaps it happens by the reverberation of the sun’s light from a strong cloud to the earth or to another cloud, where there is <term>dewy vapor</term> <note>original: "uapor roridus"; refers to the fine mist or water droplets necessary to refract light into a rainbow.</note> in between, and the sight is between the vapor and the cloud from which the reverberation happens, or on the same line, so that a reflection can be made to it: for then it is possible for entire rainbows to be seen: but the proposed discourse does not intend to speak of such things: for we have spoken of such rainbows in the 67th theorem of this book. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 77. *To find the semi-diameter of a given rainbow.*

To what height the consistency of the highest vapors can be raised we have already shown in the 60th theorem of this book: but it is not possible for a rainbow to be raised according to their entire elevation: because the matter of the rainbow is dewy vapor (according to the 66th theorem of this), which is not raised as high as dry vapor. If, therefore, we wish to find the semi-diameter of a given rainbow, and the given rainbow is semicircular, the proposition is easily had. For let its height be taken by an instrument; and let the portion or arc of its circle of altitude lying between the horizon and the <term>summit</term> <note>original: "gibbum"; the highest point or 'hump' of the rainbow's arc.</note> of the rainbow be doubled, and with the doubled arc let one enter the <term>tables of chords and arcs</term> <note>Mathematical tables used for trigonometry before the widespread use of sines/cosines.</note> placed in the first discourse of the <term>Almagest</term> <note>Ptolemy’s foundational 2nd-century work on astronomy.</note>, and let the chord be extracted by the usual art: and the found chord will be the diameter of the whole rainbow: and that divided into equal parts, half of it will be the semi-diameter of the rainbow: and thus the sine of the circle of altitude will be the semi-diameter of the rainbow, which is seen under this position at such a height. If it is said that that line is not the semi-diameter of the rainbow, but of some other circle equidistant to the rainbow but larger than the rainbow: this does not stand in the way: because those two circles fall into the same solid angle at the center of the world, which is then the center of vision: whence what is said of one can be understood of the other, as far as quantity is concerned. And because the complete proportion of rainbow to rainbow is had through the proportions of such diameters: therefore we call such a diameter the diameter of the rainbow. If, however, the rainbow is a portion smaller than a semicircle: let its height be taken. And because, as is clear through the 75th theorem of this book, the sun is then above the horizon in the same circle, let the height of the sun be taken. Since therefore, as was declared in that theorem, the distance of the center of the rainbow below the horizon is equal to the elevation of the sun above the horizon: let these two arcs of altitude be joined, namely of the rainbow and of the sun, and there will result the arc lying between the point of the circle of altitude in which the diameter falls (drawn from the center of the sun's body through the center of vision and through the center of the rainbow to the circle of altitude itself—and this is the <term>nadir of the sun</term> <note>The point on the celestial sphere directly opposite the sun's position.</note>) and the upper point of the circle of altitude of the rainbow: therefore let that arc be doubled, and let the chord be extracted as before, and let it be divided into equal parts: and the intent will be had. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 78. *A rainbow seen as a semicircle is half of a smaller circle; but a portion seen as less than a semicircle is a portion of a larger circle.*

The cause of this proposed matter is clear according to the premises of this book. For since, as is clear through the 64th theorem of this, the center of the sun and of the vision and of the rainbow always consist in the same line, which is the axis of the pyramid of illumination of the dewy vapor: because of which it is clear that in every reflection from which the rainbow appears, the center of vision is always the pole of the circle of the rainbow: it is evident, therefore, that it makes no difference in the sight...
