the elevation or tilt of the surface of the rainbow above the surface of the horizon is seen. Since a line passing through the center of the sun and the eye is always perpendicular to the surface of the rainbow, the <term>periphery of the rainbow</term> <note>The outer edge or circumference of the rainbow's arc.</note> always maintains a uniform relationship to the eye by its very nature, as is evident from the 65th theorem of the first book of this work. However, what is proposed here has its cause not in reflection, but in <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light as it passes from one medium (like air) into another (like water droplets).</note>. For as we declared in the 8th book of this work, the variation in the angles of refraction is caused by the variation in the transparency of <term>diaphanous bodies</term> <note>Materials that allow light to pass through, such as air or water.</note>, even those of the same type. Indeed, refraction toward the perpendicular line is greater in thicker water than in thinner water. 

Since, therefore, when the sun is at the edge of the horizon, the air is thicker than itself after it has been thinned by the presence of solar light, it is clear that in that thicker air there is less refraction away from the perpendicular. Thus, the rays refracted at that time are closer to the perpendicular than they are later at the surfaces of the eyes located there, than happens when the air is thinner. But when the air is thinned, refraction occurs toward those same eyes from more remote parts of the vapor itself; for it does not happen from the closer parts, since it did not happen from them before either. Nor does that refraction occur from the parts of the vapor where it occurred before, because when the medium is changed, the refraction itself is changed according to the 8th book of this work. Therefore, the refraction must necessarily occur from more remote parts of the vapor than before. Consequently, the refracted rays are longer than those that were refracted earlier; the <term>pyramid of illumination</term> <note>A cone-shaped volume of light rays spreading from the sun toward the observer.</note> is therefore larger. Thus, its base (which, as is clear from what has been established, is the periphery of the rainbow) will also be larger. 

Furthermore, when the sun is at the edge of the horizon, only the semicircle of the resulting rainbow is seen, as is clear from the 74th theorem of this book; but when the sun is raised above the horizon, a portion of the rainbow smaller than a semicircle is seen, as is clear from the 75th theorem. The proposition is therefore manifest. However, it is the experience of some that the altitude of the rainbow and the altitude of the sun together always make 42 degrees; this theorem shows that to be impossible. For if the radius of the circle of the rainbow is sometimes smaller and sometimes larger according to the variation of the transparent media and their refractions—which was shown before—then it cannot reasonably seem to anyone that the radii of all the different circles of different rainbows are equal. There could, however, be a slight difference which perhaps cannot be perceived by a small instrument that is out of proportion to the circle of altitude. And their experience also concerns portions of rainbows smaller than a semicircle, which is clear from the altitude of the sun, which such people take either by turning the instrument or by changing their sight while the instrument is fixed—which is nothing when the sun is at the edge of the horizon. And perhaps there is no sensible difference in such portions or their diameters, because even *Aristotle* wrote nothing about it, even though he made great mention of the present theorem; yet neither he nor anyone else whose writings we have seen has brought forward a declaration on this matter. As for the difference of <term>climates</term> <note>In ancient geography, "climates" referred to latitudinal zones of the Earth.</note>, let no one offer an excuse, because what happens in one climate must necessarily happen in all climates in the generation of the rainbow. For the centers of the sun, the eye, and the circle of the rainbow always consist on the same line, and the arc of the altitude of the center of the rainbow's circle below the horizon is equal to the sun's altitude in all climates; nor will anyone perceive a difference in this.

### 79. In certain regions when the sun is at noon, a sensible rainbow does not appear.

To show what is proposed, let the center of the sun first be placed in some region at noon at the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note>. It is clear from the preceding that the base of the pyramid of irradiation will then be below the horizon and parallel to the horizon. And since the altitude of the sun will then be 90 degrees, as the sun descends (whether this happens because of the motion of the sun itself, or because of the altitude of regions more distant from the equator than the region in which the sun was perpendicular at noon—such as from that which is directly under the <term>Tropic of Cancer</term> <note>original: "capite cancri"</note>), a rainbow will never occur at noon as long as the sine of the circle of the sun's altitude at noon is greater than the diameter of the rainbow, which a diligent searcher will be able to find through the 77th theorem of this book. However, by as much as the sine of the circle of the sun's altitude at noon is less than the diameter of the rainbow, that much of the diameter of the rainbow and of the rainbow itself will appear to the eye at noon. And because of this, in summer days from the spring equinox to the autumn equinox in our customary regions—which are beyond the fourth climate up to the end of the seven known climates—the rainbow does not appear at noon, even if it appears at other times of the year. We have said all this regarding the regions that are outside the climates, in which the preceding rule can be entrusted to general teaching. In all regions, however, when the sun is above the horizon, a rainbow can appear at any hour of the day except at noon; yet only in those hours in which the sine of the circle of the sun's altitude is greater than the rainbow's diameter. And let these things suffice for the intent of the rainbow, for "Saturnian Juno sent the rainbow from heaven." <note>original: "irim de cælo misit Saturnia Iuno" — A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 9, line 2, referring to Juno using Iris as a messenger.</note>

### 80. The apparent color of clouds is formed according to the disposition of the matter and the incorporation of light.

Since the consistency of clouds is made of two vapors, namely the dry and the moist, as has been declared in natural philosophy: then when the sun, by acting on the dry, completely extracts the moist, the terrestrial dry matter is scorched so that light cannot penetrate into it; and therefore the cloud then becomes black with much blackness. Such clouds are the material of winds. In aqueous vapor, however, blackness is generated from the condensation of cold, because of which the solar ray or the rays of the stars cannot penetrate it; and therefore the moist cloud remains very black. But from any scattered, thin vapor that receives the entry of solar light, a white cloud is made; hence sometimes a white mist is seen. But when a cloud has within it a smoky moisture mixed with a little scorched terrestrial matter, then when light is received in it, a red cloud is made, and sometimes a purple one, as when the rays are terminated at the lower part of a moist cloud...

seen in the morning or in the evening; and these signify future rain. Indeed, if this happens in the east, rain is brought upon the people of that habitable area. But if it occurs in the west, then rain is carried to the lower hemisphere of the world <note>The "lower hemisphere" refers to the part of the earth below the observer's horizon.</note> beneath the people watching; there will be rain there at night, and that part of the sky will perhaps return stripped of clouds in the morning. Thus, the redness of clouds in the evening signifies clear weather on the following day. However, when a low-hanging cloud has its upper part speckled with a very dark purple, then that redness comes from burnt earthy particles which are already beginning to ignite in the "belly" of the cloud; such clouds are dangerous, containing the <term>matter of thunder</term> <note>Medieval science often viewed thunder and lightning as the ignition of "exhalations" or earthy vapors trapped within clouds.</note> and similar things. But if the cloud is dewy and at the end of its dissolution, then that cloud, having received light into itself, sometimes acquires the color of a rainbow. According to its various dispositions, a great variety of colors is produced by the light present in the clouds—whether the light falling on the cloud is <term>refracted</term> to the sight because of the density of the second transparent medium, or <term>reflected</term> to the sight from the surface of the cloud itself. But in these intermediate colors of the clouds, the mixing of shadows has no small effect, as when a higher cloud is seen through a thin, shadowy cloud. For then the observed cloud is colored with various hues according to the mixture of those shadows. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 81. Sunbeams are formed by the refraction of solar rays to the sight from some cloudy consistency, distinguished unequally by rarity and thickness.

<term>Virgae</term> <note>Latin for "rods" or "staves." These are crepuscular rays—the "beams" of light seen radiating from the sun through gaps in clouds.</note> are what we call the extensions of rays through clouds, which are commonly called "tent ropes" <note>original: "funes tentorij." A vivid medieval description of sunbeams looking like the supporting cords of a large pavilion.</note>. For when some watery cloud is interposed between the sun and our sight, a refraction of the solar rays to the sight occurs; and this happens in the middle of the second transparent medium. Because of this, the colors of the rainbow are sometimes seen there, stretched out according to certain straight lines, because they have some thinner and some thicker consistency in which the mixed light of the sun creates the illusion of color. However, the more powerful cause in these is the mixing of shadows, which, being mixed with the light in different ways, represent different colors to the eyes. And because a solar ray falling perpendicular to the surface of the cloud penetrates the cloud and is not bent toward the eyes, the cloud appears white and colorless in the middle. The sun seen through it appears without a distinct shape, but reddish in color or having some other color; for the sun presents different colors to the eyes through the thicker and misty consistency of a cloud. There is, however, no difference in this whether the sun is seen through the cloud (such that a refraction of its rays to the sight occurs) or if the rays of the sun are reflected to the sight. To one looking at the sides of the sun, a "striped" rainbow color is sometimes seen when the cloud is thick in one part and thin in another, and more watery in one part and less in another; and sometimes one part appears reddish-purple, another green or yellow. <term>Virgae</term>, therefore, occur because of the irregularity of the different positions and qualities of the "mirrors" <note>Vitello treats water droplets in clouds as tiny mirrors or refracting bodies.</note>, not because of an anomaly of shape. For there are certain mirrors which, because of their own anomaly, show anomalous and changed shapes of the forms seen through them—about which some discussion was held in the ninth book of this science. Hence, the cloud does not show the shape of the sun because the "mirrors" of the cloud are not properly suited to showing a shape due to their smallness, but they do show color, which is consistent with the transparency of the mirrors and the whole cloud. Those colors are distinguished according to the disposition of the matter in which the light is incorporated and according to the mixing of shadows. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

### 82. Parhelia are formed from the reflection of solar rays to the sight from a uniform cloudy consistency.

<term>Parelia</term> <note>Commonly known as "sun dogs" or parhelia. The term comes from the Greek "παρήλιοι" (parelioi), meaning "beside the sun."</note> are named as if they were "peers to the sun," for in Greek they are called *parelioi*, and in Latin they are called "watery suns" which are seen in a cloud. For when a cloud is interposed between the sun and the eyes, and it is uniform according to its "mirrors"—being neither denser nor thinner, nor more watery nor less in its various parts—then when a solar ray falls upon them, an illusion of a single color is created because of the similarity and uniformity of the mirrors and their regularity. It appears white in color because of the thickness of the consistency and the regularity of the cloud itself. For rays falling upon a cloud so disposed and reflected from it to the eyes (especially if that cloud is not watery or black, yet near to water) are reflected to the sight without the mixture of any shadow. Because of this, they make the sun’s own color, which is luminous and white, appear to the eyes throughout the entire consistency of the cloud. These parhelia become white, just as the light of the sun is reflected to the sight from any polished body because of the thickness of its consistency, as was shown in the 11th theorem of the 5th book of this work. Parhelia, however, are a greater sign of rain than <term>virgae</term> are, because the uniform consistency of clouds, which is the material for parhelia, is a sign that the air is in a state suitable for change and for the generation of water. And because southern air is more easily changed into water due to its readiness to be affected than northern air (which is drier due to the constriction of the cold), therefore southern parhelia are a greater sign of rain than northern ones. Parhelia, like <term>virgae</term>, occur more when the sun is in the east or the west than at midday; for the sun, being in the middle of the sky, dissolves such consistencies of clouds and greatly separates them. They occur neither above the sun nor below it, but at the slanted sides of the sun, which are toward the poles of the world. Nor do they occur very close to the sun, because a consistency of clouds is quickly dissolved from nearby; nor do they occur very far from the sun, because reflection to the sight is not possible from there. For a reflection made from a small mirror is weak; hence, when stretched far, it is weakened and vanishes before it reaches the sight. For these same reasons, these parhelia do not occur above the sun, nor below the sun: because those cloud consistencies existing near the sun are dissolved, while those distantly removed do not reach the eyes according to their reflection. Along the side of the sun, however, one can find a moderate distance in which the consistency is not dissolved, and yet reflection to the sight occurs—as long as that consistency of the cloud is not descending too close to the earth. For when clouds are too close to the horizon, then the rays reflected from those clouds do not reach the eyes because of a shorter distance that is disproportionate to the reflection of light. Since the eyes are at the earth, it is clear that then the reflection of light from the cloud does not converge with the eyes. A parhelia also cannot occur below the sun, because then the cloud, being near the earth and facing the perpendicular ray of the sun...

### 83. The colors of the rainbow are generated from a hexagonal crystal placed opposite the sun.

For colors of this kind are generated from the weakening of light due to <term>refraction</term> toward the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The "perpendicular" refers to the normal line, an imaginary line at a right angle to the surface where light enters.</note> drawn from the center of the sun's body to the surface of one of the parallelograms on the sides of the crystal. And since (as we have declared in the 27th theorem of the 4th book of this science) it is manifest that more than half of a cylinder opposite the sun is illuminated by it if the cylinder is round; however, this cannot happen in an angled cylinder (with the angles coming into the diameter of the body, dividing the base into equal parts), for then only half is illuminated due to the incidence of the rays, as we said in that same place. 

But if that columnar body is <term>transparent</term> <note>original: "diaphanū"; refers to any medium that allows light to pass through.</note>, then the other half of that body is illuminated due to the refraction of the rays. If, therefore, the surface of the transparent body opposite the sun is a single one, as in quadrangular bodies, then one strong refraction of light occurs, and the light will pass to the opposite part of the body in the form of light, and will gather outside the body in the form of light. This happens even more strongly in a spherical transparent body that is not hollow, because from the surface of the greater part of that entire spherical body, refraction occurs toward the ray that falls perpendicularly upon the surface tangent to the spherical body—which is a surface equidistant to the one cutting through the center of the sun according to the aspect from which the body to be illuminated is seen, as we showed in theorem 48 of this book. 

From the gathering of so many and such rays—even if not to a single point (since this is impossible due to the diversity of the surfaces of incidence)—nevertheless, a gathering of light occurs at a natural place, with the light itself remaining without coloration in the form of light. That gathered light heats the opposite body and, through its delay, suddenly ignites an inflammable body, such as <term>tinder</term> <note>original: "stupam"; literally "tow" or flax fibers used as kindling.</note> or anything else having the potential in itself for inflammation. 

However, if the transparent body opposite the sun has more than one flat or circular surface on that side facing the sun—for instance, if a quadrangular body is placed with one of its angles facing the sun—then refraction of the incident rays will occur through one surface to both opposite surfaces, and similarly for the rays incident to the other surface. And when the air (which is a thinner transparent body) is encountered on the side opposite the refracted light, the rays will be refracted from both surfaces away from that perpendicular which, drawn from angle to angle in the body, would divide its base into equal parts (or another line equidistant to it). Then, in another dense body placed beneath that transparent body, such as the earth or any other body, sometimes two clear lights will appear, and sometimes colored ones. This is clear to one who experiments: there will then be two mixed colors there, not more—namely the color red and another mixed color, appearing green—which are more intense or faint according to the disposition of the crystal or other small body. 

But if there are three surfaces of the body (on the part opposite the sun), as there are in a hexagonal crystal, then the light received from each of the three surfaces opposite the sun is rendered to the opposite body, such as the earth or any other body, from each of the three [bottom] surfaces. The middle of these three lights remains on the very perpendicular of the crystalline column that divides its base equally (or is equidistant to the divider), and that light becomes visible unless the sun’s light hinders it. The other two, however, are refracted away from the said perpendicular due to the nature of the second, thinner transparent medium, namely the air (for it was said in the 4th theorem of this book that when the second medium is thinner, refraction occurs away from the perpendicular), and it is like a certain scattering of rays. 

Colors appear in these lights thus reflected and refracted because of the mixing of the "blackness" of the crystalline color with the penetrating light, and because of the admixtures of the shadows of the parts of the crystal itself protruding according to the sharpness of its angles, which are projected to the side opposite the incidence of the rays (according to theorem 11 of book 2). The number of these shadows causes the diversity of colors when they are mixed with the light. Since the mixed color of the crystal and the shadows is reflected where the ray of light is more perpendicular with respect to the surface of incidence (around which a gathering of many rays occurs in the vicinity)—because that ray is more luminous—then the color red is produced. 

In other rays, however, according to their weakness and the mixing of the color of the body and more shadows, other middle colors are generated. Three colors are produced because rays are collected from the three upper surfaces to each of the lower surfaces. The color red will always be seen on that side where the ray perpendicular to the surface of the crystal (on the opposite side of the rainbow generated across from the sun) falls on its surface after the gathering of all the rays and after the refraction caused by the transparency of the intervening air. 

Then sometimes three rainbows are generated, because of the triple nature of refraction in the second, thinner transparent medium, as mentioned before. And because three times three makes a square, which is 9, there will then be 9 individual colors in number, from the multiplicity of the three upper surfaces into the number of the three lower ones. There will, however, be three specific differences of colors. No sensible distinction of these colors occurs through the angles of the body, because rays reflected or refracted from the line of the angles—which is actually indivisible—are themselves indivisible and produce nothing sensible. These colors of the rainbow produced through a crystal do not occur entirely through the nature of the colors of a "true" rainbow (whose distinction exists formally only in the eye); rather, they occur through the nature of light reflected from the shape of the said body. Hence, the cause of them is not a reflection made to the eye; for they are not seen by way of reflection, but by way of simple vision like other visible things offered to the sight, which are seen by anyone in the same place. Thus, the distinction of colors is made by the shape of the body, since from any other crystal or transparent body of a different shape, various colors...

<summary>Witelo explains how hexagonal crystals create rainbow-like colors through refraction and the mixing of light with the "shadows" of the crystal's edges. He distinguishes these physical projections from the optical illusion of a natural rainbow seen in the sky.</summary>

--- Page 789 ---
<meta>This page concludes Witelo’s monumental work on optics. It finishes Theorem 83 regarding hexagonal crystals, presents Theorems 84 and 85 on water-filled vessels and submerged mirrors, and ends with a formal prayer of thanks and the publication colophon from 1572.</meta>

# BOOK TEN OF WITELO’S OPTICS

[The colors] appear, which are not distinct according to that sequence of the rainbow's colors. And a sign of this is: if a hexagonal crystal is taken, and two of its surfaces are covered with red wax or another substance, so that between those two a third surface remains non-opaque; then, with the other three surfaces placed opposite the sun passing through a small opening—provided the place of operation is not otherwise very luminous and some black [surface] is placed beneath—then a very large, beautiful, and most clear rainbow will be seen even from a small crystal. This occurs because of the aggregation of the rays of the entire light falling from all the upper surfaces to the lower ones, which are gathered into a single nearby place. But if those three surfaces, which were just now opposite the sun, are made the lower ones, and conversely the other three are made the upper ones, then a rainbow will appear sometimes as one, and sometimes not at all. And he who ponders this playful game will find what we have written here, and even more than what has been discovered by us in such a pastime. And if the experimenter makes one of the six said surfaces opaque, he will find similar results through the rotation of the crystal to different positions. And if he places the crystal before the eye, so that the three non-opaque surfaces are turned toward the eye, he will see that red wax through all three surfaces opposite the eye. And if he rotates the crystal before the eye, many variations will occur, which one will be able to apply to the generations of colors—always considering the mixing of shadows—since the nature of the <term>reflection</term> <note>Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface.</note> of forms to the sight is the same as that of light to the things upon which it falls. For color or a visible form is not carried to the sight except through the nature of the light that is in it; and a diligent inquirer will be able to add many things to these statements through experience. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 84. Under a round glass vessel, full of water, exposed to the sun: colors similar to the colors of the rainbow are seen.

Suppose a round glass vessel, shaped like a <term>urinal</term> <note>original: "urinalis"; in medieval science, this referred to a gourd-shaped glass vessel used for both medical and chemical experiments.</note>, full of pure water, is exposed to the sun: I say that what is proposed is true. For colors similar to the colors of the rainbow are seen on the surface of a body placed beneath that vessel, such as on the surface of the earth or on another body. The generation of these colors is due to the various <term>refractions</term> <note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium (like air) into another (like glass or water).</note> of the sun's light. For as is clear from the 4th theorem of this book, one refraction occurs from the air to the glass, another also from the glass to the water; and likewise another from the water to the glass, and another from the glass to the underlying air. The angles of these refractions are different, as is clear from the 8th theorem of this book. Therefore, according to these modes of refraction, with the admixture of the color of those <term>transparent</term> <note>original: "diaphanorum"; refers to materials that allow light to pass through.</note> bodies and the shadows cast by the bodies, the light penetrates. Being diffused circularly or perhaps irregularly according to the convex surfaces of the transparent bodies, it presents various colors to the sight, distinct according to the previously mentioned causes. If that vessel is moistened on the outside with water, it will present more beautiful colors to the sight; for then the number of refractions is somewhat increased, and similarly the number of shadows. However, these colors are not truly the colors of the rainbow, because they are counted in a different number of colors than those of the rainbow, and they do not reach the sight through reflection as the colors of the rainbow do, but are seen directly, just like the light itself and other colors. Thus the proposition is clear.

### 85. With any mirror placed under water and exposed to the sun: the figure of the sun will appear as if doubled.

In a mirror, the light of rays perpendicular to the surface of the water, but falling obliquely on the surface of the mirror, is reflected from the surface of the mirror to the sight existing in the place of reflection; and thus it offers the figure of the sun to the sight. But the light of rays falling obliquely on the surface of the water is refracted at the surface of the water toward the perpendicular drawn from the point of incidence to the surface of the water, according to the 4th theorem of this book. Therefore, when that refracted form reaches the surface of the mirror, it is reflected again from that surface (which it hits obliquely) to the sight. Two figures of the sun appear: one larger because of simple reflection; and another smaller because of refraction, which diminishes the form in a denser medium before it is reflected. That second figure of the sun is seen as if it were the form of a star following the body of the sun. But it is itself a form of the sun, which is clear because outside the sun's ray, it is not reflected by itself from the surface of the mirror with the figure of the sun. And it happens that this refracted form is seen. And if a plane mirror is brought under the water into the sun's ray, then the very same form, which was previously seen under a lesser light, will be seen to be more luminous than before; and it will appear to move around the reflected figure of the sun according to the movement of the water. Therefore, the proposition is clear. And since we, with the help of divine grace, have run through the three proposed modes of seeing according to all their diversity as far as we were able, and it is not possible for us to return anything worthy of such great bounty to the divine goodness, we nevertheless rise up to those thanksgivings which we can offer to Him, who truly is Three and One: estimating nothing in existing things to be conformable, nothing co-eternal, nothing equally good as He, to whom be honor and glory through infinite ages. Amen.

Atop the ornate, circular head of the staff stands a crane on one leg, holding a small stone in its raised left claw—a traditional symbol of vigilance. The word "EPISCOP." is printed across the center of the image, split by the staff of the crosier.</image-desc>

->BI SHOP.<- <note>original: "EPISCOP." This is a shortened form of the Latin *Episcopus*, meaning "Bishop." This is a visual pun on the name of the printer, Eusebius Episcopius (also known by the German name Bischoff), a prominent publisher in Basel.</note>

<note>The crane holding a stone is a classical and Renaissance symbol for **vigilance**. Legend held that a crane would hold a stone while sleeping so that if it drifted off, the stone would drop and wake the bird, ensuring it remained an "overseer" (the literal meaning of the Greek *episkopos*).</note>

<vocab>Bishop/Overseer, pastoral staff, crane, watchfulness, symbolic image</vocab>

# Front Cover of the Volume

<note>The volume is bound in dark brown leather, showing a natural grain and signs of age and handling.</note>

->**IHS**<-

<note>original: "IHS". This is a **Christogram**, a symbolic monogram for the name of **Jesus**. While it is derived from the first three letters of the Greek name for Jesus (ΙΗΣΟΥΣ), it is used here as the official seal of the **Society of Jesus** (the Jesuits). It is often interpreted in Latin as *Iesus Hominum Salvator*, meaning **Jesus, Savior of Mankind**.</note>

<note>The emblem is rich with symbolism: the horizontal bar of the letter 'H' is surmounted by a **cross**, and below the letters are **three nails**, representing the nails used in the Crucifixion. The entire monogram is encased in a **sunburst**, or "glory," which represents the light of divine truth.</note>
